Public Prosecutor v Angappan Arivalagan and another

Public Prosecutor v Angappan Arivalagan and another
[2026] SGMC 98

Case Number:Magistrate's Arrest Case No 900155 of 2025 and others, Magistrate's Appeal No MA-9163-2026-01, Magistrate's Arrest Case No 900142 of 2025 and another, Magistrate's Appeal No MA-9164-2026-01
Decision Date:27 August 2026
Tribunal/Court:Magistrate's Court
Coram: Terence Tay
Counsel Name(s): Teng Yin Hang/Daphne Lim (Attorney-General's Chambers) for the Public Prosecutor; Ram Chandra Ramesh (C Ramesh Law Practice) for Angappan Arivalagan and Durairaj Kulothungan.
Parties: Public Prosecutor — Angappan Arivalagan — Durairaj Kulothungan

CRIMINAL PROCEDURE AND SENTENCING – Sentencing – Payment Services Act 2019

CRIMINAL PROCEDURE AND SENTENCING – Sentencing – Computer Misuse Act 1993

[LawNet Editorial Note: An appeal to this decision has been filed in MA 9163/2026/01 and MA 9164/2026/01.]

27 August 2026

District Judge Terence Tay:

Introduction

1       The appellants, Angappan Arivalagan (“Angappan”) and Durairaj Kulothungan (“Durairaj”), were Indian nationals who had claimed trial to the following related charges pertaining to two different time periods in Singapore:

Period

Angappan

Durairaj

Jan

to

12 March 2023

(“Period 1”)

Did abet by engaging with one Said in a conspiracy to carry on a business of providing a payment service in Singapore, namely, a cross-border money transfer service, and in furtherance of that conspiracy and in order to the doing of that thing: (a) Angappan arranged for individuals in Singapore who wanted to remit monies to recipients in India to transfer monies to various bank accounts: (b) pursuant to the arrangement in (a), Angappan withdrew a total of S$4,099,305 from various bank accounts and made arrangements for specific items to be purchased with the monies; (c) Angappan coordinated with tourists to bring the items purchased into India and provided them with the receipts of these items to make Goods & Services Tax refunds in Singapore; (d) Angappan liaised with Said to receive the items from these tourists in India; and (e) Said would re-sell these items in India and disburse the proceeds to the intended recipients in India, when Angappan did not have in force a licence that entitled him to carry on a business of providing a cross-border money transfer service, and when Angappan was not an exempt payment service provider in respect of the cross-border money transfer service, and Angappan had thereby committed an offence under Section 5(1) of the Payment Services Act 2019 (“PSA”), punishable under Section 5(3)(a) of the PSA read with Section 109 of the Penal Code 1871 (“PC”). (“Charge A1”)

 

13 Mar

to

3 Jul 2023

(“Period 2”)

Did abet by engaging with one Said and Durairaj in a conspiracy to carry on a business of providing a payment service in Singapore, namely, a cross-border money transfer service, and in furtherance of that conspiracy and in order to the doing of that thing: (a) Angappan arranged for individuals in Singapore who wanted to remit monies to recipients in India by having them transfer monies to 33 bank accounts; (b) pursuant to the arrangement in (a), Durairaj withdrew a total of S$6,166,515 from these 33 bank accounts and passed the monies to Angappan; (c) Angappan made arrangements for specific items to be purchased with the monies; (d) Angappan coordinated with tourists to bring these items into India and provided them with the receipts to make Goods & Services Tax (“GST”) refunds in Singapore; (e) Angappan liaised with Said to receive the items from these tourists in India; and (f) Said would re-sell these items in India and disburse the proceeds to the intended recipients in India, when Angappan did not have in force a licence that entitled him to carry on a business of providing a cross-border money transfer service, and when Angappan was not an exempt payment service provider in respect of the cross-border money transfer service, and Angappan had thereby committed an offence under s 5(1) and punishable under s 5(3)(a) of the PSA read with s 109 of the PC. (“Charge A2”)

Did abet by engaging with one Said and Angappan in a conspiracy to carry on a business of providing a payment service in Singapore, namely, a cross-border money transfer service, and in furtherance of that conspiracy and in order to the doing of that thing: (a) Angappan arranged for individuals in Singapore who wanted to remit monies to recipients in India to transfer monies to various bank accounts; (b) pursuant to the arrangement in (a), Durairaj withdrew a total of S$6,166,515 from these bank accounts and passed the monies to Angappan; (c) Angappan made arrangements for specific items to be purchased with the monies; (d) Arivalagan coordinated with tourists to bring these items into India and provided them with the receipts to make GST refunds in Singapore; (e) Angappan liased with Said to receive the items from these tourists in India; and (f) Said would re-sell these items in India and disburse the proceeds to the intended recipients in India, when Angappan did not have in force a licence that entitled him to carry on a business of providing a cross-border money transfer service, and when Durairaj was not an exempt payment service provider in respect of the cross-border money transfer service, and Durairaj had thereby committed an offence under s 5(1) and punishable under s 5(3)(a) of the PSA read with s 109 of the PC. (“Charge D1”)



2       The trial proceeded on a joint statement of agreed facts (“SOAF”), there being no dispute as to the material facts underlying the charges. The gravamen of the appellants’ common defence was that the system of money transfers carried out by them – commonly referred to as the hawala system – did not constitute an offence under s 5(1) of the PSA.

3       After hearing the parties’ submissions at the conclusion of the trial, I found that the system of money transfers carried out by the appellants fell within the rubric of a “cross-border money transfer service” under the PSA, and that the appellants were neither licensed to provide such a service nor exempted from the requirement to hold a licence. Accordingly, I convicted the appellants.

4       Following their conviction, the appellants pleaded guilty to the following charges relating to Period 2:

Period

Angappan

Durairaj

Period 2

Did abet by engaging in a conspiracy with Durairaj to do a certain thing, namely to knowingly cause a computer to perform a function for the purpose of securing access without authority to the banking system of Development Bank Singapore (“DBS”), and in pursuance of the conspiracy, and in order to the doing of that thing, an act took place, to wit Angappan instructed Durairaj to make withdrawals amounting to a total of S$6,166,515 from various ATMS in Singapore using DBS issued cards linked to 33 bank accounts as set out in Annex B, without being so authorized by DBS to do so, and Angappan had thereby committed an offence under s 3(1) read with ss 12 and 14 of the Computer Misuse Act 1993 (“CMA”). (“Charge A3”)

Did abet by engaging in a conspiracy with Angappan to do a certain thing, namely to knowingly cause a computer to perform a function for the purpose of securing access without authority to any program held in any computer, to wit, the banking system of DBS, and in pursuance of the conspiracy, and in order to the doing of that thing, an act took place, to wit Durairaj made withdrawals amounting to a total of S$6,166,515 from various ATMS in Singapore using DBS issued cards linked to 33 bank accounts as set out in Annex B on the instructions of Arivalagan, without being so authorized by DBS to do so, and Durairaj had thereby committed an offence under s 3(1) read with ss 12 and 14 of the CMA.(“Charge D2”)



5       Angappan also consented to the following charge being taken into consideration for the purpose of sentencing:

Period

Angappan

Period 1

Did knowingly cause a computer to perform a function for the purpose of securing access without authority to the banking system of DBS by making withdrawals amounting to a total of S$4,099,305 from various ATMS in Singapore using DBS issued cards linked to 28 bank accounts as set out in Annex A, without being so authorized by DBS to do so, and Angappan had thereby committed an offence under s 3(1) read with s 14 of the CMA. (“Charge A4”)



6       The court imposed the following sentences on the appellants:

 

Angappan

Charge A1

Seven months and three weeks’ imprisonment and $3,000 fine, in default of which two weeks’ imprisonment (consecutive)

Charge A2

Twelve months and three weeks’ imprisonment and $3,000 fine, in default of which two weeks’ imprisonment (concurrent)

Charge A3

Eight months’ imprisonment (consecutive)

Aggregate Sentence

Fifteen months and three weeks’ imprisonment and $6,000 fine, in default of which four weeks’ imprisonment

 

Durairaj

Charge D1

Eight months and three weeks’ imprisonment (concurrent)

Charge D2

Four months’ imprisonment (concurrent)

Aggregate Sentence

Eight months and three weeks’ imprisonment



7       The appellants have appealed against their sentences.

The facts

8       The SOAF was as follows:

STATEMENT OF AGREED FACTS

1.    This document is prepared in accordance with the provisions of s 267(1) of the Criminal Procedure Code 2010 (“CPC”).

THE PARTIES

2.    The accused persons are:

a.    Durairaj Kulothungan (“Durairaj”), Male/26 years old, Indian National FIN: [redacted], D.O.B.: 13/05/1999.

b.    Angappan Arivalagan (“Angappan”), Male/31 years old, Indian National FIN: [redacted], D.O.B.: 20/06/1993.

3.    Durairaj and Angappan are cousins.

BACKGROUND FACTS

4.    Angappan has been working as a driver in Singapore since 2012.

5.    In January 2023, while visiting his family in India, Angappan was approached by an acquaintance known to him as “Said”, who proposed that they set up a system for the families (in India) of Indian workers working in Singapore to receive monies. The business would proceed as follows:

a.    Workers in Singapore who wanted their families in India to receive monies will either transfer money to bank accounts under Angappan’s control or provide their ATM cards to Angappan to withdraw money from their accounts.

b.    Angappan would make arrangements for these withdrawn funds to be used to purchase specific items such as gold or laptops. Prior to purchasing these items, Said would tell Angappan what to buy.

c.    Said’s role would also include providing Angappan with the contact information of tourists who were returning to India from Singapore. Angappan would then coordinate with these tourists to bring these items into India and provided them with the receipts to make Goods & Services Tax refunds in Singapore. These tourists would be remunerated for their services through these tax refunds.

d.    Thereafter, these tourists would transport the purchased items to India and deliver them to Said. Said would then sell the items in India at higher prices in India. From the proceeds of these sales, Said would arrange for the disbursement of funds to the intended recipients referred to at [a]. Additionally, Angappan’s family members in India would also receive payments from the profits generated through this business.

6.    Durairaj started working for Angappan on 13 March 2023. Durairaj would assist Angappan to make daily withdrawals from the ATM cards under Angappan’s instructions. Angappan would instruct Durairaj to withdraw money from ATMs of the main DBS branches because of the higher withdrawal limit of S$10,000 a day. After withdrawing the money, Durairaj would meet Angappan on the same day to pass him the monies so that the latter could make arrangements for specific items to be purchased with the monies. These items would subsequently be transported to India by tourists. In addition to Durairaj, Angappan also enlisted the help of his wife, brother and 3 cousins in the business. They would assist Angappan in the administrative matters, such as the tabulation of monies that were coming in and withdrawn from the various accounts under Angappan’s control.

7.    Angappan received a salary of at least S$1,000 each month from Said. Durairaj was not paid by Said. However, Angappan portioned approximately S$2,400 to Durairaj in the form of payment for the latter’s transport, food and rental expenses in the period that he was assisting Angappan. Durairaj was also allowed by Angappan to withdraw small sums of monies for groceries and other personal expenses from some of the accounts under Angappan’s control.

8.    Further investigations revealed that various people would hand over their bank cards with the corresponding PINs to Angappan so that the latter may access the monies accordingly. Angappan would further extend these bank accounts to other customers who were not the account holder and allowed them to deposit monies into these accounts so that their monies could be transferred to their families in India as per [5].

9.    In total, Angappan managed to obtain bank cards linked to 33 bank accounts and had a total of about 200 customers who sent monies to their families in India through the arrangement at [5].

10.    On 3 July 2023, a member of the public called the police after observing Durairaj withdrawing large amounts of money using different ATM cards from a DBS ATM machine located at Plaza Singapura Basement 1. Upon his arrest, the police found 51 ATM cards bearing various names and cash of S$74,750 on Durairaj. When Durairaj was asked by the police officers about the cash and the cards, he initially answered “my money, my cards”. He also claimed that the money belonged to him and that he had withdrawn the money for the purpose of investing in a company in Singapore. Durairaj was unable to provide a satisfactory account for possessing the bank cards and he was placed under arrest. The bank cards and cash of S$74,750 were seized.

11.    Upon finding out that Durairaj was arrested through one of his colleagues, Angappan deleted all the chat logs with Said, Durairaj and the customers in his phone. Angappan was subsequently arrested on 11 July 2023.

12.    At all material times, neither Said, Angappan nor Durairaj had in force a licence that would entitle them to carry on such cross-border money transfer service or were exempt payment service provider of cross-border money transfer service. Durairaj also knew that the monies withdrawn would be transferred to India as part of Angappan’s business as set out at [5]

WITHDRAWALS FROM JANUARY 2023 TO 12 MARCH 2023

Facts relating to the 3rd Charge viz MAC-900155-2025 involving Angappan

13.    Between January 2023 and 12 March 2023, Angappan withdrew a total of $4,099,305 from the 28 accounts as set out in Annex A from DBS ATMs at various locations in Singapore. The following acts also took place, to wit,

(a)    Angappan arranged for individuals in Singapore who wanted their families in India to receive monies in India to transfer monies to designated bank accounts;

(b)    Pursuant to the arrangement in (a), Angappan withdrew a total of $4,099,305 from these bank accounts and made arrangements for specific items to be purchased with the monies;

(c)    Said’s role would also include providing Angappan with the contact information of tourists who were returning to India from Singapore. Angappan would then coordinate with these tourists. These tourists would be remunerated for their services through these tax refunds.

(d)    Thereafter, these tourists would transport the purchased items to India and deliver them to Said. Said would then sell the items in India at higher prices in India. From the proceeds of these sales, Said would arrange for the disbursement of funds to the intended recipients referred to at [a].

(e)    Angappan coordinated with tourists to bring the items purchased into India and provided them with the receipts of these items to make Goods & Services Tax refunds in Singapore;

(f)    Angappan liaised with Said to receive the items in India; and

(g)    Said would resell these items in India and disburse the proceeds to the intended recipients in India.

WITHDRAWALS FROM 13 MARCH 2023 TO 3 JULY 2023

Facts relating to 2nd Charge MAC-900142-2025 involving Durairaj and 4th Charge MAC-900156-2025 involving Angappan

14.    Between 13 March 2023 and 3 July 2023, Durairaj withdrew a total of S$6,166,515 from the 33 accounts set out in Annex B from DBS ATMS at various locations in Singapore. The following acts took place, to wit,

(a)    Angappan arranged for individuals in Singapore who wanted their families in India to receive monies in India to transfer monies to designated bank accounts;

(b)    Pursuant to the arrangement in (a), Durairaj withdrew a total of S$6,166,515 from these bank accounts and passed the monies to Angappan;

(c)     Angappan made arrangements for specific items to be purchased with the monies;

(d)    Said’s role would also include providing Angappan with the contact information of tourists who were returning to India from Singapore. Angappan would then coordinate with these tourists. These tourists would be remunerated for their services through these tax refunds.

(e)    Thereafter, these tourists would transport the purchased items to India and deliver them to Said. Said would then sell the items in India at higher prices in India. From the proceeds of these sales, Said would arrange for the disbursement of funds to the intended recipients referred to at [a].

(f)    Angappan coordinated with tourists to bring the items purchased into India and provided them with the receipts of these items to make Goods & Services Tax refunds in Singapore;

(g)    Angappan liaised with Said to receive the items in India; and

(h)    Said would resell these items in India and disburse the proceeds to the intended recipients in India.

Events following arrests

15.    In the course of investigations the following statements were provided to the Police by Angappan and Durairaj voluntarily, and without any threat, inducement, or promise.

The above facts are not disputed and are agreed upon between the Prosecution and the Defence under section 267 of the CPC.

Annex A

Annex B

The above facts are not disputed and are agreed upon between the Prosecution and the Defence under section 267 of the CPC.

9       The appellants also agreed to the following joint statement of facts for Charge A3 and Charge D2 without qualification:

Statement of Facts

1.    The accused persons are:

a.    Angappan Arivalagan (“Angappan”), Male/32 years old, Indian National FIN: [redacted], D.O.B.: 20/06/1993.

b.    Durairaj Kulothungan (“Durairaj”), Male/26 years old, Indian National FIN: [redacted], D.O.B.: 13/05/1999.

2.    Durairaj and Angappan are cousins.

3.    Angappan has been working as a driver in Singapore since 2012.

4.    During the Covid period, Angappan began assisting the workers living in the same dormitory as him to remit monies in India. They would hand over their ATM cards and the corresponding pin number to Angappan and Angappan would then withdraw the monies on their behalf and arrange for their remittances. Angappan initially went to Western Union to remit the monies on behalf of these workers.

5.    Subsequently, Angappan got to know one “Said” and set up business for the families in (India) of Indian workers working in Singapore to receive monies.

6.    In January 2023, while visiting his family in India, Angappan was approached by an acquaintance known to him as “Said”, who proposed that they set up a system for the families (in India) of Indian workers working in Singapore to receive monies.

7.    Further investigations revealed that various people would hand over their bank cards with the corresponding PINs to Angappan so that the latter may access the monies accordingly. Angappan would further extend these bank accounts to other customers who were not the account holder and allowed them to deposit monies into these accounts so that their monies could be transferred to their families in India as per [5].

8.    In total, Angappan managed to obtain bank cards linked to 33 bank accounts, and a total of about 200 customers, who had transferred monies to their families in India through Angappan as per [5].

9.    Durairaj started working for Angappan on 13 March 2023. Durairaj would assist Angappan to make daily withdrawals from the ATM cards under Angappan’s instructions. Angappan would instruct Durairaj to withdraw money from ATMs of the main DBS branches because of the higher withdrawal limit of S$10,000 a day. After withdrawing the money, Durairaj would meet Angappan on the same day to pass him the monies so that the latter could purchase the items to be transported to India by the tourists. In addition to Durairaj, Angappan also enlisted the help of his wife, brother and 3 cousins in the business. They would assist Angappan in the administrative matters, such as the tabulation of monies that were coming in and withdrawn from the various accounts under Angappan’s control.

Withdrawals from January 2023 to 12 March 2023

10.    Between January 2023 and 12 March 2023, Angappan did knowingly cause a computer to perform a function for the purpose of securing access without authority to the banking system of DBS, by making withdrawals amounting to a total of $4,099,305 from various ATMs in Singapore using DBS issued cards linked to 28 bank accounts as set out in Annex A, without being so authorised by DBS to do so.

Withdrawals from 13 March 2023 to 3 July 2023

Facts relating to 1st Charge MAC-903854-2023 involving Durairaj and 2nd Charge MAC-900154-2025 involving Angappan

11.    Between 13 March 2023 and 3 July 2023, Durairaj did abet by engaging in a conspiracy with Angappan to knowingly cause a computer to perform a function for the purpose of securing access without authority to any program held in any computer, to wit, the banking system of the DBS, and in pursuance of the conspiracy, and in order to the doing of that thing, an act took place, to wit Durairaj made withdrawals amounting to a total of $6,166,515 from various ATMs in Singapore using DBS issued cards linked to 33 bank accounts set out in Annex B on the instruction of Angappan, without being so authorized by DBS to do so.

12.    Between 13 March 2023 and 3 July 2023, Angappan did abet by engaging in a conspiracy with Durairaj to knowingly cause a computer to perform a function for the purpose of securing access without authority to any program held in any computer, to wit, the banking system of the DBS, and in pursuance of the conspiracy, and in order to the doing of that thing, an act took place, to wit Angappan instructed Durairaj to make withdrawals amounting to a total of $6,166,515 from various ATMs in Singapore using DBS issued cards linked to 33 bank accounts set out in Annex B, without being so authorized by DBS to do so.

13.    Durairaj and Angappan have thereby each committed an offence under s 3(1) read with ss 12 and 14 of the Computer Misuse Act 1993.

Annex A

Total withdrawals made by Angappan from the accounts as part of the arrangement to carry out the illegal cross-border money transfer service: $4,099,305

Annex B

Total withdrawals made by Durairaj from the accounts as part of the arrangement to carry out the illegal cross-border money transfer service: $6,166,515

Sentencing Submissions

Prosecution’s address on sentence

10     The Deputy Public Prosecutor (“DPP”) told the court that both Angappan and Durairaj had no antecedents, and sought a global sentence of 18½-24 months’ imprisonment and $6,000 fine for Angappan and 11-14 months’ imprisonment for Durairaj based on the following individual sentences:

 

Angappan

Charge A1

8½-12 months’ imprisonment and $3,000 fine

Charge A2

15-20 months’ imprisonment and $3,000 fine

Charge A3

10-12 months’ imprisonment

 

Durairaj

Charge D1

11-14 months’ imprisonment

Charge D2

6-8 months’ imprisonment



11     For the offences under the PSA, the DPP referred to the guidance of the High Court in Vijay Kumar v PP [2023] 5 SLR 983 (“Vijay’s Case”) and referred to a number of other sentencing precedents, as follows:

(a)      PP v Saw Yu Wai [2023] SGMC 55 (“Saw’s Case”): The offender was a director of a company that offered unlicensed and non-exempted cross-border money transfer and money-changing services. from Singapore to Myanmar for a service fee. For a period of almost three months from 1 April 2020 to 28 June 2020, the company remitted a total of $889,077 from Singapore to Myanmar and earned a profit of $4,632. The offender who pleaded guilty on the first day of trial was sentenced to 8 weeks’ imprisonment.

(b)      PP v Tan Khoon Yong [2022] SGMC 43 (“Tan’s Case”): The offender received a total of $208,890 into his bank account over a period of about one month and across 38 transactions for the purpose of transmitting the monies to persons outside Singapore; $6,000 of the monies received were established to be proceeds from an e-commerce cheating scam. The offender received a total commission of $5,165.32 for his services. He pleaded guilty and was sentenced to 10 weeks’ imprisonment.

(c)      PP v Zhu Yu [2022] SGDC 172 (“Zhu’s Case”): The offender conspired with an accomplice to provide an unlicensed payment service involving the exchange of CNY150,000 for Singapore dollars. The intended exchange was ultimately not completed because the transaction formed part of a scam of which the offender was unaware. The offender played a secondary role in the conspiracy and was promised between $1,000 and $3,000 for his participation. He pleaded guilty and was sentenced to five weeks’ imprisonment.

(d)      Chang Jiunn v PP [2025] SGHC 225 (“Chang’s Case”): The offender was involved in an arrangement to provide cross-border money transfer services, under which US dollars were received in Singapore in exchange for the transfer of an equivalent value in Chinese yuan to various recipients in China. The first transaction involved USD999,967.41, which was remitted to Singapore through an Indonesian remittance company. The second transaction involved USD800,000, although the intended transfer was ultimately unsuccessful. Following a trial, the offender was convicted and sentenced to six weeks’ imprisonment on each charge, with the sentences ordered to run concurrently. His appeals against conviction and sentence were dismissed.

(e)      PP v U Sun Tint (2021, unreported) (“U’s Case”): The offender operated an unlicensed and non-exempt cross-border money transfer service over a period of five months, during which he transacted a total of $5,147,609.23 and earned a profit of $26,189.80. A further charge under the Money-changing and Remittance Businesses Act (Cap 187, 2008 Rev Ed) (“MCRBA”) was taken into consideration for sentencing. The offender pleaded guilty and was sentenced to six months’ imprisonment and a fine of $100,000.

(f)      PP v Javiour Chia Kit Hou (2025, unreported) (“Javiour’s Case”): The offender assisted the principal offender in providing an unlicensed cross-border money transfer service over a period of three weeks, during which transactions totalling $35 million were carried out. He received a monthly salary of $3,500 for his involvement. A further charge under the PSA and a charge under the Corruption, Drug Trafficking and Other Serious Crimes (Confiscation of Benefits) Act 1992 were taken into consideration for sentencing. The offender pleaded guilty and was sentenced to 10 months’ imprisonment.

(g)      PP v Zin Nwe Nyunt [2025] SGDC 184 (“Zin’s Case”): The offender opened several corporate bank accounts and handed the internet banking tokens for those accounts to an accomplice, who controlled and conducted the money transfer transactions. The offending spanned an aggregate period of 14 months, and the offender received significant remuneration for her role. Of the proceeds involved, $480,000 was tainted by illegality. The offender pleaded guilty to two charges involving transactions of USD152 million and USD251 million, respectively, and was sentenced to nine months’ imprisonment on each charge, with the sentences ordered to run consecutively. A further charge involving USD127 million and a charge under the MCRBA were taken into consideration for sentencing. The aggregate sentence was 18 months’ imprisonment.

12     The DPP then pointed out the following facts in Angappan’s case:

(a)     Large number of transactions and high aggregate value involved.

(b)     Substantial period of offending.

(c)     Significance of Angappan’s role and elevated degree of culpability.

(d)     Sophisticated nature of the offence.

(e)     Difficulty of detection.

(f)     Another charge – Charge A4 – which was taken into consideration for the purpose of sentencing.

13     In relation to Durairaj, the DPP considered that Durairaj was involved only in Period 2 and his role was significantly less aggravating than that of Angappan. That said, the DPP took the view that Durairaj’s involvement was still significant as he had made systemic withdrawals using the bank cards and handed over $6,166,515 to Angappan in the course of four months.

14     Additionally, the DPP noted the following:

(a)     Durairaj had received some proceeds from Angappan.

(b)     Durairaj had been untruthful to the police initially although he eventually cooperated with the police.

Angappan’s mitigation plea

15     Defence counsel sought a fine for Angappan.

16     Defence counsel mitigated on the basis of Angappan’s personal and family circumstances, and submitted that Angappan had been unaware that his conduct was unlawful. Defence counsel further highlighted that Angappan had no antecedents and suffered from kidney stones which caused him considerable pain. Leniency was sought on the basis that, although Angappan had claimed trial, his defence had essentially been confined to a point of law.

17     Defence counsel also told the court that the monies that were seized by the police were not paid to the workers’ families in India and Angappan had to sell his land in India to repay the workers and their families. This was not disputed by the DPP.

Durairaj’s mitigation plea

18     Defence counsel sought a fine for Durairaj.

19     Defence counsel mitigated on the basis of Durairaj’s personal and family circumstances. Defence Counsel submitted that Durairaj had felt obliged to assist Angappan when asked to do so because he regarded Angappan as an elder brother, and was grateful to Angappan and Angappan’s family for the assistance they had rendered to Durairaj and Durairaj’s family.

20     Defence counsel further submitted that Angappan had assured Durairaj that his conduct was not unlawful, and that Durairaj had received only some “pocket money” for his involvement in the offences. It was also submitted that the monies involved were not themselves tainted by illegality, as they represented the salaries of Indian workers employed in Singapore, and there had been neither complaints from the workers nor financial loss.

Court’s decision

PSA offences

21     The PSA establishes a regulatory and oversight framework to address the risks associated with cross-border money transfers, including the potential use of such transactions for money laundering and terrorism financing, losses suffered by remitters, and difficulties in tracing funds and assets, when necessary.

22     The licensing and regulatory requirements under the PSA enable the relevant authorities to exercise oversight over money transfer businesses and to ensure that such businesses operate within prescribed safeguards. This is particularly important in Singapore, given its position as an international financial centre. The integrity of the financial system and confidence in Singapore as a trusted financial hub may be undermined if cross-border money transfer activities are conducted outside the regulatory framework. The licensing regime therefore serves not merely to regulate individual money transfer businesses, but also to safeguard broader financial, law-enforcement and public interests.

23     Against this regulatory backdrop, deterrence assumes particular importance in the sentencing offenders for offences involving the provision of unlicensed payment services under the PSA. Effective deterrence is necessary both to discourage individual offenders from circumventing the licensing regime and, more broadly, to deter others from providing payment services outside the regulatory framework.

24     Nevertheless, a custodial sentence is not inevitable in every case. At [71] of Vijay’s Case, See Kee Oon J (as he then was) recognised that a fine may remain appropriate in exceptional circumstances:

Fines remain an appropriate sentencing option in exceptional cases, eg, where the offender commits an “unknowing” breach or where there are exceptional mitigating factors which justify a departure from the custodial benchmark.

25     In cases falling outside such exceptional circumstances, where an accused person claims trial, the custodial benchmark identified in Vijay’s Case is an imprisonment term of three weeks, subject to adjustment upwards or downwards having regard to the applicable aggravating and mitigating factors.[note: 1]

26     In calibrating the appropriate sentence, See J identified a non-exhaustive list of offence-specific and offender-specific factors.[note: 2] The offence-specific factors concern both the harm caused by the offending and the offender’s culpability:

Offence-specific factors

Factors going towards harm

Factors going towards culpability

(a) Number of transactions involved

(b) Total value involved

(c) Actual loss to customers/business

(d) Period of offending

(e) Involvement of a syndicate

(f) Involvement of tainted monies, money- laundering or terrorism financing

(g) Involvement of transnational element

(a) Benefit to the offender

(b) Level of sophistication

(c) Degree of pre-meditation and planning

(d) The offender’s role

(e) Degree of suspicion, negligence, recklessness, or wilful blindness on the involvement of tainted monies, money laundering or terrorism-financing

Offender-specific factors

Aggravating

Mitigating

(a) Offences taken into consideration for sentencing purposes

(b) Relevant antecedents

(c) Evident lack of remorse

(a) Guilty plea

(b) Voluntary restitution

(c) Co-operation with authorities



27     Turning to the facts of the present case involving the appellants, the offences took place over months and the scale of the offences – an aggregate sum in excess of $10,000,000 – was significant not only because of the sheer amount of monies involved, but also because the transactions were conducted in cash. The modus operandi, which involved the transfer of funds to India through goods purchased in Singapore and subsequently sold in India, demonstrated that the offences were carried out systematically and with a high degree of coordination and organisation. Indeed, the fact that there were no complaints from the workers who engaged the appellants’ services, notwithstanding the scale of the transactions and the coordination required, was itself indicative of the degree of organisation with which the scheme was carried out.

28     Angappan played an instrumental role in the cross-border money transfers. While Said operated from India, Angappan was his principal operative and counterpart in Singapore, and was responsible for carrying out material aspects of the operations, in particular:

(a)     Workers transferred monies to bank accounts under Angappan’s control or provided their ATM cards to Angappan for him to make withrawals from their bank accounts.[note: 3]

(b)     Angappan extended the use of these bank accounts to other customers who were not the bank account holders.[note: 4]

(c)     Angappan made arrangements to purchase specific items such as gold or laptops with the monies that he withdrew from the bank accounts.[note: 5]

(d)     With the contact information of tourists who were returning to India from Singapore, provided by Said, Angappan would coordinate with the tourists to bring the items to India and provide them with the receipts for GST refunds in Singapore.[note: 6]

29     Angappan further streamlined the withdrawal process during Period 2 by instructing Durairaj to make withdrawals from ATMs at the main DBS branches, where the daily withdrawal limit was higher at $10,000.[note: 7]

30     With the offence-specific factors in mind and given Angappan’s role, I decided that a fine was not appropriate in the present case. Instead, I adopted the starting point of three weeks’ imprisonment and applied the following uplifts to arrive at indicative sentences:

Uplift

Reason

Charge A1

Three months’ imprisonment

The significant scale of the transactions which amounted to more than $4,000,000 and conducted in cash.

Two to three months’ imprisonment

The systematic nature of the offences with a high degree of coordination and organization.

One month’s imprisonment

Transnational element.

Two months’ imprisonment

Angappan’s role.

Total

Eight to nine months and three weeks’ imprisonment

Charge A2

Five months’ imprisonment

The significant scale of the transactions which amounted to more than $6,000,000 and conducted in cash.

Three months’ imprisonment

The systematic nature of the offences with a high degree of coordination and organization.

One month’s imprisonment

Transnational element.

Four to five months’ imprisonment

Angappan’s role.

Total

Thirteen to 14 months and three weeks’ imprisonment



31     While there was nothing of material weight in Angappan’s mitigation plea that warranted a meaningful downward reduction of his indicative sentence, I gave due credit to the fact that his defence was confined to a point of law. This obviated the need for the Prosecution’s witnesses to attend in court to give evidence and resulted in a corresponding saving of time and resources.

32     Accordingly, I sentenced Angappan to seven months and three weeks’ imprisonment for Charge A1, and 12 months and three weeks’ imprisonment for Charge A2.

33     Additionally, I imposed a fine of $3,000, in default of which Angappan is to serve two weeks’ imprisonment, for each of Charge A1 and Charge A2. The fines serve to disgorge the undisputed benefits of $1,000 a month which Anggapan received for his involvement in the offences. [note: 8]

34     Turning to Durairaj, even though I agreed with the DPP that Durairaj played an integral role in the operations during Period 2, there were several factors which distinguished his culpability from that of Angappan:

(a)     Angappan was the instigator who recruited Durairaj into the operations;

(b)     Durairaj acted primarily on Angappan’s instructions; and

(c)     There was no evidence that Durairaj had been promised any structured remuneration for his participation, apart from “pocket money” apportioned from the benefits received by Angappan.

35     Therefore, I found that Durairaj’s culpability was lower than Angappan’s, and I imposed a sentence of eight months and three weeks’ imprisonment for Charge D1. This would reflect lower uplifts for Durairaj’s subordinate role and more limited contribution to the operations.

36     Although the sentencing precedents relied upon by the DPP were not binding on this court, I nevertheless considered whether the sentences imposed for Charges A1, A2 and D1 were broadly consistent with the sentencing outcome of those cases:

(a)     The facts of Saw’s Case, Tan’s Case, Zhu’s Case and Chang’s Case paled in comparison with those of the present case. In particular, the sums involved in each of those cases were significantly lower than the sums involved in either Period 1 or Period 2, and lower still than the aggregate sum involved in Angappan’s offences. The higher sentences imposed on Angappan and Durairaj for their respective charges reflected the substantially greater sums involved in the present case.

(b)      U’s Case was of limited assistance as it was an unreported sentencing decision for which no written reasons were available. Nonetheless, based on the charge sheets and statement of facts which the DPP had usefully furnished, there did not appear to be any exceptional feature which materially distinguished the offending in that case. The sentence imposed on the offender in U’s Case was therefore broadly consistent with the sentences imposed in the present case.

(c)     The charge sheets and statement of the facts provided by the DPP for Javiour’s Case disclosed that the value of the transaction involved was substantially greater than that in the present case. However, there was an important distinguishing feature – the offender and the principal offender in Javiour’s Case were operating autonomously within a payment institution licensed to provide money-changing and cross-border money transfer services.[note: 9] As Javiour’s Case was an unreported sentencing decision for which no written reasons were available, it was not possible to ascertain what weight, if any, the sentencing court attributed to this feature. Consequently, I could not draw any meaningful comparison with the sentencing outcome in Javiour’s Case.

(d)      Zin’s Case was more instructive in relation to the significance of an offender’s role and relative culpability on his or her sentence. There, the court found that the offender, who had pleaded guilty at an early stage, was less culpable than her accomplice because she was not the mastermind and had little or no control over the corporate bank accounts after relinquishing control of them to her accomplice. The court had observed at [24] and [26]:

24    Other than the obviously large amounts involved, the calibration of the individual sentence per charge must take into account the lower culpability and involvement of the Accused. The Accused was not the mastermind and had little to no control over the number of transactions and the amounts of the funds being transferred through the corporate accounts. Of course, since she had given up control to Nyan Win, she cannot escape criminal liability for the offences committed and is being duly punished with a severe custodial sentence that is more than twice the total sentence proposed by her counsel. However, she should not be over-punished, bearing in mind her lesser role in the offences and the fact that she played no part in coming up with the illegal arrangements. The key person in Singapore involved in the arrangement was Nyan Win and it made no sense that the Prosecution would ask for the Accused to be punished to the same extent as Nyan Win – the principal perpetrator in Singapore.

…

26    The Accused had pleaded guilty early and was given the full 30% sentencing discount. If she had been convicted after a trial, I would have assessed her sentence to be in the region of 12 to 15 months per charge.

37     Having regard to these precedents, I was satisfied that the sentences imposed for Charges A1, A2 and D1 were broadly consistent with the usual sentencing range and appropriately reflected the particular and relative harm and culpability involved in the present case.

CMA offences

38     The offence under s 3(1) of the CMA was punishable with up to 2 years’ imprisonment and/or $5,000 fine for a first-time offender.

39     In the present case, Angappan and Durairaj committed the offences as a corollary to their unlicensed cross-border money transfer operations. However, this did not detract from the seriousness of their conduct as s 3(1) of the CMA was concerned principally with protecting the integrity of access controls over computer systems and against the deliberate exploitation of such systems beyond their intended purpose.

40     The facts of the present case were egregious as could be discerned from the number of accounts involved and the aggregate value of cash withdrawn – SGD6,166,515 across 33 bank accounts.

41     Given the limits imposed on cash withdrawals from ATMs, even adopting the higher withdrawal limit of $10,000 on the assumption that all the withdrawals were made at ATMs located at main DBS branches, the scale of the offending spoke for itself – at least 616 withdrawals. Furthermore, Angappan had allowed other customers to use the bank accounts to deposit monies even though they were not the account holders.

42     As Angappan had pleaded guilty to Charge A3, albeit at a late stage, I imposed a sentence of eight months’ imprisonment. Charge A4 was taken into consideration for the purpose of sentencing. Charge A4 involved the use of 23 bank accounts and the aggregate value of withdrawals was $4,099,305.

43     Durairaj similarly pleaded guilty to Charge D2 at a late stage. However, unlike Angappan, he was not involved during Period 1. In addition, his culpability in relation to Period 2 was lower, as he had acted on Angappan’s instructions. I therefore imposed a sentence of four months’ imprisonment for Charge D2.

Aggregate sentences

44     Since Angappan was sentenced to imprisonment terms for three distinct offences, s 307(1) of the CPC required the sentences for at least two of those offences to run consecutively. In this regard, there is no rule that the two longest individual sentences must run consecutively or that the longest individual sentence must be one of the consecutive sentences insofar as the aggregate sentence exceeds the longest individual sentence.[note: 10]

45     Although the offences in Charge A1 and Charge A2 took place during different periods, they essentially concerned the same legally protected interest under the PSA. On the other hand, while the offences in Charge A2 and Charge A3 protected different legal interests, they arguably formed part of the same transaction in furtherance of the cross-border money transfers during Period 2. In these circumstances, I ordered the sentences for Charges A1 and A3 to run consecutively, with the sentence for Charge A2 to run concurrently. This resulted in an aggregate sentence of 15 months and three weeks’ imprisonment and a fine of $6,000. In my view, this aggregate sentence was sufficient to reflect Angappan’s overall criminality without offending the totality principle.

46     As for Durairaj, I ordered the sentences for Charge D1 and Charge D2 to run concurrently, resulting in an aggregate sentence of eight months and three weeks’ imprisonment given that the offences arguably formed part of the same transaction.

[note: 1]Vijay’s Case at [73].

[note: 2]Vijay’s Case at [76]–[77].

[note: 3]SOAF at [5(a)].

[note: 4]SOAF at [8].

[note: 5]SOAF at [5(b)].

[note: 6]SOAF at [5(c)].

html:
Asia Excel Pte Ltd v Chua Poh Hiok

Asia Excel Pte Ltd v Chua Poh Hiok
[2026] SGDC 281

Case Number:Originating Claim No 2219 of 2024
Decision Date:31 August 2026
Tribunal/Court:District Court
Coram: Chiah Kok Khun
Counsel Name(s): Che Wei Chin (Folich LLC) for claimant; defendant in person.
Parties: Asia Excel Pte Ltd — Chua Poh Hiok

Tort – Defamation – Defamatory statements – Whether statements defamatory

Tort – Defamation – Justification – Whether substance of statement justified

Tort – Defamation – Fair Comment – Whether statements comprised fair comments based on facts and of public interest

31 August 2026

Judgment reserved.

District Judge Chiah Kok Khun:

Introduction

1       The claimant (“AE”) is in the business of retail sale of household electrical appliances and equipment; and online marketing and sales of goods. The defendant (“Ms Chua”) was a customer who purchased a cooker hood from AE through a popular online shopping platform own by Shopee Pte Ltd (“Shopee”).[note: 1]

2       AE is claiming against Ms Chua for publishing a defamatory statement (the “Review”) against AE in the review section of a page listing one of AE’s products on Shopee (“AE Listing Page”). Ms Chua, who acts in person, denies the Review is defamatory and relies on the defences of justification and fair comment.[note: 2]

3       For the reasons below, I am dismissing the claim.

Issues to be determined

4       The issues to be determined by me in this application are as follows:

(a)     Whether the Review bear a defamatory meaning.

(b)     Whether the substance or gist of the Review is true.

(c)     Whether the Review is a fair comment of public interest that can be honestly made on the facts.

Analysis and findings

The Review is not defamatory

5       The elements of the tort of defamation are trite. To establish a tort of defamation, there must be:

(a)     a statement bearing a defamatory meaning;

(b)     reference made to the claimant; and

(c)     publication to a third party.

6       Once the above is established, defamation is made out and the question of the applicability of defences such as justification, qualified privilege and fair comment arises. See: Golden Season Pte Ltd v Kairos Singapore Holdings Pte Ltd [2015] 2 SLR 751 at [34]-[35] & [39].

7       In regard to the first element, a statement is defamatory in nature if:

(a)     it lowers the claimant in the estimation of right-thinking members of society generally or ordinary reasonable people;

(b)     it causes the claimant to be shunned or avoided; or

(c)     it exposes the claimant to hatred, contempt or ridicule.

(Golden Season at [36]).

8       Turning to the present case, I note at the outset that the Review comprised the entire text of a review posted by the defendant on Shopee. It is undisputable that buyers would post ratings and reviews on products and sellers on the pages of Shopee. Such ratings and reviews form an integral part of the ecological system of e-commerce platforms. In the course of the trial, it is established that Shopee in fact actively encourages buyers of goods on its platform to post reviews on sellers. On 13 November 2024, Ms Chua posted the Review in the review section of the AE Listing Page, the text of which is as follows:[note: 3]

Please do not buy from this seller. They will call u and keep saying once delivered, no damaged to exterior means cannot return of refund. On top of it, they insist n insist u must wait at home for delivery and make sure u sign d delivery, once signed, no refund/return. Now, what if after installation, it is faulty? How to receive and make sure immediately it is not faulty? It is very frustrating that they n their delivery man will keep reminding u, once acknowledged receipt means everything is acceptable and cannot return. And they give u delivery time like 10am to 1pm n tell u, someone must check n sign once delivered or else charge u $35 for a re-delivery if no one at home. Consider the above before you buy.

9       It is not disputed that the Review was directed at AE as it was posted on the AE Listing Page.[note: 4]

10     The claimant’s case is that Ms Chua’s publication of the Review resulted in the following:[note: 5]

(a)     The Review to be read or readable by any third parties who visit the AE Listing Page.

(b)     The third parties to instantly identify that the Review relates to alleged actions performed by AE.

(c)     A large but unquantifiable number of users in Singapore and worldwide who accessed the AE Listing Page via Shopee would have read the Review.

11     The claimant contends that in their natural and ordinary meaning, the Review is understood to mean:[note: 6]

(a)     That customers should not buy items from AE.

(b)     That AE would continuously call customers to state that once delivery is done, any damage to the exterior of the product would not be subject to return or refund.

(c)     That AE would continuously insist that customers must be home for the delivery and once customers signed, there would be no return or refund for the product “no matter what”.

(d)     That AE’s delivery man would continuously remind customers of (b) above, causing frustration.

(e)     Upon giving a delivery time, someone must sign upon delivery, failing which a $35 delivery fee will be charged if no one is at the stated delivery address.

12     I consider first whether the Review is defamatory. To determine whether it is clear that the Review is defamatory, I turn to the question of the meaning of the Review

13     In this regard, caselaw provides guidance on the approach in determining meaning. In Goh Chok Tong v Jeyaretnam Joshua Benjamin and another action [1998] 2 SLR(R) 971, the Court of Appeal held at [44] that the law of defamation is concerned with the meanings of the alleged defamatory words as conveyed to the ordinary man, and ascribes two types of meanings to the words:

(a)     the natural and ordinary meaning; and

(b)     the innuendo meaning.

14     In reference to the two types of meanings, it was stated by the Court of Appeal at [44] as follows:

44    … In both cases, the meaning is that as understood by the ordinary man: in the case of the ordinary meaning such meaning is derived from the words themselves, read or heard in their proper context and in the circumstances in which they were said; and in the case of the innuendo meaning such meaning is arrived at with the aid of extrinsic facts known to the ordinary man. …

15     In another Court of Appeal decision, Chan Cheng Wah Bernard v Koh Sin Chong Freddie and another appeal [2012] 1 SLR 506 (“Chan Cheng Wah”) at [18], the Court of Appeal set out the rules applicable to the construction of words based on their natural and ordinary meanings:

(a)     the natural and ordinary meaning of a word is that which is conveyed to an ordinary reasonable person;

(b)     as the test is objective, the meaning which the defendant intended to convey is irrelevant;

(c)     the ordinary reasonable reader is not avid for scandal but can read between the lines and draw inferences;

(d)     where there are a number of possible interpretations, some of which may be non-defamatory, such a reader will not seize on only the defamatory one;

(e)     the ordinary reasonable reader is treated as having read the publication as a whole in determining its meaning, thus “the bane and the antidote must be taken together”; and

(f)     and the ordinary reasonable reader will take note of the circumstances and manner of the publication.

16     Pausing at this juncture, it is seen above that the law is clear that the question of whether a statement is defamatory is a wholly objective test. It is trite that it is so. In more than one defamation cases filed in the State Courts however, it appears that claimants have a misapprehension of the law. In the present case for instance, the claimant’s representative, who is represented by counsel, took pains to state in his affidavit of evidence in chief (“AEIC”) what he understood the Review to mean.[note: 7] He also stated that, in his mind, the Review lowers the reputation of the claimant.[note: 8] The AEIC went on in the same vein in regard to his understanding of the Review to be a statement of fact and not comment; that in his mind, the Review referred to the claimant.[note: 9] These elements of the tort of defamation are questions of law for the court. These questions do not turn on the claimants’ own beliefs and understanding. No amount of earnest belief on the part of the claimants will advance their case on meanings. Often, such misguided approach extends to evidence and pervades in the conduct of the trial, manifesting in cross-examination questions put to defendants of the defendants’ own understanding of meanings of words and their views on the question of whether they are defamatory. For completeness, it is likewise for the question of intention. The meaning which the defendant intended to convey is irrelevant in the determination of meaning, which remains an objective test.

17     Returning to the question of meaning in the present case, as discussed above, in construing the meaning of the Review, the ordinary reasonable reader will take note of the circumstances and manner of the publication of the Review (see Chan Cheng Wah at [18]). The circumstances would include the content of the Review, as well as the context of the posting of the Review. In this regard, it is not disputed that Shopee encourages buyers of goods on its platform to post reviews. Buyers regularly post ratings and reviews on products and their sellers on the pages of Shopee. Such ratings and reviews form an integral part of the Shopee platform. It was in the context of this ecological system of e-commerce that the defendant posted the Review. With the context in place, I examine the text of the Review. For ease of reference, it is set out here again:

Please do not buy from this seller. They will call u and keep saying once delivered, no damaged to exterior means cannot return of refund. On top of it, they insist n insist u must wait at home for delivery and make sure u sign d delivery, once signed, no refund/return. Now, what if after installation, it is faulty? How to receive and make sure immediately it is not faulty? It is very frustrating that they n their delivery man will keep reminding u, once acknowledged receipt means everything is acceptable and cannot return. And they give u delivery time like 10am to 1pm n tell u, someone must check n sign once delivered or else charge u $35 for a re-delivery if no one at home. Consider the above before you buy.

18     I will begin with the end. It is noted that the defendant ended the Review with the words, “Consider the above before you buy.” It is therefore clear when reading the Review as a whole that the defendant is asking the reader to consider the Review before purchasing items from the defendant. As discussed above, the ordinary reasonable reader would be treated as having read the Review as a whole in determining its meaning and the ordinary reasonable reader would take note of the circumstances and manner of the posting of the Review (Chan Cheng Wah at [18]). The ordinary reasonable reader reading the last line of the Review would understand the Review in its context and manner of posting for what it is – a review of the claimant as a seller of items on Shopee based on the defendant’s experience of making a purchase from the claimant.

19     With the context, circumstances and manner of posting of the Review in mind, I re-cap the claimant’s pleaded meanings of the Review. The claimant pleaded that the Review is understood to mean as follows:

(a)     That customers should not buy items from AE.

(b)     That AE would continuously call customers to state that once delivery is done, any damage to the exterior of the product would not be subject to return or refund.

(c)     That AE would continuously insist that customers must be home for the delivery and once customers signed, there would be no return or refund for the product “no matter what”.

(d)     That AE’s delivery man would continuously remind customers of (b) above, causing frustration.

(e)     Upon giving a delivery time, someone must sign upon delivery, failing which a $35 delivery fee will be charged if no one is at the stated delivery address.

20     Starting with the first pleaded meaning, it would be seen from the above that reading the Review as a whole that the defendant is not telling readers outright not to purchase items from the claimant. Instead, she is telling readers to consider her Review before doing so. Further, she sets out her personal experience making a purchase from the claimant for the reader to consider, before deciding whether or not to buy any items from the claimant. As alluded to above, the defendant ended the Review with the line, “Consider the above before you buy.” Contrary to the claimant’s assertion, the defendant is not saying that customers should not buy items from the claimant. Instead, the defendant is saying that they ought to consider her Review before doing so. On plain reading, the Review does not bear the first meaning pleaded by the claimant.

21     As for the second, third, fourth and fifth pleaded meaning, the claimant would be referring to the following portion of the Review:

… They will call u and keep saying once delivered, no damaged to exterior means cannot return of refund. On top of it, they insist n insist u must wait at home for delivery and make sure u sign d delivery, once signed, no refund/return. Now, what if after installation, it is faulty? How to receive and make sure immediately it is not faulty? It is very frustrating that they n their delivery man will keep reminding u, once acknowledged receipt means everything is acceptable and cannot return. And they give u delivery time like 10am to 1pm n tell u, someone must check n sign once delivered or else charge u $35 for a re-delivery if no one at home. …

22     First, a scrutiny of this portion of Review will show that nowhere does the defendant say that the claimant would “continuously call customers”. The claimant has no basis for pleading so in its second pleaded meaning. Second, the claimant has not pleaded how the other portion of its second pleaded meaning is defamatory. As discussed above, a statement is defamatory in nature if it lowers the claimant in the estimation of right-thinking members of ordinary reasonable people, causes the claimant to be shunned or avoided, or exposes the claimant to hatred, contempt or ridicule (Golden Season at [36]). I do not see how, by the claimant’s own pleaded second meaning that the Review is defamatory. The same analysis applies to the third, fourth and fifth pleaded meaning. The claimant has not pleaded in what way these meanings are defamatory. An examination of the meanings pleaded by the claimant (paras 19(b)-(e) above) will show that the claimant has in fact largely paraphrased the text of the Review without pleading the defamatory meanings. I am thus not able to make any determination of defamatory meanings. By the claimant’s own case, the Review is objectively not defamatory.

The gist of the Review is true

23     I therefore find that the claimant has failed to prove that the Review is defamatory. That is sufficient to dispose of the claim. For completeness only, I turn to the defence of justification, which the defendant has pleaded. It is trite that the defence of justification is established if the substance or gist of the offending words (as opposed to those parts of the offending words which do not add to the sting of the alleged defamation) are proven to be true. The Court of Appeal held as follows in Qingdao Bohai Construction Group Co, Ltd v Goh Teck Beng [2016] 4 SLR 979 (“Qingdao Bohai”) at [168] in regard to the defence of justification:

168    It is not controversial that the burden of proof in establishing the defence of justification lies squarely on the defendant (Gatley ([34] supra) at para 11.4; Gary Chan ([34] supra) at para 13.003; Evans ([35] supra) at pp 85–86). To successfully establish the defence of justification, the defendant need only prove the truth of the substance or gist of the offending words (as opposed to those parts of the offending words which do not add to the sting of the alleged defamation) (Review Publishing Co Ltd v Lee Hsien Loong [2010] 1 SLR 52 at [134]). Thus, some leeway is given for exaggeration and error (Chan Cheng Wah Bernard v Koh Sin Chong Freddie [2012] 1 SLR 506 (“Bernard Chan”) at [44]). However, in no way does this leeway suggest that the burden is easily discharged.

[emphasis added]

24     As seen, the defendant needs only prove the truth of the substance or gist of the offending words. Likewise, in Chan Cheng Wah at [44] the Court of Appeal held as follows:

44    The defendant has only to prove the “sting” of the charge, and some leeway for exaggeration and error is given. As stated by Burrough J in Edwards v Bell (1824) 1 Bing 403 at 409:

… it is sufficient if the substance of the libellous statement be justified; it is unnecessary to repeat every word which might have been the subject of the original comment. As much must be justified as meets the sting of the charge, and if anything be contained in a charge which does not add to the sting of it, that need not be justified.

See also Gatley on Libel and Slander (Patrick Milmos & W V H Rogers eds) (Sweet & Maxwell, 11th Ed, 2005) at para 11.9 and Aaron Anne Joseph v Cheong Yip Seng [1996] 1 SLR(R) 258 at [73].

25     In each case therefore, it is always the sting of the defamation that has to be justified. Further, it so doing, some leeway is given to the defendant for exaggeration and error.

26     In the present case, the substance of the Review would be the defendant’s delivery team calling the defendant to inform her that once the item is delivered without no damage to its exterior and the delivery is signed off, no refund will be given for any return of the item. The Review also referred to the defendant giving delivery timings such as 10 am to 1 pm, and the defendant must wait for the delivery, failing which, the claimant will charge $35 for a re-delivery if no one is at home to receive the delivery.

27     With the substance of the Review distilled, I turn to the claimant’s case as to how delivery of its goods is carried out. The claimant says that it communicated to the defendant information regarding the delivery of the cooker hood in the following manner:[note: 10]

(a)     On 13 September 2024, at around 11:52am, the claimant’s delivery team texted the defendant stating the following:

(i)       someone needs to be at the defendant’s premises to check the electrical appliance upon delivery; and

(ii)       only visible damages like scratches or dents need to be reported upon delivery. Functional defects are covered by the product warranty itself;

(b)     On 12 September 2024, around 1:13pm, the claimant’s customer service team made clear to the defendant the following points:

(i)       delivery will be on 13 November 2024, between 10am to 3pm;

(ii)       delivery staff will call the defendant about 30 minutes before arrival;

(iii)       any visible defects must be raised on the spot upon delivery and no claims for visible defects will be accepted after the delivery staff left the defendant’s premises;

(iv)       change of delivery dates should be notified two days in advance; and

(v)       only a no-show or last-minute changes for delivery timings will incur a fee of $35 to re-arrange a new delivery date.

28     It is immediately plain analysing the above that the substance of the Review is wholly justified. The substance sets out the above communication from the claimant to the defendant. By the claimant’s own case, the gist of the Review reflects the information communicated by the claimant’s delivery team to the defendant prior to the delivery.

29     For completeness, I refer to the claimant’s case that it had communicated to the defendant that functional defects of the cooker hood are covered by the product warranty issued by the manufacturer of the item. The claimant makes much of its case that the content of the Review is inconsistent with the fact that the manufacturer of the appliance provides a product warranty. However, it is clear from a plain perusal of the Review that the defendant is referring to a refund by the claimant. There is no reference in any manner in the Review regarding product warranty or refund by the manufacturer. In fact, there is no mention of the manufacturer at all in the Review. The substance of the Review concerns the delivery and refund policy of the claimant. And as discussed above, the substance is clearly justified by the claimant’s own case.

The Review comprises comments which a matter of public interest

30     As well for completeness only, I turn to consider briefly the defence of fair comment, which the defendant has also pleaded.

31     The four elements of a defence of fair comment are as follows:

(a)     the words complained of are comments, though they may consist of or include inference of facts;

(b)     the comment is based on facts;

(c)     the comment is one which a fair-minded person can honestly make on the facts; and

(d)     the comment is on a matter of public interest.

(See: Gary Chan Kok Yew and Lee Pey Woan, The Law of Torts in Singapore (Academy Publishing, 2nd Ed, 2016) at para 13.013)

32     In my view, the texts in the Review are capable of being characterised as comments, which are based on facts. The Review comprised deductions, inferences, conclusions, remarks or observations made by the defendant from the facts. The facts that the Review are based on would be the information communicated by the claimant to the defendant regarding the delivery of the cooker hood as set out above. The information communicated by the claimant provided a sufficient substratum of facts on which the defendant could base her comments. As noted above, the Review can be deemed to consist of comments, though they may include inferences of facts. I find that her comments are those which a fair-minded person can honestly make on the facts. As the claimant is selling merchandise on a popular online shopping platform, I also find that the comments are a matter of public interest. I therefore find that the defence of fair comment would apply in any event in the present case.

Conclusion

33     It is seen in this case that ratings and reviews are part and parcel of the ecological system of e-commerce platforms. Platform owners actively encourage buyers of goods to give ratings and post reviews on products and sellers on their platforms. Such ratings and reviews contribute to the pool of accessible information that buyers can have resort to when shopping on these platforms. Ratings and reviews are necessary for the efficacious operation of such e-commerce platforms. Sellers who use e-commerce platforms must accept ratings and reviews on their goods and services as part of conducting business online. It also means that they must be prepared to take the bad with the good when buyers give their ratings and reviews. Negative reviews are necessarily part and parcel of conducting business online. The tort of defamation protects the reputation of individuals and businesses. But not every negative review is defamatory. With the proliferation of online shopping, we need to guard against any increase in unmeritorious defamation actions stemming from negative online reviews posted on e-commerce platforms.

34     In the present case, I have found that the Review is not defamatory; and that in any event, the defence of justification applies. Further, I also find that the Review comprises comments which are a matter of public interest, and the defence of fair comment applies in any event. In the premises, the claim is dismissed.

35     As regards the question of costs, there is no reason for costs not to follow the event in this case. The claim is dismissed and the claimant is to pay costs. As for the quantum of costs, taking into consideration the nature of the claim, the work done by parties for the action, the time spent for the trial, the respective submissions on costs, and the defendant acting in person; I fix costs at $4,000 (inclusive of disbursements), to be paid by the claimant to the defendant.
