html:
Tan Sze Shan v Gain City Best-Electric Pte Ltd

Tan Sze Shan v Gain City Best-Electric Pte Ltd
[2026] SGDC 273

Case Number:Originating Application for Enforcement Order No 140 of 2026
Decision Date:26 August 2026
Tribunal/Court:District Court
Coram: Lewis Tan
Counsel Name(s): The applicant in person; Sheam Zenglin (Shen Zenglin) and Lee Soo Chye (Oaks Legal LLC) for the respondent.
Parties: Tan Sze Shan — Gain City Best-Electric Pte Ltd

Civil Procedure – Judgments and orders – Enforcement – Whether judgment remains capable of enforcement after attempted performance by judgment debtor

Civil Procedure – Judgments and orders – Enforcement – Whether judgment debtor’s inputs can be obtained before determining application for an enforcement order made without notice

26 August 2026

Deputy Registrar Lewis Tan (delivering the judgment of the court ex tempore):

Introduction

1       The present enforcement application arises from an order requiring the enforcement respondent to provide the enforcement applicant with a replacement laptop or, in default of that obligation, to pay him $1,586. The respondent tendered a replacement laptop within the stipulated time, but the applicant rejected it because it apparently did not carry the requisite warranty.

2       More than four years later, the applicant seeks to enforce the alternative monetary obligation. Interpreting the order, I find that the monetary obligation never arose. The respondent duly tendered performance of the obligation to provide a replacement laptop, and the applicant’s rejection of that performance did not place the respondent in default. There is therefore no outstanding obligation capable of enforcement, and the application for an enforcement order is dismissed.

Facts and Procedural History

3       On 14 March 2021, Mr Tan Sze Shan (“Applicant”) purchased a laptop, an ASUS Laptop Ryzen 7 4700U, from Gain City Best-Electric Pte Ltd (“Respondent”) for $1,586.00. Subsequently, the Applicant successfully brought a claim in the Small Claims Tribunal (“SCT”) against the Respondent in respect of the laptop, with the learned Tribunal Magistrate ordering as follows (the “SCT Order”):[note: 1]

(1)    The Respondent to provide a one-to-one replacement of the [Applicant’s] laptop by 25 February 2022. [“First obligation”]

(2)    In default, the Respondent do pay the [Applicant] the sum of $1,586.00 … by 25 February 2022, failing which the [Applicant] may enforce the Order accordingly. [“Second obligation”]

4       Sometime on or before 25 February 2022,[note: 2] the Respondent attempted delivery of a replacement laptop. However, the delivery was rejected by the Applicant as it apparently did not come with the full manufacturer warranty.[note: 3]

5       The matter was left dormant for more than four years, until May 2026, when the Applicant issued two Letters of Demand to the Respondent, demanding payment of $1,586. The Respondent rejected the demands as it considered that it had complied with the SCT Order by attempting delivery of a replacement laptop within the stipulated timeframe, and in so doing “diligent[ly] fulfilled what was asked by the SCT [O]rder”.[note: 4]

6       The Applicant thus took out the present enforcement application, wherein he sought to attach up to $2,586 in the Respondent’s bank accounts, with this sum comprising $1,586 of the sum apparently outstanding under the SCT Order, $500 due to the Bailiff, and $500 due to Applicant. In accordance with O 22 r 2(3) of the Rules of Court 2021 (“ROC”), which provides that “[a]n enforcement applicant may apply to the Court by summons without notice for an enforcement order” [emphasis added], the enforcement application was made without notice.

Obtaining Respondent’s Inputs before Determination of the Enforcement Application

7       While the application was appropriately made without notice, O 22 r 2(3) of the ROC does not require the Court to determine it without first hearing from the enforcement respondent; the rule merely provides that the application “may” be made without notice. Pursuant to the Court’s general case-management powers under O 3 r 2(2) of the ROC to ensure that justice is done and having regard to the Ideal of achieving fair and practical results suited to the needs of the parties under O 3 r 1(2)(e) of the ROC, I directed that the Respondent be given an opportunity to respond.

8       This was appropriate because the Applicant’s own affidavit disclosed that the Respondent had tendered a replacement laptop within the time stipulated by the SCT Order, which the Applicant rejected. Whether the Respondent was “in default”, and hence whether any obligation remained capable of enforcement, was therefore an anterior issue which ought to be determined before any enforcement order was made. Determining the application without first resolving that issue risked unnecessary expenditure of time and costs, as it would merely defer the determination of this anterior issue to a later stage when the decision was subsequently challenged by the party adversely affected by my decision.

No Outstanding Obligation to Enforce

9       Having heard from parties, I find for the Respondent on this anterior issue. As the First obligation was performed, the Second obligation – which only arose if the Respondent was in default of the First obligation – did not arise. Accordingly, there is no outstanding obligation under the SCT Order capable of enforcement, and the application is dismissed. I elaborate.

10     In Hoban Steven Maurice Dixon and another v Scanlon Graeme John and others [2007] 2 SLR(R) 770 (“Hoban”), the appellants sued the respondents for minority oppression but subsequently decided on an exit mechanism for the appellants’ shares in the third respondent company to be purchased by the first and second respondents. With broad agreement from the parties, the trial judge ordered parties to appoint an expert to value the shares in the third respondent so that the first and second respondents could “purchase” the appellants’ shares (“June 2004 Order”). The appointed expert valued the company’s shares at nil, and the trial judge declined to adjust this valuation. Given the nil valuation, the Court of Appeal declared the trial judge’s June 2004 Order inoperative as any share transfer would have been a gift rather than a “purchase” as envisaged in the order. According to the Court, “[i]t would be wholly unreasonable and unjust to attribute to the trial judge an intention that in circumstances where the subject shares are valued at nil value, the [a]ppellant is under an obligation to effectively give away its shares to the [f]irst and [s]econd [r]espondents” (Hoban at [41]). Accordingly, the order was rendered “inoperative by reason of the legal fact that the subject shares could not be purchased by the [f]irst and [s]econd [r]espondents at nil value. This means that the parties are restored to the status quo ante, as if the June 2004 Order had never been made” (Hoban at [46]).

11     I pause at this juncture to observe that while the June 2004 Order in Hoban was an order made with broad agreement from parties, it was not a contractual consent order, but an ordinary order of court. This can be seen from [41] of Hoban, where the Court of Appeal interpreted the order from the perspective of the trial judge rather than that of the parties; the latter would have been the case if the order was a contractual consent order (Turf Club Auto Emporium Pte Ltd and others v Yeo Boong Hua and others and another appeal and other matters [2017] 2 SLR 12 at [172]). Hoban is therefore instructive as to the proper interpretation of the SCT Order, which is likewise an ordinary court order.

12     I return to the facts of this case. The Applicant accepts that the Respondent “attempted delivery [of a replacement laptop] on 25 February 2022”, but that he rejected it because it “did not come with the full manufacturer warranty that is standard for all new laptops”.[note: 5] Before me, he also acknowledged that the Respondent attempted delivery of a brand new laptop, but he did not accept it as he wanted a “brand new [replacement laptop] with warranty”. Crucially, the Applicant has not asserted that the offered replacement laptop was of a different make or model from the one that he had purchased.

13     Hence, on the Applicant’s own case, the offered replacement laptop was rejected solely because it lacked the requisite warranty, not because it was physically different from the laptop purchased. Since “provide” ordinarily means to make available (Oxford English Dictionary, “Provide” <oed.com> (accessed 26 August 2026); Meriam-Webster Dictionary, “Provide” <merriam-webster.com/dictionary> (accessed 26 August 2026); and Cambridge Dictionary, “Provide” <dictionary.cambridge.org> (accessed 26 August 2026)), the Respondent performed the First obligation by making a “one-to-one replacement” available to the Applicant within the stipulated time.

14     The fact that the Applicant declined to take possession because of the apparent lack of warranty did not detract from that performance. Nowhere in the SCT Order is it stated that the replacement laptop “must be a brand-new laptop with full manufacturer warranty equivalent to the original unit”,[note: 6] nor are there words to such effect. In fact, the original purchase order for the Applicant’s laptop also did not expressly provide for such a warranty.[note: 7] I have also not been provided with the transcript of the proceedings before the Tribunal Magistrate that would support such an interpretation. It would thus be “wholly unreasonable and unjust to attribute to the [Tribunal Magistrate] an intention” (Hoban at [41]) to impose a warranty requirement which finds no expression in the SCT Order or the underlying purchase order. To read such a requirement into the SCT Order would impermissibly enlarge its terms and, more fundamentally, allow the Applicant to treat the Respondent as being in default by reference to a condition which the Tribunal Magistrate never imposed.

15     By insisting on the warranty, the Applicant is essentially seeking an improvement to the SCT Order which goes beyond its terms. This cannot be countenanced. As the Court recently explained in GNC Holdings LLC v ONI Global Pte Ltd and another [2026] SGHC(I) 11 at [11]:

The role of the Court is to enforce the Award or not as the case may be, not to begin hearing a case on what might be seen as improvements to the orders to be now sought by a party. … That is the role of the Court: to enforce the award, not to rehear an application to vary the award as to relief. [emphasis added]

I therefore find that the Respondent was not “in default” of its First obligation “to provide a one-to-one replacement of the [Applicant’s] laptop by 25 February 2022”. The Applicant’s rejection of the replacement based on a requirement not imposed by the SCT Order did not place the Respondent in default. The Second obligation to pay the Applicant $1,586 therefore did not arise.

16     There is consequently no outstanding obligation under the SCT Order capable of enforcement, and no basis to make an enforcement order under O 22 r 2(1) of the ROC. This is consistent with the scheme of O 22: O 22 r 2(6) contemplates continued enforcement where the amount due has not been fully satisfied or the enforcement respondent has not complied with all the terms of the order, while O 22 r 2(8)(a) contemplates the cessation of enforcement where the enforcement respondent has complied with all the terms of the Court order that is being enforced. There is therefore no unsatisfied obligation remaining under the SCT Order upon which an enforcement order can operate.

Conclusion

17     In summary, the Respondent did what the SCT Order required: it duly provided a one-to-one replacement within the stipulated time. The Applicant’s rejection of that replacement on a basis not found in the SCT Order did not place the Respondent “in default”. The alternative monetary obligation therefore never arose, leaving no unsatisfied obligation capable of enforcement.

18     The application for an enforcement order is thus dismissed. I will now hear parties on costs.

[note: 1]Affidavit of Tan Sze Shan dated 10 July 2026 (“TSS”) at p 3.

[note: 2]While the Applicant asserts that the delivery was attempted on 25 February 2022, the Respondent’s records indicate that the delivery was attempted on 22 February 2022. On either case, the delivery was attempted before the deadline for performance of the First obligation.

[note: 3]TSS at [4].

[note: 4]TSS at p 10.

[note: 5]TSS at [4].

[note: 6]TSS at [4].

[note: 7]TSS at p 5.

html:
Public Prosecutor v Steven Gan Teck Guan

Public Prosecutor v Steven Gan Teck Guan
[2026] SGDC 269

Case Number:LTA Case No 3241488913, Magistrate's Appeals No 9134 of 2026-01
Decision Date:26 August 2026
Tribunal/Court:District Court
Coram: Koh Jiaying
Counsel Name(s): Elaine Ng, Jarren Wong and Hoi Min Fah for the Land Transport Authority; Accused in Person.
Parties: Public Prosecutor — Steven Gan Teck Guan

Criminal Law – R 22A(1)(a) Road Traffic (Public Service Vehicles) (Vocational Licences and Conduct of Drivers, Conductors, Trishaw Riders and Passengers) Rules  – Loitering for the purpose of soliciting passengers

Criminal Procedure and Sentencing – Sentencing

[LawNet Editorial Note: An appeal to this decision has been filed in MA 9134/2026/01.]

26 August 2026

District Judge Koh Jiaying:

Introduction

1       The accused, Mr Steven Gan Teck Guan, claimed trial to the following charge (“Charge”):

LTA-3241488913-1

You…are charged that you, on 31 March 2024 at about 5.58pm at Harbourfront Centre Taxi Point being a licensee, when acting as a driver of chauffeured private hire car no. SML8689T did loiter for the purpose of soliciting for passengers at the said location, in contravention of Rule 22A(1)(a) of the Road Traffic (Public Service Vehicles) (Vocational Licences and Conduct of Drivers, Conductors, Trishaw Riders and Passengers) Rules and you have thereby committed an offence under Section 131(1) of the Road Traffic Act 1961 and punishable under Section 131(2)(a) of the said Act.

2       After the trial, I found the accused guilty of the Charge and convicted him. He was sentenced to a fine of $650, in default 2 days’ imprisonment. I ordered a stay of execution on the payment of the fine pending the hearing of his appeal and granted bail pending appeal.

Elements of the Charge

3       The elements of the Charge are:

(a)     the accused was a licensee, when acting as a driver of chauffeured private hire car no. SML 8689T on 31 March 2024 (“First Element”); and

(b)     the accused loitered for the purpose of soliciting passengers at the Harbourfront Centre Taxi Point (“Location”) on 31 March 2024 at about 5.58 pm (“Second Element”).

The First Element was undisputed

4       Rule 22A(1) of the Road Traffic (Public Service Vehicles) (Vocational Licences and Conduct of Drivers, Conductors, Trishaw Riders and Passengers) Rules (“Rules”) applies to “a person licensed to drive a specified vehicle”. Pursuant to Rule 22A(3) of the Rules, “specified vehicle” includes a “chauffeured private hire car”, which Rule 2 of the Rules defines as a motor car that is the subject of a chauffeured private hire car licence granted under the Road Traffic (Public Service Vehicles) Rules.

5       For the First Element to be satisfied:

(a)     the accused must have been licensed to drive a chauffeured private hire car;

(b)     the vehicle SML 8689T (“Vehicle”) must have been the subject of a chauffeured private hire car licence; and

(c)     the accused must have acted as a driver of the Vehicle (as a chauffeured private hire car), on 31 March 2024.

The Prosecution’s evidence on the First Element is set out below. As the accused did not challenge this evidence, it was undisputed that he was a licensee, when acting as a driver of the Vehicle, which was a chauffeured private hire car, on 31 March 2024.

6       The Prosecution produced a Certificate under Section 139(2) of the Road Traffic Act[note: 1] (“Certificate”) in respect of the Vehicle as at 31 March 2024. By way of the Certificate, the Assistant Registrar of Vehicles certified the particulars of the Vehicle as recorded in the register of vehicles kept in accordance with Rule 12 of the Road Traffic (Motor Vehicles, Registration & Licensing) Rules. The Certificate reflected the owner of the Vehicle as L.H. Car Rental Pte Ltd, with the effective date of ownership being 10 June 2019 to 13 March 2025. The “Class Description” and the “Body Description” of the Vehicle were recorded as “Private Hire (Chauffeur)” and “Z11 – Private Hire (Chauffeur) Station Wagon/Jeep/Land Rover” respectively. Investigation Officer Bryan Tan[note: 2] (“IO Tan”) testified that Z11 is a classification in Singapore for chauffeured private hire cars such as those operated under Grab and Gojek, and such classification allows both private use and chauffeured services[note: 3]. It was therefore clear that the Vehicle was a chauffeured private hire car as at 31 March 2024.

7       The Charge refers to the accused as a licensee, when acting as a driver of the Vehicle (a chauffeured private hire car). Rule 2 of the Rules defines:

(a)     “chauffeured private hire car driver” as a person who is authorised by a licence to drive a chauffeured private hire car for reward (whether or not as an employee);

(b)     “licence” as “a vocational licence granted under section 110 of the [Road Traffic] Act authorising the holder (a) to drive one or more classes of vehicles (excluding trishaws)”, among others; and

(c)     “licensee” to mean the holder of a licence[note: 4].

8       The Prosecution produced the accused’s Driver Profile generated from the Land Transport Authority’s Public Transport Licensing System[note: 5] (“Driver Profile”). IO Tan gave evidence, based on the Driver Profile, that the accused possessed a Bus Driver’s Vocational Licence and Taxi Driver’s Vocational Licence, which were valid as at 31 March 2024[note: 6]. IO Tan also testified that where a private hire chauffeur car was hired out with the driver to convey passengers for hire and reward, the driver must possess a valid taxi driver vocational licence or a private hire car driver vocational licence issued by the Land Transport Authority (“LTA”).[note: 7] Law James[note: 8], the manager of L.H. Car Rental Pte Ltd, gave evidence that the Vehicle was rented to the accused from 24 November 2021 to 18 May 2024, which the accused confirmed[note: 9].

9       It was therefore clear that the accused was a licensee when acting as a chauffeured private hire car driver of the Vehicle on 31 March 2024.

The Second Element

10     The sole issue to be determined was whether the accused loitered for the purpose of soliciting passengers at the Location on 31 March 2024 at about 5.58 pm.

Meaning of “loiter for the purpose of soliciting passengers, by any means”

11     Rule 22A(1)(a) of the Rules provides that subject to Rule 22A(2), a person licensed to drive a specified vehicle shall not, in a public place loiter for the purpose of soliciting passengers, by any means, for any specified vehicle. Rule 22A(2) of the Rules provides that Rule 22A(1) does not apply where the said person loiters or solicits passengers with the consent in writing of the owner or operator of the public place, in accordance with the terms of such consent. Given that there was no evidence of such consent from the owner or operator of the Location, Rule 22A(2) of the Rules did not apply in the present case.

12     In order to determine if the Second Element of the Charge was made out, it was necessary to consider the meaning of the phrase “loiter for the purpose of soliciting passengers, by any means” in Rule 22A(1)(a) of the Rules.

13     The Prosecution submitted that while “loiter” was not statutorily defined in the Rules, the Oxford Advanced Learner’s Dictionary defines the term as “to stand or wait somewhere especially with no obvious reason”. As for the term “soliciting passengers”, the Prosecution referred to PP v Tan Khong Leng Jackson [2015] SGDC 68 (“Jackson Tan”) at [38], where the Court had considered what amounted to soliciting for the purposes of Rule 23(o) of the Rules (as at 25 December 2013, being the date of the offence in that case). Rule 23(o) provides that “[a] licensee, when acting as a taxi driver, shall not solicit passengers”. The Court in Jackson Tan found that for a taxi driver to solicit for passengers under that rule, he would be offering or inviting them to purchase services and conveying towards the potential passenger the idea that he is offering to that passenger his taxi services or inviting the passenger to consume his services: at [38]. Given that the conduct targeted by Rule 23(o) of the Rules and Rule 22A(1)(a) was substantively the same, I found the Court’s definition of “soliciting” in Jackson Tan to be persuasive.

14     I also found the Court’s views on “soliciting custom” (as part of a test on whether drivers of private hire vehicles were “plying for hire”) in Sulaiman bin Mohd Hassan v PP [2021] 5 SLR 763 (“Sulaiman”) and R (United Trade Action Group Ltd) v Transport for London [2023] 1 WLR 367 (“UTAG”) helpful.

15     In Sulaiman, one of the charges faced by the accused was for using a chauffeured private hire car as a taxi, otherwise than in accordance with the licence issued for the vehicle, in contravention of s 101(1) of the Road Traffic Act (“RTA”), an offence punishable under s 101(2) of the RTA: see Sulaiman at [3(a)]. The pivotal issue for the RTA charge was the meaning of “ply for hire” in the Second Schedule of the RTA because it was only if the accused was plying for hire that he would have used the vehicle as a taxi and not as a private hire car: see Sulaiman at [48]. The Court in Sulaiman referred to Cogley v Sherwood [1959] 2 QB 311, where Lord Parker CJ considered that the essence of “plying for hire” was that the vehicle in question should be on view, the owner or driver should expressly or impliedly invite the public to use it and the member of the public should be able to use that vehicle if he wanted to: see Sulaiman at [52]. The Court in Sulaiman also discussed Rose v Welbeck Motors Ltd [1962] 2 All ER 801, where Lord Parker CJ found that in Cogley, it was held that it was essential before one could say that a vehicle was plying for hire, first that it should be exhibited or be on view to the public, and secondly, that it should while on view expressly or impliedly solicit custom in the sense of inviting the public to use it: see Sulaiman at [55].

16     The Court in Sulaiman found that the test of when a vehicle is plying for hire enunciated in Cogley is really an application of common sense to a particular set of facts and that the inquiry has to be fact-sensitive because there can be many variations as to how a driver sources for passengers, particularly in the context of modern-day technology: see Sulaiman at [64]. The Court noted that there may also be situations where the vehicle is not within sight of members of the public (because it is parked at another location nearby) but the driver is away from the vehicle asking potential passengers whether they need transport and when they say they do, the driver then brings them to the vehicle or drives the vehicle to meet them, and it would be fair and logical in all these situations to say that the vehicle was in truth plying for hire: see Sulaiman at [66].

17     In considering such situations as falling within the definition of “plying for hire”, the Court in Sulaiman appeared to take a practical approach in the context of modern-day technology where exhibition was not a necessary ingredient of the offence in all cases and the focus would be on the second question of soliciting custom of the Cogley test, ie. asking potential customers whether they needed transport. This approach is similar to that taken by the Court in Nottingham City Council v Woodings [1994] RTR 72, which was discussed in Sulaiman at [58] to [60]. The focus on the second question in Sulaiman can also be seen when the Court discussed a scenario of a vehicle waiting at a location where taxis or other public service vehicles usually pick up or drop off passengers, that would point to the vehicle being there for the purpose of picking up passengers at random, and emphasised that the material consideration in determining whether the vehicle was plying for hire was that the driver is willing to make the agreement, express or implied, to ferry anyone needing transport and willing to pay the fare: see Sulaiman at [70].

18     In UTAG, the issue was whether London private hire vehicles (“PHVs”) using an operator’s smartphone app were plying for hire. If they did so, the trade association for hackney carriage drivers contended that this would be unlawful as only licensed hackney carriages could lawfully ply for hire under section 7 of the Metropolitan Public Carriage Act 1869. The English Court of Appeal found that the two-stage test of exhibition of the vehicle and solicitation of passengers set out in Cogley was clear and intelligible and stood the test of time: see UTAG at [44]. The English Court of Appeal rejected the submission that a PHV or its driver solicits business simply by driving towards or remaining in an area of high demand (see UTAG at [47]) and stated that there was nothing else the operator’s driver was doing which amounted to solicitation of any prospective passenger to take a ride in the car without having previously booked through the operator as they did not solicit passers by to step into the vehicle and reach an agreement on the spot, among other things: see UTAG at [48].

19     In view of the authorities cited above, I found that the phrase “loiter for the purpose of soliciting passengers, by any means” in Rule 22A(1)(a) of the Rules means to wait or stand around for the purpose of expressly or impliedly inviting members of the public to use the relevant vehicle for reward, using any means or methods. Similar to the views expressed by the Court in Sulaiman, the test is an application of common sense to a particular set of facts and the inquiry has to be fact-sensitive.

The Prosecution’s case

20     The Prosecution’s case was that the Second Element was established because:

(a)     the CCTV footage of the Location[note: 10] at the material time showed the accused loitering at the Location;

(b)     the accused did not have any bookings assigned by the ride hail operators to pick up any passengers at Harbourfront Centre on 31 March 2024 between 5 and 6.30 pm; and

(c)     one Mr Ranjit Singh s/o Manjit Singh (“Mr Ranjit”) testified that the accused had tried to get the attention of the people queuing at the taxi stand by saying that the queue was long and his vehicle was the one with the boot open, and had proceeded to provide a fare price upon Mr Ranjit’s request.[note: 11]

The Defence’s case

21     The accused’s position was that LTA had fabricated the story[note: 12], and conspired with Mr Ranjit to entice him though he did not fall into the trap.[note: 13] His case was that he did not solicit passengers because it was Mr Ranjit who had started to communicate with him and offered him a fare, which he rejected.[note: 14]

Reasons for conviction

22     It is trite that the principle of proof beyond a reasonable doubt can be conceptualised in two ways. First, a reasonable doubt may arise from within the case mounted by the Prosecution. As part of its own case, the Prosecution must adduce sufficient evidence to establish the accused person’s guilt beyond a reasonable doubt on at least a prima facie basis. Failure to do so may lead to a finding that the Prosecution has failed to mount a case to answer, or to an acquittal. The second way in which a reasonable doubt may arise is on an assessment of the totality of the evidence. What the Defence needs to do to bring the Prosecution’s case below the requisite threshold is to point to such evidence as would generate a reasonable doubt: see PP v GCK and another matter [2020] 1 SLR 486 at [134] to [149].

23     I was satisfied that the Prosecution has adduced sufficient evidence to establish the accused’s guilt beyond a reasonable doubt on at least a prima facie basis for the following reasons.

24     First, the first CCTV footage of the Location from 17:35:00 to 18:15:00[note: 15], which is exhibit P6, showed that the accused remained at the Location for more than 30 minutes, during which he repeatedly walked around the taxi bay area, near persons waiting in the taxi queue and the adjacent area, and around his Vehicle. The Vehicle fully entered the frame of exhibit P6 at 17:39:51. The accused parked the Vehicle in a lot at the Location, alighted and opened the boot of the Vehicle at 17:40:58. He remained outside the Vehicle until 17:49:26, at times walking near the taxi queue and the adjacent area where people were waiting with luggage. The accused alighted again at 17:49:55 and remained outside the Vehicle[note: 16] until the end of P6. During this time, he continued to walk around the taxi stand and the adjacent area where people were waiting with luggage, as well as around the Vehicle. The accused confirmed that he had driven the Vehicle to the Location as seen in P6 and remained there during the rest of P6.[note: 17] It was therefore clear that the accused was walking around the Location for slightly more than 30 minutes from 5.40 pm onwards on 31 March 2024.

25     As was stated in Sulaiman, if the vehicle was waiting at a location where taxis or other public service vehicles usually pick up or drop off passengers, that would point to the vehicle being there for the purpose of picking up passengers at random although the material consideration is that the driver is willing to make the agreement, express or implied, to ferry anyone needing transport and willing to pay the fare: see Sulaiman at [70].

26     Secondly, it was clear from the evidence put forward by the Prosecution that the accused had no ride-hailing bookings at the material time. It followed that the accused was not at the Location for the purpose of fulfilling any ride-hailing booking at the time of the offence. IO Tan testified that he had confirmed with the four ride-hail companies, namely Grab, Gojek, TADA and Ryde Technologies that the accused did not have any passenger bookings on 31 March 2024 between 5 and 6.30 pm at the Location.[note: 18] This was not disputed by the accused. The accused also asked IO Tan during cross-examination whether he had the right to provide his own personal service and not just doing e-hailing jobs, and IO Tan agreed that he had the right to do so.[note: 19]

27     Thirdly, Mr Ranjit’s evidence established on a prima facie basis that the accused was soliciting passengers.

28     Mr Ranjit’s evidence was that on 31 March 2024, he had returned from Batam and had joined the queue at the taxi stand at the Location. While he was in the queue, the accused was walking along and saying something like “The queue is long. You need a ride? My vehicle is over there, the one with the boot open.” Mr Ranjit therefore approached the accused and asked “Are you a taxi?”, to which the accused told him to look at his app on Grab, and whatever was the premium price, that was the price of the accused’s ride. Mr Ranjit then looked at his app and saw that the price was about $65 and thereafter asked the accused if he was touting. There was a subsequent exchange of words, including the accused saying that he studied law.[note: 20] Before leaving the Location, Mr Ranjit took photographs of the Vehicle and subsequently submitted a feedback with the photographs through the LTA portal on the same day.[note: 21]

29     Mr Ranjit had stated in the feedback that “I encountered a private hire driver touting at Harbourfront Center taxi stabd (sic)…He asked me to look at by (sic) grab app for premium fare ($76) and that was his price. When I asked him if he is touting he got defensive and started challenging me. He (sic) vehicle was also parked at the taxi bay. I hope LTA take (sic) action against such drivers who hustle tourist.”[note: 22] During cross-examination, Mr Ranjit confirmed that he had seen the Grab rate was $65, using the app on his phone.[note: 23] He disagreed with the accused’s position that he had approached the accused first, and testified that he was responding to the accused’s call-out.[note: 24] He also disagreed that he had pointed his finger at the Vehicle and asked if it was available for service.[note: 25] His evidence was that at 17:58:27 of the second CCTV footage of the Location[note: 26], he was looking in the direction of the two cars which were parked at the far end of the taxi bay and had asked the accused whether the accused’s car was the one in white which he understood to be an official taxi.[note: 27] He further testified that he only pointed to the Vehicle after the accused told him that the accused’s car was the silver car.[note: 28] He then clarified that the reason why he pointed to the two cars was that he knew it was the general direction but the minute the accused confirmed that it was the car in silver, he knew that it was not an authorised vehicle to do such a pick-up and he did not know that the silver car was the accused’s vehicle initially.[note: 29] Mr Ranjit also disagreed with the accused’s position that he had offered the accused $50 and the accused had rejected him, telling him that he had an appointment and that Mr Ranjit should go to the Grab app to get transport.[note: 30]

30     Mr Ranjit’s evidence was in essence that the accused was soliciting passengers by asking those in the taxi queue if they needed a ride, with Mr Ranjit responding to the accused’s call-out leading to an exchange between the accused and Mr Ranjit on the fare for the use of the Vehicle. Mr Ranjit’s evidence was substantively consistent with the feedback that he had filed on the same day of the incident, which served as a contemporaneous record of the incident.

31     I found Mr Ranjit’s evidence to be credible notwithstanding an inconsistency regarding whether the premium fare displayed on the Grab app was $76 as reflected in the feedback or $65, which was Mr Ranjit’s evidence at trial. I did not think that this was a material inconsistency for two reasons. First, Mr Ranjit’s evidence was consistent on a material aspect, which was that the accused had asked him to look at the premium fare in the Grab app, which would be the price of the accused’s ride. Secondly, it was reasonable for Mr Ranjit to not have recalled the exact premium fare on the Grab app that he had seen more than one and a half years after the incident. I also found that the second CCTV footage to be a neutral piece of evidence as it had no accompanying audio and did not therefore capture the call-out made by the accused as testified by Mr Ranjit. There was also an inconsistency between the evidence of Mr Lim Lai Huat[note: 31] (“Mr Lim”) (the former LTA officer who had looked into Mr Ranjit’s feedback[note: 32]) and that of Mr Ranjit, as Mr Lim testified that the accused had shown the phone app to Mr Ranjit[note: 33] but Mr Ranjit’s evidence was that he had checked the fare on his own phone app. However, I placed little weight on Mr Lim’s evidence in this regard because he had given his answer based on the second CCTV footage shown to him, and was not present at the Location at the material time.

32     On an assessment of the totality of the evidence, I did not think that the accused had pointed to such evidence as would generate a reasonable doubt.

33     The accused’s evidence was that Mr Ranjit had approached him and he did not approach Mr Ranjit, as could be seen from the CCTV footage of the Location. The accused further testified that Mr Ranjit had asked the accused if the vehicle parking at the lot was his and the accused had confirmed it and told Mr Ranjit that he could not serve Mr Ranjit and that Mr Ranjit could ask the “big taxi parking there” (referring to the taxi parked next to the accused’s Vehicle) or call Grab, TADA or Gojek. The accused’s evidence was that Mr Ranjit offered him a price, to which the accused told Mr Ranjit that he had a personal job to do and he could not help Mr Ranjit.[note: 34] During cross-examination, he testified that Mr Ranjit told him that the app on Mr Ranjit’s phone showed that the cost of the ride was $60 to Ang Mo Kio, and that he only gave “courtesy suggestions” that Mr Ranjit could call Grab, TADA, Gojek or a taxi company.[note: 35] The accused also gave evidence that his personal customer did not show up and he drove off.[note: 36]

34     The accused also claimed that he was at the Location to wait for a personal job[note: 37] and was not loitering, but had to walk around instead of sitting in the Vehicle due to his medical conditions of diabetes[note: 38], arthritis and gout.[note: 39] He also mentioned that he sometimes prayed when he was walking.[note: 40] In the statement he had given to LTA on 15 April 2024[note: 41] (“Statement”), the accused stated that he had parked at the Location to “wait for [his] personal booking passengers and to standby [his] ride-hail bookings”[note: 42]. While the accused confirmed that the Statement was given voluntarily, he alleged that the Statement was partially untrue[note: 43] but did not identify the portions he disputed or put this position to Mr Lim, who recorded the Statement.

35     First, I did not think that the accused’s evidence that Mr Ranjit had approached him first and made him an offer for a ride was credible. While the second CCTV footage did not have audio, it was clear that the accused had started walking towards the taxi queue at 17:57:49 and had stopped at a spot a short distance away from Mr Ranjit at 17:58:07. During this time up to 17:58:16, Mr Ranjit’s back was to the accused, and he only started walking towards the accused at 17:58:23. The accused was dressed in an orange tee shirt and bermudas, and given that he was standing far away from his Vehicle, there would have been no reason for Mr Ranjit to approach a stranger to ask for transport to be provided. The only plausible explanation was Mr Ranjit’s account that he had responded to the accused’s call-out. Accordingly, the accused was waiting or standing around for the purpose of expressly or impliedly inviting members of the public to use the Vehicle for reward, by calling out to the people in the taxi queue at the Location to ask if they needed a ride and indicating where his Vehicle was.

36     Secondly, I rejected the accused’s explanation that he was merely waiting for a personal job at the Location at the material time. The accused could not prove that he was not at the Location to expressly or impliedly invite members of the public to use the Vehicle for reward. As the Court in Sulaiman explained, a driver accused of waiting for potential passengers and therefore plying for hire may be able to show the contrary by proving that he was waiting to pick up his family or friend without payment, or that he had stopped for a toilet break or to buy something and in weighing the truth in such matters, one would have to consider factors such as the particular location that the vehicle was at and the length of time taken for the professed purpose: see Sulaiman at [71]. In this regard, while the accused’s position was that he was at the Location at that time for his personal job, and that he had told Mr Ranjit that he could not serve Mr Ranjit because he had a personal job, he did not put forward any evidence in this regard.

37     When asked during cross-examination whether he agreed that he had no evidence to show that he had customers arriving at the Location on 31 March 2024, the accused testified that he had many passengers from Indonesia many years back when he was driving his minibus who would just appear randomly and they would want their privacy[note: 44]. Apart from his unwillingness or inability to identify the specific passenger who he was waiting to pick up, when the Court sought clarification on whether he had a confirmed booking from one of these passengers, the accused could not answer clearly. His evidence was that he had met his customer in the toilet who told the accused he was coming, and the accused had responded “Okay, I see you”. The accused could not remember the date he had met his customer and also testified that his customer did not give any precise time for his arrival in Singapore.[note: 45] The accused’s failure to adduce any evidence of a confirmed personal booking, in the context of his having parked the Vehicle in a location where taxis pick up and drop off passengers and having walked around the area for more than 30 minutes, did not assist the accused in raising a reasonable doubt.

38     Finally, I rejected the accused’s allegation that LTA had fabricated the charge or conspired with Mr Ranjit to implicate him. The allegation was entirely unsupported by the evidence. The accused could not identify any prior connection between Mr Ranjit and LTA before 31 March 2024 nor did he adduce any evidence to show that Mr Ranjit was not merely an interested member of the public who had independently decided to provide feedback on what he had deemed to be a touting incident. I also found Mr Ranjit to be a candid and independent witness. This was illustrated when Mr Ranjit, upon being informed of Mr Lim’s evidence (Mr Lim being the LTA officer who handled Mr Ranjit’s feedback) that the accused had shown him the fare on the app using the accused’s phone, did not hesitate to contradict Mr Lim and confirmed that he had in fact viewed the fare on his own phone (see [31] above).

39     The evidence clearly established that on 31 March 2024 at about 5.58 pm, the accused was waiting or standing around the Location for the purpose of expressly or impliedly inviting members of the public to use his Vehicle for reward, and was therefore loitering for the purpose of soliciting passengers.

Finding of Guilt

40     Having carefully scrutinised the totality of the evidence, I was satisfied that the Prosecution had proven the Charge beyond a reasonable doubt. As such, I found the accused guilty and convicted him accordingly.

Sentencing

41     The offence under the Charge is punishable under section 131(2)(a) of the RTA, which provides that for a first offence, the prescribed punishment is a fine not exceeding $1,000 or to imprisonment for a term not exceeding 3 months or to both.

42     The Prosecution sought a fine of at least $700 to be imposed. It was submitted that the composition fine that LTA had previously offered was $500 and the Prosecution indicated it would have sought a fine of at least $600 had the accused pleaded guilty before trial but sought a higher fine of $700 following conviction after trial. The accused disagreed with the Prosecution’s submissions and made no further submissions in respect of the sentence.

43     In Jackson Tan, the Court imposed a fine of $600 where the solicitation was unsuccessful and no actual harm was caused to any passenger: at [41] to [42]. In the present case, Mr Ranjit testified that the accused had become defensive and said that he studied law after Mr Ranjit had accused him of touting, though Mr Ranjit did not pursue the matter further so as not to escalate the situation.[note: 46] The accused had also testified during examination-in-chief that he had told Mr Ranjit that he studied the law, just that he did not have a certificate, although his evidence was that he had said this after Mr Ranjit had approached him and offered him a price, which he rejected.[note: 47] As stated in [35] above, I did not think that the accused’s evidence that Mr Ranjit had approached him first and made him an offer for a ride was credible. However, it is nonetheless not disputed that there was an exchange of words between the accused and Mr Ranjit. In my view, this exchange was unpleasant. Considering the accused’s conduct at the time of the offence, and that Mr Ranjit was placed in a position where he felt that the situation could escalate, I imposed a fine of $650, in default 2 days’ imprisonment.

Public Prosecutor v Vig Anjali

Public Prosecutor v Vig Anjali
[2026] SGDC 203

Case Number:District Arrest Case No 925381 of 2025 & Ors, Magistrate's Appeal No 9136-2026-01
Decision Date:18 June 2026
Tribunal/Court:District Court
Coram: Salina Ishak
Counsel Name(s): Mark Chia Zi Han (Attorney-General's Chambers) for the Public Prosecutor. R Kalamohan (R Kalamohan Law LLC) for the accused.
Parties: Public Prosecutor — Vig Anjali

Criminal Procedure and Sentencing – Statutory offences – Section 47(2)(a) Moneylenders Act 2008 – Harassment on behalf of an Unlicenced Moneylender – Debtor notes written on walls using a permanent marker

[LawNet Editorial Note: The appeal in MA 9136/2026/01 was withdrawn on 22 June 2026.]

18 June 2026

District Judge Salina Ishak:

Introduction

1       The present case involves acts of harassment committed on behalf of unlicenced moneylenders where property damage was caused.

2       The accused, Miss Vig Anjali, a 25-year-old female Indian national, pleaded guilty to two charges of harassment punishable under s 47(2)(a) and s 47(3)(b)(i) of the Moneylenders Act 2008 (“MLA”) read with s 34 of the Penal Code 1871 (“PC”) namely:

DAC 925383-2025

3rd Charge (Amended)

You are charged that you, on 9 December 2025, at about 2.15am, at Blk 759 Woodlands Avenue 6, Singapore 730759, together with one Kumar Dishant, in furtherance of the common intention of you both, acting on behalf of an unlicensed moneylender, did commit an act likely to cause alarm to the occupants of Unit #XX-XX, in connection with a loan purportedly taken by the said occupants, and in the course of committing the said act did cause property damage to certain property, to wit, by writing the words “750 WOODLANDS AVENUE 6 #XX-XX AHMAD MAHADI BIN AHMAD NORDIN XXXXXXXX FIRST TIME!!! O$P$ BETTER YOU FIND XXXXXXXX” on the wall of the 11th-floor lift landing, and you have thereby committed an offence punishable under s 47(2)(a) and s 47(3)(b)(i) of the Moneylenders Act 2008, read with s 34 of the Penal Code 1871.

DAC 925381-2025

5th Charge (Amended)

You are charged that you, on 9 December 2025, at about 4.25am, at Blk 347A Yishun Avenue 11, Singapore 761347, together with one Kumar Dishant, in furtherance of the common intention of you both, acting on behalf of an unlicensed moneylender, did commit an act likely to cause alarm to the occupants of Unit #XX-XXX, in connection with a loan purportedly taken by the said occupants, and in the course of committing the said act did cause property damage to certain property, to wit, by: (a) (b) writing the words “347A YISHUN AVENUE 11 #XX-XXX DANIS BIN IZMAN XXXXXXXX O$P$ I WILL PLAY WITH U. ROYSTON – XXXXXXXX” on the wall of the third-floor lift landing; and writing the words “347A YISHUN AVENUE 11 #XX-XXX DANISH BIN IZMAN XXXXXXXXX O$P$ I WILL PLAY WITH U!! ROYSTON – XXXXXXXX” on the wall outside Unit #XX-XXX, and you have thereby committed an offence punishable under s 47(2)(a) and s 47(3)(b)(i) of the Moneylenders Act 2008, read with s 34 of the Penal Code 1871.

3       Four remaining charges namely, one similar charge punishable under s 47(2)(a) and s 47(3)(b)(i) of the MLA and three charges of vandalism under s 3 Vandalism Act 1966 (“VA”) read with s 34 of the PC were taken into consideration for the purpose of sentence.

4       On 4 June 2026, after considering the Prosecution’s Address on Sentence and the Defence’s Mitigation Plea, I imposed a sentence of 12 months’ imprisonment for each of the charges and ordered them to run concurrently. Although caning was mandatory for the present offence, pursuant to s 325 (1)(a) of the Criminal Procedure Code, I did not order any caning as the accused is a woman. The global sentence imposed was therefore 12 months’ imprisonment.

5       The Defence sought a deferment of the commencement of the accused’s sentence until 12 June 2026 to enable her to complete her projects as part of her course. I allowed her application and extended her court bail.

6       Nevertheless, on 9 June 2026, the accused filed a Notice of Appeal against her sentence. Bail Pending Appeal of $20,000 was offered on 10 June 2026 but was not furnished. She is presently serving her sentence.

7       I now set out the grounds of my decision in full. 

Statement of Facts

Introduction

8       The accused is a 25-year-old female Indian national. The co-accused is Kumar Dishant, a 23-year-old male Indian national (“Dishant”). At the material time, the two were students and were flatmates together at Blk 86 Redhill Close #XX-XXX, Singapore 150086 (“their residence”).

9       The accused arrived in Singapore on 5 July 2025 and Dishant on 4 December 2025. Both had entered Singapore to study.

Police Reports

10     On 9 December 2025, the Singapore Police Force (“SPF”) received reports of harassing messages being written with marker on the walls of HDB buildings at various locations.

Facts pertaining to the 3rd and 5th charges (DAC-925381-2025 and DAC-925383-2025)

11     On 8 December 2025, the accused responded to a message in a WhatsApp group offering a freelance job. She wanted to make some extra money, as she had school fees to pay for. The person she began communicating with was introduced to her as “Sid”. “Sid” offered her entailing writing on walls at specified addresses, promising her $50 in exchange. As she was unsure of the legality of the job, the accused asked “Sid” if it was legal. “Sid” assured her that it was, and the accused agreed to perform the job. She asked Dishant if he wanted to join her and they would split the proceeds equally between themselves. While Dishant initially refused, he ultimately agreed. The accused renegotiated a rate of $60 with “Sid”, given that Dishant would be with her. The two then went to purchase permanent markers on “Sid’s” instructions.

12     On 9 December 2025, from 1:00am to 6:00am, the pair went to six addresses that were provided by “Sid”. At each location, the accused wrote harassing notes at the walls of the lift landings while Dishant stood next to her. They would book private hire vehicles to each subsequent location. In total, the accused wrote seven notes across the six locations.

13     In particular, at about 2.15am, the pair went to Blk 759 Woodlands Avenue 6, Singapore 730759. At the ninth-floor lift landing, the accused used a permanent marker purchased to write the words “750 WOODLANDS AVENUE 6 #XX-XX AHMAD MAHADI BIN AHMAD NORDIN XXXXXXXX FIRST TIME!!! O$P$ BETTER YOU FIND XXXXXXXX” on a wall. The words were in relation to a loan taken by a borrower, who resided at the named unit. A photograph of the note is appended herein:

14     At about 4.25am, the pair went to Blk 347A Yishun Avenue 11, Singapore 761347. This time, on Sid’s instructions, the accused used a permanent marker to write two notes, which were in relation to a loan taken by the same borrower. In reality, the named borrower no longer lived at the named unit. At the third-floor lift landing, the accused wrote the words “347A YISHUN AVENUE 11 #XX-XXX DANIS BIN IZMAN XXXXXXXX O$P$ I WILL PLAY WITH U. ROYSTON – XXXXXXXX” on a wall. A photograph of the note is appended herein:

15     She also wrote the words “347A YISHUN AVENUE 11 #XX-XXX DANISH BIN IZMAN XXXXXXXXX O$P$ I WILL PLAY WITH U!! ROYSTON –XXXXXXXX” on the wall outside Unit #XX-XXX. A photograph of the note is appended herein:

16     After they had finished at all six locations, the pair returned home. In the afternoon, police officers arrested them at their residence. They did not receive any money from “Sid”.

17     From the notes that they wrote, the pair knew that the named persons were debtors. However, they did not inquire into whether they were acting for unlicensed moneylenders.

18     The accused, together with Dishant, in furtherance of the common intention of them both, acting on behalf of an unlicensed moneylender, wrote words likely to cause alarm to the occupants of the named units, in connection with loans purportedly taken by the occupants of the units. She did so at two different locations. She has thereby committed two offences punishable under s 47(2)(a) and s 47(3)(b)(i) of the Moneylenders Act 2008, read with s 34 of the Penal Code 1871.

Ancillaries

19     The accused and Dishant were arrested on 9 December 2025. They were produced in Court 4A on 11 December 2025 and remanded for further investigations. They were offered bail on 18 December 2025. The accused was released on bail on 18 December 2025, while Dishant was released on bail on 22 December 2025. Dishant’s matter is fixed for a FM(PG) on 3 August 2026.

20     The accused admits to the offence(s) and is charged accordingly.

Antecedents

21     The accused is a first offender.

Prescribed Punishment

22     The offence of harassment of borrowers on behalf of unlicenced moneylenders is punishable with mandatory imprisonment of up to 5 years and discretionary fine of not less than $5,000 and not more than $50,000. If damage was caused to any property, s 47(3)(b)(i) of the MLA provides for caning of not less than 3 strokes and no more than 6 strokes.

23     As a permanent marker was used in the present case, s 47(7)(a) of the MLA provides that any person is deemed to have caused damage to any property if the person defaces the property by means of any pen, marker or other delible or indelible substance.

Prosecution’s Submissions on Sentence

24     The Prosecution sought an aggregate sentence of 12 months’ imprisonment to be imposed on the accused.

Benchmark sentence for non-fire harassment cases

25     The Prosecution highlighted that in Public Prosecutor v Nelson Jeyaraj s/o Chandran [2011] 2 SLR 1130 at [46] and [47] (“Nelson Jeyaraj”), the High Court held that the benchmark sentence for non-fire harassment cases with property damage is 12 months’ imprisonment and 3 strokes of the cane. Nelson Jeyaraj was also cited by the High Court in Public Prosecutor v Quek Li Hao [2013] 4 SLR 471 (“Quek Li Hao”) at [23].

Application of the benchmark sentence

26     The Prosecution asserts that in the present case, the accused was not a debtor-turn-runner. She had accepted the offer because she needed quick cash. She had also visited six locations and left seven notes (the rest of which form the subject matter of the TIC charges). The alarm and disquiet caused was therefore extensive.

27     The Prosecution further asserts that the accused had also done so in the cover of night, in the wee hours of the morning. Being a woman, she cannot be caned. Hence, an uplift from the benchmark sentence was therefore more than justified.

Mitigating factors

28     The Prosecution highlighted that it had considered the following factors:

(a)     The accused’s relatively young age;

(b)     Her clean record;

(c)     The damage was not as permanent as compared to the usual modes of splashing paint or using fire;

(d)     Her early plea of guilt.

29     The Prosecution asserts that the benchmark sentence of 12 months’ imprisonment per charge was just and fair in the circumstances. It was highlighted that while not expressly stated, the benchmark sentence of Nelson Jeyaraj appears to be on a plead guilty basis. The offender in Nelson Jeyaraj pleaded guilty and the High Court’s discussion of the benchmark sentences was held in that context. The Prosecution further asserts that no further reduction based on the Sentencing Advisory Panel’s Guidelines on Reduction in Sentences for Guilty Pleas (“SAP Guidelines”) should be imposed.

30     The Prosecution asserts that it had no objections to the sentences for both charges to run concurrently, given that they all formed part of the same transaction. For the reasons above, the Court was urged to impose a global sentence of 12 months’ imprisonment.

Mitigation Plea

Personal circumstances

31     The accused is a 25-year-old Indian national who was residing in Singapore as a full-time student at All-Spice Institute. She has been in Singapore for approximately 10 months. She came to Singapore with the genuine intention of pursuing her studies and improving her future. She completed the course in January 2026 and was presently completing some projects.

32     The Defence asserts that the accused has been a law-abiding individual throughout her time in Singapore. The accused also suffers from anxiety, a medical condition which affects her breathing. During her period of remand, she experienced anxiety attacks and required medical attention and medication.

Circumstances of the offence

33     At the material time, the accused received a message from an individual known as “Sid” offering her what she believed to be legitimate employment. Prior to carrying out the act, the accused specifically enquired whether the job was legal, and she was assured that it was lawful.

34     Believing the representations made to her, the accused proceeded to carry out the instructions given, which involved writing on walls and sending photographs as proof. The accused did not set out with the intention of assisting an unlicensed moneylender. She was unaware that the instructions originated from an unlicensed moneylending operation and did not fully appreciate the seriousness of her actions. She did not receive any payment for the work done.

Remorse and plea for leniency

35     The accused fully understood the seriousness of her actions and expressed genuine remorse for the offence committed. She cooperated fully with the authorities and pleaded guilty at the earliest opportunity. Her early plea of guilt demonstrates her acceptance of responsibility and saved valuable judicial time and resources.

36     In the circumstances, the Defence sought the Court's leniency in sentencing, considering her clean record, her status as a young foreign student and first-time offender, her mistaken belief that she was undertaking legitimate employment, her medical condition, and her genuine remorse.

37     The Defence asserts that the accused was not a debtor seeking to evade repayment of loans, nor was she involved in the management or operation of any unlicensed moneylending activities. Her role was limited and she did not stand to derive any significant benefit from the offences. She derived no financial benefit from the offences.

38     The Defence further asserts that the Prosecution accepted that the damage caused was not permanent and was less serious than cases involving paint splashing or the use of fire. The accused is also a young first-time offender with no antecedents and possessed strong rehabilitative prospects. The accused had already experienced the hardship of remand. She also suffers from anxiety and experienced anxiety attacks during her remand period, requiring medical attention and medication. The custodial process has therefore had a particularly severe impact on her.

39     The Defence urged the Court to impose a sentence of three months' imprisonment, which would adequately reflect the seriousness of the offences while giving due weight to the accused's mitigating circumstances and rehabilitative prospects.

40     The Defence orally asserts that it was very tragic that the accused had committed the offence. While ignorance of our laws is not justifiable but looking at the country she has come from and from the All India journals and law reports, the Defence highlighted that there are no similar cases in India. The Defence further asserts that this kind of incident was not foreseeable for an Indian student came from India and spent some months here. That was why she has enquired whether it was illegal or not.

41     The Defence further asserts that it did not justify her going around to other people’s house and writing on their doors, whatsoever. Even if it was not vandalism, it was harassment. One cannot go to somebody else’s house; it is not her job. That is, even if it is not vandalism, it is harassment. Although one is being paid for it, one should not do it. That she understands. But she did not understand the severity of her acts would lead her to such an offence before this and such a sentence. Although the accused’s instruction was to request for a fine, she had been advised that that there was no room for a fine and the sentence quantum would be decided by the Court. The Defence sought a lower sentence as the accused would be going back to India. Her family is deeply upset with what has happened and she promises that she will not have anything to do with the other side of the law anymore. It was her stupidity and ignorance that led her to this.

42     The accused informed the Court that her father just had a heart attack, and he is alone in India. If she had known that it is an offence, she would not have done this just for $30. She urged the Court to impose a fine as after this she will return to India. The days she spent on bail were nothing less than a custodial sentence for her. She highlighted that she does get panic attacks. She did get one while in remand and had to be given medication for that. She urged the Court to send her back to India as she has learnt her lesson.

Prosecution’s Reply

43     In response to the Defence’s assertion on the accused’s role, it was the Prosecution’s disagreed that the accused’s role was limited. The Prosecution asserts that the charge is not one for conducting unlicensed moneylending activities. Her role was harassing borrowers on behalf of an unlicensed moneylender. Her role cannot be considered as limited given that she was the one who wrote the notes themselves. The harm and the alarm that would have been caused to those who had seen the notes, especially the borrowers were extensive. There were seven notes across six locations, and one of the charges in fact pertained to two notes.

44     The Prosecution asserts that while it was undisputed that the accused is of a relatively young age, that was not strictly mitigating. There is still a level of deterrence that should be achieved. The Prosecution further asserts that ignorance of the law is not a defence and should be little mitigating value. The alarm and the distress caused was extensive.

45     The Prosecution highlighted that its sentencing position had considered her relatively young age. The Prosecution asserts that the three month’s imprisonment sought by the Defence was unjustified and no justification was provided. Nelson Jeyaraj was not a debtor turned harasser just like the accused. The sentence would have been higher, but the Prosecution sought the sentence of 12 month which sufficiently accounts for all the mitigating factors in her credit. The Prosecution asserts that a sentence of three months’ imprisonment would be too low.

Reasons for the sentences

Parliament’s approach towards loan shark offences

46     In Quek Li Hao at [22], the High Court citing Ong Chee Eng v Public Prosecutor [2012] 3 SLR 776 at [10] (“Ong Chee Eng”) held that that Parliament’s approach towards loan shark offences is clear – it has prescribed mandatory imprisonment and caning even for first-time offenders. Parliament’s intention is clearly to deter the commission of loan shark offences. Hence, the offence of harassment on behalf of unlicensed moneylenders is considered a serious offence as both general and specific deterrence are the main sentencing considerations.

47     In Quek Li Hao, it was observed that the High Court in Ong Chee Eng at [14] and [18] grouped accused persons into two categories:

(a)     the first category consists of those who turn to loan sharks not to pay off their gambling debts but because of genuinely desperate needs such as sudden sickness and prolonged retrenchment. (“genuine financial need” category).

(b)     The second category consists of those less deserving of sympathy such as youth harassers lured by the easy money and the thrill of gamblers who harass for the easy money, they can obtain to repay their gambling debts (“greed and self-interest category”).

Benchmark sentence for non-fire harassment

48     In Nelson Jeyaraj, the High Court at [47] stated that the benchmark sentence for non-fire harassment cases with property damage is 12 months imprisonment and three strokes. This is so as such an offence affects public safety, causes significant alarm and distress not only to those affected but to other members of the public.

Application of the benchmark sentence

Aggravating factors

Multiple charges of harassment

49     The present case was not a one-off incident but one where the accused faced three charges of non-fire harassment as well as three charges of vandalism under s 3 of the VA. At the day in question from 1:00am to 6:00am, the accused and the co-accused went to six housing units in Woodlands Avenue 6, Yishun Street 11, Woodlands Avenue 4, Tengah Garden Avenue, Buangkok Crescent and Lengkok Bahru. The accused herself wrote seven notes using a black permanent marker across the six locations. She pleaded guilty to two charges of harassment resulting in property damage.

Offence committed for financial benefit

50     It was clear that the accused fell under the second category of offenders considered by the High Court in Ong Chee Eng as she had committed the offences for financial gain. She was not a debtor-turn-runner because of genuinely desperate needs. The accused responded to a message in a WhatsApp group offering a freelance job as she wanted to make some extra money to pay her school fees. She had roped in the co-accused Dishant, a fellow student and her roommate to commit the harassment.

Nature of harassment

51     On “Sid’s” instructions, the accused and her co-accused visited six different locations and left seven notes written by her using a black permanent marker. They would book private hire vehicles to travel to each subsequent location. I disagreed with the Defence’s assertion that she played a limited role. It was clear that she played an active part in the harassment of the debtors by her own acts. Furthermore, from the photographs at [13] to 15] above the debtor notes were very prominent as the size of the letters, numbers and symbols were large.

Extensive alarm and disquiet caused

52     On 9 December 2025 itself, the police received reports of harassing messages being written with marker on the walls of HDB buildings at various locations. Under such circumstances. I agreed with the Prosecution that the alarm and disquiet caused to members of the public who saw the notes and in particular, the borrowers were therefore extensive.

53     In fact, for the 5th amended charge, the accused left two debtor notes - one at the third-floor lift landing and one outside the target unit itself. She had also done so in the wee hours of the morning. Notably, the named borrower no longer lived at the unit.

54     In addition, I considered that there was also no evidence before me that the accused took steps to minimise the damage caused to the various targeted properties. Under such circumstances, there is a need for a strong deterrent sentence in the present case.

Presence of TIC charges

55     In the present case the accused consented to a similar non-fire harassment charge and three other charges of vandalism to be taken into consideration with the accused’s consent.

Ignorance of the law is not a defence

56     While the Defence accepts that ignorance of Singapore laws is not justifiable, the Defence asserts that there are no similar cases in India. According to the Defence, such offences were not foreseeable for an Indian student came from India and spent some months here. That was why she has enquired whether it was illegal or not. In my view, ignorance of Singapore laws is not a valid defence and has no mitigating value. The fact that the Defence was unable to find similar cases or offences in India is of little assistance as the applicable law is Singapore law.

57     Instead, the fact that the job offered “Sid” entailed writing on walls at specified addresses in exchange for $50 would have been a red flag to anyone. Instead of asking “Sid” on the legality of the offence, she should have made her own enquiries. Furthermore, it was undisputed that the pair knew that the named persons were debtors. However, they did not inquire into whether they were acting for unlicensed moneylenders. Accordingly, I placed no weight on the fact that she enquired from “Sid” the legality of such acts.

Mitigating factors

58     In sentencing, I considered the accused’s relatively young age, her clean record, the type of property damage and her early plea of guilt. In my view, as non-fire harassment is a serious offence, I was of the view that the benchmark sentence of 12 months’ imprisonment is just and appropriate in the circumstances. I did not think an uplift from the benchmark sentence was necessary in view of the mitigating factors.

59     All things considered, in respect of the offences in DAC-925381-2025 and DAC-925383-2025, I sentenced her to 12 months’ imprisonment for each charge. I ordered the sentences to run concurrently and to take effect from the date of arrest and to exclude the period on she was on bail.

25 August 2026

District Judge Samuel Wee:

Introduction

1       On the evening of 9 January 2024, four dogs – two Cane Corsos and two Rottweilers – escaped from a landed property (“Property”) and attacked a Labrador Retriever along the road. The Labrador Retriever sustained serious injuries (a deep open wound on the neck, a puncture wound on the right rump, a deep puncture wound on the left pre-scapular area, and a puncture wound on the left middle ear), while its owner, who had intervened to assist her dog, developed pain in her feet.[note: 1]

2       The four dogs (one male and one female of each breed) were owned by both Mr Tay Wei Yuan, Lionel (“Mr Tay”) and his wife, Ms Leow Hwee Li, Merissa (“Ms Leow”), and are specified dogs under the Second Schedule of the Animals and Birds (Dog Licensing and Control) Rules (Cap 7, R 1) (“Dog Rules”). The licensing arrangement under the Dog Rules for the four dogs is as follows:[note: 2]

(a)     Mr Tay was the licensee (“Dog Rules Licensee”) of the male Cane Corso (“Dog 1”) from 5 October 2021 until the licence lapsed on 4 October 2023, after which Dog 1 continued to be kept at the Property without a valid licence.[note: 3]

(b)     Mr Tay was the Dog Rules Licensee of the female Cane Corso (“Dog 2”) from 5 October 2021 until the licence lapsed on 4 October 2023, after which Dog 2 continued to be kept at the Property without a valid licence. Mr Tay had registered Dog 2 under his name but used his cousin’s address (“Neighbouring Unit”, which was a 3-minute walk from the Property), as Dog 2 apparently resided at the Neighbouring Unit “for the most part” and was not kept at the Property “on a permanent basis at the material time”.[note: 4]

(c)     Ms Leow was the Dog Rules Licensee of the male Rottweiler (“Dog 3”) from 25 March 2019 until the licence was cancelled on 29 May 2020, after which Dog 3 continued to be kept at the Property without a valid licence. The licence had been cancelled at Ms Leow’s own request, on the basis that her family purportedly could not get along with Dog 3 and did not wish to keep it.[note: 5]

(d)     The female Rottweiler (“Dog 4”) was never licensed to either Mr Tay or Ms Leow under the Dog Rules after they “adopted” it from one of Mr Tay’s colleagues sometime in 2018.

3       Mr Tay has pleaded guilty to three charges under the Dog Rules (“Mr Tay’s Proceeded Charges”), and has admitted and consented to two charges being taken into consideration (“TIC”) for the purposes of sentencing (“Mr Tay’s TIC Charges”):

(a)     Mr Tay’s Proceeded Charges relate to:

(i)       One offence under r 3(1) punishable under r 16 of the Dog Rules (“Rule 3(1) Offence”) for owning Dog 1 without a valid licence from 4 October 2023 to 9 January 2024 (“Mr Tay’s Rule 3(1) Charge”).[note: 6]

(ii)       One offence under r 3(2) punishable under r 16 of the Dog Rules for keeping more than three dogs at the Property from sometime in June 2023 to 9 January 2024 without the prior permission of the Director-General (“Mr Tay’s Rule 3(2) Charge”).[note: 7]

(iii)       One offence under r 3(4) punishable under r 16 of the Dog Rules for keeping more than one specified dog at the Property from 5 October 2021 to 9 January 2024 without the prior permission of the Director-General (“Mr Tay’s Rule 3(4) Charge”).[note: 8]

(b)     Mr Tay’s TIC Charges relate to:

(i)       One Rule 3(1) Offence for owning Dog 2 without a valid licence from 4 October 2023 to 9 January 2024.[note: 9]

(ii)       One Rule 3(1) Offence for owning Dog 4 without a valid licence from sometime in 2018 to 9 January 2024.[note: 10]

4       Ms Leow has pleaded guilty to two charges under the Dog Rules (“Ms Leow’s Proceeded Charges”), and has admitted and consented to seven TIC charges (“Ms Leow’s TIC Charges”):

(a)     Ms Leow’s Proceeded Charges relate to:

(i)       One offence under r 9(1)(a) punishable under r 9(2)(a) of the Dog Rules (“Rule 9(1)(a) Offence”) for being the owner in charge of Dog 1, which was found at large on 9 January 2024 (“Ms Leow's Rule 9(1)(a) Charge”).[note: 11]

(ii)       One Rule 3(1) Offence for owning Dog 3 without a valid licence from 29 May 2020 to 9 January 2024 (“Ms Leow's Rule 3(1) Charge”).[note: 12]

(b)     Ms Leow’s TIC Charges relate to:

(i)       Three Rule 9(1)(a) Offences for being the owner in charge of Dogs 2 to 4, each of which was found at large on 9 January 2024.[note: 13]

(ii)       Four offences under r 9(1)(c) punishable under r 9(2)(b) of the Dog Rules as each of the four dogs was found in a public place without a securely fitted muzzle on 9 January 2024.[note: 14]

5       I impose the sentences set out in the following table, which includes the parties’ respective positions:

Charge

Prosecution’s Position

Mr Tay’s Rule 3(2) Charge

Mr Tay’s Rule 3(4) Charge

Total for Mr Tay:

$5,400 fine

(in default 18 days’ imprisonment)

Ms Leow’s Rule 9(1)(a) Charge

$2,250 fine
