(in default 4 days’ imprisonment)

Total for Ms Leow:

$3,100 fine

(in default 11 days’ imprisonment)



Ownership of the dogs

6       The issue of ownership of a dog is relevant to the Rule 3(1) Offence and Rule 9(1)(a) Offence.

(a)     Rule 3(1) of the Dog Rules states:

No person shall own or keep a dog unless that person has taken out a licence in respect of the dog.

[Emphasis added.]

(b)     Rules 9(1)(a) and 9(2)(a) of the Dog Rules state:

(1)    A dog (whether or not licensed) may be seized, impounded, destroyed or otherwise dealt with in such a manner as the Director-General thinks fit if it is found –

(a)    at large;

…

(2)    The owner of any dog that is found under any situation referred to in paragraph (1)(a), (b) or (c) shall be guilty of an offence and shall —

(a)    in the case of a situation referred to in paragraph (1)(a) or (b), be liable on conviction to a fine not exceeding $5,000 …

[Emphasis added.]

7       Under r 2 of the Dog Rules read with s 41 of the Animals and Birds Act (Cap 7, 2002 Rev Ed), the “owner” of an animal “includes a person in charge of the animal”.

8       Consequently, it is permissible to treat both Mr Tay and Ms Leow as the owners of the four dogs for the purposes of the Dog Rules, even though they may not have been the Dog Rules Licensee for each of the four dogs. In this regard, it is apt to point out that in Tan Huey Kuan (alias Chen Huijuan) v Tan Kok Chye and another [2011] 3 SLR 960, the High Court determined in the context of a dispute concerning the possession of a dog, that the dog had been jointly owned by two persons, which indicates that a dog can have more than one owner.

Mr Tay’s sentence

9       Mr Tay is fined a total of $5,400 (in default 18 days’ imprisonment).

Mr Tay's Rule 3(1) Charge

10     Mr Tay's Rule 3(1) Charge carries a maximum fine of $5,000.

11     I sentence Mr Tay to a fine of $1,100 (in default 4 days’ imprisonment) in light of the following:

(a)     The degree of harm or potential harm involved, taking into account that Dog 1 is a specified dog, which the Prosecution explained during the hearing covers dogs that are typically more aggressive in nature.

(b)     The period of offending of more than 3 months from 4 October 2023 to 9 January 2024.

(c)     Mr Tay’s failure to renew the licence appears to have been a “genuine oversight” rather than a deliberate attempt to avoid compliance.[note: 15]

(d)     Mr Tay’s TIC Charges (see [3(b)] above).

12     In deriving this sentence, I note that the case of Public Prosecutor v Chng Leng Khim [2018] SGMC 41 indicates that a fine of $600 has typically been imposed in previous unreported cases involving offenders who plead guilty,[note: 16] and that the Prosecution conveyed that it would have sought a fine of $600-$800 for a first-time offender if a non-specified dog was involved (ie. one that is not a specified dog under the Second Schedule of the Dog Rules).[note: 17]

Mr Tay's Rule 3(2) Charge

13     Mr Tay's Rule 3(2) Charge carries a maximum fine of $5,000.

14     I sentence Mr Tay to a fine of $1,800 (in default 6 days’ imprisonment) in light of the following:

(a)     Mr Tay exceeded the quota of three dogs by one.

(b)     The period of offending under the charge of more than 6 months from sometime in June 2023 to 9 January 2024 (although I appreciate that Dog 2 may not have been kept at the Property “on a permanent basis at the material time” (see [2(b)] above)).[note: 18]

15     In deriving this sentence, I placed no weight on Mr Tay’s argument that he had no other “viable option” but to take on the caregiving role for Dog 2 because his cousin was ill and could not look after Dog 2 in the Neighbouring Unit,[note: 19] as there is no evidence of any impediment preventing Mr Tay from caring for Dog 2 within the Neighbouring Unit rather than at the Property. In this regard, it is apt to reiterate that Dog 2 was licensed to Mr Tay (albeit using his cousin’s address at the Neighbouring Unit), and that Mr Tay himself asserts that Dog 2 apparently resided at the Neighbouring Unit “for the most part” and was not kept at the Property “on a permanent basis at the material time” (see [2(b)] above).

16     For clarity, I have not taken into account the fact that the four dogs were specified dogs, as this factor forms the substratum of the Rule 3(4) Charge.

Mr Tay's Rule 3(4) Charge

17     Mr Tay's Rule 3(4) Charge carries a maximum fine of $5,000.

18     I sentence Mr Tay to a fine of $2,500 (in default 8 days’ imprisonment) in light of the following:

(a)     Mr Tay exceeded the quota of one specified dog by three, which the sentence must adequately account for.

(b)     The period of offending of more than 2 years from 5 October 2021 to 9 January 2024, which the sentence must also adequately account for (although I appreciate that Dog 2 may not have been kept at the Property “on a permanent basis at the material time” (see [2(b)] above)).

19     In deriving this sentence, I placed no weight on Mr Tay’s argument that he had no other “viable option” but to take on the caregiving role for Dog 2 because his cousin was ill and could not look after Dog 2 in the Neighbouring Unit,[note: 20] for the same reasons set out at [15] above.

Ms Leow’s sentence

20     Ms Leow is fined a total of $3,100 (in default 11 days’ imprisonment).

Ms Leow's Rule 9(1)(a) Charge

21     The Rule 9(1)(a) Charge carries a maximum fine of $5,000.

22     I sentence Ms Leow to a fine of $2,000 (in default 7 days’ imprisonment) in light of the following:

(a)     The degree of harm involved, taking into account that the four dogs caused serious injuries to another dog, and that the injured dog’s owner, who had intervened to assist her dog, developed pain in her feet (see [1] above).

(b)     The four dogs escaped the Property (through a faulty gate),[note: 21] and Ms Leow rushed out of the Property to try to restrain them thereafter,[note: 22] which is mitigating. This is therefore not a situation where the dogs were deliberately permitted by the owner to be at large.

(c)     Ms Leow’s TIC Charges (see [4(b)] above).

Ms Leow's Rule 3(1) Charge

23     As mentioned at [10] above, the Rule 3(1) Charge carries a maximum fine of $5,000.

24     I sentence Ms Leow to a fine of $1,100 (in default 4 days’ imprisonment) in light of the following:

(a)     The degree of harm or potential harm involved, taking into account that Dog 3 is a specified dog.

(b)     The period of offending of more than 3.5 years from 29 May 2020 to 9 January 2024.

(c)     The fact that Ms Leow had kept Dog 3 despite having applied to cancel the licence of her own accord (see [2(c)] above). In this regard, I place no weight on her assertion that she was confused about whether the cancellation had taken effect,[note: 23] as any genuine confusion would have prompted her to verify the position – particularly given that the period of offending spanned over 3.5 years.

25     While the circumstances of the offending in Ms Leow’s case are more severe than those in relation to Mr Tay's Rule 3(1) Charge, the sentences are identical as her higher culpability is balanced out by Mr Tay’s TIC Charges.

Conclusion

26     Mr Tay and Ms Leow are fined a total of $5,400 (in default 18 days’ imprisonment) and $3,100 (in default 11 days’ imprisonment) respectively.

27     For completeness, I placed no weight on Mr Tay’s and Ms Leow’s repeated references in their Mitigation Plea to the “economic pressures” allegedly faced by their household (arising from their retrenchments, which are unrelated to the offences, and a potential claim for damages by the owner of the Labrador Retriever),[note: 24] as financial hardship has no mitigating value unless there are exceptional circumstances (Lai Oei Mui Jenny v Public Prosecutor [1993] 2 SLR(R) 406 at [10]). To this end, Mr Tay’s and Ms Leow’s solicitors confirmed during the hearing that this information was raised for “background purposes” and not as a mitigating factor.

html:
Tan Seng Kiat v Lim Kim Wee Nigel

Tan Seng Kiat v Lim Kim Wee Nigel
[2026] SGDC 272

Case Number:Originating Claim No 1164 of 2025
Decision Date:25 August 2026
Tribunal/Court:District Court
Coram: Evans Ng
Counsel Name(s): Sameer Bin Amir Melber (Gabriel Law Corporation) for the claimant; The defendant in person.
Parties: Tan Seng Kiat — Lim Kim Wee Nigel

Contract – Contractual terms

Contract – Breach

Contract – Termination

Contract – Remedies – Damages

Contract – Variation

25 August 2026

Judgment reserved.

District Judge Evans Ng:

1       While Mr Lim Kim Wee Nigel (“Lim”) was working as a financial adviser at a local bank, he came to know Mr Tan Seng Kiat[note: 1] (“Tan”) and became Tan’s insurance agent. Some years later, Lim solicited Tan to retain him to provide freelance financial trading services.[note: 2] Tan agreed. On the afternoon of 22 January 2025, they signed a handwritten agreement (“Agreement”), under which Lim was to trade in unspecified financial instruments using Tan’s money. The full Agreement read as follows:

Tan Seng Kiat will invest $10,000 SGD with Lim Kim Wee Nigel through IG Planform. LIM Kim Wee Nigel has to provide Tan Seng Kiat with 10% monthly income of $1,000 every month at the end of 22th of every month with capital of $10000. If less than $10000 Lim Kim Wee Nigel will has to top up back to $10000. In exchange, Lim Kim Wee Nigel will be receiving the exceed profits / excess profits from the capital as his profits & reserve to protect the capital.

[All errors are in the original]

2       That evening, Tan created an online trading account (“Trading Account”) with a platform called IG. Tan held the Trading Account in his sole name.[note: 3] Outward money transfers from the Trading Account could only be made to Tan’s bank account registered with IG. He gave Lim the password to the Trading Account, thereby enabling Lim to make trades. Pursuant to the Agreement, Tan transferred $10,000 to the Trading Account.

3       The Agreement obliged Lim to provide Tan with monthly returns of 10% on $10,000, ie $1,000 on the 22nd day of each month, starting from 22 February 2025. If the Trading Account’s balance falls below $10,000, Lim “will has to top up back to $10000 [sic]” (see [1] above). This meant that Lim was required to restore the Trading Account’s balance to $10,000 (“Restoration Obligation”). The Agreement did not state the dates on which, or intervals at which, the Trading Account’s balance was to be measured against $10,000 to trigger the Restoration Obligation. The Agreement also did not contain provisions to regulate the termination or variation of the contractual relationship.

4       Lim started to trade with the $10,000. He seemed to find his range at once. Two days later, on 24 January 2025 at 2.40pm, he reported gains of $3,492.86 to Tan by sending him a screenshot of the Trading Account’s dashboard.[note: 4] Lim instructed that those gains be withdrawn from the Trading Account and transferred to Tan’s bank account by the following Monday, 27 January 2025. Lim informed Tan that the sum was to be split between them — $1,000 to Tan and $2,492.86 to Lim. Tan was therefore due to receive $1,000 substantially earlier than the payment date stipulated in the Agreement.

5       The parties communicated mainly by WhatsApp. According to their WhatsApp logs, after receiving the good news, Tan called Lim at 3.30pm, 4.22pm and 4.42pm on 24 January 2025.[note: 5] Tan’s affidavit of evidence-in-chief (“AEIC”) did not mention what was discussed during the three calls. When asked about the contents of those calls at trial, Tan replied, “we are doing---doing some transactions, then with---need this [Lim] to do the confirmation with the IG account of this, if they have received the supporting documents. Something like that.”[note: 6] Shortly after the calls, Tan made several transfers totalling $49,000 to the Trading Account.

6       In all, after the initial $10,000 was transferred to the Trading Account on 22 January 2025, Tan made four tranches of transfers totalling $100,000 for Lim to trade with: the aforesaid $49,000 on 24 January 2025, $20,000 on 7 February 2025, $15,000 on 12 February 2025, and $16,000 on 13 February 2025.

7       Where Tan’s money went, wishfulness followed. Tan asked Lim to increase the rate of monthly returns first from 10% to 12% (in a text message to Lim at 5.45pm on 24 January), then to 15% (in another text message at 7.22pm on 24 January), and finally to 20% (in yet another text message at 2.52pm on 6 February).[note: 7] On 6 February 2025 at 5.01pm, the parties agreed that Tan was to receive an 18% monthly rate of return.[note: 8] It was not clear from their text messages whether this rate of return was supposed to apply to $100,000 or $110,000. Tan’s pleaded case is the former (see [10] below]). I refer to Lim’s obligation to provide Tan with monthly returns as the “Returns Obligation”.

8       On 7 February 2025, they met at a café.[note: 9] On 12 February 2025, they met at Tan’s workplace.[note: 10] Tan’s AEIC and his evidence under cross-examination did not give a useful account of what was discussed at either meeting.

9       When Tan checked the Trading Account on 14 February 2025,[note: 11] he found that “most of the funds in the [Trading Account] had been depleted”.[note: 12] Tan testified that he recalled its balance to be around $5,000 at that point.[note: 13] Against that backdrop, Tan averred that on or around 22 February 2025 he requested Lim to “return” $110,000 to him, ie the total sum that Tan had transferred to the Trading Account.[note: 14] Lim did not comply with the request and gradually became unresponsive. Tan instructed solicitors to send a demand letter to Lim on 20 May 2025.[note: 15] He sued Lim on 25 June 2025.

Tan’s claims

10     Tan claims that Lim breached the Restoration Obligation and Returns Obligation.[note: 16] He does not allege misrepresentation. His statement of claim seeks the following sums from Lim: $110,000, 10% monthly returns on $10,000 from March 2025 to the date of judgment, and 18% monthly returns on $100,000 from March 2025 to the date of judgment. Before the trial, a learned deputy registrar informed Tan’s solicitors that the pleaded claim exceeded the District Court’s jurisdictional limit of $250,000. By letter to the Court dated 3 December 2025, Tan elected under s 22(1) of the State Courts Act 1970 to abandon his claim to returns accruing after September 2025. Tan did not need to amend his pleadings for that purpose: Tan Chee Heong v Chen Hua [2023] 5 SLR 1190 at [23] and [65(b)]. The total sum claimed at trial was limited to $243,000, excluding interest and costs. This comprised: $110,000, $7,000 being 10% monthly returns on $10,000 from March to September 2025, and $126,000 being 18% monthly returns on $100,000 from March to September 2025. I deal with the claim for the monthly returns first.

The Returns Obligation

11     Because the Agreement was of indefinite duration and contained no express termination provision, the law presumes that either party could terminate it by giving reasonable notice: Teh Guek Ngor Engelin née Tan v Chia Ee Lin Evelyn [2005] 3 SLR(R) 22 at [20].

12     Tan’s demand on or around 22 February 2025 for the return of the entire $110,000 (see [9] above) was incompatible with continuation of the Agreement and therefore constituted notice of termination.[note: 17] Immediate termination was reasonable in the circumstances — Lim did not testify that he did not understand the import of Tan’s demand or that there were impediments to an immediate cessation of trading. Thus, no winding-down period was reasonably required. Upon termination, Lim was no longer obliged to provide Tan with returns that had not accrued. It follows that Tan has no basis to claim returns for March 2025 onwards.

The Restoration Obligation

13     It is indisputable that, under the original Agreement, the Restoration Obligation applied to the specified amount of $10,000. Tan contends that it was later extended to the further sums that he transferred to the Trading Account from 24 January to 13 February 2025. There are three ways in which this could have occurred. Two of them can be disposed of briefly.

14     First, there was no rescission and substitution of the Agreement with a new agreement under which the Restoration Obligation covered all amounts transferred to the Trading Account. To establish a discharge and replacement of the Agreement, “there should have been made manifest the intention in any event of a complete extinction of the first and formal contract, and not merely the desire of an alteration, however sweeping, in terms which are still subsisting”: Morris v Baron & Co [1918] AC 1 applied in Plevin v Paragon Personal Finance Limited [2017] 1 WLR 1249 at [13]. This did not take place.

15     Second, the parties did not enter a supplemental agreement after the Agreement. Tan’s AEIC alluded to such an agreement:[note: 18] he referred to a text message sent by Lim on 15 February 2025 which allegedly showed that Lim was aware of his obligations under “the [Agreement] and the oral agreement”, thereby implying the existence of a separate “oral agreement”. But my reading of the text message is that it did not refer to any such oral agreement. Tan gave no further particulars of the purported oral agreement. There is insufficient evidence to support a finding of a supplemental agreement.

16     Tan’s case is most consistent with a variation of the Agreement. His AEIC stated:[note: 19]

As I had duly received 10% in accordance with the [Agreement], I had also noticed that [Lim] had profited a total of $3,492.86 using my capital of S$10,000.00. In light of this, I had asked [Lim] on 24 January 2025 by way of WhatsApp at 7.22pm to increase my percentage of return to 15%. My WhatsApp message and [Lim’s] response on the same day at 8.49pm is as follows:

“Can give 15 percent”

“13% ok”

As [Lim] had agreed to raise my monthly return to 13%, I had also agreed to increase the capital investment. However, this is the only term that was varied on the [Agreement] i.e, the capital amount and the monthly return. Each and every other term of the [Agreement] was to remain. [Lim] was fully aware that but for [Lim’s] guarantee of my capital, I would under no circumstances agree to deposit and/or invest any sum of money to [Lim].

[Emphasis added]

17     Tan’s closing submissions likewise advanced his case on the basis that the Agreement had been varied.

18     Whether the parties agreed to vary the Agreement, and the terms of any variation, are determined objectively. This means that “the language used by one party, whatever his real intention may be, is to be construed in the sense in which it would reasonably be understood by the other”: Tribune Investment Trust Inc v Soosan Trading Co Ltd [2000] 2 SLR(R) 407 at [40].

19     The express terms of the Agreement are the starting point. Its language linked the term “capital” to the figure of $10,000 and concluded by providing that excess profits could form a reserve “to protect the capital”. The wording of the Restoration Obligation fixed both the triggering shortfall and the amount to which the account balance was to be restored by reference to $10,000. The original contractual text did not provide that the protected amount would automatically increase with each subsequent injection of funds. It was also not proven that, at the point of signing the Agreement, the parties had contemplated that Tan would be making any transfers in addition to the initial $10,000. Whether the $10,000 figure in the Restoration Obligation was enlarged therefore depends on the parties’ later agreement.

20     I first review the parties’ communications leading up to the further transfers of $49,000 made on 24 January 2025, because this is the first occasion on which Tan argues that the Restoration Obligation was enlarged. There was nothing in the text messages exchanged between Lim and Tan from 22 to 24 January 2025 to indicate that Tan had proposed to increase the amount covered by the Restoration Obligation and that Lim concurred. Their text messages merely showed that Tan was eager to transfer additional funds to the Trading Account for Lim to trade with and that Tan was concerned with securing a higher rate of return. Tan did not once mention the Restoration Obligation or — to use Tan’s more evocative terminology — the “guarantee” of his further transfer of $49,000. Their telephone calls (see [5] above) likewise did not establish a variation of the Restoration Obligation.

21     Next, I examine the parties’ communications from 25 January to 13 February 2025 — when the second, third and fourth tranches of further transfers were made. Those communications did not support a variation of the Restoration Obligation either. Two text messages sent by Lim on 7 February 2025 stated: “I need to protect your capital”. But the statement did not identify the amount of capital then said to require protection, nor did it state that the contractual figure of $10,000 had been replaced by a larger figure. Most importantly, it simply echoed the last line of the Agreement, which was not part of the Restoration Obligation. Read in context, these two text messages are insufficient to prove that the Restoration Obligation was varied to cover a larger specific amount. They are also too vague to be treated as an admission of liability: Qingdao Bohai Construction Group Co, Ltd v Goh Teck Beng [2016] 4 SLR 977 at [87].

22     Tan, in turn, sent messages asserting that his investment was “capital protected”, including: “Capital protected and enjoyed 15% every month” (10 February 2025, 7.41am) and “Pls note that my investment with you is capital protected” (10 February 2025, 11.26am). After receiving these messages, Lim did not challenge or qualify those assertions. Lim’s omission did not, without more, amount to an acceptance of Tan’s alleged understanding that there was a guarantee over the entire capital sum that Tan had transferred. The real question is whether his omission, viewed together with the parties’ subsequent conduct, objectively evinced assent to an alleged variation to the Restoration Obligation: R1 International Pte Ltd v Lonstroff AG [2015] 1 SLR 521 at [53]-[55]. I note that Tan transferred a further $31,000 after making those assertions on 10 February 2025. To the extent that Lim thereafter continued to trade with those funds, his conduct is relevant. I nevertheless do not regard it as establishing Lim’s assent to an enlarged Restoration Obligation, for it was also consistent with the parties’ undisputed agreement to increase the trading capital and the rate of return payable to Tan, and no communication expressly identified the new amount that Lim was allegedly obliged to restore.

23     The parties’ post-13 February 2025 communications carry negligible significance. Those communications could not vary the Agreement because Tan made no further fund transfers to satisfy the requirement for consideration: Ma Hongjin v SCP Holdings Pte Ltd [2021] 1 SLR 304 at [93]. Further, the post-13 February 2025 conduct is generally not admissible merely to construe the meaning of contractual terms already agreed (or subsequently varied): Lian Hwee Choo Phebe v Maxz Universal Development Group Pte Ltd [2009] 2 SLR(R) 624 at [11]. In the premises, I find that the Restoration Obligation was not varied and that it covered the initial $10,000 only.

Breach of the Restoration Obligation

24     I am unable to determine precisely when the Restoration Obligation was triggered. The Agreement did not specify a periodic measurement date, and Tan did not adduce the Trading Account statements to prove its balance at any time. It is nevertheless unnecessary to decide whether every dip below $10,000, regardless of when it occurred, would have triggered the obligation. On Tan’s evidence, by 14 February 2025 the depletion of the balance was substantial, with the balance at about $5,000 (see [9] above). I find that the Restoration Obligation was triggered by that point. As the Agreement did not stipulate a timeline for performance after that triggering event, Lim was required to restore the balance within a reasonable time: Max Master Holdings Ltd v Taufik Surya Dharma [2016] SGHC 147 at [98]. What constituted a reasonable time is a question of fact. As Lim accessed the Trading Account daily during the material period, he kept abreast of its balance. I determine that Lim was required to satisfy the Restoration Obligation by 22 February 2025 at the latest, but he failed to do so. Lim’s accrued liability under the Restoration Obligation was not extinguished by the ensuing termination of the Agreement: Diamond Glass Enterprise Pte Ltd v Zhong Kai Construction Co Pte Ltd [2023] 1 SLR 1451 at [60] to [62].

Damages for the breach of the Restoration Obligation

25     Tan’s prayers for relief set out claims for specific sums only. He did not seek an assessment of damages. But he did plead that he suffered loss, and the issue of compensatory damages was raised in the evidence and submissions. Lim appreciated that the issue was in play and addressed it without objection. I am satisfied that granting Tan an assessment of damages would not cause Lim unfair prejudice, provided that damages are assessed within this trial.

26     I have found that the date of breach was 22 February 2025. The general rule is that contractual damages are assessed at the date of breach. That rule is produced from the interaction between the principles of mitigation and causation — where the claimant could reasonably crystallise his position at or after breach, later market movements resulting from his decision not to do so are ordinarily not attributable to the contract-breaker. Tan had control over the Trading Account and could reasonably have closed any open positions and revoked Lim’s access to crystallise the balance in the Trading Account. He did none of that. So there is no reason not to apply the general rule.

27     Since Lim is obliged to restore the Trading Account’s balance to $10,000, Tan is required to prove the measure of loss with evidence of the Trading Account’s balance as of 22 February 2025. He accepted that account statements were available but did not adduce them.[note: 20] His rough recollection of the Trading Account balance on 14 February 2025 (see [9] above) does not assist the Court with determining the value of the Trading Account balance, including any open positions, on the different occasion of the date of breach. A learned deputy registrar previously alerted Tan’s solicitors to this lacuna in his case when dismissing his application for summary judgment against Lim. They ignored the deputy registrar to Tan’s peril.

28     A breach of contract is actionable without proof of damage, but substantial damages require proof of loss. Where the claimant fails to prove either the fact or the quantum of loss, the court may award only nominal damages: Biofuel Industries Pte Ltd v V8 Environmental Pte Ltd [2018] 2 SLR 199 at [44]. Hence, even if I had accepted Tan’s case that the Restoration Obligation was varied to cover the entire $110,000, his failure to prove the Trading Account’s balance at the date of breach would have led to the same result.

Disposal

29     I make no finding on whether Lim’s solicitation of Tan to engage him to provide “freelance financial trading services” and his discretionary trading with Tan’s funds contravened the Securities and Futures Act 2001. The parties did not raise the issue of illegality. Although the Court may take cognisance of illegality that has not been pleaded (Ting Siew May v Boon Lay Choo [2014] 3 SLR 609 at [31]), the evidence before me is too rudimentary to establish the necessary facts, including Lim’s licensing status, the instruments he traded, or whether his activities formed part of a business carried on with sufficient system and continuity.

30     I order Lim to pay Tan nominal damages of $50 in respect of Lim’s breach of the Restoration Obligation. I dismiss Tan’s remaining claims. I will hear the parties on costs.

Public Prosecutor v Mohammad Sharulnaim Bin Miswan

Public Prosecutor v Mohammad Sharulnaim Bin Miswan
[2026] SGDC 271

Case Number:District Arrest Case No. 917932 of 2025 and others
Decision Date:25 August 2026
Tribunal/Court:District Court
Coram: Samuel Wee
Counsel Name(s): Niranjan Ranjakunalan (Attorney-General's Chambers) for the Public Prosecutor; S Balamurugan (Regal Law LLC) for the Defendant.
Parties: Public Prosecutor — Mohammad Sharulnaim Bin Miswan

Criminal Law – Offences – Section 204A(b) of the Penal Code 1871 (2020 Rev Ed) – Offender pressured victim to withdraw police report and lie to the investigating officer

Criminal Law – Offences – Section 342 of the Penal Code 1871 (2020 Rev Ed) – Offender locked victim in his car and refused to allow her to leave

Criminal Law – Offences – Section 385 of the Penal Code 1871 (2020 Rev Ed) – Offender used a covertly recorded video of victim engaging in sexual acts as a tool of extortion

Criminal Procedure and Sentencing – Sentencing – Section 204A(b) of the Penal Code 1871 (2020 Rev Ed) – Offender pressured victim to withdraw police report and lie to the investigating officer

Criminal Procedure and Sentencing – Sentencing – Section 342 of the Penal Code 1871 (2020 Rev Ed) – Offender locked victim in his car and refused to allow her to leave

Criminal Procedure and Sentencing – Sentencing – Section 385 of the Penal Code 1871 (2020 Rev Ed) – Offender used a covertly recorded video of victim engaging in sexual acts as a tool of extortion

25 August 2026

District Judge Samuel Wee:

Introduction

1       Mr Mohammad Sharulnaim Bin Miswan (“Mr Sharulnaim”) committed a series of offences involving two victims over approximately 14 months, from January 2024 to February 2025. His offending began when he covertly recorded five videos of the first victim (“Victim 1”) engaging in sexual acts. He then used one of the videos (“Victim 1 Extortion Video”) as a tool of extortion against Victim 1, and attempted to obstruct the course of justice by pressuring Victim 1 to withdraw her police report and to lie to the Investigation Officer (“IO”). After he was arrested and released on bail, he covertly took a photograph of the second victim (“Victim 2”) engaging in a sexual act, and wrongfully confined her in his car after confronting her.

2       Mr Sharulnaim has pleaded guilty to three charges:

(a)     One charge under s 385 of the Penal Code 1871 (2020 Rev Ed) (“Penal Code”) for putting Victim 1 in fear of harm to her reputation in order to commit extortion on 6 May 2024, by threatening to report the Victim 1 Extortion Video to the police or make it go viral unless he was paid $1,300 (“Attempted Extortion Charge”).[note: 1]

(b)     One charge under s 204A(b) of the Penal Code for obstructing the course of justice on 9 October 2024, by (i) asking Victim 1 to inform the IO that she no longer wished to pursue the matter against him; (ii) offering Victim 1 gifts and financial assistance to induce her to drop the case; and (iii) asking Victim 1 to lie to the IO that they were family members (“Obstruction Charge”).[note: 2]

(c)     One charge under s 342 of the Penal Code for wrongfully confining Victim 2 on 5 February 2025, by locking Victim 2 in his car and refusing to allow her to leave (“Wrongful Confinement Charge”).[note: 3]

3       He also admitted and consented to two additional charges being taken into consideration (“TIC”) for the purposes of sentencing:

(a)     One charge under s 377BB(3) punishable under s 377BB(7) of the Penal Code for recording five videos of Victim 1 engaging in sexual acts on 15 January 2024 without Victim 1’s consent (“TIC Voyeurism Charge”).[note: 4]

(b)     One charge under s 204A(b) of the Penal Code for obstructing the course of justice on 12 September 2024, by asking Victim 1 to inform the IO that she no longer wished to pursue the matter against him (“TIC Obstruction Charge”).[note: 5]

4       The individual and aggregate sentences I impose are set out in the following table, which includes the Prosecution’s[note: 6] and Mr Sharulnaim’s[note: 7] positions:

Facts

Events relating to Victim 1

5       On 15 January 2024, Mr Sharulnaim saw Victim 1 with her male partner acting intimately at the rooftop garden of a multistorey carpark. Suspecting that they might engage in sexual acts, Mr Sharulnaim hid behind some plants. He then used his mobile phone to make five video recordings after Victim 1 started engaging in sexual acts with her male partner (including the Victim 1 Extortion Video, which clearly showed Victim 1’s face).[note: 8] This conduct is the subject of the TIC Voyeurism Charge.

6       On 6 May 2024, Mr Sharulnaim approached Victim 1 and informed her of the Victim 1 Extortion Video. Victim 1 agreed to meet Mr Sharulnaim at his car, where he threatened to post the Victim 1 Extortion Video on social media platforms, and they exchanged phone numbers. A few hours later, Mr Sharulnaim called Victim 1 and threatened to report the Victim 1 Extortion Video to the police or make it go viral unless he was paid $1,300 by the following day (which Victim 1 did not pay). During the call, Mr Sharulnaim also indicated that he was interested in having sexual intercourse with Victim 1.[note: 9] This conduct is the subject of the Attempted Extortion Charge.

7       On 7 May 2024, Victim 1 lodged a police report, following which Mr Sharulnaim was arrested on 8 May 2024 and released on bail on 10 May 2024, with conditions that he was “Not to commit any offence while released on bail” (“No Offence Bail Condition”) and “Not to interfere with any witness or otherwise obstruct the course of justice” (“No Obstruction of Justice Bail Condition”).[note: 10]

8       On 12 September 2024, Mr Sharulnaim approached Victim 1 and requested that she inform the IO that she no longer wished to pursue the matter so that the police would cease investigations, and asked her not to tell the IO about their conversation.[note: 11] This conduct is the subject of the TIC Obstruction Charge and was a breach of the No Obstruction of Justice Bail Condition and the No Offence Bail Condition.

9       On 9 October 2024, Mr Sharulnaim approached Victim 1 and begged her to drop the case, claiming that it would impact his family and that he wanted to commit suicide. He also asked Victim 1 to lie to the IO that they were family members, and offered her gifts and financial assistance (including payment for her household necessities) if she agreed to drop the case.[note: 12] This conduct is the subject of the Obstruction Charge and was a breach of the No Obstruction of Justice Bail Condition and the No Offence Bail Condition.

Events relating to Victim 2

10     On 5 February 2025, Mr Sharulnaim saw Victim 2 engaging in sexual acts with her partner in a rental car parked at a multistorey carpark. He used his mobile phone to take a photograph, before approaching the car and gesturing for Victim 2 and her partner to step out. He then lied to Victim 2 and her partner that he was a former police officer with a video recording of them engaging in sexual acts, and threatened to lodge a police report and to inform the car rental company.[note: 13]

11     When Victim 2 and her partner attempted to leave, Mr Sharulnaim drove his car to obstruct them and compelled Victim 2 to enter his car. Fearing that Mr Sharulnaim was a former police officer, Victim 2 complied, following which Mr Sharulnaim locked the car doors and prevented her from leaving while he spoke to her about the purported video recording and made comments about her physical appearance. The confinement lasted for around 10 minutes[note: 14] and persisted despite Victim 2’s repeated requests to be released.[note: 15] This conduct is the subject of the Wrongful Confinement Charge and was a breach of the No Offence Bail Condition.

12     On 6 February 2025, Victim 2 lodged a police report, following which Mr Sharulnaim was arrested on 17 February 2025 and released on bail on 18 February 2025.[note: 16]

Sentence

Attempted Extortion Charge

13     The Attempted Extortion Charge carries a mandatory imprisonment term of 2-5 years and mandatory caning.

Sentencing approach

14     While there is no established sentencing framework for the Attempted Extortion Charge, some relevant principles can be gleaned from the following cases:

(a)      Teo Hee Heng v Public Prosecutor [2000] 2 SLR(R) 351 (“Teo Hee Heng”), where the offender was sentenced to 48 months’ imprisonment and 6 strokes of the cane for one charge of attempted extortion under s 385 of the Penal Code (Cap 224, 1985 Rev Ed), with a charge of insulting the modesty of a woman under s 509 of the Penal Code (Cap 224, 1985 Rev Ed) taken into consideration for the purposes of sentencing.

(i)       The offender attempted to extort $100 from a 44-year-old woman whose 12-year-old daughter was missing. Having learnt of the missing daughter from newspaper advertisements, the offender made several phone calls to the victim over approximately 21 hours, telling her: (A) his friends were currently holding her daughter and were “playboys” who preyed on young girls; and (B) she would have to wrap $100 in her panties (after meeting him to spread her legs wide open for him to peep at her panties before she took them off) if she wanted to know the whereabouts of her daughter. The victim reported the matter to the police, following which the offender was arrested.[note: 17]

(ii)       The offender pleaded guilty and was originally sentenced to 30 months’ imprisonment and four strokes of the cane.[note: 18]

(iii)       The offender subsequently filed a petition for criminal revision, arguing that he was acting under the threat and instructions of another person.[note: 19]

(iv)       The High Court determined that the defence of duress was not made out and dismissed the petition.[note: 20] The High Court also enhanced the sentence to 48 months’ imprisonment and 6 strokes of the cane, taking into account: (A) the offender’s retraction of his plea of guilt; and (B) the offender’s “cruel exploitation of the victim’s situation and his contemptible demands for the victim to perform those demeaning and degrading acts”.[note: 21]

(b)      Public Prosecutor v Ramasamy Ashwin [2012] SGDC 38 (“Ramasamy”), where the offender pleaded guilty and was sentenced to 30 months’ imprisonment and 3 strokes of the cane for one charge of attempted extortion under s 385 of the Penal Code (Cap 224, 2008 Rev Ed).

(i)       The offender attempted to extort $2,500 from the director of a company by sending 16 text messages (using a stolen SIM card to avoid detection) over a period of five hours, wherein he threatened to detonate six bombs in two dormitories housing 200 workers if the money was not placed in a toilet cubicle by 10pm that day. The matter was reported to the police, following which the offender was arrested.[note: 22]

(ii)       In deriving the sentence of 30 months’ imprisonment and 3 strokes of the cane, the court indicated that “The usual tariff for the offence of attempted extortion is a starting point of 2 years’ imprisonment term (which was the mandatory minimum) and 3 strokes of the cane”,[note: 23] and that an uplift was necessary because of the following aggravating factors:[note: 24]

(A)       The threats were repeated in 16 text messages over a period of five hours, which placed the victim in constant fear and anxiety.

(B)       The nature of the harm threatened could have resulted in death or serious injury to 200 workers.

(C)       The offence was premeditated as the offender had stolen the SIM card to avoid detection.

(D)       The offender had attempted to extort $2,500, which was not insignificant.

(E)       The 200 workers had to be evacuated, and valuable state resources and manpower were expended to search for the non-existent bombs.

(c)      Public Prosecutor v Kumaresan s/o Raman [2017] SGDC 203 (“Kumaresan”), where the offender pleaded guilty and was sentenced to 2 years’ imprisonment and 6 strokes of the cane for one charge of attempted extortion under s 385 of the Penal Code (Cap 224, 2008 Rev Ed), with a similar charge of attempted extortion in relation to a second victim taken into consideration for the purposes of sentencing.

(i)       The offender impersonated a government officer and threatened to arrest a teenage couple for alleged activities in a public toilet, unless they complied with his demand for money, valuables, or sexual intercourse with the female victim. The victims reported the matter to the police, following which the offender was arrested.[note: 25]

(ii)       In deriving the sentence of 2 years’ imprisonment and 6 strokes of the cane, the court took into account the following aggravating factors:[note: 26]

(A)       The offender had impersonated a government officer, which undermines the trust vested by the general citizenry in persons in authority.

(B)       The offender had exploited vulnerable victims – he preyed on the naivety of the two victims who were both 19 years old.

(C)       The offender had demanded sexual favours from the female victim, which the court found “thoroughly repugnant and insulting to the dignity of the female victim”.

15     These three cases were discussed in Public Prosecutor v Muhammad Nazri bin Sapar [2022] SGDC 273 (“Nazri”) that concerned the more serious offence of extortion under s 384 of the Penal Code (Cap 224, 2008 Rev Ed), which carries a maximum of 7 years’ imprisonment (compared to the maximum of 5 years’ imprisonment for the Attempted Extortion Charge). The court in Nazri set out the following sentencing principles for extortion offences:

(a)     The seriousness of extortion lies in the harm it causes, as it preys on victims’ fears and compels them to act against their will.[note: 27] The harm can be ascertained from:[note: 28]

(i)       The nature and severity of the harm threatened.

(ii)       The nature and value of the property extorted.

(iii)       The level of fear and other harm suffered by the victim due to the extortion, including any lasting psychological impact.

(b)     The gravity of the offence is also affected by the offender’s culpability, which can be gleaned from the following non-exhaustive factors:

(i)       The offender’s purpose for making the threat, such as whether the offender was motivated by malice beyond mere financial gain.

(ii)       The way the offender conveys his threat, such as: (A) repeating the threat; (B) displaying weapons; (C) causing property damage or hurt; (D) representing himself as a member of a secret society or criminal group; or (E) representing himself as a public officer who can exercise legal powers to the victim’s prejudice.

(iii)       Whether the offence is premeditated and planned, or is part of an organised criminal activity.

(iv)       Whether the offender targets a vulnerable victim.

16     Based on these authorities, it is apparent that the following offence-specific factors are relevant:

Harm

Culpability

(a) The nature and value of the attempted extortion, including the amount of money demanded, and whether sexual favours are sought.

(b) The nature and severity of the harm threatened.

(c) The impact of the threat, including whether state resources are expended to avert the threat.

(d) The level of fear and other harm suffered by the victim, including any lasting psychological impact.

(a) The offender’s purpose for making the threat, including whether the offender was motivated by malice beyond mere financial gain.

(b) The way the threat is conveyed, including the duration and frequency of the demands, and whether the offender impersonated a public officer.

(c) The degree of premeditation and planning.

(d) The involvement of a vulnerable victim.



The appropriate sentence

17     A sentence of 2 years’ and 3 months’ imprisonment and 3 strokes of the cane for the Attempted Extortion Charge is appropriate for Mr Sharulnaim.

18     The indicative starting point sentence (for a conviction after a trial) is 2 years’ and 10 months’ imprisonment and 3 strokes of the cane in light of the following offence-specific factors:

Harm

Culpability

(a) Mr Sharulnaim attempted to extort $1,300 from Victim 1, and also indicated that he was interested in having sexual intercourse with Victim 1.

(b) Mr Sharulnaim’s threat was severe as it encompassed posting the Victim 1 Extortion Video (which clearly showed Victim 1’s face) on social media platforms, which if carried out could have caused lasting distress to Victim 1 given the potential for rapid and widespread dissemination.

(c) Victim 1 was sufficiently alarmed to lodge a police report.

(a) Mr Sharulnaim’s actions were premeditated and planned, as the Victim 1 Extortion Video was recorded a few months before he approached Victim 1 to make his demands.

(b) Mr Sharulnaim conveyed the threat over a phone call a few hours after he had confronted Victim 1 in person.



19     This should be adjusted to 2 years’ and 3 months’ imprisonment and 3 strokes of the cane to account for the following offender-specific factors:

(a)     An uplift of 3 months to account for the TIC Voyeurism Charge.

(b)     A reduction of 10 months as Mr Sharulnaim indicated his intention to plead guilty at Stage 1 of the Sentencing Advisory Panel’s Guidelines on Reduction in Sentences for Guilty Pleas (“PG Guidelines”).

20     This sentence is not inconsistent with the precedent cases at [14] above.

(a)     It is lower than the sentence of 48 months’ imprisonment and 6 strokes of the cane in Teo Hee Heng, which involved: (i) significantly higher culpability as the threats concerned the victim’s missing 12-year-old daughter and took place over approximately 21 hours; and (ii) the absence of mitigating factors since the offender retracted his plea of guilt.

(b)     It is lower than the sentence of 30 months’ imprisonment and 3 strokes of the cane in Ramasamy, which involved significantly higher harm as the bomb threat could have resulted in death or serious injury to 200 workers, necessitating the expenditure of state resources and manpower.

(c)     It is comparable to the sentence of 2 years’ imprisonment and 6 strokes of the cane in Kumaresan, as the lower degree of harm in Kumaresan is balanced out by the offender’s higher culpability.

(i)       The harm in Kumaresan is lower, as Mr Sharulnaim’s case involved the potential dissemination of the Victim 1 Extortion Video on social media, which could have caused lasting distress to Victim 1.

(ii)       However, this is balanced out by the lower culpability in Mr Sharulnaim’s case, which does not involve the impersonation of a government officer or the exploitation of vulnerable victims. Moreover, the court in Kumaresan imposed a higher number of strokes of caning (rather than an uplift in the imprisonment term) to account for the offender’s impersonation of a government officer,[note: 29] which is not present in Mr Sharulnaim’s case.

   Obstruction Charge

21     The Obstruction Charge carries an imprisonment term of up to 7 years, a fine, or both.

Sentencing approach

22     In Parthiban a/l Kanapathy v Public Prosecutor [2021] 2 SLR 847 (“Parthiban”), the Court of Appeal made several observations concerning offences under s 204A of the Penal Code (Cap 224, 2008 Rev Ed) which are relevant to sentencing:

(a)     General deterrence ought to be the primary sentencing consideration, as such offences are “against the institutions of justice”, “contaminate the rule of law”, and “strike at the very fundamental ability of the legal system to produce order and justice”.[note: 30]

(b)     There are two broad groups of offences under s 204A of the Penal Code (Cap 224, 2008 Rev Ed):[note: 31]

(i)       Situations where offenders seek to obstruct the course of justice by eradicating or fabricating evidence of their own wrongdoing or that of others, whether to conceal acts of another or of one’s own transgressions, such as suborning witnesses.

(ii)       Situations where offenders ask others to assume criminal responsibility voluntarily.

(c)     The following offence-specific and offender-specific factors may be considered in determining the relevant sentence to be imposed:[note: 32]

(i)       The nature of the predicate charge upon which the offender sought to thwart the course of justice – the more serious the predicate charge, the more serious the act of perverting the course of justice will be.

(ii)       The effect of the attempt to pervert the course of justice, including whether the obstruction was successful.

(iii)       The degree of persistence, premeditation and sophistication in the commission of the offence.

23      Parthiban concerned an offender who, while in remand and in the midst of a capital drug importation trial, passed a handwritten note to the co-accused (through an intermediary) containing detailed instructions for the co-accused to give false testimony to exonerate both of them from their respective capital charges.[note: 33] The Court of Appeal sentenced the offender (who pleaded guilty) to 1 year’s and 9 months’ imprisonment for an offence under s 204A of the Penal Code (Cap 224, 2008 Rev Ed) in light of the following factors:[note: 34]

(a)     The predicate offence was of the most serious conceivable nature – a capital charge of drug importation under s 7 of the Misuse of Drugs Act (Cap 185, 2008 Rev Ed), which both he and the co-accused faced.

(b)     The offender’s conduct only came to light through the co-accused’s voluntary disclosure.

(c)     The offender’s instructions to give false testimony could have potentially led the trial court to make an erroneous finding on matters lying at the heart of the trial court’s determination.

(d)     There was extensive planning and premeditation – the offender circumvented the difficulty of meeting the co-accused in remand by arranging for an intermediary to pass the handwritten note to the co-accused.

(e)     The note was lengthy and detailed, spanning 11 paragraphs, and set out an entire false story for the co-accused to recite.

24     The decision of Parthiban was referred to in Rajendran s/o Nagarethinam v Public Prosecutor and another appeal [2022] 3 SLR 689 (“Rajendran”) and Public Prosecutor v CHJ [2024] SGHC 240 (“CHJ”).

(a)      Rajendran concerned two offenders who asked two reluctant performing artistes at their entertainment club to provide sexual services to customers, subsequently discovered that the two performing artistes had fled the lodging they provided and lodged a police report, and immediately arranged for their assistant (who was privy to the events) to leave Singapore to evade arrest and prevent him from implicating them in the investigations.[note: 35] The General Division of the High Court affirmed the sentence of 8 months’ imprisonment imposed by the District Court on each offender (which the District Court reduced from 9 months’ imprisonment on account of the totality principle) for an offence under s 204A of the Penal Code (Cap 224, 2008 Rev Ed) in light of the following factors:[note: 36]

(i)       The predicate offences the offenders sought to subvert were prostitution-related offences under the Women’s Charter (Cap 353, 2009 Rev Ed), which carried a maximum of 5 years’ imprisonment at the time of the offences.

(ii)       The offenders acted quickly and with deliberation after discovering that the performing artistes had fled, and took steps to ensure that their assistant remained out of Singapore.

(iii)       The offenders’ conduct was clearly intended to deprive the enforcement agency of important evidence relevant to the investigations, and could have resulted in the offenders evading the law had the assistant not returned to Singapore to assist with investigations.

(b)      CHJ concerned an offender who was arrested and released on bail for offences of sexual assault by penetration against his wife, and made four calls over a week (using a prepaid SIM card and a newly purchased phone to make three of the calls to avoid detection) to his wife’s mother to pressure his wife into withdrawing her sexual assault allegations.[note: 37] The General Division of the High Court sentenced the offender (who claimed trial) to 12 months’ imprisonment for an amalgamated charge under s 204A(b) of the Penal Code (Cap 224, 2008 Rev Ed) read with s 124(4) of the Criminal Procedure Code 2010 (Cap 68, 2012 Rev Ed) and punishable under s 124(8)(a)(ii) of the Criminal Procedure Code 2010 (Cap 68, 2012 Rev Ed) in light of the following factors:[note: 38]

(i)       The predicate offences the offender sought to subvert were charges of sexual assault by penetration under s 376(2)(a) of the Penal Code (Cap 224, 2008 Rev Ed), which carries a maximum of 20 years’ imprisonment.

(ii)       There was a degree of persistence, premeditation and sophistication as the offender made four calls over a week, and used a prepaid SIM card and a newly purchased phone to make three of the calls to avoid detection.

(iii)       The offender’s conduct could have led to him escaping accountability for the predicate offences.

(iv)       The offences were committed while the offender was on bail.

(v)       However, the General Division of the High Court considered the offender’s culpability to be tempered as he had made the calls with the hope of saving his marriage.

The appropriate sentence

25     A sentence of 6 months’ imprisonment for the Obstruction Charge is appropriate for Mr Sharulnaim.

26     The indicative starting point sentence (for a conviction after a trial) is 7 months’ imprisonment in light of the following offence-specific factors:

(a)     The predicate offence relates to the Attempted Extortion Charge, which carries a maximum of 5 years’ imprisonment.

(b)     Mr Sharulnaim’s attempt to pervert the course of justice was unsuccessful.

(c)     Mr Sharulnaim’s conduct was not sophisticated – he essentially implored Victim 1 to drop the case (see [9] above). While he made requests for her to drop the case on 12 September 2024 as well, this conduct is the subject of the TIC Obstruction Charge, for which I consider an appropriate uplift in sentence at [28] below, and which I will not take into account at this stage to avoid double counting.

27     I have calibrated this indicative starting point sentence by taking reference primarily from the sentence of 12 months’ imprisonment (for a conviction after a trial) in CHJ, which also involved the offender imploring the victim (through the victim’s mother) to drop the case against him in circumstances that are more serious than those in Mr Sharulnaim’s case, as: (a) CHJ involved an amalgamated charge in respect of four calls from the offender; (b) the predicate offence in CHJ carried a maximum of 20 years’ imprisonment, which is four times that of the Attempted Extortion Charge; and (c) the offender’s acts in CHJ were more sophisticated as he used a prepaid SIM card and a newly purchased phone to make three of the calls to avoid detection (although his culpability was tempered by the fact that the calls were made with the hope of saving his marriage) (see [24(b)] above). Consequently, the indicative starting point sentence for Mr Sharulnaim must necessarily be lower, with 7 months being appropriate.

28     The indicative starting point sentence should be adjusted to 6 months’ imprisonment to account for the following offender-specific factors:

(a)     An uplift of 1 month and 2 weeks to account for the TIC Obstruction Charge.

(b)     A reduction of 2 months and 2 weeks as Mr Sharulnaim indicated his intention to plead guilty at Stage 1 of the PG Guidelines.

29     This sentence is not inconsistent with the other precedent cases at [23]-[24] above.

(a)     It is lower than Parthiban, which involved: (i) a predicate offence of drug importation under s 7 of the Misuse of Drugs Act (Cap 185, 2008 Rev Ed) that carried the death penalty; and (ii) more sophisticated means of obstructing justice (see [23] above).

(b)     It is lower than Rajendran, which involved: (i) the offenders initially succeeding in helping their assistant evade arrest; and (ii) more sophisticated means of obstructing justice (see [24(a)] above). For completeness, I note that, like the Obstruction Charge, the offences under the Women’s Charter (Cap 353, 2009 Rev Ed) also carried a maximum of 5 years’ imprisonment at the time of the offences.

Wrongful Confinement Charge

30     The Wrongful Confinement Charge carries an imprisonment term of up to 3 years, a fine, or both.

31     In Chua Siew Peng v Public Prosecutor and another appeal [2017] 4 SLR 1247 (“Chua Siew Peng”), the offender was sentenced to 21 weeks’ imprisonment for an offence of wrongful confinement under s 342 read with s 73(2) of the Penal Code (Cap 224, 2008 Rev Ed), which carried a maximum of 18 months’ imprisonment at the time of the offence.[note: 39]

(a)     The offender faced a charge concerning a single day of confinement where she had locked both the door and the gate of her residence, leaving the victim (her foreign domestic helper, who had been subjected to prolonged physical abuse and wrongful confinement throughout her employment) with no means of exit. The victim fell after escaping through a window and suffered multiple fractures that left her wheelchair-bound for 4-6 weeks.[note: 40] The offender was convicted after a trial and originally sentenced to 2 months’ imprisonment, which was increased to 21 weeks’ imprisonment by the High Court (on appeal).

(b)     The High Court observed that a sentencing court ought to consider the following aspects of the offence:[note: 41]

(i)       the total duration of the wrongful confinement;

(ii)       the conditions in which the victim was wrongfully confined;

(iii)       whether the wrongful confinement was committed to facilitate the commission of another offence; and

(iv)       the consequences of the confinement on the victim.

32     A sentence of 1 month’s imprisonment for the Wrongful Confinement Charge is appropriate for Mr Sharulnaim.

(a)     The indicative starting point sentence (for a conviction after a trial) is 1 month’s imprisonment in light of the following offence-specific factors (see [11] above):

(i)       The duration of the wrongful confinement was a relatively short period lasting around 10 minutes.[note: 42]

(ii)       The physical conditions of confinement were unremarkable – it took place in the interior of Mr Sharulnaim’s car, and there is no indication of Victim 2 reacting adversely to the small space (eg. there is no evidence that she suffered from claustrophobia).

(iii)       During the period of confinement, Mr Sharulnaim confronted Victim 2 about the purported video recording (after he had already threatened to lodge a police report) and made comments about her physical appearance.

(iv)       The consequences of the confinement on Victim 2 were not trivial, as she was placed in a state of fear (although there is no evidence of lasting psychological trauma).[note: 43] This is particularly so given that she perceived Mr Sharulnaim to be a former police officer, and she continued to be confined despite her repeated requests to be released.

(b)     The indicative starting point sentence does not need to be adjusted as the uplift and reduction arising from offender-specific factors balance out:

(i)       An uplift of 1 week as Mr Sharulnaim committed the Wrongful Confinement Charge while he was on bail, in clear breach of the No Offence Bail Condition.

(ii)       A reduction of 1 week as Mr Sharulnaim indicated his intention to plead guilty at Stage 1 of the PG Guidelines.

Aggregate sentence

33     In line with the general rule of consecutive sentences for unrelated offences (Public Prosecutor v Raveen Balakrishnan [2018] 5 SLR 799 at [41]), the sentences for the Attempted Extortion Charge, the Obstruction Charge and the Wrongful Confinement Charge should run consecutively, for an aggregate sentence of 2 years’ and 10 months’ imprisonment.

34     While the Prosecution was open to having the sentence for the Wrongful Confinement Charge run concurrently,[note: 44] there is no principled basis to do so, as the one-transaction rule does not apply – the offences were all committed on different occasions and have different legally protected interests (Mohamed Shouffee bin Adam v Public Prosecutor [2014] 2 SLR 998).

35     Further, the aggregate sentence does not offend the totality principle as it is not significantly above the norm for the Attempted Extortion Charge (being the most serious offence), is not crushing, and is sufficient and proportionate to Mr Sharulnaim’s overall criminality (Goh Chin Soon v Public Prosecutor [2026] 3 SLR 736 at [163]).

Conclusion

36     Mr Sharulnaim is sentenced to an aggregate of 2 years’ and 10 months’ imprisonment and 3 strokes of the cane.

37     The sentence is backdated to 8 May 2024 (date of first arrest) and will take into account the periods of custody and exclude the periods on bail.[note: 45]
