-   Charges involving Chen:

15     Chen became acquainted with Ms Yang around 2010 when they worked at the same fashion shop. Sometime around July 2020, Ms Yang contacted Chen and asked if Chen was interested in working as a masseur in Singapore. Ms Yang stated that she could arrange for Chen’s entry and stay in Singapore on a work permit, but that Chen had to make a one-time payment to her for the “visa” to come to Singapore and pay a monthly levy to her. Ms Yang also stated that she could arrange for Chen’s accommodation in Singapore, but that Chen would have to pay her for the rent. Chen agreed to the proposals and proceeded to pay CNY35,000 (equivalent to about S$7,285.36) to Ms Yang for her “visa” to come to Singapore. Subsequently on 23 August 2020, Chen arrived in Singapore from China. Ms Yang and Lim then ferried Chen from the airport to the #04-07 Geylang Unit where Chen served her stay home notice (issued due to the Covid19 pandemic). On or around 3 September 2020, Ms Yang and Lim arranged for Chen to be moved to another residential unit [address redacted and hereafter referred to as the “#08-03 Geylang Unit”]. Ms Yang then assisted Chen in obtaining a work permit and on or about 18 September 2020 an “Application for a Work Permit” form was submitted to the Controller of Work Passes in which it was declared that Chen would be employed by Li Li Shun Woodwork Pte. Ltd. (UEN: xxxxxxxxxx [redacted]) (“LLS”) as a sales associate, and the work permit was approved. Chen however did not work for LLS and instead started work as a masseur. By virtue of the foregoing, Ms Yang received directly from Chen, a foreign employee, a sum of CNY35,000 (equivalent to about S$7,285.36) as consideration for Chen’s employment by LLS, and had thereby committed an offence under section 22A(1)(a) and punishable under section 22A(2) of the EFMA (subject matter of MAC 905925/2021; Penalty: Fine up to $30,000, or Imprisonment up to 2 years, or to both).

16     Pursuant to the agreement between the parties, Chen rented the #08-03 Geylang Unit from Ms Yang and Lim for a daily rental fee of S$150, due every 10 days; premises which Lim had leased at a monthly rent of only $1,900. On or around 26 September 2020, Chen went to Ms Yang’s residence at the #07-09 Geylang Unit, where she informed Ms Yang that she did not wish to continue working in Singapore any more due to amongst others, the costs of rental and the levies. Ms Yang then suggested that Chen should provide sexual services to customers to attract more customers. Because Chen could no longer afford the rental payments, she agreed. Ms Yang taught Chen how to advertise on vice websites like www.xxxxxxxxxx.com [redacted], how to conduct checks on prospective customers to avoid detection by the authorities, and provided advice on the pricing of her sexual services. Between 20th and 28th October 2020, Chen then provided sexual services to several clients at the #08-03 Geylang Unit. By virtue of the foregoing, Ms Yang procured Chen to have carnal connection for the purpose of prostitution within Singapore. Ms Yang had thereby committed an offence punishable under section 140(1)(b) and punishable under section 140(1A)(a) of the WC (subject matter of DAC 922376/2020; Penalty: Imprisonment up to 7 years, and shall also be liable to a Fine of up to $100,000/-).

17     In addition, Ms Yang and Lim had engaged in a conspiracy to allow the #08-03 Geylang Unit to be used as a brothel, and in pursuance of that conspiracy, Lim, as the tenant of the #08-03 Geylang Unit, allowed Chen to use the #08-03 Geylang Unit as a brothel between 20th and 28th October 2020. Ms Yang had thereby engaged in a conspiracy with Lim to allow the #08-03 Geylang Unit to be used as a brothel and had thereby committed an offence under section 148(2) and punishable under section 148(5)(a) of the WC, read with section 109 of the PC (subject matter of DAC 904784/2021; Penalty: Fine of up to $100,000/-, or Imprisonment up to 5 years, or to both).

18     On 26th October 2020, Ms Yang collected $1,500 from Chen, being rent for the #08-03 Geylang Unit. Ms Yang knew that part of the said moneys she collected from Chen were Chen’s earnings from prostitution. By virtue of the foregoing, Ms Yang had knowingly lived, in part, on Chen’s earnings from prostitution and had thereby committed an offence under section 146(1) and punishable under section 146(1AA)(a) of the WC (subject matter of DAC 922067/2020; Penalty: Imprisonment up to 7 years, and shall also be liable to a Fine of up to $100,000/-).

Pursuant to the arrangement between Ms Yang and Chen, Chen had to pay Ms Yang between $2,500 and $2,700 every month, part of which was used to pay for Chen’s foreign worker levy in order for Chen to continue working in Singapore. Ms Yang would then keep the balance amount for her own use. Sometime in October 2020, Ms Yang received directly from Chen a sum of $2,700 in cash, out of which $246.60 was used to pay for Chen’s levy and the balance $2,453.40 was retained by Ms Yang. The monthly payment of Chen’s levy allowed Chen to maintain a valid Work Permit to be employed by LLS as a sales associate from 18 September 2020 to 30 October 2020. By virtue of the foregoing, Ms Yang received directly from Chen, a foreign employee, the sum of $2,453.40 as consideration for Chen’s continued employment by LLS, and had thereby committed an offence under section 22A(1)(b) and punishable under section 22A(2) of the EFMA (subject matter of MAC 905928/2021; Penalty: Fine up to $30,000/-, or Imprisonment up to 2 years, or to both).

19     The table below sets out the amounts Ms Yang collected from Chen for the various purported purposes. No restitution has been made by Ms Yang to Chen.

-   Ms Yang’s further offending whilst claiming trial and on bail.

20     Investigations revealed that Ms Yang had made various posts on the vice website “www.xxxxx.com” [redacted]. She was arrested on 7 February 2025 for investigations and released on agency bail. Thereafter, she was found to have continued to have made various posts on another vice website “www.xxxxx.com” [redacted] and was again arrested on 8 May 2025 and released on agency bail (those events form part of the subject matter of the TIC charges in DAC 902958/2026 and DAC 902959/2026). Notwithstanding her prior arrests (both in 2025 and earlier in 2020), investigations revealed that Ms Yang continued and caused to be made a post with the alias “Xiao Fang- 小 小”, on another vice website “https://xxxx.xx/xxxxxxx/xxxxx.xxxxxxx=xxxx” [redacted] offering sexual services for $140. That said post was accessible in Singapore. Following the scheduling of an appointment with Ms Yang through that post, the SPF arrested Ms Yang at the residential unit located at [address redacted and hereafter referred to as the “Pasir Ris Unit”] on 11 February 2026. By virtue of the foregoing, Ms Yang had, in the course of business, used a remote communication service with a Singapore link to offer the provision by a woman of sexual services in Singapore in return for payment, and had thereby committed an offence under section 146A(1)(a) and punishable under section 146A(1)(c) of the WC (subject matter of DAC 902971/2026; Penalty: Fine up to $100,000/-, or Imprisonment up to 5 years, or to both).

21     Following Ms Yang’s re-arrest on 11 February 2026, she was produced in Court 4A on 13 February 2026 on the fresh charges, and upon the prosecution’s application given the context, her bail was revoked and no bail was ordered. MITIGATION

25     During the taking of the plea, the Mitigation took an initial form which appeared to retain some reservations regarding Ms Yang’s full responsibility under the charges. When queried, learned Defence Counsel confirmed that was not the intention and that an Amended Mitigation Plea would be filed within the same day.[note: 5] That Amended Mitigation Plea set out the facts as to what Ms Yang did in substantially similar terms to the Statements of Facts.[note: 6] It then urged leniency as Ms Yang was untraced and was pleading guilty in contrition. I summarize the main arguments made.

26      The Impecunious Argument: In response to the Prosecution’s submissions for fines, the Defence submitted that concurrent custodial terms would be more appropriate as the accused was unable to pay as she was “impecunious and impoverished” and would end up serving a protracted period in custody because default terms for fines must run consecutively.[note: 7]

27      The Third Parties Argument: The Defence also stated that the Statements of Facts only “told half-the-story” on what happened in relation to the Work Permits arranged for the PRC women who ended up working in vice.[note: 8] The Defence stated that “3rd parties are likely to be very much involved such that her [Ms Yang’s] role is possibly or likely minimal”.[note: 9] The Defence then added that whilst Ms Yang was committed to her admission to the facts sustaining the conviction on the charges against her and had received the various monetary sums from the PRC women, it would be unfair to impose disgorgement fines on Ms Yang since she ‘did not receive all the benefits’ as there were others involved.[note: 10]

28      The Overlap Argument: The Defence cited substantial overlap in the charges and simply urged minimal custodial terms to run concurrently.[note: 11]

29     In closing, the Defence did not condescend to specific sentences which it would deem reasonable for the various charges, and simply urged the court to backdate the sentence to cover the extended prior period Ms Yang had already spent in remand during the earlier investigations so as to allow Ms Yang to “swiftly return to her home”.[note: 12]

REASONS FOR SENTENCE

30     The task of sentencing requires an accurate grasp of the facts, a review of the applicable sentencing frameworks and/or precedents and applying them to the facts of the present case and the present offender to arrive at the appropriate sentence for what she has done. It was unfortunate that the Mitigation declined to approach the submissions on sentence in that manner. The plea for “minimal custodial terms to run concurrently” for all the charges really ought to have been justified on the basis of applicable sentencing frameworks and/or precedents to see if the plea was at all realistic and justifiable. After all, this offender was – regrettably – not the only one to have committed such offences here, and our fidelity to the Rule of Law requires that like offences & offenders be treated alike.

31     Therefore, taking the proper approach requires starting with a review of the admitted facts as set out earlier. Efforts were made in these grounds to consolidate them and set them out in broad chronological order because that affords a proper sensing as to what happened, and the nature of the offender that we are dealing with. A review of those facts shows two prominent aspects.

-   The offending was persistent over an extended period.

32     To recap, after her initial arrest on 17 June 2020 for peddling vice (MAC 909424/2020[note: 13], MAC 909422/2020 & MAC 909423/2020), she was allowed to remain on bail as investigations were on-going. Whilst on bail, she moved to another property and continued peddling vice (DAC 904787/2021, DAC 904786/2021, & DAC 904788/2021). She also went on to work with others to arrange for at least 4 other PRC women to also work in vice (MAC 905924/2021, DAC 922377/2020, DAC 904785/2021, MAC 905925/2021, DAC 922376/2020, DAC 904784/2021, MAC 905928/2021, MAC 905923/2021, MAC 905921/2021, MAC 905922/2021, MAC 905926/2021, MAC 905927/2021, DAC 904790/2021, & DAC 904783/2021) and profited from doing so (DAC 922375/2020, DAC 922067/2020, DAC 922374/2020, & DAC 904789/2021). When she was re-arrested on 29 October 2020 for those further activities whilst on bail, a sum of $138,177/- was seized from her – actions which were never challenged. She opted to claim trial instead and that eventually led to her being released on bail again. Even as the trial was on-going, she was found to have returned to peddling vice whilst on bail and was re-arrested a third time on 7 February 2025 (DAC 902958/2026). She was again allowed out on bail but returned again to peddling vice soon after whilst on bail and was re-arrested a 4th time on 8 May 2025 (DAC 902959/2026). That pattern repeated once more and she was re-arrested a 5th time on 11 February 2026 (DAC 902971/2026). That pattern of re-offending despite arrests, despite increasingly stringent bail conditions, despite pending enforcement actions by the authorities, stopped only because further bail was finally refused by the courts. All that shows the measure of the offender we are dealing with, her true attitude towards the law and the authorities here, and that the penchant to be involved in vice was deeply rooted. Culpability – at least from the 2nd episode of offending onwards – was aggravated and ought to find expression in the individual sentences.

-   The offending was broad and varied.

33     The facts show that she familiarized herself with the vice trade to know where to advertise so as to reach potential clients and how much to charge for her services. She also took actions to find suitable premises to carry out her activities – premises which were accessible in the residential areas of the community. She knew from an early stage – not least from the date of her admitted charges from 17 June 2020 – that all those actions were illegal. Despite that, she went on to repeat them and did so at scale. She worked with as yet still unknown individuals to facilitate sham passes for two PRC women to be in Singapore before ultimately procuring those women for the vice trade in rental properties which she helped arrange. She profited all round by collecting inflated sums for the passes, levies, and rent, before also living off their prostitution earnings; doing the same for a further two other PRC women as well. The breadth of offending spanned several distinct categories and the actions all showed calculated deliberation and shrewd planning; factors which ought to find expression in the aggregate sentence.

34     After firmly grasping the facts surrounding the charges, one turns next to the applicable sentencing frameworks and/or precedents for the individual charges to arrive at the indicative starting points.

-     Ms Yang’s own sexy massage activities:

■        MAC 909424/2020: For being a self-employed foreign masseur without a valid work pass on 17 June 2020. Offence under s 10(1) & p/u s 10(2)(a) of the EFMA. Penalty: Fine up to $20,000/-, or Imprisonment up to 2 years, or Both. Prosecution submitted for a fine of at least $8,000/-. Prosecution justified this with reference to the precedent case in PP v Rahman Mohammed Ataur [2020] SGMC 17 which involved a foreigner who was fined $8,000/- for the same offence after pleading guilty to have illegally worked as a self-employed food delivery worker and construction worker for a period of around 18 months. That precedent case was persuasive. Though the period of employment here was shorter at about 6 months, the nature of the employment – being the kind of massage services which appeared on a vice website – aggravated the offence since the harm to society was on a different level altogether. The Prosecution’s suggested start point fine of $8,000/- was thus reasonable if a little on the low side. Additionally, there was another similar charge being taken into consideration: DAC 904788/2021; that was when she continued the exact same offence at the #07-09 Geylang Unit after being released on bail. Specific deterrence was activated and I determined that the fine ought to be adjusted higher to a start point of $10,000/- instead.

■        DAC 904787/2021: For carrying on her business of unlicensed massage services at the #07-09 Geylang Unit between 20 June 2020 and 29 October 2020. Offence under s 5(1) p/u s 5(4)(a) MEA. Penalty: Fine up to $10,000/-, or Imprisonment up to 2 years, or Both. Prosecution submitted for the maximum fine of $10,000/-. Prosecution justified this based on the precedent case in Huang Xiaoyue v PP [2023]5 SLR 1609 (“Huang Xiaoyue”). In that precedent the High Court set down a benchmark sentence of $10,000/- for an “archetypal vice case” after conviction at trial. I accepted that some credit ought to be given for her late indication that she was not contesting this charge and that the fine amount should be adjusted slightly down. However, when one takes into account that the offence here was committed whilst on bail and that she had committed the exact same offence earlier for 6 months at the Sims Avenue Unit and that offence was being taken into consideration for sentencing (MAC 909422/2020), then it was clear that the penalty ought to be adjusted higher. Specific deterrence was activated and I determined that a fine of $10,000/- would adequately cater to the facts.

■        DAC 904786/2021: For advertising her business of unlicensed massage services on the vice website between 20 June 2020 and 29 October 2020. Offence under s 5(2) p/u s 5(4)(a) MEA. Penalty: Fine up to $10,000/-, or Imprisonment up to 2 years, or Both. Prosecution submitted for a fine of between $8,000/- to $10,000/-. Prosecution justified this based on the Huang Xiaoyue precedent. Applying the benchmark established and adjusting it on account of this offender’s late indication of her intention not to contest the charge meant that the fine ought to be adjusted down slightly. However, when one takes into account that the offence here was committed whilst on bail and that she had committed the exact same offence earlier for 6 months at the Sims Avenue Unit and that offence was being taken into consideration (MAC 909423/2020), then it was clear that the sentence here ought to be adjusted higher. Penalty: Fine up to $30,000/-, or to Imprisonment up to 2 years, or Both. Prosecution submitted for a fine of between $10,000/- and $11,000/- with a similar justification as that for MAC 905924/2021 & MAC 905925/2021 above. After undertaking the same review of the precedents and making the same adjustments with reference to the lower amount of money taken here, the fact that no restitution had been made, that this offence was committed whilst on bail, and that some credit ought to be given for the offender’s late indication that she was no longer contesting this charge, I agreed that a fine of $10,000/- would have been appropriate.

■        Penalty Order under s 23A(1)(a) EFMA: Additionally, the MOM Prosecutor sought a penalty of $14,913.71 under s 23A(1)(a) EFMA. That amount was the total received by the offender in the three proceeded charges. The Defence made no address on this in response. A review of the provision indicates that the making of the penalty order is mandatory, and I determined that such an order ought to made in each of the three proceeded charges for their respective amounts.

-     Ms Yang’s further offending whilst claiming trial and on bail:

■        DAC 902971/2026: for using the remote communication service, a vice website, to offer her paid sex services on 11 February 2026. Offence under s 146A(1)(a) & p/u s 146A(1)(c) WC. Penalty: Fine up to $100,000/-, or Imprisonment up to 5 years, or Both. Prosecution submitted for a fine of between $10,000/- to $12,000/-. Prosecution justified this based on the sentencing framework laid out in the Poh Boon Kiat v PP [2014]4 SLR 892 and extended in Koh Jaw Hung v PP [2019]3 SLR 516 to the present offence provision. Whilst I agreed that the sentencing framework applied and that it needed to be proportionately scaled up since the maximum penalty had since been increased from 3 years to 5 years, I found that not enough consideration had been accorded to the fact that this offence here represented a persistent return to offending whilst on bail, and that there were two other similar charges being taken into consideration as well (DAC 902958/2026 & DAC 902959/2026). Given the facts of the offence, I determined that the custodial threshold was comfortably crossed and that specific deterrence was firmly engaged. It was my judgment that a term of imprisonment of 3 months ought to be imposed instead.

35     Having arrived at the indicative starting points for each charge, I next considered if there were any offender specific factors which required an adjustment of those starting points. Where applicable, the sentencing discounts had already been accorded to the offender for her late indication that she was not contesting her charges. There was very little credit to be accorded to her being untraced since the facts indicated that this was not an aberration in any otherwise unblemished record; quite the opposite, the history shows that this was a sustained spree and that specific deterrence was firmly activated, and that has already been factored in for the relevant charges.

36     The next step was to consider which offences ought to run consecutively and whether the aggregate sentence was proportionate to the totality of her actions. Here, the Prosecution sought only to have two sentences run consecutively: DAC 922375/2020 and DAC 904785/2021, to arrive at an aggregate of 14-15 months imprisonment. I did not agree with that position. First, the two charges DAC 922375/2020 (living on earnings) and DAC 904785/2021 (conspiracy to use the unit as a brothel) both involved the same PRC woman Li when the facts and charges clearly indicated that there were two PRC women being impacted by Ms Yang’s offending. At the very least, each of the women ought to be represented in the aggregate. Next, out of the 13 proceeded charges, the Prosecution sought imprisonment terms for only 6 of them, with fines being sought for the rest. Given the breadth of the offending as recounted earlier, and the persistence of that offending, I determined that the aggregate imprisonment term ought to see representation for her actions in relation to the two PRC women (DAC 904785/2021 & DAC 922067/2020) and also for her own actions in having returned to peddling vice whilst on bail (DAC 902971/2026). Those three offences were separate and distinct and involved different legally protected interests. I was prepared to impose fines for the rest knowing that these would find their bite since fines had to be satisfied lest a term in prison be served in default of payment. I therefore arrived at the following adjusted positions for each of the charges:

-     Ms Yang’s own sexy massage activities:

■        MAC 909424/2020: For being a self-employed foreign masseur without a valid work pass on 17 June 2020. Offence under s 10(1) & p/u s 10(2)(a) of the EFMA. Penalty: Fine up to $20,000/-, or Imprisonment up to 2 years, or Both. Prosecution submitted for a fine of at least $8,000/-. Indicative starting point fine of $10,000/-.

■        DAC 904787/2021: For carrying on her business of unlicensed massage services at the #07-09 Geylang Unit between 20 June 2020 and 29 October 2020. Offence under s 5(1) p/u s 5(4)(a) MEA. Penalty: Fine up to $10,000/-, or Imprisonment up to 2 years, or Both. Prosecution submitted for the maximum fine of $10,000/-. Indicative starting point fine of $10,000/-.

■        DAC 904786/2021: For advertising her business of unlicensed massage services on the vice website between 20 June 2020 and 29 October 2020. Offence under s 5(2) p/u s 5(4)(a) MEA. Penalty: Fine up to $10,000/-, or Imprisonment up to 2 years, or Both. Prosecution submitted for a fine of between $8,000/- to $10,000/-. Indicative starting point fine of $10,000/-.

-     The vice related charges involving the PRC women:

■        DAC 922377/2020: For engaging with Lim in the common intention to procure Li for the purpose of prostitution on 10 September 2020. Offence under s 140(1)(b) & p/u s 140(1A)(a) WC r/w s 32 PC. Penalty: Imprisonment up to 7 years and shall also be liable to a Fine of up to $100,000/-. Prosecution submitted for 9-10 months’ imprisonment. Indicative starting point of 10 months’ imprisonment.

■        DAC 922376/2020: For procuring Chen on 26 September 2020 to have carnal connection for the purpose of prostitution. Offence under s 140(1)(b) & p/u s 140(1A)(a) WC. Penalty: Imprisonment up to 7 years and shall also be liable to a Fine of up to $100,000/-. Prosecution submitted for 9-10 months imprisonment. Indicative starting point of 10 months’ imprisonment.

■        DAC 904785/2021: For engaging in a conspiracy with Lim for Li to use the #04-07 Geylang Unit as a brothel from 10 to 28 September 2020. Offence under s 148(2) & p/u s 148(5)(a) WC r/w s 109 PC. Penalty: Fine up to $100,000/-, or Imprisonment up to 5 years, or Both. Prosecution submitted for 5 months’ imprisonment. Indicative starting point of 6 months’ imprisonment.

■        DAC 904784/2021: For engaging in a conspiracy with Lim for Chen to use the #08-03 Geylang Unit as a brothel from 20 to 28 October 2020. Offence under s 148(2) & p/u s 148(5)(a) WC r/w s 109 PC. Penalty: Fine up to $100,000/-, or Imprisonment up to 5 years, or Both. Prosecution submitted for 5 months’ imprisonment. Indicative starting point of 6 months’ imprisonment.

■        DAC 922375/2020: For living on the earnings of the prostitution of Li when Ms Yang collected $1,500 and CNY13,000 from Li between 15th and 23rd September 2020, which were, in part, Li’s earnings from prostitution. Offence under s 146(1) & p/u s 146(1AA)(a) WC. Penalty: Imprisonment up to 7 years and shall also be liable to a Fine of up to $100,000/-. Prosecution submitted for 9-10 months’ imprisonment and a disgorgement fine of $3,000/-. Indicative starting point of 10 months’ imprisonment with the disgorgement fine of $3,000/-.

■        DAC 922067/2020: For living on the earnings of the prostitution of Chen when Ms Yang collected $1,500 from Chen on 26 October 2020, which were, in part, Chen’s earnings from prostitution. Offence under s 146(1) & p/u s 146(1AA)(a) WC. Penalty: Imprisonment up to 7 years and shall also be liable to a Fine of up to $100,000/-. Prosecution submitted for 9-10 months’ imprisonment and a disgorgement fine of $3,000/-. Indicative starting point of 10 months’ imprisonment with the disgorgement fine of $3,000/-.

-     The employment related payments received from the PRC women:

■        MAC 905924/2021: For receiving CNY25,000 (S$5,174.95) from Li on or about 13 August 2020 as consideration for Li’s employment by JM. Offence under s 22A(1)(a) & p/u s 22A(2) EFMA. Penalty: Fine up to $30,000/-, or Imprisonment up to 2 years, or to Both. The MOM Prosecutor submitted for a fine of between $14,000 to $15,000. Indicative starting point of fine of $14,000/- together with the applicable penalty.

■        MAC 905925/2021: For receiving CNY35,000 (S$7,285.36) from Chen in July 2020 as consideration for Chen’s employment by LLS. Offence under s 22A(1)(a) & p/u s 22A(2) EFMA. Penalty: Fine up to $30,000/-, or Imprisonment up to 2 years, or to Both. Prosecution submitted for a fine of between $14,000 to $15,000. Indicative starting point of fine of $15,000/- together with the applicable penalty.

■        MAC 905928/2021: For receiving $2,453.40 from Chen in October 2020 as consideration for Chen’s continued employment by LLS. Offence under s 22A(1)(b) & p/u s 22A(2) EFMA. Penalty: Fine up to $30,000/-, or to Imprisonment up to 2 years, or Both. Prosecution submitted for a fine of between $10,000/- and $11,000/-. Indicative starting point of fine of $10,000/- together with the applicable penalty.

-     Ms Yang’s further offending whilst claiming trial and on bail:

■        DAC 902971/2026: for using the remote communication service, a vice website, to offer her paid sex services on 11 February 2026. Offence under s 146A(1)(a) & p/u s 146A(1)(c) WC. Penalty: Fine up to $100,000/-, or Imprisonment up to 5 years, or Both. Prosecution submitted for a fine of between $10,000/- to $12,000/-. Indicative starting point of 3 months’ imprisonment.

37     The above positions resulted in an indicative total imprisonment term of 19 months’ imprisonment (DAC 922067/2020, DAC 904785/2021 & DAC 902971/2026 running consecutively) with a total fine of $75,000/- and the mandatory penalty totaling $14,913.71 under s 23A(1)(a) EFMA.

38     A last look to ensure that this aggregate was proportionate to the totality of her offending was then done. In this regard, I return to address the defence submissions in the Mitigation. First was the “Impercunious Argument”. That did not appear to be at all credible since a substantial sum was found on her and seized from her during her second arrest for the spate of additional vice charges. That argument appeared to be aimed at trying to avoid the effects of the monetary penalty and I was not impressed. An offender ought not to be able to choose their penalty. Second was the “Third Parties Argument”. I do not see how this submission assists the offender. After all, if there were third parties involved, the facts show that this offender certainly did nothing to cough them up. It remains the unequivocal position before me that this offender has admitted to the charges and facts recounted and that she ought to be met with the full consequences for her offences as a result. It would be perverse to reward her with leniency for her intentional reticence. Third was the “Overlap Argument”. This was unclear and unsubstantiated as a result. An objective review of the charges will show that each was separate and distinct. Further, the aggregate consisted of clearly distinct offences with different legally protected interests. I could not find any merit to this argument as a result. Therefore, no adjustments were made to the individual sentences or the indicative aggregate sentence on those counts.

39     That said, I was mindful that the indicative aggregate sentence was higher than the aggregate sentence sought by the Prosecution, and I was prepared to temper the extent of the uplifts on account of the facts recounted earlier. I thus arrived at the final adjusted sentences as follows with the corresponding fine default terms:

■    MAC 909424/2020: Fine adjusted down from $10,000/- to $8,000/- in default 8 weeks’ imprisonment.

■    DAC 904787/2021: Fine remains at $10,000/- in default 10 weeks’ imprisonment.

■    DAC 904786/2021: Fine adjusted down from $10,000/- to $8,000/- in default 8 weeks’ imprisonment.

■    DAC 922377/2020: Imprisonment adjusted down from 10 to 9 months.

■    DAC 922376/2020: Imprisonment adjusted down from 10 to 9 months.

■     DAC 904785/2021[note: 14]: Imprisonment adjusted down from 6 to 5 months.

■    DAC 904784/2021: Imprisonment adjusted down from 6 to 5 months.

■    DAC 922375/2020: Imprisonment adjusted down from 10 to 9 months. Disgorgement fine of $3,000/- unchanged with an in-default period of 3 weeks.

■     DAC 922067/2020: Imprisonment adjusted down from 10 to 9 months. Disgorgement fine of $3,000/- unchanged with an in-default period of 3 weeks.

■    MAC 905924/2021: Fine remains at $14,000/- in default 14 weeks’ imprisonment, with the applicable penalty of $5,174.95 in default 5 weeks’ imprisonment.

■    MAC 905925/2021: Fine remains at $15,000/- in default 15 weeks’ imprisonment, with the applicable penalty of $7,285.36 in default 7 weeks’ imprisonment.

■    MAC 905928/2021: Fine remains at $10,000/- in default 10 weeks’ imprisonment, with the applicable penalty of $2,453.40 in default 2 weeks’ imprisonment.

■     DAC 902971/2026: Imprisonment term remains at 3 months.

40     The adjusted aggregate sentence was thus 17 months’ imprisonment and a total fine of $71,000/- in default 71 weeks’ imprisonment with the applicable penalty for a total amount of $14,913.71 under s 23A(1)(a) EFMA in default 14 weeks’ imprisonment. I found this aggregate to be entirely reasonable for her extended spree and not excessive or crushing and not in keeping with her prospects. Given that fines & penalties were being imposed and knowing that substantial monies had earlier been seized from the accused during her re-arrest on further offending, I invited the parties to submit as to whether those monies ought to be directed towards the payment of the fines & penalties. The Prosecution submitted that they should. The Defence, including the offender herself, pleaded to be able to keep the entirety of the monies and to serve the default in prison instead. It made little sense to sanction that deliberate consumption of public resources to house this offender for longer when she clearly had means to pay the fines and penalties. An offender should not be able to choose their punishment. The court had powers to make relevant orders under section 319(1)(b)(iv) of the Criminal Procedure Code. I therefore directed that the Prosecution pay the sum of the fine and penalties from the monies seized from the accused, and that they were at liberty to do with the balance in any manner they deemed fit thereafter. As at the date of these grounds, that payment has since been made. The 17 months’ imprisonment term was also ordered to be backdated to the date of her re-arrest on 29 October 2020 so as to take into account the periods she spent in custody but to exclude the periods on bail. The records show that the offender was on bail from 15 January 2021 till her re-arrest on 6 February 2025, and on bail from 7 February 2025 till her final arrest on 11 February 2026.[note: 15]

CONCLUSION

41     The offender Ms Yang has since filed an appeal against her sentence; she did so on the last day of the relevant period. Thereafter, through counsel, she sought bail pending her appeal. I saw parties and heard the arguments. After careful consideration, I determined that given the previous proven history of her cynical conduct in repeatedly breaching fundamental bail conditions in accumulating multiple non-bailable offences whilst on bail, we should not sanction yet another opportunity and allow Ms Yang to do as she pleases free again in society. After all, that offending behaviour just referred to was recent and this offender has only just started on her reformative journey in the sentence. It was obvious that this offender has not found it in her character to resist peddling her vice and that it would do her – and society – good if she continued to stabilize and reform in custody instead. The proper course for this offender was to make arrangements to have her appeal expedited, and that has been done. These grounds were issued in that context.

[note: 1]For the purposes of the trial, the Prosecution proceeded with three charges: DAC 922375/2020, DAC 922377/2020 and DAC 904785/2021. The other charges were stood down.

Public Prosecutor v K. N. Puventhra Reddiyar and another

Public Prosecutor v K. N. Puventhra Reddiyar and another
[2026] SGDC 237

Case Number:District Arrest Case No. DAC-924432-2018 and Others, Magistrate's Appeal No. MA-9120-2026-01 and MA-9121-2026-01
Decision Date:20 July 2026
Tribunal/Court:District Court
Coram: Chay Yuen Fatt
Counsel Name(s): DPPs Kang Jia Hui, Cheng You Duen, Vincent Ong & Louis Ngia for Prosecution; K Jayakumar Naidu (Jay Law Corporation) for Accused Persons
Parties: Public Prosecutor — K. N. Puventhra Reddiyar — Puvana Puventhra

Criminal Law – Offences – Abetment by Conspiracy – Cheating – Criminal Breach of Trust – Agent

Criminal Procedure and Sentencing – Sentencing - Principles

[LawNet Editorial Note: An appeal to this decision has been filed in MA 9120/2026/01 and MA 9121/2026/01.]

20 July 2026

District Judge Chay Yuen Fatt:

Introduction

1       The two accused persons are husband and wife. Mr K.N. Puventhra Reddiyar (the “Husband”) is a 45-year-old male Singaporean and his wife, Madame Puvana Puventhra (the “Wife”) is a 44-year-old female Singaporean. They were insurance agents with Manulife (Singapore) Pte Ltd (“Manulife”) at the material times.

2       Between 2006-2007, the accused persons sold at least six investment -linked insurance policies (“Six Policies”) to the Husband’s maternal elderly aunt, Visalatchi D/O Awani Paspathy[note: 1] (“Visa”). They promised Visa that she would be able to cash out the policies for a tidy sum of money when she retired at 62 years old. That was not to be. In breach of her trust over a period of four years, the Husband pocketed various sums of money which Visa had entrusted to him to pay Manulife as premiums for her policies. The accused persons also conspired and forged Visa’s signature to deceive Manulife into transferring the Six Policies to the Wife who then surrendered them and pocketed the proceeds of the surrender. Visa was left with nothing when she finally retired.

3       The Husband faced five proceeded charges under s 409 of the Penal Code (Cap 224, 2008 Rev Ed) (“PC”) (“CBT Charges”). Additionally, he also faced six proceeded charges under s 420 read with 109 PC (“Cheating Charges”). Being the Husband’s co-conspirator, the Wife also faced the same six Cheating Charges.

4       The two accused were jointly represented by Counsel and claimed trial to their respective charges. At the conclusion of the trial, the two accused were convicted of the said charges. The Husband, who was convicted of 11 charges, was sentenced in total to 38 months’ imprisonment. Pursuant to s 359 of the Criminal Procedure Code (2010)(“CPC”), he was also ordered to pay a compensation of $117,906 to Visa, in default to serve another six months’ imprisonment. The wife, who was convicted of six charges, was sentenced in total to 16 months' imprisonment and ordered to pay compensation of $23,906, in default to serve an additional two months’ imprisonment. The Prosecution withdrew the remaining charges against the Husband.

5       They have both appealed against their convictions and sentences and have been released on bail pending this appeal. The compensation orders have also been stayed.

Eleven Charges Against the Husband

6       The Prosecution proceeded to trial against the Husband with 11 charges, comprising five CBT Charges and six Cheating Charges (“collectively, “Proceeded Charges”). Each CBT Charge consolidates the offences committed within a calendar year.[note: 2]

7       Another six charges for forgery offences were stood down (“stood down charges”).[note: 3]

8       The Proceeded Charges against the Husband are set out as follows:

7th Charge[note: 4]

You, … are charged that you, between 24 July 2009 and 28 October 2009, in Singapore, having been entrusted with property, to wit, $15,000, whilst in the way of your business as an agent, to wit, as a Financial Planner of Manulife (Singapore) Pte Ltd, did commit criminal breach of trust in respect of the said property by dishonestly misappropriating the said property and you have thereby committed an offence punishable under Section 409 of the Penal Code, Chapter 224, 2008 Rev Ed.

8th Charge[note: 5]

You, … are charged that you, between 11 June 2010 and 21 July 2010, in Singapore, having been entrusted with property, to wit, $15,000, whilst in the way of your business as an agent, to wit, as a Financial Planner of Manulife (Singapore) Pte Ltd, did commit criminal breach of trust in respect of the said property by dishonestly misappropriating the said property and you have thereby committed an offence punishable under Section 409 of the Penal Code, Chapter 224, 2008 Rev Ed.

9th Charge[note: 6]

You, … are charged that you, between 1 March 2011 and 11 October 2011, in Singapore, having been entrusted with property, to wit, $28,500, whilst in the way of your business as an agent, to wit, as a Financial Planner of Manulife (Singapore) Pte Ltd, did commit criminal breach of trust in respect of the said property by dishonestly misappropriating the said property and you have thereby committed an offence punishable under Section 409 of the Penal Code, Chapter 224, 2008 Rev Ed.

10th Charge[note: 7]

You, …are charged that you, between 21 June 2012 to 11 September 2012, in Singapore, having been entrusted with property, to wit, $25,500, whilst in the way of your business as an agent, to wit, as a Financial Planner of Manulife (Singapore) Pte Ltd, did commit criminal breach of trust in respect of the said property by dishonestly misappropriating the said property and you have thereby committed an offence punishable under Section 409 of the Penal Code, Chapter 224, 2008 Rev Ed.

11th Charge[note: 8]

You, …are charged that you, between 24 March 2013 to 26 March 2013, in Singapore, having been entrusted with property, to wit, $10,000, whilst in the way of your business as an agent, to wit, as a Financial Planner of Manulife (Singapore) Pte Ltd, did commit criminal breach of trust in respect of the said property by dishonestly misappropriating the said property and you have thereby committed an offence punishable under Section 409 of the Penal Code, Chapter 224, 2008 Rev Ed.

12th Charge[note: 9]

You, …are charged that you, on or before 24 April 2013, in Singapore, did engage in a conspiracy with Puvana Puventhra (formerly known as Puvaneswari d/o Muthayah) to cheat Manulife (Singapore) Pte Ltd by deceiving Manulife (Singapore) Pte Ltd into believing that Visalatchi D/O Awani Paspathy had executed a Notice of Assignment and entered into a Deed of Assignment with Puvana Puventhra to assign Manulink Investor Policy Number xxxxxxxxxxx to Puvana Puventhra, and in pursuance of that conspiracy, and in order to the doing of that thing, an act took place, to wit, on or before 24 April 2013, you submitted the said Notice of Assignment and Deed of Assignment in which Visalatchi D/O Awani Paspathy purported to consent to the assignment of Manulink Investor Policy Number xxxxxxxxxxx to Puvana Puventhra when you knew that the said documents were not executed by Visalatchi D/O Awani Paspathy, and by such manner of deception, Manulife (Singapore) Pte Ltd was dishonestly induced to deliver property, to wit, Manulink Investor Policy Number xxxxxxxxxxx to Puvana Puventhra, and you have thereby committed an offence punishable under Section 420 read with Section 109 of the Penal Code (Cap 224, 2008 Rev Ed).

13th Charge[note: 10]

You, …are charged that you, on or before 13 June 2013, in Singapore, did engage in a conspiracy with Puvana Puventhra (formerly known as Puvaneswari d/o Muthayah) to cheat Manulife (Singapore) Pte Ltd by deceiving Manulife (Singapore) Pte Ltd into believing that Visalatchi D/O Awani Paspathy had executed a Notice of Assignment and entered into a Deed of Assignment with Puvana Puventhra to assign Manulink Investor Policy Number xxxxxxxxxxx to Puvana Puventhra, and in pursuance of that conspiracy, and in order to the doing of that thing, an act took place, to wit, on or before 13 June 2013, you submitted the said Notice of Assignment and Deed of Assignment in which Visalatchi D/O Awani Paspathy purported to consent to the assignment of Manulink Investor Policy Number xxxxxxxxxxx to Puvana Puventhra when you knew that the said documents were not executed by Visalatchi D/O Awani Paspathy, and by such manner of deception, Manulink (Singapore) Pte Ltd was dishonestly induced to deliver property, to wit, Manulink Investor Policy Number xxxxxxxxxxx to Puvana Puventhra, and you have thereby committed an offence punishable under Section 420 read with Section 109 of the Penal Code (Cap 224, 2008 Rev Ed).

14th Charge[note: 11]

You, …are charged that you, on or before 8 July 2013, in Singapore, did engage in a conspiracy with one Puvana Puventhra (formerly known as Puvaneswari d/o Muthayah) to cheat Manulife (Singapore) Pte Ltd by deceiving Manulife (Singapore) Pte Ltd into believing that one Visalatchi D/O Awani Paspathy had executed a Notice of Assignment and entered into a Deed of Assignment with Puvana Puventhra to assign Manulink Investor Policy Number xxxxxxxxxxx to the said Puvana Puventhra, and in pursuance of that conspiracy, and in order to the doing of that thing, an act took place, to wit, on or before 8 July 2013, you submitted the said Notice of Assignment and Deed of Assignment in which Visalatchi D/O Awani Paspathy purported to consent to the assignment of Manulink Investor Policy Number xxxxxxxxxxx to Puvana Puventhra when you knew that the said documents were not executed by Visalatchi D/O Awani Paspathy, and by such manner of deception, Manulife (Singapore) Pte Ltd was dishonestly induced to deliver property, to wit, Manulink Investor Policy Number xxxxxxxxxxx to Puvana Puventhra, and you have thereby committed an offence punishable under Section 420 read with Section 109 of the Penal Code (Cap 224, 2008 Rev Ed).

15th Charge[note: 12]

You, …are charged that you, on or before 8 July 2013, in Singapore, did engage in a conspiracy with Puvana Puventhra (formerly known as Puvaneswari d/o Muthayah) to cheat Manulife (Singapore) Pte Ltd by deceiving Manulife (Singapore) Pte Ltd into believing that Visalatchi D/O Awani Paspathy had executed a Notice of Assignment and entered into a Deed of Assignment with Puvana Puventhra to assign Manulink Investor Policy Number xxxxxxxxxxx to Puvana Puventhra, and in pursuance of that conspiracy, and in order to the doing of that thing, an act took place, to wit, on or before 8 July 2013, you submitted the said Notice of Assignment and Deed of Assignment in which Visalatchi D/O Awani Paspathy purported to consent to the assignment of Manulink Investor Policy Number xxxxxxxxxxx to Puvana Puventhra, when you knew that the said documents were not executed by Visalatchi D/O Awani Paspathy, and by such manner of deception, Manulife (Singapore) Pte Ltd was dishonestly induced to deliver property, to wit, Manulink Investor Policy Number xxxxxxxxxxx to Puvana Puventhra, and you have thereby committed an offence punishable under Section 420 read with Section 109 of the Penal Code (Cap 224, 2008 Rev Ed).

16th Charge[note: 13]
