The Offences and the Law

31     The legal provisions and principles relevant to the Proceeded Charges are not controversial.

Cheating Charges

Offence of Cheating As Agent

32     The essential elements of an offence of cheating are that the victim (in this case Manulife) was deceived by a misrepresentation flowing from the accused persons, and that the victim was dishonestly induced by such deception to deliver any property to any person: see Gunasegeran s/o Pavadaisamy v Public Prosecutor [1997] 2 SLR(R) 946 at [41] – [43].[note: 45]

33     “Deception” is defined as the inducement of a person to believe something to be true which the person making the representation knows is in fact false: Leck Kim Koon v Public Prosecutor [2022] 3 SLR 1050 at [27].

34     “Inducement” means that the deception operates on the victim’s mind and, by reason of that deception, the victim is induced to part with property. Such inducement need not be the “sole, operative reason” for the delivery of property and need only to play “some part” in inducing the delivery: Seaward III Frederick Oliver v Public Prosecutor [1994] 3 SLR(R) 89 at [28].

35     “Dishonestly” is defined in s 24 of the PC as follows:

Whoever does anything with the intention of causing wrongful gain to one person, or wrongful loss to another person, is said to do that thing dishonestly.

36     “Wrongful gain” and “wrongful loss” are defined in s 23 of the PC as follows:

Wrongful gain” is gain by unlawful means of property to which the person gaining it is not legally entitled; “wrongful loss” is loss by unlawful means of property to which the person losing it is legally entitled.

37     The Cheating Charges further incorporate the additional element of abetment by way of conspiracy. The Prosecution accepts that it has to prove, beyond reasonable doubt, the following four elements:

(a)     The accused persons abetted each other in a conspiracy to cheat Manulife by submitting forged Assignment Documents to Manulife;

(b)     Manulife was deceived into believing that Visa had signed the Assignment Documents;

(c)     Manulife was thereby induced into assigning the Six Policies to the Wife; and

(d)     The accused persons acted “dishonestly” by causing wrongful gain to them and/or wrongful loss to Manulife.

Abetment by Conspiracy

38     Section 120A(1) of the PC defines a criminal conspiracy to be when a person agrees with another to commit an offence or cause an offence to be committed. An abetment by conspiracy as provided in s 107(1)(b) entails a further act or illegal omission to take place pursuant to the conspiracy.

39     The essence of a “conspiracy” is agreement. Conspiracy requires that there must be knowledge of a common design. It is not necessary that all the co-conspirators should be equally informed as to the details of the conspiracy but they must at least be aware of the general purpose of the plot and that plot must be unlawful: Nomura Taiji and others v Public Prosecutor [1998] 1 SLR(R) 259 (“Nomura Taiji”) at [105]-[110].

40     Caselaw further provides guidance on how a criminal conspiracy may be proved:

(a)     Proof of a conspiracy is generally a matter of inference of the apparent criminal purpose in common between the accused parties: Er Joo Nguang v Public Prosecutor [2000] 1 SLR(R) 756 (at [35]). In Goldring, Timothy Nicholas v Public Prosecutor and other appeals [2015] 4 SLR 742 (at [47]), the Court of Appeal held that a conspiracy need not be proved by direct evidence, and in fact, is often proved by the cumulative circumstantial evidence. This is because conspirators mostly agree in private and direct evidence is rarely available;

(b)     A frequent method of proving a conspiracy is to show that the words and actions of the parties indicate their concert in pursuit of a common object or design, giving rise to the inference that their actions must have been co-ordinated by arrangement beforehand. These acts do not of themselves constitute the conspiracy but constitute evidence of the conspiracy: Lai Kam Loy v Public Prosecutor [1993] 3 SLR(R) 143 (at [31]);

(c)     The essence of a conspiracy is agreement, and it suffices to show the conspirators’ awareness of the general purpose of the plot, or an agreement in principle to carry out the common design: Nomura Taiji (at [110]);

(d)     Accordingly, there is no need to prove: (i) a physical meeting of the conspirators; (ii) that the conspirators remained in each other’s company throughout or at all; (iii) communication between each conspirator and every other; (iv) or that the conspirators knew all the details of the unlawful plot: Ang Ser Kuang v Public Prosecutor [1998] 3 SLR(R) 316 (at [30]); Nomura Taiji (at [110]); and

(e)     It is not essential for a conspirator to have been a party to the agreement from the start, provided that at some stage prior to the unlawful act being carried out, he or she joins in the agreement: Saleemuddin v State (1971) ILR 1 Delhi 432 (at [16]).

CBT Charges

41     The Prosecution accepted that for the CBT offences against the Husband under s 409 of the PC, it has to prove beyond reasonable doubt the following elements identified in Public Prosecutor v Ewe Pang Kooi [2020] 3 SLR 851 (“Ewe Pang Kooi”) at [29]:

i.     The Husband was entrusted by Visa with the monies;

ii.     The entrustment was done by way of the Husband’s business as an agent, namely, a financial planner of Manulife;

iii.     He misappropriated the said monies; and

iv.     He did so dishonestly.[note: 46]

42     As for the term “agent” in s 409 of the PC, it was held in Ewe Pang Kooi at [46] that insurance agents are considered such a professional agent within the meaning of s 409 of the PC. The Husband was identified by Manulife’s CCO Ng as a financial advisor or insurance agent of Manulife.[note: 47] CCO Ng further testified that as a financial planner of Manulife, the Husband was authorised to receive premium payments from his client (in this case Visa) and forward the premiums to Manulife.[note: 48] There was accordingly no dispute that he was an “agent” within the meaning of s 409 of the PC.

43     The singular issue for the CBT Charges was whether Visa had entrusted the monies to the Husband as premiums to be paid to Manulife. If this court accepts that she did entrust the monies to him for that purpose, and since it was not in dispute that the monies were not paid to Manulife, the Husband would have misappropriated the monies dishonestly in causing a wrongful loss to Visa. Simultaneously, by using the monies for his own purposes and not paying the premiums to Manulife, he would have secured a wrongful gain to himself.

Reasons for Conviction

Visa’s Evidence Accepted

Visa trusted the accused persons

44     Visa was the main witness for the Prosecution.[note: 49] She identified the Husband as her nephew and the Wife as his wife. Visa resided at Blk xxx Empress Road #xxx (“Empress Road address”). She has always lived there and nowhere else.[note: 50] This fact, the relevance of which will become clearer below, was not in dispute.

45     She lodged a police report on 28 July 2015[note: 51]informing that she had purchased insurance policies (including four of the Six Policies) from the accused persons who had promised her that she would receive $120,000 from the said policies when she retired at 62 years old. Visa produced as evidence a table entitled “Financial Summary” with regards to her insurance policies.[note: 52] It was not disputed that this table had been prepared by the Husband to represent to Visa, inter alia, that “approx $120,000 including interest” would be available to her at 62 years old from the policies purchased with her CPF Ordinary Account savings.[note: 53] I accepted Visa’s evidence that the accused persons promised that she would receive $120,000 when she turned 62 years old.[note: 54] The fact that such a representation was made by the Husband to Visa was not seriously challenged by the Defence.

46     However, when she turned 62 years old, she did not receive any statement or update from Manulife regarding her policies. She went to Manulife on 11 August 2014 to make inquires only to find out that the Six Policies had been assigned to the Wife with the purported reasons that (i) she (Visa) was emigrating and (ii) the Husband needed capital for business ventures. Visa categorically testified that she did not assign the Six Policies (or any policy for that matter) to the Wife or to any other person. She did not instruct Manulife to do so.[note: 55]

47     Visa also testified that the purported reasons given to Manulife for the assignments were completely untrue. Visa confronted the Husband who gave her excuses and promised to return her the money. He kept delaying payment and even promised to pay Visa a larger sum of money if she waited longer. When she still did not receive her payout, she asked her brother to speak to the Husband. Finally, there was a meeting of the family members on 12 July 2015 at Perumal Temple. At the said meeting, the Husband agreed to pay Visa the money as promised when she purchased the policies from him. However, when no payment from the Husband was forthcoming even after a week, Visa lodged the said police report.

48     Visa told the court the reason for lodging the police report against the Husband:[note: 56]

Q    And why did you make this police report?

A    Because I---I invested, I mean, in Manulife and they promise me at age 62, I’m supposed to get certain amount, but I don’t receive anything, you see?

Q    Who promised you that at age 62 you will receive a certain amount?

A    Both husband and wife.

49     I believed Visa’s testimony that had invested her hard-earned money to purchase the Six Policies from Manulife because she trusted the accused persons.[note: 57] The Husband was her nephew and it was only natural for her to trust him and his wife. She entrusted him with the payment of the premiums whenever he told her that the premiums were due.[note: 58] Whenever she received letters from Manulife, she also trusted him to deal with whatever needed to be done for her policies.[note: 59] With regards to the letters from Manulife concerning premium holidays, I accepted her evidence that she did not know what it was all about and she would call the Husband to ask him to settle it for her. He promised that he would deal with the matter. Visa’s evidence was as follows:

Q    Okay. Do you remember receiving this letter?

A    When I received this letter saying that “premium holiday”, I don’t know what is it---they are giving me holiday or what.

Q    Okay.

A    So, I don’t know what is it all about. So, I---I will call my nephew and tell him, “I got a letter stating there’s a premium holiday or what. I think you better settle it---settle for me this one.” Whenever I get letter or what, I will just call him and then tell him to settle because he is my agent, you see.

50     At the end of the day when she turned 62 years old, Visa did not receive any of the investment proceeds which the Husband had promised her.[note: 60] It was not because the investments underlying her policies were doing badly, but because the accused persons transferred the polices to enrich themselves thereby depriving her of what would have been her retirement nest egg.

Cheating Charges

51     It was in dispute that Visa purchased the Six Policies from the accused persons. She purchased four of those policies from the Husband and the remaining two from the Wife. The singular issue before the court was whether Visa had signed the Assignment Documents that were submitted to Manulife to transfer the Six Policies to the Wife.

52     I believed her evidence that she had no reason to transfer any of her policies to the Wife and I found that she did not do so. I believed her testimony that she did not sign any of the Assignment Documents.[note: 61] I observed that she remained steadfast in her testimony which remained consistent under cross-examination by Counsel for the Defence. She was certainly indignant when Counsel suggested that no monies were owed by the accused persons to her. Her indignation did not detract from the truth of her allegations against the accused persons but rather underscored her honest disbelief that they had betrayed her trust.

53     I also believed her evidence that she did not give any instructions to the accused persons or to Manulife to surrender, either partially or fully, any of the Six Policies. The reasons purportedly given to Manulife as stated in the Assignment Documents were that Visa was emigrating and she wanted to provide capital to the Husband for his business. These reasons were completely and clearly false. It was not even suggested by the Defence that these reasons were even real.

54     Visa’s evidence regarding the falsity of her signatures was strongly corroborated by the handwriting expert witness from the Health Science Authority (“HSA”) who testified for the Prosecution. In his opinion, he found no evidence that Visa had signed the Assignment Documents.[note: 62] I will elaborate on his expert opinion below.

55     I accepted Visa’s evidence and found that she did not sign the Assignment Documents and that her purported signatures looked different.[note: 63] As is usually the case, there was no direct evidence of an express conspiratorial agreement between the two accused persons to forge Visa’s signatures. However, the following circumstances (much of which were not in dispute) would inexorably point to a conspiracy between Husband and Wife acting in concert to forge Visa’s signatures to cheat Manulife:

(a)     It was not disputed that the Assignment Documents were not personally submitted by Visa but by the Husband;

(b)     The Wife signed the Assignment Documents as the “assignee” with the full knowledge that the Husband would be submitting the Assignment Documents to Manulife;[note: 64]

(c)     The Husband then submitted the Assignment Documents to Manulife;

(d)     Manulife received the Assignment Documents as confirmed by CCO Ng;[note: 65]

(e)     The Six Policies were assigned to the Wife;

(f)     If Manulife had known that Visa did not sign the Assignment Documents, it would not have assigned the Six Policies.[note: 66]

(g)     The Wife surrendered and cashed out the Six Policies almost immediately after the policies were assignment to her; and

(h)     The Wife received the cheques for the proceeds of the surrender of the Six Policies.

56     As rightly pointed out by the Prosecution, the accused persons were in such a rush to cash out the polices that they had prepared the applications to surrender Policy 1094 and the 3k Policy even before Manulife formally confirmed the assignment of these policies to the Wife.

57     I would also add that I found that the Parents who were stated to be “witnesses” did not in fact witness Visa signing the Assignment Documents. I found that their signatures of the Parents were also forged. I will elaborate on this finding below.

58     These enumerated circumstances when considered as a whole, would prove a concerted and pre-arranged scheme between the Husband and Wife to deceive Manulife into assigning the Six Policies to the Wife.

59     I therefore had no difficulty finding that the signatures appearing on the Assignment Documents purporting to be signed by Visa, were in fact forged by either the Husband or the Wife, pursuant to their conspiracy to deceive Manulife into transferring the Six Policies to the Wife. By their own admission, they were working in concert claiming to have met Visa together for her signature,[note: 67] and that the Husband or the Wife would get the signatures of the Parents as witnesses.[note: 68]

60     I found that the Assignment Documents were submitted by the Husband, acting in concert with the Wife, to misrepresent to Manulife that Visa had consented (by way of the forged signatures) to the assignment of her policies to the Wife. It was not controversial and I accepted the evidence Manulife’s representative, CCO Ng, that Manulife was deceived and induced into approving the assignment of the Six Policies to the Wife, on the basis that the owner of the policies (in this case Visa) had indeed signed the Assignment Documents.

61     I accepted Visa’s rejection of all suggestions by the Defence that the Six Policies were assigned on her instructions and that all the proceeds had been returned to her. I believed her evidence that she had no idea that her policies had been assigned in 2013 and 2014.[note: 69] She did not even understand the terms “assignee” and “assignor”.[note: 70]

62     I accepted that she was telling the truth because the Defence did not challenge her evidence that she only found out about the assignments when she visited the Manulife office for the first time in 2015 and spoke to the Husband’s supervisor (one Jeffery Ho) who informed that her policies had been assigned to the Wife and surrendered thereafter.[note: 71] She then confronted the Husband regarding her policies and finally lodged the police report on 28 July 2015.

63     It was not in dispute that the Husband changed the policy holder’s (Visa’s) correspondence address from the Empress Place address to the Husband’s address[note: 72]. Even though a letter from Manulife dated 12 March 2013[note: 73] was sent to Visa’s Empress Place address to formally inform of the change of correspondence address, I accepted Visa’s evidence that she would not concern herself with any correspondence from Manulife since she left it to the Husband, who was her financial advisor, to deal with whatever was required by Manulife.[note: 74] After her correspondence address was changed, the accused persons then orchestrated the assignment and subsequent surrender of her policies. All correspondence and notices from Manulife were diverted away from Visa to the Husband. Thus, Visa was kept completely in the dark until she visited the Manulife office.

64     Her visit to the Manulife office, which was undisputed, utterly deflated the Defence’s position that the assignments were instructed by her and that she had signed the Assignment Documents. I found that she would not have paid a visit to the Manulife office if that was true. The Defence’s position that Visa had intentionally and voluntarily assigned the Six Policies to the Wife is absolutely false and untenable.

65     Visa’s evidence was also strongly corroborated by the SMS and WhatsApp exchanges (generally “text exchange(s)”) between the parties which showed that Visa was questioning the Husband about her (investment-linked) policies and pressing him for the returns that the Husband had promised she would receive when she turned 62 years old. He promised to account to her but kept procrastinating and giving her excuses. In short, he was giving her the runaround. It was telling that there was no denial from the Husband (or the Wife) that he had to account to her for her policies. I will elaborate on the text exchanges below.

CBT Charges

66     With regards to the CBT Charges, the sole issue in dispute was whether Visa had entrusted the monies (as set out in Table 4 above), to the Husband in his capacity as Manulife’s financial planner, to be paid to Manulife as premiums for the 13K and 3K Policies. Given his defence, the Husband did not dispute that the monies were not paid to Manulife as premiums and that Manulife did not receive the premiums.[note: 75] As highlighted above, it was not in dispute that ultimately, these policies went into a “premium holiday” because Manulife did not receive the premiums that were due pursuant to the policy contracts. As explained by CCO Ng, a premium holiday essentially meant that the policy (being starved of its premiums) would cannibalise itself, reducing its investment value to keep the policy alive.[note: 76]

67     With regards to the sole issue for the CBT Charges, I believed Visa and accepted her oral testimony that she did in fact give the various sums of money set out in Table 4 to the Husband to pay her premiums. She trusted the Husband who was her nephew and also her financial planner from Manulife. There was no question that the Husband was authorised, by virtue of his capacity as Manulife's agent, to receive Visa's monies for the specific purpose of paying her premiums. I accepted her evidence that she dutifully handed over, or transferred, the monies to the Husband because he told her the premiums were due.[note: 77] The monies were given and entrusted to him for this reason alone and not for any other reason or purpose. As I will explain below, the monies were not given to the Husband for the reasons suggested by the Defence.

68     I agreed with the Prosecution’s submission, which is consistent with my own observation, that Visa was not financially sophisticated and who trusted and relied on the Husband’s advice as to what policies to buy. She was therefore at his mercy and vulnerable to his dishonest intentions.[note: 78] Even the Defence acknowledged that she bought whatever policies the Husband had chosen for her.[note: 79] It was probably because the Husband saw that she trusted him completely that he saw the opportunity and decided to take advantage of her.

69     I found Visa’s evidence to be internally consistent as well as externally consistent with the objective evidence. She was resolute in her testimony and remained unshaken by Counsel’s cross-examination. Her evidence was corroborated by the objective evidence of her POSB Passbook (“Passbook”).[note: 80]

70     She pointed out the transfers and payments made to the Husband. She recognised the relevant transfers and payments because she had painstakingly made handwritten notes against these transactions as a record and a reminder to herself of the purpose of the transaction. She testified that every time she transferred money to the Husband for him to pay the premiums for her policies, she would write “To Manulife” against the transaction. As pointed out by the Prosecution, Visa showed to the court where she had written on her Passbook.

71     For example, she pointed out to the following (highlighted in yellow) three transfers over 1-3 March 2011 for $5,000, $5,000 and $500 totalling $10,500:[note: 81]

72     She explained that that she had written (“To Manulife”) “7,500 (Visa)” and “3,000 (Kas)” to mean that $7,500 was meant for her 15k policy whereas $3,000 was intended for the 3k policy that she had purchased for her nephew, Kasman’s, benefit.[note: 82] As rightly pointed out by the Prosecution, the Passbook was admitted in evidence by consent as part of the AB. The Defence did not challenge Visa’s explanations that it was her usual practice to write these contemporaneous records. The Defence did not dispute the accuracy of her contemporaneous records either.[note: 83]

73     Visa testified that all the transactions in her Passbook where she had annotated with her handwriting, were transfers to the Husband for him to pay her premiums to Manulife. The annotations therefore strongly corroborated her testimony that the transfers were intended as payments for her insurance policies and not for other purposes.

74     I found that Visa had penned these annotations contemporaneously following each transaction. I accepted and found that these handwritten notes in her Passbook were contemporaneous records of every transaction of her giving money to the Husband trusting that he would use the money to pay her premiums.

(1)   Misappropriation

75     The Prosecution went through Manulife’s internal records[note: 84] of all the monies received for the 15k and 3k Policies with CCO Ng.[note: 85] He explained, with reference to other Manulife records, that some premiums for the 15k and 3k Policies were at times paid with partial surrenders of other policies.[note: 86] Crucially, he testified that the sums of money material to the CBT Charges were never received by Manulife. The only inference, in the absence of any explanation from the Defence, is that the Husband did not use Visa’s monies for their intended purpose. Instead, his bank statements show that he spent or withdrew the funds for other purposes. This was in stark contrast to Visa’s Passbook which showed, undeniably, that her money was transferred to the Husband’s account. In short, the Husband had misappropriated Visa’s money which were meant as premiums for the 3K and 13K policies.

Dishonesty

76     On the basis of Visa’s evidence, I found that the Husband knew that Visa had entrusted the monies to him as premiums for her policies. He knew that the monies were to be used exclusively to pay her policy premiums to Manulife. The definitions under ss 23 and 24 of the PC clearly state that conduct undertaken with the intention of causing wrongful loss to one person or wrongful gain to another would be "dishonest". Therefore, by failing to pay over the monies to Manulife as premiums but instead using the monies for himself, the Husband had dishonestly misappropriated Visa’s monies.

Handwriting Expert’s Evidence

77     The Prosecution called PW1 Yap Bei Sing (“Mr Yap”), a Consultant Forensic Scientist at the Document Examination Office of the HSA, to testify as a Prosecution expert witness. Mr Yap has been a document examiner since 1989 and has handled more than 4500 criminal and civil cases comprising mostly of handwriting examinations and signature verifications.[note: 87] He has also given expert evidence in court in Singapore in more than 100 cases.[note: 88]

78     In the present case, Mr Yap testified as to the authenticity of the signatures of Visa and those of the Husband’s parents who allegedly signed the Assignment Documents as “witnesses”. The written report of Mr Yap was admitted in evidence.[note: 89]

79     Mr Yap was tasked to examine and compare Visa’s purported signatures found on the Assignment Documents[note: 90] (“Visa’s questioned signatures”) with the signatures Visa provided[note: 91] (“Visa’s specimen signatures”) for the purpose of comparison. Visa’s specimen signatures comprised her normal signatures (i.e. signatures already in existence) and requested signatures (i.e. signatures signed as requested by Mr Yap for comparison). These were compared with a total of twelve of Visa’s questioned signatures.

80     Mr Yap concluded that Visa’s specimen signatures (comprising normal and requested signatures) showed consistency in stroke fluency and slant, with a range of natural variations in respect of the formation and relative positioning of the strokes.[note: 92] Essentially, this meant that there was no attempt by Visa to falsify her specimen signatures. Indeed, there was no suggestion from the Defence that she did.

81     Comparing the specimen signatures with Visa’s questioned signatures, Mr Yap noted differences in stroke fluency, slant and the formation and relative positioning of strokes between the two sets of signatures. In view of the differences noted, Mr Yap concluded that there is no evidence to indicate that the writer of Visa’s specimen signatures had written Visa’s questioned signatures.[note: 93]

82     I carefully looked at and considered the comparison charts enclosed in the Expert Report. I was of the view that the differences between Visa’s questioned signatures and her (normal) specimen signatures are very obvious even to a lay person like me. I noted, in particular, that the “slant” of the signatures was patently different as may be seen from the following snapshot of the comparison of two blocks of signatures which I selected for illustration:

83     The left side shows a block of six of the Visa’s questioned signatures and the right side shows a block of nine of Visa’s specimen signatures. As may be seen, the signatures on the left are consistently slanted to the right. Mr Yap described this as a “forward slant”.[note: 94] In comparison, the signatures on the right are consistently slanted to the left. Mr Yap described this as a “back slant”. This is but only one notable difference. Mr Yap noted other material and consistent differences including:[note: 95]

(a)     Pen pressure is heavier in Visa’s questioned signatures;

(b)     The hook in Visa’s questioned signatures is not present in Visa’s specimen signatures;

(c)     The letter “V” is not joined to the letter “i” in Visa’s questioned signatures but the two letters are joined in Visa’s specimen signatures;

(d)     The terminal “a” has a hook in Visa’s questioned signatures;

(e)     The baseline (referring to the underlining) of Visa’s questioned signatures is tapering and short compared to the long baseline in Visa’s specimen signatures; and

(f)     The presence of a dot in the baseline of Visa’s questioned signatures but none in Visa’s specimen signatures.

I certainly appreciated and accepted the differences identified by Mr Yap which were not challenged by the Defence.

84     The parents of the Husband (“Parents”) are PW2 Sarasa d/o Paspathy (“Sarasa”) and PW4 Kaja Nathan s/o Krishna Reddiar (“Kaja Nathan”). Turning to the Parents’ signatures, Mr Yap compared the purported signatures of the Parents appearing on the Assignment Documents[note: 96] (“Parents’ questioned signatures”) and the signatures they provided for comparison[note: 97] (“Parents’ specimen signatures”).

85     After comparing the two sets of signatures, Mr Yap concluded that that there was no evidence that the Parents’ questioned signatures were signed by them.[note: 98]

86     In respect of Kaja Nathan’s signatures, Mr Yap found that his questioned signatures were signed differently from his specimen signatures. Mr Yap identified a number of differences but I highlight three clear ones: (i) the formation of the initial alphabet “K” was signed differently in that the “K” in his questioned signatures ends with a terminal loop (“flourished K”) but not so in his specimen signatures; (ii) the positions of “K” and “N” are spaced out in the questioned signatures but squished together in the specimen signatures; and (iii) the difference in the formation of the last letter “T”.[note: 99] These differences, which would be obvious even to the most casual observer, are illustrated in the following signature comparison:

87     Finally, it was telling that the Defence did not put to Mr Yap (or to any of the other Prosecution witnesses for that matter) that Visa’s questioned signatures or the parents’ questioned signatures were genuine. The Defence also did not call any expert evidence to dispute Mr Yap’s opinion. Therefore, I had no difficulty accepting Mr Yap’s conclusions as stated in the Expert Report which he affirmed in court. In the final analysis, all the questioned signatures were forged.

88     The evidence was clear and I found that Manulife would not have processed the assignment of the Six Policies to the Wife had it known that Visa did not sign Assignment Documents or that her signatures were forged.[note: 100] Likewise, Manulife would not have allowed the Six Policies to be assigned to the Wife if it knew that the Parents did not sign the Assignment Documents or that their signatures were forged.[note: 101]

Evidence of the Parents

89     As mentioned above, the Assignment Documents were apparently “witnessed” by the Parents. The Defence claimed that the Husband (or both accused persons) had brought the Assignment Documents to the Parents at their residence at Blk xxx McNair Road xxxx, to sign as witnesses. The claim that the Parents purportedly "witnessed" Visa's signatures was contradicted by the Parent’s revelation in court that they did not in fact see Visa sign the said documents.[note: 102] In other words, even if it is accepted (which is not) that the Assignment Documents were brought to them for their signatures, Visa’s purported signatures were already there on the documents. I therefore found that they were not in fact witnesses to the signing of the Assignment Documents by Visa.

90     Sarasa’s evidence went even further that she did not sign any of the Assignment Documents.[note: 103] This evidence transpired when I allowed the Prosecution’s application to cross-examine her as a hostile witness. She accepted that she had never seen the Assignment Documents prior to trial. Crucially, she conceded that she did not sign the documents as a witness.[note: 104]

91     Sarasa’s concession regarding the falsity of her signatures was corroborated by the handwriting expert’s opinion that there is no evidence that Sarasa signed the documents.[note: 105] Her revelation cast even greater doubt on the authenticity of the Assignment Documents.

92     Kaja Nathan also proved to be a hostile witness for the Prosecution. He claimed that he did sign the Assignment Documents and that he had even spoken to Visa on the phone before he signed, to check that Visa had indeed signed the documents. However, his testimony in this regard materially contradicted his police statements. I allowed Prosecution’s application to confront him with his previous two statements to impeach his credit. The first statement (P2) was recorded by ASP Pong Wei Lin (“ASP Pong”) on 12 April 2016 at Tanglin Division and the second statement (P3) was recorded by Insp Spencer Tan on 20 July 2020 at Kaja Nathan’s residence. It transpired that he had provided at least two other different versions of events in his two statements and was unable to give to this court any credible or reasonable explanation for the different versions.

93     In the version in P2, he was first shown the Assignment Document for Policy 2201 to which he replied:[note: 106]

I do not know anything about this document. I have never seen this before. There is my name on it however the signature on it is not mine. I did not sign this document.

94     Kaja Nathan then proceeded to explain and demonstrate to ASP Pong how his signature was different:[note: 107]

I do it differently. I can see the difference. I will sign my old signature once and show you the difference. The K is one thing. It has different strokes. There should be a tail on the bottom left side of the K. For the T I will pull it downwards. I do not just leave it like that.

95     He was then shown the rest of the Assignment Documents and he maintained that he did not sign them and that the signatures therein were not his signatures.[note: 108]

96     Subsequently in the version in P3, when he was asked if he or Sarasa witnessed Visa signing the Assignment Documents, he said “no”.[note: 109] He explained that he only now remembered that the Husband (who was his son) had brought the Assignment Documents either to his workplace or his residence.[note: 110] He explained that when P2 was recorded, he had just undergone a bypass surgery in 2016 and was in bad health and therefore could not remember signing the documents. However, it does not explain why, when P2 was recorded, he could not recognise his own signature and even proceeded to demonstrate to the recorder that his true signature was different.

97     I also considered that the version in P2 was in fact consistent with Mr Yap's expert opinion, which was highlighted earlier and which I accepted, that there was no evidence that the signatures were those of Kaja Nathan.[note: 111]

98     Presumably, his memory had improved when P3 was recorded. Even then, he said that there were not so many documents, “[p]robably just one or two sets of documents only.”[note: 112] Crucially, he had this to say:

Q7)    You mentioned that when your son brought the documents to sign at your place, he gave your sister-in-law [i.e. Visa] a call to explain that your wife and yourself would be signing as witnesses. Did you speak to your sister-in-law on the phone during that conversation?

A7)    No, I did not.

99     He had no explanation why the version in P3 was vastly different from his court testimony when he said he had checked with Visa before signing the Assignment Documents.

100    Given that the version in P2 was more likely to be closer to the truth, I found that his credit as a witness in court was materially impeached. I therefore gave absolutely no weight to his court testimony that he either signed the Assignment Documents or that he had spoken to Visa beforehand. I found that not only Visa’s signatures, but also those of Sarasa and Kaja Nathan were all forged.

118    Parenthetically, I rejected the Defence’s submission that the Prosecution had failed to call Rani as a witness.[note: 125] I disagree that there was any obligation or necessity for the Prosecution to call her as a Prosecution witness to prove its case. It was not suggested that Rani had any personal knowledge of the Six Policies, the signing of the Assignment Documents or Visa’s payment of premiums. She may have been part of the chat group but she did not take part in the exchange of messages. She may also have been there at the meeting at the Perumal Temple but what transpired at that meeting was not material to the Prosecution’s case. In any event, Lingam was also there at the meeting and he was called as a witness.

119    Finally, as regards Visa asking the Husband for the investment returns, Lingam’s evidence would be more relevant and material. Ultimately, the Defence could have called Rani as its witness but did not do so. It does not lie in the mouth of the Defence only now to cast aspersions on the Prosecution for not calling Rani. I agreed with the Prosecution’s submission that it has no duty to call any particular witness so long as it was able to discharge its evidential burden:[note: 126]Muhammad Nabill bin Mohd Fuad v PP [2020] 1 SLR 984 at [58] and [71].

Defence’s Case Rejected

120    The Husband and Wife presented a joint, but at times inconsistent, defence that Visa had assigned the Six Policies to the Wife and that all the money she received from surrendering the policies were returned to Visa. The Husband also denied misappropriating the premiums that Visa gave him.

Cheating Charges

121    The accused persons denied that there was a conspiracy to cheat Manulife. They claimed that Visa had instructed them to assign the Six Policies to the Wife. They claimed she signed the Assignment Documents with the intension to transfer the Six Policies to the Wife. They claimed that the Parents signed the Assignment Documents as witnesses. They also claimed that after the policies were transferred to the Wife and thereafter surrendered, all the proceeds were given to Visa.

122    Having already found that Visa’s and the Parents’ signatures on the Assignment Documents were forged, this would effectively debunk their defence.

123    Putting aside, the authenticity of the signatures, their claim (that Visa had effectively assigned the policies to the Wife and that the investment returns were given to Visa) was completely at odds with the text messages between the parties which showed that they strung her along promising that her policies would pay her even greater investment returns than originally projected when in fact the said policies had already been surrendered. When confronted with these text messages, they did not deny sending the messages but claimed they were merely playing along.

124    They claimed in their defence that they thought that the messages were sent by someone else and not Visa.[note: 127] Somehow, this led to them sending Visa those messages in reply. Thus, the Husband claimed that “[a]lthough it’s her phone number, her name is there, it is not her who is texting all these, because Visa will clearly know she has taken everything already.[note: 128] The Wife similarly said she replied to Visa as reflected in the messages “[b]ecause that was not her who was messaging.”[note: 129]

125    I rejected their explanations which I found to be both preposterous and nonsensical. Apart from merely claiming that it was a mere suspicion[note: 130], the accused persons did not explain whether they thought someone else was texting for Visa or that someone had somehow was using Visa’s phone to impersonate her. Neither scenario made any sense.

126    It would appear to be the latter scenario since they claimed that the person did not have the same knowledge as Visa i.e. that nothing was owing to Visa. They appeared to be blaming Lingam for instigating Visa to ask them for money.[note: 131] However, the accused stopped short of alleging that Visa’s messages were in fact sent by Lingam.

127    The Defence did not put this suspicion to Lingam. Even if they thought it was not Visa who was communicating with them, they could and should have simply reached out to Visa to get to the bottom of their suspicion. However, they did not do so. I therefore found that their claims defied logic and were entirely baffling. Further, Counsel also did not put to Visa that the messages sent to the Husband (asking for her investment returns) were not her messages. Neither were these claims stated in the Case for the Defence (“CFD”) filed by his previous counsels.[note: 132] Therefore, this was yet another instance of the accused persons embellishing their defence after the close of the Prosecution’s case.

128    I found that there was no credible or plausible reason why Visa would want to assign her policies to the Wife. The Prosecution rightly pointed out that the reasons provided by the accused persons were mutually inconsistent and therefore unbelievable.[note: 133]

129    On the one hand, the Husband claimed that the reason for the transfer was because Visa found it tedious “to do withdrawals and banking in cheques and all”, and she also had issues with Manulife because her signatures were inconsistent.[note: 134]

130    In contrast, the Wife provided no less than four different reasons for transferring the policies to her:

(i)     Initially, she claimed that Visa wanted to emigrate to Australia (which was clearly false), and the assignment would make it easier for her to conduct her Manulife transactions.[note: 135]

(ii)     She then gave another reason that Visa was starting an import and export business (which was also false), and she needed to surrender the policies as capital for her business.[note: 136]

(iii)     When probed further, she changed her testimony and said “it’s not about her capital because she [Visa] actually owes me money” and that Visa assigned the policies to her to repay the “loan”.[note: 137]

(iv)     When asked about the loan, the Wife changed her evidence again and claimed that as of April 2013, Visa had repaid most of the money owed.[note: 138] She further claimed that she had returned to Visa all the money from the surrender of the policies.[note: 139]

131    In short, the accused persons were all over the place trying to come up with reasons as to why Visa would willingly assign her policies to the Wife. I found that they were unable to come up with any credible reason because there was none.

132    In contrast, I believed Visa’s unchallenged evidence at trial that she had never considered migrating, was never told by the Husband that she needed capital for business,[note: 140] and has never borrowed money from the accused persons.[note: 141]

133    I found that the accused’s testimony at trial is inconsistent with their CFD which stated that the policies were assigned and subsequently surrendered because Visa needed monies to repay loans of about $100,000 that she borrowed from the accused persons.[note: 142] They also stated that “[g]iven the nature and manner in which the sums received were used, there were no balances thereafter to be transmitted by [the Husband] to [Visa]”.[note: 143]

134    With regards to the handwriting expert, Mr Yap’s evidence, the Defence contended that “the analysis is inconclusive.”[note: 144] This contention was premised on Mr Yap’s agreement to Counsel’s suggestion, during cross-examination, that a person’s signature, if not signed in an ideal seated position, may be different in formation and slant if signed in a standing position or inside or on top of (the bonnet or boot of) the Husband’s vehicle.[note: 145]

135    I rejected this argument as being entirely vague and speculative. It is not clear from the argument whether the Defence was referencing to the signing of the specimen signatures or the Assignment Documents. In any case, the witnesses were not asked and it was not established that they were standing up, signing on the bonnet or boot of, or seated inside the car or otherwise, when signing any particular signature or document.

136    Next, the Defence raised the argument that Manulife did not spot the alleged forged signatures and hence did not lodge a police report for any wrongdoing.[note: 146] Hence, the Defence argued that the signatures were authentic and therefore, there was no deception. I rejected this argument as being irrelevant and circular. I found that Visa’s (and the Parents’) signatures on the Assignment Documents were forged. I also accepted the evidence of CCO Ng of Manulife that if Manulife knew that the assignor (Visa) had not signed the Assignment Documents, Manulife would not have assigned the policies.[note: 147] I reiterate that CCO Ng’s evidence was not disputed by Counsel.

137    Therefore, it was entirely irrelevant that Manulife’s representatives did not spot the forged signatures because they are not handwriting experts and were not put on specific notice that Visa’s signatures may well be forged. In other words, Manulife would not have scrutinised the signatures to the same extent that was carried out in court. Further, Manulife would not be able to know if the Parents’ signatures were forged, since Manulife would not have specimens of the Parents’ signatures in its files. Manulife was therefore deceived into believing that the material signatures were authentic and hence no police report was lodged.

138    Relatedly, the Defence argued that it would be Visa who ultimately suffered the losses for the Cheating Charges and not Manulife.[note: 148] It was my finding that Manulife had been induced, because of the deception of the forged Assignment Documents, to deliver property (i.e. assign the Six Policies) to the Wife. If the inducement was done dishonestly, the offence of cheating would be committed. As discussed above, to do something “dishonestly” is to do it with the intention of causing wrongful gain to one person, or wrongful loss to another person. In the present case, there was certainly wrongful gain to the Wife who was transferred Visa’s policies and who then cashed them out and received the cheque payments. At the same time, there was also wrongful loss to Manulife who would now be liable to account to Visa for assigning her policies without her consent. Therefore, the Defence’s argument that only Visa suffered losses was misconceived and plainly wrong.

139    I further agreed with the Prosecution’s submission that the Defence’s miscellaneous arguments were without merit and therefore ought to be rejected. One such argument which I rejected was the inaccurate claim that prior statements of the accused were not served on the Defence.[note: 149] The Prosecution pointed out that this was wrong because the statements of the accused persons that were not included in the Case for the Prosecution[note: 150] were served on the Defence in the Prosecution’s Supplementary Bundle.[note: 151]

140    The Defence also argued that the Prosecution ought to have obtained the Wife’s bank statements.[note: 152] I rejected this argument simply because the Defence has not provided any basis for its argument or the relevance of the bank statements.

CBT Charges

141    The CBT Charges pertain to the various sums of money reflected in Table 4 above that were paid to the Husband. As noted earlier, these sums of money were given to the Husband by way of Cash payments (having withdrawn from the bank) or ATM transfers. The Husband raised different defences in respect of the two modes of payment.

142    First and foremost, it was correctly pointed out by the Prosecution that the Defence had failed to challenge Visa’s testimony as regards (i) her payments (whether by cash or ATM transfers) of the monies to the Husband to be used as premiums for her policies and (ii) her handwritten notes in her Passbook which recorded the purpose of the transfers against the transactions.[note: 153]

143    This failure was an infringement of the rule in Browne v Dunn: Hong Leong Singapore Finance Ltd v United Overseas Bank Ltd [2007] 1 SLR(R) 292 at [42] (citing Browne v Dunn (1893) 6 R 67 in approval). The rationale of this rule is to grant a witness the opportunity to “explain and clarify his or her position or version of facts before any contradictory version is put forth to the court as one of fact”: Parti Liyani v Public Prosecutor [2020] SGHC 187 at [44]. I fully agreed with the Prosecution’s submission that the Husband is now precluded from alleging that the monies that were transferred to him by Visa were not premiums to be paid to Manulife.[note: 154]

Cash payments

144    I rejected his convenient claim that he did not receive the Cash payments from Visa.

145    Quite apart from the rule in Browne v Dunn, this claim flew in the face of his CFD[note: 155]which stated (at [24]) that Visa had transferred to him “some S$100,000…in tranches from 24 July 2009 to 26 March 2013”. In his CFD, the only qualification he made was that the monies were for repayment of loans which he allegedly made to Visa, and not to meet her premium obligations. When giving his defence on the witness stand, he has belated decided to even deny receiving the payments themselves. Therefore, an adverse inference must be drawn against him for his vacillating defence.

146    I also disbelieved the Husband’s testimony and rejected his defences for another cogent reason. He denied receiving the $7,500 Cash payment on 11 October 2011. Coincidentally, the exact sum of money was deposited into his POSB bank account the same day.[note: 156] When confronted with this seeming coincidence by the learned DPP, he was unable to provide an explanation.[note: 157] The Husband was therefore not a credible witness.

ATM transfers

147    At trial, the Husband did not deny the ATM transfers to his account. He would not have been able to refute the bank transactions which are clearly stated in the Passbook which corresponded to the transfers to his POSB bank account. His defence at trial was that the ATM transfers were made by Visa to repay loans he had extended to her.[note: 158]

148    In its closing submissions however, the Defence sought to dispute the accuracy of Visa’s handwritten notes in her Passbook[note: 159]to bolster the Husband’s claim that he did not receive the premiums from Visa,[note: 160]or that he was unaware of the ATM transfers.[note: 161] However, at trial, the Defence did not dispute Visa’s written notes in her Passbook which was also admitted in evidence by consent. Therefore, it was both disingenuous and behindhand to now dispute the accuracy of her handwritten notes, and the underlying ATM transfers to the Husband.

149    I also rejected his defence that any money given to him by Visa were loan repayments. This was yet another infraction of the rule in Browne v Dunn which precluded him from now asserting that the ATM transfers were to repay any loan to him. Further, the accused persons did not provide any evidence or details of the alleged loan(s) owed by Visa to them. As rightly pointed out by the Prosecution, there was no mention of any loan in the Defence’s closing submissions.[note: 162]

150    In any case, the Husband has admitted in his own statement that Visa would transfer money to his bank account to be used to pay her premiums for the 15k and 3k policies, and that his wife “knows about this arrangement between Visa and me which is Visa is transferring money to my bank account for the policy premium payment signed under my wife’s name”.[note: 163] When cross-examined as to the apparent inconsistency, he claimed that he was pressured by the recording officer to sign his statement and that what he had told the recording officer was not recorded.[note: 164] I rejected this claim because his statement was admitted by consent and the voluntariness of the statement was not in dispute.[note: 165] Further, he attested to the final accuracy of the statement after making amendments in his own handwriting and signing every page.[note: 166] Accordingly, it was clear to me that his admission in his statement contradicted his defence in court which I rejected as a last-ditch attempt at fabrication.

151    The truth was that Visa did lend the Husband two sums of money totalling $5,000 on 11 July 2012. She recorded in her Passbook that the money was “For Puven Personal” and that the loan was “Return on 17/01/13”.[note: 167] The Defence did not dispute this and in fact confirmed with Visa during cross-examination that the loan had been repaid as reflected in her Passbook.[note: 168] On the contrary, Visa did not owe the Husband any money. Apart from the Husband’s bald assertions, he failed to provide any objective evidence of any debt owed to him by Visa.

152    Contrary to the Husband’s claim that the ATM transfers represented Visa repaying him money she owed, the SMS messages (considered above) showed otherwise i.e. that Visa was chasing him to repay her for the returns he had promised but he kept apologising and giving her the runaround.

153    Ultimately, I found Visa to be a truthful and credible witness who gave cogent and consistent testimony. She had trusted the Husband, who was both her kin and insurance agent, with her money to pay the premiums for her Manulife policies. In sharp contrast, the Husband was shifty, unconvincing and inconsistent in his evidence. It was also apparent that in respect of the Cash payments, his instructions to both his previous and present Counsel had materially shifted after the close of the Prosecution’s case when he started to deny receiving the Cash payments, when there was no dispute before that. I agreed with the Prosecution that this change was nothing more than a desperate, belated and all too convenient last-ditch attempt to deny receiving the Cash payments.

Manulife Deceived to Assign the Six Policies

154    The explanation to the definition of “cheating” under s 415 of the Penal Code states as follows:

Explanation 4.—A person that is a company or association or body of persons, whether incorporated or not, can be deceived for the purposes of this section, even though none of its individual officers, employees or agents is personally deceived.

The ambit of the offence of cheating is sufficiently wide to encompass the scenario where Manulife, which necessarily functions through its officers, can be deceived even if its officers were not personally deceived.

155    In the present case, I found that Manulife’s officers were in fact deceived by the forged Assignment Documents. Accordingly, I found that the accused persons had abetted one another by way of their conspiracy to induce Manulife into approving the assignment of the Six Policies. They did so by deceiving Manulife’s representatives by forging Visa’s and the Parents’ signatures on the Assignment Documents and submitting the same to Manulife. I accepted Manulife’s representative’s evidence that the company would not have approved the assignments if it was made aware that Visa’s (or the Parents’) signatures had been forged. I found that both accused persons had a dishonest intention to deceive Manulife. In other words, I found that they had the requisite intention to enrich themselves wrongfully and to cause a wrongful loss to Manulife and consequently, also to Visa.

Conclusion

156    In conclusion, I ultimately believed and accepted Visa's evidence that she did not assign the Six Policies to the Wife and that she did not sign the Assignment Documents. Her evidence is corroborated by the handwriting expert's evidence, which was unchallenged, that the signatures in question were not Visa’s. I also disbelieved the Parents’ evidence and found that they neither signed nor saw Visa signing the Assignment Documents. I further accepted the expert’s evidence to the effect that the Parents’ signatures were also forged. Visa's evidence was also consistent with and corroborated by the text exchanges between the parties.

157    I rejected both accused persons’ defence that it was merely a family dispute. It was certainly more than that. I was satisfied beyond reasonable doubt that the accused persons had abetted each other in a conspiracy to forge all the questioned signatures to deceive Manulife into believing that Visa had intended to assign the Six Policies to the Wife. As a result of the deception, Manulife transferred the Six Policies to the Wife who then cashed them out almost immediately.

158    I believed Visa’s evidence that she gave the monies in Table 4 to the Husband, as her financial advisor, to be paid over to Manulife as premiums. I found that the Husband dishonestly misappropriated the premiums which Visa had entrusted to him. He has therefore committed CBT as an agent in respect of the said premiums.

159    Given all the evidence and my findings above, the accused persons were convicted of all the Proceeded Charges beyond reasonable doubt.

Defence’s Position on Sentence

164    In contrast, Counsel for the Defence asked that the court impose an aggregate sentence of only 18 months’ imprisonment on the Husband and only six months’ imprisonment on the Wife.[note: 172] The Defence did not provide a breakdown of the proposed sentences for the individual charges. Therefore, I derived little to no assistance from Counsel’s mitigation with regards to the proper calibration of the appropriate sentences to be imposed on his clients.

165    Curiously, Counsel concluded his mitigation by urging the court to impose a fine (as opposed to a custodial sentence) for the Wife because she needed to care for her youngest son.[note: 173] I will state at the outset that the Cheating Charges against the wife carried a mandatory imprisonment sentence. Therefore, a ‘fine only’ sentence was not legally permissible. Counsel would do well to explain this clearly to his client.

Sentencing Principles

166    I set out what I considered to be the general sentencing principles applicable to the present offences. I also identified the material offence-specific and offender-specific principles relevant to the facts of the case and to the accused persons.

Deterrence

167    Deterrence was the principal sentencing consideration in the present case for all the offences. I could see that Counsel for the Defence also agreed that general deterrence was the applicable and predominant sentencing objective as noted by the Court in Public Prosecutor v Sim Chon Ang Jason and other appeals [2024] SGHC 1695 at [63].[note: 174]

168    I considered that the twin facets of the principle of deterrence (i.e. general and specific deterrence) were relevant and engaged in the present case. General deterrence aims to deter other like-minded members of the public by making an example of a particular offender: Meeran bin Mydin v Public Prosecutor [1998] 2 SLR 522. On the other hand, specific deterrence aims to persuade the offender to refrain from re-offending by fashioning an appropriate sentence which takes into account the nature of the offence and the accused’s peculiar disposition or propensity for reoffending: Public Prosecutor v Low Ji Qing [2019] 5 SLR 769.

(1)   General deterrence

169    In the present case, the accused persons have cheated Manulife, a global financial and investment services provider with a large international footprint which included Singapore. I considered it an aggravating factor that cheating offences against financial institutions would have the tendency to undermine the integrity of such institutions in general and affect the provision of financial services in Singapore in particular: Public Prosecutor v Law Aik Meng [2007] 2 SLR(R) 814 (“Law Aik Meng”) at [24(e)]. This concern was further explained in Tan Thiam Wee v Public Prosecutor [2012] 4 SLR 141 where the Court highlighted at [11] the harmful effects of offences of fraud committed against financial institutions which included downstream compliance costs being passed on to the public:

Financial institutions form a key part of the economic system and any abuse results in a loss of confidence requiring additional safeguards to be taken. This will lead to increased costs which will be passed to all users of the system. Thus, not only do such crimes cause direct monetary loss to the financial institution concerned, the resultant loss of confidence and increase in compliance cost is borne by the community as a whole.

(emphasis added)

170    The principle of general deterrence is particularly engaged for offences against vulnerable victims because such offences create deep judicial disquiet: Law Aik Meng at [25(b)]. In this case, the victim was also and ultimately Visa who was the owner of the policies. She was a retiree and was financially illiterate. As pointed out by the Prosecution, she was prepared to support the accused persons when they joined Manulife as financial planners.[note: 175] She did so by trusting them and investing her CPF funds by purchasing the policies recommended by them. She intended to build up her nest egg for financial security in her retirement years. Now, her retirement plan has been destroyed by the greed and selfishness of the accused persons. Instead of protecting her investments in their capacity as her financial advisors, they betrayed her absolute trust and left her with no money for her retirement.

171    General deterrence must therefore necessarily constitute an important consideration in sentencing the accused persons.

(2)   Specific deterrence

172    I considered that specific deterrence was also engaged because there was a high degree of premeditation on the part of the accused persons in the commission of the cheating offences. As observed by the Court in Public Prosecutor v Fernando Payagala Waduge Malitha Kumar [2007] 2 SLR(R) 334 (“Fernando Payagala”) at [39], a deterrent sentence ought to be de rigueur where an offence is committed with premeditation and planning. Specific deterrence seeks to instil in an offender the fear of re-offending through the potential threat of re-experiencing the same sanction previously imposed: Law Aik Meng at [21].

173    In the instant case, there was no doubt that there was much premeditation involved in that the accused persons had conspired with one another to deliberately forge the material signatures in the Assignment Documents to deceive Manulife into transferring the Six Policies to the Wife. There was deliberate and careful planning and execution of the conspiracy to cheat Manulife and its officers. They also diverted all relevant notices and correspondence (sent by Manulife) to themselves so as to cover their tracks and keep Visa in the dark about what they were doing to her policies.

Offence-Specific factors

(1)   Significant harm caused

174    The Honourable the Chief Justice Sundaresh Menon (“Menon CJ”) stated in Gan Chai Bee Anne v Public Prosecutor [2019] 4 SLR 838 (“Gan Chai Bee”) at [42] that:

There is a well-established general principle that in sentencing for financial and property offences, the greater the economic value involved in the offence, the heavier the sentence.

Menon CJ further held in Gan Chai Bee at [48] that “[t]he primary yardstick will often be the value of the property involved.” This is because economic value in such offences is seen as a proxy for the degree of criminal benefit received by the offender and the degree of harm caused to the victim, both of which are relevant sentencing considerations.

175    In the context of CBT offences in general and all things being equal, it stands to reason that the larger the amount misappropriated, the greater the culpability of the offender and the more severe the sentence of the court”: Wong Kai Chuen Philip v Public Prosecutor [1990] 2 SLR(R) 361 at [18]. In the specific context of CBT committed by the Husband in his professional capacity of a financial planner, the High Court held in Ewe Pang Kooi (at [28]) that it is of “utmost importance” that the law come down harshly to deter conduct involving CBT by those entrusted with property in the way of their business as professional agents.

176    In the context of cheating offences in general, Menon CJ held in Idya Nurhazlyn bte Ahmad Khir v Public Prosecutor [2013] SGHC 238 at [47] that a custodial sentence will generally be appropriate for an offence under s 417 of the PC as long as the offence in question causes a victim to part with property that has more than negligible value. This sentiment would be amplified for the present cheating offences under s 420 which are more serious and which attract a mandatory imprisonment sentence. Hence, the Court stated in Fernando Payagala at [47] that for cheating offences under s 420, “the higher the quantum, the heftier the sentence”.

177    In respect of the Cheating Charges, between April 2013 and April 2014, the Six Policies were assigned to the Wife pursuant to their conspiracy to cheat Manulife. She then surrendered the said policies and pocketed the surrender proceeds amounting to $47,813.48. This was a significant sum of money and represented illicit gains to the accused persons which they would not have gotten if not for their conspiracy to cheat Manulife.

178    In respect of the CBT Charges, the Husband had, in the course of more than three and a half years, repeatedly and dishonestly misappropriated the money which Visa had entrusted him to be used to pay her premiums. In total, he misappropriated $94,000 from Visa. This was also a substantial sum of money.

179    In the context of Visa who was deprived of her retirement nest egg, the High Court in Huang Ying-Chun v Public Prosecutor [2019] 3 SLR 606 held at [110] that the harm caused to a victim (such as Visa) would be exacerbated where the victim was “generally elderly” for the simple reason that an elderly victim would suffer the unease that comes with their financial affairs becoming more precarious in their advanced years.

180    I disagreed with any suggestion that there was no loss to Manulife and I have already explained above why this submission was misconceived. I did not consider this to be a valid point for mitigation.

(2)   No restitution

181    There was no restitution made by the accused persons which would have been a relevant mitigating factor because it reduces the harm suffered by the victim or that it may evidence genuine remorse on the part of the offender: Gan Chai Bee at [61]–[63].

182    The lack of restitution would typically be a neutral factor, save in the case of an offender who fails to make restitution despite having the means to do so in which case, the lack of restitution may well be considered an aggravating factor: Chua Ya Zi Sandy v Public Prosecutor [2021] SGHC 204 at [8]. In the present case, there was no evidence or suggestion that the accused persons were not able to repay what they owed Visa. They are certainly not impecunious seeing that they were able to brief successive counsels in the conduct of their defence. They have simply refused to acknowledge their guilt or make any restitution to Visa. I was also of the view that it was proper to treat their failure to make restitution as aggravating given the facts of the case i.e. that the accused persons had taken advantage of and betrayed the trust of a family member thereby depriving the said family member of her precious retirement nest egg that they had promised.

(3)   Exceptional abuse of trust

183    Notwithstanding that there is already an element of an abuse of trust in the CBT Charges, I would agree with the Prosecution’s submission that in the present case, the abuse of the trust reposed in the Husband was exceptional.[note: 176] It was most certainly over and above the baseline level of abuse required of an offence under s 409 of the PC. In the present case, Visa trusted the Husband not simply because he was her financial advisor but more importantly, she was familiar with and trusted him as her nephew. It was not disputed that she trusted him so much that she left it entirely to him to pick which investment policy best suited her needs.[note: 177]

(4)   Offences were difficult to detect

184    I considered that the offences were difficult to detect because the accused persons had changed the address which Manulife corresponded with Visa, the policy owner. Visa was thereafter cut off from all further correspondence pertaining to her policies which were sent to the accused persons’ address. They then forged Visa’s signatures on the Assignment Documents which easily fooled Manulife’s representatives who would merely have carried out a routine verification. The accused persons also forged the Parents’ signatures to effectively bypass an additional safeguard in Manulife’s policy transfer process. Furthermore, the Assignment Documents were submitted by the Husband who was Manulife’s financial advisor thereby rendering the assignments even less suspicious.

185    Manulife did not know that it had been duped into transferring the policies to the Wife and thereafter allowing her (as the new policy owner) to surrender the policies. Therefore, it was an aggravating factor that the offences were difficult for Manulife to detect because of the how the accused persons had covered their tracks.

Offender-specific factors

186    There were no mitigating factors to be considered in favour of the accused persons. On the contrary, there was at least one aggravating offender-specific factor.

(1)   Lack of remorse

187    The accused persons decided to contest their charges. Whilst this would not be an aggravating factor by itself, it would mean that they have shown no remorse and therefore would have forfeited any discount which they would have been entitled had they pleaded guilty to the charges.

(2)   Not strictly first offenders

188    Next, the accused persons could not be considered as first offenders even though they have no previous similar criminal antecedents.[note: 178] It is well-settled law that the court may decline to regard an offender as a first-time offender if he faced multiple offences: Chen Weixiong Jerriek v Public Prosecutor [2003] 2 SLR(R) 334 at [17].

189    This was certainly the case here since both accused persons have been convicted of multiple Cheating Charges, and the Husband was additionally convicted of multiple CBT Charges.

(3)   Motive was financial gain

190    I next considered the accused persons’ motive for committing the offences. In Zhao Zhipeng v Public Prosecutor [2008] 4 SLR(R) 879 at [37], the High Court reiterated the principle that motive affects the degree of an offender’s culpability for sentencing purposes, and that persons who act out of pure self-interest and greed will rarely be treated with much sympathy.

191    In the context of CBT offences, it was observed in Lim Ying Ying Luciana v Public Prosecutor and another appeal [2016] 4 SLR 1220 at [55] that such an offences essentially involves the transgression of two distinct legally-protected interests, the first is the protection of the victim’s property rights, and the second is the protection of the standards of probity, integrity, and right-dealing expected of persons placed in positions of trust. The Court stated at [56] that “[a]n offender who breaches this obligation for the sake of personal enrichment is appreciably more culpable than one who does not.”

192    There was little doubt in this case that the Husband, who was under a fiduciary duty to manage Visa’s investment-linked policies, was motivated by self-interest and greed when he misappropriated her premiums. In respect of the Cheating Charges, both accused persons were also motivated by avarice when they acted in concert to cheat Visa of her Six Policies and misappropriated the surrender proceeds.

Sentence for CBT Charges

193    In respect of the Husband’s CBT Charges, I accepted the Prosecution’s calibration of the indicative sentences with reference to Ewe Pang Kooi where the Court imposed the following sentences in respect of charges under s 409 of the PC:[note: 179]

(a)     For offences involving $10,000 – about 9 months’ imprisonment; and

(b)     For an offence involving $25,000 – about 13.3 months’ imprisonment.

194    I also agreed that a slight uplift was justified on account of the aggravating offence-specific and offender-specific factors highlighted above, thereby resulting in the following indicative sentences:[note: 180]

(a)     For the CBT Charge involving $10,000 – 11 to 12 months’ imprisonment;

(b)     For the CBT Charge involving $15,000 – 12 to 13 months’ imprisonment; and

(c)     For the CBT Charges involving $25,500 and $28,500 – 15 to 16 months’ imprisonment.

Adopting the lower end of the indicative range of sentences, I sentenced the Husband as indicated at [10] above in respect of his CBT Charges.

Sentence for Cheating Charges

195    Turning to the Cheating Charges against both accused persons, I agreed with the sentences proposed by the Prosecution which were proportionate to the value of the policies cheated and which represented the gain obtained by the accused persons and the corresponding harm ultimately suffered by Visa:[note: 181]

(a)     For the Cheating Charge(s) involving around $4,000 – 2 to 3 months’ imprisonment;

(b)     For the Cheating Charge involving around $5,000 – 3 to 4 months’ imprisonment;

(c)     For the Cheating Charge involving around $6,800 – 4 to 5 months’ imprisonment;

(d)     For the Cheating Charge involving almost $8,700 – 5 to 6 months’ imprisonment; and

(e)     For the Cheating Charge involving almost $18,900 – 11 to 12 months’ imprisonment.

Adopting the lower end of the indicative range of sentences, I sentenced the Husband and Wife as indicated respectively at [10] and [12] above in respect of their Cheating Charges.

196    I accepted that the proposed sentences for the Cheating Charges were consistent with the precedents cited by the Prosecution.[note: 182] For instance, in Public Prosecutor v Jeffrey Han Tsair Ding [2021] SGDC 31, the accused had cheated the victim into investing various sums of money for certain projects. The victim issued eight cheques to that accused in the following amounts: $62,500, $6,500, $6,445, $35,000, $14,150, $4,500, $30,000 and $240,000, for a total of $399,095. The accused was convicted of eight cheating charges under s 420 of the PC corresponding to the eight cheques. In respect of the cheque for $4,500, he was sentenced to two months’ imprisonment. In respect of the cheques for $6,500 and $6,445, he was sentenced to three months’ imprisonment per charge. In respect of the cheque for $14,150, the sentence imposed was 10 months’ imprisonment.

197    In another precedent of Public Prosecutor v Lim Bee Teck Frederick [2018] SGDC 28, the accused was a renovation contractor who deceived his client into believing that he needed more money (in addition to the contract sum) to procure raw materials for the renovation works on one occasion and furniture on a second occasion. The client paid him $10,000 on each occasion. He was convicted after trial of two charges of cheating under s 420 of the PC and was sentenced to six months’ imprisonment for each charge. Unlike the present case, the sentencing court in that case found no particular aggravating or mitigating factors and considered that there was no planning or sophistication involved.

Aggregate sentences

198    The present accused persons were each convicted of more than three charges. Section 307 of the CPC mandates that at least two of the imprisonment sentences imposed on them must run consecutively.

199    In respect of the Husband, the Prosecution submitted for the sentences of only three charges (DAC-924433-2018, DAC-924435-2018 and DAC-933377-2019) to run consecutively adding up to 38 months’ imprisonment. In respect of the Wife, the Prosecution submitted for the sentences for only two charges (DAC-933497-2019 and DAC-933498-2019) to run consecutively adding up to 16 months’ imprisonment.

200    I had no difficulty agreeing with the proposed number of consecutive sentences which was fair if not restrained. After all, the Prosecution could have submitted for many more consecutive sentences given that all the offences were distinct and related to different investment policies. Therefore, as a general rule, all the sentences ought to run consecutively because the offences pertain to invasions of distinct legally protected interests: Public Prosecutor v Raveen Balakrishnan [2018] 5 SLR 799.

201    The submitted aggregate sentences were justified given the number of offences committed over several years which caused significant economic harm to Visa. The accused persons were indeed fortunate that the Prosecution did not see it fit to press for the sentences of more charges to run consecutively given their gross betrayal of Visa’s trust in them. The offenders were also cruel in stringing her along for many months promising enhanced investment returns when in fact they had already bled her dry. Therefore, I agreed with the Prosecution’s submission to order consecutive sentences against the Husband for at least three charges and against the wife for at least two charges. Nothing less would adequately reflect their overall culpability or do justice to Visa.

202    I was of the view that the respective aggregate sentences did not infringe the one-transaction rule and the totality principle laid down in Mohamed Shouffee bin Adam v Public Prosecutor [2014] SGHC 34. Ultimately, I was satisfied that the overall sentences were neither crushing nor inconsistent with the accused persons’ past records and future prospects. In my judgment, the aggregate imprisonment sentences were consonant with and appropriate to their culpability.

Conclusion - Sentence

203    The accused persons shamelessly took advantage of an elderly aunt and greatly abused her trust in them, by cheating Manulife thereby stealing her insurance policies and depriving her of her retirement nest egg.

204    For the above reasons, I imposed the individual and aggregate sentences respectively against the accused persons as submitted by the Prosecution. The Defence provided no assistance in the calibration of the appropriate sentences.

205    I was satisfied that the respective final aggregate sentences were neither crushing nor disproportionate to the accused persons’ culpability and the circumstances of the offences.

Compensation

206    Finally, I agreed with the Prosecution’s submission that a compensation order ought to be made against the accused persons under s 359 of the CPC in respect of the losses caused to Visa in respect of both the CBT and Cheating Charges.[note: 183] Counsel for the Defence did not disagree with this submission.

207    I therefore ordered that the Husband pay $117,906 (comprising the losses for the CBT Charges and his share of the losses for the Cheating Charges) to Visa in default to serve another six months’ imprisonment. I ordered the Wife to pay a compensation of $23,906 (comprising her share of the losses for the Cheating Charges) to Visa in default to serve two months’ imprisonment.
