Chan Wan Qi, Angela v Price Anthony Thomas and another

Chan Wan Qi, Angela v Price Anthony Thomas and another
[2026] SGDC 270

Case Number:Suit No 236 of 2025, Summons No 532 of 2026
Decision Date:24 August 2026
Tribunal/Court:District Court
Coram: Andrew Tan Shao Weng
Counsel Name(s): Tan Jinwen Mark (NLC Law Asia LLC) for the plaintiff; Price Anthony Thomas (in person) (for 1st the defendant and on behalf of the 2nd defendant)
Parties: Chan Wan Qi, Angela — Price Anthony Thomas — Bundleluxe Pte. Ltd

Striking out

24 August 2026

Deputy Registrar Andrew Tan Shao Weng:

Introduction

1       Price Anthony Thomas (“Mr Price”) is one of two directors of Bundleluxe Pte Ltd (“Bundleluxe”). As of the hearing of this summons, Bundleluxe is a dormant company with no revenue, assets or bank account.[note: 1] Chan Wan Qi, Angela (“Ms Chan”) is the owner of 35 Burnfoot Terrace, Singapore 459827 (“the property”). Ms Chan and Bundleluxe entered into a tenancy agreement vis-à-vis the property on 29 December 2023. The period of tenancy was 1 January 2024 to 31 December 2024, at a monthly rent of $8,500. The authorised occupants of the property were Mr Price and four members of his family.

2       Rent owed pursuant to the tenancy agreement was unpaid from at least May 2024. Despite rent being unpaid, Mr Price and his family continued residing at the property and did not vacate the premises by 29 December 2024 – the date on which the tenancy agreement expired. Instead, they moved out only on 18 March 2025. In short, Mr Price and his family resided at the property without rent being paid to Ms Chan for two thirds of the lease duration and continued to do so for approximately two and a half months beyond expiration of the lease. Their continued residence occurred notwithstanding Ms Chan’s requests for payment of arrears and repossession of the property at the expiration of the lease.

3       Through DC/OC 236/2025, Ms Chan pursues causes of action against both Bundleluxe and Mr Price, despite the fact that Mr Price was not a party to the tenancy agreement. The causes of action are breach of contract, and the torts of trespass and conspiracy. In short, Ms Chan’s main contention is that that Mr Price deliberately utilised Bundleluxe as the contracting vehicle to shield himself from personal liability when he was aware that Bundleluxe was in dire financial straits. In addition, trespass occurred because Mr Price and his family were unwanted guests at the property after the lease had expired.

4       By way of DC/SUM 532/2025 Mr Price sought to strike out several portions of the Statement of Claim (“SOC”). If he is successfully in this application, Ms Chan’s options for legal remedy would be limited to recovering damages solely from Bundleluxe. The prayers are as follows:

1.    Pursuant to Order 9 Rule 16 of the Rules of Court 2021, that the following portions of the Statement of Claim (Amendment No. 1) be struck out:

a.    Paragraphs 2A and 2B (alleged "modus operandi");

b.    Paragraphs 14, 14.1—14.6 (allegations of sham / fagade) (sic);

c.    Paragraphs 15 and 15.1—15.5 (veil-piercing and alter ego allegations);

d.    Paragraph 16A (conspiracy to defraud / injure).

2.    That the entire claim against the 1st Defendant be struck out, the 1st Defendant not being a party to the Tenancy Agreement and no material facts having been pleaded capable of establishing personal liability.

3.    That the claims for fraud and conspiracy against the 2nd Defendant be struck out on the grounds that they:

a.    disclose no reasonable cause of action;

b.    are scandalous, frivolous or vexatious; and

c.    constitute an abuse of the process of the Court.

4.    That the action, if it continues at all, proceed only as a contractual tenancy dispute between the Claimant and the 2nd Defendant.

5       I dismissed the summons in its entirety and now provide my reasons below.

The law

6       Any part of pleadings may be struck out pursuant to one of the following three grounds stated in Order 9 Rule 16 of the Rules of Court 2021:

(a)    It discloses no reasonable cause of action or defence;

(b)    It is an abuse of process of the Court; or

(c)    It is in the interest of justice to do so.

7       The bar for a successful striking out application is high. In short, it is only in “plain and obvious cases”[note: 2] which are wholly devoid of merit” that striking out is warranted. In this regard, the High Court in Leong Quee Ching Karen v Lim Soon Huat [2023] 4 SLR 1133 made the following observations (at [25] – [28]):

25    First, it is trite that the bar for succeeding in a striking out application is a high one. Thus, it has been said in Wing Joo Loong Ginseng Hong (Singapore) Co Pte Ltd v Qinghai Xinyuan Foreign Trade Co Ltd and another and another appeal [2009] 2 SLR(R) 814, where the Court of Appeal cited its previous decision in Ko Teck Siang v Low Fong Mei [1992] 1 SLR(R) 22, which in turn endorsed the English Court of Appeal case of Wenlock v Moloney [1965] 1 WLR 1238, (at [172]) that the power to strikeout is “very sparingly exercised, and only [applied] in very exceptional cases” and would not be justified “merely because the story told in the pleadings was highly improbable, and one which it was difficult to believe could be proved”. Indeed, the Court of Appeal put this in the well-known case of Gabriel Peter & Partners (suing as a firm) v Wee Chong Jin and others [1997] 3 SLR(R) 649 (“Gabriel Peter”) (at [18]) in the following manner:

In general, it is only in plain and obvious cases that the power of striking out should be invoked. This was the view taken by Lindley MR in Hubbuck &Sons, Limited v Wilkinson, Heywood & Clark, Limited [1899] 1 QB 86 at 91. It should not be exercised by a minute and protracted examination of the documents and facts of the case in order to see if the plaintiff really has a cause of action. The practice of the courts has been that, where an application for striking out involves a lengthy and serious argument, the court should decline to proceed with the argument unless, not only does it have doubts as to the soundness of the pleading but, in addition, it is satisfied that striking out will obviate the necessity for a trial or reduce the burden of preparing for a trial. [emphasis added]

The court’s power to strike out is therefore a draconian one to be exercised in plain and obvious cases, and it should not be exercised too readily unless it is clearly shown that the claimant’s case is wholly devoid of merit (see Gabriel Peter at [39]).

26    Second, pursuant to the above, the applicant in a striking out application bears the burden of proving that the claim is “obviously unsustainable, the pleadings [are] unarguably bad and it must be impossible, not just improbable, for the claim to succeed before the court will strike it out” (see the High Court decisions of Koh Kim Teck v Credit Suisse AG, Singapore Branch [2015] SGHC 52 at [21] as well as Bank of China Ltd, Singapore Branch v BP Singapore Pte Ltd and others [2021] 5 SLR 738 at [21]).

27    Third, there are three alternative grounds under O 9 r 16(1) of the ROC 2021 which would justify a striking out, namely: (a) no reasonable cause of action; (b) abuse of process; or (c) it is in the interests of justice to do so. In the context of the Kroll Framework, it is the abuse of process ground under O 9 r 16(1)(b) that is relevant. In this regard, the Court of Appeal in Gabriel Peter had explained the ambit of this ground as follows (at [22]):

The term, “abuse of the process of the Court”, in O 18 r 19(1)(d) [ie,O9 r 16(1)(b) of the ROC 2021], has been given a wide interpretation by the courts. It includes considerations of public policy and the interests of justice. This term signifies that the process of the court must be used bona fide and properly and must not be abused. The court will prevent the improper use of its machinery. It will prevent the judicial process from being used as a means of vexation and oppression in the process of litigation. … A type of conduct which has been judicially acknowledged as an abuse of process is the bringing of an action for a collateral purpose …

28    Thus, there would be an abuse of process if a claimant knowingly pursues a case that is “doomed to fail” (see the High Court decision of Kim Hok Yung and others v Cooperative Centrale Raiffeisen-Boerenleenbank BA (trading as Rabobank) (Lee Mon Sun, third party) [2000] 2 SLR(R) 455 at [17]). In such a case, the claimant would be, in effect, wasting the court’s time and this would amount to an abuse of process as the proceedings serve no useful purpose...

The applicant’s contentions

8       Pared to its essence, Mr Price’s main contention is encapsulated in prayer 4 of his summons: that the Court should only allow Ms Chan’s action to proceed against Bundleluxe vis-à-vis breach of tenancy. The pleadings pertaining to the remaining causes of action ought to be struck out. Upon close analysis, the causes of action sought to be struck out largely pertain to Mr Price’s personal involvement. I turn now to the consider the basis of his arguments.

9       First, Mr Price was not the contracting party. In this regard, he states that he “executed the contract solely and strictly in his corporate capacity as a Director…and [t]he contract contains no personal guarantee, indemnity or suretyship clause binding him”.[note: 3] As such, he “remains fully protected by separate corporate personality and the clear boundaries of director immunity affirmed by the Court of Appeal in PT Sandipala”.

10     Second, Mr Price contends that Ms Chan’s case in piercing the corporate veil is bound to fail as “the 2nd Defendant operates within an established corporate framework. The 2nd Defendant is held by a parent company under multi-shareholder ownership and is governed by a board that includes an independent local Director who owes strict statutory duties under the Companies Act 1967”. In further buttressing his case that Bundleluxe was a “genuine operating business”,[note: 4] Mr Price highlights that Bundleluxe had revenue of $974,986 and inventory holdings valued at $458,000 in FY2024.[note: 5]

11     Third, Mr Price contends that the tort of trespass cannot be sustained as a cause of action because Bundleluxe was the tenant of the property, and he was an authorised occupant pursuant to the tenancy agreement. As such, Mr Price says, “any dispute regarding possession arises between landlord and tenant under the tenancy agreement”.[note: 6]

12     Fourth, an objection was raised to portions of the Statement of Claim which refer to a past suit, which was eventually settled, involving Mr Price. At paragraph 2B, the claimant pleaded facts pertaining to DC/412/2020 which material facts are as follows. On 11 February 2020, Mr Price and Noranth Ventures (“Noranth”) were sued in relation to a tenancy agreement. Mr Price is a director and shareholder of Noranth. In addition, Lizzy Hashim Price – the wife of Mr Price – is also a shareholder of the company. The claimant in that suit alleged that Noranth breached the tenancy agreement “by failing to pay rent shortly after the commencement of the…tenancy and refusing to deliver vacant possession…to the landlord”.[note: 7] Mr Price argues that including these facts are prejudicial and that they constitute “legally irrelevant” “similar-fact narratives”.[note: 8]

My decision

13     It was not plain and obvious to me that any of Ms Chan’s pleadings ought to be struck out. To the contrary, there are more than sufficient grounds for them to proceed to trial. I elaborate below.

Piercing the corporate veil

14     I briefly summarise the law vis-à-vis Ms Chan’s causes of action against Mr Price personally. The corporate veil may be lifted where a company is used by a person as his or her alter ego. This is well established. In this regard, the key consideration is whether the act in question pertained to the company’s business or that of the individual.[note: 9] Further, lifting of the corporate veil takes place where sham structures or transactions are involved.[note: 10]

15     Ms Chan’s contention that Mr Price acted as the alter ego of Bundleluxe is not unsustainable. At the outset, I observe that Mr Price was one of only two directors of Bundleluxe. According to Michael Blaine Evanoff, the only other director of Bundleluxe, Mr Price “was the person who always interfaced with the Claimant and her Agent”.[note: 11] Thus, of the two directors of Bundleluxe, only one was involved with dealings pertaining to the property – and that was Mr Price. Further, he effectively acted as the authorised representative of Bundleluxe in negotiating and contracting with Ms Chan vis-à-vis the tenancy agreement for the benefit of him and his family.

Deliberate avoidance of personal liability by Mr Price

16     Part of Ms Chan’s case against both defendants vis-à-vis lifting the corporate veil and the tort of conspiracy revolve around two contentions. First, that Mr Price used Bundleluxe as the contracting vehicle despite knowing that the company would be unable to fulfil rental obligations. Second, that Mr Price would then rely upon Bundleluxe’s “insolvency or cessation of activity to avoid paying rent and to evade liability for arrears”.[note: 12]

17     In countering this facet of Ms Chan’s case, Mr Price points to Bundleluxe’s revenue and inventory around the time of contract (at [10] above). However, what Mr Price did not highlight in his submissions was the fact that that in the very same financial year Bundleluxe paid no tax, had a net loss of $577,359, and also had accrued losses amounting to $1,339,892. These facts make it plain that the financial health of Bundleluxe at the time of contract is clearly questionable. Despite being aware of this fact, Mr Price utilised Bundleluxe as the contracting vehicle. A few months into the tenancy agreement, rent was no longer forthcoming. Further, even if Bundleluxe had revenue and inventory as of FY2024, a question arises as to why its finances degenerated so quickly such that it could not even pay for housing – which is regarded by most as an essential necessity. In Ms Chan’s pleaded case, she alleges that Mr Price caused Bundleluxe to dissipate its assets resulting in the company being unable to meet its rental obligations, with the result being that he and his family “would enjoy the usage of the [the property] without having to pay for rent under the Tenancy Agreement”.[note: 13] The rapid deterioration of Bundleluxe’s finances – even taking Mr Price’s case at its highest – is an incontrovertible fact, which gives credence to Ms Chan’s case.

18     The facts above clearly demonstrate that Ms Chan’s two contentions (at [16] above) are clearly not without basis and hence are not liable to be struck out.

The tort of trespass

19     The tort of trespass is established when the following three elements are established:[note: 14]

(a)     The defendant commits an act of interference with the plaintiff’s land;

(b)     The act was committed voluntarily and directly; and

(c)     The plaintiff had possession of the land at the material time.

20     Ms Chan’s case is that by remaining on the property past the expiration of the tenancy agreement, Mr Price had committed trespass. His conduct took place notwithstanding Ms Chan having demanded – by way of a letter dated 24 December 2024 from her solicitors – that Mr Price handover possession of the property. Her pleadings vis-à-vis this cause of action clearly pass muster for the purposes of this striking out action. It is undisputed that Mr Price and his family continued residing at the property until 18 March 2025, which was beyond the expiration of the tenancy agreement.

21     Mr Price advanced two arguments in contending that Ms Chan’s pleadings vis-à-vis the tort of trespass should be struck out. First, that the “pleaded facts establish only that [Bundleluxe] was the sole contractual tenant and that [Mr Price] was an authorised occupant deriving his right of occupation entirely through that corporate tenancy”.[note: 15] In other words, only Bundleluxe can be held liable for trespass, and not Mr Price. This argument is entirely misconceived. The individuals who deliberately elected to remain on the property premises are most certainly liable for their actions in tort.

22     Mr Price’s second argument was that his conduct amounted to holding over, giving rise to contractual damages. As such, given that the contract provided for this situation he cannot be liable in tort. This argument is also misconceived as Ms Chan is entitled to choose which cause of action to pursue. The right of a claimant to such selection was stated in Gary Chan Kok Yew and Lee Pey Woan, The Law of Torts in Singapore (Academy Publishing, 2nd Ed, 2016) at p. 195):

There can be concurrent liability in both contract and tort based on Henderson v Merrett Dyndicates Ltd, that is a contracting party can choose to sue another in either contract or tort provided he can establish the requisite elements for each cause of action. This principle of concurrent duties in contract and tort has been specifically applied in Singapore.

Similar fact evidence

23     Finally, I address Mr Price’s contention that the pleaded facts pertaining to his previous lawsuit should be struck out. At the outset, I note that similar fact evidence is admissible in certain circumstances. Section 15 of the Evidence Act 1893 provides the statutory basis for admissibility, and reads:

Facts bearing on question whether act was accidental or intentional

15.    When there is a question whether an act was accidental or intentional or done with a particular knowledge or intention, the fact that such act formed part of a series of similar occurrences, in each of which the person doing the act was concerned, is relevant.

24     Ms Chan’s pleadings allege that Mr Price has a modus operandi of contracting through corporate vehicles for tenancy agreements, with the specific objective of shielding himself from personal liability upon default of obligations vis-à-vis those agreements. Towards this end, her pleadings contain details of a previous transaction (discussed at [12] above) in which a company which Mr Price was a director of tenanted a property and defaulted on its obligations. The legal relevance of these facts is patently obvious and fall within the ambit of section 15 of the Evidence Act. Whether the evidence is subsequently ruled to be admissible at trial is a separate matter to be determined. For the purposes of the matter before me, these pleadings are not liable to be struck out as they are relevant and not bound to fail.

Conclusion

25     The arguments mounted by Mr Price in support of this summons are not without irony. He is effectively contending that Ms Chan’s only legal remedy is to seek damages from a company with no assets, revenue, or even a bank account. As a corollary, notwithstanding the fact that he and his family resided at the property his personal assets ought to be shielded. This is precisely what the claimant is alleging of Mr Price’s intent by contracting through Bundleluxe. Whether he manifested such intent is a matter for trial. For now, Ms Chan has provided more than sufficient basis for her causes of action to deal with the striking out application. Her pleadings pass muster for the purposes of this summons, which is dismissed.

Costs

26     In dismissing the summons, I awarded costs to Ms Chan to be borne jointly and severally by both defendants. In doing so, I applied the following dicta from the Court of Appeal in BCBC Singapore Pte Ltd and another v PT Bayan Resources TBK and another [2024] 1 SLR 1:

77    We start with the general position, which is that where an unsuccessful suit was brought by two or more claimants, they will be jointly and severally liable for costs. …

…

80    Although Wing Joo Loong and Mike Gaffikin both discussed the rule in relation to a case where there were two or more defendants, we do not see why, in principle, this general rule should differ in a situation where there are two or more claimants. In a case where the joint claimants, or joint defendants, as the case may be, have lost, the general rule is that they will be jointly and severally liable for costs.

81    In our view, the best explanation for the general rule seems to be the fair allocation of risk. For the successful party, it is fairer that any risk of non-collection (for example, from one defendant’s insolvency) falls on the other unsuccessful party than the successful party: see Mike Gaffikin at 3–4; Rushcutters at [2]. As for the unsuccessful parties, they would have had the opportunity to address the risk of liability for costs and prepare for the worst-case scenario in which they lose.

27     This is a case where [81] of the dicta above is of clear application. Ms Chan should not be made to bear the burden of non-collection in light of the fact that she has effectively no chance of recovery against Bundleluxe. Further, as this summons was prosecuted primarily for Mr Price’s benefit – insofar as limiting his personal liability – it is just and equitable that he bears the costs of this application.

[note: 1]See affidavit of Mr Price dated 25 May 2025 at [35].

[note: 2]Leong Quee Ching Karen v Lim Soon Huat [2023] 4 SLR 1133 at [25].

[note: 3]Submissions of Mr Price dated 10 June 2026 at [7].

[note: 4]Affidavit of Mr Price dated 12 March 2026 at p.2.

[note: 5]Ibid at [19] – [20].

[note: 6]Ibid at [42]-[43].

[note: 7]Statement of Claim (Amendment No. 1) at [2B].

[note: 8]Submissions of Mr Price at [25].

[note: 9]Alwie Handoyo v Tjong Very Sumito and another and another appeal [2013] 4 SLR 308 at [96].

[note: 10]Win Line [UK] Ltd v Masterpart (Singapore) Pte Ltd and another [1999] 2 SLR(R) 24 at [38].

[note: 11]Affidavit of Mr Evanoff dated 29 March 2025.

[note: 12]Submissions of Ms Chan at [19].

[note: 13]Statement of Claim (Amendment No. 1) at [14.5].

[note: 14]Gary Chan Kok Yew and Lee Pey Woan, The Law of Torts in Singapore (Academy Publishing, 2nd Ed, 2016) at p. 408.

[note: 15]Submissions of Mr Price at [44].

Public Prosecutor v Nor Muhamad Syafriq Bin Saffri

Public Prosecutor v Nor Muhamad Syafriq Bin Saffri
[2026] SGDC 266

Case Number:DAC 902414/2025 and others, Magistrate's Appeal 9178/2026/01
Decision Date:24 August 2026
Tribunal/Court:District Court
Coram: Carol Ling
Counsel Name(s): Matthew Choo (Attorney-General's Chambers) for the Prosecution; Muhammad Taufiq bin Suraidi (Public Defender's Office) for the Accused
Parties: Public Prosecutor — Nor Muhamad Syafriq Bin Saffri

Criminal Procedure and Sentencing – Young Offender – Offences under Moneylenders Act 2008 – Assisting an unknown unlicensed moneylender in carrying on of the business of moneylending – Harassment – Probation Report called – Reformative Training Report called – Sentence

[LawNet Editorial Note: An appeal to this decision has been filed in MA 9178/2026/01.]

24 August 2026

District Judge Carol Ling:

Introduction

1       The Accused is 20 years old (Date of birth: 28 February 2006). He pleaded guilty to three offences, committed when he was 18 years old.

2       The proceeded charges are reproduced below:

DAC 902414/2025

You, are charged that you, on 9 February 2025, at about 6:18 PM, at Block 112 Edgefield Plains, #xx xxx, Singapore xxxx112, Singapore, acting on behalf of an unlicensed moneylender, did commit an act likely to cause alarm to the borrower, Norasyuhadah Binte Rahmat, in connection with the loan to the borrower, to wit, by affixing a debtor’s note on the wall beside the unit door, and you have thereby committed an offence punishable under s 47(2)(a) read with s 47(3)(a) of the Moneylenders Act 2008.

MAC 920049/2025

You, are charged that you, sometime in August 2024, in Singapore, did assist an unknown unlicensed moneylender in the carrying on of the business of moneylending, to wit, by relinquishing your POSB bank account bearing account number xxx-xxxxxx-x to the said unlicensed moneylender, in order to facilitate the unlicensed moneylending business, knowing that the said unlicensed moneylender was not an excluded moneylender or an exempt moneylender or authorised to do so by license, and you have thereby assisted in the contravention of s 5(1) of the Moneylenders Act 2008 and committed an offence punishable under s 19(1)(b)(i) read with s 19(2)(a) of the said Act.

DAC 920050/2025

You, are charged that you, sometime in May 2024, in Singapore, on 10 separate incidents, did assist an unknown unlicensed moneylender in the carrying on of the business of moneylending, to wit, by purchasing and selling 10 post-paid Subscriber Identification Module cards from SIMBA Telecom Pte Ltd to the said unlicensed moneylender, in order to facilitate the unlicensed moneylending business, knowing that the said unlicensed moneylender was not an excluded moneylender or an exempt moneylender or authorised to do so by license, which incidents taken together amount to a course of conduct, and you have thereby assisted in the contravention of s 5(1) of the Moneylenders’ Act 2008 and committed an offence under s 19(1)(b)(i) read with s 19(2)(a) of the said Act, which charge is amalgamated under s 124(4) and punishable under s 124(8)(a)(ii) of the Criminal Procedure Code 2010.

3       Two other similar charges under the Moneylenders Act were taken into consideration for the purposes of sentencing.

4       Given the Accused’s age at the time of the offences as well as at the point of his guilty plea, I called for a probation suitability report and a reformative training (RT) report. The Accused was found suitable for both probation and RT (at Level 1 intensity of rehabilitation). I eventually placed the Accused on probation.

5       This is the Prosecution’s appeal against the order of probation imposed on the Accused.

Key Facts of the Case[note: 1]

6       The Accused admitted to the Statement of Facts without qualification.

Facts relating to DAC 920050/2025

7       Sometime in May 2024, the Accused was offered an opportunity by an unlicensed moneylender to earn money. He was offered between $5 and $10 for every mobile phone line provided to the unlicensed moneylender. The Accused agreed. On 13 May 2024, on 10 separate occasions, the Accused purchased and obtained a total of 10 post-paid Subscriber Identification Module (“SIM”) cards from SIMBA Telecom Pte Ltd.[note: 2] The Accused provided his NRIC to register each of the post-paid SIM card. He then sold the 10 SIM cards to the unlicensed moneylender for profit. The Accused did so in order to facilitate the carrying on of the unlicensed moneylending business, knowing that the unlicensed moneylender was not an excluded moneylender, an exempt moneylender, or authorised to do so by a licence. His offending was uncovered when he was investigated for the relinquishing of his bank account to an unknown unlicensed moneylender in August 2024.[note: 3]

Facts relating to DAC 920049/2025

8       Sometime in July or August 2024, the Accused obtained a loan of $300 from an unlicensed moneylender. Subsequently, sometime in August 2024, the Accused was unable to make repayment of the debt. The Accused requested for an alternative method of repayment. He was made an offer to clear his debts by relinquishing bank accounts to the unlicensed moneylender for a week. The Accused agreed and relinquished his POSB account bearing account number xxx-xxxxxx-6 (the “POSB account”). He handed over his Automatic Teller Machine card associated with the POSB account and details relating to another POSB account bearing account number xxx-xxxxxx-3[note: 4] to a courier arranged by the unlicensed moneylender. The Accused was instructed to conceal the card in a Styrofoam box and wrap the box with plastic wrapping.

9       On 29 August 2024, several amounts were transacted through the POSB account.[note: 5] In particular, the POSB account received a total of $6,680 from two individuals who reported that they had made transfers into the POSB account in order to obtain a loan. The POSB account was seized with a balance of $880.01.

Facts relating to DAC 902414/2025

10     The victim is Norasyuhadah Binte Rahmat, a 38-year-old female. On 9 February 2025, at about 6:24 PM, the Singapore Police Force received a report from the victim with the following message “got Malay or Chinese person wearing black hoodie, pants and black cap pasted a note beside my unit. It is from the Ah Long. Happened 5 mins ago.” The address given was one in Block 112 Edgefield Plains (“victim’s unit”).

11     Sometime in September or October 2024, the Accused took a $200 loan from an unlicensed moneylender known to him as “Jay”. Subsequently, the Accused was unable to repay the loan which outstanding balance had increased to $1000. The Accused was offered a job by “Jay” to offset the loan. The Accused was instructed by “Jay” to proceed to various units and affix debtor’s notes at the units. He was to take a video or photograph of the units with the affixed debtor’s notes and transmit the same to “Jay”. The Accused was offered $70 to be deducted from his outstanding loan for each unit that he visited. He agreed to “Jay’s” offer.

12     On 9 February 2025, the Accused was provided with the addresses of three units by “Jay”, one of which included the victim’s unit. He was instructed to proceed to the units and affix debtor’s notes at the units. The Accused prepared the debtors’ notes at his home before leaving for the three units. At about 6:18 PM, the Accused arrived at the victim’s unit. He affixed a debtor’s note on a wall beside the unit’s door. The note contained the words “O$P$” with the victim’s name, NRIC number and address written in red ink over a white piece of paper. He took a photograph of the debtor’s note and transmitted it to “Jay”. The Accused removed the debtor’s note and threw it away before leaving the victim’s unit. He then proceeded to another unit located at Canberra View, Singapore, where he affixed a debtor’s note on “Jay’s” instructions.[note: 6]

13     The victim made the police report as at [10] above after she received a notification from her digital doorbell of the Accused’s presence outside of her unit. She was inside her unit at the material time and frightened by the Accused’s presence. Subsequently, the victim received the photograph that the Accused had taken of her unit with the debtor’s note affixed from one “Alex”, an unlicensed moneylender. The victim had obtained a loan from “Alex”, an unlicensed moneylender. The Accused committed this offence whilst he was being investigated and on agency bail in respect of the two charges as set out above.

The Approach to Sentencing Young Offenders

14     The approach to sentencing young offenders is well-established in case-law.[note: 7] It involves a two-step approach:

a)     Step One: The court must first ask whether rehabilitation is the dominant sentencing consideration, or had the emphasis on rehabilitation been displaced;

b)     Step Two: If rehabilitation remained the dominant sentencing consideration, the court is to consider if probation, reformative training or some other type or combination of community-based sentences would achieve it.

15     Rehabilitation was the dominant sentencing consideration in this case. The Accused was 18 years old at the time of the offences. He was a first offender. The overall facts and circumstances of the case did not displace the Court’s focus on rehabilitation as its objective in sentencing.

16     Since rehabilitation remained the dominant sentencing consideration, both probation and RT were viable sentencing options for the Court.[note: 8] I thus called for both probation and RT suitability reports. The Accused was found suitable for both probation and RT at level one intensity of rehabilitation.

Parties’ Position

17     The Prosecution submitted that the Accused ought to be ordered to undergo a term of RT, given the heightened need for deterrence:[note: 9]

a)     The Accused’s offending under the Moneylenders Act 2008 was serious. Further, the Accused’s acts of assisting by providing bank accounts and SIM cards were a critical component in facilitating the operations of unlicensed moneylenders. The Prosecution drew a similarity between the present offences and scam-related offences and argued that since probation is generally inappropriate for the latter due to deterrence and public interest considerations as set out in the Sentencing Advisory Panel’s Guidelines for Scams-Related Offences (the “Scam Guidelines”), the same should apply in the Accused’s case, given the similar nature of offending;

b)     There was a persistence in and escalation of the Accused’s offending. He displayed a pattern of financially motivated offending, escalating from providing SIM cards to an unlicensed moneylender in May 2024, to surrendering his POSB account to clear debts in July or August 2024, and ultimately committing harassment by affixing debtor's notes at multiple units in February 2025;

c) The Accused offended whilst on bail. Despite being arrested in November 2024 and released on bail, the Accused re-offended by committing harassment in February 2025. The Prosecution submitted the need for an “added measure of deterrence” as the Accused had demonstrated a disregard for authority.

18     Defence Counsel, on the other hand, submitted that probation was sufficient for the Accused’s rehabilitation:[note: 10]

a)     Specific deterrence did not feature strongly as both the probation report and the RT Report assessed the Accused’s risk of re-offending as low;

b)     Both the pre-sentence reports showed that the Accused had insight into his conduct and had learnt his lesson. He had shown genuine remorse and insight into his conduct. The Accused’s motivation in committing these offences was not criminal in nature but stemmed from immaturity and a misguided desire not to burden his financially struggling parents; and

c)     The Accused had strong community support for rehabilitation, including improved family relationships, dissociation from negative peers, pro-social networks, and positive performance in National Service. His parents were also supportive and were willing to be bonded.

19     Defence Counsel emphasized that the intervention needs identified in the RT report could be adequately addressed through the probation action plan outlined in the PSR, making community-based rehabilitation a viable and proportionate option.

20     In his final plea to the Court, Defence Counsel submitted that since specific deterrence did not feature strongly in this case, sentencing the Accused to a term of RT solely to meet the ends of general deterrence would be disproportionate, reducing the Accused to a “means to a policy end”[note: 11] while ignoring factors unique to his case.

Probation is an Appropriate Sentence

21     I agreed with the Defence that probation would be the appropriate sentence in this case. To start with, the Accused was a young, first-time offender with no prior antecedents or history of conflict with the law prior to the present offences.[note: 12] He pleaded guilty and I accepted that as an expression of remorse for his offending.

The Accused demonstrated strong rehabilitative potential

22     From both the probation and RT reports, it was clear that the Accused possessed the capacity for change and was suited for rehabilitation which could take place within the community, not necessarily within a regimented and structured environment like the RTC:

a)     The Accused had remorse and insight into his offending. Plea of guilt aside, the Accused expressed genuine regret for his offences, acknowledged the harm caused to his family and victims, and reflected that he should have sought help from his parents or school rather than taking the easy way out. He accepted responsibility for his actions. [note: 13]

b)     The Accused’s risk of re-offending was low. The probation report assessed his risk of re-offending as low compared to other male offenders on probation orders,[note: 14] with no current attitudes supportive of re-offending. This was corroborated by the RT report where it was stated that the Accused did not present with personality and behavioural patterns associated with antisocial behaviour[note: 15] or attitudes supportive of offending. The Accused’s account also reflected “a positive shift in his permissive thinking” since his last arrest in February 2025;[note: 16]

c)     The Accused exhibited a genuine commitment to change. In addition to expressing a clear and unconditional willingness to comply with all conditions and requirements imposed upon him in the course of his probation,[note: 17] the Accused’s overall compliance with time restrictions and supervision requirements showed his capacity for reflection and motivation for positive change.[note: 18] The Probation Officer reported that the Accused abided by her instructions to send his live location daily; he was also present for all video call checks conducted during the social investigation. [note: 19] When electronic monitoring breaches were detected, the Accused answered call checks promptly.[note: 20] The Accused has also remained offence-free since his last arrest in February 2025; and

d)     Obvious positive behavioural changes were evident in the Accused’s life. He had ceased contact with gang members and negative peers[note: 21] and instead, has now surrounded himself with pro-social peers, including a close friend from the mosque who encourages him to change, and a supportive girlfriend who advises him to stay out of trouble.[note: 22] The Accused also demonstrated good discipline, a positive mindset, and the ability to follow instructions and complete tasks punctually during National Service[note: 23] – areas which reflected his capacity for structure and self-improvement. The Accused has also recognised the importance of education and now has plans to pursue a work study diploma after completing his National Service.[note: 24]

The Accused has the support of his community

23     The Accused’s family environment is stable, supportive, and well-placed to provide the supervision and guidance necessary for his rehabilitation to succeed within the community. He shares a close relationship with his parents who are engaged and committed to his rehabilitation.[note: 25] Both parents have expressed their willingness to sign the probation bond, attend family intervention programmes, improve communication within the family, and guide the Accused on financial management.[note: 26] The family's willingness to be active participants in the Accused’s rehabilitation is a strong indicator that probation conditions can be meaningfully observed.

24     The Court acknowledges that multiple risk factors are present in the Accused’s life, such as poor consequential thinking, susceptibility to negative peer influence, a tendency to resolve problems independently, and limited parental supervision. Weaknesses were identified in both the Probation report and RT report. However, the existence of risk factors does not preclude probation; rather, it is the very purpose of probation to meaningfully address these risks and weaknesses in the Accused’s life so that he may be rehabilitated within the community.

Gravity of the Offence does not Preclude Probation

25     The gravity of the offences committed by the Accused was not overlooked. I agree with the Prosecution that offences under the Moneylenders Act are serious in nature which attract considerations of deterrence.[note: 27] However, the gravity of the offence alone cannot determine whether RT ought to be preferable to probation.

26     In Public Prosecutor v Mohammad Al-Ansari bin Basri [2008] 1 SLR(R) 449 at [66]-[67], the court stated:

“In all cases, therefore, the key is always to find the most appropriate sentencing option to give effect to the dominant principle of rehabilitation, which is also balanced against the need for deterrence that might arise for particular offences. In cases involving young offenders, the sentencing options that give dominant consideration to the principle of rehabilitation invariably boil down to either probation orders or reformation training. The presence of more than one sentencing option which equally advances the rehabilitative principle must mean that the courts’ hands are not tied when it comes to giving effect to this principle. Any other view cannot be right, and the courts would be remiss in the discharge of their judicial duties by abdicating their function to determine the appropriate sentence in consideration of the unique facts of each case.

In determining the balance to be struck between the dominant consideration of rehabilitation and the need for deterrence, the courts must of course pay utmost attention to the unique facts and circumstances of each case.”

27     Therefore, the court must undertake a consideration of the unique facts and circumstances in each case in order to determine which rehabilitative sentence would be more appropriate. Whilst this Court accepts that a term of RT would generally be the more appropriate sentence where the offences are serious and a measure of deterrence is necessary,[note: 28] a term of RT cannot be the default sentence simply because the offences are serious.

Limited Reliance on the Scam Guidelines

28     The Prosecution's reliance on the Scam Guidelines is not apt in the present context. The Scam Guidelines were specifically formulated to address scams-related offences, and the principles and policies underpinning them were developed with that particular category of offending in mind. Even though the Accused had relinquished bank accounts to facilitate unlicensed moneylending in this case, he was not convicted of scams-related offences. The Scam Guidelines cannot be directly transposed to his case. That said, even if I am wrong on this point and the Scam Guidelines may be applicable, fundamentally, within the scams-related sentencing framework, the Scam Guidelines do not operate as an absolute bar to probation.[note: 29]

29     The fact that the Accused reoffended whilst on bail is not lost on this Court. I viewed it as a period during which his consequential thinking remained under-developed and his financial pressures continued to drive his poor decision-making. However, critically, the probation as well as RT report both confirm that the Accused has remained offence-free from his arrest in February 2025. This is an indication that the Accused’s offending behaviour is not deeply entrenched and that he is capable of turning away from crime.

The Need for Deterrence is Adequately Met

30     It is well-established that where there is a need for both rehabilitation and deterrence in respect of a young offender, a term of reformative training is generally considered the more appropriate sentence. This is because the deterrent effect of probation has been recognised to be “penumbral at best” and “generally speaking ... relatively modest in nature”[note: 30]. However, to my mind, the need for deterrence did not automatically preclude probation as an appropriate sentence.

31     The totality of circumstances in this case favoured a community-based rehabilitation for the Accused in the form of probation over a closed and structured environment in the RTC. As Defence Counsel highlighted, specific deterrence “does not feature strongly”[note: 31] in this case, given the Accused's strong rehabilitative potential as evidenced by his genuine insight into his offending, the meaningful behavioural changes and the progress he has already made since his arrest. There was no necessity for close monitoring within the regimented and structured environment of the RTC.

32     The need for general deterrence in this case is adequately met even with an order of probation. The length of probation was for a substantial term of 18 months. The proposed probation conditions consisted of strict time restrictions and community service of 90 hours. Coupled with an experience of the court process which included a period of remand, I was satisfied that a term of probation was not manifestly inadequate as a sentence for this young offender and he has not gone unpunished.

Conclusion

33     I ordered the Accused to undergo 18 months' supervised probation with the following conditions:

a)     Time restriction from 10pm to 6am;

b)     90 hours of community service;

c)     To attend substance abuse assessment and treatment, if assessed necessary;

d)     Parents bonded for a sum of $5,000 to ensure the Accused’s good behaviour.

34     It was made plain to the Accused that should he fail to comply with the terms and conditions of the probation and/or commit another offence in the course of this probation, the term of probation may be revoked. At that point in time, the Accused may still be liable to a term of RT (or an imprisonment term) in respect of which the probation order was made.

35     On the Prosecution’s application, the execution of the terms of the probation order has been stayed pending the outcome of this appeal.

Public Prosecutor v Quek Yeong Kang

Public Prosecutor v Quek Yeong Kang
[2026] SGMC 90

Case Number:Magistrates' Arrest Case No.900985-2025 to 900987-2025
Decision Date:21 August 2026
Tribunal/Court:Magistrate's Court
Coram: Luke Tan
Counsel Name(s): Ms Daphne Lim and Mr Joel Fun Wei Xuan (Attorney-General's Chambers) for the Public Prosecutor; Mr Alain Abraham Johns and Ms Emira Binte Abdul Razak for the accused
Parties: Public Prosecutor — Quek Yeong Kang

Criminal Law – Outrage of modesty – Elements of offence – Criminal force – Intent to outrage modesty – Victim below 14 years of age

Evidence – Child witnesses – Competency – Corroboration – Unusually convincing standard – Section 159 Evidence Act 1893 (2020 Rev Ed)

Evidence – CCTV footage – Reliance – Limitations – Corroborative value

Criminal Procedure and Sentencing – Sentencing – Aggravated outrage of modesty – Section 354(2) Penal Code 1871

21 August 2026

District Judge Luke Tan:

Introduction

1       The accused is Quek Yeong Kang, also known as "Alex", a 49-year-old male Singaporean. He faced three charges of outrage of modesty against the alleged victim ("VM"), a female who was below 14 years of age at the material time, by using criminal force against VM intending to outrage her modesty. The charges were brought under s 354(1) and punishable under s 354(2) of the Penal Code 1871 (“the Penal Code”). The accused was alleged to have touched the vagina area of VM, who was then about 10 years old, on three separate occasions, namely 14 October 2023, 21 October 2023, and 28 October 2023.

2       At the material time, the accused was a swimming coach and taught swimming classes at Heartbeat @ Bedok Swimming Complex located at No. 11 Bedok North Street 1, Singapore ("Heartbeat @ Bedok"). VM was taking swimming lessons under the accused at that time. Her classes with the accused were on Saturdays from about 5.00pm to 6.00pm.

3       The accused claimed trial to all three charges. The Prosecution called a total of seven witnesses, including VM, VM's sister ("VS"), VM's brother ("VB"), VM's father ("VF"), a psychiatrist who examined VM (“Dr Woo”), another swimming coach (“Desmond”), and an investigation officer (“IO Chia”). CCTV footage was also produced showing occasions during the swimming classes when the accused was in close proximity to VM on 14 October 2023, 21 October 2023, and 28 October 2023 in the swimming pool. The accused testified in his own defence. He did not call any witnesses.

4       After assessing the evidence and submissions of parties, I found the accused guilty on all three charges and convicted him accordingly. I sentenced him to an aggregate sentence of 24 months' imprisonment and 3 strokes of the cane. The accused is currently serving his sentence. These are my grounds of decision.

The Charges

5       The accused faced the following charges:

(a)     The first charge (MAC-900985-2025) alleged that on 14 October 2023, at Heartbeat @ Bedok Swimming Complex, the accused did use criminal force on VM, a person below 14 years of age (Date of Birth: XX XXXX 2013), intending to outrage her modesty, by touching her vagina area, an offence under s 354(1) and punishable under s 354(2) of the Penal Code 1871.

(b)     The second charge (MAC-900986-2025) alleged that on 21 October 2023, at the same location, the accused committed the same offence against VM in the same manner.

(c)     The third charge (MAC-900987-2025) alleged that on 28 October 2023, at the same location, the accused again committed the same offence against VM in the same manner.

Agreed Facts

6       At the commencement of the trial, parties tendered a Statement of Agreed Facts ("SOAF") pursuant to s 267(1) of the Criminal Procedure Code 2010.

7       The agreed facts established the following. The accused conducted swimming classes at Heartbeat @ Bedok. His co-coach for the Saturday 5.00pm to 6.00pm class was one Yong Teck Yeow Desmond ("Desmond”). VM attended this class together with VS and VB, as well as six other students. The statements of four of these students, as well as a statement from the father of two of them, can be found in the SOAF (SOAF, Annex 2, pp. 15–21).

8       VM, VS, and VB attended the class on 14 October 2023, 21 October 2023, and 28 October 2023. Their swimming classes were captured on CCTV cameras at Heartbeat @ Bedok. The CCTV screenshots and their agreed descriptions were tendered as Annex 1 to the Statement of Agreed Facts.

9       VM's father made a police report on 29 October 2023 at or around 9.17pm via a "999" call.

10     In the course of investigations, the accused provided four statements to the Police voluntarily and without any threat, inducement, or promise. These were: a statement recorded by SSSgt Sophia Sim Shi Mei on 3 November 2023 pursuant to s 22 of the Criminal Procedure Code 2010; and three statements recorded by IO Chia Ji Ji on 27 January 2025 pursuant to s 23 of the Criminal Procedure Code 2010.

11     VM was seen by psychiatrist Dr Bernardine Woo Siew Choo ("Dr Woo") on 26 April 2024, and Dr Woo prepared a Medical Report dated 24 June 2024 in relation to VM.

12     Statements were also given to the Police by four other students in the class (SOAF, Annex 2(a)–(d), pp. 15–20), as well as by the father of two further students in the class, who confirmed on their behalf that they had not been touched inappropriately (SOAF, p. 21). However, three of these students made observations about the accused tickling students during lessons, which they found unusual. The first student stated that the accused had tickled his feet and his brother's feet, that this was for playing, and that he found it unusual because the accused pressed his feet (SOAF, Annex 2(a), p. 15). The second student stated that he had observed the accused tickling other students, though he could not recall who or where, and that he found it unusual because he felt only family members should tickle others in such a manner (SOAF, Annex 2(b), p. 16). The third student specifically noted that the accused would tickle him and his sister on the stomach after they finished their laps, that this lasted a few seconds, that the accused did this to others in the class as well, and that he found it unusual because Coach Desmond never did that (SOAF, Annex 2(c), pp. 17–18).

13     CCTV footage from Heartbeat @ Bedok was produced covering all three dates. The agreed descriptions of the CCTV screenshots, as set out in Annex 1 to the SOAF, showed the following.

(a)     On 14 October 2023, the footage showed, among other things, the accused swimming underwater towards VM at 17:34:39, and at 17:47:26, the accused being positioned behind VM and appearing to guide her freestyle stroke using both hands.

(b)     On 21 October 2023, the footage showed the accused assisting VM up to the wall at 17:27:51, assisting VM with wearing her swim cap at 17:28:27, and being in close physical proximity to VM at multiple points including 17:29:17, 17:33:38, 17:43:01, 17:47:01, 17:49:48, 17:52:55, 17:57:58, and 17:58:36.

(c)     On 28 October 2023, the footage showed the accused in close physical proximity to VM at 17:29:22, holding VM at her waist at 17:35:19, carrying VM up to the wall at 17:35:22, and positioned behind VM in close physical proximity at 17:35:40, as well as at 17:40:44 and 17:44:24.

Overview of the Prosecution's Case

14     The Prosecution called seven witnesses to establish their case. The Prosecution's case was that on each of the three occasions — 14 October 2023, 21 October 2023, and 28 October 2023 — the accused used the swimming lesson as an opportunity to touch VM's vagina area while in the pool, under the guise of providing swimming instruction. The Prosecution sought to establish that the accused's physical contact with VM went beyond legitimate coaching and constituted criminal force used with the intent to outrage her modesty.

Evidence of PW1 — IO Chia Ji Ji

15     The first witness was IO Chia Ji Ji (“IO Chia”), an investigation officer at Bedok Division. Upon taking over the file from the previous investigation officer, SSSgt Sophia Sim Shi Mei, IO Chia reviewed the CCTV footage from Heartbeat @ Bedok.

16     IO Chia also conducted a scene investigation at Heartbeat @ Bedok Swimming Complex. He testified that the CCTV camera capturing the relevant footage was located at the corner of the outdoor swimming pool, and that the distance between the camera and the nearest edge of the pool was approximately eight metres. He further testified that the depth of the pool near the handrails was approximately 1.2 metres.[note: 1] This was consistent with the accused's own evidence that the pool was 1.2 metres deep at both ends, sloping to 1.8 metres at the centre. Significantly, IO Chia testified that before interviewing VM, he had been unable to identify her from the CCTV footage, as the students all wore yellow caps, looked similar, and had no visible facial features[note: 2]. This was relevant to the assessment of VM's ability to identify herself and the accused in the footage, as discussed below.

Evidence of PW2 — Dr Woo Siew Choo Bernardine

17     The second witness was Dr Woo Siew Choo Bernardine ("Dr Woo"), a senior consultant at the Child Guidance Clinic of the Institute of Mental Health, where she has worked since 2000 and has been a psychiatrist since 2002. Dr Woo prepared a Medical Report dated 24 June 2024 (Exhibit P4) following her forensic assessment of VM on 26 April 2024. Her medical notes of the assessment were admitted as Exhibit P5.

18     Dr Woo testified that she documented her medical notes as she was interviewing VM, and thereafter prepared the medical report based on those notes[note: 3]. Before the interview, she had read through the Summary of Facts provided by the Police “just to get a rough idea of what the case is about”. The interview was conducted in two parts: the first part with VM's father present, during which only background questions were asked, and the second part with VM alone, during which the alleged incidents were discussed. The total duration of the assessment was less than 37 minutes, as reflected in the electronic timestamp on the clinical notes.[note: 4]

19     Dr Woo testified as to the account VM gave her of the alleged incidents. In respect of the first incident, VM told Dr Woo that on a Saturday, the accused asked the class to swim laps. After swimming a few laps, VM rested at the side of the pool. The accused asked her to continue swimming and touched her vagina over her swimsuit just before she started on the next lap. This occurred again after she swam a few more laps and rested. VM told Dr Woo that the accused touched her vagina three times on that occasion. VM also told Dr Woo that when she tried to sit by the side of the pool, the accused pulled her back into the water and subsequently carried her by the waist to sit at the side of the pool[note: 5].

20     In respect of the second incident, VM told Dr Woo that the following Saturday, the same pattern occurred, with the accused touching her vagina over her swimsuit. VM told Dr Woo that the accused touched her vagina two times on that occasion, and that she got out of the pool herself [note: 6].

21     In respect of the third incident, VM told Dr Woo that on the next Saturday, the accused again asked the class to swim laps, and after she rested at the side of the pool, he touched her vagina over her swimsuit when he asked her to continue a new lap. VM told Dr Woo that the accused touched her vagina two or three times on that occasion. VM also told Dr Woo that she and her sister told their elder brother about the incidents after the lesson.[note: 7]

22     Dr Woo further testified that VM understood that what the accused had done was wrong, explaining that he should learn about personal space and that it constituted molest[note: 8].

23     In paragraph 13 of her report (Exhibit P4), Dr Woo stated that VM is consistent in her account of events and understands the nature of the alleged abuse. She also assessed that VM was fit to give testimony in court and diagnosed her as having suffered from adjustment disorder as a result of the alleged abuse. On the question of fitness to testify, Dr Woo elaborated in court that she assessed VM's ability to give a consistent account of events, her understanding of the alleged abuse, and her demeanour during the interview, noting that VM spoke spontaneously and naturally and did not change her account.[note: 9]

24     On the diagnosis of adjustment disorder, Dr Woo testified that VM had experienced fear, anger, insomnia, nightmares, recurrent thoughts about the alleged abuse, fear of males, being easily startled, and difficulty focusing in class following the alleged incidents. However, by the time Dr Woo assessed VM approximately six months after the alleged events, these symptoms had been gradually decreasing. Dr Woo clarified that the more accurate formulation was that VM had been diagnosed with adjustment disorder, in that she had met the diagnostic criteria from the time of the alleged incidents until the symptoms resolved, rather than that she was actively suffering from it at the time of the assessment.[note: 10]

25     During cross-examination, Dr Woo acknowledged that she could not recall with certainty whether VM had used the word "vagina" or "private part" during the interview, and that she may have paraphrased the child's words in her clinical notes. She also acknowledged that the Summary of Facts provided by the Police had used the word "vagina", and accepted that it was possible, though she could not confirm, that her use of the word in her notes was influenced by the Summary of Facts rather than solely by what VM had said. However, Dr Woo maintained that VM had conveyed to her that the vagina area was the part of the body that had been touched.[note: 11]

26     Dr Woo also confirmed that she had separately assessed VM's younger sister, VS, on 3 May 2024, and assessed her to be fit to testify in court.[note: 12]

27     Before turning to the evidence of VM and VS, I address the question of their competency to testify. Under s 120 of the Evidence Act 1893 (2020 Rev Ed) ("Evidence Act"), all persons are competent to testify unless the court considers that they are prevented from understanding the questions put to them or from giving rational answers by reason of tender years, extreme old age, disease, or any other cause of the same kind. In line with the words of the provision, it is clear that a child is not rendered incompetent merely by reason of young age. Consistent with the illustration,[note: 13] it would appear that the question to consider is whether the child is able to understand the questions put and give rational answers to them.

28     In the present case, I was satisfied that both VM and VS were competent witnesses. In respect of VM, Dr Woo had assessed her on 26 April 2024 and concluded that she was fit to give testimony in Court, having found her able to give a consistent account of events, to understand the nature of the alleged abuse, and to explain why it was wrong. Before VM commenced her evidence, I also posed a series of preliminary questions to her to assess her understanding and competency. In answer to my questions, VM confirmed that she was studying at YYY Secondary School[note: 14], that English was her favourite subject, that she was comfortable speaking in English, and that she understood she was in court to tell the truth. She confirmed that she understood the questions put to her and that she should only answer questions she understood, ask for clarification if she did not, and say so if she could not remember rather than guess[note: 15]. I was satisfied that VM understood the nature of the proceedings and the obligation to tell the truth, and that she was able to give rational answers to questions. In respect of VS, aside from Dr Woo’s views (see [26]), I similarly posed preliminary questions before she commenced her evidence. VS confirmed that she was studying at XXX Primary School,[note: 16] that her favourite subject was English, that she understood she was in court, and that she understood the obligation to give truthful and accurate answers. She also understood she should not guess and should ask for clarification if she did not understand a question.[note: 17] I was satisfied that VS was likewise a competent witness. I accordingly permitted both VM and VS to give evidence on affirmation. I will set out their evidence in greater detail below.

Evidence of PW3 — The alleged victim (VM)

29     The third witness was the alleged victim, VM, who was about to turn 13 years old at the time of trial. At the material time of the alleged offences in October 2023, VM was 10 years old. VM confirmed that at that time, the accused was her swimming coach at Heartbeat @ Bedok.

30     VM testified that her first class with the accused was on 7 October 2023, which was held in the indoor pool as it was raining, and that nothing happened on that occasion. The subsequent classes on 14, 21 and 28 October 2023 were held at the outdoor open pool.

Testimony about the incidents and informing her family members

31     As regards the first incident on 14 October 2023, VM testified that on that day, after swimming a couple of laps, she and her sister were standing in the water at the side of the pool when the accused came up behind her and touched her vagina. She initially thought it was an accident as his hands may have accidentally touched her private part, but it kept going on two to three times,[note: 18] meaning two or three separate occasions.[note: 19] She described the accused as standing behind her while she faced the opposite direction, with their bodies touching,[note: 20] and explained that after swimming a few laps, she would rest at the side, and when she was about to continue, he would go behind her and touch her. VM also demonstrated the positions of herself and the accused using two dolls, with the male doll placed behind the female doll, both facing the same direction with their bodies touching. She demonstrated the touch as a rubbing motion on the vagina area of the female doll. These demonstrations were photographed and admitted as Exhibit P11.[note: 21] VM confirmed that the touch was over her swimming costume and that the accused's hand was under the water when he touched her. [note: 22]

32     As regards the second incident on 21 October 2023, VM testified that the same thing happened again. Outline of submissions by parties

74     At the end of the trial, both the Prosecution and Defence tendered written submissions and replies. I summarise the essence of their submissions below.

Prosecution’s submissions in brief

75     The Prosecution submitted that the evidence proved each of the three charges beyond a reasonable doubt. The Prosecution submitted that this was not a case where the conviction rested solely on the uncorroborated testimony of VM, because VM's evidence was corroborated by multiple other witnesses and by the objective CCTV evidence. In any event, the Prosecution submitted in the alternative that VM's evidence was so credible and compelling that it independently met the "unusually convincing" threshold.

76     On VM's evidence, the Prosecution submitted that her account bore a strong ring of truth. Despite being cross-examined across multiple video clips and subjected to detailed questioning about the positions and actions of herself and the accused at different times, VM maintained her core account consistently throughout, namely that the accused stood behind her after she completed laps and touched her vagina area over her swimming costume on each of the three dates. In addition, the Prosecution highlighted that VM did not overstate her evidence on the CCTV footage. Instead, when shown clips in which the accused was closely behind her with his hands underwater — positions consistent with how the molest occurred — she did not simply assert that the accused must have touched her vagina at those points, but she candidly testified that she did not want to "accuse" when she was not sure, and explained that while she knew the accused had touched her, she was unable to pinpoint specifically when in the footage he did so and did not wish to "anyhow say." The Prosecution submitted that this degree of restraint was a hallmark of a truthful witness, and that a witness intent on fabrication would have seized every clip showing the accused behind her to assert that the touching occurred.

77     The Prosecution further submitted that VM's evidence was internally consistent. She consistently maintained that the accused would position himself behind her, that the touching occurred while his hand was underwater, that the touching was on her vagina area over her swimming costume, that it would happen after she completed laps and stopped at the side of the pool, and that the accused repeated this conduct on 14, 21 and 28 October 2023.

78     The Prosecution also submitted that VM's evidence was externally consistent with the evidence of four other witnesses.

(a)     First, VS confirmed that VM had asked her during the class on 28 October 2023 whether the accused had touched her vagina, and that VS had replied yes.

(b)     Second, VB's evidence corroborated VM's account of a prompt disclosure after class, in that VB testified that VM told him soon after a class that the accused had touched her at her private part. The Prosecution acknowledged the discrepancy between VM's evidence (that she told VB after the class on 28 October 2023) and VB's evidence (that VM told him after the class on 14 October 2023), but submitted that this minor discrepancy did not undermine the corroborative value of VB's evidence, as both accounts established that VM had made a prompt disclosure to VB about the accused touching her private part.

(c)     Third, VF's evidence corroborated VM's disclosure to him on 29 October 2023 and the immediate police report that followed.

(d)     Fourth, Dr Woo's evidence was consistent with VM's account, in that VM gave Dr Woo a consistent account of the incidents during the forensic psychiatric assessment on 26 April 2024.

79     On the question of motive to fabricate, the Prosecution submitted that there was no credible motive for VM to have fabricated the allegations. The only motive suggested by the Defence was that VM disliked the accused and wanted to change coaches. The Prosecution submitted that a desire to change swimming coaches did not provide a plausible reason for a 10-year-old child to fabricate repeated and specific allegations of sexual touching, involve her younger sister in the fabrication, and put herself through the ordeal of a police investigation and court proceedings. The Prosecution further submitted that the evidence negated this suggested motive: VM herself explained that if she had wanted to switch coaches, she would have told her parents directly; VS confirmed there had been no conversations with VM about changing coaches; and VF confirmed that neither daughter had said she wanted to change coaches before 29 October 2023.

80     On the accused's evidence, the Prosecution submitted that it was inherently improbable and internally inconsistent, and that the accused had demonstrated himself to be an unreliable and untruthful witness. The Prosecution highlighted the accused's pattern of initial denial followed by concession when confronted with footage replayed at half speed, pointing in particular to his initial denial of making contact with VM's buttock at the 17:29:18 timestamp on 21 October 2023 and his initial denial of making contact with VM's lower back at the 17:35:32 and 17:35:33 timestamps on 28 October 2023, both of which he conceded only after the footage was replayed at half speed. The Prosecution submitted that this pattern of denial followed by reluctant concession was the hallmark of an untruthful witness who was tailoring his explanations to fit the footage only after being confronted with it. The Prosecution also relied on the accused's equivocal response to both VF and Desmond on the evening of 29 October 2023 as evidence of consciousness of guilt, submitting that an innocent person who had been falsely accused of molesting two young girls would have been expected to deny the allegation clearly and immediately.

81     In short, the Prosecution submitted that all three charges against the accused had been proven beyond a reasonable doubt.

Defence's submissions and replies in brief

82     The Defence submitted that the Prosecution had not proven any of the three charges beyond a reasonable doubt, and that the accused should be acquitted on all three charges.

83     Broadly, the Defence's case rested on several principal submissions. First, the CCTV footage did not corroborate VM's evidence and was in certain respects inconsistent with it. Second, VM's evidence was internally inconsistent and was not "unusually convincing." Third, there was no corroborating evidence capable of supporting a conviction. Fourth, Desmond testified that in the 13 years he had known the accused, he had never received any complaints from parents or students about the accused, and that it would be difficult for the accused to molest any student given the number of people present in and around the pool during classes. Fifth, the statements of four other students who attended the same class, as well as a statement from the father of two further students, were consistent with the accused's denial. Sixth, VM had expressed a desire to be coached by Desmond rather than the accused, yet had never asked her parents to change coaches, even though she claimed she would have done so if she had wanted to — but instead made allegations of molestation which would have had the obvious effect of causing her parents to change her coach. Seventh, on the Defence's preferred version of events — namely, that VM told VB after the first class on 14 October 2023 — VB would have been keeping a watchful eye on the accused, VM and VS during the subsequent classes on 21 and 28 October 2023 precisely because of what VM had told him. Yet VB confirmed that he did not observe anything improper or inappropriate during those classes. The Defence submitted that this was significant because VB was in close proximity to VM and VS at the coaching area at the shallow end of the pool, and was therefore well-placed to have noticed any inappropriate conduct by the accused.

84     On the first charge, the Defence submitted that when VM was taken through the CCTV footage for 14 October 2023, she admitted that nothing had happened in the footage at the first, second, fourth and fifth timestamps, was unsure whether anything had happened at the third timestamp, and ultimately conceded that nothing had happened at the sixth timestamp — the only timestamp at which she had initially suggested the Accused might have touched her while teaching her a swimming stroke. The Defence submitted that VM's evidence-in-chief had appeared clear and cogent, but that when confronted with the CCTV footage, she changed her evidence and was unable to identify any specific moment in the footage when the Accused had touched her. 

85     The Defence also submitted that the Summary of Facts attached to Dr Woo's clinical notes, which had been prepared by IO Chia, was inconsistent with VM's oral testimony in court and with the CCTV timestamps. In particular, the Defence pointed to the description in the Summary of Facts that the accused had approached VM while she was "resting in the corner" and touched her vagina while speaking to her, and submitted that this differed from VM's oral account that the accused had touched her while teaching her a swimming stroke. The Defence also submitted that VM's statement during cross-examination — "ever since he started, like, touching me, like, since from day — from 21 October onwards, I feel uncomfortable" — was inconsistent with her evidence that the first incident had occurred on 14 October 2023, and suggested that the commencement date of the alleged touching was in fact 21 October 2023 rather than 14 October 2023.

86     In addition, the Defence relied on the discrepancy between VM's evidence and VB's evidence on the question of when VM told VB about the alleged touching. VM testified that she told VB after the class on 28 October 2023, while VB testified that VM told him after the class on 14 October 2023. The Defence submitted that VB's evidence was to be preferred. The Defence argued that if VB had been told on 28 October 2023 as VM claimed, he would have had no particular reason to recall the date, whereas if he had been told on 14 October 2023, the date would have been memorable because the disclosure to VF and the police report followed the very next day on 29 October 2023. The Defence further relied on VB's own evidence that VM did not speak to him about the accused after the classes on 21 or 28 October 2023, and submitted that if VB was told on 14 October 2023, he would have been keeping an eye on the accused, VM and VS during the subsequent classes on 21 and 28 October 2023 — which he confirmed he did — and that he did not observe anything improper or inappropriate. The Defence argued that this was a material external inconsistency that impacted VM's credibility and whether her evidence could be said to be unusually convincing.

87     On the second charge, the Defence submitted that the relevant timestamps in the CCTV footage for 21 October 2023 did not corroborate VM's evidence. In particular, the Defence submitted that at the second timestamp (17:27:51), VM had not mentioned in her evidence-in-chief that the accused had touched her vagina, and that this only emerged during cross-examination, after which VM conceded that she could not remember and rationalised her answer by saying it was because the accused's hand was underwater. The Defence submitted that this amounted to an internal inconsistency in VM's evidence, as her account in cross-examination differed materially from her evidence-in-chief in which she had said only that the accused had held her waist. The Defence further submitted that at the sixth timestamp (17:43:01), the accused's explanation that he had brought VM back to the edge of the pool because he believed she was showing signs of drowning was not an impossibility, and that there would not have been the opportunity for the accused to touch VM's vagina at that timestamp, given that his hands were occupied with holding VM's hands to teach her the freestyle stroke and Desmond had been in close proximity to the accused and VM at that point. The Defence also submitted that VM's evidence-in-chief did not state that the accused had touched her vagina at the sixth timestamp, and that this only emerged during cross-examination, after what the Defence characterised as "C1's Acknowledgement" — VM's acknowledgment during cross-examination that the accused had not touched her vagina at any of the other timestamps.

88     On the third charge, the Defence submitted that VM was unsure whether the accused had touched her vagina at both the second timestamp (17:29:22) and the third timestamp (17:34:37) for 28 October 2023, describing herself as "50/50" at the second timestamp and saying "I think so, but I don't think also" at the third timestamp. The Defence further submitted that at the second timestamp, Desmond had been in close vicinity to the accused and VM, and that the accused's hands had been holding VM's hands to teach her the freestyle stroke, making it physically impossible for him to have simultaneously touched her vagina. In support of this, the Defence relied on the accused's own evidence during cross-examination, where he stated: "I'm holding her hand, how to touch her vagina?"[note: 81]. The Defence submitted that VM's uncertainty at these timestamps, which were the only timestamps she identified as possible instances of touching on 28 October 2023, meant that her evidence on the third charge was not "unusually convincing" and was uncorroborated.

89     More broadly, the Defence submitted that VM's evidence was highly doubtful when considered against the totality of the evidence, relying on the following matters in support of this submission: the CCTV footage was inconclusive; there was a discrepancy over when VM told VB about the accused touching her inappropriately; VB's subsequent observations disclosed nothing untoward; the other students' statements did not support any allegation of inappropriate touching; and Coach Desmond's evidence was that he had never seen the accused act inappropriately towards any student.

90     The Defence also relied on what it termed "C1's Desire" — VM's stated preference to be coached by Coach Desmond instead of the accused — and the fact that VM had never asked her parents to change coaches, even though she claimed she would have done so if she had wanted to. The Defence argued that the allegation of molestation would have had the obvious effect of causing her parents to change her coach, which was the very outcome VM sought, and that she could have achieved this more simply by asking her parents directly. The Defence submitted that it was entirely possible that VM had fabricated the allegation in order to bring about a change of coach, and that a ten-year-old child would not have appreciated the cascading consequences of such a fabrication.

91     In the Defence Reply Submissions, the Defence developed this argument further. The Defence submitted that the discrepancy between VM's evidence and VB's evidence on when VM told VB about the alleged touching was not a "minor discrepancy" as the Prosecution characterised it, but was significant when viewed in its proper context. The Defence submitted that if VB's evidence is preferred — namely, that VM told him after the first class on 14 October 2023 — the Prosecution's argument that there was a "natural and incremental pattern of disclosure" by VM is substantially undermined. On VB's version, VM made no disclosure to VB after the classes on 21 or 28 October 2023, and the Defence submitted that this gives rise to the prospect that VM's disclosure to VB on 14 October 2023 was not a genuine complaint arising from the touching, but was influenced by her dislike of the accused's swimming class.
