The Defence further pointed to what it characterised as an internal tension in VM's own evidence: she told VB after the first class on 14 October 2023 when, on her own account, she did not yet feel uncomfortable and still thought the touching might have been accidental; yet she said nothing to VB after the second class on 21 October 2023, when on her own account she knew the touching was deliberate and felt uncomfortable. The Defence submitted that this sequence was difficult to reconcile with a genuine complaint.

92     The Defence further submitted that VS's evidence of the conversation between VM and VS during the class on 28 October 2023 was of little additional evidential value, as there was no CCTV footage showing VM and VS stopping at the side of the pool to have that conversation. Relying on Lee Kwang Peng v Public Prosecutor and another appeal [1997] 2 SLR(R) 569 (“Lee Kwang Peng”) at [80], the Defence submitted that numerous complaints by complainants cannot amount to corroboration. As for VF's evidence, the Defence submitted that VM's disclosure to VF does not fall within the ambit of s 159 of the Evidence Act 1893 (2020 Rev Ed) as it was not made at or about the time the alleged facts took place, and that in any event, relying on Khoo Kwoon Hain v Public Prosecutor [1995] 2 SLR(R) 591 (“Khoo Kwoon Hain”) at [49], corroboration by virtue of s 159 alone was not corroboration by independent evidence and it would be dangerous to equate it with corroboration in the normal sense of the word.

93     In addition, the Defence submitted in its Reply that the accused's reaction when first confronted by VF — described by VF as "incoherent" and "stuttering" — was of no assistance to the Prosecution, as the accused was simply in shock upon hearing the allegations made against him. On Dr Woo's evidence, the Defence submitted that she had interviewed VM for less than 37 minutes, appeared to be heavily influenced by the Summary of Facts attached to her clinical notes and by VM's demeanour, and could not remember the interview well as it had taken place some time ago. The Defence submitted that if there is a danger that VM concocted the alleged incidents, there would equally be a danger that she was merely repeating a fictional story to Dr Woo, and that Dr Woo's evidence cannot therefore amount to corroborative evidence The Defence also submitted that VM's evidence was not unusually convincing because, across all three dates, she was unable to identify a single timestamp in the CCTV footage at which she could say with certainty that the accused had touched her vagina area; and that if she had genuinely felt uncomfortable on 21 October 2023, she should have been able to point to at least one of the nine timestamps for that date when the touching occurred, but she could not. Finally, the Defence submitted that once the court has identified a flaw internal to the Prosecution's case, weaknesses in the Defence's case cannot ordinarily shore up what is lacking in the Prosecution's case, relying on Public Prosecutor v GCK and another matter ("GCK") [2020] 1 SLR 486 at [140], and that it would be unsafe to convict the accused on any of the three charges.

Elements of the charges and relevant legal principles

94     The elements of a charge under s 354(1) of the Penal Code are: first, that the accused assaulted or used criminal force against the victim; and second, that he did so intending to outrage, or knowing it to be likely that he would thereby outrage, the modesty of that person. Where the victim is below 14 years of age, the enhanced punishment provision under s 354(2) applies.

95     "Criminal force" is defined under s 350 of the Penal Code as the intentional use of force to any person without that person's consent, in order to cause the commission of an offence, or intending by the use of such force to cause, or knowing it to be likely that by the use of such force he will cause, injury, fear, or annoyance to the person to whom the force is used. The culpable intention of the accused is the crux of the matter. While the victim's reaction is relevant, its absence is not always decisive, as much depends on the facts of the case: Lee Siew Boon Winston v Public Prosecutor [2015] 4 SLR 1184 ("Winston Lee") at [83].

96     The Prosecution bears the legal burden of proving guilt beyond a reasonable doubt, and this remains the ultimate question the court must determine after a holistic examination of all the relevant evidence, including the evidence of the victim and the other Prosecution witnesses, the accused and the evidence adduced by the Defence: Winston Lee at [63] and [75]. As the Court of Appeal observed in GCK at [135], a reasonable doubt may arise from the totality of the evidence, which necessarily involves a holistic assessment of both the Prosecution's and the Defence's cases and the interactions between the two. Further, as explained in the subsequent case of GII v Public Prosecutor [2025] 3 SLR 578 ("GII") at [27]–[28], the assessment of whether reasonable doubt exists proceeds in two stages: first, whether the Prosecution's case is internally and externally consistent such that there is sufficient evidence to establish guilt beyond a reasonable doubt at least on a prima facie basis; and second, whether, on the totality of the evidence including the Defence's case, there remains no reasonable doubt as to the accused's guilt. I bore in mind that weaknesses in the Defence's case cannot ordinarily be called in aid to shore up what is lacking in the Prosecution's case: GII at [27].

97     In the absence of corroboration, the burden of proof may nonetheless be discharged if the trial court finds the victim's evidence to be unusually convincing, such that it is safe to convict solely on her evidence. In making this assessment, the court weighs the demeanour of the victim alongside both the internal and external consistencies found in her testimony. Even where the evidence of the victim is not unusually convincing, the legal burden may still be discharged if there is sufficient corroboration: Winston Lee at [62] and [73]. A complainant's testimony would be considered "unusually convincing" only if the testimony, "when weighed against the overall backdrop of the available facts and circumstances, contains that ring of truth which leaves the court satisfied that no reasonable doubt exists in favour of the accused": Public Prosecutor v Mohammed Liton Muhammed Syeed Mallik [2008] 1 SLR(R) 601 (“Liton”) at [39]. The court must assess the victim's testimony against that of the accused, such that the victim is found to be "unusually convincing" to the extent that the court can safely say her account is to be unreservedly preferred over that of the accused: XP v Public Prosecutor [2008] 4 SLR(R) 686 at [34].

98     On the question of corroboration, the High Court in Lee Kwang Peng noted at [80] that complaints made by a victim to others are capable of amounting to corroboration in Singapore law by virtue of s 159 of the Evidence Act. That said, the High Court caveated that complaints made so long after the alleged incidents as to fall outside the ambit of s 159 of the Evidence Act cannot amount to corroboration; and even if that difficulty could be circumvented, such corroboration, not being independent, could only be of little additional evidential value.

99     As for child witnesses, there is no special rule requiring a trial judge to direct himself as to the dangers of convicting without corroboration where the only evidence is that of a child witness, although the court must remain sensitive to the requirement of corroborative evidence or alternatively consider that corroboration is not required because of the maturity and reliability of the witness: Lee Kwang Peng at [62] and [67].

100    On the question of how victims of sexual offences may be expected to behave, the High Court in GBR v Public Prosecutor [2018] 3 SLR 1048 ("GBR") at [20], made it clear that “victims of sexual crimes cannot be straitjacketed in the expectation that they must act or react in a certain manner”. The High Court in that case dismissed the appeal against conviction, noting that the victim "was young, sexually inexperienced and was thus likely to have been taken aback by the appellant's unexpected but brazen conduct", and that her reaction "was well within the realm of possibilities and indeed would have been perfectly foreseeable" (at [20]).

101    Finally, on the question of consciousness of guilt, the court is entitled to take into account lies told by an accused person as part of the holistic assessment of the evidence. Such lies may amount to corroboration of the accused person's guilt if they are shown to have been told out of a motive that can only be linked to his guilt. However, even when established, such lies are only employed to support other evidence adduced by the Prosecution and cannot by themselves make out the Prosecution's case: GCK at [141].

Decision on whether the charges have been made out

102    Before turning to the assessment of the evidence of the material witnesses, and whether the charges are made out, I make some preliminary observations about the CCTV evidence as a whole, which was evidence that both the Prosecution and the Defence relied on extensively in their submissions.

General observations on the CCTV evidence

103    I first note that the footage from all three dates did not show the accused's hands touching VM's vagina area. This was unsurprising given that the alleged touching occurred under the water and lasted only seconds.

104    Nevertheless, the footage was of considerable evidential value. It confirmed the physical setting described by VM — the interactions took place at the shallow end of the pool, with the accused repeatedly positioning himself directly behind VM and in close physical proximity to her. It also showed the accused making physical contact with VM in areas for which he could offer no credible coaching justification — namely her buttock on 21 October 2023 and her lower back on 28 October 2023 — both of which he initially denied and conceded only after the footage was replayed at half speed.

105    Further, it captured VM's contemporaneous reactions — including kicking the accused away at the 17:47:01 timestamp on 21 October 2023 — which are consistent with her account of growing discomfort. Finally, VM's careful and restrained approach to the footage — declining to assert that touching occurred at a particular timestamp unless she was certain — was itself a hallmark of her reliability as a witness, an issue I will elaborate on in greater detail in the course of discussing my findings.

106    I should, however, note the inherent limitations of the CCTV evidence. The footage was recorded from a fixed camera positioned approximately eight metres from the nearest edge of the pool. The images of persons in the pool were correspondingly small, and the resolution did not permit a clear view of the precise positions or movements of hands and fingers under the water. These limitations were compounded by the fact that the footage was being reviewed at trial some two and a half years after the events. I therefore approached with caution any submission — whether by the Prosecution or the Defence — that invited the court to draw precise conclusions from the footage as to the exact duration of a particular interaction, the precise position of a person's hands at a given moment, or the specific sequence of events within a short window of time. That said, where the accused himself conceded contact with VM after the footage was replayed at half speed, those findings rested on his own admissions rather than on the court's independent reading of the footage, and were accordingly on a firmer footing.

107    I also make one further observation about the nature of the Prosecution's case on the CCTV evidence. The Prosecution did not rely on the footage to establish that the touching occurred at any specific timestamp. The charges alleged that the accused touched VM's vagina area on each of the three dates; they did not allege that the touching occurred at any particular moment captured in the footage. The agreed timestamps represent selected moments identified by the parties for the purpose of the trial and, as was apparent from the SOAF, did not purport to be a comprehensive record of every interaction between the accused and VM during each class. It followed that VM's inability to identify the touching as occurring at any specific timestamp — or her uncertainty about whether touching occurred at a particular clip — did not necessarily contradict her evidence that the touching occurred during the class. The question was not whether the touching could be pinpointed to a specific moment in the footage, but whether, on the totality of the evidence, the court was satisfied beyond a reasonable doubt that the touching occurred on each of the three dates. I bore this in mind throughout my analysis of the individual charges.

108    I turn now to address two specific submissions by the Defence concerning the CCTV evidence. First, I rejected the Defence's consolidated submission in its Reply at [30] that the CCTV evidence offered no corroborative evidence to confirm VM's account. The fact that the selected footage does not show the accused's hands touching VM's vagina area did not diminish its corroborative value, for the reasons I have already set out above. Second, I rejected the Defence's submission in its Reply at [43]–[44] that there was no CCTV footage showing VM and VS stopping at the side of the pool to have their conversation on 28 October 2023, and that VS's evidence was therefore of little additional evidential value. The absence of CCTV footage of the conversation did not mean the conversation did not take place. The footage captured only selected timestamps and did not purport to be a comprehensive record of every interaction during the class. VS's evidence was not merely a repetition of VM's complaint. As I explain at [130]–[131] below, I relied on VS's evidence for the specific and limited purposes of corroborating the thumbs-up/thumbs-down signal that VM described, and providing context for the events of 28 October 2023 as regards the allegations relating to VM. I did not rely on it as evidence of the accused's propensity or as similar fact evidence going to his guilt on the charges involving VM.

109    I have borne the above considerations in mind throughout my analysis of the evidence.

110    Having made the above general observations on the CCTV footage, I will set out my analysis of the credibility of the Prosecution’s witnesses, before assessing the accused’s account. I will then analyse each charge in turn to ascertain if the Prosecution had successfully proven its case against the accused beyond a reasonable doubt on each charge.

Assessment of the evidence of the Prosecution witnesses

VM was an unusually convincing witness

111    I found VM to be an unusually convincing witness. Her evidence was clear, consistent, and compelling, and I was satisfied that it bore the ring of truth. In applying the legal standard set out in GII at [25]–[28], I have weighed VM's demeanour alongside both the internal and external consistencies in her testimony, and assessed her evidence against that of the accused, bearing in mind that demeanour alone is an unreliable basis for assessing the credibility of testimony: Sandz Solutions (Singapore) Pte Ltd and others v Strategic Worldwide Assets Ltd and others [2014] 3 SLR 562 ("Sandz") at [46]; AOF v Public Prosecutor [2012] 3 SLR 34 ("AOF") at [115].

112    VM gave a detailed and coherent account of how the accused touched her vagina area on each of the three occasions. The pattern she described was consistent across all three incidents: the accused would position himself behind her while she was standing in the water at the side of the pool after completing laps, and touch her vagina area over her swimming costume, with his hand under the water. She demonstrated the motion as a rubbing action using the dolls in Exhibit P11. The consistency of this account across three separate incidents, and across her evidence in court and her account to Dr Woo, was not the product of rehearsal, but reflected the repetitive nature of the conduct she was describing.

113    A notable feature of VM's evidence was what it did not include, as much as what it did. This was apparent both in her account of the incidents themselves and in her approach to the CCTV footage. On the incidents themselves, VM testified that her first class with the accused on 7 October 2023 was uneventful and she made no complaint about anything that occurred on that occasion. Her complaints were confined to the three subsequent classes on 14, 21 and 28 October 2023. A witness motivated by dislike of the accused or a desire to change coaches would have had every opportunity to include the 7 October 2023 class within the scope of her allegations, and the fact that she did not was a strong indicator that she was reporting what actually happened rather than constructing a false narrative.

114    The same restraint was evident in her approach to the CCTV footage. When shown clips in which the accused was closely behind her with his hands underwater — positions consistent with how the molest occurred — she did not simply assert that the accused must have touched her vagina at those points. Instead, she candidly testified that she did not want to "accuse" when she was not sure, and explained that while she knew the accused had touched her, she was unable to pinpoint specifically when in the footage he did so and did not wish to "anyhow say" (see [36] above). This careful and measured approach to the footage demonstrated that VM was acutely aware of the distinction between what she knew and what she could not be certain of, and that she was not prepared to assert more than she knew to be true even when the footage provided an obvious opportunity to do so. Far from undermining her evidence, this consistent pattern of restraint significantly reinforced her credibility as a witness.

115    VM's evidence was also internally consistent in the way she described her evolving understanding of what was happening to her. She testified candidly that on the first occasion on 14 October 2023, she initially thought the touch might have been accidental, but that it kept going on two to three times. By the second occasion on 21 October 2023, she felt uncomfortable. This progression — from initial uncertainty to growing discomfort — was entirely believable and consistent with the experience of a 10-year-old child who had no prior frame of reference for such conduct. Her candid acknowledgment of her initial uncertainty, far from undermining her credibility, actually reinforced it.

116    I also found VM's conduct during and after the incidents to be consistent with her account and with what one would expect of a child in her circumstances. Rather than immediately raising an alarm or confronting the accused, she first mentioned what had happened to her siblings, VB and VS. After speaking to VS, VM told her father on 29 October 2023. This sequence — an initial tentative disclosure to her siblings, and then escalation to a parent after the conduct recurred — was consistent with the behaviour of a young child who was confused and uncertain about what was happening to her, and who was unsure how adults would respond.

117    In its Reply, the Defence argued that the discrepancy between VM's evidence and VB's evidence on when VM first told VB undermined the Prosecution's case that there was a "natural and incremental pattern of disclosure." I will address the discrepancy between VM's and VB's accounts, and explain my finding that VB's evidence is to be preferred, at [132] below. On VB's version, VM told him after the very first class on 14 October 2023. The Defence argued that this earlier disclosure, made at a time when VM said she did not yet feel uncomfortable and still thought the touching might have been accidental, was more consistent with a fabricated complaint than with a genuine report of abuse. I did not accept this. A child who has just been touched on her vagina by her coach for the first time, and who was uncertain whether it was intentional, may well mention it to an older sibling without fully understanding the gravity of what has happened. VB's response — brushing it off as a possible accident — was entirely consistent with this. The fact that VM only escalated the matter further after the touching recurred was itself consistent with a genuine account rather than a fabricated one. The disclosure pattern, whether on VM's version or VB's version, reflected the behaviour of a confused and uncertain child, not a child with a calculated agenda.

118    The Defence also sought to suggest that VM's motive for making the complaint was her desire to change coaches, given that she had expressed a preference for Coach Desmond. I reject this suggestion, and instead accepted the Prosecution's submission on this point. VM addressed this directly and sensibly in cross-examination, explaining that if she had wanted to change coaches, she would simply have told her parents "straight up". This explanation was entirely credible. Moreover, VF confirmed that prior to 29 October 2023, neither VM nor VS had ever told him that they wanted to change coaches. The Defence's argument was in any event circular: a child who has been repeatedly touched on her vagina by her coach would naturally want to avoid him, and that desire cannot be transformed into evidence of fabrication simply because it coincided with what a false complaint would have achieved.

119    I also rejected the accused's suggestion, made in his own evidence, that VM fabricated the allegations because she disliked him and considered him an irresponsible or poor coach. A generalised dislike of a coach, or dissatisfaction with his coaching style, did not begin to explain why a 10-year-old child would fabricate specific, repeated, and serious allegations of sexual touching, involve her younger sister in the fabrication, and subject herself to a police investigation and court proceedings. Applying the legal framework set out in AOF at [215]–[216] and GCK at [102], where an accused person raises the suggestion that a complainant had a motive to bring false allegations against him, the accused bears an evidential burden to establish that the complainant had a plausible motive to do so — general assertions without more will not ordinarily suffice. The accused's suggestion that VM disliked him and considered him a poor coach was precisely the kind of general and unspecific assertion that fell well short of that threshold.

120    The Defence also sought to undermine VM's credibility by pointing to her uncertainty during cross-examination about specific CCTV clips, where she was unable to confirm whether the accused had touched her in particular clips. For the reasons I have already set out at [114] above, I did not find this uncertainty damaging to her credibility. VM's careful refusal to assert that touching occurred at a particular clip unless she was certain was a hallmark of her reliability, not a weakness in her evidence.

121    As for the Defence's characterisation of VM's evidence as a "recantation" when confronted with the CCTV footage, this was, with respect, a misreading of what occurred. VM's examination-in-chief was that the accused touched her vagina area on multiple occasions during each class. She did not assert that the touching occurred at any specific timestamp. When taken through the footage clip by clip, her answers — that nothing happened at certain clips, and that she was unsure about others — did not contradict her examination-in-chief. A witness who said that she knows the touching occurred during the class but could not pinpoint the exact moment on camera was not recanting her evidence; she was being precise and careful about the limits of what she could say with certainty, particularly given that the touching was brief, had occurred underwater, and the events had taken place more than two years before she testified. The same analysis applied to the second timestamp on 21 October 2023 (at 17:27:51). VM did not assert in her examination-in-chief that the touching occurred at that specific moment, and her subsequent qualification during cross-examination was consistent with her general approach rather than the "internal inconsistency" the Defence characterised it as.

122    Before turning to the corroborative evidence, I address three further points raised by the Defence.

123    First, the Defence submitted that Desmond had never received any complaints about the accused in 13 years, and that it would have been difficult for the accused to molest any student given the number of people present. I did not accept that this casts doubt on VM's account. Desmond's evidence was that his attention during class was focused on his own group of beginner students. He was not monitoring the accused's interactions with his students at all times. His confirmation that he had never personally observed the accused behaving inappropriately was therefore of limited probative value. Desmond's observation that there were "many eyes" in and around the pool during classes also did not assist the accused for the same reason: the presence of other persons in the general vicinity did not mean that the specific, covert, and brief touching described by VM would have been visible to them. The same reasoning applied to the presence of parents at the poolside, members of the public in adjacent lanes, and the absence of prior complaints from other students. The accused's conduct, as described by VM, was inherently covert — the touching always occurred under the water, with his hands concealed from view, in a context where physical contact between a coach and a student was not inherently unusual. The accused himself conceded under cross-examination that underwater outlines could only be seen "not clearly." If the accused — who was in the pool and directly involved in the interaction — accepted that underwater visibility was limited even at close range, the suggestion that swimmers in adjacent lanes several metres away, focused on their own swimming, could have detected the precise movements of his hands at the level of VM's lower body was simply not credible. It was therefore entirely consistent with this modus operandi that other students may not have noticed, or may not have been sufficiently sure of what had occurred to report it.

124    Second, the Defence submitted that VS's evidence was of little additional evidential value. I address VS's evidence in detail below. For present purposes, I note only that VS's evidence was not merely a repetition of VM's complaint. VS independently confirmed that the accused had also touched her vagina. This was relevant not as evidence of the accused's propensity or disposition — I expressly do not rely on it for that purpose, as I have stated at [108] and [130] — but as context for the events of 28 October 2023 and as corroboration of the specific and independently verifiable detail of the thumbs-up/thumbs-down signal that VM described.

125    I also address the Defence's related submission that VM’s disclosure to VB should be treated with circumspection because VM's own evidence showed she did not feel uncomfortable on 14 October 2023 and therefore the disclosure to VB on that date was not a genuine complaint arising from the touching. I rejected this submission for the reasons I have already set out at [117]. In brief, the fact that VM did not yet feel uncomfortable on 14 October 2023 did not mean her disclosure to VB was not genuine. A child who has just been touched on her vagina for the first time, and who was uncertain whether it was intentional, may well mention it to an older sibling without yet feeling the full weight of what has happened. The specificity of the disclosure — using an anatomical term to describe what the accused had done — was far more consistent with a genuine report than with a fabrication motivated by a desire to change coaches.

126    Third, the Defence submitted at DRS at [52] that VM's disclosure to VF did not fall within s 159 of the Evidence Act 1893 because it was not made at or about the time the relevant facts took place, and relied on Khoo Kwoon Hain at [49] for the proposition that s 159 corroboration was self-serving and should not be equated with corroboration in the ordinary sense. While I note that the incident in the third charge occurred just a day before VM spoke to VF, I would also add that VM's disclosure to VF was relevant as part of the overall picture of VM's conduct following the incidents, which was consistent with her account and inconsistent with fabrication. The promptness and spontaneity of the sequence of events on 29 October 2023 — disclosure to VF, confrontation of the accused, and police report all within the same evening — was strongly consistent with a genuine complaint. I will deal further with VF's evidence below.

127    I also address the Defence's overarching submission that the court should first identify whether there is a flaw internal to the Prosecution's case before considering the Defence's case, and that weaknesses in the Defence's case cannot ordinarily shore up what is lacking in the Prosecution's case (citing GCK at [140]). I accept this as a correct statement of the law, and I have applied it. However, the submission presupposed that there was a flaw internal to the Prosecution's case. For the reasons set out in this judgment, I did not find any such flaw. VM's evidence was internally consistent, externally corroborated, and unusually convincing. The Prosecution's case did not depend on the CCTV footage establishing the precise moment of touching; it depended on the totality of the evidence, including VM's account, the corroborating evidence of VS, VB, VF, and Coach Desmond, and the evidence of Dr Woo. The Defence's submission that the Prosecution was "unnecessarily pedantic" in its analysis of the accused's evidence did not assist the accused. The question was not whether the Prosecution's analysis was pedantic, but whether, on the totality of the evidence, the accused's guilt has been proved beyond a reasonable doubt. For the reasons set out in this judgment, it has.

128    In short, my finding that VM was an unusually convincing witness rested not on her demeanour alone, but on the cumulative weight of her internally consistent account, its external consistency with the evidence of VS, VB, and VF, Dr Woo’s evidence, the absence of any credible motive to fabricate, and her careful and restrained approach to the CCTV footage. I accepted her evidence that the accused touched her vagina area on each of the three occasions.

VS, VB, VF and Desmond corroborated VM's account on material particulars

129    Although I have found VM's evidence to be unusually convincing, her evidence was also amply corroborated by the other Prosecution witnesses.

130    As regards VS, VM's younger sister, she confirmed that the accused had also touched her vagina during the class on 28 October 2023. VS’s evidence was relevant for two specific and limited purposes, and I relied on it for those purposes only. I did not rely on it as similar fact evidence going to the accused's propensity or disposition. First, VS's evidence corroborated VM's account of the thumbs-up/thumbs-down signal that the two sisters devised during the class on 28 October 2023. This was a specific and independently verifiable detail of VM's account. Second, VS's evidence was relevant to the context and circumstances of the class on 28 October 2023. It explained why VM devised the signalling system with VS during that class, and it was consistent with VM's account of what occurred between the two sisters on that occasion.

131    I was mindful that VS's memory of the events had faded by the time of trial, and that her memory was refreshed pursuant to s 161 of the Evidence Act. VS confirmed that her memory had been better at the time she gave her statement on 29 October 2023, and her evidence after refreshing her memory was consistent with VM's account on the material points. I also noted that there was no suggestion of any independent motive for VS to have fabricated or embellished her account. She was about nine years old at the time of the alleged events and had no apparent reason to make a false complaint against the accused. Her corroboration of VM's account on the material points therefore carried independent weight.

132    Next, VB provided further corroboration of VM's account.

(a)     VB confirmed that VM had spoken to him about the accused touching her inappropriately near the vagina area, using a word to refer to the private part, and that his initial reaction was that it could have been a mistake or accident.

(b)     There was a discrepancy between VM's and VB's evidence on the date of VM's disclosure to VB. VM testified that she told VB after the class on 28 October 2023, while VB testified that the disclosure was made after the class on 14 October 2023. I preferred VB's evidence on this point. His account was clear and specific: he testified that following VM's disclosure, he began observing the interactions between the accused, VM and VS during the subsequent classes on 21 and 28 October 2023. The events of 29 October 2023 — the disclosure to VF, the phone call to the accused, and the police report — were sufficiently significant that VB would have had reason to anchor his memory of VM's disclosure to the class that preceded them. I accepted the Defence's reasoning on this point.

(c)     I acknowledged that VM's failure to mention in her evidence-in-chief that she had told VB on 14 October 2023 — rather than after the class on 28 October 2023 — was a genuine inconsistency between her evidence and VB's. However, it was an immaterial one. The discrepancy concerned only the date of the disclosure to VB and had no bearing on the facts in issue, namely whether the accused had touched VM's vagina area on 14, 21 and 28 October 2023. The substance of what VM told VB — that the accused had touched her at her private part — was consistent across both accounts. As Yong Pung How CJ observed in Ng Kwee Leong v Public Prosecutor [1998] 3 SLR(R) 281 at [13], an immaterial discrepancy is one that has "no direct bearing on the facts in issue" and has "nothing to do with the question whether it was the [accused] who committed the offence"; the trial judge is "perfectly entitled to find that these discrepancies did not detract from the general veracity of the prosecution witnesses on the material issues." Further, as V K Rajah J (as he then was) observed in Jagatheesan s/o Krishnasamy v Public Prosecutor [2006] 4 SLR(R) 45 at [82], a court is perfectly entitled, notwithstanding minor inconsistencies, to hold that a particular witness is in fact a witness of truth and to accept the other aspects of the witness's testimony which are untainted by discrepancies.

(d)     The discrepancy was in any event entirely understandable. VM was a 10-year-old child recounting events across three consecutive Saturdays, with disclosures made to multiple family members over a short period, some two and a half years before trial.

(e)     I was mindful that on VB's version, he was observing the accused's interactions with VM and VS during the classes on 21 and 28 October 2023 and did not see anything untoward. However, this did not undermine VM's account. VB was a 13-year-old boy watching from within the pool during a swimming class. The accused's conduct, as described by VM, was inherently covert — the touching occurred under the water, lasted only seconds, and took place in a context where some physical contact between a coach and a student was not unusual. It was entirely consistent with this modus operandi that VB, who was not positioned directly beside VM at all material times and who would also have been occupied with his own swimming, would not have detected the touching. VB's own evidence was that he was only closer to VM when he was at the coaching area, and not during laps. Even then, a sibling in the same general area would not necessarily have detected conduct that was, by its very nature, covert and concealed from view.

(f)     In any event, VB's evidence established that VM made a complaint to him on 14 October 2023 itself — the very day of the first incident. A complaint made at the first reasonable opportunity after the commission of an offence may amount to corroboration under s 159 of the Evidence Act: Lee Kwang Peng at [80]. I treated it as such. Critically, the fact that VM disclosed the touching to VB on 14 October 2023, before any of the subsequent incidents had occurred, was difficult to reconcile with any suggestion that her account was shaped by events that came later.

(g)     The Defence submitted in its Reply that the disclosure to VB on 14 October 2023 was not a genuine complaint but was instead influenced by VM's dislike of the accused. I rejected this submission. The Defence itself relied on VB's evidence that VM used a specific anatomical term to describe what the accused had done — language that was inconsistent with a child motivated simply by a desire to change coaches. The specificity and immediacy of the disclosure on the very day of the first incident are far more consistent with a genuine complaint. Moreover, VM's initial reaction was that the touching might have been accidental — was a reaction entirely inconsistent with a calculated plan to make false allegations. A child with such a plan in mind would have had no reason to qualify her disclosure with the suggestion that the touching might not have been intentional.

(h)     As for the Defence's argument that VM's silence after the second class on 21 October 2023 was inconsistent with a genuine complaint, I did not accept this. VM was a 10-year-old child processing repeated and confusing conduct by an adult in a position of authority over her. The law was clear that victims of sexual offences cannot be straitjacketed into an expectation that they must act or react in a particular way: GBR at [20]. VM's decision to act after the third incident — by devising the thumbs-up/thumbs-down signal with VS during the class itself, and then disclosing to VF that same evening — was entirely consistent with a child who was gradually building the certainty and courage needed to escalate the matter. It was wholly inconsistent with a child executing a calculated fabrication, who would have had every reason to complain earlier and more loudly.

133    The evidence of VF and Desmond about the events of 29 October 2023 was also significant. VF testified that when he called the accused and asked whether he had touched or molested his daughters, the accused stuttered and was incoherent, and could not provide a clear answer despite VF raising his voice and demanding a response. This account was corroborated by Desmond, who testified that when he subsequently spoke to the accused and asked what had transpired in his conversation with VF and why VF was insisting on making a police report, the accused told him that he could not remember specifically and clearly whether he had touched the girls or not. Desmond testified that he was surprised by this response, as the accused should have said very convincingly that he did not touch the girls. I found both VF and Desmond to be credible witnesses. Their evidence was internally consistent, mutually corroborative, and unshaken in cross-examination. In particular, in respect of Desmond, who was the accused’s friend, he would have no reason to lie about this aspect of his evidence.

134    This evidence was highly damaging to the accused. An innocent person who had been falsely accused of molesting young girls in his swimming class would be expected to deny the allegation clearly and immediately. The accused's equivocal response to Desmond — that he could not remember whether he had touched the girls — was wholly inconsistent with innocence. It was also inconsistent with the accused's own evidence in court that he had told VF "No" and was shocked by the allegation. If the accused had already clearly denied the allegation to VF, there would have been no reason for him to tell Desmond that he could not remember whether he had touched the girls.

135    I also noted Desmond's evidence about his personal guidelines on physical contact with students — that coaches should only hold students' hands or arms above the water level so that the contact remains visible, and that physical contact under the water should be avoided. This evidence provided important context for assessing the accused's conduct. The accused's repeated positioning of himself behind VM with his hands under the water, as captured in the CCTV footage and as described by VM, was precisely the kind of conduct that Desmond identified as problematic and to be avoided.

Dr Woo's evidence was credible and corroborated VM's account

136    I turn now to the evidence of Dr Woo. She is a senior consultant at the Child Guidance Clinic of the Institute of Mental Health with over two decades of experience as a psychiatrist. I found her to be a credible and reliable expert witness.

137    Dr Woo's assessment of VM was conducted in a structured and methodologically sound manner. She interviewed VM in two parts — with VM's father present only for background questions, and VM alone for the substantive discussion — using an open-ended approach that allowed VM to narrate freely before asking clarifying questions. VM's account was spontaneous, chronological, and consistent, and did not change when clarifying questions were asked.[note: 82]. Importantly, Dr Woo confirmed that although she had read the Summary of Facts prepared by IO Chia before the assessment, she used it only for background purposes and thereafter conducted her own independent interview. This methodology reduced the risk that VM's account was shaped by leading questions or by the Summary of Facts.

138    VM’s account to Dr Woo during the forensic psychiatric assessment on 26 April 2024, some six months after the events, was consistent with her evidence at trial. The core features of her account — the pattern of the accused positioning himself behind her after she completed laps, and touching her vagina area over her swimsuit — were consistent across her testimony in court and her account to Dr Woo.

139    While Dr Woo acknowledged under cross-examination that she could not recall with certainty whether VM had used the word "vagina" or "private part" during the interview, and that her use of the word "vagina" in her clinical notes may have been influenced by the Summary of Facts, this did not undermine the reliability of her assessment. The critical point was not the precise anatomical term VM used, but the body part she was describing. Dr Woo maintained clearly that VM had conveyed to her that the vagina area was the part of the body that had been touched,[note: 83] and this was consistent with VM's own evidence at trial. The terminological uncertainty in the clinical notes went to the precise word recorded, not to the substance of what VM communicated. I accepted Dr Woo's evidence on this point.

140    I now address the Defence's submissions on Dr Woo's evidence together, as they share a common thread: that Dr Woo's assessment was unreliable because it was influenced by the Summary of Facts and that it was too brief. I rejected both submissions.

141    As to the Summary of Facts, the Defence submitted that it was inconsistent with VM's oral testimony and the CCTV timestamps, and that this undermined the reliability of Dr Woo's assessment. I did not accept this. The Summary of Facts was not a verbatim record of VM's account; it was a document prepared by the investigation officer to provide general background before the assessment. It was not prepared by VM, not adopted by her as her own account, and not put to her in cross-examination as a prior inconsistent statement. As such, it could not be used to challenge VM's credibility. Separately, the consistency of VM's account to Dr Woo rested on what VM said during the independent interview, not on what was in the Summary of Facts. Minor differences in detail between a police summary and a witness's oral testimony did not, without more, establish that the oral account was unreliable.

142    As to the duration of the assessment, the Defence submitted that the assessment lasted less than 37 minutes rather than the hour Dr Woo had initially estimated, and that this brevity undermined its reliability. With respect, there was no evidence tendered that the duration of a forensic psychiatric assessment is determinative of its reliability. Further, Dr Woo is an experienced senior consultant who affirmed her opinion on oath and was able to explain and justify her conclusion under cross-examination. I saw no reason not to accept her evidence.

143    I also rejected the Defence's submission that Dr Woo was heavily influenced by the Summary of Facts and VM's demeanour, such that VM may have been repeating a fictional story. This argument was speculative. As explained above, Dr Woo's methodology reduced the risk of contamination from the Summary of Facts, and the consistency of VM's account rested on what VM said during the independent interview. The Defence's argument did not engage with the substance of Dr Woo's evidence and was accordingly rejected.

Assessment of the accused's evidence

144    I have applied the two-stage framework in GII at [27]–[28], which requires first an assessment of whether the Prosecution's case is internally and externally consistent, and second a comparative analysis of the competing accounts on the totality of the evidence. As the Court of Appeal observed in GCK at [144], the Prosecution prevails if, after considering all the evidence, no reasonable doubt remains as to the accused's guilt. For the reasons below, I found the accused's evidence to be unconvincing and unreliable.

The accused's shifting evidence on the CCTV footage

145    The most striking feature of the accused's evidence was his repeated pattern of denying physical contact with VM, only to concede it when the footage was replayed at half speed. I accepted the Prosecution's submission that, unlike VM who was careful not to overstate what the footage showed, the accused's evidence shifted repeatedly when confronted with the objective evidence, and that the irresistible conclusion was that the accused was tailoring explanations to fit the footage only after being confronted with it. This is the hallmark of an untruthful witness.

146    On 21 October 2023, he denied making contact with VM's buttock at the 17:29:18 timestamp — until the footage was replayed, whereupon he conceded the contact and claimed he was rushing her to wear her goggles faster. He agreed this had no legitimate coaching basis. What was particularly telling was that having just denied the contact entirely, he then claimed to "clearly remember" the specific reason for it — an event that took place approximately two and a half years earlier.[note: 84] These two positions were logically irreconcilable: a witness who cannot recall making contact at all cannot credibly claim, in the same breath, a clear and specific memory of why he made it. The inference was irresistible that this explanation was fabricated on the spot.

147    The same pattern repeated itself in respect of the incident on 28 October 2023, where he denied making contact with VM's lower back at the 17:35:32 and 17:35:33 timestamps, again conceding only after the footage was replayed. This was not an isolated lapse of memory. His default position throughout was to deny physical contact with VM unless the footage made denial impossible.

148    Beyond the denials, several of the accused's explanations were positively contradicted by the footage itself:

(a)     At the 17:43:01 timestamp on 21 October 2023, he claimed he had approached VM from behind because he saw her with both hands raised above the water — a sign of possible drowning. When it was pointed out that the two raised hands belonged to two different persons, he could only say that he “couldn’t differentiate if it is from the same person.”[note: 85] An experienced coach of 20 years should have had a clear recollection of what he personally observed. His inability to do so strongly suggested the explanation was constructed after the fact.

(b)     At the 17:47:01 timestamp, he said VM appeared tired and was floating outside the group, so he had to bring her back. When it was pointed out that VM was holding a float and was not in danger, he agreed, but maintained he could not leave her "just floating outside".[note: 86] This was illogical. A student holding a float and not in danger did not require a coach to approach her from behind with his hands under the water.

(c)     At the 17:34:37 timestamp on 28 October 2023, he claimed VM had jumped into the pool, water had splashed on him, he had no time to clean his face, and he had to "save her".[note: 87] This is implausible on its face, and inconsistent with his own evidence that he had simply brought VM up to check she was safe and passed her a board.

(d)     At the 17:33:38 timestamp, he conceded that guiding VM from the front was an available option, but said he guided her from behind because they were close to the starting point and he needed to monitor other students.[note: 88] His own concession that a visible, front-facing approach was possible — but not taken — was consistent with the Prosecution's case that his repeated positioning behind VM was not for coaching purposes.

149    The accused also testified that he would avoid touching the "main body" of a student when teaching. Yet he admitted to regularly tickling students at the waist or belly button area, explaining this as a form of discipline. This admission was not made in a vacuum. Multiple students in the class independently confirmed in their statements — recorded in the SOAF at pages 15, 16, 17 and 18 — that the accused had tickled them during lessons. In particular, the first student (SOAF, Annex 2(a), p. 15) stated that the accused tickled his feet; the second student (SOAF, Annex 2(b), p. 16) stated that he had observed the accused tickling other students, though he could not recall who or where; and the third student (SOAF, Annex 2(c), pp. 17–18) stated that the accused would tickle him and his sister on the stomach after they finished their laps, that this lasted a few seconds, that the accused did this to others in the class as well, and that he found it unusual because Coach Desmond never did that. The fact that multiple students independently found the tickling unusual was significant: it confirmed that the accused's physical contact with students in the waist area was not a one-off incident but a pattern of behaviour that was perceived by the students themselves as going beyond what was normal or expected of a coach.

150    The Defence relied on these same statements to suggest that the accused's physical contact with students was merely playful in nature, and that the absence of any complaint about inappropriate touching of private parts from the other students was consistent with the accused's denial. I did not accept this argument for three reasons.

(a)     First, the tickling described by the third student (SOAF, Annex 2(c), pp. 17–18) and the first student (SOAF, Annex 2(a), p. 15) involved the stomach and feet respectively — body parts entirely different from the vagina area. The fact that the accused engaged in uninvited physical contact with students in those areas did not make it less likely that he also touched VM's vagina area. The two categories of conduct were not mutually exclusive. If anything, the tickling evidence pointed in the opposite direction from what the Defence suggested: it established that the accused was willing to initiate unnecessary and uninvited physical contact with students in areas he himself said he would avoid, and that multiple students independently found this conduct unusual precisely because Coach Desmond never behaved in that way. This was not the profile of a coach who scrupulously observed appropriate boundaries with his students.

(b)     Second, the other students' statements established only that those particular students did not personally experience or observe inappropriate touching of their private parts. This was neutral evidence at best. The accused's conduct towards VM, as she described it, was inherently covert — it occurred under the water, lasted only seconds, and took place in a context where some physical contact between a coach and a student was not unusual. It was entirely consistent with this modus operandi that other students in the class would not have noticed, or would not have been sufficiently certain of what they had seen to report it. The absence of complaints from other students therefore carried little weight.

(c)     Third, and most fundamentally, the Defence's argument tried to prove too much. If the absence of complaints from other students was treated as evidence that the accused did not touch VM's vagina area, it would effectively require corroboration from other victims before any aspect of complainant's evidence could be accepted. That was not the law. VM's evidence stood on its own merits and must be assessed on its own terms, having regard to its internal consistency, its external corroboration, and the overall credibility of her account — all of which I have addressed above.

151    Moreover, the accused's admission to tickling students was significant on two counts. First, it showed the accused was prepared to initiate unnecessary physical contact in areas he said he would avoid. The accused's own admission that he tickled students at the waist or belly button area — and that multiple students independently found this unusual precisely because Desmond never did so — confirmed that the tickling served no legitimate coaching purpose. Second, the waist area was precisely the area from which he could reach VM's vagina. An accused who admitted to regular contact at the waist, and who conceded contact with VM's buttock and lower back only when the footage left him no choice, could not credibly insist that he never touched VM's vagina area, whether deliberately or accidentally. This conclusion was reinforced by the accused's own definition of the 'main body' as the area from below the chin to the upper thighs — a definition that plainly encompassed the waist and belly button, and that made his assurance that he would never touch a student's private parts all the more difficult to believe.

152    Separately, the accused's claim that it was "almost impossible" for him to have touched VM's vagina area due to the height difference between them was equally unconvincing. The pool depth at the starting point was 1.2 metres. He adduced no evidence of his own height or VM's height, and pointed to nothing in the footage to support his assertion. On the contrary, the footage at the 17:29:22 and 17:34:37 timestamps on 28 October 2023 showed him positioned directly behind VM with his hands under the water at the level of her waist and lower body — precisely the position VM described. I accepted the Prosecution's submission that the footage showed it was indeed physically possible for his hand to reach VM's vagina area while underwater.

153    On underwater visibility, the accused insisted that members of the public swimming in adjacent lanes — more than 6 metres away — would still have been able to see what his hands were doing underwater. However, he himself conceded that underwater outlines could only be seen "not clearly." The suggestion that swimmers at that distance, focused on their own swimming, could detect the precise movements of his hands at the level of VM's lower body was simply not credible.

154    In short, the accused's case was that the alleged touching was either physically impossible or would inevitably have been detected. I rejected both. As I have repeatedly noted, the touching occurred under the water, lasted only seconds, and took place in a context where some physical contact between a coach and a student was not unusual. It was inherently covert by design. The accused's categorical denial that he had never touched VM's vagina area, whether deliberately or accidentally, sat uneasily with his concessions regarding contact with VM's buttock and lower back, and his admission to regular contact at the waist — all areas in close proximity to VM's vagina, and all conceded only when the footage left him no room to deny. The absoluteness of his denial, in the face of these concessions, was a further and telling indicator of his unreliability as a witness.

The accused's conduct after the alleged offences

155    The accused's response when first confronted with the allegations was also telling. VF testified that when he called the accused and asked whether he had touched his daughters, the accused stuttered and was incoherent, and could not provide a clear answer despite VF raising his voice and demanding a response. VM similarly recalled that the accused could not answer and was "stuttering." The accused's own evidence was that he told VF "No" and was shocked.

156    These accounts could not be reconciled. If the accused had already clearly denied the allegation to VF, there would have been no reason for him to tell Desmond "I don't know" moments later. The accounts of VF, VM and Desmond together painted a consistent picture of an accused who, when first confronted, was unable to deny the allegation clearly. His attempt in court to characterise his response as a clear "No" was a further indicator of his unreliability.

157    The Defence submitted that the accused's incoherence when confronted by VF was explicable by shock, and that any innocent person suddenly accused of a serious offence would naturally be flustered. In support of this, the Defence relied on VF's own evidence that he had been angry, had raised his voice, and had demanded answers from the accused.

158    I rejected this explanation. The accused's subsequent response to Desmond — his colleague and a person with whom he would have been comfortable — was equally equivocal. When Desmond asked him about the allegations, the accused said "I don't know." A man who had just clearly denied the allegation to VF moments earlier would naturally have repeated that denial to his colleague. He did not. The accused's inability or unwillingness to do so went beyond what shock could explain, and was more consistent with consciousness of guilt. I accepted the Prosecution's submission on this point. As I have found above at [133]–[135], Desmond was a credible witness with no motive to falsely implicate the accused, and his evidence was consistent with VF's account. Had the accused truly not touched VM's vagina area — and could not even have done so accidentally, as he contended — one would have expected him to respond to Desmond with an immediate and unequivocal denial. His failure to do so was telling. I relied on the accused's equivocal conduct on the evening of 29 October 2023, and his evidence in court about the encounter, not as an independent basis for conviction, but as part of the holistic assessment of the evidence, in support of VM's account and the other corroborating evidence: GCK at [141].

159    I also noted a further instance of the accused providing a misleading account to the authorities in circumstances where disclosure of the truth would have been against his interests. In his recorded statement of 3 November 2023, his explanation for not disclosing VF's complaint — that he thought the investigating officer was asking about complaints relating to how the swimming lessons were conducted, and not about the molest allegations — was implausible, especially since he had known for five days that VF had accused him of molesting his daughters and had made a police report. This was a further indicator of an accused who was willing to present a misleading picture to the authorities when the truth was inconvenient.

160    I note further that in the same statement, the accused told the police he had a valid coaching licence without disclosing that his National Registry of Coaches ("NROC") membership had lapsed during the COVID-19 period and had not been renewed as of October 2023. This was relevant not to the charges themselves, but to the accused's general candour with the authorities. Taken together with his failure to disclose VF's complaint when asked about complaints in his recorded statement, it formed part of a consistent pattern of the accused presenting a misleading picture to the authorities when the truth was inconvenient. I did not rely on it as an independent basis for any adverse finding, but noted it as part of the holistic assessment of the accused's credibility.

161    For all the above reasons, I reject the accused's evidence on all material issues, including his denial of the charges and his bare assertion that VM had fabricated the allegations against him. Having set out my views on the overall assessment of the witnesses and the accused, I now turn to focus on each individual charge.

Analysis of the First Charge — 14 October 2023

162    The first charge alleged that on 14 October 2023, the accused touched VM's vagina area at Heartbeat @ Bedok Swimming Complex.

163    VM's evidence was that after swimming a couple of laps, she was standing in the water at the side of the pool when the accused came up behind her and touched her vagina. She initially thought it was an accident, as his hands may have accidentally touched her private part, but the touching recurred. She described the accused as standing behind her while she faced the opposite direction, with their bodies touching, and demonstrated the touch as a rubbing motion on the vagina area of the female doll using Exhibit P11.

164    The CCTV footage for 14 October 2023 showed the accused swimming underwater towards VM at 17:34:39, and at 17:47:26, the accused being positioned behind VM and appearing to guide her freestyle stroke using both hands. While the footage does not show the accused's hands touching VM's vagina area — the touch having occurred under the water — the footage was consistent with VM's account of the accused repeatedly positioning himself behind her during the class.

165    I rejected the Defence's submission that VM's concessions during cross-examination on the CCTV footage amounted to a recantation of her examination-in-chief, and that the footage did not corroborate her account. For the reasons I have set out above in [103], [120] and [121], VM's inability to identify the touching at any specific timestamp does not contradict her evidence that the touching occurred during the class, and her careful and restrained approach to the footage was a hallmark of her reliability, not a weakness in her evidence.

166    I also rejected the Defence's submission that the accused could not have committed the offence around the 17:47:26 timestamp because he was behind VM for only six seconds and was occupied with guiding both her arms. The material issue was that the charge did not allege that the touching occurred at this or any other specific timestamp. The Defence's argument therefore missed the mark: the question was not whether the accused could have committed the offence within the six seconds captured at this timestamp, but whether the totality of the evidence established that he touched VM's vagina area during the class on 14 October 2023. In any event, as I have set out at [106] above, the underwater positioning provided both the opportunity and the concealment to commit the act without detection, and the accused's hands were not continuously occupied in the manner the Defence suggested. Further, as Desmond had confirmed, a coach guides each arm in sequence through the catch, pull and push phase, meaning that one hand is periodically free. The Defence's premise that both hands were simultaneously occupied throughout the entire interaction was therefore not borne out by the evidence.

167    I further rejected the Defence's submission that VM's evidence was internally inconsistent on the question of when she first realised the touching was not accidental. At its core, this argument conflated two distinct things: the date of the first touching, and the date from which VM felt uncomfortable. These are not the same. VM's evidence was that she initially thought the first touch on 14 October 2023 was accidental, and it was only when the touching recurred on 21 October 2023 that she felt uncomfortable and knew it was not accidental.[note: 89] Both passages relied upon by the Defence speak to when VM felt uncomfortable, not to when the touching first occurred, and were therefore entirely consistent with her account. The reference to "28 October 2023" in her evidence-in-chief was, as the Defence itself acknowledged in its Reply at [73], likely a misstatement for 21 October 2023 — a minor date confusion of the kind I have addressed in [132] above.

168    VM's account was also corroborated by VB's evidence that she told him after the class, near the exit of the swimming complex, that the accused had been touching her at her private part. This contemporaneous disclosure on the very day of the incident is significant. VB's initial reaction — that it could have been a mistake or accident — mirrored VM's own evidence that she initially thought the touch might have been accidental. The fact that VM made this disclosure before any subsequent incident had occurred made it impossible to suggest that her account was a fabrication constructed after the fact (see [132(f)] above).

169    For all the reasons set out above, I was satisfied beyond a reasonable doubt that the accused touched VM's vagina area on 14 October 2023 as alleged. The foundation of this finding was VM's testimony, which I have found to be unusually convincing for the reasons set out above. Her account of the first incident was internally consistent: she described the accused positioning himself behind her after she had swum laps, touching her vagina area, and her initial uncertainty about whether it was accidental — an uncertainty that was entirely understandable in a 10-year-old child experiencing this for the first time. The CCTV footage was consistent with her general account of the accused's modus operandi, showing him repeatedly positioning himself behind her in the pool during the class. The Defence's submission that the footage makes it impossible for the accused to have touched VM at the sixth timestamp has been addressed and rejected above. For completeness, VM’s account was also corroborated in the manner described above.

Analysis of the Second Charge — 21 October 2023

170    The second charge alleged that on 21 October 2023, the accused again touched VM's vagina area at Heartbeat @ Bedok Swimming Complex.

171    VM's evidence was that the same thing happened again — after swimming laps and resting at the side, the accused went behind her and touched her vagina in the same position as before. By this occasion, she felt uncomfortable. She said the accused touched her vagina two to three times during this class.

172    The CCTV footage showed the accused in close physical proximity to VM at multiple points during the class on 21 October 2023. Significantly, as I have noted in [146] above, he denied making contact with VM's buttock at the 17:29:18 timestamp — contact he conceded only after the footage was replayed at half speed and which he agreed had no legitimate coaching justification. This concession was consistent with VM's evidence that the accused was using the swimming lesson as an opportunity to make inappropriate physical contact with her, and provides objective support for the finding that his repeated positioning behind VM was not for legitimate coaching purposes.

173    The Defence submitted that VM's evidence on the 17:27:51 timestamp was internally inconsistent, in that she did not mention in examination-in-chief that the accused had touched her vagina at that point, and only raised this during cross-examination before qualifying her answer. I did not accept that this undermined her account. The material question was whether VM's core evidence — that the accused touched her vagina two to three times during the class — remained consistent throughout, and it did. Her qualification of her answer at the 17:27:51 timestamp reflected the same careful regard for accuracy that I have addressed at [120] and [121] above, and does not amount to an internal inconsistency.

174    VM also testified that at the 17:47:01 timestamp, she kicked the accused away because she felt his hands below her waist and felt uncomfortable, and that she had told her father about this. This reaction was entirely consistent with her evidence of growing discomfort and is corroborative of her account.

175    I rejected the Defence's submissions that Desmond's proximity at the 17:43:01 timestamp made it less likely that the accused could have touched VM inappropriately, and that the drowning explanation was not impossible. As I have explained in [53] and [123] above, Desmond's attention was focused on his own group of students and his physical proximity is therefore of no assistance to the accused. As for the drowning explanation, I have addressed this in [148(a)] above: the accused's inability to identify whether it was one student who had both hands raised, or whether each of the two raised hands belonged to different people, strongly suggested the explanation was constructed after the fact, and I did not accept it as credible in the context of his overall pattern of conduct.

176    I also reject the Defence's submission that VM's failure to assert in her evidence-in-chief that the touching occurred at the sixth timestamp undermines her account, and the broader submission that VM's inability to identify a single timestamp across all three dates at which she could say with certainty that the touching occurred means her evidence is not unusually convincing. Both submissions are addressed and rejected at [120] and [121] above.

177    All in all, I was satisfied beyond a reasonable doubt that the accused touched VM's vagina area on 21 October 2023 as alleged. The second charge was accordingly proved.

Analysis of the Third Charge — 28 October 2023

178    The third charge alleged that on 28 October 2023, the accused again touched VM's vagina area at Heartbeat @ Bedok Swimming Complex.

179    VM's evidence was that after completing a set of laps, the accused again touched her vagina in the same manner, three to four times. It was during this class that VM spoke to VS, confirmed that VS had also been touched by the accused, and devised the thumbs-up/thumbs-down signal with her.

180    The CCTV footage showed the accused in close physical proximity to VM at multiple points during the class on 28 October 2023, including holding VM at her waist at 17:35:19 and carrying her up to the wall at 17:35:22. As I have noted in [147] above, the accused conceded contact with VM's lower back only after the footage was replayed at half speed, and his explanation — that he was rushing her to wear her goggles faster — had no legitimate coaching basis. This reflects his general tendency to offer after-the-fact justifications for physical contact with VM that he could not deny, justifications which I did not accept.

181    I also rejected the Defence's submission that it was physically impossible for the accused to have touched VM's vagina at the second timestamp on 28 October 2023 because his hands were occupied holding VM's hands to teach her the freestyle stroke. The accused's own evidence on this point was: "I'm holding her hand, how to touch her vagina?"[note: 90] This argument rested on the premise that the accused was holding both of VM's hands simultaneously throughout the entire interaction, but this was not borne out by the evidence. Desmond confirmed that a coach guides each arm in sequence through the catch, pull and push phase, meaning one of the accused's hands was periodically free and underwater in close proximity to VM's lower body. As I have explained at [104] and [166] above, the underwater positioning of the accused's hands during freestyle coaching provided both the opportunity and the concealment to commit the act that VM described.

182    I also rejected the Defence's submission that Desmond's proximity at the second timestamp made the commission of the offence highly improbable, and that VM's uncertainty at that timestamp undermined her account. The significance of Desmond's proximity has been addressed at [175] above. VM's uncertainty at the second timestamp is addressed at [120] and [121] above and did not undermine her account for the reasons set out there.

183    I also rejected the Defence's arguments concerning the third timestamp (17:34:37). As I had noted at [148(c)] above, the accused's explanation — that he brought VM up to check on her after she jumped in and then passed her the swimming board — was implausible and inconsistent with his own evidence. It did not preclude the opportunity to touch her vagina area in the process, and reflects the same general tendency to offer post-hoc justifications for physical contact with VM that I have addressed throughout. VM's uncertainty at this timestamp did not undermine her account for the reasons set out at [120] and [121] above.

184    The third charge was further corroborated by VS's evidence. VS confirmed, after refreshing her memory, that on 28 October 2023, the accused had touched her vagina while she was floating. As I have explained at [130] above, I relied on VS's evidence for the specific and limited purposes of corroborating the thumbs-up/thumbs-down signal that VM described, and providing context for the events of 28 October 2023. On these two specific points, VS's evidence provided direct and independent corroboration of VM's account of the third incident.

185    I was satisfied beyond a reasonable doubt that the accused touched VM's vagina area on 28 October 2023 as alleged. The third charge was accordingly proved.

186    In summary, for the reasons set out above, I found VM to be an unusually convincing witness whose evidence was amply corroborated by VS, VB, VF, and Desmond. I rejected the accused's evidence as unreliable. I was satisfied that the Prosecution had proven its case beyond a reasonable doubt on all three charges. The accused was accordingly found guilty and convicted on all three charges.

Sentencing Preliminaries

187    I will now turn to sentencing.

Prescribed penalties and antecedents

188    Each of the three charges under s 354(1) of the Penal Code 1871, punishable under s 354(2), was punishable with imprisonment for a term not exceeding five years, or fine, or caning, or any combination of such punishments.

189    The accused has no prior criminal antecedents.

Prosecution's submissions on sentence

190    The Prosecution submitted that the applicable sentencing framework was the three-step framework established in GBR and affirmed by the Court of Appeal in BRJ v Public Prosecutor [2020] 1 SLR 849 ("BRJ"). The Prosecution submitted that the present case fell within Band 2 of the GBR framework, at the lower to middle end, and sought a primary sentence of 15 to 18 months' imprisonment and three to four strokes of the cane per charge. The Prosecution had no objections to running only two sentences consecutively, and agreed that the totality principle may be engaged to arrive at an overall sentence of 24 to 30 months' imprisonment and three to six strokes of the cane, translating to 12 to 15 months' imprisonment and one to two strokes of the cane per charge after the totality adjustment (see [35] of Prosecution’s Sentencing Submissions).

191    On the offence-specific factors, the Prosecution highlighted the following. First, the touching in each instance was directed at the victim's vagina area. While the contact was over her swimming costume and did not involve skin-to-skin contact with her private parts, it was repeated multiple times within each class and across three consecutive Saturdays. Second, the accused was the victim's swimming coach and was in a position of responsibility towards her, making the abuse of trust a significant aggravating factor. Third, the victim was 10 years old at the material time, materially younger than the 14-year age ceiling in s 354(2) of the Penal Code. Fourth, the victim suffered psychological harm as a result of the accused's conduct, having been diagnosed by Dr Woo with adjustment disorder, and having experienced fear, anger, insomnia, nightmares, recurrent intrusive thoughts, fear of males, being easily startled, and difficulty focusing in class.

192    On the offender-specific factors, the Prosecution submitted that the accused claimed trial and showed no remorse throughout the proceedings. His clean record was a neutral factor.

Mitigation

193    The Defence tendered written submissions on sentencing dated 17 July 2026. In those submissions, the Defence raised three matters.

(a)     First, the Defence submitted that the touch was fleeting and over her clothes.

(b)     Second, that the accused is untraced and that this is his first offence.

(c)     Third, the Defence tendered a medical report from Ng Teng Fong General Hospital (Exhibit D1), which stated that the accused has hypertension, diabetes mellitus, hyperlipidaemia, acute ischaemic stroke, ischaemic heart disease and stage 2 chronic kidney disease.

194    The Defence also tendered four sentencing precedents, namely PP v ABO [2016] SGDC 80 ("ABO"), PP v GDC [2020] SGDC 57 ("GDC"), PP v GFL [2023] SGDC 38 ("GFL"), and PP v GHI [2023] SGDC 295 ("GHI"), and submitted that the appropriate sentence was 12 months' imprisonment and three strokes of the cane per charge, with two charges running consecutively and one concurrently, for what the Defence submitted to be a global sentence of 24 months' imprisonment and six strokes of the cane. I address these cases in my decision below.

195    At the outset, I note that strokes of the cane are not subject to the concurrent/consecutive framework that applied to imprisonment terms. Where an accused is convicted of multiple charges and caning is imposed on more than one charge, the strokes are cumulative and are served in aggregate, subject to the statutory maximum of 24 strokes under s 328(6) of the Criminal Procedure Code 2010. The concurrent/consecutive distinction applies only to imprisonment terms by virtue of s 307(1) of the Criminal Procedure Code 2010.

Court's Decision on Sentence

196    I now deal with the sentencing proper, starting with the applicable sentencing framework.

Applicable sentencing framework

197    There was no dispute between the parties that the applicable sentencing framework is the three-step GBR framework. I applied that framework in determining the appropriate sentence for each of the three charges.

Step 1: Offence-specific factors

198    I agreed with the Prosecution that there were multiple offence-specific aggravating factors present in this case.
