199    On the degree of sexual exploitation, the accused touched the victim's vagina area on each of the three occasions. While there was no skin-to-skin contact with her private parts, it was not fleeting as described by the Defence. Moreover, the conduct was repeated multiple times within each class and across three consecutive Saturdays. The repetitive and deliberate nature of his actions elevated the degree of exploitation beyond what would be expected of a single, momentary act.

200    There was also a significant element of deception and concealment. The accused exploited the cover of the water to conceal his conduct from the other persons present in and around the pool. As I found in the conviction analysis above, the touching was inherently covert by design — it occurred under the water, and took place in a context where some physical contact between a coach and a student was not inherently unusual. This deliberate exploitation of the cover of the water as a means of concealment was an aggravating feature of the circumstances of the offence.

201    Further, there was a clear abuse of a position of trust. The accused was the victim's swimming coach. The victim was in his charge during the lesson, in the water, and dependent on him for instruction and safety. The trust reposed in him by the victim and her family was a direct enabler of the offending. As the Court observed in GBR at [29(c)], the abuse of a position of trust is a significant aggravating factor, and the present case fell squarely within the category of cases where the accused was in a position of responsibility towards the victim by virtue of his office or employment.

202    The victim was also a particularly vulnerable victim. She was 10 years old at the material time, four years below the stipulated age ceiling of 14 years in s 354(2) of the Penal Code. As the court in GBR observed at [29(f)], the aggravating factor of young age applies in a graduated manner depending on how much younger the victim was than the stipulated age ceiling. A victim who was four years below the ceiling was materially younger, and I gave appropriate weight to this factor. The victim's vulnerability was further compounded by the fact that she was in the water during the offences and was in no position to easily extricate herself from the accused's conduct.

203    Finally, the victim suffered psychological harm as a result of the accused's conduct. Dr Woo diagnosed her with adjustment disorder, and testified that she had experienced fear, anger, insomnia, nightmares, recurrent thoughts about the abuse, fear of males, being easily startled, and difficulty focusing in class. While these symptoms had been gradually decreasing by the time of Dr Woo's assessment approximately six months after the events, the harm caused to a 10-year-old child by repeated sexual touching by a trusted adult was not to be minimised.

Step 2: Indicative sentencing band and calibration against precedents

204    Taking the offence-specific factors together, I was satisfied that this case fell within Band 2 of the GBR framework. As noted above, there were multiple aggravating factors: the touching was directed at the victim's vagina area, the conduct was repeated across three separate occasions and multiple times within each class, there was an abuse of a position of trust, the victim was materially younger than the stipulated age ceiling, and there was deliberate exploitation of the cover of water to conceal the conduct. The absence of skin-to-skin contact with the victim's private parts placed the case at the lower to middle end of Band 2, rather than the higher end.

205    I considered the sentencing precedents cited by both parties. The Prosecution relied on PP v Nawas Khan bin Kassim [2020] SGDC 250 ("Nawas Khan") (appeal withdrawn), PP v GEE [2022] SGDC 14 ("GEE") (appeal withdrawn), PP v JDM [2025] SGDC 39 ("JDM") (appeal against conviction dismissed; appeal against sentence allowed), PP v CGA [2024] SGHC 131 ("CGA") (appeal dismissed), and PP v BNO [2018] SGHC 243 ("BNO") (appeal dismissed). The Defence relied on ABO, GDC, GFL, and GHI. I address these cases in turn.

206    In Nawas Khan, a 60-year-old male offender pleaded guilty to one charge of using criminal force on a 13-year-old female victim by touching her left thigh and rubbing her vagina over her pants with his right hand, before attempting to slip his hand inside her pants. The accused also gave the victim $50 and told her not to tell anyone. The court imposed a sentence of 18 months' imprisonment and three strokes of the cane. As the accused was above 50 years of age and therefore exempt from caning, the court further imposed an additional two months' imprisonment in lieu of the three strokes of caning, for a total sentence of 20 months' imprisonment. The present case warranted a sentence in a similar range. The touching here was over the victim's swimming costume, whereas the accused in Nawas Khan rubbed the victim's vagina over her pants and then attempted to slip his hand inside. The accused in Nawas Khan also compounded his offending by giving the victim money to buy her silence. Notwithstanding this, the present case involves its own significant features: the accused exploited the concealment of the water, the victim was younger (10 years old compared to 13 years old), and the accused did not plead guilty.

207    In GEE, the offender was convicted after trial of two charges of outrage of modesty and one charge of attempted outrage of modesty under s 354(2) of the Penal Code against a 12-year-old boy. The most serious charge involved skin-on-skin touching of the victim's penis, which attracted a sentence of 24 months' imprisonment and three strokes of the cane. The charge of tapping the penis over the shorts attracted 12 months' imprisonment, and the charge of attempting to touch his penis over his shorts attracted six months' imprisonment, for a total of 30 months' imprisonment and three strokes of the cane. The present case involved touching over clothing without skin-to-skin contact, and the present case was consistent with the lower end of the range in GEE for charges involving touching over clothing.

208    In JDM, the offender was convicted after trial of three charges under s 354(2) of the Penal Code against a female victim who was between 10 and 13 years old. The individual sentences ranged from four months' imprisonment for the first charge of slapping the victim's buttock once over her clothes, to 24 months' imprisonment (reduced to 21 months on appeal) for the second charge of pressing his penis against the victim's body over clothing, and six months' imprisonment for the third charge of touching the victim's stomach skin-on-skin, for a total of 30 months' imprisonment (reduced to 27 months on appeal). The present case was broadly comparable in terms of the nature of the touching — both involve contact with or near the victim's private parts over clothing, without skin-to-skin contact, and the present case was consistent with the lower end of the range in JDM.

209    In CGA, the offender rubbed the victim's vagina skin-on-skin with his fingers while she was sleeping. The court imposed two years' imprisonment and three strokes of the cane after accounting for the offender's plea of guilt. The present case was less serious than CGA in several respects: the touching was over clothing rather than skin-on-skin, and the abuse in CGA spanned years with eight charges taken into consideration. The present case was appropriately calibrated below the sentence in CGA.

210    In BNO, the offender faced, among other charges, a charge of touching a nine-year-old male victim's penis skin-on-skin. The court found the case within the middle to higher end of Band 2 and agreed with the Prosecution that the indicative starting point should be two years' imprisonment and three strokes of the cane. The present case involved touching over clothing without skin-to-skin contact, and the present case sat appropriately below the sentence in BNO.

211    I turn now to the four Defence cases.

212    In ABO, the offender pleaded guilty to three charges involving his 10 to 11-year-old stepdaughter. The sentences were enhanced on appeal: see GBR at [33]. The first charge involved touching the victim's vagina and buttocks over her shorts, for which 18 months' imprisonment was imposed on appeal. The second charge involved rubbing his penis over her shorts at her vagina area, for which 21 months' imprisonment and three strokes of the cane were imposed on appeal. The most serious third charge involved skin-to-skin contact — the rubbing of the accused's exposed and erect penis against the victim's vagina — for which two years' imprisonment and three strokes of the cane were imposed on appeal. The present case was broadly comparable to the first charge in ABO in terms of the absence of skin-to-skin contact and the targeting of the victim's vagina area. I noted that the offender in ABO had pleaded guilty, which would have ordinarily attracted a sentencing discount not available to the present accused who claimed trial. This distinction, if anything, supported rather than undermined the sentence I intended to impose.

213    In GDC, the charge involved the offender touching the victim's left breast under her bra (skin-on-skin) for about one minute, pulling her hair and forcing her head towards his groin, and slapping her face twice when she resisted. This was a charge under s 354A(2)(b) of the Penal Code — the aggravated form of outrage of modesty involving the voluntary causing of hurt to facilitate the commission of the offence. On appeal, the offender was convicted on an amended charge and sentenced to two years' imprisonment and three strokes of the cane. GDC was of limited assistance to the present case. It involved a different and more serious provision (s 354A(2)(b) rather than s 354(2)), skin-to-skin contact, the use of force, and a significantly higher degree of sexual exploitation. The present charges under s 354(2) involved touching over clothing without any use of force, and were materially less serious than the offence in GDC. I accordingly give GDC little weight in calibrating the sentence here.

214    In GFL, the offender was convicted after trial and was sentenced to 18 months' imprisonment and three strokes of the cane. The charge involved the accused pulling the victim towards him on the sofa twice, causing his genital area to touch the victim's genital area over clothing. The degree of sexual exploitation was moderate — not prolonged but neither fleeting — and the contact between their respective private parts was fairly intrusive as it simulated the act of sexual intercourse. The present case is less serious than GFL in one material respect: the contact in GFL involved the accused's own genital area pressing against the victim's genital area, which is a more intrusive form of contact than the touching of the victim's vagina area with the accused's hand over her swimming costume in the present case.

215    In GHI, the offender was a tutor who claimed trial to one charge of outrage of modesty under s 354(2) of the Penal Code. The victim was 10 years old at the material time. The charge involved the offender touching the victim's right breast, placing his hand on her left thigh, touching her crotch area, and kissing the back of her neck. The contact on her breast was prolonged, less than five minutes by the victim's estimation. The court found the offender to be in a position of trust as the victim's tutor and that the level of intrusion was significant. As the offender was above 50 years of age and exempt from caning, the court imposed 14 months' imprisonment and an additional two months' imprisonment in lieu of three strokes of the cane, for a total of 16 months' imprisonment. The present case shared the key features of GHI: a 10-year-old victim, an abuse of a position of trust by a person in charge of the victim's instruction, and touching of the victim's private area over clothing without skin-to-skin contact. The offender in GHI was, however, exempt from caning by reason of age, which resulted in an enhancement of two months' imprisonment in lieu of caning. The present accused was not exempt from caning.

Step 3: Offender-specific factors

216    The accused has no prior criminal antecedents. This was a neutral factor and did not operate as a mitigating factor.

217    The accused claimed trial and has shown no remorse throughout these proceedings. He maintained a bare denial, sought to impugn the victim's credibility by suggesting she had fabricated the allegations in order to change coaches — a motive I rejected entirely in the conviction analysis above — and put the victim through the ordeal of testifying in court. He was not entitled to any sentencing discount for a plea of guilt.

218    I turn to the medical evidence tendered by the Defence. The accused's conditions — acute ischaemic stroke, ischaemic heart disease, diabetes mellitus, hyperlipidaemia, and stage 2 chronic kidney disease — are serious and I do not minimise them. However, they do not warrant any reduction in sentence or the exercise of judicial mercy.

219    On judicial mercy, the applicable principles are set out in Chew Soo Chun v Public Prosecutor [2016] SGHC 6 ("Chew Soo Chun") at [22], where the court held that judicial mercy had been exercised in two situations: where the offender was suffering from a terminal illness, and where the offender was so ill that a sentence of imprisonment would carry a high risk of endangering his life. Neither situation was present here. The medical report confirmed that the accused's conditions are chronic and are being actively managed with medications and rehabilitation. There was no evidence that they are terminal or that imprisonment would endanger his life. Judicial mercy does not apply.

220    On whether the accused's medical conditions constitute a mitigating factor — a conceptually distinct question — the court in Chew Soo Chun at [34] held that the relevant question was whether imprisonment would give rise to a real likelihood of significant deterioration in the offender's health or a significant exacerbation of his pain and suffering. Even where such an impact might otherwise arise, the court held at [39] that the conditions would be a neutral factor if the prison has the capability of addressing them to an acceptable standard, or if the consequences would transpire independently of whether the offender is in or outside prison. In the present case, there was nothing to show that the Singapore Prison Service could not manage the accused's conditions, and no such allegation had been made. There was therefore insufficient evidence to establish a real likelihood of significant deterioration in his health by reason of imprisonment. His medical conditions accordingly carried no mitigating weight.

Calibration of the individual sentences

221    Having regard to the offence-specific and offender-specific factors set out above, I agreed with the Prosecution's primary per-charge position of 15 months' imprisonment and two strokes of the cane, which places the case at the lower to middle end of Band 2 of the GBR framework.

Consecutive sentences and the totality principle

222    By virtue of s 307(1) of the Criminal Procedure Code 2010, at least two of the imprisonment terms must be ordered to run consecutively. The Prosecution had no objections to running only two of the sentences consecutively, and I agreed that this was the appropriate course.

223    I considered the totality principle as set out in Mohamed Shouffee bin Adam v PP [2014] 2 SLR 998 ("Shouffee") and PP v Raveen Balakrishnan [2018] 5 SLR 799 ("Raveen"). The totality principle encompasses two limbs. The first limb is that the aggregate sentence should not be substantially above the normal level of sentences for the most serious of the individual offences committed: Shouffee at [54]. The second limb considers whether the effect of the sentence on the offender is crushing and not in keeping with his past record and his future prospects: Shouffee at [57].

224    As a general rule, an offender who has committed multiple unrelated offences should be separately punished for each offence, and this should be achieved by an order that the individual sentences run consecutively: Raveen at [41]. However, where the offences form part of a series of similar acts committed against the same victim over a short period, the one-transaction rule and the totality principle must be applied with care to ensure that the aggregate sentence was proportionate to the overall criminality of the accused's conduct.

225    In the present case, I agreed with the Prosecution's approach that the primary per-charge sentence of 15 months' imprisonment and two strokes of the cane should be adjusted downward on a totality basis. As the Prosecution correctly submitted, running two sentences consecutively at the primary per-charge rate would yield 30 months' imprisonment and six strokes of the cane, which would place the imprisonment sentence at the higher end of Band 2 and the caning at a level that, in aggregate, would be disproportionate to the overall criminality of the accused's conduct given that the three offences were committed against the same victim in the same manner across three consecutive Saturdays. Applying the totality principle as set out in Shouffee and Raveen, I accordingly adjusted the per-charge sentence downward and sentenced the accused to 12 months' imprisonment and one stroke of the cane in respect of each of the three charges. I noted that this sentence fell at the lower end of the Prosecution's adjusted per-charge range after the totality principle was applied, was consistent with the Defence's own position on the imprisonment term, and even comprised fewer strokes of the cane than the Defence itself initially submitted was appropriate.

226    I ordered the sentences for MAC-900985-2025 (the first charge) and MAC-900987-2025 (the third charge) to run consecutively, with the sentence for MAC-900986-2025 (the second charge) to run concurrently. The aggregate sentence imposed was therefore 24 months' imprisonment and three strokes of the cane, with effect from the date of conviction.

227    In summary, the accused was the victim's swimming coach. She was 10 years old, trusted him, and was in the water under his instruction. He abused that trust by touching her vagina area over her swimming costume on three separate occasions across three consecutive Saturdays, each time exploiting the concealment of the water to avoid detection. He had shown no remorse. He claimed trial, maintained a bare denial throughout, sought to impugn the victim's credibility with a motive that I rejected, and put the victim through the ordeal of testifying in court. I was satisfied that the total sentence of 24 months' imprisonment and three strokes of the cane was fair and proportionate and in line with the facts of the case and authorities cited.

228    Finally, I wish to record my appreciation to both the Prosecution and the Defence for their thorough and well-structured submissions, which were detailed and addressed the relevant legal and factual issues.

html:
Public Prosecutor v Lee Kum Meng

Public Prosecutor v Lee Kum Meng
[2026] SGDC 268

Case Number:District Arrest Case No 910849 of 2025, Magistrate's Appeal No 9181-2026-01
Decision Date:21 August 2026
Tribunal/Court:District Court
Coram: Salina Ishak
Counsel Name(s): Stephen Yeo (Attorney-General's Chambers) for the Public Prosecutor; Kelvin Ong Kai Min (Contigo Law LLC) for the accused.
Parties: Public Prosecutor — Lee Kum Meng

Criminal Procedure and Sentencing – Statutory offences – Road Traffic Act – Driving without due care and attention – Grievous hurt caused – Harm factors in Chen Song engaged – Repeat offender

[LawNet Editorial Note: An appeal to this decision has been filed in MA 9181/2026/01.]

21 August 2026

District Judge Salina Ishak:

Introduction

1       The present case occurred when a lorry driver ran a red traffic light signal at a signalised pedestrian crossing and collided into a cyclist who was cycling across.

2       The accused, Mr Lee Kum Meng, a 58-year-old male Singapore citizen pleaded guilty to the following charge under s 65(1)(a) punishable under s 65(3)(b) read with s 65(6)(d) of the Road Traffic Act 1961 (“RTA”):

are charged that on 14 March 2023 at or about 6.59 pm, at the signalised pedestrian crossing at Toh Guan Road East towards Old Toh Tuck Road, Singapore, you did drive a motor lorry bearing registration number YM68R on a road without due care and attention by failing to notice the red light signal and the victim, who was cycling across the pedestrian crossing and had the right of way, and grievous hurt was caused to the victim, and you had thereby committed an offence under 65(1)(a) of the Road Traffic Act 1961 (“RTA”),

and further, before the commission of the said offence, you were convicted on 6 December 2000 at State Court No. 21 of an offence of speeding under s 63(4) of the Road Traffic Act (Cap 276) vide report number R00212193VD, which conviction has not been set aside, and you are thereby liable to be punished under s 65(3)(b) read with s 65(6)(d) of the RTA.

Background

3       The accused was first charged in Court 7B for the present offence on 25 June 2025. He first indicated his intention to plead guilty on 2 August 2025 and his plead guilty mention was originally scheduled on 21 October 2025. After multiple adjournments in Court 7B as well as applications to leave the jurisdictions, the accused finally pleaded guilty on 27 July 2026 and admitted to the Statement of Facts[note: 1] without any qualification.

4       After carefully considering the Prosecution’s address on sentence as well as the plea in mitigation including the video footages tendered by the Defence, I sentenced the accused to four months and two weeks’ imprisonment and disqualified him from holding or obtaining all classes of driving licences for a period of five years with effect from the date of release. The accused was granted a deferment of the commencement of his sentence until 28 August 2026 to settle his business and personal affairs.

5       Nevertheless, the accused, being dissatisfied with my decision filed a Notice of Appeal against his sentence on 5 August 2026. He is on bail pending the hearing of his appeal.

6       I now set out the grounds of my decision in full. 

Salient Facts

7       The accused was the driver of a motor lorry bearing registration number YM68R.

8       The victim is Palermo Gregorio III Chato, a 44-year-old male. At the material time, he was riding a bicycle.

9       On 14 March 2023, at about 6.59pm, the accused was driving along Toh Guan Road East towards Old Toh Tuck Road. He was headed to an industrial building located along Toh Guan Road East to collect a parcel.

10     As the accused was nearing the signalised pedestrian crossing, the applicable traffic light signal was red. The accused failed to notice this as he was occupied with looking for the correct industrial building that he needed to go to. At this time, the victim was cycling across the signalised pedestrian crossing.

11     By the time the accused realised, he immediately applied his brakes but could not stop his motor lorry in time. The front portion of his motor lorry collided into the victim. This caused the victim to fall off his bicycle and land on the road.

12     At the time of the incident, the weather was fine, the road surface was dry, traffic flow was light, and visibility was clear. There was no mechanical fault to the accused’s vehicle.

13     The accused immediately alighted and attended to the victim. A passerby called the ambulance. The victim was conveyed by ambulance to the National University Hospital (“NUH”) for treatment.

14     The victim was seen at the Accident & Emergency Department of NUH. As stated in the medical report dated 23 July 2023 prepared by Dr Zulkarnain bin Ab Hamid, a senior consultant with the Emergency Medicine Department at NUH, the victim was diagnosed with a right ankle fracture, a right foot Lisfranc joint fracture dislocation and a right big toe proximal phalanx fracture. The fractures were immobilised with backslab application, and the victim was administered analgesia. The victim was then admitted to the Orthopaedics Surgery general ward on the same day for further management of his injury.

15     As stated in the medical report dated 22 April 2023 prepared by Dr S Hema Viganeshwari, the victim underwent a CT scan and was diagnosed with the following injuries, which amount to grievous hurt:

(a)     Comminuted fracture of the distal fibula below the level of the syndesmosis;

(b)     Fracture of the anterolateral tibial plafond at the expected insertion of the AITFL;

(c)     Bony fragment at the lateral base of the first metatarsal bone with widening of the space between the intermediate cuneiform bone in keeping with a Lisfranc ligament complex injury;

(d)     Fracture of the distal aspect of the medial cuneiform bone, distal aspect of the intermediate cuneiform bone, distal aspect of the lateral cuneiform bone, base of second metatarsal bone and base of third metatarsal bone; and

(e)     Comminuted fracture of the proximal phalanx of the right big toe with extension into the metatarsal phalangeal joint.

16     The victim underwent surgical fixation of the fractures stated above on 20 March 2023. He was discharged on 22 March 2023 with plans of non-weight bearing on the right lower limb until further review. The victim was reviewed again on 4 April 2023. He was prescribed with hospitalisation leave from 14 March 2023 to 22 May 2023.

17     In the clarificatory medical report dated 18 August 2024, Dr Wang Chongyan, a physician and senior resident with NUH stated that the victim had a mild midfoot deformity resulting from the Lisfranc fracture with an assessed permanent incapacity of 2%. Additionally, he had a 12% permanent incapacity due to an intraarticular fracture with displacement. He also had a 2% permanent incapacity from a big toe phalangeal fracture with angulation. The total permanent incapacity was assessed at 16%. The victim was prescribed hospitalisation leave from 28 August 2023 to 13 September 2023 and outpatient sick leave on 20 March 2024.

18     In total, the victim8 was prescribed with the following periods of medical

(a)     14 March 2023 to 22 May 2023 (70 days);

(b)     28 August 2023 to 13 September 2023 (17 days); and

(c)     20 March 2024 (1 day).

19     On 16 November 2025, the victim informed the Police that he no longer felt pain in his sole, ankle and big toe. He also informed the Police that his big toe was still tight and not as flexible. The victim further shared that his injuries had recovered and was no reduced mobility to his daily walking.

20     By virtue of the foregoing, the accused did, on 14 March 2023 at or about 6.59pm, at the signalised pedestrian crossing at Toh Guan Road East towards Old Toh Tuck Road, Singapore, drive a motor lorry bearing registration number YM68R on a road without due care and attention by failing to notice the red light signal and the victim, who was cycling across the pedestrian crossing and had the right of way, and grievous hurt was caused to the victim, he had thereby committed an offence under s 65(1)(a) of the Road Traffic Act 1961 (“RTA”).

21     And further, before the commission of the said offence, he was convicted on 6 December 2000 at State Court No. 21 of an offence of speeding under s 63(4) of the RTA (Cap 276) vide report number R00212193VD, which conviction has not been set aside, and he is thereby liable to be punished under s 65(3)(b) read with s 65(6)(d) of the RTA.

22     The accused was arrested on 11 June 2025 at about 12pm. He was released on bail on the same day.

Antecedents

23     On 6 December 2000, the accused was convicted and fined $500 for of an offence of speeding under s 63(4) of the RTA (Cap 276).

Prescribed Punishment

24     The offence of driving without due care and attention and causing grievous hurt as a repeat offender is punishable with a fine not exceeding $10,000 or to imprisonment for a term not exceeding 4 years or to both. The offender also faces a mandatory disqualification period of at least 5 years unless there are special reasons.

Prosecution’s Submissions on Sentence

25     The Prosecution sought a sentence of between four to five months and two weeks’ imprisonment[note: 2] and a disqualification order of 5 years.

Applicable Sentencing Framework

26     In support of their sentencing position, the Prosecution relied on the sentencing framework set by the High Court in Chen Song v Public Prosecutor and other appeals [2025] 3 SLR 509 (“Chen Song”) at [123] to [146].

27     The Prosecution asserts that in the present case, the offence is punishable under s 65(3)(b) of the RTA as the accused is a repeat offender. As such, the Prosecution further asserts that while taking reference from the sentencing bands in Chen Song, the eventual sentence must consider the fact that the accused was being sentenced as a repeat offender.

28     The Prosecution asserts that in Chen Song, the court adopted a modified “sentencing bands” approach in Tang Ling Lee v Public Prosecutor [2018] 4 SLR 813 at [134]) namely:

(a)     First, identify the number of offence-specific harm and culpability factors.

(b)     Second, based on the number of offence-specific factors present, determine the degree of harm caused and the offender’s culpability, and thereafter arrive at the applicable sentencing band.

(c)     Third, identify an indicative starting point sentence within the indicative sentencing band that the offence falls within, taking into account: (i) all the primary harm and culpability factors identified; and (ii) the secondary harm factors; and

(d)     Fourth, make adjustments to the starting point to take into account the usual gamut of offender-specific aggravating and mitigating factors.

29     The Prosecution further asserts that in Chen Song it was stated that, generally, if there are 0 – 1 primary harm or culpability factors, this leads to a finding of “lesser harm” and “lower culpability” respectively: at [123]. Conversely, if there are 2 or more harm or culpability factors, this leads to a finding of “greater harm” and “higher culpability” respectively.

Offence-specific factors

30     The Prosecution assessed the present case to be placed in the “lesser harm” and “lower culpability” bands.

Harm factors

31     The Prosecution asserts that in the present case, as regards the harm, all three factors in Chen Song were engaged:

(a)      Nature and location of the injury: The victim suffered several fractures to his lower limb areas. Surgical intervention was necessary.

(b)      Impact of injury: The victim suffered total permanent incapacity that was assessed to be at 16%.

(c)      Degree of permanence: The victim was prescribed with 87 days of hospitalisation leave and one day of outpatient sick leave. He was also hospitalised from 14 March 2023 to 22 March 2023, for a period of 9 days. Nevertheless, the Prosecution noted the there is no reduced mobility to his daily walking, and he no longer felt pain in the injured areas.

Culpability factors

32     The Prosecution further asserts that one offence-specific factor was engaged. The accused flouted traffic regulations by failing to conform to a traffic light signal: Chen Song at [131(b)(iv)].

Applicable sentencing band

33     Based on the above, as the Prosecution asserts that the present case involved greater harm and lower culpability, the indicative sentencing range is a fine and/or up to 6 months’ imprisonment.

34     The Prosecution asserts that in Chen Song, the High Court observed at [137] that the custodial threshold is typically crossed where there are two or more offence-specific harm and/or culpability factors present. As all three “harm” factors were engaged (though not fully) while one “culpability” factor is applicable, the custodial threshold was clearly crossed and that the present case fell within the highest end of Band 1 of Chen Song.

Indicative starting point sentence

35     The Prosecution further asserts that as the appropriate indicative sentence account for the accused’s status as a repeat offender, a starting sentence of 6 to 8 months’ imprisonment was appropriate. This indicative sentence is on the assumption that the accused had claimed trial to the charge.

Offender-specific factors

36     The Prosecution asserts that as the accused pleaded guilty within Stage 1 of the timeline prescribed in the Sentencing Advisory Panel (SAP) Guidelines on Reductions in Sentences for Guilty Pleas, he was entitled to a reduction in sentence of up to 30%.

The appropriate sentence

37     Applying the reduction based on the SAP Guidelines, the Prosecution’s sought a sentence of 4 months to 5 months and 2 weeks’ imprisonment.

38     The Prosecution also asserts that limited weight should be given to the restitution of $1,000 made by the accused to the victim in July 2025. As the offence occurred in 2023, and it was made when the accused already had legal representation, it was more a strategic move than a show of real contrition.

Disqualification order

39     The Prosecution further asserts that there were no special reasons for the Court to deviate from the default position that an offender punished under s 65(6)(d) RTA should be disqualified from holding or obtaining a driving licence for a period of not less than 5 years.

Plea in Mitigation

40     In the written plea in mitigation[note: 3], the Defence provided the accused’s personal background as well as the circumstances leading to the present charge as well as his antecedent.

Circumstances of the offence

41     The Defence asserts that at the material time, the accused drove the motor lorry along Toh Guan Road East towards Old Toh Tuck Road, in the course of a work delivery for his company Bikers World.sg Pte Ltd (BW). BW's regular driver had been unexpectedly placed on medical leave that day.

42     The Defence further asserts that as the accused approached the said signalised pedestrian crossing, his attention was momentarily diverted as he searched for the correct industrial building for his delivery. He failed to notice that the traffic light was red, and his vehicle collided with the victim who was cycling across the crossing with the right of way. The accused applied his brakes immediately upon noticing the victim but was unable to stop his vehicle in time.

43     The accused immediately stopped his vehicle, alighted, and rendered assistance to the victim including moving him to the side of the road, and remained at the scene until an ambulance arrived. The weather was fine, the road surface was dry, traffic was light and visibility was clear; there was no mechanical fault with the accused’s vehicle. He deeply regrets the momentary lapse in attention that led to this incident, and the harm caused to the victim.

Mitigating factors

44     The Defence asserts that the accused was genuinely remorseful. He wrote to the Traffic Police on 8 July 2025, and to the victim on 17 July 2025, to express his apology and take full responsibility for his actions. He also voluntarily transferred $1,000 to the victim on 18 July 2025 as compensation, over and above any sums that may separately be payable through third-party insurance coverage.

45     He cooperated fully with the police investigations from the outset and pleaded guilty at the earliest opportunity. As his plea fell within Stage 1 of the timeline prescribed under the SAP Guidelines on Reductions in Sentences for Guilty Pleas, he was entitled to a reduction in sentence of up to 30%.

46     The Defence further asserts that the video footages[note: 4] showed the accused rendering assistance at the scene. He did not flee the scene. He personally attended to the victim and remained until help arrived, which conduct which reflects genuine concern for the victim's welfare.

47     The Defence relied on his family circumstances, the impact of a custodial sentence on his business and employees and his long-standing contribution to society as mitigating factors.

Applicable Sentencing Framework

48     The Defence agreed with the Prosecution’s adoption of the Chen Song sentencing framework and their assessment for the present case to be placed in the “lesser harm” and “lower culpability” bands. Nevertheless, the Defence disagreed that the case should be placed at the highest end of the Band 1.

Harm factors

49     The Defence asserts that the harm should be placed at the lower to moderate range instead. While the Defence accept that the three harm factors identified in Chen Song - nature and location of injury, degree of permanence, and impact of injury – were technically engaged, each of these factors were present only to a limited degree for the following reasons:

(a)      Nature and location: the injuries, while properly classified as grievous hurt, were confined to the victim's right ankle and foot — not areas typically associated with life-threatening or catastrophic harm;

(b)      Degree of permanence: although the victim was assessed with 16% permanent incapacity, the victim informed the Police on 16 November 2025 that he no longer experiences pain and that his mobility for daily activities is unaffected (save that the victim’s big toe is still tight and not as flexible); and

(c)      Impact: notwithstanding an aggregate of approximately 88 days of hospitalisation and outpatient leave, there is no evidence that the victim's livelihood or ability to carry out his daily activities was materially affected, nor is there any continuing need for rehabilitation.

Culpability factors

50     The Defence asserts that culpability should be assessed as low, without the additional weight urged by the Prosecution as only one culpability factor was present: his failure to notice the red traffic light signal. He did not speed, drive against the flow of traffic, or otherwise exhibit any of the forms of dangerous driving behaviour identified in Chen Song at [131(a)].

51     The Defence highlighted that the High Court in Chen Song cautioned at [132] against classifying a basic failure to keep a proper lookout as demonstrating a “high degree of carelessness” absent “something more”. The Defence also asserts that there was nothing more than the accused’s momentary lapse in attention. While rightly the subject of this charge, it does not warrant the additional, culpability-enhancing weight the Prosecution sought to place on it in support of a sentence at the highest point of Band 1.

The appropriate sentence

52     The Defence asserts that the custodial threshold has not been clearly crossed. It was highlighted that in Chen Song at [137] the custodial threshold is “typically” crossed where two or more offence-specific harm and/or culpability factors are present. On the proper, holistic assessment set out above, the Defence further asserts that the present case does not clearly cross this threshold, and that a fine remains an available and appropriate sentencing option consistent with the Court's direction in Chen Song at [135] that sentencing courts should remain “alive” to the fine option.

53     In the alternative, the Defence asserts that a substantially reduced custodial term — in the region of 2 to 3 months' imprisonment — would be more appropriate than the Prosecution's proposed range of 4 months to 5 months and 2 weeks, having regard to:

(a)     The lower to moderate (rather than highest) placement of harm within Band 1;

(b)     The absence of any “something more” going towards culpability;

(c)     His genuine remorse;

(d)     His willingness to pay compensation to the victim;

(e)     His full cooperation with the Police;

(f)     His early plea of guilt;

(g)     The dated and unrelated nature of his antecedent; and

(h)     The extensive personal mitigating factors.

Disqualification order

54     The Defence further asserts that that the accused does not contest the Prosecution's position that the mandatory minimum period of 5 years' disqualification from holding or obtaining a driving licence should apply.

Prosecution’s Reply

55     In response to the Defence’s assertion that the victim informed the police that he no longer experiences pain and that his mobility for daily activities is unaffected, the Prosecution asserts that this factor should be given limited weight. It has been two years since the accident, and it is normal that the victim would have some level of recovery from that point. The Prosecution further asserts that in any event, the 16% permanent incapacity is a medical finding. Ultimately what the victim tells the police was still a layman understanding of what his injuries were.

56     The Prosecution asserts that as the video footage has been placed in evidence, as noted by the Court, there were other pedestrians crossing at the time. In that context, the potential harm was also not just a hypothetical as two people were already crossing. The Prosecution further asserts that the Defence’s submissions that it was a momentary lapse in attention by its client would not be quite accurate. From the video footage, it was quite a long moment of inattention to miss all three pedestrians.

57     It was the Prosecution’s position that even on account of the Chen Song framework, without considering his status as a repeat offender, the sentencing position of 4 to 5½ months’ imprisonment was very much justified.

REASONS FOR THE SENTENCE

Applicable sentencing framework

58     The accused drove without due care and attention causing grievous hurt as a repeat offender. As such, he is liable to be punished under s 65(3)(b) of the RTA. I took reference from the sentencing framework in Chen Song for s 65(3)(a) of the RTA albeit for first offenders, as it provides useful guidance on the approach to be taken in sentencing.

59     As set out at [134 (a)] of Chen Song, the first step is for the court to identify the offence-specific harm and culpability factors.

Offence-specific harm factors

60     The foremost inquiry was for me to assess holistically whether the totality of the harm suffered by the victim is classified as “greater harm” or “lesser harm”. In doing so, I considered the intensity of each harm factor.

Primary harm factors

61     In the present case, it was undisputed that all three primary harm factors were engaged:

(a)      Nature and location of the injury

The victim suffered fractures in his lower right limb ie his leg and foot namely, comminuted fracture of the distal fibula, an acute fracture of his medial cuneiform bone and comminuted fracture of the proximal phalanx of his big toe. This factor was engaged to a limited degree in view of its location and did not involve a vulnerable part of the body.

(b)      Degree of permanence

The victim’s total permanent incapacity was assessed at 16% - his mild midfoot deformity from the Lisfranc fracture at 2%, the intraarticular fracture with displacement at 12% and a big toe phalangeal fracture with angulation at 2%.

(c)      Impact of injury

i.       The victim was hospitalised for 9 days and was given 87 days of hospitalisation leave and one day of outpatient sick leave. He underwent various surgical procedures to treat the injuries he suffered. He was discharged with his right lower limb in a cast with plans to non-weight bear until his review at the clinic.

ii.       Two weeks after the surgery, during his review he was advised to continue with non-weight bearing status for another two weeks before it was changed to an aircast boot. He was recommended to avoid sports and heavy impact activities in view of the risk of displacement.

iii.       During his review in March 2024, he reported occasional start-up pain over the right forefoot dorsum when waking up in the morning and after siting for prolonged periods. Otherwise, he was doing well and had resumed activities such as cycling and swimming.

62     In my view, the impact on the victim’s quality of life was not insignificant in view of his hospitalisation period as well as lengthy hospitalisation leave. He was on a non-weight bearing status for about four weeks while his right leg was in a cast and thereafter in an aircast boot. He was unable to carry out his ordinary activities during this period. As set out at [61(c)] above, significant rest and recuperation was required before he was able to resume activities such as cycling and swimming. Even so, he continued to suffer from residual pain from his injuries even one year after the accident. In November 2025, he informed the police that his big toe was still tight and not as flexible.

Secondary harm factors

63     Apart from the primary harm factors, I also considered the secondary harm factor that was present in this case. These are factors unrelated to the physical injuries suffered by the victim(s) but nonetheless go towards the extent of harm caused in the particular case. These factors include potential harm and property damage (see [125] of Chen Song).

Potential harm

64     At [129] of Chen Song, it was held that potential harm refers to harm that was likely to have been caused to other road users, but which ultimately did not eventuate. It was highlighted that in Wu Zhi Yong v Public Prosecutor [2022] 4 SLR 587 (“Wu Zhi Yong”), the High Court endorsed the pronouncement in Neo Chuan Seng v Public Prosecutor [2020] 5 SLR 410 at [22] (“Neo Chuan Seng”) that the level of potential harm may be assessed against facts such as the condition of the road, the volume of traffic or number of pedestrians actually on or which might be reasonably be expected to be on the road at the relevant time, the speed and manner of driving, visibility at the relevant time, the type of vehicle, and any particular vulnerabilities (eg, a truck or car colliding into a motorcycle or pedestrian). It was observed that these relate to the circumstances of driving that could increase the danger posed to road traffic users (Wu Zhi Yong at [36(a)]).

65     It was further held at [130] that a sentencing court may take into account potential harm as being a factor going towards either harm or culpability in the sentencing process but exercise due caution to ensure there is no double counting. In the present case, at the material time, the weather was fine, the road surface was dry, traffic flow was light, and visibility was clear. Prior to the collision at the signalised pedestrian crossing, the victim and two other pedestrians could be seen crossing from the accused’s right shortly before the accident as the traffic light signal were in their favour. In fact, the accused narrowly missed colliding into one of the pedestrians.

66     Based on the above factors, I was of the view that there was significant potential harm to other road users at the material time. As the potential harm as set out above presented itself in a significant manner, this should be considered in the determination of where the present offence falls within the indicative sentencing band.

67     In the present case, as reflected in the vehicle damage report, there was damage caused to the victim’s bicycle. Nevertheless, as there were no details of the damage caused to the victim’s bicycle in the Statement of Facts, I regarded it as a neutral factor and did not place any weight on this factor.

68     I was mindful that at [126] of Chen Song, the High Court held that each harm factor would count as one offence-specific factor going towards harm. However, where a secondary factor presents itself in a significant manner, this should be considered in the determination of where the offence falls within the indicative sentencing band.

69     Hence, on a holistic assessment of the above “harm” factors, I assessed the present case to fall within the “lesser harm” category. Given that all three “harm” factors were applicable, I placed the case in the moderate range of the “lesser harm” band.

70     Next, I considered whether the offender’s culpability should holistically be classified as either “lower culpability” or “higher culpability”.

Offence-specific culpability factors

Flouting of traffic rules and regulations

71     As driving is an inherently a dangerous activity, every driver in Singapore should always be alert to the prevailing traffic conditions and be aware of his or her responsibilities towards other road users. To ensure the safety of road users, it is imperative that there be strict compliance with traffic rules and regulations through observance of traffic signals and signs, adherence to speed limits and proper lane discipline.

72     In the present case, I agreed with the Prosecution that one offence-specific factor is engaged, namely the flouting of traffic rules and regulations: Chen Song at [131(b)(iv)]. From the video footage at time stamp 0:32/0:56, it could be seen that the first set of traffic lights for traffic along Toh Guan East Road was red when he executed the right turn from the junction into Toh Guan East Road. As the accused proceeded along Toh Guan East Road, at time stamp 0:42/0:56 the traffic light was similarly red when he approached the pedestrian crossing in question.

73     Accordingly, I did not accept the Defence’s assertions that that there was nothing more than a momentary lapse in attention. His attention was diverted as he was searching for the correct industrial building for his delivery. Instead, I agreed with the Prosecution that from the video footage, it was quite a long moment of inattention to have missed all three pedestrians. Furthermore, the traffic light had already been red for a few seconds as he travelled along Toh Guan Road East itself. Clearly, this was not a momentary lapse of attention, a distraction which was unavoidable nor a reasonable misjudgment.

74     Hence, the accused failed to comply to the red-light signal and flouted s 120(3) of the RTA but also Rules 5 and 7 of the Road Traffic (Pedestrian Crossing) Rules. Additionally, the accused also failed to slow down when he approached the pedestrian crossing as well as give precedence to the victim cyclist as well as the two pedestrians who were already crossing the road. S 120(3) of the RTA provides:

Duty to comply with traffic directions and traffic signs

120 (3)    Where any traffic sign, being a sign for regulating the movement of traffic or indicating the route to be followed by traffic, has been lawfully placed on or near any road pursuant to section 119, any person driving or propelling any vehicle must comply with the indication given by the sign.

While Rules 5 and 7 of the Road Traffic (Pedestrian Crossing) Rules provide:

Vehicle approaching crossing to slow down

5.    The driver of every vehicle approaching a pedestrian crossing must proceed only at such speed as will enable him to stop his vehicle before reaching the crossing.

Precedence at controlled crossing

7.    Wherever there is a pedestrian crossing at a road intersection or junction where traffic is controlled by a police officer or by light signals, every pedestrian, cyclist, mobility vehicle user and PMD rider who is about to enter or has entered such crossing shall be permitted free and uninterrupted passage over the crossing by all drivers of vehicles who are approaching the crossing notwithstanding that such drivers may have already received a signal to proceed either from the light signals or the police officer, as the case may be.

75     Accordingly, based on a holistic assessment of the facts before me, I found based on the accused’s manner of driving, his culpability was at the upper end of the low category. I disagreed with the Defence’s assertion culpability should be assessed as low without the additional weight urged by the Prosecution.

Applicable sentencing band

76     The second step was for me to arrive at the applicable sentencing band based on the number of offence-specific factors present after determining the degree of harm caused and the offender’s culpability.

77     As the case was one involving lesser harm and lower culpability, it fell within Band 1 of the Chen Song framework. At Band 1, the applicable sentencing range on a claim trial basis is a fine and/or up to 6 months’ imprisonment. As set out at [137] and [140] of Chen Song, the custodial threshold would typically be crossed where there are 2 or more offence-specific harm and/or culpability factors present. Fines are only appropriate for Band 1 cases where one or no offence-specific harm and/or culpability factors is present.

78     In determining whether a custodial sentence is warranted, I was mindful of the emphasis in Chen Song at [122] that the classification of harm and culpability should proceed in totality. In the present case, all three “harm” factors were engaged (although the nature and location of the injury to a limited degree) and one “culpability” factor was applicable. As I found the harm to be at the moderate end of the “lesser harm” band and his culpability at the upper end of the “low category”, after a holistic assessment of the harm and the culpability factors, I agreed with the Prosecution that the custodial threshold had been crossed. Hence, I disagreed with the Defence that the imposition of a fine would be appropriate in the present case.

Indicative starting point

79     The third step was for the court to identify an indicative starting point sentence within the indicative sentencing band that the offence falls within, taking into account: (i) all the primary harm and culpability factors identified; and (ii) the secondary harm factors.

80     After considering all the harm factors and culpability factors identified above, I agreed with the Prosecution that the indicative starting point should be 6 to 8 months’ imprisonment. An uplift in the indicative starting point was necessary as the accused was liable to double the prescribed fine and imprisonment term as a repeat offender. This indicative sentence is on the assumption that the accused had claimed trial to the charge. In my view the Defence’s alternative proposed sentence 2 to 3 months’ imprisonment was inappropriate as it did not properly account for the totality and intensity of the level of harm and the culpability of the accused.

81     At the fourth step, I was to adjust the indicative starting point after considering the mitigating and aggravating factors present in this case.

Adjustments to the starting point to account for aggravating and mitigating factors

Aggravating factor

Poor driving history

82     Apart from the accused’s conviction for speeding on 12 December 2000, his traffic offending history was poor. He had compounded four speeding offences and one charge of failing to conform to red light signal. The present case is the second instance where the accused failed to conform to a red-light signal, an identical offence except that it resulted in grievous hurt being caused. This reflected the accused’s propensity to flout road traffic rules and regulations.

83     The Court of Appeal in Teo Seng Tiong v Public Prosecutor [2021] SGCA 65 ruled affirmatively at [103] – [104] that courts may consider any compounded Road Traffic Act offence as an aggravating factor when sentencing for: (a) Road Traffic Act offences; and (b) non-Road Traffic Act offences, without legislative intervention.

Mitigating factors

84     I considered the following factors raised by the Defence as mitigating:

(a)     The accused was genuinely remorseful. He wrote to Traffic Police and the victim to express his apology and to take full responsibility for his actions.

(b)     He voluntarily transferred $1,000 to the victim on 18 July 2025 as compensation, over and above any sums that may separately be payable through third-party insurance coverage.

(c)     He cooperated fully with police investigations from the outset. He indicated he was pleaded guilty at the earliest opportunity – within Stage 1 of the timelines prescribed under the SAP Plead Guilty Guidelines.

(d)     He rendered assistance at the scene. The accused did not flee the scene. He personally attended to the victim and remained until help arrived. His conduct reflects genuine concern for the victim's welfare.

85     Based on the above and the factual matrix of the charge before me, I was of the view on a claim trial basis the appropriate sentence should be adjusted to 6 months’ imprisonment.

Appropriate sentencing discount

Stage of Guilty Plea

86     As the accused indicated his intention to plead guilty at Stage 1, I applied the maximum sentencing discount of 30% to the indicative starting point which would give a sentence of 4 months and 2 weeks imprisonment.

87     It was undisputed and I was also of the view that the mandatory minimum disqualification period of 5 years for all classes was appropriate in the present case. Further, no special reasons were raised nor were there any exceptional circumstances before me not to order any disqualification or which warranted a departure from the mandatory minimum period.

Conclusion

88     All things considered, in respect of the offence in DAC-910849-2025 under s 65(1)(a) punishable under s 65(3)(b) of the RTA, I sentenced him to 4 months and 2 weeks’ imprisonment and disqualification for a period of 5 years for all classes, with effect from the date of release.

Public Prosecutor v Jia Chenke

Public Prosecutor v Jia Chenke
[2026] SGDC 264

Case Number:District Arrest Case No. 910593 of 2026 and others
Decision Date:20 August 2026
Tribunal/Court:District Court
Coram: Samuel Wee
Counsel Name(s): Esther Tan (Singapore Customs) and Debra Ann Tan Mei Ling (Health Sciences Authority) for the Prosecution; The Defendant in person.
Parties: Public Prosecutor — Jia Chenke

Criminal Law – Offences – Section 128F of the Customs Act 1960 – Importation of duty unpaid cigarettes

Criminal Law – Offences – Section 16(1) of the Tobacco and Vaporisers Control Act 1993 – Importation of vaporiser components

Criminal Procedure and Sentencing – Sentencing – Section 128F of the Customs Act 1960 – Importation of duty unpaid cigarettes

Criminal Procedure and Sentencing – Sentencing – Section 16(1) of the Tobacco and Vaporisers Control Act 1993 – Importation of vaporiser components

20 August 2026

District Judge Samuel Wee:

Introduction

1       On 28 May 2026, Mr Jia Chenke (“Mr Jia”) travelled from Shanghai to Singapore with two suitcases and two bags containing duty unpaid cigarettes and vaporiser products on the instructions of an acquaintance, Mr Fu Kai Wen (“Mr Fu”).[note: 1] He arrived at Changi Airport, where he and the co-accused, Mr Xu Yunyang (“Mr Xu”), were approached by Customs Officers. Mr Jia was found to be in possession of 17.685 kg of duty unpaid cigarettes (comprising 122 cartons x 200 sticks and 11 packets x 20 sticks of assorted brands of cigarettes), 129 disposable vaporisers and 51 boxes of pods (comprising 153 pods), while Mr Xu was found to be in possession of 18.381 kg of duty unpaid cigarettes (comprising 133 cartons x 200 sticks and 1 carton x 160 sticks of assorted brands of cigarettes).[note: 2]

2       Mr Jia pleaded guilty to two charges:

(a)     One charge under s 128F punishable under s 128L(4) of the Customs Act 1960 (2020 Rev Ed) (“CA”) for being concerned in the importation of uncustomed goods – 17.685 kg of duty unpaid cigarettes (comprising 122 cartons x 200 sticks and 11 packets x 20 sticks of assorted brands of cigarettes) – on which excise duty of $14,501.18 was not paid (“Customs Charge”).[note: 3]

(b)     One charge under s 16(1) punishable under s 16(4) of the Tobacco and Vaporisers Control Act 1993 (2020 Rev Ed) (“TVCA”) for importing components of a vaporiser – 51 boxes of pods (comprising 153 pods) (“HSA Charge”).[note: 4] The Prosecution indicated that this was the first prosecution of an offence under s 16(1) of the TVCA.[note: 5]

3       He also admitted and consented to two additional charges being taken into consideration for the purposes of sentencing:

(a)     One charge under s 128F of the CA read with ss 26 and 77 of the Goods and Services Tax Act 1993 (2020 Rev Ed), punishable under s 128L(4) of the CA, for being concerned in the importation of the same 17.685 kg of duty unpaid cigarettes, on which Goods and Services Tax of $1,483.70 was not paid (“TIC Customs Charge”).[note: 6]

(b)     One charge under s 16(1) punishable under s 16(4) of the TVCA for importing 129 disposable vaporisers (“TIC HSA Charge”).[note: 7]

4       The Prosecution sought a sentence of 4 to 5 months’ imprisonment for the Customs Charge and 9 weeks’ imprisonment for the HSA Charge, with both sentences to run consecutively.[note: 8] Mr Jia was self-represented and did not make any specific submissions on sentence aside from pleading for leniency.

5       For the reasons set out below, I sentenced Mr Jia to an aggregate of 4 months’ and 9 weeks’ imprisonment (4 months’ imprisonment for the Customs Charge and 9 weeks’ imprisonment for the HSA Charge, with both sentences to run consecutively), backdated to 28 May 2026 (the date of arrest).

Customs Charge

6       The Customs Charge carries a fine of between $217,517.70 and $290,023.60 (being 15 to 20 times the amount of excise duty evaded), an imprisonment term of up to 3 years, or both.

7       The applicable sentencing framework for the Customs Charge is set out in Yap Ah Lai v Public Prosecutor [2014] 3 SLR 180 (“Yap Ah Lai”).

(a)     The High Court established the following starting point sentencing benchmarks for first-time offenders whose role was confined to pure importation of more than 2 kg of tobacco products and who pleaded guilty at the earliest chance:

Quantity of Tobacco Product (kg)

Sentencing Range (Months)

2-50

3-6

51-100

6-12

101-200

12-18

201-300

18-24

301-400

24-30

>400

30-36



(b)     The High Court also identified four non-exhaustive factors that are relevant to sentencing for customs offences:[note: 9] (i) the quantity of tobacco product involved; (ii) the repetition of the offence; (iii) the involvement of a criminal syndicate; and (iv) the role of the offender.

8       Applying the framework in Yap Ah Lai, a sentence of 4 months’ imprisonment was suitable as:[note: 10]

(a)     17.685 kg of duty unpaid cigarettes were involved, which fell within the sentencing range of 3-6 months for between 2-50 kg of tobacco product.

(b)     Mr Jia was a first-time offender, who pleaded guilty at Stage 1 of the Sentencing Advisory Panel’s Guidelines on Reduction in Sentences for Guilty Pleas (“PG Guidelines”).

(c)     Mr Jia’s role was limited to that of a courier acting on the instructions of Mr Fu – he did not have any management control or profit share in the operations, and there was no evidence of the involvement of a syndicate.

(d)     There was no need for an uplift in sentence to account for the TIC Customs Charge, as had the Prosecution proceeded with the charge, any sentence would have been ordered to run concurrently in line with the one-transaction rule (Yap Ah Lai at [56]).

9       This sentence was consistent with the principle of parity, as the co-accused, Mr Xu, had already been sentenced to 4 months’ imprisonment for importing a comparable (albeit marginally higher) quantity of 18.381 kg of duty unpaid cigarettes,[note: 11] and there was no reason to depart from that sentence in Mr Jia’s case.

HSA Charge

10     The HSA Charge carries a mandatory imprisonment term of up to 9 years and a discretionary fine of up to $300,000. Based on the Parliamentary Debates during the Second Reading of the Tobacco (Control of Advertisements and Sale) (Amendment) and Other Matters Bill, the penalties (which came into force on 1 May 2026) reflect Parliament’s intention to take a strong stance against the importation of vaporisers and their components into Singapore, in light of the growing prevalence of vaporiser use and its associated public health risks (see Singapore Parl Debates; Vol 96, Sitting No 26; 6 March 2026).[note: 12]

11     A sentence of 9 weeks’ imprisonment (as sought by the Prosecution) was suitable.

(a)     The starting point sentence had Mr Jia been convicted after a trial would have been 12 weeks’ imprisonment taking into account the following:

(i)       The 153 pods involved were empty shells that did not contain any vaporiser liquid. In this regard, the Prosecution confirmed during the hearing that it considered the harm in the present case to be very low.

(ii)       Mr Jia’s role was limited to that of a courier acting on the instructions of Mr Fu – he did not have any management control or profit share in the operations, and there was no evidence of the involvement of a syndicate (see [8(c)] above). In this regard, the Prosecution confirmed during the hearing that it considered Mr Jia’s culpability to be very low.

(iii)       An uplift to account for the TIC HSA Charge, which related to the importation of 129 disposable vaporisers.

(b)     This was reduced by 3 weeks in light of Mr Jia’s indication of his intention to plead guilty at Stage 1 of the PG Guidelines.

The aggregate sentence

12     The sentences for the Customs Charge and the HSA Charge were ordered to run consecutively. This was in line with the general rule of consecutive sentences for unrelated offences (Public Prosecutor v Raveen Balakrishnan [2018] 5 SLR 799 at [41]), as the two offences involved different substances and had different legally protected interests – the interests protected under the Customs Charge relate to the loss of revenue to the Government and the reduction of the consumption of harmful goods through the imposition of higher costs on users (Yap Ah Lai at [23]-[26]), whereas the interest protected under the HSA Charge relates to the protection of public health (Singapore Parl Debates; Vol 96, Sitting No 26; [6 March 2026]).

13     The aggregate sentence of 4 months’ and 9 weeks’ imprisonment did not offend the totality principle, as it was not substantially above the normal level of sentences for the most serious of the individual offences committed (ie. the Customs Charge), and the sentence could not be said to be crushing.

14     The sentence was backdated to 28 May 2026 (the date of arrest).

Li Hua v Farooq Mann and another

Li Hua v Farooq Mann and another
[2026] SGMC 97

Case Number:Disposal Inquiry DI-900037 of 2023, HC/CR 6/2026
Decision Date:21 August 2026
Tribunal/Court:Magistrate's Court
Coram: Crystal Tan
Counsel Name(s): Deputy Senior State Counsel David Koh and State Counsel Sarah Thaker (Attorney-General's Chambers) for the State; 1st Claimant Mr Li Hua (self-represented); Counsel Tham Li Jing and Lim Rui-Qi Rochelle (Tham Lijing LLC) for the 2nd Claimant; Counsel Derek Tan and Nadine Neo (Quahe Woo & Palmer LLC) for the 3rd Claimant.
Parties: Li Hua — Farooq Mann — Wong Joo Wan

Criminal Procedure and Sentencing – Disposal of property – Section 370(2) of the Criminal Procedure Code (Cap 68, 2012 Rev Ed)

21 August 2026

District Judge Crystal Tan:

Introduction

1       This case involved a disposal inquiry over 33 items that were seized for investigations by the Commercial Affairs Department (“CAD”) from (a) Mr Li Hua, (b) Sunmax Global Capital Pte Ltd (“SMGC”) and (c) Sunmax Global Capital Fund Pte Ltd (“Sunmax Fund”) (to be referred to as “the seized items”)[note: 1]. Mr Li Hua, the first claimant, was dissatisfied with the disposal orders by the Court and filed a criminal revision on the disposal orders.

Background

2       Briefly, for context, Mr Li Hua was the former director of SMGC. Sunmax Fund was an approved fund under the Global Investor Programme that was managed by SMGC at the material time.[note: 2] Sunmax Fund shared the same office premises as SMGC.[note: 3] The seized items were seized by CAD on 3 April 2014 for investigations into a case of possible offences for false trading and market rigging transactions under Section 197 of the Securities and Futures Act (Cap 289, 2006 Rev Ed) (“SFA”), employment of manipulative and deceptive devices under Section 201 of the SFA and cheating under Section 420 of the Penal Code (Cap 224, 2008 Rev Ed), arising from trading irregularities in the shares of Blumont Group Limited, Asiasons Capital Limited and LionGold Corp Limited.[note: 4]

3       Mr Li Hua was adjudged a bankrupt on 28 June 2022 while SMGC has been in liquidation since 2018.

4       The claimants involved in the disposal inquiry are as follows:

(a)     Mr Li Hua, the first claimant;

(b)     Mr Farooq Mann, the Private Trustee in Bankruptcy (“PTIB”) of the estate of Mr Li Hua, the second claimant; and

(c)     Mr Wong Joo Wan (“Mr Wong”), the liquidator of Sunmax Fund, the third claimant.

5       All the parties agreed[note: 5] that the governing provision for the seized items fell under Section 370(2) of the Criminal Procedure Code (Cap 68, 2012 Rev Ed) (“CPC”):

(2)    Subject to subsection (3), the Magistrate's Court must, upon the receipt of such report referred to in subsection (1), make such order as it thinks fit respecting the delivery of the property to the person entitled to the possession of it or, if that person cannot be ascertained, respecting the custody and production of the property.

[emphasis added in bold]

6       The key dispute between the three claimants was who was entitled to the possession of the seized items. Briefly, the parties’ position was as follows:

(a)     Mr Li Hua claimed the seized items on the basis that they were his “personal items without any commercial value”[note: 6] and they were seized before he became a bankrupt;

(b)     PTIB claimed the seized items on the basis that Mr Li Hua was now a bankrupt and all his property vested with PTIB under Section 369(1) of the Insolvency, Restructuring and Dissolution Act 2018 (“IRDA”);

(c)     Mr Wong claimed the seized items on the basis that they belonged to Sunmax Fund. In addition, Mr Wong had an Order of Court vide HC/ORC 3519/2023 (“ORC 3519”) that he submitted required Mr Li Hua to produce to Mr Wong any documents belonging to and/or relating to Sunmax Fund. However, Mr Wong was willing to relinquish his claim and rights to these properties if the seized items were released to PTIB;

(d)     The State did not take a position on which claimant was legally entitled to the seized items. The State was of the view that no offence was committed in respect of the seized items.[note: 7]

7       At the first hearing of the disposal inquiry on 9 January 2025, the State had listed the seized items in the Investigation Report, P1, as follows:

8       On 3 April 2014, CAD had seized the items in Annex A and Annex B1 above from 80 Raffles Place #30-23, which was the registered address of both SMGC and Sunmax Fund. On the same day, the items in Annex B2 were seized from Mr Li Hua’s personal residence or from him directly.

9       After the Court had considered the parties’ affidavits, submissions and the evidence canvassed in the disposal inquiry hearing itself, the Court made the following disposal orders:

(a)     Seized items in Annex A and Annex B1 (Items no. 1 to 10) to be delivered to the third claimant, Mr Wong as the liquidator of Sunmax Fund;

(b)     Seized items in Annex B2 (Items no. 1 to 13) to be delivered to the second claimant, PTIB.

Summary of parties’ positions

Disposal Inquiry (“DI”) Hearing on 9 January 2025

10     Before the DI Hearing on 9 January 2025, the three claimants filed affidavits and written submissions. Their positions are summarised below.

11     Briefly, the first claimant, Mr Li Hua, submitted as follows:

(a)     Both PTIB and Mr Wong were acting against the first claimant “in retaliation for Mr Song”[note: 8];

(b)     Conflict of interest between the group of Mr Song, PTIB and Mr Wong[note: 9], and including Quahe Woo & Palmer LLC[note: 10];

(c)     Section 369(1) of the IRDA “contradicts” the principles governing a disposal inquiry[note: 11] and PTIB failed to comply with elements of Section 369(1) IRDA[note: 12];

(d)     The seized items do not fall under the bankrupt’s estate but consist of his “personal records”[note: 13];

(e)     He is the last possessor of the seized items because CAD’s seizure letter stated that they were searching for items belonging to Mr Li Hua and not SMGC or Sunmax Fund[note: 14];

(f)     The premises that the seized items were seized from belonged to SMGC and not Sunmax Fund[note: 15]. In his affidavit, he stated that Sunmax Fund “did not have its own office, but its registered address was the same as SMGC’s. In other words, SMGC allowed Sunmax Fund to use SMGC’s office address as its registered address”[note: 16].

12     For the second claimant, PTIB submitted as follows:

(a)     PTIB’s role as a court-appointed officer was to recover assets to compensate Mr Li Hua’s creditors;

(b)     Mr Li Hua declared liabilities totalled $81,367,951.70 and no assets but he appeared to lead “a very good life” and lived “in a luxury District 9/ District 10 condominium”. Mr Li Hua refused to disclose his source of funds[note: 17];

(c)     Mr Li Hua was the sole shareholder and director of an investor fund that solicited up to $65,700,000 in investments from third parties and only a fraction was returned to investors. PTIB’s task was to identify where the bulk of the monies went so as to return to the creditors. Hence, it was critical for PTIB to conduct a “full and thorough investigation into the Bankrupt’s business and affairs”[note: 18];

(d)     PTIB’s claim is premised on Sections 369(1) and 370 of the IRDA[note: 19] because they are “relevant to the Bankrupt’s estate and affairs”[note: 20];

(e)     Under Section 369(1) of the IRDA, PTIB “must” take possession of “the deeds, books and documents which relate to the bankrupt’s estate or affairs, and which belong to the bankrupt or are under the bankrupt’s control” and “all other parts of the bankrupt’s property capable of manual delivery”[note: 21];

(f)     Section 370(1) of the IRDA gives effect to Section 369(1) of the IRDA by empowering PTIB to “take an inventory of and seize any property comprised in the bankrupt’s estate”[note: 22];

(g)     Mr Li Hua had not claimed that the seized items contain “purely personal documents” (italics in original) and has “remained conspicuously quiet about the contents of the items”[note: 23];

(h)     PTIB claimed all the items in Annex A. PTIB understood that Mr Wong inspected the items and managed to identify No. 1, 3 and 5 of Annex A as being relevant to the dealings of Sunmax Fund. However, the rest of the items in Annex A have not been identified because PTIB did not have an opportunity to inspect the items[note: 24];

(i)     Without having the opportunity to inspect, PTIB identified a few items in Annex A[note: 25] that appeared to belong to Mr Li Hua, for example, Item no. 2 “Stack of miscellaneous legal and court documents with cover titled “Tony’s own notes for 63b/12”;

(j)     PTIB claimed all the items in Annex B. For the items seized from SMGC/Sunmax Fund, PTIB identified at least 3 items which “presumably belong” to Mr Li Hua and not SMGC and/or Sunmax Fund, for example, “Tony’s Personal Investment UOB Account”, “Li Hua” and “Family II”[note: 26];

(k)     For the items seized from Mr Li Hua, PTIB submitted that it was entitled to take possession in its capacity as the PTIB over Mr Li Hua’s estate[note: 27];

(l)     Mr Li Hua could not “hide behind an excuse” that it was a matter of privacy for his items to be returned to him as he had failed to prove that the contents were “merely personal to him and have no connection to his affairs and estate”[note: 28];

(m)     In any event, PTIB was willing to make copies of the items and or contents of the seized items, return the originals to Mr Li Hua and undertake to delete whichever items were unrelated to Mr Li Hua’s affairs and estate.[note: 29]

13     For the third claimant, Mr Wong submitted as follows:

(a)     There are “several suspicious dealings” between Mr Li Hua, SMGC and Sunmax Fund. The seized items should not be released to Mr Li Hua because he may likely “surreptitiously dispose of and/or tamper with the same, to cover up his wrongdoings”[note: 30];

(b)     On 27 July 2023, the High Court granted ORC 3519 which ordered for Mr Li Hua to produce to Mr Wong “any and all documents that are within his possession, custody or power belonging to and/or relating to [Sunmax Fund]…”[note: 31];

(c)     On 3 June 2024, the High Court clarified that ORC 3519 required Mr Li Hua to deliver to Mr Wong “the Visa Application Form and all documents belonging to and/or relating to [Sunmax Fund] that may be released by [the CAD in respect of the Disposal Inquiry]”[note: 32];

(d)     The seized items in Annex A and Annex B fell within the ambit of ORC 3519 and are documents that Mr Li Hua has to provide to Mr Wong as liquidator of Sunmax Fund[note: 33];

(e)     The items in Annex A were seized from SMGC and/or Sunmax Fund. Sunmax Fund is the only claimant who has a proprietary interest in the items in Annex A and was in lawful possession of the items before they were seized[note: 34];

(f)     For the items in Annex B, it was submitted that they fell within the scope of ORC 3519 and Mr Li Hua is required to produce them to Mr Wong.[note: 35]

14     Subsequently, the first claimant filed reply affidavits to the second and third claimants’ affidavits, whilst the second and third claimants also filed reply affidavits to the first claimant.

15     At the DI hearing itself, parties addressed the Court orally on their written submissions and the State stated that they did not have a position on who was entitled to the possession of the seized items.[note: 36]
