Public Prosecutor v Rashid Bin Amin

Public Prosecutor v Rashid Bin Amin
[2026] SGMC 91

Case Number:Magistrate's Arrest Case No. 903932 of 2026, Magistrate's Appeal No. 9171 of 2026-01
Decision Date:29 July 2026
Tribunal/Court:Magistrate's Court
Coram: Vince Gui
Counsel Name(s): State Prosecuting Officer Zakir Hussain (Attorney General's Chambers) for the Public Prosecutor; Mohamed Sarhan s/o Mohamed Ikhbar (Public Defender's Office).
Parties: Public Prosecutor — Rashid Bin Amin

Criminal Procedure and Sentencing – Sentencing – Principles – Ex-inmate breaching conditions while on remission – Section 50Y Prisons Act 1933

29 July 2026

District Judge Vince Gui:

Introduction

1       The accused pleaded guilty to one charge under s 50Y(1)(a) of the Prisons Act 1933 for committing a serious breach of a mandatory aftercare condition (“MAC”) of his remission order by failing to remain indoors at Selarang Halfway House (“SHH”) for a cumulative period of 286 hours and 45 minutes.

2       Applying the guidelines laid down in Abdul Mutalib bin Aziman v Public Prosecutor and other appeals [2021] 4 SLR 1220 (“Abdul Mutalib”), I imposed a sentence representing 60% of the remaining duration of the accused’s remission order which yielded an imprisonment term of 516 days. The accused appealed against the sentence. These are my grounds of decision.

Background facts

3       The accused, a 50-year-old Singaporean male, was released from prison on 4 April 2026 and became subject to a remission order running until 2 September 2028 (the “Remission Order”).[note: 1] He was concurrently placed on the Mandatory Aftercare Scheme (“MAS”) and was subjected to the MACs as specified under s 50V(3) of the Prisons Act 1933.[note: 2] The MACs, which were set out in the Remission Order, required the accused to amongst others remain indoors in SHH between 10 pm and 6 am unless otherwise authorised.[note: 3]

4       The Remission Order further specified that:[note: 4]

(a)     failure to remain indoors for a cumulative period of 24 hours would constitute a “serious breach” of the MAC; and

(b)     it is an offence to commit a serious breach of a MAC. In accordance with s 50Y of the Prisons Act, he would be liable on conviction to an imprisonment term not exceeding the remaining duration of the Remission Order at the date he commits the serious breach.

5       The accused acknowledged these conditions by signing on the Remission Order on 4 April 2026.[note: 5]

6       On 25 April 2026, the accused was granted authorised time off until 10.00 pm. He was granted a period of authorised leave on 26 April 2026. However, after leaving SHH to visit his mother, he failed to return after the expiry of both authorised periods. Attempts by SHH staff to contact him were futile. He remained uncontactable. A SHH staff lodged a police report on 27 April 2026.[note: 6]

7       The accused remained at large until he was arrested by police officers on 8 May 2026. By then, he failed to remain indoors at SHH for 286 hours and 45 minutes. He did not provide any valid reason during investigations for his failure to return to the SHH.[note: 7]

Parties’ submissions

Prosecution’s submissions

8       The Prosecution submitted that the present case was comparable to the case of Amanshah in Abdul Mutalib who failed to remain indoors at SHH for 279 hours and 25 minutes. The breach took place just over two months from his release from prison. The court pegged his case at the higher end of Band 2 of the applicable sentencing framework and sentenced him to 490 days’ imprisonment representing approximately 60% of his remaining remission period.[note: 8]

9       The Prosecution submitted that the present offence similarly fell at the higher end of Band 2 and sought a sentence of 516 days’ imprisonment, representing approximately 60% of the remaining remission period. They highlighted that the accused committed the breach barely 21 days after his prison release showing his lack of commitment to rehabilitation.[note: 9]

Defence’s submissions

10     The Defence likewise accepted that the offence fell within Band 2 of the applicable sentencing framework. However, they submitted a sentence of 40% to 50% of the remaining remission period (344 to 430 days’ imprisonment) would suffice. They submitted that the accused’s rehabilitative prospects were good as he did not reoffend whilst on the run. In contrast, Amanshah in Abdul Mutalib surrendered himself for drug-related offences.[note: 10]

11     The Defence also sought to explain why the accused committed the breach, alleging that he had witnessed other residents in SHH consuming drugs secretly and was uncomfortable with the situation.[note: 11] Moreover, he wanted to spend more time with his 81-year-old wheelchair bound mother who wanted his company.[note: 12]

Decision

12     It was common ground that the principal sentencing factors to consider under the applicable framework in Abdul Mutalib are:

(a)     the gravity of the breach;

(b)     the offender’s rehabilitative prospects; and

(c)     all other relevant circumstances.

13     It was further common ground that the offence fell under Band 2 of the said sentencing framework. The main issue was where within the sentencing band the offence fell.

14     Guidance on this can be found in the case of Abdul Mutalib which involved broadly similar facts. The offender, Amanshah bin Omar (“Amanshah”) failed to remain indoors for 279 hours and 25 minutes. The High Court described that breach as “relatively grave” because it was a substantial period of time. The court went on to find that his rehabilitative prospects were “not optimistic” because he committed the breach slightly more than two months after his release and ignored repeated requests to return. This demonstrated a “lack of commitment to rehabilitation and reintegration on his part”. These factors led the court to situate the case at the higher end of Band 2. The court imposed a sentence of 490 days’ imprisonment, which was about 60% of the remaining remission period of 823 days (at [120]).

15     In the present case, the gravity of the present breach was comparable to Amanshah’s case. The accused absconded for 286 hours and 45 minutes, a slightly longer duration. He was uncontactable during that period. I similarly regarded the breach as relatively grave. The Defence accepted as much.

16     I assessed the accused’s rehabilitative prospects as poor for two main reasons.

17     First, the breach was committed shortly after his prison release. The High Court in Abdul Mutalib emphasised that the timing of the breach is material. An offender who commits a breach just fresh out of prison on remission would show a “greater disregard for the conditions of his remission order and perhaps the law in general” (at [58]). The present breach, committed just three weeks out of prison, falls squarely within this category. In fact, the accused committed the breach even earlier than that in Amanshah’s case which was more than two months after his prison release.

18     Second, the accused remained uncontactable throughout his absence and failed to surrender himself. His custody was only secured when he was released by police officers on 8 May 2026. While I accept that the accused did not commit fresh offences whilst on the run whereas Amanshah had consumed drugs during that period, Amanshah eventually surrendered himself (at [22]). The accused did not take that step and had to be apprehended. His attitude reflected poorly on his commitment to rehabilitation and reintegration. In my view, his conduct amounted to a swift and unequivocal rejection of the rehabilitative regime.

19     I was unable to accord much weight to the reasons advanced by the Defence for why he committed the breach. The Defence submitted that the accused absconded from SHH after witnessing other residents consuming drugs and wanting to spend more time with his aged mother. These allegations were not properly substantiated. The first allegation is a serious one which should have been properly investigated but was not because the accused did not surface this allegation until the plead guilty mention. But even taking the allegation at face value, it does not justify his abscondment. If he had genuine concerns about drug consumption by other residents, the appropriate course of action would have been to raise the matter with his supervisors for investigation, rather than taking matters into his own hands by absconding.

20     As for his desire to spend time with his mother, this cannot be a valid justification for breaching the MAC. The accused was well-aware of the obligations having signed the Remission Order. The MAS was intended to facilitate an offender’s rehabilitation and reintegration into the community in a structured environment and programme. Offenders are not entitled to disregard the undergirding conditions simply because they regard their personal circumstances as being more important or pressing. To condone unilateral breaches on such grounds would be to undermine the efficacy of the MAS. If the accused had wanted to spend more time with his mother, the appropriate course of action would have been to request official time off from his supervisors.

Conclusion

21     Taking all the circumstances into account, I was satisfied that the offence was just as serious if not more so than the offence committed by Amanshah in Abdul Mutalib. A sentence representing 60% of the remaining remission period accorded with the sentence imposed in that case.

22     For these reasons, I sentenced the accused to 516 days’ imprisonment. I backdated the sentence to 8 May 2026, being the date of his arrest and remand. The accused is presently serving his sentence.

Public Prosecutor v Jessy Kyra Malhotra

Public Prosecutor v Jessy Kyra Malhotra
[2026] SGDC 253

Case Number:District Arrest Case No 909315 of 2024 and Others, Magistrate's Appeals No 9109 of 2026-01
Decision Date:29 July 2026
Tribunal/Court:District Court
Coram: Koo Zhi Xuan
Counsel Name(s): Chong Kee En and Yeo Kee Hwan (Attorney-General's Chambers) for the Prosecution; Yong Hong Kit Clement (Beyond Legal LLC) for the Accused.
Parties: Public Prosecutor — Jessy Kyra Malhotra

Criminal Law – Making false declarations to banks to open corporate bank accounts – Section 417 Penal Code (Cap 224, 2008 Rev Ed)

Criminal Procedure and Sentencing – Making false declarations to banks to open corporate bank accounts – Section 417 Penal Code (Cap 224, 2008 Rev Ed)

Criminal Procedure and Sentencing – Failing as director to use reasonable diligence to monitor transactions – Section 157(1) Companies Act (Cap 50, 2006 Rev Ed)

[LawNet Editorial Note: An appeal to this decision has been filed in MA 9109/2026/01.]

29 July 2026

District Judge Koo Zhi Xuan:

1       Jessy Kyra Malhotra (“the Accused”) claimed trial to the following four charges:

(a)      Cheating OCBC charge: you, on or about 24 December 2019, in Singapore, did cheat Overseas Chinese Banking Corporation Limited (“OCBC”), by deceiving OCBC into believing that you were the sole beneficial owner of Future Traders Pte Ltd (“the Company”), by declaring on the account-opening form that you were such, when you knew this to be false, and by such manner of deception, you intentionally induced OCBC to open a corporate bank account in the name of the Company (account no. xxx) (“OCBC Account”), which OCBC would not have done had it not been so deceived, and which act is likely to cause harm to the reputation of OCBC, and you have thereby committed an offence punishable under section 417 of the Penal Code (Cap 224, 2008 Rev Ed) (“PC”);

(b)      Cheating Maybank charge: you, on or about 23 December 2019, in Singapore, did cheat Maybank Singapore Limited (“Maybank”), by deceiving Maybank into believing that you were the sole beneficial owner of a corporate account for the Company, by declaring on the account-opening form that you were such, when you knew this to be false, and by such manner of deception, you intentionally induced Maybank to open a corporate bank account in the name of the Company (account no. xxx) (“Maybank Account”), which Maybank would not have done had it not been so deceived, and which act is likely to cause harm to the reputation of Maybank, and you have thereby committed an offence punishable under section 417 of the PC;

(c)      Cheating UOB charge: you, on or about 24 December 2019, in Singapore, did cheat United Overseas Bank Limited (“UOB”), by dishonestly concealing from UOB during the account-opening process any mention of one “Sachin” whom you knew would be an operator (i.e., maker of transactions) of the account, thereby deceiving UOB into believing that you would be the sole operator of the Company’s bank account, when you knew this to be false, and by such manner of deception, you intentionally induced UOB to open a corporate bank account in the name of the Company (account no. xxx) (“UOB Account”), which UOB would not have done had it not been so deceived, and which act is likely to cause harm to the reputation of UOB, and you have thereby committed an offence punishable under section 417 of the PC; and

(d)      Companies Act charge: you, between 24 December 2019 and 2 March 2020, in Singapore, while being a director of the Company, did fail to use reasonable diligence in the discharge of the duties of your office, by failing to take reasonable steps to monitor the transactions in the following accounts held in the name of the Company: (a) [UOB Account]; (b) [Maybank Account]; (c) Standard Chartered Bank Limited (“SCB”) account no. [xxx] (“SCB Account”); and (d) [OCBC Account]; and you have thereby contravened section 157(1) of the Companies Act (Cap 50, 2006 Rev Ed) (“Companies Act”), which is an offence punishable under section 157(3)(b) of the Companies Act.

2       At the conclusion of the trial, I convicted the Accused of all four charges, and sentenced the Accused as follows:

Charge

Sentence Imposed (Imprisonment)

Cheating OCBC Charge

5 months 2 weeks (consecutive)

Cheating Maybank Charge

5 months 2 weeks

Cheating UOB Charge

5 months 2 weeks

Companies Act Charge

2 months (consecutive)

 

Global Sentence Imposed:

7 months and 2 weeks



3       Dissatisfied, the Accused has filed a Notice of Appeal against both conviction and sentence.

4       I now set out my grounds of decision, which supersede my oral remarks delivered on 9 April 2026 and 5 May 2026.

Agreed facts

5       At the start of the trial, a Statement of Agreed Facts (“P1”) signed off by both the Deputy Public Prosecutor and the Defence Counsel was tendered by the Prosecution and admitted under section 267 of the Criminal Procedure Code 2010 (“CPC”) as P1. The material portions of P1 are set out as follows:

…

2.    Sometime in or before December 2019, the Accused agreed to help one Mr Sachinkumar Amrutlal (“Sachin”), an Indian national to set up a company in Singapore, which she was told was to conduct an import and export business, known as Future Traders Pte Ltd [“the Company”]. Sachin was working with one Patel Harsh Hareshkumar (“Harsh”).

3.    The parties also agreed that the Accused would open corporate bank accounts with herself as the sole authorised signatory, and she would then hand over the internet banking credentials for those accounts to Sachin, so that he could use those accounts through internet banking. In return, the Accused was to be paid a monthly salary. Later, when she met Harsh, the Accused came to understand that Sachin would pass the internet banking credentials to Harsh so that Harsh could use those accounts. She was also told that Harsh would be paying her salary.

4.    Pursuant to her agreement with Sachin, on 22 December 2019, the Accused registered the Company with the Account and Corporate Regulatory Authority (“ACRA”) …

5.    At around this time (22 December 2019), the Accused also obtained a SIM card with telephone number [xxx] (“the SIM Card”) for use in connection with the Company, which was to be handed over to Sachin. The Accused did hand over the SIM Card to Sachin sometime in early January 2020, who in turn handed the SIM Card to Harsh.

6.    In end-December 2019, the Accused applied in person to open four corporate/business bank accounts in the name of the Company with four banks in Singapore, all with internet banking facilities. When applying for these accounts, the Accused indicated [xxx] as the Company’s contact telephone number. The applications were approved, as set out below:

34.    … Only $100 was transacted through the SCB account.

Annexed Documents

35.    All of the annexed Exhibits A to N are not disputed as to their contents, accuracy, provenance and admissibility. The parties agree that they may be admitted into evidence.

Statements

36.    Two of the Accused’s statements were recorded by Commercial Affairs Officer Theresa Goh under section 22 of the Criminal Procedure Code (Cap 68, 2010 Rev Ed) on 24 June 2020 and 10 November 2020. They are annexed as Exhibits O and P respectively.

37.    The Accused does not dispute that the statements were given voluntarily and without threat, inducement and promise.

38.    The Accused reserves the right to challenge the statements for the purposes of accuracy.

Issues in Dispute

39.    The actus reus of the alleged offences is not generally in dispute. The Accused does not dispute she opened up the four corporate bank accounts as listed above, and that she had acknowledged and signed on the account opening forms.

40.    Among other things that may be in dispute, the Accused contends that:

a.    She did not have an illicit mens rea for the purposes of the opening of the accounts. She asserts that the banks’ protocols are also independent of her actions.

b.    She did not have an illicit mens rea when she surrendered the internet banking credentials to Sachin/Harsh, and she had no awareness that the accounts would be used for illicit purposes.

c.    She was not only intended to be a nominal shareholder or director or a figurehead. She asserts she was led to by Sachin and Harsh to believe that her involvement in the Company would be legitimate.

Material evidence

Timeline of key events
