P1-C2



Evidence of the bank witnesses

7       The Prosecution called a total of seven witnesses, six of them from the respective banks (OCBC, Maybank and UOB), and the last witness being the Investigation Officer (“IO”) and statement recorder of the two investigation statements recorded from the Accused on 24 June 2020 and 10 November 2020 (ie, P1-O and P1-P respectively).

8       The three bank officers who assisted the Accused in opening of the bank accounts in person (PW1 from Maybank, PW3 from OCBC and PW4 from UOB) testified that:

(a)     The respective account opening forms (see P1 at paragraphs 9, 17 and 26) had been filled out in such a manner as to affirm that only the Accused was the beneficial owner and/or operator of the Company or the bank account in question; and

(b)     The forms would have been filled up as recorded at the Accused’s behest after they had confirmed that the Accused understood the nature of the declaration that was made. In particular:

(i)       PW1 from Maybank testified that she would have explained to the Accused that a beneficial owner is “someone who actually operate[s] the account or have control over the account, and he or she is [the one who] actually benefit[s] from the fund inside the account”;[note: 1]

(ii)       PW3 from OCBC explained that he would have gone through every section of the form with the Accused after it was completed to ensure that the fields were filled in correctly and to give the Accused an opportunity to clarify any doubts she had.[note: 2] The Accused had declared to PW3 that she alone ultimately owned and controlled the management of the Company.[note: 3]

(iii)       PW4 from UOB testified that based on how the form was filled up, the Accused would have instructed that there was no other person who could handle the bank account.[note: 4] He would have specifically asked the Accused whether anybody else would be operating the bank account.[note: 5]

9       These testimonies were further corroborated by the testimonies of the respective bank supervisors or personnel in charge of training (ie, PW2 from Maybank, PW5 from OCBC and PW6 from UOB), who all affirmed that what PW1, PW3 and PW4 had done was a matter of standard operating procedure at the respective banks.

Evidence of the Investigating Officer

10     The IO explained her investigations against the Accused and the statement taking process for P1-O and P1-P. During cross-examination, she disagreed with the Defence’s case that the Accused was the sole beneficial owner of the Company as at 23 December 2019 or 24 December 2019.[note: 6] She also disagreed with the Defence’s case that the Accused did not know that Sachin would be operating the UOB Account until or after 7 January 2020.[note: 7]

Evidence of the Accused

11     During her examination-in-chief (“EIC”), the Accused testified as follows:

(a)     She came to know of Sachin in October 2019 and was not very close to him. She did not know much about his work or financial situation.

(b)     She had two conversations with Sachin about setting up an import and export business, before December 2019.

(c)     Sachin told her that the Company would be about importing and exporting “Indian spices, clothing and Indian textiles”.[note: 8] She was told by Sachin that she would be “mostly involved with the day-to-day transactions, the business activities, having frequent meetings with the buyers … and sellers”.[note: 9]

(d)     Sachin told her to open up the various bank accounts so that these accounts could be segregated based on “employees’ salaries, the incoming amount coming from the sellers, the buyers and the expenditures of the company”.[note: 10]

(e)     She did not deny that when opening the various bank accounts, the relevant bank staff would have explained to her, or asked her questions on the parts she had to fill up, on who was the beneficial owner or operator of the Company or the respective accounts.[note: 11]

(f)     She met Sachin and Harsh in Thailand, and they had discussions about their “proposed plan [on] how the business [was] going to be operated, and how [they were] going to communicate with the buyers and the sellers”.[note: 12]

(g)     She did not expect to be handing over the bank credentials to Sachin and Harsh.[note: 13] The Accused first claimed that this “change of plan” occurred “somewhere in early December” though it was “not confirmed yet”.[note: 14] The Accused later clarified that this change only concretised after she opened the bank accounts.

(h)     She had tried to fulfil her responsibilities as a director by trying to seek out information from Sachin, but he was not able to provide her with the information.[note: 15] After a while, she realised that both Sachin and Harsh had decided not to pick up her calls and had blocked her number.[note: 16] She lost contact with Sachin and Harsh in February or March 2020.[note: 17]

(i)     Despite losing her access to the bank accounts, the Accused did not return to Singapore from Thailand because she “had something on in India at that point of time”, though at trial, she couldn’t recall what she was involved in in India at the material time which required her to stay in India.[note: 18]

(j)     When she found out that the Maybank Account was used for illicit purposes, she decided to “call the rest of the banks and asked the staff to either close down the account or [suspend] the account”.[note: 19]

Prosecution’s Case

The cheating charges

12     For the cheating charges, the Prosecution’s case was that the Accused had falsely declared herself to be the sole beneficial owner of the Company, and/or the sole beneficial owner or operator of the corporate bank accounts opened in the Company’s name. In doing so, the Accused had dishonestly induced the banks to open up the respective corporate bank accounts.

13     The Prosecution submitted that all of the relevant elements of the cheating charges have been made out:

(a)     The Accused had deceived the banks that she was the sole beneficial owner of the Company and/or that she would be the sole beneficial owner or operator of the bank accounts she was seeking to open in the Company’s name.

(b)     At the material time, the Accused was not the sole beneficial owner of the Company, nor was there any intention for her to be the sole beneficial owner or sole operator of the bank accounts that were to be opened in the Company’s name.

(c)     Induced by her misrepresentations, the banks omitted to consider the beneficial owner or operator in their decisions to open the bank accounts in question. They would not have opened the bank accounts had they been privy to the truth.

(d)     The Accused’s actions were likely to cause reputational harm to the banks.

14     The Prosecution submitted evidence showing the Accused was not the sole beneficial owner of the Company and/or the sole operator of the bank accounts, and that she had never intended to do so:

(a)     The Accused admitted in P1-P that she was the Company’s director and shareholder “purely in name”, and that she had been offered $1,500 by Sachin to play this role. Her defence that there was a “change of plans” in January 2020 where she became the director and shareholder “purely in name” only emerged at trial, and was both inconsistent and inconceivable.

(b)     The Accused did not possess any concrete information about the Company’s business operations throughout her stint as its director. She was utterly reliant on Sachin for all directions and information, and admitted at trial that she had been parroting whatever Sachin had instructed her to say to the banks.

(c)     The Accused never intended to capitalise the Company’s shares with her own money. She had admitted that the $100,000 declared in share capital was supposed to be paid by Sachin, and the Accused did not know even by 10 November 2020 whether the shares had ultimately been paid up.

(d)     The evidence showed that the Accused did not have beneficial ownership of the bank accounts and she never intended to. She had opened the four bank accounts solely on Sachin’s instructions, did not have beneficial ownership of the funds within the bank accounts, and had intended to surrender the accounts to Sachin from the beginning.

15     The Prosecution submitted that due to the Accused’s false declarations, the banks were intentionally induced to omit to consider the ultimate beneficial owner in their decision to open the bank accounts for the Company, pointing to the testimonies of the various bank officers, and also the Accused’s admission that she knew that the banks would not have opened the bank accounts for her if they knew she had concealed Sachin’s involvement. There was also likely to be reputation harm caused to the banks if the Accused’s deception and the consequent scam proceeds which flowed through the implicated accounts were made known to the public.

The Companies Act charge

16     For the Companies Act charge, the Prosecution’s case was that after opening up the bank accounts, the Accused had failed to use reasonable diligence to discharge her duties as the director of the Company by having failed to monitor the transactions in four corporate accounts held in the Accused’s name, in contravention of s 157(1) of the Companies Act.

17     The Prosecution highlighted the following:

(a)     The Accused surrendered all points of access to the bank accounts to Sachin and Harsh shortly after she opened up the bank accounts.

(b)     Having lost access, the only steps the Accused took from 7 January 2020 to 2 March 2020 in monitoring the transactions were as follows:

(i)       For the UOB Account, the Accused requested for the Landlord to collect letters that were sent on 3 February 2020, followed by asking a “friend’s friend” to take pictures of the various remittance advice enclosed within. The Accused however had no explanation when queried what steps she had taken after seeing the large amounts in the remittance advice received. There was no evidence of the Accused calling UOB to ask about the transactions.

(ii)       For the Maybank Account, the Accused agreed that she had not taken any steps to monitor the account between her surrendering access on 7 January 2020 till 30 March 2020, when her first call to Maybank was logged. Even after she was told to call the Commercial Affairs Division’s (“CAD”) number with respect to the illegal proceeds inside the account, the Accused did not do so and claimed to have misplaced the number, without ever trying to search for CAD’s hotline.

(iii)       For the SCB Account, the Accused did not attempt to contact the bank, and admitted it was not reasonable for her not to do so just because she thought the cost of calling was high.

(iv)       For the OCBC Account, the Accused cared so little about monitoring the transactions that when she made the call to OCBC on 13 March 2020, she did not know if the account was still active. She also failed to cite a recent transaction for identity verification purposes and did not follow up with the bank until the next call on 30 March 2020.

(c)     Furthermore, if the Accused was at all serious about carrying out her duties as a director, she could and should have returned to Singapore after losing access to the bank accounts. However, she offered no good reason why she did not do so. All in all, the Accused’s actions showed that she could not care less as she never intended to be a director in any form, much less one who would take reasonable steps to discharge her duties as a director.

18     The Prosecution concluded by highlighting that because of the Accused’s actions, she had allowed over S$1.6 million in scams proceeds and illicit monies to flow through the bank accounts which she cheated the banks into opening and/or failed to monitor the transactions of even after finding something amiss.

Defence’s Case

19     The Defence’s case was that the Prosecution had not proven guilt beyond reasonable doubt on all the proceeded charges. The Defence submitted that the evidence established at its highest poor judgment, a lack of sophistication, and an unfortunate willingness to follow instructions from others on the part of the Accused.

20     The Defence’s version of the key facts was as follows:

(a)     The Accused believed that the Company was intended to be a legitimate business and it was not her understanding or agreement prior to or on the days she had opened the bank accounts that she would be the shareholder and director in name only. She was misled and manipulated by Sachin and Harsh.

(b)     The Accused had handed over the SIM Card and UOB bank token upon Sachin and Harsh’s request on 7 January 2020 in Thailand, as she thought she could really trust Sachin to update her on the Company’s business activities.

(c)     After handing over the SIM Card and UOB bank token to Sachin and Harsh, she found out she was unable to obtain bank statements or operational information from them. She had been told that she did not need to be involved in the running of the business as Sachin and Harsh would be entirely in charge. When she became suspicious after viewing the Maybank transactions, the Accused had called Maybank and OCBC, and might also have called SCB.

21     The Defence submitted the following for the Court’s consideration:

(a)     The evidence from the bank officers disclosed a genuine ambiguity and a serious evidential gap – the forms adduced at trial did not support a clean, simple finding that the Accused made a knowingly false declaration of “beneficial ownership” in “the compliance sense”.

(b)     The bank officers could only speak to what the bank would like to know, but not on what the Accused understood “beneficial owner” to mean, or why she answered the way she did. The evidence led from the bank officers was also limited in showing that there was actual inducement.

(c)     The Accused’s evidence was that she had intended to be involved with the business operations and believed the business to be legitimate; she was not just the shareholder and director “in name only” during the incorporation of the Company and the opening of the bank accounts. Even if the Court finds that the Accused had followed misguided instructions, that does not without more prove beyond reasonable doubt that the Accused had acted with the dishonest intent required for the cheating charges to be made out.

(d)     The Accused should not be judged guilty by her actions subsequent to 7 January 2020 because her delay and poor follow-up actions were consistent with panic, confusion, lack of sophistication and being overseas with limited resources and blocked contacts. They do not prove that she had dishonestly cheated the banks a few weeks before that. At its highest, the Accused’s handover of the banking access reveals that the Accused was naïve and had been exploited.

(e)     The Accused’s surrender of banking access to Sachin resulted in her ability to “monitor transactions” to be practically eliminated. The Prosecution could not demand verification against documents that the Accused never had and could not obtain. Furthermore, the Accused was overseas throughout much of the period stated in the Companies Act charge.

(f)     There was no evidence that the Accused had benefited from the alleged criminality.

The Court’s Decision on Conviction

The cheating charges

22     With respect to the cheating charges, the relevant portions of section 415 of the PC provide that:

Whoever, by deceiving any person, whether or not such deception was the sole or main inducement … intentionally induces the person so deceived to do or omit to do anything which he would not do or omit to do if he were not so deceived, and which act or omission causes or is likely to cause damage … to any person in body, mind, reputation or property, is said to “cheat”.

23     For the cheating charges to be made out, the Prosecution bore the burden of proving beyond reasonable doubt that:

(a)     The Accused declared that she was:

(i)       the sole beneficial owner of the Company to OCBC,

(ii)       the sole beneficial owner of the corporate bank account to Maybank, and

(iii)       the sole operator of the corporate bank account to UOB.

(collectively, “the Declarations”);

(b)     The Declarations were false, and the Accused knew at the material time (ie, 23 and 24 December 2019) that the Declarations were false;

(c)     The Accused made the false Declarations with the intention of inducing the banks to open the corporate bank accounts for the Company;

(d)     The banks were induced to open the bank accounts in the name of the Company, which they would not have done had they not been deceived; and

(e)     The Accused’s actions were likely to cause harm to the reputation of the banks.

24     I deal with each of these issues in turn.

The 1st issue: Did the Accused made the Declarations in the corporate bank account forms?

25     On the first issue, there was no dispute that the Accused did make the said Declarations to the banks in the respective bank account opening forms. The Accused did not dispute that the forms were filled up by the bank officers on her instructions and in her presence, and that she had signed off on them.

26     The Prosecution led evidence from various bank officers who testified that the forms would have been filled up after confirming that the Accused understood the nature of the Declarations:

(a)     The witnesses from OCBC testified that it would have been explained to the Accused that “sole beneficial owner” meant that it was the Accused who owned and controlled the management of the Company. The Accused admitted that the OCBC bank staff would have asked her this, and that she would have answered that she was indeed the person who owned and controlled the management of the Company.[note: 20]

(b)     The witnesses from Maybank testified that it would have been explained to the Accused that by declaring that she was the sole beneficial owner of the Maybank Account, it meant that it was the Accused who actually operated and controlled the bank account, and benefited from the funds inside the account.[note: 21] The Accused admitted that in filling up the Maybank form as she did, she had declared to Maybank that she ultimately owned and controlled the management of the Maybank Account.[note: 22]

(c)     The witnesses from UOB testified that the Accused must have instructed that no other person could handle the UOB Account,[note: 23] and that she had the sole ability to make transactions and control this account. The Accused admitted that this was explained to her, and that by filling up the UOB form as she did, she had declared to UOB that only she would have the sole ability to make transactions on this account.[note: 24]

27     I therefore found that the Accused had, on 23 and 24 December 2019, made the Declarations to the three banks via the respective bank account opening forms which were explained to her in detail by the respective bank officers. Contrary to the Defence’s submissions, I saw no “genuine ambiguity [or] serious evidential gap” as to what was declared,[note: 25] given the Accused’s acceptance that the bank officers would have provided the aforesaid explanations to her.

The 2nd Issue: Were the Declarations false, and did the Accused know at the material time that the Declarations were false?

28     The 2nd Issue was the key issue in dispute in the trial. For this element to be made out, the Prosecution must prove beyond reasonable doubt that at the material time when the Accused opened the bank accounts, the Accused was not and did not intend to be:

(a)     the sole person who owned and controlled the management of the Company; and

(b)     the person who would be the sole operator and/or controller of the bank accounts opened.

29     In my view, the following pieces of evidence cumulatively established that the Declarations were false, and this was known to the Accused when she made the Declarations on 23 and 24 December 2019.

30     First, I found that the Accused had admitted in P1-P that she was the Company’s director and shareholder “purely in name”.[note: 26] This admission materially contradicted the Declarations and what was explained to her by the bank officers. As the Company’s director and shareholder “purely in name”, she was not the person who owned or controlled the management of the Company, and neither was she the person who would be the sole operator and/or controller of the bank accounts opened.

31     The Accused provided inconsistent explanations at trial on what was in her mind when she gave the said answers to the IO in P1-P. During her EIC, she tried to explain that she had thought the IO’s questions were in relation to her situation after 7 January 2020, in that because she had handed over control of the bank accounts to Sachin, she had then become the shareholder and director of the Company “purely in name” after 7 January 2020.[note: 27] This was an explanation which presupposed that the Accused did in fact understand the meaning of being a shareholder and director “purely in name”; and that she would have answered the IO more accurately had the IO been more precise about the time period the IO was inquiring about. However, during cross-examination and re-examination, the Accused’s account changed and she tried to portray herself as someone who did not understand what a shareholder and director “purely in name” meant and that she was “confused with the questions”.[note: 28] Some of her responses – both during cross-examination and re-examination – even appeared to suggest that she thought she was the shareholder and director “purely in name” even in December 2019.[note: 29]

32     I found both these positions proffered by the Accused to be inconsistent and on either account, contradicted by the surrounding evidence. It is important to understand the Accused’s answers in P1-P within the context of both the preceding and subsequent questions the IO had been asking the Accused. The context clearly shows the IO asking the Accused about her understanding of and position within the Company’s business not at the point of the interview on 10 November 2020, but when the Company was incorporated and the bank accounts opened (ie, in December 2019). For example, just prior to questions 168 and 169 (ie, the critical questions about whether the Accused was the Company’s director and shareholder “purely in name”), the IO had asked the Accused why she had not gone down to the registered office of the Company “before [she] left Singapore on 7 January 2020”.[note: 30] When asked about when the Company’s office was set up, the Accused had also answered “somewhere in December 2019”.[note: 31] Right after question 169, the IO had also questioned the Accused on whether she was paid a sum of money to open the corporate bank accounts for the Company (ie, events which took place on 23 and 24 December 2019),[note: 32] and the circumstances in which she had gone to Thailand in January 2020.[note: 33] Read in context, the IO was clearly asking the Accused about her position in the Company in December 2019, and this would have been clear to the Accused given her responses to the IO’s questions.

33     The IO also did not suddenly just ask whether the Accused was the shareholder and director of the Company “purely in name” out of the blue without any explanation or context. Within questions 168 and 169 themselves, the IO had reasonably contextualised her questions by asking the Accused if she was the director and shareholder “purely in name” because the Accused did “not seem to be involved in [the Company’s] operations or know much about its business” and was paid $1,500 monthly “not…to be involved in [the Company’s]’s operations”. This state of affairs – ie, the Accused being uninvolved in the Company’s operations, and not knowing much about the Company’s business – was present from December 2019, and not only after 7 January 2020. To these questions, the Accused had answered “yes”. This was a clear admission made as early as 10 November 2020 that the Declarations were false.

34     Second, I found that the Accused had such a glaring lack of knowledge of the Company and its supposed business, from the very beginning (in December 2019) and even up till the time of the trial (in January 2026), that the Declarations could not have been truthfully made. The Accused could not give any concrete, detailed evidence in court of the Company’s supposed business and plans. She did not even realise that the Company’s registered address was a fictitious one, and did not know anything about the Company’s operations in Singapore, for example, who was going to hire its employees, or how the office was going to be set up. Essentially, she knew absolutely nothing about the Company’s business or how it was going to be run. Critically, the Accused conceded during cross-examination that under such circumstances, and given her lack of knowledge, she could not be said to have been in control of the Company when she opened the bank accounts:[note: 34]

DPP:

How are you in control of a company when you never met its employees?

Accused:

I am not able to have the control because I do not---I am not able to see the employees.

DPP:

Exactly. So, when you open up these bank accounts, you cannot say that you are in control of this company, agree?

Accused:

Agree.



35     Third, I found that Sachin was, and was always intended to be, the ultimate beneficial owner of the Company and the bank accounts, not the Accused. There were multiple, independent strands of evidence which pointed to this same conclusion:

(a)     Firstly, it was clear that the Accused had blindly followed all of Sachin’s instructions for everything she had done in relation to the Company, even on her own account. She had registered the company address without knowing what it was simply because Sachin instructed her to do so. She travelled to various locations to open 4 corporate bank accounts on Sachin’s instructions, without being able to provide a sensible explanation as to why this was necessary. When she opened the various bank accounts, she had merely parroted whatever Sachin told her to say to the bank officers. The Accused also admitted during cross-examination that she was “following Sachin’s instructions and not simply seeking his advice”,[note: 35] and she agreed that if she was simply following a person’s instructions, that person would be the person in control, not her.[note: 36] Throughout the trial, the Accused never mentioned a single instance in which she had done something different from what Sachin had instructed, or even on her own accord, in relation to the Company prior to 7 January 2020. It was abundantly clear from the Accused’s own evidence during the trial that Sachin was the person who always had ultimate control over the Company since its incorporation, and not her.

(b)     Secondly, the Accused had claimed that the monies initially deposited in the respective bank accounts were borrowed from a friend of hers named Amrit,[note: 37] who was the person who had introduced her to Sachin, and whose mobile phone happened to be mysteriously in India in 2020 which the Accused could use to contact the Landlord for the bank documents sent to the Landlord’s address. I found the Accused’s unconvincing attempts to distance Amrit from this entire episode to be highly suspicious. In my view, the only reasonable inference to be drawn was that that the monies initially deposited in the bank accounts must have been Sachin’s, even if they came through Amrit’s hands.[note: 38] Thus, the reason why the Accused did not withdraw the $1,000 in the Maybank Account before surrendering all banking access to Sachin must be because Sachin was the real beneficial owner of the account generally and of the sum of money within the account specifically. On the other hand, the Accused was only allowed to withdraw $1,500 as per their agreement, and she did so from the OCBC and UOB bank accounts. The Accused’s contrived explanations that she did not withdraw the $1,000 because she might have forgotten about it, or because they belonged “to some of [her] friends”[note: 39] (without stating who), or that she might have needed to use these monies in case of emergency when abroad[note: 40] were so inconsistent and unconvincing that it was clear to me she was simply making up excuses on the stand.

(c)     Thirdly, the Accused had also admitted in P1-P,[note: 41] and also during her EIC,[note: 42] that the $100,000 meant to be used to capitalise the Company was to come from Sachin. The Accused’s subsequent attempt during cross-examination where she tried to suggest that she would have made plans to borrow money from friends to come up with the $100,000 after Sachin failed to contribute the amount[note: 43] was entirely unconvincing. She did not substantiate who she had planned to ask, and why anyone would be willing to lend her $100,000 to launch and manage a business which she knew absolutely nothing about. Furthermore, she simply could not provide a meaningful response to the Prosecution’s questions as to why she had to state “$100,000” as the share capital value when registering the Company if she was no longer going to rely on Sachin to come up with the monies.[note: 44] There was therefore no reason for me to doubt that the Accused had either simply parroted Sachin’s directions to state the share capital of $100,000 when registering the Company, or she had declared the $100,000 with the belief that Sachin would provide the funds. On either account, Sachin was the ultimate beneficial owner of the Company, not the Accused.

(d)     Fourthly, the Accused was given a chance by Defence Counsel to explain during re-examination how the Declarations could be true, given her concession that Sachin was indeed the person in control at all material time. She failed to provide any explanation whatsoever,[note: 45] and her lack of a reasoned response firmly established that at the point when she declared that she was the sole operator or ultimate beneficial owner of the Company or the bank accounts in question, she knew that the Declarations were false.

36     Fourth, the Accused’s actions subsequent to 24 December 2019 strongly corroborated the Prosecution’s case theory that she never had the intention to be in control of either the Company or the bank accounts in question on 23 or 24 December 2019.

(a)     The Accused conceded during cross-examination that if she had harboured genuine intentions of acting as a real (as opposed to nominal) director of the Company, and she was the party responsible for coming up with the $100,000 share capital, it would have made no sense at all that she would surrender her access to the bank accounts of the Company to Sachin within two weeks of the Company’s incorporation.[note: 46] Thus, even on her own account, her actions in surrendering her access to the bank accounts to Sachin were inexplicable and contradicted her defence that she was or had intended to be the ultimate beneficial owner of the Company or the respective bank accounts.

(b)     Not only did the Accused surrender all points of access to the bank accounts on or around 7 January 2020, it was clear to me that the Accused was wholly lackadaisical in finding out what had indeed happened to the accounts subsequent to 7 January 2020. Even after she was informed by Maybank to contact CAD as her Maybank account had been frozen, the Accused did not do so, and the reasons she offered for not doing so were entirely farcical. The Accused claimed that she had “misplaced” CAD’s number, but she did not and could not explain why she couldn’t have simply searched online for CAD’s number to contact them as directed by Maybank if she was indeed concerned about the transactions that had taken place in the bank account.[note: 47] The Accused’s actions (or lack thereof) after 7 January 2020 revealed that it was never her intention all along to be the owner or controller of either the Company or its bank accounts.

(c)     Furthermore, I found it incredible that the Accused would coincidentally lose both her personal email log-in password (which was linked to the UOB Account) and her personal handphone around the same time she had surrendered the SIM Card and UOB bank token to Sachin, such that she would immediately have no means of either accessing the bank accounts or being contacted by the banks for the transactions in these accounts. When her actions and the situation she had claimed to be in were viewed holistically, it was clear to me that the Accused’s intention all along – ie, from the incorporation of the Company – was to surrender all points of access to the bank accounts to Sachin. In fact, there was a moment during the trial where the Accused let slip that the plan to hand over access of the bank accounts to Sachin was discussed in “early December [2019]”.[note: 48] I found this to be a rare moment of truth in the midst of all of her otherwise untruthful and/or contradictory claims.

37     Fifth, contrary to the Defence’s submissions, I found that the Accused was financially motivated to make the Declarations falsely to the banks. She was promised $1,500 to do so and she had in fact withdrawn that amount from two of the bank accounts before she flew to Thailand to meet Sachin to pass him the SIM Card and UOB bank token. There was no credible explanation provided by the Defence as to why she would draw down an amount resembling the $1,500 promised, and not more, just before she left Singapore to meet Sachin on 7 January 2020.

38     In summary, I found that the weight of the evidence cumulatively pointed to the Declarations not only being false, but that the Accused had made the Declarations knowing that they were false.

The 3rd Issue: Did the Accused make the false Declarations with the intention of inducing the banks to open the bank accounts for the Company?

39     On the 3rd issue, I found that the Prosecution had proven beyond reasonable doubt that the Accused did make the false Declarations with the intention of inducing the banks to open the bank accounts for the Company. The material evidence supporting this finding are set out as follows.

40     First, on the Accused’s own account, she was already well aware that it would be harder for a foreigner like Sachin to open bank accounts compared to her.[note: 49] She was thus not someone who was clueless as to why Sachin would request for her to be the one opening the bank accounts. The Accused was clearly motivated not to mention Sachin’s involvement when opening the bank accounts, and she in fact did not do so.

41     Second, the surrounding context of the Accused’s actions matters. She had taken the effort to physically visit three different banks in the space of two days (ie, 23 and 24 December 2019) with the clear goal of opening up bank accounts for Sachin’s use. The Accused also did not deny that the bank officers had taken time to explain what it meant for her to be the sole beneficial owner or operator of either the Company or the bank accounts in person. By making the false Declarations in such settings, it was abundantly clear that the Accused had acted with sufficient intentionality of inducing the banks to open the bank accounts. The Defence did not provide any credible alternative interpretation of the Accused’s actions on 23 and 24 December 2019.

The 4th Issue: Were the banks induced to open the bank accounts in the name of the Company, which they would not have done had they not been deceived?

42     On the 4th issue, I found that the banks were indeed induced to open up the bank accounts as a result of the false Declarations, which they would not have done had they not been deceived.

43     First, the bank officers had convincingly testified that if they had known that the Accused had made a false declaration in relation to who the ultimate beneficial owner of the Company, or operator of the account was, they would not have proceeded to open the respective bank accounts. The Defence had not provided the court any reason to think why these bank officers might not have been speaking the truth; and had offered nothing in response to contradict their testimonies in court.

44     Second, the Accused herself agreed that if the banks knew that she had lied to them about who the ultimate beneficial owner or operator of the Company or the accounts was, they would not have opened the bank accounts.[note: 50]

45     It bears mention that under s 415 of the PC, the deception by the Accused need not be the “sole or main inducement”. In this regard, given the bank officers’ testimonies which were not contradicted by the Defence, and the Accused’s own admission, there was simply no need for the Prosecution to prove that “but for the specific alleged [false Declaration], approval would have been denied” by the banks.[note: 51]

The 5th Issue: Were the Accused’s actions likely to cause harm to the reputation of the banks?

46     On the 5th issue, it is common knowledge and undisputed that banks have a duty to know who the ultimate beneficial owners of their bank accounts are, and that the process of obtaining such declarations is a pre-requisite to mitigating the risk of the banks’ systems being used for money laundering and terrorism financing (see Tang You Liang Andruew v Public Prosecutor and another appeal [2023] 3 SLR 229 at [44]). This important step in turn mitigates the likelihood of risk of reputational harm to the banks, which would manifest if their bank accounts were used for illegal purposes. The Prosecution’s witnesses testified to this:

(a)     PW2 from Maybank testified that when an account is linked to unexplained transactions which turned out to be scams, Maybank might end up facing potential financial penalties which the Monetary Authority of Singapore (“MAS”) may impose. In the worst-case scenario, MAS may even revoke the bank’s licence to operate in Singapore.[note: 52] Such penalties if imposed could hurt the image of the bank.[note: 53]

(b)     PW5 from OCBC testified that reputational damage would be suffered by OCBC for scam proceeds to flow through its accounts.[note: 54]

(c)     PW6 from UOB testified that the reputation of UOB would be affected if UOB was deceived on who had control over the bank account and the bank account ended up being used for some criminal activity.[note: 55]

47     In the present case, it was undisputed that the bank accounts created by the Accused as a result of her false Declarations were used eventually to commit scam and/or money-laundering offences.[note: 56]

48     In my view, the Accused’s deception (which facilitated significant scam proceeds flowing through the implicated bank accounts) clearly resulted in a significant likelihood that harm would be caused to the reputation of the banks. Throughout the trial, the Defence had not put forth any evidence or submission to the contrary. This final element of the Accused’s actions being likely to cause harm to the reputation of all three banks was therefore made out beyond reasonable doubt.

Conclusion on the cheating charges

49     For all the foregoing reasons, I was of the view that the three cheating charges were proven beyond reasonable doubt and I therefore convicted the Accused of all three cheating charges.

The Companies Act charge

50     I now turn to the Companies Act charge. Given my finding earlier that the Accused was lackadaisical in finding out what had happened to the bank accounts she had surrendered to Sachin, it would follow that she had indeed failed to use reasonable diligence to monitor the transactions in all four corporate bank accounts held in the Company’s name. In fact, as the plan all along was that she was only to be a director “purely in name”, it was clear to me that the Accused never had any intention to play any substantive role as a director to begin with, much less one who would diligently monitor the transactions in the respective bank accounts she had opened only to hand over to Sachin.

51     It is critical to note that the dates in which the Accused had allegedly failed to carry out her duties were from 24 December 2019 to 2 March 2020, as stated in the Companies Act charge. It would thus be erroneous for the Court to assess whether the Accused had carried out her duties as a director only from the point she had surrendered access to the bank accounts (ie, on or after 7 January 2020), as if her surrendering all banking access to Sachin had nothing to do with the Companies Act charge. In reality, her act of surrendering all access to the bank accounts to Sachin, even though she was the sole director of the Company, ought to be core to the Court’s analysis of whether she had indeed carried out her duties with reasonable diligence from 24 December 2019. In my view, having committed the “irresponsible”[note: 57] and “unreasonable”[note: 58] act of surrendering access, her duty to monitor the transactions of the accounts was heightened, and the standard she had to meet ought to be higher – not lower – than a director who had not surrendered access to the bank accounts she was supposed to be a sole controller or operator of.

52     The facts however showed that the Accused did not meet any of these standards. The Accused simply did not take any meaningful step at all to monitor the accounts of the four bank accounts stated in the charge:

(a)     First, it was not disputed that the Accused had not monitored the transactions of the various bank accounts during the material period stated in the charge.[note: 59] The Defence had merely submitted that she had lost practical control and access to the bank accounts after 7 January 2020, but simply offering this excuse did not satisfy the statutory duty imposed on the Accused. There was also no objective evidence corroborating the Accused’s claim that she had chased Sachin for meaningful updates of the transactions in the bank accounts subsequent to 7 January 2020.

(b)     Second, I found the Accused’s act of calling some banks only in March 2020, purportedly to check on the transactions, to be unreasonably late. It was not an act of “reasonable diligence” for someone who was supposed to be the sole operator or controller of the bank accounts. There was no satisfactory reason provided as to why the Accused could not have called the banks earlier, given that she was already in possession of a handphone with a local line, and was using it to text the Landlord quite frequently as early as 31 January 2020.[note: 60] Furthermore, the Accused admitted in court that she could have asked to see the letters from UOB sent to the Landlord as early as 6February 2020 if she had wanted to.[note: 61] She had also claimed in P1-P that upon viewing certain bank documents which were sent to her, she had begun “to feel suspicious about the amount and … decided to call [Maybank] about this”.[note: 62] Critically, no reasonable explanation was provided by the Defence as to why the Accused had to wait until 13 March 2020 before making her first call to OCBC, and 30 March 2020 before making her first call to Maybank.[note: 63] There was also no evidence placed before the Court that she had called either UOB or SCB. The Accused essentially conceded during cross-examination that her excuse for not calling some of the banks because of the supposed high cost of international calls was unsound; as “even if the cost [was] high, [she ought to have called] the banks … to monitor the transactions”.[note: 64]

(c)     Third, the call logs with OCBC and Maybank revealed that even after the Accused finally called two of the banks, she had expressed no concern about the various transactions which had taken place which had caused the accounts to be frozen. The call logs revealed that there was no query raised to the bank officers as to who had made the prior transactions, and where the monies had been transferred from or to. There was also no request that the banks prevent any further access or transaction by other individuals except herself. Instead, the Accused was fixated solely on the remaining monies in the accounts and how she could effect their release. Indeed, she was so concerned about being returned these monies (even though they were not even hers to begin with) that she thought it fit to verbally threaten the Maybank officer on the line that she would call her lawyer to sue Maybank.[note: 65] In my view, the contents of the call logs completely contradicted the Accused’s belated and unsubstantiated claims in court that she had called the banks to “find out more details about the [monies] reflected in the bank statement”,[note: 66] “request [the bank] staff to suspend [the] account”,[note: 67] and “[ask] the staff to either close down the account or [suspend] the account”.[note: 68] The contemporaneous, objective evidence tendered in court revealed that even when she was finally in contact with the banks, the Accused did not show any interest whatsoever or take any step to monitor the transactions in the accounts. As correctly suggested by the Prosecution, which the Defence had no meaningful response to, the contents of the call logs were entirely consistent with the possibility that the Accused was still working under Sachin’s directions in March 2020.[note: 69]

(d)     Fourth, the Accused could not offer any good reason why she could not return to Singapore to carry out her duties as a director, after she had surrendered access to the bank accounts to Sachin. Despite multiple opportunities given for her to do so at trial, she offered no convincing explanation as to why she had to stay in India for so many months, even though she had already lost her handphone and was unable to access the bank accounts. Her claim that there was some kind of lockdown preventing her from returning to Singapore from India due to COVID-19 between January to March 2020 turned out to be either false or completely unsubstantiated.

53     For all of the foregoing reasons, I concluded that the Accused did indeed fail to take reasonable steps to monitor the transactions in the four corporate bank accounts held in the Company’s name, between 24 December 2019 and 2 March 2020, and even after she had been put on notice that something was amiss. The Accused had failed to use reasonable diligence in the discharge of her duties as a director, and the Companies Act charge was thus made out beyond reasonable doubt.

Further findings of the Court

54     In my view, the evidence presented at trial did not only prove that the Accused had cheated the banks and failed in her duty as a director of the Company, they also revealed the Accused to be at best wilfully blind to, and at worst a knowing enabler of, the criminal acts of Sachin and his associates. In other words, the Defence’s narrative that the Accused was just a naïve person who had unwittingly and unfortunately stumbled into a criminal enterprise run by others was not borne out by the evidence.

55     First, as I had alluded to earlier, the contents of the Accused’s call logs with OCBC and Maybank suggested that, as late as 30 March 2020, the Accused’s primary motivation was to secure the release of the remaining funds in the bank accounts. By March 2020, the Accused would already have known that the transfers into and out of the respective bank accounts were, in her own words, “fishy because the remittance advices were of large amounts”,[note: 70] and that the bank accounts had been frozen. Yet, the call logs showed the Accused being only interested – if not, desperate – in having the remaining funds released. The Accused provided no explanation why she was so desperate in having the funds released, when she already had reason to believe at the material time that these funds were likely tainted with criminal proceeds. There was thus good reason to infer that as late as 30 March 2020, the Accused was still acting under Sachin’s instructions to secure the release of the frozen funds, and she had complied with those instructions despite already having already known about the “fishy” transactions which had taken place in the bank accounts.

56     Second, I found the entire episode of the Accused having someone whose name she apparently did not even know to collect letters from the Landlord on her behalf to be highly suspicious. Before she left for Thailand on 6 January 2020, the Accused had already pre-empted the Landlord that her “[fiancé’s friend]” would be collecting the letters sent to the Landlord’s address.[note: 71] When asked by the IO about this on 24 June 2020, the Accused claimed that it was Sachin who had asked his friend to collect the letters.[note: 72] But when asked again by the IO on 10 November 2020, the Accused then claimed that it was one “Pali’s friend” who had collected the letters instead.[note: 73] These unexplained inconsistencies strongly suggested that the Accused was likely lying about who exactly had collected the letters from the Landlord and/or deliberately evasive in explaining how this arrangement had come about. In my view, there is good reason to believe that whoever was sent to collect the letters from the Landlord was likely associated with Sachin; if not Sachin himself.[note: 74] But more importantly, the contemporaneous text messages exchanged between the Landlord and the Accused pointed to the conclusion that even after she was put on notice of the “fishy” transactions in some of the bank accounts, the Accused was still instructing the Landlord over text messages to keep the letters for her “fiancé” (on 10 March 2020 and 13 April 2020).[note: 75] These messages to the Landlord completely contradicted the Defence’s narrative that the Accused had taken defensive actions immediately upon learning about the “fishy” transactions, and after allegedly being ignored by Sachin after she had surrendered all banking access on 7 January 2020. Rather, the fact that the Accused was still instructing the Landlord to pass the letters to her “fiancé” as late as 13 April 2020 – which was similar to the instructions she had given the Landlord on 6 January 2020 – strongly suggested that she was likely still in cahoots or communication with Sachin or whoever Sachin was associated with even as late as 13 April 2020.

57     All in all, I was of the view that the evidence presented at trial pointed not only to the Accused’s guilt in relation to the four charges, but also to her sustained involvement with Sachin’s criminal activities, even after she had been put on notice that illicit activities had taken place in relation to the bank accounts. I therefore did not find it believable at all that the Accused was someone who was simply “misled and exploited” by Sachin, or who had taken “precautionary steps when suspicion arose”, as suggested by the Defence.[note: 76] These observations of mine were not necessary – and were in fact not relied on – in finding that the four proceeded charges had been proven beyond reasonable doubt; but they would be relevant in sentencing.

58     In conclusion, I was of the view that the Prosecution had established beyond reasonable doubt all the elements of all four charges. I therefore found the Accused guilty and convicted her of all four charges.

Antecedents

59     The Accused was untraced.

Prosecution’s address on sentence

60     The Prosecution sought a global sentence of 8 to 9 months’ imprisonment, with the breakdown as follows:

Charge

Proposed sentence (imprisonment)

Cheating OCBC charge

6 to 7 months

Cheating Maybank charge

6 to 7 months

Cheating UOB charge

6 to 7 months

Companies Act charge

2 months (to run consecutively with one of the cheating charges)

Total Sentence: 8 to 9 months’ imprisonment



The cheating charges

61     For the cheating charges, the Prosecution highlighted that the Accused’s conduct epitomised the harms caused by the facilitation of scams, in the following manner:

(a)     The Accused had deliberately circumvented the three banks’ checks and balances by concealing Sachin’s involvement in the Company during the account opening process, opening bank accounts in three different banks to facilitate illicit transactions, and making false declarations to induce the banks to open up bank accounts.

(b)     The banks were induced to open the Company’s bank accounts by the Accused’s deception.

(a)     The bank accounts were eventually used to commit scams-related or money-laundering offences. Were this to be made known to the public, there is a significant likelihood that this would cause reputational harm to the banks implicated.

62     The Prosecution referred to the Sentencing Advisory Panel’s Guidelines for Scams-related offences (“Scams Guidelines”). Although the Scams Guidelines did not explicitly apply to “old regime” offences (ie, offences committed before 8 February 2024), the sentencing philosophy and approach in the Scams Guidelines should still be considered relevant when calibrating the sentence for such offences. The Prosecution submitted that making a necessary downward calibration (ie, the “Modified Guidelines” approach) would strike a balance between preserving a consistent approach in the sentencing regimes that apply to these offences generally while also extending some leniency to those whose offences were dated.

63     The Prosecution submitted a number of cases which had applied the Modified Guidelines approach, with the starting point sentence for s 417 PC offences under the “old regime” being pegged at 4 months’ imprisonment. An uplift was necessary in the present case given that the Accused had opened bank accounts for personal gain, and the quantum involved in each charge was between approximately $400,000 to $650,000.

64     The Prosecution noted the case of Public Prosecutor v Siraj Munir Bin Mohamed Basheer [2025] SGMC 13 (“Siraj Munir”), where the learned District Judge had explicitly declined to apply the Modified Guidelines approach for “old regime” offences. Instead, the Court in Siraj Munir considered the full range of sentencing factors (including those set out in the Scams Guidelines) and the sentences imposed in similar cases, to determine the appropriate sentence (ie, the “Siraj Munir” approach). It was observed in Siraj Munir that for sums ranging between $22,511 and $511,982.71, plead guilty sentences between 2 months’ imprisonment and 6 months and 1 week’s imprisonment had been imposed for s 417 PC offences. The Prosecution reasoned that if the 30% sentencing discount was absent, the estimated range of the claim trial sentences for sums ranging between $22,511 and $511,982.71 would have been between 3 months’ imprisonment to 9 months and 2 weeks’ imprisonment under the Siraj Munir approach.

65     The Prosecution submitted that whether the Court chose to apply the Modified Guidelines approach or the Siraj Munir approach, the outcome would be similar.

66     Under the Modified Guidelines approach:

(a)     The starting sentence should be 4 months’ imprisonment.

(b)     The sentence should be calibrated upwards by 2 months given that the Accused had opened an account for a third party for gain: Scams Guidelines at [13(d)].

(c)     Further uplifts were warranted for the respective inflow quantum to the bank accounts in questions:

(i)       3 months’ uplift for the Cheating OCBC charge (involving $532,176.27);

(ii)       2.5 months’ uplift for the Cheating Maybank charge (involving $412,270.60); and

(iii)       3.5 months’ uplift for the Cheating UOB charge (involving $666,672.25).

(d)     A further 0.5 months’ uplift should apply given the presence of one vulnerable victim being scammed, as recommended at [29] of the Scams Guidelines.

67     This would lead to a sentence of around 9 to 10 months’ imprisonment, on a claim trial basis, for each of the cheating charges. Considering the inflows of between $400,000 to $600,000 to each of the bank accounts, the Prosecution submitted that the sentencing tariff of 9 to 10 months’ imprisonment per cheating charge would also be consistent with the sentences referred to and imposed in Siraj Munir.

The Companies Act charge

68     For the Companies Act charge, the Prosecution submitted that the Court should apply the 3-step framework set out in Public Prosecutor v Zheng Jia [2025] 3 SLR 1290 (“Zheng Jia”).

69     For the first step, the Prosecution identified the following offence-specific factors:

(a)     No due diligence had been undertaken by the Accused in relation to the activities of the Company at all.

(b)     Even after suspicious transactions had taken place and the accounts had been closed, the Accused failed to make the proper inquiries and was more concerned with seeking the release of the monies in the bank accounts. She also did not care to return to Singapore to rectify the situation and provided no believable reason as to why she was unable to do so.

(c)     The Accused should have known from the outset that her role as the shareholder and director purely in name without any real knowledge of the Company’s business dealings or operations – necessarily entailing a failure to exercise reasonable diligence to oversee the Company – would enable the abuse of corporate structure. Her actions showed that she was at least wilfully blind to, and might have been an enabler of, the criminal activities which the Company was implicated in.

(d)     There was a transnational element, with all the victims being based overseas.

(e)     In total, $1,611,219.12 flowed through the Company’s corporate bank accounts, of which at least $804,076.14 were traced to scam proceeds.

70     Under the second step, the Prosecution submitted that the Accused’s offence fell within the mid to high Band 1 range of the table at [53] in Zheng Jia, warranting 2 to 4 months’ imprisonment. This was primarily because the Accused had deliberately abdicated her duties from the start. The present case fell squarely within the facts described at [45] of Zheng Jia which would warrant an imprisonment sentence, as this was not a case where the Accused had merely made a negligent error in the discharge of her duties as a director. At the same time, the Accused was not on par with a professional chartered accountant who made a business of committing such offences with numerous companies.

71     Under the third step, no further adjustment was necessary based on offender-specific factors, as the Accused had claimed trial and did not show remorse. The Prosecution thus submitted that a 2 to 4 months’ imprisonment sentence would be appropriate for the Companies Act charge.

Discount due to delay

72     Even though the Accused had not pleaded guilty, the Prosecution submitted that the Accused should be accorded a one-third reduction in sentence, and that the Court should run the sentence for the Companies Act charge with one of the sentences for the cheating charges consecutively (leading to the lowest possible global sentence). This was because the Prosecution acknowledged that some time had passed between the Accused’s last interview with CAD (on 10 November 2020) and the Accused’s first mention in court on 16 May 2024. Considering that the Accused had also undergone “significant life changes” in the interim, the Prosecution was of the view that a one-third reduction of sentence was justified.

73     In conclusion, the Prosecution’s final submission was that:

(a)     For each of the cheating charges, the claim trial sentence of 9 to 10 months’ imprisonment should be reduced to 6 to 7 months’ imprisonment.

(b)     For the Companies Act charge, the claim trial sentence of 2 to 4 months’ imprisonment should be reduced to 2 months’ imprisonment.

(c)     The Court should impose a global sentence of 8 to 9 months’ imprisonment.

Mitigation

74     The Defence highlighted the following culpability-reducing or mitigating factors:

(a)     The Court should not apply the Scams Guidelines as these guidelines were not framed for “old-regime” cheating offences arising from the opening of accounts which occurred before 8 February 2024.

(b)     The Accused was not the archetypal scam-enabler the Prosecution sought to paint. Her conduct after suspicion arose was inconsistent with a hardened offender.

(c)     There was no proven personal enrichment in the Accused’s offences. She did not receive the promised benefit and was used by others and left to bear the criminal consequences.

(d)     The Accused was a first offender with no antecedent. There was no evidence before the Court that she was part of a continuing criminal network, or that she posed any ongoing risk requiring a heavy disabling sentence. She had cooperated with the authorities during investigations.

(e)     The Accused was, at the point of sentencing, in a state of acute financial distress:

(i)       All her bank accounts had been closed;

(ii)       she was on social services financial assistance;

(iii)       she was living in a rental flat with no house of her own; and

(iv)       she was seeking treatment at IMH, having been diagnosed with major depressive disorder in 2024.

(a)     The Accused is a mother of a two-year-old daughter, who she is responsible to care for. A substantial custodial term would not only punish the Accused, it would destabilise a family already surviving on assistance and precarious housing.

75     The Defence submitted in its written mitigation plea that the Court should not impose consecutive sentences as proposed by the Prosecution. When queried during oral submissions about this, the Defence conceded that if the Court were to impose custodial sentences on all four proceeded charges, it would have to run at least two out of the four sentences consecutively. The Defence then highlighted that the Accused’s instruction was to seek either a probation order or a fine for her offences.

76     When queried by the Court as to why the Prosecution’s calibration of the individual sentences was flawed or mistaken, the Defence chose not to do so, but merely reiterated the “mitigating factors in [the Accused’s] case”.[note: 77] The Defence finally submitted that if a custodial sentence was warranted, the Court should impose a global sentence materially lower than the 8 to 9 months’ imprisonment sentence sought by the Prosecution.

The Court’s Decision on Sentence

The claim trial sentence for the cheating charges

77     For each of the cheating charges, the Accused was to be punished with imprisonment of up to three years, or a fine, or both.

78     The predominant sentencing consideration in the present case was that of general deterrence, given how the inflow of large sums of illicit funds to the respective bank accounts had been enabled as a result of the Accused’s cheating offences. Such offences committed against financial institutions are serious offences because they not only cause financial misery to many scam victims (as had occurred in the present case), they could also end up hurting Singapore’s reputation as an internationally respected financial and commercial centre.

79     Given the seriousness of the offences the Accused was convicted of, and in particular, the large sums of illicit funds which flowed through the accounts opened by the Accused by cheating the respective banks, it was clear to me that a fine or a probation order sought by the Defence was out of the question. The Defence did not submit any authority or precedent justifying why a fine or a probation order would suffice for these serious offences. The Accused was not even a young offender at the material time, and the Scams Guidelines has stated very clearly at [7(c)] that “fines, probation and community sentences are generally not appropriate” for scams-related offences, such as those committed by the Accused. A custodial sentence had to be imposed in the present case for the purpose of general deterrence, and the only relevant issue was the appropriate length of the custodial sentence.

The relevant sentencing factors

80     I considered the following aggravating offence-specific factors in coming to my decision on sentence for the cheating charges:

(a)     First, the Accused’s culpability was heightened by these actions:

(i)       The Accused had deliberately circumvented the checks and balances of three banks by concealing Sachin’s involvement. As I had noted when convicting the Accused, she knew that it would be hard for Sachin to open the bank accounts, yet she was determined not to mention Sachin’s involvement when opening the bank accounts, even though she was merely parroting and following all of Sachin’s instructions. There was no ambiguity that she knew full well at the material time that Sachin was and would be the true beneficial owner and/or controller of the bank accounts, and not her.

(ii)       The Accused had also taken the effort of visiting three different banks in the space of two days with the clear goal of opening the bank accounts for Sachin’s use. The Accused’s offences were not committed out of a moment of greed or folly, as the evidence showed her being involved with Sachin’s activities for a sustained period of time. Her culpability was therefore to be pegged higher compared to an offender who truly knew or suspected nothing and had simply handed over one bank account in a single moment of folly.

(b)     Second, the Accused was financially motivated to commit these offences. She was promised $1,500 and was in fact remunerated with the same by withdrawing the said sum from two bank accounts before she left for Thailand to meet Sachin and Harsh in January 2020.

(c)     Third, the bank accounts were eventually used to commit scam-related or money-laundering offences. Substantial amounts (between $412,270.60 to $666,672.25) which were likely to be illicit funds flowed through each of these bank accounts, with reported scams ranging between $120,000 to $426,000 for each bank account. This had to be treated as a weighty aggravating factor given that the checks conducted by the banks were designed precisely to avoid such adverse outcomes, yet these checks were circumvented because of the Accused’s false declarations.

81     In contrast, I found no valid culpability-reducing or mitigating factors raised by the Defence.

(a)     The Defence’s submissions that the Accused was someone who had sought to prevent further abuse of the bank accounts after learning about the fund transfers and that she had committed the offences without receiving any financial benefit were contrary to my findings at trial.

(b)     Even if the Accused was currently suffering from major depressive disorder, there was no evidence that her current psychiatric condition had a contributory link to her commission of the offences back in 2019 or 2020.

(c)     It is also trite that the personal predicament the Accused now finds herself in (such as her bank accounts being closed) as a result of her criminal activities should not be treated as a mitigating factor. While the Defence took pains to emphasize the dependency of the Accused’s two-year-old child on the Accused, I did not find her present predicament so dire or exceptional such that the sentence should be altered or reduced. There was evidence before the Court that the Accused’s child could be taken care of by the Accused’s husband, and the Accused also had a social worker looking into her family’s situation.

82     In the circumstances, I could not attribute any mitigatory weight to the mitigating factors put forth by the Defence.

The appropriate sentences

83     In calibrating the sentences for the cheating charges, I agreed with the Prosecution that whether the Modified Guidelines approach or the Siraj Munir approach was applied, a similar sentencing outcome would be reached. In the circumstances, I did not see a need to take a firm view as to which approach the Court should apply to these “old regime” offences (ie, s 417 PC offences committed against banks prior to 8 February 2024), given that the Defence did not make any extensive submissions on this particular issue. I now set out the reasons why both approaches would lead to the same sentencing outcome.

84     I applied the Modified Guidelines approach in the following manner:

(a)     The starting point sentence for each of the cheating charges would be 4 months’ imprisonment: see Public Prosecutor v Yip Kong Fai Clement [2024] SGDC 284 at [21].

(b)     For each of the cheating charges, the Accused had committed the offence for gain. This is recognised as an offence-specific aggravating factor under the Scams Guidelines at [13(d)]. On the other hand, as it is usually inherent in such s 417 PC offences for an offender to be opening or attempting to open a new bank account, I did not consider this to be a distinct aggravating factor against the Accused under the Modified Guidelines approach (see Public Prosecutor v Muhammad Ryan Rosmani [2024] SGDC 239 at [17]). In my view, the uplift for the factor of committing the offence for gain should be no more than 1 month’s imprisonment, representing an appropriate downwards adjustment from the uplift of 3 months’ imprisonment which would apply with respect to a s 55A Corruption, Drug Trafficking and Other Serious Crimes (Confiscation of Benefits) Act 1992 offence where the offender had opened a new bank account and was motivated by gain: see illustration 1 at [20(b)] of the Scam Guidelines.

(c)     I then applied a further uplift of 3 months and 2 weeks’ imprisonment given the significant funds transferred into each of these accounts. Under the Scams Guidelines, an uplift of at least 25% of the starting sentence (ie, 1 month’s imprisonment) should be considered when significant funds of $100,000 or more were received or transferred out of the bank account. In the present case, substantial amounts between $412,270.60 to $666,672.25 flowed into each of these accounts, more than four times than of $100,000 for each account. The uplift of 3 months and 2 weeks’ imprisonment was thus in my view entirely justified.

(d)     This led to a sentence of 8 months and 2 weeks’ imprisonment for each of the cheating charges, under the Modified Guidelines approach.

85     Under the Siraj Munir approach, I noted that on the facts of Siraj Munir itself, in relation to the “SCB Charge” where a s 417 PC charge was preferred, the Court had calibrated the claim trial sentence to be 4 months’ imprisonment (at [80]), even though for that particular offence, there was no transaction flowing through the bank account in question (at [75]), and it was also not clear what the offender had actually gained from the offending (at [76]). In the present case, there were illicit transactions amounting to more than $400,000 for each of the bank accounts in question, a vulnerable victim was involved in the Maybank Account, and the Accused had also made a financial gain of at least $1,500. In my view, if a 4 months’ imprisonment sentence was justified on the facts of Siraj Munir, the sentence of at least 8 months and 2 weeks’ imprisonment for each of the cheating charges would be well justified given the significantly weighty aggravating factors in the present case. Such a sentence was also not excessive when compared to the s 417 PC precedents referred to in Siraj Munir at [83].

86     For the foregoing reasons, I was of the view that a claim trial sentence of 8 months and 2 weeks’ imprisonment was appropriate for each of the cheating charges when considering the offence-specific factors alone.

The claim trial sentence for the Companies Act offence based on offence-specific factors

87     For the Companies Act offence, the Accused was liable to a fine not exceeding $5,000 or to imprisonment for a term not exceeding 12 months.

The sentencing framework in Zheng Jia

88     In Zheng Jia, the High Court set out a sentencing framework under s 157(3)(b) of the Companies Act which can be applied to a situation when a director of a company failed to act with reasonable diligence and thus breached his duty under s 157(1) of the Companies Act.

89     Under the first step, the court may consider a non-exhaustive list of factors (Zheng Jia at [51]), including:

(a)     the extent of due diligence undertaken by the director in relation to the activities of the company and/or the client;

(b)     efforts made by the director to monitor or review transactions in the company's bank accounts;

(c)     the extent to which the director knew or should have known that failing to exercise reasonable diligence could enable abuse of the corporate structure;

(d)     the duration of offending;

(e)     whether the offending conduct was pursued as part of a business or profit-driven scheme;

(f)     whether the director made any efforts at concealing his wrongdoing;

(g)     whether there was a transnational element to the offence; and

(h)     the nature and extent of the harm that resulted to the company and/or third parties.

90     Having identified the salient offence-specific factors, the second step is to place the offence within the appropriate sentencing band to arrive at an indicative sentence (Zheng Jia at [53]). The sentencing bands are as follows:

(a)     Band 1 (one to three offence-specific factors): an indicative sentence of up to four months' imprisonment;

(b)     Band 2 (four to five offence-specific factors): an indicative sentence of five to eight months' imprisonment; and

(c)     Band 3 (more than six offence-specific factors): an indicative sentence of nine to twelve months' imprisonment.

91     After deriving an indicative sentence at the second step, the third and final step would be to adjust that indicative sentence based on offender-specific factors relevant to the case (Zheng Jia at [56]). These would include matters such as:

(a)     other offences taken into consideration for sentencing;

(b)     the offender's relevant antecedents;

(c)     the offender’s remorse or the lack thereof;

(d)     whether the offender entered into a timeous plea of guilt;

(e)     the extent of voluntary restitution made; and

(f)     whether the offender voluntarily co-operated with the authorities during investigations.

Application of Zheng Jia to the present case

92     In the present case, although the Accused was not a “professional chartered accountant whose business model was predicated on [her] being registered as a locally resident nominee director of numerous companies incorporated for foreign clients” (Zheng Jia at [45]), she was definitely a director who had “assumed [her office] with every intention of abdicating [her] duty under s 157(1) of the [Companies Act]” (Zheng Jia at [47]). Actions like the Accused’s “present serious risks to [the implicated companies] specifically, and Singapore’s corporate and financial ecosystem generally” (Zheng Jia at [47]). The sentencing framework in Zheng Jia should therefore apply to the present case.

93     In my view, there were at least three offence-specific factors present:

(a)     First, the Accused had undertaken no due diligence at all in relation to the activities of the Company. In convicting the Accused, I had found that the Accused’s intention when opening the bank accounts was always to surrender her banking access to Sachin. Even after suspicious transactions had taken place and the accounts had been closed, the Accused did not make any proper inquiries and was more concerned with seeking the release of the monies within the accounts.

(b)     Second, the Accused must have known from the outset that her failure to exercise reasonable diligence would enable the abuse of the corporate structure by Sachin. As I had found above at [54], her actions suggested that she was at least wilfully blind to, or might have been a knowing enabler, of Sachin and his associates committing the scams-related and/or money-laundering offences which the Company was implicated in. It was aggravating that she appeared to have continued to act on Sachin’s instructions even as late as 30 March 2020 and 13 April 2020 (see above at [55] – [56]).

(c)     Third, the harm caused as a result of the Accused’s failure to carry out her duties was significant. Large amounts of scams proceeds (ie, more than S$800,000) were allowed to flow through the bank accounts, to the detriment of all of the banks and the many victims who were scammed.

94     Given the presence of at least three salient and weighty offence-specific factors, I was of the view that this case fell under the higher end of Band 1 of the Zheng Jia framework. An indicative starting sentence of 3 months’ imprisonment was therefore more than justified, given the Band 1 range which stretches to 4 months’ imprisonment.

95     I now turn to the offender-specific factors I had considered, which would apply to both the cheating charges and the Companies Act charge.

Calibrating the eventual sentences after considering offender-specific factors

96     Given that the Accused had been convicted after trial, there was no plead guilty sentencing reduction to be accorded to her.

97     Nevertheless, I accepted the Prosecution’s submission to accord the Accused a one-third reduction in each of the individual sentences to account for the delay between her last interview with CAD on 10 November 2020, and the filing of the charges against her in court on 16 May 2024. During oral submissions, I had highlighted that objectively speaking, the gap of time between November 2020 and May 2024 was not exactly lengthy or inordinate, given that there were transnational elements to the offences committed by the Accused, in that most of the victims were based overseas.

98     However, I noted that in the present case, it was the Prosecution – who would be privy to investigative facts or steps not known to the Court – who had sought a sentencing reduction for the factor of delay. I also acknowledged the Prosecution’s submission that the Accused had undergone significant life changes in the interim (ie, having given birth to her two-year-old daughter and taken on the responsibility as her daughter’s primary caregiver). For these reasons, I agreed to accord a substantial degree of leniency to the Accused and reduced each of the individual sentences as follows:

(a)     For each of the cheating charges, the sentence was reduced to 5 months and 2 weeks’ imprisonment;

(b)     For the Companies Act charge, the sentence was reduced to 2 months’ imprisonment.

99     Under s 307(1) of the CPC, at least two of the four imprisonment sentences imposed must run consecutively. I accepted the Prosecution’s proposal to run the sentence for the Companies Act charge (ie, 2 months’ imprisonment) consecutively with one of sentences for the cheating charges (ie 5 months and 2 weeks’). This led to a global sentence of 7 months and 2 weeks’ imprisonment, which was a sentence I found just and appropriate in the circumstances, and could not be said to be excessive considering the manner in which the Accused had committed the offences, and the significant harm caused by the Accused’s irresponsible actions for personal gain.

Conclusion

100    In conclusion, I imposed a sentence of 7 months and 2 weeks’ imprisonment on the Accused.

101    The Accused is on bail pending appeal.
