Public Prosecutor v Chan Bingyi

Public Prosecutor v Chan Bingyi
[2026] SGDC 248

Case Number:DAC 915576-2022, Magistrate's Appeal No 9116 of 2026-01
Decision Date:27 July 2026
Tribunal/Court:District Court
Coram: Ong Hian Sun
Counsel Name(s): DPP(s) Jiang Ke Yue, Ng Jun Chong, Thaddeus Tan & Teo Lu Jia (Attorney-General's Chambers) for the Prosecution; Mr Adrian Wee Heng Yi & Lynette Chang (Lighthouse Law Sg)
Parties: Public Prosecutor — Chan Bingyi

Criminal Law – s 304A(b) of the Penal Code (Cap 224, 2008 Rev Ed)

Criminal Procedure – Sentencing

[LawNet Editorial Note: An appeal to this decision has been filed in MA 9116/2026/01.]

27 July 2026

Senior District Judge Ong Hian Sun:

Introduction

1       The Accused claimed trial to the following charge (DAC-915576-2022):

“…that you, on 8 March 2019, sometime between 11.39am and 12.20pm, at Revival Medical & Aesthetics Centre located at 90 Bras Basah Road, #B1-24, Esplanade Xchange, Singapore, did cause the death of one Lau Li Ting (female / 31 years old at time of death) (“the deceased”) by doing a negligent act not amounting to culpable homicide, to wit, you administered ethylenediaminetetraacetic acid (“EDTA”) to the deceased intravenously when there were no indications for using it on her, and at too high a concentration and too quickly, and your negligent act did cause the deceased to develop EDTA toxicity, which in turn led to her cardiac arrest and eventual death, and you have thereby committed an offence punishable under section 304A(b) of the Penal Code (Cap 224, 2008 Rev Ed).

2       At the close of the trial, the accused was found guilty and convicted of the proceeded charge. He was sentenced to 18 months’ imprisonment.

3       Being dissatisfied, he has appealed against his conviction and sentence. He was granted a stay of the execution on his sentence of imprisonment. He is currently released on bail pending the hearing of his appeal.

The Prosecution’s case

4       The accused is Dr Chan Bingyi, a 38-year-old male Singaporean bearing NRIC No. SXXXX717F. At the material time, he was a medical doctor practicing at Revival Medical & Aesthetics Centre located at at 90 Bras Basah Road, #B1-24, Esplanade Xchange, Singapore (“the clinic”).

5       The deceased is Ms Lau li Ting. She was 31 years old at the time of her death.

6       On 8 March 2019, Ms Lau visited the clinic for aesthetic treatment. She was attended to by the accused, who agreed to perform “chelation” treatment involving the administration of ethylenediaminetetraacetic acid (“EDTA”). Shortly after receiving this treatment, Ms Lau collapsed and subsequently died at Singapore General Hospital (“SGH”).

7       Amongst other evidence, the Prosecution relied on the retracted admission provided by the accused to the Ministry of Health (“MOH”)[note: 1] on 18 March 2019, ten days after the incident, where the accused gave a detailed account of the incident, admitting that, despite informing the deceased that she was not a suitable candidate to undergo this “chelation treatment of removing various metals including heavy metal” from her body, the accused nevertheless agreed to provide this “chelation treatment” to her upon her insistence.

8       According to the accused’s answer in his own words: “…After the consultation, Ms Lau was asked to proceed to "Procedure Room 1". Inside the room, she was asked to sit on the treatment bed. After she had sat down, I applied one plug on her right cubital fossa to prepare her for the "chelation" treatment. Inside the room with me were Claire and Sabrina. Sabrina was bringing the Botox, fillers and saline into the room and Claire was washing Ms Lau's face. Sabrina also assisted me to set up the drip lines for 500cc and 100cc saline to be IV into Ms Lau to prevent the line from clotting. I believed that Claire was the staff who had applied the numbing cream on Ms Lau's face after she had washed Ms Lau's face.

9       While waiting for Sabrina to set up the tubing and for Claire to finish applying the numbing cream. Ms Lau told me that she had an appointment for her manicure and later in the same evening, she was flying to China.

10      I then left the room and went to "Recovery Room" to draw 12.5cc of Sodium Bicarbonate and 12.5cc of Disodium Ethyl-diamine-tetra-acetic acid (150 mg/cc) in a 25cc syringe. I then returned to Procedure Room 1 and slowly pumped in both these 2 drugs into the 100cc bag. After pumping in these 2 drugs, I was monitoring the drip rate and speed to time it for at least an hour duration and at the same time, monitoring side effects like burn sensation and nausea. Ms Lau was still talking about her plan for the day. About 5 minutes of talking, Ms Lau suddenly stopped talking. I tried to speak to her but there was no response. I checked on her and realised that she was having a seizure. At that time, Ms Lau was sitting inclined on the treatment bed. I put her in a safe position to make sure that she does not injure herself and allowed the seizure to self-abort. About a minute or 2 later, her seizure stopped. I told my staff to bring in the resuscitation kit. When Ms Lau was having her seizure, I immediately switched off both the drips..” [emphasis in bold and underlined].

11     In addition to accused’s retracted admission, the Prosecution also relied on the corroboration evidence by the accused’s two clinic assistants - Ms Ng (also known as Sabrina)[note: 2] and Ms Chew (also known as Claire)[note: 3] whom accused could not think of any reason why any of them will lie in court to get him into trouble and they have testified that the accused was administering EDTA to Ms Lau.

12     Ms Chew testified that the accused had asked her to apply numbing cream on the deceased’s face and that she saw the accused check the drip chamber of the drip treatment set up while doing so.[note: 4] According to Ms Chew, the entire treatment would have been completed after 45 minutes to one hour.[note: 5] According to Ms Chew,[note: 6] based on her experience one would look only at the drip chamber to check the speed of the drip, and in this case, Ms Chew testified that the accused had done so because the deceased was on the IV drip and she believed the IV lines were running.[note: 7]

13     Ms Ng testified that the accused informed the clinic assistants that the deceased wanted to receive drip treatment after his consultation with the deceased.[note: 8] On the accused’s instruction,[note: 9] Ms Ng then primed the IV lines required for the drip treatment and brought them into the treatment room.[note: 10] Shortly after, Ms Ng placed the chemicals needed for the drip treatment on a preparation table in the accused’s consultation room[note: 11] and went in and out of the treatment room several times while preparing a consent form for the deceased to sign as well as the supplies for other treatments which the deceased requested – such as Botox and dermal fillers.[note: 12]

14     On these occasions, Ms Ng confirmed while under cross-examination and re-examination that she saw that the IV lines were connected to the deceased and were running.[note: 13] Ms Ng also testified that she heard the accused asking the deceased whether the treatment was causing her pain.[note: 14] In response, the deceased told the accused that she did not feel pain and requested for more EDTA. Hearing this, the accused left the room and came back with a syringe which Ms Ng thought contained EDTA. The accused then administered the contents of the syringe into the 100ml bag of saline connected to the deceased before continuing to speak to the deceased.[note: 15]

15     According to Ms Ng, the deceased collapsed less than 5 minutes later.[note: 16] Ms Ng testified that the drip had been running for about 10 minutes before she entered the room with the supplies for the Botox and dermal fillers[note: 17] and that the 100ml saline packet would have been completed in less than 45 minutes based on the rate it was dripping at.[note: 18]

16     According to the evidence adduced by the Prosecution, the deceased was assessed to be fit and healthy at the Clinic prior to her treatment.

17     The Prosecution also adduced evidence from the deceased’s family members that the deceased was healthy and physically well when they last saw her. The deceased did not have any pre-existing conditions which could explain her collapse.

18     Mr Lau Yau Sui (“Mr Lau”), the deceased’s father, testified that the deceased was physically fine when he left for work at about 8.00am on 8 March 2019.[note: 19] According to Mr Lau, the deceased was very healthy and did not have any chronic illnesses or health issues such as heart problems.[note: 20] Neither did the deceased suffer any issues after consuming her psychiatric medication or health supplements.[note: 21]

19     Mr Lau Jun Hao (“Jun Hao”), the deceased’s brother, testified that the deceased seemed perfectly fine when she left home between 11.00am and 12.00pm on 8 March 2019. According to Jun Hao[note: 22] and the deceased’s mother Mdm Tan Ah Kuan[note: 23], the deceased did not have a history of heart problems or seizures nor did she suffer any adverse health effects from consuming her health supplements and psychiatric medication.

20     The Prosecution also tendered the photographs taken by the deceased at the accused’s clinic at 12.05pm[note: 24] (marked P15 and P20) which show an IV apparatus that was fully assembled and likely in operation.

21     The type of equipment needed for the administration of EDTA is undisputed and has been produced and marked as exhibits D10- D16. The process by which the equipment is set up is also undisputed: First, the apparatus components must be connected. Second, the IV lines must be primed to remove air bubbles within the IV line. This involves releasing some liquid from the connected bottles of saline so that the air bubbles are carried out of the IV line. Once this is done, the lines are hung up using an S-hook. Finally, the accused would decide on the quantity of EDTA to be administered and pump it into the saline bottles. The EDTA would then be administered to the patient via the drip line which is connected to a cannula on the patient.

22     Firstly, the photographs show that the IV lines were hung up in the treatment room. This would only be done after the lines were primed as agreed by the accused under cross-examination.[note: 25]

23     Secondly, the photographs show that the protective caps of the IV needles were taped to the IV line. According to Ms Chew, the IV needle caps would only be taped to the IV line after the IV line is primed and the IV line ready to be used.[note: 26]

24     Thirdly, the IV needles themselves are not visible in P15 and P20. Ms Ng’s evidence is that if the needles are not visible, they would usually be connected to the cannula on the patient’s body.[note: 27] This is corroborated by the accused’s admission that he wouldn’t have left the needles dangling.[note: 28]

25     Fourthly, the photographs in P20 show water droplets in the drip chambers of the IV set up and the appearance of these water droplets changes between the photographs which were taken roughly 1 second apart. When Ms Chew and Ms Ng were shown these photographs, they both testified that the IV-line looked like it was running. Ms Chew inferred this based on the droplet that can be seen in the drip chamber and her experience that this was an indicator that the drip was running.[note: 29] Similarly, Ms Ng testified that a drop in the drip chamber indicated that the drip was running.[note: 30]

26     Ms Ng,[note: 31] Ms Chew[note: 32] and the accused[note: 33] himself testified that the deceased suffered a seizure, became unresponsive, and was foaming at the mouth at the clinic after the treatment.

27     The Singapore Civil Defence Force’s (“SCDF”) incident report (marked P11) indicated that the SCDF personnel who attended to the deceased at the Clinic found no detectable pulse or breathing upon arrival[note: 34].

28      Upon arriving at the Department of Emergency Medicine, SGH, the deceased’s condition was critical.[note: 35] Blood tests conducted on 8 March 2019 revealed that the levels of ionic calcium in the deceased’s blood ranged from 0.70 MMOL/L to 0.87 MMOL/L[note: 36] and that the deceased was hypocalcemia.[note: 37] Dr Juliana Poh (“Dr Poh”), the attending physician, could not identify an underlying cause for the cardiac arrest.[note: 38] However, she confirmed that hypocalcemia causes numbness, tetany, and cardiac arrhythmias.[note: 39]

29     The deceased was subsequently transferred to the Department of Cardiothoracic Surgery, National Heart Centre Singapore (“NHCS”). Based on the deceased’s medical records with NHCS (marked P29), Dr Sivaraj Pillai Govindasamy (“Dr Sivaraj”), the attending physician, testified that the ECG results combined with the deceased’s young age suggested that the deceased’s circulatory collapse was not caused by blockages in the vessels in the heart.[note: 40] There was also no evidence that the deceased’s circulatory collapse was caused by a pulmonary embolism - a clot in the arteries.[note: 41]

30     According to Dr Tan Hock Heng (“Dr Tan”), the rapid bolus administration of EDTA causes sudden hypocalcemia, seizures, heart failure, cardiac arrhythmia, tetany and respiratory arrest.[note: 42] The deceased displayed these symptoms and no alternative explanation for these symptoms have been identified other than that the deceased’s symptoms must have been caused by the accused administering EDTA to the deceased.

31     Further the Prosecution relied on the results of the analysis conducted by the Analytical Toxicology Laboratory (“ATL”) of the Health Sciences Authority (“HSA”) on blood samples obtained from the deceased to establish that EDTA was administered to the deceased. According to both Dr Tan[note: 43] and Prof Duflou,[note: 44] the detection of EDTA in these samples can be due to the administration of EDTA.

32     A postmortem sample of peripheral blood (plain) was taken from the deceased during the autopsy performed on 14 March 2019. According to a report produced by the ATL (marked P12), < 2mg/ml of EDTA was found in the postmortem sample.

33     An antemortem sample of blood taken from the deceased on 8 March 2019 was sent to HSA for analysis on 25 March 2019. According to a report produced by the ATL (marked P13), 89/ml of EDTA was found in the antemortem sample. The Prosecution has prepared a table detailing the unbroken chain of custody of the antemortem sample for the HSA analysis which was unchallenged and there was no basis for the antemortem sample to be tampered with.[note: 45]

34     The Prosecution submitted that the evidence adduced show that there is an unbroken chain of causation between the accused’s administration of EDTA to the deceased and the clinical symptoms of EDTA toxicity found on the deceased which ultimately led to the deceased’s death.

35     Following the accused's administration of EDTA, the deceased collapsed and experienced seizures that lasted several minutes. When these seizures ceased, she did not have any pulse nor was she breathing.[note: 46]

36     The deceased's condition remained critical upon arrival at SGH. According to Dr Poh, the deceased had a pulse but was unable to breathe by herself[note: 47] and would have died without medical intervention.[note: 48] As Dr Poh was unable to identify a reversible cause for the deceased’s condition, the deceased was referred to NHCS to be placed on an extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (“ECMO”) to support her heart and lung function.[note: 49]

37     Upon deceased’s arrival at NHCS, her prognosis was poor.[note: 50] Dr Sivaraj opined that the deceased was “dead along the way” and that the only thing keeping her alive at that point was the ECMO.[note: 51] The deceased passed away five days later.

38     An autopsy was conducted on the deceased on 14 March 2019. According to the autopsy report (marked P40) the interim cause of death was stated as cardiorespiratory failure pending further investigations. The pathologists who conducted the autopsy – Dr Benjamin Kuek Jia Wei (“Dr Kuek”)[note: 52] and Dr Lee Chin Thye (“Dr Lee”)[note: 53] – testified that they arrived at this conclusion because there was no obvious cause of death identified from the autopsy. As a result, they ordered ancillary investigations including toxicological analysis, histological examinations, bacterial studies and virological studies.

39     After studying the results of the ancillary investigations, a subsequent report (marked P41) was issued by Dr Lee certifying the final cause of death to be EDTA toxicity. Dr Lee explained that none of the ancillary investigations revealed an obvious cause of death except the toxicological investigations which showed the presence of EDTA in the deceased’s antemortem and postmortem samples.[note: 54] Dr Lee therefore concluded that the final cause of death was EDTA toxicity[note: 55] – a conclusion concurred by Dr Kuek.[note: 56]

40     The Prosecution relied on the evidence adduced from the witnesses and the opinion of Dr Tan to establish that the accused’s administration of EDTA to the deceased was negligent. Dr Tan reached this opinion having considered that: (i) the use of disodium EDTA is prohibited; (ii) there were no legitimate clinical indications for administering EDTA to the deceased; and (iii) the concentration and rate of EDTA administered was too high.

41     According to Dr Tan, EDTA is recognised as a dangerous drug that was withdrawn from the US market following fatalities associated with its use.[note: 57] In Singapore, EDTA is prohibited for medical use[note: 58] and is not considered for any treatments, nor is it described in the Ministry of Health's guidelines for the management of poisoning.[note: 59] The Ministry of Health has issued a circular specifically instructing hospitals and clinics not to perform chelation treatment using EDTA.[note: 60] While the accused claimed ignorance of this circular prior to the deceased's collapse, the Prosecution submitted that that does not change the fact that he had administered a prohibited drug to the deceased.

42     Chelation treatment involves the use of EDTA to bind to metallic ions and extract them from the body.[note: 61] Disodium EDTA, which the accused used in this case, binds preferentially to calcium – a mechanism that makes it inherently dangerous.[note: 62] This is because ionic calcium plays a critical role in essential bodily functions including neurotransmission and neuromuscular function. When EDTA depletes calcium levels and causes hypocalcemia, patients can suffer heart failure and impaired muscle function leading to tetany.[note: 63] Given these serious risks, there must be legitimate reasons for the administration of EDTA.

43     EDTA should only be used for specific indications such as heavy metal poisoning or elevated calcium levels,[note: 64] and must only be administered by clinicians trained in its use.[note: 65] Comprehensive testing before treatment, including calcium or renal panels to confirm conditions like heavy metal poisoning or hypercalcemia, should also be done.[note: 66] During administration, clinicians must also actively monitor the patient's cardiac status and serum calcium levels to prevent dangerous complications.[note: 67]

44     The Prosecution submitted that in the present case, there were no legitimate clinical indications for administering EDTA to the deceased and the accused violated the necessary pre-administration safety precautions. Under cross-examination, the accused conceded that the deceased displayed none of the conditions that he thought would justify EDTA treatment, including heart disease, diabetes, or heavy metal poisoning.[note: 68] Neither did the accused perform any preliminary tests or screening, nor did he monitor the deceased’s heart rate or serum calcium levels during the chelation treatment[note: 69]

45     The accused told the deceased that she was not suitable to receive EDTA because there were no indications for it and because he knew the risks involved in chelation.[note: 70] Despite this, the accused proceeded to administer EDTA to the deceased exposing the deceased to life-threatening risk without any valid justification.

46     EDTA must be administered under strictly controlled conditions to prevent adverse effects. Dr Tan testified that safe administration requires a concentration level of 6mg/ml and an infusion rate of 15-16.7mg/min – parameters that the accused exceeded.[note: 71]

47     According to Dr Tan, the concentration of EDTA administered to the deceased was too high. The accused injected 12.5ml of EDTA with a concentration of 150mg/ml into the 100ml saline bag, creating a total EDTA dose of 1,875mg.[note: 72] Dr Tan confirmed that this concentration level exceeded safe recommendations.[note: 73]

48     The rate at which the accused administered EDTA to the deceased was also too fast. If the 100ml saline bag was administered within one hour, the deceased would have received 31mg/min of EDTA – nearly double the safe rate of 15-16.7mg/min.[note: 74] Prof Duflou agreed with this calculation and confirmed that administration within 45 minutes would have delivered 41.67mg/min – almost three times the recommended rate.[note: 75] These calculations demonstrate that regardless of the timeframe, the accused administered EDTA at a rate that was too fast.

49     Dr Tan opined that the accused's administration of EDTA to the deceased would not be accepted as proper by any responsible body of medical practitioners skilled in chelation treatment.183 Prof Duflou has disagreed with Dr Tan. He acknowledges that the safe administration of any drug depends on the rate of delivery, which in turn depends on the concentration of the drug and the duration over which the drug is administered.184

50     Dr Tan opined that the accused's administration of EDTA to the deceased would not be accepted as proper by any responsible body of medical practitioners skilled in chelation treatment. 183 Prof Duflou has disagreed with Dr Tan. He acknowledges that the safe administration of any drug depends on the rate of delivery, which in turn depends on the concentration of the drug and the duration over which the drug is administered.184

The Defence

51     The main crux of accused’s defence is that he did not in fact administer EDTA to the deceased. He did not challenge the voluntariness of his statements but attempted to retract his admission that he administered EDTA to the deceased. The accused further attempted to challenge the final cause of death by contending that the EDTA present in the deceased’s antemortem sample and postmortem sample were due to contamination and that the Prosecution has failed to prove beyond a reasonable doubt that the deceased’s cardiac arrest and eventual death was caused by the administration of EDTA.

52     The accused testified that he was not in a clear state of mind when he gave the statement to MOH IO. The accused further testified that he was the one responsible for injecting the EDTA and did not administer the EDTA contrary to what the clinic assistants have testified. For the first time in court he mentioned that IV lines were primed twice and not once as indicated in his statements to IO.

53     It is undisputed that he did not inform the SCDF personnel, deceased’s family members and the SGH doctors about the victim’s request for chelation treatment at his clinic and his alleged non-administration of the EDTA to the deceased prior to her sudden collapse.

54     He did not provide any evidence that he has been properly trained to administer EDTA via the IV drip. He did not provide any justifications for agreeing to administer EDTA to the deceased at deceased’s request. He also did not provide any evidence that the EDTA was properly obtained for an approved purpose for his clinic. He also did not challenge the Prosecution expert’s evidence on the requirements for proper monitoring of the patient during the course of administration of EDTA. His did not provide any substantiation for his claim that he was not informed about the the notice by MOH on the prohibition of the administration of EDTA and that it did not apply to his clinic.

55     He engaged his expert, Prof Duflou to suggest that there could be other possibilities of causation of the cardiac arrest and that the presence of EDTA was not the only possible cause of death on the premise that he did not administer EDTA to the deceased.

The Court’s Decision on Conviction

56     There are two contradicting versions before this court. The first version that implicated accused and consistent with his initial statements to MOH of his administration of EDTA which is corroborated by the testimonies of his clinic assistants, the photographs taken by the deceased at the clinic, the symptoms displayed by the deceased prior to and after her collapse and the objective results of the presence of EDTA on the antemortem and postmortem blood samples taken from the deceased. The second version was the version given by the accused in his testimony in court denying administering EDTA to the deceased.

57     The main issue to be decided by this court is whether there was in fact any administration of EDTA by the accused to the deceased and whether the accused’s defence that he did not administer EDTA to the deceased and that he gave his initial statements to MOH implicating himself while he was in an unstabilised state and was falsely implicated by his clinic assistants could be believed.

58     As a preliminary point, the Defence urged this court not to accept the testimonies of Ms Chew and Ms Ng as they did not give entirely consistent accounts and fail to satisfy the “unusually convincing standard”. The Defence is clearly misconceived on this preliminary point in law and I agree with the Prosecution’s submission that there is no requirement for the eyewitness’s testimony to be “unusually convincing” in order for the accused to be found guilty as the standard is only required if the eyewitness’s uncorroborated evidence had formed the sole basis for the conviction: see, eg, Public Prosecutor v GCK and another matter [2020] 1 SLR 486 at [87] and Public Prosecutor v Mohammed Liton Mohammed Syeed Mallik [2008] 1 SLR(R) 601 at [37].

59     It is clear that the Prosecution’s case does not rest solely on the uncorroborated evidence of the clinic assistants as their versions in court supported each other’s version and were corroborated by accused’s admission in his statement to the MOH, the undisputed symptoms displayed by the deceased as observed prior to and after her collapse at the clinic, the objective evidence of the photographs taken by the deceased and the presence of EDTA found in the blood samples of the deceased.

60     The Defence also raised another preliminary point that the Defence has suffered prejudice during the trial as the Prosecution has run an inconsistent case with regards to the administration of the EDTA at too high a concentration and too quickly especially when Ms Ng testified to a second dose and faster administration time by the accused.

61     I agree with the Prosecution that the case run by the Prosecution has been consistent throughout in reliance of the evidence of the clinic assistants and the retracted admission by the accused as well as the expert opinion of Dr Tan. I fail to see how the Defence has suffered any prejudice when all along in court the accused has claimed that he did not administer the EDTA and the accused has ample opportunities to cross examine the clinic assistants and attempted to impeach, in particular, Ms Ng’s credibility with her prior inconsistent statements.

62     I also find that the Defence Expert’s evidence could not have been “blunted” in any way as his opinion must have been premised on the accused’s defence that he did not administer any EDTA to the deceased.

63     Having observed the clinic assistants in giving their evidence and after evaluating their evidence in the light of their prior statements given to MOH and the reasons they gave regarding the inconsistences highlighted by the Defence and the admission by the accused in P18, I found no cogent reasons why they would want to fabricate evidence to implicate the accused in their testimonies in court that he has administered EDTA to the deceased.

64     In my view, the clinic assistants gave a credible and largely corroborated account that they understood that the accused had administered EDTA to the deceased as the procedure has started and the IV line was running even though they may not be the person who personally administered the EDTA on the deceased.

65     Ms Chew observed the accused checking the drip chamber and testified that this is only done when one checks the speed of the drip.[note: 76] Ms Chew concluded through her peripheral vision that accused was pumping something into the IV bottle which she assumed was EDTA and that the procedure had started and the IV lines were running as there was no other reason for the accused to check the drip chamber.[note: 77]

66     Ms Chew admitted lying to the IO initially on her own accord when giving her statements to the IO to protect the clinic and everyone involved but she was later overcome with guilt to tell the truth about the administration of EDTA to the deceased.[note: 78] Her testimony is consistent with the accused’s admission in P18 that he was checking the drip rate and speed because he was administering EDTA to the deceased.

67     The Defence also attempted to impeach and to cast doubt especially on Ms Ng’s version of the second dosage administered by the accused to the deceased upon deceased’s request for more EDTA as Ms Ng failed to mention this in her statements to MOH and it only came out of her evidence in court regarding the second dosage of the EDTA administered by the accused which further incriminate the accused in terms of the concentration of the dosage of EDTA administered by him.

68     The main inconsistencies on Ms Ng’s evidence raised by the Defence relate to who primed the IV lines, whether Ms Ng saw the deceased being administered EDTA and whether she observed the deceased asking for more EDTA and the accused administering a second dose of EDTA.

69     The Prosecution submitted that Ms Ng has provided a satisfactory explanation for these inconsistencies, and her credibility should not be impeached: PP v Sri Tharean Muthalagan [2022] SGHC 96[note: 79] at [67]. Ms Ng explained that she lied in the prior inconsistent statements for self-preservation, fear of being implicated for the deceased’s death and potential job loss, she deliberately tried to “not think about and not know about anything”.[note: 80]

70     It is clear to this court that the clinic assistants were aware that the chelation treatments done by the clinic were not proper. As a matter of practice, they were not required to obtain the written consent of the patients for the chelation treatment. According to Ms Ng’s unchallenged evidence, the accused had told the clinic assistants that drip treatment would no longer be provided at Revival Medical Clinic after the deceased’s collapse.[note: 81] I accepted that Ms Ng has provided a satisfactory reason for her prior inconsistent statements, and her credibility was not impeached.

71     In my view there are no cogent reasons for Ms Chew and Ms Ng to fabricate evidence in court to falsely implicate the accused. Their testimonies implicating the accused in administering EDTA were corroborated by the accused’s own admission, the seizures displayed by the deceased prior to her collapse, the photographs taken by the deceased and the presence of EDTA in the blood samples of the deceased.

72     I accepted the evidence indicating that the deceased was assessed to be fit and healthy to receive the chelation treatment by the accused and the evidence of her family members that deceased did not have any prior heart condition. In my view there is no other apparent or cogent reason for the deceased to have suddenly collapsed and displayed symptoms consistent with EDTA toxicity if she had not been administered EDTA.

73     I accepted the evidence adduced by the Prosecution of the photographs taken by the deceased showing the IV equipment that was fully assembled with the lines hung up as further proof that the lines were already primed and ready to be used and seemed like the lines were running according to the clinic assistants when shown the photographs.

74     I accepted the toxicology reports and the evidence of the forensic pathologists that the cause of death was due to EDTA toxicity arising from the presence of EDTA in both the premortem and postmortem blood sample.

75     In my view it was very unlikely that the presence of EDTA in the deceased’s blood samples could have been caused by contamination of the blood samples of the test tubes used by the SGH.

76     Having heard the evidence, in my view there is no conclusive evidence before this court to show that contamination of the test tube containing the ante-mortem blood sample had occurred. This is a red herring raised by the Defence as this court is of the view that there is ample evidence to establish that accused had administered EDTA to the deceased prior to her collapse at the clinic.

77     I accepted the opinion of Dr Tan that the act of administration of the EDTA by the accused on the deceased was clearly negligent and would not have been accepted as proper by a responsible body of medical practitioners skilled in carrying out chelation using EDTA especially when accused knew that the use of disodium EDTA was prohibited as shown in the absence of consent forms for chelation treatments in his clinic, the lack of any legitimate clinical indications for EDTA treatment to the deceased, the lack of any proper training of the accused in chelation treatment and the failure to closely monitor the concentration and rate of the administration of the EDTA.

78     The accused’s defence is one of bare denial in administering EDTA to the deceased.

79     The accused’s denial cannot be substantiated in the light of his own admission in P18 which was recorded ten days after the incident. The accused did not challenge the voluntariness of the statements and claimed that his mind was unstable at the time of the giving of his statement.

80     The accused has sufficient time to prepare for himself when he gave the voluntary statement to the IO in P18. IO testified that accused was coherent[note: 82] in his answers and had many opportunities to amend the statement before he affirmed the truth of the statement.[note: 83]

81     The accused also had many opportunities to make clarifications and amendments in at least 7 other occasions prior to the recording of his statement in P51on 3 January 2022 at 10.40 am where he again stated that he obtained the EDTA and injected it into the saline bag after he had fully set up the IV drip. The whole period from the time the accused set up the IV drip on the deceased till she went into a seizure was probably about 15 to 20 minutes according to the accused.[note: 84]

82     There are no cogent reasons for the IO to falsely implicate him during the course of the recording of his statement in P18 when the accused himself gave a very detailed description of what happened in the clinic on that fateful day.

83     The accused attempted to explain that he could not have started the procedure as the consent form has not been signed and that he merely carried out an additional priming without releasing the clamp were clearly afterthoughts especially the latter which was not mentioned in any of his subsequent statements to the IO and appeared to be an attempt to counter Ms Ng’s evidence of a second dosage administered by the accused.

84     That accused did not administer the EDTA because the deceased has not signed the consent form is clearly an afterthought as it is clear to this court there was no requirement for the accused to obtain consent for chelation treatment although he had the practice of obtaining consent for the other legitimate aesthetic treatments performed by him. It was also clear from his clinical notes that he did not make any reference on the provision or the lack of it regarding the chelation treatment of the deceased.

85     If the accused had indeed not commenced any chelation treatment on the deceased prior to the collapse of the deceased, he should have been upfront with the SCDF personnel, the SGH doctors, the family members of the deceased, his clinic assistants and the MOH IO that the deceased collapsed before he could commence the chelation treatment on her. Instead of getting rid of the evidence, he should have preserved the scene, made a report to the police on his own accord and asked for the scene of the fateful incident to be preserved with proper photographs taken at the scene after the sudden collapse of the deceased.

86     His omissions to inform all the persons involved immediately after the deceased’s collapse and his failure to make an immediate police report on his own accord and to preserve the scene thereafter only reinforced this court’s finding that he knew he had done something so palpably wrong which led to the deceased’s collapse due to his administration of EDTA and his failure to closely monitor the concentration and rate of the administration of the EDTA on the deceased.

87     While the expert engaged by the Defence attempted to show that there may be other possibilities that could explain the sudden collapse of the deceased, I did not attach any weight to his opinion as it was necessarily premised on the Defence’s brief that the accused did not administer any EDTA to the deceased, and also this court has found that accused did in fact administered EDTA based on the evidence adduced by the Prosecution and disbelieved the accused’s defence.

88     There is clear and incontrovertible evidence against the accused on his administration of EDTA on the charge and the accused acts were the sole and direct cause of the deceased’s death.

89     There are no merits raised by the accused that he did not administer the EDTA to the deceased and that the cause of death could be due to other possible causes. Accordingly, I convicted the accused on the charge.

The Court’s Decision on Sentence

90     This court accepted the evidence adduced by the Prosecution and disbelieved his defence that he did not administer EDTA to the deceased at the material time. He was found guilty and convicted of the offence punishable under section 304A(b) of the Penal Code (Cap 224, 2008 Rev Ed) (“PC”) and is liable to be punished with imprisonment for a term which may extend to 2 years, or with fine, or with both.

91     In 2008, the Parliament amended the punishment for section 304A PC into two separate limbs for rash and negligent acts, with the former attracting the higher maximum term of five years’ imprisonment and the latter attracting a maximum of two years’ imprisonment.

92     On the appropriate approach to be taken in sentencing of a case of this nature, both parties agree that this court is not the right forum to formulate any sentencing framework and refer this court to existing precedents to serve as useful guidance on the offence specific factors of harm and culpability, and the offender specific factors of mitigating and aggravating factors as relevant for consideration of the appropriate sentence.

93     Where an offence under section 304A(b) PC envisages only one type of harm, namely death, causation would still be a relevant consideration. Whether the deceased’s death was a direct consequence of the accused’s act or whether there were other contributing causes to the deceased’s death which may lessen the severity of the offence specific factor of harm would be relevant for consideration by this court.

94     Having heard and accepted the oral testimonies of Sabrina Ng and Claire Chew as witnesses of truth without any cogent reasons to falsely implicate the accused, especially the evidence of Sabrina Ng on the second dose of EDTA and the administration of “less than 45 minutes” on the deceased by the accused, the admission by the accused in exhibit P80 that he administered EDTA on the deceased, the photographs taken by the deceased prior to her collapse at the clinic, the incontrovertible fact that EDTA was found in the antemortem sample of the deceased and the lack of credibility in the deceased’s defence that he did not administer the EDTA, I accordingly find that the accused’s acts were the sole and direct cause of the deceased’s death.

95     There is an option for a fine under section 304A(b) of the PC, however, both parties agree that the custodial threshold has been crossed in the present case. The Prosecution sought an imprisonment term of 18 to 24 months while the Defence sought an imprisonment term of 6 to 8 months.

96     The main issue before this court in determining the appropriate sentence will depend mainly on the finding of the level of culpability of the accused within the prescribed spectrum of punishment.

97     The Defence having referred to the case of PP v Putra Nur Iman Bin Muhammad Danial Zhang [2026] SGMC 14 (“Putra”) at [9] citing PP v Hue An Li [2014] 4 SLR 661 has proposed an approach for the court to consider as a first step the offence-specific factors and place the case into three sentencing ranges comprising low, moderate and high culpabilities. This is quite similar to that proposed by the Prosecution although the sentencing ranges proposed by the Prosecution vary slightly from the Defence. I prefer to adopt an equal distribution of the 24-month sentencing bands across three equal categories of low, moderate and high culpabilities with their corresponding ranges of fine to 8 months’ imprisonment, 8 to 16 months’ imprisonment and 16 to 24 months’ imprisonment respectively.

98     The Prosecution has identified a list of culpability enhancing offence-specific factors gathered from existing precedents to assist the court in assessing where to place the present case in the three sentencing bands and to derive an indicative starting sentence. The culpability enhancing factors are: (a) the foreseeability of the risk of harm; (b) abuses of position or trust; (c) motive for his acts; (d) the duration of the negligence; (e) the degree of training received as regards the procedure carried out; (f) The degree of departure from the expected standard of care; and (g) the offender’s post-offence conduct (e.g in concealing the offence).

99     Based on the above culpability enhancing factors, the Prosecution submitted that the present case falls within the high culpability sentencing band with an indicative starting sentence of between 1 year and 6 months to 2 years’ imprisonment.

100    On the other hand, the Defence submitted that the accused’s culpability falls at the most at the highest end of the low or the lowest end of the moderate culpability band and hence attracting an indicative starting sentence of between 6 to 8 months’ imprisonment.

101    Of the medical negligence cases referred to this court by both parties to assess what should be the appropriate indicating starting sentence, I find only two cases are relevant for this court’s consideration.

102    First is the unreported case of Wong Meng Hang (“Wong”) where Wong, a former aesthetics doctor, in 2022, pleaded guilty to a charge of committing a rash act causing death. Wong performed a liposuction procedure on the patient and administered an excessive amount of Propofol, an anaesthetic drug and potent sedative, which led to the death of the patient. As highlighted by the Defence, this case involved several aggravating factors, including his lack of qualification to administer the drug and subsequent history of dishonesty to paramedics and hospital staff.

103    Wong was sentenced to 4 months’ imprisonment for causing death by the rash act. Defence recognised this is an unreported case but nevertheless submitted that it serves as a useful data point.

104    I agree with the Prosecution that as Wong is an unreported decision and without the benefits of the full reasoning compared to a reported case, it would be unsafe to rely on Wong’s case. Moreover, the Prosecution submitted that there was a considerable delay in Wong’s prosecution which may be a factor taken into consideration in the sentencing by the court in Wong’s case.

105    The Prosecution urged this court to consider the only reported High Court decision on medical negligence in Lim Poh Eng v PP [1999] 1 SLR(R) 428 (“Lim Poh Eng”) as most relevant for assessment on the appropriate sentence to be meted out in the present case.

106    In Lim Poh Eng, the offender was a practitioner of traditional Chinese medicine. The victim visited his clinic, and he prescribed a course of treatment of colon washouts. The victim self-administered the colon washouts without any supervision on three occasions. After each occasion she complained to the offender that she felt unwell. But the offender did not examine her and assured her everything was normal. The day after the third occasion, the victim's family brought her to see the offender. The victim looked distinctly unwell. The offender gave her some medicine but her pulse remained weak and he had reservations about her recovery. Yet he did not refer her to a hospital and did not follow up on the victim after sending her home. The victim's condition deteriorated and she was admitted to hospital where she was found to have a perforation in her anal canal caused by the colon washouts. The district judge convicted the offender under section 338 of the PC which has the maximum punishment of 2 years’ imprisonment term and sentenced the offender to 10 months' imprisonment. The High Court upheld the custodial sentence on appeal.

107    The High Court at [37] to [39] in Lim Poh Eng held that the benchmarks set for road traffic cases (where fines were imposed for negligent acts) were not applicable. This was because unlike such cases which were mostly caused by a momentary lapse, the appellant’s negligence occurred over a period of time in the context of a doctor-patient relationship. The appellant’s offence was serious: he (a) prescribed colonic washouts without training in the procedure and use of the equipment, and without understanding the risks involved; and (b) took extremely poor care of victim. The normal sentence for a first offender who pleaded guilty to a charge under section 338 PC was nine months’ imprisonment.

108    As a doctor bound by his vocation to save lives, the accused should not have used the EDTA, which was prohibited by MOH, to treat the deceased without regard to the known risks involved. It is neither mitigatory for the accused that the deceased did not suffer any harm in her previous treatment nor that he may have carried out such prohibited treatments to various other patients without any harm in the past prior to this tragic incident.

109    I agree with the Prosecution that the accused knew that the risk of hypocalcaemia, seizures, cardiac arrhythmias and even death arising from chelation treatment was foreseeable and yet he did not take any precaution to ensure that the deceased was a suitable candidate for chelation treatment or to ensure that the deceased’s condition was properly monitored in the course of the chelation treatment.

110    In a doctor-patient relationship, the patient’s life and wellbeing is at the mercy of the doctor treating the patient. The accused has clearly betrayed the trust reposed on him by the deceased by agreeing to administer EDTA to her despite knowing that there was no indications for its use on her. He was merely motivated by monetary gain in treating her without taking the necessary safeguards to ensure her safety.

111    In addition, the accused has not undergone any proper training on the administration of EDTA for chelation treatment and this has resulted in him administering the EDTA at too high a concentration and too quickly causing the deceased to develop EDTA toxicity, which in turn led to her cardiac arrest and eventual death.

112    As observed in Lim Poh Eng, the negligence in medical negligence cases usually occurred over a period of time and not due to a momentary lapse. In the present case, the accused was actively involved in administering the EDTA despite knowing that he is administering a treatment which is prohibited by the Ministry of Health and the risks involved in doing so. Notwithstanding this, the accused administered a second dose to the deceased which he ought to know would further increase the risk of any potential harm to the health of the deceased if there was no proper monitoring by the accused during the treatment.

113    The accused’s conduct after the deceased’s collapse is also a relevant culpability enhancing factor. He wilfully chose to conceal the EDTA treatment administered to the deceased from the deceased’s family members, the paramedic SCDF officers and the treating doctors depriving them of the critical life-saving information needed to help to revive the deceased. He also deliberately omitted keeping proper clinical notes about the administration of the EDTA to the deceased, knowing that he had administered a prohibited substance which had caused the deceased to collapse suddenly in his clinic. For his own self-preservation, he did not preserve any of the items he had used for the EDTA treatment on the deceased at the material time in question.

114    As observed by the High Court in Lim Poh Eng, the normal sentence for a first offender who pleaded guilty to a charge under section 338 PC was nine months’ imprisonment. In my view, the starting sentence for a first offender who pleaded guilty under section 304A(b) PC involving medical negligence akin to that of gross negligence in Lim Poh Eng, the starting sentence should be around 12 months’ imprisonment.

115    In our present case, considering the offence-specific enhancing factors highlighted above, the starting sentence for a claimed rial case should be a fifty percent uplift from the 12 months imprisonment for a plead guilty case which would yield the starting sentence of 18 months imprisonment and this would place the accused near the beginning of the high culpability band of 16 to 24 months’ imprisonment.

116    Applying the second step of considering the mitigating and aggravating factors of the offender-specific factors that are not directly related to the commission of the offence, since the accused did not show any remorse and the accused has been convicted after trial and the other charges which the accused is facing has been stood down, I agree with the Prosecution that no further adjustments are necessary.

117    Having considered the accused’s conduct which represents a blatant breach of his basic duty owed by every medical practitioner to their patients, his action to administer the EDTA without express approval from the authority, careful screening of the patient’s needs, safety protocols and monitoring process, and thereby causing fatal consequence to the deceased, and his subsequent deplorable conduct of wilfully concealing critical information to the treating doctors, this court is of the view that a sentence of 18 months imprisonment would be appropriate and commensurate with his culpability

Public Prosecutor v Thum Choong Onn

Public Prosecutor v Thum Choong Onn
[2026] SGDC 240

Case Number:District Arrest Case No. 905866 of 2026, Magistrate's Appeal No. 9173/2026/01
Decision Date:27 July 2026
Tribunal/Court:District Court
Coram: Shawn Ho

Introduction

1       The Accused, Mr Thum Choong Onn, pleaded guilty to one charge of driving without reasonable consideration for other persons using the road and causing grievous hurt under s 65(1)(b) punishable under s 65(3)(a) of the Road Traffic Act 1961.

2       He was sentenced to 10 days’ imprisonment and a mandatory 5-year driving disqualification for all classes of driving licences.

3       The Defence has appealed against the sentence. The Accused is currently on bail pending appeal. His imprisonment term and driving disqualification order have been stayed.

4       I set out my reasons.

Charge

5       The Accused pleaded guilty to the following charge:

You,

Name: Thum Choong Onn

Gender/ Age: Male/ 55 Years Old

Nationality: Singaporean

are charged that you, on 23 October 2024, at about 4:05 pm, at the signalised cross junction of Tanjong Katong Road and Dunman Road, Singapore, did drive a motorcar bearing registration number SKT386B on a road without reasonable consideration for other persons using the road, to wit, by failing to keep a proper lookout and encroaching into the travel path of a motorcycle bearing registration number FBS4249A, which was travelling straight from the opposite direction on a traffic green light signal and had the right of way, resulting in a collision with the said motorcycle, and grievous hurt was caused to the motorcycle rider, one Tan Choon Mong (male, 67 years old), by your driving of the said motorcar, and you have thereby committed an offence under Section 65(1)(b) punishable under Section 65(3)(a) of the Road Traffic Act 1961.

Statement of facts

Facts of the Case

9       On 23 October 2024, at about 4:05p.m., the Accused was driving the Motorcar on the rightmost lane of the 3-lane road on Dunman Road in the direction of Koon Seng Road, while approaching the signalised cross junction of Tanjong Katong Road and Dunman Road, Singapore (“Junction”). In so doing, the Accused drove the Motorcar without reasonable consideration for other persons using the road. This resulted in a collision between the Motorcycle and the left side of the Motorcar, and the victim fell off his Motorcycle onto the ground in the Junction. The collision was captured in video footage from another motorcyclist’s in-vehicle camera, a copy of which is annexed hereto as Annex A and forms a part of this Statement of Facts (SOF). After the collision, the Accused assisted in helping the victim up to the pedestrian pavement.[note: 5]
