Prescribed punishment

20     The prescribed punishment for causing grievous hurt under s 65(1)(b) punishable under s 65(3)(a) of the Road Traffic Act 1961 (“the Act”) is:

(a)      s 65(3)(a):

(i)       A fine not exceeding $5,000 or to

(ii)       Imprisonment for a term not exceeding 2 years or to both.

21     The two components of the overall sentence generally are not to be regarded as mutually compensatory. Hence, an increase in the fine or custodial sentence should not be taken to mandate the imposition of a reduced disqualification period than would otherwise have been ordered: Edwin s/o Suse Nathen v Public Prosecutor [2013] SGHC 194 at [13]-[14].

22     While the different types of punishment are not fungible, there is a positive correlation between the length of the imprisonment term and/or quantum of the fine imposed and the period of the disqualification ordered. This direct relationship arises from the overlapping considerations of harm and culpability underlying the determination of the length of imprisonment or quantum of fine, and the length of the disqualification period: Chen Song v Public Prosecutor [2025] 3 SLR 509 at [141].

23     An offence’s statutory maximum sentence signals the gravity in which Parliament views such offences. A sentencing judge ought to take this into account when determining precisely where the offender’s conduct falls within the entire range of punishment set by Parliament: Public Prosecutor v Kwong Kok Hing [2008] 2 SLR(R) 684 at [44].

(Benny Tan, Assessing the Effectiveness of Sentencing Guideline Judgments in Singapore Issued Post-March 2013 and A Guide to Constructing Frameworks, (2018) 30 SAcLJ 1004 at [46])

24     The court should ensure that the full spectrum of sentences enacted by Parliament is carefully explored in determining the appropriate sentence, viz. Completeness principle (Poh Boon Kiat v Public Prosecutor [2014] 4 SLR 892 at [60]).

Prosecution’s submissions on sentence

25     The Prosecution asked for around 2 - 3 weeks’ imprisonment (PG basis) and a driving disqualification for 5 years (mandatory minimum).[note: 15]

26     The Prosecution argued that the present case involved lesser harm on a holistic assessment, and the offender is of lower culpability, as the following factors are present:[note: 16]

(a)      Nature and location of the injury: the victim sustained a closed left scaphoid wrist fracture, which required surgical fixation on 7 November 2024 and four further clinic reviews thereafter (up till 8 January 2025), and in respect of which the victim was advised for splint immobilisation. While the fracture was not in a location proximate to vital organs, the victim’s left wrist is relatively critical to his daily mobility and movement, considering in particular the victim’s work as a delivery rider.[note: 17]

(b)      Impact of injury: the victim was granted a total of 78 days of Hospitalisation Leave from 23 October 2024 to 8 January 2025, and certified “unfit for duty” in that period.[note: 18]

(a)      Flouting of traffic rules and regulations: the Accused made an unauthorised U-turn at the time of the accident. In addition, the Accused made the U-turn while without giving way to any oncoming vehicles, nor waiting for a safe opportunity to complete the turn.[note: 19]

27     As the present case involves lesser harm, and the offender is of lower culpability, the applicable sentencing range is Band 1 in Chen Song (i.e., a fine and/or up to 6 months’ imprisonment).[note: 20]

28     On the third step, the indicative starting point sentence within the applicable sentencing range ought to be a short custodial sentence of 2-3 weeks’ imprisonment (on a claim-trial basis) for the following reasons:

(a)     The court in Chen Song stated that the custodial threshold would typically be crossed where there are 2 or more offence-specific harm and/or culpability factors present (see paragraphs [137] and [140]). In the present case, there are at least two offence-specific harm and culpability factors present.

(b)     In addition to the primary harm factors and culpability factors recited in detail in the Prosecution’s Address on Sentence at [5], the Accused did not bring the Motorcar to a complete stop at the Junction before proceeding to make the U-turn, which slightly increases his culpability.

(c)     In terms of potential harm (going towards culpability): the victim was riding a motorcycle at the time of the collision, and he fell onto the ground in the junction (when traffic conditions were moderate).

(d)     Some damage was sustained to both the Motorcar and Motorcycle.[note: 21]

29     On the fourth step, the indicative starting point sentence ought to be adjusted by a one-week uplift to 3-4 weeks’ imprisonment (on a claim-trial basis), taking into account the following offender-specific aggravating and mitigating factors:

(a)     The Accused has two recent compounded offences of failing to conform to a red-light signal under s 120(4) of the Act, which may be taken into account as an aggravating factor under s 139AA of the Act, as follows:

(i)       1 February 2022 – composition fine of $380.00, and issuance of 12 demerit points; and

(ii)       25 November 2022 – composition fine of $400.00, and issuance of 12 demerit points.

(b)     The Accused assisted in helping the victim up after the collision, and readily co-operated with the authorities.[note: 22]

30     The Accused had indicated his plea of guilt within Stage 1 of the Sentencing Advisory Panel’s Guidelines for Reduction in Sentences for Guilty Pleas. Accordingly, a maximum of 30% reduction in the Accused’s imprisonment sentence may be considered. The final sentence that should be imposed in the event of a maximum 30% reduction would therefore be around 2-3 weeks’ imprisonment and a driving disqualification of 5 years (mandatory minimum).[note: 23]

Mitigation plea

31     The Defence asked for a fine of $5000 and the mandatory 5-year disqualification order.[note: 24]

32     The Defence made the following arguments:

(a)     The Accused cooperated with the authorities and indicated his intention to plead guilty at the earliest stage (stage 1). His plea saved judicial time and resources.[note: 25] He assisted after the collision.[note: 26]

(b)     He had no prior convictions for careless or dangerous driving. The Defence accepted that the Prosecution highlighted two compounded red-light offences in 2022. However, these composition offences should be accorded little to no weight, as a payment of composition is not an indication of guilt (Re Lim Chor Pee [1990] 2 SLR(R) 117). In any case, the prior compounded offences are not section 65 offences.[note: 27]

(c)     The Accused accepted that he failed to keep a proper lookout. He is genuinely remorseful and understands the seriousness of the consequences.[note: 28]

(d)     There was an absence of aggravating driving behaviour. There was no speeding, intoxication, mobile phone use, sleepy driving, racing, or sustained inattention. The lapse was momentary.[note: 29]

(e)     The matter falls within Band 1 of the Chen Song framework: lesser harm and lower culpability.[note: 30]

(f)     The custodial threshold is not crossed. Although Chen Song observes that the custodial threshold would typically be crossed where there are two or more offence-specific harm and/or culpability factors, the court must still assess the totality of the harm and culpability holistically and consider whether the factors present themselves to a limited degree (Chen Song at [123] – [127]).[note: 31]

(g)     For the “nature and location of injury” limb, the Prosecution stated that “While the fracture was not in a location proximate to vital organs, the Accused’s left wrist is relatively critical to his daily mobility and movement, considering in particular the victim’s work as a delivery rider”. The Defence disagreed with this proposition.[note: 32]

(h)     The Prosecution’s reliance on the victim’s particular occupation over-particularised the analysis. The harm inquiry should not turn on a granular comparison of victims’ occupations. If it did, the same injury would be treated differently depending on whether the victim was, for example, an office worker (stationary at work, not requiring to expend any bodily effort other than typing on keyboards) or a construction worker (who would have high physical exertion daily at work). The proper focus remains the nature, severity, permanence, and actual impact of the injury, rather than a speculative assessment of how the victim’s occupation may make the injury more or less serious.[note: 33]

(i)     While the Defence does not seek to belittle the victim’s injury and is cognisant of the victim’s need for surgery, a wrist fracture is not to a vulnerable and sensitive part of the body.[note: 34]

(j)     The 77 days of “Hospitalisation Leave” should not be treated as if the victim had been warded throughout that period. There is no evidence that he was warded for 77 days. The label “Hospitalisation Leave” is therefore evidence of certified unfitness for work, but not evidence of prolonged inpatient hospitalisation or a severe life-threatening injury. This is a factor that ought to be considered as the limb “impact of injury” lies on a spectrum: a victim having to be warded and not able to move from his hospital bed suffers a greater impact than if he was simply given leave but could stay at home and go about his daily activities.[note: 35]

(k)     The 77 days of medical leave is not high such as to warrant a custodial sentence, as can be seen from the table of precedents.[note: 36]

(l)     Accordingly, the Defence’s position is that no primary harm factor is engaged such as to constitute an aggravating factor contributing to the quantitative assessment as set out in Chen Song.[note: 37]

(m)     The Prosecution submits that potential harm is present because the victim was a motorcyclist who fell onto the ground in the junction when traffic conditions were moderate. The Defence respectfully submits that a more detailed assessment of the Video would reveal that potential harm is minimal.[note: 38]

(n)     The Defence accepts that the culpability factor of “flouting traffic rules” is present as the Accused made an unauthorised U-turn.[note: 39]

(o)     The video footage shows that before the Accused made the U-turn, another car ahead of the Accused had already turned right across the victim’s direction of travel. This was a clear indication that vehicles were making discretionary right turns across the victim’s path. A reasonably prudent motorcyclist approaching the junction ought therefore to have slowed down and exercise heightened caution, particularly since the victim was proceeding straight through a junction where vehicles were visibly turning across him.[note: 40]

(p)     The victim’s failure to slow down despite visible turning traffic is part of the factual matrix against which the Accused’s culpability should be calibrated. It supports the conclusion that the Accused’s culpability remains at the low end of lower culpability.[note: 41]

Sentencing

The Law

(1)   Legislative history of s 65 of the Act

33     As was observed by Sundaresh Menon CJ in Wu Zhi Yong v Public Prosecutor [2021] SGHC 261 at [15] (albeit in the related context of s 64 of the Act), the Road Traffic (Amendment) Act 2019 (Act 19 of 2019) envisaged a new scheme of penalties for careless or inconsiderate driving in a tiered structure calibrated according to the degree of hurt caused. This is codified in the Act as ss 65(2) to 65(5). The maximum punishments which may be imposed for each category of harm increase concomitantly with the seriousness of the harm caused; this translates into wider ranges of punishments where more serious harm is occasioned (Sue Chang v Public Prosecutor [2022] SGHC 176 at [38]).

34     For instance, where death is caused, s 65(2)(a) provides that a first-time offender is liable to a fine not exceeding $10,000 or to imprisonment for a term not exceeding three years or to both. In contrast, the residual category (where no actual physical harm is caused, but which includes cases of non-personal injury or potential harm) captured in s 65(5)(a) provides that a first-time offender is liable to a fine not exceeding $1,500 or to imprisonment for a term not exceeding six months or to both (Sue Chang at [38]).

35     By tiering the punishment provisions in accordance with the type of harm suffered, Parliament has given clear expression to the need to give explicit consideration to the outcomes that result from instances of careless or inconsiderate driving. This is a stark departure from the structure of s 65 of the pre-2019 Act, where there was a single range of punishment with no differentiation based on the type and/or degree of harm caused (Sue Chang at [39]).

36     In addition, while Parliament has retained the distinction between reckless or dangerous driving under s 64 of the Act and careless or inconsiderate driving under s 65 of the Act, this distinction has been made more pronounced through the refining of the punishment provisions. These two provisions reflect the differing circumstances under which an irresponsible driving offence can occur. The former offence (s 64) is regarded as being more serious than the latter (s 65), reflecting primarily the differing levels of culpability of the offenders. Accordingly, the current architecture of the Act concerning irresponsible driving offences tiers the punishment provisions according to both harm and culpability, not dissimilar to the Penal Code (Sue Chang at [40]).

(2)   Driving disqualification order

37     Driving disqualification orders meld the three sentencing objectives of punishment, protection of the public and deterrence: Edwin s/o Suse Nathen v Public Prosecutor [2013] 4 SLR 1139 at [13]-[14], Public Prosecutor v Koh Thiam Huat [2017] 4 SLR 1099 at [64] and Chen Song v Public Prosecutor [2024] SGHC 129 at [143].

38     The most important sentencing principles engaged in driving disqualification orders are to:

(a)      protect society, because disqualification orders are meant to prevent future harm that the offender may cause to the public, and to

(b)      deter, because such orders deprive offenders of the freedom to drive: Public Prosecutor v Ong Heng Chua [2018] SGHC 95 at [61].

39     As stated in Public Prosecutor v Mohd Isa [1963] MLJ 135, the “most satisfactory penalty for most motoring offences is disqualification” because a fine is paid once and then forgotten. For instance, a 12-month disqualification order would mean that for the entire year in which the order is in effect, the offender is reminded every day of his offence and the unwarranted risks in which he had placed ordinary members of the public: Sivakumar s/o Rajoo v Public Prosecutor [2002] 1 SLR(R) 265 at [28].

40     Where a person is disqualified for a period of 12 months or longer, that person’s driving licence shall be “of no effect” and the person is further prevented from driving a motor vehicle after the disqualification period unless he passes the prescribed test of competence to drive: s 43(1)(b) of the Road Traffic Act.

Decision on sentence

41     For driving without due care or attention causing grievous hurt, the applicable case is Chen Song v Public Prosecutor [2024] SGHC 129.

Framework in Chen Song

42     A quantitative factors-based approach, where the indicative sentencing band is determined at the first step, based on the number of offence-specific harm and culpability factors is especially useful: Chen Song at [123].

43     “Lesser harm” is caused and the offender’s culpability is deemed as “lower culpability” where at most one harm or culpability factor applies in respect of each category: Chen Song at [123].

44     “Greater harm” would be caused and the offender’s culpability deemed as “higher culpability” where there are 2 or more harm and culpability factors respectively: Chen Song at [123].

45     This is a general guideline which is not to be applied mechanistically in every case. The foremost inquiry is to assess holistically whether the totality of the harm suffered by the victim should be classified as either “greater harm” or “lesser harm” and whether the offender’s culpability considered as a whole should be classified as either “lower culpability” or “higher culpability”: Chen Song at [123].

(1)   Harm factors

46     Primary harm factors are factors which pertain directly to the bodily injury suffered by the victim(s) in each case. These factors include:

(a)     the nature and location of the injuries;

(b)     the degree of permanence of the injuries; and

(c)     the impact of the injuries: Chen Song at [124].

47     The three broad primary harm factors are:

(a)      Nature and location of the injury: This factor focuses on the precise nature and the location of the injury. This requires a consideration of:

(i)       the nature and severity of injury (eg, simple or complex and extent of injury, etc);

(ii)       the number of injuries;

(iii)       whether surgical intervention was necessary (or whether the injuries were treated conservatively);

(iv)       the disposition of the victim post-surgery (eg, general ward, high dependency or intensive care unit); and

(v)       the location of the injury (eg, vulnerable location).

(b)      Degree of permanence: This factor considers whether the injury or injuries caused to the victim are permanent or transient. Permanent injuries include loss of a limb or permanent privation of the sight of either eye or the hearing of either ear, etc.

(c)      Impact of injury: This factor contemplates the impact of the injury on the victim’s quality of life. Here, considerations of:

(i)       the duration of stay in the hospital/rehabilitation centre;

(ii)       duration of any hospitalisation/medical leave;

(iii)       ability to carry out daily tasks and maintain livelihood; and

(iv)       duration of rehabilitation (if any), are relevant: Chen Song at [127].

48     There is an inevitable overlap between the factors of nature and location of injury on the one hand, and impact of injury on the other. The period and nature of hospitalisation may be an indicium of both the nature and severity of the injury and perhaps even the number of injuries suffered, and its impact on the victim’s quality of life. The period and nature of hospitalisation may be relevant to both factors: Habeeb Zaleena d/o Pallivilakam Kader Habeeb Mohamed v Public Prosecutor [2026] SGHC 99 at [35].

49     As to whether an injury is at a vulnerable location, the High Court in Ling Zhao Bin v Public Prosecutor [2026] SGHC 107 stated at [27]:

It seems to me that the parts of the body were regarded as vulnerable because the injuries were to, or in locations proximate to, vital organs. The common thread is that these locations are vulnerable because an injury suffered in any of these locations, may result in a risk to life or permanent or long-term loss of function that impairs the victim’s ability to live independently and without assistance (eg loss of cognitive ability or paralysis). Vulnerability is defined with the reference to the severity of the harm that could result from an injury in a location. Without being prescriptive and in any way comprehensive, this common thread could serve as a working definition of a vulnerable location. It is consistent with why an injury to a vulnerable location was identified in Chen Song as relevant to the harm analysis under the “nature and location” factor, and the purpose of the central inquiry in the harm analysis (which is to ascertain the extent of physical harm that is suffered by the victim as a result of the injury in question as stated at [22] above).

[Emphasis added]

50     I bore in mind that there may be cases where even if two or more primary harm factors apply, if they present themselves to a limited degree, the court may nevertheless consider that “lesser harm” had been caused based on a holistic assessment of the harm caused: Chen Song at [127].

51     Secondary harm factors are unrelated to the physical injury suffered by the victim(s), but which nonetheless go towards the extent of harm caused in a particular case. These factors include:

(a)     property damage; and

(b)     potential harm: Chen Song at [125].

52     Consideration of actual harm focuses on the moment of a collision. Potential harm looks at the wider circumstances before and after a collision (Public Prosecutor v Cheng Chang Tong [2023] SGHC 119 at [57]).

53     Potential harm refers to harm that was likely to have been caused to other road users but which ultimately did not eventuate: Chen Song at [129] and Public Prosecutor v Johnson Tan Wee Kiat [2026] SGHC 59 at [13].

54     The level of potential harm may be assessed against facts such as the condition of the road, the volume of traffic or number of pedestrians actually on or which might reasonably be expected to be on the road at the relevant time, the speed and manner of driving, visibility at the relevant time, the type of vehicle, and any particular vulnerabilities (eg, a truck or car colliding into a motorcycle or pedestrian). It was observed that these relate to the circumstances of driving that could increase the danger posed to road users (Wu Zhi Yong at [36(a)]): Chen Song at [129].

55     It would only be appropriate to have regard to potential harm if there was a sufficient likelihood of the harm arising and this in turn should be assessed in the light of the gravity of the harm risked (Neo Ah Luan v Public Prosecutor [2018] 5 SLR 1153 at [67]): Chen Song at [129].

56     The potential for harm has to be assessed with reference not only to the actual distance travelled, but the distance which the offender intended to travel (Chan Chow Chuen v Public Prosecutor [2024] SGHC 294 at [24]). In Fan Lei v Public Prosecutor [2024] SGHC 278 at [10], travelling a distance of 17km was not enough to point to increased potential harm. In Fan Lei, there was no evidence that the offender was driving in a careless manner over that 17km.

57     I was mindful that in assessing the level of harm or potential harm, the sentencing court should be careful not to double-count any factors which may already have been taken into account in assessing the level of culpability: Ye Lin Myint v Public Prosecutor [2019] 5 SLR 1005 at [58] (see also Andrew Ashworth, Sentencing and Criminal Justice (6th Ed, 2015, Cambridge University Press) at [4.3] and [4.5]).

58     Each primary harm factor would count as one offence-specific factor going towards harm. However, where a secondary harm factor presents itself in a significant manner, this should be considered in the determination of where the particular offence falls within the indicative sentencing band: Chen Song at [125].

(2)   Culpability factors

59     A non-exhaustive list of factors which each constitute 1 offence-specific factor going towards culpability is as follows (Chen Song at [131]):

(a)      Any form of dangerous driving behaviour. For instance:

(i)       speeding;

(ii)       driving against traffic;

(iii)       driving when not fit to drive;

(iv)       driving under the influence of alcohol or drugs;

(v)       sleepy driving;

(vi)       driving while using a mobile phone;

(vii)       swerving in and out of lanes;

(viii)       using a vehicle in a dangerous fashion; and

(ix)       street racing.

(b)      Flouting of traffic rules and regulations. For instance:

(i)       failing to stop at a stop line;

(ii)       failing to conform to traffic signal;

(iii)       not forming up correctly to execute a turn;

(iv)       changing lanes across a set of double white lines/chevron markings; and

(v)       making an illegal U-turn/right turn.

(c)      High degree of carelessness: This is demonstrated where there was a prolonged or sustained period of inattention (as opposed to a momentary lapse of attention), and where the offender was deliberately cavalier about certain mitigatable risks. As stated in Sue Chang at [95], it would also be relevant to consider the extent to which the offender’s distraction was avoidable and the extent to which the offender’s misjudgment was reasonable.

(3)   Sentencing framework for driving offences causing grievous hurt punishable under s 65(3)(a)

60     The following sentencing framework applied for careless driving offences causing hurt punishable under s 65(3)(a) where the offender elects to claim trial (Chen Song at [134]).

61     First, the court is to identify the number of offence-specific factors under the broad categories of “harm” and “culpability” (Chen Song at [134(a)]).

62     Second, based on the number of offence-specific factors present, the court is to determine whether the harm caused is “lesser harm” or “greater harm” and whether the culpability of the offender is “lower culpability” or “higher culpability” and thereafter arrive at the sentencing band the offence falls within (Chen Song at [134(b)]).

63     “Lesser harm” is caused, and the offender’s culpability is deemed as “lower culpability” where there are 0–1 harm or culpability factors respectively. “Greater harm” is caused, and the offender’s culpability is deemed as “higher culpability” where there are 2 or more harm or culpability factors respectively (Chen Song at [134(b)]).

Circumstances

64     Third, after determining the indicative sentencing band that the offence falls within, the court should identify an indicative starting point sentence within that range, taking into account: (a) all the primary harm factors and the culpability factors identified; and (b) the secondary harm factors (Chen Song at [134(c)]).

65     Fourth, the court is to make adjustments to the starting point to take into account the usual gamut of offender-specific aggravating and mitigating factors (Chen Song at [134(d)]).

66     The High Court stated that with reference to the proposed sentencing bands for s 65(3)(a), the custodial threshold would typically be crossed where there are 2 or more offence-specific harm and/or culpability factors present. Therefore, for Band 1 cases, fines would ordinarily be reserved for cases where 0–1 offence-specific harm and/or culpability factors are present (Chen Song at [137]).

67     A mandatory 5-year disqualification period applies for offences punishable under s 65(3), “unless the court for special reasons thinks fit to not order or to order otherwise”: s 65(6)(d) of the Act (Chen Song at [138]).

(see also Ivan Tang et al., Sentencing Frameworks for Consistency: A Proposed Framework, (2024) 36 SAcLJ 380 at [130])

68      Harm. For the nature and location of injury:

(a)     The victim had sustained a closed left scaphoid wrist fracture (“Fracture”) in the road traffic accident.[note: 42]

(b)     The victim underwent surgical fixation of the Fracture.[note: 43]

(c)     The X-rays of the left wrist on 4 December 2024 showed some healing at the fracture site and possible early cystic changes.[note: 44]

(d)     The victim was reviewed in the Hand Surgery clinic on 29 October 2024 for the Fracture.[note: 45] The victim remained stable in clinic reviews on 13 November 2024, 18 November 2024 and 4 December 2024.[note: 46]

69     For the impact of injury, the victim was granted a total of 78 days of Hospitalisation Leave from 23 October 2024 to 8 January 2025 (both dates inclusive) and certified “unfit for duty” in that period, across five medical certificates issued by TTSH including for some overlapping periods, as listed below:

(a)     On 23 October 2024, the Accused was granted 14 days of hospitalisation leave, from 23 October 2024 to 5 November 2024 (inclusive).

(b)     On 29 October 2024, the Accused was granted 30 days of hospitalisation leave, from 6 November 2024 to 5 December 2024 (inclusive).

(c)     On 7 November 2024, the Accused was granted seven days of hospitalisation leave, from 7-13 November 2024 (inclusive).

(d)     On 13 November 2024, the Accused was granted five days of hospitalisation leave, from 14-18 November 2024 (inclusive).

(e)     On 4 December 2024, the Accused was granted 51 days of hospitalisation leave, from 19 November 2024 to 8 January 2025 (inclusive).[note: 47]

70     The Defence argued that “‘Hospitalisation Leave’ should not be treated as if the Victim had been warded throughout that period”.[note: 48] To be clear, this was not done. I was aware that for “impact of injury”, Chen Song at [127(c)] differentiates between “duration of stay in the hospital/ rehabilitation centre” and “duration of any hospitalisation/ medical leave”.[note: 49]

71     The victim’s Motorcycle sustained some damage, and was towed away from the site of the collision to be transported to a workshop for repairs.[note: 50]

72     Given that it was a single fracture to the wrist (not a vulnerable location), the primary harm factor of “nature and location of injury” was present to a limited degree.

73     The primary harm factor of impact of injury was engaged. The victim was granted a total of 78 days of Hospitalisation Leave and certified “unfit for duty” in that period, across five medical certificates issued by TTSH.[note: 51]

74     On a holistic assessment, there was lesser harm (lower end).

75     To be clear, I was mindful that the damage to the Accused’s own vehicle should not be treated as an aggravating factor: Ching Kelvin v Public Prosecutor [2024] SGHC 297 at [15].

76     I turn next to the Accused’s culpability in the present case.

77      Culpability. The Accused flouted traffic rules by making an illegal U-turn (Chen Song at [131]).

78     The Accused made an unauthorised U-turn at the Junction at about 4:05p.m., without having brought the Motorcar to a complete stop at the Junction.[note: 52] He made the U-turn without giving way to any oncoming vehicles nor waiting for a safe opportunity to complete the turn.[note: 53]

79     As a result, while the Accused was still in the midst of completing the U-turn, the Motorcar encroached into the travel path of the on-coming Motorcycle, which was travelling straight from the opposite direction on a traffic green light signal and had the right of way.[note: 54] This resulted in a collision between the Motorcycle and the left side of the Motorcar, and the victim fell off his Motorcycle onto the ground in the Junction.[note: 55]

80     The Defence argued that:

(a)     The video footage shows that before the Accused made the U-turn, another car ahead of the Accused had already turned right across the victim’s direction of travel. This was a clear indication that vehicles were making discretionary right turns across the victim’s path. A reasonably prudent motorcyclist approaching the junction ought therefore to have slowed down and exercised heightened caution, particularly since the victim was proceeding straight through a junction where vehicles were visibly turning across him.[note: 56]

(b)     The victim’s failure to slow down despite visible turning traffic is part of the factual matrix against which the Accused’s culpability should be calibrated. It supports the conclusion that the Accused’s culpability remains at the low end of lower culpability.[note: 57]

81     However, what the defence stated are not factors that reduced the Accused’s culpability and should not be regarded as a relevant mitigating factor: Guay Seng Tiong Nickson v Public Prosecutor [2016] 3 SLR 1079 at [70].

82     The Defence also argued that there was an absence of aggravating driving behaviour.[note: 58] There was no speeding, intoxication, mobile phone use, sleepy driving, racing, or sustained inattention.[note: 59] However, these were neutral factors since the mere absence of an aggravating factor is a neutral factor for sentencing: Edwin s/o Suse Nathen [2013] 4 SLR 1139 at [24] and Poh Boon Kiat v Public Prosecutor [2014] 4 SLR 892 at [99].

83     For the mitigation plea’s table of cases, I noted the following points:

(a)      Public Prosecutor v Paul Raj Arokiasamy [2026] SGDC 201:

(i)       Unlike the Accused’s one culpability factor, there was no culpability-increasing factor in Paul Raj Arokiasamy at [86].

(ii)       Unlike the Accused’s two compounded offences for failing to conform to the red-light signal, the offender in Paul Raj Arokiasamy at [92] had a clean driving record.

(b)     The case of Erh Zhi Huang Alvan v Public Prosecutor (MA 9204 of 2022) is analysed in this judgment below at [113]-[123].

(c)     Imprisonment was given in Ling Zhao Bin v Public Prosecutor [2026] SGHC 107, Public Prosecutor v Chin Wei Guang [2026] SGDC 101 and Public Prosecutor v Lee Thiang Jiang [2026] SGDC 88:

(i)       Unlike the Accused’s one culpability factor, there was no culpability-increasing factor in Ling Zhao Bin at [65].

(ii)       The victim’s hospitalisation leave of 78 days[note: 60] was longer than the 25 days of hospitalisation leave in Lee Thiang Jiang. In Lee Thiang Jiang at [81], the court stated that “…considering that it is a dated antecedent, limited weight should be given to the conviction”.

84     The Supreme Court has repeatedly emphasised a fact-sensitive approach for traffic cases:

(a)     The highly fact-specific nature of traffic offences means that sentencing, being ultimately a matter of discretion, must be approached judiciously with the highest level of attention to the facts and circumstances of each case (Public Prosecutor v Ganesan Sivasankar [2017] 5 SLR 681 at [57]):

(i)       The High Court was reiterating the point made in Public Prosecutor v Chia Hyong Gyee (Oral Judgment, 25 May 2017, Magistrate’s Appeal No 001/2017/01).

(ii)       The High Court in Stansilas Fabian Kester v Public Prosecutor [2017] 5 SLR 755 stated at [46] and [73]: “In the final analysis, the appropriate sentence to be imposed will be the product of a fact-sensitive exercise of discretion, taking into account all the circumstances of the case.”

(b)     It bears repeating that the facts of each traffic case must be carefully evaluated, weighed and assessed: Lee-Teh Har Eng (Oral Judgment, 15 December 2016, Magistrate’s Appeal 9099/2016) referred to in Koh Thiam Huat at [36].

85     The High Court in Koh Thiam Huat at [39] stated that the facts and circumstances which give rise to traffic offences are so infinitely varied that a blind and rigid adherence to precedents is inadvisable:

… Indeed, the facts and circumstances which give rise to traffic offences are so infinitely varied that a blind and rigid adherence to precedents and sentencing norms by default is inadvisable….

[Emphasis added]

86     In the present case, the Accused flouted traffic rules by making an illegal U-turn (Chen Song at [131]). He made an unauthorised U-turn at the Junction, without having brought the Motorcar to a complete stop at the Junction.[note: 61] He made the U-turn without giving way to any oncoming vehicles nor waiting for a safe opportunity to complete the turn.[note: 62]

87     The foremost inquiry is to assess holistically whether the offender’s culpability considered as a whole should be classified as either “lower culpability” or “higher culpability”: Chen Song at [123]. On a holistic assessment, the present case involved lower culpability.

88     Given the lesser harm and lower culpability, the case fell within Band 1 of Chen Song.

89     The custodial threshold would typically be crossed where there are two or more offence-specific harm and/or culpability factors present: Chen Song at [137].

90     In the present case, the custodial threshold was crossed as there are two or more offence-specific harm and/or culpability factors.

91     The indicative starting point was a custodial sentence of about 2 to 3 weeks. Taking into account the offender-specific aggravating and mitigating factors, the custodial sentence was calibrated downwards to 10 days’ imprisonment.

92     To be clear, I was mindful of the High Court’s decision in Vasentha d/o Joseph v Public Prosecutor [2015] 5 SLR 122, which stated at [48] that indicative starting points are not rigid or inflexible categories and the precise sentence to be imposed in each case would depend on the specific circumstances of that case (see also Aw Soy Tee v Public Prosecutor [2020] 5 SLR 453 at [31]).

93     The 3-Judge Panel in Lee Shing Chan and another v Public Prosecutor and another appeal [2020] 4 SLR 1174 at [34] made clear its preference for a more holistic approach since sentencing is not a scientific exercise and does not demand mathematical precision,[note: 63] which is quite impractical in any case when dealing with human beings and the multifarious situations in the cases.

94     This emphasis on a more holistic approach to sentencing was echoed in S Elamparithi v Public Prosecutor (oral judgment, MA 9238/2019) at [20], i.e. sentencing is not a scientific exercise demanding mathematical precision; it is a matter of judicial discretion to be approached with a judicious measure of pragmatism and common sense, having regard to the offender-specific and offence-specific factors.

95     Sentencing is ultimately an exercise in evaluative ethical judgment — there might well be cases which will eventually be assessed to straddle the border between the bands: Ng Kean Meng Terence v Public Prosecutor [2017] 2 SLR 449 at [48] (see Sir Anthony Hooper, Sentencing: Art or Science, (2015) 27 SAcLJ 17).

96      Antecedents. The Accused’s driving record was not unblemished.

97     He had driving-related compounded offences. An offender’s compounded offences are a relevant sentencing consideration for road traffic violations: Teo Seng Tiong v Public Prosecutor [2021] SGCA 65 at [80]-[81] and [99]-[108].

(See also Public Prosecutor v Ong Heng Chua [2018] SGHC 95 at [39]-[47] and Public Prosecutor v Koh Thiam Huat [2017] SGHC 123 at [56]-[60])

98     Under s 139AA of the Act, a court may take offences that have been compounded (on or after 1 November 2019) into account as an aggravating factor.

99     This is based on the wording and legislative history of s 139AA, including the Explanatory Statement to the Road Traffic (Amendment) Act 2021 (Act 12 of 2021).

100    I was aware that the Court of Appeal in Teo Seng Tiong v Public Prosecutor [2021] SGCA 65 at [17] considered an earlier version of s 139AA of the Act:

139AA.    For the purpose of determining the appropriate sentence for an offence committed by a person under this Act, a court may take into account, as an aggravating factor, any offence that has been compounded (whether before, on or after the date of commencement of section 21 of the Road Traffic (Amendment) Act 2019) under this Act before the date of the sentencing. (emphasis added)

101    The Road Traffic (Amendment) Act 2021 (Act 12 of 2021) amended s 139AA of the Act as follows:

Section 139AA of the principal Act is amended by deleting the words “whether before,” (emphasis added)

102    Importantly, the Explanatory Statement to the Road Traffic (Amendment) Act 2021 (Act 12 of 2021) stated:

Clause 28 amends section 139AA so that a sentencing court, when determining the appropriate sentence for an offence committed by a person under the Act, may take into account as an aggravating factor, any offence that has been compounded on or after (and not before) the date of commencement of section 21 of the Road Traffic (Amendment) Act 2019). (emphasis added)

103    The amendments to s 139AA by the Road Traffic (Amendment) Act 2021 – specifically deleting the words “whether before” – militated against the argument that the sentencing court may take into account as an aggravating factor, any offence that has been compounded (including those before 1 November 2019).

104    In Public Prosecutor v Cheng Chang Tong [2023] SGHC 119 at [60], the High Court considered the offender’s compounded offences in the 1990s and 2012. However, neither the Prosecution nor the Defence appeared to have brought to the court’s attention the fact that the Road Traffic (Amendment) Act 2021 (Act 12 of 2021) had amended s 139AA of the Act.

105    In the present case, I gave due weight to the Accused’s two compounded offences in 2022 for failing to conform to the red-light signal.

106    For completeness, as it took place before 1 November 2019, I did not take into account his compounded offence for failing to conform to a “No U Turn” sign.

107     Guilty plea. The SAP Guidelines for Guilty Pleas applied: Ng En You Jeremiah v Public Prosecutor [2025] SGHC 135 at [110]-[111] and [115]-[117] (see also Edwin Lim Wei Keat, A Critical Analysis of the Application of Guidelines on Reduction in Sentences for Guilty Pleas in Singapore, SAcLJ (10 October 2025, e-First) at [37]-[43]).

108    I gave full weight to the Accused’s guilty plea: Angliss Singapore Pte Ltd v Public Prosecutor [2006] 4 SLR(R) 653 at [77]. This saved the criminal justice system resources that would have been expended with a full trial.

109    Accordingly, I gave the Accused the full 30% discount (Stage 1) for his early plea of guilt.

110    All things considered, including the harm and culpability factors, the starting point for the sentence was about 2 to 3 weeks’ imprisonment. After considering the mitigating factors and the PG discount, in the round, the sentence would be 10 days’ imprisonment.

111     Cooperation with the authorities. I gave due weight to the Accused’s cooperation with the authorities: Public Prosecutor v Siew Boon Loong [2005] 1 SLR(R) 611 at [16]-[18].

112    I also considered the fact that after the collision, the Accused assisted in helping the victim up to the pedestrian pavement.[note: 64]

(4)    Erh Zhi Huang Alvan’s Case

113     Erh Zhi Huang Alvan v Public Prosecutor (“Erh”) (MA 9204 of 2022) was one of the cases heard in the Chen Song decision. The High Court allowed the appeal in Erh and substituted a sentence of 10 weeks’ imprisonment with a fine of $4,000. There was also the minimum 5-year driving disqualification.

114    The offender in Alvan Erh was driving his motor car along an expressway. Due to heavy traffic, the car travelling in front of Erh braked and came to a stop. Consequently, Erh abruptly switched lanes, failing to keep a proper lookout. This led to a collision between Erh’s motor car and the victim who was travelling on his motorcycle: Chen Song at [163].

115    In relation to harm, the victim in Erh suffered from: (a) a traumatic amputation of the right little finger; and (b) a right-sided clavicle fracture. He was given hospitalisation leave of 58 days: Chen Song at [165].

116    It was undisputed that permanent injury was caused to the victim in Erh, although there was no evidence before the High Court that the victim would suffer from any permanent hand disability as a result and he was assessed to be likely to be able to return to work. Therefore, in the High Court’s view, taking into consideration also the victim’s right-sided clavicle fracture, the damage caused to his motorcycle and the potential harm arising from his abrupt lane-change on the expressway during peak hour, this would place the harm caused in the higher end of the “low” category. This was so bearing in mind that the range of injuries classified as grievous hurt is broad and are by their nature serious: Chen Song at [165].

117    Erh’s culpability was low. His offending conduct was simply a manifestation of the basic elements of the careless driving offence: Chen Song at [165] (see also Adri Satryawan Pratama v Public Prosecutor [2024] SGHC 258 at [14]).

118    Based on the High Court’s determination that the harm caused was at the higher end of low and Erh’s culpability was low, the indicative sentence ought to be a fine based on the Sue Chang framework: Chen Song at [167].

119    After taking into account that Erh pleaded guilty and readily co-operated with the authorities, the High Court allowed the appeal in MA 9204 of 2022 and substituted Erh’s sentence of 10 weeks’ imprisonment with a fine of $4,000: Chen Song at [169].

120    I noted that in Erh’s case:

(a)     There was no evidence before the High Court that the victim would suffer from any permanent hand disability as a result and he was assessed to be likely to be able to return to work: Chen Song at [165] and Ling Zhao Bin at [54(a)].

(b)     Erh’s culpability was low. His offending conduct was simply a manifestation of the basic elements of the careless driving offence: Chen Song at [165]. In Erh, the lane change was a reactive, split-second response to avoid colliding with the car in front that had braked and stopped due to heavy traffic (see Ling Zhao Bin at [54(c)].

121    While the victim in Erh suffered a permanent loss of his little finger, the High Court noted that there was no indication of any permanent disability that resulted from this injury and that he had in fact been medically assessed as being likely to be able to return to work. Apart from this, he also suffered a right-sided clavicle fracture, though it was not apparent that there was any surgical intervention required for this injury. While the victim in Erh was given 58 days of hospitalisation leave, this included only one day of hospitalisation, as he was discharged the day after the accident (Public Prosecutor v Johnson Tan Wee Kiat (Johnson Chen Weiji) [2026] SGHC 59 at [21]).

122    For completeness, it may be argued that Erh’s sentence was based on the framework in Sue Chang (instead of Chen Song): see Chen Song at [165] and [167]. However, as the High Court observed in Chen Song at [120], applying both frameworks would likely result in the same or similar outcomes. A similar observation was made by the High Court in Adri Satryawan Pratama v Public Prosecutor [2024] SGHC 258 at [3] and [15] and in Loh Kaine Tong Nicholas v Public Prosecutor (HC/MA 9037/2023/01).

123    In the present case:

(a)     The Accused’s culpability was higher than Erh. In Erh, the lane change was a reactive, split-second response to avoid colliding with the car in front that had braked and stopped due to heavy traffic. In contrast, the Accused had flouted traffic rules by making an unauthorised U-turn at the Junction, without having brought the Motorcar to a complete stop at the Junction.[note: 65]

(b)     The victim underwent surgical fixation of the Fracture.[note: 66] In Erh’s case, surgery was required for the amputation of the motorcyclist’s little finger; for the right-sided clavicle fracture, it was not apparent that there was any surgical intervention required for this injury.

(c)     The victim’s hospitalisation leave for 78 days was longer than the 58 days of hospitalisation leave in Erh.

(5)   Special reasons

124    An offender would be disqualified from driving unless he shows “special reasons”.

125    In this connection, the two-stage framework for “special reasons” is as follows:

(a)     First Stage: Show special reasons, viz. reasons relating to the facts or circumstances of an offence and not to the offender herself; and

(b)     Second Stage: Even if special reasons are established, the court will consider whether the discretion not to disqualify must be exercised in favour of the offender.

126    Under the two-stage framework, the first stage is offence-specific (not offender-specific). When an offender seeks to come within the special reasons exception, the facts to back up such circumstances must be proved to the court’s satisfaction: Toh Yong Soon v Public Prosecutor [2011] 3 SLR 147 at [5].

127    Even if special reasons are established, it does not automatically follow that the offender would not be disqualified from driving. For the second stage, the court’s discretion not to disqualify can only be made in very exceptional circumstances: Sivakumar s/o Rajoo v Public Prosecutor [2002] 1 SLR(R) 265 at [25] (see also Prathib s/o M Balan v Public Prosecutor [2017] SGHC 303 at [9]-[11]).

(i)   First Stage

128    What are “special reasons” not to impose a driving disqualification? The special reasons have to be reasons relating to the facts or circumstances of an offence and not to the offender himself – this would be the clearest means of giving effect to Parliament’s intention: M V Balakrishnan v Public Prosecutor [1998] 2 SLR(R) 846 at [9], Muhammad Faizal bin Rahim v Public Prosecutor [2012] 1 SLR 116 at [41] and Rafael Voltaire Alzate at [38].

129    In other words, a special reason is a mitigating or extenuating circumstance, not amounting in law to a defence to the charge, yet directly connected with the commission of the offence, and one which the court ought properly to take into consideration when imposing punishment: Whittall v Kirby [1947] 1 KB 194 at 201, as endorsed by Muhammad Faizal bin Rahim at [30].

130    Offender-specific factors, such as the fact that the defendant is of a good character or has a good driving record, cannot be accepted as special reasons: Wilkinson’s Road Traffic Offences, Sweet & Maxwell, (32nd Ed, 2025, General Editor: Kevin McCormac) at [21-10]. Circumstances peculiar to the offender do not go towards reducing his moral culpability; they are essentially extrinsic facts about the offender which are unrelated to the offence but are produced to elicit sympathy from the court. These circumstances are morally distinguishable from circumstances peculiar to the offence: Muhammad Faizal bin Rahim at [43].

131    Even if an offender requires his driving licence for his livelihood, this would not constitute a special reason (see also Tan Yock Lin and S. Chandra Mohan, Criminal Procedure (LexisNexis: March 2019; Binder 3, Loose-leaf, Chapter XVII: Sentencing) at [3751]).

132    This is because in the Malaysian Criminal Appeal Court case of Public Prosecutor v Hiew Chin Fong [1988] 1 MLJ 467 – which was endorsed in Chua Chye Tiong v Public Prosecutor [2004] 1 SLR(R) 22 at [61] and [62] – a 12-month disqualification period was imposed on the offender despite the fact that his livelihood depended on him having a driving licence.

133    The Criminal Appeal Court in Public Prosecutor v Hiew Chin Fong laid down several statements of law on what should not be considered special reasons:

(a)     Financial hardship to the offender;

(b)     The offender knew no other means of earning his livelihood;

(c)     That the effect of the disqualification must necessarily and consequently deprive the offender of his livelihood or occupation; and

(d)     That the offender was a poor man and would have difficulty to get to his work.

134    The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs, Ms Sun Xueling, had stated as follows (Singapore Parliamentary Debates, Official Report (8 July 2019) vol 94):

… Actually, if an individual depends on driving to make a living, that is all the more reason for him to drive safely and for him to be off the roads if he is unable or unwilling to do so.

135    Before an emergency is capable of amounting to a special reason under law, a crucial prerequisite is for the offender to show that there was no alternative but for him to drive, and that he had explored every reasonable alternative before driving: Sivakumar s/o Rajoo v Public Prosecutor [2002] 1 SLR(R) 265 at [17], affirmed in Siti Hajar bte Abdullah v Public Prosecutor [2006] 2 SLR(R) 248 at [13] (see also Fan Lei v Public Prosecutor [2024] SGHC 278 at [16]).

136    When an offender seeks to come within the special reasons exception, the facts to back up such circumstances must be proved to the court’s satisfaction: Toh Yong Soon v Public Prosecutor [2011] 3 SLR 147 at [5]. The onus lies on an accused to raise special reasons for the court’s consideration, if such reasons exist: Chue Woon Wai v Public Prosecutor [1996] 1 SLR(R) 725 at [13], Prathib s/o M Balan v Public Prosecutor [2017] SGHC 303 at [12] and Siti Hajar bte Abdullah v Public Prosecutor [2006] 2 SLR(R) 248 at [12].

(See also Wilkinson’s Road Traffic Offences, Sweet & Maxwell, (32nd Ed, 2025, General Editor: Kevin McCormac) at [21-62])

137     Cheong Wai Keong v Public Prosecutor [2005] SGHC 126 stands for the proposition that the shortness of distance travelled cannot in itself be a “special reason” (Rafael Voltaire Alzate at [41]). A court should be able to have regard to the distance travelled as part of its overall analysis (Rafael Voltaire Alzate at [42]).

138    The High Court in Lee Shin Nan v Public Prosecutor [2023] SGHC 354 at [79] stated that special reasons will generally be found only if the court is satisfied that the offender drove in circumstances that reasonably suggest:

(a)     it was necessary to do so in order to avoid other likely and serious harm or danger; and

(b)     there was no reasonable alternative way to achieve this end.

(see also Chen Song at [138] and Ng En You Jeremiah v Public Prosecutor [2023] SGHC 354 at [82])

(ii)   Second Stage

139    Even if special reasons are established, it does not automatically follow that the offender would not be disqualified. In this regard, there must be a separate process of considering whether the discretion must be exercised in favour of the offender: Sivakumar s/o Rajoo at [22]. The limited discretion not to disqualify can only be made in very exceptional circumstances, having regard to the special circumstances as well as to the whole of the circumstances surrounding the commission of the offence, including the manner in which the offender drove and the alcohol content in the offender’s body: Sivakumar s/o Rajoo at [25].

140    Pulling the various strands together, the test for special reasons is stringent and is only satisfied in very exceptional circumstances (see also Prathib s/o M Balan v Public Prosecutor [2017] SGHC 303 at [9]-[11]).

141    The Act is construed strictly to preserve its policy of protecting road users: Chua Chye Tiong v Public Prosecutor [2004] 1 SLR (R) 22 at [53]. A less restrictive approach would negate the legislative stipulation of mandatory disqualification and defeat its underlying objectives: Siti Hajar bte Abdullah v Public Prosecutor [2006] 2 SLR(R) 248 at [8]. Widening the special reasons exception would encourage frivolous defences: Muhammad Faizal bin Rahim at [41].

(See also Tan Yock Lin and S. Chandra Mohan, Criminal Procedure (LexisNexis: March 2019; Binder 3, Loose-leaf, Chapter XVII: Sentencing) at [3702], [3751] and [3752])

142    In the present case, I found no special reason to dispense with the 5-year disqualification, which is mandatory as well as appropriate.

143    Accordingly, I imposed a driving disqualification for 5 years.

144    I kept in mind the proportionality principle in sentencing: Public Prosecutor v Law Aik Meng [2007] 2 SLR(R) 814 at [30].

145    Under the proportionality principle, the sentence to be imposed must not only bear a reasonable proportion to the maximum prescribed penalty, but also to the gravity of the offence committed (Kow Keng Siong, Sentencing Principles in Singapore (Academy Publishing, Second Ed, 2019) at [06.091]-[06.093]).

Conclusion

146    For the above reasons, the Accused was sentenced to 10 days’ imprisonment and a driving disqualification for all classes of driving licences for 5 years.

html:
Public Prosecutor v Tey Shi Hui

Public Prosecutor v Tey Shi Hui
[2026] SGDC 251

Case Number:District Arrest Case No 919073 of 2025 & 1 Other
Decision Date:25 July 2026
Tribunal/Court:District Court
Coram: Paul Quan
Counsel Name(s): Lee Cheng Wah (Attorney-General's Chambers) for the Public Prosecutor; Raphael Louis (Ray Louis Law Corporation) for the Accused.
Parties: Public Prosecutor — Tey Shi Hui

Criminal Law – Offences – Property – Theft

Criminal Procedure and Sentencing – Sentencing

25 July 2026

District Judge Paul Quan:

Introduction

1       This is another case where the court has to decide whether a community order should be made in respect of an offender diagnosed with kleptomania who committed shop theft.

2       I adopt the same reasoning and language that I used in my previous decision in PP v Teo Hui Lan [2026] SGDC 206 (“Teo”) mainly for consistency, while being deeply cognisant of the differences between the two cases.

Brief facts and charges

3       The accused, Tey Shi Hui (“Ms Tey”), a 32-year-old Singaporean, stole two boxes of collagen health products valued at S$142.70 from a retail store in February 2025. She committed a second and subsequent shop theft offence in May 2025. Full restitution has been made for the stolen items.[note: 1]

4       On 23 June 2026, upon her plea of guilt, I convicted Ms Tey on a charge of shop-theft under section 380 of the Penal Code 1871 (2020 Rev Ed) (“PC”). She also consented to have a similar charge taken into consideration for the purpose of sentence (“TIC”).

Parties’ sentencing positions

5       Ms Tey is a first-time offender.[note: 2] The defence asked for a pre-sentence report (“PSR”) to be called on her for the court to consider making a mandatory treatment order (“MTO”) under section 339(1) of the Criminal Procedure Code 2010 (2020 Rev Ed) (“CPC”),[note: 3] on the basis of her diagnosis of kleptomania that had a causal link to the commission of the offences.[note: 4] The prosecution did not dispute this but reserved its sentencing position until having sighted the MTO PSR. [note: 5]

6       I called for a mandatory PSR under section 339(2) CPC on Ms Tey. Pursuant to section 339(6) CPC, I ordered her to attend at the Institute of Mental Health (“IMH”) for assessment to enable an MTO PSR to be submitted by the appointed psychiatrist to the court.

7       I received the PSR from the appointed psychiatrist on 14 July 2026 well ahead of today’s mention,[note: 6] with her recommendation for an MTO for a duration of 18 months. The parties have now submitted that this is the sentence I should impose on Ms Tey.

Court’s decision

8       As the statutory restrictions enumerated under section 337(1) CPC either do not apply in Ms Tey’s case in and of themselves or by virtue of section 337(2) CPC, it is open to me to make an MTO. Having reviewed the MTO PSR, I agree with the parties and explain in this ex tempore judgment why I now make an MTO requiring Ms Tey to undergo psychiatric treatment for a period of 18 months under section 339(1) CPC.

MTO PSR called on Ms Tey

9       I delivered brief reasons on 23 June 2026 explaining why I decided to call for an MTO PSR on Ms Tey. Doing so for me to consider MTO as a community based sentencing option is consistent with both the broader rationale underlying community based sentencing and the particular considerations for calling an MTO PSR. For context, I first outline these reasons.

Rationale underlying community based sentencing

10     In Ms Tey’s case, she was diagnosed with kleptomania that has a direct causal link to the commission of the shop theft offences. Such offences involving persons with specific and minor mental conditions, which are traditionally viewed by the courts to be on the rehabilitation end of the spectrum, are targeted for community based sentencing that allows greater flexibility in balancing the various sentencing principles: Sim Wen Yi Ernest v PP [2016] 5 SLR 207 (“Ernest Sim”) at [33], by essentially considering whether rehabilitation should be given prominence in the case at hand notwithstanding any countervailing need for deterrence, retribution or prevention: Kalaiarasi d/o Marimuthu Innasimuthu v PP [2012] 2 SLR 774 (“Kalaiarasi”) at [39]. The offender is rehabilitated by identifying and addressing the root causes of the offending behaviour, whilst preventing the offender from being dislodged from his family, employment and society, whereas the public interest is served by reducing recidivism through correction and rehabilitation: Kalaiarasi at [35] and [36].

Particular considerations for calling MTO PSR

11     This is similarly echoed in the court’s approach in GCX v PP [2019] 3 SLR 1325 at [47] that provides specific guidance on when an MTO PSR should be called, depending on the offender’s rehabilitative potential and whether other sentencing principles were so dominant that rehabilitation should be rejected out of hand.

Need for deterrence attenuated in Ms Tey’s case

12     First, I identified and balanced the relevant sentencing principles, giving each its appropriate weight, in order for me to have some sense of the offender’s rehabilitative potential: GCX at [47]. On the face of Ms Tey’s case, the principle of deterrence, both general and specific deterrence is engaged; so is the retributive principle.

13     As recent as the end of last month, I reiterated the point I made in PP v Tham Quan Hui [2026] SGDC 79 at [21] that we should continue to press the principle of general deterrence into service for shop theft offences so as not to undo the modest decrease of 3% in the number of shop theft cases in 2025 as compared to 2024 and to prevent a reversal of this encouraging but nascent trend: Teo at [12]. Ms Tey also showed apparent recalcitrant behaviour attracting specific deterrence, by committing another subsequent shop theft offence, which is the subject-matter of the TIC charge, barely three months after her first shop theft.

14     Retributive sentencing demands that the court metes out punishment that is proportionate to the nature of the offence and the offender to tamper any untrammelled deterrence. Shop theft should not be regarded as petty crime with its significant opportunity costs and punishment must be pegged at a sufficiently high level to drive home the point that crime does not pay. Ms Tey’s culpability lies in her apparent deliberate conduct in removing the stolen items from the display standee, holding on to them, moving around to make sure she was not being observed and exiting the supermarket without making payment at the opportune moment.[note: 7] Indeed, she was not discovered and was only subsequently traced as her offence was captured on surveillance footage.[note: 8]

15     But a person suffering from a mental illness that leaves him unable to fully appreciate the nature and consequences of his actions will not be deterred by the prospect of a custodial sentence; similarly general deterrence does not function to make an example of an offender who did not possess full cognitive normalcy and rationality: GCX at [54]. The weight to be given to retribution also depends on the culpability of the offender, and the offender can bear a lower level of culpability for his actions depending on the extent to which his psychiatric condition has contributed to the offence: GCX at [55] and [56].

16     In this regard, the defence relied on Ms Tey’s medical reports from her psychiatric specialist at Raffles Hospital. Although they do not appear to comply with the new requirements under rule 4(3) of the Criminal Procedure (Expert Opinion) Rules 2025, I took them at face level because the prosecution did not object to relying on them for Ms Tey’s diagnosis of kleptomania that had a causal link to the commission of the shop theft offences as the basis to call for an MTO PSR on her. Her risk of reoffending was also assessed by her specialist to be low, given that she was compliant with her medication regime and her committed participations in WE CARE Community Service’s Atypical Theft Offending (“ATO”) programme, and the counselling sessions at the Singapore Association for Mental Health (“SAMH”).[note: 9]

17     The need for deterrence, both general and specific, therefore appears to be attenuated; so too the need to punish in the light of Ms Tey’s reduced culpability.

Real prospect of rehabilitation exists in Ms Tey’s case

18     Next, I should not apply an overly restrictive threshold as to the offender’s rehabilitative potential and needed only to be persuaded that rehabilitation is a real prospect: GCX at [47].

19     I found that there was a real prospect of rehabilitation in Ms Tey’s case. She continued to keep up with her medication regime and completed six ATO and five SAMH counselling sessions.[note: 10] In particular, she had received positive feedback from her ATO counsellor on the insights she had demonstrated and the coping strategies she had been actively adopting that are positive protective practices.[note: 11] She did not re-offended since she completed the SAMH programme on 1 October 2025 and the ATO programme on 9 January 2026. She also expressed genuine contrition and remorse for her offending behaviour[note: 12] and has cooperated fully with the authorities during investigations.[note: 13]

20     Given that the need for deterrence and retribution in this case is attenuated, rehabilitation should be given prominence. There is sufficient rehabilitative potential or a real prospect of rehabilitation, such that an MTO might realistically be ordered on the facts: GCX at [39]-[41]. Calling for a PSR is a mandatory first step if I wish to consider making an MTO and I did not rule out such a possibility then on 23 June 2026: GCX at [45]. At that stage, I was cognisant that I lacked the necessary facts to apprise myself fully of Ms Tey’s true rehabilitative potential and I was therefore slow to lightly find that other sentencing principles so substantially trumped the principle of rehabilitation such that there was simply no need to call for an MTO PSR.

MTO recommended by appointed psychiatrist in PSR

21     In Ms Tey’s PSR, the appointed psychiatrist has recommended an MTO for a period of 18 months on the basis that Ms Tey is suitable for an MTO (presumably health-wise) and she has no objections being placed on an MTO, as well as her assessment that an MTO is viable for Ms Tey.[note: 14]

Section 339(3) CPC satisfied

22     The appointed psychiatrist has had regard to Ms Tey’s medical reports,[note: 15] and she opined that:[note: 16]

(a)     she has kleptomania at and around the material time of the offences. Being an impulse-control disorder, her kleptomania was a contributory link to her committing the shop thefts as her exercise of self-control was impaired;

(b)     she has gained insight into her condition and she expressed a desire to continue treatment and her commitment is evidenced by her completion of the WE CARE programme; and

(c)     kleptomania is treatable with a combination of medication and psychotherapy.

She also noted that Ms Tey was amenable to MTO.[note: 17] Her examination of Ms Tey’s mental state to assess Ms Tey’s suitability for MTO was also unremarkable.[note: 18]

23     Having considered the matters set out under section 339(3) CPC, the appointed psychiatrist’s view was that Ms Tey was suitable to be placed on an MTO.[note: 19] Section 339(9) CPC makes clear that the PSR is final and conclusive as to these matters and pertinently, the appointed psychiatrist did not raise any issues in relation to these matters that would proscribe the making of an MTO: GCX at [40].

24     The appointed psychiatrist’s opinion is not determinative of the court’s assessment and the PSR itself will not be accepted without question as it is still the court’s role to examine the internal consistency and cogency of the report once produced: GCX at [46] and [61]. Ms Tey’s PSR did not draw erroneous conclusions that are obviously at odds or internally inconsistent with the remainder of the report: Low Geok Hong v PP [2016] SGHC 69 at [11].

Expedient to make MTO in Ms Tey’s case

25     At this stage, even if section 339(3) CPC were satisfied, I still have to address the legal question of whether an MTO should be ordered and undertake a balancing exercise between the various sentencing principles again: GCX at [42] and [82], based on the nature of the disorder, the extent to which it contributed to the commission of the offence and the offender’s potential for treatment as informed by the PSR: GCX at [46]. Ultimately, I will have to be satisfied that it is expedient to make an MTO, having regard to the circumstances including Ms Tey’s offences and her character: section 339(1) CPC.

26     It is not necessary for a causal link to be shown between Ms Tey’s psychiatric condition and the commission of her offences before an MTO could be ordered, although such a link was shown in her case: GCX at [81]. MTO is an appropriate sentencing option in Ms Tey’s case because like the facts in GCX at [83] and [85]:

(a)     the principles of deterrence and retribution receded in significance because Ms Tey was suffering from an impulse-control disorder at and around the material times of her offences: see [22(a)], above, which impaired her exercise of self-control. In any event, the harm caused by her offence is also decidedly low because full restitution has been made and the supermarket has suffered little or no loss as such;

(b)     the PSR also indicated that Ms Tey would be susceptible to treatment and this would take place over 18 months. This militated against simply a short term of imprisonment that would not have allowed for meaningful medical intervention. Instead, it suggested that treatment via MTO was the better response rather than punishment; and

(c)     this was not a case where rehabilitation had such diminished importance that it was outweighed by deterrence and retribution. Indeed, rehabilitation is the dominant sentencing principle.

Conclusion

27     I have explained to Ms Tey:

(a)     that the MTO is passed in lieu of any sentence of imprisonment and fine which I may impose for the shop theft offence;

(b)     the purpose, effect and obligations specified in section 340 CPC and the consequences that may follow if any of such obligations of the MTO are not met; and

(c)     the power of the court to vary or revoke the MTO upon the application of the appointed psychiatrist.

Ms Tey has indicated to me that she accepts and is willing to comply with the MTO.

18-month MTO made

28     Having regard to the circumstances, including the nature of the offence and Ms Tey’s character, I find it expedient to make an MTO under section 339(1) CPC requiring Ms Tey to undergo psychiatric treatment for a period of 18 months from today. I am optimistic about Ms Tey’s rehabilitation with the MTO because she had indicated that this is something she would like to “navigate through in the long run” and to make it her “way of life”.[note: 20] Far from ringing hollow, I am confident that she will be able to succeed in this regard as she has already completed her WE CARE programme and continues to see her SAMH psychologist on a monthly basis via virtual consultation. She also keeps up with practising coping strategies, such as meditation, and also has familial support from her father. I have high hopes for her in controlling and overcoming the challenges of her kleptomania.

29     I also commend Mr Raphael Louis for putting up a detailed mitigation plea from which I have derived considerable assistance in reaching my decision.
