He was unable to satisfactorily explain these inconsistencies pursuant to questions posed by the court,[note: 116] and my view was that this betrayed a lack of any reasonable explanation for the payment in cash, apart from a desire to reduce a paper trail.

84     Further, as noted at [66(d)], there also was no objective evidence that any LEW services had been performed by Goh for NEC. The text/WhatsApp messages of 4 and 11 May 2018 that Goh relied on as proof of such work did not state that the drawings were from NEC, and the message of 11 May 2018 in fact only reflected Tay wishing to seek advice from Goh, instead of wishing him to endorse the drawings. Goh’s CFD also stated that the LEW services he performed were around 20 June 2018, which was clearly inconsistent with the position he took at trial.[note: 117] In this regard, Goh claimed that he told the recorder of his statements as well as his lawyer about the LEW services rendered on 4 and 11 May 2018, but that they both somehow omitted to reflect this in his statements and CFD.[note: 118] I found this double omission to be incredible and too convenient. It was more likely that his assertion in paragraph 141 of his statement P17, that he never signed off on any jobs for NEC, was the truth.

85     While it was claimed that further work would have been referred but for the fact that the CPIB’s investigations started and the accused persons were not allowed to communicate with each other, I found this to be a weak claim. The money was received on 4 May 2018, and Goh was first brought to the CPIB only on 30 May 2018. This gave Tay, Fang and NEC nearly a month to refer work to Goh, but there was no objective evidence of this, despite Fang’s claim that NEC had a few jobs from three landed properties and a condominium at the relevant time.[note: 119] In any case, this injunction from CPIB was clearly breached since Goh communicated with Fang on 20 June 2018 when he asked Fang to sign the fresh document that appointed him as a provider of LEW services to RH Creation. It was therefore clear that the accused persons paid little heed to CPIB’s injunction against communicating with each other, and it would not have formed any real impediment to them communicating if they wished.

86     As noted above, Goh’s act of asking Fang to sign a fresh letter of appointment was also a clear attempt to change the justification for the payment after the fact. Goh claimed that he asked this of Fang because he initially thought that he was providing his services to NEC based on what Tay told him,[note: 120] but thereafter thought that it was RH Creation based on what the CPIB officer told him. However, he dropped the matter when Fang did not sign the new appointment letter. If the agreement was genuine, I found it difficult to believe that Goh’s attempt to right such an error thereafter would be so feeble. He was also evasive when asked whether his evidence made sense insofar as he claimed that Fang had declined to sign the backdated letter of appointment.[note: 121] Assuming that it was true that the party that engaged him was RH Creation instead of NEC, this also meant that he had not been paid for the endorsement work he did for NEC on 4 and 11 May 2018. He stated that he did not ask to be paid for that although he estimated the work to be worth $8,000 to $10,000, claiming once again that it was because he was not permitted by CPIB to speak to anyone.[note: 122] As above, I did not believe this aspect of his evidence, since this injunction from CPIB did not stop him from communicating with Fang on 20 June 2018. In any case, I also noted that Goh’s explanation for this 20 June 2018 communication was inconsistent with Fang’s, as Fang claimed that he was referring LEW to Goh that was unrelated to the $50,000 that had been paid to Goh.[note: 123]

87     In all, this led me to the conclusion that no LEW services were rendered by Goh to NEC pursuant to the $50,000 paid to him, that it was not a genuine contract, and that Goh therefore knew that the payment to him was a corrupt reward for his introduction of Lantro to Pico.

Tay

88     In respect of Tay, he immediately asked Goh for a loan of $6,000 upon handing him the money. If, as Tay claimed, Goh had been angry with him for initially not wanting to give Goh a referral fee, and if Goh then needed help to get LEW, it meant that Goh wanted or needed this money, so it would not have made sense for Tay to then be so bold as to ask Goh for a loan. To my mind, this also pointed to an understanding between the parties, that Tay and Goh knew of the nature of the payment as a corrupt gratification. Thus, Tay knew that his request was not likely to be rejected since Goh would accede to it as an act of reciprocity.

89     Tay also handed the $50,000 to Goh in cash and did not tell anyone in Lantro that he was doing this. I earlier rejected the claim that it was normal industry practice to pay a single person $50,000 in cash in an above-board transaction. Further, if the transaction was legal, there was no reason why Tay could not have informed Lantro or Poh about it. The fact that he did not, indicated his knowledge that it was not above-board. He also admitted in his statements that he knew it was not right to give Goh referral fees in the form of LEW fees. I accepted those portions of his statements, and my finding was that Tay also knew that what he did was corrupt.

Fang

90     As for Fang, he seemingly decided, without prompting, to pay Goh in cash instead of a bank transfer. As noted above, he was unable to give a satisfactory reason for this, which suggested that he must have known that what he was doing was not above-board, and was corrupt. He, too, admitted in his statements to knowing that it was wrong to pay a referral fee in this manner to Goh.

91     As for his belated attempt in late June 2018 to refer LEW to Goh, Fang claimed that he had only been told not to communicate with the other accused persons about the case, and thus it was permissible to communicate with Goh about LEW services that were not under the NEC contract.[note: 124] I was unable to accept that this was a genuine attempt to help Goh or refer work to him, especially since Fang’s account was that he knew that Goh had uttered the threat to Tay, and that he felt it suspicious that the referral fee that Goh had initially asked for and the eventual amount paid for LEW services were the same. Given that he would have known by June that he and Tay were in trouble with the law over their dealings with Goh, I found it difficult to believe that he would still attempt to “help” Goh by referring work to him. It was far more likely that this was a late attempt to lend an air of authenticity to their earlier dealings by purportedly referring LEW to Goh. In all, I also find that Fang knew that what he did was corrupt.

92     Given these findings on Tay’s and Fang’s knowledge that their act was corrupt, I also concluded that there was an agreement between them to carry out this illegal act, and that they thus did engage in a conspiracy with each other to corruptly give Goh the $50,000 as a reward for advancing Lantro’s business interests with Pico.

Other points

93     Both the prosecution and defence raised a number of other points for their respective cases and against the opposing parties’ cases. I did not find it necessary to deal with all of them, save for the following three which I address for completeness.

Witnesses related to NEC

94     The first point concerned what transpired between Fang and NEC that led NEC to make the payment of $50,000 to RH Creation, which amount Fang subsequently encashed and handed to Tay. To be clear, since it was not disputed that the funds came from NEC and given my findings that no LEW services were rendered to NEC and there was no genuine agreement between it and Goh, I did not find it strictly necessary to examine what Fang told NEC to have them agree to disburse the funds to him. Nevertheless, I addressed it for completeness. In this regard, the testimonies of Kalam and DW6 Hasanuzzaman (“Hasan”) were relevant. It should also be noted that one Esther/Vinge, who was Kalam’s wife, was also named as being involved in NEC, though she was not called as a witness as she had moved to Australia and declined to return to Singapore to testify.[note: 125]

95     On how he procured the $50,000, Fang asserted that he initially told Kalam, whom he said was NEC’s boss, that Goh wanted the $50,000 as a referral fee, but Kalam reacted strongly and refused. Later, when Goh offered his LEW services, Fang relayed this to Kalam, who agreed and did not ask why the cost of the LEW services was the same as the previously sought referral fee.[note: 126]

96     Kalam denied the above, stating that he was not the boss of NEC at the material time, as he was then working with a company named KSM Construction and Engineering Pte Ltd (“KSM”). He claimed that he knew of the Lumina project only after he was called to CPIB for an interview, and denied that in mid to end April 2018, Fang had spoken to him about the request for a referral fee of $50,000 from someone from the Zoo. He also denied that about a week later, Fang told him that the person from the Zoo was now offering unlimited LEW services for a year for $50,000, and that he had agreed to engage this person for $50,000.[note: 127] The defence sought to show that Kalam was not truthful about his non-involvement in NEC, by adducing evidence of emails that had been forwarded to him by Hasan, as well showing that he was in certain WhatsApp chat groups with Fang.[note: 128] Where these were undated or dated after 2018, I did not give them much weight in showing Kalam’s involvement in NEC at the material time. However, there was at least one email in 2017 mentioning NEC which Hasan forwarded to Kalam, and Kalam was unable to explain why this was so.

97     Hasan had been an employee of NEC from around 2013 to 2022, and testified that when he worked there, he reported to Kalam for the sites that he worked on. Nevertheless, he stated that Vinge was “always in the office”, that “everything was handled by her”, and that when he was in the office, he saw Vinge and Kalam “always dealing with the money matters.” He also stated that he forwarded one of the emails to Kalam because the name list of workers therein had been prepared by Kalam’s office.[note: 129] In his statement to the CPIB, Hasan stated that Kalam was the husband of his lady boss, and that Kalam was not involved in NEC’s day to day business as he had a job outside of NEC.[note: 130] In court, he stated that he had lied in this statement as he had been told to do so by Kalam and Vinge.[note: 131]

98     Vinge’s statements were admitted into evidence by consent. In these, she stated that she owned NEC and was its director, while Kalam worked for KSM. She stated that although she had no expertise in the work to be done for the Lumina project, NEC worked with Fang and Lantro to bid for the project as NEC had workers to supply. She stated that Fang told her that the $50,000 was needed for LEW fees for a year as they were doing the electrical work for the Lumina project and needed the “licence”, and that they could not start the project without the fee.[note: 132] The defence’s case was that Vinge was lying in her statements to protect Kalam, and that Kalam (who was called by the defence but treated as a hostile witness) was lying in his testimony as well, because he was a long-term visit pass holder at the time, and thus did not want to admit to running the operations at NEC.

99     My views were as follows. I found Kalam to be somewhat evasive, and that his credibility was suspect. Further, when the hearing broke for the evening and he was to return to continue his testimony the next day, he contacted Hasan overnight to ask why Hasan forwarded the emails to him.[note: 133] Although he did not press when Hasan declined to engage with him, his act of contacting Hasan was quite inappropriate, as he had been directed not to contact Hasan. As for Hasan, he was an admitted liar insofar as he claimed that he had lied in his statement to the CPIB, despite knowing that he could get into serious trouble for doing so.[note: 134] He had left NEC as he was not only unhappy about the salary he was paid, but said that it was also sometimes paid late, and he took the view that Kalam was not someone who would tell the truth in court.[note: 135] His motivations for testifying against Kalam and Vinge were therefore questionable. Finally, as Vinge was not present in court, the veracity of her account could not be tested. Ultimately, I did not think that it was safe to place weight on the testimonies of Kalam and Hasan, or the statements of Vinge. It nevertheless remained that NEC provided the funds at Fang’s request and did not appear to take issue either with the erroneous LEW invoice that Fang prepared or that they had paid this money but had not received the LEW services from Goh.

Tay’s and Fang’s “incentive” to give a bribe of $50,000

100    The second point, put forward by the defence, was that Tay and Fang objectively had little “incentive” to give Goh a substantial bribe of $50,000 just for his recommendation for the Lumina project.[note: 136] However, such a “kickback” to Goh was precisely what Tay had suggested to Poh. Even by Tay’s and Fang’s account in trial, they had been prepared to facilitate such a payment as Tay asked Poh to engage Goh for undefined “consultant” work and when Poh refused, Fang then asked the boss of NEC to fund this payment as well but was also rejected. They then braced themselves to “standby to get in trouble” when they initially thought that they could not pay Goh the money. Tay had even admitted that the $50,000 was eventually paid in part to prevent Goh from making trouble in the Lumina project. Thus, putting aside the quantifiable financial benefits that Lantro or NEC could earn from the Lumina project, Tay and Fang were clearly prepared to facilitate and pay such a bribe, so there were clearly benefits that they perceived they could receive from this payment. I therefore rejected the defence’ argument on this point.

101    Relatedly, the defence also submitted that since Goh was not an employee of Pico, his influence was limited such that it was illogical that Tay and Fang would believe that his sway was so great as to justify a $50,000 payment just for a recommendation.[note: 137] However, it was clear from the evidence that Goh’s recommendation of Lantro to Soh in fact worked, because Soh passed Tay’s contact to his colleagues, Boo then contacted Tay, and the appointment of Lantro followed. As noted above, without Goh’s referral, Pico’s employees would not even have known about Lantro, much less gotten in touch with them such that Lantro’s appointment could result. The facts thus did demonstrate the effectiveness of Goh’s recommendations, and it was therefore not illogical that contractors would be willing to pay him for this. Since the said companies would henceforth be known to each other, this also presented future opportunities for working together, and the benefits of the recommendation were therefore not necessarily limited to just the Lumina project.

CPIB’s omission to consider certain evidence

102    Third, the defence noted that the messages on Goh’s mobile phone appeared not to have been taken into consideration during the CPIB’s investigations, and that Tay’s and Fang’s mobile phones had not been seized during the investigations. It was submitted that this led to certain events in the timeline such as the 26 March meeting having been omitted in the Case for the Prosecution, and an investigation conducted with a “preconceived notion” that the $50,000 must have been a bribe to Goh, with only “feeble attempts” made to investigate into whether the $50,000 was truly for LEW services.[note: 138]

103    My view was that this overstated the matter. This was because even if the WhatsApp or text messages between the parties had not been considered during investigations, this was not fatal since they had been produced at trial, addressed by the parties in testimony, and considered by this court. Similarly, even if there had been insufficient attempts by the CPIB to look into whether the payment of $50,000 was genuinely for LEW services instead of being a bribe, this had been canvassed at the trial, and the accused persons had their opportunity to produce satisfactory evidence to show that the LEW endorsement work had been done, but failed to do so.

104    These three points therefore did not serve to raise any reasonable doubt in my mind about the accused persons’ guilt. Ultimately, I was satisfied that the prosecution had proven its case against all three accused persons beyond a reasonable doubt, and I convicted them as charged.

Sentencing

105    The three accused persons were liable to be punished with a fine not exceeding $100,000, or to an imprisonment term not exceeding five years, or both. Before the present series of offences, Goh was untraced. Tay had dated antecedents from 1996, when he was just under 21, and the prosecution was not regarding these as relevant for the present purposes. Fang was untraced.

106    The parties’ positions on sentencing were as follows:

(a)     The prosecution’s position was that:

(i)       Goh should receive a sentence of at least eight months’ imprisonment;

(ii)       Tay should receive a sentence of at least seven months’ imprisonment; and

(iii)       Fang should receive a sentence of at least six months’ imprisonment.[note: 139]

(b)     The defence’s position was that:

(i)       Goh should receive a sentence of four to six months’ imprisonment;[note: 140] and

(ii)       For Tay and Fang, while the custodial threshold was not necessarily crossed, if it was crossed, then an imprisonment term of not more than four months for each of them would suffice.[note: 141]

Relevant sentencing considerations

107    It was not disputed that in sentencing for corruption offences, deterrence is key. The High Court held in Ching Hwa Ming (Qin Huaming) v Public Prosecutor [2024] 3 SLR 547 at [79], that in sentencing an offender for an offence under s 5 of the PCA, the framework in Public Prosecutor v Syed Mostofa Romel [2015] 3 SLR 1166 (“Romel”) applies, but that the court may also consider the offence-specific factors going towards harm and culpability set out in Goh Ngak Eng v Public Prosecutor [2023] 4 SLR 1385 (“Goh Ngak Eng”).

108    The case of Romel (at [26]) sets out three non-exhaustive categories in private sector corruption cases. Category 1 is where the receiving party was paid to confer on the paying party a benefit that is within the receiving party’s power to confer, without regard to whether the paying party ought properly to have received that benefit. In such cases, whether the custodial threshold is crossed depends on the facts. I agreed with the prosecution that the facts of the present case were closest to Category 1, albeit a step removed, since Goh did not have the power to confer the benefit of granting the contract to Lantro.

109    On the point of whether the custodial threshold was breached, case law has noted that where the amount of gratification was significant, where the gratification was received over a lengthy period of time, or where there was a compromise of one’s duty or a serious betrayal of trust, the starting point was likely to be a custodial sentence (Romel at [23], citing Sentencing Practice in the Subordinate Courts). In the present case, it was not disputed that the amount of gratification, at $50,000, was significant and substantial. My view therefore was that the starting point should be a custodial sentence.

Factors for calibration of sentence

110    As for the offence-specific factors used to calibrate the sentence, I had reference to the factors set out in Goh Ngak Eng which went towards harm and culpability. The prosecution submitted that the level of harm in the present case was “slight”, but in the middle of that band. The three factors cited by the prosecution that went towards harm were:

(a)     Loss suffered by third parties;

(b)     Benefit to the givers of the gratification; and

(c)     Public disquiet and reputational loss caused to Goh’s employer, WRS, in part due to the media attention on the case.[note: 142]

111    On culpability, the prosecution submitted that Goh’s culpability fell in the “medium” band, but at its lower end, while Tay’s and Fang’s culpabilities fell under the “low” band, but on its higher end. The five factors cited by the prosecution that went towards culpability were:

(a)     The amount of gratification;

(b)     The degree of planning and premeditation;

(c)     The abuse of trust;

(d)     The offenders’ motives in committing the offences; and

(e)     The roles played by the offenders in the corrupt transaction.[note: 143]

Analysis

Harm

112    I began my analysis with the factors going towards harm.

113    First, on the matter of loss suffered by third parties, I accepted that other companies lost the opportunity of contracting with Pico due to Goh’s intervention in introducing Lantro to Pico. That said, I balanced this against the fact that Lantro appeared to have won the job on its own merit after it had put in its quotation.

114    Second, on the benefit to the givers of the gratification, my view was that there were clear benefits in this regard, even if they could not be precisely quantified. In Tay’s case, the award of the contract by Pico to Lantro meant that he could secure a large contract for his new employers which went towards meeting his sales target. As a direct consequence of the payment of this bribe, he also obtained a loan of $6,000 from Goh, which loan he would not otherwise have gotten. In Fang’s case, he managed to work on the Lumina project and earned a salary from NEC for it.

115    Third, I accepted that Goh’s acts would have caused some reputational loss to WRS, in that they would have caused WRS to gain a reputation that its employees would solicit bribes in exchange for showing favour to others. However, I agreed with the defence[note: 144] that the prosecution overstated the point on the alleged public disquiet caused by the offences – media attention did not mean public disquiet. Further, while WRS or the Zoo might be a “stalwart within Singapore’s tourism industry”,[note: 145] my view was that corruption in such an organisation was of not of the order of magnitude, say, of corruption in the defence industry which could compromise Singapore’s security, or in the transport industry where bribery could compromise the safe construction of tunnels for the Mass Rapid Transit system.

116    A fourth factor not cited by parties, but which I noted, was that Tay and Fang acted together to procure and then give the gratification to Goh. While it was only two of them and not a larger enterprise or syndicate, it remained that such joint action emboldened co-conspirators to further a common criminal end, and in the present case, the offence would not have been completed without Tay and Fang working together.

117    On balance, I agreed with the prosecution that the harm caused in this case was slight. I did not pitch it at the bottom/middle/top of the “band”, because while the offence-specific factors listed in Goh Ngak Eng could be considered in the present case, I did not consider myself strictly bound by the sentencing ranges in the bands set out therein since that case concerned a different offence under the PCA.

Culpability

118    As for the factors going towards culpability, even the defence accepted that the amount of gratification involved was significant,[note: 146] and I agreed that this was the most aggravating factor in this case.

119    On the degree of planning and premeditation, this was clearly not gratification paid on the spur of the moment. My finding was that Tay raised the matter of a “kickback” for Goh with Poh immediately after Poh’s first meeting with Goh on 26 March. This meant that Tay already knew then of the need to pay Goh the gratification, had contemplated it, and was taking steps to effect this. This also meant that there was already an understanding between Goh and Tay of the need to pay Goh some gratification. Goh thereafter introduced Lantro to Pico, and gave Soh’s contact information to Tay. In my view, this was evidence of premeditation on the part of Goh and Tay.

120    I agreed with the prosecution that evidence of planning could be seen in the creation of the cover story that the payment to Goh was meant for LEW services, and in the subsequent creation of the documentation to support this fiction. Goh provided his LEW licence information to Tay, Tay passed Goh’s particulars to Fang, and Fang then created the false LEW invoice. The defence contended that since the transaction left a “substantial documentary trail”,[note: 147] it could not be said that the accused persons took deliberate steps to avoid detection. I disagreed with this contention. As I noted at [77] above, the documentation was created to give the movement of money a cloak of legitimacy. Put another way, the documentation was not a demonstration of transparency in their conduct. In this regard, I also agreed with the prosecution that the passing of the gratification in cash, in an envelope, in a car park and with no acknowledgment of receipt, smacked of surreptitiousness.[note: 148]

121    The next factor concerned abuse of trust. In this regard, while Goh’s offence was not directly in relation to WRS as his principal, it could not be denied that he took advantage of his position within WRS to gain the $50,000 for himself, contrary to WRS’s policies. Since it was not disputed that Goh’s views and recommendations carried weight with the Zoo’s contractors, I rejected his contention that he could not be said to have had much trust vested in him only because he did not occupy a “senior position” within WRS.[note: 149] As for Tay and Fang, they also acted contrary to what their respective employers would have permitted. It was submitted for Tay and Fang that the severity of this point needed to be moderated for them, as they were not senior executives within their respective companies.[note: 150] However, given that they were the key players for Lantro and NEC in the acquisition and execution of the Lumina project, great trust was reposed in them by the respective companies. I therefore did not think that the mere fact that they were not senior executives meant that there was only limited abuse of trust.

122    The final factors concerned the offenders’ motives and the roles played by them. I agreed with the prosecution that all three accused persons were motivated by personal gain. There was thus no mitigating feature here. As for their roles, it was contended by Goh that he played a passive role in the transaction,[note: 151] while it had been Tay’s and Fang’s case that they paid the money only because Goh asked for it. I disagreed with any suggestion that all of them played passive roles. As noted above, I found that as at the 26 March meeting between Goh, Tay and Poh, there was an understanding between Goh and Tay of the need to pay Goh some gratification. Thereafter, Goh provided his LEW licence information for the creation of the LEW invoice, and Tay conveyed this information to Fang, who prepared the invoice, obtained the money from NEC, and withdrew the cash. Tay then passed the cash to Goh. Each man thus played his respective role in facilitating the movement of the money and cloaking the transaction, and none of them could be said to have been passive.

123    In the round, I agreed with the prosecution that the culpability of Goh was in the “medium” band, while Tay and Fang’s culpabilities were in the “low” band, with Tay’s culpability higher than Fang’s, since he brought Fang into this enterprise. Given the amount of gratification and the clear premeditation and planning that went into this, my view was that a custodial sentence was appropriate for each accused person.

124    On the offender-specific factors, given that the three accused claimed trial to their charges, there was no issue of any discount in sentencing to be granted on account of a guilty plea.

Precedents

125    The prosecution cited a few sentencing precedents to guide this court. I agreed with the defence[note: 152] that the precedents were mostly distinguishable. The two cases which had scenarios closest to the present case in terms of the number of charges or quantum of gratification were Kannan s/o Kunjiraman v Public Prosecutor [1995] 3 SLR(R) 294 (“Kannan”) and Public Prosecutor v Koh Puay Boon [2016] SGDC 159 (“Koh Puay Boon”). However, the case of Kannan was very dated, and concerned match fixing with the national football team. I noted Counsel’s observation that the offence implicated the integrity of national sport, and I agreed that it was in a different league from the present case.

126    As for Koh Puay Boon, it concerned offences under s 5(a)(i) of the PCA, similar to the present case. It involved the receipt by the offender (who was a shareholder and director of a company named Artmazement (Global) Pte Ltd [“Artmazement”]) of funds totalling $49,500 to hand to an employee of Louis Vuitton Asia Pacific / Louis Vuitton (Singapore) Pte Ltd [“LV”], as an inducement for the said employee to further Artmazement’s business relationship with LV. Artmazement was a renovation contractor specialising in fitting out luxury boutiques. The appellant had claimed in his defence that the funds received by him were his commission for projects he brought to Artmazement, but this was rejected by the trial judge. Although the case of Koh Puay Boon involved five charges and corrupt acts which spanned eight months, the total amount involved in the charges was $49,500, which was comparable to the amount of gratification in the present case. The individual amounts involved in the charges ranged from $6,500 to $13,000. Sentences of six months’ imprisonment were imposed for the charges concerning gratifications of $10,000 to $13,000, while a sentence of three months’ imprisonment was imposed for the charge concerning gratification of $6,500. The total sentence was nine months’ imprisonment. The prosecution’s submission was that balancing these factors, Goh’s sentence should be slightly lower, at eight months’ imprisonment, and that the sentences for Tay and Fang should be correspondingly lower, at seven and six months’ imprisonment respectively.

Starting point sentence

127    Based on Koh Puay Boon as a guide, given the shorter time-frame involved in the present case and the single transaction, and bearing in mind the offence-specific and offender-specific factors set out above, I broadly agreed with the prosecution that a starting point sentence of seven to eight months’ imprisonment for Goh was appropriate. For Tay and Fang, since my view was that their culpabilities were slightly lower than Goh’s, I agreed that the starting point sentence for them should be lower, and I pegged it at about six months’ imprisonment.

128    I noted that there were no notable offender-specific aggravating or mitigating factors for all three accused persons, that would cause me to move substantially from the starting point sentences. I thus disagreed with Counsel’s oral submission made on the day of sentencing that a high fine of $80,000, being close to the maximum fine permissible fine, was a suitable alternative punishment for Tay and Fang.[note: 153]

Decision on sentence

129    In the final analysis, given the slightly different roles that each man played in this enterprise and their slightly different overall culpabilities, I calibrated their sentences to reflect this, and I sentenced them as follows:

(a)     For Goh, on DAC 903794/2022, to eight months’ imprisonment;

(b)     For Tay, on DAC 903808/2022, to seven months’ imprisonment; and

(c)     For Fang, on DAC 903809/2022, to six months’ imprisonment.

130    For Goh, since he was the recipient of the gratification, he was additionally liable to have a penalty imposed on him, of a sum equal to the amount of gratification received. In this regard, s 13 of the PCA applied, along with the case of Chang Peng Hong Clarence v Public Prosecutor [2024] 2 SLR 722. The penalty that I imposed on Goh for DAC 903794/2022 was therefore $50,000. Goh’s total sentence, including what was imposed by the District Judge in DAC 903786/2022 as well as what I imposed on him for the charges that he pleaded guilty to, was 29 months’ imprisonment. Penalties totalling $200,000 (in default 22 weeks’ imprisonment) were also imposed on him. I do not elaborate further herein on the reasons for the global sentence imposed on Goh, since his sentences are not the subject of the present appeals. Goh began serving his imprisonment sentence on 22 June 2026 and has not paid the penalties as at this time of writing.

Conclusion

131    Tay and Fang are on bail pending their appeal, and a stay of execution has been granted on their respective imprisonment terms.
