Sentencing Considerations

General Deterrence

166    The sentencing approach for the offence under the EA is well established in Sakthikanesh. The High Court in Sakthikanesh observed at [47] that the underlying principles affecting NS are national security, universality and equity, making reference to the Ministerial Statement by then Minister for Defence, Mr Teo Chee Hean made in Parliament in 2006[note: 51], which this court has also referred to in the previous oral judgment on conviction at [61]. The High Court held at [48] that,

“When a person refuses to serve NS at the time that he is required to and instead returns to serve at a time of his own choosing, or worse, at an age when he can no longer serve, his actions strike at the very core of the principles of national security, universality and equity. As his peers put aside their individual pursuits to serve NS when they were called upon to, the NS defaulter makes an exception for himself, where no exceptions are permitted. Lenient treatment of NS defaulters can create strong feelings of unfairness and resentment in those who have made personal sacrifices to serve NS and over time, lower their morale and eventually also erode public support for NS. The punishment for NS defaulters must also be sufficiently severe, so as to deter potential offenders from evading their obligations or opting to postpone them to a time of their own convenience. Were it otherwise, the perception that NS can be done on one’s own terms would undermine the strength of our defence force and thus our national security. We therefore reiterated what had been said in previous decisions, that general deterrence is the key sentencing objective in the sentencing of NS defaulters: see Lim Sin Han Andy v Public Prosecutor [2000] 1 SLR(R) 643 at [18]; Seow Wei Sin at [36] and Mohammed Ibrahim at [22].”

167    The High Court held at [57] that the length of the period of default would, as a general rule, be the key consideration in the determination of the appropriate sentence for an NS defaulter, with all the circumstances surrounding the commission of the offence to be considered as well. The High Court further held at [62] that the statutory maximum sentence of 36 months’ imprisonment should be the starting point for NS defaulters whose period of default was around 23 years or more, as they would not only have evaded the whole of their full-time NS obligations, but also their post-ORD reservist obligations. In this regard, the High Court explained at [64] that,

“The conduct of an NS defaulter who defaulted for such a long period of time, such as when he returned past the age of 40 and it was no longer possible for him to serve any of his NS obligations, would fall within the range of conduct which characterises the most serious instances of the offence. Such an offender would not only have refused to serve at the time that he was required to, he would also have evaded his NS obligations in their entirety. Currently, every male Singapore Citizen who is required to serve NS must serve two years of full-time NS. He must also serve his post-ORD reservist obligations, which, according to MINDEF, may potentially add up to 400 days of service during peace-time (based on ten years’ of reservist cycles and a maximum annual call-up of 40 days). The NS defaulter thus gains an unfair advantage over his peers in being able to pursue his personal interests during the more than three year period that his peers were serving NS. In our judgment, to adopt anything less than the statutory maximum sentence of 36 months’ imprisonment as the starting point in the sentencing of this category of NS defaulters would be inadequate.”

168    The Accused was past the age of 40 when he was arrested on 1 September 2021. His period of default, calculated from the date he failed to report for enlistment on 24 January 1997 to his 40th birthday on 31 October 2018 when the Accused became no longer a person subject to the EA, is 21years, 9 months and 7 days. The Accused had therefore evaded the whole of his full-time NS obligations and his post-ORD reservist obligations.

169    While the period of default may have been slightly less than the period of default of 23.5 years in Ang Lee Thye, I was of the view that the appropriate starting point should still be the maximum prescribed sentence of 36 months’ imprisonment. The Accused falls squarely within the worst category of NS defaulters as described in Sakthikanesh. The High Court in Sakthikanesh had referred to Sim Gek Yong v Public Prosecutor [1995] 1 SLR(R) 185 where CJ Yong had held at [13] that “a court, in deciding when to impose the maximum sentence, need only identify a range of conduct which characterises the most serious instances of the offence in question”, and held at [64] that “the conduct of an NS defaulter who defaulted for such a long period of time, such as when he returned past the age of 40 and it was no longer possible for him to serve any of his NS obligations, would fall within the range of conduct which characterised the most serious instances of the offence.” I was of the view that the conduct of the Accused falls within the same range and therefore, there is no basis for adopting a lower starting point.

Absence of Mitigating Factors

170    The mitigation plea comprised essentially the following planks:

a.     that the Accused had honestly believed himself justified in not serving NS given his Indonesian citizenship as doing so will result in him losing his Indonesian citizenship;

b.     that there had been no, or negligible harm caused as the Accused had not exercised, enjoyed or benefitted from any material rights and privileges in respect of the education he received in Singapore;

c.     that no enforcement action had been taken against him between the date he had failed to report for enlistment, i.e. 24 January 1997 and his arrest in September 2021 even though he had travelled in and out of Singapore on multiple occasions during this period;

d.     that the sentencing framework in Sakthikanesh does not apply given that the Accused’s failure to report for enlistment was in 1997 and that the case law pre-dating the 2006 amendment to the EA should apply instead;

The Accused’s dual citizenship

171    There is no dispute that MINDEF was fully aware of the Accused’s Indonesian citizenship when the Enlistment Notices were issued to him to report for enlistment for NS. There is also no dispute that MINDEF had also been informed that the Accused, as an Indonesian citizen, was not allowed to serve in the armed forces of another country. The inference to be drawn, as such, would be that MINDEF had considered the Accused’s position and decided as a matter of policy that the Accused was still obliged to fulfil his NS obligation as a Singapore citizen.

172    In Sakthikanesh at [70], the High Court, in rejecting the view that the sentence to be meted out to an NS defaulter should be calibrated based on whether he has a substantial connection to Singapore, or the amount of benefits he has enjoyed as a Singapore citizen, had held that it was clear that MINDEF was the agency that had the statutory responsibility for administering the EA, which made it an offence for anyone required by MINDEF to serve NS to default on his NS obligations. The High Court held that the determination of substantial connection to Singapore was a matter with policy implications that was within the prerogative of MINDEF and that as long as MINDEF has issued the enlistment papers to a male Singaporean, that person would need to serve NS and he would be liable for an offence under the Act if he fails to comply. As such, questions as to the extent of connection to Singapore would generally be irrelevant and that “any other view would severely undermine the principle of universality and equity by differentiating between classes of Singapore citizenship, when in truth, no such differentiation exists.”

173    The same principle apply with equal force in the present case. The issues concerning the Accused’s Indonesian citizenship and the impact serving NS would have on it, would similarly be a matter with policy implications which would be within MINDEF’s prerogative. These issues would similarly be of no relevance to the calibration of sentence. Otherwise, it would effectively amount to differentiating the Accused from other Singapore citizens when there is no basis for doing so. This would be an afront to the principle of universality and equity underpinning NS.

174    The Defence has submitted in oral submissions that the prosecution’s prayer for a custodial sentence totally disrespected the Accused’s need to keep his citizenship, which by extension, also disrespected Indonesia. With respect, this court was unable to see how a sovereign state enforcing its domestic laws against its own citizen could amount to any form of disrespect to a foreign state or its citizen.

The Defence’s Claim That There Was No or Negligible Harm

175    The Defence’s submission that there had been no, or negligible harm caused by the Accused’s failure to enlist as he had not exercised, enjoyed or benefitted from any material rights and privileges in respect of his education in Singapore should similarly be rejected on the ground that the questions of whether the Accused had exercised, enjoyed or benefitted from these rights and privileges is ultimately of no relevance to sentencing as they would also fall within the prerogative of MINDEF.

176    It would also not be correct for the Defence to submit that no harm has been caused by the Accused’s failure to report for enlistment. In Sakthikanesh, the High Court held at [52] that,

“There are multiple facets to the harm occasioned by NS defaulters. At one level, by choosing to serve their NS obligations not when they are required but only when it is convenient for them (or in some cases evading part of or the whole of their NS obligations), NS defaulters harm the operational readiness of the armed forces. At another level, they also harm the morale of fellow citizens who have made personal sacrifices to serve their NS obligations when they were called upon to do so. This can in turn lead to repercussions such as growing resentment and the loss of public support for NS, threatening the ability of our armed forces to ensure Singapore’s national security (see [48] above). Each and every member of the Singapore public would then become a victim.”

177    The High Court held at [51] that “the culpability of NS defaulters lies in the unfair advantage that they gain over their law-abiding peers by being able to pursue their personal goals (such as education or career advancements), while their peers were serving their NS obligations… NS defaulters thus violate the fundamental principles of universality and equity.”

Alleged Delay in Enforcement Action & Prosecution

178    The Defence’s main contention is that the Accused had been allowed to travel freely in and out of Singapore during the material period on multiple occasions and would have afforded opportunities for enforcement action to be taken against him. Opportunities for enforcement action would also have arisen when the Accused applied firstly to renounce his Singapore citizenship, secondly for permanent residence, and thirdly when he applied for a Short-Term Visit Pass. The failure by MINDEF to do so had caused prejudice to the Accused.

179    In Tan Kiang Kwang, CJ Yong held that,

“Delay in prosecution simpliciter may not even be a mitigating factor. Nonetheless, in appropriate cases, the court may exercise its discretion to order a `discount` in sentence, if there has been a significant delay in prosecution which has not been contributed to in any way by an accused person, if it would otherwise result in real injustice or prejudice to the accused.”

180    In Randy Chan, the High Court, in reference to Tan Kiang Kwang, held at [22] that,

“the significance of a delay in prosecution, if any, in the context of criminal justice hinges primarily on the effect of such a delay on the accused. This can be categorised for easier analysis under two headings: (a) considerations of fairness; and (b) the repercussions of delay on the offender’s effective rehabilitation and reintegration into society.”

181    The High Court in Randy Chan further held at [32] that “in cases of inordinately delayed prosecution, the first and foremost inquiry should always be whether the accused was in any way responsible for the delay.” The second, at [35] would be “the rehabilitative progress of the offender must be considered in the light of the nature and the gravity of the offence, as well as the wider public interest in each individual case.” The High Court further held that “considerations of fairness to an accused may in certain circumstances be substantially irrelevant – or, indeed, even outweighed by the public interest.”

182    In the present case, a house visit had been conducted at the Accused’s residence on 23 January 1997 after he had failed to report for enlistment on the same day – see [29]. The Accused was not at his residence. The police gazette against the Accused had been raised on 28 January 1997, which was less than 5 days after his failure to report for enlistment on 24 January 1997. Although the Accused had travelled in and out of Singapore during the period prior to his eventual arrest in September 2021, he had done so using his Indonesian passport. The Accused’s Indonesian passport reflected his name as “Edmond Ming Siang Jauw”. The police gazette, however, bore the name “Yao Zhi Hai Edmond”, which was the name reflected in the Accused’s Singapore NRIC and the enlistment notices issued by CMPB. In other words, the Accused had travelled in and out of Singapore as an Indonesian foreigner bearing a different name.

183    It is probable, as such, that that had been a key contributing factor why the Accused had not been apprehended on those occasions. Between 31 December 2008 and 16 March 2020, the Accused had used his Indonesian passport to enter Singapore on 13 occasions in breach of s 5A(1)(a) IA, which formed the basis for 13 of the charges under the IA to which the Accused had pleaded guilty to 3 and consented to the remaining being TIC. The fact that he had not apply for and therefore did not have a Singapore passport at the material time is not a valid defence to the offences under s 5A(1)(a) IA. It would also not provide a valid excuse for travelling in and out of Singapore using his Indonesian passport.

184    As such, notwithstanding the Defence’s submission that both the ICA and MINDEF ought to have been aware that “Edmond Ming Siang Jauw” was the Accused, it could not be gain said that the Accused had clearly contributed to his non-apprehension through his own actions.

185    It is also important to note that CMPB has consistently made clear to the Accused and his parents that the Accused had to fulfil his NS obligations as a Singapore citizen notwithstanding the fact that he is also an Indonesian citizen. The Accused had, in blatant disregard of the enlistment notices, knowingly and intentionally failed to report for enlistment. Up until his arrest in September 2021, the Accused had made no attempt to contact CMPB regarding his outstanding NS obligations. This was despite having been informed by ICA in December 2003 that his application to renounce his Singapore citizenship was being withheld under Article 128(2)(b) of the Constitution of the Republic of Singapore which provides that the Singapore Government may withhold registration of any declaration of renunciation of citizenship unless the person has, inter alia, discharged his NS liabilities. This was also despite the Accused’s mother DW2 Koh having been informed by ICA in 2004 to liaise directly with CMPB to resolve the Accused’s NS obligations. In 2005, ICA had also written to the Accused that they were unable to proceed with his application for permanent residence as the Accused is still a Singapore citizen.

186    Given the above, it would have been palpably clear to the Accused that the issues concerning his outstanding NS liabilities had not been resolved. Although a house visit was conducted in March 2005, the Accused was again not at the address[note: 52]. The Accused’s failure to contact CMPB to resolve the issue concerning his NS liabilities could, therefore, only be attributed to deliberate and outright refusal on the part of the Accused to acknowledge and accept his NS obligation as a Singapore citizen, a position which the Accused had maintained to date.

187    Given the circumstances, it was, in my view, perverse logic on the part of the Accused to now claim that he had been prejudiced as a result of no enforcement action having been taken against him until his arrest in September 2021. It was the Accused who had persistently refused to contact CMPB regarding his NS obligations when the onus was on him to do so. He had also contributed to his non-apprehension by using his Indonesian passport which bore a different name to travel in and out of Singapore in breach of the IA. The Accused’s claim that he had been deprived of the opportunity to fulfil his NS obligation as a result of delayed enforcement action and prosecution, when it was the Accused himself who had blatantly refused to accept his NS obligations in the first place, reeked somewhat of hypocrisy and demonstrated, in my view, a complete absence of remorse on his part.

188    Having considered the totality of the circumstances, I was of the view that any delay in enforcement action was contributed materially by the Accused’s own actions or inaction. I was also of the view that there was no delay in prosecution as the period between the Accused’s arrest and him being eventually charged in court, a period of about 1 year and 5 months was not unreasonable given the nature of the offences involved and the facts and circumstances of the case. I was therefore of the view that there had been no unfairness or injustice occasioned upon the Accused brought about by any delay in prosecution.

Argument Against Application of Sakthikanesh

189    The Defence had submitted that the sentencing approach in Sakthikanesh should not apply in the present case given that the Accused’s failure to report for enlistment took place in 1997. This was a submission which, in my view, is devoid of any merit.

190    In Ang Lee Thye, the offender had been charged with 2 counts of remaining outside of Singapore without a valid exit permit. The 2 charges covered the period between 24 May 1990 and 23 November 2013. The High Court had applied the same sentencing approach even though the offence dated back to 1990. There was no reason why the present case should be viewed any differently.

191    The Defence had referred to the case of Seow Wei Sin in support of their submission for a non-custodial sentence. The High Court had held in Sakthikanesh at [71] that Seow Wei Sin needed to be considered in the context of its unusual facts. The court had held at [37] – [39] that the three fundamental principles underpinning the NS policy in Singapore, viz, national security, universality and equity, did not apply to the offender. The offender in that case was born in 1961 and had left Singapore with his family when he was one year old and had not lived in Singapore since. At that time, NS in its present form had not been implemented. The court had observed that the offender had not left Singapore to evade his NS liability but had no choice as the family had decided to migrate to Malaysia. The court also found that to the offender’s mind, his father had sorted things out with the Singapore authorities regarding his NS liability and had no reason to think that it had not been resolved.

192    Given the exceptional facts and circumstances, I am of the view that the case of Seow Wei Sin has no application in the present case.

193    The Defence had cited the case of Chang Kar Meng in support of their submission. In that case, the Court of Appeal (“CA”) had held at [75] that the offender was entitled to rely on the sentencing range established by the relevant precedents and that there was no basis for ignoring his legitimate expectations, having regard to the general range of sentences previously meted out in similar cases. The CA’s holding must be understood in the proper context of the case, which is the comparison of the sentence meted out against the offender with the sentencing range in similar precedents.

194    In Adri Anton Kalangie v PP [2018] SGCA 40 (“Adri Anton”), the CA held at [57], that “it is not entirely clear if an individual can even, at the time of commission of the offence, be said to have a legitimate expectation as to the sentence that he will receive in the event that he is subsequently successfully prosecuted for the offence, save that the sentence should be within the relevant statutorily-prescribed range.” The CA further agreed with the High Court in Ding Si Yang v PP and another appeal [2015] 2 SLR 229 that “little weight should be given to the expectations of one who deliberately flouted the law and later found the expected costs or consequences were worse than anticipated.” In Pua Om Tee v PP and another appeal [2022] SGHC 116, the High Court held at [79] that “accused persons generally could not argue that they had a “legitimate expectation” as to the sentencing framework that would be applicable to them. Little weight ought to be given to the expectations of a person who flouts the law and later finds out that the expected costs or consequences are worse than anticipated. The only legitimate expectation that accused persons could rely on here was that they would be sentenced within the statutorily prescribed range.”

195    The Defence’s submission that the Accused should be sentenced in accordance with the “sentencing landscape” before the 2006 amendment to the EA is therefore misconceived. In any case, other than Seow Wei Sin, which has been distinguished, the Defence had not cited any other pre-2006 amendment case where a non-custodial sentence had been meted out against a NS defaulter in similar circumstances.

196    In view of the above and given that the Accused had claimed trial to the EA charge, I was unable to see any mitigating factor in the present case which would warrant any downward adjustment to the starting point sentence.

The IA Charges

197    I agreed with the Prosecution’s sentencing position with respect to the 3 charges under the IA proceeded with for the following reasons:

(a)     the similar charges TIC;

(b)     the Accused’s plea of guilt;

(c)     the unreported precedents referred to by the Prosecution.

198    The Defence had also not challenged the Prosecution’s sentencing position in respect of these 3 charges.

Sentence Imposed

199    The total sentence is therefore 36 months imprisonment and $3,000 fine in default 12 days’ imprisonment.

Public Prosecutor v Lin Qiaoming

Public Prosecutor v Lin Qiaoming
[2026] SGDC 235

Case Number:District Arrest Case No 909054 of 2026
Decision Date:20 July 2026
Tribunal/Court:District Court
Coram: Justin Yeo
Counsel Name(s): ASP Zhang Huawei (Immigration & Checkpoints Authority) for the Prosecution; Accused in person.
Parties: Public Prosecutor — Lin Qiaoming

Immigration – Criminal Offences

Criminal Procedure and Sentencing – Sentencing – Statutory Offences – Section 15(3) Immigration Act (Cap 133, Rev Ed 1997)

Criminal Procedure and Sentencing – Sentencing – Statutory Offences – Section 57(1)(k) Immigration Act (Cap 133, Rev Ed 2008)

Criminal Procedure and Sentencing – Sentencing – Statutory Offences – Section 28(4)(d) Immigration Act (Cap 133, Rev Ed 2008)

20 July 2026

Judgment reserved.

District Judge Justin Yeo:

Introduction

1       Ms Lin Qiaoming (“the Accused”), a national of the People’s Republic of China (“China”), committed multiple offences under the Immigration Act arising from a prolonged course of conduct spanning more than two decades. Eleven charges were brought against her, of which she pleaded guilty to three and admitted and consented to the remaining eight being taken into consideration (“TIC”) for the purposes of sentencing.

2       Both general and specific deterrence are dominant sentencing considerations in this case, given that the offences are committed against a public institution – being the Immigration & Checkpoints Authority (“ICA”) – and involve premeditated and repeat offending (Public Prosecutor v Law Aik Meng [2007] 2 SLR(R) 814 at [21], [22] and [24(a)]).

3       For the reasons explained in this judgment, I impose an aggregate sentence of six months’ and six weeks’ imprisonment, and a fine of $2,500 (in default, 15 days’ imprisonment)

Background Facts

4       The following facts are based on the Statement of Facts,[note: 1] to which the Accused admitted without qualification. A brief chronological overview of the facts is as follows:

(a)     On 18 March 2002, the Accused first arrived in Singapore as a tourist, using a passport issued under her actual identity (“P1”), namely, “Lin Qiaoming”, and stating her actual birthday. She was granted a Visit Pass (“VP”) until 1 April 2002. During this time, she became acquainted with Mr Tan Kim Lam (“Tan”), who is presently the Accused’s husband and co-accused.

(b)     After expiry of her VP on 1 April 2002, she remained unlawfully in Singapore in order to seek illegal employment. During this time, she knew that she had overstayed, and was afraid of the legal consequences. She therefore engaged a Chinese agent and paid a fee between $2,000 to $3,000 to facilitate her departure from Singapore.

(c)     On 1 May 2002, she left Singapore by car, without submitting the completed embarkation form relating to her entry into Singapore on 18 March 2002, and without producing P1 to the immigration officer on duty.

(d)     After returning to China, the Accused was unsuccessful in applying for a Singapore visa under her actual identity. She thus assumed her younger sister’s identity, “Lin Liming”, and obtained a new China passport (“P2”), which was issued on 1 July 2009. The biodata page of P2 bore the Accused’s photograph, with the name “Lin Liming” and Lin Liming’s date of birth.

(e)     On 12 August 2009, the Accused used P2 to apply for a Singapore visa, with Tan acting as her sponsor. She wanted to enter Singapore to seek gainful employment, and better life opportunities. A Singapore visa was eventually issued to her.

(f)     On 30 August 2009, the Accused arrived at Singapore Changi Airport.

(i)       She presented a disembarkation form in which she falsely declared that her name was “Lin Liming”, that her date of birth was Lin Liming’s date of birth, and that she had never used a passport under a different name to enter Singapore. She knew that the statements were false but made them so that the immigration officer on duty would grant her a VP and allow her entry into Singapore. These false statements were material considerations for the ICA in its consideration for the grant of a VP on arrival.

(ii)       She also produced P2 to the immigration officer on duty for arrival immigration clearance. In doing so, she knew that P2 was a misleading document as it contained her photograph but bore Lin Liming’s particulars.

(iii)       Unaware of the deception on both the disembarkation form and P2, the immigration officer granted her a VP and allowed her to enter Singapore.

(g)     On 27 October 2009, the Accused produced P2 to the immigration officer on duty for departure immigration clearance, knowing that P2 was a misleading document. The officer was unaware that P2 was a misleading document, and accorded departure immigration clearance to the Accused, thus allowing her to leave Singapore.

(h)     Between 17 February 2011 and 5 June 2015, the Accused travelled into and out of Singapore on 34 occasions using the assumed identity and P2. During this period, she married a Singapore citizen, Mr Poh Meng Hwee, on 3 May 2011 (the marriage ending in divorce in April 2015), and was issued a Work Pass on 21 June 2011 (which was initially valid until 20 June 2015, but was cancelled on 2 June 2015).

(i)     On 5 June 2015, she returned to China after cancellation of her Work Pass. She thereafter resumed her actual identity of “Lin Qiaoming” and obtained a new China passport under her actual identity (“P3”). P3 was issued on 16 May 2017.

(j)     On 28 April 2023, the Accused and Tan registered their marriage in China.

(k)     On 26 May 2023, the Accused used P3 to apply for a Singapore visa, with Tan acting as her sponsor. A Singapore visa was issued to her.

(l)     On 22 June 2023, the Accused arrived in Singapore and was granted a VP on the same day to enter Singapore.

(m)     Subsequently, relying on P3 and with Tan as her sponsor, the Accused obtained a Long-Term Visit Pass (“LTVP”) on three occasions: from 14 August 2023 to 14 August 2024; 10 July 2024 to 10 September 2025; and 12 September 2025 to 12 September 2028.

(n)     On 6 August 2025, while conducting further screening on the Accused’s LTVP application (made on 2 June 2025), officers of the ICA Services Centre traced the Accused’s fingerprint to “Lin Liming”. The screenings revealed that there was no arrival record for “Lin Liming” after “Lin Liming” had departed Singapore on 5 June 2015. The Accused and Tan were thus referred to the ICA Investigation Branch for further investigations. The investigations revealed the prolonged course of immigration offences spanning more than two decades, as briefly summarised above.

5       For completeness, I note that on 10 July 2026 (after the hearing of this matter but before this decision was rendered), Tan was convicted under s 57(1)(ka) read with s 57(1AAA) of the IA for falsely stating, in the Accused’s LTVP application of 2 June 2025, that the Accused did not possess any other identity documents bearing different particulars. Tan made the declaration in his capacity as the Accused’s local sponsor. He was sentenced to a fine of $2,000 (in default, one week’s imprisonment) for an offence punishable by a fine of up to $4,000.

The Charges

6       The Accused pleaded guilty to three charges, as follows:

(a)     Charge DAC-909054-2026 (“the Overstaying Charge”), concerning the Accused remaining unlawfully in Singapore from 2 April to 1 May 2002, a period of 30 days, in contravention of s 15(1) of the Immigration Act (Cap 133, 1997 Rev Ed) (“IA 1997”) (see [4(b)] and [4(c)] above). She thereby committed an offence under IA 1997 s 15(3), which carries punishment under IA 1997 s 15(3)(a) of a fine of up to $4,000 or imprisonment for up to six months or both.

(b)     Charge DAC-909056-2026 (“the False Statement Charge”), concerning the Accused’s obtaining of a VP by knowingly making a false statement in her disembarkation form on 30 August 2009 (see [4(f)(i)] above). She thereby committed an offence under Immigration Act (Cap 133, 2008 Rev Ed) (“IA 2008”) s 57(1)(k), which carries punishment under IA 2008 s 57(1)(vi) of a fine of up to $4,000 or imprisonment for up to 12 months or both.

(c)     Charge DAC-909059-2026 (“the Misleading Passport Charge”), concerning the Accused knowingly producing P2 to an immigration officer for immigration clearance on 30 August and 27 October 2009 (see [4(f)] and [4(g)] above). She thereby committed an offence under IA 2008 s 28(4)(d). The offence is subject to punishment under IA 2008 s 28(4)(ii) of a fine of up to $6,000 or imprisonment for up to two years or both. The charge is also amalgamated under s 124(4) of the Criminal Procedure Code 2010 (“CPC”).

7       The eight TIC charges are as follows:

(a)     One charge[note: 2] under IA 1997 s 6(2) for failure to submit a completed embarkation form together with her passport when departing Singapore on 1 May 2002, which carries punishment under IA 1997 s 6(3)(b) of a fine of up to $4,000 or imprisonment for up to 12 months or both. This charge will be taken into consideration when sentencing for the Overstaying Charge.

(b)     One charge[note: 3] under IA 2008 s 57(1)(k) for making a false statement in an application for Singapore permanent residency on 5 March 2013. As with the False Statement Charge, this charge carries punishment of a fine of up to $4,000 or imprisonment for up to 12 months or both. This charge will be taken into consideration when sentencing for the False Statement Charge.

(c)     One charge[note: 4] under Immigration Act 1959 (“IA”) s 57(1)(ka) read with 57(1AAA), for making a false statement in an application for a LTVP on 2 June 2025, which carries punishment under IA s 57(1AA)(gb) of a fine of up to $4,000. This charge will be taken into consideration when sentencing for the False Statement Charge.

(d)     Five amalgamated charges[note: 5] under IA 2008 s 28(4)(d) for knowingly producing P2 to an immigration officer on (i) nine occasions between 17 February to 7 November 2011; (ii) four occasions between 11 June and 6 October 2012; (iii) ten occasions between 10 February and 4 October 2013; (iv) six occasions between 29 January and 9 October 2014; and (v) five occasions between 11 February and 5 June 2015. As with the Misleading Passport Charge, each of these amalgamated charges carries punishment of a fine of up to $6,000 or imprisonment for up to two years or both. These charges will be taken into consideration when sentencing for the Misleading Passport Charge.

The Overstaying Charge

Statutory Provisions

8       For the Overstaying Charge, the relevant statutory provisions are IA 1997 ss 15(1) and 15(3)(a), which carry punishment of a fine of up to $4,000 or imprisonment for up to six months or both. The provisions are as follows:

Unlawful entry or presence in Singapore

15.—(1)    A person shall not remain in Singapore after the cancellation of any permit or certificate, or after the making of a declaration under section 14(4) or after the expiration or notification to him, in such manner as may be prescribed, of the cancellation of any pass relating to or issued to him unless he is otherwise entitled or authorised to remain in Singapore under the provisions of this Act or the regulations.

…

(3)    Any person who contravenes, without reasonable cause, this section shall be guilty of an offence and —

(a)    in the case where he remains unlawfully for a period not exceeding 90 days, shall be liable on conviction to a fine not exceeding $4,000 or to imprisonment for a term not exceeding 6 months or to both;

Sentencing Factors and Precedents

9       A fine is the sentencing norm for the offence of remaining unlawfully in Singapore for less than 90 days (Public Prosecutor v Pham Thi Loan [2013] SGDC 68 (“Pham Thi Loan”) at [7]; Public Prosecutor v Nguyen Thanh Xuan [2013] SGDC 71 (“Nguyen Thanh Xuan”) at [9]). The quantum of the fine is generally calibrated according to the length of overstay (Pham Thi Loan at [8], Nguyen Thanh Xuan at [10]). In addition, the manner in which the period of overstay came to an end is also a relevant sentencing factor. For instance, it is aggravating if the overstay was terminated by the accused’s arrest, rather than voluntary surrender to the authorities (see, eg, Public Prosecutor v Chen Jialing [2019] SGDC 65 (“Chen Jialing”) at [94]; Nguyen Thanh Xuan at [10]).

10     A summary of several precedents concerning overstaying is as follows:

(a)     For periods of overstaying ranging from 15 to 30 days, the usual sentence is a fine of between $1,000 and $2,000 (see Public Prosecutor v Gary Tan Kwan Hui [2021] SGDC 267 (“Gary Tan”) at [36]–[37]).

(i)       In Nguyen Thanh Xuan, the offender overstayed for 16 days, a period which was ended when she was arrested by the police. The offender was untraced. The court specifically noted that the offender’s overstaying was ended solely because she was arrested by the police, and opined that she would otherwise have continued to overstay in Singapore. In the circumstances the court imposed a fine of $2,000 (in default, two weeks’ imprisonment).

(ii)       In Gary Tan, the offender overstayed for 17 days, a period which was ended when he was arrested for moneylending-related offences.[note: 6] The court imposed a fine of $1,000 (in default, one weeks’ imprisonment).

(iii)       In Gary Tan, the court noted (amongst other unreported decisions) the case of Public Prosecutor v Lee Yong Shin (DAC-923102-2019) (“Lee Yong Shin”). In that case, the offender’s period of overstay commenced after his employer cancelled his work permit when he became uncontactable following the discovery that he had used company funds to discharge his personal debts.[note: 7] The period of overstay came to an end 30 days later when he was arrested. The court imposed a fine of $2,000 (in default, ten days’ imprisonment).

(b)     In Chen Jialing, the offender overstayed for 46 days. The period of overstay came to an end when she was arrested following checks conducted by ICA officers at her residential unit. The offender was untraced. She pleaded guilty very late in the day, after the close of the entire case. In those circumstances, the court imposed a fine of $3,000 (in default, 15 days’ imprisonment), and the sentence was upheld on appeal to the High Court.

(c)     In Pham Thi Loan, the offender overstayed for 80 days. She remained unlawfully in Singapore until she was arrested by the police. The offender was untraced. In those circumstances, the court imposed a fine of $4,000 (in default, four weeks’ imprisonment), and the sentence was upheld on appeal to the High Court.

Application to the Overstaying Charge

11     In the present case, the Accused overstayed for 30 days. This period ended when she left Singapore unlawfully. She had taken steps to evade detection – specifically, she engaged a Chinese agent to facilitate her departure, and left Singapore without submitting the completed embarkation form, and without producing P1 to the immigration officer on duty. The latter two points are the subject matter of the TIC charge under IA 1997 s 6(2), and necessitate an uplift in the sentence. In terms of mitigating factors, I note her early plea of guilt, and her cooperation with the authorities.

12     An appropriate sentence for the Overstaying Charge on a plead guilty basis is therefore $2,500 (in default, 15 days’ imprisonment).

The False Statement Charge

Statutory Provisions

13     For the False Statement Charge, the relevant statutory provisions are IA 2008 ss 57(1)(k) and 57(1)(vi), which carry punishment of a fine of up to $4,000 or imprisonment for up to 12 months or both. The provisions are as follows:

Offences

57.—(1)    Any person who —

…

(k)    by making a false statement obtains or attempts to obtain an entry or a re-entry permit, pass, Singapore visa or certificate for himself or for any other person; …

shall be guilty of an offence and —

…

(vi)   in the case of an offence under paragraph (f), (g), (h), (i), (j), (k) or (l), shall be liable on conviction to a fine not exceeding $4,000 or to imprisonment for a term not exceeding 12 months or to both.

Sentencing Factors and Precedents

14     A custodial sentence is the norm for offences under IA 2008 s 57(1); punishment by fine is warranted only under exceptional circumstances (Goh Chin Soon v Public Prosecutor [2026] 3 SLR 37 (“Goh Chin Soon”) at [118], citing Abu Syeed Chowdhury v Public Prosecutor [2002] 1 SLR(R) 182 (“Abu Syeed Chowdhury”) at [26]). In Abu Syeed Chowdhury, the court established the following four guiding considerations for calibrating an appropriate sentence:

(a)     First, the materiality of the false representation on the mind of the decision-maker (Abu Syeed Chowdhury at [28]). The greater the extent to which the falsehood induced or was capable of inducing the decision-maker to approve the application, the more severe the sentence should be. Conversely, where the false representation relates to a matter of little or no significance to the outcome of the application, this may, in exceptional circumstances, justify some measure of leniency (Abu Syeed Chowdhury at [28]).

(b)     Second, the nature and extent of the deception. Greater culpability arises where the offender undertook elaborate measures to deceive or acted in conscious defiance of the authorities (Abu Syeed Chowdhury at [29]). The use of methods that are more difficult to detect, or the production of forged corroborating documents, likewise warrant a more severe sentence (Abu Syeed Chowdhury at [29]).

(c)     Third, the consequences of the deception. Relevant considerations include any detriment suffered by the deceived party as a result of the deception, as well as broader implications on other third parties (Abu Syeed Chowdhury at [30]).

(d)     Fourth, personal mitigating factors applicable to the offender. However, limited weight should be accorded to hardships that are attributable to the offender’s own illegal entrance to Singapore (Abu Syeed Chowdhury at [31]). For instance, where an offender enters Singapore illegally and starts a family, despite knowing that the family would be adversely affected should he or she be arrested, this would be considered a “self-induced” hardship with “little mitigation value” (Abu Syeed Chowdhury at [31]).

15     The starting point sentence for making false statements in disembarkation forms, in relation to an offender who (a) is not barred from entering Singapore but (b) is subject to an outstanding arrest warrant, is five to six weeks’ imprisonment (Lin Lifen v Public Prosecutor [2016] 1 SLR 287 (“Lin Lifen”) at [66], cited in Goh Chin Soon at [147]). The significance of the outstanding arrest warrant lies in the fact that the offender’s false declarations in the disembarkation forms would, in such cases, have served to conceal his or her true identity and thereby reduced the likelihood that the authorities would discover his or her fugitive status and thus execute the arrest warrant (see Lin Lifen at [60]).

16     In establishing this indicative sentencing range, the High Court considered several precedents, which all involved sentences in claim trial scenarios (Lin Lifen at [57]–[59]). On the facts of Lin Lifen itself, which concerned an offender who was the subject of an outstanding arrest warrant, the High Court imposed a sentence of five weeks’ imprisonment. This should be understood in the context that (a) the High Court found that the offender had “entered Singapore partly to be with her son” (see Lin Lifen at [65]–[66]); and (b) Lin Lifen was a case involving a guilty plea (see Lin Lifen at [1]; and see Goh Chin Soon at [151]).

Application to the False Statement Charge

17     In the present case, the Accused was not subject to any outstanding arrest warrant. However, as observed in Goh Chin Soon at [148], the absence of an outstanding arrest warrant does not warrant a starting point that is “far below” the benchmark identified in Lin Lifen. In Goh Chin Soon, although there was no outstanding arrest warrant, the false declarations allowed the accused to bypass travel restrictions in contravention of the Bankruptcy Act (Goh Chin Soon at [148]). In the present case, the Accused’s false declarations were calculated to conceal her true identity and prevent the authorities from discovering that she had previously overstayed in Singapore and had unlawfully departed Singapore. By assuming a different identity, she was able to circumvent the immigration regime and obtain entry into Singapore under a false identity, without her adverse immigration history being disclosed to the authorities. While this may be less aggravated than a direct evasion of an outstanding arrest warrant, it nevertheless involves a serious attempt to frustrate the authorities’ ability to accurately identify the Accused and assess her admissibility into Singapore.

18     I now analyse the four guiding conditions in Abu Syeed Chowdhury:

(a)     First, in relation to the materiality of the false representation on the mind of the decision-maker, the immigration officer would not have granted the Accused a VP to enter Singapore had the officer known that the disembarkation form contained false declarations. The Accused’s false representation was therefore very material to the officer’s decision to grant her a VP. This is akin to the situation in Goh Chin Soon.

(b)     Second, in relation to the nature and extent of the deception, the Accused made multiple false declarations relating to (i) her identity; (ii) her date of birth; and (iii) the fact that she had never used a passport under a different name to enter Singapore. She corroborated this with the use of P2, thus making her deception even harder to detect. This renders the present case more aggravated than Lin Lifen (where the false declaration related only to the fact that she had never used a passport under a different name to enter Singapore) and analogous to the situation in Goh Chin Soon (see Goh Chin Soon at [152]).

(c)     Third, in relation to the consequences of the deception, the Accused’s false declarations enabled her to obtain a VP and gain entry into Singapore when she otherwise would not have been permitted to do so. In particular, the deception concealed the fact that she had previously overstayed in Singapore and had departed Singapore unlawfully. By doing so, the Accused was able to circumvent the immigration regime and evade detection for immigration offences that she had previously committed.

(d)     Fourth, offender-specific factors.

(i)       In relation to offender-specific mitigating factors, I note the Accused’s early plea of guilt, and her cooperation with the authorities – factors which are similar to that in Lin Lifen, but absent in Goh Chin Soon. For completeness, I note that in Lin Lifen, the High Court considered that the offender had entered Singapore partly to be with her son (see Lin Lifen at [66]), but no similar personal circumstance arises on the present facts – indeed, the Accused admitted that she had entered Singapore at the material time to seek gainful employment and better life opportunities in Singapore.[note: 8]

(ii)       Against the identified mitigating factors stands the offender-specific aggravating factor of the two TIC charges concerning the making of false declarations in various other immigration-related applications (see [7(b)] and [7(c)] above).

19     In view of [15] to [18] above, and comparing the various aggravating and mitigating factors with Goh Chin Soon and Lin Lifen, the appropriate sentence for the False Statement Charge, on a plead guilty basis, is six weeks’ imprisonment. There is no further additional reduction accorded for the plea of guilt under the Sentencing Advisory Panel’s “Guidelines on Reduction in Sentences for Guilty Pleas” (“Guilty Plea Guidelines”), given that the precedent in Lin Lifen already concerned a guilty plea scenario (see [16] above and Guilty Plea Guidelines at paragraph 10).

The Misleading Passport Charge

20     For the Misleading Passport Charge, the relevant statutory provisions are IA 2008 ss 28(4)(d) and 28(4)(ii), which carry punishment of a fine of up to $6,000 or imprisonment for up to two years or both. The provisions are as follows:

Interrogation of travellers

28.— …

(4)    Any person who —

(d)    knowingly produces any false or misleading document,

shall be guilty of an offence and shall be liable on conviction —

…

(ii)   in the case of an offence under paragraph (d), to a fine not exceeding $6,000 or to imprisonment for a term not exceeding 2 years or to both.

21     The Misleading Passport Charge is amalgamated under CPC s 124(4), but the doubled sentencing limit under CPC s 124(8)(a)(ii) does not apply because the offence took place before 31 October 2018 (see CPC s 124(10)). That said, I agree with the Prosecution’s submission that the analytical framework in Prakash s/o Mathivanan v Public Prosecutor [2025] 4 SLR 1386 (“Prakash”) remains relevant. I recently summarised the Prakash framework in Public Prosecutor v Loh Guang Ze [2026] SGDC 211 (“Loh Guang Ze”) at [100], and set out that summary while omitting reference to the doubled sentencing limit:

(a)    At the first stage, the court identifies the punishment prescribed for a single instance of offending, ie, the “base offence” (Prakash at [42] and [129(a)]). The court applies the relevant sentencing framework or benchmark for the “base offence”, or draws on analogous precedents where no such framework or benchmark exists. The sentencing factors considered at this stage are offence-specific in nature, encompassing the harm caused and the manner and mode in which the offence was committed (Prakash at [42]).

(b)    At the second stage, the court determines the appropriate starting point sentence for the amalgamated offence, based on a holistic assessment of the offence-specific factors bearing on the aggregate harm caused and the offender’s overall culpability over the entire course of conduct (Prakash at [43] and [129(b)]). The court … considers the following factors in this assessment:

(i)    First, in addition to the culpability-related factors identified at the first stage, the court considers the duration and frequency of the offending conduct (Prakash at [45(a)] and [129(b)(i)]). Where an offender has repeated the offence multiple times over a sustained period, this demonstrates greater recalcitrance, which is an aggravating factor.

(ii)   Second, in assessing the harm caused by the course of conduct, the court has regard to the factors identified at the first stage (Prakash at [45(b)] and [129(b)(ii)]).

(iii)   Third, the court considers whether the nature of the aggregate offending warrants a different type of sentence altogether, such as crossing the custodial threshold (Prakash at [45(c)] and [129(b)(iii)]).

(c)    At the third stage, the court adjusts the starting point sentence to account for offender-specific aggravating and mitigating factors (Prakash at [46] and [129(c)]). These are the same factors as those applicable to non-amalgamated offences (Prakash at [46] and [129(c)]).

Prakash First Stage – Starting point sentence for “base offence”

22     Taking as the “base offence” one of the two occasions of knowingly producing a misleading document (ie, P2) to an immigration officer for immigration clearance, the starting point sentence for the “base offence” on a claim-trial basis would be four months’ and three weeks’ imprisonment. I elaborate.

23     In Goh Chin Soon (at [141]), the High Court held that where the false or misleading document knowingly produced is a passport, and the offender claims trial, the appropriate starting point sentence is four months’ imprisonment. Such a starting point takes into consideration the “sacrosanct nature of a passport”, given its integral function as proof of identity and its role in maintaining border security (Goh Chin Soon at [142]).

24     An uplift of three weeks’ imprisonment is warranted in view of the following two offence-specific aggravating factors:

(a)     First, the Accused exhibited a high degree of premeditation in obtaining P2. She came up with the plan to obtain P2 after she was unsuccessful in applying for a Singapore visa under her actual identity. Using P2, she could also circumvent immigration-related restrictions in re-entering Singapore occasioned by her earlier unlawful departure from Singapore. This is similar to the situation in Goh Chin Soon (see [123(a)] read with [137]).

(b)     Second, the Accused committed the offence for personal gain, namely, to re-enter Singapore under a false identity so that she could seek gainful employment and better life opportunities in Singapore.[note: 9] In Goh Chin Soon, the High Court treated as aggravating the offender’s use of a passport bearing a false identity to facilitate travel into and out of Singapore without detection by the authorities, thereby enabling him to evade the travel restrictions arising from his status as an undischarged bankrupt (at [123(b)] and [137]).

25     This uplift is proportionate when viewed against the one-month uplift imposed in Goh Chin Soon (at [143]). While the present case shares with Goh Chin Soon the aggravating factors discussed at [24] above, there was an additional aggravating factor in Goh Chin Soon: the offender had continued the passport bearing a false identity despite having lawful means of travel available to him, including after he had obtained a Singapore passport (see Goh Chin Soon at [137] and [143]). For completeness, I note a further aggravating factor in Goh Chin Soon which is not present here, ie, that the offender lacked remorse, as evidenced by the fanciful explanations he advanced at trial (Goh Chin Soon at [123(c)]. However, the lack of remorse is a consideration that falls to be addressed at the third stage of the Prakash framework in the present case.

Prakash Second Stage – Starting point sentence for amalgamated charge

26     The Prosecution submitted that the uplift at the Prakash second stage should be nine months’ imprisonment, after taking into consideration that the Accused had travelled in and out of Singapore on a total of 36 occasions.[note: 10]

27     In my view, this approach erroneously conflates the second and third stages of Prakash. At the second stage of Prakash, the court considers only the aggregate offending for the amalgamated charge itself. It does not also further consider the aggregate offending for the TIC charges, which is a matter properly considered at the third stage of Prakash.

28     Given that the Misleading Passport Charge concerned two occasions of offending in total, I find that an uplift of three weeks’ imprisonment is appropriate, thus bringing the indicative claim trial sentence to five months’ and two weeks’ imprisonment.

Prakash Third Stage – Offender-specific factors

29     At the third stage of the Prakash framework, the court considers offender-specific factors.

30     The relevant offender-specific aggravating factor in the present case relates to the five TIC charges mentioned at [7(d)] above, which are all amalgamated charges under IA 2008 s 28(4)(d). They involved a total of 34 instances of the Accused illegally travelling in and out of Singapore with P2. Each of the TIC charges is more aggravated than the Misleading Passport Charge in terms of the number of occasions of offending encapsulated by each of those charges. Collectively, they warrant an uplift of three months’ imprisonment, thus bringing the claim trial sentence to eight months’ and two weeks’ imprisonment.

31     The relevant offender-specific mitigating factor concerns the Accused’s early plea of guilt. This is a distinguishing factor from Goh Chin Soon, where the offender was found to have lacked remorse. Here, the Accused pleaded guilty within Stage 1 of the Guilty Plea Guidelines and has also been cooperative with the authorities. Granting her a 30% sentencing reduction in line with the Guidelines, the final sentence for the Misleading Passport Charge is six months’ imprisonment.

Global Sentence

32     I now turn to consider the global sentence. Sentences for related offences forming part of a single transaction should generally run concurrently (ie, the “one-transaction rule”), while sentences for unrelated offences should run consecutively (ie, the “general rule”). See Public Prosecutor v Raveen Balakrishnan [2018] 4 SLR 799 (“Raveen”) at [39] and [41].

33     The Prosecution submitted that the imprisonment terms for the False Statement Charge and the Misleading Passport Charge should run consecutively.[note: 11] The Prosecution acknowledged that the offending conduct in these two charges may arguably constitute a single transaction (and thus should run concurrently under the “one-transaction rule”), but contended that the offences concerned the invasion of different legally protected interests.[note: 12] Specifically, the Prosecution contended that the False Statement Charge concerned an undermining of the security and integrity of the immigration system, while the Misleading Passport Charge compromised the sacrosanct nature of a passport as prima facie proof of a passport holder’s identity, which is indispensable to international travel and border security (citing Goh Chin Soon at [39] to [40]).[note: 13]

34     I am not persuaded by this argument. In Goh Chin Soon, the offender contended that the charges in that case (which were similar to the False Statement Charge and the Misleading Passport Charge) concerned the same legally protected interests in having travellers provide truthful information and documents regarding their identity (Goh Chin Soon at [158]). The High Court did not express disagreement with this submission, but pointed out that the invasion of interests in Goh Chin Soon “plainly occurred on distinct dates”; they therefore did not constitute a “single invasion of the same legally protected interest” (Goh Chin Soon at [158], emphasis in original). In contrast, in the present case, there is a substantial degree of factual proximity between the False Statement Charge and the Misleading Passport Charge – the False Statement Charge and the first instance of offending under the Misleading Passport Charge were committed in the course of the same immigration clearance process at Singapore Changi Airport on 30 August 2009. That said, I note that the position in Goh Chin Soon would have applied squarely to the present case had the Prosecution proceeded with any of the five TIC charges mentioned at [7(d)] above, instead of the Misleading Passport Charge. This is because the five TIC charges concerned the invasion of interests on “distinct dates” from the False Statement Charge, as was the case in Goh Chin Soon.

35     In my judgment, a strict application of the one-transaction rule in this case would allow the Accused to avoid consideration of her enhanced culpability as reflected in the multiplicity of offences she committed. To borrow the language of Goh Chin Soon at [160] albeit in a slightly different context, this is “a case where the one transaction rule ought not to be rigidly applied”. Having the imprisonment terms for the False Statement Charge and the Misleading Passport Charge run consecutively, rather than concurrently, would more appropriately reflect the Accused’s aggregate criminality.

36     For completeness, I address the Accused’s seeking of concurrent sentences on the basis that she had already received punishment in China for assuming a fake identity and obtaining a fake passport.[note: 14] In response, the Prosecution explained that the punishment imposed in China concerned the Accused’s use of a false identity to apply for and obtain P2.[note: 15] The Accused did not dispute this. In any event, the False Statement Charge and the Misleading Passport Charge relate to the Accused’s conduct in seeking to enter and entering Singapore by making false declarations and producing a misleading passport to Singapore immigration authorities. Punishment imposed in China for assuming a fake identity and obtaining a fake passport does not amount to punishment for these offences in Singapore.

37     I now take a “last look” at all the facts and circumstances as required by the “totality principle” (see Raveen at [73]). There are two limbs to the principle (Raveen at [73], citing Mohamed Shouffee bin Adam v Public Prosecutor [2014] 2 SLR 998 at [54] and [57]), which I analyse as follows:

(a)     First, the aggregate sentence is not substantially above the normal level of sentences for the most serious of the individual offences committed (ie, the Misleading Passport Charge).

(b)     Second, the aggregate sentence is neither crushing nor out of keeping with the Accused’s past record or future prospects. Indeed, the sheer number of immigration offences that the Accused committed over an extended period of time warrants a deterrent sentence.

38     I therefore order that the imprisonment terms for the False Statement Charge and the Misleading Passport Charge run consecutively. I am satisfied that the aggregate sentence of six months’ and six weeks’ imprisonment, and a fine of $2,500 (in default, 15 days’ imprisonment), is sufficient and proportionate to the Accused’s overall criminality.
