Public Prosecutor v Han Teng Kwang

Public Prosecutor v Han Teng Kwang
[2026] SGDC 228

Case Number:District Arrest Case 902199-2024 and 3 Others, Magistrate's Appeal Nos 9138/2026/01
Decision Date:20 July 2026
Tribunal/Court:District Court
Coram: Luke Tan
Counsel Name(s): Mr Leong Kit Yu and Mr Law Yan An (Attorney-General's Chambers) for the Public Prosecutor; The accused in person
Parties: Public Prosecutor — Han Teng Kwang

Criminal Law – Statutory offences – Corruption, Drug Trafficking and Other Serious Crimes (Confiscation of Benefits) Act – s 47AA(1) – possession of property reasonably suspected of being benefits from criminal conduct

Criminal Procedure and Sentencing – sentencing – principles – lack of remorse as an aggravating factor

Evidence – Admissibility – statements – voluntariness

[LawNet Editorial Note: An appeal to this decision has been filed in MA 9138/2026/01.]

20 July 2026

District Judge Luke Tan:

Introduction

1       The accused, Han Teng Kwang, a 72-year-old male Singaporean, faced four charges under section 47AA(1) and punishable under section 47AA(2)(a) of the Corruption, Drug Trafficking and Other Serious Crimes (Confiscation of Benefits) Act (Cap 65A, 2000 Rev Ed) ("CDSA") for possessing property that may be reasonably suspected of being benefits from criminal conduct, and failing to account satisfactorily how he came by such property.

2       The Prosecution's case was that the accused received the property reflected in each charge through various bank accounts linked to companies he controlled, including Sun Mode Holding Pte Ltd (“Sun Mode”).The accused exercised sole control over Sun Mode's UOB Bank Account No. XXX-XXX-XXX-X[note: 1] (the "Sun Mode Bank Account"). The moneys were also received through the bank accounts of Kunlun Mountains Enterprise ("Kunlun"), a sole proprietorship owned by PW4 Mr Teo Seng Liang ("Mr Teo"), and Business Ventures Corporation Pte Ltd ("BVC"), whose director, PW9 Madam Yeo Chor Cher ("Mdm Yeo"), acted at the accused's behest. Between April and September 2020, various love scam victims transferred substantial sums to bank accounts controlled by third parties, who then handed cash to the accused or transferred funds to the Sun Mode Bank Account at his behest. The moneys were directly traceable to these victims.

3       The accused denied any involvement in the transactions the subject of the charges, claiming ignorance of the moneys received into the relevant accounts and denying that he had met or had any dealings with most of the Prosecution witnesses. As will be seen, his evidence was incoherent, internally inconsistent, and contradicted by the documentary evidence and the testimony of multiple witnesses.

4       After a full trial, I convicted the accused on all four charges and sentenced him to an aggregate of 14 months’ imprisonment. The accused, being dissatisfied, has appealed against his conviction and sentence. The sentence has been stayed, and the accused is currently on bail. These are my Grounds of Decision.

The Charges

5       The accused faced the following charges:

(a)     The first charge (DAC-902199-2024) alleged that between 2 July 2020 and 3 July 2020, the accused possessed property that may be reasonably suspected of being in whole directly representing benefits from criminal conduct, to wit, S$15,500 in the Sun Mode Bank Account, which he had control over, and that he failed to account satisfactorily how he came by the same.

(b)     The second charge (DAC-902200-2024) alleged that sometime between August 2020 and September 2020, the accused possessed property that may be reasonably suspected of being in whole directly representing benefits from criminal conduct, to wit, S$58,000 in cash from Teo Seng Liang, and that he failed to account satisfactorily how he came by the same.

(c)     The third charge (DAC-902201-2024) alleged that on or about 27 July 2020, the accused possessed property that may be reasonably suspected of being in whole directly representing benefits from criminal conduct, to wit, S$43,700 in cash from Yeo Chor Cher, and that he failed to account satisfactorily how he came by the same.

(d)     The fourth charge (DAC-904166-2024) alleged that on or about 16 April 2020, the accused possessed property that may be reasonably suspected of being in whole directly representing benefits from criminal conduct, to wit, S$23,750 in the Sun Mode Bank Account, which he had control over, and that he failed to account satisfactorily how he came by the same.

Overview of the Prosecution's Case

6       The Prosecution's case rested on evidence from multiple sources: bank records, WeChat message exchanges, ACRA documents, and statements recorded from the accused in the course of police investigations. The central thrust of the Prosecution's case was that between April and September 2020, the accused received funds totalling S$140,950 that were directly traceable to victims of romance scams. These victims had no legitimate dealings with the accused or any of the entities through which the funds were channelled. The accused received these funds through a combination of direct deposits into the Sun Mode Bank Account and cash deliveries arranged through third parties acting at his direction. When questioned by officers from the Commercial Affairs Department ("CAD"), the accused was unable to provide any satisfactory account of how he came by these funds.

Deposits and transfers of moneys by alleged victims

7       The Prosecution's case commenced with evidence from multiple victims who had transferred substantial sums to bank accounts of various companies. I set out the material aspects of these witnesses’ evidence below.

8       The first witness, PW1 Lau Siew Leng [“Mdm Lau”], a housewife, testified that she had been deceived into making cash deposits totalling $6,500 to a UOB account belonging to Sun Mode on 3 July 2020. She testified that she deposited $3,500 at 0850 hours and $3,000 at 1112 hours on 3 July 2020 into UOB account number XXX-XXX-XXX-X, explaining that she believed she was paying "delivery fees" as instructed by someone who claimed that items being sent required delivery fee payments. Her police report dated 7 July 2020 (Exhibit P1) documented these transactions. This document, and the cash deposit receipt (Exhibit P2), corroborated her testimony about the deposits made to the Sun Mode account. Mdm Lau confirmed that she had no prior knowledge of Sun Mode or of the accused and had never conducted any business with either party. When shown the company registration documents for Sun Mode (Exhibit P3), she confirmed she did not recognise the company or its registered director, the accused.

9       The second witness, PW2 Ong Yik Huay [“Mdm Ong”], who worked at a provision shop, provided similar evidence about online deception. She testified that she had been approached for an online friendship and was persuaded to transfer money. Mdm Ong made two cash deposits to the Sun Mode account: $7,000 at Paya Lebar Quarter, followed by an additional $2,000. Her police report dated 7 July 2020 (Exhibit P4) detailed how she was deceived by someone who asked her to transfer money after befriending her online. Like the first witness, Mdm Lau, Mdm Ong also confirmed she had no prior knowledge of Sun Mode or of the accused and had never conducted any business with these parties. When shown the Sun Mode company documents, she similarly confirmed that she did not recognise the company or the accused.

10     The third witness, PW3 Seow Yin Khoi [“Mr Seow”], a retiree, testified about extensive financial losses suffered through a love scam.

(a)     Mr Seow described being deceived by a woman who claimed to need money for purchasing materials and equipment for her business operations. His police report dated 28 August 2020 (Exhibit P5) documented his victimisation and the substantial sums that he had transferred. Mr Seow's transfers were also methodically documented through his bank statements (Exhibits P6 and P7). On 23 July 2020, he transferred $16,000 to BVC’s UOB account. Two days later, on 25 July 2020, he transferred an additional $30,000 to the same BVC account. The bank statements showed these withdrawals from his personal UOB account corresponding to the dates and amounts stated in his police report.

(b)     Mr Seow further testified that on 7 August 2020, he transferred $40,000 to Kunlun’s Maybank account, and on 26 August 2020, he transferred $10,000 to Kunlun’s UOB account. His bank statements corroborated these transactions, showing a total of $96,000 transferred to various corporate accounts over the course of several months.

(c)     When shown the company registration documents of BVC (Exhibit P8) and Kunlun (Exhibit P9), Mr Seow confirmed that he had no knowledge of these companies, their officers, or their business activities prior to making the transfers. He testified that he had never conducted any legitimate business with these entities. Further, when shown the company registration documents for Sun Mode (Exhibit P3), Mr Seow similarly confirmed that he had no prior knowledge of Sun Mode or of the accused, and had never conducted any business dealings with either party.

11     PW5 Lee Wei Sean (“Ms Lee Wei Sean”), a person who assisted a doctor with facial therapy, testified about being defrauded of $25,000. Her police report dated 16 April 2020 (Exhibit P13) documented how she had been deceived and subsequently asked her elder sister to transfer money on her behalf to a Maybank account. The report specifically stated that the transfer was made to pay an "admin fee". This was requested by her online contact. Ms Lee Wei Sean’s evidence was supported by PW6 Lee Wei Siew (“Ms Lee Wei Siew”), an accountant who was Ms Lee Wei Sean's elder sister. Ms Lee Wei Siew confirmed that she had transferred $25,000 to a Maybank account on 15 April 2020 at 1745 hours at her sister's request, as documented in the police report. Both sisters testified that they had no prior knowledge of Pro-Health Water Technologies (“Pro-Health”) (Exhibit P14), Sun Mode, one Chew Soo Yan, or of the accused, and had never conducted any business with these parties.

12     There was a further victim, Mdm Seah Hwee Khin (“Mdm Seah”), who had passed away before the trial and whose police report was admitted in evidence under s 32(1)(j)(i) of the Evidence Act 1893. This was done through the evidence of PW7 Ms Nur Athirah Binte Mohamad Ashmoni [“Ms Nur”], a senior assistant executive from the Registry of Births and Deaths at the Immigration and Checkpoints Authority, who testified that Mdm Seah had passed away on 26 September 2022 from pancreatic cancer. Her death certificate (Exhibit P1(A)) was admitted following a formal ancillary hearing, during which the accused accepted that Mdm Seah had passed away. The Prosecution was thus able to tender Mdm Seah's police report under s 32(1)(j)(i) of the Evidence Act 1893. Mdm Seah’s police report dated 12 October 2020 (Exhibit P15) documented her deposit of $10,000 to Kunlun’s OCBC bank account on 11 September 2020 at 1315 hours.

Money flow connected with the accused

13     Several witnesses gave evidence pertaining to the transfers of money to the accused and their interactions with him. I have summarised the main features of their evidence below.

Evidence of Mr Teo Seng Liang

14     Critical evidence linking the accused to the money flows came from PW4 Teo Seng Liang [“Mr Teo”], a taxi driver who was the registered business owner of Kunlun.

15     Mr Teo testified that he incorporated Kunlun on 26 March 2020 after meeting the accused at the Singapore Expo, where they discussed potential business collaborations involving Indonesian products. The company registration documents (Exhibit P9) confirmed his status as its business owner and the incorporation date of Kunlun.

16     He testified that he allowed the accused to use Kunlun's bank accounts to receive and process funds, believing he was assisting with legitimate trading activities and hoping to earn fees from the accused for doing so. Mr Teo said that all moneys received into Kunlun's accounts were arranged by the accused, and that the accused had assured him the funds came from legitimate sources.[note: 2]

17     Mr Teo provided detailed evidence of three separate transactions supported by bank statements.

(a)     First, he testified that $39,978 was credited to Kunlun's Maybank account, as shown in the bank statement (Exhibit P10). He subsequently withdrew $38,000 in cash on 20 August 2020 and handed it directly to the accused at his residence. The bank statement clearly showed both the credit entry and the corresponding cash withdrawal.[note: 3]

(b)     Second, Mr Teo confirmed that $10,000 was credited to the company's UOB account on 26 August 2020, as documented in the UOB bank statement (Exhibit P11). The statement showed the credit entry with the notation "TRF FRM Mr Seow Yin Khoi", directly linking this deposit to Mr Seow's transfer. Mr Teo testified that the crediting of this money into Kunlun’s account was arranged by the accused. Mr Teo further said that he withdrew this amount in cash the following day and delivered it to the accused at his home.[note: 4]

(c)     Third, Mr Teo testified that $10,000 was deposited into Kunlun’s OCBC account on 11 September 2020, as shown in the OCBC bank statement (Exhibit P12). The statement recorded this as a cash deposit. He immediately withdrew this amount and handed it to the accused.[note: 5]

(d)     Mr Teo testified that the accused had arranged all these money transfers and that he had provided the account numbers for all three bank accounts to the accused. He further testified that the accused had specifically requested him to open the Kunlun Maybank account for the purpose of receiving these funds.[note: 6]

Evidence of Ms Wong Lye Leng Lynn

18     PW7 Wong Lye Leng Lynn [“Ms Wong”] was a witness who had previously worked for Pro-Health. Ms Wong provided detailed evidence about extensive WeChat communications (Exhibits P17 (and Exhibit P17T – the certified translated version)), [note: 7] between herself and one Mr Sun Jian Ping[note: 8], who claimed to be an investor with 15 years of experience at A*STAR and connections to NTU professors.

19     Ms Wong testified that Pro-Health was a legitimate start-up company that had invented a new water treatment machine at Ngee Ann Polytechnic, validated by Enterprise Singapore in 2019. The company was founded by Mr Chew Soo Yan, who had been registered as its director since 20 October 2017. Ms Wong had worked for the company since 2019, selling water filtration systems before joining the water machine project.

20     According to Ms Wong, Mr Sun Jian Ping was introduced to Pro-Health through an NTU professor as a potential investor for their water treatment technology. Mr Sun Jian Ping claimed to have connections to investors and represented himself as having extensive experience in the field. He conducted due diligence by visiting Ngee Ann Polytechnic to examine their water machine and requesting company registration documents and bank account details.

21     Ms Wong testified that Mr Sun Jian Ping arranged a physical meeting between Pro-Health and the accused in March 2020. The meeting took place at the lobby of Bugis Plus Hotel at Bencoolen and subsequently moved to the OG restaurant on the second floor nearby. Present at this meeting were Ms Wong, Mr Chew Soo Yan, Sun Jian Ping, and the accused, whom Mr Sun Jian Ping referred to as "CEO Han".[note: 9] Ms Wong identified the accused in court as the person she met at this meeting.

22     The WeChat communications, produced in court, also revealed an elaborate scheme where Mr Sun Jian Ping, acting on behalf of "CEO Han," instructed Pro-Health to open a US dollar bank account with Maybank for receiving investment funds. Mr Sun Jian Ping provided detailed instructions on how to complete the bank application forms, including specifying the purpose as "buying, selling and investment" and the source of funds as "investors." He even provided the name of a purported major buyer, "Fujian Feiyadi Industry and Trade Development Company," to be included in the application.

(a)     When Pro-Health encountered difficulties opening the US dollar account due to a required $3,000 deposit, Mr Sun Jian Ping shifted the plan to use their existing Singapore dollar corporate account. He promised substantial business deals involving $20.6 million worth of garlic ($3.6 million), disposable masks ($13 million), and water machines ($4 million), with a 50% prepayment of $10.3 million. This occurred during the COVID-19 period when such products were in high demand.

(b)     Mr Sun Jian Ping provided contact details for Indonesian suppliers, including "Super Manggis" and "Rodeo Fresh," and instructed Ms Wong to prepare multiple supply agreements for garlic, disposable masks, and water systems. However, none of these agreements was ever signed by the purported Indonesian parties, and no legitimate business transaction ever materialised.

23     On 15 April 2020, $25,000 was unexpectedly transferred into Pro-Health’s Maybank account from Ms Lee Wei Siew. Ms Wong testified that Mr Sun Jian Ping called repeatedly and urgently to confirm whether this amount had been received, claiming that "CEO Han was rushing every 3 minutes to check on this amount." Ms Wong, however, did not know why the matter was so urgent. The bank statement (Exhibit P16) showing the Maybank account transactions, confirmed this transfer from Ms Lee Wei Siew.[note: 10]

24     Mr Sun Jian Ping then instructed Pro-Health to immediately transfer $23,750 to Sun Mode Bank Account, claiming this was a service fee payment. When Ms Wong questioned the purpose of these transactions, Mr Sun Jian Ping explained that Ms Lee Wei Siew was paying consultation fees to Pro-Health for water systems and water treatment services related to an Indonesian water project, and that Pro-Health would pay service fees to Sun Mode as a trading company representative.[note: 11]

25     Ms Wong prepared consultation agreements and invoices for Ms Lee Wei Siew's purported $25,000 consultation fee, but these documents were never finalised or signed. No actual consultation services were ever provided to Lee Wei Siew.[note: 12] When Sun Jian Ping later instructed another transfer of $4,275 to Sun Mode, the transaction could not be completed because Pro-Health’s Maybank account was frozen by the police.

26     Ms Wong testified that on 30 April 2020, Mr Chew Soo Yan, Mr Sun Jian Ping and she were summoned to Cantonment Police Station by PW15 Station Inspector Tan Hong Seng ["SI Tan"], who informed them that the money they had received was from romance scam victims and ordered them to return the funds immediately. The accused did not attend. Mr Sun Jian Ping claimed that "CEO Han" could not attend due to a hospital appointment.[note: 13]

27     After the meeting with the police on 30 April 2020, Ms Wong testified that Mr Sun Jian Ping sent further messages attempting to influence how Pro-Health should characterise the transactions to the police. Specifically, Mr Sun Jian Ping instructed Pro-Health to write a memorandum stating that the $23,750 transferred to Sun Mode was Pro-Health's own pre-investment in an Indonesian water treatment project, which it now wished to withdraw, so that Mr Sun Jian Ping could then return the amount to the victim as the police had instructed. Ms Wong testified that she pushed back against this, telling Mr Sun Jian Ping that if the $23,750 was said to be from Pro-Health, this was inconsistent with the company's financial position, as they could not even afford an $800 ticket to Wuhan, let alone funds to invest in Indonesia. Notwithstanding this, Mr Sun Jian Ping continued to send messages asking Pro-Health to present the transactions as a normal business dealing when speaking to the police, so as not to affect future business. Ms Wong further testified that in Mr Sun Jian Ping's subsequent messages, he claimed to have introduced "CEO Han" to Pro-Health to assist with their water treatment project, and that "CEO Han" had set up a company in Indonesia and acquired land for Pro-Health's water treatment technology projects. Mr Sun Jian Ping further conveyed that "CEO Han" was angry that Pro-Health had gone to the police station and placed responsibility on him. Ms Wong testified that Mr Sun Jian Ping continued to send messages asking Pro-Health not to say anything further, referring to pages 211 onwards of the WeChat messages.[note: 14]

Evidence of Madam Yeo Chor Cher and Ms Edna Lee

28     The evidence from PW9 Madam Yeo Chor Cher [“Mdm Yeo”], director and shareholder of BVC, provided further corroboration of the accused's receipt of the moneys the subject of the third charge. Mdm Yeo testified that she had previous dealings with the accused regarding trading in agricultural products, seafood, and other commodities, though no successful transaction had ever been completed.

29     Mdm Yeo explained that the accused had proposed that her company's bank account be used to receive payments from buyers, explaining that he had no accountant while BVC had accounting staff, and that buyers would deposit money into her company's account for purchasing goods from Indonesia. She could retain a service fee of 5% to 10% for facilitating these transactions. Mdm Yeo thus provided BVC’s bank account details to the accused accordingly.[note: 15]

30     On 23 July 2020, $16,000 was transferred into BVC’s UOB account from one Seow Yin Khoi, followed by $30,000 on 25 July 2020 from the same source. Mdm Yeo testified that the accused had informed her by telephone that buyers would be depositing money to purchase seafood from Indonesia. She was told that Indonesians would be coming to collect the cash for purchasing goods.[note: 16]

31     On 27 July 2020, Mdm Yeo and her accountant Ms Edna Lee withdrew $43,700 in cash from the UOB bank branch near Fu Lu Shou Complex. The withdrawal was made using multiple cheques to avoid the $5,000 limit requiring two signatures, as they needed to withdraw the cash urgently. Mdm Yeo testified that she immediately handed this cash to the accused at Fu Lu Shou, as he had claimed that Indonesians were nearby and needed to collect the money immediately for purchasing goods.[note: 17]

32     Subsequent WhatsApp messages between Mdm Yeo and the accused, admitted as Exhibit P21 (and Exhibit P21T – the certified translated version)[note: 18], revealed the aftermath of these transactions. After police contacted Mdm Yeo informing her that the money received was "not clean," she repeatedly messaged the accused demanding either delivery of the promised goods or return of the money. These messages showed Mdm Yeo's growing concern as she was told by police that the money needed to be returned to the victims, and her unsuccessful attempts to get the accused to respond to her demands.[note: 19]

33     During cross-examination of Mdm Yeo, in relation to the present charges, the accused challenged Mdm Yeo only on the payment voucher, stating that he had not signed it and seldom visited the UOB branch at Fu Lu Shou Complex. However, Mdm Yeo maintained her evidence that she had handed the cash to the accused outside the UOB bank at Fu Lu Shou Complex.[note: 20]

34     Mdm Yeo’s evidence was largely corroborated by the evidence of PW14 Lee Hui Hoon Edna [“Ms Edna Lee”], who had worked at the same Burlington Square office as Mdm Yeo from 2018 to 2021. Ms Edna Lee testified as to the cash withdrawal and handover on 27 July 2020, and said that Mdm Yeo had asked her to withdraw $43,700 from the UOB bank branch at Fu Lu Shou Complex. Ms Edna Lee confirmed that she withdrew the money first and waited at the bank for Mdm Yeo to arrive. When both Mdm Yeo and the accused arrived at approximately the same time, the three of them stood at a corner near the bank's ATM area, where Mdm Yeo handed the cash to the accused. Ms Edna Lee witnessed Mdm Yeo asking the accused to sign a voucher as acknowledgement of receiving the money.[note: 21]

Evidence of Mr Chew Soo Yan

35     PW8 Mr Chew Soo Yan (“Mr Chew Soo Yan”), the founder and sole director of Pro-Health, provided detailed testimony about how his company became involved with the accused through the intermediary Mr Sun Jian Ping.

36     Mr Chew Soo Yan testified that Pro-Health was a legitimate start-up company that had co-developed a water treatment machine with Ngee Ann Polytechnic under an Enterprise Singapore grant. The company faced financial difficulties in paying outstanding amounts to Ngee Ann Polytechnic before the machine could be released. It was in this vulnerable state that Mr Sun Jian Ping approached them, claiming to be a former A*STAR researcher with 20 years of experience and connections to potential investors.

37     On 14 March 2020, Mr Sun Jian Ping arranged a meeting between Pro-Health and the accused. The meeting began at the lobby of Bugis Plus Hotel at Bencoolen and subsequently moved to the OG restaurant on the second floor nearby. Present at this meeting were Mr Chew Soo Yan, Ms Wong, Mr Sun Jian Ping, and the accused, whom Mr Sun Jian Ping referred to as "CEO Han."[note: 22] This was the first time Mr Chew Soo Yan had met the accused, though he subsequently met him on three or four further occasions at the same Bencoolen location.

38     Following this initial meeting, Mr Sun Jian Ping instructed Pro-Health to provide their Maybank bank account details, ostensibly for receiving investment funds for their water treatment project. [note: 23] Mr Sun Jian Ping claimed that the accused had projects in Indonesia and Sumatra requiring water treatment technology, and that substantial business deals worth millions of dollars were in prospect.

39     On 15 April 2020, $25,000 was unexpectedly transferred into Pro-Health’s Maybank account from Ms Lee Wei Siew. Mr Chew Soo Yan testified that Mr Sun Jian Ping contacted him to ask whether his company had received this amount.[note: 24]

40     Mr Sun Jian Ping then instructed Pro-Health to immediately transfer $23,750 to Sun Mode Bank Account, claiming this was a service fee payment to Sun Mode as a trading company representative, and that the accused needed this money urgently.[note: 25] Mr Chew Soo Yan complied with this instruction. When Mr Chew Soo Yan inquired about the source and purpose of this money, Mr Sun Jian Ping explained that Ms Lee Wei Siew was paying consultation fees to Pro-Health, and Pro-Health paid a service fee to Sun Mode. However, no actual consultation services were ever provided to Ms Lee Wei Siew, and Sun Mode did not provide any services to Pro-Health. No consultancy agreement was ever executed.[note: 26]

41     A second payment of $4,500 was received on 20 April 2020, and Mr Sun Jian Ping again instructed Mr Chew Soo Yan to transfer $4,275 to Sun Mode. However, this second transfer could not be completed because Pro-Health’s account was frozen.[note: 27]

42     When Mr Chew Soo Yan inquired at Maybank about the account freeze, he received an SMS from the CAD Anti-scam centre directing him to report to the Cantonment Police Station. At the police station, SI Tan informed Mr Chew Soo Yan, Ms Wong, and Mr Sun Jian Ping that the money they had received was from romance scam victims and ordered them to return the funds immediately. At that meeting, SI Tan asked Mr Chew Soo Yan to whom he had given his bank account, and he replied that he only gave it to Mr Sun Jian Ping. Then Mr Sun Jian Ping, who was also there, said that he gave the same bank account to the accused.[note: 28]

43     After the police meeting, Mr Sun Jian Ping also sent Mr Chew Soo Yan a message asking him to tell the police that this was a normal commercial transaction and to avoid saying anything that could not be proven, stating that if this was done, future business would not be affected.[note: 29]

44     Mr Chew Soo Yan also said that SI Tan had issued two letters addressed to the accused and to Sun Mode, informing the accused of the police's concerns regarding the two sums of money deposited into Pro-Health’s account and requesting him to attend an interview. Mr Chew Soo Yan and Ms Wong accompanied Mr Sun Jian Ping to a meeting with the accused outside Bugis Plus Hotel at Bencoolen, where Mr Sun Jian Ping passed the letters to the accused. The accused read the letters but refused to accept them, passing them back to Mr Sun Jian Ping. When Mr Chew Soo Yan informed the accused that SI Tan required the $23,750 to be returned, the accused acknowledged this and said that he needed time to arrange a transfer of funds from Indonesia to make the repayment. Through Mr Sun Jian Ping, the accused also requested that Mr Chew Soo Yan prepare a withdrawal memorandum to facilitate this transfer. Mr Sun Jian Ping then sent Mr Chew Soo Yan a draft withdrawal memorandum by PDF and instructed him to amend, sign and return it. The memorandum stated that the $23,750 transferred to Sun Mode was Pro-Health's investment in an Indonesian water treatment project at Padang, Sumatra, which Pro-Health now wished to withdraw on account of financial difficulties.[note: 30]However, the accused never returned the $23,750. A cheque for this amount issued by Sun Mode was received by Mr Chew Soo Yan but, on Mr Sun Jian Ping's instructions, was never banked in, and was subsequently returned to Mr Sun Jian Ping at a further meeting at Bencoolen on 27 May 2020. The $23,750 was never recovered by Pro-Health.[note: 31]

45     During cross-examination, Mr Chew Soo Yan maintained his evidence despite the accused's challenges on the meeting locations and business arrangements. In particular, Mr Chew Soo Yan consistently maintained that he had met the accused four to five times at Bencoolen locations.[note: 32]

Evidence of Mr Sun Jian Ping

46     PW16 Mr Sun Jian Ping (“Mr Sun Jian Ping”) is a retired senior research engineer who worked at A*STAR for 20 years before retiring in July 2016. He testified that he came to know the accused around 2018 through a social introduction by mutual friends, and that the accused had told him he had previously served in the Singapore Police Force and had worked in Indonesia for a long time doing trading in seafood and agricultural products. Mr Sun Jian Ping knew that the accused had a company named Sun Mode but he did not know what Sun Mode did or the accused’s role in Sun Mode.[note: 33]

47     Mr Sun Jian Ping testified that he made a small investment of S$18,000 in Sun Mode sometime between 2018 and 2019, after the accused proposed that they cooperate on trading activities involving Indonesian products. However, no trading activity ever materialised and he received no returns on his investment, and the investment has not been returned to him.

48     Mr Sun Jian Ping came to know Mr Chew Soo Yan around 2020 through a mutual acquaintance at a law firm in Chinatown. He testified that Mr Chew Soo Yan was conducting research using his own funds on a water treatment machine co-developed with Ngee Ann Polytechnic, and that Mr Chew Soo Yan needed approximately S$30,000 to pay Ngee Ann Polytechnic before the machine could be released to him. After various attempts to raise funds through other channels failed, Mr Sun Jian Ping mentioned Mr Chew Soo Yan's situation to the accused. The accused expressed interest in the project, and Mr Sun Jian Ping arranged a meeting between them at a café at the second level of OG near the Goddess of Mercy temple at Waterloo Street. Also present at this meeting were a lady [Ms Wong] and Mr Sun Jian Ping himself. Mr Sun Jian Ping said that he did not pay close attention to what was discussed at the meeting.[note: 34] I note that Mr Sun Jian Ping's description of the meeting location — a café at the second level of OG near the Goddess of Mercy temple at Waterloo Street — differed from Mr Chew Soo Yan's description of the same meeting as having commenced at the lobby of Bugis Plus Hotel at Bencoolen before moving to the OG restaurant on the second floor nearby. Nothing material turns on this discrepancy, as both witnesses were consistent on the substance of what was discussed and agreed at the meeting.

49     Following this meeting, Mr Sun Jian Ping became the conduit for passing messages between the accused and Pro-Health, primarily through Ms Wong. He testified that he did not know the specific reason why the accused and Mr Chew Soo Yan could not communicate directly, but speculated that the accused's physical condition may have made long-distance travel difficult.[note: 35] Mr Sun Jian Ping confirmed that the WeChat communications in Exhibit P17 comprised his messages with Ms Wong at pages 162 to 209, and his messages with Mr Chew Soo Yan were at pages 210 to 216.[note: 36]

50     Mr Sun Jian Ping testified that through him, the accused instructed Mr Chew Soo Yan's company to open a US dollar Maybank account for receiving remittance. The accused provided the name of a purported major buyer, Fujian Feiyadi Industry and Trade Development Company, to be included in the Maybank account application. The accused further instructed Mr Sun Jian Ping to convey to Mr Chew Soo Yan that the trading scope should be expanded to include garlic and disposable masks in addition to water systems, and supply agreements for all three items were prepared by Ms Wong at the accused's direction and conveyed to the accused through Mr Sun Jian Ping.[note: 37]

51     Mr Sun Jian Ping said that on 15 April 2020 the accused had asked him to check with Ms Wong on whether S$25,000 had been credited into Pro-Health's Maybank account. Mr Sun Jian Ping confirmed that while there was no direct record of the accused making this request, based on logical deduction, it was the accused who had asked him to make this inquiry, as he himself would have had no reason to do so. He did not know what this sum of $25,000 was for. The accused repeatedly chased for confirmation that the sum had been received into the Pro-Health account, but Mr Sun Jian Ping did not ask the accused what the urgency was about.[note: 38]

52     Shortly afterwards, the accused instructed Mr Sun Jian Ping to tell Ms Wong to immediately transfer S$23,750 to the Sun Mode Bank Account. Mr Sun Jian Ping confirmed that this was the accused's company's bank account, as the bank information provided by the accused bore the name "Sun Mode." Mr Sun Jian Ping testified that he did not know the purpose of this transfer and did not ask the accused, as he did not wish to be involved too deeply in the business between the accused and Mr Chew Soo Yan.[note: 39] He further conveyed to Mr Chew Soo Yan the accused's answer that the arrangement was that Ms Lee Wei Siew had paid a consultation fee to Pro-Health, and Pro-Health was paying a service fee to Sun Mode as an Asian trade agency representative company.[note: 40]

53     A second sum of S$4,500 was subsequently received into Pro-Health's account, and the accused again instructed Mr Sun Jian Ping to tell Mr Chew Soo Yan to transfer S$4,275 to Sun Mode.[note: 41] However, this transfer could not be completed because Pro-Health's bank account was frozen by the police. 60     The Sun Mode statement (Exhibit P22) showed cash deposits totalling $15,500 from victims Mdm Lau and Mdm Ong Yik Huay, relating to the first charge, and the Sun Mode statement (Exhibit P23) showed the $23,750 GIRO transfer from Pro-Health credited on 16 April 2020, relating to the fourth charge.

This relates to the moneys handed to the accused by Mr Teo, which forms part of the second charge.

63     PW17 ASP Suraya Binte Kasman ("ASP Suraya"), who retired from the Singapore Police Force on 31 January 2026 after serving with the CAD since October 2008, gave evidence in her capacity as the investigation officer who had taken over the case from her predecessor. ASP Suraya testified that she had facilitated the administrative aspects of the case, including preparing the fourth and final charge for service on the accused, and that she had met the accused on one occasion for this purpose, accompanied by PW13 ASP Nick Lie Daicheng ["ASP Nick"], who served the charge in Mandarin.

64     ASP Suraya also testified that she had conducted ACRA screenings of the relevant entities through an internal CAD system linked to the ACRA database, and that she had done so on 5 December 2025 in preparation for the first tranche of the trial. The accused did not raise any valid objection to the admissibility of any of these documents, and did not challenge ASP Suraya's evidence in any material respect during cross-examination.

Long statements of the accused recorded by SI Tan

65     SI Tan, who was at the material time on loan to the CAD's Transnational Commercial Crime Task Force, testified that he recorded two long statements from the accused: the first on 14 October 2020 (Exhibit P28), and the second on 10 August 2021 (Exhibit P29), in the course of investigating a series of love scam cases in which victims had transferred money to various bank accounts connected to the accused. The statements were recorded in Mandarin and typed in English. SI Tan confirmed that he made various handwritten amendments to both statements during the recording process, with the accused's knowledge and acknowledgement of each amendment by signature, and that the accused did not make any complaints during or after the statement recording.[note: 51]

66     In Exhibit P28, the accused admitted, amongst other things, that: (a) he was the director of Sun Mode; and (b) he did not know who Mr Chew Soo Yan of Pro-Health was, but that Mr Chew Soo Yan had been introduced to him by his "China friend", Mr Sun Jian Ping. The accused had claimed that the $25,000 deposited into Pro-Health's bank account and subsequently transferred to the Sun Mode Bank Account was sent by him to Indonesia to develop land. He further claimed that the money deposited into BVC's bank account and handed to him by Mdm Yeo at the Fu Lu Shou UOB branch was for buying fish from Indonesia.

67     SI Tan issued a production order dated 27 July 2021 (Exhibit P30) requiring the accused to furnish documents relating to specific transactions. In the second statement recorded on 10 August 2021 (Exhibit P29), the accused said that he was unable to provide the invoices from his suppliers (except for those that his girlfriend had sent to him) sought in the production order and that his company’s records were in a mess. He further claimed not to keep any of his company’s records in Singapore, and denied having told Mr Teo to delete the messages that they had previously exchanged.

68     During cross-examination, the accused denied ever meeting SI Tan and claimed that the statements were not made by him. The accused also alleged that a Malay police officer had threatened to close his accounts if he did not cooperate fully, but SI Tan denied this. SI Tan maintained that he was the officer who recorded both statements from the accused, and that proper procedures were followed throughout. I note that the accused did not, at any point during SI Tan's cross-examination, allege that SI Tan had threatened him into making the statement recorded as Exhibit P28 by stating that he could not leave and could not see a doctor unless he signed. The latter allegation was raised for the first time during the accused's own cross-examination at Day 12 and will be addressed below.

Cautioned Statements of the accused recorded in 2024

ASP Nick confirmed that he conducted all statement recordings in Mandarin, notwithstanding that the formal documentation indicated that interpretation was provided from English to Mandarin.

As he wrote down each response, ASP Nick would simultaneously verbalise what he was writing to the accused in Mandarin, so that the accused could confirm the accuracy of each sentence as it was recorded.[note: 52] The accused was permitted to read each statement before signing.

For the fourth cautioned statement recorded on 28 February 2024, the location was changed from the intended level 4 interview room to the Bukit Merah East Neighbourhood Police Centre on the ground floor of Police Cantonment Complex Tower D, as the accused did not wish to take the lift upstairs. ASP Nick served photocopies of all four cautioned statements to the accused upon completion of all four recording sessions.

72     During cross-examination, the accused challenged ASP Nick's evidence by claiming he had been told to sign documents before being allowed to see a doctor, and that a Malay ASP had been present during the statement recording process and had brought him water and medicine. ASP Nick denied these allegations, and confirmed that no other person was present in the interview room during the statement recordings.[note: 53]

73     As regards the contents of the cautioned statements, the accused stated the following in response to the allegations pertaining to each charge:

(a)     As regards the first charge involving the possession of the $15,500 in Sun Mode Bank Account ( 2 to 3 July 2020), the accused claimed that he was not aware of the existence of three of the four sums of money that constituted the $15,500. (b)     For the second charge involving the possession of the $58,000 in cash from Teo Seng Liang (August to September 2020), the accused admitted that he received the two sums of money from Mr Teo through his lawyer, as he claimed that Mr Teo owed him money. However, the accused said that he did not know that these two sums of moneys were “dirty monies”.

However, he said that the company that Mr Chew Soo Yan worked for owed the accused money related to their business transactions. The accused also said that he did not verify the source of the moneys.

Challenge to the admissibility of the statement recorded by SI Hafit

74     Aside from the statements recorded by SI Tan and ASP Nick, there was another statement recorded on 16 September 2019 by PW18 Station Inspector Hafit Bin Ismail (“SI Hafit”). At the time of the statement recording, SI Hafit held the rank of Senior Staff Sergeant.

75     The accused challenged the admissibility of all the statements recorded from him during the investigation.

76     The accused's position was that the contents of the statements did not come from him, which went to the issue of accuracy rather than voluntariness. As no issue of involuntariness arose, no ancillary hearing was required under section 279(1)(d) of the Criminal Procedure Code 2010 (“CPC”), and these six statements were accordingly admitted into evidence.

77     However, in respect of the long statement recorded on 16 September 2019 (initially marked Exhibit P32i for identification), which was recorded by SI Hafit, the accused raised a challenge related to voluntariness. The accused's position was that: (a) the contents of the statement did not come from him; (b) the pages were largely blank or contained different contents when he signed, though his account of the state of each page shifted materially during his evidence; and (c) his signatures had been obtained involuntarily in that he alleged that a male Chinese officer, in the presence of a Malay female superior officer, had told him he would only be permitted to seek medical attention after signing the document. He further alleged that throughout the process, he had been accompanied by a separate figure, namely an elderly retired Malay male officer who had not given evidence in court, and that he had signed because he was anxious to go to the hospital and trusted that investigation officers would not act improperly.[note: 54]An ancillary hearing was accordingly convened. I have set out the evidence adduced during the ancillary hearing and my findings in relation to the admission of this statement.

Evidence and submissions

78     The Prosecution called three witnesses for the purposes of the ancillary hearing.

79     SI Hafit, the statement recorder, and the interpreter AH-PW2A, former Inspector Foo Kum Wai (“Insp Foo”), gave consistent evidence on all material points. Both confirmed that the statement was recorded on 16 September 2019, with the accused speaking in a mixture of English and Mandarin, at the CAD, and that no other person, including any Malay female officer or Chinese male officer, was present during the statement recording. SI Hafit further confirmed that the accused's signatures were appended at the end of the statement recording, after the statement had been read back to the accused through Insp Foo, and that the accused was invited to make any amendments before signing. Insp Foo confirmed that SI Hafit had administered the warning, which he had translated into Mandarin for the accused, and that the accused had acknowledged it. Both SI Hafit and Insp Foo confirmed that no inducement, threat or promise was made to the accused, and that the accused had signed the statement voluntarily.[note: 55]

80     ASP Nick also gave evidence on two matters. First, that the accused was placed under arrest on only one occasion, namely 29 January 2024, and the bail bond executed on that date (Exhibit P34) was the only bail bond ever executed in relation to the accused, in relation to his arrest on that date. Aside from this arrest, the accused was not arrested on any other date.[note: 56] ASP Nick also confirmed that the only documents the accused ever signed in connection with the investigations were his statements, any acknowledgement slips for seized exhibits, and the bail bond executed on 29 January 2024. No document was signed by the accused in 2023. Second, ASP Nick denied the accused's specific allegations that he had told the accused that unless he pleaded guilty, they would not release him, and that a bailor would only be called to sign the bail bond upon the accused pleading guilty.[note: 57]

81     The accused gave evidence as AH-DW1. He confirmed that the signatures on the statement (Exhibit P32i) were his but raised two substantive challenges: first, that the contents did not come from him and/or were not there when he signed; and second, that his signatures had been obtained involuntarily in that he alleged that a young male Chinese officer had told him he would only be permitted to seek medical attention after signing the document. He further alleged that the pages were largely blank or contained different contents when he signed, and that he had done so because he was anxious to go to the hospital and trusted that investigation officers would not act improperly.[note: 58] The accused also alleged that throughout the process, he had been accompanied by an elderly retired Malay male officer who was not SI Hafit and who had not given evidence in court. He further alleged that when he asked a lady officer about the purpose of the signatures, the male officer told him the signatures were merely to confirm that an interpretation had been provided to him.

82     At the end of the evidence-giving stage of the ancillary hearing, the Prosecution submitted that Exhibit P32i ought to be admitted on two grounds.

83     First, no inducement, threat or promise had been made to the accused. His claim that he signed the statement quickly to obtain medical attention amounted to self-inducement at best, and he had, in any event, confirmed during cross-examination that he had not been subject to any inducement, threat or promise. His allegations that the statement did not reflect what he had signed, or that he had not made it at all, went to accuracy rather than voluntariness, were unparticularised, and were inconsistent with SI Hafit’s and Insp Foo’s evidence.

84     Second, and in the alternative, even if there had been some form of inducement, threat or promise, the accused had not established any causal link between such conduct and the making of the statement. Moreover, the accused had been unable to identify any of the Malay officers he described when shown the relevant photo board, and ASP Nick's evidence that the accused had only ever been arrested once — on 29 January 2024 — directly contradicted the accused's claim that he had signed a document under duress in 2023.

85     As for the accused, he maintained that he had not given any statement to the recording officers. He claimed that he had attended the CAD on the first occasion merely to assist with a case, and that on a second occasion, a male police officer had threatened to close down all his accounts. He stated that he had sought to leave as he was unwell but was told he needed a bailor before he could do so, that a retired or near-retired Malay officer had accompanied him throughout, and that upon leaving, he had gone directly to the hospital where he remained for approximately three to four days.

My findings on the admissibility of Exhibit P32

86     I rejected the accused's challenges to the admissibility of Exhibit P32.

87     First, the accused placed the alleged inducement in 2023, yet the statement was undisputedly recorded on 16 September 2019, a date confirmed consistently by both SI Hafit and Insp Foo. The accused offered no credible explanation for how a statement dated 16 September 2019 and bearing his signatures could have been signed in 2023. Further, when shown the photo board of Malay officers attached to the Transnational Commercial Crime Task Force from 2020 to 2023 (Exhibit P33), the accused was unable to identify any officer as the Malay superior he had described. Since the accused himself placed the alleged inducement in 2023, the photo board's coverage of that period was directly relevant, and his failure to identify any officer on it further undermined his account.

88     Second, the bail bond evidence directly contradicted the accused's account. The accused was placed under arrest on only one occasion, on 29 January 2024, and no bail bond was ever executed in connection with any statement recording in 2023.

89     Third, I rejected the accused's specific allegations against ASP Nick. ASP Nick denied them clearly and consistently, and his role as lead investigation officer who took over only after ASP Suraya's retirement meant he was not involved in the recording of the statement on 16 September 2019. The allegations were therefore not only denied but also inconsistent with the established facts of the investigation.

90     Fourth, despite having made specific allegations about a retired ASP and a Malay female superior officer throughout the ancillary hearing, the accused was expressly invited to call witnesses in connection with the statement at the conclusion of the ancillary hearing, but declined to do so. No witness was called to support any of these allegations. This further undermined his account.

91     Fifth, I accepted the evidence of SI Hafit and Insp Foo that no inducement, threat or promise was made and that the accused had signed the statement voluntarily. Their evidence was consistent with each other and was not shaken in cross-examination. I further noted that SI Hafit’s evidence in the main trial confirmed that the accused's signatures were obtained for specific and distinct purposes — to acknowledge the warning administered to him, to confirm the contents of the statement, and to confirm that the statement was true and correct. This directly contradicted the accused's claim in re-examination that he had been told the signature was merely to confirm interpretation.

92     Sixth, the accused proved himself an inconsistent witness whose evidence kept changing and whose claims could not be believed. For one, his account was internally inconsistent in several material respects. He initially denied ever having met SI Hafit, yet confirmed that the signatures on the statement were his. When asked whether the statement was one of the documents put in front of him for signature, he first said it was not, then confirmed that it was. His description of the officers involved shifted materially: he initially described the Malay officer as a young female superior,[note: 59] but later referred to an elderly retired Malay male officer.[note: 60] Further, during the ancillary hearing, the accused's account of the contents of the statement when he signed also shifted. He initially said the pages were blank when he signed, but when pressed page by page, he said there were "some contents" on the first page, "not so many things" on pages 2 and 3, and that the words on page 4 were there, but the other two signatures were not. His account of page 5 was similarly inconsistent: he first said the words and numbers were not there when he signed, but then said "these things were already there" before reverting to saying the printed words did not exist. In addition, during re-examination, he had stated that a "retired officer" had accompanied him throughout the entire process and that a "lady officer" had been present, to whom he had directed a question about the purpose of the signature, and claimed that the male officer had told him the signature was merely to confirm interpretation.[note: 61] These further details were inconsistent with his earlier account and were also not put to SI Hafit or Insp Foo during cross-examination.

93     Finally, and most significantly, during cross-examination, the accused agreed that he had not been subject to any inducement, threat or promise in relation to the recording of the statement. Specifically, when asked by the Prosecution whether he agreed that he was not subject to any inducement, threat or promise in relation to the recording of the statement at tab 1, the accused replied "Agree."[note: 62] His only qualification concerned the signing procedure, which went to accuracy at most and not to voluntariness. Further, whatever the accused may have assumed about whether the officers would record his statement properly, such a self-induced assumption did not emanate from any person in authority and cannot, as a matter of law, constitute an inducement, threat or promise rendering the statement involuntary.

94     For these reasons, I found that Exhibit P32i was given by the accused voluntarily and that it was his statement. This exhibit was accordingly admitted into evidence as Exhibit P32.

95     In Exhibit P32, the accused confirmed that he was the director of Sun Mode, that UOB bank account number XXX-XXX-XXX-X was his company's bank account, and that he remained in control of the account and its ATM card. At Question 11, the accused was expressly informed that funds received in his bank account were derived from fraudulent activities, was advised of the risk of receiving moneys from foreign sources where he had no prior relationship with the sender, and was specifically warned to refrain from receiving or dealing with funds from unknown and/or dubious sources, which acts may render him liable to Prosecution under the Penal Code and/or the CDSA. The accused confirmed that he understood this warning and signed the statement voluntarily. Notably, this warning was administered some seven months before the earliest offence in April 2020.

96     With the admission of Exhibit P32, the Prosecution closed its case. Thereafter, having considered the evidence adduced by the Prosecution, I was satisfied that there was sufficient evidence against the accused to require him to give his defence. I accordingly called upon the accused to enter his defence.

Overview of the Defence’s Case

97     The accused elected to give evidence and was the only witness called for the defence. In summary, the accused claimed ignorance of the receipt of moneys, and essentially offered no defence to the first charge, made a bare denial of the second charge, and gave explanations for the third and fourth charges that contradicted his own investigative statements. Further, in his examination-in-chief, the accused made wide-ranging allegations against several witnesses. He alleged that Mr Teo was involved in money laundering and had exploited his knowledge of the accused's international trading business, and that Mdm Yeo was similarly involved in money laundering and had dealings with a China state-linked entity called "Mayflower." He also alleged that Mr Sun Jian Ping had connections to China's public security apparatus and could not be trusted. Notably, these allegations were not put to the respective witnesses during cross-examination. Further, the accused did not produce any evidence to support any of his various accounts. I elaborate on material aspects of his testimony in the paragraphs that follow.

98     At the outset, I note that the accused testified that he had never met most of the Prosecution witnesses. For some of the female witnesses who testified, his account was that they were deceived by love scammers and that he was not the one who cheated them of their money, and the scamming had nothing to do with him.[note: 63] Regarding Sun Mode, the accused testified that this was his company, which he had incorporated for trading purposes. He admitted during cross-examination that he had control over the Sun Mode Bank Account.[note: 64]

99     The accused also gave more detailed evidence about some of the witnesses who testified.

He further claimed that it was Mr Teo who had sought his assistance by asking him to accompany him to the Cantonment Police Complex for a police interview, at which a Chinese male ASP had provided the accused with a name list of accounts with dealings, which the accused said he returned two days later with full details of all his business transactions. The accused insinuated that Mr Teo's own lawyer had cautioned him against making unguarded statements.[note: 65]

101    In relation to Mdm Yeo Chor Cher, the accused acknowledged having known her for close to 30 years and referred to her as "Winnie." The accused claimed that it was Mdm Yeo who had approached him to borrow money and had sought his assistance with various business ventures, all of which he said he had either rejected or discontinued.[note: 66]

102    The accused admitted knowing Mr Sun Jian Ping, stating that he had known him for about 15 years, and that he had helped Mr Sun Jian Ping, although they did not have monetary dealings.[note: 67]

103    When cross-examined on his charges, the accused’s responses can be summarised as follows:

(a)     For the first charge involving the possession of the $15,500 in the Sun Mode Bank Account (2–3 July 2020), the accused's evidence on this charge was incoherent and persistently inconsistent. He gave shifting accounts as to whether he had received the moneys at all and was unable to reconcile his oral evidence with his cautioned statement Exhibit P24. (b)     For the second charge involving the possession of $58,000 in cash from Teo Seng Liang (August–September 2020), the accused denied receiving $58,000 in cash from Mr Teo, asserting instead that it was Mr Teo who owed him money. His oral evidence was irreconcilable with his cautioned statement Exhibit P25, in which he had stated that he had received two sums of money from Mr Teo through his lawyer. When confronted with Exhibit P25, the accused equivocally accepted at one point that he had received money from Mr Teo through a lawyer, whom he subsequently described as a retired ASP, before reverting to saying he did not know if he had received this, and then saying that he did not know how much he had received.
