When asked how he could have instructed Mr Sun Jian Ping to represent to Ms Wong that Ms Lee Wei Siew had paid a consultation fee to Pro-Health if he had no knowledge of Ms Lee Wei Siew, he gave no answer.[note: 76]

Elements of the Charge

104    From the wording of the provision, the core elements of a charge under section 47AA(1) of the CDSA are as follows:

(a)     the person (A) possesses any property;

(b)     the property may be reasonably suspected of being, or of in whole or in part, directly or indirectly, representing, benefits from criminal conduct; and

(c)     A fails to account satisfactorily for how he came by the property.

105    I broadly agree with the Prosecution’s analysis of the elements of each charge,[note: 77] which I will elaborate on below.

106    Turning to element (a) of a charge under this provision:

(a)     The term "property" is defined in s 2(1) of the CDSA to mean "money and all other property, movable or immovable, including things in action and other intangible or incorporeal property". It is well established that the right to moneys standing in a bank account constitutes a thing in action: Skandinaviska Enskilda Banken AB (Publ), Singapore Branch v Asia Pacific Breweries (Singapore) Pte Ltd and another and another suit [2009] 4 SLR(R) 788 at [335]. In the present case, the moneys received by the accused and deposited into the Sun Mode Bank Account therefore fell squarely within the statutory definition of "property" in the CDSA.

(b)     As for the term "possesses", s 2(1) of the CDSA defines "possession", in relation to any property, to mean actual and constructive possession of the property. The word "possesses" as used in s 47AA(1) bears the same meaning. This follows from s 2(2) of the Interpretation Act (Cap 1, 2002 Rev Ed), which provides that where a word is defined in a written law, other grammatical forms of that word carry corresponding meanings unless a contrary intention appears. No such contrary intention is discernible from the CDSA. Indeed, the structural parallels between ss 46(3) and 47(3) of the CDSA, which employ the phrase "possession of … such property", and s 47AA(1), which uses the phrase "possesses … any property", reinforce the conclusion that both formulations are intended to carry the same meaning. I accordingly find that "possesses" in s 47AA(1) encompasses constructive possession, which I agree with the Prosecution, means the exercise of “control or dominion over property without actual physical possession or custody of it”[note: 78].

107    As regards element (b):

(a)     The phrase "criminal conduct" is defined in s 2(1) of the CDSA to mean "doing or being concerned in, whether in Singapore or elsewhere, any act constituting a serious offence or a foreign serious offence". A "serious offence" includes an offence of cheating,[note: 79] such as that perpetrated against each victim of a love scam in this case. Moneys scammed from victims would accordingly constitute "benefits from criminal conduct".

(b)     I also agreed with the Prosecution that the test for whether property "may be reasonably suspected of being benefits from criminal conduct" is purely objective. My reasons are as follows:

(i)       The provision uses the phrase "any property that may be reasonably suspected of being" benefits from criminal conduct, as opposed to requiring that the accused himself "reasonably suspects" the property of being such. To require the accused to have subjectively suspected the property would render otiose the distinction between s 47AA(1) and s 47(3) of the CDSA. The latter provision makes it an offence for a person to possess property which he knows or has reasonable grounds to believe constitutes benefits from criminal conduct, and carries a maximum punishment of a fine not exceeding S$500,000 or imprisonment not exceeding 10 years or both (s 47(6)(a) of the CDSA). By contrast, s 47AA(1) carries a lower maximum punishment of a fine not exceeding S$150,000 or imprisonment not exceeding three years or both (s 47AA(2)(a) of the CDSA). This graduated sentencing structure reflects a lower mens rea requirement under s 47AA(1), namely the accused's failure to account satisfactorily for how he came by the property, rather than actual knowledge or reasonable belief. To read a subjective suspicion requirement into s 47AA(1) would render it tautologous with s 47(3), an outcome that should be avoided in view of the canon that Parliament shuns tautology and does not legislate in vain: Tan Cheng Bock v Attorney-General [2017] 2 SLR 850 at [38].

(ii)       My interpretation above is further supported by the parliamentary intention behind s 47AA. At the second reading of the Serious Crimes and Counter-Terrorism (Miscellaneous Amendments) Bill (No 43 of 2018), the Second Minister for Home Affairs, Mrs Josephine Teo, explained that the Government had observed syndicates targeting locals and using their bank accounts to launder criminal proceeds, with money mules being trained not to make any admission during police investigations. She stated that "[u]nder our current laws, the Prosecution must prove that these money mules know the moneys are linked to criminal conduct. This is challenging, especially against mules trained to claim ignorance." Section 47AA was therefore introduced so that "the Courts will be able to decide, based on the circumstances of the case, whether the accused could be reasonably expected to suspect that moneys are linked to criminal conduct".[note: 80] A test that requires the factfinder to assume the accused's position — including his knowledge of the relevant facts and circumstances — would defeat this parliamentary intention. The correct test is therefore whether a reasonable person, armed with the objective facts and evidence, would suspect that the property is or represents benefits from criminal conduct.

108    Element (c) requires an evaluation of the purported offender’s account about how he came by the property.

Decision of the Court on whether the charges have been proven

109    Having set out the elements and requirements necessary to prove the charges against the accused, I will next set out my analysis of the credibility of the Prosecution’s witnesses, before assessing the accused’s account. I will then analyse each charge in turn to ascertain if the Prosecution had successfully proven its case against the accused beyond a reasonable doubt on each charge.

Credibility of the Prosecution witnesses

110    I found the Prosecution witnesses to be credible and reliable. The witnesses, who were victims of the scams, gave consistent and detailed accounts of how they were deceived into transferring money to various accounts. Their evidence was corroborated by documentary evidence, including police reports, bank statements, and transaction records.

111    In addition, Ms Wong and Mr Chew Soo Yan from Pro-Health provided detailed and consistent testimony about their interactions with Mr Sun Jian Ping and the accused. Their evidence was supported by extensive WeChat communications and banking records showing the flow of funds through their company’s account.

112    As for Mdm Yeo and Ms Edna Lee, they provided credible and mutually corroborating evidence about the cash handover on 27 July 2020, consistent with the BVC bank statement (Exhibit P19) and the payment voucher. Both witnesses identified the accused in court.

113    I also found Mr Teo to be a credible witness. His evidence was unchallenged in any material respect during cross-examination, was detailed and consistent with the banking records, and explained how funds from victims were channelled through Kunlun's accounts to the accused. When the accused was asked whether Mr Teo had any motive to falsely implicate him, he could identify none, saying only that he "don't know". I accordingly accept Mr Teo's evidence in its entirety.

114    As for Mr Sun Jian Ping, I found him to be a credible witness on the material aspects of his evidence. His account of acting as a conduit between the accused and Pro-Health was consistent with the WeChat communications in Exhibit P17T and with the evidence of Ms Wong and Mr Chew Soo Yan. Significantly, Mr Sun Jian Ping confirmed that it was the accused who had instructed him to check whether the S$25,000 had been received into Pro-Health's account, to instruct the immediate transfer of S$23,750 to the Sun Mode Bank Account, and to convey to Pro-Health the characterisation of the transactions as a consultation fee and service fee arrangement. Mr Sun Jian Ping also confirmed that after the police meeting on 30 April 2020, it was the accused who instructed him to ask Mr Chew Soo Yan to prepare a withdrawal memorandum and to tell the police that the transactions were normal business dealings. Of particular significance, Mr Sun Jian Ping confirmed that it was the accused who had instructed him to send a message to Mr Chew Soo Yan stating "The police did not ask you, then you need not say" (Exhibit P17T, p 51). This instruction, conveyed at the accused's direction after the police had intervened, was consistent with a consciousness of guilt and an awareness that the transactions were not legitimate. The accused declined to challenge any of this evidence in cross-examination — despite being expressly reminded by the court of the consequences of failing to do so — and thus failed to cast any doubt on Mr Sun Jian Ping's evidence. I accordingly accept it in its entirety.

115    For completeness, the banking witnesses provided objective evidence about the various transactions, and their testimony was consistent with the documentary evidence presented.

Assessment of the accused’s evidence

116    In contrast to my general conclusion that Prosecution witnesses’ evidence was largely consistent and corroborated, I found the accused's evidence to be unreliable and lacking in credibility. His blanket denials were inconsistent with the overwhelming documentary and witness evidence.

117    For one, his claim that he had never met many of the Prosecution witnesses, including CAD officers, was contradicted by multiple witnesses who identified him in court and provided detailed accounts of their interactions with him. Further, the accused's denial of making the police statements was not credible given the detailed content of the statements and the proper procedures followed by the recording officers.

118    In addition, the accused's explanations that the moneys were received by him for legitimate business purposes were not supported by any documentary evidence, and there was no evidence of any legitimate business activities ever conducted despite the substantial sums involved.

119    I also found that the accused's defence to the charges shifted incessantly during cross-examination, and at no point did he produce any documentary evidence in support of any of his accounts. In summary, in relation to the first charge, he offered no substantive defence. In relation to the second charge, he made a bare assertion that the charge was "untrue" and "fake". In relation to the third and fourth charges, his explanations in examination-in-chief squarely contradicted his investigative statements and the objective evidence that was produced. I will discuss his evidence in greater detail when I assess the individual charges.

Analysis of the charges

120    I now turn to analyse each charge in turn. In doing so, I was mindful that the Prosecution bore the burden of proving beyond a reasonable doubt each element of the charge under s 47AA(1) of the CDSA. I also considered that the accused's failure to offer any clear, credible and consistent explanation as to how he came by the moneys was itself a relevant consideration going to element (c) of each charge. Where the accused's account was shifting, internally inconsistent, or contradicted by objective evidence, that failure may also lend further support to the inference that the moneys were reasonably suspected of being benefits from criminal conduct.

121    Before turning to the individual charges, I note one matter of significance that bears particularly on the analysis of moneys that were received and possessed by him in the Sun Mode Bank Account. This was contained in Exhibit P32, the statement recorded from the accused on 16 September 2019 by SI Hafit. Notably, this exhibit contained an express warning administered to the accused at Question 11, in which the accused was informed that the funds he had received in his bank accounts were derived from fraudulent activities, was advised of the risk involved in agreeing to receive moneys into his bank accounts, including from foreign sources where he had no previous relationship with the sender, and was specifically warned to refrain from receiving or dealing with funds from unknown and/or dubious sources, which acts may render him liable to prosecution under the Penal Code and/or the CDSA (Exhibit P32, p 3, Answer to Question 11). The accused confirmed that he understood this warning. This warning was administered approximately seven to eight months before the earliest of the four offences was committed in April 2020. The accused's acknowledgement of this warning was directly relevant to the objective element under s 47AA(1)(b) of the CDSA.

122    In this regard, a reasonable person who had received such an express warning from the CAD in September 2019 would, when subsequently receiving substantial sums of money from strangers into the same bank account in 2020, have had all the more reason to suspect that those moneys were benefits from criminal conduct. The accused's prior knowledge of this risk, confirmed by his own signed acknowledgement in Exhibit P32, reinforced the objective inference that the moneys he possessed, which were received directly into the Sun Mode Bank Account, may be reasonably suspected of being benefits from criminal conduct, particularly given that they came from unknown and/or dubious sources of the kind against which he had been expressly warned.

123    I now turn to the individual charges.

First Charge - $15,500 in Sun Mode Bank Account

124    For this charge, the evidence clearly established that $15,500 was deposited into Sun Mode Bank Account on 2 and 3 July 2020. Mdm Lau testified that she lodged police report Exhibit P1 dated 7 July 2020 stating she was cheated into depositing $3,500 at 0850 hours and $3,000 at 1112 hours on 3 July 2020 into UOB account number XXX-XXX-XXX-X (Sun Mode Bank Account). She produced cash deposit receipts (Exhibit P2) evidencing these deposits. Similarly, Mdm Ong testified that she lodged police report Exhibit P4 stating she was cheated into depositing $7,000 and $2,000 into the Sun Mode Bank Account. Both victims confirmed they had no prior knowledge of Sun Mode or the accused and had never conducted any business with either party.

125    These deposits are evidenced by Sun Mode Bank Account statement Exhibit P22 for 1–3 July 2020, showing credit entries of $7,000, $3,500, $3,000 and $2,000, totalling $15,500, between 2–3 July 2020, with the moneys subsequently withdrawn in cash at bank ATMs. The accused exercised sole control over the Sun Mode Bank Account as established in Exhibit P32 (p 2, Answer to Question 5), giving him constructive possession of these funds for the period they were in the account.

126    The circumstances surrounding these deposits pointed clearly to the conclusion that the moneys were benefits from criminal conduct (ie, cheating under section 419 or 420 of the Penal Code 1871). Both Mdm Lau and Mdm Ong were complete strangers to the accused and to Sun Mode. Each had been deceived into making the deposits. There was no legitimate reason for the accused to have received these sums, and no legitimate reason for him to have subsequently withdrawn them in cash. On any objective assessment, these moneys were reasonably suspected of being benefits from criminal conduct.

127    When questioned by SI Tan about how he came by the moneys, the accused offered only a bare and unsatisfactory explanation in Exhibit P29 dated 10 August 2021, pp 3–4, Answer to Question 18, stating simply that he "had remit [them] to [his] supplier". When charged, he said in Exhibit P24 dated 29 January 2024 that for three of the four sums that constituted the $15,500 in the Sun Mode Bank Account, he "was totally unaware of their existence".

128    At trial, the accused's evidence on this charge was incoherent and persistently inconsistent. He initially denied receipt of the moneys, but after being confronted with bank statements and being repeatedly questioned about money credited into the Sun Mode Bank Account, he then agreed that he had full control of the account, that he had made multiple withdrawals from it after the moneys had been deposited into that account.[note: 81] He then claimed that Sun Mode had received the moneys from buyers as deposits for goods,[note: 82] before denying receipt again, before finally admitting receipt once more when confronted with his long statement Exhibit P29, stating that he had received the $15,500 and had allegedly remitted it to a Singaporean with a New Zealand passport who was residing in Malaysia, purportedly to purchase masks.[note: 83] When confronted with his cautioned statement Exhibit P24, in which he had said he was "totally unaware" of the existence of three of the four sums of money constituting the $15,500, he was unable to reconcile this account with his earlier oral evidence.[note: 84] The accused then reverted to denying receipt of the moneys altogether, before ultimately saying he did not know whether he had received them.[note: 85] In any event, the accused confirmed that he did not know either Mdm Lau or Mdm Ong and had no dealings with them,[note: 86] meaning that the moneys would have come from unknown or dubious sources.

129    Notably, given the prior warning administered to him by SI Hafit in Exhibit P32 (see [121]), the accused was on notice of the possible illicit nature of funds received into the Sun Mode Bank Account, especially funds from unknown or dubious sources.

130    Having assessed all the relevant evidence, I found that the Prosecution had proven the first charge beyond a reasonable doubt.

Second Charge - $58,000 from Teo Seng Liang

131    The evidence established that the accused had received $58,000 in cash from Mr Teo Seng Liang in three separate transactions.

132    As regards these moneys transferred to the accused, there were two sources of funds.

(a)     First, Mr Seow testified that he lodged a police report stating that he was cheated into transferring two sums of money, S$40,000 and S$10,000, to two bank accounts of Kunlun on 7 August 2020 and 26 August 2020. He confirmed in court that he made these transfers and produced his bank statement to corroborate this account. He also confirmed that he had no prior knowledge of, and no dealings with, Kunlun, Mr Teo, the accused or Sun Mode.

(b)     Second, Mdm Seah, who passed away on 26 September 2022, lodged a police report on 12 October 2020 stating that she was cheated into depositing a sum of S$10,000 into a bank account bearing account number YYY-YYY-YYY-Y[note: 87] (belonging to Kunlun/Mr Teo) on 11 September 2020. This bank account statement showed that a cash deposit of S$10,000 was made on 11 September 2020, consistent with the details stated in Mdm Seah's police report.

133    Mr Teo testified that the accused had sought his help to receive moneys in the Kunlun account and to hand them over to the accused. Mr Teo had agreed to help him, given their relationship and the accused's assurance that the moneys came from legitimate sources. Mr Teo then provided the bank account numbers for three bank accounts of Kunlun to the accused, and the accused arranged for each of the three sums of money to be transferred to these bank accounts. After the moneys were transferred, the accused informed Mr Teo and instructed him to withdraw the moneys in cash and hand them over to the accused at the accused's home. Mr Teo did not know who transferred the three sums of money to the said bank accounts and what the moneys were for. In any event, he withdrew three sums of money, S$38,000, S$10,000 and S$10,000, in cash from the said bank accounts, and handed over the cash to the accused at his home, on or around the same day the moneys were received in these accounts ie, on or around 20 August 2020, 27 August 2020 and 11 September 2020. The cash withdrawals were evidenced by the statements of accounts for the three bank accounts of Kunlun. As highlighted by the Prosecution, Mr Teo’s evidence was unchallenged during cross-examination, and the accused also did not provide any motive for Mr Teo to falsely implicate him.

134    In court, while the accused disputed receipt of the moneys, his oral denial of having received any moneys from Mr Teo was directly contradicted by his own prior statements. As set out at [136] and [137] below, his prior statements in Exhibits P28, P29 and P25 contained three separate and mutually inconsistent accounts of how he came by the moneys, each of which was irreconcilable with his oral denial at trial. The accused offered no satisfactory explanation for any of these inconsistencies. I therefore found that the accused did receive S$58,000 in cash from Mr Teo, as Mr Teo had testified.

135    The accused therefore had actual possession of S$58,000 in cash handed to him by Mr Teo. These moneys were directly traceable to the sums lost by Mr Seow and Mdm Seah through love scams and therefore constituted benefits from criminal conduct. The accused himself accepted in cross-examination that he had no reason to possess moneys belonging to either Mr Seow or Mdm Seah, as he had no dealings with either of them. Beyond this, the manner in which the moneys changed hands was itself objectively suspicious. There was no apparent reason why the accused needed to route the funds through Mr Teo's Kunlun accounts rather than receiving them directly into the Sun Mode Bank Account. The most natural inference, which I accepted, was that the accused deliberately interposed Mr Teo as an intermediary in order to distance himself from the scam victims and avoid any direct paper trail linking the funds directly to him.

136    Turning to element (c) of the charge, when questioned by SI Tan about the moneys traceable to Mr Seow, the accused explained in Exhibit P28, Answer to Question 13, that:

"[he] got to know a female New Zealanders thru a Malaysia contacts thru phone calls and she told [him] they have stocks for mask. She told [him] that her boyfriend needs support in the transaction and requires a company bank account. [He] told Teo [ie, Mr Teo] that there is 2 amounts of money to be send into his [(Teo's)] account and [he] had told him [(Teo)] the money is to buy mask. The goods have yet to arrive."

He further explained in Answer to Question 14 that he "went to the money changer at People's Park and send to her as payment." When asked about the $10,000 deposited into Kunlun's account on 11 September 2020, he said in Exhibit P29, p 4, Answer to Question 19 that "it was to pay supplier and [he] had remitted to them." However, the accused was unable to furnish any documentary records to substantiate any of these explanations (Exhibit P30, items 9–11 and 14).

137    When subsequently charged, the accused abandoned these explanations entirely. In court, the accused denied receiving $58,000 in cash from Mr Teo, or that Mr Teo had provided him with the bank account numbers of three bank accounts belonging to Kunlun.[note: 88] Instead, the accused asserted that it was Mr Teo who owed him money and who had come to his house to borrow money, not to deliver it.[note: 89] He alleged that Mr Teo was involved in money laundering and had exploited his knowledge of the accused's international trading business. However, when confronted with his cautioned statement Exhibit P25, in which he stated that he had received two sums of money from Mr Teo through his lawyer because Mr Teo owed him money, the accused equivocally accepted this at one point, saying the money had been passed to him through a lawyer who was a retired ASP, before reverting to saying he did not know how much, if anything, he had received.[note: 90] He was unable to explain the contradiction between this account and his oral denial of having received any money from Mr Teo,[note: 91] and could not offer a consistent account of how he came by the moneys at any stage of the proceedings. When asked whether Mr Teo had any motive to falsely implicate him, he said he did not know. The accused also confirmed that he did not know Mr Seow Yin Khoi or Mdm Seah Hwee Khin and had no dealings with either of them, and that he had no reason to possess money belonging to them.[note: 92]

138    For completeness, I should address a belated allegation raised by the accused. This was the claim made by him for the first time during his own cross-examination on Day 12 that SI Tan had told him he could not leave and could not see a doctor unless he signed Exhibit P28. I rejected this allegation for the following reasons. First, and most significantly, this allegation was not put to SI Tan at any point during SI Tan's cross-examination. The accused therefore had no basis for raising it for the first time during his own cross-examination, especially since SI Tan had no opportunity to respond to it. Further, the failure to put this allegation to SI Tan was a significant procedural omission that undermined the credibility of the allegation entirely. Second, SI Tan gave clear and consistent evidence that no inducement, threat or promise was made during the recording of Exhibit P28, and that proper procedures were followed throughout. His evidence was not shaken in cross-examination. Third, the accused's belated allegation was inconsistent with his own conduct during the recording process: SI Tan confirmed that the accused had acknowledged each handwritten amendment by signature and had not made any complaints during or after the statement recording. Fourth, the accused's shifting and contradictory accounts across the proceedings — from the explanations given in Exhibit P28, to the entirely different account in his cautioned statement Exhibit P25, to his outright denial at trial — were themselves inconsistent with the suggestion that Exhibit P28 was made involuntarily. A person who had been coerced into making a false statement would not subsequently offer yet further inconsistent accounts in his cautioned statement and at trial. I accordingly found that Exhibit P28 was made voluntarily and that its contents accurately reflected what the accused had said to SI Tan.

139    I also accepted the Prosecution’s argument that the circumstances in which the three sums of money (ie, S$38,000, S$10,000 and S$10,000) were transferred from Mr Teo to the accused were objectively suspicious, since there was no reason why the accused had to enlist Mr Teo’s help to receive the moneys, instead of receiving them in his own bank account(s) or the Sun Mode Bank Account directly from Mr Seow or Mdm Seah. Thus, the inference could be drawn that the accused wanted to avoid a direct connection of funds from Mr Seow and Mdm Seah to him owing to the illicit nature of the moneys.

140    All in all, I found that the Prosecution had proven the second charge beyond a reasonable doubt. The accused had actual possession of S$58,000 in cash handed to him by Mr Teo. These moneys were directly traceable to the sums lost by Mr Seow and Mdm Seah to love scams and therefore constituted benefits from criminal conduct. The circumstances in which the moneys changed hands were objectively suspicious, in particular, as there was no reason for the involvement of Mr Teo for him to receive the funds from Mr Seow and Mdm Seah. These circumstances thus showed that the accused possessed moneys that may be reasonably suspected of being benefits from criminal conduct. Finally, the accused's shifting accounts across the various stages of investigations and the proceedings plainly failed to constitute a satisfactory explanation, and his numerous contradictory positions in his statements to the police, and his accounts in court, showed that he had no satisfactory explanation as to how he came by and possessed the moneys.

141    I was therefore satisfied beyond a reasonable doubt that all three elements of the second charge were made out.

Third Charge - $43,700 in cash from Yeo Chor Cher

142    The evidence established that $46,000 was transferred from victim Mr Seow to BVC's UOB account. Mr Seow testified that he transferred $16,000 on 23 July 2020 and $30,000 on 25 July 2020 to the BVC Bank Account, evidenced by his bank statement Exhibit P6 and BVC's bank statement Exhibit P19.

143    Mdm Yeo testified that: (a) the accused was in the seafood business and she helped find buyers; (b) she agreed to use BVC's account to receive the moneys on the accused's behalf, earning a 5 to 10% service fee; and (c) on 27 July 2020, she and Ms Edna Lee withdrew $43,700 in cash using multiple cheques and immediately handed the cash to the accused outside the UOB bank branch near Fu Lu Shou Complex. The cash withdrawal is evidenced by BVC bank statement Exhibit P19 showing ten withdrawal entries on 27 July 2020.

144    Crucially, Mdm Yeo's account was corroborated by the accused's own admission to SI Tan in Exhibit P28, p. 3, Answer to Question 11, that "[t]he old lady Winnie hand over me the S$46,000/-. It was not her in fact her PA who passed me the money, they were together." In court, Mdm Yeo confirmed that her English name was Winnie.[note: 93] Ms Edna Lee provided independent corroboration, testifying that she witnessed the cash handover and saw Mdm Yeo ask the accused to sign a voucher acknowledging receipt.

145    The objective circumstances strongly indicated these moneys were benefits from criminal conduct. The accused enlisted Mdm Yeo's company to receive funds from a romance scam victim, with Mdm Yeo testifying that she was told "Indonesians would be coming to collect the cash for purchasing goods". However, no legitimate business transactions ever materialised. When the police informed Mdm Yeo that the money was "not clean", she repeatedly messaged the accused demanding either delivery of promised goods or return of the money as evidenced by Exhibit P21T, pp. 2–5, but received no response.

146    Regarding the accused's failure to account satisfactorily for these funds, when questioned by SI Tan, the accused said the moneys were "for buying fish from Indonesian" in Exhibit P28, p. 2, Answer to Question 9, and claimed he sent the money to his company in Indonesia. However, he was unable to furnish any documentary record to substantiate his explanations, as shown by Exhibit P30, items 7 and 8. When charged, he disavowed his earlier explanations and said he had "no idea that [he] had receive this sum of money from Yeo Chor Cher" (see Exhibit P26).

147    The accused's evidence at trial on this charge was equally shifting. He initially denied receiving the money from Mdm Yeo, then admitted receiving it, explaining that it was a fee to be passed to a Chinese organisation he referred to as "Mayflower" in connection with business dealings he had facilitated on Mdm Yeo's behalf.[note: 94] However, when confronted with his inconsistent answer (given to Question 9) in his earlier statement Exhibit P28, the accused then changed his account again, saying the money was used to buy fish from Indonesia.[note: 95]He subsequently denied once more that Mdm Yeo had given the money to him before saying instead that it was handed to him by an unidentified member of her staff.[note: 96] He ultimately confirmed that he had received $43,700 in cash and that both Mdm Yeo and Ms Edna Lee had been present at the UOB bank branch at Fu Lu Shou Complex when the handover took place,[note: 97]before denying any connection between the money and Mayflower.[note: 98] The accused also confirmed that he did not know Mr Seow and had no dealings with him, and that he had no reasons to possess moneys from Mr Seow.[note: 99]Finally, the accused offered no satisfactory explanation for his failure to respond to Mdm Yeo's repeated messages demanding the return of the money or the delivery of goods.[note: 100] Instead, when asked why he had not replied to Mdm Yeo's messages, he simply said he had ignored her because she had no credibility.

148    Based on the evidence adduced, I found that the Prosecution had proven the third charge beyond a reasonable doubt. The accused had actual possession of S$43,700 in cash, as established by the evidence of Mdm Yeo and Ms Edna Lee. These moneys were directly traceable to the sums lost by Mr Seow to love scams and therefore constituted benefits from criminal conduct. As Mr Seow neither knew nor had any dealings with the accused or Sun Mode, there was no reason for the accused to possess these moneys.

149    It is also significant that the accused chose to route the funds through Mdm Yeo's company rather than receiving them directly. He gave Mdm Yeo the impression that the moneys were payments from buyers for Indonesian goods, and instructed her to deliver the cash to him urgently. No legitimate business transaction ever materialised. When the police informed Mdm Yeo that the moneys were not clean, she repeatedly messaged the accused demanding either delivery of the promised goods or return of the funds. The accused did not respond. His silence in the face of these demands, for which he offered no satisfactory explanation at trial, was itself telling. The inference I drew was the same as for the second charge: the accused interposed Mdm Yeo as an intermediary to avoid a direct connection between himself and the scam victim, Mr Seow. The accused's assertion that it was Mdm Yeo who had sought his help in relation to dealings with a Chinese entity he referred to as "Mayflower" was plainly contradicted by the content of Mdm Yeo's messages to him, which made no reference to any such dealings and were concerned solely with the delivery of goods or the return of money. Mdm Yeo herself testified that she had "nothing to do with the China Mayflower."

150    As for element (c), the accused's account of what the moneys were for was internally inconsistent and constantly shifting — from claiming the moneys were "for buying fish from Indonesian" (Exhibit P28, p 2, Answer to Question 9), to denying any knowledge of having received the moneys (Exhibit P26), to attributing the moneys at trial to dealings with "Mayflower" while simultaneously reverting to his earlier explanation that the money was used to buy fish. He adduced no evidence to support any of these contradictory accounts. I was therefore satisfied beyond a reasonable doubt that all three elements of the third charge were made out.

Fourth Charge - $23,750 from Pro-Health

151    The evidence established that $23,750 was transferred from Pro-Health to the Sun Mode Bank Account at the accused's direction through Mr Sun Jian Ping. The original $25,000 came from Ms Lee Wei Siew, who was deceived by a romance scammer who was targeting her sister into believing she was paying an "admin fee" as documented in Exhibit P13.

152    The scheme involved the accused using Mr Sun Jian Ping as an intermediary to approach Pro-Health, a legitimate start-up facing financial difficulties. Mr Chew Soo Yan and Ms Wong, both linked to Pro-Health, testified that Mr Sun Jian Ping introduced the accused as "CEO Han" at a meeting on 14 March 2020. The accused then orchestrated an elaborate deception involving false promises of $20.6 million in business deals for garlic, masks, and water machines, with detailed instructions for opening foreign currency accounts as evidenced by Exhibit P17T, pp 5–20.

153    When $25,000 was received from Ms Lee Wei Siew on 15 April 2020, Mr Sun Jian Ping immediately called Pro-Health repeatedly, claiming "CEO Han was rushing every 3 minutes to check on this amount" as evidenced by Exhibit P17T, pp 32–33. Within 15 minutes, he instructed the immediate transfer of $23,750 to Sun Mode as a "service fee payment" (Exhibit P17T, pp 33–35). Mr Sun Jian Ping testified that he carried out these actions on the accused's instructions.

154    Two further matters reinforced the objective inference that the moneys may be reasonably suspected of being benefits from criminal conduct.

(a)     First, after the police meeting on 30 April 2020, the accused instructed Mr Sun Jian Ping to caution Mr Chew Soo Yan to say less to the police and to present the transactions as a normal commercial dealing so as not to affect future business (Exhibit P17T, pp 50–52). This conduct was consistent with a consciousness of guilt and an awareness that the moneys were not from legitimate sources.

(b)     Second, the accused read the letter from SI Tan informing him that the moneys deposited into the Pro-Health Bank Account were believed to be criminal proceeds and requesting him to attend an interview at the CAD, but refused to take it. His refusal to accept the letter, taken together with his instruction to Mr Sun Jian Ping to discourage Mr Chew Soo Yan from making full disclosure to the police, reinforced this inference.

155    A further matter of significance was the accused's conduct following the police's intervention. After Mr Chew Soo Yan prepared the written withdrawal memorandum at the accused's request, the accused issued a cheque to Mr Chew Soo Yan or Pro-Health for S$23,750. However, this cheque was subsequently returned to the accused through Mr Sun Jian Ping and was never banked in. The accused returned only S$4,000 in cash to Mr Chew Soo Yan at a physical meet-up in Bencoolen, retaining the balance of S$19,750. This conduct was consistent with an unwillingness to make full restitution and a consciousness that the moneys were not legitimately his to keep, and further reinforced the objective inference that the moneys he possessed (as per the charge) were reasonably suspected of being benefits from criminal conduct.

156    In summary, the accused had constructive possession of the $23,750 through his sole control of the Sun Mode Bank Account as established in Exhibit P32, p 2, Answer to Question 5. The objective circumstances overwhelmingly indicated these moneys were benefits from criminal conduct: the funds were directly traceable to a romance scam victim, the elaborate scheme involved false business representations, and the accused's instruction to Mr Sun Jian Ping to represent to Ms Wong that Ms Lee Wei Siew had paid "consultation fees" to Pro-Health (Exhibit P17T, p 37) was demonstrably false, as both Ms Lee Wei Siew and Ms Lee Wei Sean testified they had no dealings with Pro-Health.

157    When questioned by SI Tan, the accused provided inconsistent explanations, initially stating in Exhibit P28, p 2, Answers to Questions 5–7, that "this was for water dispenser" and that he would "send to Indonesia to develop the land," but furnished no documentary evidence as shown by Exhibit P30, item 6. His explanations changed multiple times: initially claiming involvement in water projects, then stating in Exhibit P27 that Pro-Health "owed him money," and finally denying any knowledge of the transactions at trial.

158    In court, the accused’s evidence on this charge was similarly incoherent.

(a)     In examination-in-chief, he stated that he did possess the $23,750 and had used it to purchase a burial ground for a deceased Indonesian worker. However, in cross-examination, he denied having said this and claimed he could not remember whether he had possessed the sum at all. [note: 101]

(b)     He then offered a series of further inconsistent explanations, including that the money was used to pay fees and expenses for purchasing fish and gold from Indonesian officials.[note: 102]

(c)     When confronted with his long statement Exhibit P28, in which he had acknowledged receiving $25,000 from Pro-Health and had stated that the money was for a water dispenser and had been sent to Indonesia to develop land, the accused alleged for the first time that the statement had been made involuntarily under threat, claiming that SI Tan had told him he could not leave and could not see a doctor unless he signed. Notably, this allegation had not been put to SI Tan during SI Tan’s cross-examination. I rejected this belated allegation for the reasons set out at [138] above, which apply with equal force here. I accordingly found that Exhibit P28 was made voluntarily and that its contents accurately reflected what the accused had said to SI Tan. In addition, the accused confirmed that he did not know Ms Lee Wei Siew and had no dealings with her or with Pro-Health and had no reasons to possess her money.[note: 103] The accused was unable to explain how he could have instructed Mr Sun Jian Ping to represent to Ms Wong that Ms Lee Wei Siew had paid a consultation fee to Pro-Health if he had no knowledge of Ms Lee Wei Siew. When this was put to him directly in cross-examination, the accused said only "I do not know" and declined to provide any explanation. He also denied having instructed Mr Sun Jian Ping in this regard, suggesting instead that Mr Sun Jian Ping was not telling the truth, but offered no basis for this suggestion.[note: 104]

159    Based on the evidence adduced, I found that the Prosecution had proven the fourth charge beyond a reasonable doubt. To summarise, the accused had constructive possession of the right to the sum of S$23,750 that was transferred into the Sun Mode Bank Account, by reason of his sole control of that account. This sum was directly traceable to the sum lost by Ms Lee Wei Siew as a result of a love scam perpetrated against Ms Lee Wei Sean and therefore constituted benefits from criminal conduct. As both Ms Lee Wei Sean and Ms Lee Wei Siew neither knew nor had any dealings with the accused or Sun Mode, there was no reason for the accused to possess this sum.

160    Critically, the objective circumstances surrounding the transfer of this sum into the Sun Mode Bank Account strongly suggested that it was reasonably suspected of being benefits from criminal conduct. In particular, the accused was somehow able to instruct Mr Sun Jian Ping to inform Ms Wong that "Lee Wei Siew" had paid a consultation fee of S$25,000 to Pro-Health — a representation that was plainly untrue, as Ms Lee Wei Siew testified that she had no dealings with Mr Chew Soo Yan or Pro-Health. However, the accused accepted that he did not know Lee Wei Siew and had no dealings with her, and when pressed as to how he could have instructed Mr Sun Jian Ping to make the representation about Ms Lee Wei Siew if he had no knowledge of her, he gave no answer. The obvious and irresistible inference is that the sum was reasonably suspected of being benefits from criminal conduct.

161    Further, as noted at [121] above, the accused had been expressly warned by the CAD in September 2019 that funds received in his bank accounts were derived from fraudulent activities and that he should refrain from receiving or dealing with funds from unknown and/or dubious sources. A reasonable person who had received such a warning and who subsequently received a sum of money from a stranger through an elaborate chain of intermediaries — involving false representations about consultation fees and service fees for transactions that never materialised — would have had all the more reason to suspect that those moneys were benefits from criminal conduct.

162    As for element (c), the accused's account of what the moneys were for constantly changed — from claiming the moneys were "for water dispenser" and sent "to Indonesia to develop the land" (Exhibit P28, p 2, Answers to Questions 5–7), to claiming in his cautioned statement that Pro-Health "owed him money" (Exhibit P27), to testifying in examination-in-chief that the moneys were used to buy a burial ground for a deceased Indonesian worker, before denying this in cross-examination. He adduced no evidence to support any of these accounts. I was therefore satisfied beyond a reasonable doubt that all three elements of the fourth charge were made out.

Conclusion

163    I was satisfied beyond a reasonable doubt that the Prosecution had proven all elements of the four charges against the accused. The evidence established that the accused was in possession of funds totalling $140,950 that may be reasonably suspected of constituting benefits from criminal conduct. The accused's systematic use of multiple intermediaries to receive and process funds from love scam victims was objectively suspicious and consistent with a deliberate attempt to avoid a paper trail linking him to the criminal proceeds.

164    The accused had failed to provide any clear, credible and consistent explanation as to how he came by any of the moneys across all four charges, and produced no documentary evidence to support any of his shifting accounts.

165    I therefore found the accused guilty on all four charges and convicted him accordingly.

Sentencing: Preliminaries

Prescribed Penalties

166    Each of the four charges under s 47AA(1) of the CDSA is punishable under s 47AA(2)(a) of the CDSA with a fine not exceeding S$150,000, imprisonment for a term not exceeding three years, or both.

Antecedents

167    The accused has one prior conviction, namely for possession of an obscene book on 13 February 1984, for which a fine of $500 was imposed. This antecedent is unrelated to the present charges and was not relied upon by the Prosecution. The accused has no prior related convictions.

Prosecution's Submissions on Sentence

168    The Prosecution sought a global sentence of 14 to 17 months' imprisonment, with the sentences for the second, third and fourth charges running consecutively and the first charge running concurrently. Details of the sentences sought are set out in the table below.

Global Sentence: 14 to 17 months’ imprisonment



169    On harm, the Prosecution highlighted that the amounts involved were significant, ranging from S$15,500 to S$58,000, most of which were dissipated, with only S$8,544.69 recovered and returned to the victims. The predicate offences took the form of love scams, which the Sentencing Advisory Panel has noted have increased more than seven-fold over the past five years, with amounts lost quadrupling. On culpability, the Prosecution pointed to the accused's persistence in offending and, more significantly, his high degree of planning and premeditation — in particular, his use of unsuspecting third parties to receive and deliver moneys in cash to avoid a paper trail, and his orchestration of an elaborate ruse involving false business representations to deceive Pro-Health, which he doubled down on even after being informed that the moneys were criminal proceeds.

170    On offender-specific factors, the Prosecution submitted that the accused demonstrated a palpable lack of remorse — he maintained untenable positions to the end despite overwhelming evidence, and cast multiple baseless allegations against CAD officers and witnesses, conduct which the Court of Appeal in Lian Hoe Heng v Public Prosecutor [2026] SGCA 25 (“Lian Hoe Heng”) at [132] described as especially egregious. There were no mitigating factors: the accused claimed trial; his clean record was neutral; his age of 73 did not warrant a reduction; and his medical conditions did not justify one as the Singapore Prison Service confirmed it could adequately manage them.

Mitigation

171    At the hearing on 2 June 2026 (Day 13), following the delivery of the verdict, I adjourned the matter to 17 June 2026 to deal with sentencing. At the hearing on 2 June 2026, and in line with matters highlighted by the Prosecution about the accused’s possible health conditions, I drew the accused's attention to the potential mitigating value of tendering his updated medical documents, and expressly invited him to obtain updated medical reports from his doctors before the next hearing date. I explained to the accused that such documents could have mitigating value and that there was even a possibility, depending on their contents, of judicial mercy being invoked.[note: 105]I also made it clear that the matter was already adjourned to 17 June 2026 for sentencing, and that he should use the intervening period to obtain updated medical documents if he wished to avail himself of that opportunity. The accused confirmed that he would obtain them.[note: 106]

172    However, at the sentencing hearing on 17 June 2026 (Day 14), the accused did not provide any updated medical documents. Further, when invited to mitigate, the accused declined to do so in any substantive sense. Instead of addressing the charges or offering any mitigating factors, he made wide-ranging allegations against the Prosecution witnesses, asserting that they had committed criminal offences overseas and that he was "merely a scapegoat"[note: 107] When I pointed out that mitigation was an opportunity to say things that might lighten his sentence, and asked if there was anything else he wished to say, the accused responded: "I did not make any mistake, why must I mitigate?"[note: 108] Thus, in short, the accused made no substantive mitigation and provided no medical documents or other material which may be of mitigating value.

Court’s Decision on Sentence

Sentencing framework

173    In approaching the sentence to impose, I considered what sentencing framework to apply. The CDSA does not prescribe a specific sentencing framework for offences under s 47AA(1), and there are no appellate decisions directly on point. I thus found it appropriate to have regard to the framework set out in Huang Ying-Chun v Public Prosecutor [2019] 3 SLR 606 ("Huang Ying-Chun") at [98], which was developed for offences under s 44(1)(a) of the CDSA involving the assistance of another person in retaining benefits from criminal conduct.

174    In this regard, while s 44(1)(a) and s 47AA(1) are distinct provisions, I agreed with the Prosecution that they were directed at the same underlying mischief, namely the laundering of criminal proceeds, and the factors relevant to assessing harm and culpability were materially the same. The principal difference between the two provisions laid in the degree of the offender's involvement and the mens rea requirement, which was reflected in the lower maximum punishment prescribed for s 47AA(1) offences. This difference did not displace the Huang Ying-Chun harm and culpability factors as a useful analytical guide, though the specific sentencing bands set out in that case would not be directly transposable to s 47AA(1) offences, given the difference in the prescribed maximum punishment.

Offence-specific factors: Harm and Culpability

175    Turning to the harm factors, I took into account two main considerations. First, the amounts involved across all four charges were significant, ranging from S$15,500 to S$58,000, and most of these sums were dissipated. The authorities were only able to recover a total of S$8,544.69, which has since been returned to the victims as follows: S$1,978 to Mr Seow (second charge); S$1,316.69 to Mr Seow (third charge); and S$5,250 to Ms Lee Wei Siew (fourth charge). Second, the predicate offences took the form of love scams, which are serious. As the Sentencing Advisory Panel observed in the Guidelines for Scams-Related Offences at [5], reported scam cases have increased more than seven-fold over the past five years, with amounts lost quadrupling.

176    As for the culpability factors, I found the following to be relevant.

177    First, the accused demonstrated persistence in his offending. In relation to the first charge, he received moneys from two victims through the Sun Mode Bank Account on four occasions over just two days, and subsequently withdrew these moneys in cash on multiple occasions. In relation to the second charge, he received moneys from Mr Teo on three occasions over approximately three weeks.

178    Second, and more significantly, the accused displayed a high degree of planning and premeditation in relation to the second, third and fourth charges. In relation to the second and third charges, he enlisted the help of unsuspecting third parties — Mr Teo and Mdm Yeo — to receive moneys from the victims on his behalf, instructed them to deliver the moneys to him in cash urgently, and assured them that the moneys came from legitimate sources. As stated earlier, the obvious inference, which I accepted, was that the accused wished to avoid a paper trail linking the scam victims to him. In relation to the fourth charge, the accused devised and executed a multi-layered scheme through Mr Sun Jian Ping to induce Pro-Health to believe that legitimate overseas customers wished to procure goods and services from them. He directed Pro-Health to open a USD account and to prepare supply and consulting agreements, and caused a false representation to be made to Pro-Health that Ms Lee Wei Siew had paid a consultation fee. When he was informed that the S$25,000 comprised criminal proceeds, rather than making prompt restitution, he conditioned any refund on Pro-Health first issuing a written withdrawal memorandum — a further act of deception that served to obscure the true nature of the transaction.

Offender-specific factors

179    The accused's conduct throughout the trial was a significant aggravating factor. He maintained his denials in the face of overwhelming objective evidence, including his own signed statements and banking records that directly contradicted his oral evidence. He insisted, for instance, that he had not received the moneys deposited into the Sun Mode Bank Account, notwithstanding that he had sole control over that account and the deposits were proven by objective banking evidence. An accused person who claims trial is, of course, entitled to do so, and no adverse inference is drawn from that election alone. However, where an accused person advances positions that are plainly untenable and persists in them to the end of trial despite being confronted with clear and uncontroverted evidence to the contrary, that conduct reflects a complete absence of remorse and is properly treated as an aggravating factor: Lee Foo Choong Kelvin v Public Prosecutor [1999] 3 SLR(R) 292 (“Lee Foo Choong Kelvin”) at [36].

180    I also took into account the accused's conduct in making multiple unsubstantiated allegations against the CAD officers and several Prosecution witnesses. These included allegations of fabrication of statements, improper treatment during investigations, and complicity in money laundering. None of these allegations was put to the relevant witnesses during cross-examination, and none were substantiated by any evidence. The making of such allegations without any evidential foundation was not a matter to be taken lightly. As the Court of Appeal observed in Lian Hoe Heng at [132], dishonest and baseless allegations against those who participate in the criminal justice system are especially egregious, as they undermine the integrity of the system and erode public confidence in it. I treated this conduct as a further aggravating factor.

181    In giving effect to the accused's lack of remorse as an aggravating factor, I considered whether to reflect it in the individual sentences or at the global sentence stage. I concluded that the latter approach was more appropriate. The accused's conduct — his persistent denials, his shifting accounts, and his baseless allegations against officers and witnesses — was not confined to any single charge but pervaded the entirety of the proceedings. It was therefore more logical to give effect to this aggravating factor when calibrating the aggregate sentence, rather than artificially apportioning it across individual charges. This approach was consistent with the guidance of the Court of Appeal in Lian Hoe Heng at [64], which observed that where an offender's lack of remorse was relevant to all charges, it was preferable to consider its effect in the round at the aggregate sentence stage.

182    There were no offender-specific mitigating factors that would justify a downward calibration of his sentences. The accused claimed trial and was not entitled to a sentencing discount. The absence of prior related convictions was a neutral factor, not a mitigating one: BPH v Public Prosecutor and another appeal [2019] 2 SLR 764 at [85].

183    As for the accused's age of 73, I was mindful that a discount for advanced age was not a matter of mercy, but may be warranted where an offender's particular circumstances would make his punishment significantly more onerous, so as to avoid making him suffer more than others who are similarly situated: Yap Ah Lai v Public Prosecutor [2014] 3 SLR 180 (“Yap Ah Lai”) at [87]–[91]. The key consideration was whether the sentence would be disproportionate and crushing, having regard to the accused's past record and future life expectancy. In the present case, on neither count did I consider a reduction warranted. Based on sentences that I was minded to impose, even if all four sentences were ordered to run consecutively, the accused would be released before he turned 75, and the aggregate sentence would not result in the accused spending a substantial portion of his remaining years in custody.

184    As for his past record, while Yap Ah Lai at [89] recognised that some credit may be given to a mature first-time offender for having passed most of his life without offending, I accorded this factor limited weight in light of the accused's persistent offending, the significant sums involved across four charges, and his complete absence of remorse.

185    As for the accused's medical conditions as set out in his medical report dated 12 November 2024,[note: 109] there was no clear evidence that a sentence of imprisonment would carry a high risk of endangering his life, nor was there any evidence that he is terminally ill. The exercise of judicial mercy was thus not warranted: Chew Soo Chun v Public Prosecutor [2016] 2 SLR 789 ("Chew Soo Chun") at [22].

186    Turning to whether the accused's medical conditions even constitute a mitigating factor, the applicable question — which was conceptually distinct from judicial mercy — was whether an imprisonment term would have a markedly disproportionate impact on the accused by reason of his ill health, in the sense of giving rise to a real likelihood of significant deterioration in his health or a significant exacerbation of his pain and suffering: Chew Soo Chun at [34] and [38]. Even where an offender's ill health might otherwise have such an impact, it will be a neutral factor if the prison has the capability of addressing his medical conditions to an acceptable standard, or if the consequences of his conditions would transpire independently of whether he is in or outside prison: Chew Soo Chun at [39(a)] and [39(b)]. In the present case, the Singapore Prison Service has confirmed that it has an adequate system of healthcare delivery in place and manages inmates with a variety of medical conditions, including those with complex and serious medical conditions.[note: 110] There was therefore insufficient evidence to establish a real likelihood of significant deterioration in the accused's health or a significant exacerbation of his suffering by reason of imprisonment. His medical conditions accordingly carry no mitigating weight.

187    Finally, no mitigatory weight should be attached to the partial recovery of S$8,544.69. Of this sum, S$4,000 was returned by the accused to Mr Chew Soo Yan, who in turn surrendered it to the authorities. However, the accused did not do so out of remorse — he returned the sum only after Mr Chew Soo Yan requested a refund of the investment sum of S$23,750. The remaining S$4,544.69 was recovered due to the timely intervention of the authorities in freezing the relevant bank accounts, for which no credit should be given to him.

Individual sentences and the global sentence

188    I note that imprisonment terms of between three weeks and five months have been imposed on offenders who pleaded guilty to offences under s 47AA(1) of the CDSA involving amounts between S$5,000 and S$64,800: Public Prosecutor v Faizal Bin Mustaffa [2022] SGDC 232 at [55] and [101]–[102]. The present accused claimed trial and the starting sentences should accordingly be calibrated upwards from those imposed in guilty plea cases.

189    Having regard to the offence-specific and offender-specific factors, I agreed with the sentence sought by the Prosecution for the individual charges. I therefore imposed the following sentences, based on the lowest end of the Prosecution’s suggested sentencing range per charge, namely two months' imprisonment for the first charge; five months' imprisonment each for the second and third charges; and four months' imprisonment for the fourth charge.

190    As the accused was convicted of at least three distinct offences, the court was required under s 307(1) of the CPC to order the sentences for at least two of the offences to run consecutively. In deciding which sentences should run consecutively, I bore in mind the one-transaction rule, which contemplates that where two or more offences are committed in the course of a single transaction, all sentences in respect of those offences should run concurrently: Public Prosecutor v Raveen Balakrishnan [2018] 5 SLR 799 at [39]. Whether offences form part of a single transaction depends on whether they entail a single invasion of the same legally protected interest.

191    In the present case, the offences underlying the second, third and fourth charges were clearly distinct from one another and did not form part of a single transaction. Each involved a separate set of victims, a separate scheme, and a separate invasion of the legally protected interest. I accordingly ordered the sentences for those three charges to run consecutively, with the sentence for the first charge running concurrently. The aggregate sentence was thus 14 months' imprisonment. The individual and global sentences are set out in the table below for easy reference.

192    I was satisfied that the aggregate sentence of 14 months' imprisonment did not offend the totality principle. Under the first limb, the question was whether the aggregate sentence is substantially above the normal level of sentences for the most serious individual offence: Mohamed Shouffee bin Adam v Public Prosecutor [2014] 2 SLR 998 ("Shouffee") at [54]. Given the relative novelty of s 47AA(1) offences and the limited sentencing precedents available, I found it useful to take the midpoint of the prescribed maximum sentence as a proxy for the normal sentencing level: Ye Lin Myint v Public Prosecutor [2019] 5 SLR 1005 (“Ye Lin Myint”) at [94], an approach in line with what was suggested by the Prosecution. The maximum sentence for an offence under s 47AA(1) is three years' imprisonment, giving a midpoint of 18 months. The aggregate sentence of 14 months thus fell comfortably below this midpoint and did not offend the first limb.

193    Under the second limb, the question was whether the aggregate sentence is crushing and not in keeping with the offender's past record and future prospects: Shouffee at [57]. I was satisfied that the aggregate sentence was not crushing and was proportionate to the accused's overall criminality. His offending was sustained over approximately six months and involved four separate schemes targeting multiple victims through different intermediaries. The total amount involved was S$140,950, most of which was dissipated and not recovered. His complete absence of remorse throughout the proceedings, as discussed above, was a further consideration that weighed against any reduction. Accordingly, an aggregate sentence of 14 months' imprisonment was, in my judgment, a fair and proportionate reflection of the totality of his conduct.

194    Finally, I would like to record my appreciation for the thorough and detailed submissions tendered to this court, which have been very useful in deciding on the verdict and sentence in the present case.

Deputy Registrar Ng Tee Tze Allen:

1       The Claimant in this action is the Management Corporation of a subdivided building known as Regis Mansions.[note: 1] The Defendant is one of the registered subsidiary proprietors.[note: 2]

2       The Claimant started MC/OC 6632/2025 (“this action”) for what it asserted to be outstanding contributions to the management fund and sinking fund as well as interest due from the Defendant.[note: 3] The Defendant denied liability, alleging inter alia, that parts of the Claimant’s claim were time-barred and that he had overpaid the Claimant. On the same basis, the Defendant filed MC/SUM 256/2026 to strike out the Claimant’s claim.

3       I heard the parties substantively on 8 April 2026 and 18 June 2026. Having heard them and considered their evidence and submissions, I allow MC/SUM 256/2026 to strike out the Claimant’s claim for the reasons below.

Procedural history

4       I start with a summary of the procedural history given that it has a direct bearing on the substantive issues before me (e.g. the limitation defence), the affidavits I am prepared to consider, and why I ultimately decided to strike out the Claimant’s claim.

The second substantive hearing

23     This brings me to the second substantive hearing of MC/SUM 256/2026 on 18 June 2026. At that hearing, it transpired that, amongst other things, the Claimant’s proposed amendments to its Statement of Claim remained defective. It was also apparent that the Claimant had not put its case in order (see [90]-[110] below).

24     When this came to light, the Claimant’s solicitors requested permission to file yet another affidavit on the basis that there were inconsistencies in the Claimant’s case.

25     I did not grant the Claimant permission to file a further affidavit. As I explained at the second substantive hearing, I had already granted the Claimant an indulgence by permitting it to file a further affidavit at the first substantive hearing to include its proposed amendments to its Statement of Claim. Indeed, given that the Claimant was resisting a striking out application and it sought to amend its Statement of Claim, it behoved the Claimant to ensure that its proposed amendments were correct.

26     I would further add that under Order 3 r 5(6) of the Rules of Court 2021, the Claimant needed to establish a “special case” before the Court would allow any further affidavit to be filed. This is because the rules intend for there to be only one round of affidavits from each party, except in a “special case”. This would include the situation where there is a new issue that could not reasonably have been within the Claimant’s contemplation when it filed its affidavit: CZD v CZE [2023] 5 SLR 806 (“CZD”) at [19]–[21].

27     In the present case, the Claimant identified no such special case. The only rationale identified by the Claimant was that its statement of accounts was contradictory. This is certainly no reason to give permission for the filing of a further affidavit especially given the following matters:

(a)     It was evident early in the proceedings that a key dispute between the parties was an accounting one. Indeed, it was for that reason that I directed the Claimant to furnish a fresh statement of accounts (see [8] above).

(b)     If it was not clear that this was an issue then, it should have been amply clear, at the latest, from the first substantive hearing when the Claimant heard the Defendant’s submissions on its accounts (see [17]-[19] above).

(c)     Further, I had already granted the Claimant an indulgence in the first substantive hearing to rectify the deficiencies in its case. Any failure to do so does not qualify as a “special case”.

28     For the foregoing reasons, I declined to grant the Claimant permission to file a further affidavit. The Claimant had ample opportunity to ensure the necessary evidence was before me and had already been granted an indulgence to do so. Accordingly, the affidavits which I take into account for this application are limited to:

(b)     Chng Hui Ru’s responsive affidavit dated 3 February 2026;

(c)     Chng Hui Ru’s further affidavit dated 19 February 2026;

(d)     Defendant’s reply affidavit dated 18 March 2026;

(e)     Chng Hui Ru’s further affidavit dated 6 May 2026; and
