29     I turn to the substantive merits of MC/SUM 256/2026.

The Claimant’s preliminary objections

30     I start with the Claimant’s preliminary objections. Essentially, the Claimant argued that the Defendant’s striking out application was made pursuant to the Rules of Court 2021, O 9 r 19, and it was precluded by O 65 r 3:

Excluded interim applications (O. 65, r. 3)

3.    Without affecting the Court’s powers under Order 9, no application under Order 9, Rule 17 or 19 or Order 11 may be made in any case to which this Order applies.

31     I do not accept these submissions. There was no doubt that the Defendant’s application was made pursuant to O 9 r 16, not O 9 r 19:

(a)     First, prayers 1 and 2 of MC/SUM 256/2026 which sought to strike out the Statement of Claim on the basis that “it is an abuse of process of the Court” and in the alternative that “it is in the interest of justice to do so” tracked the grounds in Order 9 rule 16(1)(b) and rule 16(1)(c) respectively.

(b)     Second, the very first paragraph of his written submissions stated that this application was made “pursuant to Order 9 rule 16(1)(b) and rule 16(1)(c)”.

(c)     Finally, the Claimant had itself proceeded on the above basis in its initial set of written submissions. Section II of the Claimant’s submissions which was titled “The Law on Striking Out” started at [13] with a reproduction of O 9 r 16 before continuing at [14]-[23] with a discussion of the case law on the same.

32     It was thus not clear to me why the Defendant’s application is precluded by O 65 r 3. To do so would be to compel the Defendant to rely on O 9 r 19 when he could rely on, and was in fact relying on, another provision. No authority was identified for this proposition.

The law on striking out

33     I turn to the substantive arguments raised, starting with the law on striking out.

34     Order 9 rule 16(1) of the Rules of Court 2021 provides:

Striking out pleadings and other documents (O. 9, r. 16)

16.—(1) The Court may order any or part of any pleading to be struck out or amended, on the ground that —

(a)    it discloses no reasonable cause of action or defence;

(b)    it is an abuse of process of the Court; or

(c)    it is in the interests of justice to do so,

and may order the action to be stayed or dismissed or judgment to be entered accordingly.

35     It is well established that the authorities that pre-date the Rules of Court 2021 remain relevant in assessing the merits of a striking out application: Leong Quee Ching Karen v Lim Soon Huat and others [2023] 4 SLR 1133 (“Leong Quee Ching”) at [23].

36     It is also well established that the bar for striking out is a high one, and is to be exercised in plain and obvious cases where it is shown that the claimant’s case is wholly devoid of merit: Leong Quee Ching at [25]-[26].

37     In this regard, there is no doubt that a claim can be struck out if it is time-barred pursuant to O 9 r 16(b) and (c). As the High Court stated in Djony Gunawan v Christina Lesmana [2026] SGHC 112 at [99]:

99.    … An action that is clearly time-barred may be struck out as an abuse of process: see Singapore Civil Procedure 2020 Vol 1, para 18/19/10, commentary on “Limitation”; moreover, it would be in the interests of justice to do so.

38     A claim can also be struck out under O 9 r 16(c) when the claim is frivolous and vexatious, or obviously unsustainable: Singapore Civil Procedure 2025 (Sweet & Maxwell) at [9/16/3]. As the Court of Appeal explained in The “Bunga Melati 5” [2012] 4 SLR 546 at [39], a case is “plainly or obviously” unsustainable if it is either legally or factually unsustainable and this would be the case if:

(a)    Legally unsustainable: if “it may be clear as a matter of law at the outset that even if a party were to succeed in proving all the facts that he offers to prove he will not be entitled to the remedy that he seeks”; or

(b)    Factually unsustainable: if it is “possible to say with confidence before trial that the factual basis for the claim is fanciful because it is entirely without substance, [for example, if it is] clear beyond question that the statement of facts is contradicted by all the documents or other material on which it is based”.

39     In this regard, while the defendant bears the burden of proving that the claimant’s case is liable to be struck out, the claimant has the responsibility of showing that it has a reasonable cause of action with a prospect of success. As the Court explained in Chandra Winata Lie v Citibank NA [2015] 1 SLR 875 (“Chandra Winata”) “a plaintiff who is not in a position to plead, particularise and point to the necessary proof from the very outset of his suit is at risk of having his suit struck out”:

34    A plaintiff who commences a suit takes on, by that very act, the burden of pleading, particularising and proving every essential element of each cause of action which he chooses to pursue against the defendant in that suit. A plaintiff who is unable to discharge any one of these three burdens will fail at trial. More importantly for present purposes, a plaintiff who is not in a position to plead, particularise and point to the necessary proof from the very outset of his suit is at risk of having his suit struck out under O 18 r 19 of the Rules of Court (Cap 322, R5, 2014 Rev Ed).

35     A plaintiff can resist such an application: (i) by demonstrating that he has pleaded every essential element of a known cause of action; (ii) by showing that he has furnished sufficient particulars for the defendant to have reasonable notice of the case he has to meet and not thereby to be embarrassed at trial; and (iii) by pointing to proof for each element of his cause of action. The proof which a plaintiff points to on a striking-out application can be nothing more than his own uncorroborated and self-serving testimony as to facts within his personal knowledge. Whether it is sufficient evidence for the plaintiff ultimately to succeed is, of course, a matter to be determined at trial after weighing all the evidence, including evidence obtained during discovery. But a plaintiff cannot get past the striking-out stage if either: (i) he fails properly to plead a cause of action; or (ii) the proof he points to in support of an essential element of his cause of action in fact has no rational connection to it.

(emphasis mine)

40     Finally, in a striking out application, a claimant is bound by its pleadings and cannot be allowed to shift the metaphorical goalposts: Tahnoon Pasha v Hill, Avere Mark and another [2026] SGHC 36 at [42].

41     I turn to the Claimant’s case with these principles in mind.

The Claimant’s original claim is liable to be struck out

The parties’ respective positions

42     The Claimant’s original case was for the sum of S$36,838.32. On the Claimant’s case, this represented outstanding contributions to the management fund and sinking fund and interest. In its Statement of Claim, the particulars of the S$36,838.32 were claimed to be set out in a Statement of Accounts dated 12 May 2025.[note: 11] The following can be observed of the 12 May 2025 Statement of Accounts:[note: 12]

(a)     The first entry, dated 31 October 2019, purports to consolidate interest charges from August 2007 to October 2017. The second and third entries are payments made on 2 June 2024 and 29 October 2024 for $810 and S$820 respectively.

(b)     This is followed by a list of entries dating from November 2019 to 1 May 2025 which purport to record alleged management fund, sinking fund and interest charges.

(c)     There is only one other payment from the Defendant recorded. Interspersed in the entries described at (b) above is an entry dated 3 February 2025 which recorded a payment of S$1,000.

(d)     The 12 May 2025 Statement of Accounts ends off by stating that “Amount Due” is S$36,838.32.

43     At the first substantive hearing, the Defendant submitted that the Claimant’s entire claim should be struck out because:[note: 13]

(a)     All amounts allegedly incurred before 18 July 2019 are time-barred. In this regard, he submitted that his solicitors’ letter of 10 May 2023 was not an acknowledgment of debt that reset limitation.

(b)     The 12 May 2025 Statement of Accounts is incorrect and manufactured for this claim.

(c)     Only claims for interest after 22 February 2024 are valid.

(d)     The Defendant has paid more than his maintenance and sinking fund and other contributions from 18 July 2019.

44     My views are as follows.

The Claimant’s claim for debts arising before 18 July 2019 is time-barred

The six-year time bar imposed by section 6(1) of the Limitation Act 1959 applies to the Claimant’s claims for interest

45     I start with the limitation issue. In my view, all amounts allegedly due before 18 July 2019 (i.e., more than six years prior to the commencement of this action on 18 July 2025) are time-barred. As noted above, this applies to the Claimant’s claim for interest allegedly charged from August 2007 to October 2017.

46     In this regard, the Claimant argued that the right to charge interest was imposed by section 40(6) of the Building (Strata Management) Act 2004 (“BSMA”). I accept this proposition. It is clear from its text that section 40 of the BSMA expressly permits a management corporation to levy contributions and to charge interest for late payment. Sections 40(1) and (6), BSMA provide:

Contributions by subsidiary proprietors

40.—(1)    A management corporation may levy the contributions determined by it in accordance with section 39(1) or (2) or 41, and the contributions mentioned in section 39(3), by serving on the subsidiary proprietors written notice of the contributions payable by them in respect of their respective lots.

…

(6)     Any contribution levied under this section or section 41 —

(a)     becomes due and payable to the management corporation without any deduction whatsoever in accordance with the decision of the management corporation to make the levy;

(b)     if not paid on or before the 30th day after it becomes due and payable, bears interest at the rate determined by the management corporation and the interest accrues from the expiry of 30 days after the date when the contribution becomes due and payable unless the management corporation determines in a general meeting (either generally or in a particular case) that any unpaid contribution bears no interest; and

(c)     may, together with the interest due, be recovered as a debt by the management corporation in any court of competent jurisdiction.

(emphasis mine)

47     However, that does not preclude the application of the Limitation Act 1959 which provides at section 6(1)(d) that “actions to recover any sum recoverable by virtue of any written law” “shall not be brought after the expiration of 6 years from the date on which the cause of action accrued”:

Limitation of actions of contract and tort and certain other actions

6.—(1)    Subject to this Act, the following actions shall not be brought after the expiration of 6 years from the date on which the cause of action accrued:

(a)    …

…

(d)     actions to recover any sum recoverable by virtue of any written law other than a penalty or forfeiture or sum by way of penalty or forfeiture

(emphasis mine)

For completeness, it should be noted that neither party argued that the interest chargeable was a “penalty or forfeiture” which attracts a limitation period of “one year from the date on which the cause of action accrued”: section 6(4) of the Limitation Act 1959.

48     I am also not convinced by the Claimant’s argument that section 40(6) of the BSMA excludes the application of section 6(1) of the Limitation Act 1959 because “contributions are payable to the management corporation ‘without any deduction’ and late payment interest can only be waived by the general body”. As I understood it, the crux of this argument is that allowing the limitation defence would extinguish the Claimant’s right to outstanding contributions and this would contradict section 40(6) of the BSMA. I do not agree.

(a)     It is recognised that the expiry of a limitation period may have one of two results: extinguishing the claimant’s right, or barring the claimant’s remedy: Andrew McGee, Limitation Periods (Sweet & Maxwell, Thomson Reuters, 9th Ed, 2022) at [2-051].

(b)     In the present case, the express wording of section 6(1) of the Limitation Act 1959 makes clear that it does not extinguish the alleged debt. Instead, it simply bars the commencement of an action after the expiration of six years. And section 40(6) of the BSMA says nothing about the time within which court proceedings must be commenced.

(c)     This interpretation is also supported by section 26(2) of the Limitation Act 1959, which deems the right of action to recover a debt to have accrued on the date of an acknowledgment of the same or the last part payment. The Court of Appeal made the same point in Chuan & Company Pte Ltd v Ong Soon Huat [2003] 2 SLR(R) 205, albeit in the context of a contract claim governed by section 6(1)(a):

36    Under our statutory scheme, where the limitation period has expired, what it means is that the debt is irrecoverable. If the debtor is sued, he may plead the defence of limitation. However, this defence must be expressly pleaded: see s 4 of the Act, O 18 r 18(1) of the Rules of Court and the House of Lords’ decision in Ketteman v Hansel Properties [1987] AC 189 at 219. Thus, a judgment may be entered on such a claim unless the debtor raises the limitation defence. A judgment may also be entered if there is a subsequent acknowledgment of the debt. Therefore, our scheme of things does not render a debt which is time-barred non-existent; it only renders the debt irrecoverable if limitation is pleaded.

49     Finally, the Claimant had also submitted that section 40(10) of the BSMA makes it a criminal offence not to pay the MCST’s contributions.[note: 14] This may be so. However, it is not clear how this impacts the MCST’s ability to commence a civil claim, or why it should displace the operation of the Limitation Act 1959. Section 40(10) is reproduced:

(10)  A subsidiary proprietor who fails to pay any contribution or interest due and owing to a management corporation before the 14th day after the date of service of any written demand mentioned in subsection (9) shall be guilty of an offence and shall be liable on conviction to a fine not exceeding $10,000 and, in the case of a continuing offence, to a further fine not exceeding $100 for every day or part of a day during which the contribution or interest or both remain unpaid after conviction.

50     For these reasons, I find that the six-year limitation period under section 6(1) of the Limitation Act 1959 is applicable to an MCST’s claims for interest. I turn to consider whether it applied to the Claimant’s claims.

The Claimant has no good answer to the time bar defence

51     Once a limitation defence is pleaded, the burden lies on the Claimant to prove that its claim was brought within the applicable limitation period: IPP Financial Advisers Pte Ltd v Saimee bin Jumaat [2020] SGCA 47 at [37] to [41].

52     In the present case, the Claimant submitted that the Defendant caused time to run afresh by acknowledging the debt or making partial payments pursuant to section 26 of the Limitation Act 1959. The Claimant asserted the following in support of its submission:

(a)     the Claimant had lodged a charge on the Defendant’s property on 4 February 2015 (the “Charge”) and pursuant to section 26(1) of the Limitation Act 1959, the right of action to enforce the Charge is deemed to have accrued on the date of last payment;[note: 15]

(b)     the Defendant had acknowledged the Claimant’s claim pursuant to section 26(2) of the Limitation Act 1959:

(i)       through his solicitors’ letter of 10 May 2023;[note: 16]

(ii)       by failing to challenge the Charge;[note: 17] and

(c)     the Defendant had made partial payments from 9 March 2015 to 12 August 2025.[note: 18]

53     I am not convinced by any of these arguments for the following reasons.

(1)   Section 26(1) of the Limitation Act 1959 does not apply because the Claimant is not enforcing a charge

54     I start by reproducing section 26(1) and (2) of the Limitation Act 1959:

Fresh accrual of action on acknowledgment or part payment

26.—(1)    Where any right of action has accrued to recover land or to enforce a mortgage or charge in respect of land or personal property, and —

(a)    the person in possession of the land or personal property acknowledges the title of the person to whom the right of action has accrued; or

(b)    in the case of any such action by a mortgagee or chargee the person in possession as aforesaid or the person liable for the debt secured by the mortgage or charge makes any payment in respect thereof, whether of principal or interest,

the right shall be deemed to have accrued on and not before the date of the acknowledgment or the last payment.

(2)    Where any right of action has accrued to recover any debt or other liquidated pecuniary claim, or any claim to the personal estate of a deceased person or to any share or interest therein, and the person liable or accountable therefor acknowledges the claim or makes any payment in respect thereof, the right shall be deemed to have accrued on and not before the date of the acknowledgment or the last payment.

55     The Claimant’s reliance on section 26(1) fails at the outset. The text of section 26(1) of the Limitation Act 1959 makes clear that it applies to the “right of action” to “recover land or to enforce a mortgage or charge”. In the present case, however, the Claimant is not seeking to enforce any such right. The reliefs sought by the Claimant in its Statement of Claim are as follows:

AND the Claimants claim: -

(a)    the said sum of S$36,838.32;

(b)    interest at the rate of 12% per annum from the date of this Originating Claim to the date of judgment;

(c)    costs on an indemnity basis;

(d)    further or other relief which this Honourable Court deem fit.

(2)   The Defendant did not acknowledge the alleged debt

56     I turn to the Claimant’s submissions on there being an acknowledgment of the Claimant’s claims. In this regard, it is well established that for there to be an acknowledgment of the alleged debt, there must be a clear admission of liability or the debt in question: Chuan & Company Pte Ltd v Ong Soon Huat [2003] SGCA 15 at [12] and [18].

57     Applying these principles, it is clear that the Defendant’s solicitors’ letter of 10 May 2023 contained no such acknowledgment. Indeed, reading the letter, I was unable to find any admission of liability (and indeed, the Claimant did not identify any specific paragraph to that effect). On the contrary, the Defendant’s solicitors disputed the alleged debt in their letter. Consider the following extracts of the letter:[note: 19]

3.    First, all contributions and interest allegedly accrued and owing prior to May 2017 are time barred and should be discounted.

4.    Second, he had paid all maintenance and sinking fund contributions due and even had overpaid.

…

14.    We now refer to your client’s statement of accounts dated 17 August 2020.

15.    First, it included amounts allegedly due from January 2008. As stated above, this raises the impossibility that our client allegedly neglected to make maintenance and sinking fund payments in a condominium of less than 50 units for more than 10 years without the managing agent, council and auditors detecting it.

16.    Second, we note that your client only included $23,049.28 as interest owed on 31 October 2019 without giving any reference to the principal on which this sum was calculated substantiates our client’s position that its accounting /record system is flawed.

58     As for the Defendant’s alleged failure to challenge the Charge, this submission must fail. First of all, the Defendant’s silence (without more) is at most equivocal and does not amount to an acknowledgment of the alleged debt. In any event, section 27 of the Limitation Act 1959 provides that any such acknowledgment must be in writing and signed by the person making the acknowledgment or his agent. Any failure by the Defendant to challenge the Charge does not meet these formal requirements:

Formal provisions as to acknowledgments and part payments

27.—(1)    Every such acknowledgment as is referred to in section 26 shall be in writing and signed by the person making the acknowledgment.

(2)    Any such acknowledgment or payment as is referred to in section 26 may be made by the agent of the person by whom it is required to be made under that section, and shall be made to the person, or to an agent of the person, whose title or claim is being acknowledged or, as the case may be, in respect of whose claim the payment is being made.

(3)   The Defendant did not make part payments of the alleged debt

59     I turn to the Claimant’s submission that the Defendant had made part payments of the alleged debts. In support of this submission, the Claimant argued that pursuant to section 43(9) of the BSMA, “all management funds, sinking funds, accrued interest and legal costs secured under the Charge are not distinct debts but instead form a single debt that the Defendant owes the Claimant”[note: 20] and that the Defendant had made part payments from 9 March 2015 to 12 August 2025.

60     I reject this submission.

61     First, the wording of section 43(9) does not support the effect which the Claimant contends. It simply makes clear that section 43 does not affect the rights and powers conferred by sections 30 and 40:

(9)    This section does not affect the rights and powers conferred on the management corporation by sections 30 and 40 to recover the amount or contribution due and all interest thereon including any legal costs and incidental charges necessarily incurred for the recovery of the amount or contribution in respect of any lot as a debt from the subsidiary proprietor of, or the subsidiary proprietor’s successor in title to, the lot.

62     On my reading of the provision, section 43(9) is simply a savings provision that preserves the management corporation’s rights under sections 30 and 40. It says nothing about whether the various sums owed by a subsidiary proprietor constitute a single debt or distinct debts for the purposes of the Limitation Act 1959. It also does not operate to combine into a single debt the various sums, which even on the Claimant’s case, accrued on different dates.

63     In the affidavit of Chng Hui Ru, the Claimant exhibited a subsequent Statement of Accounts dated 17 October 2025 which purported to show the “Management and Sinking Funds accounts of billing and payment starting in December 2003 when the Defendant bought the unit”.[note: 21] This 17 October 2025 Statement of Accounts showed that the first entry of the 12 May 2025 Statement of Accounts, to which the limitation defence applied, (see [42] above) arose from multiple invoices issued on various dates. These invoices spanned pages 2 to 4 of the same document. The relevant portion of page 2 of the 17 October 2025 Statement of Accounts is reproduced for illustration purposes:

64     Flowing from the above, even if the Claimant had applied the Defendant’s payments to sums owing chronologically, that does not operate to reset the limitation period for subsequent debts that had accrued but remained unpaid. Further, the Claimant’s evidence did not identify any partially paid debts.

65     Accordingly, to the extent that there are outstanding debts due from August 2007 to October 2017, they remain time-barred and any such claim should be struck out.

The 12 May 2025 Statement of Accounts is deeply flawed

66     As noted at [43] above, the Defendant’s position at the first substantive hearing was not simply that parts of the Claimant’s claim were liable to be struck out because it was time-barred. The Defendant’s position at the first substantive hearing was also that the Claimant’s entire claim should be struck out because:

(a)     The 12 May 2025 Statement of Accounts is incorrect and manufactured for this claim.

(b)     Only claims for interest after 22 February 2024 are valid.

(c)     The Defendant has paid more than his maintenance and sinking fund and other contributions from 18 July 2019.

67     I do not intend to make any finding as to whether the Claimant had “manufactured” the 12 May 2025 Statement of Accounts for this claim. For the purposes of this application, it is sufficient to find that:

(a)     the Claimant’s 12 May 2025 Statement of Accounts was a poor basis to support a claim because it was a deeply flawed document which was contradicted by the Claimant’s own accounts; and

(b)     as of the first substantive hearing on 8 April 2026, the Claimant was not in a position to plead, particularise and point to proof of each element of its cause of action. The original Statement of Claim was therefore liable to be struck out (see Chandra Winata discussed at [39] above).

68     I explain my reasons for my findings above.

The 12 May 2025 Statement of Accounts was contradicted by the Claimant’s own records

69     As elaborated at [42] above, the 12 May 2025 Statement of Accounts purported to record the debts due from the Defendant and the payments he made starting from August 2007 to 1 May 2025.

70     However, the 12 May 2025 Statement of Accounts did not record all the payments made by the Defendant. On its face, the Defendant had made only three payments to the Claimant. These are the sums of S$810 and S$820 which were paid on 2 June 2024 and 29 October 2024 respectively (see the second and third entry above) as well as the sum of S$1,000 which was paid on 3 February 2025.[note: 22]

71     This was incorrect. The Claimant exhibited a subsequent Statement of Accounts dated 17 October 2025[note: 23] which it described as “showing the Management and Sinking Funds accounts of billing and payment, starting in December 2003 when the Defendant bought the unit”.[note: 24] This statement showed numerous payments made by the Defendant that were not reflected in the 12 May 2025 Statement of Accounts.

72     For example, the 12 May 2025 Statement of Accounts stated that the Defendant had not paid the sums of S$531 and S$45 for the management and sinking fund for the period August 2020 to October 2020 and that these sums remained payable. However, the Claimant’s 17 October 2025 Statement of Accounts showed that those sums were paid:

12 May 2025 Statement of Accounts at p.1[note: 25]

17 October 2025 Statement of Accounts at p.5[note: 26]



73     This was material. The basis of the Claimant’s claim was that the Defendant failed to make payments due to the management fund and sinking fund. However, the Claimant’s own accounts completely undermined this.

74     Indeed, the 17 October 2025 Statement of Accounts demonstrated that the 12 May 2025 Statement of Accounts’ failure to record the Defendant’s payments was not a one-off error. Instead, the 17 October 2025 Statement of Accounts appeared to show that the Defendant had paid off all of the sums due to the management fund and sinking fund up to and including the month of July 2025 when the Claimant commenced this action (see [5] above). According to the 17 October 2025 Statement of Accounts, as of 31 July 2025, only interest (starting from 30 September 2004) and legal fees of S$725.78 (incurred on 1 May 2015) were outstanding.

75     This inadequacy of the 12 May 2025 Statement of Accounts was confirmed at the second substantive hearing. In that hearing, I had reviewed with Claimant’s counsel the 17 October 2025 Statement of Accounts. After that review, the Claimant’s counsel accepted that the sums outstanding up to July 2025 appeared to comprise only interest and legal fees. This was also the very point made by the Defendant right from the start in his first written submissions of 1 April 2026. In those submissions, the Defendant had submitted that the 17 October 2025 Statement of Accounts “support[ed] his position that he has paid all his maintenance and sinking fund contributions”.[note: 27]

The Claimant did not particularise and point to proof of its interest claim

76     I turn to the Claimant’s claim for interest. As noted at [42] above, the 12 May 2025 Accounts purported to record outstanding interest from August 2007.

77     There are two main difficulties with the Claimant’s claim for interest.

78     First, and as discussed, the 12 May 2025 Statement of Accounts stated that the Defendant had not paid the management fund and sinking fund contributions that became due. However, this was contradicted by the Claimant’s subsequent 17 October 2025 Statement of Accounts which stated that the Defendant had made these payments and that primarily interest remained outstanding.

79     Now, even assuming that the Defendant had made these payments between May and October 2025, the onus was on the Claimant to particularise when these payments were made. Without these particulars, the Defendant could not ascertain whether the Claimant’s position was correct, whether interest had been correctly charged, or whether there was any basis to challenge it. However, these particulars could not be discerned from either Statement of Accounts.

80     Second, it was not entirely clear that the Claimant had the right to charge interest of 12% per annum for the entire period which it sought to do. In this regard, the Defendant did not dispute that a management corporation such as the Claimant is entitled to charge and sue for outstanding interest pursuant to section 40(6)(b) of the BSMA (reproduced for ease of reference):

(6)    Any contribution levied under this section or section 41 —

(a)    becomes due and payable to the management corporation without any deduction whatsoever in accordance with the decision of the management corporation to make the levy;

(b)     if not paid on or before the 30th day after it becomes due and payable, bears interest at the rate determined by the management corporation and the interest accrues from the expiry of 30 days after the date when the contribution becomes due and payable unless the management corporation determines in a general meeting (either generally or in a particular case) that any unpaid contribution bears no interest; and

(c)    may, together with the interest due, be recovered as a debt by the management corporation in any court of competent jurisdiction.

(emphasis mine)

81     What the Defendant’s counsel took issue with was that the Claimant relied only on a resolution dated 22 February 2024. He submitted that “interest charges are authorised and only imposed after a resolution is passed” and “as the Claimant relies only on a resolution dated 22 February 2024 … all interest charges prior to 22 February 2024 are void”. [note: 28]

82     The Claimant’s counsel did not contest the legal premise of the Defendant’s submission. Instead, he submitted that there were resolutions which authorised this 12% rate. However, he conceded that save for the 22 February 2024 resolution, these resolutions were not before the Court.

83     I see the force of the Defendant’s submission. Critically, the only paragraph of the Claimant’s original Statement of Claim which provides any basis for this 12% interest rate is [7]. In that paragraph, the Claimant pleaded that it had “in force a resolution which entitles [it] to … recover interest at 12% per annum until payment is made”. This cohered with the Defendant’s submissions that the Claimant was only relying on one resolution to ground its interest claim and contradicted the Claimant’s response.

84     Furthermore, even taking the Claimant’s submissions at face value, the law is clear that a claimant must plead every essential element of its cause of action, furnish sufficient particulars so that the defendant has reasonable notice of the case he has to meet, and point to proof for each element of the claim (see [39] above). However, for the reasons at [78]-[83], the Claimant failed to do so. Its interest claim was therefore embarrassing, unsupported by the necessary proof, and liable to be struck out under O 9 r 16(b) and/or O 9 r 16(c) of the Rules of Court 2021.

The original Statement of Claim could not stand

85     For the reasons above, the original Statement of Claim could not stand. The Claimant’s original case was premised on the 12 May 2025 Statement of Accounts. However, that Statement of Accounts omitted material payments, was contradicted by the Claimant’s own later accounts, and did not provide a proper basis for the Claimant’s claim for interest. The net effect of this was that as of the end of the first substantive hearing, the Claimant was not in a position to plead, particularise and point to proof for the essential elements of its claim. Its claim was liable to be struck out.

86     Nevertheless, due to the draconian nature of a striking out application, I gave the Claimant the opportunity to propose amendments to its Statement of Claim. Indeed, the law recognises that if the defects of the Claimant’s Statement of Claim could be cured by an amendment, that would be preferable to striking it out (see Ching Mun Fong (executrix of the estate of Tan Geok Tee, deceased) v Liu Cho Chit and another appeal [2000] 1 SLR(R) 53 at [12]). In this regard, I also stated that:

(a)     If the Claimant’s position was that interest had accrued because of late payments, the dates of the relevant payments and how the interest was computed should be particularised in its amended Statement of Claim; and

(b)     If the Claimant was seeking to rely on Annual General Meetings to ground its right to charge interest at a rate of 12% per annum, the relevant minutes should be exhibited in that further affidavit.

87     As noted at [19]-[23], this led to the Claimant filing Ms Chng Hui Ru’s affidavit dated 6 May 2026, the Defendant filing a further affidavit on 3 June 2026, and the parties filing further written submissions on 11 June 2026 ahead of the second substantive hearing on 18 June 2026.

The Claimant’s proposed amended case remains liable to be struck out

88     Notwithstanding the indulgence given to the Claimant, its claim remained liable to be struck out. I explain.

The time-barred claims remained unsustainable

89     First and foremost, although the Claimant’s counsel sought to revisit the time bar issues at the second substantive hearing, no new arguments were made and no fresh authority was tendered. As such, for the reasons at [45]-[65] above, I remain of the view that the Claimant’s claims which arose more than six years prior to the commencement of this action on 18 July 2025 are time-barred and should be struck out.

The Claimant failed to put its case in order despite being given the opportunity

90     Second, the Claimant failed to put its case in order despite having been given a clear opportunity to do so. It would be recalled that at the first substantive hearing, the difficulties with the Claimant’s accounts and interest claim were squarely identified. Amongst other things, the Defendant had challenged both:

(a)     the correctness of the Claimant’s records; and

(b)     the Claimant’s entitlement to charge interest at 12% per annum before 22 February 2024.

91     At that hearing, I was prepared to proceed on the basis that the Claimant might be able to save its claim if it could put its accounts in order and properly address the Defendant’s criticisms. I had also set out what I expected the Claimant’s further affidavit to address (see [86] above).

92     However, the Claimant failed to take up this opportunity. Not only did the Claimant’s proposed amended Statement of Claim refer to a non-existent 18 July 2025 Statement of Accounts, the Claimant also failed to put its accounts in order and point to proof of the relevant AGM resolutions. The effect of this was that as at the second substantive hearing, the Claimant remained unable to plead, particularise, or point to the necessary proof of its case. This rendered its claim liable to be struck out (see Chandra Winata at [39] above). I elaborate.

Proposed amendments to the Statement of Claim referred to a non-existent Statement of Accounts

93     I start with the defects in the Claimant’s proposed Statement of Claim (Amendment No.1). Therein, the Claimant sought to rely on a Statement of Accounts dated 18 July 2025 instead of the original 12 May 2025 Statement of Accounts. The proposed Statement of Claim (Amendment No.1) states at [3]: [note: 29]

3. The Claimants’ claim is for the sum of S$36,838.32 S$32,256.81 being outstanding contributions to the management fund and sinking fund [imposed pursuant to sections 39 and 40 of the Building Maintenance And (Strata Management) Act 2004] and interest, full particulars have been rendered to the Defendant and short particulars are as follows:

PARTICULARS

Date

Particular

Amount (S$)

128/057/25

Statement of Account

36,838.32

32,256.81



94     However, there was no such document. This was confirmed by the Claimant’s counsel at the second substantive hearing. When asked to identify the 18 July 2025 Statement of Accounts, Claimant’s counsel referred me instead to the 17 October 2025 Statement of Accounts exhibited at pp 17–24 of Ms Chng’s 6 May 2026 affidavit. He then confirmed that there was no 18 July 2025 Statement of Accounts and that the proposed amended Statement of Claim should have referred to the 17 October 2025 Statement of Accounts instead.

95     I might have been prepared to overlook this failing assuming the incorrect date was a simple typographical error and the 17 October 2025 Statement of Accounts was in fact the correct document. However, this was not the case. Contrary to the proposed amendments which reflected an outstanding sum of S$32,256.81, the 17 October 2025 Statement of Accounts reflected an outstanding sum of S$32,310.07.

96     For completeness, I would add also that the Claimant had, in Ms Chng’s affidavit, introduced yet another Statement of Accounts dated 4 May 2026. However, this was also not the Statement of Accounts referred to in the proposed Statement of Claim (Amendment No.1). Quite apart from the different date, the 4 May 2026 Statement of Accounts ends off with a balance of S$35,251.60. This is approximately S$3,000 more than the S$32,256.81 which the Claimant purported to claim in its proposed amendments.

The Claimant failed to put its accounts in order

97     Next, the Claimant had also failed to put its accounts in order. In the second substantive hearing, the Claimant sought to rely on the 4 May 2026 Statement of Accounts to show that payments made by the Defendant were appropriated first to earlier accrued interest before being applied to management fund, sinking fund and special levies. In support, the Claimant relied on resolutions passed starting from the Annual General Meetings held on 26 February 2022 wherein it was resolved that:[note: 30]

5.0    Payment Appropriation

It was unanimously resolved that all payments made by subsidiary proprietors to the Management Corporation shall be appropriated strictly in the following manner and the subsidiary proprietors shall have no rights to appropriate otherwise.

a.    Firstly, in payment of Interests charges.

b.    Secondly, in payment of Goods and Service Taxes.

c.    Thirdly, in payment of any Legal costs owing to the Management Corporation by the subsidiary proprietors and/or their tenant.

d.    Fourthly, in payment of all outstanding Levies and any other Monies due from the subsidiary proprietors to the Management Corporation.

e.    Fifthly, in payment of all outstanding payments of any nature for services of amenities or services provided by the Management Corporation to the subsidiary proprietors and/or the tenants.

f.    Lastly, in payment to the Management Funds followed by the Sinking Funds.

98     On the Claimant’s case, the effect of this resolution was that, notwithstanding the Defendant’s instructions to apply his payments to the sums due for the management fund and sinking fund, the Defendant’s payments were instead first applied towards outstanding interest (which the Defendant contended was time-barred). On that basis, the Claimant submitted that the outstanding amounts owed by the Defendant for the management fund, sinking fund and special levies were S$16,985.78 as at 18 July 2025, and S$22,430.78 as at 29 April 2026.

99     As no arguments were made on the legality (or otherwise) of the aforesaid resolution, I make no comment on the same and proceed on the assumption that it is legal and that the Claimant’s case was not legally unsustainable.

100    I am also prepared to accept that the Claimant’s case would not be factually unsustainable assuming the 4 May 2026 Statement of Accounts properly explained the Claimant’s accounts. If so, the fact that it departed from the 17 October 2025 Statement of Accounts would not have been a sufficient reason to strike out the Claimant’s case. Such issues would ordinarily be tested at trial.

101    But that was not the position here. Taking the Claimant’s case at its highest, it was only from the 26 February 2022 Annual General Meeting that the Claimant had a resolution requiring payments to be applied to interest first. The resolution before that was framed only as an authority to offset interest against payments received. It did not require the Claimant to apply every payment first to interest. The 27 February 2021 resolution stated:[note: 31]

5.0    Offset Interests against Payment received

It was unanimously resolved that the Management Corporation be authorised to offset interest for late payment of Management Fund and Sinking Fund contributions and any other contributions or any other amount owed to the Management Corporation by a subsidiary proprietor against payment received from subsidiary proprietor concerned.

102    This mattered because the Claimant had changed how it applied payments received from the Defendant before 2022 in its 4 May 2026 Statement of Accounts. In particular, the Claimant reallocated payments which it had previously applied towards management fund and sinking fund contributions to earlier interest charges.

103    To take the example discussed at the second substantive hearing, the 4 May 2026 Statement of Accounts showed an outstanding management fund contribution of S$531 for the period February to March 2020 under Invoice INMFMC14337. However, the 17 October 2025 Statement of Accounts showed no such outstanding principal sum. Further, the Claimant’s own spreadsheet showed that the Defendant’s payment of S$585 on 23 August 2021 (i.e., before the 26 February 2022 resolution) had been applied to Invoice INMFMC14337. This is seen from the following extracts of the aforesaid documents, with highlights added for ease of reference:

4 May 2026 Statement of Accounts, p.1[note: 32]

17 October 2025 Statement of Accounts, p.15[note: 33]

Claimant’s Excel spreadsheet of payments received from the Defendant[note: 34]



104    The Claimant was also unable to explain this discrepancy at the second substantive hearing. Nothing was said of the point in Ms Chng’s 6 May 2026 affidavit, and no explanation was given by counsel at the hearing. Instead, counsel sought permission to file a further affidavit to explain the inconsistencies in the Claimant’s accounts.

The Claimant failed to point to proof of its pre-2021 interest charges

105    The same difficulty arose in relation to the Claimant’s alleged entitlement to interest at 12% per annum. Even though the Claimant was suing for interest arising from the early 2000s and it bore the burden of properly substantiating its claim, the Claimant only exhibited resolutions from 27 February 2021 onwards in the affidavit of Ms Chng Hui Ru dated 6 May 2026 at Tab 3 of CHR-1.

106    Unsurprisingly, the Defendant renewed his submissions that the Claimant’s claim for interest was unsupported for most of the period claimed.[note: 35]

107    In response, the Claimant’s counsel submitted that the Claimant could not trace the relevant resolutions because it had changed its managing agent. The Claimant’s counsel also sought to rely on the invoices issued for interest which reflected this 12% rate.

108    In my view, the Claimant’s explanation was insufficient to stave off a striking out application. In saying this, I am aware that the evidential threshold that the Claimant has to cross at the striking out stage is not high. As explained in Chandra Winata at [35] (reproduced at [39] above), “[t]he proof which a plaintiff points to on a striking-out application can be nothing more than his own uncorroborated and self-serving testimony as to facts within his personal knowledge.”

109    However, the Claimant does not even cross this low threshold.

(a)     The Claimant’s explanation about the Annual General Meeting resolutions is set out in Ms Chng Hui Ru’s 6 May 2026 affidavit. However, the Claimant did not point to any evidence showing that the 12% rate had been determined by the management corporation. Further, nowhere in this affidavit did the Claimant say that it was unable to obtain the earlier resolutions because of a change in managing agent. On the contrary, on the face of the affidavit, the Claimant appeared to have exhibited all the resolutions it intended to rely on. The sole paragraph on the point was [3(c)] which stated:

(c)    The relevant AGM resolutions on late interest charges, claiming costs on an indemnity basis and apportionment of payment. The resolutions in the Claimants’ possession are exhibited at Tab 3 of CHR-1

(b)     A similar issue arises vis-à-vis the Claimant’s attempt to rely on the invoices. Nowhere in Ms Chng Hui Ru’s 6 May 2026 affidavit did she say that the Claimant was relying on these invoices as proof that the Claimant had determined the 12% interest rate in accordance with section 40(6)(b) of the BSMA. Instead, she stated at [4] that the invoices were exhibited as evidence that they had been issued to the Defendant for the relevant quarters:

4.    I also exhibit herewith at TAB 4 of CHR-1 copies of the quarterly invoices / statements issued by the previous managing agent (Focal Property Services), for the period 2009 to 2020, to the Defendant. These invoices / statements are enclosed as evidence that the said invoices / statements were issued to the Defendant for the relevant quarters.

110    As such, I am of the view that the Claimant’s interest claim remained unsupported for a substantial part of the period claimed (i.e., before 27 February 2021). It was thus liable to be struck out. This is especially so given that this issue had already been flagged at the first substantive hearing, and the Claimant had been given a further opportunity to adduce the necessary evidence.

Conclusion

111    The net effect of the two substantive hearings before me is that, even by the second substantive hearing, the Claimant remained unable to properly plead and particularise its case, or point to the necessary proof in support of it. In particular, the Claimant could not state:

(a)     the amount of management fund and sinking fund contributions (if any) that remained outstanding;

(b)     assuming the Claimant’s case was that the Defendant had paid these contributions late, when they were in fact paid; and

(c)     what interest, if any, was properly chargeable.

112    Applying Chandra Winata, the Claimant’s claim was liable to be struck out.

113    The next question is whether I should give the Claimant another chance to amend its Statement of Claim. In this regard, I draw guidance from EA Apartments Pte Ltd v Tan Bek and others [2017] 3 SLR 559. In that case, the High Court refused a further opportunity to amend after the plaintiff had already been given prior opportunities and was effectively offering its case “in dribs and drabs”: at [50]–[51].

114    The same reasoning applies here. It is possible that the Claimant might be able to fix some of the deficiencies in its case. But that is not the question now. The question is whether, after the opportunity already given, it is just to give the Claimant another attempt. I did not think it was. In this case, the relevant issues had already been identified at the first substantive hearing. The Claimant was then given a further opportunity to amend and to adduce the necessary evidence. However, it did not use that opportunity to put forward a proper case. To give the Claimant yet another chance to amend its Statement of Claim would drag out these proceedings and unfairly prejudice the Defendant.

115    For the reasons above, the Claimant’s Statement of Claim is struck out in its entirety under O 9 r 16(1)(b) and/or O 9 r 16(1)(c) of the Rules of Court 2021. Further, to the extent that the Claimant sought to rely on its proposed amendments, I decline to grant permission to amend.

116    I will hear parties on the appropriate consequential orders, including the further conduct of the Defendant’s counterclaim. The parties are directed to file written submissions on costs (limited to 5 pages) within seven days of this decision.

Public Prosecutor v Lew Jun De

Public Prosecutor v Lew Jun De
[2026] SGDC 192

Case Number:District Arrest Case No. 912750 of 2025, Magistrate's Appeal No. 9137/2026/01
Decision Date:13 July 2026
Tribunal/Court:District Court
Coram: Shawn Ho
Counsel Name(s): Heershan Kaur (Attorney-General's Chambers) for the Prosecution; B. Rajendraprasad (Regent Law LLC) for the Defence.
Parties: Public Prosecutor — Lew Jun De

Criminal Law – Statutory Offences – Road Traffic Act

Criminal Law – Careless driving – Grievous hurt

[LawNet Editorial Note: An appeal to this decision has been filed in MA 9137/2026/01.]

13 July 2026

District Judge Shawn Ho:

Introduction

1       The Accused, Mr Lew Jun De, pleaded guilty to one charge of careless driving causing grievous hurt to a pedestrian under s 65(1)(a) punishable under s 65(3)(a) read with s 65(6)(d) of the Road Traffic Act 1961.

2       The Prosecution asked for 3 to 4 weeks’ imprisonment (PG basis) and a 5-year driving disqualification. The Defence asked for imprisonment of no longer than 15 days and a disqualification period of no longer than 5 years.

3       He was sentenced to 15 days’ imprisonment and a mandatory 5-year driving disqualification for all classes of driving licences.

4       The Defence has appealed against the sentence. The Accused is currently on bail pending appeal. His imprisonment term and driving disqualification order have been stayed.

5       I set out my reasons.

Charge

6       The Accused pleaded guilty to the following charge:

You,

Name: Lew Jun De

Gender/ Age: Male/ 28 Years Old

Facts relating to the charge DAC 912750 2025

11     On 9 December 2023, at about 6.30pm, the victim was conducting foot patrol along Maude Road towards King George’s Avenue before Townshend Road Lamp Post 4 to check for parking coupons on parked vehicles. 18     By virtue of the foregoing, the Accused had driven his Car, a motor vehicle, on a road, without due care and attention, and had caused grievous hurt to the victim. Prescribed punishment

19     The prescribed punishment for causing grievous hurt under s 65(1) punishable under s 65(3)(a) read with s 65(6)(d) of the Road Traffic Act 1961 (“the Act”) is:

(a)      s 65(3)(a): a fine not exceeding $5,000 or to imprisonment for a term not exceeding 2 years or to both;

(b)      s 65(6)(d): for an offender or a repeat offender in s 65(3)(a) or s 65(3)(b) – a driving disqualification for a period of not less than 5 years.

20     The two components of the overall sentence generally are not to be regarded as mutually compensatory. Hence, an increase in the fine or custodial sentence should not be taken to mandate the imposition of a reduced disqualification period than would otherwise have been ordered: Edwin s/o Suse Nathen v Public Prosecutor [2013] SGHC 194 at [13]-[14].

21     While the different types of punishment are not fungible, there is a positive correlation between the length of the imprisonment term and/or quantum of the fine imposed and the period of the disqualification ordered. This direct relationship arises from the overlapping considerations of harm and culpability underlying the determination of the length of imprisonment or quantum of fine, and the length of the disqualification period: Chen Song v Public Prosecutor [2025] 3 SLR 509 at [141].

22     An offence’s statutory maximum sentence signals the gravity in which Parliament views such offences. A sentencing judge ought to take this into account when determining precisely where the offender’s conduct falls within the entire range of punishment set by Parliament: Public Prosecutor v Kwong Kok Hing [2008] 2 SLR(R) 684 at [44].

(Benny Tan, Assessing the Effectiveness of Sentencing Guideline Judgments in Singapore Issued Post-March 2013 and A Guide to Constructing Frameworks, (2018) 30 SAcLJ 1004 at [46])

23     The court should ensure that the full spectrum of sentences enacted by Parliament is carefully explored in determining the appropriate sentence, viz. Completeness principle (Poh Boon Kiat v Public Prosecutor [2014] 4 SLR 892 at [60]).

Sentencing

The Law

(1)   Legislative history of s 65 of the Act

28     As was observed by Sundaresh Menon CJ in Wu Zhi Yong v Public Prosecutor [2021] SGHC 261 at [15] (albeit in the related context of s 64 of the Act), the Road Traffic (Amendment) Act 2019 (Act 19 of 2019) envisaged a new scheme of penalties for careless or inconsiderate driving in a tiered structure calibrated according to the degree of hurt caused. This is codified in the Act as ss 65(2) to 65(5). The maximum punishments which may be imposed for each category of harm increase concomitantly with the seriousness of the harm caused; this translates into wider ranges of punishments where more serious harm is occasioned (Sue Chang v Public Prosecutor [2022] SGHC 176 at [38]).

29     For instance, where death is caused, s 65(2)(a) provides that a first-time offender is liable to a fine not exceeding $10,000 or to imprisonment for a term not exceeding three years or to both. In contrast, the residual category (where no actual physical harm is caused, but which includes cases of non-personal injury or potential harm) captured in s 65(5)(a) provides that a first-time offender is liable to a fine not exceeding $1,500 or to imprisonment for a term not exceeding six months or to both (Sue Chang at [38]).

30     By tiering the punishment provisions in accordance with the type of harm suffered, Parliament has given clear expression to the need to give explicit consideration to the outcomes that result from instances of careless or inconsiderate driving. This is a stark departure from the structure of s 65 of the pre-2019 Act, where there was a single range of punishment with no differentiation based on the type and/or degree of harm caused (Sue Chang at [39]).

31     In addition, while Parliament has retained the distinction between reckless or dangerous driving under s 64 of the Act and careless or inconsiderate driving under s 65 of the Act, this distinction has been made more pronounced through the refining of the punishment provisions. These two provisions reflect the differing circumstances under which an irresponsible driving offence can occur. The former offence (s 64) is regarded as being more serious than the latter (s 65), reflecting primarily the differing levels of culpability of the offenders. Accordingly, the current architecture of the Act concerning irresponsible driving offences tiers the punishment provisions according to both harm and culpability, not dissimilar to the Penal Code (Sue Chang at [40]).

(2)   Driving disqualification order

32     Driving disqualification orders meld the three sentencing objectives of punishment, protection of the public and deterrence: Edwin s/o Suse Nathen v Public Prosecutor [2013] 4 SLR 1139 at [13]-[14], Public Prosecutor v Koh Thiam Huat [2017] 4 SLR 1099 at [64] and Chen Song v Public Prosecutor [2024] SGHC 129 at [143].

33     The most important sentencing principles engaged in driving disqualification orders are to:

(a)      protect society, because disqualification orders are meant to prevent future harm that the offender may cause to the public, and to

(b)      deter, because such orders deprive offenders of the freedom to drive: Public Prosecutor v Ong Heng Chua [2018] SGHC 95 at [61].

34     As stated in Public Prosecutor v Mohd Isa [1963] MLJ 135, the “most satisfactory penalty for most motoring offences is disqualification” because a fine is paid once and then forgotten. For instance, a 12-month disqualification order would mean that for the entire year in which the order is in effect, the offender is reminded every day of his offence and the unwarranted risks in which he had placed ordinary members of the public: Sivakumar s/o Rajoo v Public Prosecutor [2002] 1 SLR(R) 265 at [28].

35     Where a person is disqualified for a period of 12 months or longer, that person’s driving licence shall be “of no effect” and the person is further prevented from driving a motor vehicle after the disqualification period unless he passes the prescribed test of competence to drive: s 43(1)(b) of the Road Traffic Act.

Decision on sentence

36     For driving without due care or attention causing grievous hurt, the applicable case is Chen Song v Public Prosecutor [2024] SGHC 129.

Framework in Chen Song

37     A quantitative factors-based approach, where the indicative sentencing band is determined at the first step, based on the number of offence-specific harm and culpability factors is especially useful: Chen Song at [123].

38     “Lesser harm” is caused and the offender’s culpability is deemed as “lower culpability” where at most one harm or culpability factor applies in respect of each category: Chen Song at [123].

39     “Greater harm” would be caused and the offender’s culpability deemed as “higher culpability” where there are 2 or more harm and culpability factors respectively: Chen Song at [123].

40     This is a general guideline which is not to be applied mechanistically in every case. The foremost inquiry is to assess holistically whether the totality of the harm suffered by the victim should be classified as either “greater harm” or “lesser harm” and whether the offender’s culpability considered as a whole should be classified as either “lower culpability” or “higher culpability”: Chen Song at [123].

(1)   Harm factors

41     Primary harm factors are factors which pertain directly to the bodily injury suffered by the victim(s) in each case. These factors include:

(a)     the nature and location of the injuries;

(b)     the degree of permanence of the injuries; and

(c)     the impact of the injuries: Chen Song at [124].

42     The three broad primary harm factors are:

(a)      Nature and location of the injury: This factor focuses on the precise nature and the location of the injury. This requires a consideration of:

(i)       the nature and severity of injury (eg, simple or complex and extent of injury, etc);

(ii)       the number of injuries;

(iii)       whether surgical intervention was necessary (or whether the injuries were treated conservatively);

(iv)       the disposition of the victim post-surgery (eg, general ward, high dependency or intensive care unit); and

(v)       the location of the injury (eg, vulnerable location).

(b)      Degree of permanence: This factor considers whether the injury or injuries caused to the victim are permanent or transient. Permanent injuries include loss of a limb or permanent privation of the sight of either eye or the hearing of either ear, etc.

(c)      Impact of injury: This factor contemplates the impact of the injury on the victim’s quality of life. Here, considerations of:

(i)       the duration of stay in the hospital/rehabilitation centre;

(ii)       duration of any hospitalisation/medical leave;

(iii)       ability to carry out daily tasks and maintain livelihood; and

(iv)       duration of rehabilitation (if any), are relevant: Chen Song at [127].

43     There is an inevitable overlap between the factors of nature and location of injury on the one hand, and impact of injury on the other. The period and nature of hospitalisation may be an indicium of both the nature and severity of the injury and perhaps even the number of injuries suffered, and its impact on the victim’s quality of life. The period and nature of hospitalisation may be relevant to both factors: Habeeb Zaleena d/o Pallivilakam Kader Habeeb Mohamed v Public Prosecutor [2026] SGHC 99 at [35].

44     As to whether an injury is at a vulnerable location, the High Court in Ling Zhao Bin v Public Prosecutor [2026] SGHC 107 stated at [27]:

It seems to me that the parts of the body were regarded as vulnerable because the injuries were to, or in locations proximate to, vital organs. The common thread is that these locations are vulnerable because an injury suffered in any of these locations, may result in a risk to life or permanent or long-term loss of function that impairs the victim’s ability to live independently and without assistance (eg loss of cognitive ability or paralysis). Vulnerability is defined with the reference to the severity of the harm that could result from an injury in a location. Without being prescriptive and in any way comprehensive, this common thread could serve as a working definition of a vulnerable location. It is consistent with why an injury to a vulnerable location was identified in Chen Song as relevant to the harm analysis under the “nature and location” factor, and the purpose of the central inquiry in the harm analysis (which is to ascertain the extent of physical harm that is suffered by the victim as a result of the injury in question as stated at [22] above).

[emphasis added]

45     I bore in mind that there may be cases where even if two or more primary harm factors apply, if they present themselves to a limited degree, the court may nevertheless consider that “lesser harm” had been caused based on a holistic assessment of the harm caused: Chen Song at [127].

46     Secondary harm factors are unrelated to the physical injury suffered by the victim(s), but which nonetheless go towards the extent of harm caused in a particular case. These factors include:

(a)     property damage; and

(b)     potential harm: Chen Song at [125].

47     Consideration of actual harm focuses on the moment of a collision. Potential harm looks at the wider circumstances before and after a collision (Public Prosecutor v Cheng Chang Tong [2023] SGHC 119 at [57]).

48     Potential harm refers to harm that was likely to have been caused to other road users but which ultimately did not eventuate: Chen Song at [129] and Public Prosecutor v Johnson Tan Wee Kiat [2026] SGHC 59 at [13].

49     The level of potential harm may be assessed against facts such as the condition of the road, the volume of traffic or number of pedestrians actually on or which might reasonably be expected to be on the road at the relevant time, the speed and manner of driving, visibility at the relevant time, the type of vehicle, and any particular vulnerabilities (eg, a truck or car colliding into a motorcycle or pedestrian). It was observed that these relate to the circumstances of driving that could increase the danger posed to road users (Wu Zhi Yong at [36(a)]): Chen Song at [129].

50     It would only be appropriate to have regard to potential harm if there was a sufficient likelihood of the harm arising and this in turn should be assessed in the light of the gravity of the harm risked (Neo Ah Luan v Public Prosecutor [2018] 5 SLR 1153 at [67]): Chen Song at [129].

51     The potential for harm has to be assessed with reference not only to the actual distance travelled, but the distance which the offender intended to travel (Chan Chow Chuen v Public Prosecutor [2024] SGHC 294 at [24]). In Fan Lei v Public Prosecutor [2024] SGHC 278 at [10], travelling a distance of 17km was not enough to point to increased potential harm. In Fan Lei, there was no evidence that the offender was driving in a careless manner over that 17km.

52     I was mindful that in assessing the level of harm or potential harm, the sentencing court should be careful not to double-count any factors which may already have been taken into account in assessing the level of culpability: Ye Lin Myint v Public Prosecutor [2019] 5 SLR 1005 at [58] (see also Andrew Ashworth, Sentencing and Criminal Justice (6th Ed, 2015, Cambridge University Press) at [4.3] and [4.5]).

53     Each primary harm factor would count as one offence-specific factor going towards harm. However, where a secondary harm factor presents itself in a significant manner, this should be considered in the determination of where the particular offence falls within the indicative sentencing band: Chen Song at [125].

(2)   Culpability factors

54     A non-exhaustive list of factors which each constitute 1 offence-specific factor going towards culpability is as follows (Chen Song at [131]):

(a)      Any form of dangerous driving behaviour. For instance:

(i)       speeding;

(ii)       driving against traffic;

(iii)       driving when not fit to drive;

(iv)       driving under the influence of alcohol or drugs;

(v)       sleepy driving;

(vi)       driving while using a mobile phone;

(vii)       swerving in and out of lanes;

(viii)       using a vehicle in a dangerous fashion; and

(ix)       street racing.

(b)      Flouting of traffic rules and regulations. For instance:

(i)       failing to stop at a stop line;

(ii)       failing to conform to traffic signal;

(iii)       not forming up correctly to execute a turn;

(iv)       changing lanes across a set of double white lines/chevron markings; and

(v)       making an illegal U-turn/right turn.

(c)      High degree of carelessness: This is demonstrated where there was a prolonged or sustained period of inattention (as opposed to a momentary lapse of attention), and where the offender was deliberately cavalier about certain mitigatable risks. As stated in Sue Chang at [95], it would also be relevant to consider the extent to which the offender’s distraction was avoidable and the extent to which the offender’s misjudgment was reasonable.

(3)   Sentencing framework for driving offences causing grievous hurt punishable under s 65(3)(a)

55     The following sentencing framework applied for careless driving offences causing hurt punishable under s 65(3)(a) where the offender elects to claim trial (Chen Song at [134]).

56     First, the court is to identify the number of offence-specific factors under the broad categories of “harm” and “culpability” (Chen Song at [134(a)]).

57     Second, based on the number of offence-specific factors present, the court is to determine whether the harm caused is “lesser harm” or “greater harm” and whether the culpability of the offender is “lower culpability” or “higher culpability” and thereafter arrive at the sentencing band the offence falls within (Chen Song at [134(b)]).

58     “Lesser harm” is caused, and the offender’s culpability is deemed as “lower culpability” where there are 0–1 harm or culpability factors respectively. “Greater harm” is caused, and the offender’s culpability is deemed as “higher culpability” where there are 2 or more harm or culpability factors respectively (Chen Song at [134(b)]).

59     Third, after determining the indicative sentencing band that the offence falls within, the court should identify an indicative starting point sentence within that range, taking into account: (a) all the primary harm factors and the culpability factors identified; and (b) the secondary harm factors (Chen Song at [134(c)]).

60     Fourth, the court is to make adjustments to the starting point to take into account the usual gamut of offender-specific aggravating and mitigating factors (Chen Song at [134(d)]).

61     The High Court stated that with reference to the proposed sentencing bands for s 65(3)(a), the custodial threshold would typically be crossed where there are 2 or more offence-specific harm and/or culpability factors present. Therefore, for Band 1 cases, fines would ordinarily be reserved for cases where 0–1 offence-specific harm and/or culpability factors are present (Chen Song at [137]).

62     A mandatory 5-year disqualification period applies for offences punishable under s 65(3), “unless the court for special reasons thinks fit to not order or to order otherwise”: s 65(6)(d) of the Act (Chen Song at [138]).

(see also Ivan Tang et al., Sentencing Frameworks for Consistency: A Proposed Framework, (2024) 36 SAcLJ 380 at [130])
