71     At this juncture, I paused to note that on 3 September 2025 (“1st PG mention”), the Accused had qualified his plea before me, and his conviction was set aside.

72     At the 1st PG mention:

(a)      Degree of Permanence. The Statement of Facts did not mention that based on the Certificate of Order Made Under the Work Injury Compensation Act 2019 (WICA) dated 30 September 2025, the victim was found to have 6% permanent incapacity. This was because WICA’s Certificate of Order was made on 30 September 2025, i.e. after the 1st PG mention on 3 September 2025. Consequently, this fact on the degree of permanence was not present at the 1st PG mention.

(b)      Surgery. The Statement of Facts did not mention that the victim had undergone a plate implant surgery,[note: 50] which was removed after a year.[note: 51]

(c)      Dental Treatment and Costs. The Statement of Facts did not mention that the victim underwent root canal treatment of her broken teeth (number 31 and 32) and replacement of a missing tooth number 41, and she paid RM5,000 for her broken teeth repair. This was because the receipt of payment of the broken teeth treatment was uploaded by the Prosecution on 4 June 2026, i.e. after the 1st PG mention on 3 September 2025.[note: 52]

(d)      Prosecution’s Sentencing Position. At the 1st PG mention, the Prosecution asked for 3 to 4 weeks’ imprisonment (claim trial basis) and a 5-year driving disqualification. This was lower than the sentence of 3 to 4 weeks’ imprisonment (plead guilty basis) and a 5-year driving disqualification sought by the Prosecution on 5 June 2026.

73     The 1st PG mention had initially proceeded uneventfully. He was given 1 week’s imprisonment and a 5-year driving disqualification. On the same day, the Accused (who was unrepresented) denied driving carelessly or negligently, and he maintained that he had no choice but to swerve suddenly due to the taxi’s sudden jam-braking.[note: 53] The Prosecution averred that the Accused had qualified his plea.

74     Section 301(1) of the Criminal Procedure Code 2010 (“CPC”) stated:

Where a court has delivered its judgment, it may rectify a clerical error at any time, and any other error, including an error in the exercise of its sentencing powers, may be rectified by the court by the next working day after the delivery of the judgment.

75     Section 301(1) of the CPC applies to all courts – it empowers the court to correct non-clerical errors by the next working day after delivery of the judgment (Jennifer Marie and Mohamed Faizal Mohamed Abdul Kadir, The Criminal Procedure Code of Singapore: Annotations and Commentary (Academy Publishing, 2012) at [15.003] and [15.029]).

76     Section 301(1) of the CPC has remained substantially the same as s 217(2) of the Criminal Procedure Code (Cap 68), which stated:

A clerical error may be rectified at any time and any other mistake may be rectified at any time before the court rises for the day.

77     Section 217(2) of the Criminal Procedure Code (Cap 68) was analysed by Chief Justice Yong Pung How in Public Prosecutor v Oh Hu Sung [2003] 4 SLR(R) 541.

78     The Chief Justice in Oh Hu Sung stated at [21]-[22] and [26]-[28]:

21    Thus, it was clear from the authorities that while the general rule is that the court is functus officio after sentence is pronounced, s 217(2) of the CPC is an exception to this general prohibition against the alteration of judgments. The district judge rejected counsel’s submissions and authorities on the point as they dealt with alterations in sentence, and not a conviction. However, this should not make any difference. There was no reason to restrict “judgment” in s 217 to orders on sentence.

22      Therefore, I was unable to agree with the district judge when he took the view that s 217(2) of the CPC had no application because he was functus officio after sentence was pronounced. On the contrary, if the requirements of s 217(2) were satisfied, the court was fully entitled to alter or review its judgment, whether or not sentence was pronounced. Therefore, I next considered if s 217(2) applied on the facts of this case.

26     In considering what suffices as a “mistake” under s 217(2), I was prepared to hold that it includes errors by a party as well as by the court… …

27     It is clear that “mistake” in s 217(2) is construed expansively. It clearly encompasses more than mere clerical errors, for otherwise the first limb of the subsection would be otiose. It also goes beyond mere accidental slips and omissions: Chiaw Wai Onn, supra. “Any other mistake” in s 217(2) includes not only mistakes by the court (as was the case in Monteiro v PP [1964] 1 MLJ 338, where the judge had found the accused guilty before his counsel addressed the court), but also unilateral mistakes by the parties. It covers not only errors of law but also errors of fact.

28    However, such a wide construction is clearly open to abuse by accused persons, who could seek to use s 217(2) as a backdoor to overturn convictions. The principle of finality of proceedings, as encapsulated in s 217(1), should generally be observed unless it is clear that a miscarriage of justice will otherwise result. Accused persons should not be permitted merely at whim to change their pleas, and the court must take care not to encourage such responses, where no valid and sufficient grounds have been shown. Therefore, the condition I set down in Virgie Rizza V Leong – that the mistake must be obvious to the court or admitted by all parties – should be strenuously observed before s 217(2) can apply.

[emphasis added]

79      Oh Hu Sung was applied by the High Court in Karthigeyan M Kailasam v Public Prosecutor [2016] SGHC 193 at [7]-[10].

80     In Karthigeyan M Kailasam, the High Court stated at [9]-[10] and [20]:

9.    In their submissions, the prosecution relied on the broad definition of the words “any other mistake” that was set out in Public Prosecutor v Oh Hu Sung [2003] 4 SLR(R) 541 (“Oh Hu Sung”). In that case, Yong Pung How CJ held that “any other mistake” in s 217(2) was to be construed expansively and encompassed more than mere clerical errors for otherwise the first limb of the subsection (which refers to clerical errors) would be otiose (at [27]). “Any other mistake” included not only mistakes by the court, but also unilateral mistakes by the parties. It covered both errors of law and errors of fact. However, in the interest of finality of proceedings, Yong CJ stressed that s 217(2) would only apply if the mistake was obvious to the court or admitted by all parties (at [28]). I pause here to note that this expansive definition of the term “any other mistake” could conceivably cover the present situation since the “mistake” in question (that an MTO was the more appropriate punishment) was one which both the prosecution and the defence apparently felt ought to be corrected.

10    There are a few pertinent points to note. First, although the word “mistake” (in s 217(2) of the CPC 1985) was replaced with “error” in the CPC 2012, this does not substantively alter the scope of the provision … …

…

20      At the end of the day, there is a clear public interest in ensuring that appropriate decisions are made and the right sentences are passed at first instance, just as there is a public interest in finality in proceedings which should not be lightly disturbed except on appeal, or in appropriate cases, through invoking the court’s revisionary jurisdiction or through the use of s 301 of the CPC 2012 where circumstances permit. Erroneous decisions made at first instance can of course be set right on appeal or on revision, but not all such instances of error will be the subject-matter of appeal or revision. It is therefore crucial that the first instance courts are properly assisted to the fullest possible extent in order to arrive at the right conclusions.

[emphasis added]

81      Oh Hu Sung was referred to by the Court of Appeal in Public Prosecutor v Dinesh s/o Rajantheran [2019] SGCA 27 at [49]:

… As Yong CJ noted in Public Prosecutor v Oh Hu Sung [2003] 4 SLR(R) 541 (in discussing the statutory prohibition against the alteration of judgments in s 217 of the Criminal Procedure Code (Cap 68, 1985 Rev Ed) which in modified form can now be found in s 301 of the CPC), the “principle of finality of proceedings, as encapsulated in s 217(1), should generally be observed unless it is clear that a miscarriage of justice will otherwise result” (at [28]).

82     In sum, for s 301(1) of the CPC:

(a)     While the general rule is that the court is functus officio after sentence is pronounced, s 301(1) of the CPC is an exception to this general prohibition against the alteration of judgments (Oh Hu Sung at [21]).

(b)     The principle of finality of proceedings, as found in s 301(1) of the CPC, should generally be observed unless it is clear that a miscarriage of justice will otherwise result; the mistake must be obvious to the court or admitted by all parties (Oh Hu Sung at [28]; Karthigeyan M Kailasam at [9]; Dinesh s/o Rajantheran at [49]).

(c)     “Judgement” covers both conviction and sentence (Oh Hu Sung at [21]-[22]; Public Prosecutor v Ng Guan Hup [2009] 4 SLR(R) 314 at [30]).

(d)     It is clear that “error” is construed expansively – it clearly encompasses more than mere clerical errors (Oh Hu Sung at [27]; Karthigeyan M Kailasam at [9]).

(e)     “Any other error”:

(i)       Includes not only errors by the court, but also unilateral errors by the parties (Oh Hu Sung at [26]-[27]; Karthigeyan M Kailasam at [9]);

(ii)       Covers both errors of law and errors of fact (Oh Hu Sung at [27]; Karthigeyan M Kailasam at [9]).

(See also Kow Keng Siong, Sentencing Principles in Singapore (Academy Publishing, Second Ed, 2019) at [34.047]-[34.062])

83     In the present case, s 301(1) of the CPC was engaged for the 1st PG mention on 3 September 2025.

84     The Accused (who was unrepresented) at the 1st PG mention had denied driving carelessly or negligently, and he had maintained that he had no choice but to swerve suddenly due to the taxi’s sudden jam-braking. What the Accused said went towards the charge and he did not admit without qualification the offence alleged against him. The Prosecution averred that the Accused had qualified the plea of guilt. Taken together, the error of allowing such a conviction to stand was obvious to the court or admitted by all parties (Oh Hu Sung at [28]; Karthigeyan M Kailasam at [9]).

85     Allowing the conviction to stand at the 1st PG mention would clearly be a miscarriage of justice (Oh Hu Sung at [28]; Dinesh s/o Rajantheran at [49]).

86     Accordingly, pursuant to s 301 of the CPC, his conviction at the 1st PG mention on 3 September 2025 was set aside on the same day.

87     I turn next to the Accused’s culpability in the present case.

88      Culpability . The Accused had swerved to the left side of the road to change lane at fast speed and collided into the victim (pedestrian).[note: 54]

89     The foremost inquiry is to assess holistically whether the offender’s culpability considered as a whole should be classified as either “lower culpability” or “higher culpability”: Chen Song at [123]. On a holistic assessment, the present case involved lower culpability.

90     Given the lesser harm and lower culpability, the case fell within Band 1 of Chen Song.

91     The custodial threshold would typically be crossed where there are two or more offence-specific harm and/or culpability factors present: Chen Song at [137].

92     In the present case, the custodial threshold was crossed as there are two or more offence-specific harm and/or culpability factors.

93     The indicative starting point was a custodial sentence of about 3 to 4 weeks. Taking into account the offender-specific aggravating and mitigating factors, the custodial sentence was calibrated downwards to 15 days’ imprisonment.

94     This sentence was close to the 3-week imprisonment given in Hee Kwee Choy:

(a)     Compared to Hee Kwee Choy, there was a longer period of hospitalisation leave, some permanent incapacity, and culpability-increasing factors such as speeding and swerving.[note: 55]

(b)     But unlike Hee Kwee Choy, the injury was not caused to a vulnerable part of the victim’s body (fractures of the right acetabular and an undisplaced fracture of the right inferior pubic ramus)[note: 56] and the victim was only admitted in hospital for a day before she sought treatment in Malaysia and was admitted in hospital for 5 days (after implant surgery).[note: 57]

(c)     In Hee Kwee Choy, the victim acquired pneumonia post-surgery and had to undergo physiotherapy for at least 3 months thereafter.[note: 58] The court considered that the degree of carelessness was not low as it was remarkable that the offender had completely failed to notice the victim at a signalised pedestrian crossing with a green signal.[note: 59]

(d)     Both the offender in Hee Kwee Choy and the Accused were untraced.[note: 60]

95     To be clear, I was mindful of the High Court’s decision in Vasentha d/o Joseph v Public Prosecutor [2015] 5 SLR 122, which stated at [48] that indicative starting points are not rigid or inflexible categories and the precise sentence to be imposed in each case would depend on the specific circumstances of that case (see also Aw Soy Tee v Public Prosecutor [2020] 5 SLR 453 at [31]).

96     The 3-Judge Panel in Lee Shing Chan and another v Public Prosecutor and another appeal [2020] 4 SLR 1174 at [34] made clear its preference for a more holistic approach since sentencing is not a scientific exercise and does not demand mathematical precision, which is quite impractical in any case when dealing with human beings and the multifarious situations in the cases.

97     This emphasis on a more holistic approach to sentencing was echoed in S Elamparithi v Public Prosecutor (oral judgment, MA 9238/2019) at [20], i.e. sentencing is not a scientific exercise demanding mathematical precision; it is a matter of judicial discretion to be approached with a judicious measure of pragmatism and common sense, having regard to the offender-specific and offence-specific factors.

98     Sentencing is ultimately an exercise in evaluative ethical judgment — there might well be cases which will eventually be assessed to straddle the border between the bands: Ng Kean Meng Terence v Public Prosecutor [2017] 2 SLR 449 at [48] (see Sir Anthony Hooper, Sentencing: Art or Science, (2015) 27 SAcLJ 17).

99      Antecedents. The Accused had a clean driving record.

100     Guilty plea. The SAP Guidelines for Guilty Pleas applied: Ng En You Jeremiah v Public Prosecutor [2025] SGHC 135 at [110]-[111] and [115]-[117] (see also Edwin Lim Wei Keat, A Critical Analysis of the Application of Guidelines on Reduction in Sentences for Guilty Pleas in Singapore, SAcLJ (10 October 2025, e-First) at [37]-[43]).

101    I gave full weight to the Accused’s guilty plea: Angliss Singapore Pte Ltd v Public Prosecutor [2006] 4 SLR(R) 653 at [77]. This saved the criminal justice system resources that would have been expended with a full trial.

102    Accordingly, I gave the Accused the full 30% discount (Stage 1) for his early plea of guilt.

103    All things considered, including the harm and culpability factors, the starting point for the sentence was about 3 to 4 weeks’ imprisonment. After considering the mitigating factors and the PG discount, in the round, the sentence would be 15 days’ imprisonment.

104     Restitution. I gave due weight to the fact that the Accused made restitution of RM 2,000. The fact that the offender made restitution is one of the “ambient circumstances” that a court can and should take into account in assessing whether the plea of guilt itself indicates remorse and if the offender should accordingly receive a discount in the sentence: Angliss Singapore Pte Ltd v Public Prosecutor [2006] 4 SLR(R) 653 at [76].

105     Cooperation with the authorities. I gave due weight to the Accused’s cooperation with the authorities: Public Prosecutor v Siew Boon Loong [2005] 1 SLR(R) 611 at [16]-[18].

106     Personal circumstances. Given that the Accused is his household’s sole breadwinner,[note: 61] he alluded to the fact that incarceration would bring hardship to the family.

107    However, personal circumstances such as financial difficulties and hardship caused to family by their incarceration have no mitigating value save in the most exceptional cases: Lai Oei Mui Jenny v Public Prosecutor [1993] 2 SLR(R) 406 at [10]-[11] and Chua Ya Zi Sandy v Public Prosecutor [2021] SGHC 204 at [11]-[14].

108    Hardship to the family is a natural consequence when a family’s breadwinner decides to commit an offence and is imprisoned for it: Kannan s/o Birasenggam v Public Prosecutor [2021] SGCA 15 at [10]. In the present case, I saw no cogent reasons to consider his personal financial and family circumstances as valid mitigating factors.

(4)    Erh Zhi Huang Alvan’s Case

109     Erh Zhi Huang Alvan v Public Prosecutor (“Erh”) (MA 9204 of 2022) was one of the cases heard in the Chen Song decision. The High Court allowed the appeal in Erh and substituted a sentence of 10 weeks’ imprisonment with a fine of $4,000. There was also the minimum 5-year driving disqualification.

110    The offender in Alvan Erh was driving his motor car along an expressway. Due to heavy traffic, the car travelling in front of Erh braked and came to a stop. Consequently, Erh abruptly switched lanes, failing to keep a proper lookout. This led to a collision between Erh’s motor car and the victim who was travelling on his motorcycle: Chen Song at [163].

111    In relation to harm, the victim in Erh suffered from: (a) a traumatic amputation of the right little finger; and (b) a right-sided clavicle fracture. He was given hospitalisation leave of 58 days: Chen Song at [165].

112    It was undisputed that permanent injury was caused to the victim in Erh, although there was no evidence before the High Court that the victim would suffer from any permanent hand disability as a result and he was assessed to be likely to be able to return to work. Therefore, in the High Court’s view, taking into consideration also the victim’s right-sided clavicle fracture, the damage caused to his motorcycle and the potential harm arising from his abrupt lane-change on the expressway during peak hour, this would place the harm caused in the higher end of the “low” category. This was so bearing in mind that the range of injuries classified as grievous hurt is broad and are by their nature serious: Chen Song at [165].

113    Erh’s culpability was low. His offending conduct was simply a manifestation of the basic elements of the careless driving offence: Chen Song at [165] (see also Adri Satryawan Pratama v Public Prosecutor [2024] SGHC 258 at [14]).

114    Based on the High Court’s determination that the harm caused was at the higher end of low and Erh’s culpability was low, the indicative sentence ought to be a fine based on the Sue Chang framework: Chen Song at [167].

115    After taking into account that Erh pleaded guilty and readily co-operated with the authorities, the High Court allowed the appeal in MA 9204 of 2022 and substituted Erh’s sentence of 10 weeks’ imprisonment with a fine of $4,000: Chen Song at [169].

116    I noted that in Erh’s case:

(a)     There was no evidence before the High Court that the victim would suffer from any permanent hand disability as a result and he was assessed to be likely to be able to return to work: Chen Song at [165] and Ling Zhao Bin at [54(a)].

(b)     Erh’s culpability was low. His offending conduct was simply a manifestation of the basic elements of the careless driving offence: Chen Song at [165]. In Erh, the lane change was a reactive, split-second response to avoid colliding with the car in front that had braked and stopped due to heavy traffic (see Ling Zhao Bin at [54(c)].

117    While the victim in Erh suffered a permanent loss of his little finger, the High Court noted that there was no indication of any permanent disability that resulted from this injury and that he had in fact been medically assessed as being likely to be able to return to work. Apart from this, he also suffered a right-sided clavicle fracture, though it was not apparent that there was any surgical intervention required for this injury. While the victim in Erh was given 58 days of hospitalisation leave, this included only one day of hospitalisation, as he was discharged the day after the accident (Public Prosecutor v Johnson Tan Wee Kiat (Johnson Chen Weiji) [2026] SGHC 59 at [21]).

118    For completeness, it may be argued that Erh’s sentence was based on the framework in Sue Chang (instead of Chen Song): see Chen Song at [165] and [167]. However, as the High Court observed in Chen Song at [120], applying both frameworks would likely result in the same or similar outcomes. A similar observation was made by the High Court in Adri Satryawan Pratama v Public Prosecutor [2024] SGHC 258 at [3] and [15] and in Loh Kaine Tong Nicholas v Public Prosecutor (HC/MA 9037/2023/01).

119    In the present case:

(a)     The Accused’s culpability was higher than Erh. In Erh, the lane change was a reactive, split-second response to avoid colliding with the car in front that had braked and stopped due to heavy traffic. In contrast, the Accused had swerved to the left side of the road to change lane at fast speed and collided into the victim (pedestrian).[note: 62]

(b)     The victim underwent a plate implant surgery, which was removed after a year.[note: 63] In Erh’s case, for the right-sided clavicle fracture, it was not apparent that there was any surgical intervention required for this injury.

(c)     The victim was hospitalised from 10 to 15 December 2023, which was longer than the one day of hospitalisation in Erh.

(d)     The victim’s hospitalisation leave for 127 days[note: 64] was longer than the 58 days of hospitalisation leave in Erh.

(5)   Special reasons

120    An offender would be disqualified from driving unless he shows “special reasons”.

121    In this connection, the two-stage framework for “special reasons” is as follows:

(a)     First Stage: Show special reasons, viz. reasons relating to the facts or circumstances of an offence and not to the offender herself; and

(b)     Second Stage: Even if special reasons are established, the court will consider whether the discretion not to disqualify must be exercised in favour of the offender.

122    Under the two-stage framework, the first stage is offence-specific (not offender-specific). When an offender seeks to come within the special reasons exception, the facts to back up such circumstances must be proved to the court’s satisfaction: Toh Yong Soon v Public Prosecutor [2011] 3 SLR 147 at [5].

123    Even if special reasons are established, it does not automatically follow that the offender would not be disqualified from driving. For the second stage, the court’s discretion not to disqualify can only be made in very exceptional circumstances: Sivakumar s/o Rajoo v Public Prosecutor [2002] 1 SLR(R) 265 at [25] (see also Prathib s/o M Balan v Public Prosecutor [2017] SGHC 303 at [9]-[11]).

(i)   First Stage

124    What are “special reasons” not to impose a driving disqualification? The special reasons have to be reasons relating to the facts or circumstances of an offence and not to the offender himself – this would be the clearest means of giving effect to Parliament’s intention: M V Balakrishnan v Public Prosecutor [1998] 2 SLR(R) 846 at [9], Muhammad Faizal bin Rahim v Public Prosecutor [2012] 1 SLR 116 at [41] and Rafael Voltaire Alzate at [38].

125    In other words, a special reason is a mitigating or extenuating circumstance, not amounting in law to a defence to the charge, yet directly connected with the commission of the offence, and one which the court ought properly to take into consideration when imposing punishment: Whittall v Kirby [1947] 1 KB 194 at 201, as endorsed by Muhammad Faizal bin Rahim at [30].

126    Offender-specific factors, such as the fact that the defendant is of a good character or has a good driving record, cannot be accepted as special reasons: Wilkinson’s Road Traffic Offences, Sweet & Maxwell, (32nd Ed, 2025, General Editor: Kevin McCormac) at [21-10]. Circumstances peculiar to the offender do not go towards reducing his moral culpability; they are essentially extrinsic facts about the offender which are unrelated to the offence but are produced to elicit sympathy from the court. These circumstances are morally distinguishable from circumstances peculiar to the offence: Muhammad Faizal bin Rahim at [43].

127    Even if an offender requires his driving licence for his livelihood, this would not constitute a special reason (see also Tan Yock Lin and S. Chandra Mohan, Criminal Procedure (LexisNexis: March 2019; Binder 3, Loose-leaf, Chapter XVII: Sentencing) at [3751]).

128    This is because in the Malaysian Criminal Appeal Court case of Public Prosecutor v Hiew Chin Fong [1988] 1 MLJ 467 – which was endorsed in Chua Chye Tiong v Public Prosecutor [2004] 1 SLR(R) 22 at [61] and [62] – a 12-month disqualification period was imposed on the offender despite the fact that his livelihood depended on him having a driving licence.

129    The Criminal Appeal Court in Public Prosecutor v Hiew Chin Fong laid down several statements of law on what should not be considered special reasons:

(a)     Financial hardship to the offender;

(b)     The offender knew no other means of earning his livelihood;

(c)     That the effect of the disqualification must necessarily and consequently deprive the offender of his livelihood or occupation; and

(d)     That the offender was a poor man and would have difficulty to get to his work.

130    The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs, Ms Sun Xueling, had stated as follows (Singapore Parliamentary Debates, Official Report (8 July 2019) vol 94):

… Actually, if an individual depends on driving to make a living, that is all the more reason for him to drive safely and for him to be off the roads if he is unable or unwilling to do so.

131    Before an emergency is capable of amounting to a special reason under law, a crucial prerequisite is for the offender to show that there was no alternative but for him to drive, and that he had explored every reasonable alternative before driving: Sivakumar s/o Rajoo v Public Prosecutor [2002] 1 SLR(R) 265 at [17], affirmed in Siti Hajar bte Abdullah v Public Prosecutor [2006] 2 SLR(R) 248 at [13] (see also Fan Lei v Public Prosecutor [2024] SGHC 278 at [16]).

132    When an offender seeks to come within the special reasons exception, the facts to back up such circumstances must be proved to the court’s satisfaction: Toh Yong Soon v Public Prosecutor [2011] 3 SLR 147 at [5]. The onus lies on an accused to raise special reasons for the court’s consideration, if such reasons exist: Chue Woon Wai v Public Prosecutor [1996] 1 SLR(R) 725 at [13], Prathib s/o M Balan v Public Prosecutor [2017] SGHC 303 at [12] and Siti Hajar bte Abdullah v Public Prosecutor [2006] 2 SLR(R) 248 at [12].

(See also Wilkinson’s Road Traffic Offences, Sweet & Maxwell, (32nd Ed, 2025, General Editor: Kevin McCormac) at [21-62])

133     Cheong Wai Keong v Public Prosecutor [2005] SGHC 126 stands for the proposition that the shortness of distance travelled cannot in itself be a “special reason” (Rafael Voltaire Alzate at [41]). A court should be able to have regard to the distance travelled as part of its overall analysis (Rafael Voltaire Alzate at [42]).

134    The High Court in Lee Shin Nan v Public Prosecutor [2023] SGHC 354 at [79] stated that special reasons will generally be found only if the court is satisfied that the offender drove in circumstances that reasonably suggest:

(a)     it was necessary to do so in order to avoid other likely and serious harm or danger; and

(b)     there was no reasonable alternative way to achieve this end.

(see also Chen Song at [138] and Ng En You Jeremiah v Public Prosecutor [2023] SGHC 354 at [82])

(ii)   Second Stage

135    Even if special reasons are established, it does not automatically follow that the offender would not be disqualified. In this regard, there must be a separate process of considering whether the discretion must be exercised in favour of the offender: Sivakumar s/o Rajoo at [22]. The limited discretion not to disqualify can only be made in very exceptional circumstances, having regard to the special circumstances as well as to the whole of the circumstances surrounding the commission of the offence, including the manner in which the offender drove and the alcohol content in the offender’s body: Sivakumar s/o Rajoo at [25].

136    Pulling the various strands together, the test for special reasons is stringent and is only satisfied in very exceptional circumstances (see also Prathib s/o M Balan v Public Prosecutor [2017] SGHC 303 at [9]-[11]).

137    The Act is construed strictly to preserve its policy of protecting road users: Chua Chye Tiong v Public Prosecutor [2004] 1 SLR (R) 22 at [53]. A less restrictive approach would negate the legislative stipulation of mandatory disqualification and defeat its underlying objectives: Siti Hajar bte Abdullah v Public Prosecutor [2006] 2 SLR(R) 248 at [8]. Widening the special reasons exception would encourage frivolous defences: Muhammad Faizal bin Rahim at [41].

(See also Tan Yock Lin and S. Chandra Mohan, Criminal Procedure (LexisNexis: March 2019; Binder 3, Loose-leaf, Chapter XVII: Sentencing) at [3702], [3751] and [3752])

138    In the present case, I found no special reason to dispense with the 5-year disqualification, which is mandatory as well as appropriate.

139    Accordingly, I agreed with the Defence that a driving disqualification for 5 years should be imposed.[note: 65]

140    I kept in mind the proportionality principle in sentencing: Public Prosecutor v Law Aik Meng [2007] 2 SLR(R) 814 at [30].

141    Under the proportionality principle, the sentence to be imposed must not only bear a reasonable proportion to the maximum prescribed penalty, but also to the gravity of the offence committed (Kow Keng Siong, Sentencing Principles in Singapore (Academy Publishing, Second Ed, 2019) at [06.091]-[06.093]).

Conclusion

142    For the above reasons, the Accused was sentenced to 15 days’ imprisonment and a driving disqualification for all classes of driving licences for 5 years.

143    I am grateful for the hard work and submissions of both sides.

Public Prosecutor v Ahmad Faraz

Public Prosecutor v Ahmad Faraz
[2026] SGDC 234

Case Number:District Arrest Case No 907887 of 2024, Magistrate's Appeals No 9153 of 2026-01
Decision Date:20 July 2026
Tribunal/Court:District Court
Coram: Ong Hian Sun
Counsel Name(s): DPPs Eugene Phua and Suriya Prakash (Attorney-General's Chambers) for the Public Prosecutor; Mr Ashvin Hariharan and Mr Prakash Otharam (Ashvin Law Corporation) for the Accused.
Parties: Public Prosecutor — Ahmad Faraz

Criminal Procedure and Sentencing  –  Sentencing – s 6(a) of the Prevention of Corruption Act (Cap 241, 1993 Rev Ed) 

20 July 2026

Senior District Judge Ong Hian Sun:

Introduction

1       The accused pleaded guilty to the following charge in DAC-907887-2024: -

“…that you, in Singapore, in 2020, being an agent, to wit, the Head of Information Systems & Technology at Mapletree Investments Pte Ltd (“Mapletree”), did corruptly obtain from one Mehta Anant, Senior Business Development Manager at Hexaware Technologies Asia Pacific Pte Ltd (“Hexaware”) gratification, to wit, facilitation of employment of one Siti Filzah Binte Sulaiman for the role of Project Management Officer for the Mapletree PMO & Data Architect Services contract, as inducement for doing acts in relation to your principal’s affairs, to wit, advancing the business interests of Hexaware with Mapletree, and you have thereby committed an offence punishable under section 6(a) of the Prevention of Corruption Act (Cap 241, 1993 Rev Ed) (“PCA”).”

2       The accused consented for one other similar charge under section 6(a) of the PCA in DAC-907888-2024 in relation to his corruptly obtaining from Mehta Anant gratification, to wit, the facilitation of employment of one Fahad, to be taken into consideration (“TIC”) for purpose of sentencing.

3       Having considered the submissions by the parties, I sentenced the accused to serve a 6 months’ and 2 weeks’ imprisonment term.

4       Dissatisfied, the accused has filed an appeal against the sentence imposed. Stay on the execution of his sentence of imprisonment has been granted and he is currently released on bail pending his appeal.

5       I now set out the reasons for my decision.

Facts

6       The accused admitted to the Statement of Facts without qualification as outlined below.

7       The first accused is Ahmad Faraz (“Faraz”), a 49-year-old male Chinese (HK SAR) national with date of birth: XX August 19XX and FIN No.: GXXXX075N. At the material time, Faraz was married to his first wife. Faraz had a second wife, Siti Filzah Binte Sulaiman (“Siti”), with whom he had a romantic relationship with since 2019 and with whom he was married from XX January 2021. Faraz also had a friend by the name of Fahad Muhammad (“Fahad”) from Pakistan.

8       At all material times, Faraz was the Head of Information Systems & Technology (“IST”) at Mapletree Investments Pte Ltd (“Mapletree”). Faraz joined Mapletree as Head of IST sometime in July 2020. Faraz’s role as Mapletree’s Head of IST included overseeing major operations within IST and he was central in approving Information Technology (“IT”) related procurement, both in terms of deciding which vendors could bid in IT contracts and who would be awarded the IT contracts. Faraz was dismissed from Mapletree in August 2022.

9       The second accused is Mehta Anant (“Anant”), a 46-year-old male Indian national with date of birth: XX February 19XX and FIN No.: GXXXX675X. At all material times, Anant was a Senior Business Development Manager at Hexaware Technologies Asia Pacific Pte Ltd (“Hexaware”). At all material times, Anant knew that Faraz was the highest-ranking person in Mapletree’s IST department.

10     Prior to July 2020, Hexaware was not on Mapletree’s Preferred Vendor List (“PVL”). Being on the PVL is a pre-requisite for any vendor to submit quotes and tender for contracts for IT related items or services from Mapletree. At all material times, Faraz would have to approve the IT vendor that was applying to be on Mapletree’s PVL. In terms of the usual procurement process, Faraz would also have to approve the selected IT vendors to bid in IT contracts and the IT vendor that was to be eventually awarded the IT contracts.

11     Sometime around July 2020, Anant went to Faraz’s office at Mapletree to do a presentation to Faraz’s IST team on Hexaware’s IT capabilities. Subsequently, Anant applied for Hexaware to be placed on Mapletree’s PVL. Hexaware’s application to join the PVL was approved by Mapletree’s management on or about 31 August 2020. Faraz was involved in the approval process of Hexaware’s application to join the PVL.

12     Sometime around September or October 2020, Anant met Faraz and asked whether there were any IT contracts which Hexaware could fulfil. Faraz told him that there was this Project Management Officer and Data Architect Services (“PMODA”) contract which Hexaware might be interested in. This contract required Hexaware to provide three employees to Mapletree – a Senior Project Management Office (“PMO”) Manager, a PMO Manager and a Data Architect. Faraz then told Anant that he had a personal relationship with Siti and Fahad, and sought Anant’s help to get Hexaware to employ both Siti and Fahad for two of the three roles, in return for Faraz providing the IST approval for the Mapletree contracts to Hexaware, namely, the PMODA contract and the 150 Man Day SAP Development contract (“150MD contract”). Anant agreed to facilitate the employment of Siti and Fahad in return for Faraz providing the IST approval for the said two Mapletree contracts to Hexaware. Anant agreed as he wanted to keep a good business working relationship with Faraz and Mapletree and Anant wanted to secure the PMODA contract and 150MD contract from Mapletree. Anant knew that if he submitted a competitive price quote and managed to put forward Faraz’s two preferred candidates, ie, Siti and Fahad, in Hexaware’s PMODA contract bid, the PMODA contract would likely be awarded to Hexaware. Anant would benefit personally as the award of contracts from Mapletree to Hexaware would allow him to hit his annual sales target. In this regard, Anant further asked Faraz to recommend Hexaware to Mapletree’s management and push for business deals between Hexaware and Mapletree, ie, to advance the business interests of Hexaware with Mapletree. Faraz agreed to Anant’s request and introduced Hexaware to his IST team.

13     Faraz had recommended to Mapletree that the Senior PMO Manager, PMO Manager and Data Architect roles be outsourced through the PMODA contract rather than Mapletree hiring the three employees directly to fill these three roles so that he would be able to conceal his relationship with Siti and Fahad. Further, and to ensure that Hexaware stood the best chance of winning the PMODA contract by virtue of being the cheapest vendor to tender a bid, Faraz directed his staff at Mapletree to invite Hexaware, Ernst & Young (“EY”) and KPMG to tender a bid for the PMODA contract. EY and KPMG were established and reputable vendors likely to price higher than Hexaware.

14     Pursuant to the corrupt arrangement at [12] above, from on or before 15 October 2020, even before the bids for the PMODA contract were to be put in by Hexaware, EY and KPMG, Anant facilitated the employment of Siti and Fahad by taking steps to ensure that Siti and Fahad would be the candidates that Hexaware put up for consideration for the purposes of the PMODA contract. Prior to the PMODA contract award, both Faraz and Anant also made edits on Siti’s resume prior to the submission of her resume for the PMODA contract.

15     Subsequently, Anant put in Hexaware’s bid for the PMODA contract sometime around October 2020 and put forward resumes of several candidates, including the resumes of Siti and Fahad. Faraz then ensured that he participated in the interviews of the candidates, including the interviews of Siti and Fahad with his team. In the interviews of Siti and Fahad, Faraz was the most senior Mapletree employee on the interview panel. Despite Siti’s lack of experience for the PMO role, Faraz attested to Siti’s suitability during her interview. As Faraz was the Head of IST and the most senior employee of Mapletree on the interview panel, he made the final decision after discussions with his team as to the suitability of the candidates put up by Hexaware. Faraz did not at any point declare his relationship with Siti and Fahad to Mapletree.

16     The director of finance of Mapletree had questioned Faraz’s IST department on the review of the candidates and their qualifications and questioned whether there was any prior experience working with Hexaware as a vendor or whether any informal checks on the quality of Hexaware’s personnel had been conducted. Faraz attested to his first-hand experience working with Hexaware and the quality of their deliverables. Subsequently and in November 2020, Faraz provided the IST approval for Hexaware as the vendor of choice. On 9 December 2020, Mapletree awarded the PMODA contract to Hexaware. The PMODA contract awarded to Hexaware was valued at $637,200. Hexaware’s profit margin for the PMODA contract was about 34% to 40%.

17     At around the same time, in or around September 2020 and in relation to the 150MD contract, Faraz had been informed that previous vendors had bid for a rate of $400 per man day whereas Hexaware’s quoted rates were $428 per man day. Sometime between September 2020 and the award of the 150MD contract to Hexaware in or around 30 October 2020, Anant and Faraz met in relation to the 150MD contract. Pursuant to the corrupt arrangement at [12] above and prior to the award of the PMODA contract to Hexaware and subsequent employment of Siti and Fahad, Faraz provided Anant with the historical bid price. In doing so, Faraz advanced the business interests of Hexaware with Mapletree. Faraz did not tell this information to the other competing vendors for the 150MD contract. This gave Hexaware an unfair advantage over the other vendors, bidding in the same tender. By virtue of Faraz’s telling Anant this information, and not to the other competing vendors, in October 2020, Hexaware submitted the lowest bid of $399 per man day among the vendors bidding for the 150MD contract. Hexware’s bid was $1 per man day less than the next lowest bid price placed by Avensys Consulting Pte Ltd (at $400 per man day). Hexaware was eventually awarded the 150MD contract; during the approval process, Faraz had directed for his staff to award the 150MD contract to Hexaware. The 150MD contract awarded to Hexaware was valued at $59,850 (150 man days x $399 per man day bid price). Hexaware’s profit margin for the 150MD contract was about 30% to 40%.

18     Faraz knew that it was wrong to agree to the above corrupt arrangement at [12] above as his decision to approve Hexaware for the PMODA contract and 150MD contract would be biased. Yet, Faraz had agreed to the corrupt arrangement and revealed the bid price as he was in a romantic relationship with Siti at the material time and he wanted to secure a better job for her with better prospects and remuneration.

19     Anant had facilitated the employment of Siti and Fahad by Hexaware and Capita Pte Ltd (a recruitment company) respectively and their subsequent deployment to Mapletree pursuant to the PMODA contract as a PMO Manager with a monthly salary of about $12,000 for 12 months and a Data Architect with a monthly salary of about $12,000 for 12 months respectively. As a result of the corrupt arrangement, Siti was paid a total of not less than $240,000 from December 2020 to August 2022 and Fahad was paid a total of not less than $228,000 from March 2021 to September 2022. Shortly after Siti secured the employment contract in December 2020, Faraz married Siti on XX January 2021.

20     By virtue of the foregoing, Faraz, in Singapore, in 2020, being an agent, to wit, the Head of IST at Mapletree, did corruptly obtain from one Anant, a senior business development manager at Hexaware, gratification, to wit, the facilitation of employment of Siti for the role of Project Management Officer for the Mapletree PMODA contract, in which Siti would be paid about $144,000 over 12 months, as inducement for doing acts in relation to his principal’s affairs, to wit, advancing the business interests of Hexaware with Mapletree, and Faraz has thereby committed an offence punishable under section 6(a) of the Prevention of Corruption Act (Cap 241, 1993 Rev Ed).

Parties’ Submissions on Sentence

21     The Prosecution and the Defence referred this court to the sentencing framework as set out in Goh Ngak Eng v Public Prosecutor [2023] 4 SLR 1385 at [45]-[47] (“Goh Ngak Eng”) in relation to private sector corruption offences under s 6 of the PCA in arriving at the appropriate sentence for the proceeded charge against the accused.

22     The High Court in Goh Ngak Eng developed a sentencing framework for private sector corruption offences, namely, offences under section 6(a) and section 6(b) of the PCA based on the two-stage, five-step framework adopted in Logachev Vladislav v Public Prosecutor [2018] 4 SLR 606.

23     At the first stage of the framework, the court arrives at an indicative starting sentence for the offender which reflects the intrinsic seriousness of the offending act. It involves three steps (Logachev at [76]-[79]):

Step 1: The court will have regard to the relevant offence-specific factors and identify (a) the level of harm caused by the offence; and (b) the level of the offender’s culpability (Goh Ngak Eng at [59]-[95] in relation to corruption-related offence-specific factors):

Offence-specific factors

Factors going towards harm

Factors going towards culpability

(a) Actual loss caused to principal

(a) Amount of gratification given or received

(b) Benefit to the giver of gratification

(b) Degree of planning and Premeditation

(c) Type and extent of loss to third parties

(c) Level of sophistication

(d) Public disquiet

(d) Duration of offending

(e) Offences committed as part of a group or syndicate

(e) Extent of the offender’s abuse of position and breach of trust

(f) Involvement of a transnational element

(f) Offender’s motive in committing the offence

(g) Whether the public service rationale is engaged

(g) Presence of threats, pressure or coercion

(h) Presence of public health or safety risks

(h) The role played by the offender in the corrupt transaction

(i) Involvement of a strategic industry

 

(j) Bribery of a foreign public official

 



Step 2: The court identifies the applicable indicative sentencing range by reference to the level of harm caused by the offence and the level of the offender’s culpability based on the following sentencing matrix (Goh Ngak Eng at [103]):

Step 3: The court identifies the appropriate starting point within the indicative sentencing range that was identified in step two for the accused.

24     At the second stage, the court makes adjustments to the starting point sentence identified under the first stage and arrives at a sentence that reflects the personal circumstances of the offender, by taking into account the relevant aggravating and/or mitigating circumstances unique to the offender and considering if the sentence arrived at is proportionate and consistent with the overall criminality of the offender. This stage consists of two steps: (a) The court makes adjustments to the identified starting point as may be necessary to consider factors personal to the offender’s particular circumstances (ie, offender-specific factors). (b) Where an offender has been convicted of multiple charges, the court considers if further adjustments should be made to the sentence for the individual charges, taking into account the totality principle.

25     In applying the sentencing framework, the Prosecution submitted that the harm caused by the offence falls within the higher end of the “Slight” harm category as Mapletree suffered the loss of not having the best vendor with the most competent employees engaged for the PMODA and 150MD contracts, and in addition Hexaware’s profit for the PMODA contract was about 34% to 40% arising from the corrupt arrangement and the profit margin for the 150MD contract was about 30% to 40%.

26     In addition, there was benefit gained by the giver of the gratification, Anant in securing the Mapletree contracts and allowing him to hit his annual sales targets. There was also loss to third parties who were deprived of fair competition in quoting for the jobs with Mapletree.

27     The Prosecution further submitted that the culpability of the accused falls within the lower range of the “Medium” culpability category as the amount of gratification received by the accused through the facilitation of Siti’s employment contract resulted in her being paid $144,00 over 12 months. Siti became accused’s wife shortly after the employment contract was confirmed and it was clear that the primary motivation of the corrupt arrangement was to ensure that Siti secure a job with better prospects and remuneration with a steady stream of income for the family.

28     In addition, the accused had abused his position and breached the trust placed on him by Mapletree as he occupied an influential position as its Head of IST and was instrumental in overseeing operations within IST and played an important role in the approving process for the Information Technology related procurement contracts. Throughout the whole procurement process, accused failed to disclose his relationships with Siti and Fahad to Mapletree as Mapletree relied on his recommendations.

29     In comparison with Anant, the accused played a far more culpable role as he initiated the corrupt arrangement and planned to obtain gratification from Anant in the form of the facilitation of employment for Siti and Fahad.

30     Following the sentencing matrix as set in Goh Ngak Eng at [103], the indicative starting sentences for an accused person who is convicted for offences under ss 6(a) and 6(b) of the PCA after trial and having regard to the offence-specific factors identified by the Prosecution with the level of harm as “Slight” (at the higher end of the range), and accused’s level of culpability as “Medium” (on the lower end of the range), the indicative sentencing range is an imprisonment term of between 6 and 12 months.

31     After considering accused’s role and the harm caused by the offence, the Prosecution submitted that accused’s sentence should fall in the middle level of the indicative sentencing range of 8 to 9 months’ imprisonment.

32     The Prosecution further submitted that the following offender-specific factors are relevant in the present case. Firstly, the accused faced a TIC charge in relation to him corruptly obtaining from Anant gratification, to wit, the facilitation of employment of Fahad; and secondly, accused is untraced.

33     Having considered the above offender-specific factors, the Prosecution submitted that appropriate claim-trial sentence would be 8 to 9 months’ imprisonment.

34     Since accused has pleaded guilty at Stage 4 of the SAP PG Sentencing Guidelines, which warrants a reduction of up to 5%, the Prosecution sought a sentence of between 7.5 and 8.5 months’ imprisonment.

35     The Defence contended that Hexaware’s profit should not be equated with Mapletree’s loss as Hexaware may earn a higher margin because of its own cost structure, efficiencies, or pricing model which does not necessarily translate into financial loss to Mapletree. Further the Defence argued that there is no clear evidence of the cost that Mapletree would have incurred had it filled the roles of Siti and Fahad by direct hire. This is also not a case where the profit margin represented a wrongful mark-up to the contract value to fund the bribes or that Mapletree was made to pay above the market rate for the services obtained.

36     The Defence submitted that the harm caused in this case should fall within the lower to middle band of the “Slight” harm category. The harm lies mainly in the compromise of Mapletree’s internal process, the unfair advantage conferred on Hexaware, and the suborning of the agent-principal relationship, rather than in any proven tangible financial loss or clear third-party prejudice.

37     As for culpability, the Defence submitted that the accused’s culpability falls within the lower to middle band of “Low” culpability. The Defence argued that the salary of $144,000 paid to Siti over a 12-month period does not provide a principled measure of the gratification received as work was duly performed by Siti and there was no evidence any of these monies flowing into the pockets of the accused and therefore it does not justify a finding of medium culpability.

38     The Defence further contended that the additional benefit of Siti gaining work experience and better prospect from employment at Mapletree should not be given independent aggravating weight and the duration of offending should not be assessed in the light of Siti’s salary being paid over a 12-month period but rather this case should be considered as arising from a single corrupt arrangement.

39     The Defence further submitted that for the PMODA contract, the accused was not the final approver as he merely provided the IST approval and the final approval was provided by the Director of Finance. In respect of the 150MD contract, during the approval process, the accused directed his staff to award the 159MD contract to Hexaware only because Hexaware had submitted the lowest bid.

40     Nevertheless, the Defence conceded that there was some abuse of position and breach of trust, but the culpability of the accused overall fell within the lower to middle band of “Low” culpability.

41     The Defence submitted that this case falls within the slight harm and low culpability sentencing framework matrix with an applicable indicative sentencing range of a fine or up to 6 month’s imprisonment and considering that the substance of the corrupt arrangement was the remuneration paid to Siti pursuant to an employment contract where work and services were performed by Siti, the Defence further submitted that the appropriate indicative starting sentence would be a fine and /or up to 2 months’ imprisonment at the lower end of the indicative sentencing range.

42     The Defence agreed with the Prosecution that with the one TIC charge and accused’s lack of antecedents, there should be no further uplift to the indicating starting sentence.

43     The Defence, however, disagreed with the Prosecution on the appropriate discount to be given to the accused for his plea of guilt. The accused pleaded guilty before the conclusion of the first ancillary hearing but the Defence contended that several of the documents filed in the numerous s 231 CPC Notices should have been filed earlier with the Prosecution’s supplementary Bundle at the close of the CCDC process and hence the matter would be classified at Stage 3 of the SAP guidelines, allowing for a 10% reduction in sentence.

Decision on Sentence

44     It was accepted by both parties that the applicable sentencing framework is that laid down in Goh Ngak Eng for private sector corruption offences under s 6 of the PCA.

45     There was also no question that the dominant sentencing consideration is that of general deterrence given the public interest in relation to private sector corruption as identified by the Court in Goh Ngak Eng at [54], that “the public interest is in the private sector maintaining a reputation for being corruption free, with business being conducted in a fair and transparent manner so as to ensure that the public’s legitimate expectations of bona fides, commercial even-handedness and economic welfare are not prejudiced, and that the efficient operation of the market is not disrupted.”

46     In respect of the offence-specific factors relating to harm, both parties are in general agreement that for this case, the level of harm fell in the “Slight” band with the Prosecution arguing that it should fall at the higher end of “Slight” band and the Defence contending that it should be somewhere between the lower to middle of “Slight” band.

47     I am of the view that there was actual harm caused by the accused to his principal, Mapletree, although the actual quantum may be difficult to compute as contended by the Defence since it cannot be denied that Siti did render her work and services pursuant to the award of the contract to Hexaware by Mapletree.

48     In addition, there was clearly benefit derived by the giver of the gratification, Anant who successfully bid for the contract and gained profit margin of up to about 34% to 40% of the PMODA contract for Hexaware.

49     In my view, Hexaware was not a bona fide bidder as Anant was given insider information by the accused and there was clearly prejudice occasioned to any third party in the procurement process, although the actual loss would be difficult to quantify but the contractual quantum involved was not insignificant.

50     Having considered the offence-specific factors relating to harm, this court is of the view that the level of harm fell somewhere between middle and high end of the “Slight” band.

51     In respect of the offence-specific factors relating to culpability there is disagreement between the Prosecution and the Defence with the Prosecution classifying the accused’s level of culpability as “Medium” (falling on the lower end of the range) and the Defence contending that it should fall at the lower to middle band of the “Low” culpability.

52     I am unable to accept Defence’s categorisation of the level of the accused’s culpability in this case. In my view the accused has planned and orchestrated the corrupt arrangement with Anant by abusing his position as the Head of IST at Mapletree where he played an influential role of getting Hexaware’s application to join the PVL of Mapletree to be approved and subsequently making recommendation for Hexaware to be approved as the vendor of choice for the PMODA contract; ensuring that Anant facilitated the employment of Siti and Fahad by participating in the interviews of the Siti and Fahad as the most senior representative of Mapletree in the assessment of their suitability as candidates put up by Hexaware.

53     The accused further abused the trust reposed on him by Mapletree in disclosing sensitive historical insider information of the per man day rate for the 150MD contract to Anant and by failing to disclose his relationships he had with Siti and Fahad to Mapletree throughout the procurement and approval process for the award of the contracts.

54     In my view the level of culpability of the accused fell within the “Medium” category at the lower end of the range as submitted by the Prosecution.

55     Based on the Goh Ngak Eng framework, the indicative sentencing range should be an imprisonment term of between 6 and 12 months.

56     This court is of the view that the appropriate starting point within this indicative range for the accused after considering the offence-specific factors, should fall within the range of 7 to 8 months’ imprisonment which is a slight calibration downwards to the range of 8 to 9 months sought by the Prosecution.

57     After taking into account the offender-specific factors highlighted by both parties regarding the accused’s one TIC charge and his lack of antecedents, I agree with the parties that there should not be any uplift to the indicative starting sentence and the appropriate claim-trial sentence would be in the range of 7 to 8 months’ imprisonment for this case.

58     There is disagreement between the Prosecution and the Defence on whether the sentencing discount of up to 5% should apply to the accused’s plea of guilt at Stage 4 of the proceedings according to the Prosecution or whether the discount should be 10% at Stage 3 of the proceedings according to the Defence, pursuant to the sentencing guidelines on reduction in sentences for guilty pleas issued by the Sentencing Advisory Panel.

59     This court is prepared to accord the accused the 10% reduction from the appropriate claim-trial sentence of between 7 to 8 months’ imprisonment and based on the circumstances of this case I have calibrated the final sentence of 6 months and 2 weeks’ imprisonment to be imposed on the accused which in my view would be commensurate with his culpability and appropriate to serve as a deterrence to other like-minded individuals from perpetrating such crimes.
