Public Prosecutor v Abdullah Questanie Bin Ibrahim

Public Prosecutor v Abdullah Questanie Bin Ibrahim
[2026] SGDC 231

Case Number:District Arrest Case No 901477 of 2026 & 7 Others
Decision Date:17 July 2026
Tribunal/Court:District Court
Coram: Paul Quan
Counsel Name(s): Valerie Lim (Attorney-General's Chambers) for the Public Prosecutor; Accused self-represented.
Parties: Public Prosecutor — Abdullah Questanie Bin Ibrahim

Criminal Law – Offences – Property – Theft

Criminal Law – Statutory Offences – Corrosive and Explosive Substances and Offensive Weapons Act – Being found in the company of person who possessed offensive weapon

Criminal Law – Statutory Offences – Motor Vehicles (Third-Party Risks & Compensation) Act – Driving without third party insurance coverage

Criminal Law – Statutory Offences – Road Traffic Act – Unqualified driving

Criminal Procedure and Sentencing – Sentencing – Young offenders

17 July 2026

District Judge Paul Quan:

Introduction

1       This is a case which lies at the cusp of the intersection between rehabilitative and deterrent concerns involving a young offender, who committed a spate of offences. Both probation and reformative training (“RT”) have been assessed to be suitable sentencing options. The question before me is which sentencing option, if at all, should be exercised in this case.

Brief facts

2       The accused, Abdullah Questanie Bin Ibrahim (“Mr Abdullah”), an 18-year-old Singaporean, stole a car with three other minors aged 17, 16 and 14 and took the car for a joyride on two successive occasions. He did not possess a driving licence at the time and consequently was uninsured. For one of the rides, the 16-year-old minor brought along a fruit knife and Mr Abdullah knew he had done so.

Charges

3       Mr Abdullah has pleaded guilty to two charges of committing theft of a motor vehicle under section 379A(1) of the Penal Code 1871 (2020 Rev Ed) (“PC”).[note: 1] He has also consented to have six other charges taken into consideration for the purpose of sentence (“TIC”), namely:

(a)     four accompanying charges of unqualified driving and driving without third-party insurance coverage under section 35(1) of the Road Traffic Act 1961 (2020 Rev Ed) and section 3(1) of the Motor Vehicles (Third-Party Risks & Compensation) Act 1960 respectively;[note: 2]

(b)     a charge of theft under section 379 PC for stealing a debit card from a wallet inside the vehicle;[note: 3] and

(c)     a charge of being found in the company of the 16-year-old minor who possessed an offensive weapon under section 8(1) of the Corrosive and Explosive Substances and Offensive Weapons Act 1958 (2020 Rev Ed) (“CESOWA”).[note: 4]

Parties’ positions

4       I convicted Mr Abdullah on 19 May 2026. Agreeing with the prosecution,[note: 5] I called for both a probation pre-sentence report (“PSR”) and an RT PSR on Mr Abdullah, rather than only a probation PSR, which was what Mr Abdullah asked me to do so that he can continue with his studies if he were placed on probation.

5       I have since received his PSRs from the Singapore Prison Service (“SPS”) and his probation officer on 3 July 2026[note: 6] and 15 July 2026 respectively.[note: 7] SPS has recommended him to undergo “Level 1 intensity of rehabilitation” if he were sentenced to RT, whereas his probation officer has recommended 18 months’ split probation (16 months’ intensive, two months’ supervised), including a residential condition at the Singapore Boys’ Hostel (“SBHL”) for 12 months. Despite a moderate risk of reoffending and on account of his young age and that he is untraced, the prosecution does not object to Mr Abdullah undergoing probation under section 5 of the Probation of Offenders Act 1951 (2020 Rev Ed) (“POA”), according to the length, intensity and conditions recommended by his probation officer. It has also sought a prohibition on Mr Abdullah against driving as an additional condition during the probation period.[note: 8] Mr Adullah, who remains self-represented, has asked me to allow him to undergo probation.

Court’s decision

6       I explain in this ex tempore judgment why I now decide that it is expedient to make a split probation order requiring Mr Abdullah to be under the supervision of a probation officer for 18 months (16 months’ intensive, two months’ supervised), having regard to the circumstances, including the nature of Mr Abdullah’s offences and his character: section 5(1) POA.

Why both RT and probation PSRs called

7       I delivered brief reasons on 19 May 2026 explaining why I called for both an RT and probation PSRs on Mr Abdullah. I outline these reasons by way of background.

8       I am cognisant that I should generally call for a probation PSR before sentencing a young offender who is aged 21 or below. In Mr Abdullah’s case, the basic prerequisites for probation are met and I did not think probation is unviable or unrealistic so as to rule it out as a sentencing option altogether: A Karthik v PP [2018] 5 SLR 1289 at [20] and [21].

Basic prerequisites for probation met

9       In Mr Abdullah’s case, the basic prerequisites for probation are met:

(a)     Mr Abdullah’s offences are not offences for which the sentences are “fixed by law”: section 5(1) of the Probation of Offenders Act 1951 (2020 Rev Ed) (“POA”) –

(i)       for each of his offence under section 379A PC, Mr Abdullah faces mandatory imprisonment for a term which may extend to seven years that can be coupled with a fine, and

(ii)       the sentences are fixed in type but not in quantum; the court must impose imprisonment with or without a fine, but has the discretion to decide on the length of imprisonment and the quantum of the fine: Mohamad Fairuuz bin Saleh v PP [2015] 1 SLR 1145 at [17(c)]; and

(b)     the proviso to section 5(1) of the POA also does not apply as the offences are not punishable with either a specified minimum sentence or mandatory minimum sentence. Mr Abdullah also does not have any previous convictions.

Probation viable or realistic

10     Be that as it may, I must still preliminarily assess whether probation is viable or realistic on the facts of Mr Abdullah’s case, and the court should order a probation PSR if the accused is young (that is, between 16 and 21 years old), a first offender and convicted of a relatively less serious crime: Wong Shan Shan v PP [2008] SGHC 49 at [20]-[21].

11     In this case, Mr Abdullah is a young offender being 18 at the time of the offences, conviction and sentencing. He is also a first-time offender. In assessing the severity of his offences, I drew a comparison with the offences faced by the offenders in A Karthik and Wong Shan Shan. These offenders were arguably convicted of more serious charges or more charges: Cheah Bernice [2024] SGDC 220 at [14]. In both cases, the appellate court thought that probation PSRs ought to have been called on the offenders.

12     I did not consider this to be a case where probation should be altogether excluded as a viable or realistic sentencing option for Mr Abdullah. In exceptional circumstances an offender, who appears, on the face of it, suitable for probation (in that he satisfies the basic prerequisites for probation) can nonetheless be sentenced without the court ordering a probation PSR: Wong Shan Shan at [23]. Such circumstances do not exist in this case.

13     Where rehabilitation is the dominant sentencing consideration, probation would be one of the typical options at the court’s disposal, given that probation places rehabilitation at the front and centre of the court’s deliberation: A Karthik at [67].

RT PSR should also be called

14     Having said that, the context in which the offences were committed as highlighted by the prosecution troubled me:

(a)     they were group offences, involving other minors aged 14 to 17, with Mr Abdullah being the oldest among the lot;

(b)     Mr Abdullah’s 17-year-old relative and the 16-year-old minor first found the car key remote that the owner misplaced and the car to that remote. Being the oldest in the group, Mr Abdullah ought to have known better but decided to steal the car for a joyride with the other two. Mr Abdullah and the 16-year-old minor took turns to drive the car around the vicinity for nearly two hours and the car was seen jerking repeatedly; [note: 9]

(c)     Mr Abdullah then brought the car key remote home. Emboldened by this first attempt, he decided to steal the car again for yet another joyride the next night, this time around with a 14-year-old minor, and picked up the 16-year-old minor, after which he drove around the vicinity;[note: 10]

(d)     the alarm caused to the complainant, who was the car owner’s husband, and the need for him to give chase and intercept them on the second occasion, upon which they evaded apprehension by abandoning the car by the roadside and fled the scene on foot;[note: 11] and

(e)     Mr Abdullah was an unqualified driver at the time and was therefore uninsured to drive.[note: 12] He needlessly exposed his younger accomplices and innocent road users to the potential harm of such unqualified and uninsured driving. It was purely fortuitous that no such harm materialised.

There were also theft and CESOWA TIC charges. On the face of it, there appears to also be a need for deterrence, both specific (because of the nature of Mr Abdullah’s reoffending behaviour) and general (because stealing vehicles for joyrides in a group, engaging in unqualified and uninsured driving and encouraging minors to commit crime are brazenly dangerous, and like-minded youths have to be generally deterred), and the consequent need to consider RT as a possible sentencing option to incorporate a sufficient element of deterrence within the overarching focus on the goal of rehabilitation with a minimum incarceration period of six or 12 months that is not a feature of probation: PP v Koh Wen Jie Boaz [2016] 1 SLR 334 at [34] and [39]. Where there is a need for both deterrence and rehabilitation, RT may be the most suitable sentence, given that it offers a useful middle ground between sending the offender to prison and meeting the desire to rehabilitate a young offender: A Karthik at [67].

15     I was therefore also not closed to RT as a possible rehabilitative-deterrent/punitive sentencing option. The offences stand at the cusp of the intersection between rehabilitative and deterrent concerns. I therefore called for a report pursuant to section 305(3) of the Criminal Procedure Code 2010 (2020 Rev Ed) on Mr Abdullah’s physical and mental condition, his suitability for RT, and the nature of the rehabilitation that is recommended for him, in order for me to assess RT as a sentencing option. I ordered for him to be remanded for a week at the reformative training centre (“RTC”) to enable his PSR to be submitted to the court and for him to be released thereafter to continue to be placed on bail.

Approach to sentencing young offender

16     When sentencing a young offender, the first stage is to identify and prioritise the primary sentencing considerations appropriate to the offender having regard to all the circumstances including those of the offence. The second stage is to select the appropriate sentence that would best meet those identified and prioritised sentencing considerations: PP v Mohammad Al-Ansari bin Basri [2008] 1 SLR(R) 449 at [77]-[78] and PP v Koh Wen Jie Boaz [2016] 1 SLR 334 (“Boaz Koh”) at [28] as affirmed and explained in PP v ASR [2019] 1 SLR 941 at [94], [101]-[102]. The inquiry proceeds from the foremost question of whether rehabilitation remains the dominant sentencing principle.

Stage 1: Identify and prioritise primary sentencing considerations

17     At the first stage, the question is whether in all the circumstances, the presumptive emphasis on rehabilitation has been displaced: See Li Quan Mendel v PP [2020] 2 SLR 630 (“Mendel See”) at [15]. If an offender is 21 years old or below at both the time of the offence and the time of sentencing, the law takes the presumptive view that the primary sentencing consideration in such cases will generally be rehabilitation, because both the retrospective and prospective rationales underlying such presumptive primacy of rehabilitation would apply: A Karthik v PP [2018] 5 SLR 1289 at [44].

Presumptive primacy of rehabilitation not displaced in Mr Abdullah’s case

18     In this case, Mr Abdullah is 18 at the time of the offences and sentencing today. The primacy of rehabilitation is therefore presumptive. But the focus on rehabilitation can be diminished or even eclipsed by such considerations as deterrence or retribution where the circumstances warrant, where:

(a)     the offence is serious,

(b)     the harm caused is severe,

(c)     the offender is hardened and recalcitrant, or

(d)     the conditions do not exist to make rehabilitative sentencing options viable: Boaz Koh at [30].

19     Mr Abdullah’s offences are serious, it was fortuitous that the harm caused by his offences were not severe, and he displayed reoffending behaviour: see [14], above.

20     Mr Abdullah is a first-time offender and he is not a hardened and recalcitrant offender as such. However, specific deterrence appears to be engaged in this case, given that Mr Abdullah committed the theft offence not once but twice and back-to-back. Against this are the circumstances in which he found himself that drove him to commit the offences. According to his account to his probation officer,[note: 13] his 17-year-old relative had, on the first occasion, repeatedly asked him to enter the stolen car and he did so without much consideration of his actions. He then drove out of negative peer influence from the 16-year-old minor. He brought the car remote home because his relative had asked him to and he did so without giving due consideration to his actions. He reoffended on the second occasion because his relative had asked him to and he did not wish to leave him alone in the car because he feared for his relative’s safety if he drove and got into an accident. He drove again because his relative had asked him to pick up the minor who lived nearby.

21     I am satisfied that the presumptive primacy of rehabilitation has not been displaced in that the focus on rehabilitation is not diminished or eclipsed by deterrent or retributive considerations.

Stage 2: How sentencing considerations ought to be achieved

22     Having determined that Mr Abdullah should be rehabilitated, I next have to ascertain how rehabilitation ought to be achieved and his suitability to undergo a specific form of rehabilitation: ASR at [99]. The second stage is to select the appropriate sentence that would best meet this concern of prioritising rehabilitation.

Probation is appropriate sentence to meet rehabilitative needs

23     Where rehabilitation is the dominant sentencing consideration, probation would be one of the typical options at the court’s disposal: see [13], above. In this case, the conditions exist to make probation a viable rehabilitative sentencing option as is evident from Mr Abdullah’s probation PSR. The opinion of the probation officer is not and should not be conclusive on the issue of sentencing, nor does it bind the court to a certain decision: Praveen s/o Krishnan v PP [2018] 3 SLR 1300 at [65]. However, I am slow to depart from the recommendations of Mr Abdullah’s probation officer in her comprehensive report because there is nothing to suggest that there was no proper basis for them, or that they were based on circumstances that were factually incorrect or have since materially changed: A Karthik at [79].

Mr Abdullah assessed to be suitable for probation

24     The recommendation for probation by Mr Abdullah’s probation officer is supported by her assessment based on the Youth Level of Service/ Case Management Inventory (“YLS/CMI”) that is “a reliable and validated structured instrument designed to assess the risk of re-offending and rehabilitation needs of youth offenders aged 12 to below 19”.[note: 14] The sources of information from which to make her assessment are also sufficiently broad-based.[note: 15]

(1)   Mr Abdullah’s risk of re-offending moderate

25     Mr Abdullah’s risk of re-offending was assessed to be moderate based on the YLS/CMI upon balancing the risk and protective factors.[note: 16] On that basis, the recommendation is that he is suitable to undergo a period of 18 months’ split probation (16 months’ intensive, two months’ supervised) with:[note: 17]

(a)     a time restriction from 10pm to 6am imposed on him,

(b)     a 12-month residency period in SBHL: sections 5(3)(a) and 5(4) POA,

(c)     electronic monitoring for four months after discharge from SBHL,

(d)     the performance of 90 hours of community service as he is also assessed to be physically and mentally fit to perform such community service and suitable arrangements can be made for him to do so: sections 5(5), 5(6) and 5(7) POA,[note: 18]

(e)     attendance of any necessary substance use assessment and treatment,

(f)     his parents bonded to ensure his good behaviour during the probation period, and

(g)     a court-ordered review in six months.

(A)   Existence of risk factors

26     Significant among the identified risk factors as highlighted by the prosecution are Mr Abdullah’s poor consequential thinking, propensity for risk-taking, susceptibility to negative influence, lack of discipline and poor regard for rules, as well as a history of permissive parenting that impacts on the effectiveness of parental supervision.[note: 19]

(B)   Some protective factors

27     Against these is the existence of some protective factors, namely Mr Abdullah’s adherence to the time curfew imposed by the court as a bail condition since end-January 2026, and trial time restriction imposed by the probation officer from 26 May 2026, where he was present at home when three video-calls were made in June and July 2026; as well as the presence of familial support in the form of renewed parental commitment to supervision.[note: 20]

28     He is currently enrolled in the National Institute of Technical Education (“ITE”) Certificate (“Nitec”) in Mechanical Technology course and although he reportedly lost interest after he committed the offences and the consequent court proceedings,[note: 21] he has conveyed his desire to study to me and his probation officer. He plans to pursue a work study diploma in ITE in order to command a higher pay. [note: 22] There are no current significant derailers in the form of negative peer influences, undesirable leisure activities or substance use.[note: 23]

29     Crucially, Mr Abdullah has also gained insights into his offences.[note: 24] At first blush, it would appear that Mr Abdullah’s account as to how he came to commit the offences “belies a lack of personal accountability for the severity of his actions”,[note: 25] including attributing his conduct to his relative’s influence. However, his mother has also confirmed such onfluence.[note: 26] His relative has since been ordered by the Youth Court to reside at the Singapore Boys’ Home for 21 months under a juvenile detention centre order for mirror theft offences among others.[note: 27] Ultimately, Mr Abdullah reflected that his actions were foolish and impulsive as he could have handed the car remote to the police instead of keeping it, and that the 16-year-old minor, whom he thought was a positive peer, was bad company because he influenced him to drive.[note: 28]

30     He has also accepted responsibility and held himself accountable for his actions by expressing:[note: 29]

(a)     willingness to attend programmes, reside in a hostel and be electronically monitored, if necessary;

(b)     willingness to accept supervision by the probation officer and his parents;

(c)     intention to avoid reoffending by keeping a smaller social circle and spending more time at home with his family to keep him meaningfully occupied, remind him of behavioural expectations and distracted him from misbehaving;

(d)     intention to ensure regular school attendance, cope with negative emotions and manage potential conflicts; and

(e)     plans to manage boredom and his desire for fun, as well as manage potential negative influence from his relative.

31     He now has more focused familial support as well, with his parents committed to supervise and support his rehabilitation.[note: 30]

(2)   Concrete plan to address risk factors

32     There is also a concrete action plan for intervention in various key areas during the probation period for Mr Abdullah and I am satisfied that 18 months is the sufficient time period to rehabilitate him in a semi-structured environment like SBHL.[note: 31] Mr Abdullah is willing to attend programmes[note: 32] to address key areas for intervention in his attitudes, peer relations, meaningful engagement and personality/behaviour. His parents will also be guided on more effective parenting and enhancing communications with him.

Similar criminogenic needs identified in RT PSR

33     I mention in passing that the RT PSR identified similar criminogenic needs.[note: 33] Crucially, he did not present with personality and behavioural patterns associated with antisocial behaviour;[note: 34] neither did he present with criminal attitudes but rather limited consequential thinking and susceptibility to negative influences: [note: 35]

(a)     during the first occasion, he did not give much thought to his actions and was misguided by his relative without reflecting on the reality of the situation; and on the second occasion, he felt pressured by his relative to participate again and could not assert himself by saying no;

(b)     he expressed guilty and remorse for his actions and accepted personal responsibility. He also spoke of the negative impact of his actions on himself and the victim after his arrest; and

(c)     his attitudes demonstrate support for conventional norms – he has not re-offended, reported disengagement from negative influences and consulting pro-social connection, and plans to complete his Nitec course and desire to progress to polytechnic.

34     The consequential recommendation of an RT level 1 intensity of rehabilitation programme over six months that will focus on interventions to:[note: 36]

(a)     strengthen his ability to assert positive choices in the face of peer pressure and practise longer term consequential thinking, and

(b)     enhance his ability to ask for help when faced with problems and expand his prosocial network to support his continued desistance from offending,

though in a structured RTC environment, coheres with the intervention plan set out in the probation PSR to be administered in the main in SBHL.

Conclusion

35     I am therefore satisfied that it is expedient to make a probation order, having regard to the circumstances including the nature of Mr Abdullah’s offence and his character: section 5(1) POA. I have explained the recommendations in the probation PSR to Mr Abdullah and to his parents. Having understood the effect of the order and proposed conditions and that if he fails to comply with the order or commit another offence, he will be liable to be sentenced for his original offences, Mr Abdullah is willing to comply with the requirements: section 5(9) POA. His parents have also agreed to execute a bond to give security for Mr Abdullah’s good behaviour during the probation period: section 5(2) POA.

Split probation of 18 months with conditions ordered on Mr Abdullah

36     I order Mr Abdullah to undergo a period of 18 months’ split probation (16 months’ intensive; two months’ supervised) from today, in particular with:

(a)     a daily time restriction for him to remain indoors from 10pm to 6am,

(b)     a 12-month residency period in SBHL,

(c)     electronic monitoring for four months after discharge from SBHL,

(d)     the performance of 90 hours of community service,

(e)     the attendance of any necessary substance use assessment and treatment,

(f)     prohibition from driving during the probation period,

(g)     his parents to execute a bond in the sum of S$5,000 to give security for Mr Abdullah’s good behaviour during the probation period, and

(h)     a court-ordered review in six months on 6 January 2027 at 2.30pm in Court 18C.

The other usual conditions relate to Mr Abdullah being of good behaviour and to keep the peace, to report to and receive visits from his probation officer, to notify her immediately of any change of residence or employment and not to change his employment without her prior approval, as well as to carry out any of her lawful instructions.

37     This is not only a viable and feasible but the appropriate sentence to impose that is both sufficient and proportionate in Mr Abdullah’s case. A probation period of 18 months will suffice, given the nature and extent of the intervention plan that has been put in place for his rehabilitation; a punitive or deterrent-based sentence, such as a sentence of RT, will be less helpful for his rehabilitation. He has already experienced some semblance of this during his one-week remand at RTC for his PSR assessment in any event.

38     The main concern for Mr Abdullah and his parents is the ability for him to continue his studies. The probation officer has confirmed that this will be possible even if he resides in SBHL. The consequent requirement to maintain regular attendance and positive conduct can be covered under the condition to carry out the probation officer’s lawful instructions. This is now entirely in Mr Abdullah’s good hands and I am cautiously optimistic of his rehabilitation, which I look forward to see in six months’ time when I review his progress.

html:
Haweina Trading Co Ltd v Bling Blink SG Pte Ltd and another

Haweina Trading Co Ltd v Bling Blink SG Pte Ltd and another
[2026] SGDC 230

Case Number:Originating Claim No 1255 of 2025, Assessment of Damages No 100 of 2026
Decision Date:17 July 2026
Tribunal/Court:District Court
Coram: Evans Ng
Counsel Name(s): Fong Wei Li, Tiffanie Lim Jing Wen and Leng Ji En Paul (Forward Legal LLC) for the claimant; The first defendant absent and unrepresented; The second defendant in person.
Parties: Haweina Trading Co Ltd — Bling Blink SG Pte Ltd — Ng Hui Fen

Tort – Defamation – Damages

17 July 2026

Judgment reserved.

Deputy Registrar Evans Ng:

1       The Claimant is a foreign company and runs a business providing eyelash beautification services and related products and training courses. The 1st Defendant is a Singapore company and, nomen est omen, it too provides eyelash products and services. The 2nd Defendant is its sole shareholder and director. The disputants had no dealings with each other until April 2025. The Defendants had a misunderstanding with a supplier whom they had in common with the Claimant. They put it down to the Claimant’s doing. Disgruntled, they dashed off a series of posts about the Claimant, its representatives or employees on their social media accounts.

2       Those louche publications attracted a libel action from the Claimant. Because the Defendants did not file and serve a notice of intention to contest or not contest, a default judgment was entered against them. The issues of defamatory meaning and identification became incontestable. The matter proceeded to this assessment of damages hearing, at which the Claimant sought general damages only.

3       Unlike a natural person, a corporate claimant is not presumed to have a reputation. It must prove that it has a reputation that is capable of being injured by the libel. Therefore, when assessing damages, there is a threshold question of whether the claimant had a trading or business reputation within Singapore, at the time of the libellous publications. This is a question of fact to be established by evidence: Qingdao Bohai Construction Group Co, Ltd and others v Goh Teck Beng and another [2016] 4 SLR 977 at [50], [51], [58] and [59]. If the answer is negative, it is not entitled to damages.

4       The Claimant pleaded that it “operates outside of Singapore, from Taiwan” but has clients and customers “across Asia, including […] Singapore” and a reputation “within the beauty community, particularly in Taiwan and Singapore”. I examine whether the evidence fulfils this pleading.

5       Ms Yeh Yi-Wei is a director of the Claimant and appeared as its sole witness. She says that the Claimant has clients in Singapore, based on the number of “followers” that its social media accounts have accumulated. Her affidavit of evidence-in-chief affirmed on 30 January 2026 stated:

The Claimant is a company based in Taiwan […]. Given that the Claimant has clientele across Taiwan, Hong Kong, Malaysia and Singapore, the Claimant has, to date, amassed approximately 13,700 followers on Instagram and 2,517 followers on Threads [which are social media platforms]. The Claimant primarily relies on social media to conduct and promote their business.

In my view, her reasoning lacks discrimination and her numbers are short of explanatory power. There is no certain or necessary relationship between the number of followers that a company has gathered on its social media accounts and the existence of its business or trading reputation in a particular jurisdiction. Further, there is no evidence in the affidavit to show whether any, and if so, how many, of the Claimant’s social media followers were from Singapore, and when they were cultivated.

6       Ms Yeh’s affidavit also alleged, “On or around I was also informed by a potential client of mine from Singapore that she had seen the [defamatory statements] […] Evidence of this is exhibited […] herein.” The allegation is missing a date. The exhibited evidence consists of screenshots of some text messages exchanged between Ms Yeh and the said “potential client”, which are meant to prove the allegation. I cannot determine from the screenshots when those text messages were exchanged — I suppose the Claimant’s solicitors faced the same problem when drafting the affidavit, inserted a placeholder in the text, and forgot about it. The bigger problem is that the Claimant is unable to demonstrate from the contents of the text messages that the said “potential client” hailed from Singapore and not elsewhere (for example, Hong Kong or Malaysia).

7       That is the entire gamut of the Claimant’s affidavit evidence to prove that it had a business or trading reputation within Singapore as of April 2025, and it is insufficient.

8       When cross-examined by the 2nd Defendant, Ms Yeh said the Claimant:

(a)     did not have any physical premises in Singapore,

(b)     did not employ any staff in Singapore,

(c)     did not know how many alleged Singapore customers it had served,

(d)     had not produced any records showing the number of alleged Singapore customers it had served,

(e)     had not shown how much business revenue was derived from alleged Singapore customers,

(f)     did not conduct any physical courses in Singapore,

(g)     did not know how many alleged Singapore customers attended its online courses,

(h)     did not keep attendance records of its online courses because they were pre-recorded videos,

(i)     had not produced any invoices or receipts relating to alleged Singapore customers who had signed up for its courses,

(j)     did not know how many of its social media followers were from Singapore,

(k)     did not receive any industry awards in Singapore,

(l)     was not invited by any Singapore organization to speak as an industry expert, and

(m)     was not featured by any Singapore media outlets.

9       When given another opportunity to show the Court any documents regarding the extent of the Claimant’s reputation in Singapore, Ms Yeh stated:

In terms of the number of Instagram followers, there are 14,100 [as of 16 June 2026, the date of the hearing], which I would say it is rather reputable with this number of followers. And I believe be it Singapore, Hong Kong or Taiwan, the number of followers in my case, I belong to the top tier.

Her answer made clear that the Claimant is indeed relying purely on the strength of its online social media presence to prove its business or trading reputation in Singapore, which I cannot accept (see [5] above). The oral evidence given on behalf of the Claimant does not advance its case.

10     Since the Claimant has failed to establish that, at the material time, it had the requisite reputation in this jurisdiction, it is not entitled to an award of damages. I will hear the parties on costs.

Public Prosecutor v JIY

Public Prosecutor v JIY
[2026] SGDC 229

Case Number:District Arrest Case No. DAC-906016-2025 & 10 Ors, Magistrate's Appeal No. MA-9158-2026-01
Decision Date:17 July 2026
Tribunal/Court:District Court
Coram: Shaiffudin Saruwan
Counsel Name(s): DPP Cheronne Lim (Attorney-General's Chambers) for the Prosecution; Teo Choo Kee (CK Teo & Co.) for the Accused
Parties: Public Prosecutor — JIY

Criminal procedure and sentencing – Sentencing – Misuse of Drugs Act 1973 – s 8(b)(ii) p/u s 33A(1) – LT-1 consumption of methamphetamine – s 8(a) p/u s 33(3B) – Enhanced possession of methamphetamine

Criminal procedure and sentencing – Sentencing – s 7 Corrosive and Explosives Substances and Offensive Weapons Act 1958 – Possession of knuckle duster

Criminal procedure and sentencing – Sentencing – s 55A(1)(a)(i) r/w s 55A(1)(b)(ii) p/u s 55A(5) of the Corruption, Drug Trafficking and Other Serious Crimes (Confiscation of Benefits) Act 1992 – Sharing details of one’s bank account with another

[LawNet Editorial Note: An appeal to this decision has been filed in MA 9158/2026/01.]

17 July 2026

District Judge Shaiffudin Saruwan:

Introduction

1       This is an appeal against sentence.

2       The accused was represented by Mr Teo Choo Kee of CK Teo & Co. DPP Cheronne Lim was the prosecutor.

3       There was a gag order prohibiting the publication of the name, address, photograph, any evidence or any other thing likely to lead to the identification of the victim in relation to the charge under s 377BE(2) of the Penal Code 1871 (“PC”) which was taken into consideration (DAC-918423-2025).

The charge(s)

4       The accused pleaded guilty to the four charges below –

(a)      DAC-906016-2025:

LT1 consumption of methamphetamine under s 8(b)(ii) punishable under s 33A(1) of the Misuse of Drugs Act 1973 (“MDA”)(“the LT1 consumption charge”). There was also a breach of the basic condition of the remission order punishable under s50T(1)(a) Prisons Act 1933 (“PA”). The accused was liable to an enhanced sentence not exceeding 58 days.

(b)      DAC-908319-2025:

Enhanced possession of methamphetamine under s 8(a) punishable under s 33(3B) MDA (“the enhanced consumption charge”). There was also a breach of the basic condition of his remission order punishable under s50T(1)(a) PA. The accused was liable to an enhanced sentence not exceeding 58 days.

(c)      DAC-918509-2025:

Possession of a knuckleduster without authority under s 7(1) of the Corrosive and Explosives Substances and Offensive Weapons Act 1958 (“the offensive weapon charge”). There was also a breach of the basic condition of his remission order punishable under s50T(1)(a) PA. The accused was liable to an enhanced sentence not exceeding 58 days.

(d)      DAC-921201-2025:

Enabling one Lennard Lee to operate his UOB bank account by sharing his banking details, and failing to take reasonable steps to ascertain the purpose of Leonard Lee being able to operate the said bank account under s 55A(1)(a)(i) read with s 55A(1)(b)(ii) punishable under s 55A(5) of the Corruption, Drug Trafficking and Other Serious Crimes (Confiscation of Benefits) Act 1992 (“the CDSA charge”). There was also a breach of the basic condition of his remission order punishable under s50T(1)(a) PA. The accused was liable to an enhanced sentence not exceeding 377 days.

5       The following seven charges were taken into consideration –

(a)     Two counts of robbery under s 392 PC.

(b)     One count of possession of drug-taking utensils under s 9 punishable under s 33(1) MDA and punishable under s 50T(1)(a) PA.

(c)     One count of threatening to distribute an intimate video recording of the victim engaging in sexual intercourse under s 377BE(2) punishable under s 377BE(3) PC.

(d)     One count of possession of a truncheon under s 22A(2) of the Miscellaneous Act 1906 (“MOA”).

(e)     One count of using insulting behaviour on the victim by making him kneel in a compromising position to apologise under s 3(1)(a) punishable under s 3(2) of the Protection from Harassment Act 2014 (“POHA”).

(f)     One count of providing the internet banking user ID and password for his UOB account to one Lennard Lee resulting in multiple unauthorised transactions punishable under s 3(1)(a) read with s 12(1) of the Computer Misuse Act 1993 (“CMA”) and punishable under s 50T(1)(a) PA.

The facts

6       The salient facts as extracted from the statement of facts were –

Introduction:

a.    From 24 May 2023 to 20 March 2025, the accused was subject to a remission order.

The CDSA charge:

b.    On 9 March 2024, the accused opened an account with UOB bearing account number XXXXXXX774.

c.    Sometime on or before 9 March 2024, one Lennard Lee, whom the accused claimed was his secondary school classmate, purportedly asked to ‘borrow’ the accused’s bank account as Lennard resided overseas in Thailand and did not have a Singapore bank account. The accused agreed and sent the UOB account’s internet banking user ID and password to Lennard via WhatsApp message. The accused did not take any steps to ascertain Lennard’s true purpose of being able to operate the UOB account.

d.    After the accused had relinquished control of the UOB account, he did not carry out any transactions. However, from 9 March 2024 to 22 March 2024, a total of S$424,058.61 flowed through the UOB account. A sum of S$292,887.70 was traced to scam proceeds. The victims included an elderly victim aged 77 years old who transferred an unascertained amount to the UOB account.

The LT1 consumption charge and the enhanced possession charge:

e.    On 22 January 2025, at about 8.30 am, police officers searched the car which the accused and his girlfriend were in. They seized various drug taking paraphernalia, empty ziplock bags and two packets containing crystalline substances. The latter were analysed and found to contain not less than 0.94 grams of methamphetamine. The accused admitted that the methamphetamine belonged to him and was for his own consumption.

f.    The accused’s urine sample was also tested and found to contain methamphetamine. The accused admitted that he had consumed “ice”, the street name for methamphetamine, the night before his arrest.

The offensive weapon charge:

g.    The police also seized a knuckleduster from the car. The accused admitted that he had bought the said item from a Telegram group for about S$200. A knuckleduster was a scheduled weapon under the Second Schedule to the Corrosive and Explosive Substances and Offensive Weapons Act 1958. The accused had it in his possession without any lawful purpose.

h.    After his arrest on 22 January 2025, the accused underwent medical examination/observation at the Drug Rehabilitation Centre (“DRC”) on 23 January 2025. He was discharged on 28 January 2025 whereupon he was directed by the Central Narcotics Bureau (“CNB”) to attend at Tanglin Police Division on 4 February 2025 at 11.00 am. However, the accused absconded failed to do so. On 24 February 2025, a warrant for the accused’s attendance at Tanglin Police Division on 13 March 2025 at 11.00 am, was issued. Again, the accused failed to do so. On 2 April 2025 at about 11.05pm, the accused was arrested and taken into custody. He was produced in Court on 4 April 2025 and has been held in remand since.

Antecedents

7       On 20 December 2011, the accused was placed on 24 months’ probation for committing theft in dwelling and extortion. On 13 January 2014, he re-offended by committing another extortion offence. His probation order was revoked and he was sentenced to undergo Reformative Training.

8       On 25 October 2017, he was put on 12 months’ SAF detention for consumption and possession of methamphetamine charges.

9       On 3 July 2020, he was sentenced to a total of five years’ and six months’ imprisonment and fined $3000 for consumption and possession of methamphetamine and for unlawful possession of a scheduled weapon. Multiple charges of methamphetamine consumption and possession, possession of drug-taking utensils and failure to report for urine tests, and unlawful possession of a scheduled weapon, were taken into consideration.

The sentence

Prosecution’s sentencing submissions

10     The prosecution sought the following sentences –

Charge

Offence

Prosecution’s Proposed Sentences

Defence’s Proposed Sentences

921201-2025

CDSA

7 to 8 months and enhanced sentence (ES) 75 days

(consecutive)

6 months and ES 56 days

(consecutive)

906016-2025

LT1 consumption

5 years and 3 strokes and ES 29 days

(consecutive)

5 years and 3 strokes and ES 12 days

(consecutive)

908319-2025

Enhanced possession

2 years and ES 29 days

(concurrent)

2 years and ES 12 days

(concurrent)

918509-2025

Possession of knuckleduster

6 months and 6 strokes and ES 9 days

(consecutive)

6 months and 6 strokes and ES 6 days

Total sentence

6 years 1 month to 6 years 6 months and 9 strokes and ES 142 days

5 years 12 months and 9 strokes and ES 88 days



The LT1 consumption and enhanced possession charges

11     In so far as these two charges were concerned, the facts surrounding the commission of these offences did not warrant any uplift from the mandatory minimum sentences prescribed for these offences. As such, for the LT1 consumption charge, I imposed a sentence of five years’ imprisonment and three strokes of the cane. For the enhanced possession charge, I imposed a sentence of two years imprisonment.

12     On the issue of the enhanced sentences (ES), the defence submitted that for the LT1 consumption and enhanced possession charges, the accused was at the tail-end of the remission period, therefore the ES should be calibrated at 20% of the remaining remission period (RRP) of 58 days each, thereby putting the ES at 12 days each. I respectfully disagreed. For both these charges, they fell into Band 2 of the framework in Abdul Mutalib bin Aziman v PP and other appeals [2021] 4 SLR 1220 (“Abdul Mutalib bin Aziman”). These offences were serious offences, and they were similar to the offences for which he was granted remission. Also, he had re-offended within one and half years after his conditional release. This showed that there was a lack of commitment towards rehabilitation and reintegration. As such, I agreed with the prosecution that an ES sentence calibrated at 50% of the RRP of 58 days was appropriate. This would put the ES at 29 days each.

The CDSA offence

13     Applying the SAP guidelines for scam-related offences, the starting point for the offence was at six months’ imprisonment. A total of S$424,058.61 had flowed through the account in question. This represented a significantly high amount which warranted an uplift of 3 months. Further, one of the scam victims was a vulnerable person which warranted a further uplift of one month. This placed the sentence at 10 months’ imprisonment. After factoring the 30% sentencing discount for his early plea of guilty, the final sentence imposed was seven months’ imprisonment. The defence’s submission for six months’ imprisonment was inappropriate as it did not address the uplifts that were warranted.

14     With regard to the ES, I noted that the offence was not similar to the offences in respect of which he was granted remission. And it was committed almost a year after his release. Under these circumstances, I agreed with the prosecution that the case fell into Band 1 of the framework in Abdul Mutalib bin Aziman, and therefore an ES of 20% of the RRP of 377 days was appropriate, putting the ES at 75 days.

The offensive weapon offence

15     The circumstances of the offence did not warrant any uplift or downward revision from the usual benchmark for such offences. As such, I impose the sentence of six months’ imprisonment and six strokes of the cane. I noted that the sentence had taken into account the sentencing discount of 30%: PP v Teo Kok Wah [2022] SGDC 136 at [22]).

16     With regard to the ES, the offence was not similar to the offences in respect of which he was granted remission. Under the circumstances, I agreed with the prosecution that the case fell into Band 1 of Abdul Mutalib bin Aziman framework. The appropriate calibration should be in the region of 15% of the RRP of 58 days which put the ES at 9 days.

Consecutive/concurrent sentences

17     I disagree with both the prosecution’s and the defence’s submissions that the imprisonment sentences in the LT1 consumption charge, the CDSA charge and the offensive weapon charge, should run consecutively.

18     The accused had not just re-offended when he was under a conditional remission which ended on 20 March 2025. He continued with his offending behaviour after that date. On 26 March 2025, he committed another series of offences which included two counts of robbery under s 392 PC involving one victim, threatening to distribute an intimate recording of the same robbery victim engaging in sexual intercourse under s 377BE(2) PC, using insulting words on the same victim under s 3(1)(a) POHA, and unlawful possession of a truncheon under s 22A(2) MOA. Overall, the level of criminality demonstrated by him was very high and this should be reflected in the overall sentence. As such, I ordered the sentences in the LT1 consumption charge, the enhanced possession charge and the CDSA charge to run consecutively. The total aggregate sentence was therefore seven years’ and seven months’ imprisonment and an ES of 142 days’ imprisonment.

19     The imprisonment sentence is backdated to the date of his arrest, 22 January 2025, to take into account the periods he was in custody and/or remand, and to exclude the period he was on bail. He was on bail from 28 January 2025 to 2 April 2025. I noted that after the arrest, the Accused was directed to undergo medical examination at the Drug Rehabilitation Centre (DRC) from 23 January 2025 to 28 January 2025. As the admission into DRC was in relation to the arrest for the proceeded drug charges before me, I was of the view that this period should be taken into account as the period he was in custody/remand for the purpose of computing his earliest date of release.

Conclusion

20     The Accused has lodged an appeal against sentence. He is presently serving sentence.
