html:
Public Prosecutor v Teo Soon Piak

Public Prosecutor v Teo Soon Piak
[2026] SGDC 225

Case Number:Summons No 259025197611-1, Magistrate's Appeal No 9140-2026-01
Decision Date:13 July 2026
Tribunal/Court:District Court
Coram: Cheng Yuxi
Counsel Name(s): Lee Yan Yi (Traffic Police) for the Public Prosecutor; Chua Jun Qian and Tham Kok Leong (Tactica Law) for the accused.
Parties: Public Prosecutor — Teo Soon Piak

Criminal Procedure and Sentencing – Sentencing – Road Traffic Act – Dangerous driving – Failure to conform to red light signal – Disqualification order

[LawNet Editorial Note: An appeal to this decision has been filed in MA 9140/2026/01.]

13 July 2026

District Judge Cheng Yuxi:

Introduction

1       Driving is an “inherently dangerous activity”. The licence to drive is a “privilege accorded to persons who have demonstrated…that they are capable of meeting the standards expected of a reasonably competent driver”. A disqualification order thus “serves to remove the privilege to drive from those who have abused it, and…reinforces the notion of shared usage of the roads”: Kwan Weiguang v Public Prosecutor [2022] 5 SLR 766 (“Kwan Weiguang”) at [61]. Where a driver fails to obey even the most basic of traffic rules – stopping at a red light signal – and causes injury to two other road users as a result, such a privilege should be taken away from him.

2       In the present case, the accused, Teo Soon Piak, was charged as follows:

You…are charged that you, on the 31st day of January 2025, at about 2 pm, did drive motorcar… at the signalized cross junction of Buangkok Drive, Hougang Avenue 10, and Punggol Road, Singapore, on a road, in a manner which was dangerous to the public, having regard to all the circumstances of the case, including the nature, condition and use of the road, and the amount of traffic which was actually at the time on the road, to wit, by failing to conform to the traffic red light signal while travelling straight across the signalized junction of Buangkok Drive and resulted in a collision with motor taxi…which was travelling straight from your left to right side on traffic green light signal, and hurt was caused to one Lim Kian Yew, male, 24 years old, and one Lim Seng Chew, male, 64 years old, by such driving, you have thereby committed an offence under Section 64(1) punishable under Section 64(2B)(a) of Road Traffic Act 1961 (“RTA”).

3       The accused pleaded guilty to the proceeded charge.

4       After considering parties’ submissions, I sentenced the accused to a fine of $4,000 and a disqualification from all classes of driving licences (“DQAC”) for a period of 15 months with effect from 12 June 2026, the date of sentence.

5       The Defence filed an appeal against the sentence imposed. At the time of the appeal, the accused had already paid the fine in full. The Defence confirmed that the appeal was only against the DQAC imposed. On the Defence’s application, I granted a stay of execution on the order of disqualification.

6       These are the full reasons for my decision.

Facts

7       The following facts are taken from the Statement of Facts, which the accused admitted to without qualification.

8       The accused was the driver of his motorcar at the time of accident.

9       The first victim was Lim Seng Chew, male, 65 years old. He was the driver of his motor taxi at the time of accident.

10     The second victim was one Lim Kian Yew, male, 25 years old. He was the rear passenger of the taxi at the time of accident.

11     On 31 January 2025, at about 2pm, the accused was driving his car at the signalised cross junction of Buangkok Drive, Hougang Avenue 10, and Punggol Road, Singapore, in a manner which was dangerous to the public, having regard to all the circumstances of the case, including the nature, condition and use of the road, and the amount of traffic which was actually at the time on the road, by failing to conform to the traffic red light signal while travelling straight across the signalised junction of Buangkok Drive. This resulted in a collision with the first victim’s taxi, which was travelling straight from the accused’s left to right side on a traffic green light signal. Hurt was caused to the first victim and the second victim by the accused’s driving.

12     The first victim’s in-vehicle camera footage revealed that the traffic light signal was already showing red in the accused’s direction (at timestamp 13:57:18). The first victim’s vehicle subsequently proceeded to travel straight into the junction after the traffic light signal in his direction turned green. The accused’s car was seen travelling from the first victim’s right side (at timestamp 13:57:45). The front-left corner of the accused’s car collided into the front-right corner of the first victim’s taxi.

13     Due to the collision, the accused’s car sustained scratches on its front-left corner, and the first victim’s taxi sustained scratches on its front-right corner.

14     On 1 February 2025, the first victim and the second victim sought medical treatment at Our Family Physician Clinic & Surgery, where they were each granted medical leave for three days from 1 February 2025 to 3 February 2025. The first victim reported that he sustained pain in his shoulder and neck. The second victim reported that he sustained slight pain in his neck.

15     At the time of the accident, the weather was clear, the road surface was dry, the visibility was clear, and the traffic condition was moderate.

16     The accused had thereby committed an offence of dangerous driving causing hurt under Section 64(1) punishable under Section 64(2B)(a) of the RTA.

Relevant provisions

17     The relevant provisions of the RTA at the time of the offence read as follows:

Reckless or dangerous driving

64.—(1)    If any person drives a motor vehicle on a road recklessly, or at a speed or in a manner which is dangerous to the public, having regard to all the circumstances of the case, including the nature, condition and use of the road, and the amount of traffic which is actually at the time, or which might reasonably be expected to be, on the road, the person (called the offender) shall be guilty of an offence…

(2B)  If hurt is caused to another person by the driving of a motor vehicle by the offender, the offender shall on conviction of an offence under subsection (1) —

(a)    be liable to a fine not exceeding $10,000 or to imprisonment for a term not exceeding 2 years or to both…

Disqualification for offences

42.—(1)    Where a person (called in this section the offender) is convicted of —

(a)    an offence under this Act or any other written law in connection with the driving of a motor vehicle…

the court may, in addition to imposing on the offender the punishment provided for such offence, make an order disqualifying the offender from holding or obtaining a driving licence for life or for any period that the court thinks fit.

Antecedents

18     The accused had dated traffic antecedents, including compounded offences for inconsiderate driving on 14 August 2001 and speeding on 24 February 2019.

Parties’ submissions on sentence

19     The Prosecution submitted that a fine of $4,000 to $5,000 and a DQAC of 18 to 24 months should be imposed.[note: 1] The Prosecution argued that the accused’s culpability was low, as the only factor was that he failed to conform to a red light signal which had been red in his direction for a significant period. Harm was caused to two victims who sustained injuries. Each received three days of medical leave. The first victim’s taxi also sustained damage, although no repair was required.[note: 2]

20     In mitigation, the Defence argued that this was not a case involving excessive speed, racing, aggressive driving, intoxication, mobile phone usage, or any deliberate flouting of traffic rules. Instead, the accused immediately applied his brakes when he noticed the taxi, in an attempt to avoid the collision, but was unable to do so. The collision resulted in relatively minor vehicle damage and the victims suffered minor injuries. This case thus fell within the lower end of the spectrum of dangerous driving causing hurt cases.[note: 3]

21     The Defence urged the court not to impose a DQAC against the accused. This was because the accused operated a speciality lubricants business on his own, which required him to travel to various locations to meet his clients. He could not afford to hire another driver if his license were suspended. A DQAC would severely impair or destroy his livelihood, as he was the primary breadwinner of the family. The Defence stated that the accused was willing to pay a fine at the higher end of the Prosecution’s sentencing submissions ($5,000), without any disqualification order.[note: 4]

22     The Defence also highlighted the accused’s remorse, cooperation with the authorities, and clean driving history of over 40 years without being convicted in a traffic court.[note: 5]

23     In response, the Prosecution pointed out that it was inaccurate to characterise the accused’s driving record as unblemished, as he did have some dated traffic antecedents. The Prosecution also highlighted that in a case of failing to conform to a red light signal, a DQAC of 12 months would be the general starting point. In the present case, there was the additional aggravating factor of personal injury caused to two victims.[note: 6]

Decision on sentence

24     In determining the appropriate sentence, I considered the harm caused and the culpability of the accused.

25     In terms of actual harm, the two victims fortunately suffered relatively minor injuries. The first victim stated that he sustained pain in his shoulder and neck. The second victim reported that he sustained slight pain in his neck. Each of them was given three days of medical leave. The right-front corner of the first victim’s motor taxi sustained scratches Furthermore, given that the traffic volume was moderate, there was some degree of potential harm to other road users. The in-vehicle camera footage showed that other cars travelling in the same direction as the first victim had also begun to enter the junction. This was especially because the traffic light had been red for some time before the accused proceeded across the junction.

26     In terms of culpability, the fact that the accused had failed to conform to the traffic light signal was an element of the offence of dangerous driving and I did not separately regard this as an aggravating factor. There were no other culpability-enhancing factors.

Fine

27     Parties were aligned as to the fine to be imposed. In my view, a fine of $4,000 was appropriate in light of the harm and culpability factors. This was lower than what the Defence had sought. The accused had also paid the fine imposed. The Defence confirmed that the appeal was only in relation to the 15-month DQAC,[note: 7] which I will now address.

Disqualification order

28     For an offence punishable under s 64(2B)(a) of the RTA, there was no mandatory minimum period of disqualification. The Court could nonetheless impose a DQAC pursuant to s 42(1) of the RTA as the accused had been convicted of an offence under the RTA in connection with the driving of a motor vehicle.

29     In Kwan Weiguang at [59], the High Court opined that a disqualification order served three sentencing objectives: punishment, protection of the public by removing a dangerous driver from the roads and deterrence. For first-time traffic offenders with a clean driving record (especially those without any history of compoundable offences or speeding tickets), the disqualification period should be set at 12 months or below. This was assuming that the degree of potential harm posed to other road users was relatively low. However, the Court should also consider relevant circumstances of the commission of the offence, including driving when the traffic volume was heavy, driving within residential or school zones, driving a heavy vehicle, etc. The extent of any property damage caused and the potential harm that could have resulted from the act of dangerous or reckless driving would also be relevant: Kwan Weiguang at [56] and [66]-[67].

30     Having considered the fact that the accused was convicted of an offence of dangerous driving, specifically, failure to conform to a red light signal, and the circumstances of the present case, I was of the view that a disqualification order should be imposed in this case. This was to remove the privilege of the accused’s continued use of the roads and to protect the public. Driving is an inherently communal activity in addition to being an inherently dangerous one. Stopping at a red light signal is one of the most basic traffic rules that all drivers are expected to obey. This is especially so when a red light governs the safe and effective flow of traffic at junctions where vehicles were moving in different directions. Drivers are entitled to expect that this fundamental traffic rule would be followed by other road users. A driver who drives dangerously (such as by beating the red light signal) places other road users at immediate risk of hurt and property damage: see Seah Ming Yang Daryle v Public Prosecutor [2024] 4 SLR 1561 at [1].

31     As to the period of disqualification, in my view, a DQAC of 15 months was fair and appropriate in the present circumstances, for the following reasons:

(a)     Actual harm was caused to not one, but two victims who were both injured. There was property damage caused to the first victim’s taxi. There was also potential harm given that the traffic flow was moderate, and multiple cars in the first victim’s direction had already begun entering the junction where the accused failed to conform to the red light signal.

(b)     The accused could not be considered to have a clean driving record, as he did have a history of compounded offences for (among others) inconsiderate driving and speeding.

(c)     An order for disqualification of 12 months had already been imposed in other cases where the offender failed to conform to a red light signal, even where the accused had a clean driving record, traffic flow was light and no injuries were caused to any person: see for example, Public Prosecutor v Shahram Jowkar [2024] SGDC 166 (upheld on appeal). A higher period of disqualification was justified in the present case, given the factors in (a) and (b) above.

(d)     The Defence’s argument that the accused should be allowed to pay a higher fine ($5,000) in exchange for no order of disqualification was fundamentally flawed. In Kwan Weiguang at [73] and [74], the High Court made clear that there was no necessary link between the period of disqualification and fine and/or imprisonment sentence imposed. The Court should calibrate the disqualification order separately. This was because the disqualification order was concerned with a different set of objectives, and took effect above and beyond the primary punishment. A sufficiently long disqualification order might need to be imposed to send a strong signal even if there was low harm (as reflected in the lower primary punishment). Consequently, disqualification orders were also not meant to be inversely proportional to the primary sentence imposed. When deciding on the appropriate period of disqualification, the disqualification order and the fine imposed would not be mutually compensatory. In other words, an increase in the punishment imposed (such as a fine) should not be taken to mandate the imposition of a reduced period of disqualification than would otherwise have been ordered. It would be unprincipled to discount the period of disqualification in such a manner.

(e)     It was well-established that the impact of a sentence such as a disqualification order on the accused’s livelihood and financial circumstances would not be a relevant mitigating factor save in very exceptional or extreme circumstances: Lai Oei Mui Jenny v Public Prosecutor [1993] 2 SLR(R) 406 at [10]. No exceptional circumstances were present on the facts of this case.

Conclusion

32     For the above reasons, I sentenced the accused to a fine of $4,000 and a DQAC for 15 months, which were in my view fair and reasonable. On the application of the Defence, I granted a stay of execution on the DQAC. The accused had already paid the fine imposed.

[note: 2]NEs (12 June 2026) p 3 lines 14-23.

[note: 4]NEs (12 June 2026) p 5 lines 5-9.

html:
Public Prosecutor v Tan Kim Song Michael

Public Prosecutor v Tan Kim Song Michael
[2026] SGDC 224

Case Number:District Arrest Case No 902828 of 2024 & 4 Others
Decision Date:10 July 2026
Tribunal/Court:District Court
Coram: Paul Quan
Counsel Name(s): Jonathan Tan/Ashley Chin (Attorney-General's Chambers) for the Public Prosecutor; Manoj Nandwani/Sameer Melber (Gabriel Law Corporation)/Ling Ying Hong, Samuel (LVM Law Chambers LLC) for the Accused.
Parties: Public Prosecutor — Tan Kim Song Michael

Criminal Law – Offences – Documents – Falsification of paper

Criminal Law – Statutory Offences – Prevention of Corruption Act – Corruptly giving gratification to agent as inducement

Criminal Procedure and Sentencing – Sentencing

10 July 2026

Judgment reserved.

District Judge Paul Quan:

Introduction

1       This is a case of a senior company officer who abetted a falsification offence by conspiring with a fellow senior officer to falsify an entertainment claim to defraud the company.

Brief facts

2       At the time of the offence in December 2016, the accused, Tan Kim Song Michael (“Dr Tan”), a 52-year-old Singaporean, was a director and group chief executive officer (“CEO”) of Fullerton Healthcare Corporation Limited (“FHC”). He conspired with Chan Pai Sheng, Daniel (“Dr Chan”), who was a fellow director and also deputy group CEO at the time, to falsify an entertainment claim to seek disbursement for an inflated entertainment expense from FHC, so as to provide financial assistance to a third-party individual, Chiew Collin (“Mr Chiew”). Dr Tan and Sin David (“Mr Sin”) approved the claim that Dr Chan submitted, knowing that it was false and done wilfully and with intent to defraud FHC.

3       At the time, Mr Sin was also a fellow FHC director and chairman/deputy chairman of FHC’s board of directors and later FHC’s president. He was CEO of Sin Capital Group Private Limited (“Sin Capital”) as well. Sin Capital became FHC’s major shareholder when Mr Sin decided to invest in FHC through Sin Capital after Dr Tan and Dr Chan approached him to be an investor. With other investors, Mr Sin incorporated FHC as a holding company to buy over Fullerton Healthcare Group Pte Ltd (“FHG”) co-founded by Dr Tan and Dr Chan. FHG functioned as FHC’s subsidiary in Singapore. FHC expanded its business in China through Fullerton Health China Limited (“FHCL”). Dr Chan was also FHCL’s president and Mr Sin its chairman. Tei Chu Pink (“Mr Tei”), the director of Sin Capital’s investment team, was seconded to FHCL as its head of mergers and acquisitions (“M&A”).

4       Separately, Dr Tan also allegedly abetted corruption offences by conspiring with Dr Chan and Mr Sin, to corruptly give gratification to Mr Chiew, who was the CEO of Aon Singapore Private Limited (“Aon Singapore”), to induce him to advance FHG’s business interests with Aon Singapore. In 2014, FHC was contracted as the third-party administrator of Aon Care, which was Aon Singapore’s employee health and well-being management product, where six insurance companies agreed to use FHC as the healthcare service provider. The contract was renewable every five years.

Charges

5       Dr Tan faces a single charge of abetting by conspiracy an offence of falsification under section 477A of the Penal Code (Cap 224, 2008 Rev Ed) (“PC”) and four charges of abetting by conspiracy offences of corruptly giving gratification as an inducement to an agent under section 6(b) of the Prevention of Corruption Act (Cap 241, 1993 Rev Ed) (“PCA”).

6       Dr Tan pleaded guilty to the falsification charge at the last mention on 8 July 2026. I convicted him and reserved my judgment on sentence.

Discharge not amounting to acquittal granted on PCA charges

7       At the end of the last mention, in exercise of its prosecutorial discretion as part of a plea offer to Dr Tan that he accepted, the prosecution applied for a discharge not amounting to an acquittal (“DNATA”) under section 232(1) of Criminal Procedure Code 2010 (2020 Rev Ed) (“CPC”) on all four of his PCA charges, District Arrest Case Nos (“DAC”) 902839-42 of 2024.

8       The prosecution submitted that the presumptive position of a DNATA under section 232(2) CPC is not displaced in this case. There is no prejudice to Dr Tan because the prosecution confirmed that there is evidential basis for the PCA charges to be brought and maintained against him, but that the prosecution is declining to prosecute him on these charges at this stage. There is also some element of finality as the prosecution undertook to review its position at the conclusion of Mr Chiew’s trial.

9       In deciding whether I should exercise my discretion to grant a discharge amounting to an acquittal (“DATA”) instead, I am cognisant that there is an initial presumption in favour of granting a DNATA which an accused person must show sufficient reasons to displace: Ahmad Danial bin Mohamed Rafa’ee v PP [2023] 5 SLR 824 (“Danial”) at [25]. The defence did not contest the prosecution’s application. I must still decide the matter on the merits, balancing the public interest and the rights of the accused person: Danial at [25].

10     I am satisfied that I should not exercise my discretion to grant a DATA because there is no prejudice to Dr Tan outweighing the public interest in ensuring that a suspect is not cleared of an offence without trial: Danial at [33], on the basis of:

(a)     the prosecution’s confirmation, the upshot of which is that there is reason to believe that Dr Tan is in some way involved in the offences that are the subject matter of his PCA charges and there are grounds to bring the charges against Dr Tan: Danial at [28], [33], [42(b)]. I am not required to make an objective assessment of the evidential basis for these charges that the prosecution spoke of: Danial at [42(d)]; and

(b)     the prosecution’s undertaking to review its position at the conclusion of Mr Chiew’s trial, which means that Dr Tan will not be subject to the indefinite apprehension of potential criminal proceedings because the prosecution is simply hitting a finite pause in the proceedings: Danial at [30] and [42(a)].

11     I therefore now grant a DNATA on Dr Tan’s four PCA charges.

Prescribed punishment

12     For a falsification offence under section 477A PC, Dr Tan must be imprisoned for a term that may extend to ten years and/or fined. The maximum fine that a district court can impose is S$30,000: section 303(2)(b) CPC.

Parties’ sentencing positions

13     Dr Tan is a first-time offender.

Prosecution’s sentencing position: fine of S$30,000

14     The prosecution has submitted that the custodial threshold has not been crossed in Dr Tan’s case. It sought the maximum fine of S$30,000 to be imposed on him on the basis of the parity principle, given that it sought the same sentence on Dr Chan’s mirror charge (PP v Chan Pai Sheng, Daniel [2026] SGDC 223 (“Daniel Chan”)), and this was also a significant downward adjustment to Mr Sin’s global fine of S$160,000 (PP v Sin David [2025] SGDC 218) to account for the shorter period of offending and the significantly lower falsified amount involved in Dr Tan’s case.

15     In calibrating its proposed sentence, the prosecution has considered the substantial amount involved in the falsification; the crucial role Dr Tan played in approving the inflated claim; the abuse of trust reposed in him as FHC’s director and group CEO by approving the inflated claim; the absence of personal gain; and his guilty plea.

Defence’s sentencing position: fine of $5,000

16     The defence also submitted that the custodial threshold has not been crossed. It sought a fine of $5,000 to be imposed on Dr Tan instead on the basis of the significantly lower amount involved; Dr Tan’s single charge; the absence of personal enrichment; Dr Tan’s plea of guilt and cooperation; his otherwise exemplary personal circumstances and longstanding charitable contributions; and the need to maintain proportionality while giving full effect to general deterrence and retribution. As compared to Sin David that involved six charges, an aggregate falsified sum exceeding S$213,000, repeat offending for almost a year, abuse of a senior approving position, and coordinated offending involving multiple false claims, Dr Tan’s case merits a markedly lower financial penalty according to the defence.

Court’s decision

17     Applying the parity principle in respect of the fine of S$25,000 I have imposed in Daniel Chan on Dr Chan’s mirror charge and the aggregate fine of $160,000 imposed in Sin David, I agree with the parties that the custodial threshold has not been crossed in Dr Tan’s case. Having reserved my judgment on sentence at the last mention on 8 July 2026, I now impose a fine of S$25,000 on Dr Tan on his single falsification charge.

18     I set out the reasons for my decision.

Deterrence and retribution as operative sentencing principles

19     The deterrent considerations for group offences in criminal conspiracies and harsher punishment premised on the difficulty in detection of financial crimes that I articulated in Sin David at [15] apply equally in Dr Tan’s case. The gravamen in his case was that as co-founders of FHC, he, Dr Chan and Mr Sin could approve claims for business expenses without obtaining any approval from their finance teams. As a matter of practice, Dr Tan and/or Mr Sin approved Dr Chan’s claims. Because the trio were members of a group that effectively checked itself, their nefarious activities were difficult to detect: Sin David at [16].

20     Dr Tan can still be specifically deterred even if he did not commit the offence for personal gain because he is capable of rational thought: Sin David at [16]. He knew that the entertainment expense claim was inflated and was to be paid by FHC to provide financial assistance to Mr Chew. Yet he proceeded to approve the claim.

21     Deterrent sentencing must not, however, be disproportionate and is to be suitably tampered by retributive concerns that relate to the gravity of the offence and the culpability of the offender: Sin David at [17].

Harm caused by Dr Tan’s offence

22     The amount of money involved is a relevant sentencing factor for falsification offences that cause a wrongful disbursement of funds: Sin David at [19]; see also Tan Puay Boon v PP [2003] 3 SLR(R) 390 (“Tan”) at [50].

Claim sum and falsified amount not insubstantial

23     In Dr Tan’s case, the purported entertainment expense claimed was S$82,476.81, nearly twice the actual expense of S$42,512.79. The falsified amount was S$39,964.02, which was wrongly disbursed to Dr Chan. Both values are not insubstantial.

Dr Tan’s culpability

24     I assess Dr Tan’s culpability by considering his motive for offending; the scale of the falsification; the manner and level of planning, premeditation and sophistication of the falsification; and the extent of his abuse of trust: Sin David at [21].

Motive

25     In Dr Tan’s case, he was driven to approve Dr Chan’s false claim so that Dr Chan could provide financial assistance to Mr Chiew on the pretext of incurring an entertainment expense that had in fact been inflated. Prior to the offence, sometime in 2015, Mr Chiew had asked Dr Chan for financial assistance for his children and house. Dr Chan then informed Dr Tan of Mr Chiew’s request. The wrongful disbursement was paid to Mr Chiew. The falsification was therefore not committed for personal gain: Tan at [47].

Scale of falsification

26     The falsification offence was a one-off occurrence where Dr Tan had approved one false entertainment expenses claim that was inflated on one occasion on 7 December 2016.

Manner and level of planning, premeditation and sophistication of falsification

27     It is aggravating that Dr Tan had acted in conspiracy with Dr Chan; premeditation features in the group offence of criminal conspiracy: Sin David at [24]. In this case, Dr Chan would get hold of receipts that Mr Tei would arrange from KTVs in Hong Kong where Dr Chan met various potential investors bi-monthly to help with FHC’s Hong Kong business. After getting these receipts, he would submit them to FHC to claim for the KTV expenses incurred. With Dr Tan’s knowledge, Dr Chan submitted inflated claims to obtain monies from FHC to provide financial assistance to Mr Chiew.

28     In the case of a conspiracy, the offender’s role in the conspiracy is a relevant sentencing factor: Sin David at [26]. Rather than personally devising or implementing an elaborate scheme, the defence characterised Dr Tan’s role as a failure to discharge his executive responsibility because his responsibilities were directed towards the operational management of the group as it expanded into an increasingly sophisticated corporate structure. I agree with the prosecution that Dr Tan played a crucial role in the conspiracy in approving the false claim when he knew that it was inflated and it was for the purpose of providing financial assistance to Mr Chiew. Indeed, he, Dr Chan, and Mr Sin played their respective roles – Dr Chan was to submit the inflated receipt to support the inflated claim and Dr Tan and Mr Sin were to approve it – they were similarly culpable in bringing the scheme into fruition in that regard.

Abuse of trust

29     Dr Tan had abused the trust reposed in him as FHC’s director and group CEO by approving Dr Chan’s inflated claim in that capacity. The falsification offence was more serious as it was committee by a senior officer: Sin David at [28]. Not only that, Dr Tan was also a fellow co-founder with Dr Chan and Mr Sin who could approve business expenses claims without obtaining any approval from their finance teams. Yet he took advantage of the very approval process which he was entrusted to gatekeep by a deliberate and adject dereliction of his duty to check against his fellow co-founders in precisely such an instance: Sin David at [28].

Personal aggravating and mitigating factors

30     Leaving the harm-culpability analysis, I turn to consider the aggravating and mitigating factors personal to Dr Chan that present themselves in his case.

No personal aggravating factors

31     There are no personal aggravating factors in this case.

Absence of criminal antecedents neutral factor

32     Mr Sin is a first-time offender. But the absence of criminal antecedents is at best a neutral factor; it is an absent aggravating factor, not a mitigating factor: BPH v PP [2019] 2 SLR 764 at [85]. The defence sought to persuade me that this one-off occasion of offending was an aberration and out of character for him: PP v BWJ [2023] 1 SLR 477 at [102]. His charitable works and professional contributions, though commendable, do not provide any relevant baseline insight into Dr Tan as a professional and how the departure by his remiss conduct on this occasion should be regarded: see eg PP v Xie Jianfeng [2026] SGDC 173 at [46].

Guilty plea

33     Like Dr Chan and Mr Sin, Dr Tan too has pleaded guilty after the prosecution extended a revised plea offer that involved applying for a DNATA on his PCA charges at this stage of the proceedings. I have also taken this into account in sentencing.

Application of parity principle

34     I agree with the parties that the parity principle applies and I should have regard to the sentences passed in Daniel Chan and Sin David:

(a)     the sentence in Daniel Chan imposed on a mirror charge is a par excellence situation where co-offenders are charged with the same offence arising from the same transaction or events but are dealt with in separate criminal proceedings: PP v Ng Sae Kiat [2015] SGHC 191 (“Ng”) at [74],

(b)     that mirror charge was withdrawn in Sin David. Be that as it may, parity should not only apply to cases where the co-offenders were involved in the same transaction and they are charged for the same offence: Ng at [75]. Formal identity of charges against the offenders whose sentences are compared is not a necessary condition: Ng at [76], and

(c)     the principle can apply for the purposes of sentencing offenders who, as a matter of substance, can be said to be participants in a common criminal enterprise: Ng at [78]. The fact that Dr Chan submitted the inflated receipt to support the inflated claim which Dr Tan and Mr Sin subsequently approved is sufficient to make the trio participants in a common criminal enterprise with their guilty knowledge.

35     It is not the law that every co-offender in a common criminal enterprise must be identically charged or sentenced: Chong Han Rui v PP [2016] SGHC 25 (“Chong”) at [52]. The principle of parity in sentencing between co-offenders urges that sentences meted out to co-offenders who are party to a common criminal enterprise should not be unduly disparate from each other: those of similar culpability should receive similar sentences, while those of greater culpability should generally be more severely punished: Chong at [1].

Dr Tan, Dr Chan and Mr Sin’s culpabilities similar in common criminal enterprise

36     In this case, Dr Tan, Dr Chan and Mr Sin each played their respective roles in the common criminal enterprise. Dr Tan knew that Dr Chan’s claim was inflated and approved it as FHC’s director and group CEO. So did Mr Sin in his executive position. Dr Tan’s approval was essential for the claim to go through as was Mr Sin’s, which was in turn wholly dependent on Dr Chan submitting the inflated receipt to support the inflated claim in the first place. All of their roles were essential and critical. Their culpabilities in the common criminal enterprise were therefore similar.

37     Dr Chan was fined S$30,000 on a mirror charge, whereas Mr Sin was fined an aggregate of S$160,000 on six similar falsification charges. The defence made the point that Dr Tan’s fine should be markedly lower because the overall harm in Sin David was materially greater. Essentially, Dr Tan and Mr Sin are equally placed in terms of culpability – they did the same wrong by approving a claim they knew was inflated. Mr Sin might have approved more claims and over a longer period of time but this is already reflected in the substantially heavier fines imposed on him: Ng at [72] and [82]. This is all the more so considering the compounding effect of multiple sentences of fine imposed that must run consecutively, along with their default terms if they are unpaid. A fine of S$5,000 that the defence sought would be unduly disparate from that imposed on Mr Sin.

38     The other point that the prosecution made about its proposed fine of S$30,000 being more proportionate also has some persuasive force. That fine quantum is 18.75% of the aggregate sentence of S$160,000 imposed in Sin David, and is proportionate when compared to the falsified sum of S$39,964.02 in Dr Tan’s case being about 18.69% of the overall sum of S$213,827.65 falsified in Sin David. The defence’s proposed fine of S$5,000 would only have yielded a meagre 3%.

Sentencing precedents of Leow and Ong

39     The sentence of a high fine is consistent with two sentencing precedents cited by the prosecution, PP v Leow Ban Leong [2018] SGDC 157 (“Leow”) and PP v Ong Teck Liam [2017] SGDC 317 (“Ong”) (where the individual sentences passed were fines of S$30,000), discussed in Sin David at [34] and [35(a)].

Desperation as motive in Leow and passive inheritance of illegal practice in Ong absent in Dr Tan’s case

40     I will only add that:

(a)     the accused persons in Leow were found to have been driven by desperation and not pursuant to any sophisticated or meticulous planning when they committed three falsification offences to cover up inadvertently overcharging the government S$102,238.50. The conspiracy was not highly planned, premeditated or even moderately sophisticated: Leow at [161]; and

(b)     the accused person in Ong was a passive inheritor of an illegal practice of using cash vouchers for entertainment expenses to pay commission. She was not privy to the exact details of such payments and did not know they were bribes: Ong at [90]. Ten falsification charges were proceeded against her with 108 TIC. Her predecessor was also given an individual fine of S$30,000 on each of the seven proceeded charges with 31 TIC.

These features, namely desperation as motive and passive inheritance of an existing illegal practice, were absent in Dr Tan’s case.

41     It is also pertinent that having regard to the parity principle, the court in Ong found at [70] that role and involvement of the accused person’s predecessor in facilitating the falsification offence is exactly the same as, if not more culpable than her: Ong at [93]. Notwithstanding that she faced a higher number of charges, the court nevertheless found that imposing an individual fine of S$30,000 per charge, resulting in an aggregate fine of S$300,000, which would be S$90,000 higher than the sentence meted out to her predecessor, would be adequate: Ong at [94].

Conclusion

Fine of S$25,000 imposed

42     I therefore sentence Dr Tan to a fine of S$25,000 on his falsification charge. If he does not pay the fine, he will serve two months’ imprisonment in default.

Public Prosecutor v Chan Pai Sheng, Daniel

Public Prosecutor v Chan Pai Sheng, Daniel
[2026] SGDC 223

Case Number:District Arrest Case No 902843 of 2024 & 12 Others
Decision Date:10 July 2026
Tribunal/Court:District Court
Coram: Paul Quan
Counsel Name(s): Jonathan Tan/Ashley Chin (Attorney-General's Chambers) for the Public Prosecutor; Navin Thevar/Uday Duggal (RCLT Law Corporation) for the Accused.
Parties: Public Prosecutor — Chan Pai Sheng, Daniel

Criminal Law – Offences – Documents – Makes false entry in paper

Criminal Law – Statutory Offences – Prevention of Corruption Act – Corruptly giving gratification to agent as inducement

Criminal Procedure and Sentencing – Sentencing

10 July 2026

Judgment reserved.

District Judge Paul Quan:

Introduction

1        PP v Sin David [2025] SGDC 218 was a case of a senior company officer who abetted falsification offences by conspiring with a fellow senior officer to falsify entertainment claims to defraud the company. This is the case involving that fellow senior officer.

Brief facts

2       At the time of the offences, the accused, Chan Pai Sheng, Daniel (“Dr Chan”), a 52-year-old Singaporean, was a director and deputy group chief executive officer (“CEO”) of Fullerton Healthcare Corporation Limited (“FHC”). He was also president of Fullerton Health China Limited (“FHCL”), a subsidiary of FHC. He submitted inflated and false receipts for entertainment claims to be processed in his name to seek disbursements of inflated and fictitious entertainment expenses from FHC and FHCL, so as to provide financial assistance to a third-party individual, Chiew Collin (“Mr Chiew”) and pay for his ‘consultancy services’ to FHC.

3       Tan Kim Song Michael (“Dr Tan”), a fellow FHC director and group CEO, and Sin David (“Mr Sin”) approved the claims, knowing that they were false and submitted wilfully and with intent to defraud FHC. At the time, Mr Sin was also a fellow FHC director and chairman/deputy chairman of FHC’s board of directors and later FHC’s president. He was FHCL’s president and CEO of Sin Capital Group Private Limited (“Sin Capital”) as well. Sin Capital became FHC’s major shareholder when Mr Sin decided to invest in FHC through Sin Capital after Dr Chan and Dr Tan approached him to be an investor. With other investors, Mr Sin incorporated FHC as a holding company to buy over Fullerton Healthcare Group Pte Ltd (“FHG”) co-founded by Dr Chan and Dr Tan. FHG functioned as FHC’s subsidiary in Singapore. FHC expanded its business in China through FHCL. Tei Chu Pink (“Mr Tei”), the director of Sin Capital’s investment team, was seconded to FHCL as its head of mergers and acquisitions.

4       Separately, Dr Chan also allegedly abetted corruption offences by conspiring with Dr Tan and Mr Sin to corruptly give gratification to Mr Chiew, who was the CEO of Aon Singapore Private Limited (“Aon Singapore”), to induce him to advance FHG’s business interests with Aon Singapore. In 2014, FHC was contracted as the third-party administrator of Aon Care, which was Aon Singapore’s employee health and well-being management product, where six insurance companies agreed to use FHC as the healthcare service provider. The contract was renewable every five years.

Charges

5       Dr Chan faces eight charges of abetting an offence of falsification under section 477A of the Penal Code (Cap 224, 2008 Rev Ed) (“PC”) and five charges of abetting by conspiracy offences of corruptly giving gratification as an inducement to an agent under section 6(b) of the Prevention of Corruption Act (Cap 241, 1993 Rev Ed) (“PCA”).

6       At the last mention on 8 July 2026, he pleaded guilty to five falsification charges. He also consented to have two similar falsification charges under section 477A PC taken into consideration for the purpose of sentence (“TIC”). I convicted him and reserved my judgment on sentence.

Discharge amounting to acquittal granted on falsification charge

7       Upon his conviction and in exercise of its prosecutorial discretion as part of a plea offer to Dr Chan that he accepted, the prosecution applied for a discharge not amounting to an acquittal (“DATA”) under section 147 of the Criminal Procedure Code 2010 (2020 Rev Ed) (“CPC”) on one of the falsification charges, District Arrest Case No 902828 of 2024, at the end of the last mention.

8       I now grant a DATA on that charge in recognition of the prosecution exercising its constitutional discretionary powers.

Discharge not amounting to acquittal granted on PCA charges

9       In the same vein, the prosecution also applied for a discharge not amounting to an acquittal (“DNATA”) under section 232(1) of the Criminal Procedure Code 2010 (2020 Rev Ed) (“CPC”) on all five of his PCA charges, District Arrest Case Nos (“DAC”) 902851-55 of 2024.

10     The prosecution submitted that the presumptive position of a DNATA under section 232(2) CPC is not displaced in this case. There is no prejudice to Dr Chan because the prosecution confirmed that there is evidential basis for the PCA charges to be brought and maintained against him, but that the prosecution is declining to prosecute him on these charges at this stage. There is also some element of finality as the prosecution undertook to review its position at the conclusion of Mr Chiew’s trial.

11     In deciding whether I should exercise my discretion to grant a DATA instead, I am cognisant that there is an initial presumption in favour of granting a DNATA which an accused person must show sufficient reasons to displace: Ahmad Danial bin Mohamed Rafa’ee v PP [2023] 5 SLR 824 (“Danial”) at [25]. On the prosecution’s undertaking to review its position when Mr Chiew’s case has concluded, the defence left it to the court to decide whether the discharge should amount to an acquittal.

12     I must decide the matter on the merits, balancing the public interest and the rights of the accused person: Danial at [25]. I am satisfied that I should not exercise my discretion to grant a DATA because there is no prejudice to Dr Chan outweighing the public interest in ensuring that a suspect is not cleared of an offence without trial: Danial at [33], on the basis of:

(a)     the prosecution’s confirmation, the upshot of which is that there is reason to believe that Dr Chan is in some way involved in the offences that are the subject matter of his PCA charges and there are grounds to bring those charges against Dr Chan: Danial at [28], [33], [42(b)]. I am not required to make an objective assessment of the evidential basis for the charges that the prosecution spoke of: Danial at [42(d)]; and

(b)     the prosecution’s undertaking to review its position at the conclusion of Mr Chiew’s trial, which means that Dr Tan will not be subject to the indefinite apprehension of potential criminal proceedings because the prosecution is simply hitting a finite pause in the proceedings: Danial at [30] and [42(a)].

13     I therefore now grant a DNATA on Dr Chan’s five PCA charges.

Prescribed punishment

14     For a falsification offence under section 477A PC, Dr Chan must be imprisoned for a term that may extend to ten years and/or fined. The maximum fine that a district court can impose is S$30,000: section 303(2)(b) CPC.

17     According to the prosecution, the global fine of $140,000 to S$150,000 sought for Dr Chan (as compared to the aggregate fine of S$160,000 imposed in Sin David) is justified based on the lesser number of charges proceeded against Dr Chan as compared to Mr Sin, the comparable overall harm caused by Dr Chan’s offences, their similar culpabilities, their clean records and their guilty pleas.

18     In calibrating its proposed sentence, the prosecution considered the substantial amount involved in the falsification; the crucial role Dr Chan played in submitting the receipts for inflated and false claims to be processed in his name; the abuse of trust reposed in him as FHC’s director and deputy group CEO by such submissions in support of those claims that he knew would be approved by Dr Tan and/or Mr Sin; the absence of personal gain; the aggravating presence of two similar TIC charges; and his guilty plea.

Defence’s position: fine of no more than S$120,000

19     The defence also submitted that the custodial threshold has not been crossed and that the parity principle should apply, such that a fine that is significantly lower than the $160,000 imposed on Mr Sin, ie not more than S$120,000, should be imposed on Dr Chan because his moral culpability within the common criminal enterprise was far lower than that of Mr Sin.

20     Even if the parity principle were not applicable, the defence contended that the fine quantum should still be no more than S$120,000 on a low harm-low culpability assessment.

Court’s decision

21     Applying the parity principle and having regard to the individual and aggregate fines imposed in Sin David, I agree with the parties that the custodial threshold has not been crossed in Dr Chan’s case. Having reserved my judgment on sentence at the last mention on 8 July 2026, I now impose an aggregate fine of S$135,000 on Dr Chan.

22     I set out the reasons for my decision.

Deterrence and retribution as operative sentencing principles

23     The deterrent considerations for group offences in criminal conspiracies, and financial crimes meriting harsher punishment when they are uncovered because of the difficulty in detecting them, which I articulated in Sin David at [15] apply with equal force in Dr Chan’s case. The gravamen in his case was that as co-founders of FHC, he, Dr Tan and Mr Sin could approve claims for business expenses without obtaining any approval from their finance teams. As a matter of practice, Dr Tan and/or Mr Sin approved Dr Chan’s claims. Because the trio were members of a group that effectively checked itself, their nefarious activities were difficult to detect: Sin David at [16].

24     Dr Chan can still be specifically deterred even if he did not commit the spate of offences for personal gain because he is capable of rational thought: Sin David at [16]. He knew the receipts he had submitted were either inflated or false and therefore that the entertainment claims processed in his name using these receipts were consequently inflated or fictitious. On some occasions, he would make payments of lesser amounts (ie inflated receipts); on others, he would not make any payments (ie false receipts).

25     Deterrent sentencing must not, however, be disproportionate and is to be suitably tampered by retributive concerns that relate to the gravity of the offence and the culpability of the offender: Sin David at [17].

Harm caused by Dr Chan’s offences

26     The amount of money involved is a relevant sentencing factor for falsification offences that cause wrongful disbursements of funds: Sin David at [19]; see also Tan Puay Boon v PP [2003] 3 SLR(R) 390 (“Tan”) at [50].

Claim sums and falsified amounts not insubstantial

27     In Dr Chan’s case, the purported entertainment expenses claimed across the five proceeded charges was S$336,803.81. The falsified amounts that were wrongly disbursed to Dr Chan totalled S$253,791.67 across all the charges (including the two TIC charges). Both values are by no means insubstantial.

Overall inflation of two-and-a-half times with individual amounts inflated by between two to more than three-and-a-half times and with two fictitious amounts

Dr Chan’s culpability

29     I assess Dr Chan’s culpability by considering his motive for offending; the scale of the falsification; the manner and level of planning, premeditation and sophistication of the falsification; and the extent of his abuse of the trust reposed in him in his executive capacity: Sin David at [21].

Motive

30     The pertinent facts that Dr Chan admitted to are that:

(a)     prior to the December 2016 offence, Mr Chiew had asked Dr Chan for financial assistance for his children and house sometime in 2015. Dr Chan then informed Dr Tan of Mr Chiew’s request, and

(b)     prior to the 2019 offences, the trio agreed sometime in 2018 to claim certain business expenses from FHC which would be paid from FHCL’s accounts using inflated entertainment invoices. The understanding that they had was that this was to pay Mr Chiew for the ‘consultancy services’ that he provided to FHC.

31     In those circumstances, Dr Chan was driven to submit the impugned receipts for false or fictitious entertainment claims to be processed in his name to defraud FHC or FHCL into making wrongful disbursements to fund Mr Chiew’s financial assistance request and to pay for his ‘consultancy services’ to FHC, on the pretext of incurring entertainment expenses that had in fact been inflated or were fictitious. The wrongful disbursements were paid to Mr Chiew. The falsification was therefore not committed for personal gain: Tan at [47].

Scale of falsification

32     The offences were aggravating in that they were systematic and committed over a prolonged period over numerous occasions: Sin David at [23]. Besides an isolated occasion in December 2016, there were six occasions of falsification during the course of about a year, one every quarter in January 2019, April 2019 and September 2019 and three in the last quarter in November 2019.

Manner and level of planning, premeditation and sophistication of falsification

33     It is also aggravating that Dr Chan had acted in conspiracy with Dr Tan and Mr Sin; premeditation features in the group offence of criminal conspiracy because the essence of a conspiracy is agreement: Sin David at [24]. It is clear that there was such agreement in respect of the falsification offences in 2019 to fund the payment of Mr Chiew’s ‘consultancy services’ using FHCL’s accounts by claiming certain business expenses from FHC using inflated entertainment invoices: see [29(b)], above. As for the falsification offence in December 2016 to fund Mr Chiew’s financial assistance request, Dr Tan was privy to Mr Chiew’s request because Dr Chan had told him about it: see [29(a)], above. After collecting the receipts arranged by Mr Tei from the KTVs in Hong Kong where Dr Chan met various potential investors bi-monthly with Mr Sin and Mr Tei to help with FHC’s Hong Kong business, he would then submit the receipts to FHC or FHCL for claims to be processed in his name for the inflated or fictitious KTV expenses incurred. A number of these claims were made with Dr Chan’s knowledge to obtain monies from FHC to provide financial assistance to Mr Chiew.

34     There was some deviousness or surreptitious planning (or otherwise sophistication) involved because fictitious claims were submitted between inflated ones and the claims were also supported by a mixture of inflated and false receipts: Sin David at [25].

35     In the case of a conspiracy, the offender’s role in the conspiracy is a relevant sentencing factor: Sin David at [26]. The defence attempted to circumscribe Dr Chan’s role as merely acting on Mr Sin and Mr Tei’s instructions and arranging for the receipts to be handed to FHC or FHCL, which would then arrange for the false or fictitious claims to be made. But this blithely ignores the fact, which Dr Chan admitted to, that typically he would inform Mr Sin and/or Mr Tei that he required inflated or false KTV receipts prior to flying off. Mr Tei would then arrange for the receipts to be prepared and Dr Chan would collect them from him thereafter.

36     I therefore prefer the prosecution’s characterisation of Dr Chan’s role as crucial in submitting the receipts for the inflated or false claims to be processed in his name. He, Dr Tan, and Mr Sin played their respective essential roles in bringing the scheme to defraud FHC and FHCL into fruition to obtain monies to fund Mr Chiew’s financial assistance request and to pay for his ‘consultancy services’ to FHC – Dr Chan was to collect and submit the receipts for inflated or false claims to be processed in his name, which Dr Tan and/or Mr Sin were then to approve.

Abuse of trust

37     Although the defence did not dispute that Dr Chan held relatively senior appointments as FHC’s deputy group CEO and FHCL’s president, it sought to argue that Mr Sin held positions of greater influence and seniority. Sin Capital, of which he was CEO, was also FHC’s major shareholder. However, as the prosecution rightly pointed out, this does not give due weight to the fact that Dr Chan was a co-founder in his own right together with Dr Tan and Mr Sin. It was not a hierarchical, employer-employee, or subordinate relationship.

38     The defence also sought to argue that unlike Mr Sin who approved the claims in his executive capacity and a case of abuse of trust reposed in him in that capacity could be founded in that regard, Dr Chan merely submitted the receipts as an employee. I am unpersuaded by the niceties of that argument, which I find, with respect, to be an artificial construct. The fact of the matter is that Dr Chan, Dr Tan and Mr Sin were fellow co-founders who could approve business expenses claims without obtaining any approval from their finance teams. Dr Chan knew of the purport of the scheme to defraud FHC/FHCL using the impugned receipts by submitting them to support inflated or false claims in his name. He also knew the claims would be approved without intervention because the trio took advantage of this self-check approval process, which he was entrusted to gatekeep in precisely such an instance: Sin David at [28].

39     With respect, I am also constrained to say that the defence’s characterisation of Dr Chan as a “courier” or “messenger” of Mr Sin and Mr Tei, who merely “ferried” the receipts that Mr Tei had passed to him on their instructions for the purpose of facilitating claims that they themselves wanted to be submitted and processed, grossly understates the true nature of Dr Chan’s role. It also flies in the face of his knowledge and agreement of the purpose of the scheme and his active involvement in requesting the receipts: see [32] and [34], above. His role is also no less important than Mr Sin’s role as the final approver of the claims. While the prosecution rightly acknowledged that the false claims could only have been successfully processed and paid out with Mr Sin’s approval, there would be nothing to approve without Dr Chan submitting the receipts in the first place for claims in his name to be processed.

40     As such, I agree with the prosecution that Dr Chan had abused the trust reposed in him as FHC’s director and deputy group CEO by submitting the impugned receipts to support inflated or false claims to be processed in his name. The falsification offences were more serious as it was committed by a senior officer: Sin David at [28].

Personal aggravating and mitigating factors

41     Leaving the harm-culpability analysis, I turn to consider the aggravating and mitigating factors personal to Dr Chan that present themselves in his case.

Aggravating presence of TIC charges

42     The presence of two similar TIC charges are aggravating: PP v UI [2008] 4 SLR(R) 500 at [37]-[38], but I have already taken their aggravating facts into account when considering the harm caused by Dr Chan’s offences and the level of his culpability: [26], [27] and [31]. I have consciously avoided any effects of double-counting it as a personal aggravating factor. In any event, any aggravating effect is also cancelled out by the mitigatory effect of Dr Chan’s voluntary cooperation to the authorities: see [42], below.

Full and voluntary cooperation

43     I accept that Dr Chan rendered full and voluntary cooperation to the Corrupt Practices Investigation Bureau (“CPIB”) during investigations by admitting from the outset at his first two interviews that he had passed money to Mr Chiew, as well as collected inflated entertainment receipts from Mr Tei and submitted them for his reimbursement claims to be processed. Such forthcoming remorse and contrition, especially when it entails volunteering evidence that may be unfavourable to oneself, is to be encouraged particularly given the difficulty detecting financial crimes: see [23], above, and the specific intricacies of the scheme and approval process in this case. I made the same observation in the context of syndicated cross-border money-laundering offences: see eg PP v Ho Mun Hao [2026] SGDC 156 at [55]; PP v Chan King Vun [2026] SGDC 208 at [51].

44     I do not think it is meaningful to compare the extent and quality of the cooperation rendered by Mr Sin. I considered that in the round with his plea of guilt and more importantly, his contemporaneous behaviour (of arranging and pushing for independent investigations that precipitated a CPIB complaint that eventually saw him being implicated in the falsification offences) evincing genuine remorse and contrition, which I thought was the decisive mitigating factor: Sin David at [32].

Dr Chan not regarded as first-time offender because of multiple offending

45     Although Dr Chan has no criminal antecedents, I do not regard him as a first-time offender because he had committed multiple offences: Chen Weixiong Jerriek v PP [2003] 2 SLR(R) 334 at [17]. In any case, the absence of antecedents is at best a neutral factor: BPH v PP [2019] 2 SLR 764 at [85], and it could not be seriously argued that Dr Chan’s offending behaviour was an aberration and out of character for him in the light of the multiplicity of his offences sustained across an extended period: PP v BWJ [2023] 1 SLR 477 at [102].

Plea of guilt

46     Like Dr Tan and Mr Sin, Dr Chan too has pleaded guilty after the prosecution extended a revised plea offer that involved applying for a DNATA on his PCA charges at this stage of the proceedings. I have also taken this into account in sentencing.

Application of parity principle

47     I agree with the parties that the parity principle applies:

(a)     the par excellence situation is where co-offenders are charged with the same offence arising from the same transaction or events but are dealt with in separate criminal proceedings: PP v Ng Sae Kiat [2015] SGHC 191 (“Ng”) at [74]. For instance, Dr Chan and Dr Tan each face a mirror charge, but that charge was withdrawn against Mr Sin. For the remainder of Dr Chan’s charges, those mirror that faced by Mr Sin,

(b)     be that as it may (for the withdrawal of the mirror charge against Mr Sin), parity should not only apply to cases where the co-offenders were involved in the same transaction and they are charged for the same offence: Ng at [75]. Formal identity of charges against the offenders whose sentences are compared is not a necessary condition: Ng at [76], and

(c)     the principle can apply for the purposes of sentencing offenders who, as a matter of substance, can be said to be participants in a common criminal enterprise: Ng at [78]. The fact that Dr Chan submitted the impugned receipts to support inflated or false claims processed in his name, which Dr Tan and Mr Sin subsequently approved, is sufficient to make the trio participants in a common criminal enterprise with their guilty knowledge.

I should therefore have regard to the sentences passed in Sin David.

48     It is not the law that every co-offender in a common criminal enterprise must be identically charged or sentenced: Chong Han Rui v PP [2016] SGHC 25 (“Chong”) at [52]. The principle of parity in sentencing between co-offenders urges that sentences meted out to co-offenders who are party to a common criminal enterprise should not be unduly disparate from each other: those of similar culpability should receive similar sentences, while those of greater culpability should generally be more severely punished: Chong at [1].

Dr Chan not merely acting on instructions

49     On the facts it has presented in its mitigation plea, the defence has sought to persuade me that Dr Chan’s moral culpability within the common criminal enterprise was lower than that of Mr Sin, by drawing the necessary inferences from those facts that:

(a)     Mr Sin made the decision that money should be paid to Mr Chiew,

(b)     he initially conceived of and orchestrated the falsification, and

(c)     by contrast, Dr Chan only acted on his instructions and his role was limited to submitting the receipts that were handed to him for claims to be processed in his name.

As the prosecution did not dispute the facts presented in the mitigation plea, I did not have to call an ancillary hearing.

50     Although the defence has commendably assembled and put forth a trove of facts from Dr Chan’s perspective, they still have to be appreciated in the light of those that Dr Chan admitted to in the statement of facts. As I understand it, the defence is not putting forth a case that Mr Sin was more culpable merely because he was the progenitor of the scheme and had advised Dr Chan and Dr Tan as to the payment to Mr Chiew. But Dr Chan was less culpable because he was taking the lead from, in the words of the defence, the “general” as a “foot soldier” acting on instructions from Mr Sin.

51     The statement of facts and the instant messaging communications relied upon by the defence in its mitigation plea do not bear this out. I agree with the prosecution that any advice that Mr Sin rendered did not derogate any agency on Dr Chan’s part to agreeing to pay Mr Chiew: see [32], above. This was not a case where Dr Chan was merely acting on instructions although he might not be fully conversant with the intricacies or mechanics of the process. There is a world of difference in saying that he lacked commercial or business savviness and relied on Mr Sin’s representation that Mr Chiew’s financial assistance request was “common practice”; it is quite another to say he could not appreciate the implications of using inflated or false receipts or submitting such claims. He did not need anyone to tell him that the latter was clearly wrong in any context.

52     In this regard, the ineluctable inference from the messages where he appeared to take instructions unquestioningly, even when Mr Sin intervened to explain certain mechanics to avoid attracting the risk of scrutiny from their finance teams with “outsized” claims, was that he understood this to be the scheme they had generally discussed and broadly agreed to:

Dr Chan and Mr Sin’s culpabilities similar in common criminal enterprise

54     In this case, Dr Chan, Dr Tan and Mr Sin each played their respective roles in the common criminal enterprise. Dr Chan conspired with his fellow co-founders with the knowledge that they would approve the claims processed in his name using the inflated or false receipts he had submitted. That was simply the arrangement they had agreed to in order to get the claims through. Dr Chan was to collect and submit the receipts for inflated or false claims to be processed in his name. Dr Tan approved the claims as FHC’s director and group CEO; so did Mr Sin in his executive capacity. Mr Sin’s approval was essential for the claims to go through as was Dr Tan’s, which was in turn wholly dependent on Dr Chan submitting the impugned receipts in the first place for the inflated or false claims to be processed in his name. All of their roles were essential and critical.

55     I therefore agree with the prosecution that the culpabilities of Dr Chan and Mr Sin in the common criminal enterprise were similar. As such, the sentences that is imposed on Dr Chan should not be unduly disparate from those imposed on Mr Sin.

Sentencing precedents of Leow and Ong

56     The sentence of a high fine is consistent with two sentencing precedents cited by the prosecution, PP v Leow Ban Leong [2018] SGDC 157 (“Leow”) and PP v Ong Teck Liam [2017] SGDC 317 (“Ong”) (where the individual sentences passed were fines of S$30,000), discussed in Sin David at [34] and [35(a)].

Desperation as motive in Leow and passive inheritance of illegal practice in Ong absent in Dr Chan’s case

57     I will only add that:

(a)     the accused persons in Leow were found to have been driven by desperation and not pursuant to any sophisticated or meticulous planning when they committed three falsification offences to cover up inadvertently overcharging the government S$102,238.50. The conspiracy was not highly planned, premeditated or even moderately sophisticated: Leow at [161]; and

(b)     the accused person in Ong was a passive inheritor of an illegal practice of using cash vouchers for entertainment expenses to pay commission. She was not privy to the exact details of such payments and did not know they were bribes: Ong at [90]. Ten falsification charges were proceeded against her with 108 TIC. Her predecessor was also given an individual fine of S$30,000 on each of the seven proceeded charges with 31 TIC. Having regard to the parity principle: Ong at [70], the court found that her predecessor’s role and involvement in facilitating the falsification offense is exactly the same as, if not more culpable than her: Ong at [93]. Notwithstanding that she faced a higher number of charges, the court nevertheless found that imposing an individual fine of S$30,000 per charge, resulting in an aggregate fine of S$300,000, which would be S$90,000 higher than the sentence meted out to her predecessor, would be adequate: Ong at [94].

These features, namely desperation as motive and passive inheritance of an existing illegal practice, were absent in Dr Chan’s case.

two months’ imprisonment



59     For the fine in DAC 902843 of 2024 involving a falsified sum of about S$40,000, I have pegged this to the fine of S$25,000 imposed in Sin David for falsified sums of between S$19,000 and S$21,000. Quite apart from the absolute quanta, I recognise that they involve either higher inflation or false claims that merited heavier fines. By contrast, DAC 902843 of 2024 involved an inflated claim involving a sum that was inflated by less than twice of the actual expenses incurred.

Fine of S$135,000 imposed

60     I therefore sentence Dr Chan to an aggregate fine of S$135,000, in default, 12 months’ imprisonment.

61     In both their trademark styles, both DPP Jonathan Tan and Mr Navin Thaver engaged in incisive oral submissions before me, from which I have benefitted greatly in reaching my decision, together with the papers they have prepared for this case. I am grateful for their assistance and commend them and their respective teams for their industry.
