Prosecution’s Reply submissions

33     In response to the Defence’s submissions on sentence, the Prosecution argued that every WOF member in the criminal conspiracy had a different but important role to play in the siphoning of monies from CTPL. The Accused was integral to the scheme as he was the only person from the WOF who was external to CTPL. He had provided the WOF with the crucial first avenue for the siphoning of money out of CTPL. The fundamental difference between the Accused and the other sub-contractors was that the Accused was privy to the intricate details of the conspiracy, and even received a cut of the wrongful gain, unlike the other sub-contractors involved.

34     The Prosecution also responded to the Defence’s argument that the Accused had made more restitution than Tan. The sum returned illegally, together with the sum of his voluntary restitution of $18,000, would amount to $734,736.78, which is not far off from Tan’s restitution of $670,000. The two watches and cash amounting to $47,300 which were seized by CPIB (with a total value of $71,300) cannot be regarded as voluntary restitution.

35     The Prosecution further submitted that the actual loss suffered by CTPL cannot exclude the GST amounts paid to IRAS as they arose from the cheating offences, and any genuine service rendered to CTPL is irrelevant to the present offences.

36     The Prosecution highlighted that they are not seeking any uplift in the Accused’s eventual sentence on account of the late plea of guilt. Rather, the Prosecution submits for a lower discount for the plea of guilt. Even excluding the time taken to resolve issues with the Statement of Facts, the Accused had indicated his intention to plead guilty much later than Tan. Tan had pleaded guilty as early as 21 September 2022, whereas, the Accused had indicated his intention to plead guilty only on 3 May 2024.

Issues to be determined

37     The issues which the Court considered at this hearing were as follows:

i.     The offence specific factors relevant to the levels of harm and culpability.

ii.     The offender specific factors.

iii.     Based on the offence specific factors and the offender specific factors, the indicative starting sentence for each set of offences.

iv.     The issue of parity of sentence vis-à-vis the co-accused persons.

v.     The further adjustments to be made to account for the one transaction rule and the totality principle.

Decision on sentence

38     The offence under s 420 PC is punishable with imprisonment for a term which may extend to 10 years and shall also be liable to a fine. The offence under s 468 PC is similarly punishable with imprisonment for a term which may extend to 10 years and shall also be liable to a fine. The offence under s 465 PC is punishable with imprisonment for a term which may extend to extend to 4 years, or with fine, or with both. The offence under s 47(2)(a) CDSA is punishable with a fine not exceeding $500,000 or imprisonment for a term not exceeding 10 years or both. The hefty penalties prescribed for all four offences indicate that they are serious offences warranting significant punishment.

39     The court in PP v Law Aik Meng [2007] 2 SLR(R) 814 (“Law Aik Meng”) stated at [22] that specific deterrence is usually appropriate in instances where the crime is premeditated. The court also stated at [24] that the principle of general deterrence is engaged when the aim is to educate and deter other like-minded members of the general public by making an example of a particular offender. In the present case, both sets of factors were present which led me to conclude that the principles of both general and specific deterrence were engaged. I will first deal with the charges under s 420 PC.

Sentencing considerations for the offences under s 420 r/w s 109 PC

40     I started with the offence specific factors relevant to the levels of harm and culpability.

Offence-specific factors going towards harm

(1)   The quantum involved

41     In Gan Chai Bee Anne v PP [2019] 4 SLR 838, Menon CJ explained at [42] that in sentencing for financial and property offences, the economic value is a proxy for the degree of criminal benefit received by the offender and the degree of harm caused to the victim, and both are relevant sentencing considerations.

42     In the present case, the total amount cheated is a staggering $9,676,534.12. The actual loss to CTPL, after taking into account the amount of $5,000,000.054 which was returned to CTPL by the WOF, was $4,676,534.066.

43     The Defence argued that the actual loss suffered by CTPL was only around $3,337,552.33. This was derived by deducting the GST amounts paid to IRAS on behalf of Civil Tech ($1,016,055.56) and the cost of works done by GCE for CTPL ($322, 925.69) in addition to the amounts returned to CTPL by the WOF ($5,000,000.054). In this regard, I accepted the Prosecution’s submissions that:

a.     The actual loss suffered by CTPL cannot exclude the GST paid to IRAS because the GST amounts stemmed from the payments made against the false invoices. The GST payments were necessary collateral for the cheating offences committed by the WOF; and

b.     Any genuine service rendered to CTPL is irrelevant to the present offences and cannot serve as a proxy for restitution or be considered as a set-off against the losses suffered by CTPL

44     Therefore, the actual loss to CTPL stands at $4,676,534.66, which is a huge sum, and indicates that significant harm was caused to CTPL.

(2)   Reputational damage

45     I further agreed with the Prosecution that the present offences tarnished the image and reputation of the building and construction industry in Singapore. They also potentially increased the cost of doing business in the industry. In PP v Fernando Payagala Waduge Malitha Kumar [2007] 2 SLR(R) 334 (“Fernando”), the court at [42] explained that a sophisticated offence replete with carefully orchestrated efforts and steps to avoid detection is cause for greater consternation and would raise the ante for better protective measures in order to prevent a recurrence of similar offences. This results not only in substantial costs being incurred by potential institutional victims, but also much inconvenience, and perhaps even loss of reputation. While these remarks were made with reference to credit card cheating offences, I am of the view that they apply with equal force to the present set of offences which were sophisticated with many steps taken to avoid detection.

Offence-specific factors going towards culpability

(1)   The degree of planning and premeditation involved

46     There was a high degree of planning and premeditation involved. The offences were well orchestrated to ensure the smooth execution of the scheme. Each member of the WOF had specific tasks assigned to him which were then carefully coordinated across the five of them. The schedule of billings and the amounts to be billed were similarly well planned and coordinated. Liauw, as the Project Manager would check and endorse the payment certificates for the progress claims made by the sub-contractors, while Ong and Gan, as Project Directors would approve and sign off on the payment certificates. Tan, as the Group Finance Manager, would approve the payments and sign on the payment vouchers and CTPL’s cheques. He also obtained the second signatory for the cheque payments. Tan had also set up a WhatsApp chat group for the WOF members to facilitate discussions regarding the amounts to be billed and the sub-contractors to be used to launder the monies taken out of CTPL. In this manner, the WOF had created an elaborate web of false documents to siphon the sum of $9,676,534.12 from CTPL.

(2)   The sophistication of the offence and measures taken to avoid detection.

47     The offences were sophisticated and designed to create the impression that these were genuine transactions which had been approved by CTPL. The co-conspirators were senior employees of CTPL who were authorised to endorse and approve payments. They approved and signed off on the false progress claims submitted by GCE, TW, and Hua Rong. Thereafter, to facilitate the withdrawal of the monies which had been deposited into the accounts of GCE, TW, and Hua Rong, several sub-contractors were recruited to create the series of false invoices. Even after the scheme was discovered by THM and the WOF had agreed to return the sum of $5,000,000.54 to CTPL, the WOF members took steps to conceal their tracks. They recruited a second layer of sub-contractors to facilitate the movement of the monies back to CTPL.

(3)   The role of the Accused

48     The courts have often held that the severity of the sentence imposed should correspond to the role played by the offender. The Accused here played an active and important role in the scheme. There were a total of 17 false invoices billed to CTPL for non-existent works. The Accused signed on 12 of the false invoices as well as the progress claims issued to CTPL from GCE and TW. He was well aware that no works were carried out for these false progress claims and invoices. Consequently, GCE and TW were the recipients of most of the money transferred out of CTPL - $8,299208.88 out of $9,676,534.12.

49     The Accused had also, on the advice of Tan, raised the share capital of TW in order to reduce suspicion arising from the significant amounts that TW billed to CTPL.

50     Further, the Accused was also involved in recruiting one of the sub-contractors who was used to facilitate the withdrawal of monies from GCE, TW, and Hua Rong. He had recruited Zhuang He (“Zhuang”), who was the Director of Hong Hai Construction Pte Ltd (“Hong Hai”) and also a sub-contractor of GCE. Zhuang issued false invoices to TW to facilitate the transfer of monies from TW to Hong Hai.

51     A total of 27 false invoices were issued to GCE, TW and Hua Rong to move the monies out of the three companies. The Accused approved the payments from GCE and TW to the corresponding subcontractors, while Huang approved the payments from Hua Rong. A total of $6,364,088.06 from the siphoned monies were withdrawn from GCE, TW and Hua Rong in this manner.

52     Once the monies to be returned to CTPL were consolidated in GCE’s bank account, the Accused authorised seven false GCE credit notes, one false TW credit note, and the corresponding payment vouchers and cashier’s orders for the return of the monies totalling $5,000,000.54 to CTPL.

53     The Defence had argued that the Accused was a mere participant in the scheme who could have been easily replaced by any other subcontractor whom CTPL had engaged.[note: 1] Whether or not the co-conspirators could have recruited another sub-contractor to create the false invoices is irrelevant. The fact is, it was the Accused who had willingly and actively participated in the scheme. His culpability must be measured according to his involvement in the offences, which was not inconsiderable. It is evident that the Accused was actively involved in first siphoning the monies from CTPL and then moving it around to avoid detection.

(4)   Abuse of position of trust

54     The Accused was the director of GCE and TW. He had clearly abused his position as an officer of the two companies when he agreed to lend their names and their billing facilities to the WOF for their scheme to cheat CTPL. He had also abused his position as the director when he approved and authorised the credit notes, payment vouchers and cashier’s orders issued out of GCE and TW.

(5)   The offences were committed as a group

55     The Accused had conspired with four others to cheat CTPL. The offences were then committed as a group with each person having a distinct and separate role. They were like pieces in a puzzle where each of them performed specific tasks which were all planned and carefully coordinated to evade detection.

(6)   Motive / financial gain

56     The Accused was promised a cut of the monies cheated from CTPL. In keeping with this promise, the Accused received a total of $905,000. Very bluntly put, the Accused committed these offences out of greed.

Offender-specific factors

(1)   Remorse shown by the Accused

57     The Accused had entered a plea of guilt which I accepted as an expression of his remorse.

(2)   Number of charges involved

58     The Accused faced a large number of charges – 20 proceeded charges and 65 charges taken into consideration for the purposes of sentencing. All 85 charges related to the scheme to cheat CTPL of almost $10 million.

(3)   Accused was not a first-time offender

59     In terms of whether the Accused should be regarded as a first-time offender, given the multiple charges which he faced, I took the view that he cannot be treated as a first-time offender. In Chen Weixiong Jerriek v PP [2003] 2 SLR(R) 334, Yong Pung How CJ held that it is the court’s prerogative to refuse to consider anyone who has been charged with multiple offences as a first-time offender, even if he has no prior convictions. The courts in general, should be extremely reluctant to regard such persons as first-time offenders.

(4)   Restitution was made

60     After the offences were discovered, the Accused returned a total of $734,736.78 to CTPL. The amount of $716,736.78 was returned as part of the settlement agreement with THM and the Accused made a voluntary restitution of about $18,000.

Sentencing precedents for the s 420 PC offences

61     The Prosecution cited the following six sentencing precedents in support of their submissions on sentence.

a.      PP v Cheong Sing Whee (“Cheong”) [2005] SGDC 124. The offender pleaded guilty to one charge under s 420 r/w s 109 PC involving $1,540,000. He consented to TIC one charge of s 420 r/w s 109 PC involving $1,940,000. The offender was the managing director of Sin Yuh Industries Pte Ltd (“Sin Yuh”). He purchased machinery from Henko Industries Pte Ltd (“Henko”). In order to obtain a loan from DBS, the offender had to provide evidence to DBS that 40% of the cost of the machines had been paid. The offender and the director of Henko conspired to submit a letter stating that Henko had received the monies, when in fact they had not. DBS disbursed a loan for the amount of $1,540,000 to Sin Yuh. The offender was unable to repay the loan, and DBS had to seize the machinery to sell them off. DBS was only able to obtain $863,680 from the sale of the machinery. The total loss to DBS was $676,320. The trial judge imposed a sentence of 3 years’ imprisonment. The sentence was reduced to 2 years’ imprisonment on appeal.

b.      PP v Winnie Goh Li Ching (“Winnie Goh”) [2011] SGDC 428. The offender pleaded guilty to 30 charges under s 420 r/w s 109 PC Cap. 224 and three charges under s 420 PC. She consented to TIC 156 similar charges. The offender was a bank officer with OCBC and was part of a conspiracy to cheat the bank to disburse mortgage loans to individuals who did not meet the credit worthiness criteria for the loan application. The offender would provide the necessary salary information for each of the loan applications to real estate agents who were part of the conspiracy. The forged documents were submitted to the offender who would authenticate them before submitting them to OCBC for approval. As a result of the scheme, OCBC disbursed 179 loans exceeding $62 million. The offender received commissions amounting to $44,632.57 from OCBC, referral fees amounting to $11,257.65 from the agents, and cash benefits amounting to about $90,000 from her accomplices. The bank incurred losses amounting to $687,788.37.

The court found that the offender had played a vital role in the loan processing procedures at the bank. The cheating offences would not have materialised without her support in endorsing the forged documents submitted. The offender had initially adopted a passive role in turning a blind eye to the loan applications even though she was aware that the estate agents were submitting false income documents. Subsequently, she took on a more active role by assisting in the calculation of the income levels required in order for the applicants to be eligible for the loans. In some of the transactions, she had even sought the assistance of forgers to create the false documents required for submission to the bank.

The offender was sentenced to a total of 60 months’ imprisonment. The individual sentences for the s 420 r/w s 109 PC charges were as follows: for mortgage loans involving between $1,070,100 to $2,250,000 – 18 months’ imprisonment per charge; for mortgage loan involving $1,395,000 - 15 months’ imprisonment; for mortgage loans involving $945,000 – 12 months’ imprisonment per charge; for mortgage loans involving $824,715 & $837,000 – 10 months’ imprisonment per charge; for mortgage loan involving $540,000 – 7 months’ imprisonment; for mortgage loans involving $124,600 to $292,000 – 6 months’ imprisonment per charge. The individual sentences for the s 420 PC charges were as follows: for mortgage loans involving $1,485 to $2565 as commissions – 3 months’ imprisonment per charge.

c.      Goldring, Timothy Nicholas v PP and other appeals (“Goldring”) [2015] 4 SLR 742. The offenders claimed trial to 18 charges each under s 420 r/w s 109, PC. The offenders were director-shareholders of a company which offered investment products (Boron Products) promising a 12.5% return on the principal amount within six months of investment. They made two sets of representations to potential investors, and these investors relied on the representations when they invested in the Boron Products. At the end of the six-month window, the investors failed to receive their returns as promised. The total loss suffered by the investors was US$732,000 (about S$1,005,500). No restitution was made despite both offenders having the means and opportunity to do so. The High Court found this to be an aggravating factor. Goldring was sentenced to a total of 7 years’ imprisonment, and Nordmann was sentenced to a total of 8 years’ imprisonment. The sentences for both offenders were upheld on appeal.

d.      PP v Neo Aileen (“Neo Aileen”) [2013] SGDC 315. The offender pleaded guilty to two charges under s 420 PC Cap 224. The offender deceived the victim, a friend, into believing that she could provide an attractive US foreign currency exchange rate. She thereby dishonestly induced the victim to deliver to her a total of US$1,000,000 (equivalent to SG$1,297,000 as at September 2011). No restitution was made. The total loss caused was US$1,000,000. The offender was sentenced to 39 months’ imprisonment per charge giving an aggregate sentence of 78 months’ imprisonment. No appeal was filed against the sentence imposed.

e.      PP v Linda Lee (“Linda Lee”) [2017] SGDC 267. The offender held various senior positions in her company including head of asset management services and vice president of asset management services. The offender used her position to print false invoices and cheat her company with other co-offenders. The court found that she was one of the two masterminds of the scheme and was the prime mover of the offences. She faced a total 361 charges of which 224 were for cheating offences. She pleaded guilty to a total of 35 charges which included 6 charges under section 420 PC and 22 charges under section 420 PC r/w s109 PC. In sentencing the offender, the court held that her culpability was high and the harm caused was severe. The offences were committed over 5 years and the company suffered losses of over $10 million. The offender had made personal gains in excess of $5 million She was sentenced to a global sentence of 14 years’ imprisonment. On appeal, the global sentence was reduced to 12.5 years’ imprisonment. There was no change to the individual sentences, but the appellate court altered the charges to be run consecutively.

f.      PP v Gene Chong Soon Hui (“Gene Chong”) [2018] SGDC 117. The offender was the company finance manager who had cheated the company by creating fictitious transactions and using pre-signed company cheques to siphon monies out of the company. The offender faced 194 charges of which 165 were under s 420 PC. He pleaded guilty to 20 charges which included 15 charges under s 420 PC. In sentencing the offender, the court noted that the proceeded cheating charges involved a loss of over $1 million to the company. The offences took place over 5 years. The offender was sentenced to a global sentence of 11 years’ imprisonment. The offender’s appeal against sentence was dismissed by the High Court.

62     The sentencing precedents above showed that a wide range of sentences were imposed indicating that sentencing for cheating offences tend to be fact specific. Nonetheless, I was able to gather some useful indications from the six cases. I found that the factual matrix in Winne Goh, Linda Lee and Gene Chong were most similar to the present case and relied on them as relevant comparators. The harm caused in terms of the losses suffered in Winnie Goh ($687,788.37) and Gene Chong (over $1 million) was lower than the present case ($4,676,535.66) but higher in Linda Lee (over $10 million). The level of culpability was higher in Linda Lee (offender was one of the two masterminds and prime mover of the offences) but similar to Gene Chong (premeditation and abuse of trust) and Winnie Goh (initially turned a blind eye and only subsequently became more active but overall, the cheating offences would not have materialised without her support). The offenders in the three cases had also pleaded guilty but there was a longer period of offending and a greater number of charges in all three cases.

63     The cheating charges were the predicate offences for the CDSA charges and in a way, they were also the catalyst for the two sets of forgery charges. The largest amount of $7,407,898.90 was contained in the third cheating charge. I therefore took the view that the overall sentence imposed for the cheating offences would drive the global sentence in this case. In this regard, I relied on the High Court’s comments in Tan Thiam Wee v PP [2012] SGHC 142 at [8] and [10] that in cases involving multiple charges, the focus should be on the totality of the sentence rather than on the adequacy of the sentence for the individual charges.

64     In the present case, the need for general and specific deterrence was evident. The quantum involved was high and the level of culpability was significant too. The offences were premeditated and sophisticated, and the Accused was a key player in the commission of the offences. In light of these aggravating factors and having regard to the sentencing precedents above, I arrived at a global starting sentence of seven and a half years’ imprisonment for the three s 420 r/w s 109 PC offences.

Sentencing considerations for the offences under s 468 r/w s 109 PC

65     There was significant overlap with the sentencing factors considered for the cheating offences.

66     There were a total of 17 charges for the aggravated forgery and the Prosecution proceeded on six of them. The fraud was a serious one and had adversely affected the reputation of the building and construction industry. They were all deliberate, pre-meditated and calculated to deceive. The Accused had forged 12 out of the 17 false invoices using GCE and TW, which were existing sub-contractors of CTPL. They were intended to deceive THM and the rest of CTPL’s management into believing that the invoices represented genuine transactions. Consequently, large sums of monies were disbursed on the strength of those invoices. The quantum per false invoice involved sums of between $175,836.66 to $1,853,646,60. A sum of $5,000,000.54 was returned to CTPL. The net loss to CTPL was $4,676,534.66. This figure could have been higher if THM had been any less vigilant.

67     The Accused had abused his position as the Director of GCE and TW when he perpetrated these offences. He had committed them over a period of several months and derived significant financial benefit from them. He received a sum of $905,000 but after deducting all the monies disgorged from him, his net gain was $98,963.22, which was still a significant sum.

68     In determining the sentence for the six charges, I made reference to the following case.

69      Lim Ek Kian v Public Prosecutor (“Lim Ek Kian”) [2003] SGHC 58. The offender was the managing director of a company which was the distributor for Skoda cars in Singapore. He claimed trial to a single charge for forging documents submitted to LTA for the transfer of $9,237 worth of PARF/COE rebates accruing to a customer from her existing car. The customer intended to buy a Skoda car from the offender’s company and paid a downpayment for the new car. The customer filled up the transfer form but signed under the wrong column. The offender subsequently discovered the error and prepared a new form. He forged the customer’s signature on the new form. He also entered the details of another customer as the intended recipient of the PARF/COE rebates and again forged the signature of the other customer. All of this was not made known to either customer. The offender submitted the form to LTA and the transfer as specified in the form was registered. Subsequently, Skoda went into receivership, and the first customer did not receive the car. Instead, she lost most of her downpayment and $9,237 worth of her PARF/COE rebates. The offender was sentenced to 12 months’ imprisonment. The court observed at [35] that the Courts have always treated offences under s 468 PC seriously, and past cases have adopted a 12-month sentence of imprisonment as a benchmark. The prescribed punishment then was imprisonment for a term which may extend to seven years and shall also be liable to a fine.

70     For the present case, the prescribed punishment is imprisonment for a term which may extend to 10 years and shall also be liable to a fine. The amounts involved here were also much higher than what was seen in Lim Ek Kian. There were more charges here representing repeated instances of offending, and the offences were committed pursuant to an elaborate conspiracy. However, I took the view that the Accused’s culpability was lower than that of the offender in Lim Ek Kian. Lim had defrauded a public organisation, adversely affected the public’s perception of the rebate system, and shown a blatant disregard for his customers’ welfare and basic business ethics. I also bore in mind that the losses caused by this set of offences had already been taken into account in sentencing for the cheating charges. All considered, I found that a starting sentence from 14 months’ imprisonment per charge would be appropriate, with individual sentences to be calibrated according to the amounts involved.

Sentencing considerations for the offences under s 465 r/w s 109 PC

71     There were a total of 38 charges preferred under s 465 r/w s 109 PC. They involved a second tier of six sub-contractors. The Prosecution proceeded on six of the 38 charges. The proceeded charges involved two sets of documents. The first set were forged invoices prepared by the sub-contractors to disguise the withdrawal of the monies from the accounts of GCE, TW, and Hua Rong. The second set were forged credit notes prepared by the Accused to facilitate the return of the monies to CTPL. Both sets of charges involved largely similar sentencing considerations.

72     The offences were planned and premeditated and carefully coordinated across the six sub-contractors. The purpose of the forged documents was to conceal the true nature of the transactions and present them as legitimate claims for work done. Given that the sub-contractors involved were existing sub-contractors from the building and construction industry and not fictitious entities, it made the offences more difficult to detect. There were several charges involved with substantial amounts. For the forged invoices, the amounts ranged from $316,720 to $983,591.08. For the forged credit notes, the amounts ranged from $1,086,050 to $1,567,871.

73     I agreed with the Prosecution on the distinction drawn between the two sets of documents. The forged invoices in the first set were motivated by personal gain. This was a factor which was absent in the second set of documents. The purpose of forged credit notes was to facilitate the return of the monies to CTPL. I accepted the Prosecution’s submissions that the sentences should reflect this distinction.

74     The Prosecution cited the case against a co-conspirator, Yu Yingjie, a sub-contractor and the director of Da Ho Foundation (S) Pte Ltd, who faced a mirror charge under s 465 r/w s 109 PC to the charge in DAC-918307-2021. He pleaded guilty and was sentenced to 14 weeks’ imprisonment. The Prosecution submitted that for DAC-918307-2021, the Accused should face a sentence not too far from the sentence imposed on Yu Yingjie, with the sentences for the remaining two charges for the forged invoices to be adjusted upwards as they involve higher amounts. All three invoices were billed to GCE. In fact, 31 out of the 38 forged invoices were billed to either GCE or TW indicating that they were received and processed by the Accused. The remaining seven forged invoices were billed to Hua Rong. All considered, I arrived at a starting sentence of six months’ imprisonment for DAC-918307-2021 with the remaining sentences for the forgery charges to be calibrated according to the amounts involved.

Sentencing considerations for the offences under s 47(2)(a) CDSA

75     The offences under s 47(2)(a) CDSA are essentially money-laundering offences. I agreed with the Prosecution that deterrence was the key sentencing consideration here. In calibrating the sentence for this charge, I was guided by the High Court’s decision in Juandi in which the court adopted the sentencing bands in Ho Man Yuk but with suitable uplifts to account for the aggravating factors. The sentencing bands set out in Ho Man Yuk are as follows:

a.     For amounts of S$100,000 to less than S$300,000 – 10 to 11 months’ imprisonment; and

b.     For amounts of S$300,000 to S$500,000 – 12 to 13 months’ imprisonment.

77     The offender in Ho Man Yuk had claimed trial and was not accorded the usual discounts for an early plea of guilt. The offender in Juandi and the Accused in the present case had both pleaded guilty. Both faced similar number of charges - Juandi faced 31 charges in total, and the Accused faced 27 charges. The amounts involved in the individual charges were similar too. The key difference was the period of offending which was shorter in the present case. In Juandi, the offences were committed over almost five years whereas in the present case, the CDSA offences spanned a period of only four months from April to July 2016. All considered, I was of the view that a smaller uplift than those adopted in Juandi should apply. I therefore arrived at starting sentences of between 15 to 35 months’ imprisonment for the five CDSA charges with individual sentences to be calibrated according to the quantum involved in each charge.

Parity in sentencing

78     In Chong Han Rui v PP [2016] SGHC 25 (“Chong Han Rui”) CJ Menon remarked at [1] and [52]) that:

Consistency in sentencing is a key principle in our criminal justice system. This is rooted in the notion that all are equal before the law. The principle of parity in sentencing between co-offenders urges that sentences meted out to co-offenders who are party to a common criminal enterprise should not be unduly disparate from each other. To put it simply, those of similar culpability should receive similar sentences, while those of greater culpability should generally be more severely punished.

I emphasise however that the parity principle is not to be applied in a rigid and inflexible manner. Rather, it is an important aid to the sentencing court to ensure that sentencing of co-offenders is done in a manner that is broadly consistent and fair. But ultimately, what is consistent and fair depends on the facts of the case at hand.

79     The Prosecution cited the above remarks and argued that the Accused’s culpability is equal to or higher than Tan’s and significantly higher than Liauw’s. It was submitted that the Accused had played an active and integral role in the scheme to siphon money out of CTPL. He was the only member of WOF who was outside CTPL and so he was able to provide the WOF with the first crucial avenue for the siphoning of monies out of CTPL. The Accused was also heavily involved in the illegal return of money to CTPL where he used GCE and TW to move the monies out of GCE’s and TW’s accounts and back to CTPL.

80     The Defence on the other hand argued that the Accused had a lower level of culpability than Tan and Liauw. The Defence submitted that the scheme was masterminded by Tan and the Accused was a mere pawn who was made use of by Tan. The Accused had at all times acted on Tan’s instructions. He had no control over how the scheme would be worked. It was Tan who decided on the amounts to be stated in the progress claims and invoices issued. It was also Tan who solely decided on the division of monies received from CTPL. In fact, the Accused was not aware of what Tan had discussed with Ong, Gan, and Liauw.

81     I found no merit in the Defence’s arguments. There was no evidence to support their contention that Tan had masterminded the scheme. This was not stated in the SOF. In fact, the learned District Judge who presided over Tan’s case had stated in her Oral Judgement at [9(d)] that it is undisputed that Tan was not the mastermind of the scheme.[note: 2] As set out by the Prosecution in their Skeletal Reply to Mitigation, every member of the WOF had a different but important role to play in the scheme. The Accused provided the means to move the monies around - out of CTPL at first and then back into CTPL when the scheme was discovered. His was not a passive role. He was as much involved in the planning and organisation as Tan was, albeit at different stages in the scheme. He had no reason to be a pawn in Tan’s machinations as claimed by the Defence. The Accused had acted out of greed. He had expected huge pay outs for his efforts when he embarked on this conspiracy with the WOF. He was not disappointed and did receive the very large sum of about $905,000. I therefore found that the Accused’s level of culpability was similar to Tan’s with respect to the cheating and CDSA offences, but slightly higher for the forgery and aggravated forgery charges, given his active and direct participation in the creation of the false invoices and credit notes both at the initial stage of siphoning monies from CTPL and at the subsequent stage for the return of the monies to CTPL.

82     I found that Liauw’s overall culpability, when compared to the Accused’s culpability, was lower. Liauw was a marketing manager within CTPL and the project manager for MOT Changi Airport T5 Project. His role in this conspiracy was to sign off on the payment certificates for the progress claims submitted by the sub-contractors. He performed this function only at the first stage of the scheme when the monies were siphoned out from CTPL. He did not directly participate in the second stage of the scheme for the return of the monies to CTPL although he was part of the discussions and he did hand over his share of the monies to the sub-contractors.

83     The Prosecution had further highlighted that the Accused had indicated his intention to plead guilty very late in the day. In this regard, I accepted the Defence’s plea that this should not be treated as an aggravating factor. I simply noted that he would be granted a lower sentencing discount.

84     Finally, I took into account the benefits derived by the Accused vis-à-vis Tan and Liauw. After the offences were discovered, the Accused received about $905,000 from the monies siphoned from CTPL. He returned a total of $734,736.78 and cash and watches worth $71,300 were seized from him by the CPIB. His net gain was $98,963.22. In comparison, Tan made a wrongful gain of about $970,000 and returned $670,000. His net gain was about $300,000. Liauw made a wrongful gain of about $800,000 and returned about $660,000 and also surrendered two Rolex watches valued at about $64,000 to the CPIB during investigations. Liauw’s net gain was about $76,000. The Accused derived higher benefits than Liauw but lower than Tan.

Sentence imposed

85     I next proceeded to calibrate the sentences for the individual charges. For this, I did refer to the table of sentences imposed for Tan and Liauw which is found in Prosecution’s Submissions on Sentence at p 4-5. For ease of reference, the table is reproduced below.

Sentences for the offences under s 420 r/w s 109 PC

86     I had earlier determined that a global starting sentence of seven and a half years’ imprisonment would be appropriate for the three s 420 r/w s 109 PC offences. The Accused had pleaded guilty and I accorded him a sentencing discount to arrive at a final global sentence of 6 years’ imprisonment. This sentence was reserved for the charge involving the highest amount. The individual sentences for the remaining two charges were adjusted downwards according to the amounts involved. In this regard, I took reference from the sentences imposed for Tan for the two lesser cheating charges. Given that the harm and culpability involved was similar for both offenders, I saw no reason to depart from the sentences imposed on Tan. After considering the Accused’s plea of guilt, I arrived at a final sentence in the range of 12 to 28 months’ imprisonment. Three sentences to run consecutively

90     Where an offender is sentenced to three or more terms of imprisonment at one trial, at least two imprisonment terms must run consecutively. The sentencing court in determining which of the multiple sentences to run consecutively, will be guided by (a) the one-transaction rule, and (b) the totality principle.

91     For the one-transaction rule, where two or more offences are committed in the course of a single transaction, all sentences in respect of those offences should run concurrently rather than consecutively. In determining whether the offences form a single transaction, the court must assess whether they constitute a “single invasion of the same legally protected interest”.[note: 3] However, this rule is not rigidly applied, and suitable deviations would be considered where the final sentence does not correctly reflect the offender’s enhanced culpability due to the multiplicity of the offences that were committed.

92     As for the totality principle, it serves as a “final check” to prevent the court from imposing an excessive overall sentence and to ensure that the aggregate sentence is proportionate to the overall criminality presented. The totality principle may also serve to boost the sentences if they would otherwise result in a manifestly inadequate overall sentence.[note: 4]

93     In the instant case, I found that each species of offences - the cheating charges, the two sets of forgery charges, and the money-laundering charges under the CDSA - concerned different legally protected interest. The offending behaviour in each set of charges was different, and so I found that the offences were not committed in the course of a single transaction. Accordingly, I ordered one charge from each type of offence to run consecutively – DAC-918256-2021, DAC-918287-2021, and DAC-918333-2021. This resulted in a total sentence of 6 years' and 20 months' imprisonment. The aggregate sentence was similar to the one received by Tan with only a slight increase to account for the Accused’s later indication of his guilty plea. The consistency in the sentence for the two of them reflects their broadly similar levels of harm and culpability. The sentence imposed on the Accused was not out of the norm and cannot therefore be said to be a crushing sentence.

Conclusion

94     After a review or a last look at the sentences imposed, I was satisfied that the sentences imposed were not manifestly excessive. The Accused is presently released on bail pending appeal.

Public Prosecutor v Loh Guang Ze

Public Prosecutor v Loh Guang Ze
[2026] SGDC 211

Case Number:District Arrest Case No 914814 of 2024 and others
Decision Date:30 June 2026
Tribunal/Court:District Court
Coram: Justin Yeo
Counsel Name(s): Ms June Ngian (Attorney-General's Chambers) for the Prosecution; Mr Kelvin Tan (Linea Law LLC) for the Accused.
Parties: Public Prosecutor — Loh Guang Ze

Criminal Procedure and Sentencing – Sentencing – Statutory Offences – Section 376A(1) Penal Code

Criminal Procedure and Sentencing – Sentencing – Statutory Offences – Section 420(1) Penal Code

Criminal Procedure and Sentencing – Sentencing – Statutory Offences – Section 377BB(5) Penal Code

30 June 2026

Judgment reserved.

District Judge Justin Yeo:

Introduction

1       Mr Loh Guang Ze (“the Accused”) devised a scheme in 2018 to obtain sexual services from women by posing as a fictitious agent on Locanto (a website for classified advertisements), never intending to pay them for their services. He successfully met up with multiple victims to obtain their sexual services in various locations, including a female minor who was 15 years old at the time of the offence. He also covertly recorded videos of some of the victims performing sexual acts or engaging in sexual intercourse with him during these encounters. He was arrested when the police received an anonymous tip from a female stating that she had been cheated by an agent on Locanto, having not been paid for the sexual services she had provided to a client.

2       There is a gag order against publishing the name, address, photograph, any evidence or any other thing likely to lead to the identification of the victims in this case.

3       Beyond the sentencing analysis for each of the five proceeded charges under three different offence provisions in the Penal Code 1871 (“PC”) – namely, PC ss 376A(1)(a), 420A(1) and 377B(5) – this case raises two issues of broader sentencing significance.

(a)     First, the sentencing approach for an offence under PC s 420A involving the dishonest or fraudulent obtaining of sexual services, and in particular:

(i)       whether the framework established in Wong Tian Jun De Beers v Public Prosecutor [2022] 4 SLR 805 (“De Beers”) for cheating to procure sex and other sexual acts under PC s 417 applies, with appropriate modifications, to such an offence; and

(ii)       what non-exhaustive factors going to harm and culpability ought to guide the sentencing analysis.

(b)     Second, the sentencing approach for voyeuristic recordings of another person’s private regions without consent under PC s 377BB(5), and in particular:

(i)       whether the framework established in Nicholas Tan Siew Chye v Public Prosecutor [2023] 4 SLR 1223 (“Nicholas Tan”) for operating equipment to observe another person’s private regions without consent under PC s 377BB(4) applies, with appropriate modifications, to such an offence; and

(ii)       how the Nicholas Tan framework interacts with the framework in Prakash s/o Mathivanan v Public Prosecutor [2025] 4 SLR 1386 (“Prakash”) in the context of a PC s 377BB(5) charge that is amalgamated under s 124(4) and punishable under s 124(8)(a)(ii) of the Criminal Procedure Code (“CPC”).

Overview of Charges

4       The Accused faced ten charges in respect of his acts against six victims. He pleaded guilty to five of the charges, and consented to the remaining charges being taken into consideration for the purposes of sentencing (“TIC”), as detailed in the tables below.

(a)     One charge under PC s 376A(1)(a) punishable under s 376A(2)(b), concerning his sexual penetration of a minor:

(c)     Four charges under PC s 377BB(5) punishable under s 377BB(7), concerning his video recording of the private regions (ie, genitals, breasts and/or buttocks) of four victims during their sexual encounters with him, without their consent:

Charge

Law relating to the SPOM Charge

Statutory Provisions

21     For the SPOM Charge, the Accused is liable to imprisonment for a term which may extend to ten years, or to a fine, or to both. The relevant offence and punishment provisions (PC s 376A(1)(a) punishable under s 376A(2)) are as follows:

Sexual penetration of minor below 16 years of age

376A.—(1)    Any person (A) who —

(a)    penetrates, with A’s penis, the vagina, anus or mouth, as the case may be, of a person below 16 years of age (B);

…

shall be guilty of an offence.

…

(2)    Whoever commits an offence under this section against a person (B) who is of or above 14 years of age but below 16 years of age —

(a)    in a case where the offender is in a relationship that is exploitative of B, shall be punished with imprisonment for a term which may extend to 20 years, and shall also be liable to fine or to caning; and

(b)    in any other case, shall be punished with imprisonment for a term which may extend to 10 years, or with fine, or with both.

The AQW indicative sentencing range

22     In AQW v Public Prosecutor [2015] 4 SLR 150 (“AQW”) at [41], the court held that for an offence under PC s 376A, the starting point sentence is between ten and 12 months’ imprisonment, based on the following circumstances:

(a)     the sexual act was fellatio, ie, penile-oral penetration;

(b)     the minor is of or above 14 years of age and does not appear particularly vulnerable;

(c)     the offender did not coerce or pressure the minor into participating in the sexual act; and

(d)     there was no element of abuse of trust.

23     I further note that AQW and the precedents cited in arriving at the indicative starting point sentencing range involved guilty pleas.

Sentencing analysis and decision

24     In relation to the SPOM Charge, the Prosecution sought a sentence of 16 to 18 months’ imprisonment.[note: 6] The Defence sought a sentence of 14 months’ imprisonment.[note: 7]

Offence-specific harm and culpability factors

25     I am satisfied that a sentence beyond the indicative sentencing range in AQW is warranted. Seven offence-specific factors, going to both harm and culpability, support this conclusion.

(a)     First, the Accused had used the internet to procure sexual services from V1. As the Accused admitted, he had come up with a scheme that “would allow him to receive sexual services from girls and women on Locanto”, “a website for classified adverts”.[note: 8] The High Court has emphasised its “contempt for such predatory behaviour in the digital realm”, observing – in the context of offences under the same provision (ie, PC s 376A(1)(a)) – that using the internet with the intention of committing sexual offences is an aggravating factor (Yap Lee Kok v Public Prosecutor [2021] SGHC 78 (“Yap Lee Kok (HC)”) at [8]–[9], where the accused had used Facebook to seek females to befriend and to pursue sexual relations with them). See also the discussion at [29(a)] and [65(c)] below.

(b)     Second, the Accused had taken significant effort to conceal his identity through his use of a false online persona known as “Sherry”, making V1 wear a blindfold throughout the encounter, and arranging for the venue to be an accessible toilet at a Community Club. In Yap Lee Kok (HC), the court found that the use of false online monikers and meeting at a venue instead of the offender’s home revealed an intention to conceal identity and avoid detection (Yap Lee Kok (HC) at [10]; see also AQW at [61]). See also the discussion at [65(c)] below.

(c)     Third, there was significant premeditation and planning (see also Yap Lee Kok (HC) at [11]). As is evident from [9]–[13] above, the entire scheme was designed by the Accused to allow him to receive sexual services from his victims without payment, and with his identity concealed.

(d)     Fourth, the Accused had induced V1 to provide sexual services by informing her that she would receive $5,000 for such services.

(e)     Fifth, the Accused had shown a blatant disregard for V1’s clearly expressed boundaries. V1 had communicated beforehand that she did not wish to perform fellatio, yet the Accused proceeded to ask her to do so. This demonstrates that the Accused was not merely opportunistic but was willing to override V1’s stated wishes in pursuit of his own gratification. The fact that V1 ultimately complied does not diminish the gravity of this conduct; rather, it underscores that the Accused had exploited a blindfolded minor who found it difficult to refuse demands made of her in that toilet. Separately, the Accused’s act of placing his hand on V1’s breast while she was fellating him was an opportunistic act of additional violation.

(f)     Sixth, the Accused had reason to believe that V1 was a minor. He had instructed her to dress in her school uniform for the encounter, an instruction which she complied with by wearing her Secondary School uniform. While the Statement of Facts does not expressly state that the Accused knew that the Victim was a minor, the Defence did not disagree with the Prosecution’s argument on this point.[note: 9]

(g)     Seventh, the Accused (through his persona, “Sherry”) asked V1 “several times” to continue the agreement with the client, despite V1 informing “Sherry” that she did not wish to continue given that her wishes (not to engage in fellatio) were not respected.[note: 10] It is aggravating that the Accused had attempted to extract further sexual services from a minor, and to continue having sexual interactions with her after the offence.

Offender-specific factors

26     In relation to offender-specific factors, I make two observations:

(a)     First, there is a TIC charge involving the same victim, namely Voyeurism Charge 3. While this would ordinarily be an offender-specific aggravating factor, I do not factor it into the sentence for the SPOM Charge as it will be separately considered in the context of the Voyeurism Charges. This avoids double counting the same TIC charge.

(b)     Second, it is mitigating that the Accused had pleaded guilty to the SPOM Charge.

Comparison with precedents

27     I now turn to compare the SPOM Charge with the reported precedents. The relevant cases are AQW and the precedents cited there in, as well as Public Prosecutor v Yap Lee Kok [2020] SGDC 261 (“Yap Lee Kok (DC)”, which was appealed to the High Court in Yap Lee Kok (HC)).

(1)   AQW and precedents cited therein

28     In AQW, the 35-year-old accused became acquainted with a male minor through a Facebook account that he operated under a pseudonym. The accused knew that the minor was 14 years old at the material time. The accused met with the minor in person, and the minor eventually stayed at the accused’s home. That night, as they lay in bed, the accused hugged and kissed the minor, which the minor reciprocated. The accused then undressed both himself and the minor. He then fellated the minor, resulting in a charge under PC s 376A(1)(c). On appeal, the High Court reduced the sentence to a term of imprisonment of ten months, which was at the lower end of the indicative range of ten to 12 months (AQW at [64]). The High Court observed that there was no reason to depart from the indicative sentencing range – amongst other things, the High Court found that the offence was committed without much premeditation (AQW at [62]). In addition, the High Court imposed a sentence at the lower end of the range in view of the accused’s “good prospects of rehabilitation” (AQW at [64]).

29     There are significantly more aggravating factors in the present case than in AQW which, taken together, warrant a sentence significantly above the ten months’ imprisonment imposed in AQW. I highlight five differences:

(a)     First, unlike in AQW where there was nothing to suggest that the accused’s use of Facebook was with the intention of committing the sexual offence against the minor (see AQW at [60] and Yap Lee Kok (HC) at [8]), the Accused here had deliberately leveraged an internet platform to procure sexual services from his victims. Indeed, it was through V1’s response to the Accused’s online advertisement that led to the sexual encounter.

(b)     Second, the present case involved significant premeditation, planning, and deliberate steps to conceal the Accused’s identity. In contrast, the court in AQW found that there had not been much premeditation (AQW at [62]).

(c)     Third, the Accused had induced V1 to provide sexual services with a promise of payment of $5,000, a feature absent in AQW.

(d)     Fourth, the Accused showed a blatant disregard for V1’s clearly expressed boundaries by demanding fellatio despite her prior objections and subsequently seeking to persuade her to provide such services again. In contrast, there was no suggestion in AQW that the minor had been pressured to engage in the sexual acts (AQW at [8]).

(e)     Fifth, unlike the accused in AQW who was found to have good prospects of rehabilitation, the same cannot be said of the Accused in the present case.

30     The present case is also more aggravated than three precedents analysed in AQW, which each resulted in a sentence of 12 months’ imprisonment per charge of engaging in fellatio with a minor. These cases did not involve the elements of premeditation and planning; concealment of identity; inducement to provide sexual services; elements of coercion or exertion of pressure; or disregarding a minor’s expressed boundaries. In brief:

(a)     In Public Prosecutor v Suhaimi bin Shamsudin DAC 98971/2013 (discussed in AQW at [30]), a 23-year-old accused met a 14-year-old minor through a mobile phone application, and they engaged in consensual sexual activity which included mutual fellation.

(b)     In Public Prosecutor v Lim Zhixiang Adin DAC 22916/2013 (discussed in AQW at [31]), a 24-year-old accused met a 14-year-old minor through Facebook. They checked into a chalet and, that night, began hugging and kissing. The accused then fellated the minor.

(c)     In Public Prosecutor v Alex Fong Guo Yuan DAC 12314/2010 (discussed in AQW at [32]), a 26-year-old accused met a 13-year-old minor online, and through conversations on an instant messaging platform, the accused asked the minor if he was interested in meeting for sex, to which the minor said yes. The minor fellated the accused on two occasions.

31     The present case is materially more aggravated than all the abovementioned precedents.

(2)   Yap Lee Kok

32     In Yap Lee Kok (DC), the accused pleaded guilty to two charges under PC s 376A(1)(a). In this case, the accused had befriended the victim – a 14-year-old female – through Facebook, learnt about her age, and initiated conversations of a sexual nature. They exchanged photographs of his penis and her breasts and vagina. This eventually led to the sexual encounters that were the subject of the two proceeded charges:

(a)     The first proceeded charge concerned the accused’s penile-oral penetration of the minor in the rear of the accused’s vehicle. During fellatio, the accused rubbed the minor’s exposed vagina with his finger and exposed her breasts by pulling her brassiere and t-shirt upwards, before sucking and rubbing her right nipple. The District Court considered AQW and imposed a sentence of 12 months’ imprisonment for this charge (ie, at the high end of the indicative sentencing range). No appeal was brought against this sentence.

(b)     The second proceeded charge concerned the accused’s penile-vaginal penetration of the same female on the same occasion, after she had fellated him (which was the subject matter of the first charge). He penetrated her vagina with his penis, before she fellated him a second time. After the second fellatio, he instructed her to lie down, held her legs apart with his hands, and penetrated her exposed vagina with his penis for a second time. Following penetration, he pulled his erect penis from her vagina and ejaculated on her stomach and face. The District Court imposed a sentence of 18 months’ imprisonment for this charge. The sentence was upheld by the High Court in Yap Lee Kok (HC).

33     In imposing the above sentences, the District Court considered three TIC charges, namely – two charges under PC s 376A(1)(a) (relating to the first penile-vaginal penetration and the second fellatio), and one charge under PC s 292(1)(a) amalgamated under CPC s 124(4) (relating to the accused sending eight photographs of his penis to the minor).

34     Of the two proceeded charges in Yap Lee Kok (DC), the SPOM Charge is less egregious than the second proceeded charge. As observed by the Defence, the second proceeded charge in Yap Lee Kok (DC) involved penile-vaginal penetration of a minor and other aggravating factors (such as the lack of consent to vaginal penetration and the non-use of a condom which carried with it the unwanted risk of pregnancy).[note: 11] The first proceeded charge in Yap Lee Kok (DC) bears greater similar to the SPOM Charge, and it is against this charge that comparison should be made.

35     In relation to offence-specific factors:

(a)     On the one hand, the SPOM Charge is more aggravated than the first proceeded charge in Yap Lee Kok (DC). This is in view that:

(i)       First, the Accused had concealed his identity from V1 through the use of the “Sherry” persona, and by requiring V1 to be blindfolded throughout the encounter. Although a moniker was used in Yap Lee Kok (DC), the victim was not prevented from seeing the accused’s face or identifying him.

(ii)       Second, the Accused induced V1 to provide sexual services by promising payment of $5,000. There was no such inducement in Yap Lee Kok (DC).

(iii)       Third, the Accused went beyond V1’s indicated boundaries regarding her unwillingness to perform fellatio by asking her to fellate him when she was blindfolded and in a confined space (ie, an accessible toilet) with him. In Yap Lee Kok (DC), it appears that the victim had agreed after some persuasion to meet with the accused to perform fellatio on him (Yap Lee Kok (DC) at [6(a)] and [10(b)]).

(b)     On the other hand, the first proceeded charge in Yap Lee Kok (DC) is more aggravated than the SPOM Charge in that the accused had forged a friendship with the victim prior to the sexual encounter and had additionally made skin-to-skin contact with the victim’s vagina and nipple during the encounter (see [32(a)]).

36     In relation to offender-specific factors:

(a)     First, while there were related TIC charges in Yap Lee Kok (DC) (see [33] above), it is unclear if or how these were factored into the sentence of 12 months’ imprisonment on the first proceeded charge.

(b)     Second, on appeal, the High Court noted the accused’s efforts in voluntarily attending counselling sessions and observed that these were “indicative of his resolve to change”, and that “rehabilitation therefore factors into the sentencing equation” although deterrence and retribution ultimately remained the paramount considerations (Yap Lee Kok (HC) at [23]). In contrast, there is nothing in the present case that would similarly bring rehabilitation into the sentencing equation.

Sentence for the SPOM Charge

37     Having considered the offence-specific and offender-specific factors in relation to the SPOM Charge, as well as the various sentencing precedents, I agree with the Defence that an appropriate imprisonment term for the SPOM Charge is 14 months’ imprisonment. This is above the indicative sentencing range in AQW, and is warranted by the numerous aggravating factors in this case. No further sentencing reduction is given on account of the Accused’s guilty plea, given that the cited precedents concerned sentencing in guilty plea scenarios.

Law relating to the Fraud Charges

Statutory Provisions

58     For each of Fraud Charges 1 and 2, the Accused is liable to imprisonment for a term not exceeding ten years, or to a fine, or to both. The relevant offence and punishment provisions (PC s 420A(1) punishable under s 420A(2)) are as follows:

Obtaining services dishonestly or fraudulently

420A.—(1)    A person shall be guilty of an offence if he obtains services for himself or another person dishonestly or fraudulently and —

(a)    the services are made available on the basis that payment has been, is being or will be made for or in respect of them;

(b)    the person obtains the services without any payment having been made for or in respect of them or without payment having been made in full; and

(c)    when the person obtains the services —

(i)    the person knows that they are being made available on the basis mentioned in paragraph (a) or that they might be; and

(ii)   the person intends that payment will not be made or will not be made in full.

(2)    A person who is guilty of an offence under subsection (1) shall on conviction be liable to imprisonment for a term not exceeding 10 years, or to fine, or to both.

Whether the De Beers framework applies

59     In relation to the sentencing approach, the Prosecution submitted that guidance should be taken from De Beers, which established the sentencing framework for cases involving cheating to procure sex and other sexual acts under PC s 417.[note: 14] The Prosecution submitted that both De Beers and the Fraud Charges involved an offender posing as a freelance agent to lure victims who wanted to provide sexual services for money, and deceived them into providing sexual services to the offender himself. However, given that the maximum imprisonment term under PC s 420A(2) (ten years’ imprisonment) is more than three times higher than that under PC s 417 (three years’ imprisonment), the Prosecution submitted that an uplift ought to be imposed on the sentencing ranges set out in De Beers.[note: 15]

60     Defence Counsel disagreed with the Prosecution on the application of De Beers. Instead, Defence Counsel submitted that the applicable guidance is found in Public Prosecutor v Abdul Rahman Bin A Karim [2021] SGDC 72 (“Abdul Rahman”), where the court declined to propose a sentencing matrix for offences under PC s 420A (see Abdul Rahman at [57]–[59]).

61     I agree with the Prosecution that it is appropriate to adapt the De Beers sentencing framework in relation to the Fraud Charges, for the following reasons.

(a)     First, as the Prosecution rightly observed (see [59] above), there are close parallels between the offence of cheating to procure sex (under PC s 417) and that of obtaining sexual services dishonestly or fraudulently (under PC s 420A). I acknowledge that in De Beers, the court expressed doubt as to whether PC s 420A would have applied to the facts before it (De Beers at [35]). However, that doubt arose from two features in that case: the victims were “auditioning for a role” rather than providing sexual “services” to the accused, and were in any event not doing so with any expectation of payment (De Beers at [35]). The court was not suggesting that the sentencing framework developed for cases involving cheating to procure sex under PC s 417 cannot be suitably adapted to the dishonest or fraudulent obtaining of sexual services under PC s 420A.

(b)     Second, in Abdul Rahman, the court had declined to propose a sentencing framework for PC s 420A on the basis that such offences may arise in factually diverse situations involving varying degrees of harm and culpability (Abdul Rahman at [59(b)]). That reservation must, however, be understood in its proper context: the court in Abdul Rahman did not have the benefit of De Beers, which had yet to be decided. In De Beers, the court acknowledged that cheating offences under PC s 417 did not readily lend themselves to a sentencing framework because of the array of different scenarios that might arise, but nonetheless found it appropriate to establish a harm-culpability sentencing matrix for a “particular species of cheating” involving “cheating to procure sex and other sexual acts” (De Beers at [38]). In my view, the reasoning applies with equal force to PC s 420A: a sentencing matrix can be usefully applied to a particular species of offending under PC s 420A that involves the dishonest or fraudulent obtaining of sexual services.

(c)     Third, the harm-culpability sentencing matrix in De Beers accounts for the full range of sentences provided for in the offence-creating provision, and does not ignore the higher ranges of sentences that may be imposed (De Beers at [40]). This helps ameliorate the potential concern that prosecuting offences that involve a violation of a victim’s bodily and sexual integrity under PC s 417 may result in understating the gravity of such offences (De Beers at [40]). These observations apply with equal force to PC s 420A. As with offences involving cheating for sex under PC s 417, offences involving the dishonest or fraudulent obtaining of sexual services under PC s 420A likewise “rank at a particularly high level of odium and gravity” (De Beers at [39]) within the sentencing range prescribed for the offence.

(d)     Fourth, I acknowledge that two post-De Beers decisions involving PC s 420A did not apply the De Beers framework – namely, Public Prosecutor v Tan Chip Huat [2022] SGDC 180 (“Tan Chip Huat”) and Public Prosecutor v Ng Hui Yi [2022] SGDC 279 (“Ng Hui Yi”). Both courts instead applied Abdul Rahman (see Tan Chip Huat at [79]–[84] and Ng Hui Yi at [63]). That said, De Beers was not discussed in those cases. I therefore do not regard those decisions as foreclosing the approach I have taken.
