Public Prosecutor v Liu Emin

Public Prosecutor v Liu Emin
[2026] SGMC 84

Case Number:Magistrate Arrest Case No. 908840 of 2024
Decision Date:01 July 2026
Tribunal/Court:Magistrate's Court
Coram: Samuel Wee
Counsel Name(s): Houston Johannus (Ministry of Manpower) for the Prosecution; The Defendant in person.
Parties: Public Prosecutor — Liu Emin

Criminal Law – Offences – Section 22(1)(d) of the Employment of Foreign Manpower Act 1990 (2020 Rev Ed) – Applicability of the presumptions under section 15(1) of the Employment of Foreign Manpower Act 1990 (2020 Rev Ed)

Criminal Law – Offences – Section 22(1)(d) of the Employment of Foreign Manpower Act 1990 (2020 Rev Ed) – Whether knowledge is established when the accused person did not read the statement

1 July 2026

Judgment reserved.

District Judge Samuel Wee:

Introduction

1       Ping An Dentist Pte Ltd (“Ping An”) submitted an Employment Pass (“EP”) application for Mr Huang Hsin Yuan (“Mr Huang”), which incorrectly stated his monthly salary as $8,000 (“EP Application”).[note: 1] Ping An’s director, Ms Liu Emin (“Ms Liu”), had permitted her staff to use her CorpPass account to complete and submit the EP Application to the Ministry of Manpower (“MOM”),[note: 2] and subsequently signed a related Declaration Form without realising it reflected Mr Huang’s salary as $8,000.[note: 3]

2       Ms Liu was charged under s 22(1)(d) read with s 20(1)(a), punishable under s 22(1)(i) of the Employment of Foreign Manpower Act 1990 (2020 Rev Ed) (“EFMA”) for consenting to Ping An making a statement to the Controller of Work Passes (“Controller”) in connection with the EP Application which Ping An knew was false in a material particular (“False Statement Offence”).[note: 4] The charge states:[note: 5]

You … are charged that, on or about 10 January 2023, in Singapore, [Ping An], a body corporate of which you were a Director, in connection with an application for an Employment Pass for [Mr Huang], did make a statement which [Ping An] knew was false in a material particular to the Controller of Work Passes (the “Controller”) of the Ministry of Manpower (“MOM”) in a Declaration Form (the “Form”) which was submitted to the Work Pass Division, MOM, which offence was committed with your consent, to wit, in your capacity as Director of [Ping An], you declared for and on behalf of [Ping An] in the Form that the fixed monthly salary of the said [Mr Huang] was to be $8,000, when you knew this was false and you have thereby committed an offence under section 22(1)(d) read with section 20(1)(a) of the Employment of Foreign Manpower Act 1990 (“EFMA”), which offence is punishable under section 22(1)(i) of the EFMA.

Facts

Mr Huang seeks employment with Ping An

3       Ping An employed Mr Huang in August 2022 under a Work Permit,[note: 6] with a starting basic monthly salary of $5,000 plus potential monthly variable incentives of up to $800.[note: 7] During his recruitment interviews, Mr Huang told Ping An’s management team (“Management Team”, comprising Ms Liu and Mr Wong Leong Wei (“Mr Wong”))[note: 8] that he wanted assistance in applying for an S Pass or EP, which he believed would improve his chances of becoming a Permanent Resident in Singapore.[note: 9]

4       Mr Huang completed his probation in November 2022 and his basic monthly salary was increased to $5,500 (“5.5k Salary”).[note: 10] Ping An decided to help Mr Huang apply for an EP (rather than an S Pass) because the Management Team believed that Mr Huang’s 5.5k Salary met the requirements for both[note: 11] –the Prosecution’s witness, Mr Wong, confirmed that Ping An saw no difference between an S Pass and an EP application for Mr Huang as the 5.5k Salary “[f]its both categories”.[note: 12]

5       On 10 January 2023, Ms Liu logged into her CorpPass account and permitted her front desk staff (“FD Staff”) to complete and submit the EP Application.[note: 13]

(a)     She wrote the details for the EP Application (including Mr Huang’s 5.5k Salary) on a piece of paper (“Information Paper”) and provided it to the FD Staff to complete and submit.[note: 14] Ms Liu was unable to recall the identity of the FD Staff due to Ping An’s numerous employees.[note: 15]

(b)     At the time, the Management Team did not know that the EP Application[note: 16] submitted by the FD Staff listed Mr Huang’s fixed monthly salary as $8,000 (“8k Statement”),[note: 17] comprising a basic monthly salary of $5,500 and fixed monthly allowances of $2,500.[note: 18] In this regard, there is no evidence that Ms Liu read the EP Application to verify the details before its submission to MOM.

6       On 26 January 2023, MOM issued its in-principle written approval of the EP Application,[note: 19] following which both Ping An and Mr Huang had to sign the Declaration Form.[note: 20]

(a)     The Declaration Form comprised five pages.[note: 21]

(i)       The first page reflected Mr Huang’s details, the 8k Statement, and other declarations relating to Mr Huang.

(ii)       The second page contained further declarations relating to Mr Huang. In particular, it stated:

I declare that the information in this Application for an Employment Pass, Declaration Form and any appeals are, to the best of my knowledge, true and correct; and that all documents submitted in support for this Application, Declaration Form and any appeals, are true copies of the original.

(iii)       The third page was for Mr Huang to sign.

(iv)       The fourth page reflected declarations relating to Ping An.

(v)       The fifth page contained further declarations relating to Ping An and was for Ping An to sign. In particular, it stated:

I declare that the information in this Application for a Employment Pass, Declaration Form and any appeals are, to the best of my knowledge, true and correct; and that all documents submitted in support for this Application, Declaration Form and any appeals, are true copies of the originals.

(b)     Ms Liu signed the Declaration Form for Ping An on 26 January 2023[note: 22] without reading it and was not aware of the 8k Statement on the first page.[note: 23] Contrary to the Prosecution’s assertion, there is no evidence showing that she had read or been aware of the contents of the EP Application (particularly the 8k Statement) when she signed the Declaration Form (see [58]-[59] below).

(c)     Mr Huang signed the Declaration Form on 28 January 2023. Like Ms Liu, he did not read the Declaration Form and was not aware of the 8k Statement.[note: 24] Mr Huang also testified that Ping An never discussed a potential monthly salary of $8,000 with him,[note: 25] and there is no evidence to substantiate the Prosecution’s assertion that Ms Liu had deliberately hidden the 8k Statement from Mr Huang to get him to sign the Declaration Form.[note: 26]

7       The signed Declaration Form was submitted and Mr Huang received his EP.

8       Based on Mr Huang’s income statements, his salary did not exceed $5,500 from November 2022 to July 2023.[note: 27]

MOM’s detection of the False Statement Offence

9       Mr Huang ceased employment with Ping An in July 2023.[note: 28]

10     He filed a complaint with MOM concerning unpaid amounts relating to his 5.5k Salary,[note: 29] which resulted in MOM discovering that the 8k Statement was false.[note: 30] The details of this complaint are unrelated to the 8k Statement and the present proceedings.[note: 31]

11     After investigations by MOM, Ms Liu was charged for the False Statement Offence on 19 November 2024. She provided her statement under s 23 of the Criminal Procedure Code 2010 (2020 Rev Ed) (“Section 23 Statement”) in Mandarin, which was translated as follows:[note: 32]

The application was not made by me.

I employed a lot of workers.

I cannot recall the application was made by who.

It has been a long time since the application was made via my Singpass.

That was a mistake by the admin.

I know that since I am the boss of the company, I will be responsible. I plead with the authority to give me a chance.

The issues

12     For Ms Liu to be convicted of the False Statement Offence, the Prosecution must establish four elements:[note: 33]

(a)     Ping An must have made a statement to the Controller (“First Element”).

(b)     The statement must have been made in connection with an application for a work pass (“Second Element”).

(c)     Ping An must have known that the statement was false in a material particular (“Third Element”).

(d)     Ms Liu must have known about and consented to Ping An’s making of the false statement (“Fourth Element”).

13     The First to Third Elements deal with whether Ping An (as a primary offender) has committed an offence under s 22(1)(d) of the EFMA, while the Fourth Element addresses whether Ms Liu (as a secondary offender) should be personally liable for Ping An’s offence.[note: 34]

14     The Prosecution contends that all four elements are met.

(a)     It asserts that the First and Second Elements are apparent from the incontrovertible facts.[note: 35]

(b)     It contends that the Third Element is established, by relying on s 15(1) of the EFMA to argue that Ms Liu is presumed to have knowledge of the 8k Statement and that she bears the burden of proving its truth (“Section 15 Presumptions”).[note: 36]

(c)     It argues that the Fourth Element is established based on the following:

(i)       Ms Liu must have instructed the FD Staff to include the 8k Statement and therefore knew of its inclusion in the EP Application;[note: 37]

(ii)       Ms Liu’s signing of the Declaration Form proves her knowledge of the 8k Statement and her consent to it;[note: 38] and

(iii)       Ms Liu’s motive for making a false statement to the Controller was to reward Mr Huang, while Ping An would “likely” also benefit from not having to pay a foreign worker levy for Mr Huang.[note: 39]

15     Based on Ms Liu’s Closing Submissions, her defence centres on the following assertions:[note: 40]

(a)     She merely instructed the FD Staff to input Mr Huang’s 5.5k Salary into the EP Application, and had no knowledge that the 8k Statement was included.

(b)     The FD Staff must have keyed the 8k Statement in error.

16     I find that the Prosecution has failed to establish the Fourth Element beyond a reasonable doubt and acquit Ms Liu of the False Statement Offence.

The First and Second Elements are established – Ping An made a statement to the Controller in connection with the EP Application

17     The First and Second Elements are established.

18     It is clear from the EP Application that the 8k Statement was made to the Controller in connection with an application for an EP,[note: 41] and Ms Liu confirmed during cross-examination that it was Ping An that submitted the EP Application for Mr Huang.[note: 42]

The Third Element is established – Ping An is presumed to have known that the 8k Statement is false in material particular

The approach towards the Third Element

19     The Third Element requires Ping An to have knowledge that the 8k Statement is false in material particular.

20     Having reviewed the legislative history of s 22(1)(d) of the EFMA, there are, in my view, two factual thresholds that must be established before I can answer the main question of whether Ping An had knowledge that the 8k Statement is false in material particular:

(a)     First, that Ping An had knowledge of the 8k Statement in the EP Application (“Threshold A”).

(b)     Second, that the 8k Statement is false in material particular (“Threshold B”).

The legislative history of s 22(1)(d) of the EFMA

21     The legislative history of s 22(1)(d) of the EFMA reveals that the requirement that the applicant has knowledge of the false statement (“Knowledge Requirement”) was deliberately introduced.

22     Initially, s 22(1)(d) of the Employment of Foreign Workers Act (Cap 91A, 1997 Rev Ed) (which was the predecessor of the EFMA) did not contain the Knowledge Requirement and provided:

Any person who … makes any statement or furnishes any information to the Controller or an employment inspector under this Act which is false in any material particular or is misleading by reason of the omission of any material particular … shall be guilty of an offence …

23     Subsequently, the Knowledge Requirement was introduced on 1 July 2007 through the Employment of Foreign Workers (Amendment) Act 2007 (Act No 30 of 2007), whereupon the Act was renamed the Employment of Foreign Manpower Act (Cap 91A, 1997 Rev Ed) and s 22(1)(d) provided:

Any person who … makes any statement or furnishes any information to the Controller or an employment inspector under this Act which he knows or ought reasonably to know is false in any material particular or is misleading by reason of the omission of any material particular … shall be guilty of an offence …

24     Finally, the current iteration of s 22(1)(d) of the EFMA, which retained the Knowledge Requirement, was introduced in November 2012 through the Employment of Foreign Manpower (Amendment) Act 2012 (Act No 24 of 2012) and states:

Any person who … in connection with any application for or to renew a work pass or for any other purpose under this Act, makes any statement or provides any information to the Controller or an authorised officer or employment inspector which the person knows, or ought reasonably to know, is false in any material particular or is misleading by reason of the omission of any material particular … shall be guilty of an offence …

25     The Knowledge Requirement means that liability requires more than just making a false statement to the Controller in connection with an application for a work pass. The Prosecution must prove that the person knew that the statement was in the application and that it was false.[note: 43]

26     This view is supported by the Parliamentary Debates during the Second Reading of the Employment of Foreign Manpower Bill (Bill No 22 of 2012) on 11 September 2012, where the then Acting Minister for Manpower Mr Tan Chuan-Jin emphasised the link between a person’s innocence and his lack of knowledge of the relevant statement (albeit in the context of the Section 15 Presumptions) (see Singapore Parl Debates; Vol 89, Sitting No 7; Page 730; [11 September 2012]):[note: 44]

Second, we will prosecute foreign workers that submit forged educational qualifications to circumvent MOM's criteria for educational qualifications, especially for S Pass and EP holders. Offenders will be subject to a maximum fine of $20,000, or to a maximum imprisonment term of two years, or to both. Foreign workers have also been known to submit forged educational qualifications and subsequently feign ignorance of the submission, which hampers our enforcement efforts in proving that they had knowledge of the falsehood. Hence, we will now presume that a work pass applicant has knowledge of the information provided in his application, including that of the qualifications which have been submitted. The burden of proof will now be placed on the errant workers. My Ministry will ensure that enforcement action is targeted at culpable workers. An innocent worker can rebut the presumption by proving that he did not have knowledge of the submission of false qualifications when the declaration was made. For instance, he can prove that the employment agency or employer had submitted the forged certificate on his behalf without his knowledge. My Ministry will take action against other culpable parties, such as errant employers and employment agents, if they have abetted such acts.

[Emphasis added.]

The Section 15 Presumptions

27     The Section 15 Presumptions are set out in s 15 of the EFMA, which states:

Burden of proof, etc.

15.—(1)    For the purposes of section 7, and any proceedings in respect of any prescribed infringement or any offence under this Act —

(a)    a person who makes an application for a work pass is presumed, until the contrary is proved, to have knowledge of the information provided in the application; and

(b)    subject to subsection (2), the burden of proving the truth of the contents of an application for a work pass is on the person who makes the application.

(2)    Where any application for a work pass is made by more than one person, then for the purposes specified in subsection (1), each applicant bears the burden of proving the truth of the contents of the application that relate to the applicant.

28     The Section 15 Presumptions apply to “a person who makes an application for a work pass” (“Section 15 Applicant”) and have two aspects.[note: 45]

(a)     Under s 15(1)(a), the Section 15 Applicant is presumed to have knowledge of the information in the application unless the contrary is proven (“Knowledge Presumption”), which relates to Threshold A.

(b)     Under s 15(1)(b), the Section 15 Applicant bears the burden of proving the truth of the statement (“Falsity Presumption”), which relates to Threshold B.

The Prosecution asserts that the two aspects of the Section 15 Presumptions are disjunctive, and that the Falsity Presumption applies even if the Prosecution does not rely on the Knowledge Presumption.[note: 46]

29     Both Mr Huang and Ping An fall within the definition of a Section 15 Applicant in the present case.

(a)     Under regs 4(a), 5(a) and 6(a) of the Employment of Foreign Manpower (Work Passes) Regulations 2012, an application for a work pass would typically be made by two co-applicants:[note: 47]

(i)       the foreign employee (“Co-Applicant 1”); and

(ii)       the employer, or on behalf of the employer by a person authorised by the employer (“Co-Applicant 2”).

(b)     Co-Applicant 1 is Mr Huang (the foreign employee),[note: 48] while Co-Applicant 2 is Ping An (the employer). This is apparent from the fact that MOM addressed the in-principle written approval of the EP Application to both Mr Huang and Ping An.[note: 49]

(c)     In this regard, I disagree with the Prosecution’s argument that Co-Applicant 2 should be Ms Liu rather than Ping An.[note: 50]

(i)       The Prosecution characterised Ms Liu as “being the employer of [Mr Huang]”[note: 51] because the EP Application was submitted using her CorpPass account,[note: 52] she had given instructions for the submission of Mr Huang’s EP Application, and she was the one who signed the Declaration Form on Ping An’s behalf.[note: 53]

(ii)       This cannot be correct, as it conflates the identity of Ping An with its director, Ms Liu, which is inconsistent with the doctrine of separate legal personalities.

(iii)       The Prosecution’s position is also contradicted by the documentary evidence that shows that Ping An was Mr Huang’s employer:

(A)       The initial Work Permit application reflects Ping An under the “Name of Employer”.[note: 54]

(B)       The EP Application reflects Ping An under the “Company name”.[note: 55]

(C)       The in-principle written approval of the EP Application reflects Ping An under the “Name of Employer/Sponsor”.[note: 56]

(D)       The employment documents that the Prosecution relied on were all issued by Ping An (as the employer).[note: 57]

(iv)       The Prosecution’s position is also fundamentally inconsistent with the charge for the False Statement Offence (see [2] above), which positions Ping An as the primary offender of an offence under s 22(1)(d) of the EFMA and Ms Liu as the secondary offender under s 20(1)(a) of the EFMA in her capacity as a director of Ping An.[note: 58]

(d)     In any event, the outcome of this case would remain the same even if Ms Liu is treated as Co-Applicant 2 for the reasons set out at [56]-[57] below.

Threshold A: Ping An is presumed to have knowledge of the 8k Statement

30     The Prosecution relies on the Knowledge Presumption to argue that Ping An is presumed to have knowledge of the 8k Statement in the EP Application when it was submitted on 10 January 2023 (“10 Jan 2023 Submission”).[note: 59]

31     As set out at [29] above, Ping An is a Section 15 Applicant to whom the Knowledge Presumption applies. Ping An is therefore presumed to have knowledge of the 8k Statement in the 10 Jan 2023 Submission.

32     To rebut the Knowledge Presumption, it must be established that two categories of people were not aware of the 8k Statement in the 10 Jan 2023 Submission:

(a)     The Management Team, comprising Ms Liu and Mr Wong.

(b)     The FD Staff who submitted the EP Application using Ms Liu’s CorpPass account.

33     While there is evidence that the Management Team had no knowledge of the 8k Statement in the 10 Jan 2023 Submission, there is no evidence that the FD Staff had no knowledge.

The Management Team

34     There is sufficient evidence that both Ms Liu and Mr Wong were not aware of the 8k Statement in the 10 Jan 2023 Submission.

(a)     Ms Liu testified that she left the FD Staff to fill in and submit the EP Application, and did not know that the 8k Statement was included (see [5] above). Her testimony is consistent with and corroborated by her Section 23 Statement (see [11] above).[note: 60]

(b)     Mr Wong likewise testified that he was not aware of the 8k Statement and that it must have been an error.[note: 61]

(c)     There is no evidence of anyone from Ping An ever discussing a salary of $8,000 for Mr Huang,[note: 62] which supports Ms Liu’s position. Indeed, Mr Wong confirmed during trial that this salary was never discussed by Ping An’s Management Team (who had intended the 5.5k Salary),[note: 63] and Mr Huang maintained that it was never conveyed to him.[note: 64]

35     Furthermore, the Prosecution’s failure to establish the following two points means that there is no objective basis to cast doubt on the credibility of Ms Liu’s evidence.

36     First, the Prosecution has not proven that Ms Liu gave the FD Staff express instructions to input the 8k Statement in the 10 Jan 2023 Submission.[note: 65]

(a)     It is not disputed that Ms Liu was the one who provided the details for the EP Application to the FD Staff to fill in and submit by writing the relevant details on the Information Paper for the FD Staff to refer to (see [5] above).

(b)     However, there is no evidence that the Information Paper listed Mr Huang’s salary as $8,000 instead of the 5.5k Salary, or of anyone from Ping An ever discussing a salary of $8,000 for Mr Huang (see [34(c)] above).

(c)     Moreover, there is a reasonable possibility that the 8k Statement was keyed in error:

(i)       According to Ms Penny Lai (“Ms Lai”, the Prosecution’s witness from MOM), a primary entry is inputted for the fixed monthly salary (“Primary Entry”) before two secondary entries can be made for the basic monthly salary (“Secondary Entry 1”) and fixed monthly allowances (“Secondary Entry 2”).[note: 66]

(ii)       Ms Lai testified that she was unsure whether any data would be automatically populated in Secondary Entry 1 and Secondary Entry 2 in response to an entry into the Primary Entry.[note: 67] For example, if $8,000 was keyed into the Primary Entry, she was uncertain whether Secondary Entry 1 would automatically show $8,000 by default, or whether Secondary Entry 1 and Secondary Entry 2 would remain blank for manual input. Ms Lai was also unsure whether an entry of $5,500 in Secondary Entry 1 would result in an automatic adjustment in Secondary Entry 2 to $2,500 (to ensure the total tallied with the Primary Entry).[note: 68]

(iii)       Consequently, it remains reasonably possible that the FD Staff may have keyed the Primary Entry erroneously, and thereafter sought to “fix” the error by inputting the 5.5k Salary under Secondary Entry 1, without noticing the figure in Secondary Entry 2 or that he (or she) also had to change the Primary Entry to the 5.5k Salary.

(d)     I therefore do not agree with the Prosecution that it is “wholly unlikely that [the FD Staff] would have been mistaken in keying the relevant details”,[note: 69] and find that the Prosecution’s assertion that Ms Liu “proceeded to instruct her staff to key in [Mr] Huang’s fixed monthly salary as $8,000”[note: 70] is not substantiated.

(e)     I also do not agree with the Prosecution’s argument that Ms Liu’s testimony under cross-examination was a “volte-face from her Evidence-in-Chief where she claimed that one of her many workers had filled in the salary details in [Mr Huang’s EP Application] and she had therefore neither control nor awareness of what was being filled in”, and that she was attempting to conceal the truth.[note: 71]

(i)       The Prosecution relies on the following extract from Ms Liu’s testimony during her evidence-in-chief (“EIC Extract”) to assert that the EP Application in its entirety was submitted by the FD Staff “without [Ms Liu’s] knowledge and instruction”:[note: 72]

I don’t even have my own personal workspace. I could only work using the computer at the front desk, and there will be many staff who would use the computer at the front desk. Although this application - that is, this EP application - was made using my Corppass account, but it was my worker who had filled in the details at that time …[note: 73]

I also just want to summarise by saying there is no evidence from the Ministry of Manpower that I was the one who had filled this in, directed this information to be filled in, because I do not have any need to do so. I had many workers at that time, and it was very fluid. There were about 20 to 30 workers, including students, interns, part-timers and full-timers. I do not know which one of these workers had filled in this $2,500 allowance.[note: 74]

(ii)       I disagree with the Prosecution’s position. Viewed in context, the EIC Extract merely conveys that Ms Liu did not know what the FD Staff had inputted for a specific part of the EP Application (ie. the fixed monthly allowance of $2,500), and cannot be read to mean that Ms Liu was unaware that the FD Staff had submitted the EP Application in its entirety.

(iii)       The EIC Extract is therefore consistent with Ms Liu’s testimony during cross-examination, where she explained the following:[note: 75]

(A)       She wrote the details of the EP Application (including Mr Huang’s 5.5k Salary) on the Information Paper and provided it to the FD Staff to complete and submit (see [5(a)] above).

(B)       She was unable to recall the identity of the FD Staff due to Ping An’s numerous employees (see [5(a)] above).

(C)       She did not know that the EP Application reflected a fixed monthly allowance of $2,500 (see [5(b)] above).

37     Second, the Prosecution has not established any intention by Ms Liu to make a false statement to the Controller for Ping An’s benefit.[note: 76]

(a)     Ping An’s Management Team believed that Mr Huang’s 5.5k Salary met the requirements for an S Pass and an EP, and saw no difference between applying for either (see [4] above). While the Prosecution has adduced evidence showing that this is incorrect (see [48] below), the Management Team’s misconceived view extinguishes the possibility that Ping An was trying to gain an advantage by making a false statement to the Controller.

(b)     The Prosecution has also failed to establish actual savings by Ping An on insurance or levy payments (which do not have to be paid by employers for employees holding an EP).[note: 77]

(i)       The Prosecution provided no evidence that Ping An failed to pay insurance or levy payments for Mr Huang after the EP Application was approved. Pertinently, the Prosecution’s Closing Submissions refrained from asserting an actual benefit to Ping An and instead referred to a “likely” (and speculative) benefit arising from savings in work permit levies.[note: 78]

(ii)       In contrast, Ms Liu testified that Ping An continued to pay for Mr Huang’s insurance and believed it was still paying the foreign worker levy for Mr Huang.[note: 79] In this regard, Ms Liu’s failure to produce documentary evidence is not fatal, as the burden remained on the Prosecution to prove actual savings (s 105 of the Evidence Act 1893 (2020 Rev Ed)).

(c)     The Prosecution’s argument that Ms Liu was motivated to commit the False Statement Offence to “fulfil [a] promise” to Mr Huang to get him an EP or S Pass (see [3]-[4] above) is unconvincing.[note: 80] There is no evidence that Ms Liu guaranteed Mr Huang an S Pass or EP,[note: 81] nor evidence of any benefit that Ping An would gain (eg. there is no evidence that Mr Huang threatened to quit if Ping An’s application for an S Pass or EP failed).

(d)     I also considered whether Ping An sought to obtain Mr Huang an EP to avoid utilising its existing quotas for S Passes or Work Permits. However, the Prosecution did not raise this, and there was no evidence on this issue. Moreover, this case is unique: Ping An had already employed Mr Huang and did not need the EP to keep him employed; Ping An was applying for the EP to help Mr Huang (see [3] above);[note: 82] and both Ms Liu and Mr Huang have given evidence that they signed the Declaration Form without reading it and realising the 8k Statement existed (see [6] above).

38     While it may have been careless to leave the FD Staff’s use of her CorpPass account unsupervised[note: 83] (which conduct may arguably constitute a separate offence), such carelessness cannot equate to Ping An’s actual knowledge of the 8k Statement in the 10 Jan 2023 Submission.[note: 84]

The FD Staff

39     The Knowledge Presumption remains unrebutted in respect of the FD Staff’s knowledge of the 8k Statement in the 10 Jan 2023 Submission.

40     Ms Liu relies on the possibility that the FD Staff keyed the 8k Statement in error.[note: 85]

41     However, as the FD Staff who completed and submitted the EP Application remains unidentified (see [5(a)] above), it is not possible to ascertain whether he (or she) was unaware of the 8k Statement.[note: 86]

42     Consequently, it has not been established that the FD Staff made an error, and the Knowledge Presumption is not rebutted.

Conclusion on Threshold A

43     The Prosecution has established that Ping An is presumed to have knowledge of the 8k Statement by virtue of the Knowledge Presumption, as there is insufficient evidence to rebut the presumption (eg. by showing that the FD Staff made an error in the EP Application).[note: 87]

44     That said, the presumption of Ping An’s knowledge of the 8k Statement by virtue of the Knowledge Presumption does not equate to Ms Liu’s knowledge of the 8k Statement for the purposes of the Fourth Element, which is discussed at [52]-[62] below.

45     For completeness, had it not been for the Knowledge Presumption, I would have found that the Prosecution failed to prove Ping An’s actual knowledge of the 8k Statement in the 10 Jan 2023 Submission because:

(a)     There is sufficient evidence showing that both Ms Liu and Mr Wong did not know that the 8k Statement was in the 10 Jan 2023 Submission (see [34]-[38] above).

(b)     The evidence disclosed a reasonable possibility that the 8k Statement was keyed in error (see [36(c)] above).

Threshold B: The 8k Statement is false in material particular

46     Under the Falsity Presumption, the burden of proving the truth of the 8k Statement falls on Ping An (as the Section 15 Applicant).

47     This burden has not been discharged, as it is clear from the facts that the 8k Statement is false since Mr Huang’s salary did not exceed $5,500 from November 2022 to July 2023 (see [8] above).[note: 88]

48     Moreover, the falsehood is material because MOM would not have approved the EP Application if it had known that Mr Huang’s fixed monthly salary was $5,500.[note: 89]

(a)     The Prosecution’s witness from MOM, Ms Lai, testified that based on Mr Huang’s age of approximately 32 years in January 2023, he would have needed a fixed monthly salary of $7,250 to qualify for an EP.[note: 90]

(b)     While Ping An’s Management Team believed that Mr Huang’s 5.5k Salary was sufficient to qualify for an EP (see [4] above), this was mistaken. Ms Lai explained that whilst the form for the EP Application lists a salary range of $5,000 to $10,000, this range is merely indicative and the actual qualifying salary depends on the applicant’s age. She further explained that Ping An should have used MOM’s online self-assessment tool to determine whether the 5.5k Salary was sufficient for Mr Huang’s age.[note: 91]

Ping An is presumed to have known that the 8k Statement is false in material particular

49     Having established Thresholds A and B, I now consider whether Ping An is deemed to have known that the 8k Statement is false in material particular.

50     Since there is no evidence suggesting that Ping An did not know that the 8k Statement was false, I am bound to find that the Third Element is established.

51     The First to Third Elements are thus established, and the Prosecution has proven that Ping An (as a primary offender) has committed an offence under s 22(1)(d) of the EFMA.

The Fourth Element is not established – Ms Liu did not know about the 8k Statement and could not have consented to it

Section 20(1)(a) of the EFMA

52     Under s 20(1)(a) of the EFMA, Ms Liu would be liable for Ping An’s offence under s 22(1)(d) of the EFMA if the Prosecution proves that it was “committed with the consent or connivance” of Ms Liu.

53     In Dao Thi Boi v Public Prosecutor [2024] 6 SLR 277, the General Division of the High Court determined that the test for consent by an officer of a corporation under s 20(1)(a) of the Endangered Species (Import and Export) Act (Cap 92A, 2008 Rev Ed) is “whether the offender can be shown to have known the material facts that constituted the offence by the body corporate in which he is an officer and to have agreed to its conduct of the business on the basis of those facts”. I see no reason why a similar test should not apply under the EFMA.

54     For Ms Liu to be liable for the False Statement Offence, she must therefore have known the material facts of Ping An’s offence under s 22(1)(d) of the EFMA (namely, that the 8k Statement was part of the EP Application) and consented to its submission to the Controller.

55     There are two distinct points in time that the Prosecution relies on to argue that Ms Liu had knowledge of the 8k Statement:[note: 92] (a) in the 10 Jan 2023 Submission; and (b) when she signed the Declaration Form on 26 January 2023 (“26 Jan 2023 Signing”).

The 10 Jan 2023 Submission

56     The Prosecution has not established that Ms Liu had knowledge of the 8k Statement in the 10 Jan 2023 Submission for the reasons at [34]-[38] above.

57     As mentioned at [29] above, contrary to the Prosecution’s contention, Ms Liu does not qualify as a Section 15 Applicant and the Knowledge Presumption does not apply.[note: 93] Even if the Knowledge Presumption applied, the outcome would be the same as I would have found that Ms Liu had rebutted the presumption for the same reasons at [34]-[38] above.

The 26 Jan 2023 Signing

58     The Prosecution has not proven that Ms Liu knew about the 8k Statement during the 26 Jan 2023 Signing.[note: 94]

59     Although Ms Liu signed the Declaration Form declaring that the information was “true and correct” (see [6(a)(v)] above),[note: 95] she has given coherent and consistent evidence that she signed it without reading:

(a)     Ms Liu’s testimony that she did not read the Declaration Form before endorsing it remained steadfast throughout the trial and there was no evidential basis to doubt her evidence (see [6(b)] above).

(b)     She has given a credible explanation for why she did not read it – she was facing a heavy workload that day and was less concerned with the paperwork because Mr Huang was already employed by Ping An under a Work Permit.[note: 96] Importantly, the 8k Statement was not on the same page that Ms Liu signed (see [6(a)] above),[note: 97] which supports her explanation.

(c)     Ms Liu’s explanation is believable, given that the Prosecution’s witness, Mr Huang, himself signed the Declaration Form without reading or noticing the 8k Statement (see [6(c)] above), which suggests that such hasty signing was characteristic of the working environment.

(d)     Further, there is no evidential basis for me to doubt the credibility of Ms Liu’s evidence for the reasons set out at [35]-[37] above, and given that the following two arguments raised by the Prosecution are unfounded:

(i)       The Prosecution argues that Ms Liu’s experience as an employer means that she must have known it was the “employer’s responsibility to check through [the] documents before signing”.[note: 98] As explained at [59(b)] above, Ms Liu has given a credible explanation for why she did not read the Declaration Form before signing it. Even if she was careless, such carelessness does not amount to knowledge and consent for the purposes of s 20(1)(a) of the EFMA.[note: 99]

(ii)       The Prosecution argues that Ms Liu must have known that the 5.5k Salary would not satisfy the criteria for an EP.[note: 100] However, the evidence shows that Ping An’s Management Team believed that Mr Huang’s 5.5k Salary met the requirements for both an EP and an S Pass (see [4] above).

60     For completeness, the Prosecution indicated that it was not relying on the Knowledge Presumption in respect of the 26 Jan 2023 Signing.[note: 101]

Conclusion on the Fourth Element

61     The Prosecution has therefore failed to prove that Ms Liu was aware of the 8k Statement in either the 10 Jan 2023 Submission or during the 26 Jan 2023 Signing, and has not proven the Fourth Element.

62     For clarity and completeness:

(a)     It was not necessary to consider wilful blindness as the Prosecution did not raise this issue. In any event, wilful blindness would not have been established, as there is no evidence that Ms Liu was aware of the 8k Statement so as to arouse suspicion requiring further investigation (Tan Kiam Peng v Public Prosecutor [2008] 1 SLR(R) 1).

(b)     I placed no weight on Ms Liu’s assertion that MOM’s online EP Application system was flawed or faulty,[note: 102] as Ms Liu did not provide adequate evidence of alleged flaws relating directly to the 8k Statement.[note: 103]

(c)     I considered whether Ms Liu’s broad knowledge of and consent to the submission of the EP Application in its entirety, without knowledge of its specific contents (such as the 8k Statement), would suffice to establish the Fourth Element. This approach is unsuitable as it would render other officers of Ping An (such as Mr Wong) liable for the False Statement Offence merely for knowing of the EP Application’s submission regardless of its contents, and would also be inconsistent with the Knowledge Requirement under the Third Element.

(d)     While the evidence suggests that Ms Liu may have been careless in signing the Declaration Form without reading it (see [59(d)(i)] above), I decline to exercise my discretion under s 128(1) of the Criminal Procedure Code 2010 (2020 Rev Ed) to alter the charge to reflect the alternative fault element of neglect under s 20(1)(b) of the EFMA as this would be prejudicial to Ms Liu.

(i)       In Goh Chin Soon v Public Prosecutor [2021] 4 SLR 401 (“Goh Chin Soon”) at [84], the High Court indicated that a charge should be amended at a late stage in the trial only where the defence that the accused person would have to run for the amended charge is likely to be substantially similar to the defence run for the original charge.

(ii)       The present charge requires the Prosecution to prove the Fourth Element – that Ms Liu knew about and consented to Ping An’s making of the false statement. Ms Liu’s defence accordingly centred on showing that she did not know the 8k Statement was included in the EP Application, and was accompanied by her acknowledgment that she should have read the Declaration Form before signing it.[note: 104]

(iii)       Altering the charge to reflect the alternative fault element of neglect would therefore render Ms Liu’s current defence untenable and require her to mount an entirely different defence. Consequently, in line with Goh Chin Soon, it is not appropriate for the charge against Ms Liu to be altered to reflect the alternative fault element of neglect under s 20(1)(b) of the EFMA.

(iv)       Moreover, the Prosecution sought to alter the charge only after all sets of Closing Submissions had been filed,[note: 105] without explaining why the alternative fault element was not raised earlier.

Conclusion

63     The Prosecution has failed to establish the Fourth Element of the False Statement Offence, and I therefore acquit Ms Liu of the False Statement Offence.

html:
Thirunavukarasu Manikam v Gumanan s/o Nallathambi and others

Thirunavukarasu Manikam v Gumanan s/o Nallathambi and others
[2026] SGDC 214

Case Number:District Court Originating Claim No. 781 of 2022, District Court Assessment of Damages No. 459 of 2025
Decision Date:01 July 2026
Tribunal/Court:District Court
Coram: Sia Aik Kor
Counsel Name(s): Joseph Li Jing Xin (ReThink Legal) for the claimant; The first defendant in person; The second defendant absent and unrepresented.
Parties: Thirunavukarasu Manikam — Gumanan s/o Nallathambi — JBR Curry House Pte. Ltd. — Thomas JohnKennedy Rani — Arulsamy Thomas JohnKennedy — Wai Fong Machinery Pte. Ltd

Damages – Assessment

Evidence – Adverse inferences

1 July 2026

Judgment reserved.

District Judge Sia Aik Kor:

1       In this suit, Thirunavukarasu Manikam (“Thiru” or the “Claimant”) sues Gumanan s/o Nallathambi (“Gumanan” or the “First Defendant”), JBR Curry House Pte Ltd (“JBR” or the “Second Defendant”), Thomas JohnKennedy Rani (“Rani” or the “Third Defendant”) and Arulsamy Thomas JohnKennedy (“John” or the “Fourth Defendant”)(collectively, the “Defendants”). The claim is based on a breach of contract, in the tort of misrepresentation and in unjust enrichment. Wai Fong Machinery Pte. Ltd. had applied to add itself as a fifth defendant for the purposes of resisting an injunction application by Thiru which was dismissed when Thiru was absent from the hearing. It was subsequently not involved in these proceedings.

The Claim

2       Thiru claimed that the Defendants had agreed that in return for his injection or loan of funds to secure the tenancy of No. 9 Kian Teck Drive Singapore 628826 (“Premises”) including paying off the debts of the earlier tenants of the Premises as a condition precedent and to apply towards the running of a food and beverage business (“Business”) by JBR at the Premises, the Defendants agreed to make him a shareholder of JBR for the value of his capital input, appoint him as a director and allow him to participate in the Business, give him 50% share in the net profits of the Business at the Premises, and for Gumanan, Rani and John to repay the injection in equal shares when the Business was on an even keel and to ink a shareholders agreement setting out the same (collectively the “Representations”). The Defendants did so as they were starved of capital to begin or sustain the Business. The Defendants subsequently reneged on the agreement and refused to issue shares in JBR to him or facilitate his appointment as director of JBR or to sign the agreement. The Defendants essentially did all things to thwart his involvement in the Business and deny him his role in JBR.

3       Thiru claimed that he provided a total of $162,035.43 in reliance on the Representations which were false and made falsely at the material time, and which were either fraudulent or negligent misrepresentations.

4       Thiru claimed that the Defendants also failed and refused to provide proper accounting records of the Business or to account to Thiru the income and expenditure of JBR. The Defendants operated the Business by employing phantom employees and paying CPF contributions to them as an expense of the Business and engaged in malpractices such as not depositing cash collections of the Business into JBR’s bank account. The Defendants effectively rendered the value of the shares in JBR meaningless and worthless. The Defendants failed to make reparations to settle the loan extended to Rani and John which was received by all the Defendants and occupied the Premises to make financial gains at the expense of Thiru and JBR. Thiru claimed that the Defendants had thereby unjustly enriched themselves at the expense of Thiru and JBR.

5       Thiru therefore claimed against the Defendants repayment of $162,035.53 and damages for loss of opportunity in respect of the potential earnings of the monies so applied to seed the Business.

The Defence

6       John and Rani are husband and wife. Rani and John, together with Gumanan started the Business at the Premises and together, they operated and managed the Business at the Premises. John was the manager of JBR and Rani was a shareholder of JBR. Gumanan was a director and shareholder of JBR. Rani and John had actual authority from Gumanan and JBR to start, operate and manage the Business at the Premises.

7       The Defendants deny intending to defraud or defrauding Thiru. They deny that the funds were provided by Thiru at the Defendants’ request. They alleged that Thiru had voluntarily provided the funds to the Defendants to secure the Premises for JBR. They do not deny that JBR entered into a tenancy of the Premises for $75,085 with funds provided by Thiru. Thiru was a lender and investor to the Defendants for the Business and financier to secure the Premises. Specifically, Thiru was a lender and investor for JBR in relation to its Business within the Premises only.

8       The Defendants deny that they were starved of capital to begin or sustain the Business and claimed that they had sufficient funds to do so without Thiru’s involvement[note: 1]. They deny promising or representing to Thiru that he would be made shareholder, director and be permitted to participate in the Business. They also deny that they had represented or agreed that Thiru would receive a 50% share in the net profits of the Business. As Thiru was a lender and investor, Thiru and John had agreed that Thiru would partake in the “profits and losses” of JBR[note: 2]. The Defendants had agreed with Thiru to repay the loan/injection when the Business was on an even keel[note: 3]. However, JBR was operating at a loss.

9       The Defendants alleged that it was misconstrued that the clearance of the bad debts of the previous tenant was a condition precedent for the tenancy of the Premises for JBR. The Defendants admit that Thiru had paid Eng Lee Engineering Pte Ltd (“Eng Lee”) the required security deposit and advance rentals for the Premises but deny that he had paid off Eng Lee for the earlier tenancy to pave the way for JBR to commence the Business.

10     While the Defendants assert that JBR maintained proper accounting records, their position is that Thiru was not entitled to any confidential information of JBR, including its income and expenditure.

Entering of Judgment against Gumanan and JBR

11     On 15 January 2025, JBR’s defence was struck out following its breach of an unless order made on 19 November 2024. The unless order relates to a production order made on 17 July 2024 where JBR was ordered to disclose to Thiru its audited, or if unavailable, unaudited financial statements for its Business within the Premises for all financial years that overlap with any part of the period from April 2022 to the date of the order, as well as the supporting documents relied upon to arrive at the unaudited financial statements. Under the production order, JBR was also ordered to produce the human resource records of JBR which evidence the names and citizenship of its former and current employees and the duration of such employment for each of these employees as well as all written communication between the Ministry of Manpower and JBR regarding the employment of phantom employees in the Business and the payment of CPF contributions to these employees and JBR’s CPF contribution statements for the period from April 2022 to the date of the order. JBR did not comply with the production order at all. Accordingly, judgment was entered against JBR for it to pay Thiru the sum of $162,035.53 with interest and to pay Thiru damages for loss of opportunity, if any, to be assessed.

12     On 10 June 2025, consent judgment was entered against Gumanan in similar terms[note: 4]. The trial of Thiru’s claim proceeded only as against Rani and John and was heard over 6 days on 3 November 2025, 5 and 6 January 2026, 23, 26 and 27 February 2026.

Assessment of Damages

13     This is the assessment of damages payable to Thiru for his loss of opportunity as against Gumanan and JBR pursuant to the judgments against them. For the assessment hearing on 12 March 2026, JBR did not file any affidavits and was also absent from the hearing. On 27 December 2025, JBR’s sole director and shareholder, one Shaik Rajee Mohameed Shaik Abudullah, had informed Thiru’s counsel via email that “JBR will not be defending the AD hearings”[note: 5]. No closing or reply submissions were filed on behalf of JBR.

Thiru’s case

14     At the AD hearing[note: 6], Thiru’s claim was that he was promised 50% of the net profits of the Business[note: 7]. Thiru argued that this was evident as it was pleaded in the Defence[note: 8] that Thiru and the Fourth Defendant had agreed that Thiru would partake in the “profits and losses” of JBR. In the affidavits of the Third Defendant[note: 9] and the Fourth Defendant[note: 10], they had stated that they had agreed with Thiru that he would be entitled to only 50% of the net profits of the Business.

15     Accordingly, Thiru claimed that his 50% profit share was therefore the “potential earnings of the monies so applied to seed the Business”[note: 11] and represents his pleaded loss of opportunity.

Gumanan’s case

16     In Gumanan’s closing submissions, he challenged that he was personally liable. He claimed that John and Rani were the directing minds of JBR and that he was only a director and shareholder on paper. The day-to-day operations and management of JBR would be under the purview of Rani and John and he did not play any active part in the management of JBR. He claimed that he became a director of JBR after Rani and John had asked him for help by becoming a director in JBR and to effect this, Rani and John transferred to him 30% of the paid-up shares in JBR.

17     Gumanan claimed that he had no prior knowledge of Thiru’s investment into JBR when it was made and only came to be aware of issues with Thiru sometime around May 2022 from Rani and John.

18     Gumanan claimed that he should not be held liable for any of the losses suffered by Thiru as the proper party was JBR. There is no evidence that he was authorised by JBR to invite Thiru to invest in JBR. Gumanan claimed that he had not breached his fiduciary duties, engaged in fraudulent or wrongful trading or unlawfully paid dividends from JBR to himself. He had also not failed to act with due diligence, or made negligent misrepresentations to Thiru. Neither is Thiru able to pierce the corporate veil of JBR.

Issues

19     As consent judgment had already been entered against Gumanan for him to pay Thiru the sum of $162,035.53 as well as damages for the loss of opportunity, if any, which are to be assessed, the issue of his liability to pay such sums is no longer a live issue in the assessment hearing. What is relevant is whether Thiru suffered any damages for his loss of opportunity which Thiru states is 50% of the net profits of the Business and if so, the quantum of such damages.

20     In any event, I did not accept Gumanan’s arguments that he was only a director and shareholder on paper, given that this was not supported by the evidence[note: 12] that he was a director and shareholder of JBR since its incorporation on 3 August 2021. Rani only became a shareholder on 23 September 2021 when Gumanan transferred 70,000 of his 100,000 shares to her. These shares were subsequently transferred back to Gumanan on 23 November 2022 and Gumanan held 100% of the shares of JBR from 23 November 2022 to 5 May 2023[note: 13]. Rani did not become a director of JBR until 5 April 2022 and ceased to be a director on 29 September 2022. Hence, Gumanan was the one who incorporated JBR on 3 August 2021 and was the sole director from 3 August 2021 to 4 April 2022 and from 30 September 2022 to 6 May 2023. He was also the sole shareholder of JBR from 3 August to 22 September 2021 and from 23 November 2022 to 5 May 2023.

21     Gumanan’s claim that he had no prior knowledge of Thiru’s investment into JBR was also inconsistent with the fact that he was a signatory to the canteen service agreement at the Premises dated 4 April 2022[note: 14] as well as an authorised cheque signatory to JBR’s bank account with access to the monies in the account[note: 15]. Gumanan did not invest any monies in JBR[note: 16] and was not asked to invest any monies in JBR by Rani or John[note: 17]. Gumanan was also responsible for the use of JBR’s CorpPass[note: 18] as well as the signatory to JBR’s Annual Report for the financial year ended 31 December 2022 declaring that JBR was able to pay its debts as they fall due[note: 19]. Gumanan would therefore be well aware of JBR’s financial situation and must therefore have been aware of Thiru’s investment given that the canteen service agreement evidenced the payment of the security deposit and advance rental. In addition, as Rani testified in respect of JBR’s finances, “nothing happened without Gumanan’s knowledge”[note: 20] while John testified that both Gumanan and Rani were in charge of JBR’s finances[note: 21].

22     In my view, the sole issue which arises in the assessment hearing is whether JBR was profitable.

Was JBR profitable?

Burden of Proof

23     Section 108 of the Evidence Act provides that when any fact is especially within the knowledge of any person, the burden of proving that fact is upon that person. Thiru argued that the facts surrounding JBR’s profitability or otherwise are especially within JBR’s knowledge and Gumanan’s knowledge as a director and are not capable of being known by Thiru whose access to JBR’s financial records stopped after 13 July 2022. Accordingly, Thiru argued that the burden has shifted to Gumanan and JBR to prove that JBR has been unprofitable.

24     To deal with Thiru’s arguments, I turn to the following exposition by the Court of Appeal in Britestone Pte Ltd v Smith & Associates Far East, Ltd [2007] 4 SLR(R) 855 at [60]

To contextualise the above principles, at the start of the plaintiff’s case, the legal burden of proving the existence of any relevant fact that the plaintiff must prove and the evidential burden of adducing some (not inherently incredible) evidence of the existence of such fact coincide. Upon adduction of that evidence, the evidential burden shifts to the defendant, as the case may be, to adduce some evidence in rebuttal. If no evidence in rebuttal is adduced, the court may conclude from the evidence of the plaintiff that the legal burden is also discharged and make a finding on the fact against the defendant. If, on the other hand, evidence in rebuttal is adduced, the evidential burden shifts back to the plaintiff. If, ultimately, the evidential burden comes to rest on the defendant, the legal burden of proof of that relevant fact would have been discharged by the plaintiff. The legal burden of proof – a permanent and enduring burden – does not shift. A party who has the legal burden of proof on any issue must discharge it throughout. Sometimes, the legal burden is spoken of, inaccurately, as “shifting”; but what is truly meant is that another issue has been engaged, on which the opposite party bears the legal burden of proof.

25     In view of the above-mentioned, I did not accept Thiru’s arguments in so far as they suggest that section 108 of the Evidence Act displaces his legal burden of proving that JBR was profitable and that he has suffered damages for the loss of opportunity to participate in such profits. However, as illustrated above, while the evidential burden to produce facts in relation to JBR’s profitability may rest on Gumanan and JBR pursuant to section 108 of the Evidence Act, it is also clear that the evidential burden can shift if rebuttal evidence is adduced.

26     In the present case, Thiru argued that JBR is profitable based on the system generated sales receipts on 1, 2, 3, 4, 6 and 13 July 2022[note: 22] which he argued indicate an estimated revenue of $5,700 per day. Thiru claimed that such an estimate is conservative because the bank statements show that the NETS collections increased significantly after the opening day on Thursday, 16 June 2022[note: 23]. At the trial, Rani had agreed that an estimate of around 500 to 600 paying customers daily (prior to 6 May 2023) was conservative[note: 24] and that the price list at [4.16] of the investigative report dated 13 May 2025[note: 25] reflects the prices of the food and drinks sold at JBR prior to 6 May 2023[note: 26]. Thiru argued that based on the price list, a customer could easily spend more than $10, especially if beer is purchased. Thiru also argued that the quantification was consistent with the renewal of the canteen service agreement, the declaration of solvency in the ACRA filings, the fact that no bank loans were obtained as well as the ability of JBR to pay high salaries, given its job advertisements from 5 October 2024 to 19 October 2024 for a store assistant offering a salary of $3,000 - $5,000 and from 22 January 2025 to 5 February 2025 for a business development manager offering a monthly salary of $8,000 to $14,000.

27     However, the annual report of JBR for the financial year ending 31 December 2022 indicates that JBR’s revenue was $619,796 and after accounting for cost of sales of $335,348 and operating expenses of $342,823, JBR made a loss of $53,130.

28     Save for the revenue, Thiru did not appear to dispute the other figures in the Statement of Comprehensive Income in JBR’s Annual Report for the financial year ended 31 December 2022, given that he in fact relied on the same figures in calculating JBR’s profits. In the circumstances, I proceeded to consider if the revenue figures in the 2022 Annual Report were under-reported.

Whether the revenue figures in the 2022 Annual Report were under-reported

29     While Thiru claimed that the system generated sales receipts from JBR’s digital payments and cash terminals from 1 to 13 July 2022 show an average daily revenue or collection of around $5,781.95[note: 27], there is no evidence as to how these various receipts should be interpreted and whether there is any overlap among the various receipts. In this regard, I note that the sum of the NETS collection from Nets Terminal ID 70591101 and Nets Terminal ID 70591103 on 1, 2, 4, 6 and 13 July 2022 was close to the amounts credited into JBR’s UOB account in respect of the same days. However, there is no indication of the NETS collection from Terminal VP-POS01 in JBR’s bank account. In addition, the handwritten calculations[note: 28] appear to be reconciliation calculations. For example, the handwritten calculations[note: 29] appear to reconcile the NETS collection dated 2 July 2022 from Terminal ID 70591103 in the sum of $2,276.27 against the NETS collections generated by Terminal VP-POS01 in the sum of $1,892.10 resulting in an extra sum of $384.17. Similarly, the handwritten calculations[note: 30] appear to reconcile the NETS collection dated 4 July 2022 from Terminal ID 70591103 in the sum of $1,039.00 against the NETS collections generated by Terminal VP-POS01 in the sum of $1,009.50 resulting in an extra sum of $29.50. The calculations go on to state the total sales of the day as $2,140.40, including the cash collections, which is the output from Terminal VP-POS01. The receipt from the sale of the set meals on 4 July 2022[note: 31] were also reconciled against the cash used as well as the NETS collection from Terminal 70591101 to arrive at a total sales of $567.90 and an extra $98.90. Adding the reconciliation calculations of $2,140.40 and $567.90 together gives a revenue of $2,708.30 on 4 July 2022. Similarly, adding $3,034.10 to $730.60 gives a revenue of $3,764.70 on 6 July 2022[note: 32] and adding $2,694.10 to $781.70 gives a revenue of $3,475.80 on 13 July 2022[note: 33]. These do not support Thiru’s arguments that the average daily collections was $5,781.95.

30     The revenue is stated as $619,796 in the 2022 Annual Report. Dividing this by a total of 199 days from 16 June 2022 to 31 December 2022 yields a daily revenue of $3,114.55. Given the substantial variability in the revenue of the 6 days for which receipts are available, it is unclear if they are representative of the revenue in the months which follow. Based on the bank statements, the NETS collections appeared to have increased from July 2022. However, it is unclear whether the cash collection has correspondingly dropped. Thiru has also not shown that the average daily NETS collection for the months for which bank statements were available exceeded or was inconsistent with the average daily revenue of $3,114.55 represented by the revenue of $619,796 stated in the Annual Report.

31     While Rani did confirm that there were approximately 500 to 600 customers per day, it was unclear if they spent an average of $10 per person. Based on the bank statements of JBR[note: 34], the small value deposits paid by PayNow over 2 September to 12 September 2022 amount to $537.40 over 45 transactions. Hence, Thiru argued that the average spend by customers paying by PayNow was $12.74 per transaction. However, it is unclear whether the average spend of the 45 transactions over 11 days would be representative of the average spend of the claimed 5,500 or 6,600 customers over those days, including those who may have paid in cash.

32     In the circumstances, Thiru was unable to prove on a balance of probabilities that the revenue figures in the Annual Report in 2022 were under-reported and that JBR was profitable as at 31 December 2022.

33     In relation to the period after 31 December 2022, Thiru had relied on the investigative report dated 13 May 2025. There, it was estimated that there were between 100 and 150 customers between 0811 hours and 1021 hours on 1 May 2025, between 150 and 200 customers between 1329 and 1600 hours and between 150 and 250 customers between 1800 and 2100 hours[note: 35]. Based on the price list of the items sold at the restaurant, it is estimated each customer who purchased food at the restaurant would spend an average of $5.00 while those who bought beer would spend an average of $10.00. Other food items e.g. snacks, titbits, desserts etc would cost each customer an average of $2.00[note: 36].

34     In my view, the findings by the private investigators in 2025 did not bring Thiru very far. Based on the report[note: 37], the numbers appear to be based on discrete video footage taken from 0811 hours to 1021 hours on 1 May 2025 which was a public holiday and for which the footfall would be higher. No evidence was advanced as to how many customers would purchase food and how many would purchase beer or other items and the basis on which one can estimate the average spend of each customer. No figures were also available as to the cost of sales or the operating expenses in 2025 and it is unclear how the corresponding figures in JBR’s Annual Report in 2022 could be extrapolated to subsequent years. There was therefore insufficient evidence for the Court to make any finding in respect of the profitability of JBR after 31 December 2022.

35     I was unable to draw any inference from the circumstantial evidence highlighted by Thiru for the following reasons. First, while the canteen agreement entered into in April 2022 was with Eng Lee, the canteen service agreement entered into on 16 January 2023 was with Wai Fong Machinery Pte Ltd[note: 38] which had taken over the premises from Eng Lee. The renewal of the canteen agreement, even before it had expired, did not therefore point to the fact that JBR was profitable at the time. The desire to secure the Premises at which the Business is conducted for a longer period may indicate optimism about JBR’s prospects but this alone is insufficient indication that it was in fact profitable at that time. Secondly, the fact that JBR has filed annual returns with ACRA for financial year ending 31 December 2023 that JBR is solvent does not necessarily imply that it is profitable. The declaration that JBR is solvent simply means that JBR is able to pay its debts as they fall due. An entity which makes losses can nevertheless be solvent if there is sufficient cash, assets, financing or investor support to meet its liabilities. The fact that JBR did not take any bank loans is also not determinative of its profitability, given that there may be other sources of funds such as equity injections and director or shareholder loans. The fact that JBR posted job advertisements with high monthly salaries was also unable to assist Thiru as it was unclear whether the positions were ultimately filled, what the salaries that were eventually paid were, and what was the corresponding impact on the operating expenses and JBR’s profits.

36     Thiru argued that pursuant to section 116(g) of the Evidence Act, the Court may presume that evidence which could be and is not produced would if produced be unfavourable to the person who withholds it.

37     In this regard, the principles in relation to the drawing of an adverse inference in relation to absent witnesses set out in Sudha Natrajan v The Bank of East Asia Ltd [2017] 1 SLR 141 (“Sudha Natrajan”) at [20] – [23] are instructive:

(a)     Adverse inferences may go to strengthen the evidence adduced on that issue by the other party or to weaken the evidence, if any, adduced by the party who might reasonably have been expected to call the witness.

(b)     There must however have been some evidence, even if weak, which was adduced by the party seeking to draw the inference, on the issue in question, before the court would be entitled to draw the desired inference. In other words, there must be a case to answer on that issue which is then strengthened by the drawing of the inference.

(c)     While the inference to be drawn is not necessarily confined to the undisclosed evidence, section 116(g) does not afford the court the opportunity to speculate as to what the evidence may be without some basis for the drawing of the inference which the opposing party seeks to persuade the court to draw. In other words, the court must put its mind to the manner in which the evidence that is not produced is said to be unfavourable when drawing the adverse inference under s 116(g).

38     As set out earlier, Thiru was unable to prove on a balance of probabilities that JBR was profitable as at 31 December 2022, contrary to the indication in the 2022 Annual Report that it was loss-making. There was also no prima facie evidence that JBR was profitable subsequent to 31 December 2022 to which an adverse inference could be drawn or applied in strengthening the evidence. Applying the principles set out in Sudha Natrajan, it was not possible to speculate on the quantum of profits which JBR had made, if it was indeed profitable subsequent to 31 December 2022.

39     In respect of JBR, Thiru had sought to rely on Toh Wee Ping Benjamin & anor v Grande Corp Pte Ltd [2020] 2 SLR 308 where the Court of Appeal held at [42] that the effect of having a defence struck out is that the defendant is deemed to have admitted to all allegations of fact in the statement of claim. Hence, Thiru argued that JBR is deemed to have admitted to the facts pleaded in the Statement of Claim that Thiru will receive a 50% share in the net profits of JBR, the business at JBR is lucrative and that JBR is not operating at a loss, as alleged in the Defence.

40     Even if I accept that the Business was lucrative, such a bare statement says nothing about the quantum of profits made and was incapable of filling the evidential void in the present case in respect of the quantum of profits that JBR is alleged to be making. As held in Sudha Natrajan, section 116(g) of the Evidence Act does not afford the court the opportunity to speculate as to what the evidence may be.

Conclusion

41     In the circumstances, I find that Thiru was unable to prove on a balance of probabilities the quantum of JBR’s profits and correspondingly his damages for the loss of opportunity.

42     The parties are to file and exchange written submissions on the issue of costs (limited to 10 pages) within 14 days of this judgment.
