Defence Witnesses

23     The defence’s slate only comprised the accused persons and one other witness. Mr Loy had initially elected to remain silent after the close of the prosecution’s case but later changed his mind and opted to testify on his own behalf. Mdm Gian testified on her own behalf. Aside from the two accused persons, the only other witnesses offered was:

(1)     DW2- Jonathan Ow, a lawyer who met with Ronald in April 2016 and found him seemingly well.

(2)     DW3 — Dextan Fun, Mr Loy's cousin, who testified that he did not pay for the Rolex watch and agreed that based on the evidence Mr Loy was the customer of The Hour Glass watch boutique.

The Defence's Case

24     The defence case essentially centred on the contention that Mr Loy's actions were legitimate and stemmed from an agreement with Ronald made in May 2016, whereby Ronald, who was desperate for funds to pay his outstanding mortgage, requested Mr Loy's help to find funding, leading to their agreement to obtain a loan exceeding the mortgage amount. The claimed intent was that Ronald wished the balance to be invested in property development projects.

25     It was the defence's case that Ronald seemed mentally competent when signing the $4 million Loan Agreement with Ethoz, citing testimony from lawyer Jonathan Ow who met with Ronald and found him apparently capable of understanding complex loan agreements, as well as corroborating evidence from Ethoz employees who observed Ronald's active participation in loan discussions and his objection to certain terms.

26     The defence further contended that Mr Loy's subsequent transfer of funds to his personal account was not misappropriation but rather done in accordance with his agreement with Ronald to avoid double taxation on investments. Since there was no criminal conduct, the defence argued, the subsequent CDSA charges against both Mr Loy and Mdm Gian could not stand, with Mdm Gian having had no reasonable grounds to believe she was facilitating criminal activity through her accounts.

27     Over the 64-day trial, Mr Loy spun multiple disjointed strands of his having been a victim of deceit on the part of Ronald, which was largely unsubstantiated by any evidence. In the process, he continued to maintain serious accusations at numerous individuals, including accusing Ronald and Bhupesh of being cheats, Li-Fen of being dishonest, police officers of egregious misconduct, his former lawyers of malpractice, the prosecution of malicious prosecution, and even the DPPs and Police of fabricating evidence.

28     Upon careful analysis, I found the defence's case to be wholly unpersuasive, for the reasons I shall elaborate upon at length further in these grounds.

MEDICAL WITNESSES SUPPORTING RONALD YIP’S DEMENTIA DIAGNOSIS

Evidence of PW14 Dr Mervyn Koh

29     Ronald was deemed medically unfit to testify at trial, having been diagnosed with post-ICU delirium in 2016 and later developing dementia. His physician, Senior Consultant Geriatrician Dr Mervyn Koh (“Dr Koh”), testified that Ronald had significant cognitive deficits that would have impaired his ability to make complex financial decisions, noting Ronald exhibiting “significant deficits in terms of orientation, short term memory recall, as well as subtraction of a $100 minus seven”[note: 4].For the final aspect, Ronald returned a wrong answer on two occasions when he was given five tries.

30     Dr Koh first saw Ronald on 14 September 2016 at the Geriatric Medicine Clinic, Tan Tock Seng Hospital (TTSH), for a Cognitive Assessment after he was referred from a Polyclinic. Ronald had a past medical history of hyperlipidaemia and benign prostatic hypertrophy and had been admitted to TTSH’s Orthopaedics department from 14 July to 4 August 2016 to treat his left upper limb necrotising fascitis[note: 5], which required three surgeries and a prolonged ICU stay.

31     At the time of referral on 14 September 2016, Dr Koh diagnosed Ronald with post-ICU delirium, as he had features consistent with that condition, including short-term memory loss, aphasia (or word-finding difficulty), and disorganised thinking where he was unable to reason with his daughter logically.

32     On 22 February 2017, Dr Koh followed up and further diagnosed Ronald with Post-ICU Cognitive Impairment, with his Chinese Mini-Mental State Examination (CMMSE) scores falling in the mild dementia range. Dr Koh noted that Ronald “subsequently went on to develop mild Alzheimer’s disease or dementia in September 2017”[note: 6] and that Ronald's dementia progressed to the moderate stage by July 2020[note: 7] on account of his developing hallucinations and increasingly “profound word-finding abilities”[note: 8]. Dr Koh informed that his last review of Ronald occurred on 20 January 2021, where the latter remained in a moderate stage of Alzheimer’s dementia, and was wheelchair dependent, and dependent on his helper with most of his activities of daily living.

33     I noted that Dr Koh's professional opinion was tethered on a firm foundation, where he based his views from a specific well-recognised cognitive test on Ronald on 14 September 2016, and where he, as stated above, concluded that Ronald had significant deficits in orientation and short-term memory recall and would likely have experienced difficulties making complex financial decisions.

34     Critically, Dr Koh opined that he had serious doubts that Ronald was capable of gaining a complete understanding of the Ethoz loan documents, given that Ronald was computationally challenged and had issues with short-term recall memory[note: 9]. While Ronald would understand that he was taking a four-million-dollar loan, he would have difficulty understanding the rest of the 30-page document, especially terms involving interest calculations and his specific repayment obligations.

35     Dr Koh further noted that the effects of Ronald's cognitive impairment may not have been perceptible to a layman who only had superficial interaction with him Generally, someone who knew Ronald longer would notice clear memory lapses and difficulty with complex decisions. He added that any person engaging in in-depth financial discussions, would have to properly check Ronald's understanding, by asking him to repeat information back, as to be able to detect his cognitive deficits[note: 10].

36     The prosecution's evidence in establishing that Mr Loy had used the Balance Sum without authorisation came from a reconstruction of contemporaneous documents and the testimony of Li-Fen. Notably, the defence, notwithstanding the observations stated above, did not proffer any expert evidence to counter Dr Mervyn Koh's professional expert opinion. The defence's reliance on lay observations, (particularly the perceptions of Ethoz employees and lawyer Jonathan Ow, who had seen Ronald on 25 April 2016[note: 11], many months prior to Dr Koh’s CMMSE test), of Ronald's apparent competence, without any countervailing medical evidence, must therefore be given little weight.

Implications of Dr Mervyn Koh’s evidence to this case

37     In my judgement, Dr Koh’s evidence is enormously consequential in two respects. The first was that Ronald’s diagnosis was gradually evolving process of cognitive impairment, where he was believed by Dr Koh to merely suffer from post-ICU delirium in mid-September 2016. Dr Koh upgraded his diagnosis in February 2017 to diagnose Ronald with Post-ICU Cognitive Impairment, with his functions and traits falling in the mild dementia range, and where he was further confirmed to have mild dementia in September 2017, which unfortunately exacerbated to moderate dementia in mid-2020, and had debilitated to being wheelchair bound and entirely dependent on his helper by January 2021, even as he was deemed to have plateaued in the moderate range.

38     The evidence thus showed that Ronald’s disease followed a fairly rapid progression, and hence the cognitive features of Ronald that lawyer Jonathan Ow observed in April 2016, which impressed him that the former was competently in command of his faculties, might have no longer been the same in the later part of 2016 and early 2017, when the principal developments of this case occurred.

39     On the second aspect of Dr Koh’s evidence that only a lay person who had spent considerable time with Ronald, and who repeatedly discussed financial plans, figures and concepts with him, would have perceived the patient’s cognitive deficits, the undisputed facts of the case would show that at the time Ronald lived alone in his Telok Kurau bungalow, and only the First Accused, Mr Loy would be in such a position as to be able to sense the onset and development of his Alzheimer’s dementia. The prosecution’s case, of course, is that he exploited this knowledge.

Evidence of Dr Jerome Goh

40     To clarify on Ronald’s ability to give evidence, the prosecution called Dr Jerome Goh Hern Yee (“Dr Goh”), Chief of Forensic Psychiatry at IMH, who had been called upon to assess Ronald.

41     Dr Goh explained the substance of his report[note: 12], and his findings that Ronald at the time of his examinations on 21 September 2020 and 8 October 2020 had by then developed significant cognitive deficits affecting multiple domains, specifically planning, language, memory, attention, and orientation to time and place, Dr Goh opined that as Ronald’s cognitive condition significantly impaired his ability to accurately recall past events, he was unfit to testify in court.

42     The clinical picture Dr Goh painted was quite stark, where he revealed that Ronald scored only 4 out of 30 on the Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA) test, against a normal threshold of 26 and above. During the aforementioned two interviews conducted in September and October 2020, Ronald was unable to state his age, address, the names of his children's occupations, or even the year.

Ronald’s assessed inability to give a coherent personal account of salient events connected to the case

43     Dr Goh added that Ronald could not identify where he was, misidentifying IMH as a polyclinic on the second visit. He had difficulty recalling the names of, and his interactions with, the key individuals in the case he was involved in, and gave only vague, repetitive responses when pressed.

44     For reference, Dr Goh stated the following in his report[note: 13]:

12    (Ronald) was unable to provide details about the names mentioned in the case, apart from saying "Loy Wei Ezekiel" is a young man who "try to claim make all kinds of claims because of the accident". He said he met the latter "because of the accident” but could not provide details. In the second interview, he said "Loy Wei Ezekiel" is a young man who was trying to cheat him every now and then, but he could not furnish further details. He said he did not know "Gian Juat Ngim".

[Emphasis added]

45     At cross-examination, Dr Goh explained how he tried to get Ronald to explain his account of being “cheated” by this young man identified as “Loy Wei Ezekiel”, Ronald was, however, unable to provide coherent or detailed responses throughout the conversation.

46     When asked how the cheating happened, Ronald deflected to his helper rather than answering directly. Ronald could not recall the name of the person Dr Goh had just mentioned moments earlier and had to ask his helper for the name. When pressed on specifics as to how the cheating occurred, when it happened, how much money was involved, Ronald either gave vague, generic answers, shook his head, or failed to respond meaningfully. The only substantive thing he managed to state was that there were "all kinds of funny proposals."[note: 14]

47     Dr Goh’s overall observation from this exchange was that Ronald was unable to give a coherent personal account of events, showed significant memory difficulties, and could not provide any concrete details about the alleged cheating

48     Dr Goh expressed his view that this assessment, along with collateral history from his helper[note: 15] and daughter[note: 16], as well as his consultation of a prior specialist report[note: 17] from Dr Mervyn Koh of TTSH, corroborated a diagnosis that Ronald suffered from dementia.

No serious rebuttal by defence to show Ronald was competent to give testimonial evidence

49     From an analytical standpoint, Dr Goh's evidence was significant as his recommendation that Ronald was unfit to testify would have had major implications for the conduct of the trial as Ronald was undoubtedly intended to serve a role as a key witness. While the defence sought to undermine Dr Goh’s findings, it was a fact that they never produced a competing medical expert, prepared to take a professional stance that Ronald was competent to take the stand.

50     Given this, aside from lawyer Jonathan Ow (and also certain Ethoz employees) who had seen Ronald in April 2016, but not in October 2020, the defence was limited to giving anecdotal impressions, mostly supplied by the First Accused, to undergird their stance that Ronald was somehow cognitively competent to furnish oral evidence, and be cross-examined, at a court trial.

51     With respect, none of these witnesses could possibly stand as a serious challenge to Dr Goh’s and Dr Koh’s testimonies that Ronald had since late 2016, been suffering from progressive cognitive decline, which would have, by October 2020, developed to dementia of a level of severity as to render him profoundly unfit to testify in court. I was accordingly satisfied of Ronald’s incapacity to stand as a witness for this criminal trial.

TESTIMONY OF RONALD’D DAUGHTER PW8, YIP LI-FEN

Evidence of Yip Li-Fen

52     This would be an appropriate juncture to segue to salient aspects of Li-Fen’s testimony and why I found her to be a credible witness. Essentially, Li-Fen’s testimony was integral in filling in the gaps left by Ronald’s incapacity, and in curating and connecting the document trial left by Ronald and his friend, Kulip Singh, which included a trove of messages and letters.

53     Li-Fen was Ronald's only child and worked as an accountant at a hedge fund in New York. She described her father as a well-educated, articulate man with a master’s degree in mechanical engineering who had a long career in oil and gas before running his own marine business, YHPL. By the time of the material events, the company was largely dormant, and Ronald was burdened by a significant debt of approximately $2.5 million to RBS Coutts, which had snowballed from a failed tugboat-building venture in China that collapsed during the 2008 Lehman crisis.

Li-Fen’s account of Ronald's Hospitalisation in July 2016

54     Li-Fen entered the present milieu when she found out about her father's hospitalisation through an email from her aunt, who had coincidentally discovered Ronald was in Tan Tock Seng Hospital while visiting another relative. Li-Fen flew back to Singapore within 12 hours. Ronald had been admitted for necrotising fasciitis, which was a severe flesh-eating infection on his left arm, and which required four surgeries including skin grafting. At this first instance, she stayed for two weeks before returning to New York.

First Contact with the First Accused, Ezekiel Loy

55     Li-Fen had heard her father mention a "young man" who had a profile of successful real estate projects in Malaysia and been awarded a “Datuk-ship” by one of their states but had not paid much attention to this reference at the time. After she returned to New York, a friend named “Joanne” who had been caring for Ronald called her in a panic because she could not contact him. Through another contact, Li-Fen was given Ezekiel's number and called him. Mr Loy told her he had been bringing Ronald food, taking him to hospital appointments and his financial travails.

56     When Li-Fen spoke to Mr Loy, he told her that because of his network of business relationships, he had a group of funders that he could easily draw funds from, and that he was willing to help Ronald settle his Coutts problem. When Li-Fen asked why he was helping, Mr Loy had allegedly said, "Don't worry, he is a good friend of mine,"[note: 18] and that he was helping him find a solution to the Coutts problem. Li-Fen's initial impression was cautious she found it hard to believe someone would help a friend to the extent of lending credit for over $2 million with no formal agreement.

Observations of Ronald's Deteriorating Mental State

57     An equally cogent part of Li-Fen’s testimony was her first-person account of Ronald’s cognitive deterioration. After communication was restored through a landline and repaired handphone, Li-Fen began speaking to her father almost daily and noticed clear signs of cognitive decline which encompassed these observations:

(1)     Ronald spoke much more slowly than before and struggled to find words, which was markedly out of character for someone she described as very articulate.

(2)     Ronald had good and bad days but was never back to his former self.

(3)     In one alarming incident in late August 2016, Ronald called her in a panic believing he had been in a motorbike accident and that someone was suing him. She had to repeat the correct account of his hospitalisation twice before he calmed down. She noted that Ronald himself admitted he could not differentiate between reality and dreams.

(4)     Li-Fen’s friend “Tracey”[note: 19], who visited Ronald in person, independently confirmed that Ronald "seems kind of spaced out" and was speaking slowly with a loss of words between sentences.

58     I noted that Li-Fen’s observations were consistent with and corroborated the clinical findings in Dr Mervyn Koh's report[note: 20], which diagnosed Ronald with Post-ICU Delirium in September 2016 and later Post-ICU Cognitive Impairment in February 2017. In my judgment, Li-Fen's testimony was essential to prosecution’s case for several reasons, being:

(1)     Firstly, it provided a lay witness account of Ronald's cognitive decline from someone who knew him well and could speak to the contrast between his pre- and post-hospitalisation state.

(2)     Secondly, Li-Fen’s observations from as early as late August 2016, which was before Dr Koh's formal assessment in September 2016, and suggested that the cognitive impairment was already manifesting in Ronald’s daily life.

(3)     Thirdly, Li-Fen’s account of Ezekiel's involvement beginning almost immediately after Ronald's discharge from hospital, including bringing him food, taking him to appointments, and being present at his home, establishes the proximity and access Mr Loy had to a vulnerable and cognitively impaired Ronald during a critical period. Finally, her scepticism about Ezekiel's claimed generosity particularly his offer to help resolve the Coutts debt with no formal agreement, foreshadowed the alleged cheating that formed the basis of the charges.

Lifen’s return in September 2016 and medical appointment before Dr Koh

59     Li-Fen arrived in Singapore on 11 September 2016 and departed on 20 September 2016. She testified that her primary goal was to bring her father to see a doctor, first at the polyclinic, then at Tan Tock Seng hospital to see a geriatric specialist. Li-Fen showed up without telling her father, as she was concerned that he might not feel he needed help, given his confused state. She also discovered that Mr Loy occasionally came to the house to stay, and on her first arrival noticed a car parked outside, so she waited until the next day before going in.

60     When Li-Fen spoke to her father about Mr Loy’s presence, Ronald stated Mr Loy was helping him to get a new funder, but he could not describe where he had gone or who he had met. He said they had gone out for meetings but was unable to give any cogent description of what progress had been made.

61     She brought her father to see Dr Koh at TTSH. During the assessment, Ronald could not remember he had a master's degree. Dr Koh explained it could be post-ICU delirium and said that some people would improve to 50% of their former state, some to 100%, and some would stay as they were. He arranged a follow-up in 3 months.

Ronald’s financial circumstances and the Coutts loan

62     Li-Fen described her father as "cash poor, asset rich", and that Ronald had not had any significant income for a long time, and she had occasionally helped him pay small bills. He collected rent from shophouses and an apartment at Rangoon Road, but tenants often did not pay.

63     Li-Fen stated that her father’s travails over the Coutts credit facility was alleviated by the Ethoz loan of 4 million dollars was released, which was used to partially pay off the RBS Coutts loan, where Ronald’s Telok Kurau bungalow was used as collateral.

64     Regarding the Telok Kurau property, Li-Fen explained that selling it was never an option in her father's mind. He had explicitly told her that selling it would feel like a failure in life, as it was a prized possession passed down from his grandfather. This was one of the reasons the outstanding loan had snowballed from approximately $1 million to over $2 million between 2008 and 2016.

Li-Fen’s November 2016 trip and developments concerning the Ethoz loan

65     When Li-Fen returned in mid-November 2016, her father told her that Mr Loy, who used to come on two or three occasions a week, had not been seen for a few weeks. When they tried to get Mr Loy to come over using an excuse, he agreed to come the next day but did not show up, later messaging to say he was tied up.

66     Ronald was unable to tell Li-Fen whether there was a loan coming or whether any progress had been made on the Coutts debt. He said he had been to a few places to meet some people but could not say anything specific.

67     Li-Fen then texted Mr Loy directly asking if there was a loan. She recalled Mr Loy’s response was vague, stating "it's already settled"[note: 21] and that he would call her, but she never received that phone call.

68     While helping her father clear his mail, Li-Fen discovered two Coutts statements showing a credit of approximately $2.45 million and another of approximately $185,000. She emailed their Coutts' contact person Andrew Turner to confirm the loan had been paid off, and he confirmed the crediting of the sums on the next day[note: 22].

Ronald’s text messages of 30 December 2016

69     One of the most significant parts of Li-Fen's evidence is her recollection of Ronald’s frenzied messages on 30 December 2016. On that day, Ronald sent Li-Fen a series of text messages stating that Mr Loy had taken over Yip Holdings[note: 23], pledged the Telok Kurau property for a four-million-dollar loan from Ethoz, and that the money and property were "most probably gone."[note: 24] He also noted that Mr Loy had disconnected his phone and had not been spoken to in two weeks.

70     Li-Fen noted that the messages were not drafted in her father's usual style, as Ronald was English-educated and competently articulate. She realised that the messages contained spelling uncharacteristic grammatical errors and even gibberish, which she sensed to be consistent with the cognitive decline she had been observing. She said that whenever she received such texts during this period, she would just call him instead.

71     When she called Ronald, he explained that his friend Kulip Singh, a retired police inspector, had helped him write to One Legal LLC, the law firm that handled the Ethoz loan, demanding loan documents. They had only just realised that Mr Loy had put himself as director of Yip Holdings and potentially taken the $4 million sum, less the $2.5 million owed to Coutts. She recalled Ronald’s text stating “Kulip is helping me and we would make a police report. And we will (sic) demand Ethoz to make sure they don’t release the funds”[note: 25]. At that point, Li-Fen also recalled that they were not yet aware of the Mr Loy’s specific dispositions of the Balance sum.

Li-Fen’s May 2017 visit to help uncover the trail of monies and dispositions

72     When Li-Fen returned to Singapore in May 2017, she found that Ronald had taken extensive action, noting a considerable collection of police reports and letters, which she believed to be drafted by Kulip Singh in the house. Li-Fen herself recalled visiting the Citibank branch at Lau Pa Sat and obtaining bank statements for the Yip Holdings account, which showed that funds had come in and the very next day had been wired out to a company called "Yip & Loy Private Limited.”[note: 26] Ronald stated that he had no knowledge of this company, causing Li-Fen to wonder if her father had been victimised by “this scam even beyond what I understand”[note: 27].

73     When Li-Fen made an ACRA search, she found that the directors of Yip & Loy Private Limited were Mr Loy and another individual who was not her father, Ronald, and indeed, was not known to her.

Further discoveries upon Li-Fen’s June 2017 return and preparations for civil action

74     When Li-Fen returned in June 2017, she met with the Citibank relationship manager and obtained the account opening documents for the Yip Holdings Citibank account. These revealed that the mailing address on the account was Mr Loy’s home address, not Ronald's, and that Mr Loy was already listed as a 52.5% shareholder of Yip Holdings when the account was opened in October 2016. The account was also set up to require only one signature to release funds[note: 28].

75     Li-Fen also realised during this trip, that her father could no longer quantify numbers, and seemed not to appreciate the difference between $100,000 and $1 million. She had to type out the figures and explain what the $20,000 monthly interest meant in practical terms before he could grasp the severity of his situation. Li-Fen also added that she had been involved in a civil suit filed against Mr Loy in the High Court in connection with the sums taken.

Why Li-Fen was a critical witness

76     I have set out Li-Fen’s testimonial evidence in some detail as she was uniquely placed within the prosecution’s roster of 19 witnesses as she was there at the material time to provide a contemporaneous account of the critical events of their case, where she was able to connect the intersection between Mr Loy’s actions and her observations of her father’s concurrent deterioration while the former was taking place.

77     Essentially Li-Fen's was able to give a first-person account of the following critical aspects of the prosecution’s case:

(1)     First, Li-Fen’s testimony enabled the corroboration of documentary in establishing a clear timeline of how Mr Loy systematically gained control of Ronald's company and assets, even as she was able to see how Ronald was becoming increasingly cognitively impaired and financially desperate.

(2)     Second, Li Fen conducted her own investigations into the Citibank account, having the gumption to meet Citibank manager Heng Kwang Han and describing her discovery of troubling and suspicious details, including Mr Loy using his home address as the mailing address and setting up a single-signatory arrangement, which was suggestive of deliberate structuring efforts to facilitate the misappropriation of funds without Ronald's knowledge or meaningful consent.

(3)     Third, Li-Fen's observation that her father could no longer quantify large sums of money by mid-2017 further corroborated the medical evidence of progressive cognitive decline, from nothing less than her own lived experience.

(4)     Finally, Li-Fen was able to give direct testimony of her own encounters with Mr Loy, including his sudden disappearance from contact after the loan was disbursed. Li-Fen also testified on Mr Loy’s vague and evasive responses to Li-Fen's direct questions at that juncture, which appeared consistent with the behaviour of an individual who had already obtained what he wanted and was adroitly distancing himself.

RONALDS’S MESSAGES TO VARIOUS PARTIES, HIS REPORTS TO THE POLICE, AND LETTER TO AGC & CAD

Ronald’s document trail

78     While Ronald was assessed to be cognitively unable to give evidence for this trial, he left a considerable document trail in December 2016 and January 2017 which were quite telling in revealing his anxiety, disquiet and panic. When he suspected that Mr Loy has taken the Balance Sum, Ronald reacted by seeking help from Li-Fen and his legally trained friend Kulip Singh, a retired police prosecutor, to lodge a police report, and wrote several letters to various agencies seeking clarity and assistance in recovering the Balance Sum. To say the least, these actions are wholly inconsistent with the existence of any agreement authorising Mr Loy to deal with the Balance Sum in the manner that he did.

79     Ronald’s concerns were all too clear in his police report was filed on 31 December 2016 where Ronald reported that Mr Loy had apparently reset his Singpass password on his behalf, retained his OneKey device, and gone uncontactable. Ronald lodged the report to disclaim liability for unauthorised transactions and to void the device.

80     The prosecution's case was further supported by the tenor of Ronald's police statements, which were admitted into evidence in lieu of his oral testimony. Aside from a series of police statements[note: 29] recorded between 31 December 2016[note: 30] and 20 April 2018[note: 31], Ronald had also crafted a series of letters and statements[note: 32] with the help of Mr Kulip Singh, a retired police prosecutor, who had passed on[note: 33] prior to these proceedings, and thus could not be a witness.

81     In this series of statements, Ronald was unequivocal that he had no knowledge of any property investment in Lucky Plaza, that he was not involved in trading in commodities, and that he had no agreement with Mr Loy to develop software or applications. I will now touch on the contents of these letters and statements:

Ronald’s letter to One Legal LLC dated 29 December 2016

82     The first of these documents was a two-page letter[note: 34] dated 29 December 2016 and addressed to One Legal LLC marked "Without Prejudice, By Hand and Registered Mail" which was Li-Fen believed to have been drafted by Kulip Singh and opened with the salutation "Most Honourable Gentlemen."

83     The letter made four key points:

(1)     Firstly, Ronald stated that he is aged 74 years, was “suffering slightly from dementia”, had no knowledge or expertise with legal terms or legal contracts, and that his understanding of any contract would be dependent on the lawyers.

(2)     Secondly, Ronald stated that he had come to One Legal LLC's office on some occasions at the behest of their client[note: 35], and that legal contracts were drawn up which he could not fully understand, being dependent much more on what their client and the law firm conveyed to him.

(3)     Thirdly, Ronald stated that as One Legal LLC was acting for their client and obviously in that client’s interest, he now found on hindsight that he should have been advised to engage his own counsel to peruse the contracts and assure they were fair in the protection of his legal rights.

(4)     Fourthly, and most critically, Ronald stated that no copies of the contracts were given to him, and that if copies were given to their client, that client had failed, refused or neglected to give him copies for his retention and for his seeking legal advice on them, stating "This is not (sic) accordance to Law."

84     Ronald concluded the letter with a demand that copies of all contracts signed in One Legal LLC's office bearing his signature be given to him on or before 4 January 2017 at 5pm, reserving all his rights to legal redress if he did not receive the same by that deadline.

Reaction by Ethoz to the 29 December 2016 letter

85     PW 13 Brandan Cai Xiande (“Mr Cai”) was a team leader at Ethoz Capital Limited (“Ethoz”) who managed the relationship managers involved in the $4 million loan to Yip Holdings Pte Ltd. He was the primary point of contact between Ethoz and Mr Loy throughout the loan transaction. At trial, Mr Cai’s testimony covered the lead-up to the loan, the signing of the letter of offer, and critically, the events that followed.

86     The most significant part of Mr Cai's testimony concerned Ethoz's reaction upon receiving the 29 December 2016 letter. While the letter was addressed to One Legal LLC, there was considerable alarm at Ethoz caused by Ronald’s reference that he was suffering from dementia. Mr Cai testified that Ethoz was very concerned about the whole deal, having suddenly received a letter from one of the personal guarantors claiming to be suffering from dementia.

PW13’s attempts to contact Mr Loy in the wake of the letter

87     Following receipt of this letter, Mr Cai made repeated attempts to contact Mr Loy for updates and to arrange a meeting but testified that during this period Ethoz officers could not obtain definitive answers from Mr Loy at all with the latter not responding to their messages or their calls.

PW13’s account of Mr Loy’s evasive responses

88     WhatsApp messages tendered in evidence showed Mr Cai asking for updates on 6 January 2017, 12 January 2017, and 19 January 2017, with Mr Loy giving only vague responses such as "No update yet" and "We are in the midst of it." When asked urgently to meet to clarify loan matters, Mr Loy responded, "After CNY" and then "Not at the moment."

89     By 1 February 2017, Brendan Cai was reduced to messaging Mr Loy to beseech "Can you spare me 3 minutes? Please give me a call back. Please call your partner, Mr. Yip. He is also concerned on the whole deal."[note: 36] Mr Cai testified that no substantive response was ever received. Mr Cai described a pattern of evasion on Mr Loy’s part, which was also recounted by other witnesses and pointed to the latter’s motive of deliberately making himself scarce to avoid accountability.

Reaction by One Legal LLC to the 29 December 2016 letter

90     The final prosecution witness; PW 19, was Tracy Chen Lai Fong (“Ms Chen”), a director and corporate lawyer at One Legal LLC, where she has practised since 2005. Ms Chen testified that One Legal LLC was instructed by Ethoz and YHPL in connection with the $4 million loan facility, acting for those entities rather than for Mr Loy personally.

91     Ms Chen recalled that Ronald had attended at One Legal LLC's office on 30 December 2016, one day after the date on P101, bringing the letter with him and requesting a set of documents for the transaction. Ms Chen was not present that day, and her staff attended to Ronald and delivered the documents to him by hand.

92     Ronald returned on 10 January 2017 with a second letter[note: 37]. Ms Chen met him together with two other lawyers, including one Toh Jiawen who had handled the actual transaction. At the meeting, Ronald raised concerns about One Legal LLC acting for Mr Loy whereupon Ms Chen responded that they had not acted for him in his personal capacity. She remembered that Ronald had sought clarification on the disbursement of the loan proceeds, and that he confirmed he had no issue with the mortgage redemption but was concerned about the balance funds.

93     Ronald’s confused state of mind at the meeting is exemplified by this exchange with Ms Chen when he claimed to have met Mr Loy in a hospital after his accident, and informed that he was only recently made aware that the latter was a director of YHPL[note: 38]:

DPP:

Did Mr. Ronald mention to you anything about Mr. Ezekiel?

PW19:

Yes.

DPP:

What did he say?

PW19:

He mentioned that he had, uh, an accident 6 months ago and he met Ezekiel at the hospital. He also mentioned that the loan transaction was arranged by Ezekiel. And when we told him that---when I told him that Ezekiel was reflected as a shareholder and director of his company---of the company, Yip Holdings, he expressed that he had just recently been aware of it when he saw the business profile of the company.

[Emphasis added]



94     Strikingly, when Ms Chen asked whether Ronald remembered signing the documents or visiting the office previously, Ronald did not seem to recollect either visit. He mentioned he was suffering from memory lapses, saying he could be normal one moment and forget everything five minutes later. He broke down in tears when speaking about his accident and stated that he had been taken advantage of by Mr Loy[note: 39].

95     In my judgment, Ronald’s 29 December 2016 letter was significant in the context of this case as it corroborated Ronald's vulnerability, his lack of independent legal advice, and his acting upon a gaining awareness that something had gone wrong with the contracts he had signed, all of which were central to the prosecution's case against Mr Loy.

Ronald Yip’s 9 January 2017 letter

96     As stated above, Ms Chen had received another a two-page letter dated 9 January 2017, from Ronald, with the subject heading "Request for Full Accounts of Monies Drawn from Contract of Loan and the Dispensation Account." This letter, which was couched in a far stronger tone than the missive of eleven days earlier, stated as follows:

Your client, Loy Wei Ezekiel brought me to your office in order to conscript a loan which loan documents and processing was handled by you. The principal purpose was to clear Coutts of the outstanding loan and I was told the balance would be given to me.

In the interim, your client Loy Wei Ezekiel had brought me to make a key device and took my password and installed himself without my knowledge and consent as a 51%[note: 40] Director of my company, Yip Holdings Pte Ltd.

Have you paid Coutts and please give an account of the balance due and payable to me as it was my house that was mortgaged. Also note that Loy Wei Ezekiel did not invest a single dollar in the company and he has installed himself by deceit and fraud in order to get his hand on all monies that come out of my house mortgage.

Please give me a full account if the balance had not yet been deposited into Yips (sic) Holdings Pte Ltd, I am giving you written instructions not to do so and hold it back until my further instructions.

Any monies that he takes out of Yip (H)oldings Pte Ltd from proceeds of my mortgage clearly touch on the Criminal Law of Section 420 of the Penal Code and at this time all his actions go towards an attempt of Section 420

Please give me full statements of account soonest and into what account the balance was deposited as I am awaiting full statements before I lodge a report to the Commercial Affairs Department

Once again, if the monies are still with you, I am instructing you not to be put into Yip Holdings Pte Ltd with immediate effect.

Please forward a full statement of account to me of that transaction forthwith.

…

[Emphasis added]

Ronald’s allegations of fraud on Mr Loy’s part and communication of intent to report to CAD in his second letter represented a significant escalation

97     To say the least, Ronald’s second letter represented a significant escalation from his first. Where the letter of 30 December 2016 was primarily a request for documents with a general complaint about the lack of independent legal advice, the subsequent letter was a far more pointed and legally specific document. Ronald now explicitly named Mr Loy as the person who brought him to One Legal LLC's office, described Mr Loy’s manipulation of his SingPass credentials, and characterised Mr Loy's conduct as nothing less than deceit and fraud.

98     Ronald also invoked Section 420 of the Penal Code and made clear his intent to report the matter to the Commercial Affairs Department. This rapid escalation coheres with Li-Fen’s testimony of Ronald enlisting the help of Kulip Singh, and suggests Ronald had in the intervening period been able piece together the sequence of events and the nature and extent of Mr Loy’s alleged actions with the Ethoz loan monies.

99     The account of the SingPass incident is particularly significant as a contemporaneous written record made very shortly after the events in question. This is entirely consistent with the evidence of other witnesses including PW13 Brandan Cai, who testified[note: 41] that Ronald told him during the Chinese New Year visit to the latter’s residence, that he did not know how Mr Loy had obtained his SingPass and been able to change the shareholding of the company as to confer a majority share of 52.5% to himself, and leaving Ronald with a minority interest.

100    The most remarkable aspect of this subsequent letter was Ronald's invocation of Section 420 of the Penal Code, effectively alleging that Mr Loy had committed the criminal offence of cheating. This was notable as the allegation was in a letter written before any police report or formal proceedings had commenced and amply demonstrates that Ronald had a clear enough understanding of what had happened to characterise it in criminal law terms. This directly undermined any suggestion that Ronald consented to or was content with the arrangements Mr Loy had put in place.

101    Taken together, the letters of 29 December 2016 and 9 January 2017 to One Legal LLC, which prompted responses by both the law firm and Ethoz, constitute compelling contemporaneous evidence for the prosecution’s case that Ronald did not consent to Mr Loy's actions and was deceived into a transaction whose true purpose and consequences he did not understand.

Ronald’s direct message to Mr Loy

102    Among the documents presented by the prosecution was one-page letter[note: 42] dated 11 January 2017. It is addressed directly from Ronald to Mr Loy. The letter stated:

11th January 2017

Dear Mr. Loy,

WHEREABOUT THE S$1,268,500 COLLECTED BY YOU ON THE 10th NOVEMBER 2016 AFTER WHICH YOU COMPLETELY DISAPPEARED FROM CONTACT

You are completely aware that the above proceeds arose up of the mortgage of my house at Telok Kurau to which you have no ownership nor share.

Surprisingly, after you collected the cheque enclosed at Annex "A" of which we have evidence you chose to disappear completely. You are not contactable on the handphone and in the last two months you don't even bother to call me.

We give you till 5p.m. on the 18 of January 2017 to contact me Mr. Yip at (number stated) and arrange to meet at Mr. Kulip Singh's office failing which we have to take the next effective step to solve this mystery by referral to due authorities.

It is in your interest to meet up and resolve this issue.

We thank you.

Mr. Yip Fook Chong

[Emphasis added]

103    A perusal of the text will show that Ronald made three points:

(1)     Firstly, Ronald asserted that Mr Loy is completely aware that the sum of S$1,268,500 arose from the mortgage of his house at Telok Kurau, to which Mr Loy has no ownership nor share.

(2)     Secondly, Ronald stated that after Mr Loy collected the cheque, of which they have evidence, he chose to disappear completely, becoming uncontactable on his handphone and failing to call Ronald for the last two months.

(3)     Thirdly, Ronald imposed an ultimatum giving Mr Loy until 5pm on 18 January 2017 to make contact and arrange to meet at Kulip Singh's office, failing which they would refer the matter to “due authorities”, and underscored that it would be in Mr Loy's interest to meet up and resolve the issue.

104    In my view, this letter joins the other two prior letters of 29 December 2016 and 9 January 2017 as contemporaneous evidence that rebutted any suggestion that Ronald consented to or was content with Mr Loy's handling of the Balance Sum. Written just two months after the Ethoz loan was disbursed, it demonstrated that Ronald was acutely aware that S$1,268,500 of proceeds from the mortgage of his own home had been collected by Mr Loy, that Mr Loy had no entitlement to those funds, and that Mr Loy had deliberately made himself scarce after collecting them.

Ronald Yip’s FIR of 12 January 2017

105    Ronald did, three days after second letter to One Legal LLC, take the step of making a formal complaint to the authorities. Given Ronald’s inability to give evidence in court, it would be apropos to reproduce in full, his statement to the police, which was recorded on 13 January 2017, and which stated as follows[note: 43]:

INTERIM ANALYSIS

Reconstructing Ronald’s intentions and state of mind from his statements juxtaposed from his medical history and Li-Fen concurrent evidence

108    Absent Ronald’s court testimony, his letters and statements are the closest links to understanding Ronald’s intentions and his state of mind at the time of his apparent discovery of Mr Loy’s transfer of the balance sum, and the pattern of his subsequent actions. These would, of course, be closely related to questions of his cognitive state at the material time, which spanned 30 December 2016 to 17 January 2017.

109    Turning first to the final letter of this series, which was the one dated 17 January 2017, the letter's significance in the overall case is threefold:

(1)     Firstly, it is a contemporaneous document written just two months after the Balance Sum was disbursed, which makes it highly probative of Ronald's state of mind and understanding at the material time.

(2)     Secondly, it is addressed to both investigative and prosecutorial authorities in Singapore, the AGC and the CAD which demonstrated that Ronald understood the seriousness of what had happened and was apparently seeking the most effective possible remedy.

(3)     Thirdly, it is wholly inconsistent with the defence's case that Ronald had agreed to let Mr Loy use the Balance Sum for investments. A man who had agreed to such an arrangement would have no reason to write to the CAD alleging Criminal Breach of Trust two months later.

Ronald’s pattern of escalation was coherent and methodical, suggesting he was in control of his faculties at the material time

110    Forensically analysis Ronald's escalation from One Legal LLC to the AGC and CAD within fifteen days revealed Ronald’s coherence in the manner he progressively piecing together the extent of a fraud allegedly perpetrated against him.

111    The first letter to One Legal LLC on 29 December 2016 was tentative and procedural. Ronald asked for documents and admitted his dementia (which was to cause considerable consternation) but eschewed from naming Mr Loy as a wrongdoer. He seemed to suspect something was wrong but had not yet assembled the full picture.

112    By his second letter on 9 January 2017, Ronald’s tone had transformed entirely. Ronald now invoked Section 420 of the Penal Code, explicitly naming Mr Loy, describing the SingPass manipulation, and threatening to go to the CAD. Essentially, in just eleven days, Ronald had moved from requesting documents to making specific criminal allegations.

113    Running in parallel, Ronald’s direct letter to Mr Loy on 11 January 2017 imposed a formal ultimatum, which was to respond by 5pm on 18 January 2017 or face referral to "due authorities." This is not the behaviour of a confused man but of someone following a deliberate strategy, possibly under the guidance of his friend Kulip Singh, a retired police inspector. The logical implication being that Mr Loy's failure to respond to this ultimatum would effectively remove any remaining ambiguity about his intentions.

114    On 13 January 2017, Ronald filed his police report and simultaneously wrote to the AGC and CAD, routing the letter through his Member of Parliament, which was a sophisticated move reflecting a clear understanding of how to ensure a complaint would receive attention. In that letter, Ronald was specific in characterising Mr Loy's conduct as Criminal Breach of Trust and describing himself as "an old man suffering from slight dementia" left holding a four-million-dollar loan, which was a contemporaneous acknowledgement of his own vulnerability that was a poignant observation within a forensically significant statement as to his cognitive ability and his motivation.

115    Simply stated, Ronald seemed self-aware that he had developed “slight dementia” but appeared to demonstrate that he was sufficiently in control of his faculties as to prosecute a highly strategic pattern of escalation in his letters and statements. Ronald’s behaviour, to say the least, was wholly inconsistent with the defence's case that Ronald had agreed to let Mr Loy use the Balance Sum for investments. A man who had made such an agreement would not, upon discovering that Mr Loy had become uncontactable, respond by invoking criminal statutes, filing police reports, and writing to investigative and prosecutorial agencies within a fortnight.

116    Notwithstanding his condition, Ronald was methodical in approach as each step in the escalation was triggered by new information obtained in the previous step, and each step was calibrated to the appropriate authority. This was more the fully thought-through behaviour of an individual uncovering a fraud, not regretting an agreement.

Li-Fen corroborated Ronald’s evidence and had no motive to frame the two accused persons

117    The evidence gleaned from Ronald’s document trail was largely corroborated by Ronald’s daughter. Li-Fen testified that when she walked Ronald through Mr Loy's claims about the investment of the Balance Sum, Ronald told her he had no recollection of ever discussing these matters with Mr Loy, let alone agreeing to them, and also categorically stating that he had never been taken to Lucky Plaza to see an apartment unit[note: 45]. Li-Fen's evidence did not waver under cross-examination. She denied without qualification that Ronald had ever agreed to let Mr Loy use the Balance Sum for investment purposes.

118    By her own account, before Ronald’s health crisis in the latter part of 2016, Li-Fen had been largely resident in the United States since the commencement of her master’s degree studies in in 2004[note: 46], where she was based in New York and worked in the finance sector there as an accountant after obtaining her MBA. Li-Fen’s overseas residence even predated her parents’ divorce in 2007. Under cross-examination Li-Fen stated that she was financially independent, and indeed supported Ronald when the latter had difficulty collecting rent from his tenants, and also when her father was involved in litigation with shipping companies, before his business went into dormancy[note: 47]. Li-Fen’s evidence has already been set out in extensio earlier. Overall, I found Li-Fen to be a credible and reliable witness, and I accept her evidence. It was especially clear that Li-Fen, who spent most of her time overseas and did not know the two accused persons prior to the material time, would have had no motive to frame Mr Loy, or Mdm Gian for that matter.

Corroboration by independent witnesses PW13 Brendan Cai and PW19 Tracy Chen

119    I had set out Mr Cai and Ms Chen’s evidence earlier, as both were independent third-party witnesses, who had dealt with Ronald during the critical period of early 2017, and were thus able to provide eyewitness accounts of their interactions with Ronald that corroborated his document trail in several important respects.

120    Mr Cai’s most significant contribution was his account of the Chinese New Year visit in early 2017. When he raised matter of the loan with Ronald directly, Ronald told him he was very upset about losing control of his company and could not understand how Mr Loy had obtained his SingPass to change the shareholding. Notably, this was a spontaneous, unguarded account given to a commercial lender, and not a lawyer, a family member, or an investigator, which mapped precisely onto the grievances Ronald had set out in his escalating letters. Also remarkable was the fact that Ronald was not reciting a prepared complaint; but appeared to be expressing genuine distress to someone he had no particular reason to perform for.

121    Mr Cai’s account of Mr Loy's progressive evasiveness from January 2017 onwards in ignoring calls, deflecting meetings, and eventually going silent, also mirrored Ronald's own account in his letters and statements that Mr Loy had become uncontactable.

122    Ms Chen’s corroboration operated on a different but equally important level. She met Ronald only once, on 10 January 2017 as she had not been the One Legal LLC lawyer directly involved in the transaction and had not been present at Ronald’s earlier attendance at her law firm.

123    Ms Chen’s account was remarkable precisely because she had no prior relationship with him. She described Ronald as distraught, breaking down in tears, and unable to recall having visited the office just ten days earlier. He told her he had memory lapses and could be “normal” one moment and “forget everything” five minutes later. This is a contemporaneous, independent observation of Ronald's cognitive state made by an experienced lawyer, which corroborated both Dr Koh's medical findings and Ronald's own self-description in the CAD letter, that Ronald was quite able to comprehend and express himself, but experienced gaps of recollection where his memory recall was compromised by the nascent signs of his ultimately debilitating condition.

Ronald’s disclosures in his encounters with PW13 and PW19 were contemporaneous, unscripted and spontaneous

124    What made both Ms Chen’s and Mr Cai’s accounts so significantly valuable as corroborative evidence was their independence and informality in settings at these respective encounters. I accept that Ronald's letters were drafted with Kulip Singh's assistance and obviously professionally scripted in a manner as to be directed at formal parties and authorities to demand action. The accounts to rendered to Mr Cai and Ms Chen were unscripted and spontaneous, and clearly without any intervention from Kulip Singh. It was thus telling that their substance is entirely consistent throughout in rendering the same message that Ronald did not authorise the shareholding change, did not understand what had happened to the Balance Sum, and felt he had been exploited.

125    Overall, Ronald’s consistency was very difficult to explain away, and I thus hold that the content of his document trail from 29 December 2016 to 13 January 2017 were a truthful and reliable articulation of the facts and his situation as he understood them to be. In these two occasions, we thus heard, from the two testimonies, a contemporaneous rendition of Ronald’s direct voice on his position in relation to the Balance Sum.

The First Accused would have been put to notice on Ronald’s position by PW13’s text messages

126    Further, even if Mr Loy were to claim, as he did, that he did not receive the ultimatum of 11 January 2017, he would, from Mr Cai’s testimony have been put to notice that Ronald was deeply unhappy with his taking and handling of Balance Sum by Ethoz’s Mr Cai’s series of urgent texts coming from 6 January 2017, which culminated with his message of 1 February 2017 stating "Can you spare me 3 minutes? Please give me a call back. Please call your partner, Mr. Yip. He is also concerned on the whole deal”[note: 48].

127    Mr Loy evidently did not act on this message and instead continued to make dispositions of the Balance Sum till 11 July 2017, just over a month to the point of his arrest on 16 August 2017.

THE PROSECUTION’S CASE

128    At its core, the prosecution submitted that this case is not about whether Ronald appeared articulate to laypersons or signed a loan agreement. It is about what Mr Loy did after he gained control of the Balance Sum, which was to layer the funds through shell accounts, misrepresenting his mother as an investor and using it for luxury purchases, and all done without transparency or consent.

129    The prosecution's case was built on three main planks.

(1)     First, Mr Loy took the Balance Sum entirely out of YHPL and Ronald's control and placed it under his sole dominion. Y&L had no connection to YHPL. The learned DPPs noted that Ronald held no shares or positions in Y&L, and there was consequently no legitimate reason to route the money through Y&L's account other than to add a layer of obfuscation. The prosecutors also contended that Mr Loy also lied to bank relationship managers about the purpose of the transfers, telling Mr Leong that the funds were "from my own personal means" when they were wholly traceable to the Balance Sum.

(2)     Secondly, the DPPs observed that every single use of the Balance Sum was for Mr Loy's personal benefit. The Lucky Plaza Property and shares was purchased in his sole name. The Rolex watch and the Mercedes sports car were purchased for him. They noted that Mr Loy even used the Balance Sum for his court bail. Not a single cent was returned to YHPL or applied towards the Rangoon Road redevelopment that Mr Loy claimed was the purpose of the investment agreement.

(3)     Third, the prosecutors contended that Mr Loy failed to advance any credible explanation. He was unable to give a consistent account of the alleged oral agreement. While Mr Loy claimed in his CFD the existence of an oral agreement, at trial he pivoted to claim that the Balance Sum was his money, as he had earned it. Under cross-examination, when confronted with this inconsistency, Mr Loy sought to reconcile it by adopting the position that he had the option of investing the money or treating it as his own.

The First Accused's incorporation of Y&L and his immediate actions when the Balance Sum became available raise the index of suspicion

130    The prosecution's case against Mr Loy centred on the assertion that he has committed a criminal breach of trust involving the $1,268,500[note: 49] Balance Sum from YHPL. While it was beyond dispute that Mr Loy was validly entrusted with dominion over these funds as an authorised signatory for YHPL's bank account, the fundamental question is whether Mr Loy's actions show that he dishonestly misappropriated the money. I found the evidence of dishonest intent to be strong after considering the prosecution’s points in their submissions, which I shall liberally refer to for this section.

131    I agreed with the prosecution’s stance that the sheer immediacy of the transfer to Y&L to lend to deep suspicion. In just a single day after the funds were deposited into YHPL's account, Mr Loy transferred the entire amount to Y&L, a company he had incorporated with himself as the sole director and shareholder. It serves to remind that Y&L had no connection whatsoever to YHPL. Neither Ronald nor YHPL held any shares or positions in Y&L.

The Absence of Any Legitimate Purpose for the Transfer Through Y&L

132    It was incongruous, in my view, that the name of Y&L bore Ronald's “Yip” surname in its company name along with Mr Loy’s, when in fact Mr Loy fully owned Y&L. In this regard, the prosecution had made a valid observation[note: 50] that if the Balance Sum were truly to be used on behalf of YHPL, there was nothing stopping Mr Loy from doing so directly out of YHPL's account. This being the case, this court accepted the prosecution’s opinion that the transfer through Y&L's account served no purpose other than to add “another layer” before the Balance Sum arrived in Mr Loy's personal bank account.

The opening of the Citibank account and its dormancy before the availability of the Balance Sum

133    It is also significant that Mr Loy had incorporated Y&L on 15 August 2016 and opened its bank account with the assistance of PW3 Desmond Leong (“Mr Leong”), a relationship manager with Citibank, some months before the Balance Sum was even disbursed. The account was opened in August 2016 and lay dormant until the Balance Sum arrived. The only transaction that ever passed through Y&L's account was the through-flow of the Balance Sum itself. This is wholly inconsistent with the picture of a legitimate business vehicle that Mr Loy sought to paint.

Gross misrepresentations made about the business purpose of the funds

134    The suspicion against Mr Loy's intent is further evidenced by the multiple misrepresentations he told to bank employees about the reasons for his actions. When opening Y&L's bank account, Mr Loy told Mr Leong that Y&L was in the wholesale business of Korean cosmetic products and that he had secured a contract to distribute such products in Southeast Asia. He also told Mr Leong that he was in discussions with a Chinese company to distribute industrial equipment for palm oil extraction. The prosecution appropriately observed[note: 51] that these claims were “not only unsubstantiated by any evidence” but “were directly contradicted by the complete absence of any transactions in Y&L's account” and noting that Mr Leong’s account of what Mr Loy told him was “unchallenged” during cross-examination.

135    It was significant that Mr Loy repeated this account when asked about his transfer of the Balance Sum out of YHPL's account just one day after it was deposited. He told Mr Leong that this was because he needed urgently to start his business as he had just secured the contract to distribute Korean cosmetic products. At trial, I observed that Mr Loy studiously avoided responding directly to the DPP’s characterisation of this statement to be a lie, and when questioned by the DPP[note: 52] whether this was a convenient reason so that Mr Leong would agree to open a bank account for him, Mr Loy had cryptically stated: “He needed a reason. I gave him the reason”[note: 53].

Misrepresentations as to the origin of the funds and reasons for their transfer

136    It was similarly problematic for the First Accused that upon Citibank’s Mr Leong questioning Mr Loy about the transfer of $1,268,400.78 from Y&L's bank account into his personal Citibank account, Mr Loy had stated in a recorded phone call that "these funds are from my own personal means."[note: 54] The prosecution validly observed that “Under cross-examination, he conceded that the referenced sum was instead wholly traceable to the Balance Sum”[note: 55].

Ronald’s ignorance of the transfer

137    From the accounts covered earlier in these grounds, it was clear that Mr Loy did not inform Ronald when he transferred the Balance Sum out of YHPL's account into Y&L's and later his personal accounts, nor did he inform Ronald of the various payments he made prior to 30 December 2016. To recapitulate, on 30 December 2016, Ronald told Li-Fen that Mr Loy had apparently disconnected his phone SIM card and that he had not spoken to Mr Loy for two to three weeks. Mr Loy had disappeared and did not come to see Ronald or call him prior to and following the Balance Sum being deposited into YHPL's account and being transferred out of it. To say the least, this pattern of evasion and disappearance is wholly inconsistent with the conduct of a person acting pursuant to a legitimate agreement.

The First Accused's fund movements disclose a consciousness of wrongdoing

138    Beyond the initial transfer, the learned DPPs contended[note: 56] that Mr Loy engaged in a deliberate pattern of layering transactions through multiple bank accounts, which I agreed should found further suspicion of his dishonest intent. After transferring the money into his personal Citibank account, Mr Loy transferred a total of $850,000 from his personal Citibank account into Mdm Gian's personal bank accounts: $300,000 into her first POSB account and $550,000 into her second POSB account. This $850,000 is wholly traceable to the Balance Sum.

139    From the uncovered evidence, the prosecution described[note: 57] the layering continuing in a particularly elaborate fashion in connection with the Lucky Plaza property purchase. The movement of the $400,000 on 9 February 2017 is telling. Mdm Gian transferred the sum between her two POSB accounts, withdrew it in two cash tranches of $254,000 and $146,000, and both amounts were deposited into Mr Loy's OCBC account on the very same day. Within 24 hours, that same $400,000 had been deployed as the fixed deposit underpinning the OCBC Housing Loan for the Lucky Plaza property.

No commercial rationale presented itself for the transfer through Y&L's account

140    The elaborate sequence of cash withdrawals and redeposits served no discernible commercial purpose. If there was a genuine investment agreement between Mr Loy and Ronald, the $400,000 could have been transferred directly from YHPL's account or Mr Loy's own personal account. The decision to route the funds through Mdm Gian's accounts and move them in cash tranches was unnecessary for any legitimate purpose. The only plausible explanation for this circuitous route was to distance the Balance Sum from its origins.

141    I also found Mr Loy's explanation for routing the $400,000 through Mdm Gian's accounts was that he wanted to obtain $800 worth of Takashimaya vouchers to be implausible, and agree with the prosecution’s characterisation[note: 58] of this as a “bare” and “belated” claim, and an “afterthought” which was never mentioned in any of his police statements, nor in his Case for the Defence, which was unsupported by evidence whatsoever.

142    In my judgment, Mr Loy's observed pattern of layering transactions through multiple bank accounts, engaging in deceptive behaviour with various parties, and becoming evasive and uncontactable when questioned about his dealings with the Balance Sum served to bolster the prosecution's contention of his dishonest intent.

The Balance Sum Was Spent Solely For The First Accused's Personal Benefit

143    I turn now to the specific uses to which Mr Loy put the Balance Sum. The prosecution has demonstrated, and I accept, that every single use of the Balance Sum was for Mr Loy's personal benefit, with not a single cent ever being applied for the benefit of YHPL.

The Lucky Plaza Property

144    Every aspect of the Lucky Plaza transaction pointed in the same direction. The property was purchased solely in Mr Loy's name. The entire purchase price was funded from the Balance Sum, disbursed across three streams, comprising $116,500 from Mr Loy's personal Citibank account for stamp duties, legal fees and the deposit; $368,823.97 by cashier's order from Mdm Gian's second POSB account; and $400,000 routed through Mdm Gian's accounts as the fixed deposit for the OCBC Housing Loan. The loan was taken out in Mr Loy's personal capacity, and the monthly repayments of $18,259.95 were met from his personal account.

The Lucky Plaza transaction had little semblance to a jointly agreed investment

145    The Lucky Plaza transaction bore none of the indicia of a jointly agreed investment. From the testimonies of PW5 Charmine Yee (“Ms Yee”), Mr Loy never mentioned Ronald or YHPL to the very OCBC officer who facilitated the loan. Despite Mr Loy's claim that Ronald had agreed to the purchase, the latter was uninvolved in any viewings. The prosecution calculated[note: 59] that the property would generate a monthly loss of $651.99, with rental proceeds consistently falling short of mortgage repayments. Conspicuously, all title and contractual documentation were in Mr Loy's name alone. To recap again from the foregoing part of these grounds, Ronald told Li-Fen that he had no recollection of discussing the Lucky Plaza property with Mr Loy, nor of any agreement between them to purchase it.

Mr Loy’s misrepresentation to OCBC that a downpayment came from directorship fees, sales of investments, savings and business income rather than the Balance Sum

146    I also note PW5, Ms Yee’s, testimony[note: 60] that Mr Loy made a declaration, while completing an OCBC form that the downpayment came from directorship fees, sales of investments, savings and business income. This was, by any measure, false, as the monies would have ineluctably come entirely from the Balance Sum. When this was put to him at trial, Mr Loy’s response was that the truth of his declaration was contingent on his relationship with Ronald.

147    This is a remarkable position which was tantamount to saying that a patently false statement to a bank became true if such a private agreement could be claimed. Mr Loy was seemingly alluding to an evolving element of his defence which was that Ronald owed him money for inter alia, remuneration as a director for running the companies. It is plainly unsustainable given the clear context of OCBC’s questionnaire, and it illustrated the increasingly strained lengths to which Mr Loy was driven in attempting to justify what was, at its core, a straightforward misappropriation.

Share Purchases

148    The share purchases tell a similar story. Mr Loy used $125,519.40 from his OCBC account to purchase shares via 11 EPS payments, all through a trading account held solely in his name. No proceeds were ever returned to YHPL, and Ronald played no part in any of these transactions. The prosecution traced each of the 11 payments back to the Balance Sum with care, and I was satisfied that the sums were at least substantially, if not entirely, traceable to it.

149    The traceability issue was resolved, in part, by Mr Loy's own evidence. The defence had contested whether the EPS payments could be conclusively traced to the Balance Sum specifically. But in re-examination, Mr Loy conceded that several of these payments were made pursuant to his alleged “investment agreement” with Ronald.

Payments to Innomedia Technologies (“Innomedia”)

150    The payments to Innomedia followed the same pattern. Mr Loy paid $24,500 to Innomedia Technologies for two projects "Car Street" and "Property Street" from his personal bank account, without mentioning Ronald or YHPL to PW4, Bhupesh Kalra (“Buphesh”). The prosecution established that YHPL was not a party to either project or derived any benefit from them. The only person Mr Loy introduced to Bhupesh as an investor was his own mother, the Second Accused, Mdm Gian, whom he misrepresented in that capacity. Neither project was completed, and Mr Loy did not make full payment for either, with Bhupesh explaining that he did not hand over the source code upon the aforesaid failure to pay.

151    While Mr Loy claimed that the payments to Innomedia came from his own money, the prosecution has satisfactorily proven otherwise. A tracing exercise[note: 61] established that the funds are at least partially and substantially traceable to the Balance Sum.

152    I was also satisfied that both Mr Loy and Mdm Gian’s financial circumstances of at the material time made it implausible that these payments could have come from their own means. Mdm Gian was the sole breadwinner of the household, paying for her sons' school fees, her husband's medical bills, and household expenses, and her bank account statements reflected average monthly balances of below $10,000. Mr Loy's personal bank accounts reflected consistently low monthly balances, offering no support for his claim to have maintained a private cash reserve of between $1.9 million and $2.1 million stored in bags at home. The only evidence offered in support of this claim was a set of grainy photographs that could not be reliably attributed to him. The was not credible reason to accept his account.

Evidence of DW3, Dextan Fun

153    Before proceeding to the next two transactions concerning a Mercedes sports car and a Rolex Yacht Master, I will first turn to the evidence of DW3, Dextan Fun (“Mr Fun”).

154    Mr Fun was Mr Loy's cousin and Mdm Gian's nephew was called as a defence witness to provide exculpatory explanations for two transactions: the purchase of a Mercedes SLK sports car and the Rolex Yacht-Master watch. On the watch, Mr Fun’s account[note: 62] was that he had identified a Chinese buyer willing to pay around $18,000 for the watch, and introduced the opportunity to Mdm Gian, who purchased it at retail for $14,800 and passed it to him for onward sale, with a view to a planned profit split 50/50 between them.

155    In my view, Mr Fun’s account did not withstand scrutiny. The most damaging of the account was the fact that the tax invoice was made out solely to Mr Loy, and it was also Mr Loy who signed the receipt field confirming collection of the watch. Indeed, Mr Fun’s name appeared nowhere on the invoice.

156    When this was put to Mr Fun in cross-examination, DW3 could offer no satisfactory explanation. This thus produced a fundamental difficulty to the defence case that if the transaction were genuinely a commercial arrangement between Mr Fun and Mdm Gian, there is no reason why Mr Loy would appear as the named customer or sign for receipt of the item.

157    Mr Fun’s account was also directly contradicted by Mdm Gian's own evidence. Mdm Gian’s consistent position was that she purchased the watch on Mr Loy's instructions and passed it directly to him, and not to Mr Fun. Naturally one of these accounts must be false, and Mdm Gian's version was the more plausible as it was corroborated by the documentary record. The existence of the alleged Chinese buyer remained uncorroborated, and no evidence of the subsequent sale or profit from the timepiece was produced.

158    In relation to the Mercedes sports car, where Mr Fun claimed he had identified the Mercedes on SGCarMart, and asked Mdm Gian to take out the bank loan in her name because he could not obtain one himself after leaving the army, and that he funded the purchase by passing her approximately $40,000 to $41,000 in cash[note: 63], similar difficulties arose against Mr Fun’s account. Mr Loy's phone number appeared on the vehicle sales agreement alongside Mdm Gian's, which Mr Fun could not adequately explain. Taken together, Mr Fun’s evidence on the two transactions assumed the appearance of a constructed narrative designed to provide cover for transactions that the documentary record pointed firmly towards Mr Loy.

The Rolex Yacht-Master Watch

159    Payments toward the acquisition of the Rolex Yacht-Master was readily traceable to the Balance Sum. The purchase price of $14,800 was charged to Mdm Gian's credit card, but the tax invoice was made out solely to Mr Loy, and his signature appeared on the receipt field, which was a field the jeweller confirmed was reserved for the person who physically received the watch. As stated above, Mdm Gian's account was consistently that she made the payment on Mr Loy's instructions and passed the watch directly to him upon purchase.

160    I noted that the fund trail was unambiguous. Following the disbursement of the Balance Sum into Mr Loy's personal Citibank account, he made a series of cash withdrawals totalling $14,600 across two days in November 2016. Near-identical sums were deposited into Mdm Gian's first POSB account on the same or following day. Remarkably, this was an account that had held only $2,940.47 prior to those deposits. Mdm Gian then applied $14,900 towards her Visa credit card for the watch purchase. The withdrawals from Mr Loy's account, the near-identical deposits into Mdm Gian's account on the same or following day, and the subsequent application of those funds towards the watch purchase, taken together, admit of no other reasonable explanation than that the cash was passed from Mr Loy to Mdm Gian for that purpose.

161    Ultimately, Mr Loy's attempt to distance himself from the transaction did not withstand scrutiny. While he denied receiving the watch and sought to attribute the purchase to his cousin, Mr Fun. Mr Fun's unequivocal evidence debunked this account upon his confirmation at cross examination that he did not pay for the watch[note: 64].

The Mercedes Sports Car

162    Turning now to the Mercedes sports car, which bore registration number SKE350H. The car dealer, PW17 Tan Siong Khim (“Mr Tan”), testified that on 2 January 2017, Mr Loy had gone to his dealership in the daytime, having seen the car on sgCarMart. He went around the car, expressed interest in buying it, and asked Mr Tan to reserve it, saying he would return later that day with his mother to negotiate further.

163    Mr Loy returned with Mdm Gian, and the parties negotiated on price, agreed on a figure, went for a test drive, and then completed the paperwork. Mr Tan added that the sales agreement listed two contact numbers, one belonging to Mdm Gian and the second belonging to Mr Loy. The car was intended to be registered in Mdm Gian's name. Mr Loy, however, told Mr Tan on the day of purchase that he would be the driver of the car[note: 65].

164    Less the finance loan from Maybank, the negotiated immediately payable sum of approximately $67,000 was paid in cash ($60,000), NETS ($2,000), and cheque ($5,126). On 18 January 2017, when the car was handed over, Mdm Gian and a person identified as Mr Loy's brother were present. Mdm Gian handed over the $60,000 as a cash sum[note: 66].

165    Mr Tan also gave evidence that Mdm Gian's Notice of Assessment was insufficient to substantiate the loan, and that Mr Loy eventually came in as a guarantor. Tan recalled clearly Mr Loy provided a bank statement showing a balance of approximately $1 million.

166    When asked by the DPP, Mr Tan stated that the names “Dextan Fun”, “Ronald Yip”, “Yip Holdings”, and “Yip & Loy” were never mentioned during the transaction, and that there was no reference of the car being intended as any kind of investment. Mr Tan vividly recalled Mr Loy to be "the person that actually showed the interest to purchase the car."[note: 67]

167    Here, the prosecution was able to show that the funds for the purchase of the Mercedes are traceable to the Balance Sum, with $65,126 being wholly traceable, and a further $8,846.69 being at least partially traceable. The $150,000 transferred from Mr Loy's personal Citibank account into Mdm Gian's first POSB account on 3 and 4 January 2017 is wholly traceable to the Balance Sum, as the only deposits into Mr Loy's personal Citibank account prior to those transfers were from the Balance Sum itself.

168    The learned DPPs noted that prior to the receipt of that $150,000, Mdm Gian's first POSB account contained only $2,140.32. The subsequent payments towards the Mercedes, including a $60,000 cash withdrawal, a $5,126 cheque, and a $2,000 NETS payment were therefore wholly traceable to the Balance Sum.

169    Mr Loy's claim that he was merely paying a $2,000 deposit as a favour for his cousin Dextan Fun is wholly inconsistent with his observed conduct by PW17. The learned DPPs observed[note: 68] that Mr Loy first denied test driving the car at all, then shifted his position and claimed he drove it on a different date, and also that neither position was put to Mr Tan when he was on the stand. Their stance was that Mr Loy effectively conceded that Mr Tan's testimony was unchallenged when he said he "couldn't be bothered"[note: 69] to challenge it. Mr Fun himself also did not corroborate Mr Loy's account.

170    In my judgment, the totality of Mr Loy's conduct, where he had expressed an ardent interest, negotiating the price, test driving the car, and telling the dealer he would be its driver was wholly inconsistent with the claim that he was merely doing his cousin a favour. The evidence trail pointed to Mr Loy intending the vehicle to be a personal acquisition.

Use of Balance sum for retail purchases and court bail

171    Mr Loy also spent at least $164.45 from the Balance Sum on various retail purchases at petrol stations and supermarkets apparently for his own benefit. These sums are entirely traceable to the Balance Sum, as the only deposits into his personal Citibank account were from the Balance Sum itself. Mr Loy contended that that these were "petty expenses" required for "investment activities”[note: 70], which were stated to be petrol for transport to carry out investments, and stationery for printing investment pitches.
