Mr Loy did not attempt any further substantiation of these expenditures but conceded that he did not submit any of these expenses to the corporate secretary[note: 71].

172    Rather extraordinarily, Mr Loy applied $30,000 from the Balance Sum towards his own court bail, after his arrest. Acting on Mr Loy's instructions, Mdm Gian applied for and was issued a cashier's order on 16 February 2017 for $30,000 payable to the State Courts. This sum was wholly traceable to the Balance Sum, having been transferred from Mr Loy's personal Citibank account into Mdm Gian's second POSB account before being applied to his bail. To say the least, Mr Loy’s use of misappropriated funds to pay his own court bail does not conduce to give a good impression of his distinguishing between personal assets and corporate property held under his care.

THE DEFENCE CASE

The defence case on the central question of whether there was a dishonest misappropriation by the First Accused

173    Essentially both sides agree that the core issue is whether Mr Loy dishonestly misappropriated the Balance Sum. As can be seen from the forgoing, the prosecution framed this as straightforward proposition for the undisputed facts speak for themselves. This being that Mr Loy transferred the money out of YHPL the very next day, routed it through a company he solely controlled, moved it into his personal account, and apparently expended the monies on himself and his own interests. The defence counters that Mr Loy genuinely believed he was legally entitled to do so pursuant to an oral investment agreement with Ronald, and that genuine belief negates the dishonesty element.

174    In this regard the defence relied[note: 72] on the Court of Appeal's definition of "dishonest" in Poh Yuan Nie v Public Prosecutor [2022] SGCA 74, which requires that the accused intended to mislead or cheat, submitting that this definition cannot apply to Mr Loy because Ronald allegedly agreed to and was fully aware of the investment plan, which would include the transfer of funds to Y&L's account, the purchase of the Lucky Plaza property in Mr Loy’s personal name, and the investment in shares.

175    The defence offered two practical justifications for the property being purchased in Mr Loy’s personal name: first, it would avoid the additional buyer's stamp duty that would have applied if purchased in Ronald's name or through a corporate entity; and second, Mr Loy’s willingness to be a personal guarantor for the Ethoz loan showed he was not trying to take advantage of Ronald, since he would be personally liable if Ronald died before the loan was repaid.

Ronald's mental capacity

176    The defence then pivoted to Ronald's mental capacity as the central issue, with counsel arguing that if Ronald were mentally capable at the material time, as certain lay witnesses suggested, then the irresistible inference must be that he validly entered into the Loan Agreement and was fully aware of and consented to the investment arrangement with Mr Loy[note: 73].

177    This is where the two sides diverged most sharply. The defence devoted considerable space to arguing that Ronald was mentally competent at the material time, relying on the lay witnesses including DW2 Jonathan Ow, PW6 Javier Tan, PW13 Brendan Cai, and PW2 Heng Kwang Han who all observed nothing unusual about him.

178    In relation to these four witnesses, the defence essentially made the following points[note: 74]:

(1)     Mr Jonathan Ow (DW2), a practising lawyer of 30 years, met Ronald on three occasions in 2016. Ronald sought legal advice on a complex loan agreement involving a 1% monthly interest rate, a 3% service charge, and a mortgage over two properties. Ronald introduced Mr Loy to Mr Ow as "the person who arranged for the loan" and made clear he had appointed Mr Loy to make loan arrangements on his behalf. Mr Ow's evidence was that Ronald was able to understand complex corporate and financial matters.

(2)     Mr Tan Jin Long Javier (PW6), the Ethoz relationship manager, attended multiple meetings with Ronald and Mr Loy. He observed that Ronald's demeanour was normal, that he seemed to understand what he was signing, and that he was aware the loan was $4 million and not $5 million as originally requested.

(3)     Mr Cai Xiande (PW13), Ethoz's team leader, corroborated Mr Tan's account. He noted that Ronald was actively involved in discussions, raised concerns about the negative pledge clause in the letter of offer, and even proposed finding another financier. Mr Cai agreed that Ronald's participation showed he could comprehend and engage with the content of the discussions.

(4)     Mr Heng Kwang Han (PW2), the Citibank relationship manager who attended to Ronald and Ezekiel on 10 October 2016, testified that Ronald "looks normal to me, like any other man you would see on the street," was able to describe his business and personal experience in the industry, and signed the account opening documents without reluctance. Mr Heng also confirmed that Ezekiel being the sole authorised signatory despite Ronald being a director was "not uncommon," and that there was "nothing suspicious" arising from Citibank's due diligence.

179    Learned defence counsel[note: 75] concluded that four independent witnesses unanimously observed Ronald to be mentally capable across three different contexts, legal, financial, and banking between April and October 2016, and that this is inconsistent with the prosecution's case that he was mentally deficient and unable to make complex decisions.

Analysis of defence submissions on Ronald’s mental capacity

180    On its surface, this is the defence's strongest argument, that four independent witnesses, including two called by the prosecution had consistently observed Ronald as mentally capable. Ronald's objection to the negative pledge clause, a specific commercial concern among nineteen clauses, might have been difficult to explain away as the behaviour of someone cognitively impaired.

Submissions on Ronald’s apparent capacity are contrary to actual medical evidence

181    While I commend counsel for their assiduous analysis, their argument is vulnerable to the actual medical evidence presented. The prosecution's medical evidence from Dr Mervyn Koh was not simply that Ronald was visibly confused or incoherent, but rather that he had specific deficits in short-term memory and orientation that might not be perceptible to a layman in a brief or superficial interaction, which the encounters undoubtedly were. Dr Koh explicitly noted that the effects may not be perceptible by a layman who only had superficial interaction with Ronald, but that these would come out if the inquisitor performed due diligence in checking for understanding and asking him to repeat himself. I refer specifically to this fragment of Dr Koh’s testimony[note: 76]:

…(I)f it’s just a superficial interaction with Mr. (Ronald) Yip as if he was ordering a drink at a coffeeshop, I don’t think it would have been perceptible to any layman. However, if this was a person who knew him for a longer period of time, then it would be the evident that he would have clear memory lapses at even difficulty making complex decisions. And with regards to even complex Financial matters, taking a loan and all that, I would believe that somebody who engaged in a very in depth conversation with him with regard to financial matters and did due diligence in checking for his understanding and getting him to repeat himself to show that understanding would be able to pick up these cognitive deficits.

182    In their submissions, the defence critiqued Dr Koh's evidence[note: 77], pointing out that he never conducted a formal assessment of Ronald's decision-making capacity for financial matters and effectively conceded this under cross-examination. Counsel argued that Dr Goh's evidence is similarly unhelpful[note: 78] as he only assessed Ronald in 2020 and admitted he could not reliably extrapolate backwards to 2016.

183    Dr Jerome Goh, the IMH psychiatrist who assessed Ronald in September and October 2020, while being candid about his the limits of ability to “extrapolate backwards”[note: 79] to even just seven months of deterioration between February 2020 and September-October 2020, much less ascertain Ronald’s condition at the material time in 2016, was nevertheless clear that a person's cognitive impairment may not always be apparent to laypeople around them, and it was not a certainty that it would be picked up. Notably Dr Goh had assessed Ronald in 2020, when the latter was fully in the thrall of dementia as to be unable to give evidence in court. Dr Goh noted that since dementia was a progressive condition, Ronald's deficits in 2016 would likely have been milder[note: 80] and implicitly less perceptible.

No competing defence expert to give an opposing medical viewpoint

184    I acknowledge the points made by learned counsel, but also note the defence’s inability to produce a competing medical expert to give a contrary medical opinion on Ronald’s mental capacity, it was open for the prosecution to validly argue that the lay witnesses' observations, while genuine, might not have picked up specific cognitive deficits that would have become evident to a trained geriatric physician.

185    In my judgment, the presented evidence convinced me that there should also a clear distinction between Ronald being able to generally follow a conversation, on the one hand, and being able to make fully informed, independent decisions about complex financial arrangements, on the other. With respect, the defence conflated these two aspects. Hence, Ronald raising the negative pledge clause, for instance, seemed reflect a residual ability to engage with familiar concepts to the seasoned businessman that he was without necessarily demonstrating full comprehension of the overall transaction.

Why Ronald’s condition was only one part of the equation

186    The prosecution's position, as discerned from their submission arguments treated the medical evidence as corroborative rather than central, and without it, the objective evidence of Mr Loy’s conduct and the absence of any credible agreement was sufficient, in their estimation, to prove the charge.

187    Simply stated, the prosecution did not rest its case primarily on Ronald's incapacity, but rather on the objective conduct of Mr Loy and the absence of any credible evidence of an agreement. Hence, while the prosecution did rely on Dr Koh's and Dr Goh's evidence to establish Ronald's vulnerability, the main thrust of their argument was essentially that Mr Loy’s own behaviour, which included disappearing after the transfer, misrepresenting investment goals to bank officers, and paradoxically never mentioning Ronald to anyone involved in the alleged investments, were wholly inconsistent with a genuine agreement.

The alleged investment agreement

188    The defence asserted that there was a genuine oral agreement to invest the Balance Sum in the Lucky Plaza property, shares, and the Rangoon Road redevelopment. The prosecution systematically engaged, deconstructed and generally dismantled this claim by, inter alia, pointing out that:

(1)     the alleged agreement was entirely oral despite Mr Loy having dealt with Ronald in writing on other occasions;

(2)     that Mr Loy could not even have known the quantum of the Balance Sum in October 2016 when he claimed the agreement was made;

(3)     that none of the investments were in YHPL's name or for YHPL's benefit; and

(4)     that Mr Loy never mentioned Ronald to any of the counterparties in the alleged investments; and that no monied from the Balance Sum ever returned to YHPL.

189    The prosecution also highlighted the extraordinary number of times Mr Loy’s account of the agreement shifted, in his police statements, his Case for the Defence, his evidence-in-chief, and cross-examination.

The defence submission did not engage issues concerning the First Accused’s credibility

190    The prosecution had concentrated a considerable part of their submissions on Mr Loy’s credibility referencing his constantly evolving positions on an array of material issue, spanning the purpose of the Balance Sum, the amounts Ronald allegedly owed him, the circumstances of their meeting, the objective of the alleged agreement, and his use of the money for expenses. The learned DPP’s submission also highlighted his litany of allegations against the police, the prosecutors, his own former lawyers, and even the court registries, arguing that these reflect a witness prone to fabrication and desperate deflection (which will be covered more extensively in the later part of these grounds).

191    The defence, by contrast, did not seriously engage with Mr Loy’s credibility problems, focusing instead on the legal standard of reasonable doubt and the weaknesses in the prosecution's medical evidence.

192    As a result of the defence submissions being more reliant on reasonable doubt arguments and the lay witness evidence on Ronald's mental state, they did not adequately address the prosecution's core point, which was that even if Ronald was mentally competent, there is no credible evidence that he ever agreed to allow what Mr Loy actually did with the money.

FINAL ANALYSIS

Would Ronald have approved the First Accused’s use of the Balance Sum, if it was never used for YHPL's benefit

193    Within this hypothetical thought experiment that Ronald did not lack mental capacity, one might ask would it have been conceivable for him to let Mr Loy handle the funds in the manner he did?

194    It is telling that the defence could not rebut the prosecution's contention that nothing from the Balance Sum was ever returned to YHPL or shown to have been used for its benefit. Where all sides are clear that the Balance Sum was to be invested for the eventual purpose of redeveloping Ronald's Rangoon Road property, Mr Loy's actions was wholly at odds with any genuine intention to redevelop the Rangoon Road property.

195    While Mr Loy held the Balance Sum from 18 November 2016 to the time of his arrest in August 2017, there was no indication of any of the monies going towards the redeveloping the Rangoon Road property, nor any funds ever being returned to YHPL. Mr Loy did not draft any corporate resolution authorising any his dealings with the Balance Sum. There was no agreed investment strategy, nor discernible targets. Conspicuously too, none of the investments were made in YHPL's name. The First Accused’s uncontactability and layering of accounts cast a pall of suspicion

196    When concerned parties, including Li-Fen and representatives from Ethoz, sought answers for Mr Loy's actions, he became uncontactable and was seen to be evasive in avoiding explanations. Mr Loy's conduct towards Brandan Cai of Ethoz is exemplary in this regard: when Mr Cai questioned Mr Loy about his dealings with Ronald, Mr Loy brushed him aside and ignored his enquiries. Similarly, when Li-Fen sought to contact Mr Loy on Ronald's behalf, she noted Mr Loy to be dismissive and unresponsive. Further, Mr Loy's observed pattern of layering transactions through multiple bank accounts, engaging in deceptive behaviour with various parties, and becoming evasive when questioned are circumstantially adverse to his case. My answer to the above thought experiment is a categorical “No”, Ronald would not approve, and Ronald’s actual position is extremely clearly set out by the letters and statements that were exhibited prior to the Interim Analysis.

Analysing the First Accused as witness

197    I have already dealt with the evidence of the two defence witnesses of fact, DW2 Jonathan Ow and DW3 Dextan Fun, earlier in these grounds. I now direct my analysis to the First Accused, Mr Loy, himself.

198    The High Court in Farida Begam d/o Mohd Artham v Public Prosecutor [2001] 3 SLR(R) 592, [2001] SGHC 333 identified three domains for the assessment of a witness's credibility: demeanour, internal consistency, and external consistency. I will address each in turn, though I should say at the outset that in my view the most transparent and forensically reliable approach to demeanour is not to rely on impressionistic observations of manner or bearing, but to identify discernible patterns of forthrightness or evasion in the way a witness gave evidence and responded to questions. I will accordingly treat demeanour in that broader sense and address it after dealing with the consistency analysis.

External Consistency

199    Mr Loy's evidence was extensively contradicted by other witnesses and by the objective documentary record. The most significant areas of external inconsistency were as follows.

200    On the Lucky Plaza property, Mr Loy claimed the purchase was an investment for YHPL's benefit. Yet Ronald did not participate in any viewings, all title and contractual documentation was in Mr Loy's name alone, and the property generated a consistent monthly loss. None of these features were consistent with a jointly agreed investment made on YHPL's behalf.

201    On the Rolex watch, Mr Loy claimed the funds transferred to Mdm Gian's account were intended for share investments. The bank records told a different story: the money moved from his account to Mdm Gian's account, she confirmed she purchased the watch on his instructions and passed it directly to him, and his cousin DW3 Dextan Fun confirmed at cross-examination that he had not paid for the watch and that Mr Loy was the actual customer. Mr Loy's name appeared on the tax invoice and his signature appeared in the receipt field, yet he denied having received the watch at all.

202    On the Mercedes sports car, Mr Loy claimed he had paid the deposit merely as a favour to his cousin. The car dealer testified that Mr Loy had expressed clear personal interest in the vehicle, negotiated the price, gone on a test drive, and told him he would be the car's driver. Mr Loy contradicted himself about the test drive, first denying it entirely and then claiming he had driven the car on a different date. He did not challenge the dealer's testimony on either point, saying he "couldn't be bothered."

203    On the Car Street and Property Street software projects, Mr Loy claimed these were funded from the Balance Sum for YHPL's benefit. Yet he never mentioned Ronald to Bhupesh Kalra of Innomedia Technologies, and he introduced his own mother; who had no role in YHPL, as one of his investors. Neither claim was consistent with a genuine intention to develop these projects for the company's benefit.

204    On the OCBC housing loan declaration, Mr Loy declared to OCBC that the sources of funds for his downpayment were directorship fees, sales of investments, savings, and business income. The downpayment came entirely from the Balance Sum. When confronted with this at trial, Mr Loy maintained that the truth of his declaration was contingent on his relationship with Ronald, a position I found wholly untenable.

205    Finally, on Mr Loy's claim to have extended a $300,000 loan to Ronald secured against properties at 102 Rangoon Road and 130 Lorong J Telok Kurau, I found it wholly implausible that Ronald would have pledged properties with a combined market value of nearly $10 million as security for a loan of just $300,000. This claim was as implausible as it was unsubstantiated.

Internal Consistency

206    Mr Loy's evidence was equally lacking in internal consistency, with his account shifting fundamentally across his police statements, his Case for the Defence, his evidence-in-chief, and cross-examination.

207    On the use of the Balance Sum, his Case for the Defence asserted that he and Ronald had agreed on how the funds should be spent. At trial, he shifted to claiming the money was his own, stating that it was "earned through my personal means"[note: 81] and "It is my money. I did not commit criminal breach of trust."[note: 82] Under cross-examination, he shifted again, claiming he had the option of either investing the money pursuant to the agreement or treating it as his own, and that he had authority to choose between the two. These three positions are irreconcilable with each other.

208    On the alleged oral agreement, Mr Loy’s Case for the Defence stated that he and Ronald had agreed to secure a loan from Ethoz only. At trial, he claimed there had also been an agreement to borrow $2.55 million from one Netty Jung and then added that Ronald had also wanted a loan from ValueMax. When pressed on the latter, he claimed a "missing" document would have confirmed it. This was not the only occasion on which Mr Loy invoked absent documents when cornered by an inconsistency he could not otherwise explain.

209    On the timing of the alleged agreement, Mr Loy had sworn in an affidavit that it was entered into "on or around October 2016."[note: 83] This was impossible, as the quantum of the Balance Sum could not have been known in October 2016 as the figure of $2,450,000 required to discharge the Coutts mortgage had not yet been agreed upon at that point. When this was put to him under cross-examination, Mr Loy first conceded the point, then asserted ignorance, and in re-examination claimed there had been "a mistake" in the affidavit, which he attributed to being "very tied up with full-time national service"[note: 84] and having given his lawyers the wrong date over the phone. I would observe that a person who had genuinely entered into an agreement involving over $1.2 million would be expected to remember with reasonable accuracy when that agreement was made.

210    On the question of written versus oral agreements, Mr Loy testified that he had a written document recording a $300,000 loan to Ronald and that he habitually committed events and agreements to writing. Yet for the alleged agreement concerning the Balance Sum, effectively a sum more than four times larger, he had claimed there was no written record, saying Ronald had wanted it to be oral and that discussions had taken place over WhatsApp. Those WhatsApp messages were, predictably, "missing" and were never produced.

211    On the monies Ronald allegedly owed him, Mr Loy told the police that approximately $80,000 to $100,000 of the Balance Sum represented expenses and monies Ronald owed him. This did not appear in his Case for the Defence. At trial during evidence-in-chief, he claimed Ronald owed him "at least 300-over thousand dollars"[note: 85] and a further $500,000[note: 86]. After his counsel discharged himself, he expanded this to a list of sums totalling $882,000[note: 87], then added claims for a further $423,215, a retainer and transport allowance of $162,500, and interest on a $20,000 loan. Months later, still in evidence-in-chief, he added yet more figures. When confronted, Mr Loy produced a document containing illegible scribbles and once again alluded to a "missing" document. By the end of cross-examination, he was essentially claiming entitlement to the entire Balance Sum as an offset against $1.5 million he said Ronald owed him.

212    Finally, on the claim that his Case for the Defence had been drafted without his input, Mr Loy raised this allegation some five years after the document was filed. He did not call his former lawyers to support it. I drew an adverse inference from this failure and found that the Case for the Defence, with its omissions, must have been drafted in accordance with his instructions.

Demeanour and Overall Credibility

213    Drawing these threads together, I found Mr Loy's overall credibility to be severely and irreparably undermined. Several features of his conduct at trial were particularly damaging in this regard.

214    The most persistent was his pattern of invoking "missing" documents whenever he was confronted with an inconsistency he could not otherwise explain. This recurred across multiple aspects of his case and had the appearance of a deliberate strategy rather than a series of unfortunate coincidences.

215    Equally damaging was the escalating and entirely unsupported nature of his claims about the monies Ronald allegedly owed him. These claims expanded dramatically over the course of the trial, without any documentary foundation, and culminated in the extraordinary position that he was entitled to treat the entire Balance Sum as his own by way of offset, with Ronald said to now owe him $1.5 million[note: 88]. No credible evidence was ever produced in support of any of these figures.

216    His explanation for the wrong date in his affidavit; that he was busy with national service and gave his lawyers the wrong date over the phone, was similarly unconvincing for the reasons I have already given.

217    Perhaps most telling was his repeated use of the phrase "could not be bothered" as an explanation for the inaccuracies in his police statements. When confronted with errors in those statements, Mr Loy said he had been angry and fed up with the police and "could not be bothered to give accurate answers."[note: 89] This response, and variations of it, recurred throughout the trial. It is an alarming position for a person facing serious criminal charges to adopt, and it is one that is entirely inconsistent with the conduct of someone who genuinely had a legitimate explanation for his use of the Balance Sum. The only person who would be indifferent to the accuracy of his own police statements is one who knew that the truthful answer could not help his case.

218    Taken together, Mr Loy's evidence was rife with grave internal inconsistencies, unsupported by any credible documentary evidence, and frequently and directly contradicted by other witnesses. I found his account of the Balance Sum to be wholly unreliable

The First Accused's Tendency to make unfounded claims and personal attacks eroded his credibility

219    I was satisfied that Mr Loy had a pattern of making unproven allegations against various parties that were troublingly scattershot and scurrilous in nature. In their submissions[note: 90], the learned prosecutors noted Mr Loy accused Ronald of being a cheat[note: 91] and of even being somehow able to “control” the prosecution, the police force, and even engage gangsters[note: 92] against him, where for the last claim, he never made any police report[note: 93] against his alleged underworld harassers.

220    The First Accused also accused Li-Fen of being a liar. He made serious allegations against police investigation officers, claiming they had deleted and suppressed evidence and forged documents. He accused his former lawyers of malpractice and of drafting his CFD without his instructions. He accused the prosecution of malicious prosecution, and the DPPs and police of forging evidence.

221    Among Mr Loy’s most outlandish claims, he alleged that that DPP Eric Hu, the lead prosecutor conducting the trial had, in 2008, written a blog encouraging the communist movement to topple the Singapore government, and seemingly alluded to the DPP’s personal animus against him arising from his coming from a different school[note: 94].

First Accused: (DPP Hu) He studied at Hwa Chong Institution. He doesn’t like people coming from my school (ACS). Yes. Let him confirm where he studied.

…

In 2008, Your Honour, (DPP Hu) wrote a blog encouraging the communist movement, the Marxist conspiracies to topple the Singapore government, to study hard and get into government service and then conspire together to topple the Singapore government. The people at ACS were not happy about this and I wrote a blog against it, against having that MRT station at Hwa Chong being named as Hwa Chong station. And then the 18 Singapore government agreed, and they changed it to another name.

[Emphasis added].

222    This claim was eclipsed by Mr Loy’s allegation that DPP Hu had tried to send drugs to him in prison, where he exclaimed while the latter was cross-examining him[note: 95]:

First Accused: No, you---you had people sending drugs to me.

223    Not a single shred of evidence was produced in support of any of these allegations. Many were never put to the relevant witnesses when they were on the stand, which was a significant procedural failure on the part of Mr Loy’s defence.

224    The failure to put an allegation to a witness is not a mere technical omission as it deprives that witness of the opportunity to respond, and it deprives the allegation of whatever forensic value it might otherwise have had.

225    I am satisfied that this pattern of unsubstantiated allegations, sustained across 64 days of trial, reflected not a genuine account of events but a recurring resort to deflection whenever Mr Loy found himself without a credible answer to the evidence against him. It is itself a telling indicator of a witness who knew his substantive case to be without merit.

226    I noted too that Mr Loy was prone to making rather grandiose claims about himself, including that he had been nominated for the Forbes 30 Under 30 award, the Singapore Young Entrepreneur Award, the Singapore Spirit of Enterprise Award, and the World Tourism Award, all in 2017. These claims were equally unsubstantiated, and do not aid in establishing credibility.

227    Mr Loy also made a claim to be Singapore's youngest self-made millionaire, relying on an unsubstantiated Wikipedia extract When the court pointed out[note: 96] that the Wikipedia extract he relied upon to establish his status as Singapore's youngest self-made millionaire could not be traced to any reliable provenance, Mr Loy was unable to offer any further substantiation. For completeness, this the article[note: 97] tended by the First Accused stated:

In 2001, (Adam) Koo became Singapore’s youngest self-made 2 millionaire at the age of 26. As of 2015 the newest, youngest 3 self-made millionaire in Singapore is Ezekiel Loy, who became a self-made millionaire at the age of 21.

228    I should add that Mr Loy’s primary school report card, which he tendered as evidence of his entrepreneurial character, was not a document that this court could give any weight to in the context of the serious charges he faced. Mr Loy did nothing to help his credibility by insisting that these be exhibited for his defence.

229    When confronted with his many material inconsistencies during cross-examination, Mr Loy repeatedly told the court that he "couldn't be bothered with how accurate [his] answers were to the police"[note: 98] and that he "couldn't be bothered with how [he] answered the police."[note: 99].

230    I agreed with the prosecution’s stance that this was an “alarming position”[note: 100] to be taken by a person facing serious criminal charges, who reposed an expectation to be regarded as a reliable and trustworthy witness.

231    It would only be expected that any person who genuinely had a legitimate agreement with Ronald and a credible explanation for his use of the Balance Sum would have every reason to ensure that his answers to the police were accurate and consistent. Indeed, one would posit that the only person who would be indifferent to the accuracy of his own police statements is one who knew that the truthful response could not help his case.

The CDSA Charges Against the First Accused

232    I turn now to the CDSA charges against Mr Loy. The CBT offence forms the predicate criminal conduct for the CDSA charges. It is the prosecution's case that the Balance Sum represents Mr Loy's benefits from criminal conduct, and that his subsequent transferring and using of moneys derived from the Balance Sum therefore fulfils the elements of section 47(1) of the CDSA.

233    Having found that Mr Loy committed the CBT offence, it follows that the Balance Sum represents his benefits from criminal conduct. The prosecution has carefully traced each of the 34 CDSA charges to the Balance Sum through a detailed Aide Memoire, and I am satisfied that the tracing exercise has been properly carried out. I shall briefly address the key aspects of the tracing.

234    The transfers of $850,000 to Mdm Gian's accounts are wholly traceable to the Balance Sum, as the only deposits into Mr Loy's personal Citibank account prior to those transfers were from the Balance Sum itself. Mr Loy conceded this during cross-examination. The transfers of $113,987.89 to his personal OCBC account are similarly wholly traceable to the Balance Sum.

235    The payments of $116,500 towards the Lucky Plaza property are wholly traceable to the Balance Sum, as they were made directly from Mr Loy's personal Citibank account, which received no deposits other than from the Balance Sum. Mr Loy conceded this during cross-examination. The $400,000 fixed deposit used to satisfy the OCBC Housing Loan requirement is wholly traceable to the Balance Sum through the route of transfers and cash withdrawals and redeposits described above. The cashier's order of $368,823.97 paid from Mdm Gian's second POSB account towards the purchase price of the Lucky Plaza property is substantially traceable to the Balance Sum, as Mr Loy himself conceded during cross-examination.

236    The 11 EPS payments totalling $125,519.40 for share purchases are at least substantially, and in many cases wholly, traceable to the Balance Sum. In each instance, the prosecution has demonstrated through careful tracing that the funds in Mr Loy's OCBC account at the time of each EPS payment were substantially or wholly derived from the Balance Sum. Mr Loy's denials of traceability in respect of several of these payments were internally inconsistent: in re-examination, he claimed that several of these payments were made pursuant to his alleged investment agreement with Ronald, which would itself mean that the funds were traceable to the Balance Sum. I accept the prosecution's tracing analysis in respect of each of these payments.

237    The payments of $24,500 to Innomedia Technologies are at least partially and substantially traceable to the Balance Sum. The first payment of $2,000 can be traced through a chain of EPS credits and share purchases back to a deposit of $254,000 into Mr Loy's OCBC account that is wholly traceable to the Balance Sum. The remaining payments are traceable to cash deposits of $20,000 and $5,000 made on 3 April 2017, which are at least partially traceable to the Balance Sum.

238    The five housing loan repayments totalling $18,259.95 are at least partially traceable to the Balance Sum, having been debited from Mr Loy's OCBC account into which the Balance Sum had flowed.

239    The $30,000 applied towards Mr Loy's court bail is wholly traceable to the Balance Sum, having been transferred from his personal Citibank account into Mdm Gian's second POSB account before being applied to the cashier's order payable to the State Courts.

240    I am therefore satisfied that the prosecution has proven each of the 34 CDSA charges against Mr Loy beyond a reasonable doubt.

THE SECOND ACCUSED'S INVOLVEMENT AND CULPABILITY

241    I turn now to consider Mdm Gian's role in these events. The factual substratum of her involvement was not in dispute between the parties. What divided them was the proper characterisation of her state of mind and the inferences to be drawn from her conduct.

242    The defence portrayed Mdm Gian as a mother who acted out of filial loyalty towards a son serving full-time National Service, accepting his instructions without question and without any awareness that the funds passing through her accounts were the proceeds of criminal conduct. On the defence's case, the watch and car transactions were attributable to Mr Fun rather than to Mr Loy, and Mdm Gian was an unwitting conduit rather than a knowing participant.

243    The prosecution's case was that the surrounding circumstances placed Mdm Gian in a position where she could not reasonably have been unaware that something was amiss. She had been informed by the police that Mr Loy was under investigation for cheating.

244    Further, the sums deposited into her accounts bore no relationship to anything Mr Loy could legitimately have earned as a National Serviceman drawing a monthly allowance of some $600 to $700.

245    Perhaps the prosecution’s most cogent point was that Mdm Gian was present when Mr Loy misrepresented her to Bhupesh as one of his investors, and she said nothing to correct him.

246    The prosecution further submitted that Mdm Gian’s evidence at trial was marked by evasiveness and contradiction, and that her own words in the witness box, to the effect that she would protect her son even at cost to herself, illuminated the true nature of her participation

247    The elements of the charge against Mdm Gian under section 44(1) of the CDSA are threefold. First, that she entered into an arrangement in relation to her bank accounts. Second, that she had reasonable grounds to believe that Mr Loy was engaged in criminal conduct at the material time. Third, that she had reasonable grounds to believe that the arrangement would facilitate the retention or control of Mr Loy's benefits from that criminal conduct.

248    The phrase 'reasonable grounds to believe' has been considered by the High Court in Ang Jeanette v Public Prosecutor [2011] 4 SLR 130, where it was observed that the standard occupies a middle ground, which demands more than mere speculation but does not require the certainty of actual knowledge.

249    The inquiry is neither purely subjective nor purely objective. The court places itself in the position of the particular accused, taking into account what she knew and her personal circumstances, but then asks whether a reasonable person in that position would have drawn the relevant belief from those facts. It is the application of an objective standard of reasonableness to a subjective factual matrix.

250    The starting point is what was not in dispute. It was common ground that funds traceable to the Balance Sum passed through Mdm Gian's bank accounts, that she was aware these funds came from Mr Loy, and that she handled them in accordance with his directions. It was equally common ground that she did so through her two POSB accounts, and that the transactions she carried out using those accounts constituted an arrangement within the meaning of section 44(1) of the CDSA.

251    The question that remained for determination was therefore a narrower one: whether Mdm Gian, at the time she entered into and gave effect to this arrangement, had reasonable grounds to believe that the funds represented the proceeds of Mr Loy's criminal conduct and that what she was doing would facilitate his retention of control over those proceeds. The physical acts were not contested. What fell to be decided was the state of mind with which those acts were performed, assessed against the objective standard described above.

Mdm Gian's awareness of the police investigation into Mr Loy

252    One of the more significant pieces of evidence bearing on Mdm Gian's state of mind was her knowledge that Mr Loy was the subject of a police investigation for cheating. Inspector Kenny Lim of the Singapore Police Force gave evidence that he had telephoned Mdm Gian and informed her that he was investigating a cheating case involving her son. He explained that he was unable to discuss the details of the matter over the phone and requested that she attend at the police station to provide a statement.

253    Mdm Gian's response to this call was itself revealing. She told Inspector Lim that she was unavailable that week and asked him to call again the following week. She did not challenge or dispute what he had told her about the investigation. Inspector Lim observed that she spoke to him in a raised voice and that, unlike most parents of persons under investigation who are contacted by the police, she did not appear distressed. He subsequently attempted to reach her again but was unsuccessful, and no statement was ever recorded from her.

254    Mdm Gian did not deny that this conversation took place. She accepted that Inspector Lim had called her, though she said she had not wanted to accept what he told her. More tellingly, she recounted that Mr Loy had assured her that he had not cheated anyone, which was an account which itself confirmed that she was aware, at the material time, that he, in fact, stood accused of cheating. I regarded this awareness as a matter of considerable significance in assessing whether the circumstances were such as to give her reasonable grounds to believe that the funds passing through her accounts were the proceeds of criminal conduct.

The disproportion between the sums received and any legitimate source

255    A second and related consideration was the sheer scale of the funds that passed through Mdm Gian's accounts. Notably, Mdm Gian’s banking history prior to her involvement in these transactions showed no deposits of remotely comparable size. When pressed in cross-examination to identify any prior deposit approaching the amounts she had received, she could point only to a single deposit of $31,000, which was itself a sum she regarded as large, as against deposits of $50,000 and $450,000 that she received in connection with Mr Loy's instructions.

256    Mdm Gian acknowledged that she considered $3,000 to be a substantial sum of money, and that the amounts she received were, in her own words, 'much bigger'[note: 101] than that. When the police asked her whether it was common for her to receive a deposit of $450,000, she conceded that it was not, and she was unable to offer any explanation for where the money had come from.

257    The Second Accused’s inability to explain the source of these funds was not merely a gap in her knowledge. She admitted that Mr Loy had not told her where the money came from, and that she had not asked. This was a significant omission.

258    Mdm Gian knew that Mr Loy was serving full-time National Service at the material time, drawing a monthly allowance of around $600 to $700. There was no conceivable legitimate source from which Mr Loy could have derived sums of this magnitude. A person in her position, who was well aware that her son was under police investigation for cheating, receiving deposits wholly disproportionate to anything he could legitimately have earned, and having chosen not to enquire into their provenance, could not reasonably have avoided the conclusion that something was seriously amiss with the funds she was being asked to handle.

Mdm Gian's Silence When Mr Loy Misrepresented Her Role to Bhupesh

259    A further consideration was Mdm Gian's conduct when Mr Loy introduced her to Bhupesh as one of his investors. She was present when this representation was made. She knew it to be false. She said nothing to correct it.

260    This was not a trivial omission. The misrepresentation went directly to the nature of the arrangement, as it offered a false explanation for why funds were passing through her accounts. A person who genuinely believed she was doing nothing more than helping her son with routine financial matters would have had no reason to remain silent when her role was being mischaracterised to a third party. Mdm Gian’s silence in those circumstances is more readily explicable on the basis that she understood the true nature of what she was involved in and appreciated that it could not withstand scrutiny.

261    Drawing these threads together, I was satisfied that the mental element of the charge was established. Mdm Gian knew at the material time that Mr Loy was under police investigation for cheating. She received into her accounts sums that bore no relationship to any income Mr Loy could legitimately have earned. She asked no questions about where the money came from. And she stood by in silence while Mr Loy offered a false account of her role to a third party. Considered individually, each of these circumstances might perhaps be explained away. Considered together, they left me in no doubt that Mdm Gian had reasonable grounds to believe that the funds she was handling represented the proceeds of Mr Loy's criminal conduct and that the arrangement she had entered into with him served to facilitate his retention of control over those proceeds.

Mdm Gian's Evidence and Its Reliability

262    With respect, I did not find Mdm Gian to be a reliable witness. Her evidence on several material points was internally inconsistent, and her manner of giving evidence made it difficult to place confidence in her account.

263    The clearest illustration of this concerned her evidence about the police investigation into Mr Loy. She began by denying that she had known anything about the cheating allegations. She then conceded that she had in fact known Mr Loy was under investigation and that she had been concerned enough to ask him about it.

264    Mdm Gian sought to reconcile these positions by suggesting that there were two sides[note: 102] to the matter and that Mr Loy's version was that he had not cheated anyone, which was a concession which itself contradicted her earlier denial of knowledge. When this contradiction was pointed out to her, she shifted her position once more, maintaining that she had only come to know about the cheating investigation at some later point. The progression of her evidence on this single issue: from denial to qualified admission, to partial retraction was not at all consistent with a witness doing her honest best to recall events accurately.

265    It was also significant that when Mr Loy told Mdm Gian to disregard Inspector Lim's call, she did so without question and made no further attempt to follow up. A person who genuinely believed there was nothing to be concerned about might reasonably have sought clarification. Mdm Gian's readiness to let the matter drop entirely, on her son's instruction, was more consistent with a deliberate choice not to enquire further than with genuine ignorance of what the investigation was about

266    The Second Accused’s conduct in the witness box was also a matter I took into account. Mdm Gian was at times openly combative in response to questions that called for straightforward answers, and on one occasion questioned the prosecution's arithmetic when asked a simple question about when Mr Loy commenced National Service.

267    When Mdm Gian’s police statement was put to her in cross-examination, Mdm Gian declined to engage directly with questions that were each no more than a sentence long, requiring repeated attempts before she would respond.

268    When pressed further on the contents of her statement, Mdm Gian attributed her inability to recall to a stroke she said she had suffered at some point in the past. She could not, however, identify when this had occurred, there was no medical documentation of any such event, and she acknowledged that she had not sought any formal diagnosis. I was unable to accept this explanation. The claimed medical episode was entirely without corroboration and appeared, in the context of the proceedings, to serve as a means of avoiding answers to questions she found inconvenient.

269    Having considered Mdm Gian's evidence as a whole, I was not able to regard her as a reliable witness on the material issues. The inconsistencies in her account were not minor or peripheral. Indeed, they went to the heart of what she knew and when she knew it. Mdm Gian’s evidence shifted in ways that could not be attributed to the ordinary frailties of memory, and her manner of giving evidence reinforced rather than dispelled the concerns arising from those inconsistencies.

270    Mdm Gian’s own words in the witness box were, in the end, the most candid thing she said. When she told the court that she would protect her son even at cost to herself, she was in all likelihood speaking truthfully. That candour, however, cut against rather than in favour of her case. It offered the most coherent explanation for the pattern of her evidence, not a witness struggling to recall events accurately, but a mother doing what she had said she would do. The court does not doubt the sincerity of that impulse. It cannot, however, treat it as a basis for accepting evidence that is contradicted by the objective facts, nor can it excuse participation in conduct that the law regards as criminal.

271    On the evidence before me, I was satisfied that the prosecution had established each element of the charge against Mdm Gian beyond a reasonable doubt. The arrangement she entered into with Mr Loy, the circumstances in which she did so, and what those circumstances would have conveyed to any reasonable person in her position, together left no room for a reasonable doubt as to her guilt

The CDSA Charges Against Mr Loy

272    Both parties agreed that if the CBT charge is made out, the CDSA charges follow as a matter of course

VERDICT

273    Having considered all the evidence with care, I was satisfied that the prosecution had proven its case against both accused persons beyond a reasonable doubt.

274    In Mr Loy's case, the conclusion was, in my judgment, inescapable. The undisputed facts, encompassing the transfer of the entire Balance Sum out of YHPL within a single day of its receipt, its passage through a company he alone controlled, and its systematic application to his own personal ends without a single cent returning to YHPL, admitted of no innocent explanation. Mr Loy’s attempts to provide one only deepened his difficulty. Mr Loy’s account of an oral investment agreement shifted so fundamentally and so often, across his police statements, his Case for the Defence, his evidence-in-chief, and cross-examination, that no coherent version of it survived scrutiny.

275    When confronted with the contradictions in his evidence, Mr Loy resorted to allegations against virtually every party connected with the proceedings; allegations that were as serious as they were unsupported, and which served only to confirm that his substantive case had no answer to the evidence against him.

276    In Mdm Gian's case, I was satisfied for the reasons set out above that the circumstances in which she handled the funds were such as to give any reasonable person in her position grounds to believe that the money represented the proceeds of criminal conduct and that what she was doing would facilitate Mr Loy's retention of control over those proceeds. Her evidence did not cause me to doubt that conclusion. If anything, the manner in which she gave evidence, and what she ultimately said about her own motivations, reinforced it.

277    I accordingly convicted both accused persons on their respective charges..

SENTENCING CONSIDERATIONS

Findings at Trial Relevant to Sentence

278    I turn now to the aspects of the evidence and the conduct of the proceedings that bear on the appropriate sentences to be imposed.

279    In relation to Mr Loy, the findings at trial disclosed a pattern of offending that was both deliberate and sustained. The transfer of the entire Balance Sum out of YHPL within a single day of its receipt was not an impulsive act. Y&L had been incorporated months earlier, with Mr Loy as its sole director and shareholder, and the Citibank account through which the funds were routed had lain dormant until the Balance Sum became available. The speed and structure of the transfer reflected a degree of preparation that was inconsistent with any innocent explanation.

280    The misrepresentations Mr Loy made to bank employees about Y&L's business activities compounded this picture. He told Citibank's relationship manager that Y&L was engaged in the distribution of Korean cosmetics and palm oil equipment, which were claims that were entirely without foundation and served no purpose other than to provide a pretext for the movement of funds. Not a single transaction consistent with those declared business activities ever passed through Y&L's account.

281    The uses to which Mr Loy put the Balance Sum were entirely personal. He purchased a property at Lucky Plaza in his sole name, acquired shares for his personal trading account, paid for two software development projects that were for his own benefit, purchased a Rolex Yacht-Master watch, and contributed to the acquisition of a Mercedes sports car. No part of the Balance Sum was ever returned to YHPL or applied for its benefit.

282    A substantial portion of the funds was ultimately recovered; approximately S$1,036,758.95 in total, comprising S$30,000 held as court bail, S$400,000 in an OCBC time deposit account, and an estimated S$580,291.17 from the proceeds of the Lucky Plaza property sale.

283    I note, however, that this recovery was entirely the result of the efforts of the investigating authorities. No credit for it can be attributed to Mr Loy, who at no point took any voluntary step to return or preserve the funds.

284    Mr Loy's conduct when questioned about his dealings with the Balance Sum was also a matter I took into account. When Ronald's daughter and representatives from Ethoz sought explanations, he became progressively uncontactable and evasive. At trial, his account of the Balance Sum shifted repeatedly and fundamentally — between a claim that its use had been agreed with Ronald, and a claim that it represented his own personal funds held in cash at home. Neither version was supported by any credible evidence, and the two were irreconcilable with each other. His credibility was further eroded by the pattern of unsubstantiated allegations he directed at virtually every party connected with the proceedings, including Ronald, Li-Fen, Bhupesh Kalra, the investigating officers, his former lawyers, and the prosecutors.

285    Turning to Mdm Gian, the findings relevant to her sentence have been set out in the earlier part of these grounds. In summary, I was satisfied that the circumstances in which she handled the funds, such as her knowledge of the police investigation into Mr Loy for cheating, the wholly disproportionate sums that passed through her accounts relative to any income Mr Loy could legitimately have earned, and her silence when Mr Loy misrepresented her role to Bhupesh, together gave her reasonable grounds to believe that the funds represented the proceeds of criminal conduct.

286    Mdm Gian’s evidence at trial did not cause me to revise that assessment. The inconsistencies in her account, and her ultimate candour about her own motivations, reinforced rather than undermined the conclusion I had reached

SENTENCING PRINCIPLES

287    The dominant sentencing considerations in cases of this nature are general deterrence and retribution. Where an offender has abused a position of corporate trust to misappropriate funds from a vulnerable victim, and has done so through a course of deliberate and sophisticated conduct, the sentence must reflect both the community's condemnation of such behaviour and the need to deter others who might be minded to exploit similar positions of trust for personal gain.

288     Rehabilitation, while not irrelevant given Mr Loy's age at the time of the offending, could not be accorded significant weight in the circumstances of this case. The offending was not impulsive or opportunistic in any simple sense. It involved the incorporation of a company, the acquisition of a controlling stake in the victim's company, the securing of a substantial loan using the victim's property as collateral, and the systematic dispersal of the proceeds across multiple accounts and transactions.

289    This was not the conduct of a young person who had made a single poor decision. The weight that might otherwise attach to youth and the prospect of rehabilitation was substantially diminished by the calculated nature of what Mr Loy did and by his conduct throughout the proceedings.

Sentence for the Criminal Breach of Trust Charge

290    Section 406 of the Penal Code provides for imprisonment of up to seven years, a fine, or both. The sum misappropriated was S$1,268,500.

291    Two precedents involving comparable quanta were placed before the court. In Public Prosecutor v Tio Chee Hui [2018] SGDC 112, the offender misappropriated Singapore dollars received upfront from two Batam-based moneychangers in exchange for foreign currency he never delivered. The sums involved were S$639,473 and S$1,294,200 respectively.

292    The court took into account the deliberate nature of the offending, the trust reposed in the offender, the financial impact on the victims, the offender's non-cooperation with investigations, and his failure to attend court. The offender pleaded guilty and was sentenced to three years' imprisonment for the first charge and four years and six months' imprisonment for the second, with his appeal against sentence dismissed by the High Court.

293    In Public Prosecutor v Varusai Mohamed Bin Syed Hanifa [2022] SGDC 238, the offender was convicted after trial on seven section 406 Penal Code charges for misappropriating moneys entrusted to him by his doctor for forex trading. The court noted the considerable trust reposed in the offender and the scale of the misappropriation.

294    Sentences of three years' imprisonment for the charge involving S$599,266, three years and six months' imprisonment for the charge involving S$751,558, and 24 months' imprisonment for the charge involving £150,000 were imposed, with the offender's appeal subsequently lapsing.

295    I found both cases to be of assistance as reference points, though neither mapped precisely onto the present facts. The present case involved a more vulnerable victim than either precedent given that Ronald was elderly, cognitively impaired, and living alone at the material time, and the degree of planning and premeditation was considerably greater. At the same time, Mr Loy was 22 years of age at the time of the offending, a factor that carried some, if limited, mitigating weight.

296    Taking these matters into account, I was of the view that a starting point of five years' imprisonment, rather than the six years urged by the prosecution, was the more appropriate anchor for the section 406 charge. I was, however, satisfied that an upward adjustment of six months was warranted on account of factors that distinguished this case from the precedents, and to which I now turn.

297    I turn now to the factors that warranted an upward adjustment from the starting point I had identified.

AGGRAVATING FACTORS

298    The first and most significant was the vulnerability of the victim. Ronald was elderly, unemployed, and living alone at the material time. He had been diagnosed with post-ICU delirium in September 2016 and, as Dr Mervyn Koh's evidence established, had significant cognitive deficits that would have impaired his ability to make complex financial decisions or to appreciate the full implications of what he was agreeing to.

299    What made this factor particularly weighty was the timing of Mr Loy's actions. Y&L was incorporated during Ronald's hospitalisation. The Ethoz loan was secured shortly after his diagnosis. The inference that Mr Loy was aware of Ronald's condition and chose to act when he did precisely because of it was one I found difficult to resist.

300    The second aggravating factor was the degree of planning and premeditation involved. The offending was not opportunistic. It unfolded across a period of months and involved a sequence of deliberate steps: the incorporation of Y&L with Mr Loy as its sole director and shareholder; the acquisition of a controlling stake in YHPL; the securing of a S$4 million loan using Ronald's property as collateral; and the immediate transfer of the Balance Sum through Y&L on the very day after it was received. Each step served a purpose in the overall scheme, and the scheme as a whole bore the hallmarks of careful advance planning rather than a spontaneous decision to misappropriate funds that happened to come within reach.

301    The third factor was the abuse of the position of trust that Mr Loy occupied. As a director of YHPL, he owed fiduciary duties to the company and, through it, to Ronald as its beneficial owner.

302    The misappropriation was not merely a breach of those duties in a technical sense but nothing less than a calculated exploitation of the very position that gave him access to the funds in the first place. The courts have long recognised that offences of this kind, committed by persons in positions of corporate trust, call for sentences that reflect the seriousness with which such abuse is regarded.

303    The fourth factor was the elaborate nature of the cover-up. Mr Loy did not simply take the money and disappear. He layered the transactions through multiple accounts, misrepresented Y&L's business activities to financial institutions, became progressively uncontactable when questioned by Ronald's family and by Ethoz, and provided explanations that shifted and contradicted each other throughout the proceedings. This sustained effort to conceal and deflect was itself evidence of a consciousness of wrongdoing that went beyond the original act of misappropriation.

304    The fifth factor was that the entire Balance Sum was applied for Mr Loy's personal benefit. The Lucky Plaza property, the shares, the Rolex watch, the Mercedes sports car, with every identified use of the funds was indubitably for his own account. No monies was returned to YHPL or applied to any purpose that could conceivably have been for its benefit. The degree of personal enrichment was total.

305    The sixth factor, which I regarded as relevant specifically to the CDSA charges, was Mr Loy's decision to enlist his mother's assistance in routing the funds through her accounts. The willingness to draw a family member into criminal conduct, and to exploit the trust and loyalty that a family relationship ordinarily commands, was an aggravating feature of those charges. I applied a moderate uplift from the tariffs in Chong Kum Heng v Public Prosecutor [2020] 4 SLR 1056 on this account, though a lesser one than the prosecution had sought.

306     Finally, I took into account Mr Loy's conduct throughout the proceedings as evidence of a complete absence of remorse. His defence at trial was not merely unsuccessful, it was characterised by a pattern of shifting and irreconcilable accounts, by claims that were advanced without any supporting evidence and abandoned when challenged, and by a series of allegations directed at virtually every party connected with the case. These included allegations against Ronald, Li-Fen, Bhupesh Kalra, the investigating officers, his former lawyers, and the prosecutors.

307    Mr Loy’s claim, made some five years after the event, that his Case for the Defence had been filed without his knowledge or instructions, was a further illustration of this pattern, being an attempt to explain away inconvenient omissions by casting blame on others rather than engaging with the substance of the case against him. An offender who conducts himself in this way at trial cannot be said to have demonstrated any genuine appreciation of the gravity of what he has done

Mitigating Factors for the CBT charge

308    I turn now to the factors that counsel advanced in mitigation, and the weight I was prepared to accord them.

309    The most substantial mitigating factor was Mr Loy's age. He was 22 years old at the time of the offending and had no prior criminal record. The defence submitted that his actions could, at least to some degree, be attributed to the folly of youth. I accepted that youth is a recognised mitigating factor and that younger offenders generally retain a greater capacity for rehabilitation. I also accepted that Mr Loy's status as a full-time National Serviceman at the material time was a circumstance that the court should take into account.

310    These considerations were, however, substantially diminished by the nature of the offending itself. The scheme Mr Loy executed was not the product of an impulsive or immature decision. It involved the incorporation of a company, the acquisition of a controlling stake in YHPL, the securing of a multi-million-dollar loan using another person's property as collateral, and the systematic dispersal of the proceeds across multiple accounts and transactions over an extended period.

311    Incidentally, the defence's own submission acknowledged that an upward calibration from the starting point in Tio was necessary to account for the vulnerability of the victim and the non-financial harm caused to Ronald. A person capable of conceiving and executing a scheme of this complexity and duration cannot credibly claim that his youth and inexperience should carry significant mitigating weight.

312    The sophistication of the offending was, in my judgment, more consistent with a calculated and deliberate course of conduct than with the kind of poor judgment that youth as a mitigating factor is intended to address.

313    Mr Loy's status as a first-time offender was a further factor I considered. The absence of prior convictions is ordinarily a neutral to mildly mitigating circumstance. In the present case, however, the sheer scale and duration of the offending, with no fewer than 35 charges spanning a period from November 2016 to June 2017, meant that this was not a case of a single lapse of judgment by an otherwise law-abiding individual. It was a sustained course of criminal conduct involving multiple distinct acts of misappropriation and money laundering. The weight that might otherwise attach to a clean record was accordingly limited.

314    Mr Loy claimed trial and demonstrated no remorse throughout the proceedings. He was therefore not entitled to any sentencing discount that would ordinarily be available upon a plea of guilt.

The appropriate sentence for the CBT Charge

315    Drawing these threads together, I was satisfied that the appropriate sentence for the CBT charge was 66 months' imprisonment. The starting point I had identified was five years' imprisonment, derived from a comparative analysis of Tio and Varusai and calibrated to reflect the quantum involved.

316    From that starting point, the aggravating factors I have set out above, comprising the vulnerability of the victim, the degree of planning and premeditation, the abuse of a position of corporate trust, the elaborate cover-up, the total personal application of the misappropriated funds, and the enlisting of a family member's assistance, warranted a meaningful upward adjustment.

317    Against these, I weighed Mr Loy's youth and his status as a first-time offender, which I accorded limited but not negligible weight.

318    The defence had urged a sentence of between 54 and 60 months' imprisonment, submitting that Mr Loy's culpability fell between Tio (54 months' imprisonment) and Public Prosecutor v Tan Cheng Yew (72 months' imprisonment for each charge under section 409), and that a sentence within that range appropriately balanced the overall criminality with his youth at the material time.

319    I found this range to be too low. The present case was more serious than Tio in several material respects, where the victim was significantly more vulnerable, the degree of planning was considerably greater, and the cover-up was more elaborate. While the present case did not reach the level of egregious conduct in Tan Cheng Yew, which involved a solicitor who had actively procured the entrustment of funds he had no intention of returning and who subsequently fled the jurisdiction for six years, the aggravating features of the present case placed it well above the lower end of the range the defence proposed.

320    After much deliberation, I formed the view that a sentence of 66 months' imprisonment reflected the gravity of the offending, gave appropriate weight to the mitigating factors, and was not, in my judgment, crushing when considered in the context of the overall sentence to be imposed.

Sentences for the CDSA charges

321    I turn now to the sentences for Mr Loy's 34 CDSA charges. The starting point for each charge was derived from the sentencing bands in Chong Kum Heng v Public Prosecutor [2020] 4 SLR 1056, calibrated according to the quantum involved in each transaction.

322    The defence had proposed applying a modest uplift of one month to the Ho Man Yuk bands, submitting that the present facts were significantly less egregious than Juandi given the lower total quantum, the absence of transnational elements, the absence of syndicate involvement, and the shorter duration of offending. The prosecution, by contrast, sought sentences at a higher level, with further enhancement on account of Mr Loy's lack of remorse and conduct at trial.

323    I accepted that the present case was of lower severity than Juandi, which involved a decade-long conspiracy within a sophisticated criminal network, a total quantum of criminal benefits far exceeding the present case, and offending that caused harm to a strategic sector of Singapore's economy. Those features are not present here. At the same time, I was satisfied that several features of the present case warranted sentences above the base tariff.

324    The most significant of these was that Mr Loy was himself the perpetrator of the predicate CBT offence. He was not a secondary participant who had handled funds without full knowledge of their provenance.

325    Mr Loy was the effective architect of the entire scheme, the direct beneficiary of the misappropriation, and the person who then systematically laundered the proceeds through a series of deliberate transactions. This placed his culpability for the CDSA offences at a materially higher level than that of a person who had merely facilitated another's criminal conduct.

326    Beyond this, the layering of transactions through multiple accounts; through Y&L, through his personal accounts, and through his mother's accounts, was not incidental to the offending but was a deliberate strategy to distance the funds from their origins and to frustrate any attempt to trace them.

327    The routing of funds through Mdm Gian's accounts, including the elaborate sequence of cash withdrawals and redeposits in connection with the Lucky Plaza property purchase, served no legitimate purpose and was designed solely to obscure the money trail.

328    The total personal application of the laundered funds was also a relevant consideration. Every transaction the subject of a CDSA charge was directed towards Mr Loy's own benefit whether they involved property, shares, luxury goods, or personal expenses. There was no suggestion that any part of the funds was applied for any purpose other than his own enrichment.

329    Finally, I took into account Mr Loy's conduct at trial as a further basis for an upward adjustment. His complete absence of remorse, his shifting and irreconcilable accounts, and his sustained pattern of unsubstantiated allegations against virtually every party connected with the proceedings were matters that I regarded as warranting a moderate enhancement above the base tariff, consistent with the approach affirmed in Seng Yong Yi Lucas v Public Prosecutor [2025] SGHC 158.

330    Weighing these considerations against the mitigating factors I had already identified; principally Mr Loy's youth and his status as a first-time offender, I arrived at the individual sentences set out in the table below. The sentences reflect the quantum involved in each charge as the primary determinant, adjusted upward to account for the aggravating features I have described, and are consistent with the approach taken in the precedents placed before the court.

Sentence for Mdm Gian's CDSA Charge

331    I turn now to the appropriate sentence for Mdm Gian's charge under section 44(1)(a) of the CDSA, which concerned her facilitation of Mr Loy's control over S$850,000 in criminal proceeds through her personal DBS accounts.

332    The applicable sentencing framework is that set out in Huang Ying-Chun v Public Prosecutor [2019] 3 SLR 606, which requires the court to assess the level of harm and culpability before identifying the appropriate sentencing range from the matrix, selecting a starting point within that range, and making adjustments for offender-specific factors.

333    On the question of harm, the prosecution and defence were not far apart in their assessments, though they differed on the precise characterisation. The prosecution placed the case at the lower end of "Severe" harm, while the defence submitted that it fell within "Moderate" harm with low to medium culpability. I preferred the prosecution's characterisation.

334    The sum of S$850,000 is a substantial amount, and the court in Huang had treated a comparable sum of S$957,000 as a factor tending towards a finding of severe harm. The absence of syndicate involvement, transnational elements, and harm to public confidence meant that the case did not reach the higher end of the severe range, but the quantum alone was sufficient to place it there.

335    On culpability, I was satisfied that Mdm Gian's culpability was low. She did not devise the scheme, did not commit the predicate offence, and derived no personal benefit from the funds that passed through her accounts. Her role was essentially one of passive facilitation. Effectively, she made her accounts available to her son and acted on his instructions in receiving, depositing, and transferring funds. There was no evidence of sophistication or planning on her part, and she was not in Singapore for the purpose of committing the offence. These features distinguished her position from that of the offender in Huang, whose culpability was assessed at medium on account of his planning and premeditation, the sophistication of the criminal enterprise, and his having travelled to Singapore solely to offend.

336    The comparison with Public Prosecutor v Lim Yi Jie [2019] SGDC 128 was also instructive. In that case, the offender received 40 months' imprisonment for a charge involving S$86,400, with harm assessed at the higher end of moderate and culpability at the higher end of medium.

337    The present case involved nearly ten times that amount, which placed it firmly in the severe harm category even in the absence of the other aggravating features present in Lim Yi Jie. Mdm Gian's significantly lower culpability, however, meant that the overall sentencing range was not correspondingly higher.

338    Placing the case at the lower end of the severe harm and low culpability cell of the Huang matrix, the indicative range was 30 to 60 months' imprisonment.

339    I then considered the offender-specific factors. On the aggravating side, Mdm Gian's facilitation was not a single isolated act. It extended over a period of approximately seven months and involved multiple transactions across her accounts. Throughout this period, she had reasonable grounds to believe that Mr Loy was engaged in criminal conduct, and she was aware of the police investigations into him for cheating, she knew that the sums being deposited into her accounts were wholly disproportionate to what he could legitimately have earned on a National Service allowance, and she was present when Mr Loy misrepresented her role to Bhupesh. Her conduct at trial was also a matter I took into account. She was evasive and contradictory in her evidence, and her initial denial of knowledge of the investigations into her son; a denial she later retreated from, did not assist her.

340    On the mitigating side, I gave weight to the following. Mdm Gian did not commit the predicate offence and derived no personal benefit from the funds. She acted on her son's instructions, a circumstance that, while not exculpatory, was relevant to the assessment of her moral culpability.

341    Mdm Gian’s role was less sophisticated than Mr Loy's in every respect. She was a first-time offender with no prior criminal record. At the material time, she was working as a part-time tutor and was the primary caregiver for her husband, who had suffered a stroke. These personal circumstances did not diminish the seriousness of what she had done, but they were matters I took into account in calibrating the sentence.

342    Mdm Gian did not plead guilty and was therefore not entitled to any discount on that account.

343    Weighing all of these considerations, I was satisfied that a sentence of 30 months' imprisonment was appropriate. This placed the sentence at the lower end of the prosecution's proposed range of 30 to 40 months, and reflected the combination of severe harm, low culpability, and the mitigating personal circumstances I have described. The sentence was, in my judgment, proportionate to Mdm Gian's overall criminality and consistent with the precedents placed before the court.

Conclusion on Mdm Gian's Sentence

344    The imposed sentence of 30 months' imprisonment reflected the seriousness of Mdm Gian's facilitation of Mr Loy's control over S$850,000 in criminal proceeds, and her sustained course of conduct over approximately seven months in circumstances where she had reasonable grounds to believe that her son was engaged in criminal conduct. At the same time, it gave appropriate weight to the factors that distinguished her position from that of a person who had participated in or profited from a money laundering enterprise. Again, she derived no personal benefit, she did not conceive or direct the scheme, and she acted throughout on her son's instructions.

Conclusion on Mr Loy's Sentences and the Global Sentence

345    Before turning to the global sentence, I think it is important to record the fundamental difference in culpability between the two accused persons, because it bears directly on the overall sentencing exercise.

346    Mr Loy was the architect of everything that followed. He identified the victim, incorporated Y&L, acquired a controlling stake in YHPL, secured the Ethoz loan using Ronald's property as collateral, misappropriated the Balance Sum on 18 November 2016, and then systematically laundered the proceeds through a series of deliberate transactions over the following seven months.

347    Mr Loy committed the predicate offence against a vulnerable elderly victim with significant cognitive impairment. He used the entirety of the misappropriated funds for his own benefit. He enlisted his mother's assistance to route funds through her accounts. He was evasive and uncontactable when questioned by those who sought to understand what had happened to the money. And he conducted himself throughout the trial in a manner that demonstrated a complete absence of remorse and a willingness to make unsubstantiated allegations against virtually every party connected with the proceedings.

348    Mdm Gian's position was materially different in every one of these respects. She did not conceive the scheme, did not commit the predicate offence, derived no personal benefit, and played a role that was limited in both scope and sophistication. She was charged with a single offence. The difference in the sentences imposed on the two accused persons reflects these differences in culpability.

The Global Sentence

349    Having arrived at the individual sentences for each charge, I turn to the question of which sentences should run consecutively and whether the resulting aggregate Global Sentence is proportionate to Mr Loy's overall criminality.

350    I was satisfied that the CBT charge and the CDSA charges were not part of a single transaction. The CBT was a completed offence at the moment Mr Loy misappropriated the Balance Sum on 18 November 2016.
