351    The CDSA offences were distinct acts committed subsequently, as Mr Loy transferred and applied the criminal proceeds across a series of separate transactions over the period from November 2016 to June 2017. Each CDSA offence involved a deliberate decision to deal with the proceeds in a particular way, and the series of transactions as a whole reflected a sustained and purposeful effort to distance the funds from their origins and to convert them into personal assets. The CBT and the CDSA offences therefore violated distinct legally protected interests and arose from separate acts, notwithstanding that they were connected by the underlying scheme.

352    I identified three CDSA charges to run consecutively with the CBT charge. The first was DAC-922482-2018, involving the transfer of $450,000, which was the single largest money laundering transaction, attracting a sentence of 18 months' imprisonment. The second was DAC-922483-2018, involving the transfer of $150,000, attracting a sentence of 12 months' imprisonment. The third was DAC-922491-2018, involving the transfer of $25,000, attracting a sentence of 4 months' imprisonment.

353    Together, these three charges captured the scale and sustained nature of Mr Loy's money laundering conduct across the period of offending, and their selection for consecutive sentences appropriately reflected the distinct nature of the laundering offences, the sophistication of the scheme, and the need for adequate deterrence. The remaining sentences were ordered to run concurrently.

354    I then stood back and considered whether the aggregate sentence was proportionate to Mr Loy's overall criminality and was not crushing in the sense described in Public Prosecutor v Raveen Balakrishnan [2018] 5 SLR 799. The aggregate sentence of 100 months' imprisonment, or 8 years and 4 months, is a substantial term. I was satisfied, however, that it was warranted by the totality of Mr Loy's conduct. He was the architect of a sustained scheme that exploited a vulnerable elderly victim with significant cognitive impairment, misappropriated S$1,268,500, laundered the proceeds through 34 separate transactions, applied every cent to his own benefit, enlisted his mother's assistance, and conducted himself throughout the trial in a manner that demonstrated a complete absence of remorse.

355    The aggregate sentence reflected the gravity of that conduct. Mr Loy's youth and his status as a first-time offender had already been taken into account in arriving at the individual sentences, and I did not consider that they warranted any further reduction at the global stage. The sentence was not, in my judgment, crushing when considered in the context of the overall criminality involved and Mr Loy's personal circumstances."

357    As indicated above, I ordered the sentences for DAC-922482-2018 (18 months' imprisonment), DAC-922483-2018 (12 months' imprisonment), and DAC-922491-2018 (4 months' imprisonment) to run consecutively with the CBT charge, with all remaining sentences running concurrently. This resulted in a global sentence of 100 months' imprisonment, equivalent to 8 years and 4 months.

Backdating to take into consideration all remand dates

358    The sentence was backdated to account for Mr Loy's periods in remand and custody, excluding all periods when he was on bail. The records showed that Mr Loy was on bail from 17 February 2017 to 16 August 2017, and again from 31 August 2017 to 13 December 2021, when he absconded and remained at large until 22 April 2022. He has been in remand continuously since that date, and his sentence was backdated accordingly.

Concluding sentencing remarks

359    I was satisfied that the aggregate sentence was not crushing. It was proportionate to the totality of Mr Loy's conduct, being his systematic misappropriation of S$1,268,500 from a vulnerable elderly victim with significant cognitive impairment, his commission of 34 money laundering offences over an extended period, his application of the entirety of the criminal proceeds to his own benefit, his enlisting of his mother's assistance to route funds through her accounts, his evasive conduct when questioned, and his complete absence of remorse as demonstrated by his contradictory testimony and his sustained pattern of unsubstantiated allegations against the victim, the victim's relatives, commercial personnel involved in the transactions, police officers, and the deputy public prosecutors assigned to the case.

360    The sentence was nonetheless lower than that sought by the prosecution. In arriving at a figure below the prosecution's recommendation, I gave weight to Mr Loy's age at the time of the offending and to the fact that the criminal proceeds had not been permanently dissipated.

361    The efficient tracing efforts of the police resulted in the seizure of more than S$1,268,500, meaning that the actual monetary loss to the estate has not been made permanent. I should be clear that this was entirely the result of the authorities' investigative work and owed nothing to any cooperation or assistance from Mr Loy. Nevertheless, the absence of permanent financial loss to the victim's estate was a factor I took into account in calibrating the sentence downward from the prosecution's position.

362    The sentence also serves the purpose of general deterrence. It sends a clear signal that those who abuse positions of corporate trust to exploit vulnerable victims, and who then engage in sophisticated money laundering to conceal their gains, can expect substantial custodial terms. This is particularly important in cases involving the exploitation of elderly persons with cognitive impairment, where the victim's vulnerability is itself a feature of the offending.

363    The sentence is consistent with the relevant precedents. In Tan Cheng Yew, the offender received a global sentence of 144 months' imprisonment, but that case involved more serious charges under section 409 of the Penal Code, a higher total quantum, and the aggravating circumstance of the offender having absconded for a far longer period than Mr Loy. In Varusai, the offender received a global sentence of 102 months' imprisonment for multiple CBT charges.

364    The present sentence of 100 months sits consistently within the range established by these authorities, reflecting the serious but somewhat less egregious nature of Mr Loy's offending relative to those cases.

365    Finally, while the sentence is a substantial one, Mr Loy is still a young man. He will have meaningful opportunity for rehabilitation and reintegration upon his release, and I would encourage him to reflect on the harm his conduct has caused and to apply himself constructively to that end.

Civil proceedings were not considered in these grounds

366    I should add, for completeness, that civil proceedings arising from the same underlying facts were commenced and concluded against Mr Loy in the High Court. I wish to make clear that those proceedings have played no part in my analysis. The conviction in this case rests solely on the evidence adduced at trial, assessed to the criminal standard of proof beyond a reasonable doubt. My findings on Mr Loy's credibility are the product of my own evaluation of his evidence over the course of 64 hearing days, and are independent of any findings made in the civil forum.

html:
Public Prosecutor v Paul Raj Arokiasamy

Public Prosecutor v Paul Raj Arokiasamy
[2026] SGDC 201

Case Number:District Arrest Case No. 902246 of 2026 & Ors
Decision Date:29 June 2026
Tribunal/Court:District Court
Coram: Shawn Ho
Counsel Name(s): Steve Tan (Traffic Police) for the Prosecution; N Sreenivasan S.C. and Tan Si Xin Adorabelle (Sreenivasan Chambers LLC) for the Defence.
Parties: Public Prosecutor — Paul Raj Arokiasamy

Criminal Law – Statutory Offences – Road Traffic Act

Criminal Law – Careless driving – Grievous hurt

Criminal Procedure and Sentencing – Driving Disqualification – Length

29 June 2026

District Judge Shawn Ho:

Introduction

1       The Accused, Mr Paul Raj Arokiasamy, pleaded guilty to one charge of careless driving causing grievous hurt under s 65(1)(a) punishable under s 65(3) read with s 65(7)(a) of the Road Traffic Act 1961 (“the Act”).

2       He was fined $3,000 in default 6 days’ imprisonment and given a 3-year driving disqualification for all classes of driving licences.

3       There was no appeal. Senior Counsel N. Sreenivasan made arguments on the length of the driving disqualification, which are analysed in this written judgement.

Length of the Driving Disqualification

(1)   Defence’s Arguments

4       Mr Sreenivasan argued that for “serious offenders”, there was a 2-year mandatory minimum driving disqualification (s 65(9)(a) of the Act). Since the present case did not involve a serious offender, he sought a driving disqualification of 1 to 2 years.

(2)   Decision on Driving Disqualification

5       I did not accept Mr Sreenivasan’s arguments for six reasons:

(a)      Parliamentary intention. During the parliamentary debates of the Road Traffic (Miscellaneous Amendments) Bill on 7 January 2025, then-Minister of State Associate Professor Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim, emphasised that the “intent of these amendments is not to signal a more lenient stance towards egregious motorists, nor to let them off with lighter sentences”.

(b)      Provision (statutory). For a serious offender who visited grievous harm on a victim, the relevant provision would be s 65(9)(g) of the Act with a mandatory minimum driving disqualification of at least 7 years (not 2 years).

(c)      Principles of sentencing for driving disqualification orders. Driving disqualification orders meld the three sentencing objectives of punishment, protection of the public and deterrence.

(d)      Philosophy (mandatory minimum DQ as a “ceiling”). I had concerns about using the mandatory minimum DQ as a “ceiling” for a separate offence.

(e)      Perception (anchoring & clustering effect). The Defence’s submissions would likely lead to a clustering of sentences around the lower end of the sentencing range and may lead to an anchoring effect.

(f)      Particular facts of the case. The length of the driving disqualification would depend on the facts.

(a)   Parliamentary Intention

6       The mandatory driving disqualification period for offences under s 65(3) of the Act was removed by Parliament for offences committed after 12 June 2025.

7       The amendments took effect on 12 June 2025: Road Traffic (Miscellaneous Amendments) Act 2025 (Commencement) Notification 2025 on 4 June 2025 (S 402/2025).

8       During the parliamentary debates of the Road Traffic (Miscellaneous Amendments) Bill on 7 January 2025, then-Minister of State Associate Professor Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim, emphasised that the “intent of these amendments is not to signal a more lenient stance towards egregious motorists, nor to let them off with lighter sentences”:

Mr Yip asked if lighter sentences could embolden risky behaviour and lead to more repeat offenders. Ms Joan Pereira, Assoc Prof Razwana, Mr Dennis Tan, and Ms Hazel Poa were also concerned that the amendments would send the wrong message to offenders. I wish to reiterate that the intent of these amendments is not to signal a more lenient stance towards egregious motorists, nor to let them off with lighter sentences. We will continue to punish those who exhibit irresponsible driving behaviour. The maximum penalties are stiff and remain unchanged. Judges will have full flexibility to decide the appropriate sentence up to the maximum sentence prescribed in law, depending on the facts of each case.

[emphasis added]

(b)   Provision (Statutory)

9       Mr Sreenivasan argued that for “serious offenders”, there was a 2-year mandatory minimum driving disqualification: s 65(9)(a) of the Act.

10     However, this was not a like-for-like comparison to the present case. The Defence relied on a provision premised on “no hurt” (s 65(5) of the Act). In contrast, the present case involved grievous hurt. For a serious offender who visits grievous hurt on a victim, the relevant provision is s 65(9)(g) of the Act, which mandates a minimum DQ of at least 7 years.[note: 1]

(c)   Principles of Sentencing for DQ Orders

11     Driving disqualification orders meld the three sentencing objectives of punishment, protection of the public and deterrence: Edwin s/o Suse Nathen v Public Prosecutor [2013] 4 SLR 1139 at [13]-[14], Public Prosecutor v Koh Thiam Huat [2017] 4 SLR 1099 at [64] and Chen Song v Public Prosecutor [2024] SGHC 129 at [143].

12     The most important sentencing principles engaged in driving disqualification orders are to:

(a)      protect society, because disqualification orders are meant to prevent future harm that the offender may cause to the public, and to

(b)      deter, because such orders deprive offenders of the freedom to drive: Public Prosecutor v Ong Heng Chua [2018] SGHC 95 at [61].

13     As stated in Public Prosecutor v Mohd Isa [1963] MLJ 135, the “most satisfactory penalty for most motoring offences is disqualification” because a fine is paid once and then forgotten. For instance, a 12-month disqualification order would mean that for the entire year in which the order is in effect, the offender is reminded every day of his offence and the unwarranted risks in which he had placed ordinary members of the public: Sivakumar s/o Rajoo v Public Prosecutor [2002] 1 SLR(R) 265 at [28].

14     Where a person is disqualified for a period of 12 months or longer, that person’s driving licence shall be “of no effect” and the person is further prevented from driving a motor vehicle after the disqualification period unless he passes the prescribed test of competence to drive: s 43(1)(b) of the Road Traffic Act.

(d)   Philosophy (Mandatory Minimum DQ as a “Ceiling”)

15     As a matter of sentencing philosophy, I had concerns about the Defence’s use of the mandatory minimum DQ (s 65(9)(a) of the Act) as a “ceiling” for a separate offence.

16     The Defence viewed the two-year mandatory minimum disqualification period for a “serious offender” as an implicit maximum cap or “ceiling” for an offender who does not meet that statutory definition.

17     Such an approach conflates a statutory minimum with a sentencing ceiling. A mandatory minimum sets the baseline of punishment for an aggravated class of offenders; it does not restrict the court’s discretion to impose a similar or higher sentence on an ordinary offender.

18     The Defence’s submissions militate against the sentencing objectives of deterrence, prevention and retribution.

(e)   Perception (Anchoring & Clustering Effect)

19     The Defence’s submissions may lead to an anchoring effect (viz. anchor of 2 years) and would likely lead to a clustering of sentences around the lower end of the sentencing range (Tan Song Cheng v Public Prosecutor [2021] SGHC 138 at [26], Public Prosecutor v GED and other appeals [2022] SGHC 301 at [128], and Public Prosecutor v Lin Pengli Barrie [2025] SGHC 133 at [30]).

(see See Kee Oon, Fact-Finding and Reality: A Judicial Decision-Making Primer (Academy Publishing, 2022), “Anchoring Bias” at 16-18)

20     A clustering of sentences around the lower end of the sentencing range would be contrary to the court’s duty to consider the full spectrum of sentences in determining the appropriate sentence: Court of Appeal in Iskandar bin Jinan v Public Prosecutor and another appeal [2024] SGCA 55 at [92(b)].

(f)   Particular Facts of the Case

21     During the parliamentary debates of the Road Traffic (Miscellaneous Amendments) Bill on 7 January 2025, then-Minister of State Associate Professor Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim, stated that “Sentencing decisions are made by the Courts, which will consider the facts and circumstances of every case”:

Sentencing decisions are made by the Courts, which will consider the facts and circumstances of every case. The Bill will give the Courts more flexibility to decide on the appropriate sentences, rather than be constrained by the statutory minimums.

[emphasis added]

22     Facts matter. Facts are a kaleidoscope of the colourful vagaries of human behaviour. Each case turns on its facts.

(see Andrew Ashworth, Sentencing and Criminal Justice, Cambridge University Press (Sixth Edition, 2015), pages 425-427)

23     That is why the Supreme Court has repeatedly emphasised a fact-sensitive approach for traffic cases:

(a)     The highly fact-specific nature of traffic offences means that sentencing, being ultimately a matter of discretion, must be approached judiciously with the highest level of attention to the facts and circumstances of each case (Public Prosecutor v Ganesan Sivasankar [2017] 5 SLR 681 at [57]):

(i)       The High Court was reiterating the point made in Public Prosecutor v Chia Hyong Gyee (Oral Judgment, 25 May 2017, Magistrate’s Appeal No 001/2017/01).

(ii)       The High Court in Stansilas Fabian Kester v Public Prosecutor [2017] 5 SLR 755 stated at [46] and [73]: “In the final analysis, the appropriate sentence to be imposed will be the product of a fact-sensitive exercise of discretion, taking into account all the circumstances of the case.”

(b)     The facts and circumstances which give rise to traffic offences are so infinitely varied that a blind and rigid adherence to precedents and sentencing norms by default is inadvisable. In this class of offences, attention to the particular facts and circumstances is of paramount importance: Koh Thiam Huat at [39].

(c)     It bears repeating that the facts of each traffic case must be carefully evaluated, weighed and assessed: Lee-Teh Har Eng (Oral Judgment, 15 December 2016, Magistrate’s Appeal 9099/2016) referred to in Koh Thiam Huat at [36].

24     In the present case, the 1st victim suffered grievous hurt:

(a)     The 1st victim sustained a right distal fibula open comminuted fracture.[note: 2]

(b)     The 1st victim underwent right lower limb debridement and fixation of comminuted fibula fracture on 27 June 2025.[note: 3]

25     The Accused had consented to having another charge of careless driving[note: 4] taken into consideration for sentencing.

26     All things considered, I did not agree with the Defence’s submissions on the length of the driving disqualification (i.e. 1 to 2 years).

Charges

27     The Accused pleaded guilty to the following charge:

You,

Name: Paul Raj Arokiasamy

Gender/ Age: Male/ 35 years old

Nationality: Malaysian

are charged that on 26 June 2025 at or about 6.47 p.m., along Woodlands Crossing towards Malaysia, Singapore, did ride a Malaysia registered motorcycle, JXQ2593, on a road without due care and attention, to wit, by failing to keep a proper lookout ahead for other road users, resulting in a collision with a cyclist, who was ahead of you, and grievous hurt was caused to the cyclist, namely one KWAN MING HUA, male aged 54, by such driving, you have thereby contravened Section 65(1)(a) of the Road Traffic Act 1961 which contravention is an offence under Section 65(3) which is punishable under Section 65(7)(a) of the Act.[note: 5]

28     He consented to having another charge taken into consideration for sentencing:

You,

Name: Paul Raj Arokiasamy

Gender/ Age: Male/ 35 years old

Nationality: Malaysian

are charged that on 26 June 2025 at or about 6.47 p.m., along Woodlands Crossing towards Malaysia, Singapore, did ride a Malaysia registered motorcycle, JXQ2593, on a road without due care and attention for other persons using the road to wit, by failing to keep a proper lookout ahead for other road users, resulting in a collision with a cyclist, who was ahead of you and after which collided into another motorcycle and a car SMZ7295D, you have thereby contravened Section 65(1)(a) of the Road Traffic Act 1961 which contravention is an offence punishable under Section 65(5)(a) of the Act.[note: 6]

Statement of facts

29     The Accused is Paul Raj Arokiasamy, Male Indian, 35 years old, Malaysian Citizen. He was the rider of Malaysia registered Motorcycle JXQ2593, at the time of the incident.[note: 7]

30     The 1st victim is Kwan Ming Hua, Male Chinese, 53 years old, Malaysian Citizen. He was the Cyclist, at the time of the incident.[note: 8]

31     The 2nd victim is an Unknown rider on a motorcycle.[note: 9]

32     The 3rd Victim is Husni Bin Yusof, Male Malay, 53 years old, Singapore Citizen. He was the driver of Singapore registered Motor car SMZ7295D, at the time of the incident.[note: 10]

Facts of Case

33     On 26 June 2025 at or about 6.47 p.m., along Woodlands Crossing towards Malaysia, Singapore, the Accused was riding a Malaysia registered motorcycle, JXQ2593, on a road without due care and attention, by failing to keep a proper lookout ahead for other road users, resulting in a collision with a cyclist, who was ahead of the Accused, after which collided into the 2nd and 3rd victims’ vehicles who were travelling on the Accused’s right, and grievous hurt was caused to the 1st victim by the Accused’s driving.[note: 11]

34     Footage from ICA shows that the 1st victim was travelling ahead of the Accused on the extreme left along the double yellow continuous lines when the Accused collided into the 1st victim’s rear, and due to the impact, the Accused fell to his right and collided with the 2nd and 3rd victims’ vehicles.[note: 12]

Injury

35     Due to the accident, the 1st victim was conveyed to Woodlands Health. The 1st victim had a right lower limb deformity and 1x1 cm puncture wound with active bleeding. X-rays of the lower limb showed a right distal fibular comminuted fracture with air tracking. The 1st victim sustained a right distal fibula open comminuted fracture. The 1st victim underwent right lower limb debridement and fixation of comminuted fibula fracture on 27 June 2025.[note: 13]

36     The 1st victim was warded for 5 days from 26 June 2025 to 30 June 2025 and discharged with 49 days of hospitalisation leave from 26 June 2025 to 13 August 2025.[note: 14]

37     As a result of the accident, the following damages were ascertained:

(i)     The Accused’s motorcycle sustained scratches to the front and right portions.

(ii)     The 1st victim’s bicycle sustained a slightly twisted rear wheel.

(iii)     The 3rd victim’s car did not sustain any damages.[note: 15]

Prevailing Condition

38     At the time of the accident, the weather was fine, road surface was dry, traffic flow was moderate to heavy, and visibility was good.[note: 16]

Conclusion

39     By virtue of the foregoing, the Accused has committed the offence of driving without due care and attention causing grievous hurt under section 65(1)(a) read with section 65(3) and punishable under section 65(7)(a) of the Road Traffic Act 1961.[note: 17]

Prescribed punishment

40     The prescribed punishment for causing grievous hurt under s 65(1)(a) punishable under s 65(3) read with s 65(7)(a) of the Act is:

(a)      s 65(7)(a):

(i)       Fine not exceeding $5,000 or to

(ii)       Imprisonment for a term not exceeding 2 years or to both.

41     The two components of the overall sentence generally are not to be regarded as mutually compensatory. Hence, an increase in the fine or custodial sentence should not be taken to mandate the imposition of a reduced disqualification period than would otherwise have been ordered: Edwin s/o Suse Nathen v Public Prosecutor [2013] SGHC 194 at [13]-[14].

42     While the different types of punishment are not fungible, there is a positive correlation between the length of the imprisonment term and/or quantum of the fine imposed and the period of the disqualification ordered. This direct relationship arises from the overlapping considerations of harm and culpability underlying the determination of the length of imprisonment or quantum of fine, and the length of the disqualification period: Chen Song v Public Prosecutor [2025] 3 SLR 509 at [141].

43     An offence’s statutory maximum sentence signals the gravity in which Parliament views such offences. A sentencing judge ought to take this into account when determining precisely where the offender’s conduct falls within the entire range of punishment set by Parliament: Public Prosecutor v Kwong Kok Hing [2008] 2 SLR(R) 684 at [44].

(Benny Tan, Assessing the Effectiveness of Sentencing Guideline Judgments in Singapore Issued Post-March 2013 and A Guide to Constructing Frameworks, (2018) 30 SAcLJ 1004 at [46])

44     The court should ensure that the full spectrum of sentences enacted by Parliament is carefully explored in determining the appropriate sentence, viz. Completeness principle (Poh Boon Kiat v Public Prosecutor [2014] 4 SLR 892 at [60]).

Prosecution’s submissions on sentence

45     The Prosecution asked for a fine of $4,000 to $5,000 and a 5-year driving disqualification for all classes of driving licences.

46     As this offence took place after 12 June 2025, a driving disqualification was not mandatory under the law.

Mitigation plea

47     The Defence asked for a fine of about $2,000.

48     For “serious offenders”, there was a 2-year mandatory minimum driving disqualification: s 65(9)(a) of the Act.[note: 18] Since the present case did not involve a serious offender, the Defence sought a driving disqualification of 1 to 2 years.[note: 19]

Sentencing

The Law

Legislative history of s 65 of the Act

49     As was observed by Sundaresh Menon CJ in Wu Zhi Yong v Public Prosecutor [2021] SGHC 261 at [15] (albeit in the related context of s 64 of the Act), the Road Traffic (Amendment) Act 2019 (Act 19 of 2019) envisaged a new scheme of penalties for careless or inconsiderate driving in a tiered structure calibrated according to the degree of hurt caused. This is codified in the Act as ss 65(2) to 65(5). The maximum punishments which may be imposed for each category of harm increase concomitantly with the seriousness of the harm caused; this translates into wider ranges of punishments where more serious harm is occasioned (Sue Chang v Public Prosecutor [2022] SGHC 176 at [38]).

50     For instance, where death is caused, s 65(2)(a) provides that a first-time offender is liable to a fine not exceeding $10,000 or to imprisonment for a term not exceeding three years or to both. In contrast, the residual category (where no actual physical harm is caused, but which includes cases of non-personal injury or potential harm) captured in s 65(5)(a) provides that a first-time offender is liable to a fine not exceeding $1,500 or to imprisonment for a term not exceeding six months or to both (Sue Chang at [38]).

51     By tiering the punishment provisions in accordance with the type of harm suffered, Parliament has given clear expression to the need to give explicit consideration to the outcomes that result from instances of careless or inconsiderate driving. This is a stark departure from the structure of s 65 of the pre-2019 Act, where there was a single range of punishment with no differentiation based on the type and/or degree of harm caused (Sue Chang at [39]).

52     In addition, while Parliament has retained the distinction between reckless or dangerous driving under s 64 of the Act and careless or inconsiderate driving under s 65 of the Act, this distinction has been made more pronounced through the refining of the punishment provisions. These two provisions reflect the differing circumstances under which an irresponsible driving offence can occur. The former offence (s 64) is regarded as being more serious than the latter (s 65), reflecting primarily the differing levels of culpability of the offenders. Accordingly, the current architecture of the Act concerning irresponsible driving offences tiers the punishment provisions according to both harm and culpability, not dissimilar to the Penal Code (Sue Chang at [40]).

Decision on sentence

53     For driving without due care or attention causing grievous hurt, the applicable case is Chen Song v Public Prosecutor [2024] SGHC 129.

Framework in Chen Song

54     A quantitative factors-based approach, where the indicative sentencing band is determined at the first step, based on the number of offence-specific harm and culpability factors is especially useful: Chen Song at [123].

55     “Lesser harm” is caused and the offender’s culpability is deemed as “lower culpability” where at most one harm or culpability factor applies in respect of each category: Chen Song at [123].

56     “Greater harm” would be caused and the offender’s culpability deemed as “higher culpability” where there are 2 or more harm and culpability factors respectively: Chen Song at [123].

57     This is a general guideline which is not to be applied mechanistically in every case. The foremost inquiry is to assess holistically whether the totality of the harm suffered by the victim should be classified as either “greater harm” or “lesser harm” and whether the offender’s culpability considered as a whole should be classified as either “lower culpability” or “higher culpability”: Chen Song at [123].

(1)   Harm factors

58     Primary harm factors are factors which pertain directly to the bodily injury suffered by the victim(s) in each case. These factors include:

(a)     the nature and location of the injuries;

(b)     the degree of permanence of the injuries; and

(c)     the impact of the injuries: Chen Song at [124].

59     The three broad primary harm factors are:

(a)      Nature and location of the injury: This factor focuses on the precise nature and the location of the injury. This requires a consideration of:

(i)       the nature and severity of injury (eg, simple or complex and extent of injury, etc);

(ii)       the number of injuries;

(iii)       whether surgical intervention was necessary (or whether the injuries were treated conservatively);

(iv)       the disposition of the victim post-surgery (eg, general ward, high dependency or intensive care unit); and

(v)       the location of the injury (eg, vulnerable location).

(b)      Degree of permanence: This factor considers whether the injury or injuries caused to the victim are permanent or transient. Permanent injuries include loss of a limb or permanent privation of the sight of either eye or the hearing of either ear, etc.

(c)      Impact of injury: This factor contemplates the impact of the injury on the victim’s quality of life. Here, considerations of:

(i)       the duration of stay in the hospital/rehabilitation centre;

(ii)       duration of any hospitalisation/medical leave;

(iii)       ability to carry out daily tasks and maintain livelihood; and

(iv)       duration of rehabilitation (if any), are relevant: Chen Song at [127].

60     There is an inevitable overlap between the factors of nature and location of injury on the one hand, and impact of injury on the other. The period and nature of hospitalisation may be an indicium of both the nature and severity of the injury and perhaps even the number of injuries suffered, and its impact on the victim’s quality of life. The period and nature of hospitalisation may be relevant to both factors: Habeeb Zaleena d/o Pallivilakam Kader Habeeb Mohamed v Public Prosecutor [2026] SGHC 99 at [35].

61     As to whether an injury is at a vulnerable location, the High Court in Ling Zhao Bin v Public Prosecutor [2026] SGHC 107 stated at [27]:

It seems to me that the parts of the body were regarded as vulnerable because the injuries were to, or in locations proximate to, vital organs. The common thread is that these locations are vulnerable because an injury suffered in any of these locations, may result in a risk to life or permanent or long-term loss of function that impairs the victim’s ability to live independently and without assistance ( eg loss of cognitive ability or paralysis). Vulnerability is defined with the reference to the severity of the harm that could result from an injury in a location. Without being prescriptive and in any way comprehensive, this common thread could serve as a working definition of a vulnerable location. It is consistent with why an injury to a vulnerable location was identified in Chen Song as relevant to the harm analysis under the “nature and location” factor, and the purpose of the central inquiry in the harm analysis (which is to ascertain the extent of physical harm that is suffered by the victim as a result of the injury in question as stated at [22] above).

[emphasis added]

62     I bore in mind that there may be cases where even if two or more primary harm factors apply, if they present themselves to a limited degree, the court may nevertheless consider that “lesser harm” had been caused based on a holistic assessment of the harm caused: Chen Song at [127].

63     Secondary harm factors are unrelated to the physical injury suffered by the victim(s), but which nonetheless go towards the extent of harm caused in a particular case. These factors include:

(a)     property damage; and

(b)     potential harm: Chen Song at [125].

64     Consideration of actual harm focuses on the moment of a collision. Potential harm looks at the wider circumstances before and after a collision (Public Prosecutor v Cheng Chang Tong [2023] SGHC 119 at [57]).

65     Potential harm refers to harm that was likely to have been caused to other road users but which ultimately did not eventuate: Chen Song at [129] and Public Prosecutor v Johnson Tan Wee Kiat [2026] SGHC 59 at [13].

66     The level of potential harm may be assessed against facts such as the condition of the road, the volume of traffic or number of pedestrians actually on or which might reasonably be expected to be on the road at the relevant time, the speed and manner of driving, visibility at the relevant time, the type of vehicle, and any particular vulnerabilities (eg, a truck or car colliding into a motorcycle or pedestrian). It was observed that these relate to the circumstances of driving that could increase the danger posed to road users (Wu Zhi Yong at [36(a)]): Chen Song at [129].

67     It would only be appropriate to have regard to potential harm if there was a sufficient likelihood of the harm arising and this in turn should be assessed in the light of the gravity of the harm risked (Neo Ah Luan v Public Prosecutor [2018] 5 SLR 1153 at [67]): Chen Song at [129].

68     The potential for harm has to be assessed with reference not only to the actual distance travelled, but the distance which the offender intended to travel (Chan Chow Chuen v Public Prosecutor [2024] SGHC 294 at [24]). In Fan Lei v Public Prosecutor [2024] SGHC 278 at [10], travelling a distance of 17km was not enough to point to increased potential harm. In Fan Lei, there was no evidence that the offender was driving in a careless manner over that 17km.

69     I was mindful that in assessing the level of harm or potential harm, the sentencing court should be careful not to double-count any factors which may already have been taken into account in assessing the level of culpability: Ye Lin Myint v Public Prosecutor [2019] 5 SLR 1005 at [58] (see also Andrew Ashworth, Sentencing and Criminal Justice (6th Ed, 2015, Cambridge University Press) at [4.3] and [4.5]).

70     Each primary harm factor would count as one offence-specific factor going towards harm. However, where a secondary harm factor presents itself in a significant manner, this should be considered in the determination of where the particular offence falls within the indicative sentencing band: Chen Song at [125].

(2)   Culpability factors

71     A non-exhaustive list of factors which each constitute 1 offence-specific factor going towards culpability is as follows (Chen Song at [131]):

(a)      Any form of dangerous driving behaviour. For instance:

(i)       speeding;

(ii)       driving against traffic;

(iii)       driving when not fit to drive;

(iv)       driving under the influence of alcohol or drugs;

(v)       sleepy driving;

(vi)       driving while using a mobile phone;

(vii)       swerving in and out of lanes;

(viii)       using a vehicle in a dangerous fashion; and

(ix)       street racing.

(b)      Flouting of traffic rules and regulations. For instance:

(i)       failing to stop at a stop line;

(ii)       failing to conform to traffic signal;

(iii)       not forming up correctly to execute a turn;

(iv)       changing lanes across a set of double white lines/chevron markings; and

(v)       making an illegal U-turn/right turn.

(c)      High degree of carelessness: This is demonstrated where there was a prolonged or sustained period of inattention (as opposed to a momentary lapse of attention), and where the offender was deliberately cavalier about certain mitigatable risks. As stated in Sue Chang at [95], it would also be relevant to consider the extent to which the offender’s distraction was avoidable and the extent to which the offender’s misjudgment was reasonable.

(3)   Sentencing framework for driving offences causing grievous hurt punishable under s 65(3)(a)

72     The following sentencing framework applied for careless driving offences causing hurt punishable under s 65(3)(a) where the offender elects to claim trial (Chen Song at [134]).

73     First, the court is to identify the number of offence-specific factors under the broad categories of “harm” and “culpability” (Chen Song at [134(a)]).

74     Second, based on the number of offence-specific factors present, the court is to determine whether the harm caused is “lesser harm” or “greater harm” and whether the culpability of the offender is “lower culpability” or “higher culpability” and thereafter arrive at the sentencing band the offence falls within (Chen Song at [134(b)]).

75     “Lesser harm” is caused, and the offender’s culpability is deemed as “lower culpability” where there are 0–1 harm or culpability factors respectively. “Greater harm” is caused, and the offender’s culpability is deemed as “higher culpability” where there are 2 or more harm or culpability factors respectively (Chen Song at [134(b)]).

Band

Circumstances

Sentencing range

1

Lesser harm and lower culpability

Fine and/or up to 6 months’ imprisonment

2

Greater harm and lower culpability

Or

Lesser harm and higher culpability

6 months’ to 1 year’s imprisonment

3

Greater harm and higher culpability

1 to 2 years’ imprisonment



76     Third, after determining the indicative sentencing band that the offence falls within, the court should identify an indicative starting point sentence within that range, taking into account: (a) all the primary harm factors and the culpability factors identified; and (b) the secondary harm factors (Chen Song at [134(c)]).

77     Fourth, the court is to make adjustments to the starting point to take into account the usual gamut of offender-specific aggravating and mitigating factors (Chen Song at [134(d)]).

78     The High Court stated that with reference to the proposed sentencing bands for s 65(3)(a), the custodial threshold would typically be crossed where there are 2 or more offence-specific harm and/or culpability factors present. Therefore, for Band 1 cases, fines would ordinarily be reserved for cases where 0–1 offence-specific harm and/or culpability factors are present (Chen Song at [137]).

(see also Ivan Tang et al., Sentencing Frameworks for Consistency: A Proposed Framework, (2024) 36 SAcLJ 380 at [130])

79      Harm . For the nature and location of injury:

(a)     The 1st victim (cyclist) had a right lower limb deformity and 1x1 cm puncture wound with active bleeding. X-rays of the lower limb showed a right distal fibular comminuted fracture with air tracking. The 1st victim sustained a right distal fibula open comminuted fracture.[note: 20]

(b)     The 1st victim underwent right lower limb debridement and fixation of comminuted fibula fracture on 27 June 2025.[note: 21]

80     For the impact of injury:

(a)     The 1st victim was warded for 5 days from 26 June 2025 to 30 June 2025.[note: 22]

(b)     The 1st victim was discharged with 49 days of hospitalisation leave from 26 June 2025 to 13 August 2025.[note: 23]

81     As a result of the accident:

(a)     The 1st victim’s bicycle sustained a slightly twisted rear wheel.[note: 24]

(b)     The 3rd victim’s car did not sustain any damage.[note: 25]

82     Two primary harm factors were engaged: (a) nature and location of injury and (b) impact of injury.

83     Nevertheless, I bore in mind that there may be cases where even if two or more primary harm factors apply, if they present themselves to a limited degree, the court may nevertheless consider that “lesser harm” had been caused based on a holistic assessment of the harm caused: Chen Song at [127].

84     On a holistic assessment, there was lesser harm on the lower end.

85     To be clear, I was mindful that the damage to the Accused’s own vehicle should not be treated as an aggravating factor: Ching Kelvin v Public Prosecutor [2024] SGHC 297 at [15].

86      Culpability . There was no culpability-increasing factor.

87     The foremost inquiry is to assess holistically whether the offender’s culpability considered as a whole should be classified as either “lower culpability” or “higher culpability”: Chen Song at [123]. On a holistic assessment, the present case involved lower culpability.

88     Given the lesser harm and lower culpability, the case fell within Band 1 of Chen Song.

89     The custodial threshold would typically be crossed where there are two or more offence-specific harm and/or culpability factors present: Chen Song at [137].

90     All things considered, I was of the view that the custodial threshold was not crossed and a fine would suffice.

91      TIC charge. There was one TIC charge. The effect of taking into consideration outstanding charges is to enhance the sentence that would otherwise have been imposed for the proceeded charges: Public Prosecutor v UI [2008] 4 SLR(R) 500 at [38] (see also s 148 of the Criminal Procedure Code 2010).

92      Antecedents. The Accused had a clean driving record.

93      Guilty plea. I gave full weight to the Accused’s guilty plea: Angliss Singapore Pte Ltd v Public Prosecutor [2006] 4 SLR(R) 653 at [77]. This saved the criminal justice system resources that would have been expended with a full trial.

94     That said, the evidence (including video evidence) against the Accused was overwhelming and lends itself to the conclusion that he had little choice but to plead guilty: Vasentha d/o Joseph v Public Prosecutor [2015] SGHC 197 at [71] and [73], and Public Prosecutor v BDB [2017] SGCA 69 at [74].

95      Cooperation with the authorities. I gave due weight to the Accused’s cooperation with the authorities: Public Prosecutor v Siew Boon Loong [2005] 1 SLR(R) 611 at [16]-[18].

96     The Accused received a call from the police a few days after the incident and was told to report to the Traffic Police Department at Jalan Ubi, Singapore.[note: 26] He showed up at the Traffic Police Department.[note: 27] At all times, he cooperated with the Police in their investigations.[note: 28]

Conclusion

97     For the above reasons, the Accused was fined $3,000 in default 6 days’ imprisonment and given a 3-year driving disqualification for all classes of driving licences with effect from 15 June 2026.[note: 29]

98     I am grateful for the hard work and submissions of both sides.

Public Prosecutor v Tan Thiam Ching

Public Prosecutor v Tan Thiam Ching
[2026] SGMC 83

Case Number:Magistrate Arrest Case No 903179 of 2026 & 6 Others
Decision Date:26 June 2026
Tribunal/Court:Magistrate's Court
Coram: Paul Quan
Counsel Name(s): Mavis Ng (Attorney-General's Chambers) for the Public Prosecutor; Accused self-represented.
Parties: Public Prosecutor — Tan Thiam Ching

Criminal Law – Offences – Criminal force and assault

Criminal Law – Offences – Hurt – Rash act endangering personal safety of others

Criminal Law – Offences – Offences against public servant – Refusing to sign police statement

Criminal Law – Offences – Property – Dishonest misappropriation

Criminal Law – Offences – Property – Mischief

Criminal Law – Offences – Protection from Harassment Act – Intentional harassment

Criminal Procedure and Sentencing – Sentencing

26 June 2026

District Judge Paul Quan:

Introduction

1       This is a case where an offender labouring under a psychiatric condition committed a slew of offences and the court has to decide whether it should impose a rehabilitative community order instead of a punitive sentence on him.

Brief facts and charges

2       In April 2026, the accused, Tan Thiam Ching (“Mr Tan”), a 62-year-old Singaporean, was captured on surveillance footage from his neighbour’s camera to have forcefully removed another surveillance camera belonging to that neighbour and throwing it over the ledge of the 12th floor of his neighbour’s unit. When his neighbour confronted him, he then threw a glass ball through his closed unit window, causing the window pane and glass ball to shatter. In a later incident, he also swung his arm towards this neighbour. Yet in a separate earlier incident in March 2026, he intentionally caused harassment to another neighbour by throwing unknown yellow powder towards the main gate of that neighbour’s unit. In the preceding year in April 2025, a sum of S$4,500 was erroneously transferred to his bank account via PayNow through his mobile number and he dishonestly misappropriated the sum by using it on furniture and daily necessities. After he was arrested on 15 April 2026 and during investigations on 16 April 2026, he refused to sign the police statement that was recorded from him.

3       Mr Tan has pleaded guilty to four charges, namely two of doing a rash act to endanger the personal safety of others under section 336(a) of the Penal Code 1871 (2020 Rev Ed) (“PC”), one of dishonest misappropriation of property under section 403 PC, and one of refusing to sign his police statement under section 180 PC. He has also consented to have three other charges taken into consideration for the purpose of sentence (“TIC”), namely one of mischief under section 426 PC, one of using criminal force under section 352 PC, and one of intentional harassment under section 3(2) of the Protection from Harassment Act 2014 (2020 Rev Ed) amalgamating three occasions as a course of conduct under section 124(4) of the Criminal Procedure Code 2010 (2020 Rev Ed) (“CPC”).

Parties’ sentencing positions

4       Mr Tan has no criminal antecedents. He was previously remanded by the mentions court in May 2026 for a forensic psychiatric evaluation for his section 336(a) PC offences. He was diagnosed to be suffering from delusional order at the time of the offences and there was a partial contributory link between this condition and the offences.[note: 1] Given his psychiatric condition that operated at the material time, the risk of re-offending[note: 2] and the psychiatric mitigatory steps that should be taken,[note: 3] the prosecution has asked me to call for a pre-sentence report (“PSR”) on him to assess the suitability of a mandatory treatment order (“MTO”) under section 339 CPC as a sentencing option.[note: 4] Mr Tan, who is self-represented, has indicated that he needs to seek treatment for his condition and sought an MTO to be made.

5       I convicted Mr Tan on 12 June 2026 and called for a mandatory PSR under section 339(2) CPC on him. Pursuant to section 339(6)(a) CPC, I ordered him to be remanded for observation at the Institute of Mental Health (“IMH”) for two weeks for assessment to enable an MTO PSR to be submitted by the appointed psychiatrist to the court. Time was of the essence because Mr Tan has been remanded on a no-bail order.

6       I received the PSR from the appointed psychiatrist on 24 June 2026,[note: 5] with his recommendation for an MTO for a duration of 24 months. The prosecution has now asked me to make such a community order. So too does Mr Tan.

Court’s decision

7       As the statutory restrictions against a community order enumerated under section 337(1) CPC do not apply in Mr Tan’s case, it is open to me to make an MTO. Having reviewed the MTO PSR, I agree with the parties and explain in this ex tempore judgment why I now make an MTO requiring Mr Tan to undergo psychiatric treatment for a period of 24 months under section 339(1) CPC.

8       I adopt the same analytical framework and where appropriate, the same language in my previous MTO decision in PP v Teo Hui Lan [2026] SGDC 206 in this judgment for consistency while being cognisant of the differences between the cases.

MTO PSR called on Mr Tan

9       I delivered brief reasons on 12 June 2026 explaining why I decided to call for an MTO PSR on Mr Tan. Doing so for me to consider MTO as a community based sentencing option is consistent with both the broader rationale underlying community based sentencing and the particular considerations for calling an MTO PSR. For context, I first outline these reasons.

Rationale underlying community based sentencing

10     In Mr Tan’s case, he was diagnosed with delusional order at the time of his section 336(a) offences and there was a partial contributory link between this condition and the offences. Such offences involving persons with specific and minor mental conditions, which are traditionally viewed by the courts to be on the rehabilitation end of the spectrum, are targeted for community based sentencing that allows greater flexibility in balancing the various sentencing principles: Sim Wen Yi Ernest v PP [2016] 5 SLR 207 (“Ernest Sim”) at [33], by essentially considering whether rehabilitation should be given prominence in the case at hand notwithstanding any countervailing need for deterrence, retribution or prevention: Kalaiarasi d/o Marimuthu Innasimuthu v PP [2012] 2 SLR 774 (“Kalaiarasi”) at [39]. The offender is rehabilitated by identifying and addressing the root causes of the offending behaviour, whilst preventing the offender from being dislodged from his family, employment and society, whereas the public interest is served by reducing recidivism through correction and rehabilitation: Kalaiarasi at [35] and [36].

Particular considerations for calling MTO PSR

11     This is similarly echoed in the court’s approach in GCX v PP [2019] 3 SLR 1325 at [47] that provides specific guidance on when an MTO PSR should be called, depending on the offender’s rehabilitative potential and whether other sentencing principles were so dominant that rehabilitation should be rejected out of hand.

Need for deterrence and retribution attenuated in Mr Tan’s case

12     First, I identify and balance the relevant sentencing principles, giving each its appropriate weight, in order for me to have some sense of the offender’s rehabilitative potential: GCX at [47]. On the face of Mr Tan’s case, the principle of deterrence, both general and specific deterrence is engaged; so is the retributive principle.

13     Specific deterrence is engaged because Mr Tan has committed multiple offences. It also cannot be gainsaid that defiant conduct against public servants, killer litter offences, and unneighbourly behaviour especially in our particular context of dense living, must be generally deterred. Retributive sentencing demands that the court metes out punishment that is proportionate to the nature of the offence and the offender. Mr Tan’s offences are serious, whereas his culpability lies in his apparent deliberate conduct in:

(a)     forcefully removing his neighbour’s camera and throwing it over the ledge from the 12th floor, causing it to be damaged and his neighbour suffering consequential loss of S$250;[note: 6]

(b)     throwing the glass ball through his unit’s closed window, causing the window to break and his neighbour getting injured stepping on the glass shards from the broken window and suffering a small cut on his toe when his neighbour attempted to return home;[note: 7]

(c)     dishonestly misappropriating and spending away the monies that were transferred to him erroneously;[note: 8] and

(d)     refusing to sign his statement to the police.[note: 9]

14     But a person suffering from a mental illness that leaves him unable to fully appreciate the nature and consequences of his actions will not be deterred by the prospect of a custodial sentence; similarly general deterrence does not function to make an example of an offender who did not possess full cognitive normalcy and rationality: GCX at [54]. The weight to be given to retribution also depends on the culpability of the offender, and the offender can bear a lower level of culpability for his actions depending on the extent to which his psychiatric condition has contributed to the offence: GCX at [55] and [56].

15     In this regard, the upshot of Mr Tan’s forensic psychiatric evaluation in May 2026 in relation to his section 336(a) PC offences is that he was:

(a)     diagnosed with delusional order since 2020 and was suffering from the condition at the time and there is a partial contributory link between his condition and both offences as his persecutory delusions towards his neighbour had likely led to his actions;

(b)     assessed to be at risk of re-offending as he continued to endorse persecutory ideas towards his neighbour and was socially isolated with limited external support. He displayed limited insight into his condition although he agreed to an increase of antipsychotic medication; and

(c)     recommended to continue close psychiatric follow-up for continuous titration of his medications, psychoeducation, monitoring of adherence to treatment, and a repeat referral to the Community Intervention Team.

16     The need for deterrence, both general and specific, therefore appears to be attenuated; likewise the need for retributive justice in the light of Mr Tan’s reduced culpability.

Real prospect of rehabilitation exists in Mr Tan’s case

17     Next, I should not apply an overly restrictive threshold as to the offender’s rehabilitative potential and need only be persuaded that rehabilitation is a real prospect: GCX at [47].

18     I find that there is a real prospect of rehabilitation in Mr Tan’s case. He was agreeable to an increase of antipsychotic medications,[note: 10] continue his medications as prescribed and resume psychiatric follow-up.[note: 11] He also stated that upon his return to the community, he intended to avoid any further interaction or confrontation with his neighbour, he would call the police if necessary, planned to apply for a protection order and install his own surveillance camera.[note: 12] Monitoring adherence to treatment coupled with medication and psychoeducation as recommended will target the persecutory delusions he continues to hold against his neighbours.

19     Given that the need for deterrence and retribution in this case is attenuated, rehabilitation should be given prominence. There is sufficient rehabilitative potential or a real prospect of rehabilitation, such that an MTO might realistically be ordered on the facts: GCX at [39]-[41]. Calling for a PSR is a mandatory first step if I wish to consider making an MTO and I did not rule out such a possibility then on 25 May 2026: GCX at [45]. At this stage, I was cognisant that I lacked the necessary facts to apprise itself fully Mr Tan’s true rehabilitative potential and I was therefore slow to lightly find that other sentencing principles so substantially trumped the principle of rehabilitation that there is simply no need to call for an MTO PSR: GCX at [47].

MTO recommended by appointed psychiatrist in PSR

20     In Mr Tan’s PSR, the appointed psychiatrist has recommended an MTO for a period of 24 months on the basis that: [note: 13]

(a)     Mr Tan is suitable for an MTO (presumably health-wise);

(b)     Mr Tan has no objections being placed on an MTO and that he will attend psychiatric appointments, comply with his medication, as well as subject himself to community monitoring by a social worker; and

(c)     the appointed psychiatrist’s assessment that an MTO is viable for Mr Tan.

Section 339(3) CPC satisfied

21     The appointed psychiatrist was aware of Mr Tan’s diagnosis during his last psychiatric forensic evaluation in May 2026,[note: 14] and he opined that:[note: 15]

(a)     Mr Tan has been diagnosed with delusional disorder that was present during the offence period. He has ongoing persecutory delusions against his neighbours whom he believes are monitoring, tracking him and wanting to do bad things towards him;

(b)     there is a contributory link to the offences involving his neighbours. His disorder led to him taking action against them such as throwing items and fighting with them. His ongoing persecutory delusions contributed to the loss of self-restraint resulting in his actions; and

(c)     delusional disorder is treatable. Mr Tan lacks insight into his condition but has informed that he would attend his appointments, comply with medication and agree for a social worker to monitor him in the community.

He also noted that Mr Tan was amenable to MTO.[note: 16] His examination of his mental state to assess his suitability for MTO was also unremarkable.[note: 17]

22     Having considered the matters set out under section 339(3) CPC, the appointed psychiatrist’s view was that Mr Tan was suitable to be placed on an MTO.[note: 18] Section 339(9) CPC makes clear that the PSR is final and conclusive as to these matters and pertinently, the appointed psychiatrist did not raise any issues in relation to these matters that would proscribe the making of an MTO: GCX at [40].

23     The appointed psychiatrist’s opinion is not determinative of the court’s assessment and the PSR itself will not be accepted without question as it is still the court’s role to examine the internal consistency and cogency of the report once produced: GCX at [46] and [61]. Mr Tan’s PSR did not draw erroneous conclusions that are obviously at odds or internally inconsistent with the remainder of the report: Low Geok Hong v PP [2016] SGHC 69 at [11].

Expedient to make MTO in Mr Tan’s case

24     At this stage, even if section 339(3) CPC were satisfied, I still have to address the legal question of whether an MTO should be ordered and undertake a balancing exercise between the various sentencing principles again: GCX at [42] and [82], based on the nature of the disorder, the extent to which it contributed to the commission of the offence and the offender’s potential for treatment as informed by the PSR: GCX at [46]. Ultimately, I will have to be satisfied that it is expedient to make an MTO, having regard to the circumstances including Mr Tan’s offences and her character: section 339(1) CPC.

25     It is unnecessary for a causal link to be shown between Mr Tan’s psychiatric condition and the commission of her offence before an MTO could be ordered: GCX at [81]. MTO is an appropriate sentencing option in Mr Tan’s case because like the facts in GCX at [83] and [85]:

(a)     the principles of deterrence and retribution receded in significance because Mr Tan was suffering from a disorder that was present at the time of the offences involving his neighbours and it was a contributory link for him committing the offences;

(b)     the PSR also indicated that Mr Tan would be susceptible to treatment and this would take place over 24 months.[note: 19] This militated against simply ordering a fine or a short term of imprisonment that would not have allowed for meaningful medical intervention. Instead, it suggested that treatment via MTO was the better response rather than punishment; and

(c)     this was not a case where rehabilitation had such diminished importance that it was outweighed by deterrence and retribution. Indeed, rehabilitation is the dominant sentencing principle.

Conclusion

26     I have explained to Mr Tan:

(a)     that the MTO is passed in lieu of any sentence of imprisonment and fine which I may impose for his offences;

(b)     the purpose, effect and obligations specified in section 340 CPC and the consequences that may follow if any of such obligations of the MTO are not met; and

(c)     the power of the court to vary or revoke the MTO upon the application of the appointed psychiatrist.

Mr Tan has indicated to me that he accepts and is willing to comply with the MTO.

24-month MTO made

27     Mr Tan’s MTO PSR does not express an opinion on the other offences that do not involve his neighbours. Be that as it may, it will be inconsistent to impose a punitive sentence of a fine or imprisonment for them as this will run counter to an MTO and defeat its rehabilitative purpose. Mr Tan’s diagnosis of his psychiatric condition in 2020 predates these offences in any event.

28     Having regard to the circumstances, including the nature of the offence and Mr Tan’s character, I find it expedient to make an MTO under section 339(1) CPC requiring Mr Tan to undergo psychiatric treatment for a period of 24 months from today.

Compensation not ordered

29     The compensation complainant in respect of the dishonest misappropriation charge has attended today’s proceedings. She has sought a compensation order in the sum of S$4,500, which she had erroneously transferred to Mr Tan. Proper documents have been submitted to support her claim. By his guilty plea, Mr Tan does not dispute the loss that has been quantified by her. He has informed me that he does not have any means to pay compensation. The prosecution has verified this through the investigation officer and has consequently not sought a compensation order.

30     In considering whether a compensation order is appropriate, which is a matter that I must consider under the law, and if so to make the order: sections 359 (1) and 359(2) of the Criminal Procedure Code 2010 (2020 Rev Ed) (“CPC”); PP v AOB [2011] 2 SLR 793 at [27], I am cognisant that any order I make must not be oppressive and must be realistic, in that I must be satisfied that Mr Tan either has the means available or will have the means to pay the compensation within a reasonable time: AOB at [25].

31     That said, Mr Tan’s inability to pay compensation is not an absolute bar to the making of a compensation order, since the CPC provides for an in-default term of imprisonment for failing to pay the compensation. The maximum in-default term in this case is six months’ imprisonment: section 360(4) CPC. I am equally cognisant that a compensation order does not form part of the sentence, not is it an alternative to a sentence. It should not be used as further punishment of a convicted person: AOB at [25]. It is to deter a convicted person from not paying the compensation ordered.

32     I have already made a community order in Mr Tan’s case. Mr Tan is impecunious and will have to serve a default term if he is unable to pay any compensation I order. In the same spirit of not imposing a punitive sentence of a fine or imprisonment on the dishonest misappropriation charge that would be inimical to the MTO that I made and defeat its rehabilitative purpose, I have to decline to order the compensation that is sought. The court does not make an order in vain. In other words, I will not make an MTO only to have it defeated by an in-default term if I were to order compensation and Mr Tan is unable to pay it.

33     I appreciate that the compensation complainant is looking to me for a remedy, which I cannot gives in the circumstances without rendering the MTO ineffectual and nullifying its intended rehabilitative effect. She is, however, not without remedy. She can exercise any right to a civil remedy, which in any event is also unaffected even if compensation were ordered and for recovery beyond the compensation paid under the order, except that civil damages is deemed to have been satisfied to the extent of any such amount paid: section 359(4) CPC.
