Public Prosecutor v Chan King Vun

Public Prosecutor v Chan King Vun
[2026] SGDC 208

Case Number:District Arrest Case No 916106 of 2025
Decision Date:26 June 2026
Tribunal/Court:District Court
Coram: Paul Quan
Counsel Name(s): Mohamed Riasudeen (Attorney-General's Chambers) for the Public Prosecutor; Chooi Jing Yen/ Chong Xin Zi, Claire (Chooi Jing Yen LLC) for the Accused.
Parties: Public Prosecutor — Chan King Vun

Criminal Law – Statutory Offences – Corruption, Drug Trafficking and Other Serious Crimes (Confiscation of Benefits) Act – Assisting another to control benefits from criminal conduct

Criminal Procedure and Sentencing – Sentencing

26 June 2026

Judgment reserved.

District Judge Paul Quan:

Introduction

1       This is a case of transnational money laundering across the Singapore-Malaysian borders involving a young Malaysian money mule, who was recruited by a syndicate to travel to Singapore to collect and move scam proceeds for reward.

Brief facts

2       The accused, Chan King Vun (“Mr Chan”), a 24-year-old Malaysian residing in Johor Bahru at the time, responded to an online job advertisement for work in Singapore.[note: 1] During the interview, one “Lao Da” informed Mr Chan that the job opportunity involved collecting monies from Singapore residents and delivering them to other persons in Singapore for a monthly salary of RM$8,000 and a 1% commission on the amount collected.[note: 2] Between 10 August 2025 to 13 August 2025, Mr Chan commuted daily from Malaysia to Singapore by bus and made a total of eight collections amounting to S$124,060 from five scam victims on six separate occasions over the course of four days.[note: 3]

Charge and prescribed punishment

3       Mr Chan has pleaded guilty to a single charge of abetting an offence under section 51(1)(a) of the Corruption, Drug Trafficking and Other Serious Crimes (Confiscation of Benefits) Act 1992 (2020 Rev Ed) (“CDSA”) by conspiring with Lao Da and other unknown persons to assist those persons control the criminal benefits from their scams-related offences.[note: 4]

4       By virtue of section 51(5) CDSA read with section 109 PC, he can be punished with a fine not exceeding S$500,000 and/or imprisonment for a term not exceeding ten years.

5       In recognition of the exercise of prosecutorial discretion, I also granted Mr Chan, upon the prosecution’s application, a discharge amounting to an acquittal on six other charges of cheating under section 420 of the Penal Code 1871(2020 Rev Ed) (“PC”) that he faced.[note: 5]

Parties’ sentencing positions

6       Mr Chan has no criminal antecedents in Singapore.

7       On its moderate harm-medium culpability assessment[note: 6] based on an application of the sentencing framework in Huang Ying-Chun v PP [2019] 3 SLR 606 (“Huang”), the prosecution has sought a sentence of 26 to 29 months’ imprisonment to be imposed on Mr Chan.[note: 7] On its moderate harm-low culpability assessment based on the same Huang framework,[note: 8] the defence has submitted a lower term of not more than 15 months’ imprisonment instead.[note: 9] In this regard, apart from Huang’s case, the parties have cited PP v Putra Alfian bin Ahmad Said [2024] SGDC 190 (“Putra”), PP v Liao Nuoqian [2025] SGDC 284 (“Liao”) and my recent decision in PP v Ho Mun Hao [2026] SGDC 156 (“Ho”) in support of their respective sentencing positions.

Court’s decision

8       On 12 June 2026, I convicted Mr Chan on the CDSA charge. After hearing parties on mitigation and sentence, I reserved my judgment on sentence.

9       Applying the Huang framework and on my assessment that the level of harm caused by Mr Chan’s offence is at the lower end of moderate range of harm, whereas his level of culpability is pegged at the lowest end of medium range of culpability, I now sentence Mr Chan to 20 months’ imprisonment.

10     I set out the reasons for my decision.

Deterrence as operative sentencing principle in Mr Chan’s case

11     Deterrence continues to be the dominant sentencing principle in such cross-border money laundering cases. Since my decision in Ho’s case, the worrying trend of Malaysian nationals travelling to Singapore to assist scam syndicates collect cash and valuables from scam victims remains unabated, with more than 30 being charged in Singapore since March 2026 thus far.[note: 10] The prevalence of such offences is of judicial concern and attract general deterrence: PP v Law Aik Meng [2007] 2 SLR(R) 814 at [25(a)]. Mr Chan’s offence may predate this recent development but it would be artificial to slice time so thinly, with the unintended effect of considering such offending behaviour in an unrealistic vacuum while disregarding the current and obvious state of affairs, as the basis for not making an example of his case to deter like-minded offenders. To some extent, sentencing also has to reflect current trends to achieve its full salutary effect: PP v Shawn Loh [2025] SGDC 292 at [65]. Given the numerous and separate collections that Mr Chan made, he has to be suitably deterred as well for his recalcitrant conduct, even if he would have no opportunity to re-enter Singapore after he has been dealt with as a foreigner who had committed a crime in Singapore: Liao Nuoqian v PP [2026] SGHC 92 at [84].

12     Retributive justice, which demands proportionate sentencing according to the gravity of the offence and the nature of the offender, serves as a check on any untrammelled deterrence. The Huang sentencing framework that features the familiar harm-culpability analysis, serves such a purpose, to which I now turn.

Huang sentencing framework applies to Mr Chan’s case

13     The parties have applied the Huang sentencing framework to Mr Chan’s case. Huang’s case laid down the sentencing framework for offences under section 44(1)(a) of the Corruption, Drug Trafficking and Other Serious Crimes (Confiscation of Benefits) Act (Cap 65A, 2000 Rev Ed). This is the predecessor provision of section 51(1)(a) CDSA. The Huang sentencing framework can therefore apply to Mr Chan’s case because the charge that he faces is premised on a section 51(1)(a) CDSA offence.

Application of Huang sentencing framework

14     As I did in Ho’s case, I apply the first four steps of the Huang sentencing framework in turn, omitting the fifth that pertains to the totality principle because Mr Chan also faces only a single proceeded charge: Huang at [131].

15     In this regard, I find it helpful to adopt the same analytical framework (and where appropriate the same language) in Ho’s case for consistency while being deeply cognisant of any differences it has with Mr Chan’s case.

Step 1: Identify the level of harm and level of culpability

16     I first have to consider the offence-specific factors to identify the level of harm caused by the offence and the level of the offender’s culpability: Huang at [98] and [101].

Moderate range of harm caused by Mr Chan’s offence

17     I agree with the parties that moderate harm is caused by Mr Chan’s offence. The defence has postulated this to be at the lowest end,[note: 11] whereas the prosecution clarified its position during oral submissions that this should not be higher than the harm assessed in Putra’s case,[note: 12] which the appellate court eventually pegged at the low end of moderate harm: see LawNet editorial note on the appellate decision in Magistrate’s Appeal 9138 of 2024 accompanying the district court’s Putra decision (“Putra (HC) editorial note”) at [3].

(1)   Amount of S$124,060 cheated not insubstantial

18     In Huang’s case, a substantial amount of S$957,000 was cheated that goes towards a finding of high level of harm, although not the overriding factor in the analysis: Huang at [109]. The victims were generally elderly with the youngest victim being 50, and the most elderly being 82 who suffered the most losing S$650,000. This was therefore a factor tending towards a finding of severe harm: Huang at [110].

19     In Mr Chan’s case, the amount cheated was S$124,060 from five victims, two of whom were vulnerable being 65 and above, who lost $9,500 and S$30,000 respectively, with the rest of the other victims in their early forties and the youngest being 30. In Ho’s case, I observed at [22] that the economic value of the crime in that case could not be said to be insubstantial even though it was lower than that in Huang’s case, given that the amount cheated was S$145,520 and also from five victims, two of whom were above 70 and therefore vulnerable, who lost S$6,000 and S$30,000 respectively, and another two being above 50, who lost S$4,000 and S$69,620 respectively. I say the same here, though to a slightly lesser extent, given the difference in the quanta cheated and the profile of the victims.

20     The prosecution has sought to distinguish Liao’s case on the basis that only one single victim was involved in that case.[note: 13] I accepted the same argument in Ho’s case at [48]. The defence has contended that this is incorrect because only one report involving RMB 148,225 was received but the total amount laundered was S$279,785.20, which pointed towards there being multiple victims.[note: 14] During oral submissions, the defence postulated that this would either be the merchants in respect of the cheating charges or the original scam victims.

21     As the prosecution rightly pointed out in its oral reply, the merchants had nothing to do with the CDSA charge. They might have been deceived into delivering the items paid using monies from a debit card they thought belonged to the purchaser, when in fact they were tainted monies and were cheated as such. But there was no evidence of loss suffered by the merchants. This was different from Mr Chan or Ho’s case where the scam victims actually parted with and handed their monies or property to runners and therefore identified as the victims in respect of the CDSA charges as such. In Liao’s case, the funds cheated from the scam victims already resided in the debit card account, which were then used to make the purchases of the items that were then transferred. These victims could therefore be properly regarded as those in connection with the CDSA charge. It is not unusual in scams-related offences to quantify the number of victims based on formal reports lodged traceable to, say, the accounts through which the cheated funds were laundered whilst taking cognisance of the entire magnitude of the offence, for instance its economic value represented by the entire quantum of funds flowing through the accounts. As there was only one report lodged where RMB 148,225 was transferred to the debit card account pursuant to a scam perpetrated in China where the victim transferred funds to a purported stock trading website: Liao at [5] (see statement of facts at [3]), it can therefore be said that Liao’s case involved only one victim on that basis.

(2)   Syndicated offence involving transnational element

22     The infiltration of foreign criminal elements into our borders must be strongly deterred when syndicates target Singapore citizens and residents using runners sent specifically to Singapore: Huang at [113]. It was undisputed[note: 15] that like in Huang’s case, the offence in Mr Chan’s case was also syndicated and involved a transnational element with cross-border operations: Huang at [112] and [113]. In Ho’s case, I observed at [23(a)] that the nature of such an offence in that case was more nuanced because it entailed a systemic abuse of the proximity and porosity of Singapore’s borders with Malaysia; in contrast, Huang’s case involved foreign criminal elements further away with a Taiwanese mule and syndicate. I make the same point here.

23     In Putra’s case, the appellate court was of the view that the transnational element was “engaged to a low level” in that the accused “only knew of and used a Malaysian number”: Putra (HC) editorial note at [3]. Without more (and I reiterate my caution in Ho’s case at [29] against relying on the Putra (HC) editorial note), it cannot support, much less stand for, the defence’s broader proposition that scant information about the nature of the syndicate in Putra or Mr Chan’s case, such as the number of members and the reach of their operations, does not make for any meaningful distinction between the nature of the transnational element in Putra and Mr Chan’s case respectively.[note: 16] Like in Ho’s case at [29], I continue to hold the view that the two are of different complexion and Mr Chan’s case warrants a higher harm assessment.

24     In Liao’s case, while the district court took into account the involvement of a transnational criminal syndicate as an aggravating factor at [54], nothing turns on its consequent assessment of the level of harm at the low end of the moderate range without the benefit of further explanation from the court and especially when it purported to take reference from Putra’s case at [55].[note: 17] This suffers the same limitations arising from relying on the Putra (HC) editorial note without full grounds from the appellate court in this regard.

25     The point I made in Ho’s case and reiterate here is not the physical infiltration of our borders or the distance the criminal elements have had to travel to do so per se[note: 18] as much as Mr Chan is a criminal element who has repeatedly infiltrated the uniquely proximate and porous Singapore-Malaysia borders via easy commute by bus.

(3)   Serious nature of predicate scams-related offences

26     In Huang’s case, the underlying cheating offences were serious because they exploited the public’s trust in public sector officials: Huang at [114]. In Mr Chan’s case, the predicate offences took the form of scams-related offences (job, investment and love scams) that are serious in nature because of the scams-related offences situation in Singapore, which I noted in PP v Shawn Loh [2025] SGDC 292 at [65] (and reiterated in Ho’s case at [25]):

(a)     scams are by far the most prevalent crime type in Singapore today;

(b)     between 2020 and the first half of 2025, there were about 190,000 reported cases constituting 60% of all reported crimes, with losses amounting to about S$3.7bn; and

(c)     scams-related offences reached a high watermark in 2024 with a seven-fold increase in losses to scams to at least S$1.1bn.

I also noted in Ho’s case that I acknowledged a brief reprieve in this dire situation in PP v Ayu Syakirah Binte Shahrul [2026] SGDC 111 at [15]. Although the number of scam cases fell by 27.6% to 47,308 cases in 2025 from 51,501 cases in 2024, and the losses from scams also fell by 17.9% to about S$913.1m in 2025 from about S$1,112.4m in 2024, the situation is still very concerning and tackling scams remains a key priority. The decrease in both scam cases and scam losses suggests cautiously that the anti-scam strategies and public measures introduced by the Government and industry partners have made it more challenging for scammers to succeed. In tandem with such efforts, and so as not to undo this modest improvement and to prevent a reversal of this encouraging but nascent trend, the court should continue to signal its deterrent stance against such serious offences categorically.

27     It is also noteworthy that in 2025, job and investment scams were among the top five scam types with the most number of cases (being the third and fourth highest scam types),[note: 19] with investment scams being the top scam type in terms of the amount lost.[note: 20] While there was a decrease in investment scams cases by 19.8% to 5,462 cases in 2025, such cases remained the fourth highest scam types,[note: 21] with the amount of about S$336.2m lost being the highest among the various scam types, representing a 4.8% increase from 2024.[note: 22] Internet love scams were also one of the top ten scam types in Singapore.[note: 23]

(4)   Assessing level of harm at lower end of moderate harm consistent with harm assessments in Huang, Putra, Liao and Ho

28     Having regard to the offence-specific factors, namely:

(a)     a lower amount cheated;

(b)     the less elderly victim profiles;

(c)     the specific nature of the syndicated transnational offence that abused the proximate and porous nature of our borders with Malaysia; and

(d)     the seriousness of the predicate scams-related offences; and

(e)     an absence of harm caused to confidence in public administration because there was no evidence of any impersonation of public sector officials involved,[note: 24]

pegging the harm caused by Mr Chan’s offence at the lower end of the range of moderate harm is consistent with the findings of severe harm in Huang’s case, mid-point of moderate harm in Ho’s case, and (subject to the caveat I made about the limitations of the Putra (HC) editorial note) lower end of moderate harm in Putra and Liao’s case.

Medium range of offender culpability

29     As for Mr Chan’s level of culpability, the prosecution has submitted that this should be pegged at medium culpability[note: 25] whereas the defence the highest end of low culpability.[note: 26]

(1)   Mr Chan’s role as runner in criminal enterprise critical though not expansive

30     The most important consideration is the offender’s role in the criminal enterprise or scheme: Huang at [127]. It was undisputed that Mr Chan’s role in the syndicate was a runner.[note: 27] So was the accused in Ho’s case, to which I observed at [31] that:

That label alone is unhelpful. The fact that he was a mere foot soldier and nowhere near the apex of the hierarchy should also not be overstated: Huang at [121]. The success of the entire enterprise hinges on getting the victims to part with their monies and the role that Mr Ho played in collecting the monies was therefore critical, even if not expansive, especially when the victims were based in Singapore. Mr Ho may be a cog, but he is a cog that makes the wheels of the whole operation turn.

On this basis, the prosecution similarly characterised Mr Chan as having played an “active and integral” role.[note: 28] It was an “indispensable and distinct component of the scam operation”, or put in another way: [note: 29]

the success of the syndicate depended on individuals such as [Mr Chan] who were willing to meet victims face-to-face, collect the proceeds of the scam and hand them over to other individuals to presumably transfer the proceeds further up the chain.

The direct face-to-face interactions placed Mr Chan at the critical juncture where the victims ultimately parted with their monies.[note: 30] They were induced to do so through Mr Chan’s involvement and the scams could not have succeeded without his participation.[note: 31] In that respect, the prosecution clarified during oral submissions that while Mr Chan might have been replaceable as a runner and his role in that regard might be dispensable as such, his particular function was not.

31     On the other hand, the defence argued that Mr Chan was never integral to the overall scheme and was entirely replaceable,[note: 32] unlike the accused in Putra’s case whom the district court found at [26] to have “played an integral role in the entire criminal enterprise” as he was “vital” and “indispensable” in facilitating the swift transfer and dissipation of the monies cheated from innocent victims that represent the criminal proceeds of the scammers. It is not known why the appellate court thought that the aggravating factor of the role played by the accused in Putra’s case was “engaged to a low level”: Putra (HC) editorial note at [2]. During oral submissions, the defence took the prosecution’s clarification on and submitted that runners like Mr Chan perform a dispensable function that can be performed by other runners. This was contrasted with the function of the accused in Putra’s case that only he could perform because he held on to auto-teller machine (“ATM”) cards that were specifically given to him so that he could use them to withdraw monies within a 15-minute time frame: Putra at [6] (see statement of facts at [6]) and [26].

32     With respect, I am unable to appreciate the distinction. Both Mr Chan and the accused in Putra’s case were runners who were given specific time-sensitive tasks that only they could perform at that point in time without throwing a spanner in the works and halting the wheels of the operation of the syndicate, even if briefly, for someone else to take over. Apart from specific collections to make and specific people to whom the collections were to be handed over, Mr Chan was also personally given a passphrase and a unique S$50 note for the day that were used during the verification process.[note: 33] If Mr Chan had to be replaced for any reason, it would mean a delay in collection, if not a real risk of non-collection altogether in the event of an intervention or the victims getting cold feet. In the worst-case scenario, the activities of the syndicate may be detected and thereby disrupted. Time was therefore equally of the essence in Mr Chan’s case as it was in Putra’s case. Nothing turns on how they were recruited[note: 34] – Mr Chan through an online job advertisement and the accused in Putra’s case, a debtor-turned runner who ended up working for his unlicensed moneylender when he was unable to repay his debt. Arguably, there was a ready pool of money mules in both of such cases.

(2)   Criminal enterprise fairly sophisticated

33     It is the sophistication of the scheme or criminal enterprise as a whole that is relevant and not just the role of the individual offender within the greater scheme: Huang at [59].

34     Like Huang (at [119]) and Ho’s case (at [34]), the criminal enterprise in Mr Chan’s case was fairly sophisticated. There were several distinct parts to the criminal scheme employed by the syndicate, with Mr Chan’s role confined to only one of these parts. At the upstream level, there were members who ensnared victims with job, investment and love scams; at the downstream level, there were runners like Mr Chan who collected monies from the victims and others to whom the collections were handed over. Instructions from Lao Da on the collections were conveyed via Telegram. The prosecution also held this view.[note: 35] The defence thought that the criminal enterprise was less sophisticated.[note: 36] I would have thought that if at all, the criminal enterprise was more sophisticated, given the level of coordination required for its covert authentication system[note: 37] and the arrangements put in place to avoid detection,[note: 38] including concealing Mr Chan’s identity; collections at random locations across Singapore including residential blocks, carparks and even inside vehicles; daily change of persons to whom the collections were to be handed over; and using a fake Shopee pass when doing the collections.

(3)   Mr Chan displayed planning and premeditation

35     Given that:

(a)     he responded to an online job advertisement to work in Singapore,[note: 39]

(b)     attended an interview where Lao Da told him that the collection of monies in Singapore was legal on behalf of officials who did not want to be seen doing the collections themselves,[note: 40] and

(c)     Lao Da told him not to ask too many questions and follow instructions when he tried to find out who the officials were,[note: 41]

I am prepared to accept that Mr Chan could be said to only realise once he was in Singapore that the work he was led to believe was legitimate was in fact criminal in nature: Huang at [86]. Be that as it may, by 11 August 2025, he started to suspect that the job was illegal because his wife had questioned why the officials would pay him to do the collections instead of doing this themselves if it were legal.[note: 42] The subsequent collections were therefore premeditated criminal activity: Huang at [118]. This was all the more so when his suspicion peaked when he was handed the fake Shopee pass on 12 August 2025.[note: 43]

(4)   Duration of offending in context of multiple infiltrations by Mr Chan as foreign criminal element into Singapore

36     In Ho’s case, I made the point that while the offending took place across five incidents over a week as compared to 13 incidents spread over two weeks in Huang’s case, the accused in Ho’s case shuttled between Malaysia and Singapore daily with the exception of one day to carry out the instructions from the group. This evinced a deliberate and conscious decision to offend because each entry represented a locus poenitentiae (or place of repentance) to which the accused could avail himself, but yet he doubled down and engaged in multiple offending until he was arrested and would likely have persisted for at least another week if he were not caught.

37     I make the same point here. Although the offending period was shorter across four days, Mr Chan’s conduct was no less deliberate. As the prosecution rightly pointed out during oral submissions, the intensity was greater in that there were six incidents and eight collections. On 13 August 2025, he was entrapped on the seventh incident when he was about to do his ninth collection and would have made another subsequent collection from another victim that day if he were not arrested.[note: 44] The defence made the point that he had wanted to stop working on the day he was arrested. He continued working that day not only because he was concerned that Lao Da might create trouble for him in Johor Bahru,[note: 45] but also because he had wanted to receive his reward.[note: 46] The defence did not argue that Mr Chan was forced to continue working out of fear of some form of reprisal as opposed to acting out of greed and should be treated less severely: Huang at [93], and rightly so because there is neither evidence to support this nor facts from which to make any such ineluctable inference.

38     The prosecution differentiated Liao on the basis that the offending conduct took place over a single day in that case.[note: 47] I accepted the same argument in Ho’s case at [48]. The defence pointed out during oral submissions that the offending purchases took place over two days: Liao at [5] (see statement of facts at [14]). This is undoubtedly correct but the transfer of the purchased items, which is the subject matter of the relevant CDSA charge in question, took place during the course of one day on 28 August 2024 to one Wen Chunjun: Liao at [4] (see CDSA charge) and [5] (see statement of facts at [15]).

39     I say nothing of the offending period in Putra’s case,[note: 48] or the frequency of the ATM withdrawals that the defence raised during oral submissions because this did not appear to have been taken into account by the appellate court.

(5)   No abuse of trust by Mr Chan

40     Unlike in Ho’s case at [36], there was no abuse of trust by Mr Chan[note: 49] even though he had direct face-to-face interactions with the scam victims because he did not impersonate anyone who was purportedly connected to the scams that the victims were subjected to, or make any representations to them, express or implied, that could found the basis of the victims reposing their trust in him.

(6)   Mr Chan’s less culpable mental state

41     Mr Chan has been charged under the “reasonable grounds to believe” limb of section 51(1)(a) CDSA. This mental state is a mens rea element of the offence and not an aggravating factor. I accept that his subjective belief or suspicion that the job was illegal does not elevate this to that of actual knowledge or the relevant mental state for the purposes of his CDSA charge: Huang at [123].[note: 50]

(7)   Mr Chan did not know about predicate offences

42     It was also undisputed that Mr Chan did not know about the predicate offences,[note: 51] but he did suspect the legality of the job. However, this would not be considered as a factor increasing his culpability: Huang at [125].

(8)   Mr Chan’s level of culpability assessed at lowest end of medium range of culpability

43     I assess Mr Chan’s level of culpability to be at the lowest end of the medium range of culpability, considering the offence-specific factors:

(a)     the critical role that he played,

(b)     the fairly sophisticated criminal enterprise,

(c)     the premediated nature of the offence upon his suspicion that the job was illegal,

(d)     the short but intensive duration of offending evincing a deliberate and conscious decision to offend,

(e)     the absence of any abuse of trust by him,

(f)     his less culpable mental state of reasonable belief, and

(g)     he did know about the predicate offences.

44     This is consistent with the culpability assessments pegged at the medium range in Huang’s case, the lower end of the medium range in Ho’s case, and (subject to the same caveat) the low end of the medium range in Putra’s case. Liao’s case, with its low culpability assessment, is distinguishable.

Step 2: Identify the applicable indicative sentencing range – moderate harm-medium culpability assessment corresponds to indicative sentencing range of 30 to 60 months’ imprisonment

45     A moderate harm-medium culpability assessment corresponds to an indicative sentencing range of 30 to 60 months’ imprisonment: Huang at [102].

Step 3: Identify appropriate starting point sentence within indicative sentencing range – starting point sentence assessed at 32 months’ imprisonment

46     Pegging the harm caused by the offence at the lower end of moderate range of harm and Mr Chan’s culpability at the lowest end of medium range of culpability, I assess the starting point sentence to be 32 months’ imprisonment.

Step 4: Make adjustments to starting point sentence to account for offender-specific factors

47     I next consider the offender-specific aggravating and mitigating factors personal to Mr Chan to ascertain whether any upward or downward adjustments need to be made to the starting point sentence.

No personal aggravating factors warranting upward adjustments to starting point sentence

48     There are no personal aggravating factors that warrant any upward adjustments to the starting point sentence.

Personal mitigating factors warrant overall downward adjustment of three months’ imprisonment to starting point sentence

49     The consideration of Mr Chan’s personal mitigating factors lands on the side of an overall downward adjustment of three months to the starting sentence.

(1)   Mr Chan’s full and voluntary cooperation with the authorities of some mitigatory weight

50     Genuine contrition and remorse is a question of fact and the contemporaneous documents, evidence, behaviour and conduct at the material time in question has been used as a reliable fact-finding yardstick: PP v Andy Oie Zheng Jie [2024] SGDC 238 at [32].

51     In Ho’s case, I applied a downward adjustment of three months’ imprisonment to account for the full and voluntary cooperation of the accused with the authorities: Ho at [55]. Such forthright repentant behaviour, even to the extent of volunteering not an insignificant amount of incriminating facts, evinced contemporaneous and therefore genuine contrition and remorse. By comparison, Mr Chan did not offer up as much of such information[note: 52] and his cooperation should correspondingly carry less weight.

(2)   Mr Chan’s youth also of some mitigatory weight

52     Mr Chan was 23 at the time of the offence and can avail himself to his youth as a mitigating factor. However, this cannot be overstated. There is an imperative need to deter like-minded offenders, in particular youthful ones who are being targeted by scam syndicates. The cost of crime must be sufficiently high so that these targeted youths think long and hard before becoming money mules for easy money: Cheah Bernice [2024] SGDC 220 at [22]. Indeed, Mr Chan was motivated to commit the offence for gain. Crippling the supply of enablers by denying scammers and scam syndicates the tools they need, is a key strategy that would significantly increase the difficulty for scammers to successfully conduct or profit from scams in Singapore,[note: 53] particularly enablers such as Mr Chan, who had played a significant role in actively facilitating the laundering of criminal proceeds by scam syndicates and in making it difficult for authorities to track the money trail: Galvez Mary Joe Blanco v PP [2026] SGHC 110 (“Galvez”) at [40].

(3)   Mr Chan not considered first-time offender; absence of antecedents neutral factor in any event

53     Although Mr Chan has no criminal antecedents in Singapore, he should not be regarded as a first-time offender because of the multiple collections he made from the scam victims that constituted the CDSA offence: Chen Weixiong Jerriek v PP [2003] 2 SLR(R) 334 at [17]. In any event, the absence of antecedents is at best a neutral factor; it is an absent aggravating factor, not a mitigating factor: BPH v PP [2019] 2 SLR 764 at [85]. The repeated collections militate against any argument that this is a one-off aberration and out of character for him: PP v BWJ [2023] 1 SLR 477 at [102].

Full 30% reduction in sentence for indication of early guilty plea

54     Mr Chan’s early indication of guilty plea also carries mitigatory weight. I therefore accord him the full 30% reduction in sentence as recommended by the Sentencing Advisory Panel in its guidelines in this regard.

Conclusion

55     The final sentence is based on:

(a)     the starting point sentence of 32 months’ imprisonment on a (lower end of) moderate harm - (lowest end of) medium culpability assessment;

(b)     an overall downward adjustment of three months’ imprisonment to the starting point sentence to take into account the personal mitigating factors of full and voluntary cooperation with the authorities as well as youth; and

(c)     a full 30% reduction in sentence for the early indication of guilty plea.

Sentence of 20 months’ imprisonment imposed

56     The final sentence I arrive at and impose on Mr Chan is therefore 20 months’ imprisonment, backdated to 13 August 2025 when he was first arrested. He was held in custody and subsequently held in remand after he was first charged in court on 15 August 2025.

57     I am cognisant that the parties’ respective sentencing positions should not anchor my decision by forming the floor and ceiling for sentencing: PP v S Iswaran [2025] 3 SLR 403 at [156]. The sentence I have eventually arrived is the appropriate sentence to impose that is both sufficient and proportionate, and it is mere happenstance that it lies in between the parties’ positions.

58     I thank the parties for their cogent written and oral submissions, from which I derived considerable assistance. This is the second case of such nature that Mr Chooi and Ms Chong have taken on under Pro Bono SG’s criminal legal aid scheme before me and like the first in Ho’s case, they have discharged their duties with fine distinction.
