68     Applying the framework in De Beers, it was clear to me that the harm caused by the accused and his level of culpability were at the very highest end. The accused had procured penetrative sex from the victims, which represented one of the most grievous intrusions of bodily autonomy, and which has left the victims still picking up the pieces of their destroyed lives many years after their traumatic experience. The accused also acted with clear premeditation and subterfuge, without any consideration for his victims, whom he treated as playthings for his own selfish gratification. The accused showed no remorse during his offending spree, during the trial proceedings, and even after he was convicted of the charges against him. I agree with the Prosecution on the aggravating factors they submitted, and that there were no mitigating factors in this case.

69     For completeness, I highlight that the accused pleaded guilty to two charges, one under s 417 of the Penal Code and one under s 420 of the Penal Code, involving a different victim mid-way through this trial and was sentenced to the maximum sentence of 36 months’ imprisonment for the s 417 Penal Code charge in another court.

70     The accused, having been convicted after trial here, was not entitled to any sentencing discount. I therefore impose the maximum sentence of three years’ imprisonment for each of the two s 417 Penal Code charges. In my view, any lower sentence would not adequately reflect the seriousness of the offences disclosed and the harm caused.

The extortion charges

Extortion against V1

71     For the extortion charge against V1, the minimum prescribed punishment is two years imprisonment and up to seven years imprisonment, with caning.

72     Several features of s 384 bear emphasis at the outset. First, the provision prescribes a mandatory minimum sentence of two years' imprisonment, reflecting Parliament's view that extortion is an inherently serious offence that invariably warrants a custodial sentence of some substance. Second, the maximum sentence of seven years' imprisonment is significantly higher than the maximum for attempted extortion under s 385, reflecting the greater gravity of a completed extortion offence. Third, the provision expressly permits caning as an additional punishment, signalling Parliament's intention that it should be considered in appropriate cases.

73     The Prosecution highlights that the facts of the present case are egregious and far exceed any sentencing precedent. The Prosecution seeks the maximum prescribed punishment of seven years’ imprisonment, together with 12 strokes of the cane. The following aggravating factors are highlighted:[note: 48]

(a)     The threats made to V1 were protracted and continuous, from March to October 2020.

(b)     The accused exercised significant control over V1’s life as he made her share her whereabouts (using WhatsApp’s location sharing function) with him at all times. He also conducted searches to obtain information about V1’s personal life, including the identities of her parents and employer.

(c)     The total amount extorted, $177,434.25, is large and far above any amount in the precedents.

(d)     The harm caused to V1 is severe and extends beyond the stated figure in the charge. V1 performed intensely demeaning acts for the accused’s pleasure, including finding and meeting unknown men to perform oral sex on them,[note: 49] being partially nude in a public place,[note: 50] engaging a female prostitute to have sex with her and the accused,[note: 51] engaging a transgender prostitute to have sex with her,[note: 52] having sex with a woman,[note: 53] and engaging a dominatrix to flog her.[note: 54] V1 also prostituted herself on the accused’s instructions to earn more money for him.

(e)     V1’s life has been irreparably damaged by the accused’s conduct, as elaborated in her victim impact statement.

74     In assessing the appropriate sentence, I considered the relevant harm and culpability factors. I fully agree with the aggravating factors highlighted by the Prosecution and that the present case is unprecedentedly serious, given the level of harm caused and the accused's culpability.

(1)   Harm

75     I find that the harm in this case is exceptional and falls at the very highest end of the spectrum.

76     The extortion of V1 was not a single act or a brief episode. It was a sustained campaign of terror that lasted from 29 February 2020 to 7 October 2020, approximately eight months, during which V1 was extorted into transferring a total of $177,434.25 to the accused.

77     However, the true financial devastation wrought upon V1 is even more severe than the raw figure suggests. To meet the accused's relentless demands, V1 emptied her bank account and took out bank loans. She remains in debt to this day. Furthermore, the accused did not merely take money from V1. He drove her and her family into financial ruin. The harm caused to V1's parents, who had their savings depleted by their daughter's desperate attempts to satisfy the accused's demands, is a further dimension of harm that the court must consider.

78     The harm caused to V1 extended beyond financial harm. To earn money to meet the accused's demands, V1 was forced to prostitute herself, with the accused vetting her clients and directing her activities. I find that the psychological harm suffered by V1 is severe and lasting. V1’s victim impact statement speaks for itself. The depth and permanence of V1's psychological harm are a powerful indicator of the gravity of the accused's conduct. The accused did not merely take money from V1. He destroyed her sense of safety, her capacity for trust, her ability to form relationships, and ultimately her ability to continue living in the country she called home. This is harm of the most profound and lasting kind.

(2)   Culpability

79     I find that the accused's culpability also falls at the very highest end of the spectrum.

80     The accused's conduct during the extortion phase was premeditated and unrelenting. He conducted searches on V1’s personal life to determine the identities of her parents, employer, and other personal information to make his threats more credible and more terrifying. He required V1 to share her whereabouts with him at all times via WhatsApp's location-sharing feature. He took control of her social media. He monitored and directed her activities with a level of control that far exceeded that typical in an extortion case.

81     The accused also took active steps to maximise the financial yield of his extortion. When V1 had exhausted her own resources, the accused directed her to prostitute herself to earn more money for him. He vetted her clients and directed her activities as a prostitute. This represents a level of exploitation and control that is deeply aggravating and has no parallel in typical extortion cases.

82     The accused fully exploited the power imbalance created by his possession of V1’s explicit material. He held over her the constant threat of public humiliation and the destruction of her personal and professional relationships. This gave him a degree of control over V1 that was total and suffocating, and which he exploited without mercy or restraint.

83     The present case is, by any measure, one of the most serious extortion cases that have come before the courts. There is no doubt in my mind that the appropriate sentence in the present case should fall near the highest end of the sentencing range prescribed. However, I remain slow to conclude that this case is said to be the worst of its kind that will ever come before the courts. To be clear, while I stop short of characterising this as the absolute worst case, it is nonetheless one of the most serious extortion cases to come before the courts, and the sentence imposed must reflect this.

(3)   Caning

84     I turn next to the question of caning. I am satisfied that caning is warranted in the present case, and I impose 12 strokes of the cane. My reasons are as follows.

(a)     First, the physical harm caused to V1 in the course of the extortion is a powerful factor in favour of caning. The accused's extortion drove V1 to subject herself to physical abuse, including being flogged and whipped, leaving behind numerous wounds, to satisfy his demands. It is appropriate that the accused, who caused V1 to suffer physical harm, should himself experience a measure of physical punishment.

(b)     Second, the accused's conduct was characterised by a complete and callous disregard for V1's physical and psychological well-being. He treated her as an object to be exploited and degraded for his own financial gain. Caning is an appropriate response to conduct of this nature, reflecting the court’s condemnation of the accused's behaviour and the need to impose a punishment that is commensurate with the gravity of his offending.

(c)     Third, the need for deterrence, both specific and general, strongly supports the imposition of caning. The accused's scheme was premeditated and designed to be difficult to detect. A sentence of imprisonment alone may not be sufficient to deter the accused or others from engaging in similar conduct. The addition of caning sends an unambiguous message that such extortion will be met with severe physical punishment.

85     Given the aggravating factors present, in my view, a sentence of six years and six months’ imprisonment, together with 12 strokes of the cane, is appropriate and warranted. This places the sentence in the present case near the highest end of the maximum prescribed punishment. While the harm and culpability are exceptional, the court stops short of the maximum in recognition of the fact that this is not characterised as the absolute worst case of its kind. The court must have regard to the full sentencing range provided for by Parliament, and must not shy away from imposing sentences at the higher end of the range where the facts warrant it: De Beers at [40].

Attempted extortion against V2

86     For the attempted extortion charge against V2, the minimum prescribed punishment is two years imprisonment and up to five years imprisonment, with caning.

87     The charge pertains to the accused's attempt to put V2 in fear of harm to her reputation by threatening to release her sexually explicit video online, telling her, inter alia, "I'll fucking make you the most famous person in Singapore... You will see yourself everywhere", and demanding that she transfer S$2,750 to him if she did not want him to release the explicit video. V2 ultimately did not comply with the accused's demands.

88     In assessing the appropriate sentence, I considered the relevant factors of harm and culpability.

(1)   Harm

89     Although V2 ultimately did not comply with the accused's demands, the harm caused by the attempted extortion was nonetheless severe and lasting. The fact that the extortion was not completed does not diminish the gravity of the offence. The accused had already, by the time of the extortion attempt, obtained a sexually explicit video of V2 through his prior deception. The threat to release this video was therefore not an idle one. It was a credible, targeted threat, supported by the accused's actual possession of the material in question.

90     The nature of the threatened harm was particularly grave. The accused threatened to release V2's sexually explicit video online, telling her that he would make her "the most famous person in Singapore" and that she would "see herself everywhere." The accused's threat was not vague or general. It was specific, targeted, and designed to maximise the fear and distress caused to V2. This threat was directed at V2’s reputation, dignity, and personal relationships. The potential consequences of such a release, including public humiliation, damage to personal and professional relationships, and lasting reputational harm, are severe.

91     The psychological harm caused to V2 has also been canvassed above as demonstrated by V2’s victim impact statement. While not all of this harm is attributable solely to the attempted extortion, the attempt did come after the accused had already subjected V2 to sexual exploitation. This undoubtedly compounded and deepened the psychological trauma she suffered.

92     I therefore find that the harm in this case falls at the high end of the spectrum.

(2)   Culpability

93     The accused's conduct was highly premeditated. He first exploited her by posing as a wealthy Caucasian sugar daddy, offering her financial security, and then using the sexually explicit material he had obtained through deception as a weapon against her. As Menon CJ observed in De Beers at [49(b)], the reluctance of victims to come forward when offences are committed against them, because of the stigma associated with being cheated and sexually exploited, clearly renders them vulnerable. The accused exploited this vulnerability to the fullest.

94     The accused carried out his scheme from Malaysia, targeting victims in Singapore. This cross-border dimension of his offending significantly increases his culpability, as it made detection and apprehension considerably more difficult. A joint covert operation between the Singapore Police Force and the Royal Malaysian Police Force was required to apprehend the accused.[note: 55]

95     I therefore find that the accused's culpability falls at the high end of the spectrum.

(3)   Caning

96     S 385 of the Penal Code expressly provides for caning as an additional punishment, signalling Parliament's intention that caning should be considered in appropriate cases. The accused's conduct in this case was predatory, sophisticated, and callous, having first obtained sexually explicit material through deception before weaponising it against his victims. I am satisfied that caning is warranted in the present case, and I impose 3 strokes of the cane.

97     Having considered the facts and circumstances of the case, I am satisfied that a sentence of three years' imprisonment with three strokes of the cane is justified for this charge. A sentence of three years' imprisonment represents 60% of the maximum sentence. In arriving at this sentence, I am mindful that the extortion in this case was attempted and not completed; V2 did not comply with the accused's demands. This distinguishes the present charge from the completed extortion charge involving V1, which attracted a higher sentence. The fact that the extortion was not completed provides some basis for calibrating the sentence for this charge at a level below that imposed for the completed extortion offence, while still reflecting the gravity of the accused's conduct. Nevertheless, the imposed sentence must be substantially above the minimum sentence of two years imprisonment to reflect the fact that the accused was convicted after trial and has shown no remorse.

The global sentence

98     Having determined the individual sentences for each of the four proceeded charges, I turn to consider how the sentences ought to run, and whether the resulting aggregate sentence is appropriate. In doing so, I apply the analytical framework for sentencing an offender with multiple offences set out in PP v Raveen Balakrishnan [2018] 5 SLR 799 ("Raveen").

The Raveen framework

99     The Raveen framework involves three stages as follows:

(a)     The first stage requires the sentencing court to consider the appropriate sentence for each individual offence, having regard to the relevant aggravating and mitigating factors that bear upon each discrete sentence. I have already addressed the first stage in my earlier grounds dealing with the individual charges.

(b)     The second stage of the sentencing analysis is to determine how the individual sentences should run. The starting point of the analysis is whether the offences are unrelated, and this is determined by considering whether they involve a single invasion of the same legally protected interest. As a general rule, sentences for unrelated offences should run consecutively. In contrast, sentences for offences that form part of a single transaction should run concurrently, subject to the requirement in s 307(1) of the CPC.

(c)     The third stage of the sentencing analysis is to apply the totality principle and take a "last look" at all the facts and circumstances to ensure that the aggregate sentence is sufficient and proportionate to the offender's overall criminality. Specifically, there are two limbs to the totality principle. First, the court should examine whether the aggregate sentence is substantially above the normal range for the most serious of the individual offences committed. Second, the court should examine whether the sentence's effect on the offender is crushing and not in keeping with his past record and future prospects.

100    The offences against V1 and the offences against V2 are unrelated. They were committed against different victims, at different times, and in the context of separate and distinct criminal episodes. The charges relating to each victim cannot be said to form part of a single transaction, and the prima facie position is therefore that the sentences for the charges relating to V1 and those relating to V2 should run consecutively.

101    The more nuanced question is whether the two charges relating to each individual victim can be considered unrelated. I find that they can. In particular, the cheating charge against a victim operated against the accused's invasion of the victim’s interest in not being deceived and induced to engage in sexual acts under false pretences. The extortion charge, by contrast, operated against the accused's invasion of the victim’s entirely distinct interest in not being subjected to unlawful threats and coercion designed to extract money from her. The offences therefore violate different legally protected interests. In De Beers,[note: 56] Menon CJ observed that the cheating charge pertaining to "Belle" operated against the offender’s invasion of "Belle's" interest to not be deceived and suffer loss as a result, while the criminal intimidation charge pertaining to "Belle" operated against the offender’s invasion of "Belle's" distinct interest in not being placed under unlawful duress such that she was forced or compelled to not report his acts to the police. The same reasoning applies here.

102    As a prima facie position, all four sentences ought to run consecutively. However, this is subject to the operation of the totality principle at the third stage of the Raveen framework, to which I now turn.

The totality principle

103    If all four sentences were to run consecutively, the total sentence would be 15 years and 6 months imprisonment with 15 strokes of the cane.

(1)   First limb of totality principle

104    In the present case, the most serious individual offence is the extortion charge against V1 under s 384 of the Penal Code, for which I have imposed a sentence of six years and six months' imprisonment and 12 strokes of the cane. An aggregate sentence of 15 years and six months' imprisonment and 15 strokes of the cane would be substantially above this figure. The first limb of the totality principle, therefore, provides some basis for moderation of the aggregate sentence.

(2)   Second limb of totality principle

105    Under the second limb, I am satisfied that running all four sentences consecutively would result in an aggregate sentence that, while arguably warranted given the accused's overall criminality, would violate the totality principle when considered against the accused's overall sentencing position. I am mindful that the accused has already served a sentence of 54 months' imprisonment arising from his earlier plea of guilt mid-trial in February 2025 in respect of another victim. The accused's sentence of 54 months was backdated to his arrest date on 28 January 2021. In default of the imposed compensation order, the accused also served an additional 70 days' imprisonment. He has since completed that sentence, and for the current charges, the accused has been remanded since 25 March 2025.[note: 57] As the accused will be serving a continuous period of custody, it is appropriate for this court to consider the totality of his aggregate sentence, including the sentence of 54 months that he has already served.

106    Taking into account the totality of the accused's custodial exposure across all sets of offences, I am satisfied that it is appropriate to run only three of the four sentences consecutively, rather than all four. I order the following three sentences to run consecutively: the cheating charge against V1 (three years’ imprisonment), the extortion charge against V1 (six years six months’ imprisonment and 12 strokes of cane), and the cheating charge against V2 (three years’ imprisonment). These are my reasons:

(a)     First, the cheating and extortion charges against V1, while both relating to the same victim, protect entirely distinct legally protected interests, as explained above. These are fundamentally different interests, and the offences cannot be said to form part of a single transaction. They must therefore run consecutively.

(b)     Second, the cheating charge against V2 must run consecutively with the sentences for the V1 charges because it was committed against an entirely different victim, at different times, and in the context of separate criminal episodes. Running the cheating charge against V2 consecutively with the V1 sentences is necessary to capture the full criminality of the accused's conduct in targeting multiple victims.

(c)     Third, running these three sentences consecutively is necessary to reflect the distinct yet cumulative nature of the accused's criminality. The accused did not commit a single offence or a single episode of offending. He operated a sustained and multi-faceted criminal scheme targeting multiple victims, using deception to procure sexual material and then leveraging that material for financial gain. The accused's conduct demonstrated an exploitative and simply callous disregard for his multiple victims over an extended period of time, underscoring his overall criminality. Running only two sentences consecutively would fail to reflect this adequately.

107    Finally, taking “a last look” at the overall total sentence and applying the totality principle, I make a slight downward adjustment to the extortion charge against V1, reducing it to 6 years' imprisonment instead of 6 years and 6 months' imprisonment. This reduction is made solely on account of the totality principle and not because of any reassessment of the individual sentence. The total sentence for the current set of charges is therefore 12 years and 15 strokes of the cane. When the current aggregate sentence of 12 years is considered alongside the 54 months already served, the total custodial exposure of approximately 16 years and 6 months is, in my judgment, a sentence that is condign to the accused's behaviour and prospects and that is proportionate to the totality of his criminal conduct across all three victims.

108    I order the current aggregate sentence of 12 years’ imprisonment and 15 strokes of the cane to be backdated to his date of remand on 25 March 2025.

109    For completeness, I address the accused’s submission seeking to have his current aggregate sentence run concurrently with his previous sentence of 54 months’ imprisonment. This argument was misconceived as a matter of law because, at the time of sentencing for the current charges, the accused had already completed his previous sentence. Therefore, it is not possible for the sentences for the current set of charges to run concurrently with those he has already served.

110    The accused also asked for his current sentence to be backdated to before his remand date of 25 March 2025. Under s 318(3) of the CPC, a court may direct that a sentence of imprisonment take effect on a date earlier than the date the sentence is passed. However, in doing so, the court must consider the following:

(a)     The date on which the offender was arrested for the offence;

(b)     The length of the period (if any) during which the offender was remanded in custody in relation to the offence;

(c)     The length of the period (if any) during which the offender was remanded in a psychiatric institution (whether for observation or otherwise) under Division 5 of Part 13 in relation to the offence;

(d)     the length of the period (if any), after the offender was arrested for the offence, during which the offender was not in custody.

111    In this case, the Singapore Prison Service has indicated that the accused has completed his previous sentence and that his custody status was converted to remand on 25 March 2025.[note: 58] In other words, in relation to the present offences that he has been convicted before me, his period of custody in remand starts from 25 March 2025. Therefore, it was appropriate for the accused’s current sentence to be backdated to 25 March 2025 under s 318(5)(b) CPC.

Conclusion

112    The accused's conduct in this case was predatory, calculated, and callous. He devised and executed an elaborate scheme of deception and exploitation targeting vulnerable women, using explicit material he had obtained through deception as weapons against them. He showed no remorse throughout the proceedings, forced his victims to relive their traumatic ordeals on the stand, and conducted himself at trial in a manner that was itself aggravating. The harm he has caused to V1 and V2 is severe and lasting. V1 was driven to financial ruin, forced into prostitution, and ultimately compelled to leave the country she called home. V2 was diagnosed with post-traumatic stress disorder and continues to suffer the consequences of the accused's actions years after the offences were committed.

113    The courts must not shy away from utilising the full sentencing range provided for in the offence-creating provisions where the facts warrant it.[note: 59] In my view, the sentences imposed in the present case reflect the exceptional gravity of the accused's offending, the very highest level of harm caused to the victims, and the complete absence of any mitigating factors.

114    I therefore sentence the accused to an aggregate sentence of 12 years’ imprisonment with 15 strokes of the cane, backdated to the date of remand on 25 March 2025.

Public Prosecutor v Loganathan Vijayan

Public Prosecutor v Loganathan Vijayan
[2026] SGDC 196

Case Number:District Arrest Case No. 911388-2022 and others, Magistrate's Appeal Nos. 9194-2025-01
Decision Date:09 June 2026
Tribunal/Court:District Court
Coram: Eddy Tham
Counsel Name(s): Deputy Public Prosecutors Darren Ang (Attorney-General's Chambers) for the Public Prosecutor; Defence Counsel A Revi Shanker (M/s ARShanker Law Chambers) for the Accused.
Parties: Public Prosecutor — Loganathan Vijayan

Criminal Law – Claim trial – Theft – Abet by instigation – Section 380 read with section 109 of the Penal Code 1871 – Criminal trespass under section 447 of the Penal Code 1871 – Criminal Procedure and Sentencing – Mitigation and Sentencing

[LawNet Editorial Note: An appeal to this decision has been filed in MA 9194/2025/01.]

9 June 2026

District Judge Eddy Tham:

BACKGROUND

1       The Accused claimed trial to three proceeded charges. In one charge, he was alleged to have committed one offence of theft of copper cables under section 380 read with section 109 of the Penal Code 1871 (“the Penal Code”). The remaining two charges were for committing criminal trespass onto Keppel FELS compound with the intention of committing the alleged theft of copper cables, offences under section 447 of the Penal Code.

2       At the end of the trial, the Accused was found guilty and convicted of all three proceeded charges.

3       After conviction, the Accused admitted and consented to one charge of theft under section 380 of the Penal Code and another charge of criminal misappropriation under section 403 of the Penal Code to be taken into consideration for the purpose of sentencing (“the TIC charges”).

4       The Accused was thereafter sentenced to 19 months’ imprisonment for the theft offence and three weeks’ imprisonment for each of the criminal trespass offences. The sentence for the theft offence was ordered to run consecutively with one of the criminal trespass sentence, giving a global sentence of 19 months and 3 weeks’ imprisonment.

5       The Accused being dissatisfied with the outcome of the trial, has filed an appeal against both conviction and sentence. He has been released on bail pending the hearing of the appeal.

THE CHARGES

6       The three charges are as follows:

Charge: DAC-911388-2022

are charged that you, on 15 July 2022, at about 4.19pm, at the Keppel FELS compound located at 50 Gul Road, Singapore 629351, a building used for the custody of property, did abet, by instigation, the commission of an offence under s 380 of the Penal Code 1871 (“PC”), to wit, by instructing one Karthikeyan Rajendran to drive the lorry bearing the registration number YP9291L (“the Lorry”) towards the exit of Keppel FELS while about 1,700kg of copper cables (with an estimated value of $28,667.02) (“the Copper Cables”) had been loaded onto the Lorry, intending to cause the commission of a theft of the Copper Cables in the possession of one Ramprosad Saha, a facility manager stationed at Keppel FELS (“Ramu”), without Ramu’s consent, and you have thereby committed an offence punishable under s 380 read with s 109 of the PC.

Charge: MAC-905569-2022

are charged that you, on 15 July 2022, at about 3.37pm, at the Keppel FELS compound located at 50 Gul Road, Singapore 629351, did commit criminal trespass, to wit, by entering into the said Keppel FELS compound, property in the possession of another, with intent to commit an offence of theft-in dwelling under s 380 of the Penal Code 1871 (“PC”), and you have thereby committed an offence punishable under s 447 of the Penal Code 1871.

Charge: MAC-905570-2022

are charged that you, on 13 July 2022, at about 7.24pm, at the Keppel FELS compound located at 50 Gul Road, Singapore 629351, did commit criminal trespass, to wit, by entering into the said Keppel FELS compound, property in the possession of another, with intent to commit an offence of theft-in dwelling under s 380 of the Penal Code 1871 (“PC”), and you have thereby committed an offence punishable under s 447 of the Penal Code 1871.

THE BACKGROUND FACTS

7       I will not set out some background facts which are not disputed.

The employment of the Accused

8       The Accused is Loganathan Vijayan, a 36-year-old Indian male at the time of the trial. At the material time of the offences, the Accused was a site supervisor employed by Sunseap Pte Ltd (“Sunseap”).

9       Up until 2021, Sunseap had ongoing solar panel installation works at Keppel FELS, which is a building used for the custody of property. As Sunseap’s works at Keppel FELS were completed by 2021, the Accused had no official reason to enter Keppel FELS or handle the materials inside the compound after 2021.

The arrest of the Accused

10     The undisputed facts are as follows.

11     In the evening of 13 July 2022 and into the early hours of 14 July 2022, the Accused entered and departed from the Keppel FELS premises together with two of his colleagues from Sunseap, namely PW9 Mr Meyyanathan Sathaiah (“Sathaiah”) and DW4 Mr Manimaran Vignesh (“Vignesh”). Their movements had been captured on CCTV footage of Keppel FELS. The Accused did not dispute that he and his two colleagues had been captured in this footage.

12     On 14 July 2022, PW3 Mr Ramprosad Saha (“Ramprosad”), a facilities manager at Keppel FELS, noticed that certain cables had been removed from the store and that a bundle of cables had been left unattended at Lot 2 of the shipyard. He brought this to the attention of PW4 Mr Nor Shafiq bin Mohamed Salleh (“Shafiq”), the Group Security Manager at Keppel FELS. Prior to 8.43 pm that same day, Shafiq arranged for two temporary closed-circuit cameras to be set up to keep watch over the bundle of cables.

13     The following day, 15 July 2022, at approximately 3.37 pm, the Accused and PW10 Mr Karthikeyan Rajendran (“Karthikeyan”) arrived at Keppel FELS aboard a lorry. Karthikeyan was employed by a company called DAS Recycling. He would buy scrap metal from customers. The Accused is one of his customers who would call him when he had scrap metal to be sold to him. When he received a call from such customers, he would drive his lorry to the place for scrap metal to be collected. Acting on the Accused's directions, Karthikeyan drove the lorry with the Accused as his passenger to Lot 2 and brought it to a stop there.

14     Between approximately 3.46 pm and 4.19 pm, the Accused moved about Lot 2 in search of a forklift operator who could assist in loading the bundle of cables onto the lorry. At around 4.19 pm, a forklift operator did so at the Accused's behest. After the loading onto the lorry has been completed, the Accused then directed Karthikeyan to drive the lorry towards the exit of the premises.

15     At around this juncture, Shafiq initiated a lockdown of the facility's gates. The Accused and Karthikeyan were intercepted at the delivery gate of Keppel FELS, where both were subsequently placed under arrest.

THE PROSECUTION'S CASE

16     The Prosecution's case rested principally on the oral testimonies of its witnesses and the Accused's own recorded statements made between 15 and 21 July 2022. The Prosecution's witnesses included Ramprosad, Nor Shafiq, Meyyanathan, one of the accused's co-workers who was present on the material dates and Karthikeyan.

17     The Prosecution's case was, in essence, a straightforward one. On 13 July 2022 at about 7.24pm, the Accused entered the Keppel FELS compound at 50 Gul Road together with his co-workers. On that evening, he and his co-workers had gone around and picked up cables and thereafter moved them to Lot no 2 of the shipyard. On 15 July 2022, the Accused had arranged with Karthikeyan to collect the cables. However, they were apprehended while attempting to remove approximately 1,700 kilograms of copper cables from the premises. The cables were loaded onto a lorry and were being driven out of the compound when they were stopped by security personnel. The Accused's own recorded statements, made across five separate sessions between 15 and 21 July 2022, were tendered in evidence and formed a significant part of the Prosecution's case.

18     The Defence had initially challenged the admissibility of the statements. However, after one day of ancillary hearing, the Accused changed his mind and consented to the admission of his statements.[note: 1] In any case, during the ancillary hearing, there was nothing put to the relevant witnesses from the Prosecution about any allegations of threat, inducement or promise or of any inaccuracy in the recording of the statements.

THE DEFENCE CASE

19     The Defence case centred on the existence and role of an alleged Bangladeshi Facilities Supervisor at Keppel FELS known only as "Ismail." According to the Accused, Ismail was a subordinate staff member working under Ramprosad in the Facilities Department. The Accused claimed to have known Ismail during his three years of attachment to Keppel FELS while working for Sunseap Pte Ltd, an official contractor of Keppel FELS.

20     The Accused's case was that on both 13 and 15 July 2022, he and his co-workers entered Keppel FELS at Ismail's invitation and under his instructions, for the purpose of clearing old and scrap cables and repacking used cables. The Accused maintained that only scrap cables were to be cleared, that the proceeds of any sale were to be handed to Ismail, and that Ismail would in turn pay rental for the lorry and provide tips to the workers. The Accused denied any dishonest intention, asserting that he had Ismail's consent and was merely carrying out Ismail's instructions. Essentially, the Accused alleged that all his actions in entering the premises on 13 and 15 July 2022 as well as his act of removing the cables on 15 July 2022, had been sanctioned by Ismail and thereby clothed with the veneer of legitimacy.

21     The Accused further challenged the reliability of his recorded statements, alleging that he had made false confessions arising from the stress he felt from personal financial difficulties, rental arrears, his mother-in-law's critical health condition, and pressure from Karthikeyan, who had allegedly pressed the Accused to accept sole responsibility for fear of losing his own livelihood. The Accused also contended that the investigating officers failed to follow up on the roles of Ismail and Manimaran, and that certain CCTV footage from the pass exchange gate, which would have captured Ismail's presence, was not produced in court.

22     The Defence relied on the evidence of two witnesses for the Ismail Defence in addition to the Accused. Manimaran corroborated the Accused's account to the extent of confirming that Ismail had previously approached the team about overtime work and had arranged the necessary Permits to Work. Meyyanathan, called as a Prosecution witness, also made reference to Ismail in his testimony and confirmed that the Permit to Work was arranged through Keppel FELS staff.

THE ISSUES

23     The following issues of fact arose for determination:

(a)     Whether the Accused's recorded statements ought to be accorded full weight;

(b)     Whether the Accused entered the Keppel FELS compound on 12 and 15 July 2022 with criminal intent, so as to establish the charge of criminal trespass under section 447 of the Penal Code; and

(c)     Whether the Accused dishonestly removed the copper cables from the possession of Keppel Corporation Ltd without its consent, so as to establish the charge of theft in dwelling under section 380 of the Penal Code; and

(d)     Whether there was such a person called Ismail who is a staff of Keppel Fels who had authorised the Accused to remove used cables to be sold as scrap materials as this was central to his defence of no dishonest or criminal intent.

MY FINDINGS OF FACT

The Recorded Statements

24     I deal first with the Accused's challenge to his recorded statements. The Accused made statements on five separate occasions between 15 and 21 July 2022. He sought to impugn all of them on the basis that he had falsely admitted to wrongdoing out of duress, citing the feeling of betrayal by Ismail, personal financial stress, family difficulties, and pressure from Karthikeyan.

25     I am unable to accept this submission.

26     It is important to note at the outset that the Accused accepted that his statements had been made voluntarily without any threat, inducement or promise. This was based not just on the consent conveyed by Defence Counsel during the ancillary hearing but it was personally confirmed by the Accused whilst on the stand being cross-examined. The Accused also confirmed directly that his statements had been accurately recorded by the recording officer:[note: 2]

Q.    You confirmed that you gave at least nine statements to the police for this case within a week from your arrest, correct?

A.    Yes, could be.

Q.    And during this trial, you did not dispute that you gave the statements voluntarily, and that the statements were recorded accurately.

A    Yes.

27     The Accused, having confirmed that his statements had been accurately recorded from him then argued that he had gave false confessions to the police recorder.

28     I will now deal with the reasons he gave as to why he would make false confessions to the police.

29     He claimed he felt betrayed by Ismail when he was first apprehended. He claimed he saw Ismail standing at the Keppel’s yard when he was first caught but Ismail did not speak up for him. He then tried to explain the situation to Keppel’s staff but they told him that the police were coming and he could say whatever he wanted to say to the police. He stated that was when he felt betrayed and that he was being framed.[note: 3]

30     I found it unbelievable that the sense of betrayal and feeling of being framed would cause the Accused to make a false confession to the police. If anything, such betrayal ought to have driven the Accused to point the finger at Ismail as the culprit who had misled him to think that he was authorised to enter the premises to clear the cables for sale. That would have been the most natural and obvious course of action in order to clear his name. In fact, when he was told to wait for the police to come, he testified that:

So, I thought okay, when the police comes, I would let them know what happened.[note: 4]

31     Therefore, it is wholly inexplicable for the Accused to completely make mention of Ismail, the central figure for him entering the Keppel Fels and sole defence to the charge of theft at the very first opportunity for him to do so in his first statement to the police. By failing to mention him, it also deprived him of the opportunity of securing the person of Ismail since the Accused allegedly saw him present at the scene when he was first stopped by Keppel Fels security.

32     The irresistible inference to be drawn from the Accused’s failure to cite the Ismail defence in his statements is that this was clearly an afterthought and a belated attempt raised to extricate himself after having been caught red-handed on 15 July 2022.

33     His other explanations are equally feeble and incapable of providing a sound reason for making a false confession. The Accused's financial difficulties, his mother-in-law's health condition, and the pressure allegedly exerted by Karthikeyan should instead propel the Accused to exert his innocence. I note in particular that by pleading innocent, he would also have helped to prevent Karthikeyan from being implicated. He could easily take the position that both he and Karthikeyan were not aware that their acts were without the approval of the owner of the cables. Instead in P9, he took the position that he alone was guilty and that Karthikeyan was not aware that they were committing theft. There was absolutely no need for him to take the blame in order to exonerate Karthikeyan, even if he was feeling emotionally black-mailed by Karthikeyan.

34     Furthermore, a total of 9 statements were recorded over the course of five days: P9 on 15 July, P10 -P11 and three cautioned statements on 16 July, P12 on 17 July, P13 on 18 July and P14 on 19 July 2022. The Accused would have had ample opportunity between sessions to reflect on what he had said and to retract any false statements made by him earlier, or to seek legal advice. The fact that he did not do so, and that the statements remained consistent across all the sessions, strongly suggested that they were made voluntarily and reflected his genuine account of events at the time.

35     I therefore accord full weight to the accused's recorded statements. They constitute a significant and reliable part of the evidence against him in respect of all the three charges.

36     I thus gave full weight to the admissions contained in the following parts of his statements:

(a)     P9, statement recorded on 15 July 2022

37     The admissions made it very clear that the Accused had gone into Keppel FELS yard on 13 July 2022 with the sole purpose of stealing copper cables belonging to Keppel. He had engaged the services of two of his colleagues, Sathaiah and Vignesh, to assist him to move the copper cables belonging to Keppel, to a spot which would be convenient for him to return on another day to collect. He had entered into Keppel FELS that night without changing pass. He did return 2 days later with Karthikeyan. However, after loading the cables onto the truck driven by Karthikeyan, they were stopped by Keppel FELs security when they wanted to drive out of Keppel FELs. He had admitted that he was stealing the copper cables on the 15 July 2022 at that point when he uploaded the copper cables onto the lorry. In his statements, he had also stated the pressing financial circumstances he was under which led him to commit the offence.

38     It is noted that whilst the Accused had admitted to committing theft of Keppel’s cables on two occasions, he has only been charged in relation to one theft offence.

Analysis of the Charges of Criminal Trespass

39     Turning to the charges of criminal trespass under Section 447 of the Penal Code, the Prosecution must establish that the Accused entered the property of Keppel FELS with intent to commit an offence, namely theft.

40     The elements of the offence of criminal trespass as set out in section 441 of the Penal Code are as follows:

(a)     Enter into property in the possession of another;

(b)     With intent to commit an offence.

41     The Defence argued that the Accused did not trespass because he complied with all security clearance procedures, including pass exchange and registration, and because he had Ismail's permission to enter.

42     I found that both elements of criminal trespass had been proven beyond a reasonable doubt. The first element of entering the property of Keppel FELS on both dates of the two charges are not disputed by the Defence. Factually, it would not have been possible to dispute this element given that the presence of the Accused together with his two co-workers on the night of 13 July 2022 was captured on CCTV and the Accused admitted that he was the person shown in the footage.

43     He was also stopped and arrested in the premises on 15 July 2022.

44     The only defence open to the Accused was that his entry into the premises was not for the purpose of committing an offence. His statements as highlighted above completely supported the Prosecution’s case of an intent to commit an offence. It is irrelevant whether he managed to comply with the physical security procedures in place at Keppel FELS on the material dates. The fact of entry together with the intent to commit an offence would be sufficient to establish guilt beyond a reasonable doubt.

45     The complete failure of the Accused to mention Ismail in any of his statements was fatal to his case. The CCTV footages on both 13 and 15 July 2022 also put paid to the Accused’s allegation that Ismail was present physically on those 2 dates. In any case, all the prosecution witnesses who were employees of Keppel FELS have stated that they do not know of any “Ismail” who was an employee of Keppel FELS who could have authorised the Accused to sell Keppel FELS’s cables as scrap. The security officers called by the Defence

46     Further, the absence of any official work order, written authorisation, or documentation from Keppel FELS management sanctioning the removal of 1,700 kilograms of copper cables is a critical gap in the Defence's case. There are strict requirements such as the issuance of an outward permit for anyone to bring out goods from within the Keppel FELS site.[note: 5] A worksite supervisor, even if Ismail existed and gave the instructions attributed to him, did not have the authority to sanction the removal of property of such scale and value on behalf of Keppel Corporation Ltd. The Accused, having worked at the facility for three years, ought reasonably to have known this.

47     I further note that there were multiple security lapses admitted by Shafiq. Shafiq had testified that from checking the CCTV footage, there was a discrepancy in that what had been declared by the Accused in the form when entering Keppel FELS did not match what was evident on the CCTV footage. He admitted that the security officer had endorsed on the form without checking the lorry.[note: 6] However, these security lapses do not assist the Accused in his defence as to whether there was any dishonest intent on his part. If anything, the evidence suggested that the Accused was aware of the lax security environment and took advantage of it. This is entirely consistent with, rather than inconsistent with, criminal intent.

48     I am therefore satisfied that the Prosecution had established the charges of criminal trespass beyond a reasonable doubt, and I convict the Accused accordingly on both charges of criminal trespass.

The Theft in Dwelling Charge

49     I turn now to the more serious charge of theft in dwelling under section 380 of the Penal Code. The Prosecution must establish that the Accused dishonestly took moveable property out of the possession of Keppel Corporation Ltd without its consent.

50     Besides the overwhelming evidence of the Accused’s admissions in multiple statements, the same failure of the Accused to produce evidence of the existence of Ismail would be fatal to the defence in the light of the physical evidence in this case. The Accused was caught red-handed with approximately 1,700 kilograms of copper cables belonging to Keppel FELS were found loaded onto the lorry being driven out by Karthikeyan who was acting on the Accused’s direction.

51     The Accused was also found on 15 July 2022 when he was apprehended with the Declaration Form (Exhibit P8) with the information that he had brought into Keppel FELS on 3 July 2022, three quantities of cables. He admitted in his statement P10 when questioned about P8 that “only with this document, will they allow me to go out with the items”. This declaration was earlier established to be false based on the CCTV evidence that on 3 July 2022, the Accused did not bring in any items in his lorry as well as based on the evidence of Shafiq who had looked into the matter.[note: 7] The Accused himself admitted that the lorry that he had come in on 3 July 2022 did not contain the three items. However, the Accused claimed that another vehicle from a cable company was delivering the items and the items were on the other vehicle.[note: 8] I found such an assertion absurd and rebutted by the CCTV evidence which did not show any other vehicle coming into Keppel FELS together with the Accused’s lorry.

52     It was thus put to the Accused during cross-examination that he had intended to make use of P8 to get the stolen goods out of Keppel FELS:[note: 9]

Q    Put it to you that you intended to use P8 on the 15th of July 2022 to leave Keppel FELS with stolen cables, agree or disagree?

A    That is what I accepted on the statements.

53     The Accused’s use of P8 in order to bring out the cables should he be checked by security when exiting Keppel FELS constituted further evidence of his dishonest intent of theft of the cables. His intent to rely on a false declaration form clearly showed that there was no authorisation by any Ismail for him to bring out the cables.

54     Furthermore the stated reason he gave for entering the Keppel FELS on 15 July 2022, was captured on the computer system of the security known as “EVMS” captured that there reason for entry into the shipyard was to perform a collection that was authorised by “Mr Ramo, the facility manager”.[note: 10] This was evidently false as Ramoprasad had testified that he did not authorise any collection by the Accused on that day. More pertinently, the Accused did not mention Ismail as the person who had authorised the collection. This false declaration of reason further buttressed the case of a dishonest intention on the part of the Accused.

55     I also found that it was entirely implausible that 1,700 kilograms of copper cables constituted mere "scrap" or "rubbish" to be disposed of in the ordinary course of maintenance, without any formal documentation, work order, or authorisation from Keppel FELS management. The estimated value of the copper cables was $28,667.02 based on the table (exhibit P5) prepared by the Facilities Department of Keppel FELS. The unchallenged evidence of Ramprosad was that these cables were functional and could be used.

56     Based on the Accused’s evidence, there are only three persons in court who would have known the existence of Ismail and his role in the removal of cables belonging to Keppel FELS.

Other possible eyewitnesses to the existence of Ismail

57     The Accused first claimed that there were other witnesses who could confirm that Ismail had authorised the removal of the cables from Keppel FELS.

58     First was Karthikeyan. The Accused asserted that the Karthikeyan would have seen Ismail at his shop and also the cable company vehicle that had entered together with his lorry on 3 July 2022. Karthikeyan when cross-examined denied that there was any third party present when the goods which came from Keppel FELS were weighed at his place at Das Recycling and monies were paid to the Accused.[note: 11] When it was put to the Accused that Karthikeyan had denied that they were any third parties involved in all the transactions he had with the Accused, the Accused could only lamely respond that Karthikeyan had refused to give the information in court.[note: 12]

59     As for Sathaiah, his evidence in court was that he did see a supervisor from Keppel talking to the Accused once or twice. He claimed that after speaking with the supervisor that the Accused would then tell Sathaiah about what work needed to be done. This was in respect of the work in relation to what was captured on CCTV on 13 July 2022 showing that a trolley was being used to move the materials. This supervisor had also exchanged their passes to allow he, the Accused and Vignesh to enter Keppel FELS.[note: 13]

60     Although Sathaiah did not identify this supervisor as Ismail, it is quite obvious that his evidence was corroborative of the Accused’s evidence that he was acting on Ismail’s direction. On the whole I found it dubious that Sathaiah would have failed to mention in his statement P18 that the Accused was acting under instructions of a supervisor who was from Keppel. I found that he would have naturally mentioned it even if he was not asked as that would have been part of his case that he did not know that the Accused was doing anything illegal. He had stated at A7 in P18, when asked whether he was aware that the Accused was stealing anything, that “I do not know about all these claims. If I knew he was doing illegal activities, I would not have helped him at all.”

61     Hence it would have been obvious to Sathaiah that if he saw that the Accused had been talking to a Keppel supervisor and thereafter had returned to him to tell him what to do, it would have supported his case that he would not think that the Accused was acting illegally since he was being given instructions by a Keppel supervisor.

62     When confronted with his failure to mention this supervisor, Sathaiah merely replied that he was only asked about what the Accused did and hence he did not mention anything about the supervisor.[note: 14] As I have mentioned, it would have been obvious to him that this is an important factor to his position that he did not know the Accused was stealing the cables and ought to have mentioned it. This is reinforced by the fact that in court, even when he was not asked about the supervisor, he had the sense to mention him in respect of the Accused:[note: 15]

Court:

So do you label them as scrap or you are told that these are scrap? Do you do any labelling?

Witness:

Yes, we are informed that it is scrap, Your Honour. That only---only those cables we handle.

Q

Who inform?

A

Mr Logan will inform us, but he would be informed or instructed by someone else.(my emphasis)



63     In the excerpt above, Sathaiah was being asked how he knew that the cables that he was being asked to move were “scrap”. Sathaiah’s answer was that he was so informed by the Accused but had the presence of mind without being prompted to add that Sathaiah would have been informed or instructed by someone else. I found therefore that Sathaiah’s credit was impeached as to why he had omitted any reference to the Accused being instructed by a Keppel supervisor in his statement.

64     As for DW4 Vignesh, he was the only witness other than the Accused who claimed to have seen a person by the name of Ismail. He claimed that Ismail had first offered work to him but he had declined. However, subsequently, his supervisor, the Accused then asked him to do the work given by Ismail as that would be akin to “overtime work”. He also claimed that Ismail had gotten them the entry pass to enter the premises to carry out the work.[note: 16] At the end of the work, when they exited the premises, he saw that Ismail was waiting for them and the Accused had handed their passes to him.[note: 17]

65     I found the same flaw in Vignesh’s testimony which is that despite agreeing that Ismail featured significantly in his court testimony about the overtime work he did for the Accused and that he was present on the night to issue them their passes and collected them on completion of work, he had completely failed to mention Ismail in the two statements he had given to the police.

66     I found his explanation that he did not mention Ismail because he was not asked about him[note: 18] a convenient but improbable excuse. With very little prompt, Vignesh in court had rattled on about the role played by Ismail in not just being the primary mover of this overtime work carried out by him in relation to the cables but that he was intimately involved in their being able to enter the premises in that he was the person who had obtained the entry passes and also collected them after their work. I found it improbable that he would have omitted mentioning Ismail when he was being questioned about he came to be moving the cables on that evening in Keppel FELS.

67     I found that the evidence given by Sathaiah and Vignesh about the existence of a Keppel FELS supervisor who had instructed the Accused to carry out the work a clear after-thought and had concocted this evidence in belated attempt to exonerate the Accused.

68     Given that they were caught on tape to have assisted the Accused to move the cables, their evidence would also needed to be viewed with circumspection as it would be in their self-interest to exonerate the Accused to further distance themselves from any dishonest intent.

69     The Defence further pointed to the video footage showing the Accused and his co-workers working without apparent fear or anxiety and submitted that this is inconsistent with criminal intent. I do not find this argument persuasive. The absence of visible anxiety is equally consistent with the Accused being a seasoned individual who was confident in his ability to exploit the known security lapses at Keppel FELS. As for his co-workers, the Accused had exonerated them, stating that they were not aware that he was taking the cables without authorisation and hence they would have no reason to be anxious. It did not, in my judgment, raise a reasonable doubt as to his guilt.

CONCLUSION ON THE VERDICT

70     Having considered all the evidence in its totality, I am satisfied that the Prosecution has proved its case beyond a reasonable doubt on all the charges. The "Ismail" defence, while not entirely implausible as a narrative, is insufficiently corroborated to raise a reasonable doubt. The Accused's own recorded statements, the physical evidence, the financial circumstances of the transaction, and the absence of any legitimate authorisation and documentation all point consistently and compellingly towards the guilt of the Accused.

71     For the foregoing reasons, I found the Accused guilty and convicted him on both the charges of criminal trespass under Section 447 of the Penal Code and the charge of theft in dwelling under Section 380 read with section 109 of the Penal Code.

THE SENTENCING

Antecedents

72     The Accused has no previous convictions.

Sentencing Provisions

73     The sentencing provision under section 380 of the Penal Code provides for punishment of imprisonment of up to seven years and a fine. An offence of criminal trespass under section 447 of the Penal Code is punishable with imprisonment which may extend to 3 months, or with fine which may extend to $1,500, or with both.

The Prosecution’s Submission on Sentence

74     The Prosecution sought a total sentence of approximately 22 to 24 months' imprisonment, with the theft charge and the 13 July 2022 trespass charge running consecutively. The Accused was convicted after trial on three charges, with two further charges taken into consideration (TIC).

The Theft Charge

75     The Prosecution proposed a starting point of 10 to 12 months' imprisonment based on the value of the stolen cables at S$28,667.02, drawing on two precedent cases involving copper cable theft — PP v Mia Mohammad Imran and another [2021] SGDC 116 and PP v Md Resat bin Ahmad [2017] SGMC 26— where offenders who pleaded guilty to lesser charges involving significantly lower property values received sentences of 3 to 5 months. The Prosecution argued that a substantial uplift from this starting point is warranted on three grounds.

76     First, the Accused's culpability was high. The Prosecution characterised him as the mastermind of the operation, who recruited co-workers by exploiting existing relationships of trust and seniority. He also relied on multiple layers of deception, including making false declarations on entry and exit forms between June and July 2022 to create a paper trail, and falsely representing to security officers that he was entering on the instructions of one "Ramu," whom he had not contacted in over a year. The operation was well-planned, with the cables being prepared two days in advance and arranged with Karthikeyan separately to collect them.

77     Second, the two TIC charges demonstrate persistent offending. One TIC charge relates to the dishonest misappropriation of cables valued at S$102,010 over a period from August 2021 to July 2022, and the other related to an earlier theft of 300 kilograms of cables between February and March 2022, also involving Karthikeyan.

78     Third, the Accused demonstrated a lack of remorse. While the Prosecution acknowledged that claiming trial is not in itself aggravating, it submitted that the Accused's conduct during trial crossed the line into aggravating territory. Specifically, he made serious and unfounded allegations against Prosecution witnesses, including accusing a Keppel investigation officer of concealing CCTV evidence, and he fabricated an entirely fictional character "Ismail" to construct an exculpatory narrative, which the Prosecution described as spinning “an entire fairy tale in court" that wasted valuable judicial time.

The Trespass Charges

79     The Prosecution sought two to three weeks' imprisonment for each trespass charge. The Prosecution further submitted that the sentence for the theft charge and the sentence for the 13 July 2022 trespass charge should run consecutively, yielding the total sought sentence of 22 to 24 months.

Mitigation

80     The Defence sought a global sentence of 15 months and 2 weeks' imprisonment, backdated to the date of the Accused's arrest on 15 July 2022.

Mitigating Factors

81     The Defence advanced several grounds in mitigation. First, the Accused is untraced, meaning he had no prior criminal record. Second, the Defence submitted that there was no actual loss to Keppel FELS, as the cables were recovered before they left the premises. The Defence also characterised the cables as old and loose, emphasising that Logan did not cut any new cables and only took what was already discarded or redundant.

Sentencing Principles

82     The Defence invoked three sentencing principles to anchor its position. On principle of parsimony, it was submitted that the sentence should be no more severe than is necessary to meet the purposes of sentencing. On proportionality, it was argued that the overall punishment must be proportionate to the gravity of the offending behaviour. On totality, it was submitted that where multiple sentences are to be served, the aggregate must be just and appropriate when viewed against the overall offending conduct.

Right to Claim Trial

83     The Defence made a specific plea that the Accused should not be penalised for exercising his right to claim trial, framing this as a fundamental human right and a cornerstone of a fair and just society. It urged the court not to treat the conduct of his defence as an aggravating factor.

Plea for Compassion

84     The Defence closed with a personal appeal for mercy, asking the court to give the Accused a second chance. The Defence submitted that the Accused was aware of his wrongdoing, wished to devote himself to his family, and promised not to reoffend. The Defence urged the court to reconcile the interests of justice with compassionate and humanitarian considerations.

Backdating

85     Finally, the Defence requested that any sentence imposed be backdated to 15 July 2022, the date of the Accused's arrest, noting that he was held on remand until 8 November 2022 before being released on bail.

Reasons for the Sentences

86     The sentencing principle for property-related offences is one of deterrence. The principle of proportionality had also shaped the Court’s sentencing in that the starting point would be to look at the amount or value of the stolen items. Typically, the sale value of the items stolen would be a good gauge.

The Theft Charge

87     I first deal with the principal charge of abetting theft in dwelling under Section 380 read with Section 109 of the Penal Code, which carries a maximum punishment of seven years' imprisonment.

88     On the question of the value of the stolen property, I accepted the figure of S$28,667.02 as set out in the charge, there being no dispute between the parties on this. However, I also accepted the Defence's submission that the cables were recovered before they left the Keppel FELS compound. The recovery of stolen property is a relevant mitigating consideration, as it attenuates the actual harm caused to the victim. That said, the recovery of the cables did not mean that there was no loss at all. The cables plainly retained some value at the time they were taken, and the mere fact of their recovery did not extinguish the harm inherent in the act of theft itself. As no evidence of the precise residual value of the recovered cables was led before this court, I am unable to make a precise finding on this point. I would therefore hold that there remains some value to be attributed to the stolen items, albeit of an undetermined amount, and that the loss to Keppel FELS was accordingly attenuated to some degree.

89     Taking into account the value of the property involved and the partial mitigation afforded by the recovery of the cables, I set the starting point at 11 months' imprisonment.

90     I turn now to the aggravating factors. The first and most significant is the Accused's role as the prime mover of the entire operation. The evidence at trial established clearly that the Accused was not a mere participant but the architect of the theft. He identified the opportunity, recruited his co-workers by exploiting relationships of trust and seniority, made the necessary logistical arrangements, and directed the operation from start to finish. Karthikeyan, Sathaiah, and Vignesh were all drawn into the scheme at Logan's instigation. The fact that the Accused involved others in the commission of his offences is an aggravating factor in itself, as it multiplied the harm caused and exposed others to criminal liability.

91     The second significant aggravating factor is the two TIC charges, which I am required to take into account in sentencing. These charges reveal that the Accused's offending was not an isolated lapse in judgment but part of a persistent pattern of criminal conduct directed at Keppel FELS over an extended period. In particular, MAC-900079-2023 involved the misappropriation of cables valued at S$102,010 between August 2021 and July 2022, and DAC-900092-2023 involved an earlier theft of 300 kilograms of cables between February and March 2022. Actual loss was caused to Keppel as the items stolen or misappropriated were not recovered. Taken together, these TIC charges paint a picture of sustained and deliberate exploitation of Accused's familiarity with the Keppel FELS premises and security arrangements.

92     I note the Defence's submission that the Accused is untraced and that this should be treated as a mitigating factor. I accept that the absence of prior antecedents is ordinarily a relevant mitigating consideration. However, the weight to be accorded to this factor is substantially diminished in the present case by the TIC charges, which demonstrated that the Accused's offending predated the present charges by a considerable period. His clean record is therefore of limited mitigating value in the circumstances.

93     I also note the Defence's plea for compassion and the Accused's expressed remorse and promise not to reoffend. I have considered these submissions carefully. While I do not doubt that the Accused's family circumstances are difficult and would have been exacerbated by the sentence that would be meted out, personal hardship and expressions of future good conduct are factors that carry limited weight in cases of this nature, particularly where the offending was deliberate, sustained, and involved the exploitation of others.

94     On the question of remorse, I accepted the principle, as stated PP v Ganesan Sivasankar [2017] 5 SLR 681, that the mere act of claiming trial is not an aggravating factor, and I did not hold it against the Accused that he chose to contest the charges. The Defence is correct that the right to claim trial is a fundamental one and must be protected. However, I am of the view that the Accused's conduct during the trial — in particular, his construction of an entirely fictitious exculpatory narrative centred on the character of "Ismail," and his making of serious and unfounded allegations against Prosecution witnesses, in particular an allegation that Shafiq, the Keppel staff in charge of security, had deliberately withheld CCTV evidence that would be beneficial to his case— goes beyond the legitimate exercise of the right to claim trial and reflected a genuine absence of remorse. This is a factor I would take into account in calibrating the appropriate uplift.

95     Taking all the aggravating factors into account — the Accused's role as the prime mover, his recruitment of co-workers, the planning and premeditation involved, the TIC charges, and his conduct at trial — I increase the sentence by 8 months from the starting point of 11 months, arriving at a sentence of 19 months' imprisonment for the theft charge.

The Trespass Charges

96     I turn to the two charges of criminal trespass under Section 447 of the Penal Code. Both charges relate to the Accused's entry into the Keppel FELS compound, which is a restricted area, for the purpose of committing theft.

97     I note that Logan did not enter the compound as a stranger or by force. Rather, he exploited his detailed knowledge of the security arrangements at Keppel FELS — knowledge acquired during his years of legitimate attachment to the facility — to gain entry under false pretences and to navigate the security systems in a manner calculated to avoid detection. This deliberate exploitation of insider knowledge in a restricted industrial facility is an aggravating feature of the trespass charges. However, I have calibrated the length of the sentences knowing that one of the sentences would have to be ordered to run consecutively with the theft sentence and considering that the trespass charge was for the purpose of committing the theft offence in which a substantial term of imprisonment would have been meted out.

98     I accordingly sentenced the Accused to three weeks' imprisonment on each of the two trespass charges.

Global Sentence and Backdating

99     Pursuant to Section 307(1) of the Criminal Procedure Code, at least two sentences must run consecutively. I ordered the sentence for the theft charge and the sentence for the 13 July 2022 trespass charge (MAC-905570-2022) to run consecutively, with the sentence for the 15 July 2022 trespass charge (MAC-905569-2022) to run concurrently with the theft charge.

100    The global sentence is therefore 19 months' and 3 weeks' imprisonment.

101    On the question of backdating, the Defence has submitted that the Accused was arrested on 15 July 2022 and remained on remand until 8 November 2022 before he was released on bail. I accordingly ordered the sentence to be backdated to 15 July 2022 to account for the period Logan has already spent in remand and to exclude the period for which the Accused was on bail.

CONCLUSION

102    The Accused's offending was not a momentary lapse but a calculated and sustained course of criminal conduct. He was the architect of a scheme that exploited his insider knowledge of a restricted industrial facility. He drew his subordinate co-workers and a business acquaintance into his criminal activities and his offences were repeated over an extended period as reflected in the TIC charges. The global sentence of 19 months' and 3 weeks' imprisonment reflected the full weight of these circumstances, tempered by the partial recovery of the stolen cables and the limited mitigating value of his clean record. The length of the sentence would give proper expression to the principles of deterrence and proportionality that govern property-related offences of this nature.

103    I am satisfied that the global sentence is neither crushing nor disproportionate when viewed against the totality of the Accused's conduct. While I am mindful of the hardship that a custodial sentence would inevitably visit upon the Accused and his family, the courts have consistently held that personal circumstances of this nature carry limited weight where the offending is deliberate and sustained.
