Public Prosecutor v Teo Ziqi

Public Prosecutor v Teo Ziqi
[2026] SGMC 82

Case Number:Magistrate Arrest Case No. 905438-2021 and others, Magistrate's Appeal Nos. 9004-2026-01
Decision Date:22 June 2026
Tribunal/Court:Magistrate's Court
Coram: Eddy Tham
Counsel Name(s): Deputy Public Prosecutors Ms Phoebe Tan (Attorney-General's Chambers) for the Public Prosecutor; Defence Counsel Foo Cheow Ming (M/s Foo Cheow Ming Chambers) for the Accused.
Parties: Public Prosecutor — Teo Ziqi

Criminal Law – Claim trial – Attempt to enter Casino by using another person’s identification document – Offence under section 175A of the Casino Control Act (Cap 33A, 2007 Rev Ed) read with section 511 and punishable under section 512(2) of the Penal Code (Cap 224, 2008 Rev Ed – Attempt to enter Casino while being excluded under s 165A(1)(b) read with s 165A(2) of the Casino Control Act (Cap 33A, 2007 Rev Ed) as an undischarged bankrupt – Offence under section 125(2)(a) of the Casino Control Act, read with section 511 of the Penal Code (Cap 224, 2008 Rev Ed), and punishable under section 195(2) of the Casino Control Act and section 512(2) of the Penal Code – Criminal Procedure and Sentencing – Mitigation and Sentencing

[LawNet Editorial Note: An appeal to this decision has been filed in MA 9004/2026/01.]

22 June 2026

District Judge Eddy Tham:

BACKGROUND

1       The Accused Teo Ziqi claimed trial to four proceeded charges. The charges relate to two attempts to enter Marina Bay Sands Casino (“the Casino”).

2       In the first instance, he was charged with an attempt to enter the Casino at level one entrance to the premises, using another person’s identity document, namely a driving license, an offence under section an offence punishable under section 175A of the Casino Control Act (Cap 33A, 2007 Rev Ed) (“the Act”), read with section 511 and punishable under section 512(2) of the Penal Code (Cap 224, 2008 Rev Ed) (“the Penal Code”).

3       As the Accused was also an undischarged bankrupt, he faced a second charge of attempting to enter the Casino while being excluded under section 165A(1)(b) read with s 165A(2) of Act , which is an offence under section 125(2)(a) of the Act, read with section 511 of the Penal Code (Cap 224, 2008 Rev Ed), and punishable under section 195(2) of the Act and Section 512(2) of the Penal Code.

4       After he was rebuffed in this attempt, the Accused went down to another level and made another attempt to enter the Casino. This second attempt then gave rise to two similar charges of attempting to enter using another person’s identification document and whilst being an undischarged bankrupt.

5       At the end of the trial, the Accused was found guilty and convicted of all four proceeded charges.

6       The Accused was thereafter sentenced to one week’s imprisonment in respect of the first section 175A of the Act offence, two weeks’ imprisonment for the first section 125(2)(a) of the Act offence and the second section 175A of the Act offence and three weeks’ imprisonment for the second section 125(2)(a) of the Act offence. For the global sentence, I ordered the one week’s imprisonment to run consecutively with the three weeks’ imprisonment, giving a total of four weeks’ imprisonment.

7       The Accused being dissatisfied with the outcome of the trial, has filed an appeal against both conviction and sentence. He has been released on bail pending the hearing of the appeal.

THE CHARGES

8       The four charges are as follows:

Charge: MAC-905438-2021

.. that you, on 6 March 2021, at or about 4.43 pm, at Marina Bay Sands Casino, 10 Bayfront Avenue, Singapore 018956, did attempt to enter the Marina Bay Sands Casino premises via the Level One entrance, to wit, by using one Teo Lee Wei’s driving licence, and you have thereby committed an offence punishable under Section 175A of the Casino Control Act (Cap 33A, 2007 Rev Ed), read with Section 511 and punishable under Section 512(2) of the Penal Code (Cap 224, 2008 Rev Ed).

Charge: MAC-905439-2021

.. that you, on 6 March 2021, at or about 4.43 p.m., did attempt to enter Marina Bay Sands Casino, 10 Bayfront Avenue, Singapore 018956, via the Level One entrance, while you were excluded under s 165A(1)(b) read with s 165A(2) of the Casino Control Act (Cap 33A, 2007 Rev Ed) from entering the Marina Bay Sands Casino premises as you were an undischarged bankrupt at the material time, and you have thereby committed an offence under Section 125(2)(a) of the Casino Control Act, read with Section 511 of the Penal Code (Cap 224, 2008 Rev Ed), and punishable under Section 195(2) of the Casino Control Act and Section 512(2) of the Penal Code.

Charge: MAC-905440-2021

.. that you, on 6 March 2021, at or about 4.52 pm, at Marina Bay Sands Casino, 10 Bayfront Avenue, Singapore 018956, did attempt to enter the Marina Bay Sands Casino premises via the B2M entrance, to wit, by using one Teo Lee Wei’s driving licence, and you have thereby committed an offence punishable under Section 175A of the Casino Control Act (Cap 33A, 2007 Rev Ed), read with Section 511 and punishable under Section 512(2) of the Penal Code (Cap 224, 2008 Rev Ed).

Charge: MAC-905441-2021.

.. that you, on 6 March 2021, at or about 4.52 p.m., did attempt to enter Marina Bay Sands Casino, 10 Bayfront Avenue, Singapore 018956, via the B2M entrance, while you were excluded under s 165A(1)(b) read with s 165A(2) of the Casino Control Act (Cap 33A, 2007 Rev Ed) from entering the Marina Bay Sands Casino premises as you were an undischarged bankrupt at the material time, and you have thereby committed an offence under Section 125(2)(a) of the Casino Control Act, read with Section 511 of the Penal Code (Cap 224, 2008 Rev Ed), and punishable under Section 195(2) of the Casino Control Act and Section 512(2) of the Penal Code.

9       In respect of the second set of charges, namely MAC 905440/21 and MAC 905441/21, where the Accused was alleged to have attempted to enter the Casino, the original charges stated that the attempt was made at Level “Basement 2” of the Casino. The Defence had asserted that the Accused had never attempted to enter the Casino at Basement 2 as he was never at Basement 2. This was also evident from the CCTV footage shown that the Accused was seen at level B2M. The Defence therefore submitted that the 3rd and 4th charges must fail on this basis.

10     I found that there was no dispute that the Accused was indeed at level B2M making an attempt to enter the Casino as captured by the CCTV of the Casino. He was under no misapprehension that he was being charged in relation to another entrance at level “Basement 2” given the evidence led by the Prosecution: the CCTV evidence was played out in court, and all the Prosecution witnesses as well as the Accused were questioned on the basis of that CCTV recording.

11     I therefore amended the 3rd and 4th charges to reflect that the attempt was made at level “B2M” instead of level “Basement 2” of the Casino. The amended charges were read to the Accused. He maintained his plea of not guilty and both the Prosecution and the Defence declined to recall any witnesses or adduce fresh evidence in the light of the amendment.

UNDISPUTED FACTS

12     In the Statement of Agreed Facts, marked as SOAF, Marina Bay Sands Pte Ltd was issued a casino licence C-MBS-001 dated 18 April 2019 for the period from 26 April 2019 to 25 April 2022, and the designated sites for the purposes of “casino” as defined under section 2 of the Casino Control Act are delineated within the dotted red lines in the attached maps to the SOAF.

13     The Accused is an undischarged bankrupt and he is therefore excluded under s 165A(1)(b) read with s 165A(2) of the Casino Control Act from entering the Marina Bay Sands Casino premises at the material time. The Accused’s bankruptcy status was also confirmed by a screening done by the Investigation Officer.[note: 1]

THE PROSECUTION’S CASE

14     On 6 March 2021, the Accused had obtained the driving licence of PW1 Mr Teo Lee Wei ("Teo"). Teo testified that the Accused was his nephew as well as his former employer. He testified that on his last day of work on 6 March 2021, the Accused had asked for his driving licence in order to purchase insurance, and he had accordingly handed it over. Teo claimed that he did not know what the Accused had done with his driving licence thereafter.

15     After obtaining Teo's driving licence, the Accused proceeded to Marina Bay Sands (“MBS”) Casino on the same day. At about 4.42 p.m., the Accused presented Teo's driving licence to the levy counter at Level One to purchase the levy. CCTV evidence showed the Accused presenting an identification document to the levy counter at Level One to purchase the levy. It is not disputed that the document presented was Teo's driving licence.

16     After purchasing the levy, the Accused handed an identification document to PW5 Mr Dokku Ansari Ajmalkhal ("Ajmal"), a senior security officer, at the Singaporean/PR entry lane at Level One. Ajmal asked the Accused to pull down his mask fully to verify his identity against the photograph on the identification document. It is disputed, however, what the identification document was that the Accused had presented to Ajmal at that point.

17     Ajmal assessed that the Accused's face did not tally with the photograph on the identification document produced to him. He then asked the Accused to produce a second identification document, which the Accused did. Thereafter, Ajmal directed the Accused to the levy counter.

18     PW2 Mr Mohamed Shariffuddin Bin Zainudin ("Shariffuddin"), a senior security officer and acting supervisor at Level One of the Casino at the material time, was alerted to the incident. At the levy counter, he found that the Accused had claimed that the levy had been purchased using his cousin's identification document and that he wished to transfer the levy to himself. The Accused was informed that this could not be done in his cousin's absence, and he then left the levy counter.

19     Shariffuddin alerted his manager, PW3 Mr John Seet Siuhang (“John Seet”), to the incident and was told to keep an eye on the Accused. Pursuant to this direction, Shariffuddin followed the Accused from a distance.

20     At about 4.52 p.m., CCTV footage captured the Accused presenting an identification document to a staff member at the Singaporean/PR Entry Lane at Basement Two M ("B2M"). Shariffuddin had followed the Accused to this level and spotted him presenting an identification document to the staff member at the B2M entrance. Shariffuddin called out to his colleague to stop or "hold" the Accused to prevent his colleague from admitting him and took over the identification document that the Accused had presented.

21     Shariffuddin saw that the identification document was the Accused's cousin's driving licence. He then asked the Accused why he was using the same identification document again. The Accused claimed that he needed to enter the Casino to call his cousin out. When Shariffuddin pointed out that he could have phoned his cousin to come out instead, the Accused admitted that he had been excluded under an exclusion order of the National Council on Problem Gambling ("NCPG").

22     Shariffuddin then alerted John Seet of the Accused's alleged second attempt to enter the Casino premises and was told to bring the Accused to a holding room.

23     Shariffuddin explained the Casino's entry process: a person wishing to enter the Casino must produce his identification document to pay a levy. Once the levy is paid, the information is entered into the system, linking the payment to the identification document of the person. When the person subsequently wishes to enter the Casino, he must scan his identification document at the gantry; the system will then detect whether the levy has been paid and whether the person has been excluded. The officer at the entry point will also ask the person to remove his mask — as members of the public were required to wear masks during the COVID-19 period — to conduct a visual check of the person's face against the identification document tendered. After the identification document is scanned at the gantry and the visual check completed, the person will be able to gain access to the Casino premises.

24     John Seet testified that he was the on-duty manager at the Casino on the said date and that Shariffuddin was the supervisor on duty. He corroborated Shariffuddin's evidence, confirming that he had been alerted to an incident involving a person who had claimed to have mistakenly used another person's identification document to enter the Casino at Level One through the gantry for Singaporeans. He had thereafter instructed Shariffuddin to keep a lookout for this person after the identification document had been returned to him. He was subsequently alerted a second time by Shariffuddin, who informed him that the same person had made a second attempt to enter the Casino at Basement 2.

25     John Seet then directed that the Accused be brought to the holding room and that the police be activated to attend to an impersonation case.

26     When he went to the holding room, he verified that the identification document used was a driving licence belonging to one Teo Wei Lee, whom the Accused claimed to be his cousin. The Accused informed him that he had the driving licence in his possession for the purpose of renewing his company's car insurance policy. John Seet ascertained from the Accused that the reason he had attempted to enter the Casino using another person's identification document was that he was an excluded person and was in urgent need of money. He further ascertained that the Accused's cousin was unaware that the Accused had intended to use his driving licence to enter the Casino. This information was recorded in a Casino Incident Report prepared by Shariffuddin and vetted by John Seet. The report was thereafter uploaded into the Casino's computer system by another officer, Mr Hafizuddin Bin Jaffar. A copy of Teo's driving licence was attached to the report. The report was admitted as Exhibit P3.

27     Finally, PW4 Assistant Superintendent of Police (at the material time) Mr Simon Poh Meng Jie ("ASP Poh") testified that he had recorded a statement from the Accused. The statement was admitted as Exhibit P4 without any objection from the Defence. The Defence confirmed that the statement had been recorded without any threat, inducement, promise, or oppression.

28     The contents of the statement were broadly consistent with what had been set out in the Casino Incident Report. The Accused admitted to the following:

(a)     He was aware that he could not enter any Singapore casino as he was under an exclusion order of the NCPG (paragraph 3 of P4).

(b)     He had only $300 but needed $2,000 to pay his workers. He therefore wanted to try his luck at the Casino to see if he could win enough money to pay them (paragraph 4 of P4).

(c)     He went to the first floor and purchased the levy for $150, as the staff did not check his particulars at that stage. He then tried to enter the Casino but was stopped by the officer, who noticed that his face did not match the driving licence of his cousin, Teo Wei Lee. He was denied entry and told to leave (paragraph 5 of P4).

(d)     After walking around aimlessly for about five minutes in MBS, he tried to enter the Casino again at level B2M. The officer checked his driving licence again and noticed that the photograph did not match. Three security officers then came and detained him in the holding room (paragraph 5 of P4).

(e)     He had his cousin's driving licence in his possession as he had intended to use it to apply for car insurance. He had employed his cousin as a delivery driver. His cousin did not know that he had intended to use his driving licence to illegally enter the Casino (paragraph 6 of P4).

29     ASP Poh also recorded four cautioned statements in respect of each of the four charges. The Defence similarly did not challenge the admissibility of these statements (Exhibits P5–P8). The Accused gave a similar response to each charge:

I admit my mistake and wish to be granted leniency. That is all.

30     The Defence did not challenge the accuracy of any of the Accused's statements or the contents of the Casino Incident Report, nor did they dispute the veracity and accuracy of the CCTV footages.

31     The Prosecution called Ajmal as a rebuttal witness after the Accused testified that he had produced his own NRIC to Ajmal — contrary to what was stated in his statement. Ajmal testified that the Accused had produced a driving licence to him. Upon noticing that it did not match the Accused's appearance, he had asked the Accused for further identification, whereupon the Accused produced his NRIC. Ajmal then brought the Accused to the levy counter to check.

THE DEFENCE'S CASE

32     The Defence case comprised two main prongs.

33     The first was that at the gantry, the Accused had not shown Teo's driving licence to Ajmal but had instead shown his own identity card (“NRIC”).

34     The Accused testified that he was indeed in financial difficulty, as he needed several thousand dollars to pay his employees. He decided to go to the Casino to gamble in order to earn fast cash to meet that need. It was an impulsive decision, made in part because he happened to have his cousin's driving licence with him.

35     At MBS Level One, he had used his cousin's driving licence to pay for the levy at the levy counter. He then proceeded towards the gantry and showed the levy ticket to Ajmal. Ajmal asked him to pull down his mask and enquired where his identity card was. The Accused then handed over his own identity card to Ajmal. Upon checking, Ajmal said it was not correct. At that point, the Accused changed his mind, asked for the levy ticket and his identity card back, and told Ajmal that he no longer wished to enter. He thereafter made two attempts at the levy counter to obtain a refund of the $150 levy he had paid but was told that a refund could not be processed as the levy was not in his name and that the person named in the levy would have to personally apply for the refund.

36     The Defence referred to the copy of the Accused’s NRIC contained in the Casino Incident Report and submitted that there was a stark difference between the Accused's photograph in his NRIC and his physical appearance at the time, which was also captured in the Casino Incident Report. The Defence asserted that this marked disparity was the reason why the Accused had been stopped by Ajmal and refused entry into the Casino.

37     In relation to the second set of charges, the Accused testified that after he was unable to recover the levy paid, he felt aggrieved at being worse off financially than before. He therefore decided to try his luck again at the Casino, this time at level B2M.

38     He claimed that he handed over the levy ticket and his NRIC to the staff member at the gantry. However, before the staff member could complete the check, Shariffuddin intervened and stopped the process. The Accused was thereafter detained by the security staff.

39     The first prong of the Defence was therefore that the Accused had not made use of another person's identification document in attempting to gain entry into the Casino.

40     The second main prong of the Defence was that there was no attempt in law, as the Accused had been denied entry whilst still some distance away from the Casino premises. It was also argued that his attempt had been rendered impossible by the intervention of the Casino officers, such that he had no opportunity to present his identification document for scanning at the entry gantry.

41     It was further argued that the gantry would not have opened for the Accused even if he had scanned his NRIC, as the levy had not been purchased in his name. This was said to constitute a "factual impossibility".

42     The Defence also argued that the Prosecution's case was incomplete by reason of its failure to call the two officers manning the levy counter to prove what document had been presented, as well as the officer manning the gantry at level B2M, and invited the Court to draw an adverse inference accordingly.

43     It was further argued that the charges, which originally stated that the second attempt was made at level "Basement 2" — a different location from B2M — had misled, oppressed, and embarrassed the Accused to such a degree that he had been prejudiced and denied a fair trial.

44     Finally, the Defence objected to the Prosecution calling Ajmal as a rebuttal witness after the close of the Defence case, arguing that the Prosecution had violated a fundamental principle of trial procedure by being afforded a second opportunity to shore up its case.

THE LAW

Elements of the Offences

45     To make out an offence under section 175A of the Casino Control Act, read with section 511 and punishable under section 512(2) of the Penal Code, the Accused must have attempted to enter the Casino premises by pretending to be some other person or by using another person's identification document.

46     To establish an offence under section 125(2)(a) of the Casino Control Act, read with section 511 of the Penal Code and punishable under section 195(2) of the Casino Control Act read with section 512(2) of the Penal Code, an excluded person must have attempted to enter or remain on, or take part in any gaming on, any casino premises. It is undisputed that the Accused was an excluded person, as he was an undischarged bankrupt at the material time. Accordingly, this case turns on whether the Accused had attempted to enter the Marina Bay Sands Casino premises on 6 March 2021 via the Level One and B2M entrances respectively.

The Law on Attempt

47     An attempt is defined as taking a substantial step towards the commission of an offence with the intention of committing that offence, under section 511(1) of the Penal Code. A substantial step is defined as a step that is "strongly corroborative of an intention to commit the offence" under section 511(2) of the Penal Code.

ANALYSIS AND FINDINGS

Identity of the Document Presented at Level One

48     I found that the identification document presented by the Accused at both the Levels One gantry at the material time was clearly Teo's driving licence, based on the totality of the evidence.

49     First, there was the incontrovertible evidence of the CCTV footage. From the CCTV footage at the Level One levy counter, it could be seen that the Accused had taken back a card from the levy counter officer after purchasing the levy. Thereafter, the Accused was seen presenting a card to Ajmal. The Accused had admitted that he had presented Teo's driving licence to the levy counter officer. The card in his hand would therefore have been Teo's driving licence as he walked towards the gantry. The CCTV footage showed that there was no movement of his hand to exchange the card he had taken back for his own NRIC from his wallet before presenting a card to Ajmal. Visually, it was quite clear that the Accused had presented the same card he had taken back at the levy counter to Ajmal.

50     Second, Ajmal gave clear evidence that the identification document shown to him by the Accused was a driving licence, and that upon checking, he found that it did not match the Accused's face.

51     Third, the Accused had not challenged the admissions he made to the Casino officers as recorded in the Casino Incident Report, nor those in his police statement P4, in which he admitted to having attempted to enter the Casino by presenting his cousin's driving licence at the Level One and B2M gantries.

52     He offered no explanation as to why he had not informed the Casino security officers or the police that what he had produced to the officers at the gantry was not Teo's driving licence but his own NRIC.

53     In any event, I found it implausible that he would have presented his own NRIC to the officers. The levy had been purchased using Teo's driving licence. Had he used his own NRIC and passed the facial verification, he would then have had to use the same identification document to scan at the gantry, at which point he would have been stopped because the levy had not been purchased in his name. The gantry would also not have opened, as the system would have detected him as an excluded person. It would therefore have made no sense for him to use his NRIC for the check by the security officer. A better bet would be for him to show Teo’s driving licence and gamble that he might pass the facial verification check.

54     I also found it telling that, on his own evidence, when Ajmal checked the identification document and said it was not correct, the Accused stated that he then took back the levy ticket and NRIC and said, "Oh, this is not mine. I don't want to go in already."[note: 2] If the Accused had genuinely tendered his own NRIC and Ajmal had found that his physical appearance did not match it, the Accused could have protested and confirmed that it was indeed him. He would not have conceded that the NRIC was not his if it had in fact been his own. I found that the Accused had inadvertently corroborated Ajmal's evidence: when Ajmal found that the identification document did not match the Accused's appearance, the Accused admitted that it was not him, and only at that stage produced his own NRIC.

55     The Accused also admitted that the levy ticket did not bear his name, which would have made it evident that the levy ticket would not correspond to his NRIC had he produced it. That would have been a further reason why it would have been illogical for him to hand over his NRIC together with the levy ticket to Ajmal.

Identity of the Document Presented at Level B2M

56     As to what the Accused had presented to the security officer at level B2M, Shariffuddin testified that he had taken over the identification document that the Accused had presented to the staff member at the B2M gantry. He was certain that the identification document was the Accused's cousin's driving licence. The CCTV footage captured Shariffuddin receiving the identification document from the staff member. It was never put to Shariffuddin during cross-examination that he had in fact been presented with the Accused's NRIC.

57     I therefore found that the Accused had presented another person's identification document — namely, Teo's driving licence — at the Level One and B2M gantries at the Singaporean/PR entry lanes respectively when he was stopped by MBS security.

Offence of Attempt is made out

58     I found that the Accused’s presentation of the identification document at that stage when he was stopped at the gantry constituted a substantial step towards the commission of the offence of entering the Casino premises whilst being an undischarged bankrupt at the material time.

59     The Prosecution had adduced evidence that if a patron passes through the gantry at the Singaporean/PR Entry Lanes, there are no further barriers or checks before the gaming area. The Accused himself testified that as long as he passed the gantry, he would have successfully gained entry into the Casino premises, and that there were no further barriers beyond it.

60     The Accused had clearly evinced an intention to commit the offence of entering the Casino whilst being an undischarged bankrupt and/or using another person’s identification document. He had by then purchased the levy using Teo’s driving licence. If he had cleared the facial verification check when he produced the driving licence to the security staff, he would have been allowed to use Teo’s driving licence to scan the gantry. He would have been allowed to go through as the scan would have shown that levy had been paid and assuming there was no exclusion order on Teo[note: 3]. The Accused would then have been able to freely enter the Casino thereafter and the offence would have been completed.

61     The Accused with the steps taken up to being stopped by security had clearly taken a “substantial step” towards the commission of the offence.

62     For completeness, I found the Accused’s belated assertion that he informed Ajmal that he had changed his mind after his identification document had been discovered to be not matching a mere after-thought as he had never stated so in any of his statements given to the security staff of MBS or to the police. In any case, it is irrelevant as by this time, he would have already taken a substantial step towards committing the offence and would have succeeded had he not been thwarted by the security officer.

The Defence's Procedural Arguments

Amendment of the Charges

63     As for the issue of the location of B2M in relation to the second attempt, I found that there was clearly no prejudice, as set out above, and I accordingly amended the charge to reflect the correct location. The Accused knew exactly where he had made his second attempt, and the CCTV footage had also clearly captured the location.

Failure to Call Witnesses

64     As for the failure to call the levy counter officers, I found that there was no gap in the Prosecution's case, as the Accused himself had testified that he had used Teo's driving licence to purchase the levy.

65     As for the security officer manning the gantry at level B2M, the CCTV evidence clearly captured him handing over to Shariffuddin the identification document presented by the Accused. There was accordingly no evidential gap in the Prosecution's case as to what the Accused had presented to that officer.

Calling of the Rebuttal Witness

66     As for the calling of the rebuttal witness, I found that it was proper for the Prosecution to call a rebuttal witness in the circumstances. At the close of the Prosecution's case, there was sufficient evidence, based on Exhibits P3 and P4, that the Accused had admitted to presenting Teo's driving licence to Ajmal. It was only when the Defence was called that the Accused asserted that he had presented his own NRIC to Ajmal. It was therefore a necessary and appropriate step for the Prosecution to disprove this assertion through Ajmal's testimony.

CONCLUSION ON THE VERDICT

67     On the whole, I found the evidence overwhelmingly in favour of the Prosecution's case and was satisfied that the Prosecution had proven beyond a reasonable doubt that the Accused had presented Teo's driving licence at both Level One and level B2M of the Casino in attempting to enter the Casino, and that he was an undischarged bankrupt at the material time. I accordingly found the Accused guilty and convicted him of all four proceeded charges.

THE SENTENCING

Antecedents

68     The Accused has an extensive criminal history. His relevant antecedents are summarised as follows:

(a)      February 2003 — Fined $2,000 for impersonating a public servant.

(b)      October 2003 — Sentenced to 2 months' imprisonment and fined $1,000 for cheating.

(c)      September 2007 — Sentenced to 2 weeks' imprisonment for an offence under s 182 of the Penal Code;

(d)      April 2010 — Sentenced to a global term of 42 months' imprisonment for multiple cheating offences and 6 months' imprisonment for dishonest misappropriation of property under s 403 of the Penal Code. A total of 40 charges were faced on this occasion. Charges taken into consideration for the purposes of sentencing included 11 counts of cheating under section 420 of the Penal Code, four counts under section 417 of the Penal Code, one count of attempted cheating under section 417 read with section 511 of the Penal Code, one count of cheating by impersonation, one count of forgery, and one count under section 403 of the Penal Code.

(e)      May 2014 — Fined $1,000 per count (two counts) under s 116 of the Casino Control Act for entering or remaining on casino premises without paying the entry levy;

Sentenced to 6 years' corrective training for 21 counts of cheating, with seven further cheating charges taken into consideration for the purposes of sentencing.

Sentencing Provisions

69     The first set of offences are under s 175A of the Act, read with s 511 of the Penal Code (Cap 224, 2008 Rev Ed), and punishable under s 512(2) of the Penal Code. Section 512(2) of the Penal Code provides that where no express provision is made by this Code or by such other written law for the punishment of such attempt, be punished with such punishment as is prescribed for that offence.

70     Section 175A of the Act provides that on conviction, the punishment is a fine of up to $10,000 or imprisonment up to 3 years or both.

71     The second set of offences under section 195(2) of the Act are punishable on conviction to a fine not exceeding $10,000 or to imprisonment for a term not exceeding 12 months or to both.

The Prosecution’s Submission on Sentence

72     The Prosecution having had sight of the mitigation plea asking for a fine, maintained their position that custodial sentences ought to be imposed for both the s 125(2)(a) Casino Control Act charges and the s 175A Casino Control Act charges.

73     In respect of the s 125(2)(a) charges, the Prosecution submitted that the sentencing norm for such offences is imprisonment and referred the Court to a screenshot from the sentencing repository which had been uploaded in their sentencing submissions. On this basis, the Prosecution submitted that a fine would not be appropriate.

74     In respect of the s 175A charges, the Prosecution submitted that the custodial threshold was crossed having regard to three factors:

(a)     First, the Accused had a heavy track record of cheating and impersonation offences.

(b)     Second, there was a degree of persistence in his conduct, as he had made attempts to enter the Casino on two separate levels.

(c)     Third, the Prosecution highlighted that s 512(2) of the Penal Code does not draw a distinction between a completed offence and an attempt, and instead explicitly provides that the offender shall be punished with such punishment as is prescribed for the offence. The Prosecution further submitted that there was an element of deception involved in the procurement of Teo's driving licence, as Teo had been unaware of the true purpose for which the Accused had wanted his driving licence, as was evident from his testimony in Court.

75     The Prosecution sought a short custodial sentence for the section 175A charges and a sentence of 2-3 weeks for the section 125(2)(a) charges with one sentence for each set of charges to run consecutively.

Mitigation

76     In mitigation, the Defence submitted that the Accused is a divorced man with a son, for whom he pays $500 per month in expenses, and that he also bears responsibility for his elderly mother's expenses. He was released from prison in July 2020 and had, through the Yellow Ribbon Project, secured employment as a delivery driver, working 11-hour days. He has since been employed full-time as a deliveryman by a bakery company. The Defence submitted that since his release, the Accused had been making genuine efforts to rehabilitate and stay out of trouble.

77     The Defence further submitted that the Accused had attempted to set up a catering business in order to achieve a better work-life balance and spend more time with his son, but that the business suffered setbacks due to the COVID-19 pandemic. It was in this context that he contemplated gambling as a means of generating income to pay the workers who depended on him. The Defence characterised the offences as the product of financial desperation rather than deliberate criminality and submitted that the Accused genuinely regrets his actions.

78     In respect of the facts relating to the Casino Control Act charges, the Defence submitted that on 6 March 2021, the Accused had in his possession the driving licence of his cousin, Teo, as he had intended to procure vehicle insurance for Teo, who was at the material time working as a part-time driver at the same company. The Accused had gone to the Casino intending to gamble in order to raise funds to pay his workers but recalled that he was subject to an exclusion order under the NCPG. He used Teo's driving licence to pay for the Casino levy as it happened to be on him at the time. The Defence submitted that the Accused had not set out to deceive Casino staff, and that he had eventually decided to abort his attempt to enter the Casino, though he was detained by Casino staff before he could leave.

79     In respect of the section 175A Casino Control Act charges, the Defence submitted that a fine ought to be imposed. The Defence relied on the unreported case of PP v Chua Yuxiang (MAC 907366-2015 & Ors), cited in PP v Karthigeyan M Kailasam [2015] SGDC 312 ("Karthigeyan"), where the offender who had used a victim's NRIC to attempt to enter the Casino was sentenced to a fine of $1,500 (in default 6 days' imprisonment) for the section 175A charge read with section 511 of the Penal Code. In Karthigeyan itself, the offender was sentenced to a fine of $3,000 (in default 3 weeks' imprisonment) per charge for four counts of s 175A, having entered the Casino on multiple occasions using his brother's NRIC. The Defence noted that in that case, both parties had agreed on appeal that a mandatory treatment order was appropriate given the offender's diagnosis of pathological gambling and submitted that while this would not apply to the present Accused, a similar fine ought nonetheless to be imposed.

80     The Defence also referred to PP v Teo Choon Chai [2015] 5 SLR 346, where the High Court upheld sentences of 2 weeks' imprisonment per charge for four counts of section 175A, the offender having entered the Casino on 10 occasions using a friend's NRIC which he had taken without permission. The Defence sought to distinguish that case on the basis that the Accused here had not taken Teo's driving licence without permission, that there was no premeditation, and that the Accused had only been charged with attempts rather than completed offences. The Defence emphasised that the Accused had never physically entered the Casino and that no harm had been caused to any party and submitted that a fine of $2,000 was appropriate.

81     In respect of the s 125(2)(a) Casino Control Act charge, the Defence submitted that the two Casino Control Act charges arose from a single transaction, as the Accused's attempt to enter the Casino using Teo's driving licence and his attempt to enter whilst being an undischarged bankrupt were inextricably linked. While acknowledging that the one-transaction rule does not strictly apply to offences punishable by fines, as held in Seng Foo Building Construction Pte Ltd v PP [2017] 3 SLR 201, the Defence submitted that the underlying concern of avoiding disproportionate punishment for the same criminality remained relevant and could be addressed through the totality principle. The Defence again emphasised that the offence was an attempt and that no harm had been caused and submitted that a fine of $1,000 was appropriate for this charge.

Reasons for the Sentences

The sentences

82     Having considered the submissions of the Prosecution, the mitigation plea of the Defence, and the antecedents of the Accused, I imposed the following sentences:

(a)     MAC 905438 of 2021 (first attempt, s 175A Casino Control Act) — 1 week's imprisonment

(b)     MAC 905439 of 2021 (first attempt, s 125(2)(a) Casino Control Act) — 2 weeks' imprisonment

(c)     MAC 905440 of 2021 (second attempt, s 175A Casino Control Act) — 2 weeks' imprisonment

(d)     MAC 905441 of 2021 (second attempt, s 125(2)(a) Casino Control Act) — 3 weeks' imprisonment

83     The sentences in MAC 905438 of 2021 and MAC 905441 of 2021 were ordered to run consecutively, with the remaining sentences running concurrently, resulting in a global sentence of 4 weeks' imprisonment.

Reasons

84     I accepted that, ordinarily, a fine might be an appropriate sentence for failed attempts of this nature. However, I was of the view that the particular circumstances of this case warranted a departure from that position.

85     I gave significant weight to the Accused's extensive antecedents, in particular his numerous prior convictions for cheating. Those antecedents are directly relevant because they share the same foundational elements of dishonesty and deception that underlie the present offences. The Accused sought to portray himself as a changed man, and the Defence urged the Court to view his conduct sympathetically on the basis that he had been motivated by a desire to pay his workers.

86     While I did not doubt that financial pressure played a role in his decision-making, this did not alter the character of the offences themselves. The present offences remained premised on deception and dishonesty. While it is not clear whether the Accused had deceived his cousin, Teo, in order to obtain his driving licence, the fact is that he had attempted to use that driving licence to pass himself off as Teo to Casino staff, an entirely different purpose from what he had told Teo. In committing the offence, the Accused had also attempted to deceive the Casino staff into thinking he was the same person shown in the driving licence. The motivation behind the offending did not diminish the dishonest means by which he sought to achieve his ends.

87     In these circumstances, the principle of specific deterrence came to the fore. Given the Accused's persistent pattern of dishonesty-related offending across multiple convictions spanning many years, a fine would not adequately serve the sentencing objective of deterring him from reoffending in a similar vein. It is further noted that amongst his many antecedents, there were two in 2014 closely related Casino Control Act offences for which he was fined for entering the Casino without paying the levy. He has escalated in the seriousness of his offending by attempting to enter whilst being an excluded person and also for using someone else’s identification document.

88     At the same time, I was mindful of the principle of proportionality. The present offences, being attempts that did not result in the Accused successfully entering the Casino, are of lesser seriousness than the cheating offences that feature prominently in his antecedent record. A short custodial sentence measured in weeks was therefore sufficient to meet the ends of justice, without imposing a sentence disproportionate to the gravity of the offences before the Court.

89     As regards the consecutive sentences, I ordered the sentences in MAC 905438 of 2021 and MAC 905441 of 2021 to run consecutively on account of the fact that the two sets of attempts, whilst proximate in time, constituted distinct criminal acts carried out at different entry points of the Casino. The remaining sentences were ordered to run concurrently. The global sentence of 4 weeks' imprisonment adequately reflects the overall criminality of the Accused's conduct.

CONCLUSION

90     The Accused, despite having been released from prison in July 2020 and having had the benefit of rehabilitation support through the Yellow Ribbon Project, reoffended within a relatively short period by committing offences that bore the same hallmarks of deception and dishonesty as his prior convictions. While I was sympathetic to the financial pressures he faced and accepted that his motivation was in part to meet his obligations to his workers, these considerations could not displace the need for specific deterrence given his substantial antecedent record.

91     A global sentence of 4 weeks' imprisonment was therefore imposed, reflecting both the need to deter the Accused from further dishonesty-related offending and the principle of proportionality, having regard to the fact that the present offences were attempts that fell short in seriousness of his prior convictions.

[note: 1]Notes of Evidence, 3 April 2025, 112/1-32.

[note: 2]Notes of Evidence, 4 April 2025, 12/13-24.

[note: 3]This is a presumption as no evidence had actually been led on whether there was any exclusion order on Teo.

Public Prosecutor v Thiriselvam S/O Gopal

Public Prosecutor v Thiriselvam S/O Gopal
[2026] SGMC 81

Case Number:Notice to Surety No. 901375 of 2025, Magistrate's Appeal No. 9124 of 2026-01
Decision Date:22 June 2026
Tribunal/Court:Magistrate's Court
Coram: Christopher Goh Eng Chiang
Counsel Name(s): Natalie Chew (Attorney-General's Chambers) for the Prosecution; Mahadevan Lukshmayeh (Lukshmayeh Law Corporation) for the Surety (7 Jan 2026 and 11 Feb 2026); Accused in Person (6 May 2026)
Parties: Public Prosecutor — Thiriselvam S/O Gopal

Criminal Procedure and Sentencing – Bail – Show Cause Hearing – Forfeiture

[LawNet Editorial Note: An appeal to this decision has been filed in MA 9124/2026/01.]

22 June 2026

District Judge Christopher Goh Eng Chiang:

Introduction

1       The surety, Thiriselvam S/O Gopal, (“the Surety’), stood bail in the sum of $10,000 for one Ahmmed Md Toufiq, a Bangladeshi National (“the Accused”). The Accused failed to attend at the Pre-Trial Conference Centre (“PTCC”) on 12 November 2025. A Warrant of Arrest (“WTA”) was issued for his arrest, and the Surety was required to show cause on 7 January 2026 as to why the bail sum should not be forfeited to the State.

2       On 6 May 2026, I forfeited a sum of $7,500 out of the total bail amount of $10,000. The Surety, being dissatisfied with the order of forfeiture, has now appealed against it.

Facts of the case

Background to the case

3       I first set out a brief chronology of events:

Date

Event

25 Mar 2025

Accused was charged in court an offence under the Misuse of Drugs Act 1973 (“MDA”). He was offered bail of $10,000 with one surety or $5,000 with two sureties.

3 Apr 2025

The Surety executed the bail bond and the Accused is released on bail.

15 Oct 2025

Counsel for the Accused, Mr Skandarajah S/O Selvarajahah (“Mr Rajah”) discharged himself before the PTC judge.

Matter was adjourned 4 weeks for the Accused to engage a new counsel.

12 Nov 2025

The Accused was absent at the adjourned PTC. A Warrant was issued for the Accused’s arrest (“WTA”).

A Notice was ordered against the Surety to show cause why the bail amount should not be forfeited to the State.

7 Jan 2026

The 1st Show Cause (“SC”) mention.

The Surety was present and was represented by Mr Mahadevan Lukshmayeh (“Mr Lukshmayeh”).

The SC mention was adjourned to 11 Feb 2026 to allow the Accused to surrender himself.

The Accused surrendered himself at the Police Cantonment Complex later the same day.

11 Feb 2026

The 2nd SC mention.

6 May 2026

The 3rd SC mention. Mr Lukshmayeh discharged himself.

Court finds that cause is not shown and forfeits $7,500 which is to be paid by 16 June 2026.

20 May 2026

Mr Lukshmayeh, who has been re-engaged by the Surety, filed a Notice of Appeal against the Order of Forfieture.



Execution of the bail bond and the Surety’s acknowledgement of his duties

4       On 25 March 2025, the Accused was charged in court for an offence under the MDA. He was in custody for nine days before the Surety executed the bail bond on 3 April 2025. In addition to the bail bond, the Surety also signed the “Acknowledgement of Duties as Surety” form, in which he acknowledged he understood and accepted the following obligations as well being willing and able to stand as surety for the Accused in respect of the charges against him. These were inter alia: 

(a)     to ensure the Accused’s punctual attendance at all court dates and times;

(b)     to find out in advance all dates and times when the Accused’s attendance in court was required;

(c)     to ensure that the Accused complied with all bail conditions, including the condition that the Accused would not leave Singapore except with the court’s prior permission;

(d)     to remain in constant contact with the Accused and be aware of his movements so as to ensure his compliance;

(e)     that if the Accused took ill on a court date, to ensure that the Accused consult a doctor immediately and obtain a medical certificate stating that the Accused was not fit to attend court, and thereafter to attend court on the Accused’s behalf to inform the court of the Accused’s condition and tender the medical certificate to the judge; and

(f)     to keep in daily communication with the Accused and to lodge a police report within 24 hours of losing contact with him.

5       The Surety further acknowledged that his duties would continue until the conclusion of the proceedings or until he was formally discharged as surety and declared that he would faithfully discharge his duties failing which he would forfeit the bail sum of $10,000 to the State.

The Show Cause proceedings

The 1st SC mention

6       The Surety attended the 1st SC mention on 7 January 2026. I adjourned the matter and directed that the Accused was to surrender himself at the Police Cantonment Complex (“PCC”).

7       The Accused did so later the same day, after the mention (see: NP299 arrest report A/20260107/2060).

The 2nd SC mention

8       At the 2nd SC mention on 11 February 2026, the following account emerged:[note: 1]

(a)     After the PTC on 15 October 2025 was adjourned, the Accused had asked a “friend”, one “Mr Joseph Fernandez” (“Mr Joseph”) to assist him in engaging a lawyer.

(b)     On 11 November 2025, the day before the PTC, the Accused sent a WhatsApp (“WA”) message to Mr Joseph to ascertain whether a lawyer had been engaged. Mr Joseph replied in the affirmative and asked the Accused to forward payment of $300, which the Accused did.

(c)     Also on 11 November 2025, the Surety claimed to have spoken with the Accused who told him that a lawyer had informed him that a lawyer had been engaged for the upcoming PTC.

(d)     Despite his representation to the Accused, Mr Joseph did not appear to take any step to engage a lawyer until the morning of 12 November 2025. He contacted Mr Foo Ho Choo (“Mr Foo”), an advocate and solicitor via WA.

(e)     Mr Joseph forwarded Mr Foo a sum of $200 and the Accused’s mention slip showing that the Accused’s court date was later that afternoon at 1600 hours on 12 November 2025.

(f)     The WA messages tendered did not show that Mr Foo had agreed to represent the Accused. Neither was the Surety able to show that Mr Foo had actually been engaged to represent the Accused. There was no Warrant to Act. In fact, the WA messages did not even show that the Surety had even spoken to Mr Foo.

(g)     On 12 November 2025, after 1600 hours, both the Accused and Mr Foo were not present at the PTC Chambers. Thereafter, between 1649 and 1635 hours, the IO made three calls to contact the Accused. However, there was no response. The Accused’s ICMS casefile showed that the WTA was issued against the Accused at 1649 hours.[note: 2]

The Mitigation Plea

9       Between the 2nd and 3rd SC mentions, the Surety tendered a mitigation plea (“MP”). The key contents are summarised below:

(a)     The Surety was aware that the Accused had been given until 12 November 2025 to engage a lawyer. The Accused had informed the Surety that this was being arranged by a friend.

(b)     On 11 November 2025, the Surety was informed by the Accused that he had engaged a lawyer to attend the PTC the following day, hence his (ie. the Accused) attendance was not required. The Surety claimed that he insisted on more information from the Accused. However, it was Mr Joseph who took the phone and spoke to him. Mr Joseph then informed the Surety that one Mr Foo had been engaged and that the Surety would be updated on the outcome of the PTC.

(c)     On the night of 12 November 2025, the Accused contacted the Surety and informed him that due to a “misunderstanding”, the lawyer had not attended the PTC.

(d)     On 14 November 2025, the Surety attended at State Courts to enquire about the case. He was told that a WTA had been issued against the Accused and that a Notice to Surety to Show Cause had been issued against him. Thereafter, the Surety had gone down to the Warrant Enforcement Unit (“WEU”) to check on the status of the WTA. However, he was unable to obtain any meaningful information from the WEU.

(e)     The Surety claimed to have only received the Show Cause Notice in late December 2025. He claimed that until the morning of 7 January 2026, no one had called him concerning this matter and the Accused had also informed him that no one had contacted him.

(f)     The Surety informed the court that he is a divorcee who is also looking after his 92-year-old mother who suffers from dementia. Due to her condition, he is now facing financial difficulties and has sought financial assistance.

(g)     He urged the court to show him leniency and give him a “warning” in lieu of any forfeiture.

The 3rd SC mention

10     I forfeited $7,500 out of the total bail bond of $10,000 and remitted the remainder.

The principles governing forfeiture

11     The applicable principles governing bail forfeiture are well established and were comprehensively set out by the High Court in Cher Ting Ting v Public Prosecutor [2016] SGHC 13 (“Cher Ting Ting”) where the a district court’s decision to forfeit the entire bail sum of $60,000 was affirmed on appeal.

12     In Cher Ting Ting at [24], the High Court approached the question of forfeiture in two stages:

“ …. the court will consider the question of forfeiture in two stages …. First, the court will consider whether the surety has shown sufficient cause for the non-forfeiture of the bond amount. Second, if the court finds that the surety has failed to show sufficient cause, the court will determine, in the exercise of its discretion, the extent to which the bond is to be forfeited”

The first stage: whether sufficient cause has been shown

13     At the first stage, the court is to determine whether sufficient cause has been shown.  The key consideration in determining the existence of sufficient cause is whether the surety is able to show that he exercised reasonable due diligence in the discharge of his duties as surety. This was a fact-specific inquiry, and the surety bears the burden of satisfying the court that sufficient cause exists such that forfeiture should not take place (per Chan J in Cher Ting Ting at [28], [34] and [35]).

14     The onus is therefore on the Surety to show that he had exercised due diligence. During the 2nd SC mention and subsequently in the MP, the Surety had tried to explain what happened.

15     Taking the Surety’s explanation at its highest, all he appeared to have done before the PTC on 12 November 2025 was to accept, without any verification, the Accused’s assertion that a lawyer had been engaged. The Surety made no independent checks, with the State Courts, with Mr Foo directly, or otherwise, to conform that a lawyer had indeed been engaged.

16     Now, the Surety in his MP asserted that he had spoken to Mr Joseph personally on 11 November 2025 and had been shown a receipt that monies had been paid to the engaged lawyer, Mr Foo. This version of events is, in my view, improbable and is inconsistent with the documentary evidence. The WA messages shown to the court during the 2nd SC mention showed that the the Accused and Mr Joseph had only communicated via WhatsApp. They did not meet in person. Therefore, Mr Joseph could not have taken the handphone from the Accused to speak to the Surety as asserted by the Surety. Further, the WhatsApp messages clearly showed that Mr Joseph only made some form of payment to Mr Foo on 12 November 2025, not on 11 November 2025 as asserted by the Surety in the MP. I therefore reject the Surety’s explanation in this regard.

17     Beyond this, the Surety also failed to check with the State Courts as to status of the Accused’s criminal case on 12 November 2026. The Surety acknowledged that he had received telephone calls from the IO on 12 November 2025 at 1632 and at 1634 hours but was unable return the calls to work commitments.[note: 3] Further, although he said that he had contacted the Accused on 12 November 2025 and that he was in regular communication with him, it does not appear that the Surety had kept in daily communication with the Accused as he was required to do so.[note: 4]

18     For these reasons, I found that the Surety had failed to exercise reasonable due diligence in the discharge of his duties as surety.

The second stage: the extent to which the bond is to be forfeited

19     Having found that the Surety had failed to show sufficient cause, I turned to determine the extent to which the bond is to be forfeited.

20     In Cher Ting Ting at [41], the High Court held that

“ …. the starting point where the surety has failed to show sufficient cause is therefore forfeiture of the entire amount of the bond. The court will depart from this prima facie position if, and only if, the surety satisfies the court that there are exceptional circumstances warranting such a departure…”

21     I considered the following factors:

(a)      Surety’s degree of culpability. This was considered by the High Court in Cher Ting Ting at [43] – [45]. As mentioned above, the Surety had relied solely on the Accused’s assertion that he had engaged a lawyer and that the Accused’s attendance at the PTC was not required. He made no effort to check whether this was indeed the case. Further, I noted that attempts by the Investigation Officer to contact the Surety in the afternoon of 12 November was unsuccessful. The only reason proffered by the Surety was that he was busy with work commitments. This was not a sufficient excuse.

(b)      Financial considerations and effect of dependents. In Cher Ting Ting at [56] the High Court has held that while financial considerations and means of the surety are relevant considerations,

“…..  a surety’s lack of means, taken alone, will generally be an inadequate reason for any reduction in forfeiture. Such lack of means must amount to an exceptional circumstance warranting departure from the prima facie position of full forfeiture. This is justified on the basis that (i) by executing his bond, the surety is taken to have represented that he is willing and able to suffer the potential consequences of forfeiture; and (ii) the system of bail will not perform its function effectively if the threat of forfeiture is illusory and easily eluded.”

In the present case, the Surety highlighted his financial problems due to his mother’s medical condition. However, the Surety had not provided any documentary evidence to substantiate his claim. In the absence of such evidence, I was unable to find that his financial situation amounted to an exceptional circumstance that would warrant a departure from the prima facie position of full forfeiture.

(c)      Efforts made by the Surety after the Accused’s non-attendance. In his MP, the Surety had also highlighted that after knowing that a WTA had been issued against the Accused, he had made efforts by seeking clarifications from the State Courts and WEU. He highlighted that he had only received the Show Cause Notice in late December 2025 and that he did not hear from the IO until 7 January 2026, the date of the 1st SC mention. After the 1st SC mention. The Accused surrendered to the authorities later the same day.

I accepted that facilitating the Accused’s surrender was a factor militating in favour of reduced forfeiture (per Cher Ting Ting at [61]). However, in determining the reduced forfeiture amount, this fact must be considered against the Surety’s entire conduct after the Accused’s non-attendance.

In my view, the Surety should have ensured that the Accused surrendered to the authorities as soon as possible. Even if I accepted the fact that he had only received the Show Cause Notice in late December 2025 (which I did not, as the Show Cause Notice is dated 12 November 2025, a Wednesday, and should have been received by the Surety at the latest, perhaps, by the end of the following week), the Surety could have ensured that the Accused surrendered much earlier. He was aware that the Accused had failed to attend court and that a WTA had been issued against the Accused. He was also he knew who the IO was and that the IO had been trying to contact him, yet there was no evidence that he tried to liaise with the IO between 12 November 2025 and 7 January 2026.

On balance, I agreed with the assessment of the learned Deputy Public Prosecutor that “…. it appears that he has expended little effort to ensure that the Accused actually did surrender to the police”.[note: 5]

(d)      Relationship between the Surety and Accused. The relationship between the Surety and the Accused was unclear. On the evidence, the Accused, a foreigner, appeared to be the Surety’s colleague.[note: 6] As the Accused is a foreigner, I would therefore have expected the Surety to pay closer attention to when the Accused was to attend court, to make the necessary checks and clarifications if necessary. In the present case, it did not appear that the Surety had taken his responsibilities more seriously like he should have done.

Submission by the Prosecution

22     The Prosecution submitted that the court should forfeit the bail monies but left the quantum to the court’s discretion.

My decision

23     In summary, I found the following:

(a)     The Surety had not shown sufficient cause against the forfeiture of the bond.

(b)     In determining the amount of the bond should be forfeited, I did not find his financial circumstances exceptional. However, I did consider that the Surety had made some checks regarding the status of the WTA and that the Accused had surrendered after the 1st SC mention.

24     I therefore adjudged that the appropriate amount to forfeit was $7,500 out of the total amount of $10,000, which was in my view, already a generous outcome for the Surety.

Conclusion

25     The Surety being dissatisfied with the forfeiture order, has filed an appeal against it. I note that Mr Lukskshumayeh who had discharged himself on 6 May 2026 has filed the appeal on behalf of the Surety.

26     As this was a non-monetary bail bond, the Surety was to have made the payment of $7,500 by 16 June 2026. I have stayed the payment of this amount pending the outcome of the Appeal.

[note: 1]This information is based on WhatsApp messages tendered and the Notes of Evidence (“NE”) for 11 February 2026.

[note: 2]See WTA Review report dated 7 January 2026 prepared by the IO and the ICMS Notes of Evidence for 12 November 2025. Both can be found in the ICMS casefile of the Accused. Also see NE, 11 February 2026, from 16/27 to 17/01.

[note: 3]NE, 11 February 2026, at 23/24 – 26.

[note: 4]See Surety’s “Acknowledgement of Duties as Surety” form set out at [4] of these Grounds.

[note: 5]NE, 11 February 2026, at 26/14 – 18.

[note: 6]NE, 6 May 2026, at 10/7.
