html:
Public Prosecutor v Ajiramah binte Ahmad Hassan

Public Prosecutor v Ajiramah binte Ahmad Hassan
[2026] SGMC 80

Case Number:Magistrate Court Notice 900907 of 2025
Decision Date:22 June 2026
Tribunal/Court:Magistrate's Court
Coram: Kevin Ho Hin Tat
Counsel Name(s): Johan Tay (Attorney-General's Chambers) for the Public Prosecutor; Sean Marican (M M Marican & Co) for the Accused.
Parties: Public Prosecutor — Ajiramah binte Ahmad Hassan

Criminal Law – Offences – Community Disputes Resolution Act 2015 – Breach of special direction – Disobedience of order of court

Criminal Procedure and Sentencing – Sentencing

22 June 2026

District Judge Kevin Ho Hin Tat:

Introduction

1       The Community Disputes Resolution Tribunal (“CDRT”) is a specialist tribunal that was established in October 2015 to provide an accessible and cost-effective avenue to litigants to resolve neighbour disputes. In order to ensure compliance with CDRT orders, there is a two-strike approach to enforcement under the Community Disputes Resolution Act 2015 (“CDRA”) regime. Where there is a breach of a CDRT order, the CDRT is empowered to issue a special direction to direct that the contravening party comply with the disobeyed order. This is the first strike. Breach of a special direction constitutes a criminal offence, the second strike.

2       This case concerns such an offence for the breach of a special direction issued by the CDRT. The accused pleaded guilty to a single charge under s 7(1)(a) of the CDRA (“Breach of Special Direction Offence”). I sentenced the accused to a fine of $2,500. As there does not appear to be any reported case on the Breach of Special Direction Offence, I issue these grounds of decision to set out in detail my reasons.

Facts

3       The accused is a 72-year-old lady who resided with her husband, Mr Arshard bin Mohammad (“Mr Arshard”) in the same Housing & Development flat, which I will simply refer to as the “Accused’s Unit”.[note: 1]

4       The complainant, a 55-year-old lady, was the accused’s neighbour who resided next to the Accused’s Unit (“Complainant’s Unit”).[note: 2]

5       The complainant and her family had a longstanding history of conflict with the accused and Mr Arshard over noise from the Complainant’s Unit spanning over “many years”.[note: 3]

6       In or around 2024, the accused installed a closed-circuit television (“CCTV”) camera above the doorway of the Accused’s Unit. She also placed two tables – a smaller table and a larger table (“Table 1”, “Table 2”, and the “Tables” collectively) – along the common corridor next to the Accused’s Unit. It is useful to reproduce below a photograph depicting the Accused’s Unit (left of the photograph) as well as the Tables:

7       Sometime in 2024, the complainant filed a claim against the accused and Mr Arshard. On 17 January 2025, pursuant to s 5(1) of the CDRA, the learned Tribunal Judge issued an Order of Tribunal, CDT/ORC/2006/2025 (“Order”), which contained, among others, the following orders for specific performance (“Orders for Specific Performance”):

(a)     move or adjust the Tables so that the Tables are located directly outside the main door of the Unit, ie, at the space immediately to the right of the Unit’s main door; and

(b)     either remove or adjust the CCTV camera such that it does not face the doorway of the Complainant’s Unit.

8       The accused and Mr Arshard failed to comply with the Orders for Specific Performance. This led to the complainant filing an application for a special direction on breach of court order in CDT/SD/703/2025.

9       On 14 March 2025, pursuant to s 6(2) of the CDRA, the Tribunal Judge issued a special direction in CDT/ORC/2017/2025 (“Special Direction”), directing the accused and Mr Arshard to comply with the Order.

10     On 24 June 2025, the complainant filed a police report regarding their non-compliance with the Special Direction. A police inspection on the same day confirmed that the accused and Mr Arshard had failed to comply with the Orders for Specific Performance. This was a breach of the Special Direction, which was the subject of the offence under s 7(1)(a) of the CDRA that the accused pleaded guilty to.

11     The accused was charged in Court on 27 October 2025.

12     Thereafter, between January and May 2026, the accused took the following remedial steps to comply with the Special Direction:

(a)     sometime around 23 January 2026, Table 2 was removed from the common corridor outside the Accused’s Unit;

(b)     sometime before 12 February 2026, the accused adjusted the CCTV camera such that it no longer faced the doorway of the Complainant’s Unit; and

(c)     sometime around 4 May 2026, Table 1 was removed from the common corridor outside the Unit.

13     The Prosecution did not take any action against Mr Arshard.

Submissions on sentence

14     The Prosecution sought a fine of $1,000. The Prosecution highlighted that there were no reported cases for the Breach of Special Direction Offence under s 7(1)(a) of the CDRA. A check on the State Courts’ Sentencing Information & Research Repository (“SIR”) revealed that a “median” fine of about $1,000 was imposed for such offences in two cases (where the offenders had pleaded guilty).[note: 4]

15     The Defence submitted for a fine of $400. The Defence argued that the following mitigating factors were present: (a) the accused had no antecedents;[note: 5] (b) the accused was remorseful and had undertaken “significant steps” to comply with the Special Direction;[note: 6] and (c) the accused had pleaded guilty. The Defence highlighted the accused was illiterate, senior and her native language was in Malay, which led to “difficulties” understanding the Tribunal Judge’s orders.[note: 7] The Defence also pointed out that the accused and Mr Arshard (who was suffering from “chronic illness”) were unemployed. A high fine would therefore “crush her finances”.[note: 8]

The Decision

The CDRA regime and the two-strike approach

16     The CDRA, which came into effect on 1 October 2015, introduced a new statutory tort of interference with a neighbour’s enjoyment or use of the place of residence that the neighbour resides in. This is provided for under s 4 of the CDRA, which sets out non-exhaustive instances of acts or omissions which may cause interference with a neighbour’s place of residence, including the causing of excessive noise or smell, obstructing the neighbour’s place of residence, and surveillance of the neighbour or the neighbour’s place of residence.

17     The CDRA also established the CDRT as a specialist tribunal to facilitate the resolution of such disputes. Under s 5(1) of the CDRA, the CDRT may make various orders if it is satisfied that a claim under s 4 is made out and it is just and equitable to do so. The orders that the CDRT may make include an order for damages, an injunction, an order for specific performance, and even an order that the respondent provides an apology to the neighbour.

18     In setting up the CDRT, Parliament recognised that residents should first seek to resolve the matter amicably with their neighbour, failing which, mediation should be attempted. The CDRT was intended to be an “avenue of last resort to deal with intractable” cases (see Singapore Parliamentary Debates, Official Report (13 March 2015) vol 93, Mr Lawrence Wong, Minister for Culture, Community and Youth) (“2015 Parliamentary Debates”).

19     The CDRT was designed to allow parties to represent themselves without the need for lawyers. Section 29(3) of the CDRA prohibits legal representation unless the following two requirements are met: (a) all parties to the proceedings agree to that party being legally represented; and (b) the Registrar or tribunal (as the case may be) grants leave. The CDRT is also governed by simplified and streamlined procedures in order to allow lay persons to navigate proceedings with ease. While proceedings are “less formal” (as acknowledged in Parliament – see the 2015 Parliamentary Debates), it should be stressed that this is not a license to disobey orders or directions made by the CDRT.

20     In this regard, the CDRA regime provides for a two-strike approach to enforcement:

(a)     Where there is a failure to comply with a community dispute order for the first time, the party in whose favour the disobeyed order was made may apply to the CDRT under s 6(1) of the CDRA for a direction that the contravening party must comply with the disobeyed order, ie, a special direction. The CDRT, if satisfied that the contravening party has, without reasonable excuse, failed to comply with the disobeyed order, may issue the special direction to direct that the contravening party comply with the disobeyed order within a specified time. This is the first strike. The CDRT may also order any person to enter into a bond to ensure that the contravening party complies with the special direction (see s 6(3) of the CDRA).

(b)     In the event that the contravening party, without reasonable excuse, fails to comply with the special direction, this constitutes an offence under s 7(1)(a) of the CDRA. This is the second strike, as the offender has failed to comply with the community dispute order twice in a row. Additionally, in the case of a continuing offence, the offender shall be liable to be punished under s 7(1)(b) of the CDRA with a further fine for every day or part of the day during which the offence continues after conviction (subject to a maximum of $10,000 in total).

21     The rationale for such an approach, as enunciated in Parliament, is as follows (see the 2015 Parliamentary Debates):

We agree that a strong deterrent is necessary to ensure that the community dispute orders have bite. At the same time, we also recognise that bringing the full weight of the law upon wrongdoers for one-off breaches may be too harsh. So, we really worked hard at trying to get the balance right. What the Bill provides for is a two-strike approach to enforcement. The consequences are calibrated and will become more severe with each additional breach.

[emphasis added]

22     The community dispute order under s 5(1) of the CDRA is a civil order. Generally speaking, when a civil order is breached, the court has quasi-criminal powers to punish for civil contempt. It is therefore significant that Parliament saw it necessary to go further and criminalise the breach of a special direction. The articulated rationale was that the “real possibility of criminal sanctions” would provide for sufficient deterrence to ensure compliance with the community dispute orders (see the 2015 Parliamentary Debates).

23     It is also pertinent that s 7(3) of the CDRA states that where a person is convicted of the Breach of Special Direction Offence, the failure to comply with the special direction as well as the failure to comply with the order of court under s 5 (which is subject of the special direction) is not punishable as a contempt of court. Conversely, where a person has been punished for any non-compliance as a contempt of court, that person shall not be convicted of an offence under the Breach of Special Direction Offence (see s 7(4) of the CDRA). This underscores the gravity of the Breach of Special Direction Offence, as it serves a similar, if not the same, function as contempt of court.

24     Against the backdrop above, I was of the view that the overriding sentencing consideration in this case was deterrence. At its heart, the Breach of Special Direction Offence is rooted in a person’s repeated disobedience of the CDRT’s order and direction. Such an offence, if left unaddressed, could undermine the efficacy of the CDRA regime, and potentially even the broader administration of justice. A message of deterrence was needed to be sent out to would-be offenders regarding the importance of complying with directions and orders made by the CDRT. It would be a costly mistake for anyone to assume that CDRT orders can be disregarded, or even disrespected, with impunity simply because of the CDRT’s status as a tribunal. It should be reminded that the CDRT is part of the State Courts as “full-fledged Courts presided over by District Judges” (see the 2015 Parliamentary Debates). To echo the observations of the then Minister for Law, Mr K Shanmugam in January 2020, CDRT orders “like any other court orders” are to be “taken seriously” (see Singapore Parliamentary Debates, Official Report (6 January 2020) vol 94, Mr K Shanmugam, Minister for Law).

Decision on sentence

25     The maximum sentence for the Breach of Special Direction Offence, ie the offence under s 7(1)(a) of the CDRA, is a fine of up to $5,000, or three months’ imprisonment, or both.

26     It is established law that a fine may be sufficient as a deterrent sentence if it is “high enough to have a deterrent effect” (Public Prosecutor v Cheong Hock Lai and other appeals [2004] 3 SLR(R) 203 at [43] affirmed more recently in Public Prosecutor v Lim Yee Hua and another appeal [2018] 3 SLR 1106 at [47]).

27     On the facts, I was of the view that an appropriately calibrated fine was a sufficiently deterrent sentence for two main factors. First, the fact that the accused took steps to comply with the Special Direction was a significant factor that militated against a custodial sentence. That said, the accused only complied with the special direction after she was charged in court (see [11] – [12] above). Further, it took a relatively long period of time for the accused to comply fully with the Orders for Specific Performance. Even after being charged in Court in October 2025 for the Breach of Special Direction Offence, the accused only took steps to comply between January and May 2026. The mitigating weight to be placed on the accused’s remedial measures was therefore moderated downwards.

28     The second factor that militated against a custodial sentence was the fact there was no evidence to suggest that the complainant was substantially prejudiced or suffered any material harm on account of the accused’s breach of the Special Direction.

29     I now turn to the Defence’s arguments.

30     The accused claimed that she was illiterate and that her native language was Malay resulting in “difficulties” understanding the “orders of the Tribunal”.[note: 9] This did not assist the accused. It is instructive to refer to the principles for contempt of court, where the contemnor’s motives and reasons for disobedience are relevant for mitigation (PT Sandipala Arthaputra v STMicroelectronics Asia Pacific Pte Ltd and others [2018] 4 SLR 828 at [48]). However, there was no suggestion by the Defence that there was any attempt whatsoever by the accused to comply with the Order or the Special Direction, or to make any appropriate inquiries on how to do so. Further, even if the accused did have difficulty understanding the simple Orders for Specific Performance – which were essential to move or adjust the Tables and to remove or adjust the CCTV camera – it would have been clear beyond peradventure by the time the Special Direction was issued against her for non-compliance with the Order that she needed to comply, and understand how to comply with the Order if she did not fully appreciated how to do so. Importantly, the fact remains that the accused had persisted in her non-compliance with the Special Direction even after she was charged in October 2025 (with Defence Counsel on record since November 2025). She only commenced piecemeal remedial measures from January 2026 onwards, taking up to May 2026 in order to comply with the simple orders.

31     I rejected the Defence’s argument that was premised on the accused’s financial circumstances. There was no objective evidence before me to substantiate the assertions about the accused’s financial circumstances. In any event, it is well established that financial difficulties would, in the absence of exceptional or extreme circumstances, not constitute a valid mitigating factor: Public Prosecutor v Ong Ker Seng [2001] 3 SLR(R) 134 at [30].

32     I did not place any mitigating weight on the accused’s age as a 72-year-old. It is trite law that in general, the mature age of an offender does not warrant a moderation of the punishment. It is only where the sentence is a long term of imprisonment that the offender’s age is a relevant factor, as the court should not impose a sentence that effectively amounts to a life sentence (Public Prosecutor v UI [2008] 4 SLR(R) 500 at [78]).

33     I placed some mitigating weight on the accused’s plea of guilt. I also noted the accused’s untraced record (although it was simply the absence of an aggravating factor).

34     While I found that the custodial threshold was not crossed, I disagreed with the Prosecution’s submission for a $1,000 fine. I was unable to place much weight, if at all, on the SIR results (see [14] above). Apart from there only being two previous cases (which were hardly enough to constitute a trend), unreported decisions are of limited precedential value (see Toh Suat Leng Jennifer v Public Prosecutor [2022] 5 SLR 1075 at [51] for eg), and the facts and reasoning behind the sentences in those two cases were not before me. The fine had to be sufficiently high to provide for a deterrent effect, that was commensurate to the accused’s culpability.

35     Having regard to all the facts and circumstances, I sentenced the accused to a fine of $2,500, in default 10 days’ imprisonment. At the Defence’s request (which the Prosecution did not object to), I permitted the accused to pay the fine in five equal monthly instalments of $500, with the first instalment paid on 17 June 2026, and the last instalment due on 17 October 2026.

Conclusion

36     It should be reinforced that orders and directions made by the CDRT are to be complied with and treated seriously. Insofar as there is any perception that orders and directions made by the CDRT are “all bark and no bite”, this case should put that misplaced view firmly to rest.

[note: 2]SOF at para 3(i).

[note: 3]SOF at para 4.

[note: 4]Prosecution’s Address on Sentence dated 24 May 2026 at paras 2 and 3.

[note: 5]Mitigation Plea dated 16 June 2026 (“MP”) at para 6.

[note: 6]MP at para 7.

[note: 7]MP at para 11.

[note: 8]MP at para 13.

html:
Aminah Bte Mohamed Kassim v Loch Grocer Pte. Ltd.

Aminah Bte Mohamed Kassim v Loch Grocer Pte. Ltd.
[2026] SGMC 79

Case Number:Originating Claim No 8556 of 2024
Decision Date:22 June 2026
Tribunal/Court:Magistrate's Court
Coram: Evans Ng
Counsel Name(s): Pua Lee Siang and Clarice Tan Jia Ying (Hin Tat Augustine & Partners) for the claimant; Daryl Ong Hock Chye (LawCraft LLC) for the defendant.
Parties: Aminah Binte Mohamed Kassim — Loch Grocer Pte. Ltd.

Tort – Negligence

22 June 2026

Judgment reserved.

District Judge Evans Ng:

1       The claimant, Mdm Aminah, is of a small build. She was in her mid-60s when this accident happened. She was cycling from Jurong West Street 42 towards Jurong Spring Community Club[note: 1] in the late afternoon of 15 March 2023 when she got injured.[note: 2] She claims that as she was passing the front of unit #01-156 at Block 507 Jurong West Street 52 (“Shop”), something hard hit her on her left from behind. The impact caused her to lose her balance, and she fell off her bicycle and hit her head against a wall.[note: 3]

2       The Shop is owned by the defendant company, of which Mr Lee Chee Hoon is the sole shareholder and director. It sells frozen food products.[note: 4] It has indoor and outdoor premises.[note: 5] Chests of freezers, among other things, are placed at the outdoor premises underneath a canopy. But because the Shop is west-facing, sunlight would still beat down on the freezers from around 2pm onwards on fine days.[note: 6]

3       This is an issue that affects many retail shops with ground-floor outdoor premises. It is common knowledge that many of them deal with it by installing canopies with drapes at the end, which can be rolled up when not needed. Or they might install a further retractable canopy with a greater sloping angle. The Shop prefers something more expedient. It would put up translucent panels to shield its freezers in the afternoon and remove them in the evening.

4       These are rectangular panels made of polycarbonate.[note: 7] Each one is around 2 metres high and 1.5 metres wide.[note: 8] It is undisputed that three panels were put up on the material day.[note: 9] This is a photograph[note: 10] of two of these panels serving the purpose intended by the Shop:

5       There is no direct evidence of the weight of each of those panels. Mr Lee gave oral evidence that “it is very light” and “can be picked up by a child”.[note: 11] It is unclear what specimen of a child Mr Lee has in mind. I estimate the thickness of each panel to be at least 3mm. I take judicial notice of the fact that polycarbonate is denser than water and should have a density of around 1.2 g/cm3. Based on these specifications, each panel would weigh at least 10kg.

6       I find that the defendant owes a duty to take reasonable care to secure chattels that are within the Shop’s control—such as the panels—so that they do not cause physical harm to passers-by, including Mdm Aminah. The existence of this duty of care is indisputable because it comes within or is closely analogous to the well-established duties of occupiers to take reasonable care for the safety of their visitors and the users of adjoining properties.

7       The question of whether the defendant has taken reasonable care is a mixed one of fact and law, having regard to the specific facts of each case. Reasonableness does not lie in the eye of the beholder. The courts will consider factors including the likelihood and seriousness of harm, the costs of taking precautions to avoid the harm and the social utility of the activity in assessing the standard of reasonableness.

8       The Shop puts up the panels using the following set-up (or “design”,[note: 12] whatever it may be called). The top edge of each panel is slotted into a groove in the canopy.[note: 13] Since the length of each panel exceeds the height of the groove, the person putting up the panel would press it into an arch, creating a compressed concave face and a stretched convex face. The bottom edge of the panel is then held at rest by static friction generated through contact with the ground. I find that the set-up used by the defendant, as I have just described, fails to satisfy the requisite standard of care.

9       There is no evidence that the panels were manufactured to be held in place by pressing each of them into an arch before wedging it between two objects, here the Shop’s canopy and the ground. Once erected, each panel is always in a state of uneasy equilibrium. What stops the bottom edge of each panel from slipping is only static friction. There are no other implements or features at the foot of the panel to secure it.[note: 14] Friction is seldom relied on in everyday applications to hold motile things in place. Hence, mechanics insert wheel chokes; cobblers apply glue; and Velcro became a success. The strength of the frictional force acting on the edge of each panel would also vary depending on the actual tangential angle it forms with the ground and the slipperiness of the specific patch of ground at that moment, all of which means that any one panel could be significantly more unstable than the others.

10     Sudden and rapid motion is associated with and frequently ensues from deforming an object this way and charging it with elastic potential energy. One may imagine the arm of a traction trebuchet. Those of a less martial bent may picture one curling a deck of playing cards in the palm of one’s hand until the cards spring forth. It is also central to the sport of pole vaulting, wherein the athletes do not entrust their safety to a capricious force but a plant box (a sunken receptable in the ground) that secures the base of their pole while it propels them skyward.

11     Against this reasoning, Mr Lee argues, without the support of evidence, “People outside also use the same boards to shield the sun and rain”.[note: 15] But he does not go so far as to claim that others put up such panels using the same set-up as the Shop’s. Anyway, common practice alone is not determinative of whether the said practice satisfies the standard of care: Cavanagh v Ulster Weaving Co. Ltd. [1960] AC 145. In my view, the Shop’s set-up was chosen to suit its own convenience, for it enabled its employees to put up and take down the panels quickly and without much difficulty.

12     I find that this set-up of the panels is inherently unstable and unreliable. A panel with its concave face towards the Shop is likely to fall sharply and abruptly towards the outside if it is unintentionally dislodged. Any passer-by within a metre or so is unlikely to be able to react fast enough to avoid being hit. The force upon impact is likely to be substantial given the weight and height of each panel. There are other practical and affordable ways to shade the freezers that pose less risk to passers-by.

13     Closed-circuit television video footage recorded by a camera within the Shop’s indoor premises that pointed towards the outdoor premises was adduced to resolve what caused the accident. At trial, the parties conducted multiple viewings of the video and scrutinised the screenshots taken from it.[note: 16] After this forensic exercise, the defendant accepts that the video shows that, just as Mdm Aminah was cycling past the last panel,[note: 17] it “disappeared” from view.[note: 18] That was the most that could be extracted from the video.

14     Mdm Aminah supposes a “strong” wind[note: 19] dislodged the panel. I cannot accept this theory because the outdoor fabric banners seen in the video were not fluttering much.[note: 20]

15     Mr Lee was not at the scene. It was the defendant’s other witness, Mdm Chew Bee Suat, who was at the Shop at the material time. But she was deep within its indoor premises and was not paying attention to the outdoor premises and therefore did not see or hear the accident.[note: 21] She could not offer evidence that answers the question of what caused the panel to come loose.

16     The defendant submits that the natural and probable cause of the accident was that Mdm Aminah’s bicycle had dislodged the last panel that she cycled past.[note: 22] I cannot accept this theory either. Mdm Aminah was unlikely to have cycled into that panel because a metal trolley (see the photograph at [4]) was protruding from the middle of the shopfront, and after her bicycle has cleared the trolley, she would in all likelihood have approached the last panel with a sufficient margin. I also find that the way in which the panel dropped out of view in the video was inconsistent with what would have happened had the front wheel or the handlebars of her bicycle hit its vertical edge. Without a plausible explanation from either party, the rules of evidence come to the fore.

17     Caselaw is replete with examples of the evidential rule known as res ipsa loquitur being applied in negligence cases involving objects falling from buildings or elsewhere that Charlesworth & Percy on Negligence (Sweet & Maxwell, 16th Ed, 2025) has a section of illustrations about them (at para 6-30). The defendant argues this rule cannot be applied in this matter because one of the three requirements for its application is that the cause of the accident must be unknown (Grace Electrical Engineering Pte Ltd v Te Deum Engineering Pte Ltd [2018] 1 SLR 91 at [39(c)]), whereas Mdm Aminah has advanced a positive case regarding the cause of the panel’s collapse.[note: 23] I reject the defendant’s argument. Instead, a claimant who tenders evidence directed to proving a defendant guilty of some particular negligence is not thereby precluded from relying on the rule: Anchor Products Ltd. v Hedges (1966) 115 CLR 493. The other two requirements are that the defendant must have been in control of the situation or thing which resulted in the accident; and that the accident would not have happened, in the ordinary course of things, if proper care had been taken. The defendant does not argue that they have been satisfied, which is indeed the correct position. Therefore, res ipsa loquitur applies to shift the evidential burden to the defendant to rebut the prima facie case of negligence.

18     The defendant has not managed to do so. In addition to his affidavit of evidence-in-chief, Mr Lee was given an opportunity to orally explain what caused the panel to fall, and he admits that he can only “guess”.[note: 24] The defendant also did not identify the particular employee who had put up the panel in question and get him or her to testify in respect of how exactly the panel was put up that day. This leads me to find that the panel fell and struck Mdm Aminah owing to the negligence of the defendant. As regards the remoteness of damage, it cannot be and has not been[note: 25] an issue that the defendant challenges.

19     Finally, I do not find that was any contributory negligence on Mdm Aminah’s part. The defendant argues that she should not have cycled on that pathway generally[note: 26] and taken the precise route in particular;[note: 27] and that she should have worn but failed to wear a helmet while cycling.[note: 28] However, I cannot identify any prohibition against cycling on the relevant pathway. It does not appear to be listed in the First Schedule of the Active Mobility (Pedestrian-Only Paths) Order 2018 as a “pedestrian-only” path for the purposes of the Active Mobility Act 2017. I have reviewed the photographs taken of the area too,[note: 29] and it does not seem inappropriate for cyclists to travel on the relevant pathway and take the precise route that Mdm Aminah did,[note: 30] provided they proceed at a reasonable speed and keep a proper lookout for others. Based on my viewing of the video, Mdm Aminah was cycling at a reasonable speed and did not swerve to avoid any obstacle or pedestrian right become the accident. There is also no legal requirement for cyclists to wear a helmet if they are not cycling on a road. Hence, there is no basis to apportion liability between Mdm Aminah and the defendant under s 3(1) of the Contributory Negligence and Personal Injuries Act 1953.

20     In conclusion, I hold that the defendant was negligent and shall be wholly liable for the accident on 15 March 2023 that caused Mdm Aminah to suffer personal injuries. This is a bifurcated proceeding. Costs of this trial shall be reserved until after the assessment of damages.

Public Prosecutor v Graham McKenzie Horn

Public Prosecutor v Graham McKenzie Horn
[2026] SGMC 78

Case Number:R370-CAD-2025-0711-12728, Magistrate's Appeal No 002/2026/01
Decision Date:22 June 2026
Tribunal/Court:Magistrate's Court
Coram: Lau Qiuyu
Counsel Name(s): Magdalene Huang (Attorney-General's Chambers) for the Public Prosecutor; Daniel Koh and Fernando Er (Eldan Law LLP) for Graham McKenzie Horn.
Parties: Public Prosecutor — Graham McKenzie Horn

Criminal Procedure and Sentencing – Disposal of property – Section 370(3)(b) Criminal Procedure Code 2010

[LawNet Editorial Note: An appeal to this decision has been filed in MA 2/2026/01.]

22 June 2026

District Judge Lau Qiuyu:

1       On 12 July 2024, the Commercial Affairs Department of the Singapore Police Force (the “CAD”) seized funds held in two accounts with LGT Bank (Singapore) Ltd pursuant to s 35(1)(a) of the Criminal Procedure Code 2010 (the “CPC”). The first account, maintained by Mr Graham McKenzie Horn (“Mr Graham”), bore the account number XXXXXXX (“Graham’s Account”). The second account, maintained by Ms Angela Marie Bluebell Horn (“Ms Angela”), bore the account number XXXXXXX (“Angela’s Account”). The seizure of the funds in both Graham’s Account and Angela’s Account (collectively, the “Two Accounts”) was first reported to the court on 11 July 2025, where the CAD’s application for continued seizure at that juncture was allowed. This present application concerned the second reporting by CAD in relation to the seized properties.

2       At the second reporting, the CAD filed an investigation report dated 13 January 2026 (the “CAD’s Second Report”), in which it provided an update on the status of investigations and made an application under s 370(3)(b) of the CPC for continued seizure of the funds in the Two Accounts for a further six months, pending the completion of its investigations. When the properties were first seized on 12 July 2024, the account balance in Graham’s Account was USD 7,869,331.74. This sum has since increased to USD 8,545,441.14 as at the time of the second reporting on 13 January 2026. As regards Angela’s Account, the account balance upon seizure on 12 July 2024 was GBP 3,876,943.13, with the sum increasing to GBP 3,944,466.12 as of 13 January 2026. CAD explained that as the Two Accounts held assets in bonds, equities and derivatives, the account balance would fluctuate periodically given the price movement of the underlying assets.[note: 1]

3       Mr Graham and Ms Angela resisted the CAD’s application for continued seizure each time, at both the first and second reporting. Having considered parties’ submissions in detail, I again allowed CAD’s application for continued seizure at this second reporting and, in doing so, delivered the brief reasons for my decision on 8 May 2026. As only Mr Graham has filed an appeal against my decision, the detailed grounds herein will focus on the funds seized in Graham’s Account, though given the interconnected nature of CAD’s application in respect of the Two Accounts, reference would be made to Angela’s Account where appropriate.

Background facts

4       On 6 March 2024, the CAD received information that Mr Graham received proceeds from a reclaimed dividend tax fraud committed against the Denmark Tax Agency (the “DTA”), with part of the proceeds transferred to Mr Graham and his family members, including his former wife, Ms Angela. Pursuant to the information received, on 12 July 2024, CAD commenced investigations into possible money laundering offences under s 54 of the Corruption, Drug Trafficking and Other Serious Crimes (Confiscation of Benefits) Act 1992 (the “CDSA”) committed by Mr Graham and Ms Angela. The funds in the Two Accounts were consequently seized by the CAD pursuant to s 35(1)(a) of the CPC, being property “in respect of which an offence [was] suspected to have been committed”.[note: 2]

5       Subsequently, on 14 November 2024, the CAD received a Mutual Legal Assistance (“MLA”) request from the Denmark authorities, requesting that the Two Accounts be seized. The CAD was given to understand from the MLA request that the Denmark authorities were investigating Mr Graham and five other suspects (collectively, the “conspirators”) for allegedly perpetuating a “cum-ex” trading scheme, a type of dividend arbitrage fraud that exploits tax refund systems, in defrauding the DTA. This scheme involved the creation of the appearance of multiple owners of the same shares around dividend payments dates to generate multiple tax refunds claims.[note: 3]

6       By way of background, while all Denmark-listed companies were to withhold 27% of the dividends paid to foreign entities and pay the same amount to the DTA as dividend withholding taxes, United States (“US”) pension funds were exempted from paying dividend taxes and could claim refunds for the same. The Denmark authorities alleged that the conspirators made use of custodian banks to register various US pension funds with Danish company shareholdings when those funds were not in fact the shareholders of the Danish companies and would not be entitled to the dividends. Fictitious dividend credit advice slips were then prepared by the custodian banks to fraudulently claim for refunds of withholding taxes from the DTA. This fraudulent scheme led the Denmark government to suffer losses amounting to nearly USD 149.1 million.[note: 4]

7       The Denmark authorities’ investigations and funds tracing into the custodian bank accounts, which applied for the fraudulent withholding tax refunds from the DTA revealed that Mr Graham had benefitted EUR 24,372,196.66, while Ms Angela benefitted GBP 744,352.24. As the Denmark authorities believed that the funds in the Two Accounts represented criminal proceeds derived from the fraud perpetuated against the DTA, they requested for the seizure of the same. While the conspirators (including Mr Graham) have been charged in Denmark, the Denmark authorities’ investigations remain ongoing, and the extent of benefits received by Ms Angela remains unconfirmed.[note: 5]

Procedural history

8       The CAD first reported its seizure of the funds in the Two Accounts to the court on 11 July 2025, in accordance with the one-year deadline in s 370(1)(b) of the CPC. As the CAD took the view that disclosure of certain portions of the investigation report dated 11 July 2025 (the “CAD’s First Report”) would prejudice investigations, it applied for an ex-parte hearing to seek a court order for such portions to be redacted prior to its disclosure to Mr Graham and Ms Angela. This was done in accordance with the well-established procedure laid down in the Court of Appeal decision of Mustafa Ahunbay v Public Prosecutor [2015] 2 SLR 903 (“Mustafa”) at [81]. The court allowed redactions to parts of the CAD’s First Report on 6 and 21 August 2025, and the redacted report was served on Mr Graham and Ms Angela (through their respective sets of counsel) thereafter. As both Mr Graham and Ms Angela objected to the CAD’s application for continued seizure of the funds in the Two Accounts at the time of the first reporting, an inter partes hearing was held on 7 October 2025 for the interested parties to be heard. The court delivered its decision on 27 October 2025, allowing the CAD’s application for continued seizure. The court further ordered that the next court review was to be fixed on 27 January 2026, with the CAD to file its further investigation report two weeks before the next review date (ie, by 13 January 2026).

9       The CAD’s Second Report, providing an update on the status of investigations, was filed on 13 January 2026 in accordance with the court’s directions. The CAD again took the position that disclosure of certain portions of the CAD’s Second Report would prejudice investigations and applied for an ex-parte hearing to seek an order of redaction prior to the disclosure of the investigation report. This was heard before me on 2 February 2026, where I was satisfied, on the basis of the CAD’s submissions, that there was at that stage a real risk of further investigations being prejudiced if details of the investigations at various portions of the CAD’s Second Report were disclosed to the interested parties, namely Mr Graham and Ms Angela. I hence took the view that the public interest would prevent those portions of the investigation report from being disclosed and ordered that the CAD’s Second Report be redacted accordingly as per the court’s order before its disclosure to the interested parties.

10     The redacted copy of the CAD’s Second Report was then served on Mr Graham and Ms Angela (again through their respective sets of counsel). As before, both of them objected to the CAD’s application for continued seizure, and the inter partes hearing was fixed before me on 1 April 2026. As explained at [3] above, I delivered my decision and allowed the CAD’s application on 8 May 2026, and it was from this decision at the second reporting that Mr Graham’s appeal arose.

Whether the mode of challenge should be by way of an appeal

11     Mr Graham sought to challenge the decision by lodging an appeal against the orders made on 8 May 2026. The Notice of Appeal was filed on 22 May 2026. I first considered, as a preliminary issue, whether this was the appropriate mode of challenge against the orders made herein, ie, to allow the CAD’s application for continued seizure of the funds in Graham’s Account under s 370(3)(b) of the CPC.

12     In the context of orders made in a disposal inquiry, whether convened under s 370 of the CPC or otherwise, it is well established that there is no right of appeal against such orders (see Lim Tien Hou William v Ling Kok Hua [2024] 3 SLR 457 (“William Lim”) at [2] and [29], citing earlier decisions in Sofian and another v Public Prosecutor [1968-1970] SLR(R) 782 (“Sofian”) at [14]; and Thai Chong Pawnshop Pte Ltd and others v Vankrisappan s/o Gopanaidu and others [1994] 2 SLR(R) 113 at [12]).

13     In Sofian, an order of forfeiture of various gold bars was made by the District Court as it had been satisfied, amongst others, that an offence under the Control of Imports and Exports Ordinance had been committed. The appellants were persons claiming to have an interest in these gold bars, who submitted that there would be a right of appeal against the order of forfeiture as a prosecution had been instituted in respect of these gold bars. The Court of Appeal disagreed with the appellants, holding that the forfeiture proceedings did not constitute a “criminal case or matter” giving rise to a right of appeal (at [14]):

We are of the view that the proceedings before the District Court in this case were not criminal in their nature and in their form nor did the proceedings contemplate anything other than the forfeiture of the gold bars in question. The question of the conviction or the punishment of the appellants or in fact anyone else was not then in contemplation. The appellants were never placed in jeopardy of being punished for any offence during those proceedings. Although the court concerned was a court exercising criminal jurisdiction and although the court had to be satisfied that an offence under the Ordinance had been committed before making an order for forfeiture we are satisfied that, despite the presence of these elements, which are some of the elements which are present in criminal proceedings generally, a most vital element was lacking, namely, that no one was ever liable to be convicted or sentenced to punishment such as imprisonment or fine and that the proceedings were accordingly not criminal. In our judgment, the inquiry before the District Court was not a criminal case or matter giving rise to a right of appeal under s 290(1) of the Criminal Procedure Code.

[emphasis added in bold and italics]

14     Despite the passage of time since Sofian was decided, the present procedure for appeal under s 377(1) of the CPC retains the same reference to a “criminal case or matter”. It provides as follows:

377.—(1)    … a person who is not satisfied with any judgment, sentence or order of a trial court in a criminal case or matter to which the person is a party may appeal to the appellate court against that judgment, sentence or order in respect of any error in law or in fact, or in an appeal against sentence, on the ground that the sentence imposed is manifestly excessive or manifestly inadequate.

[emphasis added in bold and italics]

15     While the present case was not a disposal inquiry and instead related to an application under s 370(3) of the CPC for continued seizure of property, I was of the view that the principles espoused in the above cases would be similarly applicable here. As with the orders made in a disposal inquiry, the orders made by the court in the present application for continued seizure under s 370(3) of the CPC lacked the same vital element of criminal proceedings, namely that no person was liable to be convicted or sentenced. The inquiry that concerned the court here was simply whether the seized properties remained relevant to investigations, following which the court must not dispose of the same.

16     Accordingly, and as held in the line of cases at [12] and [13] above, the “only available recourse is to invoke the revisionary jurisdiction of the court” by filing a “petition for revision” (William Lim at [2] and [29]). This would be consistent with how challenges have been made against the decisions of the court under s 370(3) of the CPC – see, for example, the criminal revisions that were filed in Lee Chen Seong Jeremy and ors v Public Prosecutor [2019] 4 SLR 867 (“Jeremy Lee”), Ng Siam Cheng Sufiah v Public Prosecutor [2020] 4 SLR 659 (“Sufiah Ng”), and AB Partners Pte Ltd v Public Prosecutor [2020] 4 SLR 1082 (“AB Partners”).

17     Notwithstanding that Mr Graham has filed an appeal rather than a criminal revision in this case, I was mindful that the High Court has held that it was not foreclosed, in such situations, from considering whether to nonetheless exercise its revisionary jurisdiction (William Lim at [29]). I hence considered that this issue would be one appropriately reserved to the High Court. On that basis, I proceed to set out the detailed grounds for my decision to allow the CAD to retain seizure of the funds in Graham’s Account at the second reporting.

Parties’ positions

18     The CAD submitted that the information provided in the CAD’s Second Report showed that there was a reasonable basis for the court to think that the funds seized in Graham’s Account remained relevant for investigations into possible money laundering offences under s 54 of the CDSA. In particular, the CAD’s Second Report stated that the funds tracing exercise in relation to Graham’s Account was ongoing, and it further detailed the steps taken by the CAD since investigations commenced. This was not a case where the police have failed to make any headway in its investigations after a prolonged period, and there has not been any undue delay on the police’s part.[note: 6] The court must hence not dispose of the property under s 370(3)(b) of the CPC.

19     While the CAD appeared, in its written submissions, to rely on an additional ground, ie, that the continued seizure was necessary to prevent dissipation of the funds and to preserve the same for a possible disposal order under s 364 of the CPC,[note: 7] it subsequently confirmed at the hearing that it was not relying on this additional ground. This was because the CAD accepted, upon being queried by the court, that this was not a stated ground in the CAD’s Second Report, and no facts in support of this were provided in the said report. Accordingly, the “one-report” rule, as laid down in Jeremy Lee and clarified in Sufiah Ng, would apply to disallow the CAD from relying on material not found in the CAD’s Second Report to justify its continued seizure of Graham’s Account (see Jeremy Lee at [69] and Sufiah Ng at [86] to [89]).[note: 8]

20     In response, Mr Graham submitted that the CAD’s Second Report was deficient and insufficient for the purposes of justifying yet another extension of the CAD’s seizure of funds in Graham’s Account. As this was the second reporting, CAD’s Second Report must: (a) be subject to stricter and more stringent scrutiny; (b) provide more information than the CAD’s First Report, including the reasons for delay and the progress made in between the reports; and (c) show greater justification that the seized assets remain relevant to investigations.[note: 9] However, this was not the case, and the CAD’s Second Report instead contained mere assertions and evidenced CAD’s dilatory conduct, which resulted in a delay to investigations.

21     In addition, Mr Graham relied on a judgment issued by the High Court of Justice, Business and Property Courts of England and Wales, King’s Bench Division, Commercial Court (the “English High Court”) dated 2 October 2025 (the “English Judgment”), which related to a civil action commenced by the Danish Customs and Tax Administration against Mr Graham and various other defendants.[note: 10] Mr Graham submitted that there was an overlap of facts underlying: (a) the action commenced in the Danish Court of Glostrup by way of two indictments against him for the alleged tax fraud (the “Indictments”); and (b) the issues before the English High Court in the English Judgment. In particular, the English High Court had determined each such overlapping issue entirely in Mr Graham’s favour. There were also no allegations of money laundering made against Mr Graham in the Indictments or before the English High Court. As such, there was no reasonable basis for the CAD to conduct concurrent investigations based on overlapping facts that have already been adjudged by a common law court of competent jurisdiction to be unrelated to money laundering offences or otherwise.[note: 11]

22     Finally, Mr Graham submitted that the CAD was not entitled to rely on the MLA request received from Denmark on 14 November 2024 to substantiate its present application for the continued seizure of Graham’s Account, as such MLA request would fall under the regime of the Mutual Assistance in Criminal Matters Act 2000 (the “MACMA”) and not s 370(3) of the CPC. In the present case, the Danish court has not issued any “foreign confiscation order” within the meaning of the MACMA and no proceedings have been commenced in the Singapore High Court in relation to the granting of any such restraint order over Graham’s Account. The MLA request from Denmark was hence irrelevant for the CAD’s purpose in seeking continued seizure under s 370(3)(b) of the CPC. For the avoidance of doubt, it was clarified by Mr Graham’s counsel at the hearing of this matter that this argument relating to the irrelevance of the MLA request was only limited to that received from Denmark, and not the outgoing MLA request sent by Singapore to the foreign authorities. For the latter outgoing request sent by Singapore, Mr Graham’s submission would be that this was far too delayed and displayed dilatory conduct on the part of CAD (see [20] above).[note: 12]

23     For completeness, the CAD’s Second Report also listed the Denmark Special Crime Unit (the “SCU”) as a party which potentially had interest in Graham’s Account (and Angela’s Account). This was because the Denmark government was laying claim to the funds seized in the Two Accounts. However, as the SCU consented to the CAD’s application for continued seizure of the Two Accounts, the SCU did not participate in the inter partes hearing, at which Mr Graham and Ms Angela made submissions objecting to the CAD’s application.

The court’s decision

The law on continued seizure of property

24     The funds in Graham’s Account were seized by the CAD pursuant to s 35(1)(a) of the CPC, on the basis that these were property in respect of which money laundering offences under s 54 of the CDSA were suspected to have been committed. Upon such seizure, the CAD must make a report of the seizure to the court under s 370(1) of the CPC, which provides:

370.—(1)    If a law enforcement officer seizes any property in the exercise of any power under section 35 or 78, the law enforcement officer must make a report of the seizure to the relevant court at the earlier of the following times:

(a)    when the law enforcement officer considers that —

(i)    the property is not relevant for the purposes of any investigation, inquiry, trial or other proceeding under any written law; and

(ii)   either of the following applies:

(A)    there is no pending investigation mentioned in subsection (3)(c)(i) or (ii);

(B)    there is a pending investigation mentioned in subsection (3)(c)(i) or (ii) but the law enforcement officer considers that the continued seizure of the property is no longer required;

(b)     one year after the date of seizure of the property.

[emphasis added in bold and italics]

25     Upon receiving such a report under s 370(1) of the CPC, the court must make such orders relating to the disposal of the seized property under s 370(2) as may be applicable, save that the court must not dispose of the property if any of the limbs in s 370(3) of the CPC were to apply. Section 370(3) states:

(3)    The relevant court must not dispose of the property if —

(a)    there is any pending court proceeding under any written law in relation to the property;

(b)     the relevant court is satisfied that the property is relevant for the purposes of any investigation, inquiry, trial or other proceeding under any written law; or

(c)    the relevant court is satisfied that, in a case where the law enforcement officer applies for the continued seizure of the property, there is any pending investigation —

(i)    to locate, or ascertain the identity of, any person or persons entitled to possession of the property; or

(ii)   into any absconded person reasonably suspected of having committed a relevant offence in connection with which the property mentioned in section 35(1) or 78(1) or (1A) was seized, and the continued seizure will not cause injustice to any person entitled to possession of the property.

[emphasis added in bold and italics]

26     The funds in Graham’s Account were seized on 12 July 2024, and the CAD’s First Report was made to the court on 11 July 2025, in accordance with the one-year deadline in s 370(1)(b) of the CPC. Having heard the parties at the first reporting, I allowed the CAD’s application for continued seizure of the funds in Graham’s Account under s 370(3)(b) of the CPC, and directed that the next court review be fixed on 27 January 2026, with the further investigation report to be filed two weeks prior, ie, by 13 January 2026. The CAD’s Second Report was filed on 13 January 2026, in accordance with such court directions.

27     In the CAD’s Second Report, the CAD again sought an extension of seizure for a further six months, relying on s 370(3)(b) of the CPC. This provided that the court must not dispose of the property if it was satisfied that such property was relevant for the purposes of any investigation, inquiry, trial or other proceeding under any written law. For the court to be so satisfied, there “should be enough information put before the court so that the magistrate can have a reasonable basis for concluding that these statutory requirements are met” (AB Partners at [46]). To this end, a “bland assertion from the [investigation officer] to the effect that investigations are continuing and that the seized assets are relevant will [not] suffice” and the court “would be entitled to some explanation for the delay” (Rajendar Prasad Rai v Public Prosecutor [2017] 4 SLR 333 (“Rajendar”) at [48]).

28     In addition, “sufficient information has to be put before the court, otherwise, no real purpose is served by the involvement of the court” (AB Partners at [47]). Without which, the court would be “reduced to acting in a purely formal role to endorse whatever [it] was presented with, without any basis for satisfying [itself] that these assertions were validly made, and it is meaningless in such circumstances to speak of judicial oversight of the seizure process” (Rajendar at [49]).

29     Further, the “threshold for the information required is higher than that for the initial seizure” (AB Partners at [48]). This more stringent threshold followed from the fact that time would have passed since the initial seizure, and for the judicial oversight introduced at this stage to be meaningful, the court must be “presented with enough information to assess and calibrate the balance between the private interests of an applicant who has not yet been convicted and the public interest in the contemplated prosecution” (Rajendar at [50]).

30     Having reviewed the case law in this area, the High Court in AB Partners cogently summarised the principles as follows (at [49]-[50]):

49    In summary, therefore, an extension should be supported by:

(a)    sufficient information instead of mere bland or bald assertions;

(b)    information on the state of investigations; and

(c)    timelines on the expected progress of the investigations.

50    In determining whether the information disclosed is sufficient to provide reasonable basis for thinking that the seized property is relevant to a specified purpose under s 370(3), the court is entitled to take into account, inter alia, the period which has elapsed since the property was first seized and the nature of the wrongdoing which gave rise to the investigation or inquiry ([Mustafa] at [84]). The longer the period the property has been seized and detained, the greater will be the justification needed to show that it is still relevant to the investigation or inquiry ([Mustafa] at [84]).

[emphasis added in bold and italics]

31     I now turn to the facts of the present case with the applicable legal principles in mind.

Did CAD’s Second Report contain sufficient basis?

32     As explained at [9] above, an ex-parte hearing was convened on 2 February 2026, where portions of the CAD’s Second Report were ordered to be redacted prior to its disclosure to Mr Graham and Ms Angela. This was done as I was satisfied that there was a real risk that disclosure of such portions would prejudice ongoing police investigations, and the public interest would weigh against a disclosure of such portions in the report. The copy of the CAD’s Second Report that was disclosed to Mr Graham and Ms Angela hence had various portions redacted.[note: 13] Given the reasons for redaction, I will only be making express reference to the unredacted portions in these written grounds, though I may refer broadly to the redacted portions, without reference to the specific contents therein, in explaining the reasons for my decision.

33     The background information explaining how the CAD had received information relating to the receipt of alleged criminal proceeds by Mr Graham, and how such criminal proceeds were believed to have flowed into Graham’s Account and Angela’s Account, are set out at [4] to [7] above. Pursuant to such information received, the CAD commenced investigations into money laundering offences under s 54 of the CDSA and seized the funds in the Two Accounts for this purpose. These are domestic money laundering investigations commenced separately of the MLA request received from the Denmark authorities. In fact, the CAD’s investigations commenced on 12 July 2024, prior to the receipt of the MLA request from the Denmark authorities on 14 November 2024.

34     As at the time of the CAD’s Second Report, the focus of the CAD’s investigations was on the tracing of funds held in the Two Accounts. To this end, the CAD’s investigations revealed that Graham’s Account was largely funded by transfers from certain sources. Concurrently, the SCU was also pending a response from foreign authorities to confirm which portions of Graham’s Account could be traced to the fraud perpetrated against the DTA.[note: 14] When the CAD first reported the matter to court on 11 July 2025, it stated that it was in the midst of preparing an outgoing MLA request to the foreign authorities to obtain this same information to conduct its own concurrent investigations. At the second reporting on 13 January 2026, the CAD provided an update in the CAD’s Second Report that this outgoing MLA request has since been sent on 2 January 2026. The CAD further estimated that the foreign authorities might take a number of months to respond.

35     Mr Graham submitted that the CAD had provided minimal updates as regards the progress of its investigations against Mr Graham and Graham’s Account. Notwithstanding that one period of extended seizure had already been granted by the court, the CAD could only, at the second reporting, show progress in one area of investigations, ie, that the outgoing MLA request has since been sent. Not only was this a failure on the CAD’s part to provide sufficient details on the status of investigations, but it also displayed dilatory conduct on the part of the CAD, as the MLA request was only sent on 2 January 2026, more than 17 months after the Graham’s Account was first seized. In addition, no information has been provided by the CAD as to why it had taken them so long. Given the lack of any meaningful progress, the CAD should not be granted a further extension under s 370(3)(b) of the CPC.[note: 15]

36     Having considered the CAD’s Second Report in its entirety and parties’ submissions, I was satisfied that the material provided therein contained sufficient information for the court to conclude that the funds seized in Graham’s Account remained relevant for the CAD’s investigations.

(a)     The CAD’s Second Report stated that Mr Graham and his conspirators have been charged in Denmark for offences arising out of a fraud perpetrated on the DTA, resulting in a loss of nearly USD 149.1 million to the Denmark government. The Denmark authorities’ investigations remain ongoing.

(b)     The Denmark authorities’ investigations and funds tracing revealed that Mr Graham and Ms Angela benefitted EUR 24,372,196.66 and GBP 744,352.24 respectively, though the extent of the latter remains unconfirmed. The Denmark authorities believe that the balances in both Graham’s Account and Angela’s Account represented criminal proceeds derived from the fraud.

(c)     The total amount seized in the Two Accounts (being USD 8,545,441.14 in Graham’s Account and GBP 3,944,466.12 in Angela’s Account as of 13 January 2026) amounted to an approximate equivalent of around EUR 12 million. This was less than half of what was suspected to have been Mr Graham’s and Ms Angela’s benefits of crime from the alleged tax fraud perpetrated against the DTA. There was hence a chance that the whole or part of the sums seized in the Two Accounts could represent the criminal proceeds received by Mr Graham and Ms Angela.

(d)     The CAD has commenced investigations under s 54 of the CDSA for money laundering offences and was in the midst of conducting the funds tracing exercise to verify the source of funds, including identifying the portions which could be traced to the fraud perpetrated against the DTA. As part of the CAD’s investigations, an outgoing MLA request has been sent to the foreign authorities to obtain such information, and their response remained pending.

37     While I accepted Mr Graham’s submission that the CAD has not provided any explanation in the CAD’s Second Report as to why it had taken them the time it did for the MLA request to be prepared and sent, I acknowledged ultimately that the CAD has made progress in its investigations in between the first reporting and the second reporting. This was unlike a situation where the CAD appeared to have made no progress (eg, if it was still preparing the outgoing MLA request and failed to provide any explanation as to the delay). Instead, in the intervening period, the MLA request was completed and has been sent to the foreign authorities. As regards Mr Graham’s submission about the time taken to do so, I bore in mind the observations of the High Court in AB Partners, where it recognised the complexities of cross-border crimes (at [69]):

It is appreciated that cross-border crimes may be complex, and that there will generally be some delay in communications with foreign agencies, as both the local and foreign investigative and prosecution agencies will need to work through their own structures in requesting and responding to requests, as well as in clarifying matters… On the other hand, the rights of the persons affected by the seizure also need to be considered; the court needs to balance facilitating investigations while ensuring that any release is not unduly or inappropriately held up.

[emphasis added in bold and italics]

38     Balancing the competing considerations, I did not consider this to be a case where the CAD has failed to show sufficient progress since the last reporting, or that there has been such undue delay that it could no longer be said that the funds in the Two Accounts remained relevant to investigations. Having regard to the guidance of the High Court at [68] of AB Partners, I was satisfied that, based on the CAD’s Second Report, the extension sought was bona fide, the investigations remained ongoing, and that progress has been made since the last reporting. The CAD has also provided an estimate that the foreign authorities might take a number of months to respond. I accepted that progress has been made within the local structure, both in terms of the MLA request made to the foreign authorities and the funds tracing conducted on the Two Accounts.

Requests made by the CAD for interviews

39     Another area of update provided in the CAD’s Second Report related to the requests made by the CAD to interview Mr Graham and Ms Angela in Singapore and for their statements to be recorded. CAD had first written to Mr Graham’s counsel on 19 December 2024 to request that Mr Graham attend in Singapore for the interview, but this was not acceded to. Instead, Mr Graham’s counsel proposed a meeting between themselves, the foreign lawyers and the CAD.

40     Thereafter, on 12 December 2025, the CAD wrote to both Mr Graham’s and Ms Angela’s respective counsels to request that they attend in Singapore for their statements to be recorded under s 22 of the CPC. To this, Mr Graham’s counsel replied on 19 December 2025 to state that Mr Graham was overseas and unable to travel to Singapore. Mr Graham’s counsel instead suggested for: (a) Mr Graham to prepare a written statement based on a list of questions sent by the CAD in advance; or (b) a remote video interview to be facilitated. As regards Ms Angela, her counsel replied on 22 December 2025 to inform the CAD that she had nothing further to add beyond what was stated in her affidavits filed at the first reporting of this matter.

41     During the hearing, the CAD acknowledged that at this juncture, the funds tracing was the “main focus” of the police investigations, though the update on the status of the CAD’s request for interviews was also provided in the CAD’s Second Report to inform the court of the matters that remained outstanding.[note: 16] Subsequently, when the matter was adjourned for decision, the CAD sought to supplement the above by observing that the failure of Mr Graham and Ms Angela to present themselves for investigations could lead to them being regarded as “absconded persons” for the purposes of s 370(3) of the CPC, though the CAD withdrew this submission upon acknowledging that this was not a point raised in the CAD’s Second Report. The CAD further confirmed it was not relying on this submission for the purposes of the present application for continued retention.[note: 17] I hence did not make any substantive findings on this issue of “absconded persons”, as this was not ventilated before me.

42     Mr Graham submitted that he had offered to cooperate with the CAD’s investigations by counter-proposing ways through which his statement could be taken without the need for him to attend in Singapore. However, it was the CAD who had refused such offers of cooperation, and this was evidence of the CAD’s own dilatory conduct, leading to the delay in investigations.

43     I was unable to agree with Mr Graham that the mere fact that CAD has not acceded to the alternative modes of statement-taking proposed by Mr Graham showed dilatory conduct on the part of the CAD. The CAD has explained in the CAD’s Second Report that Mr Graham’s request was inconsistent with ss 21 and 22 of the CPC, which required a witness to attend before a police officer at a police station for the purposes of statement recording. The CAD could not be said to have progressed slowly in investigations simply because it required that Mr Graham’s statement be taken in compliance with s 22 of the CPC.

44     In any event, and in light of the CAD’s submissions in relation to the status of requests for interviews, I considered this to be part of the holistic update provided by the CAD as regards the outstanding matters, ie, that as at the date of the CAD’s Second Report, neither Mr Graham nor Ms Angela have presented themselves before the CAD in Singapore for their statements to be taken. Nonetheless, and quite apart from this, I was satisfied that progress has been made by the CAD on other fronts, which provided me with sufficient basis to be satisfied that the seized funds in the Two Accounts remained relevant for investigations (see [32] to [38] above).

The English Judgment

45     As stated at [21] above, Mr Graham sought to argue that the issues decided by the English High Court in the English Judgment bore an overlap with the factual issues which were the subject of the Indictments brought against Mr Graham and his conspirators in Denmark. Crucially, the English High Court rejected the civil claims pursued by the DTA against Mr Graham and the other named defendants. In brief, the English Judgment set out the court’s findings that: (a) the misrepresentations alleged by the DTA had not been made; (b) the DTA had not understood them to have been made; (c) neither Mr Graham nor anyone else had intended to make false representations or engage in any unlawful conduct; (d) any losses suffered by the DTA had not been induced by anything said or done by Mr Graham or any of the named defendants; and (e) the alleged fraudulent documents submitted to the DTA were legitimate.[note: 18]

46     I was of the view that the decision in the English Judgment was not dispositive of the issue of whether the funds seized in the Two Accounts here remained relevant to investigations. The English Judgment recognised that there were parallel proceedings across various jurisdictions, and the English Judgment was made with reference to the claims pursued by the Danish Customs and Tax Administration at the trial in the English High Court, governed by English law, and upon the evidence and arguments placed before that court. The English High Court was careful to observe that the claims, evidence and arguments before it “may or may not be the same as or similar to the criminal charges or civil claims brought in other jurisdictions under systems of law other than English law, or the evidence and argument put to those other courts…”.[note: 19]

47     There was thus nothing before this court to suggest that the English Judgment was determinative of the CAD’s investigations in Singapore. Instead, the CAD’s Second Report provided that as of 13 January 2026, the Denmark authorities’ investigations remained ongoing.[note: 20] Mr Graham also accepted that it was not his position that the charges against him in Denmark have been withdrawn. Neither was it his position that the investigations by the Denmark authorities against him have concluded.[note: 21] From the CAD’s Second Report, the basis of the CAD’s seizure was not dependent on the English Judgment or any findings made thereunder. The funds in the Two Accounts were seized on the basis that there were properties in respect of which money laundering offences under s 54 of the CDSA were suspected to have been committed, which in turn related to whether the funds therein could be traced to the criminal proceeds derived from the fraud perpetrated against the DTA.

48     Contrary to Mr Graham’s submissions, the DTA and/or the SCU need not have made any money laundering allegations in the proceedings before the English High Court and/or in the Danish Indictments.[note: 22] The money laundering offences were the subject of the CAD’s ongoing domestic investigations, with the suspected tax fraud against the Denmark authorities being the predicate offences for the CAD’s money laundering investigations.[note: 23] I was also unable to agree with Mr Graham’s arguments that there was no reasonable basis for the CAD to conduct concurrent investigations based on overlapping facts that have already been adjudged by the English High Court to be unrelated to money laundering offences or otherwise.[note: 24] Even if the factual issues before the English High Court overlapped with that in the Danish Indictments, there was nothing before me to show that this disposed of the ongoing investigations in Denmark with finality, especially in light of Mr Graham’s own acceptance that the investigations in Denmark remained ongoing and the charges have not been withdrawn. Accordingly, there was ample basis for the CAD to continue its investigations into Mr Graham and Ms Angela for the suspected offences under s 54 of the CDSA and into the provenance of the funds seized in the Two Accounts.

The MLA request from Denmark

49     The final point made by Mr Graham was that the CAD’s reliance on the MLA request received from Denmark on 14 November 2024 was irrelevant for the present application, as the MLA request would fall within the regime of the MACMA and not the CPC. This was because the legislative regime relating to the restraining or forfeiture of assets pursuant to an MLA request was governed by the MACMA.[note: 25]

50     With respect, I considered that Mr Graham’s submissions in this regard were misconstrued. The CAD was not seeking to seize the funds in the Two Accounts pursuant to any restraining order issued under the MACMA. Instead, the basis for CAD’s seizure was under s 35(1) of the CPC, in relation to investigations under s 54 of the CDSA. These domestic money laundering investigations had commenced even prior to the MLA request from Denmark (see [33] above). The CAD had not seized the funds in the Two Accounts only after it received the MLA request from Denmark. Instead, these were seized by the CAD prior to the MLA request, pursuant to information obtained by the CAD that criminal proceeds could have flowed into the Two Accounts, leading the CAD to commence investigations into suspected money laundering offences.

Conclusion

51     In light of the foregoing reasons, I was satisfied that there was sufficient basis disclosed in the CAD’s Second Report to provide this court with reasonable basis for finding that the funds seized in the Two Accounts (and in particular, for the purposes of the present appeal, Graham’s Account) remained relevant for the purposes of the CAD’s investigations. As such, pursuant to s 370(3)(b) of the CPC, the court must not dispose of the same, and I allowed CAD’s application for continued seizure of the funds in the Two Accounts at this juncture.

52     Considering the time that had lapsed from the date of the CAD’s Second Report (ie, 13 January 2026) to when my decision was delivered on 8 May 2026, I agreed with Mr Graham and Ms Angela that this period ought to be taken into account in deciding on the length of extension to be granted to the CAD, before its next report was to be made to the court. Accordingly, I ordered that the funds in the Two Accounts be retained by the CAD for a further three months from 8 May 2026, ie, till 8 August 2026, or until CAD’s investigations were complete, whichever was earlier. In addition, the investigation officer was to file a further report on the status of investigations two weeks before the next review date (ie, two weeks before 8 August 2026).
