html:
Mobot Pte Ltd v The Management Corporation Strata Plan No 4067

Mobot Pte Ltd v The Management Corporation Strata Plan No 4067
[2026] SGDC 202

Case Number:Originating Claim No 111 of 2022
Decision Date:22 June 2026
Tribunal/Court:District Court
Coram: Chiah Kok Khun
Counsel Name(s): Tan Tiong Gee Andrew and Manickam Kasturibai (Andrew Tan Tiong Gee & Co) for the claimant; Kawal Pal Singh s/o Amarjit Singh and Adrienne Grace Milton (Tito Isaac & Co LLP) for the defendant.
Parties: Mobot Pte Ltd — The Management Corporation Strata Plan No 4067

Tort – Misrepresentation – Subsidiary proprietor of strata title property applying to management corporation for fitting out permit – Subsidiary proprietor carrying out fitting out works – Whether representations made by management corporation fitting out works approved – Whether subsidiary proprietor submitted a complete and compliant set of documents for approval of fitting out works – Whether fitting out works authorised

22 June 2026

Judgment reserved.

District Judge Chiah Kok Khun:

Introduction

1       This action arises from an application for approval to commence renovation works at a strata title property. The claimant is in the business of manufacturing, assembly and sale of bicycles[note: 1] and a subsidiary proprietor of unit #01-55 at North Spring Bizhub, 7 Yishun Industrial Street 1 (the “Unit”). The defendant is the management corporation of North Spring Bizhub. There are 453 units at North Spring Bizhub.

2       The claimant’s case is that it had submitted documents to obtain the permit to renovate the Unit, and on 16 December 2021, the defendant verbally approved the commencement of renovation works. In reliance on the assurance, the claimant commenced renovation works on 21 December 2021, but was subsequently instructed by the defendant to stop work, causing losses and disruption to its business plans and operations. The claimant contends that as a result of the defendant’s failure to process or approve the renovation permit, it suffered substantial operational delays and financial losses. The claimant commenced this action for negligent misrepresentation, claiming loss and damage resulting from delays to the renovation works and loss of use of the Unit. The claimant also claims for breach of statutory duty on the part of the defendant pursuant to the Building (Strata Management) Act 2004 (“BSMA”).[note: 2]

3       The defendant’s case is that it did not give any verbal approval, conditional or otherwise, to the claimant to renovate the Unit. The claimant has also failed to comply with mandatory requirements under the building manual of North Spring Bizhub (“Building Manual”)[note: 3] and the by-laws, including submission of complete and technically compliant documentation and approvals from relevant statutory authorities. Further, the claimant had carried out renovation works on 21 December 2021 without any approval, in breach of the by-laws of North Spring Bizhub and has caused damage to the unit. The defendant counterclaims for unspecified damages.

4       For the reasons set out below, I am dismissing the claimant’s action and allowing the defendant’s counterclaim.

Issues to be determined

5       The issues to be determined by me in this case are as follows:

(a)     Whether approval was given to the claimant before 21 December 2021 to proceed with the fitting out works:

(i)       whether the claimant submitted a complete and compliant set of documents for fitting out approval, and whether it was prior to the commencement of the works on 21 December 2021 or at all; and

(ii)       Whether the defendant provided verbal approval, assurances, or consent for the claimant to commence renovation works.

(b)     Whether approval (or a fitting out permit) ought to have been given to the claimant after 21 December 2021.

(c)     Whether the claimant is in breach of the by-laws of North Spring Bizhub and has also caused damage to the unit.

Analysis and findings

No approval was given to the claimant before 21 December 2021 to proceed with the fitting out works

6       The law in regard to negligent misrepresentation is uncontroverted. The General Division of the High Court held in the case of Low Sing Khiang v LogicMills Learning Centre Pte Ltd [2024] 3 SLR 759 at [30] as follows:

30    To make out a claim of negligent misrepresentation, the following elements have to be satisfied (IM Skaugen SE and another v MAN Diesel & Turbo SE and another [2018] SGHC 123 at [121]; Ma Hongjin v Sim Eng Tong [2021] SGHC 84 at [20]; Spandeck Engineering (S) Pte Ltd v Defence Science & Technology Agency [2007] 4 SLR(R) 100 at [77], [81], [83] and [115]; Fong Maun Yee and another v Yoong Weng Ho Robert [1997] 1 SLR (R) 751 at [52]):

(a)    The defendant must have made a false representation of fact.

(b)    The representation induced actual reliance.

(c)    The defendant must owe a duty of care to the plaintiff to take reasonable care in making the representation.

(d)    There must be a breach of that duty of care.

(e)    The breach must have caused damage to the plaintiff.

7       It is seen that not only must the alleged representation be false, but it must also induce actual reliance. With the above legal principles in mind, I turn to the facts of the present case. It is important in the analysis of a claim in misrepresentation to first determine the exact representations that the representee asserts were made by the representor. The exact representations alleged must be pleaded in the statement of claim. In the present case, the claimant’s contention is that the defendant made a series of representations about the renovation permit for fitting out works at the Unit. However, a perusal of the statement of claim (amendment no 1), the further and better particulars, and the reply and defence to counterclaim (amendment no 2) filed by the claimant shows that the representation pleaded is confined to that allegedly given by the chairperson of the defendant, Mr Lee Chang Joon (“Mr Lee”) on 16 December 2024 that the documents submitted by the claimant were sufficient for the renovation permit to be issued and that the claimant could start the renovations on 17 December 2021.[note: 4]

8       It is seen thus that the claimant’s pleaded case on misrepresentation is confined to the alleged statements made by Mr Lee on 16 December 2024. The claimant contends that it had submitted documents to obtain the renovation permit prior to 16 December 2021. On 16 December 2021 Mr Lee verbally assured and approved the commencement of fitting-out works. The claimant further alleges that such approval was linked to the solicitation of proxy votes for the pending annual general meeting (“AGM”) of North Spring Bizhub, and that Mr Lee sought the claimant’s director, Mr Lai Wei Chun’s (“Mr Lai”) support in exchange for facilitating approval of the renovation permit. The claimant claims that in reliance on the alleged assurance, it commenced renovation works on 21 December 2021, but was subsequently instructed by the defendant to stop work, causing losses and disruption to its business plans and operations. The claimant thus seeks loss of profits to be assessed; and special damages at $15,389.90.

9       The analysis of the claimant’s case in this regard starts with the claimant’s submissions of documents for purposes of its renovation works. Mr Lai came to the office of the defendant on 7 December 2021 and submitted the documents (the “7 December Documents”) to a Ms Kelly, a staff of the defendant. It is not disputed that the 7 December Documents were submitted without the endorsement of any professional structural engineer (“PE”). It is undisputable that it is a requirement under the Building Manual which governs building matters at North Spring Bizhub, that the endorsement of a PE is required for the approval of the renovations in question (under clauses 7.2.1(c)-(f) of the Building Manual).[note: 5] This requirement was recognised, and accepted by the claimant when Mr Lai signed the undertaking in form B, which was one of the documents given to Mr Lai to fill up and submit to obtain the defendant’s approval before commencing renovation works:[note: 6] The relevant portion of form B states as follows:

We understand that drilling and hacking of the structural floor slab is strictly prohibited without the written consent of the Project’s Structural Engineer. Should approval be given, prior to any drilling, all points must be marked out using ‘steel cover meter’ or appropriate equipment to determine the positions of the post-tension cables. Separate written approval must be obtained from the Management prior to commencement of the actual drilling and/or hacking activities.

10     Further, a form A was submitted without the claimant’s signature. Ms Kelly highlighted the shortfalls in the 7 December Documents to Mr Lai on 7 December 2021 and informed him that the documents must be submitted in full before it could be processed and approval could be granted.

11     The claimant appears to accept at trial that Mr Lai had undertaken that separate written approval should be obtained from the defendant prior to the commencement of actual drilling and hacking activities, based on form B. Mr Lai agreed that all drilling and hacking works were strictly prohibited without the written consent of a project structural engineer. However, he asserted that the clause did not apply to him and the Unit. The claimant’s expert Mr Ong also likewise contended, without any basis, that the requirement did not apply to the Unit. It is unclear to me why the claimant’s renovation works would be exempted from the requirement of a PE’s approval. There is no creditable evidence adduced by the claimant in support of its assertion that the requirement did not apply to the Unit.

12     I turn now to the events on 16 December 2021. The evidence shows that Mr Lee made a call to Mr Lai in the morning (the “First Call”). At the First Call Mr Lee introduced himself to Mr Lai and informed Mr Lai of the impending AGM.[note: 7] In the afternoon, Mr Lai called Mr Lee, mentioning there he had been some issues with obtaining the renovation permit, and with the managing agent of North Spring Bizhub. He requested for a meeting at the office of the defendant (the “Second Call”).

13     At the meeting at the office of the defendant Mr Lai discussed with Mr Lee the renovation works at the Unit and asked for his consent to carry out the renovation works. Mr Lee’s evidence is that as the claimant intended to create a mezzanine floor in the Unit using industrial beams,[note: 8] he noted that the 7 December Documents were incomplete and advised Mr Lai to follow the requirements under clause 7.2(f) of the Building Manual to provide all the requisite plans endorsed by a PE. He also advised Mr Lai to submit the relevant documentation to the relevant government authorities for their approval and thereafter to obtain a renovation permit issued by the defendant’s office. Mr Lai said he would submit all the required documentation as stipulated in the Building Manual and assured Mr Lee, in the presence of Ms Kelly that the claimant would not mount any racking into the ground or the wall; or create any platforms by way of installing any racking that would create a mezzanine floor; and would not hack any part of the Unit. Mr Lee informed Mr Lai that the claimant could install a standalone racking system, but he was not allowed to use industrial beams for the racking; and any form of alteration to the building’s structure was prohibited. The construction of a mezzanine floor was strictly prohibited as the authorities would not grant approval. I note that this comports with clause 7.4(c) of the Building Manual, which states that the erection of a mezzanine floor is strictly not allowed.[note: 9]

14     Mr Lee’s evidence is that Mr Lai mentioned that he held proxy voting forms and could utilise his votes to support Mr Lee at the impending AGM. Mr Lai asked if Mr Lee could overlook the requirement of URA approval to be submitted and to look no further into the required documents to be submitted to the defendant. Mr Lee however informed Mr Lai that the proper procedure set out in the Building Manual must be complied with strictly, and he would not accept any “favour trading”. Mr Lai in any case asked Ms Kelly for the Letter of Authorisation (“LOA”) for voting at the AGM, endorsed and handed it to Mr Lee. As noted by the defendant, neither Mr Lee nor Ms Kelly was cross-examined on this point and their evidence in this regard remained unassailed.

15     In this regard, I am therefore unable to accept the claimant’s version that Mr Lee had called Mr Lai on 16 December 2021 solely for the purpose of soliciting votes for the impending AGM in exchange for his approval of the claimant’s renovation works. More pertinently, the claimant’s version relies on Mr Lee having the sole decision-making power over granting the approval for the claimant’s renovation of the Unit. The claimant’s case is that Mr Lee granted the claimant approval for the renovation of the Unit in exchange for the LOA for the AGM. The claimant’s case however is dependent on Mr Lee having the authority to grant approval for the claimant’s renovation of the Unit. There is no evidence adduced by the claimant that Mr Lee had such authority, neither is it objectively reasonable that Mr Lee would ever have such authority to grant the approval on behalf of the defendant. I also note that the claimant did not plead any apparent or ostensible authority on the part of Mr Lee. I find therefore that in any event, there is no evidence that any representation by Mr Lee that the documents submitted by the claimant were sufficient for the renovation permit to be issued and that the claimant could start the renovations on 17 December 2021,[note: 10] would induce actual reliance on the part of the claimant. Further, I find that any purported reliance by the claimant on any such alleged representation by Mr Lee would in any case be unreasonable. In any event, I note that it is undisputed that Mr Lee stopped the claimant’s renovation works on 21 December 2021 (as discussed below), before the AGM (which was scheduled for 30 December 2021). This put paid to the claimant’s case that Mr Lee had granted approval to the claimant’s renovation works in return for Mr Lai’s proxy votes at the AGM. Mr Lee would have known that it was completely open to Mr Lai to revoke the LOA and the proxy votes in support of Mr Lee before the AGM after Mr Lee stopped the renovation works.

16     For completeness, I refer to the claimant’s contention that the 7 December Documents included a cheque from the claimant dated 17 November 2021, being the security deposit required as a part of the renovation application and that the banking of this cheque by the defendant is equivalent to approval of his application. I find this contention to be outright without basis, and it is inexplicable how such an argument could be made. In any event I note that Ms Kelly testified at the trial that it was merely a standard protocol for her to issue a receipt upon receiving the cheque, and the cheque itself would be passed to the defendant’s office to be banked.[note: 11] She would not be kept aware of whether the cheque had cleared, and the purpose of issuing the receipt is to “prove that [the managing agent] received the cheque”.[note: 12]

17     In my view, the approval and issuance of a renovation permit could not have been be granted on 16 December 2021 in any event because the 7 December Documents lacked the endorsement of a PE; and they showed plans for a mezzanine, which would not be permitted under the Building Manual without the prior approval of the relevant competent authorities.[note: 13] In this regard, the defendant maintains that the claimant failed to comply with mandatory requirements under the Building Manual and the by-laws, including submission of complete and technically compliant documentation and approvals from relevant statutory authorities. It is plain that erection of a mezzanine floor is specifically prohibited without the approval of the relevant authorities.[note: 14]

The claimant took no steps to obtain the requisite approvals after 21 December 2021

18     I turn next to the events of 21 December 2021. On that day, Mr Lee and Ms Kelly heard loud construction noises coming from the Unit. They were in the defendant’s office, which is located adjacent to the Unit. Mr Lee and Ms Kelly found the claimant’s contractors drilling and hacking at the Unit. They noted the following at the Unit:[note: 15]

(a)     one of the walls was hacked, such that it presented a rectangular hole;

(b)     a rectangular plate was drilled into, and mounted onto, the wall opposite to the wall with the rectangular hole;

(c)     metal plates were drilled into the ground; and

(d)     industrial beams were on the floor, contrary to the standalone racking system that had been promised and assured to Mr Lee by Mr Lai on 16 December 2021.

19     It should be noted that it is not disputed by the claimant that the works conducted in the Unit on 21 December 2021 included “drilling holes on the ground to secure the metal framework”.[note: 16] In any event, the defendant’s expert, (“Mr Ng”), observed that there was: a) drilling and hacking work done in the Unit; b) hacking in a wall; c) bolting into the wall and floor slab; and d) steel hollow sections placed on the floor.

20     Mr Lee and Ms Kelly ordered the claimant’s contractors to stop work. It is undisputable that the claimant did not possess any renovation permit conferring authorisation as of 21 December 2021 to carry out renovation works at the Unit.[note: 17] The claimant’s contractors and workers had also failed to register themselves with the North Spring Bizhub security, prior to commencing work.[note: 18] This constituted a breach of the Building Manual clauses 7.17(a)(i) and 7.17(a)(ii).[note: 19]

21     In this regard, the claimant appears to contend in the course of the cross-examination of Ms Kelly that the claimant’s contractors entering the premises of North Spring Bizhub on 21 December 2021 would be tantamount to approval having been granted for the renovation works. This is plainly an untenable contention. At the outset I note that this contention is not pleaded by the claimant. Further, I fail to see how it can be said that just because a person is found in a premises it follows that permission has been granted for him to enter. The evidence shows that North Spring Bizhub has 453 units. It is hardly unusual if the security guards might not have verified the identities of every single person entering the premises. The onus is on contractors and sub-contractors to obtain the approval to enter the premises. Ms Kelly testified that the procedure was for renovation contractors to report to the defendant’s office upon arriving at North Spring Bizhub premises. Ms Kelly would then take photos of their identity passes and send the photos to a group chat with the security guards. There is however no record of the claimant’s renovation contractors doing so. This is perhaps unsurprising, given that no renovation permit had been issued to the claimant.

22     As regards the unauthorised renovation works at the Unit, it is seen that despite the claimant’s assurance to the defendant that the works involved only standalone racking without drilling or hacking, the claimant commenced works 21 December 2021 which involved unauthorised drilling into the structural floor slab and walls, and the installation of industrial beams. These works were carried out without any approval, written or otherwise. I agree with the defendant that plainly the instruction to stop work issued by Mr Lee on 21 December 2021 was a lawful and reasonable step to enforce compliance with safety requirements, protect the structural integrity of the building, and ensure that all obligations under the Building Manual were met.

23     Following the events of 21 December 2021, Mr Richard Tang the managing agent of North Spring Bizhub (“Mr Tang”) met with Mr Lai on 22 December 2021. Mr Tang reiterated that renovation works cannot be carried out without permit; and that the documents submitted by the claimant were incorrect and inadequate. These included the approval from the Singapore Civil Defence Force (“SCDF”), a statutory requirement, carrying a wrong address. Mr Lai was told to submit rectified plans with the necessary approvals from SCDF and a PE.

24     In view of the claimant’s intended creation of a second floor in the Unit, Mr Lee advised the claimant to write to URA to obtain formal approval. If this was obtained, it would be likely that the claimant’s renovation application would be approved by the defendant.[note: 20] The claimant however did not obtain such approval or waiver of the requirement from URA. Whilst the claimant had depicted emails between Mr Lai and URA as their official approval, it is clear that these emails comprised URA’s answers to the claimant’s general enquiries. Despite amending the documents submitted, the claimant did not take steps to obtain the requisite approval from URA. In this regard, Mr Ng the defendant’s expert is of the view that the unauthorised works on 21 December were consistent with “the process of building a mezzanine floor or platform”.[note: 21] In his opinion, the approvals necessary for the construction of a such a mezzanine floor or platform are as follows:[note: 22]

(a)     Approval from SCDF in the form of:

(i)       Building Plan.

(ii)       Fire Protection submissions.

(b)     URA planning approval or waiver.

(c)     Building Construction Authority (“BCA”) submission.

25     He added that BCA would require the URA planning approval or waiver to be granted first, before proceeding to “process the structural submission for approval”. It is also noted in Mr Ng’s report that a submission to BCA would also be required for a standalone racking system, if: (a) the loading is high; and (b) the area exceeded 10 sq m (the requirement as of 2021).[note: 23] In Mr Ng’s view, the claimant’s plans involved an area that exceeded 10 sq m. For completeness, I note that during the cross-examination of Mr Ong, the claimant’s expert, he testified that it was possible for a standalone racking system to also require approval from the authorities in certain scenarios. Although he disagreed that a submission to BCA would be required in the present case, he nevertheless testified that if he were the PE appointed at the material time, he would have consulted BCA if he was unsure.[note: 24]

26     As well for completeness, I turn to the claimant’s case in regard to alleged statements made to Mr Lai by Mr Tang. As noted above, the representation pleaded by the claimant is confined to that allegedly given by the chairperson of the defendant, Mr Lee on 16 December 2024 that the documents submitted by the claimant were sufficient for the renovation permit to be issued and that the claimant could start the renovations on 17 December 2021.[note: 25] The claimant however appeared to expand its case on misrepresentation to alleged statements made by Mr Tang. In the course of the trial, the claimant makes much of the comments made by Mr Tang on WhatsApp in January 2022 that he saw no issues to hold back the renovation permit. The claimant contends that Mr Tang had told Mr Lai that he saw “no issue issuing the reno permit”.[note: 26] The claimant’s case appears to be that Mr Tang (like Mr Lee) had the final say in whether the renovation permit would be issued.

27     As with the claimant’s case as regards Mr Lee, I find the claimant’s case of its reliance on Mr Tang’s alleged representation objectively unreasonable. There is no basis for the claimant to hold the belief that the managing agent has the authority to approve renovations on behalf of the defendant. Mr Tang’s comments plainly cannot constitute the renovation permit itself. In any event, Mr Tang made it clear in his testimony in court that he could only give the site staff of the defendant “advice or guideline”, and the staff “consult [him] for whatever issue or problem they are not sure”.[note: 27] Tang stated clearly his comments to Mr Lai were not the approval. According to Tang, the permit was never issued as several matters were not in order. These included the plans that involved a mezzanine floor and the drilling of holes.[note: 28] Mr Tang made it clear as well that the reply from URA that the claimant purports to be an approval from URA was not approval of the claimant’s proposed plans. It was a reply on the general policy on installing racking systems in industrial buildings. Mr Tang reiterated in court that the site staff did not grant the requisite approval because the plans showed “drilling of holes” and the creation of “a second floor” or “one more floor”. This was described by Mr Tang as “worse than mezzanine [floor]”[note: 29] and that the site staff had “good reason not to issue [the] renovation permit”.[note: 30]

28     There is therefore no evidence of misrepresentation of fact made by the defendant. The claimants’ claim in misrepresentation must fail. Further, it is seen above that the claimant took no steps to obtain the requisite approvals after 21 December 2021. There is no reason for the defendant to issue any permit for fitting out works to the claimant. I agree with the defendant that the delays and any alleged losses were self-inflicted by the claimant through its premature actions and non-compliance; and not attributable to the defendant.

29     As regards the claimant’s claim in negligence, the claimant contends that the defendant has neglected to process its application for a renovation permit after the renovation works were stopped by the defendant on 21 December 2021. The claimant’s case in regard to the breach of duty appears to be essentially that the defendant failed to grant the permit for fitting out works.[note: 31] But it follows from my analysis above that there is no valid reason for the defendant to issue any permit for fitting out works to the claimant. The claim in negligence fails as well.

No basis for a claim in breach of statutory duty

30     In regard to the claimant’s pleaded claim for breach of statutory duty on the part of the defendant, it appears in the pleadings that the claimant is relying on s 88(1) of the BSMA.[note: 32] It also appears that it is relying on s 29(2)(b) which states that the management corporation may do all things reasonably necessary for the performance of its duties for the enforcement of the by-laws. The claimant in turn refers to various parts of the Building Manual and suggests that the defendant is to issue a renovation permit upon the satisfaction by the claimant of these parts of the Building Manual. In the course of the trial, the claimant’s counsel decided to abandon the claim for breach of statutory duty. For completeness however, I will briefly discuss why any such claim is doomed to fail in any event.

31     Section 88(1) of the BSMA states as follows:

Breaches of this Part

88.—(1)    If a management corporation or subsidiary management corporation commits a breach of any provision of this Part, or makes default in complying with any requirement of, or duty imposed on it by, any provision of this Part, a subsidiary proprietor or mortgagee in possession or occupier of a lot is entitled to apply to the court —

(a)    for an order to restrain the breach of any such provision by; or

(b)    to recover damages for any loss or injury to the subsidiary proprietor, mortgagee in possession, or occupier or property arising out of the breach of any such provision from, the management corporation or subsidiary management corporation, as the case may be.

…

32     Section 88(1) allows a subsidiary proprietor to apply to court to recover damages for any loss or injury resulting from the failure of a management corporation in complying with any duty imposed on it by the BSMA. The duties that the defendant contends the claimant has failed to comply with are those under s 29(2)(b). Section 29(2)(b) states as follows:

Duties and powers of management corporation in respect of property

29

…

(2)    Except as otherwise provided in subsection (3), a management corporation may —

…

(b)    do all things reasonably necessary for the performance of its duties under this Part and for the enforcement of the by-laws.

33     The claimant suggests that the defendant has an obligation to issue a renovation permit upon the satisfaction by the claimant of the relevant parts of the Building Manual. However, it is unclear to me on what basis the claimant is asserting such an obligation on the part of the defendant. The claimant has not shown how the Building Manual imposes any such obligation on the defendant in this regard. Furthermore, it is unclear to me how s 29(2)(b) assists the claimant in its case. The section states that the management corporation may do all things reasonably necessary for the performance of its duties for the enforcement of the by-laws. The claimant has not shown in what way this translates into an obligation on the defendant to issue a renovation permit. There is therefore no basis for a claim in breach of statutory duty against the defendant.

There is no evidence that the claimant has suffered any damage

34     I have made the finding that there was no misrepresentation, as no false representation of fact were made. The claimant has failed to fulfill the first element of the tort of misrepresentation. There is accordingly no necessity for me to consider the other elements. For completeness however, I turn to the question of damage suffered by the claimant. For an action in misrepresentation to succeed, the representee must have suffered damage by acting on the alleged misrepresentation. It is an element of the tort of misrepresentation, which is not actionable per se. In this regard, the claimant has failed in any event to show that it has suffered any damage by acting on the alleged representation. Whilst there is no requirement in law for losses to be realised before they are recognised as damage suffered, there must be evidence of actual damage. In this regard, the claimant has not shown that it has suffered any such damage. The claimant has claimed for loss of profits and special damages of $15,389.90. However, there is no evidence proffered for any such loss of profits or damages suffered by the claimant.

The claimant is in breach of the by-laws of North Spring Bizhub and has caused damage to the unit.

35     I turn finally to the counterclaim. The defendant’s case is that by carrying out the unauthorised works on 21 December 2021, the claimant is in breach of the by-laws of North Spring Bizhub and has also caused damage to the Unit. I have made the finding above that unauthorised works have taken place. I therefore hold that the claimant is liable to the defendant for any damage caused to the Unit.

36     The defendant’s further case is that the claimant’s tenant, one Foam Lab Sg Pte Ltd (the “Tenant”) had conducted fitting out works without authorisation or approval. In February 2022, the Tenant installed a round fixture on an external wall. On 26 May 2022, the Tenant conducted renovation works without authorisation. The defendant relies on para 5 of the Second Schedule of the Building Maintenance (Strata Management) Regulations 2005 which states as follows:

Alteration or damage to common property

5.—(1)    A subsidiary proprietor or an occupier of a lot shall not mark, paint, drive nails or screws or the like into, or otherwise damage or deface, any structure that forms part of the common property except with the prior written approval of the management corporation.

37     It is seen that the regulation imposes obligations on both the subsidiary proprietor and the occupier of a unit not to undertake any works that would affect any structure that forms the common property, without the prior written approval of the management corporation. In the present case, I note that it is not disputed that the Tenant had carried out unauthorised works that damaged the common property. The claimant is therefore liable to make good any damage caused by the Tenant's unauthorised works and to indemnify the defendant in respect of any resultant costs and expenses.

38     In view of the foregoing, I find that the liability of the claimant for the counterclaim is made out. As the trial before me is bifurcated, I will determine the quantum of rectification costs payable by the claimant at the assessment of damages stage.

Conclusion

39     In the premises of all of the above, I find that the claimant has failed to prove its claim against the defendant on the balance of probabilities. The claim is accordingly dismissed.

40     As for costs, it follows the event and the claimant is to pay the costs of the claim. As regards the quantum of costs, the claimant is to pay the defendant the sum of $46,000 (plus GST if any) all in. The costs order takes into consideration, among others, the following:

(a)     The costs are on a standard basis.

(b)     The nature of the claim.

(c)     The time and work expended by counsel.

(d)     The expert evidence expenses.

(e)     The costs range in Appendix H of the State Courts Practice Directions 2021, at Pt IIIA, for tort claims being a) Pre-Trial: $9,000 - $30,000; b) Trial (daily tariff): $2,500 - $6,000; and c) Post-trial work: up to $8,000.

(f)     The breakdown of costs awarded is as follows: a) Pre-Trial: $18,000; b) Trial: $16,000 and c) Post-trial work: $6,000.

(g)     Disbursements payable by the claimant is fixed at $6,000.

41     As for the counterclaim, the defendant has proved its case, and I order interlocutory judgment for the counterclaim with damages to be assessed. I will reserve the question of costs and interest in respect of the counterclaim to the assessment of damages. The defendant is to file a summons for directions in respect of the assessment of damages for the counterclaim within 21 days of the date of this judgment.

html:
Public Prosecutor v Lee Yun Han

Public Prosecutor v Lee Yun Han
[2026] SGDC 204

Case Number:District Arrest Case No 919400 of 2025 & 19 Others
Decision Date:19 June 2026
Tribunal/Court:District Court
Coram: Paul Quan
Counsel Name(s): Melissa Heng (Attorney-General's Chambers) for the Public Prosecutor; David Nayar (David Nayar and Associates) for the Accused.
Parties: Public Prosecutor — Lee Yun Han

Criminal Law – Offences – Property – Cheating

Criminal Law – Statutory Offences – Computer Misuse Act – Unauthorised access to computer material

Criminal Law – Statutory Offences – Corruption, Drug Trafficking and Other Serious Crimes (Confiscation of Benefits) Act – Concerned in arrangement by handing control of bank account to another person without taking reasonable steps to ascertain purpose of controlling account

Criminal Law – Statutory Offences – Corruption, Drug Trafficking and Other Serious Crimes (Confiscation of Benefits) Act – Possessing reasonably suspected to be benefits from criminal conduct

Criminal Law – Statutory Offences – Miscellaneous Offences (Public Order and Nuisance) Act – Unlawful provision of SIM card registered using person’s personal information

Criminal Procedure and Sentencing – Sentencing

19 June 2026

District Judge Paul Quan:

Introduction

1       This is a case involving offences related to scams, fraudulent tenancies and the unlawful provision of SIM cards.

Brief facts

2       The accused, Lee Yun Han (“Mr Lee”), a 33-year-old Singaporean, relinquished control over his personal and corporate bank accounts by disclosing his internet banking login credentials to those accounts to an unknown person “Claus”. He then abetted Claus to cheat various landlords into entering fraudulent tenancies when he knew he was not a true tenant who would observe the terms of the tenancy agreements. He also provided five SIM cards to Claus unlawfully.

Charges

3       Mr Lee has pleaded guilty to five charges, namely:

(a)     one of abetting an offence under section 55A(1)(a)(i) read with section 55A(1)(b)(ii) of the Corruption, Drug Trafficking and Other Serious crimes (Confiscation of Benefits) Act 1992 (“CDSA”) of being concerned in an arrangement with Claus to hand over control of his corporate bank account to Claus without taking reasonable steps to ascertain Claus’ purpose of controlling the account;

(b)     three of cheating under section 420 of the Penal Code 1871 (2020 Rev Ed) (“PC”); and

(c)     one of unlawful provision of SIM cards that he registered under section 39B(1) of the Miscellaneous Offences (Public Order and Nuisance) Act 1906 (2020 Rev Ed) (“MOA”) amalgamated as a course of conduct under section 124(4) of the Criminal Procedure Code 2010 (2020 Rev Ed).

4       He has also consented to have 15 other charges taken into consideration for the purpose of sentence (“TIC”), namely:

(a)     five charges of abetting an offence under section 3(1) of the Computer Misuse Act 1993 (“CMA”) of unauthorised access to the banking services of his personal bank accounts by disclosing his internet banking credentials to those accounts to Claus;

(b)     one similar CDSA charge;

(c)     two similar PC charges;

(d)     six charges of abetting the offence of cheating under section 417 PC by deceiving banks to open bank accounts in his name when he knew he would not be the sole operator of the accounts; and

(e)     one charge of possessing cash suspected to be criminal proceeds under section 55(1) CDSA.

Parties’ positions

5       Mr Lee has no similar criminal antecedents. The prosecution has sought a global sentence of 26 months’ imprisonment and a disgorgement fine of S$4,350 to be imposed on him. The defence has submitted a shorter term of 20 months’ imprisonment instead with the same disgorgement fine. While the parties agree on the individual sentences to be imposed on the charges proceeded against him, they differ on the number of consecutive sentences, with the prosecution asking for all but one of the sentences to run consecutively whereas the defence has asked for three sentences to run consecutively.

Court’s decision

6       I sentence Mr Lee to an aggregate term of 24 months’ imprisonment and also impose a total disgorgement fine of S$7,030 on him. I explain my sentencing decision on the charges proceeded against him in turn in this ex tempore judgment.

Handing over control of corporate bank account under section 55A(1)(a) CDSA

7       In November 2024, Mr Lee entered into an arrangement with Claus to hand over to Claus control of his corporate bank account, which he had opened, by disclosing his internet banking credentials to Claus in exchange for money.

Prescribed punishment

8       For the CDSA offence, Mr Lee can be punished with a fine not exceeding S$50,000 and/or imprisonment for a term not exceeding three years by virtue of section 55A(5) CDSA. Applying the Sentencing Advisory Panel’s guidelines on scams-related offences (“SAP Guidelines”),[note: 1] the parties agree that the sentence to be imposed on Mr Lee for this offence should be eight months’ imprisonment and a disgorgement fine of S$4,100.

Deterrence as operative sentencing principle

9       Deterrence is the operative sentencing principle in Mr Lee’s case, given the relevant context at the time of the offence in November 2024 of the prevalence of scams, the proliferation of money mules and the crucial role they play in equipping scam syndicates, as well as our resolute aim to effectively cut off the easy supply of new and existing bank accounts to scam syndicates: PP v Yip Kong Fai Clement [2024] SGDC 284 at [14].

10     The situation for scams-related offences was dire in 2024. The prevalence of scams remained worryingly unabated then with a 10.6% increase to 51,501 cases and a seven-fold increase in total losses to scams to at least a staggering $1.1b in 2024 as compared to 2023.[note: 2] Crippling the supply of enablers by denying scammers and scam syndicates the tools they need, such as payment accounts, is a key strategy that would significantly increase the difficulty for scammers to successfully conduct or profit from scams in Singapore.[note: 3] Preventing scammers from using bank accounts, the control of which has been ceded to members of scam syndicates, is an essential part in the fight against scams: SAP Guidelines at [6].

11     Specific deterrence also applies, given the recalcitrant nature of Mr Lee’s re-offending behaviour evinced by the spate of subsequent similar offences from November 2024 to February 2025, where he opened and/or handed control over six other bank accounts to Claus, after he committed the first offence of relinquishing his personal bank account in October 2024.

Application of SAP Guidelines

12     The corporate account was used to launder criminal proceeds obtained from two non-vulnerable scam victims involving S$15,000.

13     Applying the SAP Guidelines:

(a)     the starting sentence is six months’ imprisonment: SAP Guidelines at [11(a)]. In entering into the arrangement with Claus, Mr Lee failed to take reasonable steps to ascertain Claus’ purpose of controlling his bank account:

(i)       Claus was unknown to Mr Lee. Claus advertised fast cash for renting out bank accounts and Mr Lee responded to Claus and exchanged messages with him; and

(ii)       Mr Lee was in debt at the time and agreed to relinquish his bank account in exchange for money.

Mr Lee did so simply because Claus offered him fast cash for access to his bank account and Mr Lee was in need of money at the time. Indeed, he did receive at least $1,600 for this. Without exercising due diligence, he could neither have seriously thought that this arrangement was legitimate, nor that he could be paid not an insubstantial amount to do very little or nothing at all without any catch. In fact, he did not check with Claus as to what his account would be used for;

(b)     an upward adjustment of four months’ imprisonment to the starting sentence is warranted for opening a new corporate bank account to be handed over and being motivated to commit the offence for personal gain: SAP Guidelines at [13(a)], [13(d)]. This is higher than the illustrative uplift of three months’ imprisonment at [20(b)] of the SAP Guidelines because Mr Lee is more culpable in that he incorporated a company specifically for the purpose of opening the corporate bank account. Corporate accounts can be more heavily transacted than personal accounts and suspicious transfers should be more difficult to detect: PP v Amsyar Dinie Bin Abdul Ghafor, District Arrest Case No 9087525 of 2024 & 1 Other (26 November 2024), unreported, at [9]; PP v Jonathan Neo Choon Hian [2025] SGDC 297 at [31];

(c)     there ought to be a further upward adjustment of three months’ imprisonment to the starting sentence for opening another five bank accounts, two of which fortuitously had issues and handing over another account: SAP Guidelines at [13(a)] and [13(b)]. The harm caused by handing control over his corporate bank account and these other accounts must also be taken together in its totality. This necessarily means that the harm has to include at least the $86,898 that was traced to be laundered criminal proceeds obtained from four victims in respect of one of these accounts, even though this is the subject-matter of a TIC charge: SAP Guidelines at [13(f)]; PP v Praveen Nivash Velmurugan [2025] SGDC 45 at [15(d)];

(d)     a full 30% reduction in sentence can be accorded to Mr Lee for his guilty plea: SAP Guidelines at [17] and Illustration 1 at [20(e)]; and

(e)     a fine of S$4,100 should be imposed in addition to the custodial sentence to disgorge the financial gain from his offence: SAP Guidelines at [18]. This includes a total of S$2,500 he had received in respect of three of the TIC offences: PP v Su Jiqing Joel [2021] 3 SLR 1232 (“Joel Su”) at [98].

Sentence of nine months’ imprisonment and disgorgement fine of S$4,100 imposed

14     The final sentence I arrive at and impose for Mr Lee’s CDSA offence is therefore nine months’ imprisonment and a disgorgement fine of S$4,100.

Fraudulent tenancies

15     From December 2024 to January 2025, Mr Lee abetted Claus to cheat three landlords into entering fraudulent tenancies. He deceived the landlords into believing that he was the rightful party leasing their premises as the tenant who would observe the terms of the tenancy agreements when he had no such intention to do so. The properties were then used to perpetrate rental scams by Claus and his associates on potential tenants parting with rental deposits but unable to move into these properties because Mr Lee was the registered tenant of these properties.

Prescribed punishment

16     For the cheating offences, Mr Lee must be imprisoned for a term that may extend to ten years, which can be coupled with a fine. The parties agree that the sentence of six months’ imprisonment per charge ought to be imposed on Mr Lee. The parties also agree that I can take guidance from Woo Haw Ming v PP [2023] 3 SLR 1041 (“Woo”) in this regard.

Deterrence as operative sentencing principle

17     The private, contractual nature of tenancy agreements do not detract from the clear public interest in deterring the proliferation of fraudulent tenancies: Woo at [31]. The difficulty in detecting such tenancies also draws considerations of specific and general deterrence to the forefront of the sentencing calculus: Woo at [36].

Mr Lee’s culpability

18     That Mr Lee met the property agents, viewed the premises, signed the inventory lists and collected the keys to the premises pursuant to his agreement to assist Claus with no intention to reside in the premises, did so for S$500 for each agreement under the instructions of Claus, who did not account for why he could not do so himself, and delivered the keys to the properties to Claus through a delivery company, grounded the inference that he knew the premises would be used for illicit activities: Woo at [30]. Because Mr Lee knew he would not be the true tenant observing all the terms of the tenancy agreements and the rightful party leasing the premises, it did not lie in his mouth to say he did not know what Claus intended to do with the premises, including using them for criminal activities

Harm caused by Mr Lee’s offences

19     The harm caused should not be confined to the landlords’ pecuniary losses and should extend to consideration of the fact that the landlords did not consent to have their properties exploited for rental scams, as well as Mr Lee facilitating the later rental scams and introducing distance between law enforcement authorities and the perpetrators of the broader scheme, such as Claus and his associates: Woo at [31]. By his facilitative fraudulent criminal conduct, Mr Lee has also subverted public order by enabling others to commit further criminal offences: PP v Tan Wen Jie [2021] SGDC 183 at [50].

Mr Lee’s case more egregious than Woo’s case

20     The accused in Woo’s case faced two cheating charges proceeded against him for entering into two fraudulent tenancies on 31 January 2019 and sometime before 4 December 2019. He was paid S$100 for entering into the first tenancy. He also faced two other TIC charges where he entered into similar fraudulent tenancies on 11 January 2019 and 20 January 2019. The appellate court upheld the sentence of three months’ imprisonment imposed per charge by the district court.

21     The facts of Mr Lee’s case is decidedly more egregious. He faces three of such charges proceeded against him committed on 3 December 2024, 16 December 2024 and 22 January 2025. He was paid S$500 in respect of each tenancy and paid a total of S$2,500, including two fraudulent tenancies in respect of two similar TIC charges. He was also paid $180 for transport to the properties. I also took into account the fact that the consequent rental scams resulted in 26 victims suffering a total loss of S$185,151.60 that were not recovered:

The severity of the rental scams is underscored by the fact that they would have attracted sentences of between 12-15 months’ imprisonment if prosecuted as cheating offences.

Sentences of six to eight months’ imprisonment and disgorgement fine of $500 to S$1,180 imposed per charge

22     Mr Lee’s cheating offences should attract at least six months’ imprisonment per count. The prosecution did not seek any disgorgement fines. The jurisprudence on disgorgement fines is well established and can be found across different types of offences, even for those whose maximum prescribed punishments are capped below the District Court’s sentencing limit: PP v Lim Yung Keng Adam [2023] SLR (StC) 416 (“Adam Lim”) at [52]. As a matter of principle, I am not precluded from imposing such fines: Adam Lim at [55(c)] and [56]. The principle is that:

(a)     where an offender is sentenced to an imprisonment term, the court may, in addition to that imprisonment term, impose a fine, and

(b)     the primary purpose of doing so would be to disgorge the profits which he may have made from his illegal behaviour, subject to the maximum limit of the fine prescribed by statute: Joel Su at [37]. Such fines serve to punish and deter: Joel Su at [48] and [50].

23     I therefore impose a sentence of six months’ imprisonment and a disgorgement fine of $500 for the first cheating offence in DAC 919402 of 2025.

24     To reflect the overall recalcitrant nature of Mr Lee’s offending evinced by his multiple offending (including the two TIC charges committed on 14 December 2024 and 25 February 2025), I apply an uplift to the sentences for the subsequent offences:

(a)     seven months’ imprisonment and a disgorgement fine of S$1,000 for the cheating offence in DAC 919404 of 2025, having committed this offence when he had already committed, not one but two, recent similar offences in DAC 919402 of 2025 and DAC 919403 of 2025, the latter being just two days ago; and

(b)     eight months’ imprisonment and a disgorgement fine of S$1,180 for the offence in DAC 919405 of 2026, having committed this offence when he had already committed three previous offences and barely a month after he committed the offence in DAC 919404 of 2025 and a subsequent offence in DAC 919406 of 2025 a month later.

Unlawful provision of local SIM cards

25     In February 2025, Mr Lee agreed to register mobile lines in exchange for money at the Claus’ request. He did not enquire why Claus required these mobile lines. Subsequently, he provided five local SIM cards to Claus for S$250, without knowing why Claus needed the mobile lines, why he could not register the lines himself and why Claus paid him to do this. He therefore had reasonable grounds to believe that this was to facilitate the commission of an offence and the SIM cards would be used for such improper purposes but did not dwell further.

Prescribed punishment

26     By virtue of section 39B(4)(a) MOA, The offence of provision of SIM cards using a person’s personal particulars attracts a fine not exceeding S$10,000 and/or imprisonment not exceeding three years.

27     Taking reference from the SAP Guidelines relating to the disclosure of Singpass credentials under section 8A CMA, the parties agree that Mr Lee should be imprisoned for six months and fined S$250. As the MOA charge is amalgamated, I also have to consider sentencing within the broader approach laid down in Prakash s/o Mathivanan v PP [2025] 4 SLR 1886 for charges amalgamated under section 124(4) CPC.

Deterrence as operative sentencing principle

28     Parliament clearly intended for deterrence and accountability to undergird the criminalisation of misusing local SIM cards, with the penalties of such offences being pegged to those for the misuse of Singpass credentials under the CMA (Singapore Parl Debates; Vol 95, Sitting No 133; [2 April 2019] (Josephine Teo, Second Minister for Home Affairs):

(a)     the offence circumvents previous successful efforts to block all incoming overseas calls that spoof local numbers. In response, scammers pivoted to using local SIM cards to reach prospective victims. The locally registered numbers deceptively veil scam calls and SMSes with a cloak of legitimacy, causing prospective victims to fall prey;

(b)     local numbers have also been used to set up WhatsApp and Telegram accounts to target victims or receive their monies via PayNow; and

(c)     this was against a general backdrop from a sampling study that close to 80% of local SIM cards misused for crime were registered with another person’s particulars.

29     In 2024, messaging platforms were the most common means by which scammers contacted victims, with an increase in the number of such cases from 12,368 in 2023 to 15,145 in 2024, and with WhatsApp and Telegram being the top two messaging platforms exploited by scammers.[note: 4] The number of scams perpetrated on Telegram saw an increase of about 95.7% in 2024.[note: 5]

Guidance taken from SAP Guidelines

30     The prosecution has submitted that guidance can be taken from the SAP Guidelines on the basis that:

(a)     Parliament has pegged the penalties for a section 39B(1) MOA offence to that of sections 8A and 8B CMA, to which the SAP Guidelines apply;

(b)     the unlawful provision of local SIM cards, like the misuse of Singpass credentials and Singpass accounts, enables scammers to perpetrate their crimes. The sentencing considerations for various scams-related offences under the CDSA, CMA and PC contemplated by the SAP Guidelines are likewise relevant and therefore apply to offences under section 39B(1) MOA; and

(c)     the starting sentence of six months’ imprisonment that applies to an archetypal section 8A CMA offence should apply in Mr Lee’s case given the “similar level of culpability between both offences, and the similar potential harms” with upward adjustments to be made to account for:

(i)       Mr Lee’s motivation by gain to commit the offence,

(ii)       Mr Lee providing five different SIM cards to Claus, and

(iii)       a victim’s loss of S$8,400 to a rental scam with one of the mobile lines being used in relation to the scam.

The defence has highlighted that there is no specific SAP sentencing framework or benchmark that is directly applicable to the offence.

31     I am in general agreement with the prosecution’s approach. These courts have previously also adopted the same approach: see eg PP v Muhammad Darwiis Bin Zainudin [2025] SGDC 265 at [25] and [28]; PP v Haryani Binte Juraimi [2026] SGDC 163 at [66]. I will only make one caveat. As between a section 39B(1) MOA offence and a section 8A CMA offence, the latter offence is the more serious, given the nature of Singpass accounts, what they can do and the consequences when they are compromised: SAP Guidelines at [27]. The unlawful provision of local SIM cards is more akin to handing over control of bank accounts under section 55A(1) CDSA but is more serious because they can be used to make scam calls, send scam messages, open bank accounts or e-wallets and/or set up WhatsApp or Telegram accounts to target victims. Such unlawful provision is no less debilitating with a single local mobile line being linked to 48 job scam reports with losses amounting approximately to S$1m in a 2021 case that was cited in Parliament: see [28], above.

32     Practically, nothing turns on this in the context of the SAP Guidelines. Under the guidelines, the starting sentence of six months’ imprisonment is the same for both an archetypal case under section 55A(1) CDSA and section 8A(1) CMA. The objective mens rea requirement of reasonableness is also the same as are the relevant offence-specific factors and the recommended uplifts. Guidance can therefore be taken from the SAP Guidelines in Mr Lee’s case for his section 39B(1) MOA offence.

Application of Prakash sentencing approach for amalgamated charge

33     I apply the Prakash sentencing approach for amalgamated charges under section 124(4) CPC as is the case here.

Stage 1: Identify punishment prescribed for offence

34     At the first stage, I must identify the punishment prescribed for the MOA offence: Prakash at [42]. By virtue of section 39B(4) MOA, this is a fine not exceeding S$10,000 and/or imprisonment not exceeding three years. Sentencing factors, including the harm caused and the factors which relate to the manner and mode by which the offence is committed, and the benchmark for a unamalgamated charge (or analogous precedents where no benchmark is applicable) would generally remain relevant for sentencing in respect of the amalgamated charge: Prakash at [42].

35     Taking guidance from the SAP Guidelines, the indicative starting point sentence ought to be seven-and-a-half months’ imprisonment had the MOA charge been unamalgamated based on a starting sentence of six months’ imprisonment for an archetypal case and an upward adjustment of one-and-a-half months’ imprisonment to take into account the fact that Mr Lee was motivated by gain to commit the offence and was indeed paid S$250 for his efforts.

Stage 2: Determine appropriate starting point sentence

36     At the second stage, the court will determine the appropriate starting point sentence based on a holistic assessment of the offender’s culpability over the entire course of conduct and having regard to the aggregate harm caused and the offender’s overall culpability: Prakash at [43]. By virtue of section 124(8)(a)(ii) CPC, Mr Lee is subject to double the punishment prescribed by section 39(B)(4)(a) MOA. Generally, the criminality of an offender would be increased by virtue of the repetition of criminal behaviour, as compared to an offender who had committed a single offence, even if the total harm caused by the two offenders was otherwise identical: Prakash at [43]. Both the number of incidents and the aggregate outcome have been made known by the prosecution and I may consider both in my assessment of Mr Lee’s culpability and the harm caused: Prakash at [44].

(1)   Duration and frequency of offending conduct relevant to culpability

37     The duration and frequency of the offending conduct are relevant to the offender’s culpability. An offender who has repeated the offence multiple times over a sustained period of time would have demonstrated greater recalcitrance, which is an aggravating factor: Prakash at [45(a)]. In this case, Mr Lee provided five SIM cards over the course of a day. The upshot is that he had engaged in five occasions of unlawful provision within a single day, evincing an abject disregard for doing so.

(2)   Aggregate outcome of offence as indicative of overall harm

38     The aggregate outcome of the offence would be indicative of the harm caused by the entire course of conduct: Prakash at [45(b)]. In this case, that outcome is represented by the victim’s loss of S$8,400 to a rental scam with one of the mobile lines being used in relation to the scam.

(3)   Indicative starting point sentence of ten-and-a-half months’ imprisonment on amalgamated charge

39     A further upward adjustment of three months’ imprisonment to the indicative starting point sentence is warranted. The indicative starting point sentence is therefore ten-and-a-half months’ imprisonment on a claim-trial basis.

Stage 3: Consider offender-specific aggravating and mitigating factors

40     At the third stage, having considered the relevant offence-specific factors and having determined the appropriating starting point sentence, the court then considers the relevant offender-specific aggravating and mitigating factors before deciding on whether adjustments are required to the starting point sentence: Prakash at [46].

(1)   No personal aggravating factors

41     There are no personal aggravating factors in Mr Lee’s case.

(2)   Clean record not mitigatory because of multiple offending

42     Although Mr Lee has no previous criminal antecedents, I do not regard him as a first-time offender because he had committed multiple offences: Chen Weixiong Jerriek v PP [2003] 2 SLR(R) 334 at [17]. In any event, the absence of antecedents is at best a neutral factor: BPH v PP [2019] 2 SLR 764 at [85], and it could not be seriously argued that Mr Lee’s offending behaviour was an aberration and out of character for him because of the multiple occasions of provisioning: PP v BWJ [2023] 1 SLR 477 at [102].

(3)   Guilty plea carries mitigatory weight

43     Mr Lee’s guilty plea carries mitigatory weight and I accord him the full 30% reduction in sentence following the recommendations of the SAP in its guidelines in this regard.

Sentence of seven months’ imprisonment and disgorgement fine of S$250 imposed

44     The final sentence I arrive at and impose on Mr Lee for his MOA offence is therefore seven months’ imprisonment and a fine of S$250 to disgorge the financial gain from his offence.

Conclusion

45     The individual sentences I impose on the charges that is proceeded against Mr Lee are:

Charge

Sentence

DAC 919400 of 2025

(concerned with arrangement to hand over control of corporate bank account)

Nine months’ imprisonment and fine of S$4,100, in default four weeks’ imprisonment

DAC 919402 of 2026

(fraudulent tenancy)

Six months’ imprisonment and fine of S$500, in default five days’ imprisonment

DAC 919404 of 2026

(fraudulent tenancy)

Seven months’ imprisonment and fine of S$1,000, in default one week’s imprisonment

DAC 919405 of 2026

(fraudulent tenancy)

Eight months’ imprisonment and fine of S$1,180, in default one week’s imprisonment

MAC 908700 of 2025

(Unlawful provision of SIM cards)

Seven months’ imprisonment and fine of S$250, in default two days’ imprisonment



46     As Mr Lee has been convicted of three or more distinct offences, I am mandated by law to run the sentences for at least two of the offences consecutively. The prosecution has urged me to run four out of the five sentences consecutively. This will come close to a full cumulative sentence and running three of such sentences would suffice. I therefore order the sentences on DAC 919400 of 2025, DAC 919405 of 2026 and MAC 908700 of 2025 to run consecutively. The three CDSA, PC and MOA offences are separate, unrelated and violate different legal interests and the sentences on them should be presumptively ordered to run consecutively as such: PP v Raveen Balakrishnan [2018] 5 SLR 799 at [41] and [102].

Sentence of 24 months’ imprisonment and disgorgement fine of S$7,030 imposed

47     I sentence Mr Lee to an aggregate term of 24 months’ imprisonment and also impose a total disgorgement fine of S$7,030 on him. If Mr Lee does not pay the fine, he will serve six weeks’ and seven days’ imprisonment in default.

48     The aggregate sentence is neither excessive nor inadequate: Gan Chai Bee Anne v PP [2019] 4 SLR 838 at [20]. It is sufficient because:

(a)     it reflects the gravity of the offences involved: PP v Law Aik Meng [2007] 2 SLR(R) 814 at [56],

(b)     Mr Lee’s overall criminality cannot be encompassed in two consecutive sentences: PP v Syamsul Hilal bin Ismail [2012] 1 SLR 973 at [32], and

(c)     of the multiplicity of his offences: Mohamed Shouffee bin Adam v PP [2014] 2 SLR 998 (“Shouffee”) at [41]. In particular, the aggregate sentence should not represent some sort of bulk discount in sentencing that has the effect of conveying the unintended impression or suggestion that Mr Lee does not have to bear the full brunt of the consequence of multiple offending: Raveen Balakrishnan at [46], [75] and [81].

49     The aggregate sentence will also not be:

(a)     crushing – Mr Lee’s lack of antecedents notwithstanding given his multiple offending, and taking into account his future prospects, considering a 24-month (with an additional seven weeks if he does not pay the fine) disruption to his current station in life being 33 years old presently: Shouffee at [57], or

(b)     disproportionate – the aggregate sentence is not substantially above the normal level of sentence for the most serious of the individual sentences committed, being the CDSA offence: Shouffee at [54]. As the SAP Guidelines contemplates a starting point for an archetypal offence and not a sentencing range from which to derive the normal level of sentence: Haliffie bin Mamat v PP [2016] 5 SLR 636 at [79], I have regard to the midpoint of the maximum prescribed sentence of three years’ imprisonment for the offence as a useful proxy instead: Ye Lin Myint v PP [2019] 5 SLR 1005 at [94]. An aggregate sentence that is six months more than this midpoint cannot be said to be disproportionate. The more important point is that the aggregate sentence is commensurate with Mr Lee’s overall criminality: Shouffee at [80].

50     No ‘last-look’ adjustment to the aggregate sentence is necessary: Shouffee at [58] and [59].

51     I backdate the sentence of imprisonment when Mr Lee was first arrested on 8 March 2025 to take into account the period of police custody and exclude the period when he was out on bail from 9 March 2025 to date.

[note: 1]Sentencing Advisory Panel, “Guidelines for Scams-Related Offences” (21 August 2024), online:<https://www.sentencingpanel.gov.sg/files/Guidelines/Guidelines_For_Scams_Related_Offences.pdf>.

[note: 2]Singapore Police Force, “Annual Scams and Cybercrime Brief 2024” (25 February 2025) at [2], online: <https://www.police.gov.sg/-/media/63E8611E0D1C4F09B6AFA533260CD04F.ashx>.

[note: 3]Sim Ann, Senior Minister of State, Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Ministry of Home Affairs, Opening Speech at the second reading of the Criminal Law (Miscellaneous Amendments) Bill (4 November 2025) at [10], online: <https://www.mha.gov.sg/mediaroom/parliamentary/second-reading-of-the-criminal-law-miscellaneous-amendments-bill-opening-speech>.

[note: 4]See footnote 2 at [15].

[note: 5]See footnote 2 at [16].

html:
Public Prosecutor v Abdul Marzuq Waliyuddin Bin Abdul Majid

Public Prosecutor v Abdul Marzuq Waliyuddin Bin Abdul Majid
[2026] SGMC 76

Case Number:MAC-909726-2025
Decision Date:19 June 2026
Tribunal/Court:Magistrate's Court
Coram: Toh Han Li
Counsel Name(s): DPP Chong Kee En (Attorney-General's Chambers) for the Prosecution; Mr Sean Marican (M M Marican & Co) for the Accused
Parties: Public Prosecutor — Abdul Marzuq Waliyuddin Bin Abdul Majid

Criminal Law – Offences – Distribution of intimate recording

Criminal Procedure and Sentencing – Sentencing

Criminal Procedure and Sentencing – Compensation – Emotional trauma

19 June 2026

Principal District Judge Toh Han Li:

Introduction

1       The accused pleaded guilty to the following charge:

You…are charged that you, sometime between 12 April and 24 May 2021, in Singapore, had intentionally distributed an intimate image of one [redacted] (“the victim”), to wit, by uploading intimate recordings of the victim on the MeWe social media platform, without her consent to the distribution, and knowing that the distribution would cause the victim humiliation, and you have thereby committed an offence under Section 377BE(1) punishable under Section 377BE(3) of the Penal Code 1871.

Facts

Background

2       In 2016, the accused and the victim were in a romantic relationship. They met while attending a religious school. During their relationship, the accused persuaded the victim to exchange intimate videos and photos of themselves. The accused was then 17 years old, and the victim was then 15 years old.

3       Sometime between January to June 2016, at the accused’s urging, the victim sent to the accused photos and at least two videos of herself naked and masturbating, by touching herself at her breasts and vagina. In both videos, the victim was fully naked with her face visible as she masturbated (“the Videos”). The Videos were about two minutes in length each.

4       Sometime in 2017 or 2018, the victim broke up with the accused as she felt that he was possessive and toxic. When they broke up, she deleted any intimate photos and videos she had of him, and she asked that he do the same. The accused told her that he had deleted her intimate photos and videos. However, unbeknownst to the victim, the accused retained the videos and photos for his “viewing pleasure”.

5       After they broke up, the accused tried to contact the victim again as he wished to explain his “side of the story”, but the victim did not respond. The accused then got into a relationship with another woman.

Facts pertaining to the Proceeded Charge

6       On 12 April 2021, the accused decided to message the victim. At this time, the accused was 22 years old and the victim was 20 years old. It was the Ramadan month (13 April to 12 May 2021), and the accused wanted to seek forgiveness from the victim for his behaviour during their relationship and asking to get back together, even though he was in a relationship with someone else. The victim did not respond and decided to block him.

7       When the accused saw that the victim had blocked him, he became furious. Angered by her rejection and wanting to humiliate her, the accused decided to log on to his account on the “MeWe” social media platform. At this point, the MeWe platform had millions of users.

8       Prior to April 2021, sometime in November 2020, the accused created an account on the MeWe platform to browse pornography. The accused joined several groups on MeWe dedicated to pornography. Two of them involved non-consensual pornography – “sgnsfw” (Singapore Not Safe For Work) and “Awek Tudung” (Tudung-Wearing Girls). The Awek Tudung Group was a closed group requiring the administrator to accept one’s request to join before being able to see the content posted by all the other members in the group, whilst the sgnsfw Group was an open-access group allowing anyone on the MeWe platform to access its content.

9       On or around 12 to 14 April 2021, driven by anger at the victim’s rejection, the accused decided to rename his MeWe account as the victim’s name, i.e., “[redacted]” – which would be visible to all on the MeWe platform. Simultaneously, the accused made snippets of one of the Videos (“the Snippets”) – i.e., shorter length videos of about five seconds – featuring the victim masturbating. Using his newly named “[redacted]” account (“the [redacted] Account”), the accused posted the Snippets on the sgnsfw Group. From 12 April to 24 May 2021, the accused posted the Snippets around 10 times on the sgnsfw Group.

10     At the same time, using the [redacted] Account, the accused also began posting the Snippets on the Awek Tudung Group. The accused retrieved recent photos of the victim from her Facebook page and her Facebook header (with her full name). The accused also had a photoselfie of the victim in full religious garb, in which she was touching herself at her vaginal area. In these photos, the victim’s face could be seen.

11     Using the [redacted] Account, the accused posted the various photos of the victim together with the Snippets sometimes in side-by-side “Before/After” comparisons on the Awek Tudung Group. At other times, he posted them with captions such as “SG Madrasah Babe”. The accused knew that the victim was attending religious instruction at this time, and that many of the members on the Awek Tudung Group were Singaporean or Malaysian Malays.

12     Attracted by the accused’s posts containing the Snippets of the victim on the Awek Tudung Group, two other users “M A” and “P N” decided to follow him on MeWe, and he in turn requested to follow them. On the basis of his sharing the Snippets, “M A” and “P N” accepted his “follow” request, allowing him to view the pornographic content shared by them. The trio would often discuss rape fantasies amongst themselves. The accused also personally sent the Snippets to other users on the Awek Tudung Group such as user “P E” who would re-post/re-share the Snippets. The accused would re-post/re-share on the Awek Tudung Group using his account.

13     The accused made the posts and re-posts referred to above on the Awek Tudung Group several times throughout the period of 12 April to 24 May 2021.

14     The accused had intentionally distributed intimate recordings (the Snippets) of the victim on the MeWe social media platform without the victim’s consent, and he had done so knowing that the distribution would cause the victim humiliation.

Discovery of the Offences

15     On 22 May 2021, the victim received an Instagram message from an unknown male “[redacted]” asking if she was “[redacted]” and sexually soliciting her as he was under the impression that she had posted her own nudes on MeWe under the name “[redacted]”. The victim then realised that someone was impersonating her. The victim informed “[redacted]” that it was not her and asked where he had obtained her nudes. He in turn sent her a link to the Awek Tudung Group.

16     The victim suspected that it was the accused who had shared her nudes. For a few days, she felt deeply distressed, but she decided to gather up her courage and go incognito in order to undertake her own investigation. On 25 May 2021, the victim created an undercover account on the MeWe platform and joined the Awek Tudung Group. She was horrified to discover that the Group consisted of many posts of obscene images and videos of various tudung-clad women and that her images were amongst these posts.

The Court’s decision on sentence

68     The sentencing framework for offences under section 377BE(1) Penal Code as set out in GED was applicable here.

69     The predominant sentencing principle here was deterrence. The speeches that the Prosecution had highlighted in Parliament with regard to the passage of these amendments to deal with such offences were relevant and undoubtedly catered for factual situations such as the present case, which was a classic case of “revenge porn”.

The GED sentencing framework

70     In GED, the High Court applied a five-step framework for offences under section 377BE(1) Penal Code:

a)     First step: Consider the relevant offence-specific factors and identify the level of harm (objective and subjective) and the offender’s culpability.

b)     Second step: Identify the applicable indicative sentencing range.

c)     Third step: Identify the starting point within the range.

d)     Fourth step: Make such adjustments to the starting point as may be necessary to take into account the relevant offender-specific aggravating and mitigating factors.

e)     Fifth step: Consider whether further adjustment need to be made on account of the totality principle.
