72     I proceeded to consider the offence-specific factors pertaining to harm and culpability in the present case.

Harm

Objective aspects of harm

73     As noted in GED at [51] to [53], the three relevant objective aspects of harm were the nature of the image or recording, the identifiability of the victim and the nature and extent of the distribution.

74     This entailed a consideration of:

a)     what parts of the victim’s body were shown and how exposed the body parts were (whether bare or covered);

b)     what acts were depicted; and

c)     the medium used (whether a still image or a video recording).

75     With regard to a) and b), the more intrusive and the more overtly sexual the nature of the acts (and/or the victim’s body parts) shown in the intimate image or recording, the higher the degree of objective harm that will generally be caused, all else being equal.

76     The relevant facts relating to the objective aspects of harm were as follows. The accused had an account on the “MeWe” social media platform which had millions of users at the material time. He joined several groups on MeWe dedicated to pornography. Two of them involved non-consensual pornography namely “sgnsfw” (Singapore Not Safe For Work) and “Awek Tudung” (Tudung-Wearing Girls). Sgnsfw was an open-access group allowing anyone on the MeWe platform to access the content in the group. The Awek Tudung Group was a closed group requiring the administrator to accept one’s request to join before being able to see the content posted by all the other members in the group.

77     Between January and June 2016, whilst they were in a relationship and at the accused’s urging, the victim had sent him photos and at least two videos of herself naked and masturbating (by touching herself at her breasts and vagina). In both videos, the victim was fully naked with her face visible as she masturbated, which were about two minutes long. The accused had made Snippets of one of the videos, which were shorter length videos of about five seconds, featuring the victim masturbating with her face visible. From 12 April to 24 May 2021, he posted the Snippets around 10 times on the sgnsfw Group.

78     The accused retrieved recent photos of the victim from her Facebook page and her Facebook header with her full name. He posted a photoselfie of the victim in full religious garb, in which she was touching herself at the vaginal area and her face was visible, on the Awek Tudung Group. The accused posted the various photos of the victim together with the Snippets sometimes in side-by-side “Before/After” comparisons on the Awek Tudung Group.

79     At other times, he posted them with captions such as “SG Madrasah Babe”. The accused knew that the victim was attending religious instruction at this time, and that many of the members on the Awek Tudung Group were Singaporean or Malaysian Malays.

80     Attracted by the accused’s posts containing the Snippets of the victim on the Awek Tudung Group, two other users decided to follow him on MeWe, and he in turn requested to follow them. On the basis of his sharing the Snippets, the two users accepted his follow request, allowing him to view the pornographic content shared by them. The trio would often discuss rape fantasies amongst themselves. The accused also personally sent the Snippets to other users on the Awek Tudung Group who would re-post/re-share the Snippets. The accused would also re-post/re-share on the Awek Tudung Group using his account. The accused made the posts and re-posts referred to above on the Awek Tudung Group several times throughout the period from 12 April to 24 May 2021.

81     On 27 May 2021, data obtained by the Police showed that there were 79,348 members on the Awek Tudung Group. Sgnsfw was an open-access group allowing anyone on the MeWe platform (which had millions of users) to access the content in the group.

82     Since the distribution of her nudes, the victim continued to have strangers contacting her via social media platforms asking her if she was the person in the nude pictures they had seen and soliciting her for sexual matters. She also had friends contacting her asking her about her nudes which they have come across on the internet.

Subjective aspects of harm

83     The subjective aspects of harm included any particular aspects of the victim’s suffering that would shed light on the degree of humiliation, alarm or distress subjectively experienced by the victim as a result of the offence, including any impact on the victim’s mental health, such as the development of conditions like depression or post-traumatic stress disorder (GED at [56]).

84     The court could take into consideration the circumstances and sensitivity of the particular victim (GED at [58]). This was illustrated by the case of R v Bostan (Amar) [2018] EWCA Crim 494 (“Bostan”). In Bostan, the offender knew that the victim was from a conservative family and that her mother would be shocked and ashamed that her daughter had allowed the offender to have such a photograph of her, in which she was naked above the waist only and was not doing anything overtly sexual. The court held that it should consider the greater subjective harm that may have been suffered by this particular victim owing to her family background and circumstances.

85     The court could also consider consequential harm other than emotional and psychological consequences (GED at [59]) as well as the vulnerability of the victim where the victim is young.

86     The facts relevant to the subjective aspects of harm were as follows.

87     In the present case, the accused had uploaded the Snippets and photos of the victim from April to May 2021, when the victim was 20 years old, depicting the victim when she was 15 years old, which was when the photos and videos had been made.

88     When the victim discovered that her nudes were being distributed on the group where there were pornographic materials of other females, she felt disgusted and overwhelmed with emotions. She was distraught when she saw the number of “likes” under her image. She wanted to end her life as she was ashamed and felt that her life was over as people would recognise her and have seen her in the nude. Her sister managed to stop her in time. After that, her mother distanced herself from her. At that time, she was doing Year 2 of her degree programme. She was under a lot of stress and anxiety due to her nudes being distributed by the accused, such that it affected her Year 2 finals examination as she noticed a fall in her overall grades.

89     Before the accused uploaded her images and videos, she was considering becoming an Asatizah as she was doing her degree in Islamic Jurisprudence and Its Knowledge. After the intimate images and videos were distributed, she decided not to become an Asatizah or work in any Islam-related industry as she was afraid that people would make comments about her career choice in the Islamic industry if they discovered nude images of her.

90     Since the distribution of her nudes, she had been in constant fear that people would recognise her. She continued to have strangers contacting her via social media platforms asking her if she was the person who depicted in the nude pictures they had seen and soliciting her for sexual matters and also had friends contacting her asking her about her nudes which they have come across on the internet. Due to this incident, the victim did not enter into a relationship as she was unable to trust anyone after what happened.

Conclusion on harm

91     In my view, practically all the harm factors as set out in GED, both objective and subjective, were engaged here. Her photos and videos, in which her face was fully visible and she was naked and masturbating, had been uploaded by the accused on platforms dedicated to pornography, namely the Awek Tudung Group with 79,348 members and Sgnsfw, an open-access group allowing anyone on the MeWe platform, which had millions of users to access the content in the group. The accused had retrieved recent photos of the victim from her Facebook page and her Facebook header with her full name and the accused posted a photoselfie of the victim in full religious garb, where she was touching herself at the vaginal area, on the Awek Tudung Group.

92     It was relevant that the victim was vulnerable as she was 15 years old in the images and videos (which would feed prurient interests on these platforms) and was undergoing religious instruction at the material time, which the incident had derailed. She had decided not to become an Asatizah or work in any Islam-related industry as she was afraid that people would make comments about her career choice in the Islamic industry if they discovered nude images of her. She was distraught when she saw the number of “likes” under her image. She wanted to end her life as she was ashamed and felt that her life was over as people would recognise her and have seen her in the nude. Her sister managed to stop her in time. After that, her mother distanced herself from her.

93     In the circumstances, I found the harm to be at the lower end of severe in the present case.

Culpability

94     I considered the following factors pertaining to culpability to be relevant, namely the accused’s motive for committing the offence, the degree of planning, preparation and premeditation, the duration and persistence of offending, the use of anonymity and the breach of conditions of station bail.

95     When they broke up, the victim had deleted any intimate photos and videos she had of him, and she asked that the accused to do the same. The accused lied to her that he had deleted her intimate photos and videos. Unbeknownst to the victim, he retained the videos and photos for his “viewing pleasure”.

96     The offence was then committed by the accused out of malice and with the intention to harm and humiliate the victim. When the accused saw that the victim had blocked him, he became furious. Angered by her rejection and wanting to humiliate her, he chose two platforms dedicated to pornography, accessible to millions of users which could access it and another with 79,348 members to do so. He depicted her in religious garb with her face visible, in the act of masturbating.

97     There was a fair degree of planning, preparation and premeditation on the accused’s part. He retrieved recent photos of the victim from her Facebook page and her Facebook header with her full name. He posted the various photos of the victim together with the Snippets sometimes in side-by-side “Before/After” comparisons on the Awek Tudung Group. He also posted them with captions such as “SG Madrasah Babe”. He knew that the victim was attending religious instruction at this time, and that many of the members on the Awek Tudung Group were Singaporean or Malaysian Malays. He shared the victim’s Snippets and engaged in discussions with two other users in the Awek Tudung Group on rape fantasies. From 12 April to 24 May 2021, he made the posts and reposts on the Awek Tudung Group several times and posted the Snippets around 10 times on the sgnsfw Group.

98     The accused did all this under the cloak of anonymity, pretending that it was the victim who had uploaded such images and videos using the victim’s name. As a result, the victim continued to have strangers contacting her via social media platforms asking her if she was the person in the nude pictures they had seen and soliciting her for sexual matters and also had friends contacting her asking her about her nudes which they had come across on the internet.

99     When the news broke about the Awek Tudung Group on 27 May 2021, the accused panicked and deleted his MeWe account. He also deleted the intimate videos and photos he had retained of the victim on his cloud account.

100    While the accused remained on station bail, one of the conditions was that he was not to interfere with any witness. On 20 September 2023, he contacted the victim using an anonymous account via Telegram in an attempt to apologise to her. The victim blocked him.

Conclusion on culpability

101    The accused was out to exact revenge on the victim and to harm and humiliate her by depicting her with her face and full name as a promiscuous person in religious garb in platforms dedicated to pornography with a large number of users. This led to the victim’s images and videos going viral and the victim continued to be sexually solicited to this day and had friends contacting her asking her about her nudes which they had come across on the internet. He had also spoken of her in demeaning terms with users of these platforms. He posted and reposted her images and videos multiple times over a period of more than one month. He tried to cover his tracks by deleting his MeWe account and his cloud account and also breached one of the station bail conditions by contacting the victim.

102    In the circumstances, I found the accused’s culpability to be at the lower end of high.

Uncharged offending

103    I considered the Prosecution’s submission that there were aggravating factors of uncharged offending namely, procurement of the victim’s intimate images from her when she was 15, which could have been an offence under section 7 Children and Young Persons Act (Cap 38, 2001 Rev Ed); and possession of intimate images which could have been an offence under section 377BD Penal Code.

104    I was of the view that these were not aggravating factors on the basis that they could have constituted separate offences, but rather, that they formed part of the factual matrix in the calibration of the level of harm and culpability as these facts had a nexus with the offence for which the accused was charged (GED at [83]).

105    Simply put, I had considered the victim’s age in the intimate images and videos as a harm factor, as well as the fact that the accused had lied to the victim that he had deleted the images and videos and had in fact retained them for his viewing pleasure despite being told by the victim to delete them as a culpability factor.

Distinguishing Chan Kok Kit, GED and GEH

106    The Defence sought to rely on Chan Kok Kit, where the offender had knowingly distributed an intimate recording of the victim, by uploading a video of the offender having sexual intercourse with the victim onto a pornographic website.

107    The court in Chan Kok Kit agreed with the Prosecution’s submission that it was a moderate harm, medium culpability case. In terms of harm, the court noted that the video was widely distributed and was found on eight pornographic websites and could have been seen by both strangers and those who knew the victim. The court noted that the victim was “mentally destroyed”, suffered “sleepless nights”, and was “afraid of guys”.

108    In terms of culpability, the court noted that the distribution of the video took place after the accused and the victim had ended their relationship. The court held that it could be inferred that the accused’s intent in uploading the video onto a pornographic website was to hurt and humiliate the victim, especially as he had not only posted something which exposed her face and naked body, but he had even deliberately posted her nickname, nationality and the area where she stayed.

109    In my view, Chan Kok Kit could be distinguished, as the facts of the present case were more aggravating than those in Chan Kok Kit, both in terms of harm and culpability for the following reasons.

110    First, the victim was 15 years old in the images and videos. There was nothing to suggest in Chan Kok Kit that the victim there was anything other than an adult.

111    Second, the victim was depicted in religious garb, and the accused knew that the victim was attending religious instruction and deliberately chose a platform dedicated to pornography, namely the Awek Tudung Group, whose members were Singaporean or Malaysian Malays.

112    Third, the accused used the victim’s Facebook page and her Facebook header which displayed her full name, as opposed to Chan Kok Kit, where the offender posted her nickname, nationality and the area where she stayed.

113    Fourth, as a result of the accused’s actions, the victim’s career had been impacted as she had decided not to become an Asatizah or to work in any Islam-related industry as she was afraid that people would make comments about her career choice in the Islamic industry if they discovered nude images of her.

114    Fifth, while the court in Chan Kok Kit inferred that the offender’s intent in uploading the video on a pornographic website was to hurt and humiliate the victim, it was specifically stated in the present case that the accused was angered by the victim’s rejection and wanted to humiliate her.

115    Sixth, the accused engaged in demeaning conversations with members of the Awek Tudung Group about the victim and discussed rape fantasies with them.

116    Seventh, one of the conditions of the accused’s station bail was that he was not to interfere with any witness, nevertheless, he breached this condition by contacting the victim.

117    The court in Chan Kok Kit stated that it did not impose (nor did the Prosecution seek) caning, on account of there being no violence being involved in the commission of the offence, nor were there any other considerations that warranted such a form of punishment.

118    With respect, the court in Chan Kok Kit did not specifically consider the second situation discussed in GED at [107] where caning would presumptively be warranted, namely where the offender widely disseminates (for example, on pornographic websites) images or recordings depicting the victim’s bare skin in such intimate regions or the victim engaging in a sexual act, and where the victim is identifiable or expressly identified. That said, there were also two key points of distinction, namely that the offender in Chan Kok Kit did not use the victim’s full name, unlike in the present case, and that the victim was only 15 years old in the images and videos.

119    In the circumstances, I was of the view that the facts of the present case were more aggravating than those in Chan Kok Kit both in terms of harm and culpability.

120    Defence counsel also relied on GED and GEH in submitting that the facts were less egregious in those cases. In GED, the image was circulated on the offender’s Facebook page under the “Public” setting, which attracted approximately 1,000 comments, 3,000 “likes”, and 2,000 “shares” within the eight hours that it was made available for. Upon seeing this, the offender in GED removed the first Facebook post and published a new Facebook post containing an edited version of the image in which the victim’s face was blurred but her breasts and the supervisor’s face were fully visible, and which was removed one day later. In GEH, a video of the victim’s penis was distributed by the offender to over 500 of the victim’s own personal contacts.

121    In my view, the facts of GED and GEH could be distinguished from the present case. In the present case, the images and videos of the victim with her full name taken from her actual Facebook page were uploaded onto platforms dedicated to pornography. The accused had posted on platforms dedicated to pornography from April to May 2021, namely the Awek Tudung Group with 79,348 members and Sgnsfw, an open-access group allowing anyone on the MeWe platform, which had millions of users to access the content in the group.

122    It was also clear that the images and videos of the victim continued to be circulated, as she continued to receive propositions to this day from persons who had seen her images and videos close to five years after the offence, and had friends contacting her asking her about her nudes which they had come across on the internet.

Starting point and adjustment for offender specific factors

123    The harm was severe and the culpability was high and based on the GED sentencing framework the range was 45 to 60 months’ imprisonment with the option of caning.

124    As the harm was as the lower end of severe and the culpability was at the lower end of high, I placed the starting point at 46 months’ imprisonment.

125    Applying the full 30% reduction at Stage 1 for the accused’s plea of guilt under SAP Guidelines, the sentence was 32 months’ imprisonment (rounded down). This was within the maximum of 36 months’ imprisonment that could have been imposed on a MAC charge.

126    As there was only one sentence of imprisonment imposed on the accused, the sentence was not crushing on the accused on a totality basis.

Caning

127    In GED, the High Court held at [107] that caning will presumptively be warranted in two specific situations:

We also agree with the Prosecution that caning will presumptively be warranted in certain situations. At this stage, we highlight two such situations: (a) where the offender uses criminal or violent means to capture images or recordings of bare skin in intimate regions of the victim’s body (by which we mean the victim’s genital or anal region or breasts, as specified in ss 377BE(5)(a)(i) and 377BE(5)(a)(ii) of the Penal Code); and (b) where the offender widely disseminates (for example, on pornographic websites) images or recordings depicting the victim’s bare skin in such intimate regions or the victim engaging in a sexual act, and where the victim is identifiable or expressly identified. Other situations where caning will presumptively be warranted should be considered and developed by the courts in appropriate future cases.

[Emphasis added]

128    In my judgment, these were two distinct situations discussed by the High Court in GED where caning was presumptively warranted. I did not accept the Defence’s submission that there necessarily had to be criminal or violent means to capture images of the victim before caning could be imposed. I should add that the sentencing matrix at set out in GED at [104] had caning as an option in six out of nine harm/culpability combinations, and hence it could not be only as narrowly constrained as the Defence had submitted, namely in a scenario where there were criminal or violent means to capture images of the victim.

129    In this regard, one of the two situations discussed in GED, namely category (b) as highlighted above, had been engaged in the present case. The accused had widely disseminated the victim’s images and videos when she was 15 years old, with her face fully visible and her full name visible, on platforms dedicated to pornography, the images and videos depicting her engaging in a sexual act of masturbation. Further, while the Defence had submitted that he did not intend to distribute the victim’s image or videos when he first obtained them, the fact was that he did so later on, motivated by revenge, depicting her at a young age with her full name identified and engaging in a sexual act. When they broke up, the victim had deleted all intimate photos and videos she had of him, and she asked that he do the same. However, the accused lied to her that he had deleted her intimate photos and videos but unbeknownst to the victim, the accused retained the videos and photos for his “viewing pleasure”.

130    In the circumstances, on the basis of general deterrence and retribution, caning was warranted.

131    Taking into account the fact that the accused had pleaded guilty and had spared the victim the trauma of testifying at a trial, I imposed two strokes of the cane on the accused. This was also the number of strokes imposed in GEH for the actual distribution offence.

Compensation

The Prosecution’s submissions on compensation

132    The Prosecution sought a compensation order of $5,000 for the victim’s emotional trauma sustained from the accused’s offence.

133    It submitted that in a case of distribution of intimate images or recordings under section 377BE(1) Penal Code, a “standard sum” of $2,500 should be awarded for emotional trauma and suffering. Where there was evidence that the distribution was repeated or widespread and extensive such as in the present case, the standard sum should be doubled to $5,000.

134    The Prosecution submitted that the principles as set out by the High Court in Tay Wee Kiat and another v Public Prosecutor and another appeal [2018] SGHC 114 (“Tay Wee Kiat”) were relevant for the award of compensation.

135    The Prosecution cited the following cases where compensation was awarded for sexual offences:

a)     In Public Prosecutor v Rosdiana Binte Abdul Rahim [2021] SGMC 78 (“Rosdiana”), compensation of $500 was ordered in respect of a charge of insulting the victim’s modesty under section 509 Penal Code (Cap 224, 2008 Rev Ed), in which the offender had made the victim shower in front of her and dress herself in a room with open windows (at [170]–[172]).

b)     In Public Prosecutor v Alan Ngai (unreported) (SC-906669-2022) (“Alan Ngai”), the District Judge (“DJ”) ordered compensation in the amount of $4,500 ($500 per charge) against the offender, who had committed, inter alia, voyeurism and uttered words to insult the modesty of the domestic helper.

c)     In Public Prosecutor v Pang Zong Kang (SC-908583-2025) (“Pang Zong Kang”) heard on 23 January 2026, the DJ ordered compensation of $500 against an offender who had committed a similar offence of voyeurism (filming a victim urinating), under section 377BB(3) Penal Code.

d)     In Public Prosecutor v Rajwin Singh Shelley (SC-909073-2024) (“Rajwin Singh”), the DJ ordered compensation of $500 against an offender who had committed upskirting offences under section 377BB(5) Penal Code.

136    The Prosecution submitted that a “rough and ready” measure may be used in a case of distribution of intimate images for a “standard sum” of $2,500 to be awarded for emotional pain and suffering. This sum would be doubled to $5,000 in cases where there is multiple offending and/or widespread distribution.

137    In this regard, the Prosecution noted that in Tay Wee Kiat at [19], the High Court referred to The Guidelines for the Assessment of General Damages in Personal Injury Cases (Academy Publishing, 2010) (“the Blue Book”) which set out the following awards with respect to general psychiatric disorders that involve a “myriad of psychiatric conditions that could result from experiencing a traumatic event”.

138    In minor cases of such psychiatric conditions, a plaintiff was awarded between $1,000 and $3,000, while a moderate case would lead to an award in the $3,000–$8,000 range. In cases of post-traumatic stress disorder, a minor case would be awarded between $2,000 and $4,000, while a moderate case would be awarded between $4,000 and $10,000. The figures for minor and moderate cases of psychological harm in the Blue Book corresponded with its proposed sum of $2,500 to $5,000.

139    The Prosecution submitted that the civil courts have also awarded compensation in sexual assault cases. In Kang May Teng, Maria Olivia v Chua Jun Yang [2025] SGDC 130 (“Maria Kang”), the District Court found that the digital penetration of the plaintiff by the defendant without her consent was sufficient to make out the tort of battery. The DJ awarded S$25,000 for pain and suffering (qua mental and emotional distress) (at [111]). This was even though the plaintiff did not require psychiatric treatment or medication and had a favourable prognosis. Whilst Maria Kang was subsequently reversed on appeal by the High Court in terms of liability, the Prosecution submitted that this did not detract from the fact that damages had been awarded in the lower court for pain and suffering.

140    The Prosecution submitted that as there were no reported decisions in relation to criminal compensation for distribution of intimate images, it may be useful to consider cases in other jurisdictions where such compensation had been meted out. In an unreported decision in the Chelmsford Crown Court, United Kingdom, an order of £22,305 was made against offender Mr Stephen Bear (“Stephen Bear”) after he was convicted of voyeurism and two counts of disclosing a private sexual film on a pornographic website. Of this amount, £5,000 was ring-fenced as criminal compensation to the victim.

141    Criminal compensation for emotional pain and suffering was especially appropriate in the present case given that the victim did not seek recourse to therapy as she felt that doing so would be cost-prohibitive.

142    The Prosecution submitted that whilst criminal compensation must be considered in all offences, it was particularly appropriate in sexual offences for the following reasons:

a)     First, victims of sexual assault experience indignity, mental and emotional suffering, humiliation and/or distress from the violation. The psychological harm and mental anguish suffered could be just as acute and enduring as physical harm, if not more. To this end, compensation for pain and suffering would be a symbolic gesture of reparative justice, affirming the dignity of the victim vis-à-vis the seriousness of the wrong, and was a logical next step given the Court’s finding beyond a reasonable doubt that the accused person had committed serious wrong(s).

b)     Second, victims of sexual assault faced an inherent risk of re-traumatisation if they had to bring civil suits against their assailants. Both Parliament and the Courts have recognised that there is a need to minimise the trauma faced in the court process by victims subject to sexual abuse.

c)     Third, it was impractical and expensive to expect victims of sexual assault to bring civil suits against accused persons. The lack of historical data for such civil suits speaks for itself. The Prosecution submitted that Maria Kang had been the sole civil case where a victim had sued for general damages arising from sexual assault. Specifically, Maria Kang involved a situation where criminal charges were not preferred against a defendant.

d)     Fourth, and in that same connection, whilst it was impractical for a victim to seek civil redress it was practical for a trial or sentencing judge, who would be familiar with the case and its surrounding facts, including the effects of the crime on the victim, and the matters set out in the Victim Impact Statement to make an award for pain and suffering.

143    The Prosecution submitted that criminal compensation was not simply about money. In a victim-centred criminal justice system, criminal compensation ensured that the traditional focus on punishing an offender did not lead to the victim being ignored and abandoned. Criminal compensation thus served to acknowledge harm whilst reinforcing accountability. Most importantly, by empowering victims through a symbolic award, compensation restores dignity and autonomy to victims who have been robbed of that very dignity and autonomy by sexual offences such as the present one.

144    The Prosecution accordingly urged the court to make a compensation order of $5,000 in the victim’s favour.

The Defence’s submissions on compensation

145    The Defence did not dispute that a compensation order could be made in the present case under the principles as set out in Tay Wee Kiat but disagreed on the quantum of the compensation order.

146    It submitted that the amount $5,000 sought by the Prosecution was excessive and urged the court to make a compensation order of $500. It cited Tay Wee Kiat at [7], where the High Court held that the purpose of compensation was not to punish the accused, and thus aggravating factors relating to the offence should find expression in sentencing and not in the quantum of compensation.

147    The Defence submitted that in cases following Tay Wee Kiat, the general amount of compensation was $500 per charge. This was the amount ordered in Rosdiana, Alan Ngai and Rajwin Singh and it was in only cases of severe physical harm where compensation of $1,000 was granted as in the case of Public Prosecutor v Lim Toon Leng and Seah Lei Sie Linda [2019] SGMC 12 where the offender had instigated the victim to pour hot water on herself.

148    The Defence submitted that in cases involving physical hurt which had both physical harm and psychological harm, as observed by the High Court in Tay Wee Kiat at [19], the starting point for physical hurt of a non-severe nature was $500. As distributing intimate images online involved only psychological harm, it submitted that the starting point ought to be at or lower than $500.

149    The Defence submitted that the Blue Book provided that minor psychiatric conditions are generally awarded between $1,000 and $3,000. The Defence submitted that the prerequisite of relying on this was that the victim must first establish that she was or had been suffering from psychiatric conditions or harm and to what extent. No medical reports were obtained by the victim when the onus was on her to demonstrate such psychiatric conditions given her claim for compensation.

150    As there were no medical reports produced to demonstrate psychiatric harm or its extent but taking a common-sense approach, the victim was likely to have suffered some elements of psychiatric harm, and the Defence accordingly submitted for a sum of $500 to be ordered as compensation.

The Court’s decision on compensation

151    In Tay Wee Kiat and another v Public Prosecutor and another appeal [2018] SGHC 114 (“Tay Wee Kiat”), the High Court had set out the following principles in making an order of compensation in a criminal case:

152    First, a compensation order did not form part of the sentence imposed on the offender, nor was it an alternative to a sentence, and its purpose was not to punish. For that reason, aggravating factors relating to the offence should find expression in sentencing and not in the quantum of compensation ordered. The purpose of compensation was to allow an injured party to recover compensation where a civil suit was an inadequate or impractical remedy (Tay Wee Kiat at [7]).

153    Second, compensation ought only to be ordered in clear cases where the fact and extent of damage are either agreed or readily and easily ascertainable on the evidence. This was because compensation was an ancillary power of a criminal court and should not usurp its core functions of trying and sentencing accused persons (Tay Wee Kiat at [8]). The assessment of loss or damage had to be based on some credible evidence and not simply on the Prosecution’s representations (Tay Wee Kiat at [13]). Simply put, this was a fact-specific enquiry and should not be simply based on a “standardised amount”.

154    Third, since criminal compensation was essentially a proxy for civil damages, the amount of compensation ordered should not exceed what would be reasonably obtainable in civil proceedings. In other words, the court could make a compensation order only in respect of the injury or loss which resulted from the offence for which the accused was convicted. At the same time, the order must not be oppressive but must be realistic in that the court must be satisfied that the accused would have the means to pay the compensation within a reasonable time (Tay Wee Kiat at [10]).

155    Fourth, regarding compensation for pain and suffering, the court in Tay Wee Kiat at [19] had regard to the Blue Book. In this regard, the Blue Book at Chapter 4, pages 25 to 27 provided the following range of awards for psychiatric conditions and stated that the factors to be taken into account in valuing claims of this nature were as follows:

i)     The person’s ability to cope with life and work in general as compared to his or her pre-trauma state;

ii)     The effect on the person’s relationships with family, friends and those with whom he or she came into contact with;

iii)     Whether the persons were suicidal because of his or her psychiatric condition

iv)     Whether medical help had been sought;

v)     The extent to which treatment would be successful;

vi)     The extent to which medication affected the persons work and social life;

vii)     Whether the persons adhered faithfully to counselling sessions and take his or her medications;

viii)     The risk of relapse in the future; and

ix)     The chances of full recovery in the future.

156    For minor psychiatric conditions, the Blue Book stated that an award of $1,000 to $3000 may be awarded in the following circumstances:

In this category, full recovery is achieved within a short period of time and the risk of relapse in the future is small. The person is able to return to previous employment with little or no residual disabilities. The level of award takes into consideration the short length of the period of disability and the extent in which daily activities and sleep were affected.

157    For moderate psychiatric conditions, an award of $3,000 to $8,000 may be awarded if the person experienced problems associated with the above factors at (i) to (vi).

158    In the present case, the victim did not seek psychiatric help as she felt it would be cost-prohibitive and did not want to talk to anyone about it as it was embarrassing for her.

159    In my judgment, and on the principles set out above in Tay Wee Kiat, several of the factors under the moderate category of the Blue Book for psychiatric conditions had not been engaged, specifically factors (iv) to (vii), namely that the victim did not seek medical help nor was she under any medication.

160    In terms of overseas precedents, I did not find the unreported case precedent of Stephen Bear helpful as the reasons for the award were not stated by the court Further, under the United Kingdom’s Criminal Injuries Compensation Scheme, injury payments were made for disabling mental injury, payments were made for £1,000 and upwards where there was disabling mental injury confirmed by the diagnosis or prognosis of a psychiatrist.

161    That said, I noted that factors (i) to (iii) at Chapter 4 of the Blue Book on awards for psychiatric conditions were engaged. The victim felt disgusted and overwhelmed with emotions upon discovering the accused’s posts and wanted to end her life, and her mother had distanced herself from her. She had been in constant fear that people would recognise her and never entered into a relationship as she was unable to trust anyone after what happened.

162    All things considered, I considered that an award at the top end of the minor category (with a range of $1,000 to $3000) was appropriate. I also considered that as the Blue Book was published in 2010, account must be taken of inflation since then, warranting an upward adjustment.

163    All things considered, I made a compensation order of $4,000 (in default two weeks imprisonment) to the victim.

[note: 1]Singapore Parliamentary Debates, Official Report (6 May 2019), vol 94.

[note: 2]Singapore Parliamentary Debates at pp 12-13 of 54

Public Prosecutor v Kelvin Sunderesan s/o Retchagadas

Public Prosecutor v Kelvin Sunderesan s/o Retchagadas
[2026] SGMC 74

Case Number:Magistrate's Arrest Case No 905668 of 2025, Magistrate's Appeal No 9098-2026-01
Decision Date:19 June 2026
Tribunal/Court:Magistrate's Court
Coram: Salina Ishak
Counsel Name(s): Chew Shi Jun James and Erfendi Dhahlan (Attorney-General's Chambers) for the Public Prosecutor; The accused acting in person.
Parties: Public Prosecutor — Kelvin Sunderesan s/o Retchagadas

Criminal Law – Statutory Offences – Protection from Harassment Act 2014 – Section 6(1)(a) – Using abusive words against a public servant

Criminal Procedure and Sentencing – Protection from Harassment Act 2014 – Section 8(1)(d) – Repeat offender – Offence committed against a court interpreter

[LawNet Editorial Note: An appeal to this decision has been filed in MA 9098/2026/01.]

19 June 2026

District Judge Salina Ishak:

Introduction

1       The present case involves the use of abusive words towards a court interpreter in the State Courts.

Background

2       The accused, Mr Kelvin Sunderesan s/o Retchagadas a 42-year-old male Singapore citizen, claimed trial to a charge of using abusive words towards a public servant, namely, one Sountharavalli d/o Mudhlie (“the victim”) a court interpreter, in relation to the execution of her duty, an offence under s 6(1)(a) of the Protection from Harassment Act 2014 (“POHA”). Another charge with a similar date, time of offence and victim in MAC 904886-2025 under s 14(2) of the Liquor Control (Supply and Consumption) Act 2015 was stood down. The proceeded charge against him is as follow:

MAC 905668-2025

Charge

are charged that you, on 30 May 2025, at about 9.10am, at the State Courts, 1 Havelock Square, Singapore, did use abusive words towards a public servant, namely, one Sountharavalli d/o Mudhlie, a court interpreter, in relation to the execution of her duty, to wit, by saying the words “I am going to fuck you up” towards her, and you have thereby committed an offence under s 6(1)(a) of the Protection from Harassment Act 2014, and

further that you, before the commission of the aforesaid offence, were convicted on 24 January 2022 of an offence under s 6 of the Protection from Harassment Act, Cap 256A vide MAC-906745-2021, which conviction has not been set aside, and you are therefore liable for enhanced punishment under s 8(1)(d) of the Protection from Harassment Act 2014.

 

3       On 24 April 2026, at the conclusion of the trial, I found the accused guilty and convicted him on the charge in MAC 905668-2025. I imposed a sentence of 15 weeks’ imprisonment with effect from his date of arrest on 30 May 2025. The stood down charge in MAC 904886-2025 was withdrawn and I ordered a discharge amounting to an acquittal in respect of the charge.

4       The accused filed an appeal on 28 April 2026 against his conviction and sentence. The accused has served his sentence for the present charge as I had backdated it to the date of his arrest on 30 May 2025. He completed serving his sentence as the release date was worked out to be on 8 August 2025. He has been in remand since 24 April 2026 for his outstanding 33 charges in his case file number SC-903750-2025.

5       I now set out the reasons for my decision. 

Issues

6       In the present case, I had to determine whether the Prosecution had proven the following issues beyond a reasonable doubt:

(a)     The words used by the accused were abusive and

(b)     On 30 May 2025 at 9:10am, the accused used abusive words towards the victim who was executing her duties as a court interpreter in the State Courts.

Prosecution’s Case

7       The Prosecution asserts that on 30 May 2025, on or before 8.47am, the accused was to appear in Court 4A for new charges to be read to him. The victim, Miss Sountharavalli d/o Mudhlie (PW2) was the court interpreter assigned for duty in Court 4A that day.

8       Prior to his court mention, the accused and his bailor, were at the atrium just outside Court 4A of the State Courts building, together with several police officers who had been dispatched to attend to an incident. The police officers were activated as the accused appeared to be drunk and kept raising his voice[note: 1]. PW1 Senior Staff Sergeant Mohamad Salihin bin Ibnor testified that he observed that the accused smelled of alcohol and kept raising his voice until he was reminded by the police officers to calm down[note: 2]. They remained at the atrium area until the accused’s case was ready for mention in Court 4A.

9       The Prosecution further asserts when the accused’s name was called by the court officer and his case was mentioned, he entered the dock of Court 4A accompanied by police officers. The victim approached the accused to verify his identity. She saw from her iPad that the accused had new charges which had not been read to him. The accused spoke loudly into the microphone that he did not care about the charges, and that there was no need for them to be read[note: 3]. The court stood down the matter and ordered the new charges to be read to the accused[note: 4].

10     The Prosecution asserts that the police officers then escorted the accused to the corridor space just outside the courtroom. When the victim asked the accused his choice of language, being intentionally difficult, he first requested for a Telugu interpreter and subsequently a Mandarin interpreter[note: 5]. After confirming with the accused that he wanted a Mandarin interpreter, the victim informed him that she would arrange for a Mandarin interpreter to assist. The accused pointed at the victim and said, “Get it done!”. The victim then started walking towards the door into Court 4A[note: 6].

11     As the victim walked away and just as she opened the courtroom door, the accused said the abusive words “I am going to fuck you up. See the arrogance.”[note: 7] in an aggressive manner towards the victim, while gesturing towards her. The accused’s words were heard by the victim. She testified that she felt very humiliated as the members of the public who were seated near the door turned and looked at her[note: 8]. She also felt offended as the accused scolded her using vulgarities.

12     The Prosecution further asserts that after the police officers managed to calm the accused down, he confirmed that he wanted to use the English language[note: 9]. The police officers then brought the accused to the atrium area outside Court 4A and requested the victim to come back to read the new charges to the accused. The victim testified that she still attended to the accused as it was her job to attend to accused persons, regardless of how difficult they can be[note: 10].

13     While the victim was reading out the charges to the accused in English at the atrium area, the accused made a comment about “pretty, boobs 34B”. Upon hearing this, the victim stopped and walked away again[note: 11]. The victim testified that she stopped attending to the accused at that point to avoid further insults and not to expose her new colleague, Miss Sai Sanjhurah Nair to further potential harassment[note: 12]. The accused was placed under arrest shortly after.

14     The Prosecution asserts that the incident was captured by the body-worn camera (“BWC”) of PW1[note: 13] and relies on the footage in support of its case. The Prosecution further relies on the redacted Criminal Records of the accused[note: 14] to establish that he was a repeat offender for the present charge.

Defence’s Case

15     The accused denies the present charge. He challenged the basis of his arrest as he asserts that there was no First Information Report nor a police report lodged by the victim in respect of the proceeded charge. He further asserts that no breathalyser test was conducted and denies he was drunk at the material time. Instead, he alleges that he was suffering from alcohol withdrawal[note: 15]. He testified that he was unable to recall the material facts relating to the charge due to the side effects of alcohol withdrawal. According to him, this was his third incident of alcohol withdrawal[note: 16].

16     During his cross-examination of the Prosecution’s witnesses, the accused alleges that he was obstructed by the police from entering the courtroom for his case. He further alleges that the body-worn footage (P1) did not show him scolding the victim[note: 17]. He asserts that the victim had already gone into the courtroom and the door was closed as the incident happened[note: 18]. He also asserts that the victim had walked away for 3 seconds before the incident as shown in the footage at P1 happened[note: 19]. He further asserts that no member of the public in Court 4A heard the abusive words on 30 May 2025 at 9:07am[note: 20].

17     According to the accused, he never scolded the victim and his actions after the incident occurred at 9:14am (at the atrium), were reasonable[note: 21]. In his closing submissions, the accused asserts that he had no reason to believe that the words used or behaviour used, or the communication made by the accused would be heard, seen or otherwise perceived by the victim[note: 22].

18     During his own cross-examination, the accused asserts that he has no memory of the incident as shown in the footage captured on PW1’s BWC[note: 23]. His testimony was based on his observation of his own body language and the way he behaved. He did not accept that the footage showed what had happened and wanted confirmation from another BWC footage[note: 24].

19     Nevertheless, the accused did not dispute the following facts namely:

(a)     The victim was the interpreter on duty in Court 4A, and she was tasked to read the charges to him[note: 25].

(b)     His case in Court 4A was stood down for the new charges to be read and explained to him[note: 26].

(c)     After stepping out of the courtroom, the accused and the victim were standing at the corridor space just outside the courtroom[note: 27].

(d)     The accused did not inform the victim that he wanted to use the English language but instead told her he wanted to use Telugu and after that Mandarin[note: 28].

When asked if the accused was purposely being difficult with the victim, he testified that he did not want to see or communicate with her[note: 29]. He disagreed when the Prosecution suggested that the victim was behaving in a professional manner[note: 30].

20     When asked whether it was acceptable to say the words in question to a public officer, the accused asserts that the words in question were not abusive and that he had not used them on the victim[note: 31]. According to the accused, the words have two meanings and were in fact acronyms which were not vulgar. He testified that the first acronym is for fornication under the consent of the king. The second acronym is for friendly, understanding, caring and kind[note: 32]. In his Closing Submissions, the accused further asserts that the abusive words were not uttered at the victim but was a soliloquy[note: 33].

21     The accused asserts that he did not raise his voice at the victim and that it was his normal voice. He denies that he was facing her direction when he uttered the said words. He also denies gesturing his arm in the victim’s directions and explained that he always gesticulates when he speaks. Nevertheless, when it was suggested by the Prosecution that he was mentally sound and knew what he was doing, the accused asserts that his behaviour in the footage was different from his normal self.

22     Hence, what I had to determine was first, whether the words were abusive and second, that it was directed at the victim at the material time.

The Law

23     To prove its case beyond a reasonable doubt, the Prosecution must satisfy the following elements namely:

(a)     The victim was a public servant.

(b)     Abusive words were used towards the victim.

(c)     The victim was executing her duty as public servant at the material time.

Undisputed Facts

24     In the present case, the following facts are undisputed:

(a)     The victim is a public servant.

(b)     The victim was executing her duty as public servant at the material time.

(c)     The words as set out in the charge were uttered by the accused.

(d)     The incident occurred at the corridor space just outside the doors leading into Court 4A.

(e)     From the BWC footage (P1), lawyers, prosecutors and members of the public could be seen entering and leaving the courtroom in quick succession.

Salient Facts

My Findings

25     To prove its case on the single proceeded charge, the Prosecution led evidence from three witnesses while only the accused gave evidence in his defence. The Prosecution relies primarily on the evidence of PW1 Senior Staff Sergeant Mohamad Salihin Bin Ibnor and PW2, the victim.

26     Although the elements of the offence and the facts were fairly straightforward, throughout the trial, the accused sought to obfuscate matters with his various requests namely, for the disclosure and production of evidence including the statements of Prosecution’s witnesses and other BWC footages, the court’s assistance to issue process to summon various witnesses and for bail to be offered to him. I dealt with these requests summarily after the Prosecution provided their response. The accused also made various allegations against the Prosecution and its witnesses in his 115-page Closing Submissions.

27     I now turn to my assessment of the evidence before me.

The victim’s evidence

28     In the present case, I found that the victim gave clear and consistent evidence of the accused’s conduct and the words he uttered towards her in an aggressive manner at the material time. Her evidence was independently corroborated by the clear objective evidence of the footage from PW1’s BWC. The footage not only captured the exact words uttered by the accused but also his aggressive behaviour as PW1 was facing him at the material time.

29     I accepted the victim’s evidence that she felt humiliated by the words uttered by the accused as the members of the public who were seated near the door reacted by turning and looking at her. In addition, she was also offended as the accused scolded her using vulgarities. In my view, the accused’s rejection of the footage (P1) and his insistence for confirmation from another BWC footage from a different angle was his attempt to distance himself from the corroboration provided by the objective evidence. This is apparent from the accused’s assertion that he has no memory of the incident as shown in PW1’s BWC[note: 34] and that his testimony was based on his observation of his own body language and the way he behaved.

30     In any event, the Prosecution had checked on the availability of other BWC footages and informed the court as well as the accused that there was none. In my view, there was no merit in the accused’s assertion that footages from BWC’s were saved all the way as it is illogical in view of the amount of storage that it would entail if they were kept in perpetuity.

31     I rejected the accused’s assertion that the victim was inconsistent and gave false evidence on where she was when the accused uttered the offending words. I agreed with the Prosecution that there were no material inconsistencies in her evidence. I also agreed with the Prosecution that there was no basis for the accused’s assertion that the victim had given false evidence. The minor differences in the way the victim had explained herself in evidence does not tantamount to the giving of false evidence.

32     I next considered whether the words used by the accused were abusive.

Were the words uttered by the accused abusive?

33     In my view, whether the words uttered by the accused were abusive would depend on the context ie how and where it was used. When the words were directed to another person as a form of personal attack, such words are considered abusive as it is offensive. When used in a casual setting or used to express anger or frustration, then it may not be considered as abusive.

34     In the present case, the accused asserts that the words uttered have two meanings and were in fact acronyms which were not vulgar. Based on the evidence before me, I disagreed and did not accept the accused’s assertion that the words in question were not abusive. When taken in its proper situational context, such words when uttered towards a court interpreter who was carrying out her duty in the State Courts would clearly amount to the use of abusive words.

35     I found that it was clearly a personal attack on the victim intended to humiliate and cause her distress in a formal setting. In my view, the words used by the accused were highly offensive as it is a commonly used profanity. Furthermore, the accused had uttered the words in an aggressive manner towards the victim, while gesturing at her. By claiming that the words have two meanings and were acronyms which were not vulgar, it was clear the accused was trying to evade the consequences of his conduct at the material time.

36     I then considered whether the abusive words were directed at the victim.

Whether the words used were directed at the victim?

37     In the present case, I agreed with the Prosecution that the victim provided a clear, factual account of the events that transpired, which was entirely consistent with the footage from PW1’s body worn camera. She gave clear testimony that she heard the accused’s words and felt humiliated and offended. I further agree with the Prosecution that she was able to give a consistent recount of the accused’s use of abusive words to the police officer who approached her later.

38     The victim’s account of the events was corroborated by the evidence of PW1 who was present and within earshot as he was escorting the accused. He gave a cogent account which was consistent with that of the victim. His evidence was further corroborated by objective evidence of the footage from his body worn camera.

39     Accordingly, I rejected the accused’s assertion that the victim had not seen or heard him uttering the abusive words. I also rejected his assertion that the abusive words were not uttered at the victim but instead a soliloquy. The accused was clearly not alone nor was there any indication the accused believed he was alone from his interaction with the victim as well as the police officers.

40     It was clear from the footage that the accused was unhappy with the victim, and the abusive words were directed at her. This was evident from the time the victim tried to read the new charges in court until the second occasion when she tried to do so at the atrium outside Court 4A. In contrast, the victim could be observed to be carrying her duties professionally despite the accused’s disruptive behaviour.

41     Hence, I rejected his assertion that the victim had already gone into Court 4A and the door was closed as the incident happened or that no member of the public in Court 4A heard the abusive words. From the BWC footage (P1), lawyers, prosecutors and members of the public could be seen entering and leaving the courtroom in quick succession. As such, the doors would not have remained closed such that the abusive words directed at the victim would have been out of the victim’s earshot. I rejected the accused’s assertion that the victim had walked away for 3 seconds before the incident happened as it is inconsistent with the objective evidence from the BWC footage.

42     Additionally, I disagreed with the accused’s assertion that his conduct at the material time was reasonable and instead found him to be belligerent. It was also evident from the accused’s interaction with the victim that he was being intentionally difficult with her. The accused did not inform the victim that he wanted to use the English language but instead told her he wanted to use Telugu and after that Mandarin. Furthermore, he testified that he did not want to see or communicate with her. Consequently, I rejected his assertion that he had no reason to believe that the words used or behaviour used, or the communication made by the accused would be heard, seen or otherwise perceived by the victim.

43     In the present case, I agreed with the Prosecution that the accused’s evidence was unreliable and should not be believed. He was evasive during his testimony and was an unreliable witness. He repeatedly sought to evade answering simple questions that were put to him. Hence, I rejected his various assertions, in particular that the victim had not seen or heard him uttering the abusive words.

44     Additionally, I find his assertion he was unable to recall what happened due to the symptoms of alcohol withdrawal to be baseless. There was no medical evidence that he was labouring under such a condition at the material time. Further, from the BWC footage it was clear the accused was fully aware of what he was doing. He was able to interact with the police officers and the victim coherently. Hence, I found that the accused had deliberately said the abusive words to the victim. I also agreed with the Prosecution that the accused’s claims that he was suffering from alcohol withdrawal at the material time was a convenient afterthought to evade having to answer for his behaviour.

45     In his written submissions, the accused took issue with the fact that no breathalyser test was conducted in accordance with the Liquor Control (Supply and Consumption) Act to ascertain the fact whether the accused was indeed drunk prior to his arrest. During his cross-examination of Investigation Officer, PW3 Loe Kit Yee Celestine, he had asked whether any breathalyser tests were done to prevent the accused from his mention in the courtroom. I had stated during the trial that breathalyser tests are for drink driving offences and not to determine whether a person is drunk or not[note: 35]. Consequently, there is no requirement for such a test to be conducted. Instead, s 14(6) of the Act provides the following:

(6)    In this section, an individual is drunk if –

(a)    the individual’s speech, balance, coordination or behaviour is noticeably affected; and

(b)    it is reasonable in the circumstances to believe that the affected speech, balance, coordination or behaviour is the result of the consumption of liquor.

46     Based on the facts as well as the surrounding circumstances before me, I found that the police officers were justified in exercising their powers of arrest. Hence, the accused's challenge of the basis of his arrest was without merit. In any event, this was not an issue before me.

47     Lastly, the accused asserts that the revocation of bail, the duration of the trial to be held and the trial, was vexatious, extraneous and abuse of both prosecution power and of judicial process. Suffice to say, in my view, the issue of bail has been sufficiently ventilated and considered on several occasions by both the High Court and the State Courts.

48     After a careful consideration of the totality of the evidence before me, I was satisfied that the Prosecution had established all the elements of the charge in MAC-905668-2025 beyond a reasonable doubt. Accordingly, I found the accused guilty and convicted him on the proceeded charge under s 6(1)(a) of the Protection from Harassment Act 2014.

49     I now turn to the reasons for my sentence.

Sentence

Enhanced penalty under s 8(1)(d) POHA

50     The prescribed punishment for a subsequent offence of using abusive words against a public servant under s 6(1) of the POHA is a fine not exceeding $10,000 or to imprisonment not exceeding two years or to both.

Relevant antecedents

51     The accused’s antecedents for offences involving public servants or against public order are set out below:

(a)      4.9.2001 – s 20 Miscellaneous Offences (Public Order and Nuisance) Act Cap 184 for disorderly behaviour. He was fined $800.

(b)      26.2.2009 – s 20 Miscellaneous Offences (Public Order and Nuisance) Act, Cap 184 (MOA) for disorderly behaviour. He was fined $2000.

(c)      8.1.2018 – One charge under s 6(3) POHA Cap. 256A and one charge under s 20 MOA. He was sentenced to one week’s imprisonment for each charge. Two additional charges under s 3(1)(a) POHA were taken into consideration.

(d)      28.11.2019 – Two charges of using criminal force against a public servant under s 353 Penal Code. He was sentenced to 4 weeks’ imprisonment per charge. In addition, there were two charges under s 20 MOA, he was sentenced to 8 weeks imprisonment and 10 weeks’ imprisonment respectively.

(e)      24.1.2022 - Four charges under s 6(1)(a) and punishable under s 8(1)(d) POHA with four more taken into consideration. He was sentenced to 2 weeks’ imprisonment for each charge, with all four sentences ordered to run consecutively. In addition, he was convicted for voluntarily causing hurt to a public servant under s 332 Penal Code. He was sentenced to 5 months and 2 weeks’ imprisonment. Four charges under s 6(1)(a) and punishable under s 8(1)(d) POHA and 2 charges under s 20 MOA were taken into consideration.

Prosecution’s Address on Sentence

52     The Prosecution sought a sentence of at least 4 to 5 months’ imprisonment as the accused was a repeat offender. The Prosecution asserts that general and specific deterrence was a critical sentencing consideration given the context that the offence was committed and the following aggravating factors.

Nature of the offence

53     The Prosecution asserts that the offence was committed in the State Courts, against a court interpreter who was performing her duty. The State Courts is a critical public institution as one of the main judicial branches in Singapore where the administration of justice is carried out. By virtue of its function, persons from a wide range of backgrounds use the Courts and frequent the courtrooms, including accused persons such as the accused in the present case. Preserving the security and good order in the Courts is therefore of paramount importance.

54     There is significant public interest in ensuring that court proceedings are respected and not disrupted, and all officers and staff in the judiciary are protected from harassment and abuse. Here, the victim was a court interpreter, who, by virtue of her role, inevitably interacts with accused persons very frequently and is accordingly susceptible to such offences. In the present case, she was trying to facilitate and assist the accused as part of her duties. General deterrence must therefore be a highly significant sentencing consideration in the present case.

Harm to the victim

55     The Prosecution further asserts that there was considerable harm caused to the victim, as the accused had uttered the abusive words in a loud and aggressive manner, in full view of members of public and her colleagues, causing her to feel humiliated and offended. The accused was intentionally disruptive in the court proceedings, and was intentionally being very difficult to the victim, despite the victim and police officers genuinely trying to facilitate the process and assist him.

56     His aggressive and abusive outburst against the victim was completely unwarranted and unprovoked. This was not a case where there was a dispute or exchange between parties which escalated and in the heat of the moment, the words were uttered. The Prosecution highlighted that the accused was clearly being difficult and belligerent from the start.

Lack of remorse

57     The Prosecution asserts that the accused has demonstrated a blatant lack of remorse for his actions, even in the face of clear, objective evidence. He not only mounted an entirely frivolous defence but also made several serious and baseless allegations against the various parties involved at the trial. The allegations were completely spurious and baseless against the Prosecution. This was an aggravating factor that warrants an uplift in sentence: Thong Sing Hock v PP [2009] 3 SLR(R) 47 at [55]-[62]. It was highlighted that the accused committed the present offence while on bail.

Relevant antecedents

58     The Prosecution asserts that the accused was heavily traced especially for offences involving public servants or public order. He had been convicted on multiple times for similar offences, including not just the use of abusive words to public servants but also criminal force and even hurt to public servants.

(a)     On 8 January 2018, he was convicted for one count under s 6(3) POHA Cap. 256A and was sentenced to one week’s imprisonment. Two additional charges under s 3(1)(a) POHA were taken into consideration.

(b)     On 24 January 2022, he was convicted for four counts of s 6(1)(a) POHA and punishable under s 8(1)(d) POHA with four more taken into consideration. He was sentenced to 2 weeks’ imprisonment for each charge, with all four sentences ordered to run consecutively. In addition, he was convicted for voluntarily causing hurt to a public servant under s 332 Penal Code.

59     The Prosecution further asserts that this was in addition to numerous public order antecedents such as disorderly behaviour. He was clearly a recalcitrant offender, and specific deterrence must be emphasised here.

60     The Prosecution asserts that a significant uplift from his previous sentences must be imposed. This was especially as this was a conviction after a trial and not a plead guilty situation which was the case in 2022.

Mitigation

61     Despite being given the opportunity to provide mitigate, the accused showed his lack of remorse by refusing to do so. Instead, he indicated that he intention to file an appeal. He also maintained his denial of the charge.

Reasons for the Sentence

62     The present offence was committed in the State Courts against a court interpreter who was performing her duty. Hence, given the context that the offence was committed and the presence of aggravating factors, deterrence was the main sentencing consideration in the present case.

Offence-specific factors

Sanctity of court proceedings

63     I agreed with the Prosecution that the State Courts is a critical public institution as one of the main judicial branches in Singapore where the administration of justice is carried out. By virtue of its function, persons from diverse backgrounds use the Courts and frequent the courtrooms, including accused persons such as the accused in the present case. I also agreed with the Prosecution that preserving the security and good order in the Courts is of paramount importance.

64     As the sanctity of court proceedings requires that the administration of justice to be free of interference or disruptions, it is important that parties involved in the court processes observe proper decorum or behaviour in court. I agreed with the Prosecution that there is significant public interest in ensuring that court proceedings are respected and not disrupted, and all officers and staff in the judiciary are protected from harassment and abuse.

65     As part of her duty as a court interpreter, persons such as the victim interact with accused persons and other court users very frequently and is accordingly highly susceptible to such verbal abuse. As testified by the victim herself, it was her job to attend to accused persons, regardless of how difficult they can be. That was why when the accused was persistently belligerent and his conduct was no longer reasonable, the victim stopped reading the charges and walked away again. This was to avoid further insults and not to expose her new colleague to further potential harassment. Hence, general deterrence is a highly significant sentencing consideration in the present case.

Harm caused

66     I agreed with the Prosecution that there was considerable harm caused as the accused had uttered the abusive words to the victim in a loud and aggressive manner which could be heard by members of the public and her colleagues present in Court 4A. Not only did this cause the victim to feel humiliated and offended but it was also disruptive to the formal court proceedings.

67     I further agreed with the Prosecution that the accused’s aggressive and abusive outburst against the victim was completely unwarranted and unprovoked. This was not a case where there was a dispute or exchange between parties which escalated and in the heat of the moment, the words were uttered. Instead, this showed that the accused has little or no regard for the rule of law in general, only saw things from his own perspective and wanted things done his way.

Offender-specific factors

Lack of remorse

68     As regards offender-specific factors, I agreed with the Prosecution that the accused demonstrated a clear lack of remorse for his offence. Despite being given the opportunity to mitigate after he was found guilty, he still maintained his denial of the charge.

69     The accused had no qualms about making baseless and unsubstantiated allegations against the Prosecution and their witnesses. The attack on their integrity was another instance of his lack of remorse for his wrongdoing. This showed that the accused has little or no regard for the rule of law in general, only saw things from his own perspective and wanted things done his way.

70     In the present case, the accused was not entitled to any sentencing discount as he had claimed trial to the present charge. Furthermore, he was on agency bail when he committed the present offence.

Antecedents

71     This was the accused’s third conviction for an offence of using abusive words against a public servant. Additionally, this was also the second occasion that the accused was subject to the enhanced penalty for such an offence under s 8(1)(d) POHA. As highlighted by the Prosecution, the accused was heavily traced especially for offences involving public servants or public order. He had been convicted on multiple times for similar offences, including not just for the use of abusive words to public servants but also criminal force and even hurt to public servants.

72     Having regards to the aggravating factors as set out above, there was a need to send a strong signal that such behaviour in Court would not be tolerated and would be met with a stiff sentence. It was clear that the accused has a penchant for committing offences involving public servants or public order.

73     The Prosecution has sought a sentence of between 4 to 5 months imprisonment. I agreed with the Prosecution that a significant uplift from his previous sentences must be imposed. The accused was convicted after a trial and not a plead guilty situation which was the case in 2022. Considering that he was previously sentenced to 2 weeks’ imprisonment for each of his four similar charges which were ordered to run consecutively, I was of the view that a significant uplift to 15 weeks’ imprisonment was just and appropriate in the circumstances,

74     All things considered, in respect of MAC-905668-2025, I imposed a sentence of 15 weeks’ imprisonment which was backdated to the date of his arrest.
