Public Prosecutor v Yang Chao and others

Public Prosecutor v Yang Chao and others
[2026] SGDC 187

Case Number:District Arrest Case No 916110-2025 and others, Magistrate's Appeal No MA-9106-2026-01, MA-9107-2026-01 and MA-9114-2026-01
Decision Date:12 June 2026
Tribunal/Court:District Court
Coram: Terence Tay
Counsel Name(s): Benedict Teong and Cheronne Lim (Attorney-General's Chambers) for the Public Prosecutor; Wilson Foo (Folich LLC) for Yang Chao; Diana Foo (Messrs Legal Eagles) for Zhou Qifa; He Jiao in-person.
Parties: Public Prosecutor — Yang Chao — Zhou Qifa — He Jiao

Criminal Law – Offences – Criminal conspiracy

Immigration – Criminal offences – Harbouring – Illegal immigrant

Criminal Procedure and Sentencing – Sentencing

12 June 2026

District Judge Terence Tay:

Introduction

1       Singapore prides itself on being a safe and secure home for its residents, a reputation built upon a foundation of low crime rates and a high degree of public trust. When foreigners enter our borders with covert intent to commit crimes, they abuse our hospitality and strike at the heart of the security and way of life that we hold dear.

2       Organised crime groups that target Singapore as a lucrative hunting ground for property offences should be warned that law enforcement remains highly vigilant, and the full weight of the law will be brought to bear on those who are caught.

3       The accused persons were Yang Chao (“YC”), Zhou Qifa (“ZQF”) and He Jiao (“HJ”) who, together with three other accomplices, Zhou Yinggui (“Yinggui”), Hu Wen (“Wen”) and Zhou Ji (“Ji”), faced a combination of charges including housebreaking, being in possession of housebreaking implements and being members of a locally-linked organised criminal group (“Criminal Group”). The charges spanned the period 16 July to 8 August 2025 during which time the accused persons, Yinggui, Wen and Ji made a total of three trips to Singapore to further their collective intent to commit housebreaking:

Date of Trip

Persons Involved

16-19 July 2025

(“First Trip”)

YC, ZQF, HJ, Wen and Ji

22-24 July 2025

(“Second Trip”)

ZQF, HJ and Ji

8 August 2025

(“Third Trip”)

YC, ZQF, HJ and Yinggui



4       As at the date of sentencing, the charges against Yinggui were still pending while Wen and Ji remained at large.

Charges against YC and sentences

5       YC, who was represented by Mr Wilson Foo (“DC Wilson”), pleaded guilty to and was sentenced for the following charges:

Charge No.

Charge

Prescribed Punishment

Sentenced

DAC-916631-2025

(“YC 1”)

From 16 to 18 July 2025, in Singapore, did abet by engaging in a conspiracy with ZQF, HJ, Wen and Ji to commit housebreaking in order to commit theft, and in pursuance of that conspiracy and in order to the doing of that thing, YC and Wen, on 18 July 2025, entered a residential property at No. [redacted] Greenleaf Rise, a human dwelling, in order to commit theft, and YC and Wen dishonestly removed out of the possession of [redacted], without his consent, [items with a total value of approximately S$57,395.45], and YC had thereby committed an offence under section 451 read with section 109 of the Penal Code 1871 (“PC”), and as such conspiracy was committed in furtherance of the illegal purpose of a group which YC knew was an organised criminal group, YC was therefore liable to enhanced punishment under section 13(1)(b) read with section 13(3)(c) of the Organised Crime Act 2015(“OCA”).

Imprisonment not exceeding 15 years and also liable to a fine

Imprisonment 60 months

(Consecutive)

DAC-918084-2025

(“YC 2”)

From 16 July 2025 to 8 August 2025, in Singapore, was a member of the Criminal Group, knowing that the Criminal Group was a locally-linked organised criminal group, which had as one of its purposes, the obtaining of a financial benefit from the commission of an offence of house-breaking in order to commit theft under section 451 of the PC, to wit, YC was part of the Criminal Group during the aforesaid period which had as its members YC, HJ and ZQF from 16 July 2025 to 8 August 2025, and additionally had Yinggui as a member from 7 to 8 August 2025, which is a serious offence under the Schedule to the OCA, and YC had thereby committed an offence punishable under Section 5(1) of the OCA.

Imprisonment not exceeding 5 years or fine not exceeding $100,000 or both

Imprisonment 18 months

MAC-907163-2025

(“YC 3”)

On 8 August 2025, sometime before 8:35 pm, along the Rail Corridor near Bukit Timah Road, Singapore, together with ZQF, HJ and Yinggui and in furtherance of the common intention of them all, were found equipped with articles for use in connection with house-breaking, to wit, screwdrivers and wrenches, and YC had thereby committed an offence under section 453(1)(c) read with section 34 of the PC, and which offence was committed in furtherance of the illegal purpose of a group which YC knew was an organised criminal group, YC was therefore liable to enhanced punishment under section 13(1) (b) read with section 13(3)(b) of the OCA.

Imprisonment not exceeding 4 years or fine or both

Imprisonment 3 months

(Consecutive)

Global Sentence

Imprisonment 63 months



6       YC also consented to the following charge being taken into consideration for the purpose of sentencing:

Charge No.

Charge

Prescribed Punishment

DAC-916107-2025

From 7 to 8 August 2025, in Singapore, was a party to a criminal conspiracy, to wit, by agreeing with ZQF, HJ and Yinggui to commit an offence of house-breaking in order to commit theft, and YC had thereby committed an offence under section 451 read with sections 120A and 120B of the PC, and as such criminal conspiracy was committed in furtherance of the illegal purpose of a group which YC knew was an organised criminal group, YC was therefore liable to enhanced punishment under section 13(1)(b) read with section 13(3)(c) of the OCA.

Imprisonment not exceeding 15 years and also liable to a fine



Charges against ZQF and sentences

7       ZQF, who was represented by Ms Diana Foo (“DC Diana”), pleaded guilty to and was sentenced for the following charges:

Charge No.

Charge

Prescribed Punishment

Sentence

DAC-916632-2025

(“ZQF 1”)

From 16 to 18 July 2025, in Singapore, did abet by engaging in a conspiracy with HJ, YC, Wen and Ji to commit housebreaking in order to commit theft, and in pursuance of that conspiracy and in order to the doing of that thing, YC and Wen, on 18 July 2025, entered a residential property at No. [redacted] Greenleaf Rise, a human dwelling, in order to commit theft, and YC and Wen dishonestly removed out of the possession of [redacted], without his consent, [items with a total value of approximately S$57,395.45], and ZQF had thereby committed an offence under section 451 read with section 109 of the PC, and as such conspiracy was committed in furtherance of the illegal purpose of a group which ZQF knew was an organised criminal group, ZQF was therefore liable to enhanced punishment under section 13(1)(b) read with section 13(3)(c) of the OCA.

Imprisonment not exceeding 15 years and also liable to a fine

Imprisonment 60 months.

(Consecutive)

DAC-918116-2025

(“ZQF 2”)

From 16 July 2025 to 8 August 2025, in Singapore, was a member of the Criminal Group, knowing that the Criminal Group was a locally-linked organised criminal group, which had as one of its purposes, the obtaining of a financial benefit from the commission of an offence of house-breaking in order to commit theft under section 451 of the PC, to wit, ZQF was part of the Criminal Group during the aforesaid period which had as its members ZQF, HJ and YC from 16 July 2025 to 8 August 2025, and additionally had Yinggui as a member from 7 to 8 August 2025, which was a serious offence under the Schedule to the OCA, and ZQF had thereby committed an offence punishable under Section 5(1) of the OCA.

Imprisonment not exceeding 5 years or a fine not exceeding $100,000 or both

Imprisonment 18 months.

MAC-907164-2025

(“ZQF-3”)

On the 8th day of August 2025, sometime before 8 p.m., along the Rail Corridor near Bukit Timah Road, Singapore, together with HJ, YC and Yinggui and in furtherance of the common intention of them all, was found equipped with articles for use in connection with house breaking, to wit, screwdrivers and wrenches, and ZQF had thereby committed an offence under section 453(1)(c) read with section 34 of the PC, and which offence was committed in furtherance of the illegal purpose of a group which ZQF knew was an organised criminal group, ZQF was therefore liable to enhanced punishment under section 13(1)(b) read with section 13(3)(b) of the OCA.

Imprisonment not exceeding 4 years or fine or both

Imprisonment 5 months.

(Consecutive)

DAC-916108-2025

(“ZQF 4”)

From 7 to 8 August 2025, in Singapore, were a party to a criminal conspiracy, to wit, by agreeing with HJ, YC and Yinggui to commit an offence of house-breaking in order to commit theft, ZQF had thereby committed an offence under section 451 read with section 120B of the PC, and as such criminal conspiracy was committed in furtherance of the illegal purpose of a group which ZQF knew was an organised criminal group, ZQF was therefore liable to enhanced punishment under section 13(1)(b) read with section 13(3)(c) of the OCA.

Imprisonment not exceeding 15 years and liable to fine

Imprisonment 20 months.

Global Sentence

Imprisonment 65 months



8       ZQF also consented to the following charge being taken into consideration for the purpose of sentencing:

Charge No.

Charge

Prescribed Punishment

Conspiracy to commit house-breaking

4    Sometime in early July 2025, He Jiao and Zhou Qifa travelled to Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia (“KL”). In KL, they met Yang Chao, Hu Wen and Zhou Ji. Together, the five persons discussed and agreed to commit house-breaking in Singapore. They had seen multiple videos on Chinese social media about how wealthy Singapore is and thought that it would be easier to obtain valuable items by committing house-breaking in Singapore. Their plan was to scout out vulnerable landed residential properties in Singapore, break into these houses and steal valuable items which they would then leave Singapore with.

5    Each of the five persons was thus a member of a group, knowing that the group had as its purpose, the obtaining of a financial benefit from the commission of house-breaking in Singapore by the group (“the Group”).

6    An offence of house-breaking to commit theft under s 451 of the Penal Code 1871 (“PC”) is a serious offence under the Schedule to the Organised Crime Act 2015 (“OCA”). The Group was thus a locally-linked organised criminal group within the definition of s 2 of the OCA.

7    Pursuant to the agreement, the five persons travelled to Singapore by land from Malaysia on 16 July 2025.

First information report

House-breaking incident

9    After arriving in Singapore on 16 July 2025, Zhou Qifa purchased screwdrivers and wrenches at a hardware store. These were instruments to be used for the Group’s intended house-breaking. The flat tip of the screwdriver would make it easy to pry open windows and doors. Zhou Qifa was familiar with the use of such tools as he had experience working in the construction industry. The screwdrivers and wrenches were distributed amongst the five persons.

10    The five persons split into two separate sub-groups. One consisted of He Jiao, Zhou Qifa and Zhou Ji, and the other consisted of Yang Chao and Hu Wen. If anyone sub group was successful in bouse-breaking, they would split the stolen items amongst the other members.

11    On both 16 July 2025 and 17 July 2025, sometime in the night, the two sub-groups took private-hire vehicles to private landed properties in various neighbourhoods in Singapore to scout for houses to break into. He Jiao had reviewed the map of Singapore and identified the areas with private landed properties for scouting.

12    The five persons generally looked for houses in more secluded places which were adjacent to forested areas or parks which would therefore have fewer passersby. Parties’ Sentencing Submissions

The Prosecution’s address on sentence

12     The Prosecution’s joint address on sentence for the three accused persons highlighted general deterrence as the predominant sentencing consideration due to the following features of this case:

(a)     Difficulty of detection and apprehension as the offences were committed under the cover of night and the accused persons had targeted vulnerable houses without security features in secluded locations.

(b)     The offences were committed by the accused persons in a group.

(c)     Presence of a transnational element.

YC 1, ZQF 1 and HJ 1

13     These charges involved the housebreaking committed at Greenleaf Rise on the First Trip.

14     The Prosecution sought a similar sentence of 60-66 months’ imprisonment for each of the accused persons which took into account, amongst other considerations, their pleas of guilt within Stage 1 of the Guidelines on Reduction in Sentences for Guilty Pleas (“PG Guidelines”), their respective roles in the housebreaking and the following offence-specific factors:

(a)     The offence was syndicated with a transnational dimension;

(b)     There was significant premeditation and sophistication in the planning of the offence;

(c)     The modus operandi created challenges in detection and apprehension.

(d)     The housebreaking took place at a residential neighbourhood which would have engendered uneasiness and disquiet amongst the residents.

(e)     The victim would have suffered added emotional distress as he lost his treasured personal items.

(f)     Singapore should not be seen as a soft target by criminals.

(g)     The value of the properties stolen and the outstanding loss was not insubstantial.

15     Even though ZQF did not participate directly in the housebreaking, the Prosecution had considered the charge in ZQF 5 which was taken into consideration for the purpose of sentencing.

YC 2, ZQF 2 and HJ 2

ZQF 4 and HJ 4

22     The Prosecution adopted similar sentencing considerations as those for ZQF 1 and HJ 1, save that the conspiracy to commit housebreaking did not materialise due to police intervention.

YC’s mitigation plea

24     DC Wilson pointed out generally that:

(a)     YC had never been convicted or investigated by the police in any country;

(b)     YC’s parents were inflicted with a form of cancer that incurred medical expenses of about RMB70,000-80,000 a month;

(c)     YC had three school-going children that incurred hefty expenses of about RMB20,000-30,000 a month;

(d)     YC was the sole breadwinner; and

(e)     YC did not know that he was coming to Singapore to commit crimes until later and he had agreed to do so “in a moment of poor judgment and in view of his dire financial straits”.[note: 2]

25     In relation to YC 1, DC Wilson relied primarily on the district courts’ decisions in PP v Lee Teng Chye[note: 3] (“Lee Teng Chye”) and PP v Lim Wei Ho[note: 4] (“Lim Wei Ho”), and submitted that the indicative starting sentence would be based on the value of the stolen items and then calibrated based on various non-exhaustive factors such as:

(a)     the extent of property damage;

(b)     the abuse of trust and confidence reposed in the accused;

(c)     the harm or potential harm caused by the accused;

(d)     the timing of the offence;

(e)     the difficulty of detection or apprehension; and

(f)     the level of planning and premeditation.

26     DC Wilson submitted that YC exhibited less criminal tendencies then the offenders in Lee Teng Chye and Lim Wei Ho as YC did not have any antecedents. Furthermore, YC was instigated to commit the offences by the accomplices and his role as a look-out was relatively minor. Consequently, DC Wilson took the view that the indicative starting point of YCs sentence was 78-90 months’ imprisonment before the reduction under Stage 1 of the PG Guidelines which would bring the eventual sentence to 52 months’ imprisonment.

27     For YC 2, DC Wilson referred to two decisions of the district courts in PP v Huang Qin Zheng and others[note: 5] and PP v Tan Shay Howe[note: 6], where the district courts had considered the harm caused, the offenders’ culpabilities and the indication of plea at Stage 1 of the PG Guidelines, and imposed sentences of 16 months’ imprisonment, and 26 months and 2 weeks’ imprisonment, respectively.

28     DC Wilson submitted that the harm caused in the present case was at the low end of medium culpability given the value of the items stolen and YC’s minor role in the offence and instigation by the accomplices. In the circumstances, DC Wilson agreed with the Prosecution’s submission of 2 years’ imprisonment as the indicative starting point which would be reduced to 16 months’ imprisonment at Stage 1 of the PG Guidelines.

29     In the case of YC 3, DC Wilson referred the court to two decisions of the district courts in PP v Joseph Lau Jin Hua[note: 7] (“Joseph Lau”) and PP v Khairus Sa’aban Bin Abdullah[note: 8] (“Khairus Sa’aban”) where the offenders were sentenced to imprisonment terms of 4 months and 3 months, respectively, for possession of knives. In Joseph Lau, the district judge noted that “the usual sentence for the possession of an offensive weapon, where the offender pleaded guilty, was about three months’ imprisonment” but applied an uplift of one month as the offender was in possession of two weapons.

30     DC Wilson submitted that the present case was not exceptional and fell at the lower end of the Prosecution’s submission for 3 months’ imprisonment, where an offender had pleaded guilty.

31     Finally, DC Wilson agreed with the Prosecution’s submission for the sentences for YC 1 and YC 3 to run consecutively.

Court’s decision

YC 1, ZQF 1 and HJ 1

34     Housebreaking, particularly in residential areas, is deeply troubling as it violates people's private sanctuary. Beyond financial loss and the loss of items of sentimental value, it can cause psychological harm and potential physical harm, as the safety of one's home — so often taken for granted — is violated.

35     The circumstances of the present case were particularly egregious. The accused persons conspired to make multiple trips to Singapore with the sole intent to commit housebreaking and flee almost immediately thereafter.[note: 9] As a group, the accused persons and other accomplices had defined roles, division of labour and conducted coordinated operations. The brazen, organised, and transnational nature of the offences, coupled with patient reconnaissance to identify suitable targets, revealed the extent of their persistence, premeditation and planning to maximise their chances of success whilst evading detection and apprehension.

36     Consequently, I agreed with the Prosecution that deterrence, especially general deterrence, was the predominant sentencing consideration.

37     I also agreed with the aggravating factors pointed out by the Prosecution, but recognised that the accused persons had indicated their intention to plead guilty within Stage 1 of the PG Guidelines.

38     In Lee Teng Chye, the offender had, in the cover of darkness at night, masked in a disguise and armed with a screwdriver, committed housebreaking at the coffeeshop where he used to work. He stole almost $14,000 in cash and cheques that were eventually recovered. The district judge sentenced the offender to 10 months’ imprisonment which took into account the accused’s plea of guilt and dated antecedents to some degree but made no further adjustments arising from another charge under s 453(1)(b) of the PC which was taken into consideration for the purpose of sentence since this element already featured in the sentence.

39     The district judge in Lee Teng Chye had referred to Lim Wei Ho in his assessment of the sentencing considerations for an offence under s 351 of the PC.

40     In Lim Wei Ho, the offender had pleaded guilty to three charges under s 451 of the PC for breaking into two stalls at the Lau Pa Sat hawker centre and one stall at the Café 107 coffeeshop in the wee hours of 2 April 2023. The total amount stolen was $2,550. Notably, the offender had previously been employed, albeit for a short time, at one of the stalls at the Lau Pa Sat hawker centre that he had broken into. The offender had also consented to two similar charges involving two other stalls at the Lau Pa Sat hawker centre being taken into consideration for the purpose of sentencing.

41     The district judge had sentenced the accused to seven, eight and nine months’ imprisonment for the three charges and ordered the latter two sentences to run consecutively to arrive at a global sentence of 17 months’ imprisonment.

42     In sentencing the offender, the district judge had considered a number of case precedents from the district courts and observed that:

(a)     the sentence for housebreaking should be based not only on the value of the stolen items and also other relevant facts and circumstances; and

(b)     it would be difficult to discern the impact of the other relevant facts and circumstances on the sentence as many of the precedent cases were unreported.

43     With the foregoing observations in mind, the district judge identified the following non-exhaustive sentencing factors:

(a)     property damage;

(b)     abuse of trust;

(c)     other harm or potential harm caused;

(d)     time of the offence;

(e)     difficulty of detection or apprehension;

(f)     planning and premeditation; and

(g)     case or policy-specific factors relevant to sentencing (eg. in PP v Mohammad Iqbal Bin Mohamed Rafe (DAC-901940-2020 and others), the court remarked that there was a need to deter offenders from taking personal intimate items to gratify their own fetishistic or paraphilic desires).

44     Notably, for stolen property above $2,500, the district judge usefully identified the following case precedents:

Case

Saliant Features

Sentence

PP v Nguyen Huy Manh (DAC-900629-2020 and another)

· Offender stole $9,300 cash.

· $5,800 was recovered.

· Offender was untraced.

· Offender and victim worked in the same industrial building.

· No restitution.

· One charge under s 448 of the PC taken into consideration.

Imprisonment 13 months

Public Prosecutor v Dao Manh Toan (DAC-905325-2023 and others)

· Offender stole $2,806.51 worth of cigarettes and $9,226 cash.

· Offender was untraced.

· Offender used to be employed as a shop assistant at the store which he had broken into.

· Offender made restitution of $11,997.

· Two similar charges taken into consideration.

Imprisonment 18 months

Public Prosecutor v Yap Kok Boo (DAC-914063-2020 and others)

· Offender stole $45,807 worth of watches.

· Offender was untraced.

· The victim was the offender’s girlfriend.

· $2,500 in proceeds from the sale of one of the watches and the remaining watches were recovered.

· Two charges under s 379 of the PC taken into consideration.

Imprisonment 15 months



45     I was further guided by the Sentencing Practice in the Subordinate Courts, LexisNexis (3rd Ed, 2013) at p 923:

[T]he other considerations for assessing sentence would be the nature of the property trespassed upon (for example, a violation of someone’s home would be regarded more seriously), the circumstances attending the trespass (for example, the time of the offence, whether the offender was armed, etc) and the criminal record, if relevant. Sentences for this offence can vary radically depending on the circumstances.

…

[T]he length of custody is dependent on the severity of the offence. The factors which would determine where the method of entry (for example, putting a hand through a window which the offender has opened to take a radio is a far cry from forcible entry); the degree of sophisticated planning and organisation engaged in; whether the offender was part of a group; the time of break-in (night as opposed to day time); the type of premises (residential as opposed to non-residential); whether the offence was accompanied by acts of wanton vandalism, force or violence; whether the occupier was present; the effect on the occupier; whether the offence was directed at the elderly, disabled or sick victim; the value of property taken; the number of offences committed; and the antecedents of the offender… Whilst no distinction is drawn between the punishment prescribed for housebreaking committed in a dwelling house and those in commercial and industrial premises, for sentencing purposes, housebreaking of dwelling houses is viewed more seriously than housebreaking of commercial and industrial premises. The rationale for this distinction is set out succinctly in Sentencing and Criminal Justice (3rd ed) by A Ashworth at p 118:

The distinction is that the commercial burglaries are viewed as theft combined with damage, whereas the residential burglaries may additionally cause significant psychological harm to the householder, chiefly because of the invasion of the home and personal possessions and sometimes because of the loss of treasured mementos.

46     The authors further set out the following checklist of factors affecting sentence:

Seriousness Indicators (+)

Seriousness Indicators (-)

1 Series of similar offences

2 Premeditated and careful planning

3 Professional hallmarks

4 Forcible entry

5 Ransacking

6 Damage or vandalism

7 Occupier present

8 Actual or threatened harm to occupants

9 Vulnerable victim (eg lone young female or elderly person, etc)

10 Abuse of position (eg offender was security guard at the premises he broke into)

11 High value of property taken

12 Prior convictions

This list is not exhaustive.

1 Low value of property taken

2 Impulsive act or opportunistic

3 Amateurish

4 Occupier not present

5 No forcible entry

This list is not exhaustive.



47     There were two other case precedents of the district courts in 2025 which were similar in nature albeit without the invocation of the OCA, namely, PP v Zhang Yongxiang[note: 10] and PP v Feng Yunlong[note: 11] (“Zhang and Feng”). In Zhang and Feng, each of the offenders pleaded guilty to one charge under s 451 read with s 34 of the PC. Both offenders were Chinese nationals who had broken into a semi-detached house at Greenleaf View by accessing it via the neighbouring construction site which had no door or gate. The offenders stole two watches with a total value of $8,950. Each of the offenders had also consented to one other charge under s 451 of the PC involving $7,152 being taken into consideration for the purpose of sentencing. The offenders were sentenced to 15 months’ imprisonment each.

48     I observed that some of the charges in the case precedents were read with s 34 of the PC as they involved co-accused persons. While the legislative intents behind s 34 of the PC and s 13 of the OCA were not identical, the latter legislation being promulgated to “detect, investigate, prevent and disrupt organised crime activities…”,[note: 12] the sentences imposed in such cases could have taken into account the common consideration of a group offence to some degree.

49     Ultimately, every case must be decided on its own facts, and it is uncommon to find sentencing precedents that are factually identical. Nevertheless, case precedents — many of which may be unreported — provide useful reference points in relation to the amounts involved and other relevant sentencing considerations.

50     In this regard, the precedents cited concerned ordinary cases under s 451 of the Penal Code, which carried an imprisonment term of up to 10 years and a fine, or both. As the maximum imprisonment term for the predicate offence was four years or more, the application of s 13(3)(c) of the OCA in the present charges increased the maximum imprisonment term by five years to 15 years. Accordingly, the sentencing benchmarks established by those precedents for ordinary cases under s 451 of the PC could not be extrapolated directly to the present charges without adjustment to account for the enhanced maximum sentence.

51     With the foregoing in mind, I turned to consider the saliant facts of the present case:

(a)     The value of the stolen property, which included jewellery items, was substantial at over $55,000 — many times more than the value of stolen property in most of the precedent cases;

(b)     A large proportion of the stolen property was not recovered;

(c)     There were extensive premeditation and planning by the accused persons;

(d)     The offence was transnational in nature and the accused persons had adopted a hit-and-run strategy of travelling to Singapore to execute their plan and then leaving the day after the house-breaking, ie. on 19 July 2025, to evade arrest;

(e)     The division of labour and coordinated operations to maximise the chances of success;

(f)     The use of housebreaking implements procured by ZQF and distributed amongst the accused persons;

(g)     The accused persons had surveyed and targeted residential estates in secluded locations adjacent to forested areas and parks;

(h)     The accused persons took extra caution to identify residential properties with no closed-circuit television cameras and dogs;

(i)     The offence took place at night; and

(j)     The accused persons each had one similar charge taken into consideration for the purpose of sentencing, ie. YC 4 (Third Trip), ZQF 5 (Second Trip) and HJ 5 (Second Trip).

52     Notably, ZQF was convicted of theft in the People's Republic of China ("China") and sentenced to five months' imprisonment in 2018. HJ was convicted of house-breaking in China and sentenced to one year's imprisonment in 2015. While their antecedents in China did not constitute prior convictions in Singapore, it was evident that this was not their first property offence.

53     In light of the above, I would have considered a starting sentence of about 80-85 months’ imprisonment to be appropriate had the accused persons been convicted after trial, with HJ’s sentence falling within the lower end of the range; and YC and ZQF’s sentences falling within the upper end of the range for the following reasons:

(a)     YC’s culpability was higher than that of HJ as YC had taken the additional precaution of wearing a balaclava over his head to conceal his identity and he had participated directly in the housebreaking, albeit as a look-out; and

(b)     ZQF’s culpability was higher than that of HJ as ZQF procured the screwdriver and wrenches which were distributed to the other accused persons to facilitate the housebreaking.

54     As the accused persons had pleaded guilty within Stage 1 of the PG Guidelines, I applied the appropriate reduction in sentences and imposed a sentence of 60 months’ imprisonment on each of YC and ZQF, and 58 months’ imprisonment on HJ.

YC 2, ZQF 2 and HJ 2

55     The language of s 5 of the OCA, read with the definition of “locally-linked organised criminal group” (“OCG”) in s 2 of the OCA, did not appear to require a separate and distinct offence to be committed in order for a charge under s 5(1) of the OCA to be made out. As such, the sentencing considerations ought to centre on the nature and seriousness of the purpose of the OCG, including the impact on society and public safety, as well as the level of participation and role of the offender. In this regard, the harm-culpability matrix in Hermanto bin Abdul Talib provided useful guidance notwithstanding that the decision was not binding on this court.

56     On the facts of this case, I considered harm to be moderate.

57     The purpose of the Criminal Group to commit housebreaking in Singapore engendered grave public safety concerns not just because housebreaking is a serious offence but also because the Criminal Group had specifically targeted Singapore as “[t]hey had seen multiple videos on Chinese social media about how wealthy Singapore is and thought that it would be easier to obtain valuable items by committing house-breaking in Singapore.”[note: 13]

58     The persistence and resolve of the Criminal Group was also demonstrated by the number of trips that they made to Singapore, including the Second Trip where ZQF, HJ and Ji left when they could not identify a suitable target.

59     I considered the relative culpability of the accused persons to be materially equivalent and within the moderate range. The facts indicated that each of them contributed equally and meaningfully to the Criminal Group, with comparable levels of participation. Furthermore, the planning and preparation as a whole bore the hallmarks of seasoned housebreakers, in particular:

(a)     ZQF had purchased housebreaking implements on all the trips and also gloves on the Third Trip;[note: 14]

(b)     HJ had bought gloves on the Second Trip to avoid leaving behind fingerprints during the housebreaking;[note: 15]

(c)     HJ bought a torchlight on the Third Trip to aid in seeing in the dark during the housebreaking;[note: 16]

(d)     Some members of the Criminal Group had bought balaclavas from Malaysia to conceal their identities;[note: 17]

(e)     YC had put on a balaclava for the housebreaking committed at Greenleaf Rise;[note: 18] and

(f)     The Criminal Group had conducted reconnaissance operations to identify suitable targets.

60     In conclusion, I considered an indicative starting sentence of 25-30 months’ imprisonment to be appropriate. As the accused persons had pleaded guilty within Stage 1 of the PG Guidelines, I imposed a sentence of 18 months’ imprisonment on each of them.

YC 3, ZQF 3 and HJ 3

61     Except for Joseph Lau and Khairus Sa’aban, the parties did not specifically identify other reported or unreported case precedents involving housebreaking implements. However, they accepted that a starting sentence of about three to four months’ imprisonment was usually imposed for cases where the offenders had pleaded guilty.[note: 19]

62     The present charges involved a total of nine different items in the possession of the accused persons and Yinggui collectively and in furtherance of the purpose of the Criminal Group; and the sentence was enhanced under s 13(3)(b) of the OCA. In the circumstances, I found 3-5 months’ imprisonment to be an appropriate sentencing range after taking into account their pleas of guilt within Stage 1 of the PG Guidelines.

ZQF 4 and HJ 4

63     Each of ZQF and HJ pleaded guilty to an additional charge in ZQF 4 and HJ 4, respectively, in relation to the Third Trip to commit housebreaking.

64     Even though the accused persons were unsuccessful on the Third Trip, this was largely attributed due to the sting operation mounted by the police which resulted in their arrests. As far as the accused persons and Yinggui were concerned, they had taken all the necessary preparatory steps to commit housebreaking, in particular:

(a)     ZQF had purchased four screw drivers, two wrenches and gloves for the group, the cost of which was to be shared amongst the four of them.

(b)     HJ had purchased a torchlight to see in the dark during the housebreaking.

(c)     The quad had split up into pairs which entered forested areas to scout for houses that were suitable to break into.

65     As the offence was read with s 13(3)(c) of the OCA, I imposed a sentence of 20 months’ imprisonment as the accused persons pleaded guilty within Stage 1 of the PG Guidelines.

Global sentence

66     As the accused persons had been sentenced to imprisonment for at least 3 distinct offences, s 307(1) of the Criminal Procedure Code 2010 required the court to order the sentences for at least two of the offences to run consecutively.

67     In this regard, even though YC 2, ZQF 2, and HJ 2 were serious charges, the mischief that these charges were intended to address has been partially subsumed within the charges in HJ 1, ZQF 1 and 4, and YC 1 and 4. The remaining charges concerned distinct protected interests, except for ZQF 1 and 4, and HJ 1 and 4, which were housebreaking charges.

68     That said, ZQF and HJ were clearly relentless in their housebreaking endeavours – having succeeded on the First Trip and persisting despite failing to identify a target on the Second Trip – and it would not be inappropriate to order the sentences for ZQF 1 and ZQF 4, and for HJ 1 and HJ 4, to run consecutively since the offences took place on different occasions, involved different dynamics, and implicated other accomplices. On the other hand, I took the view that doing so would result in aggregate sentences of 80 and 78 months’ imprisonment for ZQF and HJ, respectively, which would be crushing and would offend the totality principle.

69     In my final analysis, being mindful of the need for parity in sentences based on the overall and relative criminality amongst the accused persons, I imposed the following sentences on the accused persons:

(a)     YC:

70     In my view, the global sentences imposed on the appellants reflected the slight variances in their relative criminality for the following reasons:

(a)     The overall criminality of ZQF was higher than that of YC even though ZQF was not directly involved in the housebreaking on the First Trip as ZQF was involved in and had procured housebreaking implements on all the trips;

(b)     The overall criminality of HJ was comparable to that of YC even though HJ was not directly involved in the housebreaking on the First Trip as HJ was involved in all three trips.

Public Prosecutor v Matsuura Yudai

Public Prosecutor v Matsuura Yudai
[2026] SGMC 77

Case Number:Magistrate Arrest Case No. 902630 of 2026 and others
Decision Date:18 June 2026
Tribunal/Court:Magistrate's Court
Coram: Samuel Wee
Counsel Name(s): Etsuko Lim (Attorney-General's Chambers) for the Public Prosecutor; Stephania Wong (Rajah & Tann Singapore LLP) for the Defendant.
Parties: Public Prosecutor — Matsuura Yudai

Criminal Law – Offences – Section 377BB(5) of the Penal Code 1871 (2020 Rev Ed) – Amalgamated charge relating to the recording of another person’s genital region

Criminal Procedure and Sentencing – Sentencing – Section 377BB(5) of the Penal Code 1871 (2020 Rev Ed) – Amalgamated charge relating to the recording of another person’s genital region

18 June 2026

District Judge Samuel Wee:

Introduction

1       Mr Matsuura Yudai (“Mr Yudai”) recorded upskirt videos of numerous female victims at shopping malls in Jurong East over the course of approximately 1 year. His modus operandi was as follows: he would turn on the video recording function on his mobile phone; place it in his briefcase with the camera lens facing upwards; zip his briefcase so as to allow the camera lens to peek out through a small hole whilst concealing the rest of his mobile phone; and walk around to record the upskirt videos.[note: 1] As each continuous recording would be of a relatively long duration, he would trim the videos to save storage space on his mobile phone before placing them in a password-protected folder.[note: 2]

2       Mr Yudai has pleaded guilty to two charges:

(a)     One charge for an offence under s 377BB(5) punishable under s 377BB(7) of the Penal Code 1871 (2020 Rev Ed) (“Penal Code”) (“Voyeurism Offence”) for intentionally recording a video of the victim’s (“Ms V”) genital region on 7 December 2025 (without her consent) in circumstances where the genital region would not otherwise have been visible (“Single Voyeurism Charge”).[note: 3]

(b)     One charge for Voyeurism Offences covering the period from 26 December 2024 to 6 January 2025 for intentionally recording 37 videos of 31 unidentified victims’ genital region and/or buttocks (without their consent) in circumstances where the genital region, buttocks and/or underwear would not otherwise have been visible, being an amalgamated charge pursuant to s 124(4) punishable under s 124(8) of the Criminal Procedure Code 2010 (2020 Rev Ed) (“CPC”) (“Amalgamated Voyeurism Charge”).[note: 4]

3       He also admitted and consented to two additional charges being taken into consideration (“TIC”) for the purposes of sentencing:

(a)     One charge for a Voyeurism Offence for intentionally recording a video of 26 other unidentified victims’ genital region (without their consent) in circumstances where the genital region would not otherwise have been visible, being an amalgamated charge pursuant to s 124(4) punishable under s 124(8) of the CPC (“TIC Voyeurism Charge”).[note: 5]

(b)     One charge for an offence under s 204A of the Penal Code for obstructing, preventing, perverting or defeating the course of justice by deleting videos he recorded of the victims’ genital region (without their consent) from his mobile phone (“TIC Obstruction of Justice Charge”).[note: 6]

4       The Prosecution seeks an aggregate custodial sentence of 20-22 weeks’ imprisonment (4-5 weeks for the Single Voyeurism Charge; and 16-17 weeks for the Amalgamated Voyeurism Charge),[note: 7] while Mr Yudai pleads for an aggregate sentence of 17-19 weeks’ imprisonment (3-4 weeks for the Single Voyeurism Charge; and 14-15 weeks for the Amalgamated Voyeurism Charge).[note: 8] The Prosecution also seeks a compensation order of $500 in favour of Ms V in respect of the Single Voyeurism Charge, which Mr Yudai has consented to.

5       I find that an aggregate sentence of 22 weeks’ imprisonment is appropriate (5 weeks for the Single Voyeurism Charge; and 17 weeks for the Amalgamated Voyeurism Charge). I also order Mr Yudai to make compensation of $500 in favour of Ms V (in default 2 days’ imprisonment).

Background

The Single Voyeurism Charge

6       On 7 December 2025, Mr Yudai adopted his modus operandi as set out at [1] above to capture an upskirt video of Ms V in a retail outlet.[note: 9]

7       He followed Ms V around the retail outlet and recorded her genital region (which would not otherwise have been visible). Mr Yudai accepts that he knew that Ms V did not consent to his recording of the video.[note: 10]

8       While the recording was ongoing, Ms V’s buttocks bumped against Mr Yudai’s briefcase twice as she was squatting to pick up some products from the retail outlet.[note: 11] Mr Yudai was undeterred by the first bump. He pretended to be browsing the products in the retail outlet and continued the video recording. After the second bump, Mr Yudai hurriedly tried to leave the retail outlet. However, Ms V noticed the camera lens in the briefcase and called the police.

9       While waiting for the police to arrive, the retail outlet’s staff brought Mr Yudai to wait in the outlet’s office, where Mr Yudai took steps to delete the video of Ms V and other upskirt videos from his mobile phone, and cleared the “recently deleted” folder thereafter[note: 12] – this conduct is the subject of the TIC Obstruction of Justice Charge.

10     When the police arrived, they were unable to find any incriminating material on Mr Yudai’s mobile phone, and Mr Yudai initially denied any wrongdoing.[note: 13] It was only after the police reviewed the retail outlet’s closed-circuit television recording of the events that Mr Yudai admitted to recording upskirt videos of Ms V and deleting the videos.[note: 14]

The Amalgamated Voyeurism Charge

11     After Mr Yudai was arrested for the offence under the Single Voyeurism Charge, he was found to be in possession of 37 videos that are the subject of the Amalgamated Voyeurism Charge.[note: 15]

12     The 37 videos were recorded between 26 December 2024 and 6 January 2025 based on Mr Yudai’s modus operandi as set out at [1] above. The videos captured the genital region or buttocks of 31 unidentified victims (which would not otherwise have been visible), and included four videos where the genital region of the victims was fully exposed. Mr Yudai accepts that he knew that the victims did not consent to his recording of the videos.[note: 16]

13     It was also discovered that Mr Yudai had recorded a video of 26 other unidentified victims’ genital region (without their consent) – this is the subject of the TIC Voyeurism Charge.

The applicable sentencing approach

The Single Voyeurism Charge

14     In Tan Siew Chye Nicholas v Public Prosecutor [2023] 4 SLR 1223 ("Nicholas Tan"), the General Division of the High Court established a sentencing framework in respect of an offence under s 377BB(4) of the Penal Code for the operation of equipment enabling an offender to observe (without the victim’s consent), a victim’s genital region, breasts (for females) or buttocks (whether exposed or covered) in circumstances where they would not otherwise have been visible.

(a)     Step A: Identify the level of harm and culpability by considering the offence-specific factors. Relevant factors include:

Harm

Culpability

(i) Invasion of the victim’s privacy.

(ii) Violation of the victim’s bodily integrity where there was physical contact with the victim.

(iii) Humiliation, alarm or distress.

(i) Whether the offender actually knew, or merely had reason to believe, that the victim had not consented to being observed.

(ii) The degree of premeditation and planning.

(iii) Stalking or following of the victim.

(iv) The type and sophistication of the equipment used and whether it was concealed.

(v) Any breach of relationship of trust with the victim.

(vi) Steps taken to evade detection.

(vii) The motivation for the offence.

(viii) The persistence of the offending conduct.



(b)     Step B: Identify the applicable indicative sentencing range (for a post-trial conviction) based on the matrix of harm and culpability levels determined at Step A.

(c)     Step C: Identify the appropriate starting point within the indicative sentencing range, having regard once again to the level of harm and culpability.

(d)     Step D: Adjust the starting point to account for offender-specific aggravating and mitigating factors. Relevant factors include:

Aggravating Factors

Mitigating Factors

(i) TIC charges.

(ii) Relevant antecedents.

(iii) An evident lack of remorse.

(iv) Whether the offence was committed while on bail or probation.

(i) A guilty plea.

(ii) Cooperation with the authorities.

(iii) An offender’s apology.

(iv) Psychological factors with a causal link to the commission of the offence.



(e)     Step E: Make further adjustments to account for the totality principle if the offender has been convicted of multiple charges.

15     While the sentencing framework in Nicholas Tan was crafted for an offence under s 377BB(4) of the Penal Code and benchmarks should generally be left to the appellate courts to establish (Public Prosecutor v Sindok Trading Pte Ltd (now known as BSS Global Pte Ltd) and other appeals [2022] 5 SLR 336 at [29]), I see no impediment to referencing the sentencing framework in Nicholas Tan for the Voyeurism Offence under s 377BB(5) of the Penal Code given that the General Division of the High Court indicated its preliminary view that there is “no reason why the same sentencing framework should not apply to the other offences in … s 377BB(5) [of the Penal Code]”.[note: 17]

The Amalgamated Voyeurism Charge

16     The Amalgamated Voyeurism Charge requires consideration of the three-step sentencing approach for amalgamated charges in Prakash s/o Mathivanan v Public Prosecutor and other appeals [2025] 4 SLR 1386 (“Prakash”):

(a)     Step 1: Identify the punishment prescribed for the base offence in view of the offence-specific factors and the relevant sentencing framework. This involves considering the sentencing framework in Nicholas Tan.

(b)     Step 2: Determine the appropriate indicative starting point sentence based on a holistic assessment of the offender's culpability over the entire course of conduct, having regard to the doubled sentencing limit and the relevant evidence of the offending behaviour.

(c)     Step 3: Consider the relevant offender-specific aggravating and mitigating factors before making any necessary adjustments to the indicative starting point sentence.

The individual sentences

The Single Voyeurism Charge

17     The Voyeurism Offence carries an imprisonment term of up to 2 years, a fine, and/or caning under s 377BB(7) of the Penal Code.

Steps A to C

18     The relevant offence-specific factors in the present case show that the harm was low and the culpability was at the upper end of low:[note: 18]

Harm

(Low)

Culpability

(Low – Upper End)

(a) Invasion of Ms V’s privacy – Mr Yudai observed and recorded a video of Ms V’s covered genital region for a brief period, and deleted the video shortly after.

(b) Violation of Ms V’s bodily integrity as Ms V’s buttocks bumped into Mr Yudai’s briefcase twice.

(c) Ms V suffered humiliation and alarm as she became aware that Mr Yudai had recorded the upskirt video.[note: 19]

(a) Mr Yudai knew that Ms V did not consent to the video recording.[note: 20]

(b) There was premeditation and planning by Mr Yudai, which is evident from his modus operandi[note: 21] and the fact that Mr Yudai followed Ms V around the retail outlet.[note: 22]

(c) Mr Yudai demonstrated persistence as he continued recording the upskirt video even after Ms V first bumped into his briefcase.



19     The indicative sentencing range for the Single Voyeurism Charge under the sentencing framework in Nicholas Tan is a fine or up to 4 months’ imprisonment (for a post-trial conviction), with an appropriate starting point of 7 weeks’ imprisonment.[note: 23]

20     For clarity, to avoid double-counting, I have not accounted for Mr Yudai’s deletion of the videos to avoid detection when assessing his culpability for the Single Voyeurism Charge. This factor will instead be considered as part of the appropriate uplift in sentence arising from the TIC Obstruction of Justice Charge.

Steps D to E

21     The indicative starting point sentence of 7 weeks’ imprisonment (for a conviction after a trial) should be adjusted to 5 weeks’ imprisonment at Step D to account for the following:

(a)     An uplift of 2 weeks for the TIC Obstruction of Justice Charge. As mentioned at [20] above, I have not accounted for Mr Yudai’s deletion of the videos to avoid detection when assessing Mr Yudai’s culpability, to ensure there is no double-counting.

(b)     A reduction of 2 weeks as the Prosecution concedes that Mr Yudai suffered from a diagnosed “stress and adjustment reaction” that has a sufficient causal link with the offence committed.[note: 24]

(c)     A reduction of 2 weeks as Mr Yudai indicated his intention to plead guilty at Stage 1 of the Sentencing Advisory Panel’s Guidelines on Reduction in Sentences for Guilty Pleas (“PG Guidelines”) and is entitled to a reduction of up to 30% of the sentence.

22     Step E will be considered as part of the analysis for the appropriate aggregate sentence (see [38]-[41] below).

The Amalgamated Voyeurism Charge

23     Under s 124(8) of the CPC, Mr Yudai is subject to double the punishment of the Voyeurism Offence.

Step 1

(1)   Steps A to C

24     The relevant offence-specific factors in the present case show that the harm was at the upper end of low and the culpability was also at the upper end of low:[note: 25]

Harm

(Low – Upper End)

Culpability

(Low – Upper End)

(a) Invasion of the victims’ privacy – there were 37 videos relating to 31 victims, including four videos where the genital region of the victims was fully exposed.[note: 26] Moreover, Mr Yudai retained the videos for close to a year,[note: 27] which gave rise to the potential for repeated invasion of their privacy.[note: 28]

(a) Mr Yudai knew that the victims did not consent to the video recordings.[note: 29]

(b) There was premeditation and planning by Mr Yudai, which is evident from his modus operandi.

(c) Mr Yudai took steps to evade detection – by placing the videos in a password-protected folder.



25     The indicative sentencing range for the base offence under the Amalgamated Voyeurism Charge under the sentencing framework in Nicholas Tan is a fine or up to 4 months’ imprisonment (for a post-trial conviction), with an appropriate starting point of 16 weeks’ imprisonment.

26     For clarity, I have not accounted for the duration of offending under the Amalgamated Voyeurism Charge at Step 1 as it is not apparent how the punishment for the base offence would be calibrated for multiple instances of recording based on the sentencing framework in Nicholas Tan, and I will instead consider this at Step 2. In this regard, the General Division of the High Court made it clear in Nicholas Tan at [81] that the factor for “the persistence of the offending conduct” relates to “situations where the offender continued to observe the victim even after the victim had made efforts to prevent or warn the offender against continuing the offending behaviour”[note: 30] and does not relate to an offender’s prolonged pattern of offending.

(2)   Steps D to E

27     As Step D appears to have some overlap with Step 3, I will consider it together with Step 3 to avoid double-counting of the aggravating factors.

28     Step E will be considered as part of the analysis for the appropriate aggregate sentence (see [38]-[41] below).

Step 2

29     The critical offence-specific factors relating to Step 2 are:

(a)     The 37 videos recorded by Mr Yudai.

(b)     The 31 unidentified victims involved.

(c)     The duration of offending between 26 December 2024 and 6 January 2025.

While the first two factors have already been accounted for at Step 1, it is permissible to consider them again at Step 2 (Prakash at [44]).

30     Accordingly, an uplift of 8 weeks to the starting point of 16 weeks’ imprisonment for the base offence is appropriate, resulting in 24 weeks’ imprisonment (for a conviction after a trial) as the indicative starting point sentence for the Amalgamated Voyeurism Charge.[note: 31]

Step 3

31     The indicative starting point sentence of 24 weeks’ imprisonment (for a conviction after a trial) should be adjusted downwards to 17 weeks’ imprisonment at Step 3 to account for the following:

(a)     An uplift of 6 weeks for the TIC Voyeurism Charge.

(b)     A reduction of 6 weeks as the Prosecution concedes that Mr Yudai suffered from a diagnosed “stress and adjustment reaction” that has a sufficient causal link with the offence committed.[note: 32]

(c)     A reduction of 7 weeks as Mr Yudai indicated his intention to plead guilty at Stage 1 of the PG Guidelines and is entitled to a reduction of up to 30% of the sentence.

The individual sentences are consistent with the sentencing precedents

32     The Prosecution and Mr Yudai relied on four main sentencing precedents, which I have considered in determining the level of harm and culpability and the calibration of the individual sentences.[note: 33]

33     The first sentencing precedent is Nicholas Tan, which, as mentioned at [14] above, involved offences under s 377BB(4) of the Penal Code and established the sentencing framework that I have referred to in this case.

(a)     The offender recorded upskirt videos of two victims on two separate occasions – V1 and V2. He followed V1 (a 20-year-old female student), squatted and placed his mobile phone camera under V1’s dress, was spotted by V1, and deleted the video thereafter. While on bail for the offence against V1, he followed V2 (a 17-year-old female student), squatted and placed his mobile phone camera pointing towards her thigh area, touched V2’s thigh, was noticed by V2 who shouted at him (and called her father and cried), and deleted the video thereafter.

(b)     The offender pleaded guilty to two charges under s 377BB(4) of the Penal Code, and there was a TIC charge relating to criminal trespass under s 447 of the Penal Code.

(c)     In respect of the offence relating to V1, the General Division of the High Court determined a starting point sentence of 3 weeks’ imprisonment based on the following offence-specific factors (and levels of harm and culpability):[note: 34]

Harm (Low)

Culpability (Low)

(i) Invasion of the victim’s privacy – the offender observed and recorded a video of V1’s covered genital region for a brief period, and deleted the video shortly after.

(i) The offender knew that V1 did not consent to the recording.

(ii) There was premeditation and planning, as the offender followed V1 for some distance.



(d)     For the offence relating to V2, the General Division of the High Court determined a starting point sentence of 4 weeks’ imprisonment based on the following offence-specific factors (and levels of harm and culpability):[note: 35]

Harm (Low, but higher than the offence relating to V1)

Culpability (Low)

(i) Invasion of V2’s privacy – the offender observed and recorded a video of V2’s covered genital region for a brief period, and deleted the video shortly after.

(ii) Violation of V2’s bodily integrity as the offender touched her thigh.

(iii) V2 suffered humiliation, alarm or distress as she became aware of the offending conduct, and thereafter called her father and cried. The distress was also exacerbated by V2’s relative youth.

(i) The offender knew that V2 did not consent to the recording.

(ii) There was premeditation and planning, as the offender followed V2 for some distance.



(e)     The starting point sentences were adjusted to 1 week’s imprisonment (for the offence relating to V1) and 3 weeks’ imprisonment (for the offence relating to V2) to account for the offender-specific factors, including: (i) an uplift for the TIC charge; and (ii) reductions as the offender pleaded guilty, cooperated with the authorities, and demonstrated a propensity for reform.

34     The second sentencing precedent is Public Prosecutor v Tan Wee Jian [2023] SGMC 90 (“Tan Wee Jian”), which involved an offence under s 377BB(4) of the Penal Code and the application of the sentencing framework in Nicholas Tan.

(a)     The offender followed the victim, stood behind her on an escalator, held his mobile phone stretched out towards her exposed thigh in an attempt to record an upskirt image, touched the victim’s thigh, and was noticed by the victim who confronted the offender before he ran off. The victim was distressed by the incident and testified that she avoided the route for a week.

(b)     The offender claimed trial and was convicted of one charge for attempted voyeurism under s 377BB(4) read with s 511(1) of the Penal Code. He was also convicted of a separate charge for the possession of voyeuristic images under s 377BD(1)(a) of the Penal Code.

(c)     The Magistrate’s Court determined a starting point sentence of 4 weeks’ imprisonment for the attempted voyeurism offence, based on the following offence-specific factors (and levels of harm and culpability):[note: 36]

Harm (Low – Upper End)

Culpability (Low – Middle)

(i) Invasion of the victim’s privacy – the offender attempted to record an image of the victim’s covered buttocks.

(ii) Violation of the victim’s bodily integrity as the offender touched her thigh.

(iii) The victim suffered humiliation, alarm or distress as she became aware of the offending conduct and thereafter avoided the route for a week.

(i) The offender knew that the victim did not consent to the recording.

(ii) There was premeditation and planning, as the offender followed the victim for some distance.

(iii) The offender ran off after being confronted by the victim.



(d)     The starting point sentence for the attempted voyeurism offence was adjusted to 6 weeks' imprisonment to account for one offender-specific factor – the offender's complete lack of remorse.

35     The third sentencing precedent is Public Prosecutor v Vishal s/o Kuppusamy [2025] SGMC 43 (“Vishal”), which involved an offence under s 377BB(5) of the Penal Code and the application of the sentencing framework in Nicholas Tan.

(a)     The offender stood behind the victim in a lift, bent down and placed his mobile phone camera under the victim’s dress to record an upskirt image, touched the back of the victim’s knee, was noticed by the victim, and deleted the video thereafter. The victim testified that she felt “scared” and “dirty after the incident”, and took precautions such as by standing against the side of lifts.[note: 37]

(b)     The offender claimed trial and was convicted of one charge under s 377BB(5) of the Penal Code.

(c)     The Magistrate’s Court determined a starting point sentence of 4 weeks’ imprisonment for the offence, based on the following offence-specific factors (and levels of harm and culpability):[note: 38]

Harm (Low)

Culpability (Low)

(i) Invasion of the victim’s privacy – the offender recorded an image of the victim’s covered buttocks, and deleted the image shortly after.

(ii) Violation of the victim’s bodily integrity as the offender touched the back of her knee.

(iii) The victim suffered humiliation, alarm or distress as she became aware of the offending conduct and thereafter took precautions against a recurrence.

(i) The offender knew that the victim did not consent to the recording.

(ii) The offender took steps to evade detection by deleting the image in a deliberate and blatant attempt to destroy evidence, and purchasing a new mobile phone to mislead investigators.



(d)     The starting point sentence for the offence was not adjusted due to the absence of relevant offender-specific factors.

36     The fourth sentencing precedent is Public Prosecutor v Elgin Ng [2026] SGDC 51 (“Elgin Ng”), which involved offences under s 377BB(5) of the Penal Code and the application of the sentencing framework in Nicholas Tan.

(a)     The offender worked as a photographer at the National Dental Centre of Singapore (“NDCS”). Over a period of around 3 years, he abused his position to take voyeuristic images of female patients whom he found attractive. His modus operandi included: using deception to call patients in for unauthorised photography sessions; failing to provide patients with a blue board to cover their chests and keeping the curtains closed to facilitate his conduct; surreptitiously arranging cameras at angles to capture top-down and bottom-up images of the patients' breasts; and transferring the images to a personal thumb drive and deleting them from the camera's memory card to avoid detection. He also accessed the NDCS's computer systems without authorisation to obtain the victims' personal details and facial photographs, which he used to assemble a catalogue of the victims; and also distributed some of the images to a friend.

(b)     The offender pleaded guilty to six charges for offences under s 377BB(5) of the Penal Code (one of which was an amalgamated charge), two charges of unauthorised access to computer material under s 3(1) of the Computer Misuse Act 1993 (2020 Rev Ed), and one charge of distribution of voyeuristic images under s 377BC(1) of the Penal Code. There were also 21 TIC charges – 19 relating to offences under s 377BB(5) of the Penal Code and two relating to offences under s 3(1) of the Computer Misuse Act 1993 (2020 Rev Ed).

(c)     The District Court applied the sentencing framework in Nicholas Tan to the six offences under s 377BB(5) of the Penal Code and determined the following offence-specific factors (and levels of harm and culpability), which were applicable to all six:[note: 39]

Harm (Low – Upper End)

Culpability (Borderline between Medium and High)

(i) Invasion of the victim’s privacy – each charge related to one victim and involved between 22 and 65 images of each victim’s breasts. Moreover, the offender retained the images and distributed some of them to a friend.

(i) The offender knew that the victims did not consent to the recording.

(ii) There was a high degree of premeditation and planning, which is evident from the offender’s modus operandi.

(iii) There was a severe breach of trust, which had been reposed in the offender by the NDCS and the victims.

(iv) The offender took steps to evade detection, including deleting images from the camera’s memory card and failing to attend NDCS investigations.



(d)     Based on these factors, the District Court derived the following starting point sentences and final sentences (after adjustments) based on the number of images involved for each charge.[note: 40]

No. Images

Starting Point Sentence

Final Sentence

22

4 months

4 months

26 over 2 days

5 months

5 months

29 over 3 days

5 months

5 months

37

5 months

5 months

65

7 months

6 months

31 (amalgamated charge involving one victim and three occasions)

7 months

7 months



(e)     The adjustments to the sentences accounted for the following offender-specific factors:

(i)       Appropriate uplifts to account for the 19 TIC charges relating to offences under s 377BB(5) of the Penal Code.

(ii)       A reduction of around 25% for the offender’s indication of his intention to plead guilty at Stage 1 of the PG Guidelines. The District Court declined to apply the maximum reduction of 30% as the offender had failed to cooperate with NDCS’s internal investigations and was effectively caught red-handed.[note: 41]

37     My assessment of the level of harm and culpability and the calibration of the individual sentences is consistent with the four sentencing precedents:

(a)     With regards to the level of harm:

(i)       The level of harm for the Single Voyeurism Charge is low, which is the same level as Nicholas Tan (for the offence in respect of V2) and Vishal given the similarity in the offender-specific factors relating to harm (see [18], [33(d)] and [35(c)] above). It is also lower than the level of harm in Tan Wee Jian (upper end of low) (see [34(c)] above), as unlike Tan Wee Jian, there is no evidence of the extent of distress suffered by Ms V.

(ii)       The level of harm for the Amalgamated Voyeurism Charge is at the upper end of low, which is the same level as Elgin Ng given the similarity in the offender-specific factors relating to harm (see [24] and [36(c)] above). In this regard, it must be stressed that there were four videos where the genital region of the victims was fully exposed, and Mr Yudai retained the videos for close to a year.

(iii)       There is therefore no basis for Mr Yudai’s contention that his level of harm is “at the lower end of the “low” spectrum” for the Single Voyeurism Charge,[note: 42] and “at the middle end of the “low” spectrum” for the Amalgamated Voyeurism Charge.[note: 43]

(b)     As to the level of culpability:

(i)       The level of culpability for both the Single Voyeurism Charge and Amalgamated Voyeurism Charge is at the upper end of low (see [18] and [24] above).

(ii)       This is higher than Nicholas Tan, Tan Wee Jian and Vishal (see [33(c)], [33(d)], [34(c)] and [35(c)]), as Mr Yudai’s culpability is elevated by: (A) the degree of planning and premeditation, which is evident from his modus operandi (see [1] above); (B) his persistence in respect of the Single Voyeurism Charge; and (C) the nature of the steps he took to evade detection in respect of the Amalgamated Voyeurism Charge (ie. by placing the videos in a password-protected folder). It is also lower than the culpability in Elgin Ng as there is no breach of trust involved in Mr Yudai’s case.

(iii)       There is therefore no basis for Mr Yudai’s contention that his level of culpability is “at the lower end of the “low” spectrum” for the Single Voyeurism Charge,[note: 44] and “at the middle end of the “low” spectrum” for the Amalgamated Voyeurism Charge.[note: 45]

(c)     In respect of the individual sentences:

(i)       The individual sentence for the Single Voyeurism Charge is 5 weeks’ imprisonment.

(A)       This is higher than Nicholas Tan and Vishal, but lower than Tan Wee Jian given the different levels of culpability and offender-specific factors involved.

(B)       It is not meaningful to compare the sentence with Elgin Ng due to the vastly different factual matrices involved.

(ii)       The individual sentence for the Amalgamated Voyeurism Charge is 17 weeks’ imprisonment.

(A)       This is lower than the sentence of 7 months’ imprisonment for the amalgamated offence in Elgin Ng given the lower level of culpability in Mr Yudai’s case and the different offender-specific factors involved.

(B)       It is not meaningful to compare the sentence with Nicholas Tan, Tan Wee Jian and Vishal given the different factual matrices involved.

The aggregate sentence

38     There are three main rules or principles to consider in this case when determining the appropriate aggregate sentence:

(a)     The one-transaction rule, which serves as a filter to sieve out sentences that ought not, as a general rule, to be ordered to run consecutively (Mohamed Shouffee bin Adam v Public Prosecutor [2014] 2 SLR 998 (“Shouffee”) at [27]).

(b)     The general rule of consecutive sentences for unrelated offences, which provides for a multiple offender who has committed unrelated offences to be separately punished for each offence (Public Prosecutor v Raveen Balakrishnan [2018] 5 SLR 799 at [41]).

(c)     The totality principle, which is applied at the end of the sentencing process, and involves the court performing a final check to assess whether the overall sentence is excessive (Shouffee at [58] and [81(h)]).

39     The general rule of consecutive sentences for unrelated offences applies in this case rather than the one-transaction rule, as:

(a)     There is no proximity in time – the Single Voyeurism Charge relates to an offence on 7 December 2025, whereas the Amalgamated Voyeurism Charge relates to offences between 26 December 2024 and 6 January 2025.

(b)     The victims involved are different – Ms V is the victim under the Single Voyeurism Charge, whereas the Amalgamated Voyeurism Charge relates to 31 unidentified victims.

40     Consequently, the sentences for the Single Voyeurism Charge and the Amalgamated Voyeurism Charge should run consecutively for an aggregate of 22 weeks’ imprisonment.

41     This aggregate sentence is sufficient and proportionate to Mr Yudai’s overall criminality, and does not offend the totality principle – it is not significantly above the norm for the Amalgamated Voyeurism Charge (being the most serious offence) and cannot be said to be crushing.

Compensation order in favour of Ms V

42     The Prosecution seeks a compensation order of $500 in favour of Ms V in light of the emotional trauma Ms V has suffered, which Mr Yudai has consented to.[note: 46]

43     I therefore order Mr Yudai to pay compensation of $500 in favour of Ms V (in default 2 days’ imprisonment).

Conclusion

44     Mr Yudai is sentenced to an aggregate of 22 weeks’ imprisonment (5 weeks for the Single Voyeurism Charge; and 17 weeks for the Amalgamated Voyeurism Charge), and is ordered to pay compensation of $500 in favour of Ms V (in default 2 days’ imprisonment).

45     The sentence is backdated to 7 December 2025 (the date of arrest) and will take into account the period of custody and exclude the period on bail (from 8 December 2025 to 7 April 2026 and 8 April 2026 to 18 June 2026).
