Appeal against sentence

5       The Accused, being dissatisfied with the sentence, filed an appeal against sentence.

6       In this Grounds of Decision, I shall first set out the Statement of Facts (“SOF”). Next, I will set out the Prosecution’s address on sentence and the Defence’s plea-in-mitigation. I will then conclude with my reasons for imposing the sentences stated at [3] above.

Statement of Facts

7       The SOF is reproduced below:

I      BACKGROUND

1.    The Accused is Liu Hesheng, a 50-year-old PRC-Chinese male (date of birth: 1 July 1975), bearing FIN No. [redacted]. He resided in Pattaya, Thailand at the material time.

2.    On 23 January 2025, at around 12.32 a.m., the owner of Watch Capital located at 111 Somerset Road, #01-33, Singapore 238164, lodged a police report stating that American Express (‘AMEX’) had flagged a transaction that took place at his shop as fraudulent. The credit card company informed him that the transaction that took place on 19 January 2025 at 12.45 p.m. involving an AMEX card for SGD 32,716.10 had been disputed by the card owner. As such, AMEX was holding the amount and raising a charge back.

3.    Subsequently, Police received two similar reports lodged by the owners of Sheen Enterprise and Lovelotsluxury. They each reported that AMEX had flagged fraudulent transactions for SGD 39,140 on 21 January 2024 at around 4.00 p.m. and SGD 14,763 (not inclusive of applicable surcharges) on 19 January 2025 at around 1.30 p.m. at their respective stores.

4.    Following the police reports, the Accused was traced and found to have entered Singapore on 18 January 2025 and left on 21 January 2025 at 6.13 p.m. via Changi Airport. While in Singapore, the Accused had used at least three different AMEX credit cards belonging to different individuals to make fraudulent purchases. A police gazette was issued against the Accused for his arrest. On 10 February 2025, the Accused attempted to re-enter Singapore and was arrested at Changi airport.

5.    Investigations revealed that sometime before January 2025, an individual known as “Boss Huang” had given the Accused three Japanese bank cards to purchase luxury items on his behalf using these cards while he was in Singapore. They were previously acquainted as Boss Huang had been a frequent customer at the accused’s massage parlour in Thailand. Motivated by greed as it had been intimated to him that he could accrue gains by making these purchases, the Accused agreed to act on his instructions. He was given the names of the individuals that he should use for the signing of receipts for purchases he made with these cards, and eventually, the doctored identity document he needed to substantiate his false identity when proof was required of him during a transaction. Hence, the Accused did not know whom these cards belonged to but suspected that they were stolen. He also knew these cards were “fake” and had been tampered with, thus he was unsure whether they would function, as Boss Huang had asked him to “try” them out. Nonetheless, he decided to proceed with the plan to make fraudulent purchases with the cards.

6.    Further investigations suggest that the cards had been tampered with such that the EMV chips embedded in them belonged to AMEX cards that were stolen from their original owners. The original AMEX cards were taken from the Yunomori Onsen Pattaya, Thailand, when the rightful cardmembers1 had visited the establishment between 13 and 17 January 2025. There, an unidentified individual swapped the EMV chips on the AMEX cards with those obtained from other stolen cards and embedded the AMEX EMV chips to the stolen cards in turn. Subsequently, the cardmembers reported problems with their AMEX cards such as their cards being declined and the EMV chip falling off.

7.    Between 19 and 21 January 2025, the Accused made 7 fraudulent purchases at 4 different retail stores in Singapore using the fraudulent credit cards, with a total transaction value of SGD102,227.68.

S/N 1, 2, and 7 are the subjects of the proceeded charges and the details are provided in the subsequent sections. The three AMEX cards involved have since been cancelled and disposed of by the Accused prior to his re-entry into Singapore on 10 February 2025.

8.    According to AMEX, all the fraudulent transactions flagged were performed with the physical card present at the Point-of-Sale (‘POS’). In such cases, the card used would have to be present and in the possession of the card member at POS. However, the owners of the three AMEX cards listed at [6] above have confirmed that they were not in Singapore at the time of the transactions, that they were neither aware of nor benefitted from the transactions, and that their physical AMEX cards remained in their possession.

II      FACTS RELATING TO THE 1ST CHARGE (DAC-902421-2025)

9.    On 19 January 2025, at or about 12.45 p.m., the Accused went to Watch Capital, located at 111 Somerset Road, #01-33, Singapore 238164. While there, he chose to purchase a Rolex Daytona wristwatch bearing serial number [redacted] with a gold-coloured casing, buckle, and rubber strap, valued at SGD 31,800.

10.    When making the payment of SGD 32,716.10 (including a 2.8% overseas surcharge), the Accused presented a card embedded with an EMV chip contained the details of AMEX [redacted] to one Yip Ting Ting (‘Yip’), the salesperson at the said store, and verbally confirmed that he was the owner of the card when Yip checked with him. He also signed on the charge slip that was handed to him as confirmation of the sale by Yip after the payment had been processed on the POS machine. He did so to deceive Yip into believing he was the rightful owner of AMEX [redacted] to accept it for payment, though he knew he was not, thereby dishonestly inducing Yip to deliver the Rolex Daytona to him.

11.    By virtue of the foregoing, the Accused has committed the offence under s 420 of the Penal Code 1871 (‘PC’).

III      FACTS RELATING TO THE 2ND CHARGE (DAC-902587-2025)

12.    On the same day, at around 1.30 p.m., the Accused went to another store nearby called Lovelotsluxury, located at 181 Orchard Road, #04-02, Orchard Central, Singapore 238896. After browsing the items on display, he informed one Cai Pei Xin (‘Cai’), the salesperson of the said store, that he wanted to purchase one Chanel handbag retailing at SGD 9,550 and one Hermes necklace retailing at SGD 695. The total price of the two items was SGD 10,603.58 (inclusive of a 3.5% surcharge). While making payment for these items, he tried using several cards that were declined. Finally, he presented the same card as before, AMEX [redacted], to Cai for payment purposes and employed the same manner of deception as described in [10] above to dishonestly induce Cai to deliver the two items to him.

13.    By virtue of the foregoing, the Accused has committed the offence under s 420 of the PC.

14. After making the purchases above, the Accused also purchased a bracelet, a charm and two pendants from the same store, paying for the items using AMEX [redacted] as well, with a total transaction amount of SGD 4,518. In total, the Accused performed SGD 15,121.58 worth of fraudulent transactions at the said store.

IV      FACTS RELATING TO THE 7TH CHARGE (DAC-902592-2025)

15.    On 21 January 2025, at or around 3.17p.m., the Accused went to Sheen Enterprise, located at 14 Scotts Road, #04-114, Far East Plaza, Singapore 228213. There, the Accused chose to purchase a Rolex Daytona wristwatch bearing serial number [redacted] in a gold-coloured casing and a leather strap valued at SGD 39,140.

16.    When making the payment, the Accused presented a card embedded with an EMV chip contained the details of AMEX [redacted] to one Lim Sok Tying (‘Lim’), the salesperson at the said store. When the salesperson sought verification of his identity, he showed her a photograph of a Malaysian passport. He also signed on the charge slip that was handed to him as confirmation of the sale by Lim after the payment had been processed on the POS machine. He did so to deceive Lim into believing he was the rightful owner of AMEX [redacted] and to accept it for payment, thereby dishonestly inducing Lim to deliver the Rolex Daytona to him.

17.    By virtue of the foregoing, the Accused has committed the offence under s 420 of the PC.

V      SUBSEQUENT EVENTS

18.    Thereafter, the Accused left Singapore on 21 January 2025, carrying with him all the items that he had fraudulently purchased. He then retained possession of the items and began wearing the Rolex Daytona wristwatch as he liked it, though he initially told the police that he had handed over one watch to Boss Huang and paid him for the remaining one.

19.    During his arrest on 10 February 2025, five cards and the Rolex Daytona wristwatch purchased from Sheen Enterprise were seized from him. Of the cards found in his possession, three were credit or debit cards that did not belong to him and showed signs of tampering which suggested that a similar chip-swapping had been performed on them.

20.    Across the four statements that were taken from the Accused during investigations and subsequently during the court proceedings over the last 9 months, the Accused has provided multiple contradictory accounts as to the preparatory acts leading up to the proceeded charges. The facts in contention pertained to whether the Accused had personally tampered with the credit cards, or in the alternative, whether he had acted on the instructions of a third party while nonetheless aware that the cards were forged and that he was potentially aiding a syndicate which had committed further offences relating to the forging of these cards.

21.    At one point, he had purposefully misled the police by claiming to have acted alone in tampering the cards to conceal the involvement of other parties so as to avoid allegations of syndicate involvement in the hopes of receiving a more lenient sentence. In the midst of court proceedings, he then changed his mind and implicated Boss Huang once more. He then claimed that he did not have the know-how necessary to tamper with the cards despite having provided the police with highly technical information on when POS machines will allow a transaction to go through without a PIN number and the general usage of magnetic stripes on cards, and having been found with the three cards which had been tampered with in a similar manner. As a result, the police and the Prosecution have expended significant resources to discern the facts set out above.

22.    As of 30 July 2025, all items listed in the table at [7] have been recovered. The Accused has remained in remand since his arrest on 10 February 2025.

The Accused’s Antecedents

8       As the Accused is a foreigner, he did not have any criminal record in Singapore.

Prosecution’s Address on Sentence and Defence’s Plea-in-Mitigation

9       The respective sentencing positions of the Prosecution and the Defence are summarised in the table below:

Case Number

10     The Defence provided an alternative sentencing position wherein the 1st Charge (DAC-902421-2025) and the 7th Charge (DAC-902592-2025) were assumed to run consecutively. This was the same as the Prosecution’s position. In the Defence’s alternative scenario, the Defence submitted that the aggregate sentence should be between 37 to 42 months’ imprisonment.

Prosecution’s address on sentence

11     The Prosecution’s submissions on sentence are summarised from [12] to [20] below.

Overview of Prosecution’s submissions

12     The Prosecution submitted that both general and specific deterrence are the predominant sentencing consideration and it highlighted the following aggravating factors:

(a)     The Accused is a foreigner who has entered Singapore for the purpose of committing sophisticated fraud offences;

(b)     The Accused has committed seven counts of cheating involving credit card fraud over a short span of four days with the transactions amounting to more than $100,000. The Police seized some tampered credit cards from the Accused;

(c)     The Accused’s criminal activities were premediated and meticulously planned; and

(d)     The Accused has misled the Police and the Prosecution in his attempts to avoid a harsh sentence.

Sentences for the three proceeded charges and global position

13     The Prosecution cited the case of Public Prosecutor v Fernando Payagala Waduge Malita Kumar [2007] SGHC 23 (“Fernando Payagala”) at [75] where the High Court held that:

75    In my view, the starting point of the sentencing tariffs for the various s 420 credit card cheating offences should figure in the following range:

(a)     syndicated and/or counterfeit/forged credit card and/or sophisticated offences – 24 to 36 months’ imprisonment for each charge;

(b)     non-syndicated stolen/misappropriated credit card offences – 12 to 18 months’ imprisonment for each charge.

Mitigating and aggravating factors should then be assessed in deciding whether they should be allowed to tip the balance so that the sentence is discounted or enhanced accordingly. The adoption of a spectrum of sentencing options for first-time offenders will permit consideration to be duly accorded to the many and varied imponderables that inevitably figure in the sentencing equation.

14     For ease of reference in this Grounds of Decision, I shall refer to [75(a)] of Fernando Payagala as the “Syndicate Category” and to [75(b)] as the “Non-Syndicate Category”.

15     When Fernando Payagala was decided, the prescribed maximum punishment for an offence under s 420 of the PC was seven years’ imprisonment. Section 420 of the PC is now punishable with an imprisonment term of up to ten years. The Prosecution thus submitted that, prima facie, the sentencing tariff for the Syndicated Category should be increased to 34 to 51 months’ imprisonment. But this was only another point of reference in the sentencing inquiry, and the Prosecution would not be applying any uplift in a mathematical manner.[note: 1] The Prosecution relied on the sentencing factors enunciated in Fernando Payagala at [73] for its calibration of the sentences.

16     I have reproduced the sentencing factors of Fernando Payagala at [73] below:

73    In summary, any assessment of sentencing factors in a credit cheating offence should take into account the following:

(a)    degree of planning and premeditation (see [39] – [41]);

(b)    sophistication of offence and measures taken to avoid detection (see [42] – [43]);

(c)    role of the accused (see [44] – 45));

(d)    number of offences and quantum involved (see [46] – [48]);

(e)    extent of actual loss, damage and adverse consequences (both tangible and intangible) to victims and connected parties (see [49] – [50]);

(f)    international dimension (see [66] – [67]); and

(g)    remorse shown (see [49] – 54)).

17     Relying on Fernando Payagala at [75(a)] (see [13] above) and the above sentencing factors, the Prosecution submitted that the Accused’s actions warranted a sentence within the range of 32 to 34 months’ imprisonment for the 2nd Charge (DAC-902587-2025) and a sentence of 38 to 40 months’ imprisonment for the 1st Charge (DAC-902425-2025) and the 7th Charge (DAC-902592-2025). In this regard, the Prosecution made the following arguments:

(a)     The Accused had agreed to participate in the third party’s scheme to use forged credit cards for the purpose of cheating. The Accused had full knowledge that the credit cards had been tampered with and were of dubious origins. He had participated in the criminal scheme as he was motivated by the gains intimated to him in the form of purchases he would be making with the cards.

(b)     Sophistication of the offence and measures taken to avoid detection:

(i)       The Accused had ready the names of individuals that he should use for the signing of receipts when he made purchases with the cards; and

(ii)       He also used a forged identity document – the doctored photograph of a passport which he had shown to the staff assisting him at Sheen Enterprise to ensure that he had proof of identity which matched that of the EMV chip in the system – to bolster his credibility.

(c)     The Accused had acted on the instructions of a third party[note: 2] whilst committing the cheating offences. He had used credit cards which were tampered with and probably stolen. The Accused was probably aware that he was assisting in further offences and potentially acting as part of a larger syndicate and was minimally wilfully blind to the significance of his agreement to participate in the scheme.

(d)     The Accused was involved in seven transactions causing a total loss of $102,227.68 at first instance. The items were only fortuitously recovered from the Accused’s possession because he attempted to re-enter Singapore so soon after the initial offences that they had yet to be dissipated. The Accused had a charge under s 35(1) of the MOA taken into consideration for the purpose of sentencing.

(e)     The four stores and three genuine credit card owners were greatly inconvenienced and alarmed when the transactions first surfaced.

(f)     The Accused is a foreigner who came to Singapore to commit a serious offence. During his short stay, he had committed the cheating offences on nearly every day of his stay. He returned to Singapore for a second time with more tampered cards. The Prosecution raised the concern that other foreign nationals may consider similar schemes. The Prosecution submitted that a deterrent sentence is imperative to nip this in the bud and to protect Singapore’s reputation for low crime rates, financial safety, and effective law enforcement.

(g)     There was a lack of remorse from the Accused. He was unco-operative during investigations by repeatedly giving differing accounts and attempted to downplay the extent of his knowledge of the schemes.

Prosecution’s global sentencing position

18     The Prosecution submitted that the sentences for the 1st Charge (DAC-902425-2025) and the 7th Charge (DAC-902592-2025) should run consecutively as they involved higher amounts and the offences took place on different days. This would address the fact that the Accused had brazenly repeated the same manner of deception to purchase a similar item from a different store just two days after he committed the first offence. The sentence for the 2nd Charge (DAC-902587-2025) can run concurrently as it involved a lower amount. This would avoid a global sentence that may be crushing. The notional aggregate sentence would be 76 to 80 months’ imprisonment.

19     According to the Prosecution, the next stage of the sentencing inquiry was to determine the sentencing discount applicable in this case in view of the Accused’s plea of guilt. The Prosecution highlighted that despite the Accused’s early indication to plead guilty, there were significant delay in the case that were caused by him. This resulted in the Police and Prosecution having to expend further resources to discern an accurate account of the Accused’s criminal activities. As such, the Prosecution submitted that a sentencing discount of up to 20% based on Stage 2 of the Guidelines on Reduction in Sentences for Guilty Pleas (“SAP PG Sentencing Guidelines”) should apply.[note: 3] The notional aggregate sentence was accordingly reduced to 60 to 64 months’ imprisonment. Finally, the Prosecution gave a further two months’ reduction at the upper end of the aggregate sentence to give credit to the Accused for his part in arranging for the items to be brought back to Singapore. The final aggregate sentence derived by the Prosecution was 60 to 62 months’ imprisonment.

20     To recap, the Prosecution’s sentencing position can be found at the second column of the Table at [9] above.

Accused’s mitigation plea and sentencing position

21     I shall now summarise the Defence’s mitigation plea and sentencing position based on a logical manner arranged by me but still capturing all the sentencing factors and issues and legal arguments raised by the Defence in its written mitigation plea (Exhibit D1) and its oral submissions.

22     First, the Defence highlighted the Accused’s reason for coming to Singapore. The Accused was a businessman from the People’s Republic of China who ran a business in Thailand. The Accused intended to expand his business in Singapore and arranged to come to Singapore in early January 2025.[note: 4]

23     The Accused got to know Boss Huang who told him that there was an opportunity to earn money by using certain credit cards to purchase high-value items in Singapore.[note: 5] Although the Accused was sceptical, he took the three credit cards provided to him by Boss Huang[note: 6] and used them in Singapore which led to the commission of the offences for which the Accused was caught and prosecuted in court.

24     Second, the Defence highlighted the following factors pertaining to the Accused’s role and culpability:[note: 7]

(a)     There was no planning nor premeditation by the Accused who had no idea that the credit cards given to him by Boss Huang would work;

(b)     While the offences involved counterfeit credit cards, the Accused had no knowledge as to the nature of the credit cards. He thought he was simply using stolen credit cards;

(c)     The Accused had acted on his own, albeit that he was abetted by Boss Huang to use the credit cards;

(d)     The Accused did not possess “highly technical information” regarding Point-of-Sales (“POS”) machines – whether POS machines require a PIN number depends on the local banking rules and is known by business owners who utilise POS machines. This also has no relevance to his alleged knowledge and/or expertise in chip-swapping.

(e)     There were no actual loss, damage and/or adverse consequences occasioned to victims and connected parties. This was solely due to the Accused who voluntarily arranged for the items to be brought back to Singapore. The Defence submitted that this was a strong sign of the Accused’s remorse.

25     Third, on the matter of co-operation with the investigations, the Defence submitted that the Accused was misled by a fellow inmate and hence gave false accounts to the Police and in court proceedings. The reason behind this situation was because the Accused was worried for his 6-year-old daughter whom he had left alone in Thailand. The Accused regretted his action and expended all efforts to correct his account. Subject to this explanation, the Defence argued that the Accused has been co-operative with the authorities throughout the investigations.[note: 8]

26     Fourth, the Defence provided the Accused’s explanation for the non-recovery of the credit cards provided by Boss Huang and used by the Accused in committing the offences. The Accused explained that he had thrown away the credit cards provided by Boss Huang and hence he purchased three other credit cards online for the purposes of giving them to Boss Huang.[note: 9]

27     Fifth, the Defence provided the Accused’s personal background. The Accused is divorced from his wife, and he has sole care and control of his 6-year-old daughter. The Accused was very worried for his daughter, who had no one to take care of her in Thailand. The Accused had arranged for his daughter to be taken care of by his sister in China, he hopes that he can be reunited with his daughter soon. The Accused is a first-time offender and he was genuinely remorseful for his past actions. The Accused hopes to be serve out the sentence he deserves and move on to build a better future with his daughter.[note: 10]

28     Sixth, the Defence addressed the court on the appropriate sentences to be imposed by making a comparison of the present case with three precedent cases, namely, Public Prosecutor v Mihaly Magashazie [2005] SGDC 35 (“Mihaly”), Ong Tiong Poh v Public Prosecutor [1998] 2 SLR(R) 547 (“Ong Tiong Poh”) and Public Prosecutor v Prakash s/o Mathivan [2018] SGDC 284 (“Prakash”).[note: 11]

29     I have provided a short write-up on these case precedents below:

Mihaly

The offender pleaded guilty to two counts of theft under s 379 of the PC and three counts of cheating under s 420 of the PC. In respect of the three cheating charges, the offender had used stolen credit cards to make purchases of items amounting to a total of $16,540.00. 12 other charges of theft, cheating and attempted cheating were taken into consideration for the purpose of sentencing. The offender was sentenced to one year’s imprisonment for each of the cheating charges and one month’s imprisonment for each of the theft charges. The court ordered the terms of imprisonment for two counts of cheating and one count of theft to run consecutively, making a total sentence of two years and one month’s imprisonment.[note: 12]

Ong Tiong Poh

The offender faced 68 charges of cheating, attempted cheating, and abetment of cheating of various shops by the use of counterfeit credit cards. The prosecution proceeded with ten of the charges, namely, two cheating charges under s 420 of the PC and eight abetments by conspiracy of cheating charges under s 420 read with s 109 of the PC. The other 58 charges were stood down. The offender was convicted after a trial. The offender handed counterfeit credit cards to accomplices, gave instructions to purchase goods at various shops, received the purchased goods and paid commissions to the accomplices based on the selling price of the goods. On appeal, the High Court found that the sentences imposed by the District Court to be manifestly inadequate. The offender was part of a sophisticated syndicate, capable of committing credit card fraud on a large scale and skilled at avoiding detection. The sentences were enhanced to 12 months’ and 20 months’ imprisonment for each of the cheating and abetment charges respectively. Three of the latter sentences would run consecutively making a total of 60 months’ imprisonment. If not for the offender’s young age of 21, the sentences would be more severe.

Prakash

The offender pleaded guilty to 13 charges. 54 other charges were taken into consideration for the purpose of sentencing. The 13 proceeded charge comprised:

(i)    Four charges under the Computer Misuse and Cybersecurity Act (Cap 50A)

(ii)   One charges of cheating by personation under s 419 of the PC;

(iii)   Two charges of cheating under s 420 of the PC (“Carousell scam”);

(iv)   Two charges of cheating under s 420 of the PC (“using credit details not belonging to the offender”); and

(v)    Four charges for abetment of cheating under s 420 of the PC read with s 109 of the PC.

In respect of these four abetments by cheating charges, the facts revealed that the offender, Malani Naidu d/o Prabhakar Naidu (“Malani”), and Gardi Bin Bandi (“Gardi”) had engaged in a conspiracy to cheat pursuant to which Gardi would obtain credit card information belonging to third parties. The credit card details would then be used to make purchases and the items would thereafter be sold for cash. The offender and/or Malani then made purchases, either online or in person, using the credit card details and collected the items purchased. Thereafter, the offender, Malani and/or Gardi would sell the items for cash and the cash proceeds were to be shared among the trio. The offender and Gardi also agreed to use the credit card details to make payment for hotel stays.

In all, there were 11 successful transactions. The total value of the items in the transactions (including the charges taken into consideration) was $47,707. No restitution was made.

30     The Defence submitted that Ong Tiong Poh is the most analogous to the present case. However, the Defence argued that the Accused was demonstrably less culpable than the offender in Ong Tiong Poh. The Defence further argued that the Accused was not part of any syndicate. At the most, the Accused was Boss Huang’s runner.[note: 13]

31     The Defence submitted that although the offences involved counterfeit credit cards, the Accused did not know of the nature of the credit cards that Boss Huang had provided to him. The Defence thus submitted that the applicable sentencing tariff fell between 18 to 24 months’ imprisonment.[note: 14] The Defence has therefore refrained from applying the sentencing tariffs of Fernando Payagala. Instead, the Defence has developed, what I would term, a hybrid sentencing tariff – a sentencing tariff that fitted neatly in the gap between the Syndicate Category and the Non-Syndicate Category (see [13] above). The Defence acknowledged that as the prescribed punishment for s 420 of the PC is up to ten years’ imprisonment, it called for a revision of its hybrid sentencing tariff. The Defence’s revised hybrid sentencing tariff was 24 to 36 months’ imprisonment.[note: 15]

32     Based on the factors the Defence has put forth (see [22] to [31] above), the Defence reached the following notional sentences:[note: 16]

(a)     1st Charge (DAC-902421-2025) – 24 to 28 months’ imprisonment.

·       This is because at the time of commission of the offence, the Accused had no knowledge at all that the credit cards provided by Boss Huang was going to work.

(b)     2nd Charge (DAC-902587-2025) – 24 to 28 months’ imprisonment.

·       This is in view of the relatively low value of the items involved.

·       The Defence relied on the sentence imposed in Prakash (reference: DAC-942072-2017 involving $18,036.00) to calibrate the sentence for the 2nd Charge.[note: 17]

(c)     7th Charge (DAC-902592-2025) – 30 to 32 months’ imprisonment.

·       This is in view of the high value of the items obtained, and that the Accused had produced a doctored photograph of a passport given to him by Boss Huang when the staff wanted to verify his identity.

·       Following from its calibration of the sentence for the 2nd Charge, the Defence then doubled it for the 7th Charge.[note: 18]

33     Lastly, the Defence submitted that the sentences for the 1st Charge (DAC-902421-2025) and 2nd Charge (DAC-902587-2025) ought to run consecutively.[note: 19] The notional aggregate sentence would be 48 to 56 months’ imprisonment. Next, the Defence highlighted that the Accused had indicated his intention to plead guilty on 14 February 2025 which is still within Stage 1 of the SAP PG Sentencing Guidelines.[note: 20] As such, the Defence submitted that the Accused should be afforded a sentencing discount of 30%. In the final analysis, the Defence’s position was that a just and appropriate global sentence should be between 33.5 to 39 months’ imprisonment.[note: 21]

34     To recap, the Defence’s sentencing position can be found at the third column of the Table at [9] above.

Court’s decision and the sentences imposed

35     In determining the appropriate sentence for this case, I have approached it in four steps:

Step 1:    Calibrating the starting point of the sentencing tariff for credit card cheating offences under s 420 of the PC involving syndicated and/or counterfeit/forged credit card and/or sophisticated offences i.e. the Syndicate Category

Step 2:    There are two parts at this step. The first part is to assess the weight to be attached to the relevant sentencing factors. The second part is to determine the appropriate level of sentencing discount for this case.

Step 3:    Where there are two or more sentences of imprisonment, the court must decide which sentences of imprisonment should be made to run consecutively. Where there are three or more sentences of imprisonment, the court is required by law, namely s 307(1) of the Criminal Procedure Code 2010 (2020 Rev Ed), to order at least two sentences of imprisonment to run consecutively. The court would then derive a notional aggregate sentence.

Step 4:    Review the notional aggregate sentence by applying the totality principle and make an adjustment, if desirable, so that the final sentence is not a crushing one.

Step 1 – Calibrating the starting point of the sentencing tariff

36     First, the Prosecution and Defence have correctly submitted that the sentencing tariffs and principles enunciated in Fernando Payagala are applicable to this case.

37     Second, I found that this case fell into the Syndicate Category of the sentencing tariffs of Fernando Payagala. The Accused was given counterfeit credit cards by Boss Huang. The Accused knew that these credit cards did not belong to him. He obviously knew that he had not applied for these credit cards lawfully. He knew that these credit cards weren’t issued to him by the credit card companies legitimately. Boss Huang supported him with fake ID in respect of the use of the counterfeit credit cards. Therefore, there was sufficient factual basis for the Accused to have reasons to believe that Boss Huang had given him counterfeit credit. All these factors bore the hallmarks of a criminal syndicate. In fact, the Defence has conceded that the Accused was a runner of Boss Huang, whom I found to be a key player of a criminal syndicate. I therefore rejected the Defence’s submission of a hybrid sentencing tariff.

38     When Fernando Payagala was decided, the prescribed maximum punishment for an offence under s 420 of the PC was seven years’ imprisonment. Section 420 of the PC is now punishable with an imprisonment term of up to ten years. In view of the higher prescribed punishment for offences under s 420 of the PC, there was a need to adjust the Fernando Payagala sentencing tariffs upwards. In support of this proposition, I relied on the case of Poh Boon Kiat v Public Prosecutor [2014] SGHC 186 (“Poh Boon Kiat”).

39     In Poh Boon Kiat, Sundaresh Menon CJ stated at [60]:

60    … … It is trite that the statutory maximum sentence signals the gravity with which Parliament views any individual offence and that the sentencing judge ought to note the maximum penalty imposed and then apply his mind to determine precisely where the offender’s conduct falls within the entire range of punishment devised by Parliament: Angliss Singapore Pte Ltd v Public Prosecutor [2006] 4 SLR 653 (“Angliss”) at [86]. Put another way, the court should ensure that the full spectrum of sentences enacted by Parliament is carefully explored in determining the appropriate sentence: see Ong Chee Eng v Public Prosecutor [2012] 3 SLR 776 at [24].

(Emphasis added)

40     The issue which I must resolve was to determine the amount of uplift to the starting point of the sentencing tariff for the Syndicate Category.

41     In Fernando Payagala, the starting point of the sentencing tariff for the Syndicated Category was 24 to 36 months’ imprisonment. This was about 29% to 43%[note: 22] of the prescribed maximum punishment of seven years’ imprisonment. For the uplift needed to the starting point for the sentencing tariff, the Prosecution submitted that it should be around 34 to 51 months’ imprisonment, which worked out to be about 28% to 43%[note: 23] of the prescribed maximum punishment of ten years’ imprisonment.

42     As rightly pointed out by the Prosecution, any uplift should not be applied in a mathematical manner. As such, in my assessment, the new starting point of the sentencing tariff for the Syndicated Category should be around 25% to 40% of the prescribed maximum punishment of ten years’ imprisonment and these worked out to be 30 to 48 months’ imprisonment. In my judgment, the new starting point of the sentencing tariff for the Syndicated Category would provide for an easier application than the range proposed by the Prosecution.

43     Having determined the new starting point of the sentencing tariff for the Syndicated Category at 30 to 48 months’ imprisonment, I moved on to Step 2 of the sentencing inquiry.

Step 2 – Assessment of the relevant sentencing factors and determining the appropriate sentence for each charge, and determining the appropriate level of sentencing discount

44     In Huang Ying-Chun v Public Prosecutor [2018] SGHC 269 (“Huang Ying-Chun”), the appellant is a Taiwanese national who was 52 years old at the material time. He pleaded guilty to one charge under s 44(1)(a) of the Corruption, Drug Trafficking and Other Serious Crimes (Confiscation of Benefits) Act (Cap 65A, 2000 Rev Ed). The appellant was involved as a runner for a foreign syndicate that cheated Singapore residents of their monies and laundered those monies out of Singapore. The syndicate operated what might colloquially be known as a “police impersonation scam”.[note: 24] In Huang Ying-Chun, See Kee Oon J (as he then was) held at [86]:

86    In Fricker Oliver v Public Prosecutor and another appeal and another matter [2011] 1 SLR 84, the High Court held that it would be aggravating where “foreigners who are in Singapore [are here] for the sole purpose of committing crime” (at [2]). I consider that this, too, is an aggravating factor relevant to the sentencing analysis here. But I would introduce an element of nuance. As the appellant has rightly pointed out, a useful distinction can be drawn between those offenders who come to Singapore with the intention to commit crime and duly do so; and those who only realise once they are in Singapore that the work they were led to believe was legitimate was in fact criminal in nature. In my judgment, the former category should be treated more severely than the latter. This distinction helps illuminate the different possibilities encompassed by the phrase “sole purpose”.

45     In my assessment, the Accused was clearly an offender who had come to Singapore with the intention to commit crime and duly did so. As such, I was in full agreement with the Prosecution’s submission (see [12] and [16(f)] above)[note: 25] that the sentencing principles of general and specific deterrence were engaged in this case.

46     I also agreed with and accepted most of the Prosecution’s address on sentence (see [16] above). They were well-reasoned with proper application of the facts of the case to all the Fernando Payagala’s sentencing factors. I would also add to the Prosecution’s submission that all the sentencing factors applied with equal force across the three charges. My acceptance of the Prosecution’s submissions was therefore a rejection, in toto, of the Defence’s mitigation plea except for the weight to be attached to the Accused’s plea of guilt and his assistance to bring the items cheated back to Singapore.

47     With regards to the individual sentences for each charge, the Prosecution’s sentencing position for the 1st Charge (DAC-902421-2025) and 7th Charge (DAC-902592-2025) was the same, i.e. 38 to 40 months’ imprisonment. For the 2nd Charge (DAC-902587-2025), the Prosecution submitted for a sentence of 32 to 34 months’ imprisonment. It was fortuitous that the Prosecution’s calibration of the individual sentences fell neatly into the new starting point of the sentencing tariff (see [42] and [43] above). I agreed, in general, with the Prosecution’s proposed sentence for each charge save for the observation made in the next paragraph.

48     The value of the item involved in the 1st Charge (DAC-902421-2025) was $32,716.10. The value of the item involved in the 7th Charge (DAC-902592-2025) was $39,140.00. There is a difference of around $6,400 between the value of the two items. In my assessment, the individual sentences must reflect the differential in the value of the items involved. It is a well-established general principle “that in sentencing for financial and property offences, the greater the economic value involved in the offence, the heavier the sentence” : Gan Chai Bee Anne v Prosecutor [2019] SGHC 42 at [42] which followed Fernando Payagala at [47] and Lim Ying Ying Luciana v Public Prosecutor and another appeal [2016] 4 SLR 1220 at [69]. Therefore, the sentence for the 7th Charge (DAC-902592-2025) ought to be higher than the sentence for the 1st Charge (DAC-902421-2025). As the value of the item for the 2nd Charge (DAC-902587-2025) was the lowest amongst the three charges, the sentence for the 2nd Charge would be the lowest amongst the three charges.

49     Therefore, based on the new starting point of the sentencing tariff (see [42] and [43] above) and my observation above, I made some minor adjustment to the sentences proposed by the Prosecution and arrived at the following indicative starting sentences:

(a)     1st Charge (DAC-902421-2025) – 40 months’ imprisonment;

(b)     2nd Charge (DAC-902587-2025) – 33 months’ imprisonment; and

(c)     7th Charge (DAC-902592-2025) – 42 months’ imprisonment.

50     I have considered the Defence’s mitigation plea and oral submissions before arriving at the above indicative starting sentences. Other than the Accused’s plea of guilt and his assistance to retrieve the items cheated from the stores, I did not find any mitigatory value in the rest of the Defence’s mitigation plea. The sentencing discount for the Accused’s plea of guilt and his assistance to retrieve the items cheated is dealt with in [52] to [53] below.

51     I did not give any weight to the Accused’s personal and family hardship. The Accused is a foreigner and he left his young daughter in Thailand[note: 26] to come to Singapore to commit crimes. I found that the Accused would have known of the consequences, namely, to serve jail time, should he be caught for his crimes in Singapore. He had left his daughter in Thailand by choice. After his arrest in Singapore, he had to make arrangements for his sister to look after his daughter. He cannot plead leniency on account of his daughter whom he had left behind arising from his criminal activities. It is well settled law that, except in most exceptional circumstances, hardship to the offender’s family has very little, if any mitigating value: see Lai Oei Mui Jenny v Public Prosecutor [1993] 2 SLR(R) 406. I did not find the Accused’s personal and family circumstances to be any different from other cases. This is plainly not an exceptional case.

Determining the sentencing discount for the Accused’s plea of guilt

52     I was doubtful whether the sentencing discount of up to 30% at Stage 1 of the SAP PG Sentencing Guidelines was applicable in this case. Paragraph 11 of the said guidelines state:

The maximum reduction in sentence of 30% in Stage 1 will apply as long as the accused person indicates during Stage 1 that he intends to plead guilty, without the need for the guilty plea to be taken during Stage 1. … However, the 30% maximum reduction in sentence will only operate if the accused person later follows through by pleading guilty without resiling from his initial indication of plea. The court may also apply a lower reduction in sentence if it assesses that the accused person had unreasonably delayed his guilty plea after his initial indication during Stage 1 that he would plead guilty. [Emphasis added].

I found that the Accused had forfeited his eligibility for the 30% sentencing discount based on the ground that he had declined to plead guilty on three occasions i.e. 28 March 2025, 3 June 2025 and 26 August 2025.[note: 27] Valuable resources from the Judiciary, the Prosecution and the Police were put to waste by the Accused.[note: 28] In my assessment, on account of the Accused’s plea of guilt, a sentencing discount of 10% can be applied. I was fortified in my assessment after reviewing the decision of Huang Ying-Chun. In Huang Ying-Chun (see [44] above for the brief facts), the appellant was sentenced to six years and six months’ imprisonment by the District Judge. The appellant appealed against his sentence. On appeal, See J considered the appropriate starting point to be 72 months’ imprisonment: Huang Ying-Chun at [129]. See J went on and stated:

130 Only one offender-specific factor applies here. The appellant ultimately accepted responsibility and pleaded guilty, albeit not at the first opportunity. The appellant was charged on 8 July 2017 but only pleaded guilty on 4 June 2018. An appropriate discount would be six months’ imprisonment. The adjusted sentence is thus 66 months’ imprisonment.

The sentencing discount in Huang Ying-Chun, in percentage term, worked out to be about 8%. Like the offender in Huang Ying-Chun, the Accused in the present case only had one offender-specific factor that was applicable, i.e. his delayed plea of guilt.

53     I then added a further 5% to give credit to the Accused for making the arrangement to have the items involved brought back to Singapore. In conclusion, I applied a sentencing discount of 15% to the indicative starting sentences.

54     Therefore, after providing for the 15% sentencing discount, I arrived at the following notional sentences:

(a)     1st Charge (DAC-902421-2025) – 34 months’ imprisonment;

(b)     2nd Charge (DAC-902587-2025) – 28 months’ imprisonment; and

(c)     7th Charge (DAC-902592-2025) – 36 months’ imprisonment.

Rejecting the three case precedents cited by the Defence

55     Before moving to Step 3 of the sentencing inquiry, I digress to deal with the three case precedents cited by the Defence.

Mihaly and Ong Tiong Poh

56      Mihaly was decided by the District Court in 2005. Ong Tiong Poh was a High Court decision decided in 1998. I placed no weight on these two cases as they have been superseded by the decision of Fernando Payagala.[note: 29]

Prakash

57     In Prakash, the District Judge (“DJ”) was aware of the decision of Fernando Payagala. However, in her grounds of decision, the DJ did not discuss or apply the sentencing tariffs enunciated in Fernando Payagala. The failure by the DJ to apply the Fernando Payagala’s sentencing tariffs was a serious omission as Fernando Payagala was a decision that was binding on her. Furthermore, the DJ also did not consider the revision needed to the sentencing tariffs to account for a higher prescribed punishment under s 420 of the PC. For the reasons stated, I gave no weight to Prakash as a sentencing precedent. I would like to add that the sentences imposed by the DJ were upheld on appeal. Unfortunately, the High Court did not release written grounds.

Step 3 – Concurrent and consecutive sentencing

58     Pursuant to s 307(1) CPC, I was obliged to order at least two of the three sentences of imprisonment to run consecutively.

59     The Prosecution submitted that the sentences for the 1st Charge (DAC-902425-2025) and the 7th Charge (DAC-902592-2025) should run consecutively as they involved higher amounts and the offences took place on different days. I did not agree with the Prosecution’s submission. In this regard, I was mindful of the decision of Mohamed Shouffee bin Adam v Public Prosecutor [2014] SGHC 34 (“Mohamed Shouffee”) where Sundaresh Menon CJ held at [25] that:

25    … … [t]here is no presumption or rule that the two most severe sentences should ordinarily be selected to run consecutively. Nor is it a rule that the most severe individual sentence of imprisonment must be selected as one of the sentences to run consecutively, so long as the aggregate of the sentences that are so selected exceeds the longest individual sentence.”

60     On the other hand, the Defence has submitted that the sentences for the 1st Charge (DAC-902421-2025) and 2nd Charge (DAC-902587-2025) ought to run consecutively. The Defence has selected the two charges where the value of the items involved were the lowest amongst the three proceeded charges. In my view, such a selection has downplayed the culpability of the Accused. For this reason, I rejected the Defence’s submission.

61     In my assessment, the terms of imprisonment for the 2nd Charge (DAC-902587-2025) and the 7th Charge (DAC-902592-2025) ought to run consecutively. These two offences were committed on different days. As was submitted by the Prosecution, the Accused had brazenly repeated the same manner of deception to purchase another item from a different store just two days after he had committed the first offence. In my assessment, ordering the sentences for the 2nd Charge (DAC-902587-2025) and the 7th Charge (DAC-902592-2025) to run consecutively gave a better reflection of the overall culpability of the Accused and the loss caused to the stores.

Step 4 – Aggregate sentence

62     At this stage of the sentencing inquiry, the Accused faced a notional aggregate sentence of 64 months’ imprisonment. I was mindful that my decision on aggregate sentence must not fall foul of the sentencing principles (i.e. the one-transaction rule and the totality principle) laid down by Sundaresh Menon CJ in Mohamed Shouffee.

63     I then reviewed the individual sentences and overall sentence. In my review of the individual sentences, I saw no reason to disturb my assessment of the individual sentences. As for the review of the overall sentence, I was guided by the totality principle. It was my assessment that the aggregate sentence would not be a crushing sentence on the Accused. As such, the final sentences that I imposed on the Accused are as stated at [3] above.

Backdating of the sentence

64     The Accused was arrested on 10 February 2025 and kept in Police’s custody until he was charged in court on 12 February 2025. The Accused was not allowed to be released on bail. Thus, the Accused was put in remand from 12 February 2025.

65     As the Accused had not been co-operative with the investigations, I did not see any merit in backdating the sentence to the date of his arrest. As such, I ordered his sentence to commence from 12 February 2025.

Public Prosecutor v Siah Choon Seng

Public Prosecutor v Siah Choon Seng
[2026] SGDC 185

Case Number:District Arrest Case No 909935 of 2021 and anor, Magistrate's Appeal No MA-9045-2026-01
Decision Date:12 June 2026
Tribunal/Court:District Court
Coram: Lau Qiuyu
Counsel Name(s): Claire Poh (Attorney-General's Chambers) for the Public Prosecutor; The Accused in person.
Parties: Public Prosecutor — Siah Choon Seng

Criminal Law – Offences – Property – Cheating

Criminal Law – Offences – Property – Forgery

Criminal Procedure and Sentencing – Sentencing

[LawNet Editorial Note: An appeal to this decision has been filed in MA 9045/2026/01.]

12 June 2026

District Judge Lau Qiuyu:

1       The self-represented accused person, Mr Siah Choon Seng, claimed trial before me to two charges – one charge of cheating under s 420 of the Penal Code (Cap 224, 2008 Rev Ed) (the “PC”) and one charge of forgery for the purpose of cheating under s 468 of the PC. In addition, the accused faced two other charges (one under s 420 and the other under s 468 of the PC), which were stood down for the purposes of the trial before me.

2       Upon the conclusion of the trial and having considered in detail the evidence and submissions before me, I found the Prosecution to have proven its case beyond reasonable doubt and convicted the accused accordingly on both charges.

3       After convicting the accused, I imposed a total sentence of 14 months’ imprisonment as follows:

Charge No.

14 months’ imprisonment

Concurrent



4       On the same day that sentence was passed, the accused lodged an appeal against the conviction and sentence in respect of both charges. A stay of execution on the sentence was allowed further to the lodging of the appeal. The accused is presently on bail, both pending the appeal and pending the resolution of the two stood down charges.

5       The detailed reasons for my decision are set out herein.

The charges

6       The two charges faced by the accused are reproduced in full below:

The Cheating Charge

You… are charged that you did cheat Hong Say Hoe by deceiving him into believing that you were representing Professional Investment Advisory Services Pte Ltd to purchase 55 Samsung S21 Ultra 5G mobile phones (“the phones”) with a total value of $89,705.00, a fact you knew to be false, to wit, by sending an email to the said Hong Say Hoe on 15 March 2021 at about 12.14am, in Singapore, and by such manner of deception, you dishonestly induced the said Hong Say Hoe to cause the phones to be delivered to one Abdul Hakim on 21 April 2021, and you have thereby committed an offence punishable under s 420 of the [PC].

The Forgery Charge[note: 1]

You… are charged that you, sometime between 15 to 22 March 2021, in Singapore, did commit forgery by dishonestly affixing electronic signatures on an electronic record, to wit, the electronic signatures of Choa Mei Kuen on a Quotation Form for 55 Samsung Galaxy S21 Ultra 5G mobile phones, with the intention of causing it to be believed that the electronic signatures was signed by the person, whom you know had not signed the electronic record, intending that the forged electronic record shall be used for the purpose of cheating, and you have thereby committed an offence punishable under s 468 of the [PC].

The Prosecution’s case

7       Relying on circumstantial evidence, the Prosecution submitted that there was overwhelming evidence to prove its case against the accused. A total of 11 witnesses were called by the Prosecution:

PW11



8       Of these, the five witnesses marked as PW7 to PW11 were additional witnesses called by the Prosecution in rebuttal. Further, there was a Prosecution witness called solely for the purpose of an ancillary hearing, which was convened in relation to the admissibility of the accused’s cautioned statement – this was the statement recorder, Ms Sophia Sim Shi Mei, marked as “1AH-PW1”. This said statement was eventually admitted in evidence (see [141] to [143] below).

Circumstances leading to the police report

9       On 24 May 2021, PW1 Mr Hong Say Hoe, a sales manager at Maxxmedia International Pte Ltd (“Maxxmedia”), lodged a police report,[note: 2] detailing how one “Alson Teo Hock Loo” (or “Alson”), who was purportedly working at Professional Investment Advisory Services Pte Ltd (“PIAS”), had placed an order with Maxxmedia for 55 sets of Samsung Galaxy S21 Ultra 5G mobile phones (the “55 Phones”) for PIAS’ use. Maxxmedia was a reseller of audio-visual equipment, including mobile phones.[note: 3]

10     PW1 had never met “Alson” in person and only communicated with him through “Alson’s” email address at “[email protected]” (the “Ampang Email”) over a period from March to April 2021 (the “Order Emails”).[note: 4] As part of the Order Emails, “Alson” forwarded PW1 a copy of the quotation form with the director’s stamp and signature,[note: 5] showing that PIAS had approved of the quotation and wished to proceed with the order. PW1 proceeded with the order and the 55 Phones were subsequently collected from Maxxmedia.

11     As no payment was received by Maxxmedia after the expiry of the agreed 30-day credit term,[note: 6] PW1 tried to contact “Alson” but to no avail.[note: 7] PW1 hence attended at PIAS’ office to look for “Alson”, where he was informed that no such person existed and no order for the 55 Phones was placed by PIAS. It was at this point that PW1 realised he could have been defrauded and he proceeded to make a police report on the same day.

The signature in the quotation sent to PW1 was forged

12     PW1 prepared the quotation for the 55 Phones and sent it to the Ampang Email for “Alson’s” review. In response, PW1 received an endorsed copy of the quotation from the Ampang Email on 22 March 2021, containing a signature with the following designation under the signature: “Choa Mei Kuen, Director, [NRIC number], PS Code: 1188” (the “Signed Quotation”).[note: 8] The same signature again appeared in a box at the bottom of the quotation just above the words “Client’s Acceptance (Sign and Stamp)”, along with a PIAS company stamp. Upon seeing this, PW1 believed the signatures on the Signed Quotation to be Choa Mei Kuen’s, who he thought was the “procurement authorised person”.[note: 9]

13     After receiving the Signed Quotation, PW1 proceeded to place the order with the Samsung distributor for the 55 Phones and awaited delivery of the same. If PW1 had known that: (a) “Choa Mei Kuen” was not a director of PIAS; (b) she did not sign on the Signed Quotation; (c) the signatures did not belong to her; and/or (d) the signatures and/or stamp were not authorised, he would not have proceeded to contact the distributor and order the 55 Phones.[note: 10]

14     PW2 Ms Choa Mei Kuen testified that she used to work as a financial advisor at PIAS from June 2016 to 31 January 2021. Contrary to what was indicated on the Signed Quotation, she was never a director with PIAS. However, the NRIC number reflected thereon was hers. The “PS Code” of 1188 also corresponded to the advisory code assigned to her when she worked at PIAS. PW2 unequivocally stated that she has never seen the Signed Quotation, and she did not affix her signature on it either.[note: 11] PW2 observed that her signature “look[ed] a bit like [the one in the Signed Quotation] … but it [was] really not [her] signature.”[note: 12] In other words, while it looked like her signature, it was not.

15     PW2’s unchallenged testimony was hence that she had nothing to do with the forged Signed Quotation, which contained her name and purported signatures. She did not personally affix her signatures on the Signed Quotation and had already left PIAS when the Signed Quotation was sent by way of the 22 March 2021 email from the Ampang Email to PW1.[note: 13]

The accused was using the Ampang Email

16     The Prosecution submitted that the key issue of fact was whether the accused was the one who had used the Ampang Email to liaise with PW1 in the Order Emails,[note: 14] through which the 55 Phones were ordered. This was key to both charges as the Signed Quotation was also sent by the user of the Ampang Email to PW1.

17     The user of the Ampang Email consistently signed off as “Alson Teo Hock Loo” of PIAS in the Order Emails.[note: 15] However, there was no person by the name of “Alson Teo Hock Loo” working at PIAS.[note: 16] Instead, there was an “Alson Teo Keck Wee”, who was an Associate Financial Services Director at PIAS. This was PW5 Mr Teo Keck Wee. PW5 clarified that while his registered name (as it appeared on his NRIC) was “Teo Keck Wee”, he used the name of “Alson Teo Keck Wee” at work and this was the name reflected in his PIAS stamp.[note: 17] PW5 did not know anyone by the name of “Alson Teo Hock Loo”, has never used or seen the Ampang Email, and has not seen the Order Emails before.[note: 18]

18     Against the fictitious identity of “Alson Teo Hock Loo” adopted by the Ampang Email user, it was the accused who received delivery of the 55 Phones contained in three boxes from PW4 Mr Abdul Hakim bin Anuar at Jackson Square on 21 April 2021. This was caught on CCTV.[note: 19] Shortly thereafter, the accused was caught on PolCam footage at the lift lobby of Block 54 Lorong 5 Toa Payoh carrying the same three boxes.[note: 20] This was the block of flats where the accused was residing at, and the 55 Phones were eventually seized from the accused’s flat on 27 May 2021 and 11 June 2021.[note: 21]

19     The Prosecution pointed to various instances linking the accused to the use of the Ampang Email.

Reference to the Ampang Email in a Magistrate’s Complaint filed by the accused

20     The Prosecution tendered a Magistrate’s Complaint filed by the accused with the State Courts on 22 April 2019 against his ex-wife, one Mdm Poh Hsiao Yen.[note: 22] As part of the grounds of complaint, the accused attached an email printout which was sent from himself, using the email address “[email protected]” (the “SCS Gmail”), to the Ampang Email. As a copy of this email printout accessed from the Ampang Email was attached to the Magistrate’s Complaint, it followed that the accused must have had access to and was using the Ampang Email.

The accused provided the Ampang Email as his email contact to a pharmacist

21     The Prosecution also relied on WhatsApp messages forensically extracted from a Samsung J1 mobile phone (the “J1 Phone”) which was seized from the accused at his flat on 27 May 2021.[note: 23] PW3 Mr Hairulnizam Kamsin gave evidence on how he had conducted a forensic search on 10 August 2021 on the contents of the J1 Phone,[note: 24] with the details and results of the search set out in a report drafted by PW6 Mr Aliden bin Hamad dated 30 August 2021 (the “Forensic Report”).[note: 25]

22     These extracted WhatsApp messages showed the accused communicating with a pharmacist based in Johor Bahru. On 31 July 2020, the pharmacist sent a message to the accused, asking for his particulars in relation to a medication order. He replied on the same day with his personal particulars, where he listed the Ampang Email as his email address.[note: 26] As the details of the other personal particulars (including his name, NRIC number, date of birth, contact number and delivery address) were accurate and belonged to the accused,[note: 27] it must follow that the accused had provided the Ampang Email because it similarly belonged to him and he was to be contacted at this email address.

The Ampang Email was contained in various notes drafted by the accused

23     In addition, various notes were forensically extracted from the J1 Phone, which the accused admitted were drafted by him.[note: 28] Highlighting the multiple references to the accused seeking to be contacted at the Ampang Email in these notes, the Prosecution submitted that the Ampang Email must have belonged to him.

(a)     In the first note titled “SINGPOST” dated 11 August 2019, the accused drafted an enquiry on the status of his mails sent to China. In this note, he signed off with his name, mobile phone number, and the Ampang Email.[note: 29]

(b)     In the second note titled “Appeal for Info/witnesses” dated 18 June 2019, the accused sought the assistance of witnesses to provide information on an alleged theft committed by his ex-wife. In this note, he similarly provided the Ampang Email as part of his contact details.[note: 30]

Files found in the J1 Phone pointed to the accused’s involvement

24     The Prosecution further relied on other files found in the J1 Phone, which pointed to the accused’s involvement in the Cheating Charge and the Forgery Charge. These files were either: (a) forensically extracted from the J1 Phone (see [21] above); and/or (b) tendered as photographs taken from the screen of the J1 Phone, with the files displayed thereon.[note: 31] PW6 was the one who had asked for the latter photographs to be taken and was present with the photographer at the material time.[note: 32] The Prosecution’s position was that the J1 Phone belonged to the accused, though this was denied by him (see [47] to [49] below).

Files in the J1 Phone relating to the creation of the Signed Quotation

25     As regards the accused’s involvement in the creation of the Signed Quotation, the Prosecution referred to the following documents found in the J1 Phone:

(a)     A folder titled “Maxxmedia” in the J1 Phone, which contained two PDF files therein.[note: 33] The first was a copy of the Signed Quotation and the second was a copy of the quotation prepared by PW1 and sent to the Ampang Email (ie, before the purported signatures of PW2 were affixed; see [12] above).[note: 34]

(b)     Drafts of what eventually came to be the Signed Quotation in varying permutations – one with PW2’s purported designation and the PIAS stamp but without PW2’s purported signatures, and another with the PIAS stamp and only one of PW2’s purported signature.[note: 35]

(c)     Image files of the PIAS stamp and PW2’s purported signature, which resembled those that were eventually affixed on the Signed Quotation.[note: 36]

(d)     Numerous photo-editing applications installed in the J1 Phone such as Adobe Photoshop, Add Water Mark Free, Cut Paste Photo Editor, etc.[note: 37]

26     The Prosecution submitted that the presence of the files at [25] above “inextricably pointed” to the accused being the person who had produced the Signed Quotation. He had done so by imposing PW2’s purported signature and the PIAS stamp onto the quotation sent by PW1 using the photo-editing applications and had “worked with several drafts before sending the final [Signed Quotation] to [PW1].”[note: 38]

Files in the J1 Phone relating to the delivery of the 55 Phones

27     As regards the accused’s involvement in arranging for the delivery of the 55 Phones to Jackson Square (see [18] above), the Prosecution referred to an image of a screenshot found in the J1 Phone, which pertained to the delivery of the 55 Phones.[note: 39] The screenshot showed the contact information of “Alson Teo Hock Loo” with a note to the driver to collect the items from Maxxmedia’s office and have them delivered to Jackson Square. The J1 Phone further had the GOGOX application installed,[note: 40] which was the delivery service used in this case. The 55 Phones were eventually collected by the accused at Jackson Square.

28     In addition, there was a deleted note created on 21 April 2021 at 10.32am that read “XXXX9176 Hakim”. To this end, PW4 Mr Abdul Hakim bin Anuar was the GOGOX delivery personnel who carried out the delivery as per the details in the screenshot in the J1 Phone at [27] above. PW4 arrived at Jackson Square with the 55 Phones at about 10.27am on 21 April 2021.[note: 41] PW4 then attempted to call the recipient at about 10.28am, before meeting with the accused at around 10.31am.[note: 42] PW4 was observed on CCTV to have been communicating with the accused till about 10.32am.[note: 43]

29     From the above, the Prosecution submitted that the time at which the note was created (ie, 10.32am) strongly suggested that the accused had obtained PW4’s mobile phone number when they met, which in turn pointed to the accused’s role in coordinating the delivery of the 55 Phones.[note: 44]

Files in the J1 Phone relating to the accused’s intention to sell the 55 Phones

30     Finally, the Prosecution also compared the images of the model of the 55 Phones (ie, Samsung Galaxy S21 Ultra 5G, 256GB, Phantom Silver colour) found in the J1 Phone,[note: 45] with those uploaded to the “SG Mob Mart” website as part of a sales listing of the same model by one “Teo” on 9 May 2021.[note: 46] The listing was created after the accused had acquired the 55 Phones on 21 April 2021 but before he was arrested on 27 May 2021. The Prosecution considered the presence of such images in the J1 Phone to be “strongly suggestive of the accused’s intention to take preparatory steps to sell the [55 Phones].”[note: 47]

The accused’s past dealings with PW2

31     PW2 was first acquainted with the accused in 2016, when she had introduced him to a health plan in her capacity as a financial services manager with PIAS.[note: 48] As part of this, PW2 recalled that the accused would have had access to her signature, NRIC number and PIAS code, as she would include these information in the health insurance application form before handing a copy of the completed form to the accused.[note: 49] This health plan was however eventually not approved.

32     Thereafter, PW2 also managed the accused’s unit trust investment portfolio, though this resulted in losses. This prompted the accused to make complaints against PW2, including threats to commence suit. The accused’s past dealings with PW2 hence showed that he had an “axe to grind” with PW2, or would, at the very least, lead to the drawing of an inference that the accused would have “no qualms in utilising [PW2’s] personal details to perpetrate his scams even though he knew this would eventually result in inconvenience to [PW2].”[note: 50]

The accused’s lies in his statements were corroborative of his guilt

33     Two statements were recorded from the accused on 28 May 2021, the day after his arrest. The Prosecution’s position was that the accused had lied in both these statements about the whereabouts of the remaining 54 mobile phones (as only one of the 55 Phones had been seized by this time). In essence, the accused stated in these statements that he was not in possession of the mobile phones, even though the remaining 54 mobile phones were eventually seized from his flat on 11 June 2021, after he had given these statements. The Prosecution hence submitted that these amounted to Lucas lies (from the English Court of Appeal decision of R v Lucas (Ruth) [1981] 1 QB 720; [1981] 2 All ER 1008 (“Lucas”)) and carried “significant probative weight” as to the accused’s guilt.[note: 51]

Strength of the circumstantial evidence points towards the accused’s guilt beyond reasonable doubt

34     In conclusion, the Prosecution submitted that the circumstantial evidence before the court would meet the requisite standard of “inevitably and inexorably” leading the court to a single conclusion of the accused’s guilt (see Public Prosecutor v Chee Cheong Hin Constance [2006] 2 SLR(R) 24 (“Constance Chee”) at [77]). This was the standard required to prove both the Cheating Charge and the Forgery Charge beyond reasonable doubt, which has been met here given the overwhelming evidence against the accused.[note: 52]

Close of Prosecution’s case

35     The Prosecution made an application to amend the Forgery Charge just before it closed its case. While the Forgery Charge initially provided that the act was committed sometime between “17 to 22 March 2021”, the Prosecution sought to expand this time frame slightly to “15 to 22 March 2021” given the time stamps in the Order Emails and PW1’s evidence.[note: 53] The accused had no objections to the amendment. I hence allowed the application for the Forgery Charge to be altered as per the Prosecution’s application.[note: 54] The requisite consent of the Public Prosecutor under s 10 of the Criminal Procedure Code 2010 (“CPC”) was also amended accordingly.[note: 55]

36     The altered Forgery Charge was read and explained to the accused. He maintained his intention to claim trial and stated that he did not wish to recall any witnesses pursuant to s 131 of the CPC.[note: 56]

37     In the premises, the Prosecution proceeded to close its case. The accused did not make any submissions of no case to answer. As I was satisfied that there was some evidence, not inherently incredible, that satisfied each and every element of both charges, I called upon the accused to give evidence in his own defence. The accused elected to give evidence.

The Defence’s case

38     The accused called three witnesses in support of his defence: the accused himself (who was marked as DW1), DW2 Mr Siow Kwong Ting Stanwin and DW3 Ms Ng Bee Choo. DW2 was the accused’s expert witness who testified on issues relating to data synchronisation and Internet Protocol (“IP”) addresses. DW3 Ms Ng was the accused’s mother. She lived with the accused and was present during the arrest and seizure on 27 May 2021.

39     The accused vehemently denied committing both the Cheating Charge and the Forgery Charge. He disassociated himself from the Ampang Email and the J1 Phone, both of which the accused asserted belonged to one “Ah Heng” instead. The accused explained that he was at Jackson Square to collect the 55 Phones on “Ah Heng’s” instructions and was otherwise unaware of the contents of the delivery.

The accused’s acquaintance with “Ah Heng”

40     In May 2016, the accused was deceived into depositing a sum of $2,500 into a bank account as collateral to secure a $25,000 business loan from a private moneylender known as “Ah Heng”. As the accused did not receive the said loan, he lodged a police report. The accused then learnt that he had deposited the sum of $2,500 into the bank account of one “Teo Hock Loo”, who had relinquished his ATM card to “Ah Heng”.

41     Following from that, through the investigative efforts of the accused, he managed to track down “Ah Heng” in Malaysia sometime in 2019. “Ah Heng” informed the accused that he was unable to repay the accused but offered to help the accused in whatever way required. In exchange, the accused promised not to report “Ah Heng” to the police.[note: 57]

The Ampang Email was used by “Ah Heng”

42     “Ah Heng” assisted the accused in various ways, which would on occasion involve the use of “Ah Heng’s” email address, ie, the Ampang Email. To this end, the accused averred that he was not the operator of the Ampang Email, as he instead used the following two email addresses: “[email protected]” (the “SCS Hotmail”) and the SCS Gmail. The accused was thus not privy to the emails exchanged between PW1 and the Ampang Email.[note: 58]

“Ah Heng” used the Ampang Email to provide assistance to the accused

43     As part of the assistance rendered to the accused, “Ah Heng” would print documents and information sent by the accused to “Ah Heng” at the Ampang Email. This included the grounds of complaint attached to the Magistrate’s Complaint (see [20] above). Having “Ah Heng” print would save the accused money, as he need not pay for internet surfing charges and the cost of printing. The accused had sent the grounds of complaint to “Ah Heng”, intending for “Ah Heng” to make some cosmetic edits, but “Ah Heng” printed the email directly from his Ampang Email inbox instead.[note: 59]

44     As regards the WhatsApp messages to the pharmacist, the accused had provided the Ampang Email as part of his personal particulars (see [21] and [22] above) as “Ah Heng” was helping to liaise with the pharmacist in Johor Bahru.[note: 60]

45     As regards the various notes drafted by the accused (see [23] above), the accused had signed off with the Ampang Email in the SingPost note as “Ah Heng” was coordinating with the Chinese counterpart. As for the second note on the appeal for witnesses, the Ampang Email was used in the draft note as the accused had intended for “Ah Heng” to gather evidence and secure the witnesses’ willingness to attend in court. However, in the eventual copy that was printed by Ah Heng,[note: 61] the Ampang Email was replaced with the accused’s own (ie, the SCS Hotmail) as he was worried that “Ah Heng” could not convince the witnesses successfully.[note: 62]

The user of the “Ampang Email” was based overseas

46     During his testimony, the accused conducted a demonstration using six emails he received from the Ampang Email, five of which were received on 18 June 2021 and the remaining one on 19 June 2021. As part of the demonstration, the accused accessed his email inbox, and, in respect of each of the six emails, retrieved the details of the message source, which displayed an IP address from which the email was received. Thereafter, he searched up the location of each of the six IP addresses using a website, which would display the country and city of each IP address.[note: 63] The outcome of the searches showed that the IP addresses of these six emails were tagged to Hong Kong, South Korea and Singapore.[note: 64] As the accused’s passport had already been impounded as part of his bail conditions[note: 65] by the time these emails were sent, the accused could not have been the one who operated the Ampang Email as he was in Singapore during this time.[note: 66] The accused further called an expert witness, DW2 Mr Siow Kwong Ting Stanwin, in support of his position on the IP addresses. The accused relied on DW2’s expertise in this area, as DW2 possessed a degree in computer engineering and has work experience in various technology-related roles.[note: 67]

Files extracted from the J1 Phone did not implicate the accused

The J1 Phone belonged to “Ah Heng”

47     The accused denied ownership of the J1 Phone. Instead, the J1 Phone belonged to “Ah Heng”, who loaned it to the accused.[note: 68] This was done on 21 April 2021, when the accused met “Ah Heng” at an open space in front of Block 54, Lorong 5 Toa Payoh after collecting the 55 Phones.[note: 69] There, he paid “Ah Heng” $1,100 in cash for a new mobile phone, which was one of the 55 Phones, and asked “Ah Heng” for a spare mobile phone. “Ah Heng” agreed and handed the J1 Phone to the accused.[note: 70]

48     The accused explained that the J1 Phone could not have belonged to him as:[note: 71]

(a)     it was only 3G-enabled and hence incompatible with Singapore’s 4G network;

(b)     it was not passcode-protected, which it would have been if it belonged to him, as he was particularly concerned about data security;

(c)     the “Find My Mobile Phone” feature was not activated on the J1 Phone, which it would have been if it belonged to him; and

(d)     the J1 Phone was not VoLTE-enabled, whereas the telecommunication service that the accused was subscribed to was only compatible with VoLTE-enabled handsets.

49     The accused further referred to printouts from the Samsung website in support of his position that “Ah Heng” was the registered owner of the J1 Phone.[note: 72] The accused explained that he sought the assistance of his contacts at Samsung Malaysia to obtain printouts of the account page relating to the J1 Phone, and this showed that the J1 Phone was registered to one “ah heng”.[note: 73]

The J1 Phone contained files which were both stored directly and transferred over from other mobile devices owned by the accused

50     While the J1 Phone did not belong to the accused, it contained files relating to him as he had a practice of synchronising the data across all his mobile devices. As a starting point, most of the files forensically extracted from the J1 Phone were already present in the mobile phone by the time the accused took possession of the J1 Phone from “Ah Heng” on 21 April 2021. These would include the documents highlighted by the Prosecution to be relevant to the offences. Hence, the accused could not be held accountable for any such incriminating files which were not created by him.

51     Nonetheless, for the remaining files, these were transferred over from other mobile devices belonging to the accused through the process of data synchronisation. Where there were files in the J1 Phone which appeared to relate to the accused, but were created before 21 April 2021, this was a result of the accused having synchronised the data from his other mobile devices to the J1 Phone. The mere fact that these files were in the J1 Phone did not mean that the J1 Phone belonged to the accused. DW2 explained the process of data synchronisation and opined that there was no way to tell, from the content extracted from the J1 Phone by PW3,[note: 74] which of such content were transferred over from another device.[note: 75]

52     As the Prosecution was unable to show which of the files were stored directly on the J1 Phone and which were transferred over from other mobile devices belonging to the accused, it could not be said that the J1 Phone belonged to the accused and he could not be held responsible for the files found therein.

The files extracted from the J1 Phone were unreliable

53     In any event, the accused cast doubt on the integrity of the files extracted from the J1 Phone, submitting that they had been compromised and/or tampered with. In particular, the accused took the position that all the images extracted from the J1 Phone[note: 76] were created and doctored by the police.[note: 77]

54     Further, the J1 Phone was inoperable by the time of the trial and could no longer be powered up. This prevented the accused from having the chance to show, through the use of a tool better than the one used by the police, that the files in the J1 Phone were being transferred over from other mobile devices, and were not stored directly on the J1 Phone.

55     Accordingly, since the primary evidence in the form of the J1 Phone was no longer available and the secondary evidence in the form of the extracted material had been tampered with, they were inadmissible and ought not to be relied upon by the court.[note: 78]

The accused collected the 55 Phones on “Ah Heng’s” instructions
