56     As regards his presence at Jackson Square, the accused explained that in March 2021, “Ah Heng” contacted him and offered him about $60 to collect a delivery order. The accused agreed and went to Jackson Square on 21 April 2021 for this purpose. There, he collected the three boxes from PW4.[note: 79] At the point of collection, he did not know that the delivery order was to be a heavy one, comprising the 55 Phones. Had the accused known of the contents of the delivery, he would not have agreed to collect the delivery order (or at the very least, would have brought a trolley with him) as he suffered from back problems and would not have risked injuring his back further.[note: 80]

57     When he met “Ah Heng” upon collecting the 55 Phones (see [47] above), “Ah Heng” requested for the accused’s assistance to store the remaining 54 sets of the 55 Phones at the accused’s flat as the buyer was not ready to pay for the items yet.[note: 81] That was how the 55 Phones came to be seized from the accused at his flat (ie, the one opened set that the accused purchased from “Ah Heng” and the remaining 54 unopened sets).

58     Further, it would be clear from the GOGOX booking details[note: 82] (see [27] above) that the contact information of the person who placed the order was “Alson Teo Hock Loo” with the mobile phone number “XXXX1460”. The accused did not use this number and searches conducted by the police with the telecommunications provider showed that the said number was tagged to individuals other than the accused.[note: 83]

59     In fact, the accused had known “XXXX1460” to be “Ah Heng’s” number, and he always contacted “Ah Heng” at this number. This was so as early as in May 2016, when “Ah Heng” first reached out to the accused and deceived the accused into depositing a sum of $2,500 into the bank account of “Teo Hock Loo”.[note: 84] The accused also pointed to a WhatsApp message which he sent to “Ah Heng” at this number on 17 July 2021, informing “Ah Heng” that the 54 unopened sets of the 55 Phones were seized by the police on 11 June 2021.[note: 85]

60     The accused was hence not the one who had arranged for the delivery of the 55 Phones. He merely collected them for “Ah Heng” and had stored them in his flat as a favour to “Ah Heng”.

The accused did not have access to PW2’s particulars

61     Finally, as regards the accused’s dealings with PW2 and PIAS, the accused did not have knowledge of PW2’s signature, NRIC number and PS code details, and did not know how the PIAS stamp looked like. This was because the health plan was not approved eventually (see [31] above) and the accused was not extended a duplicate copy of the completed and signed application form. The said form was also not tendered in evidence before the court.[note: 86]

The Prosecution has failed to prove its case

62     Given the multiple doubts raised by the accused and the insufficiency of the Prosecution’s evidence, the accused submitted that he must be acquitted as the Prosecution has failed to prove its case on both the Cheating Charge and the Forgery Charge beyond reasonable doubt.

My decision

Finding of guilt

Elements of the Cheating Charge and the Forgery Charge

63     The Prosecution must prove the following elements of the Cheating Charge:

(a)     the accused did deceive PW1 into believing that he was representing PIAS to purchase the 55 Phones;

(b)     this was a fact the accused knew to be false;

(c)     the accused had done so by sending an email to PW1 on 15 March 2021 at 12.14am (the “15 March Email”); [note: 87] and

(d)     by such manner of deception, the accused dishonestly induced PW1 to cause the 55 Phones to be delivered to PW4 on 21 April 2021.

64     The undisputed evidence was clear that the user of the Ampang Email was the one who had deceived PW1 into believing that he (as “Alson Teo Hock Loo”) was representing PIAS to purchase the 55 Phones and, in the 15 March Email, asked that PW1 send him the quotation as soon as possible. This fact was false as there was no “Alson Teo Hock Loo” at PIAS and no order was placed on behalf of PIAS. As a result, PW1 was deceived into confirming the order and arranging for the 55 Phones to be collected by PW4. PW1 eventually realised that he was deceived when payment was defaulted on the 55 Phones.

65     As regards the Forgery Charge, the Prosecution must prove the following elements:

(a)     that the accused did dishonestly affix the electronic signatures of PW2 on the Signed Quotation;

(b)     with the intention of causing them to be believed that they were signed by PW2;

(c)     knowing that PW2 did not sign on the Signed Quotation; and

(d)     intending that the Signed Quotation be used for the purpose of cheating.

66     Again, the undisputed evidence in this regard was that the Signed Quotation was attached to an email sent by the user of the Ampang Email (as “Alson Teo Hock Loo”) to PW1 on 22 March 2021, as part of the chain of Order Emails.[note: 88] This was done to confirm the order of the 55 Phones (purportedly on PIAS’ behalf) at a total cost of $89,705 (excluding GST),[note: 89] and to arrange for collection. Believing the two signatures on the Signed Quotation to have been signed by PW2, PW1 proceeded with the order of the 55 Phones and eventually arranged for their delivery to PW4. However, the two signatures purporting to be PW2’s as affixed on the Signed Quotation have been shown to be forged – PW2 testified that she has neither seen nor signed on the Signed Quotation before.

67     The first key factual issue in respect of both the Cheating Charge and the Forgery Charge was hence whether the accused was the one who corresponded with PW1 using the Ampang Email in the chain of Order Emails. If so, it would be the accused who had deceived PW1 by sending the 15 March Email and the Signed Quotation to PW1.

68     The second key factual issue was whether the J1 Phone and the contents therein belonged to the accused. The J1 Phone contained working documents relating to the creation of the Signed Quotation, including various drafts of the quotation, and the separate images of PW2’s signature and the PIAS stamp as they appeared on the Signed Quotation. The ownership of the J1 Phone would hence be highly probative to the issue of whether it was the accused who had dishonestly affixed PW2’s purported signatures on the Signed Quotation, as it would be difficult to see why he would have these pertinent working documents in his possession otherwise.

The law on circumstantial evidence

69     The Prosecution relied on circumstantial evidence to prove both charges. As held by the High Court in Constance Chee at [77], “[i]t is trite law that the circumstantial evidence on which the prosecution relies must in the final analysis ‘inevitably and inexorably’ lead the court to a single conclusion of the accused’s guilt”. The court continued at [85]:

… In a criminal case, proof beyond any reasonable doubt is required. Grave suspicion is no substitute for proof beyond reasonable doubt. In the same vein, moral certainty cannot replace the requirement for explicit and certain evidence. The various links in the interlocking chain of evidence must establish a complete chain that rules out any reasonable likelihood of an accused’s innocence. Guilt must be the only rational inference and conclusion to be drawn from the complete chain of evidence. In assessing the circumstances, the court should discount fanciful or speculative possibilities. However, if more than one reasonable inference can be elicited from the factual matrix, the inference most sympathetic to the accused ought to be accepted.

[emphasis added]

70     I now proceed to assess the complete chain of evidence before the court in this case, bearing in mind the court’s holding in Constance Chee.

Did the accused use the Ampang Email to correspond with PW1?

71     Considering the totality of the evidence before the court, I was satisfied that the weight of the evidence led to the finding that the accused was the person using the Ampang Email at the material time to correspond with PW1 in the Order Emails.

(1)   The accused listed the Ampang Email as his contact on multiple occasions

72     I considered it telling that the accused had listed the Ampang Email as his contact email address on multiple occasions prior to the Order Emails. While the accused alleged that the Ampang Email belonged to “Ah Heng”, I found it difficult to believe the accused’s convenient account that he had listed “Ah Heng’s” email address as his contact on each of these occasions, and that this was for “Ah Heng” to assist in a variety of ways. This was especially so given the absence of other supporting evidence or corroborative accounts.

73     The first instance was by way of the WhatsApp messages exchanged with the pharmacist in Johor Bahru. The accused sought to purchase medication from the pharmacy in Johor Bahru and have them delivered to Singapore. During the exchange, the pharmacist asked for the “patient full details” for “registration of prescription”.[note: 90] On 31 July 2020, the accused provided his name, NRIC number, date of birth, contact number, email address and delivery address. The email address provided was the Ampang Email.

74     The accused explained that he had provided the Ampang Email to the pharmacist as he wanted “Ah Heng”, who was staying in Johor Bahru, to coordinate the purchase of the medication. This was especially since there were travel and movement restrictions in place at that time, owing to the COVID-19 pandemic.

75     However, there appeared to be no reason why “Ah Heng’s” email address would need to be provided for any such coordination reasons. The other personal particulars provided, including the contact number, were admitted by the accused to be his.[note: 91] There was no reason to only have provided “Ah Heng’s” email address for coordination, while leaving the contact number as the accused’s own. In any event, there was no mention to the pharmacist of one “Ah Heng” who would be assisting to coordinate over email. There was also no evidence before the court of any communication that the accused had with “Ah Heng”, seeking “Ah Heng’s” assistance to coordinate with the pharmacist. Most crucially, it appeared from the subsequent WhatsApp messages that it was the accused himself who coordinated the order and delivery of the medication with the pharmacist, including the confirmation of the delivery schedule, payment details and eventual receipt of the medication. I hence found it difficult to accept the accused’s explanation.

76     I next considered the two “notes” which the accused admitted to drafting. The first note was dated 11 August 2019 and contained an enquiry to SingPost about the status of three mails sent to China. In signing off on the note, the accused provided his own contact number and the Ampang Email. The accused explained that he had provided the Ampang Email as “Ah Heng” was the one coordinating with the Chinese counterpart on the purchase of old China notes and coins. This was so as “Ah Heng” was Chinese-educated and “spoke well” in Mandarin.[note: 92]

77     I first observed that there was no mention of any purchase of old China notes and coins in this said note. It merely set out an enquiry on the status of three mails sent to China which were lost in transit. No further evidence was given by the accused to explain the context behind this note and why “Ah Heng’s” assistance in coordination would be required. In any event, given that this email was addressed to SingPost rather than to any such Chinese counterpart, there was no reason why “Ah Heng’s” email address would need to be provided here rather than the accused’s own. Further, if the accused’s version was that he required “Ah Heng” to converse and coordinate in Mandarin, there was no reason why the accused would then provide his own contact number along with the Ampang Email, instead of “Ah Heng’s” contact number. No explanation was provided by the accused in this regard.

78     Turning to the second note dated 18 June 2019, this related to the accused’s appeal for witnesses to step forward to assist him with his investigations against his ex-wife for an alleged offence of theft in dwelling. It was stated in the draft note that he could be “contacted via [mobile phone] or email”, and the accused’s mobile phone number was provided along with the Ampang Email. However, when the note was finalised and printed, the Ampang Email was replaced with an email address which the accused accepted to be his own, ie, the SCS Hotmail.

79     The accused explained that he had initially provided the Ampang Email as he wanted “Ah Heng” to assist him with the gathering of evidence and to secure the witnesses’ willingness to attend in court. However, he eventually decided against it and used his own email address instead as he was worried that “Ah Heng” might not be able to convince the witnesses. On the accused’s own account, “Ah Heng” stayed in Johor Bahru. The accused put up the notice in Singapore and was looking for witnesses who could assist with an alleged theft incident in his home in Sembawang. No further elaboration was given by the accused on how “Ah Heng”, who lived in Johor Bahru, was to assist with the gathering of evidence in Singapore. No other evidence of any communication with “Ah Heng” seeking his assistance in this regard was also tendered. Further, and as with the first note, the accused’s own contact number was provided together with Ampang Email, with no evidence before the court on why “Ah Heng’s” contact number was not similarly provided for the alleged purpose of gathering evidence. I was hence of the view that there was no basis for “Ah Heng’s” email address to have been included in the draft note in the first place, and it was more probable that the Ampang Email and the SCS Hotmail were both email accounts belonging to the accused, which he used alternatively.

(2)   The accused sent emails to and received emails from the Ampang Email without context

80     The evidence before the court also revealed a practice where the accused would send emails to and also receive emails from the Ampang Email, with there being no context as to the purpose of such emails being sent and forwarded, as the cover emails contained no information and content.

81     The first of such emails was found in the supporting document attached to the Magistrate’s Complaint filed by the accused against his ex-wife on 22 April 2019. This showed a printout of an email from the inbox of the Ampang Email, and the email was one sent by the accused to the Ampang Email on 22 April 2019 at 16:38.[note: 93] The email did not address the recipient of the email in any way, and merely set out the grounds of complaint relied on by the accused.

82     The accused explained that he had sent the email to “Ah Heng”, for “Ah Heng” to assist with the printing of the same in Johor Bahru.[note: 94] When the Prosecution submitted that it beggared belief that the accused would take the trouble to have this three-page document printed outside jurisdiction, the accused explained that he had been in Johor Bahru for various purposes on 8, 14 and 20 April 2019, including to collect the printout. Further, there was no need for there to have been any instructions in the cover email, as this was not the first document that the accused had asked “Ah Heng” to print.[note: 95]

83     I first observed that there was no evidence before the court of the accused’s travel records in April 2019. While the accused explained in his closing submissions that this was because his passport had been impounded by the police,[note: 96] there was no evidence of any attempt on the accused’s part to have obtained such information from the investigation officer or from the Immigration and Checkpoint Authority.

84     In any event, and as stated at [81] above, the email attached to the Magistrate’s Complaint was dated 22 April 2019. If the email was only sent to the Ampang Email on 22 April 2019, it seemed to be impossible for the accused to have collected the printout of this said email from “Ah Heng” on 8, 14 or 20 April 2019, as he alleged. In fact, given that the accused had signed on the printout and dated it 22 April 2019, it appeared to me as a matter of logic that it must have been printed on the same day that it was sent (ie, 22 April 2019), for it to have been signed and submitted as part of the Magistrate’s Complaint on that same day. It was not however the accused’s case that he had gone to Johor Bahru to collect the printout on 22 April 2019. I therefore found it difficult to accept the accused’s version that he had sent the email to “Ah Heng” at the Ampang Email, for “Ah Heng” to print the same.

85     The accused also tendered various email chains that were sent from the Ampang Email to him, in support of his point that the user of the Ampang Email was based overseas (see [46] above).[note: 97] These generally contained an email chain comprising two emails:

(a)     the first in the chain being an email sent from the accused (using the SCS Gmail) to the Ampang Email and himself (at the SCS Hotmail) on various dates from 13 March 2019 to 12 February 2021, relating to various subject matters but without otherwise containing any instructions or cover email; and

(b)     the second in the chain being a blank email sent from the Ampang Email back to the accused (at the SCS Hotmail) on 18 and 19 June 2021, each of which simply forwarded the first email as-is without any context, instructions or content in the cover email.

86     The accused explained in cross-examination that there was no need for the first email in the respective chains, which were sent to the Ampang Email on various dates from 13 March 2019 to 12 February 2021, to contain any instructions, as “Ah Heng” had been printing documents for the accused all the while.[note: 98] However, and as highlighted by the Prosecution, this could not explain the email on 12 February 2021,[note: 99] which merely contained a WhatsApp link to a telephone number and there was no explanation for why this would need to be printed. In response, the accused’s position then shifted to explain that he had asked “Ah Heng” to obtain details of the registered owner of this telephone number.

87     As to why these emails were then forwarded back from the Ampang Email to the accused on 18 and 19 June 2021 (ie, as the second email in the chain), the accused explained that he had called “Ah Heng” over WhatsApp to ask that “Ah Heng” forward these emails back to him. However, it was not clear why the accused would require these specific emails, which related to different subject matters, to be forwarded back to him over those two days. In any event, there was no evidence before the court that the WhatsApp call with “Ah Heng” had taken place prior to the forwarding of the emails. While the accused had tendered a screenshot of the WhatsApp chat between him and “Ah Heng”, there was no record of any such call(s) prior to or on 18 and 19 June 2021 in the chat.[note: 100]

88     Hence, reviewing the evidence surrounding these emails exchanged between the Ampang Email and the accused, I found it difficult to accept how these multiple emails sent without any context or cover email could lend themselves to the varied purposes as sought to be explained by the accused. There was also no evidence of any accompanying calls which would give context to these emails. Accordingly, I did not accept the accused’s explanations of “Ah Heng’s” role in these emails.

89     Instead, in the absence of any plausible evidence to the contrary, I again found it probable that the Ampang Email was an account used by the accused as an alternative to the other two accounts admitted by him to be his at the SCS Gmail and the SCS Hotmail. The accused was not sending and receiving emails from “Ah Heng” for the various reasons alleged. Rather, he was sending them to himself across the different email accounts owned by him. This would explain why the emails contained no context or cover email, as the accused was the only one sending and receiving these emails, and no explanation to a third party was required as regards his intention or purpose.

90     The accused himself admitted that he did have the habit of sending emails to himself across email accounts of different domains for security and accessibility reasons, which was why he had two email accounts under the “Hotmail” and “Gmail” domains. However, this would serve no purpose for the Ampang Email, which was under the “Outlook” domain and belonged to the “same Microsoft family” as “Hotmail”.[note: 101] The accused hence averred that the Ampang Email could not have belonged to him. I considered this to be a self-serving afterthought which did not support the accused’s claim that the Ampang Email belonged to “Ah Heng” in any way, particularly in light of what was discussed above. Instead, I found it to be more likely that the accused was using all three emails with the “Gmail”, “Hotmail” and “Outlook” domains, and he had been sending emails to himself at the Ampang Email.

(3)   The evidence did not show that the user of the Ampang Email was based overseas

91     While the accused had, in an attempt to show that he could not have been the user of the Ampang Email, taken considerable effort to demonstrate that the six emails sent from the Ampang Email to him on 18 and 19 June 2021[note: 102] were traced to IP addresses from overseas (see [46] above), such evidence was ultimately inconclusive as regards the location of the sender. To this end, the evidence of the accused’s own expert DW2 Mr Siow Kwong Ting Stanwin was useful in shedding light on what the IP address in the message source of these emails from the Ampang Email meant.

92     DW2 explained that an email message, when sent, would go through multiple email servers which themselves have different IP addresses that reside around the world. The email message would eventually enter the recipient’s incoming email server, which has yet another IP address. Hence, the IP address was merely a starting point to trace the origin of the email message but would not otherwise identify the device sending the same.[note: 103] DW2 further clarified that the IP addresses relied on by the accused would not be conclusive of where the sender was based, and only showed that the email message had gone through a server with that IP address.[note: 104] This was to be differentiated from the X-Originating-IP address, which would reflect the actual IP address of the sender.[note: 105]

93     In any event, a factual observation of the IP address locations of the six emails would also lead to the conclusion that these would not be an accurate reflection of where the sender (assuming the accused’s case that there was only one sender “Ah Heng”) was based. In the three emails sent from the Ampang Email on 18 June 2021 at 8.19pm, 8.22pm and 8.49pm,[note: 106] the IP addresses were shown to be from South Korea, Singapore and then South Korea again respectively, all within a span of 30 minutes. It would have been impossible for “Ah Heng” to send three emails from two countries in 30 minutes. This would be consistent with DW2’s expert opinion that the IP address reflected the location of the email server rather than the location of the sender.

94     While the accused nonetheless sought to explain that the sender must still have been based somewhere in or near the location of the server to ensure quicker and more efficient connectivity,[note: 107] this was not the evidence of DW2 or any other witnesses and only appeared for the first time in the accused’s closing submissions. Further, and again with reference to the three emails sent within 30 minutes of each other (at [93] above), the server from which the email was sent to the accused was itself not a constant. There was hence no factual basis for the accused to have made this submission.

95     The accused further argued that it was imperative for the Prosecution to have tendered evidence of the X-Originating-IP address of the Ampang Email during the exchange in the Order Emails, without which the Prosecution would fail to prove its case beyond a reasonable doubt.[note: 108] I did not agree with the accused that the Prosecution could never prove its case beyond reasonable doubt without such evidence. What ultimately mattered was whether the strength of the circumstantial evidence before the court pointed inexorably to the accused’s guilt.

(4)   The identities used in the Order Emails and Signed Quotation were both known to the accused

96     Finally, I did not consider it a coincidence that both identities which appeared in the Order Emails and Signed Quotation were identities known to the accused and were persons with whom he had unpleasant interactions.

97     The user of the Ampang Email had adopted the identity of one “Alson Teo Hock Loo” from PIAS in the Order Emails. On the accused’s own account, he had, in 2016, been deceived into depositing a sum of $2,500 into a bank account belonging to one “Teo Hock Loo”, who had in turn relinquished the bank account to “Ah Heng”. The accused was aggrieved that the outcome of the investigations concluded with a “mere” warning against “Teo Hock Loo”, instead of a sentence of fine and/or imprisonment.[note: 109]

98     The forged signatures in the Signed Quotation also purported to be those of PW2 Ms Choa Mei Kuen’s, with whom the accused was acquainted (see [31]-[32] above). As part of their dealings, PW2 had managed the accused’s unit trust investment portfolio sometime from 2016 to 2017, which suffered losses. The accused blamed this on PW2. He lodged a complaint against PW2 with the insurer and it was even escalated to the FIDReC (ie, the Financial Industry Disputes Resolution Centre).[note: 110] When that was not resolved in his favour, PW2 testified that the accused wanted to commence civil proceedings and lodge a complaint with the Monetary Authority of Singapore against her for mis-selling.[note: 111]

99     In contrast, there was no reason for “Ah Heng” to have used the names of both “Teo Hock Loo” or “Choa Mei Kuen” in the Order Emails and Signed Quotations. There was no evidence that “Ah Heng” knew of “Choa Mei Kuen” or PIAS. PW2 did not testify to knowing one “Ah Heng”, and the accused did not, in cross-examination, ask her any questions relating to “Ah Heng” either.

(5)   The weight of the evidence led to the inevitable conclusion that the accused was the user of the Ampang Email

100    Considering the various threads of evidence as set out above in their totality, I was satisfied that the weight of the evidence led the court to the inevitable conclusion that the accused was the user of the Ampang Email at the material time. The evidence led me to find that the accused used the Ampang Email as his contact email for various purposes and also used it as one of his alternative email accounts for him to send emails to himself. The identities used in the Order Email and the Signed Quotation were also known to the accused. There was nothing raised by the accused which could lead to the drawing of any other reasonable inferences, leaving me to conclude that the accused was the user of the Ampang Email and communicated with PW1 in the Order Emails.

Did the J1 Phone and its contents belong to the accused?

101    I was similarly satisfied, having assessed in careful detail the evidence before the court, that the J1 Phone and the contents therein belonged to the accused and were not, contrary to the accused’s claims, attributable to “Ah Heng”.

(1)   The J1 Phone was seized from the accused, who admitted in his statement that he purchased it in Johor Bahru

102    When the police arrested the accused at his flat on 27 May 2021, they seized the following items from him: (a) the J1 Phone; (b) one Samsung Galaxy S21 Ultra 5G mobile phone; (c) two Apple iPhone 4S; (c) one iPad; (d) one iPad mini; and (e) one black t-shirt. The Samsung Galaxy S21 Ultra 5G mobile phone was an “opened” set, ie, it was no longer contained in its packaging. The IMEI number of this said “opened” set matched the IMEI number of one of the 55 Phones. This was checked against the list of the IMEI numbers in respect of all 55 Phones, which was provided by PW1 to the police.[note: 112] The black t-shirt also matched that which the accused was seen to be wearing when he collected the 55 Phones from PW4 at Jackson Square on 21 April 2021.[note: 113]

103    The former investigation officer who seized the items, PW6 Mr Aliden bin Hamad, testified that while the accused had no reaction in relation to the seizure of most items, he had “a bit of hesitance” in relation to the seizure of the J1 Phone. He informed PW6 that it was an “old phone” and that “no one use[d] this phone anymore”.[note: 114] Thereafter, the accused was arrested and remained in police custody. A long statement was recorded from him the next day, on 28 May 2021 at about 1.23pm (the “28 May Statement”).[note: 115] In the 28 May Statement, the accused stated that the J1 Phone was an “old phone which [he] purchased in Johor Bahru for RM$400 back in April 2017” for which he did not have the receipt. When the statement was read back to the accused, he added that the J1 Phone was a “second handphone which [might] have document[s] not belonging to [him].”

104    While the accused did not object to the admissibility of the 28 May Statement at trial, he later resiled from this position in his closing submissions and submitted that this should be inadmissible and unreliable. As regards the grounds for inadmissibility, the accused belatedly sought to assert that the 28 May Statement was inaccurately recorded as he was under the influence of drowsy medication at the time. This was despite the accused’s assertions at trial that the 28 May Statement was “given voluntarily as the drowsiness had not taken effect”.[note: 116] In any event, the accused clarified that what he meant in the statement, in stating that the J1 Phone might have documents not belonging to him, was simply that the J1 Phone did not belong to him.

105    I considered the accused’s subsequent explanations of what was recorded in the 28 May Statement to be mere afterthoughts. The accused provided precise details of when and where he had purchased the J1 Phone, including its price. Even when the accused sought to distance himself from the contents of the J1 Phone during statement recording, he merely stated that the J1 Phone might contain documents that did not belong to him. Never once did the accused state, whether at the time the J1 Phone was seized or during the recording of the 28 May Statement, that the J1 Phone did not belong to him.

106    This was all the more curious considering the accused’s position at trial, ie, that the J1 Phone was loaned to him by “Ah Heng” on 21 April 2021. This would just have been about one month before the accused was arrested and the J1 Phone was seized. If the J1 Phone had indeed been so recently acquired by the accused at that point, there was no reason why the accused would not have stated as such in the 28 May Statement, and would instead provide details about how it was purchased in Johor Bahru for RM400 in April 2017. This point on the J1 Phone being loaned to him was not made even after the accused supplemented his statement when it was read back to him. Apart from stating in his closing submissions that he could not guarantee the accuracy of his 28 May Statement as he was under the influence of drowsy medication, the accused never provided any explanation as to why he had provided these details of his purchase of the J1 Phone in April 2017. It was also never the accused’s position that this specific portion of the 28 May Statement was inaccurately recorded. He merely insisted that he did not confess, in the 28 May Statement, that the J1 Phone belonged to him.[note: 117]

107    In the absence of any plausible explanation provided by the accused in response to the clear terms of his contemporaneous statement recorded on the day after his arrest, I gave full weight to the accused’s admission in the 28 May Statement that the J1 Phone was an “old phone” which “[he] purchased in Johor Bahru for RM$400 back in April 2017”.

108    For completeness, I did not place any weight on the accused’s explanations for why the J1 Phone could not have belonged to him, ie, that: (a) it was only 3G-enabled; (b) it was not passcode-protected; (c) the “Find My Mobile Phone” feature was not installed; and (d) it was not VoLTE-enabled (see [48] above). I found these explanations to be inconclusive as to the ownership of the J1 Phone and in any event self-serving, as these were wholly subjective explanations on the accused’s part.

(2)   The accused’s reliance on data synchronisation did not assist him

109    As some of the files extracted from the J1 Phone clearly referred to the accused and/or contained references to the accused’s name, for eg, the WhatsApp messages exchanged with the pharmacist in Johor Bahru and the notes drafted by the accused (see [72]-[79] above), the accused sought to explain this away by relying on the concept of data synchronisation. In brief, the accused’s defence appeared to be that all incriminating evidence found in the J1 Phone belonged to “Ah Heng” and was not attributable to him, whereas the files referencing the accused were found in the J1 Phone as a result of the accused’s practice in synchronising the data across all his mobile devices.

110    In his re-examination, the accused elaborated that the information was likely to have been transferred over from his Samsung J3 mobile phone (the “J3 Phone”) through the process of data synchronisation, with the J3 Phone being his “master handset”.[note: 118] The J3 Phone was not seized by the police and the accused even admitted that he was “not prepared to let the police know” that he had a [J3 Phone] as it was his personal phone and contained all the sensitive information.[note: 119] The accused further tendered a receipt to prove the existence of the J3 Phone,[note: 120] but also stated that it has since been sold on 14 June 2021 to raise funds.[note: 121] The accused further sought to place the blame on the police for failing to seize the J3 Phone from him during investigations. He claimed that this led to the investigations being incomplete as the police were unable to ascertain which files in the J1 Phone were stored directly therein, and which had been transferred over from the J3 Phone. Given the incomplete investigations, the accused alleged that the Prosecution could not prove that the materials extracted from the J1 Phone were attributable to him.

111    However, and contrary to the accused’s submissions, it was not the Prosecution’s case that the files in the J1 Phone comprised both files which were stored directly and files which were transferred over from other devices through the process of data synchronisation. The Prosecution was relying on the fact that such files were extracted from the J1 Phone, which was seized from the accused, along with the other circumstantial evidence, to prove its case. This issue of data synchronisation was one sought to be relied upon by the accused, to explain why the incriminating content in the J1 Phone was not attributable to him. Given that, it should have been incumbent on the accused to tender evidence in relation to what was stored in the J3 Phone to prove this point. Instead, and on the accused’s own account, he chose to sell the J3 Phone shortly after he was released on bail. It was difficult why the accused would choose to sell the J3 Phone if it had been so crucial to his defence. There was further no evidence of the accused having extracted the contents from the J3 Phone prior to him selling it.

112    In addition, and having admitted to actively concealing the existence of the J3 Phone from the police, it was entirely disingenuous of the accused to now blame the police for failing to seize the same from him. If, as alleged by the accused, an examination by the police of the J3 Phone would clearly show which material in the J1 Phone were transferred over from the J3 Phone and which were stored directly and not attributable to him, it would only be logical for the accused to have explained this to the police during investigations. Instead, the accused chose not to do so.

113    In light of the above, and without there being any evidence before the court on whether any of the material extracted from the J1 Phone had been synchronised from other mobile devices belonging to the accused, including the J3 Phone, the accused’s reliance on data synchronisation was wholly speculative and did not assist him.

(3)   The accused’s explanations on how he obtained access to “Ah Heng’s” Samsung account could not be believed

114    As part of his defence, the accused sought to tender a two-page printout from the Samsung website to show that “Ah Heng” was the registered owner of the J1 Phone, and not him.[note: 122] When the court asked that the accused elaborate on how this printout was obtained, he said that he asked his contacts in “Samsung Malaysia” to “pull out the data” from “backend” and “[u]nder the table” and they had done this as a “personal favour” to him.[note: 123]

115    The Prosecution objected to the admission of this printout as the maker of the same (ie, the alleged contacts from Samsung Malaysia who had extracted these information) was not before the court. In response, the accused asserted that he would procure the attendance of such persons as his defence witnesses. However, on the next day of trial, the accused updated that his Malaysian contacts could not attend in court. Instead, he would ask them to “do a duplication of similar account” in a “UAT environment” for “viewing purposes”.[note: 124] The Prosecution again raised a similar objection, submitting that the maker of such UAT environment was to take the stand before such evidence could be admitted. Upon hearing this, the accused switched tracks again and said that he would “try to get [“Ah Heng’s”] permission to give [him] the password and ID”, following which the accused would log into the Samsung account in court. The trial was then stood down for the day for the accused to contact “Ah Heng”.

116    When the trial resumed two days later, the accused offered yet another option in relation to the admission of the printout. The accused made no reference to his attempts to contact “Ah Heng” but instead said that “to save everyone[] the trouble”, he managed to “trial and error and log into the … account of Mr Ah Heng” with the “help of some IT expert”.[note: 125]

117    The accused then did a demonstration in court where he accessed the Samsung Malaysia website and logged into a Samsung account using the Ampang Email as the user identification. As regards the password, the accused explained that as part of his “trial and error”, he discovered that “Ah Heng” had initially used his mobile phone number (ie, “XXXX1460”) as the password to his Samsung account. However, at the time of the demonstration, the accused had since changed the password to something else, so that there would be “no avoidance of doubt whether there [was] some conspiracy or not.”[note: 126] Upon logging in, the J1 Phone was shown to be registered to this account, bearing the same model number, model name and serial number as that in the Forensic Report.[note: 127] The information as shown on the displayed webpage was printed out by the accused, who sought its admission as evidence before the court. This latter document was similar in content to the initial two-page printout purportedly obtained from the accused’s contacts in Samsung Malaysia (see [114] above), though the layout was different. Nonetheless, and having now shown himself to be the one who had accessed the Samsung Malaysia webpage and printed out the information therein, the document was eventually admitted in evidence through the accused.[note: 128]

118    Suffice it to say, I found the accused’s account relating both to how he had obtained the initial two-page printout and how he eventually gained access into the Samsung account entirely fanciful and incredible. There was no explanation provided by the accused at all as to how he came to be acquainted with these contacts in Samsung Malaysia who were willing to essentially breach consumer privacy and data protection rules to log into another customer’s account on his behalf and as a favour to him. No details were given as to who these contacts were and why they would be willing to do this for the accused. Unsurprisingly, the accused could not also call any such persons to give evidence at trial.

119    Further, while the accused indicated that he would be contacting “Ah Heng” to obtain his log-in details, he did not provide any further evidence of whether this was done and the outcome of the same. The inference to be drawn was hence that he never contacted “Ah Heng”. Instead, the accused claimed that he managed to guess “Ah Heng’s” log-in details with the help of an IT expert, which ended up being as simplistic and convenient as the Ampang Email and “XXXX1460”, both of which were particulars that the accused sought to attribute to “Ah Heng” as part of his defence at trial (ie, that these were “Ah Heng’s” email address and contact number). As explained at [71] to [100] above, I was satisfied that the accused was in fact the user of the Ampang Email. However, and in any event, the irresistible inference to be drawn from the circumstances surrounding the procurement of the Samsung account details associated with the J1 Phone was that the accused was the one who always had access to the log-in details. The accused was able to produce the initial two-page printout not because of any alleged contacts from Samsung Malaysia, but because the accused has always been able to log into the account that had the J1 Phone registered. It did not hence matter that the Samsung account profile appeared to be listed as “ah heng”, given that the accused was the one who had control of the account. He could have easily assigned any display name as he deemed fit.

(4)   It was safe to rely on the contents extracted from the J1 Phone despite its inoperability midway during trial

120    PW7 Mr Muhamaad Nur Hasfis bin Hashim, who was the investigation officer assigned to the accused’s matter in March 2023 and remained so at the time of the trial, gave evidence on the state of the J1 Phone as of January 2025. PW7 explained that it could not be powered up despite him purchasing new batteries. When PW7 enquired with various mobile phone shops, he was informed that the J1 Phone was an outdated model and the requisite parts for repair, such as the motherboard, were unavailable.[note: 129] This inoperability of the J1 Phone came to light as the accused sought access to the J1 Phone midway during trial to obtain the mobile phone number of a potential defence witness. However, when the accused attended at the police station to access the J1 Phone, he realised it could no longer be powered up.

121    The accused hence submitted that the contents extracted from the J1 Phone could not be relied on by the court as: (a) the primary evidence in the form of the J1 Phone was no longer available; and (b) the secondary evidence containing materials extracted from the J1 Phone as contained in the Forensic Report had been tampered with during the forensic examination by PW3 and PW6. Despite the accused’s submissions, I was satisfied, having reviewed the evidence in its totality, that it was safe to rely on the contents extracted from the J1 Phone as contained in the Forensic Report.

122    First, the process surrounding the extraction of the material from the J1 Phone was recorded in detail by PW6 in the Forensic Report,[note: 130] including that the J1 Phone was powered up with the data extracted successfully by PW3 on 10 August 2021. Thereafter, PW6 viewed the extracted data on 16 August 2021 and found content that could be related to the case. The files were then saved in the DVD-ROM attached to the Forensic Report. Thereafter, the J1 Phone was moved to the store in Bedok Police Division,[note: 131] kept under lock and key in metal cabinets, and was only drawn out by PW7 for the present trial in June 2023.[note: 132] I was satisfied that the Forensic Report contained material extracted from the J1 Phone at such point when it was still operable on 10 August 2021, and the fact that it was no longer operable by January 2025 did not by itself cast any doubt on the material extracted and reviewed in the Forensic Report. I also found no improper handling or tampering of the J1 Phone after its data extraction for the purposes of the Forensic Report.

123    Second, the Prosecution had tendered photographs taken of the J1 Phone on 2 June 2021, which displayed on its screen key documents relied on by the Prosecution as being probative of the accused’s guilt. These documents were consistent with those extracted by PW3 and set out in the Forensic Report, which included images of the Signed Quotation and its various drafts, the GOGOX booking details, PIAS’ stamp, PW2’s purported signature as it appeared on the Signed Quotation and stock images of the Samsung Galaxy S21 Ultra 5G mobile phone.[note: 133] These photographs clearly showed that the key documents were present in the J1 Phone shortly after it was seized, and could safely be relied upon by the court even if the J1 Phone was no longer operable thereafter.

124    Third, I found the accused’s allegations of any tampering of the secondary evidence as contained in the Forensic Report to be wholly speculative. The accused relied on 16 files in the DVD-ROM attached to the Forensic Report, which showed the “date and time of creation” to be on 27 May 2021 (ie, the date of the accused’s arrest).[note: 134] The accused submitted that as he had already been taken into custody by then and had no access to the J1 Phone, these files must have been tampered with by the police. From this, the accused concluded that it was highly probable that most of the files, if not all, would have been tampered with.[note: 135]

125    To this, PW3 explained that these 16 files highlighted by the accused could have been cache files that were generated by the J1 Phone itself. A cache file would be generated when a particular file was being accessed, for ease of accessing or previewing this same file subsequently. Hence, the cache files could have been created when the investigation officer accessed the files in the J1 Phone after it was seized.[note: 136] PW3 was further able to identify that these 16 files highlighted by the accused were indeed cache files by reviewing their respective file paths, which each contained the word “cache”.[note: 137] This was consistent with PW6’s evidence, who confirmed that he had looked through the J1 Phone before 2 June 2021 to search for evidence inside the mobile phone. In doing so, PW6 testified that he did not intentionally add or delete any contents therein. Similarly, PW3 stated that as far as he was aware, no one implanted any messages, images or files into the J1 Phone after it was seized.[note: 138]

126    Accordingly, I considered it safe to rely on the contents extracted from the J1 Phone despite its inoperability by January 2025. For completeness, the accused also submitted that the loss of primary evidence in the J1 Phone meant that he was deprived of the chance to show which files in the J1 Phone had been transferred over from other mobile devices. In this regard, I would repeat my findings in relation to the issue of data synchronisation, and specifically, how they did not assist the accused’s defence (see [109] to [113] above).

(5)   The weight of the evidence led to the inevitable conclusion that the J1 Phone and its contents belonged to the accused

127    Having scrutinised the evidence in relation to this issue, I came to the inevitable conclusion that the J1 Phone and the contents therein belonged to the accused. This could have been the only reason why: (a) the accused admitted to purchasing the J1 Phone in his 28 May Statement and was able to provide full details of its purchase; (b) the J1 Phone would contain information referencing him and his details; and (c) he had control over the Samsung account with the J1 Phone registered. For the reasons stated above, I was unable to accept the accused’s version that it belonged to “Ah Heng”, and I similarly did not accept that “Ah Heng” had loaned the J1 Phone to the accused on 21 April 2021.

128    Further, despite the inoperability of the J1 Phone by January 2025, I was satisfied that the contents extracted therefrom were safe to be relied on in the court’s assessment of the evidence. These included, amongst others, the Signed Quotation and its various drafts, the images of PW2’s purported signature which appeared on the Signed Quotation, the images of the PIAS stamp and the various photo-editing software.

Did the accused arrange for delivery of the 55 Phones to Jackson Square?

129    Having made my findings on the two crucial issues of fact here, namely, that: (a) the accused was the one who corresponded with PW1 using the Ampang Email in the Order Emails; and (b) the J1 Phone and the contents therein belonged to the accused, I now turn to consider the other relevant threads of evidence in this case.

130    The accused was captured on CCTV footage collecting the three boxes containing the 55 Phones from PW4 at Jackson Square on 21 April 2021 at around 10.32am. The said CCTV footage did not show when and how the accused left Jackson Square. However, PW6 testified that he had viewed other cameras, which showed the accused carrying the three boxes, leaving from the side gate of Jackson Square, and crossing the road towards Blocks 53 to 54.[note: 139] He was next captured on the PolCam footage at the lift lobby of Block 54 Lorong 5 Toa Payoh, where he was seen carrying the three boxes while waiting for and subsequently entering the lift at around 11.38am on the same day.[note: 140]

131    All 55 Phones were eventually seized from the accused’s flat on two occasions. One “opened” set (see [102] above) was seized at the time of the accused’s arrest on 27 May 2021. The remaining 54 sets, which remained packaged in their respective boxes, were seized on 11 June 2021. The IMEI numbers of all 55 sets which were seized from the accused at his flat tallied with that of the 55 Phones which PW1 had arranged for collection by the courier on 21 April 2021.[note: 141]

132    Against the backdrop of the undisputed facts above, the factual issue to be considered was whether the accused was the one who had arranged for delivery of the 55 Phones to Jackson Square, from which place he collected the 55 Phones and stored them at his flat. To this end, I was unable to accept the accused’s version (see [56] to [60] above) that he had collected the 55 Phones and stored them at his flat on “Ah Heng’s” instructions. I was instead satisfied that it was the accused who had arranged for delivery. This is elaborated below.

(1)   The Ampang Email and J1 Phone pointed to the accused’s involvement

133    The user of the Ampang Email was the one who had liaised with PW1 on the delivery of the 55 Phones. PW1 had sent an email to the Ampang Email to ask if the 55 Phones should be delivered to PIAS’ address at Shenton Way. To this, the user of the Ampang Email replied to explain that they were still working from home and arranged for a courier to collect the 55 Phones from Maxxmedia’s office on either 21 or 22 April 2021 instead.[note: 142] This led to PW4 collecting the 55 Phones on 21 April 2021 and delivering them to Jackson Square.

134    As explained at [100] above, I was satisfied that the weight of the evidence led the court to the inevitable conclusion that the accused was the user of the Ampang Email at the material time. This necessarily meant that he was the one who had communicated with PW1 and informed PW1 that he would be arranging for a courier to collect the 55 Phones from Maxxmedia’s office.

135    Turning next to the image of the GOGOX booking details which was found in the J1 Phone,[note: 143] this requested the delivery driver (ie, PW4) to collect the items from Maxxmedia’s office and to deliver them to Jackson Square. The contact information was listed as one “Alson Teo Hock Loo” with the contact number “XXXX1460”. “Alson Teo Hock Loo” was the name adopted by the user of the Ampang Email in the course of his correspondence with PW1 (ie, in the Order Emails), which identity turned out to be fictitious, as no such person was employed at PIAS.

136    The accused denied having anything to do with the GOGOX booking as “XXXX1460” was not shown to be registered to him, based on the police’s searches with the telecommunications company (at [58] above). In fact, the accused alleged that this was instead “Ah Heng’s” number, and he had been contacting “Ah Heng” at this number since May 2016. The issue of “Ah Heng’s” identity and association with this mobile phone number of “XXXX1460” is discussed in greater detail below (at [160] to [169]). Nonetheless, I found the accused’s point here to be an inconclusive one. Just as how the telecommunications screening did not show the mobile phone number as being registered to the accused, it also did not show that the mobile phone number was registered to “Ah Heng”. In any event, this mobile phone number of “XXXX1460” did not seem to be a crucial requirement for the successful completion of the GOGOX booking, as PW4 eventually handed the 55 Phones to the accused upon a collection of the delivery fee.[note: 144] There was no evidence before the court of any need for PW4 to have verified the mobile phone number before handing the 55 Phones to the accused. The mere fact that the GOGOX booking details reflected “XXXX1460” did not by itself disassociate the accused from having arranged for delivery and/or placing the GOGOX booking.

137    Further, there was a deleted note extracted from the J1 Phone which read “XXXX9176 Hakim”. This note was created on 21 April 2021 at 10.32am, around the time that the accused collected the 55 Phones from PW4 (see [130] above). The accused appeared to accept that this was “probably” PW4’s contact number. However, he denied obtaining it from PW4 and averred that this was provided to him by “Ah Heng” for the purposes of coordinating the delivery.[note: 145] This would however not explain why the note was only created at 10.32am, at the time the accused collected the 55 Phones from PW4. If “Ah Heng” had indeed provided the accused with PW4’s number for coordination purposes, this note should logically have been created by the accused before meeting PW4. There would have been no need for the accused to create this note only upon meeting PW4, as the items had been successfully delivered by then. In any event, no details were given by the accused on how and when “Ah Heng” had provided this number to him. I hence did not accept the accused’s claims that it was “Ah Heng” who had provided him with PW4’s number.

138    Accordingly, as I have found that the J1 Phone and the contents therein belonged to the accused (see [127] above), this meant that the accused had in his possession and stored in the J1 Phone, an image of the GOGOX booking details and PW4’s contact number. While the accused sought to attribute these to “Ah Heng”, I was not convinced of his account.

(2)   The accused’s lies about the remaining 54 sets of the 55 Phones

139    In a further attempt to distance himself from the delivery of the 55 Phones, the accused explained that he met with “Ah Heng” at the open space in front of Block 54, Lorong 5 Toa Payoh after collecting the 55 Phones (see [47] and [57] above). He claimed that it was there that he purchased one set from “Ah Heng” and agreed to help “Ah Heng” store the remaining 54 sets at his flat. When the police attended at the accused’s flat and arrested him on 27 May 2021, they only managed to seize the one set which was “opened” and which the accused alleged was purchased from “Ah Heng”. The police did not manage to locate the remaining 54 sets that day.

140    In response to the accused’s version as regards how he had come into possession of the 55 Phones, the Prosecution sought to rely on three statements given by the accused during the period that he was remanded for investigations. Two were recorded on 28 May 2021, the day after his arrest, namely: (a) the 28 May Statement, which was a long statement recorded from the accused from 1.23pm to 2.52pm; and (b) a cautioned statement recorded from the accused from 3.04pm to 3.15pm (the “Cautioned Statement”). The third statement was recorded from the accused on 10 June 2021 at 2.45pm (the “10 June Statement”). The 28 May Statement and the 10 June Statement were admitted in evidence without any objections from the accused. However, the accused objected to the admissibility of the Cautioned Statement, and an ancillary hearing was held for this purpose.

(A)   The Cautioned Statement was admitted after an ancillary hearing

141    The accused challenged the admissibility of the Cautioned Statement on the basis that he was on at least two sets of drowsy medication for flu, fever, cough and anxiety at the time the statement was recorded. While the accused accepted that the 28 May Statement (which was recorded just before the Cautioned Statement) was given voluntarily as the effects of the drowsy medication had not yet taken effect then, he was subsequently under the influence of the medication when the Cautioned Statement was recorded. He hence rushed through the process as he was getting drowsy and restless and wanted to end the process quickly so that he could return to his air-conditioned cell to rest. He further alleged that the investigation officer who recorded the statement did not read the Cautioned Statement back to him word-for-word.[note: 146]

142    The investigation officer who recorded the Cautioned Statement, 1AH-PW1 Ms Sophia Sim Shi Mei, was the sole Prosecution witness who gave evidence during the ancillary hearing. She testified that the accused was alert during the recording of both the 28 May Statement and the Cautioned Statement.[note: 147] In particular, as regards the Cautioned Statement, 1AH-PW1 explained that the accused was clearly able to articulate the seven points in response to the charge which was served on him. 1AH-PW1 also did not recall the accused expressing that he was drowsy or could not concentrate during the process of statement recording.[note: 148]

143    Having considered the evidence led at the ancillary hearing and the submissions made by both parties in detail, I accepted the evidence of 1AH-PW1 and admitted the Cautioned Statement after the ancillary hearing. I did not accept the accused’s account that he had been so drowsy that he could not properly provide his statement, particularly since he had the presence of mind to refuse to sign on the charge that was served on him and could explain his response to the charge in detail. He could state clearly that the facts in the charge were “materially wrong” and the reasons for why he did not commit the offence. It was a detailed and considered denial to the charge, which was plainly inconsistent with his account of being drowsy and under the influence of medication. I hence admitted the Cautioned Statement.

(B)   The positions taken by the accused in his statements

144    In the 28 May Statement, the accused stated that he “received a whatsapp phone call which [he could not] remember who, to collect some boxes from Jackson Square and deliver to the lobby area between [Block] 53 or 55 of Lorong 5 Toa Payoh.” There, he handed the boxes to a “Chinese old man”, who gave the accused a delivery fee. It was also then that the accused paid the “Chinese old man” $1,100 in cash for one set of the Samsung Galaxy S21 Ultra 5G mobile phone. The accused added that “[n]o concrete evidence was found” by the police when they ransacked his home.[note: 149]

145    In the Cautioned Statement, the accused maintained this position and stated that he was “not in possession of the [55 Phones]. The police [had] confirmed nothing concrete was found after the ransack [of his] 1-room flat at 1.15pm [the day before].”

146    During the recording of his 10 June Statement, the accused was shown an image extracted from the PolCam footage on 21 April 2021 at 11.38am, where he was seen standing at the lift lobby of Block 54 carrying the three boxes containing the 55 Phones. When asked to explain or elaborate on the said extracted image, his answer was:

These are not the alleged items. These 3 boxes are my other delivery. Because if I know that there will be CCTV footage all over the place. I wish to state that I do not wish to continue my statement and will provide my statement to the Investigation officer tomorrow.

147    The next day, on 11 June 2021, the accused informed the investigation officer PW6 that the remaining 54 sets of the 55 Phones were stored at his flat and that he would bring the police to his flat to retrieve them. Arrangements were thus made to bring the accused back to his flat on that same day, where the remaining 54 sets were found stored in three boxes, in a cupboard in the accused’s room.[note: 150]

(C)   The lies told by the accused in his statements amounted to Lucas lies

148    Given that the accused had known all along that the remaining 54 sets of the 55 Phones had been stored in his flat, his account in the 28 May Statement and the Cautioned Statement that he: (a) had handed the boxes to a Chinese old man; and (b) was not in possession of the 55 Phones, were clearly lies.

149    The Prosecution hence urged the court to find that these amounted to Lucas lies, which would be corroborative of the accused’s guilt. The explanation of what would amount to a Lucas lie was succinctly explained by the High Court in Er Joo Nguang and anor v Public Prosecutor [2000] 1 SLR(R) 756 at [52]:

… [In Lucas], the English Court of Appeal held that the mere fact that an accused told lies should not be taken as evidence of his guilt, although these lies could, in appropriate circumstances, amount to corroboration because it indicated a consciousness of guilt. Lord Lane CJ held at 724 that there were four criteria to be satisfied before an accused’s lie could amount to corroboration:

The lie … must first of all be deliberate. Secondly, it must relate to a material issue. Thirdly, the motive for the lie must be a realisation of guilt and a fear of the truth. … Fourthly, the statement must be clearly shown to be a lie by [independent] evidence …

[emphasis in original]

150    The accused categorically rejected this. He submitted that he had not been lying but was instead “not telling the truth” to protect “Ah Heng’s” interest.[note: 151] When asked in cross-examination on why he did not make any reference to “Ah Heng” in the 28 May Statement and the Cautioned Statement, the accused explained that he needed to protect “Ah Heng” as: (a) no instructions were given for him to surrender the remaining 54 sets of the 55 Phones; and (b) “Ah Heng” assisted him with many things.[note: 152] Hence, the accused submitted that the telling of false truths for “moral reasons” should not be considered as lies.

151    I agreed with the Prosecution that the four criteria set out in Lucas have been satisfied here, with the effect that I found the accused’s lies as regards the remaining 54 sets of the 55 Phones in the 28 May Statement and the Cautioned Statement to be corroborative of his guilt.

152    First, I found the lies to have been made deliberately. The accused had known, at the time he gave the 28 May Statement and the Cautioned Statement, that the remaining 54 sets of the 55 Phones were in his flat. He was also well aware that the investigations were ongoing in relation to the 55 Phones and that the police were in the process of locating the same, particularly since the 55 Phones were referenced in the charge served on him during the recording of the Cautioned Statement. Yet, he said that he had handed them to the “Chinese old man” and was not in possession of the 55 Phones.

153    Second, given that the 55 Phones were the subject of the Cheating Charge, the lies made by the accused as regards the whereabouts of the remaining 54 sets clearly related to a material issue. There was no doubt that the issue of whether the remaining 54 sets were in the accused’s possession would be material and relevant to the accused’s involvement in the offence.

154    Third, I agreed with the Prosecution that the accused’s motive for the lies must be a realisation of guilt and a fear of the truth. The accused had sought to explain that he lied to protect the interest of “Ah Heng”. However, the accused failed to provide any cogent or credible reasons for why he would need to do so. On his own account, he was deceived by “Ah Heng” in 2016, which resulted in him suffering a loss of $2,500. The accused even made a police report in this regard. Further, the accused’s account at trial was that “Ah Heng” had sought his help to store the remaining 54 sets in his flat, as the buyer was not ready to pay for the items. With an explanation as straightforward as that, and given the history between the accused and “Ah Heng”, it was difficult to discern any reason why the accused would need to protect “Ah Heng’s” interests and not inform the police as such during investigations.

155    Instead, and considering the sequence of events, I agreed with the Prosecution that it was more likely that the accused had lied in the 28 May Statement and the Cautioned Statement as he did not want to be questioned on why the 54 sets of the 55 Phones were in his possession, especially since the police had not found them when they attended at his flat on 27 May 2021. It was not until the recording of the 10 June Statement, when he was shown the image from the PolCam footage of him with the three boxes containing the 55 Phones, that he realised he could no longer maintain his version that the remaining 54 sets were not in his possession. Even during the recording of the 10 June Statement, the accused maintained that the three boxes were his “other delivery” (ie, not the 55 Phones), though he indicated that he did not wish to proceed with the statement recording. He only confessed to PW6 that the remaining 54 sets were in his flat the next day. To my mind, considering the above, and in the absence of any cogent explanation given by the accused as to his lies, I was amply satisfied that the accused’s motive for the lies must be a realisation of guilt and a fear of the truth.

156    Finally, and as regards the fourth criteria, it was evident that the accused’s words in relation to the 55 Phones in the 28 May Statement and the Cautioned Statement were clearly lies at the time they were made. The accused was fully aware that the remaining 54 sets were in his flat at the time the two statements were given but chose instead to say that they were not in his possession.

157    Given the assessment above, I agreed with the Prosecution that the accused’s lies did constitute Lucas lies. Not only did these lies cast serious doubt on the accused’s position that he had stored the 54 remaining sets of the 55 Phones at his flat upon “Ah Heng’s” request and on “Ah Heng’s” behalf, but they also carried significant probative weight as to his guilt.

(3)   The accused’s reliance on his condition of scoliosis

158    For completeness, I found the accused’s reliance on his condition of scoliosis to be inconclusive and in any event self-serving. The accused claimed that he could not have arranged for delivery of the 55 Phones as he did not even know that he was going to collect 55 Phones from PW4. The accused stated that as he suffered from scoliosis, he was advised by his doctors to refrain from carrying heavy loads, and he would never risk his life by carrying something as heavy as the 55 Phones.[note: 153]

159    The fact of the matter was that the accused did carry the 55 Phones from Jackson Square back to Block 54, where his flat was. The accused’s reliance on his condition of scoliosis at trial was simply an afterthought and an easy excuse to distance himself from the offences. It did not appear to me, based on a review of the PolCam footage at the lift lobby of Block 54, that the accused was struggling disproportionately in carrying the 55 Phones. In any event, if it were something as life-threatening as the accused made it out to be, there was no reason why he could not have sought the assistance of “Ah Heng” to meet him at Jackson Square and assist with the load, given that, on the accused’s own account, “Ah Heng” would have been in the vicinity, as he met with “Ah Heng” at the open space in front of Block 54 shortly after he had collected the 55 Phones.

“Ah Heng” was not called as a witness at trial

160    Finally, and crucially, the accused did not call “Ah Heng” as a witness at trial. Given the accused’s heavy reliance on “Ah Heng” for most parts of his defence, it would have been incumbent on the accused to have called “Ah Heng” as a witness in support of his case, or at the very least, set out in detail the steps taken to procure his attendance. Instead, the accused merely insisted that “Ah Heng” was “definitely the perpetrator of this crime but was not willing to be in Singapore as defence witness on fear of being arrested once [he] entered into Singapore.” The accused explained that he had tried to seek an assurance from the Prosecution not to make any arrest against “Ah Heng” once he entered Singapore, but this was rejected. He further put the blame on the Prosecution for failing to have secured “Ah Heng’s” extradition to Singapore, so that he could be vindicated.[note: 154]

161    The involvement of “Ah Heng” formed a key tenet of the accused’s case. The Prosecution was not relying on “Ah Heng’s” evidence in any way and did not need to call “Ah Heng” in support of their case. There was no obligation on the part of the Prosecution to make any such extradition request on the accused’s behalf, particularly since it was not the Prosecution’s case that “Ah Heng” was the perpetrator or even a relevant witness in the present proceedings.

162    In any event, based on the evidence at trial, there was serious doubt as to whether the accused was indeed in contact with “Ah Heng” at the material time of the offences and during the trial. For someone whom the accused had taken pains to locate through his own investigative work, tapping on private investigators, the Johor police and unlicensed moneylenders from Malaysia for a period of two years from 2017 to 2018, it was curious that the only identifying details that the accused could provide was the imprecise and ambiguous name of “Ah Heng”, that he was “Malaysian”, with a “Malaysian speaking accent”, and was a “middle-aged person” whose size was “a bit bigger” than the accused.[note: 155] There was no evidence of “Ah Heng’s” full name or other personal identification details, no photographs tendered of “Ah Heng”, no telephone call logs with “Ah Heng”, and no text messages received from “Ah Heng”. This was despite the accused’s version that he had been in contact with “Ah Heng” since 2019 and that he had asked “Ah Heng” to do many things for him since then.

163    While the accused claimed that he contacted “Ah Heng” at the Ampang Email, I was satisfied, as explained at [71] to [100] above, that the accused, and not “Ah Heng”, was the user of the Ampang Email. In any event, none of the correspondence with the Ampang Email showed any form of meaningful communication, given that these merely comprised the forwarding of information with a blank cover email. The accused also tendered a screenshot of a WhatsApp message, which he claimed he sent to “Ah Heng” on 17 June 2021, stating:[note: 156]

Hello, is this Ah Heng?

Your 3 boxes of items were with SIO Aliden … on 11/6/21…

Last but not least, when can you refund me the money you owed me? TQ.

164    While the screenshot displayed the name of the recipient as one “Ah Heng”, it was not clear from this screenshot the specific telephone number to which the message was sent. In any event, it appeared from the face of the screenshot that this was the only message ever sent to “Ah Heng”. There were no messages prior to this and there was no response from “Ah Heng” after. This was again curious, not least because the accused would, on his own account, have been in contact with “Ah Heng” in March and April 2021 in relation to the assignment to collect the 55 Phones from Jackson Square, and to thereafter hand them to “Ah Heng”. Accordingly, there was no evidence before the court of any correspondence from “Ah Heng” to the accused, in spite of the accused’s account of “Ah Heng’s” involvement and the multitude of things that he had asked “Ah Heng” to do.

165    Further, for someone whose involvement in this case was so crucial, the accused made no reference to “Ah Heng” during the recording of the 28 May Statement and the Cautioned Statement. In the 28 May Statement, the accused said that he had received a “whatsapp phone call which [he could not] remember who” to collect the delivery from Jackson Square. At trial, the accused said that it was “Ah Heng” who offered him this job in March 2021. The accused also said in his 28 May Statement that he handed the boxes to a “Chinese old man”. This was again inconsistent with the accused’s description of “Ah Heng” at trial, who he described to be a Malaysian middle-aged man. While these may not appear consequential when viewed in isolation, these multiple inconsistencies collectively cast doubt on the involvement of “Ah Heng” in the manner relied upon by the accused at trial.

166    The accused also claimed to have always associated the mobile phone number “XXXX1460” with “Ah Heng” since 2016. This was the number provided in the police report made by the accused in 2016, when he was first deceived by “Ah Heng” to transfer the sum of $2,500.[note: 157] During the trial, the accused showed the court that he had saved “Ah Heng’s” number in his mobile phone as “XXXX1460”. There was no reference to any other number that the accused had known “Ah Heng’s” number to be, or that the accused had contacted “Ah Heng” at. To this, I observed two anomalies. First, as discussed at [136] above, the telecommunications screening did not show this mobile phone number as being registered to “Ah Heng” (or a name which would have borne some semblance to “Ah Heng”). In fact, the searches showed that the ownership of this number had changed from 2019 to 2020 (ie, that it was registered to one individual in 2019 and then to another in 2020). It did not hence seem plausible that the accused had been contacting “Ah Heng” at this number since 2016.

167    Second, and perhaps more tellingly, WhatsApp messages extracted from the J1 Phone showed that messages were exchanged with the number “XXXX1460”, identified as “Mrs Resh” from February to September 2020.[note: 158] As explained at [101] to [128] above, I was satisfied based on the evidence before the court that the J1 Phone and its contents belonged to the accused. Accordingly, these messages would have been sent by the accused to “Mrs Resh” at “XXXX1460”. In the messages, the accused introduced himself as “Terence”, who was “helping Bedok Police Div[ision] to do crime investigations”. It was clear from the evidence and submissions before the court that the accused identified himself as “Terence”, even if this did not appear on his NRIC. The accused himself acknowledged as such in the 28 May Statement, where he said that his “family and friends know [him] as ‘Terence’”.

168    The substance of the messages clearly showed that the accused was not familiar with the user of this number, as he had asked “Mrs Resh” when she started using the number (ie, “XXXX1460”) and how she had come into possession of this SIM card. He even threatened to bring “Mrs Resh” down to Bedok Police Division for statement taking should she refuse to answer. “Mrs Resh” then responded that her friend helped her purchase the SIM card, and the accused asked that such friend contact him.

169    It was hence clear to me that, from at least 2020 onwards, the accused was not in contact with “Ah Heng” at the number “XXXX1460”, and he was certainly not in contact with “Ah Heng” in the manner described in his defence. Instead, the messages suggested that he had been trying to look for the person who sold the SIM card containing the number “XXXX1460” to “Mrs Resh”. Given the various doubts raised in evidence as regards “Ah Heng’s” involvement, and with the absence of “Ah Heng” as a witness in court to provide the key evidence which could only be provided by him, I was wholly unable to accept the accused’s account of “Ah Heng’s” involvement in the Cheating Charge and the Forgery Charge. I was instead of the view that this was merely a convenient excuse relied upon by the accused to disassociate himself from the offences.

The circumstantial evidence in this case inevitably and inexorably led the court to a single conclusion of the accused’s guilt

170    Considering the totality of the evidence as described above, I was satisfied that the circumstantial evidence in this case inevitably and inexorably led the court to a single conclusion of the accused’s guilt, and the Prosecution has proven both the Cheating Charge and Forgery Charge beyond reasonable doubt. I found that the “various links in the interlocking chain of evidence [have] establish[ed] a complete chain that rule[d] out any reasonable likelihood of [the] accused’s innocence” and that guilt was the “only rational inference and conclusion to be drawn from the complete chain of evidence” (Constance Chee at [85]).

171    To this end, as regards the first key factual issue (see [67] above), I have found that the accused was the user of the Ampang Email and was the one who corresponded with PW1 in the Order Emails. The meant that the accused was the one who sent the 15 March Email and attached the Signed Quotation to the email dated 22 March 2021. As for the second key factual issue (see [68] above), I have also found that the J1 Phone and the contents (including the incriminating contents) therein belonged to the accused. The accused hence had, stored in his J1 Phone, not just a copy of the Signed Quotation, but also working drafts of the same in varying permutations. In addition, the accused had separate image files of PW2’s purported signature and the PIAS stamp as they appeared on the Signed Quotation. Along with the photo-editing software found in the J1 Phone, the accused must have been the one who affixed the images of PW2’s purported signature and the PIAS stamp onto the quotation sent by PW1, creating the Signed Quotation. The accused then sent the Signed Quotation to PW1 using the Ampang Email.

172    As regards the remaining threads of evidence, I was also satisfied that it was the accused who had personally arranged for the delivery of the 55 Phones to Jackson Square, where he collected them from PW4. Using the Ampang Email, the accused informed PW1 that he would be arranging for a courier service to collect the 55 Phones from Maxxmedia’s office. On this basis, the 55 Phones were handed to PW4.
