PW4 in turn delivered the 55 Phones to Jackson Square and handed them to the accused, who brought them back to his flat. All 55 Phones were eventually seized from the accused’s flat.

173    As against the above, I was wholly unable to accept the accused’s version as regards “Ah Heng’s” involvement in the entire scheme. Contrary to the accused’s allegations, the evidence did not show that “Ah Heng” was the user of the Ampang Email. Neither did the evidence show that “Ah Heng” was the owner of the J1 Phone and the incriminating contents therein. “Ah Heng” was not the one who arranged for delivery of the 55 Phones and he did not ask that the accused store the remaining 54 sets of the 55 Phones in his flat. The accused’s lies in the 28 May Statement and the Cautioned Statement about the whereabouts of these remaining 54 sets further amounted to Lucas lies which were corroborative of the accused’s guilt.

174    The complete chain of the interlocking threads of evidence hence pointed to the single conclusion of the accused’s guilt, ruling out any reasonable likelihood of the accused’s innocence. The strength of the overwhelming evidence discounted any chance of this being a mere “fanciful or speculative” possibility (Constance Chee at [85]).

175    As regards the Cheating Charge, the evidence irresistibly pointed to the findings that:

(a)     the accused was the user of the Ampang Email at the material time and deceived PW1 that he was representing PIAS to purchase the 55 Phones;

(b)     the accused knew this to be false as he was neither “Alson Teo Hock Loo” nor did he work at PIAS;

(c)     the accused was the one who sent the email to PW1 on 15 March 2021 at 12.14am, being the user of the Ampang Email at the material time; and

(d)     PW1 was dishonestly induced as a result to cause the 55 Phones to be delivered to PW4.

176    As regards the Forgery Charge, the evidence similarly inevitably pointed to the findings that:

(a)     the accused was the one who affixed the electronic signatures of PW2 onto the quotation form for the 55 Phones, using the files and photo-editing software in the J1 Phone, and he sent the Signed Quotation using the Ampang Email to PW1;

(b)     the accused intended for PW1 to believe that it was signed by PW2, so that PW1 would proceed with the order of 55 Phones;

(c)     as the accused was the one who affixed the signature without PW2’s consent, he knew PW2 did not sign on the Signed Quotation; and

(d)     the accused intended for the Signed Quotation to be used for the purposes of cheating PW1 to deliver the 55 Phones to PW4, and eventually to him.

177    I was hence satisfied that the Prosecution had proven its case beyond a reasonable doubt and convicted the accused accordingly of both the Cheating Charge and the Forgery Charge.

Sentencing

Antecedents

178    The accused has one antecedent for an offence of forgery under s 465 of the PC. He was convicted in 2008 and sentenced to a fine of $4,000. While this was a relevant antecedent of a similar nature, I accepted that it was considerably dated, having taken place more than 12 years before the commission of the present offences. I did not hence place significant weight on this antecedent in my assessment of the appropriate sentence to be imposed in this case.

Prosecution’s submissions on sentence

179    The Prosecution sought a global sentence in the region of at least 14 months’ imprisonment. This comprised an individual sentence of 14 months’ each for the Cheating Charge and Forgery Charge, to run concurrently.

180    The total value of the 55 Phones here, as stated in the Signed Quotation, was $89,705 (excluding GST).[note: 159] However, PW1 testified that the cost price of the 55 Phones was $82,060.[note: 160] While the 55 Phones were recovered, they were sold at a loss by Maxxmedia. Of these, the 54 sets which were unopened and remained in their packaging were sold at $1,200 each, whereas the one “opened” set which was no longer in its original packaging was sold at $1,000.[note: 161] The total sale proceeds from the recovered 55 Phones were $65,800. Based on PW1’s testimony, the actual loss suffered by Maxxmedia was hence $16,260, being the difference in the cost price of the 55 Phones (ie, $82,060) and their eventual sale price (ie, $65,800).

181    In relation to the Cheating Charge, the Prosecution submitted that the value of the monies cheated would be the primary yardstick for sentencing. As regards harm, the Prosecution acknowledged that the 55 Phones were recovered and Maxxmedia suffered an actual loss of $16,260 after selling the 55 Phones at a discounted price. As regards culpability, the Prosecution submitted that there was a high degree of premeditation here. The accused had identified “Alson Teo” and “Choa Mei Kuen”, both of whom were associated with PIAS. He then penned emails under the guise of “Alson Teo Hock Loo” from PIAS over a considerable period in March 2021. Further, to ensure that the delivery would not be tracked to his address, the accused arranged for a third-party courier to collect the 55 Phones from Maxxmedia’s office and had them delivered to Jackson Square instead of directly to his flat.

182    The Prosecution compared the facts of the present case against various precedents involving comparable amounts cheated, and submitted that a term of 14 months’ imprisonment would be appropriate for the Cheating Charge.

183    In relation to the Forgery Charge, the Prosecution relied heavily on the decision in Toh Suat Leng Jennifer v Public Prosecutor [2022] 5 SLR 1075 (“Jennifer Toh”). Having regard to the amounts involved and relevant facts in Jennifer Toh as compared to the present case, the Prosecution submitted that a similar sentence of 14 months’ imprisonment would be suitable for the Forgery Charge.

184    The Prosecution submitted that the two sentences should run concurrently as they pertained to a single scam perpetrated on PW1 and his company, Maxxmedia. The Prosecution was also of the view that no mitigating weight ought to be given to the accused for his medical conditions, as there was no basis to show that the accused would suffer disproportionately in prison. Neither was there any basis to assert that the accused’s culpability was decreased by any medical condition (see Chew Soo Chun v Public Prosecutor [2016] 2 SLR 78 (“Chew Soo Chun”) at [39]).

Mitigation plea and the accused’s submissions on sentence

185    The accused maintained that he was not guilty and categorically rejected the conviction. Nonetheless, on the basis of the court’s verdict, he filed two sets of mitigation plea and sentencing submissions.

186    As regards the Cheating Charge, the accused accepted that the quantum involved would be a relevant starting point. He submitted that the relevant sum should be the actual loss of $16,260 and not the sum of $89,705 as stated in the charge. Further, this loss was suffered as PW1 had sold the 55 Phones in a panic and was not entirely caused by the accused’s and/or “Ah Heng’s” actions. The accused also undertook a detailed review of sentencing tariffs across various amounts involved, and submitted that:

(a)     where the amount involved was between $10,000 to $30,000, the sentencing tariff was six to 12 months’ imprisonment;

(b)     where the amount involved was between $30,000 to $60,000, the sentencing tariff was 12 to 18 months’ imprisonment; and

(c)     where the amount involved was between $60,000 to $100,000, the sentencing tariff was 18 to 24 months’ imprisonment.

187    The accused took the position that there were no aggravating factors in this case, as it was not committed with a high degree of deliberation or sophistication. Further, while the accused accepted the sentencing tariffs, these had yet to take into account the exceptional mitigating factors in his case.

188    As regards the Forgery Charge, the accused submitted that past cases had adopted a 12-month sentence of imprisonment as a benchmark for an offence of forgery under s 468 of the PC. However, this would be dependent on the aggravating and mitigating factors present in each case. There were no aggravating factors here as: (a) the forged document was not a government document; (b) the harm caused to Maxxmedia and PW1 was very minimal; (c) there was no evidence of other crimes being committed because of the offence of forgery; and (d) this was not a large-scale forgery. The accused further considered the actual loss amount of $16,260 to be a “rather small sum of monies”, especially when compared to the accused’s overall net worth at the time of the offence, which he claimed was $4.22 million as at 29 November 2017.[note: 162]

189    In addition, the Forgery Charge did not undermine the delivery and integrity of the investment advisory services of PIAS, did not cause Maxxmedia to shut down, and did not lead to PW1 being retrenched or having to suffer a pay-cut. In any event, he did not have any deliberate intention to target Maxxmedia or PW1 as he had no grievances against them. He also submitted that the degree of sophistication here was low, as there was no evidence to suggest that there had been careful planning and execution of the forgery to deceive PW1. The offences were also not difficult to detect as there was no evidence showing that the forging of the Signed Quotation was meticulously done.

190    The accused further highlighted that the period of offending was a short period of two months, and that he voluntarily returned the 55 Phones to the victim through the police, after he realised that he might have unknowingly helped to safekeep stolen goods for “Ah Heng”. This act of voluntary restitution, together with the accused’s full cooperation with the police, must hence be afforded significant mitigating weight.

191    However, and quite apart from the sentencing factors raised above, the accused emphasised that he was not suitable to be incarcerated due to the many medical conditions that he was suffering from, which were likely to worsen during incarceration and for which the Changi Prison Complex Medical Centre did not have the requisite medication. In particular, the accused was suffering from the following medical conditions: (a) asthma; (b) anxiety disorder; (c) gastroesophageal reflux disease (“heartburn”); (d) endoscopy surgery; (e) scoliosis; and (f) pneumothorax. Judicial mercy should hence be exercised due to the severity of the accused’s medical conditions, as jail time would carry a high risk of endangering his life.

192    Further, no amount of fine should be imposed on the accused as he has been unable to find employment due to the pending case, which has resulted an opportunity loss to the accused in the range of $670,000. The accused thus submitted that it would be extremely unreasonable for the court to impose a fine of any amount as the accused has made full restitution in this case.

193    Accordingly, in the absence of any aggravating factors and in view of the exceptional mitigating factors, the accused urged the court to impose a nominal custodial sentence without a fine. In support of this submission, he relied on the cases of Seaward III Frederick Oliver v Public Prosecutor [1994] 3 SLR(R) 89 (“Seaward”) and Nathan Edmund v Public Prosecutor [1997] 2 SLR(R) 926 (“Nathan Edmund”), where the court had, in each of these cases, imposed a sentence of one day’s imprisonment and a fine of $10,000 for offences of cheating under s 420 of the PC.

Decision on sentence

194    Both the Cheating Charge and the Forgery Charge carried the same prescribed punishment. For each charge, the accused faced mandatory imprisonment of up to ten years and was also liable to fine.

(1)   The Cheating Charge

195    In Idya Nurhazlyn bte Ahmad Khir v Public Prosecutor and anor [2014] 1 SLR 756 at [48], the High Court considered that the “primary yardstick [in sentencing for an offence of cheating would] often be the value of the property involved.” That said, the court must also not lose sight of the specific facts and circumstances in each case, especially the relevant offence-specific and offender-specific factors (Jennifer Toh at [60]).

196    The total value of the 55 Phones here was $89,705. While the starting point to be considered by the court as regards the value involved in the Cheating Charge must be $89,705, I accepted, as both parties did, that the actual loss to the victim here was less than this amount. The 55 Phones were recovered and resold by Maxxmedia, albeit at a loss of $16,260, being the difference between the cost price and the eventual sale price.

197    I agreed with the Prosecution that there was a significant degree of premeditation here, as the accused had taken multiple steps to distance himself from the offence by adopting the use of various aliases in dishonestly inducing PW1 to deliver the 55 Phones. The accused had liaised with PW1 over email using the identity of one “Alson Teo Hock Loo” from PIAS, using the Ampang Email which was devoid of any personal identifiers. Thereafter, the accused arranged for a third-party courier GOGOX to collect the 55 Phones from Maxxmedia’s office, thereby rejecting PW1’s suggestion for the 55 Phones to be delivered to PIAS’ office, and arranged for delivery to Jackson Square instead of his own flat. While the note to the driver (ie, PW4) in the GOGOX booking details expressly stated that PW4 was sent by “Alson Teo Hock Loo” to collect the 55 Phones, and further purported to provide “Alson Teo Hock Loo’s” contact number, it was eventually the accused who accepted delivery of the 55 Phones at Jackson Square, before carrying them back to his flat. To my mind, these were carefully planned steps to avoid detection, to ensure that the accused’s name and identifying particulars would not be featured at any step of the way.

198    The accused, in submitting that there was no premeditation on his part, said that there was no deliberate intention to target Maxxmedia and/or PW1 and he had no grievances against either of them. While I acknowledged that there was no evidence before this court that the accused had set out to specifically target Maxxmedia and/or PW1, the accused’s submission was missing the point. The crux of the premeditation here was not that the accused had targeted the victims, but rather, it was on the meticulous planning on the accused’s part to avoid detection and to distance himself from the offending acts.

199    I was also unable to agree with the accused’s submission that he had voluntarily returned the 55 Phones to the victim through the police on 11 June 2021. In my view, and having considered the evidence before the court, this was not a case of voluntary restitution due to remorse on the accused’s part, but rather, a situation where the 55 Phones were recovered by the police in the course of investigations. The accused had, in his 28 May Statement and Cautioned Statement, taken the position that the 55 Phones were handed to the “Chinese old man” and he was not in possession of the same. He was happy to maintain this position until 10 June 2021, when he was shown an image from the PolCam footage at the lift lobby of his block, which captured him carrying the three boxes containing the 55 Phones. It was only after he knew that he had been caught red-handed on camera that he decided to inform PW6 the next day that the remaining 54 sets of the 55 Phones were in his flat.

200    Further, while the accused had initially indicated that he intended to make restitution of the actual loss amount of $16,260 and would “definitely pay” as his “conscience actually told [him that he] should have paid because 16,000 [was actually not much]”,[note: 163] he ultimately decided not to make restitution as he “rejected the conviction” and should not be held accountable for the loss.[note: 164] Hence, there was no voluntary restitution made by the accused here, and no mitigating weight could be afforded to the accused for the police’s recovery of the 55 Phones.

201    Considering the totality of the facts and precedents cited by both parties, I agreed with the Prosecution that a sentence of 14 months’ imprisonment for the Cheating Charge was wholly warranted here. I found this sentence to be in line with the precedents cited by both parties and was in fact consistent with the sentencing tariffs submitted by the accused (see [186] above). To this end, I had particular reference to two cases, one cited by the Prosecution and the other by the accused.

202    In Public Prosecutor v Cao Shengliang [2020] SGDC 160 (“Cao Shengliang”), relied on by the Prosecution, the offender claimed trial to three charges under s 420 of the PC. The offender had issued cheques, which he knew would be dishonoured, to a seller to purchase some jewellery. The value of jewellery involved for the first two charges was $98,000 and $83,000 respectively, for which the offender was sentenced to 20 months’ imprisonment each (one to run consecutively and the other to run concurrently). As regards the third charge, the offender was sentenced to 12 months’ imprisonment (to run consecutively), for jewellery valued at $29,000. Partial restitution of $33,400 was made in respect of the first two charges, which related to the same victim.

203    In Syed Jafaralsadeg bin Abdul Kadir Alhadad v Public Prosecutor [1998] 3 SLR(R) 352 (“Syed Jafaralsadeg”), cited by the accused, the offender was convicted after trial of an offence of cheating under s 420 of the PC. The offender had deceived the director of a company into paying him $50,000 as agent’s commission for the purchase of a property on behalf of the company, when in fact no such payment was payable as no agent was involved in the sale. The offender was sentenced to 18 months’ imprisonment.

204    The starting point here, having regard to the value cheated, was $89,705. This was the sum stated in the Signed Quotation, upon which the fraudulent sale was concluded. This would be comparable to the first two charges in Cao Shengliang. However, I calibrated the sentence downwards to take into account the fact that the actual loss to the victim was considerably lower at $16,260. The extent of the downward calibration was nonetheless attenuated given the relatively higher culpability of the accused here, given the significant premeditation and the fact that no restitution was made. Similar factors were considered in my assessment of the facts of the present case against that in Syed Jafaralsadeg – I had adjusted the sentence downwards from that in Syed Jafaralsadeg considering the lower value of actual loss here.

205    Accordingly, I considered the sentence of 14 months’ imprisonment for the Cheating Charge to be justified and appropriate on the facts of the case.

(2)   The Forgery Charge

206    The accused had, in his sentencing submissions, referred to a 12-month imprisonment benchmark for offences under s 468 of the PC (see [188] above). However, the High Court had, in Jennifer Toh at [43], observed this benchmark sentence to be of limited utility, as the “single starting point appropriate is inappropriate for offences of forgery for the purposes of cheating under s 468 of the [PC]. There is simply no paradigmatic manifestation of the offence for which a notional starting point may be purposefully calibrated.” Ultimately, each case would have to be considered on their individual facts in arriving at the appropriate sentence.

207    To this end, I agreed with the Prosecution that the decision of Jennifer Toh was instructive, and the facts therein would serve as a useful reference. In Jennifer Toh, the offender sold fake insurance policies to unsuspecting victims. She forged the insurance policies by copying the letterhead and signatures from an existing policy. Through these forgeries, the victims were cheated into delivering the sums of $50,000 (respectively for the first and second charges) and $32,000 (for the third charge) to the offender. The offender had pleaded guilty and was sentenced to an imprisonment term of 18 months each for the first and second charges, and 16 months for the third charge. The imprisonment terms in the first and third charges were ordered to run consecutively, along with a fourth charge under s 420 of the PC which related to a separate set of facts not involving the insurance policies.

208    As with the Cheating Charge, the starting point in the Forgery Charge was $89,705, being the amount cheated by way of the Signed Quotation, which was forged by the accused. This was a higher sum than that in the first and second charges of Jennifer Toh. However, I again considered that the actual loss was considerably lower at $16,260 and factored in an appropriate downward calibration. The facts of Jennifer Toh and the present shared similarities in terms of the level of premeditation involved and the difficulty of detection. However, Jennifer Toh contained the aggravating factor of undermining the delivery and integrity of insurance services in Singapore, which was absent here. The offender in Jennifer Toh was also afforded some mitigating weight for her plea of guilt, which was not applicable to the accused as he had claimed trial. Considering all factors holistically, I agreed with the Prosecution that a sentence of 14 months’ imprisonment for the Forgery Charge was warranted on the facts of the case.

209    For completeness, I did not think that the cases of Seaward and Nathan Edmund, relied upon by the accused in his submission for a nominal custodial sentence without a fine (at [193] above), were instructive in the present case. These cases were readily distinguishable on the facts. Amongst others, the respective courts had found there to be no loss to the victims in these two cases. Here, there was actual loss to the victims amounting to a significant sum of $16,260. The manner in which the accused had committed the offences also reflected a greater extent of culpability, involving sophisticated premeditation and careful layers of deception. A nominal custodial term would be entirely inadequate to reflect the criminality of the accused’s actions here.

(3)   Medical conditions raised by the accused

210    I now turn to consider the various medical conditions raised by the accused and their relevance (if any) to the appropriate sentence to be imposed in this case. In the course of his mitigation, the accused tendered various medical documents for the court’s attention. These included:

(a)     an X-ray image with a study date of 14 March 2024, with the accused’s name indicated on the top left-hand corner;

(b)     the accused’s medication list printed from the records of Tan Tock Seng Hospital (“TTSH”) on 17 September 2025;

(c)     a memo from the Pain Management Clinic of TTSH dated 5 November 2025 (the “Pain Management Memo”);

(d)     a memo from the Department of Psychiatry of TTSH dated 19 November 2025 (the “Psychiatry Memo”); and

(e)     the accused’s written submissions titled “Unconducive Environment for Treatment of Anxiety and Depression”

(collectively, the “Medical Documents”).

211    These Medical Documents were separately forwarded by the Prosecution and the accused to the Singapore Prisons Service (“SPS”), for SPS’ input on whether it would be able to manage the accused’s medical conditions should he be incarcerated.

212    In response, SPS noted the accused’s history of scoliosis, lumbar spondylitis, mechanical back pain and anxiety disorder according to the Medical Documents. SPS explained that, upon admission to prison, the accused would be assessed by the Prisons Medical Officer. Follow-up appointments with the Public Healthcare Institutions (“PHIs”) and National Specialty Centres (“NSCs”) would be scheduled, if necessary, to ensure continuity of care during the incarceration. Further, SPS has an “adequate system of healthcare delivery in place” and “[a]ll inmates are given the appropriate level of medical care and treatment as may be required, including a referral to PHIs for treatment and management of their medical conditions if necessary.”[note: 165]

213    The relevance of ill health in sentencing and the doctrine of judicial mercy was succinctly laid down by the High Court in Chew Soo Chun at [38]:

In summary, ill health is relevant to sentencing in two ways. First, it is a ground for the exercise of judicial mercy. Judicial mercy is an exceptional recourse available for truly exceptional cases and which will likely result in an exceptional sentence. Where mercy is exercised, the court is compelled by humanitarian considerations arising from the exceptional circumstances to order the minimum imprisonment term or a non-custodial sentence where appropriate. Secondly, it exists as a mitigating factor. The cases where ill health will be regarded as a mitigating factor include those which do not fall within the realm of the exceptional but involve markedly disproportionate impact of an imprisonment term on an offender by reason of his ill health. The court takes into account the fact that ill health may render an imprisonment term that will not otherwise be crushing to one offender but may be so to another, and attenuates the sentence accordingly for the latter offender so that it will not be disproportionate to his culpability and physical condition.

[emphasis added]

214    The High Court continued at [39] to hold that: “[i]n all other cases, ill health is irrelevant to sentencing. It may be that the offender has a condition or several conditions, but unless he can satisfy the tests for exercising judicial mercy or for mitigating a sentence because of disproportionate suffering or decreased culpability, there is no proper basis to vary the sentence.”

215    Having considered the Medical Documents, and SPS’ response upon its review of the Medical Documents, I was of the view that the medical evidence before the court did not provide any basis for the accused’s medical conditions to be relevant to sentencing, and specifically, to reduce the sentences.

216    The Pain Management Memo stated that the accused “has been suffering from chronic lower back pain, scoliosis, and lumbar spondylosis and treated with analgesics and physiotherapy”. The doctor then reported that “[a]ccording to [the accused], he is unable to sleep on the hard floor due to pain. His back pain may be aggravated by hard mattress or hard floor.” As was evident from the Pain Management Memo, there was nothing here disclosing anything so exceptional or crushing, or any such markedly disproportionate impact an imprisonment term would have on the accused.

217    As regards the Psychiatry Memo, it stated that the accused has been diagnosed with anxiety disorder and was being managed as an outpatient. As of 19 November 2025, the accused was in remission of his condition, though the accused expressed concerns of relapse of his condition in prison. Based on this, there was similarly no medical evidence before the court that the accused’s anxiety disorder was something so exceptional or would have such markedly disproportionate impact on the accused should he be sentenced to imprisonment. In fact, it would be clear from the Psychiatry Memo that any concerns of relapse in prison were the accused’s own, and not the opinion of the doctor.

218    The accused also submitted that the Prison Medical Office did not stock two types of medication that he required on a daily basis, and frequent trips to the Institute of Mental Health (“IMH”) would be required should he be incarcerated.[note: 166] There was no evidence before the court as regards whether the Prison Medical Office did or did not, as a matter of fact, stock the said medication, but in any event, as SPS has stated in its response, where necessary, referrals may be made to PHIs for treatment and management of the inmates’ medical conditions. This would be consistent with any necessary referrals to the IMH, as described by the accused.

219    Further, the accused had himself acknowledged that the Prison Medical Officer would be able to access the medical records of inmates from the National Electronic Health Record (“NEHR”), save that he raised concerns with the fact that any such Prison Medical Officer would not be his regular doctor.[note: 167] As was clear from Chew Soo Chun, it would be sufficient for SPS to have the capability of addressing the medical conditions to an acceptable standard, and this meant that the SPS need not meet the best medical standard, or in this case, the accused’s preferred choice of doctor (at [39(a)]). To this end, there was again no evidence before the court showing how it would be so exceptional or markedly disproportionate for the accused to be reviewed by a doctor other than his regular doctor. This was particularly so considering that the Prison Medical Officer would have access to the accused’s medical records as reflected in the NEHR. Further, the SPS would make referrals to and schedule follow-ups with PHIs and NSCs where necessary.

220    Finally, while the accused has submitted that his anxiety was likely to worsen in prison due to factors like isolation, lack of control, fear of violence, and separation from loved ones, there was no medical evidence of this before the court, and in particular how likely this would happen to the accused. There was no evidence in relation to how likely this would eventuate, and the manner and extent to which the accused’s anxiety could worsen. In fact, the Psychiatry Memo stated that the accused’s condition was in remission and did not go further to opine about any likelihood of it relapsing in prison. There was also nothing to say that any such relapse could not be managed by SPS.

221    I therefore concluded that there was no proper basis to vary the sentence on account of the various medical conditions faced by the accused here. Based on the medical evidence before the court, the accused has failed to satisfy the tests for exercising judicial mercy and/or for mitigating a sentence due to any such disproportionate suffering or decreased culpability on the accused’s end.

(4)   Running of sentences

222    Finally, I agreed with the Prosecution that the two sentences in the Cheating Charge and the Forgery Charge ought to run concurrently, as they were part of the same fraud perpetrated on PW1 here. This resulted in a global sentence of 14 months’ imprisonment. The sentence was backdated to the date of arrest on 27 May 2021 to take into account the periods spent in remand and to exclude the periods where the accused was released on bail. The accused was on bail from 15 June 2021 and remains so to date.

Conclusion

223    In summary, I found the accused guilty of both charges and sentenced him to a total imprisonment term of 14 months.

html:
PS 23 Interior Pte. Ltd. v Andrew Tan Tong Sin

PS 23 Interior Pte. Ltd. v Andrew Tan Tong Sin
[2026] SGMC 71

Case Number:Magistrate Court Originating Claim No 3730 of 2025
Decision Date:12 June 2026
Tribunal/Court:Magistrate's Court
Coram: Tay Jingxi
Counsel Name(s): Leong Wen Wei, Michael (Christopher Chuah Law Chambers LLC) for the claimant; Chia Boon Teck (BT Law Chambers) for the defendant.
Parties: PS 23 Interior Pte. Ltd. — Andrew Tan Tong Sin

Building and Construction Law – Building and construction contracts – Renovation contracts and contracts for minor works

Contract – Breach

Contract – Contractual terms

Contract – Variation

Tort – Negligence

12 June 2026

Judgment reserved.

District Judge Tay Jingxi:

A   Introduction.

1       The Claimant, PS23 Interior Pte. Ltd., a company in the renovation and interior design business, sues the Defendant, Andrew Tan Tong Sin, its client at the material time, on the basis of unpaid invoices issued pursuant to a renovation contract. The contract in question takes the form of a quotation for design and renovation works dated 23 September 2021 (the “Quotation”), which was subsequently varied at least three times.[note: 1] These design and renovation works (the “Works”) were to be carried out at the Defendant’s landed property located at Old Upper Thomson Road, Singapore (the “Property”).

2       It is not disputed that the terms of parties’ agreement are captured in the Quotation. What is disputed, as I will discuss later on in this judgment, pertains to which document accurately captures the terms of the subsequent variations. In short, there are two versions of the said document containing the details of these variation orders,[note: 2] with material differences between the two. In this judgment, I will collectively refer to the Quotation and the three variation orders as the “Contract”. This definition will encompass the terms of the variation orders which I find parties to have agreed to later in this judgment.

B   Summary of parties’ cases.

3       The Claimant’s case is that the Defendant failed to make payment of a sum of $31,604.13 for the works done under the Contract.[note: 3] The Defendant was billed for these works via two Invoices, Invoice 22003 and Invoice 23004 (the “Two Invoices”), which the Claimant says have not been paid to date.[note: 4]

4       The Defendant denies that the Claimant completed all the works required by the Contract.[note: 5] He also counterclaims for the cost of rectification works which he says were required to fix defective works caused or created by the Claimant (in the sum of $59,271.40),[note: 6] as well as for the return of monies he had paid for works which he and the Claimant eventually agreed not to do (in the sum of $15,065).[note: 7] In respect of the allegedly defective works, the Defendant pleads a total of 12 such works at [D7] of his D&CC (henceforth, the “Alleged Defects”).

C   Issues.

5       Four key issues arise for my determination:

(a)     First, as a preliminary question, who did the Defendant contract with to renovate the Property? (“Issue 1”)

(b)     Second, which version of the variation orders accurately captures the terms of parties’ Contract? (“Issue 2”)

(c)     Third, does the Defendant owe the Claimant a total sum of $31,604.13 based on the Two Invoices? (“Issue 3”)

(d)     Fourth, did the Claimant breach the Contract by failing to complete its works and/or causing or creating the Alleged Defects? (“Issue 4”)

6       I proceed to deal with these issues in the order stated above.

7       At the end of my analysis, I allow the claim – but only in part – and I dismiss the counterclaim. My reasons are as follows.

D   Issue 1: Who did the Defendant contract with to renovate the Property?

8       There is some allusion in the Defendant’s Affidavit of Evidence-in-Chief (“DAEIC”) as to whether the Claimant was the proper contracting counterparty.[note: 8] According to the Defendant, the company he contacted to renovate his Property was not the Claimant but Oak3 Design and Build Pte Ltd (“Oak3”).[note: 9] For unknown reasons, it was the Claimant and not Oak3 that ended up issuing the Quotation to the Defendant.[note: 10] It was also the Claimant and not Oak3 that issued the Two Invoices to the Defendant.[note: 11] The Defendant then rounded all this off by stating that “Jackie was my interior designer whether she was representing Oak3 or [the Claimant]”.[note: 12] Implicit in this statement is an assertion that Ms Jackie Ong Chiew Yen[note: 13] (“Ms Ong”) ought to have been the proper contracting party instead of the Claimant.

9       Arising from all this is the suggestion there might be three potential candidates in respect of the party who actually contracted with the Defendant to perform the Works to the Property: the Claimant, Oak3, or Ms Ong. Despite this, the parties (including the Defendant) did not spend any time on this question at trial. They seemed to be content to assume that the Claimant was the correct plaintiff in this case. The Defendant also did not raise any argument to the opposite effect in his closing submissions.

10     In light of the above, and despite the somewhat unsatisfactory lack of address on this issue from either side, I take it that parties do not dispute that the Claimant was the entity who provided the design and renovation services to the Defendant under the Contract and is therefore the correct party in law to bring the claim.

11     I therefore proceed to consider the merits of the claim and counterclaim.

E   Issue 2: Which version of the variation orders accurately captures the terms of parties’ Contract?

12     A potential discrepancy regarding the number of variation orders issued by the Claimant to the Defendant must first be reconciled. In Invoice 22003, a particular line refers to the “contract plus 4 VO, 1 ommison (sic)”.[note: 14] It is not disputed that the acronym “VO” stands for variation order, and was in fact used by parties to refer to “variation orders” at the trial. However, the details and balances payable under the Contract for only three VOs were listed following that line, not four. I do not know why this is the case, and the Claimant gave no explanation for this apparent contradiction. Hence, despite that line, I will take the variation works that Invoice 22003 is referring to as only encompassing the three VOs which are explicitly listed, being VO1, VO2, and VO3. What I am therefore concerned about in this judgment are these three VOs only.

13     To set the scene, I briefly summarise parties’ cases in respect of the variation works under these three VOs before moving on to the material discrepancies in the documents alluded to at [2] above.

(a)     The Claimant argues that it had completed all the works under each VO by February 2023.[note: 15]

(b)     The Defendant disputes several aspects relating to the variation works for which the three VOs were issued. First, he denies the Claimant’s assertion that all variation works had been completed.[note: 16] Here, he raises the Alleged Defects on which his counterclaim rests.[note: 17] Second, the Defendant highlights that the version of the document titled “VO2” which he received from the Claimant[note: 18] is different from the version of “VO2” which the Claimant tendered at trial.[note: 19] Based on [36] to [45] of the DAEIC, the Defendant’s case is that the version he received ought to be followed, in terms of the work allegedly done and the cost of the same.

14     Having examined both sets of documents, it is clear to me that the versions of the “VO2” document tendered by both parties are different in several material respects. I set out some of these differences out below:

 

Claimant’s version tendered at trial

Defendant’s version received from Claimant

Sub-total (G7) for Omission 1

$28,295

$33,385

Sub-total for Omission 2

$13,680

$21,910

Omissions (total)

$41,975

$55,295



15     What is also confusing about this document titled “VO2” is that details pertaining to VO3, as well as two sets of works that were not done (i.e., “Omission 1” and “Omission 2”), also appear within that document. There was also no stand-alone document titled “VO1” adduced by the Claimant into evidence, despite VO1 being referred to in Invoice 22003 and despite the burden falling on the Claimant to prove that it is entitled to payment on the total sought in Invoice 22003 (which would include the cost of VO1). Bluntly put, the Claimant’s documentary evidence was messy and confused.

16     What is also concerning is the fact that the first time the Defendant had sight of the Claimant’s version of the document titled “VO2” was at the point Ms Ong’s AEIC was served on the Defendant.[note: 20] In his closing submissions (the “CS”), counsel for the Claimant did not dispute the existence of these inconsistences between the two versions of the “VO2” document, and also did not dispute the fact that the first time the Defendant would have been aware of these discrepancies was only after pleadings had closed, at the point AEICs were exchanged.[note: 21] Despite all this, counsel for the Claimant sought to persuade me not to consider these discrepancies on the basis that they had not been pleaded by the Defendant.[note: 22]

17     I have little difficulty in rejecting this argument. Whilst I agree that the technically correct thing for the Defendant to have done was to apply to amend his pleadings after reviewing the Claimant’s version of the “VO2” document, the more important issue is that the Claimant, being the creator of both versions of the “VO2” document and presumably being aware of that fact that it intended to adduce and rely on a different version of this document from the one it had sent to the Defendant, failed to explain why there were two versions of the said document,[note: 23] why it did not send its version of the “VO2” document to the Defendant, or why its version ought to be relied on. Equally worrying is Ms Ong’s testimony that her “omission and VO is a bit not right (sic)”,[note: 24] which I take to be her concession that the omissions and VOs – be it the Claimant’s version or the Defendant’s version of the “VO” document – are not correct. All these are important factors in my consideration of which copy of the “VO2” document accurately captures parties’ agreement as to the scope of the variation works to be carried out.

18     Going back to the point on pleadings, the case cited by the Claimant in support of its argument[note: 25] – How Weng Fun and ors v Sengkang Town Council and other appeals [2023] SGCA 21 (“How Weng Fun”) – in fact also stands for the proposition that the Court can allow an unpleaded point to be raised and determined where it would be clearly unjust for the Court not to do so (at [20]). This is precisely the result here if I do not consider this unpleaded point on the discrepancies between the two “VO2” documents. Doing so would severely limit my ability to decide on which version of the “VO2” document ought to be followed. This decision has critical consequences for my decision on the claim because Invoice 22003 bills the Defendant for the works done under these three VOs and gives credit to the Defendant for two sets of works that were not done (i.e., referred to as “Omission 1” and “Omission 2”). All this would affect the quantum of the Claimant’s award if the claim were allowed. The justice of the case, and the pursuit of the truth as to what parties’ agreement in relation to the variation works was, demand that the inconsistencies between both sets of the “VO2” document be examined. Finally, the Claimant cannot claim prejudice as a result of my decision on this matter because it was given a fair chance to explain these discrepancies and answer to which variation works the Claimant did or did not carry out in cross-examination. Counsel for the Claimant also dealt with these discrepancies in closing submissions.[note: 26]

19     I therefore proceed to consider which version of the “VO2” document accurately captures the nature and scope of the variation works which had been agreed on by parties. To avoid confusion, I will refer to the version of the “VO2” document adduced by the Claimant in the CBOD as the “CVO” and the version adduced by the Defendant in his AEIC as the “DVO”. I will refer to the terms of the second variation order contained within each document as “VO2”. In undertaking this analysis, I start by considering the three VOs to see whether these items of work have been agreed on by parties and, if so agreed, whether these agreed items of work had in fact been completed by the Claimant. I will then proceed to consider Omissions 1 and 2 to see if they correctly reflect the works that were removed from the scope of the Contract and which the Claimant did not eventually carry out.

(a)   The Claimant is entitled to payment of $13,609.73 for the works done in respect of VO3.

The items allegedly agreed on by parties in respect of the third set of variation works are identical across the CVO and DVO, save for one item pertaining to the construction of a washing machine kerb at $200. This item was only reflected in the CVO and not the DVO. Hence, in respect of VO3, the following works are what the Claimant asserts were agreed on under the third variation of the Contract:

21     To be entitled to payment of $13,809.73, the Claimant must prove that parties had agreed for the eight above-stated work items to be carried out and that it had in fact completed the works required by these eight items.

22     The evidence adduced by parties in this respect was far from helpful.

(a)     The Claimant did not adduce any objective proof of it completing these variation works. If any of the photographs or messages appended to the Claimant’s Affidavit-of-Evidence-in-Chief (“CAEIC”) do in fact depict these completed variation works, counsel for the Claimant did not draw the link between those pieces of evidence and these works. I am also unable to discern which items listed in [11] of Ms Ong’s AEIC, which asserts all the variation works that the Claimant had carried out, pertain to the items in VO3.

(b)     On the other hand, the Defendant, despite highlighting the conflicting documentary record pertaining to VO3 and despite seeking to rely on the smaller figure of $13,609.73 as being value of the works done under VO3[note: 28], did not put to Ms Ong his disagreement with any of the terms of VO3 or that the Claimant had failed to carry out any of these eight items of work.

23     I am therefore constrained by this state of affairs in making my decision on VO3. My findings in this respect are as follows:

(a)     The legal and evidential burdens of proof ultimately rests on the party bringing the claim (see Section 103 of the Evidence Act 1893 (“EA”)). In other words, the Claimant must adduce sufficient evidence to prove the agreed terms under VO3 and that the works required by VO3 to be carried out had in fact been carried out.

(b)     Given that the Defendant was content to use the figure of $13,609.73 to calculate the value of the works under VO3,[note: 29] he is arguably conceding two things: first, that he had agreed to seven out of eight terms under VO3 (excluding the term pertaining to the washing machine kerb); and second, that the Claimant had, at the very least, completed all the works required by these seven agreed terms amounting to a total value of $13,609.73. Accordingly, I find that parties had agreed for the Claimant to carry out the seven additional items of work listed at s/n 1 to 7 of the table at [20] above. I further find that the Claimant had duly completed these seven items of work.

(c)     In his pleadings, the Defendant explicitly disputes that the Claimant had completed all variation works.[note: 30] (The last sentence of [1] of the CS is therefore incorrect insofar as this is concerned.) In [37] of his AEIC, the Defendant implicitly disputes, at the very least, that the Claimant had constructed the washing machine kerb. In light of this, and given that the Claimant wishes this Court to believe that it had completed all works required by VO3, the burden of proving that parties had agreed for this kerb to be constructed and that the Claimant had in fact constructed it falls on the Claimant (see s 105 EA). The Claimant adduced no such evidence in this regard. In fact, Invoice 22003, which was issued by the Claimant, contradicts the Claimant’s own version of VO3; that Invoice reflects the total value of VO3 as $13,609.73 and not $13,809.73.[note: 31] Accordingly, I find that the term at s/n 8 of VO3 is not proved. I further find that the Claimant has failed to prove that it had in fact constructed the washing machine kerb ostensibly as required by VO3.

24     Accordingly, the Claimant is entitled to be paid $13,609.73 for the works it had carried out pursuant to VO3.

(b)   The Claimant is entitled to payment of $37,360 for the works done in respect of VO2.

25     I move on to consider the work to be done pursuant to VO2. Ascertaining the terms of VO2 was particularly confusing. On the face of the CVO and the DVO, the works under the headers “Additional 1” and “Additional 2” might have been loose references to VO1 and VO2 respectively. (d)   The Defendant has only partially proved the nature of the works omitted and the price of these works.

32     I turn now to consider the meat of the parties’ dispute in respect of the discrepancies between the CVO and the DVO. This dispute centres on the items that were actually omitted from the scope of the Contract, as well as the value of the said items, under Omissions 1 and 2. As highlighted at [14] above, the value of the excluded works under Omissions 1 and 2 are materially different across the CVO and the DVO. For now, I will generally refer to the works under Omissions 1 and 2, regardless of whose version I prefer, as the “Omitted Works”.

33     The Defendant not only argues that the individual and total values of the Omitted Works should be as stated in the CVO, but goes further than mere arithmetic by arguing that certain individual items in the Omitted Works are incorrect. The incorrectness allegedly takes the form of the Claimant deliberately failing to credit him for work it did not do in order that it might pocket the difference (the “Profit Argument”).[note: 37] Essentially, I understand the Defendant to mean that if the value of the Omitted Work in question was actually $100, the Claimant reflected it as $80 in its CVO in order that it could profit by a sum of $20 (by depriving the Defendant of that $20 credit).

34     Given the seriousness of this allegation, I had expected to see some rebuttal to the Profit Argument in the CS. Disappointingly, there was none. The only argument[note: 38] the Claimant raised in the CS in response to the discrepancies between the CVO and the DVO was an indirect one specifically referring to Invoice 22003. The Claimant argues that the Defendant had purportedly accepted the accuracy of the figures in Invoice 22003 by his statement “these are the valid amounts” (the “Statement”) in his email of 20 April 2023 at 17:38 (the “20 April Email”).[note: 39] According to the Claimant, the Defendant was in his 20 April Email replying to an earlier email one Ms Chin Mui Foong (“Ms Chin”) had sent to him on 17 April 2023 at 12:00 on behalf of the Claimant (the “17 April Email”).[note: 40] The Claimant appears to take the position that a copy of Invoice 22003 had been attached to the 17 April Email (see the line “I have attached the invoice for your reference” in that Email), and that the Statement therefore meant that the Defendant had acknowledged that all the amounts contained in Invoice 22003 were “valid amounts”.[note: 41]

35     The Defendant denies accepting the validity of the figures in Invoice 22003.[note: 42] Under cross-examination, the Defendant alleged that the copy of the Invoice 22003 at page 79 of the CBOD was not the same as the copy of Invoice 22003 he was referring to in his 20 April Email.[note: 43] In re-examination, the Defendant claimed that his Statement referred to “a VO of the painter that she said she did on behalf”, with the “valid” sum being “two times 1,900”.[note: 44]

36     In my judgment, the Claimant’s argument is not only unsubstantiated as a matter of evidence, but in fact premised on a fundamental misreading of the Statement. I therefore reject it entirely. My reasons are as follows:

(a)     First, in order for the Claimant’s argument to get off the ground, the Claimant must prove that it was the CBOD version of Invoice 22003 that was attached to Ms Chin’s 17 April Email. There is no evidence of this at all. None of the file names of the documents attached to the 17 April Email, which can be seen at the bottom of the said Email, can reasonably be interpreted to refer to Invoice 22003. Further, the only person in the position to testify on the Claimant’s behalf as to what document was actually attached to the 17 April Email is Ms Chin, who was not called as a witness at trial. Hence, the foundational fact which the Claimant must rely on to assert the accuracy of the figures in Invoice 22003, being that Invoice 22003 was attached to the 17 April Email, is not proved.

(b)     Second, even if the Claimant managed to prove that Invoice 22003 was attached to the 17 April Email, I disagree with the Claimant’s interpretation of the Statement. The Claimant has misquoted the Statement in its pleadings and in the CAEIC[note: 45] by citing the Statement as being “these are valid amounts”. But the Statement actually reads “these are the valid amounts (emphasis added)”. The meanings of these two statements are completely different. The Claimant’s erroneous version suggests an unequivocal acceptance by the Defendant of whatever figures he was looking at. The correct version, however, suggests that there are some amounts which the Defendant considered to be “valid”, and which he identified by referring to them as “the valid amounts”. In other words, the word “the” modifies the sentence by suggesting that there are specific “valid amounts” being identified. The corollary of this interpretation, which I prefer and adopt, is that there are amounts which the Defendant felt were not valid. The Claimant’s entire argument therefore falls apart. The onus lies with the Claimant to prove what these specific “valid amounts” were, and what document the Defendant was referring to in making this Statement. But the Claimant has failed to do so.

37     Having rejected the Claimant’s argument, I proceed to consider the Defendant’s argument in relation to the two Omissions. According to the Defendant, the correct value for each set of omissions is as follows:

(a)      Omission 1 - $33,385 (and not $28,295); and

(b)      Omission 2 - $21,910 (and not $15,830).[note: 46]

43     Based on Ms Ong’s own testimony, it seems that the correct way to reflect the works that were not carried out by the Claimant under Omission 1 would be to only include the three items totalling $11,570 under the wet kitchen works. The dry kitchen works, having all been performed, should not have appeared as an omission at all. Thus, the Defendant should have been given credit of $11,570 for these three omitted wet kitchen works. Instead, what that Claimant did in its own version of the CVO was to reflect the dry kitchen works as omissions – when that was not true – thereby giving the Defendant a total credit of only $9,330. In other words, the Claimant, by its CVO, purported to give the Defendant a lower credit amount via Omission 1. The illogical state of the paperwork issued by the Claimant calls for a good explanation from Ms Ong.

44     To this end, when Ms Ong was asked twice why the dry kitchen works were reflected as omissions when they were in fact carried out, her responses were meandering and difficult to follow.[note: 54] From her answers, I distil the following main points: (a) that there were many changes made to certain works after the Contract had been signed; (b) there was allegedly already an “agreement” to unknown terms; and (c) there were “measurement differences” which Ms Ong wanted to capture in her CVO.

45     None of these three points address the question and/or the Profit Argument directly. Changes to the scope of renovation works after a formal contract has been executed are, generally speaking, common in the industry. It is in no way an excuse for an interior designer to create and adduce into evidence a completely inaccurate VO. Further, I do not know what “agreement” Ms Ong was referring to in her answers. If by “agreement” she means that parties had agreed on the works to be excluded as reflected in the CVO, then it begs the question as to why the Claimant went ahead to carry out those works anyway (see [40] above). If by “agreement” she means that parties had agreed on the works to be excluded as reflected in the DVO, that still does not answer the question. Finally, differences in the measurements of structures and cabinetry do not explain why the Claimant had to generate an inaccurate document in the form of the CVO (in relation to the dry kitchen work).

46     The Claimant having failed to give a satisfactory explanation as to why the CVO contained incorrect line items under Omission 1, I agree with the Defendant that he ought to have been given a credit of $11,570 for the omitted wet kitchen works under Omission 1 and not a credit of $9,330 for the completed dry kitchen works. In this respect, it is the DVO and not the CVO that accurately reflects the works omitted under Omission 1. The Defendant was therefore shortchanged by $2,240 in respect of the credit he ought to have been given for Omission 1.

54     Neither answer assists the Claimant. It bears repeating that all the documents the Claimant issues to its clients and tenders to Court must be accurate. Where there are amendments made to the scope and/or nature of these works, the Claimant must be all the more careful to ensure the accuracy of its documentary record. This is important not just as a matter of professional standards, but also as a matter of principle. The Claimant cannot justifiably withhold a credit to the Defendant for works which parties have agreed should not be carried out and which were in fact not carried out. Further, Ms Ong’s answer pertaining to the change in location of certain works is beside the point. It again fails to address the core issue of why her CVO did not simply accurately reflect this.
