html:
Public Prosecutor v Boo-Koh Kang Xin

Public Prosecutor v Boo-Koh Kang Xin
[2026] SGDC 198

Case Number:District Arrest Case No 902364 of 2026 & 1 Other
Decision Date:12 June 2026
Tribunal/Court:District Court
Coram: Paul Quan
Counsel Name(s): Dhiraj Chainani (Attorney-General's Chambers) for the Public Prosecutor; Alain Abraham Johns/ Emira Binte Abdul Razakjr (Alain A Johns Partnership) for the Accused.
Parties: Public Prosecutor — Boo-Koh Kang Xin

Criminal Law – Statutory Offences – Corruption, Drug Trafficking and Other Serious Crimes (Confiscation of Benefits) Act – Assisting another to control benefits from criminal conduct

Criminal Procedure and Sentencing – Sentencing – Young offenders

12 June 2026

District Judge Paul Quan:

Introduction

1       This is a case of a young Singaporean offender based in Malaysia who was recruited as a money mule to move monies and gold collected from scam victims in Singapore.

Brief facts

2       The accused, Mr Boo-Koh Kang Xin (“Mr Boo-Koh”), a 20-year-old Singaporean, lived in Johor Bahru, Malaysia, with his family and would shuttle daily between Malaysia and Singapore for school.[note: 1] He was recruited as a money mule over Telegram to move monies and gold collected from scam victims based in Singapore to other persons in Singapore or Malaysia for reward.[note: 2]

3       Mr Boo-Koh started off as a runner and collected cash and gold on various occasions between October 2025 and January 2026.[note: 3] In October 2025, he collected no less than S$120,000 in cash from three scam victims in Singapore.[note: 4] His offending behaviour escalated in December 2025, which then saw him recruiting four runners.[note: 5] One of the runners was a 32-year-old Malaysian residing in Johor Bahru, whom he had previously engaged to drive him into Singapore on various occasions,[note: 6] and whom he instructed on how to be a runner as he had done between January 2026 and February 2026.[note: 7]

4       Mr Boo-Koh received S$6,000 in reward for being a runner and in respect of what his recruited runners did.[note: 8] Specifically, he received a sum of S$2,000 for what the Malaysian runner did, of which he paid that runner S$1,000 through third parties.[note: 9]

Charges and prescribed punishments

5       Mr Boo-Koh has pleaded guilty to a charge under section 51(1)(a) of the Corruption, Drug Trafficking and Other Serious Crimes (Confiscation of Benefits) Act 1992 (“CDSA”) of being concerned with an arrangement with the Malaysian runner and other unknown persons to assist these persons control their benefits from scams-related offences in respect of the collections made by the Malaysian runner.[note: 10] He has also consented to have a similar charge taken into consideration for the purpose of sentence (“TIC”) in respect of the collections he himself made.[note: 11]

6       For the CDSA offence, Mr Boo-Koh faces a fine not exceeding S$500,000 and/or imprisonment not exceeding ten years by virtue of section 51(5) CDSA. In essence, Mr Boo-Koh’s CDSA offence is a scams-related offence as rightly characterised by the prosecution.[note: 12] Predicate scams-related offences implicate it. It involves collections from scam victims and also facilitating the laundering of criminal proceeds from scams-related offences.

Parties’ positions

7       I convicted Mr Boo-Koh on 25 May 2026. The defence urged me to call for both probation and reformative training (“RT”) pre-sentence reports (“PSRs”) on him.[note: 13] While the prosecution would not object to an RT PSR being called, it would to a probation PSR.[note: 14] Agreeing with the prosecution, I called for only an RT PSR on Mr Boo-Koh. This is consistent with the approach I have taken in previous cases involving young offenders who commit scams-related offences: see eg PP v Elyana Binte Amraiy [2025] SGDC 152 and PP v Ayu Syakirah Binte Shahrul [2026] SGDC 111 (“Ayu”).

8       I have since received Mr Boo-Koh’s PSR from the Singapore Prison Service (“SPS”) on 11 June 2026,[note: 15] assessing him to be suitable for RT based on his physical and mental conditions and recommending him to undergo “Level 2 intensity of rehabilitation” if he were sentenced to RT. The parties have now sought such a sentence to be imposed on Mr Koh.

Court’s decision

9       I agree with the partis and sentence Mr Boo-Koh to RT with a minimum detention period of 12 months, or level 2 intensity of rehabilitation. I explain why in this ex tempore judgment.

Why RT but not probation PSR called

10     I have previously delivered brief reasons on 25 May 2026 explaining why I called for an RT but not a probation PSR on Mr Koh. I outline these reasons by way of background.

11     I should generally call for a probation PSR before sentencing a young offender who is aged 21 or below but I did not do so in Mr Boo-Koh’s case because I did not think probation is viable or realistic although the basic prerequisites for probation are met: A Karthik v PP [2018] 5 SLR 1289 at [20] and [21]. This is by virtue of the severity of his scams-related CDSA offence, which, to my mind, effectively rules out probation as a sentencing option altogether.

Basic prerequisites for probation met

12     In Mr Boo-Koh’s case, the basic prerequisites for probation are met:

(a)     Mr Boo-Koh’s CDSA offence is not one for which the sentence is “fixed by law”: section 5(1) of the Probation of Offenders Act 1951 (2020 Rev Ed) (“POA”) –

(i)       he faces a fine not exceeding S$500,000 and/or imprisonment not exceeding ten years by virtue of section 51(5) CDSA, and

(ii)       the sentence is therefore not fixed in type and quantum; the court can impose a fine and/or imprisonment and has the discretion to decide on the quantum of fine and/or the length of imprisonment to be imposed: Mohamad Fairuuz bin Saleh v PP [2015] 1 SLR 1145 at [17(c)]; and

(b)     the proviso to section 5(1) of the POA also does not apply as the offence is not punishable with either a specified minimum sentence or mandatory minimum sentence. Mr Boo-Koh also does not have any previous convictions.

Probation not viable or realistic

13     Be that as it may, I must still preliminarily assess whether probation is viable or realistic on the facts of Mr Boo-Koh’s case, and the court should order a probation PSR if the accused is young (that is, between 16 and 21 years old), a first offender and convicted of a relatively less serious crime: Wong Shan Shan v PP [2008] SGHC 49 at [20]-[21].

14     Mr Boo-Koh is a young offender being 20 at the time of the offences, conviction and sentencing. He is also a first-time offender. However, I found that probation is not viable or realistic given the severity of his scams-related CDSA offence. He also has a similar TIC charge. In relation to sentencing scams-related offences, the Sentencing Advisory Panel in its guidelines in this regard (“SAP Guidelines”) has observed at [7(c)] that:

[F]ines, probation and community sentences are generally not appropriate [for scams-related offences]. Imprisonment or reformative training, whichever is more appropriate should be considered given the need for deterrence and the public interest in suppressing scams. This applies to all offenders (even if below the age of 21) except juvenile offenders dealt with in the Youth Court. [Emphasis in original]

15     The High Court has recently endorsed these observations, given the pernicious nature of such offences, especially when committed against vulnerable victims above the age of 65, the significant role played by individuals in facilitating the laundering of criminal proceeds by scam syndicates in making it difficult for authorities to track the money trail, as well as deterrence and retribution being the dominant sentencing considerations for such offences: Galvez Mary Joe Blanco v PP [2026] SGHC 110 (“Galvez”) at [39]-[41].

16     In comparison, the offenders in A Karthik and Wong Shan Shan were arguably convicted of charges of comparable severity or more charges: Cheah Bernice [2024] SGDC 220 at [14]. In both cases, the appellate court thought that probation PSRs ought to have been called on the offenders. To be sure and as the defence has rightly pointed out,[note: 16] the SAP Guidelines merely state that probation is generally not appropriate for scams-related offences and do not specifically exclude probation for such offences. However, the consideration of the nature and gravity of any offence is necessarily a fact-specific exercise and the severity of Mr Boo-Koh’s offence must be properly appreciated in its particular context, quite apart from its maximum prescribed penalty: Cheah Bernice at [15].

17     The context in question is the concerning scams-related offences situation in Singapore in 2025. Although there was a brief reprieve in the dire situation of the previous year where the number of scam cases fell by 27.6% in 2025 as compared to 2024, and the losses from scams also fell by 17.9% to about S$913.1m in 2025 from about S$1.1b in 2024, I noted in Ayu at [15] that the situation is still very concerning and tackling scams remains a key priority. The decrease in both scam cases and scam losses suggests cautiously that the anti-scam strategies and public measures introduced by the Government and industry partners have made it more challenging for scammers to succeed. In tandem with such efforts, and so as not to undo this modest improvement and to prevent a reversal of this encouraging but nascent trend, there is no room for complacency and the court should continue to vigilantly signal its deterrent stance against such serious offences categorically.

18     The circumstances in which Mr Boo-Koh committed the CDSA offence are also troubling. The defence has sought to persuade me that he did not play a central coordinating role and that his involvement was not extensive.[note: 17] With respect, I hold a different view:

(a)     as the prosecution has rightly pointed out,[note: 18] Mr Boo-Koh was actively involved in facilitating the laundering of the scam proceeds not only as a runner but also a recruiter of runners,

(b)     he was not only a recruiter at that but in respect of the Malaysian runner for instance, he assured the runner that this was a “grey line job” that was neither legal or illegal,[note: 19] and yet in the same breath gave the runner, as the main point of contact, specific instructions on what he should do as one that suggested the contrary,[note: 20] specifically donning a mask and dressing professionally during collections, performing collections in less crowded areas and where there were no surveillance cameras, joining live video calls on Telegram during collections so that the runner and the collections could be tracked, and refraining from talking or entertaining the victims and to leave the area quickly upon collection, and

(c)     for the CDSA offence, not less than S$107,050 in cash, jewellery and a branded watch were collected from four victims of government official impersonation scams, two of whom were above 50 and one who was vulnerable being 76 who lost S$10,000.[note: 21] For the TIC offence, not less than S$120,000 was collected from three victims of investment scams, all of whom were above 60 and two were vulnerable being 67 and 69 who lost S$30,000 and S$80,000 respectively.[note: 22] In fact, the third was only one year shy of 65 and lost S$10,000.

Foolhardiness and unsophistication in committing the CDSA offence[note: 23] do not detract from the active role Mr Boo-Koh played facilitating the laundering of the scam proceeds.

19     There is an imperative need to deter like-minded offenders, in particular youthful ones who are being targeted by scam syndicates. The opportunity cost of crime must be sufficiently high so that these targeted youths think long and hard before becoming money mules for easy money: Cheah Bernice at [22]. Indeed, Mr Boo-Koh was motivated to commit the offence for gain and did receive a total of S$6,000. Crippling the supply of enablers by denying scammers and scam syndicates the tools they need, is a key strategy that would significantly increase the difficulty for scammers to successfully conduct or profit from scams in Singapore,[note: 24] particularly enablers such as Mr Boo-Koh, who had played a significant role in actively facilitating the laundering of criminal proceeds by scam syndicates and in making it difficult for authorities to track the money trail: Galvez at [40].

RT PSR ordered

20     In this case, there is a clear need to incorporate a sufficient element of deterrence, both general and specific, within any overarching focus on the goal of rehabilitation. RT affords a possible rehabilitative-deterrent/punitive sentencing option because it incorporates a minimum incarceration period of six or 12 months that is not a feature of probation: PP v Koh Wen Jie Boaz [2016] 1 SLR 334 (“Boaz Koh”) at [34] and [39]; it meets the goal of rehabilitation without sending the offender to prison: A Karthik at [67]. I therefore called for a report pursuant to section 305(3) of the Criminal Procedure Code 2010 (2020 Rev Ed) on Mr Boo-Koh’s physical and mental condition, his suitability for RT, and the nature of the rehabilitation that is recommended for him, in order for me to assess RT as a sentencing option. I ordered for him to be remanded for about a week at the reformative training centre (“RTC”) to enable his PSR to be submitted to the court. He continues to be in remand even though he has been offered bail because his parents made the conscious decision not to bail him out.[note: 25]

21     As Mr Boo-Koh was remanded for more than three months when I called for an RT PSR on him, SPS has promptly submitted his PSR on 11 June 2026 in slightly less than three weeks in time for today’s mention at my request, with an assessment that he was suitable for RT based on his physical and mental conditions and a recommendation that he undergo level 2 intensity of rehabilitation if he were sentenced to RT. I retain the full discretion to decide whether Mr Boo-Koo should be sentenced to RT or other forms of punishment, applying my mind based on all the information and facts before me in this case: Ng Jun Xian v PP [2017] 3 SLR 933 at [54].

Approach to sentencing young offender

22     When sentencing a young offender, the first stage is to identify and prioritise the primary sentencing considerations appropriate to the offender having regard to all the circumstances including those of the offence. The second stage is to select the appropriate sentence that would best meet those identified and prioritised sentencing considerations: PP v Mohammad Al-Ansari bin Basri [2008] 1 SLR(R) 449 at [77]-[78] and PP v Koh Wen Jie Boaz [2016] 1 SLR 334 (“Boaz Koh”) at [28] as affirmed and explained in PP v ASR [2019] 1 SLR 941 at [94], [101]-[102]. The inquiry proceeds from the foremost question of whether rehabilitation remains the dominant sentencing principle.

23     I apply the same approach and adopt the same language that I used in Elyana and Ayu mainly for consistency and I am cognisant of the differences between the cases.

Stage 1: Identify and prioritise primary sentencing considerations

24     At the first stage, the question is whether in all the circumstances, the presumptive emphasis on rehabilitation has been displaced: See Li Quan Mendel v PP [2020] 2 SLR 630 (“Mendel See”) at [15]. If an offender is 21 years old or below at both the time of the offence and the time of sentencing, the law takes the presumptive view that the primary sentencing consideration in such cases will generally be rehabilitation, because both the retrospective and prospective rationales underlying such presumptive primacy of rehabilitation would apply: A Karthik v PP [2018] 5 SLR 1289 at [44].

Presumptive primacy of rehabilitation not displaced in this case

25     In this case, Mr Boo-Koh is 20 at the time of the offences and sentencing. The primacy of rehabilitation is therefore presumptive. But the focus on rehabilitation can be diminished or even eclipsed by such considerations as deterrence or retribution where the circumstances warrant. Broadly speaking, this happens in cases where:

(a)     the offence is serious,

(b)     the harm caused is severe,

(c)     the offender is hardened and recalcitrant, or

(d)     the conditions do not exist to make rehabilitative sentencing options viable: Boaz Koh at [30].

Although Mr Boo-Koh is not hardened and recalcitrant being a first-time offender, his offence is serious and the harm caused is not low: see [14]-[15] and [18], above.

26     Rehabilitation may not have been displaced as the normative sentencing consideration in his case but there is clear need to incorporate a sufficient element of deterrence within any overarching focus on the goal of rehabilitation.

Stage 2: How sentencing considerations ought to be achieved

27     Having determined that Mr Boo-Koh should be rehabilitated, I next have to ascertain how rehabilitation ought to be achieved and his suitability to undergo a specific form of rehabilitation: ASR at [99]. The second stage is to select the appropriate sentence that would best meet this concern of prioritising rehabilitation and yet have the requisite deterrent effect.

RT appropriate sentence to meet rehabilitative and deterrent needs

28     In Mr Boo-Koh’s case, RT is appropriate because:

(a)     RT lies within the spectrum of rehabilitative sentences: Mandel See at [13]. However, it also incorporates a significant element of deterrence because there is a minimum detention period of either six or 12 months depending on the intensity of the RT ordered: Boaz Koh at [38];

(b)     where there is a need for both deterrence and rehabilitation, RT may be the most suitable sentence, given that it offers a useful middle ground between sending Mr Boo-Koh to prison and meeting the desire to rehabilitate him: A Karthik at [67]. RT allows the court to sentence him to a rehabilitative programme under a structured environment, while avoiding the danger of exposing him to the potentially unsettling influence of an adult prison environment: Boaz Koh at [38]; and

(c)     the conditions exist to make RT a viable rehabilitative sentencing option as is evident from Mr Boo-Koh’s RT PSR.

(1)   Mr Boo-Koh assessed to be suitable for RT

29     Mr Boo-Koh was found to be in general good physical condition with no known major illnesses,[note: 26] and also of normal mental condition with no current indication of any major mental illness.[note: 27] He was therefore assessed to be suitable to undergo RT. He: [note: 28]

presented with multiple needs that require intervention. He would benefit from interventions addressing his permissive attitudes towards crime, improving his coping and emotion regulation skills, strengthening communication and relationships with his family, and developing a commitment to meeting his financial needs through legal employment.

On this basis, the recommendation is for him to undergo level 2 intensity of rehabilitation if he were sentenced to RT.

30     An RT PSR does not contain a positive recommendation for an offender to undergo RT, and understandably so because the law does not confer any mandate for the prison authorities to make any such recommendation as to whether an offender ought to be sentenced to RT as opposed to other forms of punishment. Such a report is meant to reflect whether an offender is physically and mentally fit, and in that sense suitable, for RT: Ng Jun Xian at [54]. Even though Mr Boo-Koh has been found suitable for RT by SPS, I must apply my mind to whether he should be sentenced to RT as such.

(2)   Sentence of RT of level 2 intensity appropriate

31     The rehabilitation plan of the RT PSR is premised on adequate sources of information.[note: 29] I see no good reason to depart from the finding that Mr Boo-Koh presented multiple criminogenic needs[note: 30] (see [29], above) that require intervention:

(a)     permissive attitudes towards crime reflected in his justifications and minimisations of his offences.[note: 31] Worryingly, he –

(i)       rationalised that the financial gains from the offence were more consistent and lucrative than those from legitimate part-time work,

(ii)       perceived the legal consequences of his actions as disproportionate to his level of involvement, describing his actions as merely “moving money from one point to another” and that he “didn’t actually do a lot” to warrant the legal consequences. This militates against his acknowledgment of wrongdoing and the regret that he expressed towards the victims, and

(iii)       saw himself as a “good person who had not intentionally harmed anyone”, suggesting a limited understanding of the harm caused by his offending;

(b)     limited emotional regulation and coping abilities,[note: 32] reflected in his use of maladaptive strategies during periods of significant distress, as well as problem avoidance. His education suffered collaterally when he was affected by and unable to cope effectively with a series of romantic breakups.[note: 33] He has prosocial peers[note: 34] but avoidance coping prevented him from heeding his close friend’s caution about the legality of his offending behaviour;

(c)     his familial relationships were characterised by varying degrees of conflict, emotional distance and limited communication, with a strained relationship with his father, an emotionally distant but cordial relationship with his mother, and the loss of a close relationship with his sister as his primary source of familial support;[note: 35]

(d)     he completed his General Certification of Education Ordinary Level education, dropped out of a beauty and wellness course at the Institute of Technical Education and was withdrawn from another in visual merchandising because of his current case. He engaged in various previous part-time employment including stewarding, chef assistance, sales and service crew positions, with the longest-held position as a safety staff for close to a year. He has not engaged in any other long-term education or employment pursuits, ever since he perceived the “money transporting activity” to be more financially rewarding;[note: 36]

(e)     lack of structured and constructive leisure/recreation activities;[note: 37] and

(f)     history of substance (alcohol, electronic vapouriser and nicotine cigarette) use, with no current drug use.[note: 38]

32     Given his multiple intervention needs, it is clear to me that a level 2 intensity of psychology-based correctional programmes to be delivered over a 12-month period[note: 39] is necessary to course correct Mr Boo-Koh’s:

(a)     permissive attitudes towards crime, in particular that –

(i)       the ends (financial gain) do not justify the means, given that he has been observed to have a “quick and entrepreneurial mindset”, “an entrepreneurial spirit and who is “resourceful”,[note: 40] and that right/wrong is a bright line and not a relative concept, and

(ii)       money-laundering linked to scams is not a victimless crime that is merely about the movement of monies; real people are implicated who suffer losses that can be devastating and can lead to significant psychological harm if it involves the loss of retirement savings or monies which could have been channelled to other pressing needs, especially when vulnerable victims are involved such as in the present case: SAP Guidelines at [7(b)];

(b)     emotional regulation and maladaptive coping strategies, especially during periods of significant emotional distress;

(c)     fractured familial relationship through family reintegration. I am heartened to learn that he now has renewed familial support. His entire family has relocated back to Singapore and they have agreed to go for counselling so that their relationship can improve.[note: 41] His family is committed to supporting and guiding him as well as overseeing his activities;[note: 42]

(d)     lack of meaningful engagement in employment and recreational activities with vocational training aligned to his interests and through the employability skills programme; and

(e)     lack of meaningful engagement in education with shorter term academic studies.

Sentence of RT of level 2 intensity also proportionate

33     Mr Boo-Koh should undergo RT to reform him and to prevent crime, having regard to his character, previous conduct and the circumstances of the offences: section 305(1) of the CPC. Considerations of proportionality have been imported into the “circumstances of the offences” limb of this provision: PP v Saiful Rizam bin Assim [2014] 2 SLR 495 (“Saiful Rizam”) at [38]. Even if the minimum detention periods might not be proportionate to the underlying offence, the principle of proportionality legitimately takes a back seat with a view to reforming the young offender and deterring him at an early stage: Sim Yeow Kee v PP [2016] 5 SLR 936 at [95]. However, as much as the rehabilitative effect of RT is a valuable and important sentencing goal, a measure of proportionality in making orders for RT is also imperative so that offenders are not unduly punished: Saiful Rizam at [41].

(1)   Expected sentence of at least 18 months’ imprisonment if Mr Boo-Koh not sentenced to RT

34     As for the sentence that Mr Boo-Koh can expect if he were not sentenced to RT, I would have sentenced him to at least 18 months’ imprisonment for the CDSA offence based on the sentencing framework laid down in Huang Ying-Chun v PP [2019] 3 SLR 606 on a moderate harm- medium culpability assessment:

(a)     The harm caused is assessed to be moderate because –

(i)       the amount cheated is not insubstantial in the tune of at least S$$107,050 in cash with at least one vulnerable victim involved and the rest being above 50;

(ii)       the offence is syndicated and involved a transnational element with cross-border operations; and

(iii)       the predicate offences were serious taking the form of government official impersonation scams compounded by the scams situation I have outlined at [17];

(b)     I agree with the defence[note: 43] that Mr Boo-Koh’s culpability should be assessed to be at the medium level because of –

(i)       his active role: see [18(a)] and [18(b)], above;

(ii)       the planning and premeditation involved in the offence: see [18(b)], above;

(iii)       the fairly sophisticated criminal enterprise. At the downstream, there were runners to make collections from the victims; there were recruiters like Mr Boo-Koh, who would receive instructions on the collections to be performed and convey these instructions to other runners via a Telegram chatgroup; there were yet others who took what the runners collected to move them; at the upstream, there were other members who were involved in the government official impersonation scams;

(iv)       the period of offending over two weeks across four incidents that could not be said to be a momentary lapse in judgment;[note: 44] and

(v)       his less culpable mental state being charged under the “reasonable grounds to believe” limb of section 51(1)(a) CDSA and that he did not know about the predicate offences.

35     A moderate harm-medium culpability assessment corresponds to an indicative sentencing range of 30 to 60 months’ imprisonment on a claim-trial basis: Huang at [102].

36     As for the offender-specific personal and aggravating factors:

(a)     the presence of the similar TIC charge is aggravating, warranting a significant uplift considering the amount cheated,

(b)     although Mr Koo-Boo has no criminal antecedents in Singapore, he should not be regarded as a first-time offender because multiple collections were made that constituted the CDSA offence: Chen Weixiong Jerriek v PP [2003] 2 SLR(R) 334 at [17]. In any event, the absence of antecedents is at best a neutral factor; it is an absent aggravating factor, not a mitigating factor: BPH v PP [2019] 2 SLR 764 at [85]. The repeated collections militate against any argument that this is a one-off aberration and out of character for him: PP v BWJ [2023] 1 SLR 477 at [102], and

(c)     his youth and early guilty plea carry mitigatory weight.

(2)   Sentence of RT with minimum detention period of 12 months not comparatively disproportionate

37     A sentence of imprisonment does not make for easy and direct comparison with that of RT because it is fundamentally a very different and more severe punitive sentence. However, given that Mr Boo-Koh faces the prospect of a sentence of at least 18 months’ imprisonment if he were not sentenced to RT, a sentence of RT with a minimum detention period of 12 months would therefore not be comparatively disproportionate.

Conclusion

Sentence of RT for minimum detention period of 12 months imposed

38     I therefore sentence Mr Boo-Koh to RT for a minimum detention period of 12 months from today. This is to reform him and prevent crime given the specific rehabilitation plan that has been drawn up for him. It is not only a viable and feasible but the appropriate sentence to impose on Mr Boo-Koh that is both sufficient and proportionate.

39     Mr Boo-Koh is at an inflexion point and I urge him to make full use of the rehabilitation plan that has been put in place for him and for his family to continue to support his rehabilitation. If he adopts the correct values and belief system of what is objectively right/wrong, he is capable of making something of himself by tapping on his entrepreneurial potential identified by his educators.

40     Given that Mr Boo-Koh is in remand for slightly more than four months now, it remains for me to thank SPS for its prompt submission of Mr Koh’s PSR despite having less than three weeks’ lead-time with a slightly shorter remand period because of an intervening public holiday. I acknowledge the efforts of medical officer Dr Rodney Bay, psychiatrist Dr Nicholas Oh and senior correctional rehabilitation specialist Fiona Toh in this regard.

Public Prosecutor v Richard Boey Pang Sim

Public Prosecutor v Richard Boey Pang Sim
[2026] SGDC 191

Case Number:District Arrest Case No. 916698 of 2025, Magistrate's Appeal No. 9119 of 2026-01
Decision Date:11 June 2026
Tribunal/Court:District Court
Coram: Brenda Chua
Counsel Name(s): Ronnie Ang (Attorney-General's Chambers) for the Public Prosecutor; Amarjit Singh s/o Hari Singh (Amarjit Sidhu Law Corporation) for the Accused.
Parties: Public Prosecutor — Richard Boey Pang Sim

Criminal Law – Offence – Penal Code

Criminal Procedure and Sentencing – Sentencing

[LawNet Editorial Note: An appeal to this decision has been filed in MA 9119/2026/01.]

11 June 2026

District Judge Brenda Chua:

Introduction

1       The accused person, Richard Boey Pang Sim, a 62-year-old male Singapore citizen, pleaded guilty to the following charge:

DAC-916698-2025 (“the Charge”)

You…are charged that you, between 22 June 2023 and 1 December 2023, in Singapore, being an employee of RB Property Management Pte Ltd (“Company”), which was a managing agent for MCST 3733 of Matlock Residences, and in such capacity, being entrusted by the Company with money in UOB Account No: [redacted], amounting to $79,190, did commit breach of trust by dishonestly misappropriating the said property, and you have thereby committed an offence punishable under section 408 of the Penal Code 1871, read with section 124(2) and section 124(8)(a)(i) of the Criminal Procedure Code 2010.

2       There was no charge taken into consideration.

3       I sentenced the accused to an imprisonment term of 15 months. No backdating of the sentence was needed, as confirmed by the prosecution in court.[note: 1]

4       The accused is presently on bail pending appeal. The execution of the imprisonment term was stayed pending appeal. I set out here the reasons for my decision.

Facts

5       The facts relating to the Charge are set out in the statement of facts (“SOF”), which the accused admitted to without qualification. In the SOF:

1    The accused is Richard Boey Pang Sim, male, Singapore citizen, 62 years old (Date of Birth: 03/07/1963).

2    The victim is MCST 3733 ("MCST") of Matlock Residences, Singapore (the “Condominium”).

3    The complainant is Stefan Masuhr. At the material time, he was a Condominium resident and was a treasurer of the MCST.

FACTS RELATING TO DAC-916698-2025

4    In or around May 2023, the MCST appointed RB Property Management Pte Ltd (the “Company”) as the managing agent for the Condominium. The accused was an employee of the Company and was paid a salary of $4,200 a month by the Company.

5    At the material time, the accused was responsible for managing the administration and secretarial affairs of the MCST. This included managing contractors, looking into maintenance requests from Condominium residents, collecting management fees timely from residents and ensuring all expenses are duly approved by the MCST council members and paid timely.

6    The registered owner of each Condominium unit paid management fees once every 6 months which were deposited into UOB Account No: [redacted] (the “UOB Account”). The accused was an authorised signatory of the UOB Account in his capacity as an employee of the MCST’s managing agent, and was in that capacity entrusted by the Company with the monies in the UOB Account to pay expenses for the MCST.

7     In or around January 2024, the complainant noticed that the accused had not been sending invoices to the MCST for approval. The complainant then did a check with UOB bank and found that monies were misappropriated from the UOB Account. The complainant therefore filed a police report.

8    Investigations revealed that the accused started gambling at Singapore casinos since 2017 and lost about $400,000 to the casinos at the material time. After the accused became the UOB Account’s authorised signatory, he formed the dishonest intention to misappropriate the UOB Account’s money by transferring it to himself, so that he could gamble with the said money in the hope of winning back what he lost to the casinos. On occasions when the accused won money through gambling, he would deposit some money back in the UOB Account.

9     Between 22 June 2023 and 1 December 2023, in Singapore, the accused dishonestly misappropriated a total sum of $79,190 over 26 transactions from the UOB Account, with the intention of causing wrongful gain to himself. The accused spent the said monies on his gambling activities.

10    Between 17 July 2023 and 21 November 2023, the accused deposited $4,470 of his gambling winnings over six transactions back to the UOB Account. No further restitution has been made by the accused.

11    By virtue of the foregoing, the accused had committed breach of trust in respect of the sum of $79,190 in the UOB Account between 22 June 2023 and 1 December 2023, and he had thereby committed an offence punishable under section 408 of the Penal 1871, read with section 124(2) and section 124(8)(a)(i) of the Criminal Procedure Code 2010.

OTHER FACTS

12    The accused was arrested on 22 January 2024 and was released on bail the same day.

[emphasis added in underline]

Prescribed penalties

6       The prescribed punishment under section 408(1) of the Penal Code 1871 is set out as follows:

Criminal breach of trust by employees

408.—(1)    Whoever, being an employee, and being in any manner entrusted in such capacity with property, or with any dominion over property, commits criminal breach of trust in respect of that property, shall be punished with imprisonment for a term which may extend to 15 years, and shall also be liable to fine.

7       This is an amalgamated charge punishable under section 124(2) read with section 124(8)(a)(i) of the Criminal Procedure Code 2010 (“CPC”):

Details of time, place and person or thing

124.—(2)    Despite subsection (1), where the accused is charged with any offence mentioned in subsection (3) —

(a)    it is sufficient for the charge —

(i)    to specify the gross sum in respect of which the offence is alleged to have been committed without specifying particular items; and

(ii)   to specify the dates between which the offence is alleged to have been committed (being a period that does not exceed 12 months) without specifying exact dates; and

(b)    the charge so framed is deemed to be a charge of one offence.

(3)    For the purposes of subsection (2), the offences are as follows:

(a)    any offence under section 403, 404, 406, 407, 408, 409, 411, 412, 413 or 414 of the Penal Code 1871;

…

(8)    Subject to subsection (7), where a charge is framed under subsection (2) or (4), and a person is convicted of the offence specified in that charge —

(a)    the court may sentence that person —

(i)    in any case where the charge is framed under subsection (2) — to 2 times the amount of punishment to which that person would otherwise have been liable for that offence; or

…

Imprisonment 12 months (concurrent)



[emphasis added in bold]

Prosecution’s submissions on sentence

9       The prosecution sought an imprisonment term of 15 to 17 months.

10     The prosecution took reference from the case of Kalaichelven Genesan v Public Prosecutor [2025] SGHC 222 (“Kalaichelven”) where the offender was charged for one amalgamated charge of section 408 of the Penal Code (Cap 224, 2008 Rev Ed) read with sections 124(2) and 124(8)(a)(i) of the Criminal Procedure Code (Cap 68, 2012 Revised Edition). The offender, who claimed trial, was convicted and sentenced to 28 months’ imprisonment. The various criminal acts spanned from 16 November 2020 to 18 September 2021 and involved goods worth $108,339.63 from the victim employer, for whom the offender had worked as a storekeeper or warehouse assistant. The offender, who was untraced, made no restitution.[note: 2]

11     In upholding both conviction and sentence on appeal, the High Court in Kalaichelven stated (at [33]) that “in property offences such as CBT, the sum misappropriated is a key indicator of the harm perpetrated by the accused, and consequently, a weighty factor to consider in sentencing (see Wong Kai Chuen Philip v Public Prosecutor [1990] 2 SLR(R) 361 at [18]).”[note: 3]

12     On a Claim Trial basis, the prosecution’s sentencing position was 22 to 24 months, citing the following reasons:[note: 4]

(a)     The total sum misappropriated was $79,190 over six months.

(b)     The accused is traced for four counts of section 420 of the Penal Code (Cap 224, 1985 Revised Edition) and one count of section 408 of the Penal Code (Cap 224, 1985 Revised Edition) (“Criminal Breach of Trust Antecedent”) in 1993.

(c)     The accused made restitution of $4,470.

13     Applying the 30% reduction for Stage 1 Plead Guilty (“PG”) under the Sentencing Advisory Panel guidelines on reduction in sentences for guilty pleas (“the Guidelines”), the prosecution’s sentencing position was 15 to 17 months imprisonment.[note: 5]

Defence’s mitigation and submissions on sentence

14     The defence counsel sought an imprisonment term of nine months.

15     First, the defence counsel submitted that the accused co-operated with police investigations from the outset and had been extremely forthcoming during the investigations held against him. In Vasentha d/o Joseph v Public Prosecutor [2015] 5 SLR 122, it was held that “[o]ne good way to demonstrate the offender’s remorse, aside from pleading guilty at the first available opportunity, would be to cooperate fully with the authorities in their investigations”.[note: 6]

16     Second, the defence counsel submitted that the accused had elected to plead guilty and was truly remorseful for his actions. In Angliss Singapore Pte Ltd v Public Prosecutor [2006] 4 SLR 653, the High Court stated that “[a] plea of guilt can be taken into consideration in mitigation when it is motivated by genuine remorse, contriteness or regret and/or desire to facilitate the administration of justice”.[note: 7]

17     Third, the defence counsel submitted that previous residents or Management Corporation Strata Title (“MCST”) Chairman of developments, which the accused managed previously, held the accused in high regard. In support, the defence counsel attached a letter of compliment dated 29 December 2010 and a certificate of appreciation dated 31 August 2013 (“the Testimonials”).[note: 8]

18     On a Claim Trial basis, the defence counsel submitted for a starting point of 12 months’ imprisonment. He cited Chong Kum Heng v Public Prosecutor [2020] SGHC 21 (“Chong Kum Heng”) where the offender claimed trial to several charges, including three charges under section 408 of the Penal Code (Cap 224, 2008 Rev Ed). On appeal, the High Court imposed 18 months’ imprisonment for a misappropriated amount of $111,000 and ten months’ imprisonment for a misappropriated amount of $54,000.[note: 9]

19     In the present case, the accused misappropriated $79,190 which fell between these two quanta in Chong Kum Heng. The present case could be distinguished from Chong Kum Heng as the accused did not attempt to conceal the total sums of the misappropriated amount and willingly provided the relevant bank statements. Further, the accused made partial restitution of $4,470.[note: 10]

20     In court, the defence counsel pointed out that the accused’s 1993 antecedents were dated. The defence counsel also highlighted the difference between Kalaichelven (cited by the prosecution) and the present case. In Kalaichelven (where the offender claimed trial and was sentenced to 28 months’ imprisonment), the offending period was “more than a year” and “the quantum there was $108,339”.[note: 11] Here, the offending period was six months involving a lower sum of $79,190. In the defence counsel’s view, a starting point of 12 months was therefore fair and adequate.

21     Applying the 30% reduction for Stage 1 PG under the Guidelines, the defence counsel stated that nine months’ imprisonment would be an appropriate punishment which “will serve both general and specific deterrence”.[note: 12]

Decision on sentence

22     I agreed with the prosecution’s address on sentence which I found to be fair and reasonable.

23      First, I agreed with the prosecution that in this case, both general deterrence and specific deterrence are engaged and warranted.[note: 13] In terms of general deterrence, I echoed the prosecution’s point that “[w]e are talking about MCST funds being misappropriated…affecting the trust in such agents where…there are many condominiums in Singapore and all of them rely on MCST agents discharging their duties honestly”.[note: 14] In terms of specific deterrence, I informed the parties in court that whilst the accused’s antecedents were dated, he is nonetheless a repeat offender, having committed offences of the same or similar nature previously.[note: 15]

24      Second, I found the case of Kalaichelven (cited by the prosecution) to be useful and relevant as it was a recent case also involving an amalgamated charge and dealing with similar provisions. In that case, the offender faced one amalgamated charge of section 408 of the Penal Code (Cap 224, 2008 Rev Ed) read with sections 124(2) and 124(8)(a)(i) of the Criminal Procedure Code (Cap 68, 2012 Revised Edition).

25     As summarised by the prosecution, the offender in Kalaichelven, who claimed trial and was untraced, was convicted and sentenced to 28 months’ imprisonment (as upheld by the High Court). The offence duration was ten months and involved an amount of $108,339.63, with no restitution. I noted that at the sentencing mention for the present case, the defence counsel stated that the offending period in Kalaichelven was “more than a year” which is factually inaccurate.

26     By comparison, the accused pleaded guilty and is traced for the same offence, namely, the Criminal Breach of Trust Antecedent (sentenced to 12 months’ imprisonment) and other property-related offences in the form of cheating (sentenced to 18 months’ imprisonment). Notably, at that time (in 1993), the prescribed maximum punishment for the Criminal Breach of Trust Antecedent was much lower at seven years. Now, the prescribed maximum punishment for this offence has increased to 15 years.

27     Here, the offending duration was shorter at six months and involved a lower amount of $79,190, with a marginal restitution of $4,470 (i.e. only 5.6%). In other words, there was still a significant balance sum of $74,720 left. Further, the only reason the offending duration was as such was because the accused was discovered, and not because the accused had stopped committing the offence (SOF at [7]). Taking the abovementioned points into account and that the accused is traced, I agreed with the prosecution’s proposed sentence of 22 months on a Claim Trial basis. Applying the 30% reduction for Stage 1 PG under the Guidelines, this resulted in an imprisonment term of 15.4 months, rounded down to 15 months.

28      Third, I highlighted to the defence counsel at the sentencing mention that the case of Chong Kum Heng (cited by the defence counsel) did not involve an amalgamated charge, whereas the Charge in the present case was an amalgamated charge. Being an amalgamated charge, the court may sentence the accused “to 2 times the amount of punishment to which [he] would otherwise have been liable for that offence”.

29     For this case, the accused faced an amalgamated charge under section 124(2) of the CPC. I stressed to the parties in court that in addition to the amount being significant here, there were also 26 transactions involved (SOF at [9]). This demonstrated the higher criminality of the accused as well as the gravity of the course of criminal conduct, which is in line with the general principles and sentencing approach in Prakash s/o Mathivanan v Public Prosecutor and other appeals [2025] SGHC 167 (albeit for amalgamated charges under section 124(4) of the CPC).[note: 16] The defence counsel acknowledged this in court.[note: 17]

30      Fourth, the defence counsel also cited two unreported cases through news articles.[note: 18] As I explained to the defence counsel in court, caution is exercised against reliance on unreported cases. I did not refer or rely on the unreported cases because such “decisions often lack sufficient particulars to paint the entire factual landscape required to appreciate the precise sentences imposed. The lack of reasoned grounds also greatly diminishes the precedential value of these decisions”: Abdul Aziz bin Mohamed Hanib v Public Prosecutor and other appeals [2022] 5 SLR 640 at [173].

31      Lastly, I noted that the Testimonials provided by the defence counsel are from 2010 and 2013 (ten years before the offending period in 2023). I accorded no weight to them as I found them to be irrelevant.

Conclusion

32     This was a case where the accused was entrusted with monies of residents as a managing agent for a condominium and dishonestly misappropriated a very high five-figure sum over a disconcerting number of 26 transactions. The accused, who is traced for the same offence, spent the money on his gambling activities. Ultimately, the sentence reflected the criminality of the accused’s conduct.

33     Having considered the facts of the case, the prosecution’s submission on sentence and the accused’s mitigation, I sentenced the accused to an imprisonment term of 15 months.

34     The accused is presently on bail pending appeal.

html:
Public Prosecutor v Liau Wan Ting

Public Prosecutor v Liau Wan Ting
[2026] SGMC 72

Case Number:Magistrate Court Notice No 900447 of 2026
Decision Date:12 June 2026
Tribunal/Court:Magistrate's Court
Coram: Paul Quan
Counsel Name(s): Kimberly Boo Siew Hui (Attorney-General's Chambers) for the Public Prosecutor; Accused self-represented.
Parties: Public Prosecutor — Liau Wan Ting

Criminal Law – Offences – Giving false information to public servant

Criminal Procedure and Sentencing – Sentencing

12 June 2026

District Judge Paul Quan:

Introduction

1       This is a case involving a false allegation of rape made by an offender to a police officer.

Brief facts

2       The accused, Liau Wan Ting (“Ms Liau”), a 35-year-old Singaporean, lodged a false report to a police officer at the neighbourhood police centre (“NPC”) that she was raped by her former boyfriend even though they had consensual sexual relations. As a result, the NPC officer referred the case to an investigation officer (“IO”) for investigations, who in turn referred the case to the duty officer at the serious sexual crimes branch (“SSCB”). SSCB subsequently assigned a senior investigation officer (“SIO”) to follow up with the case and record statements from Ms Liau. The police then traced Ms Liau’s former boyfriend and brought him back to Police Cantonment Complex (“PCC”) for investigations. Ms Liau later recanted her false allegation as she did not wish for him to be arrested or imprisoned.

Charge and prescribed punishment

3       Ms Liau has pleaded guilty to a single charge under section 182 of the Penal Code 1871 (2020 Rev Ed) (“PC”) of providing false information to a public servant, knowing it to be likely that she would cause him to use his lawful power to conduct investigations against her former boyfriend on her rape allegation, which he would not do if he knew the allegation was false.

4       She must be imprisoned for a term that may extend to two years and/or fined for the offence.

Parties’ positions

5       Ms Liau is a first-time offender. Given that the nature of the false information entails a false allegation of rape, and on the authority of Koh Yong Chiah v PP [2017] 3 SLR 447 (“Koh”), the prosecution has sought a sentence of three weeks’ imprisonment to be imposed on Ms Liau. Ms Liau, who is self-represented, has expressed remorse for her actions and pleaded for the court’s leniency.

Court’s decision

6       I sentence Ms Liau to five weeks’ imprisonment. I explain why in this ex tempore judgment.

Deterrence as operative sentencing principle

7       Deterrence is the operative sentencing principle in Ms Liau’s case, given the nature of her false allegation of a serious sexual offence against an innocent person. In this regard, I am cognisant of the High Court’s observation in Siew Yit Beng v PP [2000] 2 SLR(R) 785 at [44] that:

Any false allegation of rape must not be taken lightly. Not only is it a serious allegation, it is often difficult to verify because, in most of such cases, it is the word of one person against the other. Given the social stigma usually attached to such offences, it could irretrievably damage the reputation of the alleged “rapist” even if the allegations were subsequently proven to be false.

8       Because all allegations of rape are held to the same high standard of evidential rigour, false allegations invariably waste investigative and public resources and those who knowingly make false reports must be dealt with firmly by the law: Singapore Parl Debates; Vol 94, Sitting No 103; [6 May 2019] (Amrin Amin, Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs).

9       False allegations of rape are also deeply detrimental to sustained efforts at encouraging genuine complainants of sexual abuse to come forward to report their perpetrators without fearing that their accounts will be met with scepticism on the one hand, and debunking rape myths surrounding such reporting on the other.

10     Given the distress that is caused to innocent persons, the drain on public resources and the great disservice it renders to genuine complainants of sexual assault, I agree with the prosecution that it is justified to make an example of Ms Liau’s case to deter like-minded offenders even as the court has to cast its watchful eyes on proportionality in her specific case demanded by retributive sentencing.

Sentencing approach

11     Whether the custodial threshold is crossed should essentially be determined based on the degree of harm caused by the offence: Koh at [50].

12     In previous cases of persons falsely reporting innocent persons to the police, imprisonment terms tend to be the norm where the provision of false information has a serious impact on both the victims of the false allegations and the investigative process, and the time the offender took to recant the false statement has a material impact on the sentence to be imposed: Koh at [22] and [23].

Custodial threshold crossed in Ms Liau’s case

13     If appreciable harm may be caused by the offence, the starting point is a custodial term: Koh at [50]. Cases in which the offender makes a police report alleging a crime against an innocent party have generally resulted in custodial terms given the risk of arrest and embarrassment those false allegations create; also, cases in which the false information has caused a significant wastage of public resources have also resulted in a custodial term: Koh at [54].

14     Such is the case here and it cannot be seriously disputed that the custodial threshold is clearly crossed in Ms Liau’s case.

Appreciable harm caused by Ms Liau’s offence

15     Appreciable harm was caused by Ms Liau’s offence. Her former boyfriend was traced in the wee hours of the morning at 12.35am and brought back to PCC and subject to investigations, including a blood test and a video-recorded interview that commenced at 3.46am and concluded at 4.29am.

16     There was also significant wastage of public investigative resources. Ms Liau falsely reported on 7 January 2026 at around 6.48pm at the NPC that she was raped, which triggered a series of actions and deployment of resources by the police:

(a)     the NPC officer referred the case to an IO;

(b)     after speaking to Ms Liau, the IO referred the case to the SSCB duty officer;

(c)     after speaking to Ms Liau, the SSCB duty officer in turn assigned an SIO to follow up with the case and record statements from her;

(d)     a team of six police officers was deployed to trace Ms Liau’s former boyfriend and to escort Ms Liau for a forensic medical examination at PCC’s One-Stop Abuse Forensic Examination (OneSAFE) Centre;

(e)     a team of three police officers from the forensic management branch was deployed to conduct documentation of the incident scene and seized items, with 63 photographs taken; and

(f)     a doctor paired with a nurse from the National University Hospital was deployed to travel to PCC to conduct the forensic medical examination on Ms Liau at PCC’s OneSAFE Centre.

Ms Liau whole culpable for offence

17     Ms Liau was also wholly culpable for the offence.

18     Ms Liau clearly knew the difference between consensual sex and rape after her sister-in-law had explained to her about consent when she asked her sister-in-law whether having sexual relations with someone who was not her partner could be considered rape. Yet, she went ahead to falsely report her former boyfriend for rape. She was motivated to do so because her birth control patch had expired on 6 January 2026 and she was concerned that he would not take responsibility if she were to become pregnant. This neither justified nor excused her actions.

19     Ms Liau not only lodged a false report with the NPC officer at the first instance but subsequently maintained her lie to the IO and SSCB duty officer. Insteading of availing herself to such locus poenitentiae (or place of repentance), she doubled down instead because she feared she would be imprisoned for making a false report. I am unpersuaded that any fear she might have experienced should be taken as negating the resolve she had shown in committing the offence.

20     Ms Liau subsequently recanted her false allegation:

(a)     on 7 January 2026 at 11.37pm when she first admitted to the SIO during the recording of her statement at the OneSAFE interview room that she had lied about being raped and that in fact, she had consensual sex with her former boyfriend;

(b)     on 8 January 2026 at 1.26am when she told the doctor during her forensic medical examination that she had consensual sexual intercourse with her former boyfriend and that there was no assault; and

(c)     on 8 January 2026 at 1.41am when she confirmed in a further statement that she had consented to having sexual intercourse with her former boyfriend.

21     The upshot is that Ms Liau only recanted her false allegation after about five to seven hours had elapsed from the time she first give false information about being raped to the NPC officer, by which time significant resources had already been expended, and the police had already traced her former boyfriend on 8 January 2026 at 12.35am and engaged him by bringing him back to PCC and subjecting him to investigations.

No personal aggravating factors; absence of antecedents neutral factor; early guilty plea accorded mitigatory weight

22     There are no personal aggravating factors that warrant an upward adjustment to the starting point custodial sentence.

23     Ms Liau is a first-time offender. The absence of antecedents is at best a neutral factor; it is an absent aggravating factor, not a mitigating factor: BPH v PP [2019] 2 SLR 764 at [85].

24     Due mitigatory weight is to be accorded to Ms Liau’s early guilty plea.

Siew’s case as comparative precedent

25      Siew’s case is a case precedent of some comparative value. In Siew’s case, cited in Koh’s case at [22(b)], the accused was convicted after trial on two counts under section 182 of the Penal Code (Cap 224, 1985 Rev Ed). She had made two false police statements alleging that her Chinese physician had molested and raped her when the truth of the matter was that they shared a consensual sexual relationship and she was afraid that her husband would divorce her if he were to find out about their liaison. She retracted the false allegations only after about eight months and even reasserted the truth of those allegations at trial. She was sentenced to four weeks’ imprisonment on each count.

26     The maximum prescribed punishment for the offence in Siew’s case then was six months’ imprisonment and/or fine of S$1,000. In response to the subsequent increase in the maximum prescribed punishment to one year’s imprisonment and/or fine of S$5,000 in 2008, the court in Koh observed at [20] that the amendment was intended to afford the courts more flexibility to impose higher sentences when the facts justified it, rather than to signal that Parliament viewed the offence with increased severity. The maximum prescribed punishment was further amended in 2019, which saw a doubling of the maximum imprisonment term to the current two-year term. It is clear that in the specific context of false allegations of rape, the doubling of the maximum punishment is meant to deal with persons, who knowingly make false reports, firmly by the law: Singapore Parl Debates; Vol 94, Sitting No 103; [6 May 2019] (Amrin Amin, Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs).

Conclusion

Sentence of five weeks’ imprisonment imposed

27     I therefore sentence Ms Liau to five weeks’ imprisonment, having regard to:

(a)     parliamentary intent of doubling the maximum prescribed punishment for section 182 PC offences latterly viewed in the particular context of false rape allegations;

(b)     the pernicious nature of the offence and its appreciable harm, both actual – on an innocent third party as well as on public resources – and potential – on genuine sexual assault victims in general;

(c)     Ms Liau’s selfish motive for implicating her former boyfriend;

(d)     her resolve in keeping up with her lie because of self-preservation as she was worried that she would be imprisoned herself, and

(e)     her belated retraction of her false allegation, by which time her former boyfriend was already subject to investigations and significant public resources had been expended.

28     Ms Liau’s sentence not only has to be proportionate to the nature of the offence and the offender in line with retributive sentencing; it also has to give effect to deterrent sentencing by making an example of her to deter like-minded offenders against crying wolf. Her sentence is backdated to 20 May 2026 when she was first charged in court. She has since been in remand.
