html:
Public Prosecutor v Chok Chet

Public Prosecutor v Chok Chet
[2026] SGDC 197

Case Number:District Arrest Case No. DAC 910753 of 2026 & Ors
Decision Date:10 June 2026
Tribunal/Court:District Court
Coram: Shawn Ho
Counsel Name(s): Lim Yee Shuen (Attorney-General's Chambers) for the Prosecution; Accused-in-Person.
Parties: Public Prosecutor — Chok Chet

Criminal Law – Statutory Offences – Road Traffic Act

Criminal Procedure and Sentencing – Driving Disqualification – Consecutive

10 June 2026

District Judge Shawn Ho:

Introduction

1       The Accused, Mr Chok Chet, pleaded guilty to two charges:

(a)     one charge of s 35(1) of the Road Traffic Act 1961 and

(b)     one charge of s 3(1) of the Motor Vehicles (Third-Party Risks and Compensation) Act 1960.

2       He was sentenced to two weeks’ imprisonment, a fine of $600 in default one day’s imprisonment, and disqualified from driving for 36 months.

3       The driving disqualification periods for both offences were ordered to run consecutively.

4       I set out my reasons.

Charges

5       The Accused pleaded guilty to the following charges:

You,

Name: Chok Chet

Gender/ Age: Male, 32 years old

Nationality: Malaysian

are charged that on 2 May 2026, at or about 8.35 A.M, along Ayer Rajah Expressway slip road into Pan Island Expressway near lamp post 488S20, Singapore, did ride a Malaysia registered motorcycle, RAV9149, on a road when you were not the holder of a Malaysia Class B2 driving licence equivalent to Singapore Class 2B driving licence authorising you to ride a motorcycle of that class, and you have thereby contravened Section 35(1) of the Road Traffic Act 1961, and you shall thereby be liable for punishment under Section 35(3)(a) of the same Act.[note: 1]

You,

Name: Chok Chet

Gender/ Age: Male, 32 years old

Nationality: Malaysian

are charged that on 2 May 2026, at or about 8.35 A.M, along Ayer Rajah Expressway slip road into Pan Island Expressway near lamp post 488S20, Singapore, did use a Malaysia registered motorcycle, RAV9149, whilst there was not in force in relation to the use of the said vehicle by you, such a policy of insurance or such a security in respect of third-party risks that complies with the requirements of the Motor Vehicles (Third-Party Risks and Compensation) Act 1960, and you have thereby contravened Section 3(1)(a) of the Act, which contravention is an offence that is punishable under Section 3(2) read with Section 3(3) of the Act.[note: 2]

Statement of facts

6       The complainant is SGT(2) Rahmah Binte Mohd Sani, attached to Traffic Police.[note: 3]

7       The Accused is Chok Chet, Male, Chinese, 32 years old, Malaysian. He was the rider of a Malaysia registered motorcycle bearing registration number RAV9149, at the time of the incident.[note: 4]

8       On 2 May 2026, at or about 8.35 A.M, along Ayer Rajah Expressway slip road into Pan Island Expressway near lamp post 488S20, Singapore, the Accused was riding a Malaysia registered motorcycle, RAV9149, when he was stopped by the complainant for checks. Upon checks, the Accused was found to be riding the motorcycle without a Malaysia class B2 equivalent Singapore 2B driving licence authorizing him to ride the motorcycle of that class.[note: 5]

9       The Accused only possessed an expired Malaysia Learner’s Driving Licence in B2 and D.[note: 6]

10     At the material time, the Accused was riding the motorcycle to his workplace at Woodlands before he was stopped by the complainant for checks.[note: 7]

11     The Accused was not a holder of a Malaysia Class B2 driving licence which is equivalent to a Singapore Class 2B driving licence authorising the Accused to ride the motorcycle of that class. Hence, the Accused had contravened Section 35(1) of the Road Traffic Act 1961, punishable under Section 35(3)(a) of the same Act.[note: 8]

12     Further, as the Accused was not a holder of a qualified Malaysia class B2 driving licence, at the time of the offence, there was no insurance policy or such a security in respect of Third-Party Risks that complies with the requirements of the Motor Vehicles (Third-Party Risks and Compensation) Act 1960, in relation to the use of motorcycle by the Accused.[note: 9]

13     The Accused has thus contravened Section 3(1)(a) of the Motor Vehicles (Third-Party Risks & Compensation) Act 1960 and thereby committed an offence punishable under Section 3(2) read with Section 3(3) of the Motor Vehicles (Third-Party Risks and Compensation) Act 1960.[note: 10]

Offences Committed

14     The Accused had hence committed the offences of:

(a)     Riding Without a Valid Driving Licence under Section 35(1) of the Road Traffic Act 1961 and punishable under Section 35(3)(a) of the Road Traffic Act 1961.

(b)     Using Vehicle without Insurance Coverage under Section 3(1)(a) of the Motor Vehicles (Third-Party Risks and Compensation) Act 1960.[note: 11]

Prescribed punishment

15     The prescribed punishment for s 35(1) of the Road Traffic Act 1961 (first offender) was a fine not exceeding $10,000 or to imprisonment for a term not exceeding 3 years or to both.

16     The prescribed punishment for s 3(1) of the Motor Vehicles (Third-Party Risks and Compensation) Act 1960 was a fine not exceeding $1,000 or to imprisonment for a term not exceeding 3 months or to both.

17     An offence’s statutory maximum sentence signals the gravity in which Parliament views such offences. A sentencing judge ought to take this into account when determining precisely where the offender’s conduct falls within the entire range of punishment set by Parliament: Public Prosecutor v Kwong Kok Hing [2008] 2 SLR(R) 684 at [44].

(Benny Tan, Assessing the Effectiveness of Sentencing Guideline Judgments in Singapore Issued Post-March 2013 and A Guide to Constructing Frameworks, (2018) 30 SAcLJ 1004 at [46])

18     The court should ensure that the full spectrum of sentences enacted by Parliament is carefully explored in determining the appropriate sentence, viz. Completeness principle (Poh Boon Kiat v Public Prosecutor [2014] 4 SLR 892 at [60]).

Prosecution’s submissions on sentence

19     The Prosecution referred to Public Prosecutor v Rizuwan bin Rohmat [2024] 3 SLR 694, Seah Ming Yang Daryle v Public Prosecutor [2024] 4 SLR 1561 and Public Prosecutor v Eng Kwan Meng Garrick [2026] SGHC 116.

20     The Prosecution sought the following sentences:

Charge

Offence

Sentence

DQ is with effect from

 

 

 

DAC 910753 2026

 

 

 

s 35(1) of the RTA

2 weeks’ imprisonment

and

DQ and Prohibition Order for all classes of driving licences for 24 months

 

 

 

10 June 2027

 

 

 

DAC 910754 2026

 

 

 

s 3(1) of the MVA

$600 i/d 1 day’s imprisonment

and

DQ and Prohibition Order for all classes of driving licences for 12 months

 

 

 

10 June 2026



Mitigation plea

21     The Defence asked for leniency and sought the shortest possible custodial sentence.

Sentencing

The Law

PP v Rizuwan bin Rohmat

22     In Public Prosecutor v Rizuwan bin Rohmat [2024] 3 SLR 694 at [39], the High Court, stated that:

(a)     Unqualified Drivers were drivers who never held a valid driving licence for the class of vehicles they were driving.

(b)     Qualified Drivers were drivers who failed to renew or validate their driving licence prior to the offence under s 35(1) of the Act.

(c)     There is an obvious distinction of substance between the drivers in the two categories. Unqualified Drivers never held a valid driving licence, and therefore were unskilled and unqualified to drive. That could not be said of Qualified Drivers.

23     The archetypal case was an Unqualified Driver caught driving not because of an accident, but because of police enforcement action: Rizuwan at [40] and [59]. It does not apply to the Qualified Driver: Rizuwan at [59].

Seah Ming Yang Daryle v PP

24     In Seah Ming Yang Daryle v Public Prosecutor [2024] 4 SLR 1561, the Court of 3 Judges stated that the harm that s 35(1) seeks to prevent is to keep unlicensed drivers off our roads:

(a)     First, it reduces the risk of harm to other innocent road users. Unqualified Drivers have no basic competence to drive a motor vehicle, as a matter of law and fact. Thus, when an Unqualified Driver drives on our roads, the offender poses a potential danger to other road users. This danger is further amplified as the offender who drives without a licence is more likely to cause an accident and result in harm: Daryle Seah at [52].

(b)     Second, keeping unlicensed drivers off our roads reduces the risk of innocent road users having to suffer without adequate compensation from the unlicensed drivers, who will not be covered by insurance (due to them driving without a licence) when there is an accident: Daryle Seah at [54].

(c)     Third, the nature of s 35(1) offences, similar to many other road traffic offences, is that they are difficult to detect: Daryle Seah at [55].

25     The benchmark sentence for the offence is 2 weeks’ imprisonment with a disqualification order of two years: Daryle Seah at [75] and [91].

26     An additional two years of disqualification is appropriate to adopt for the s 35(1) RTA benchmark sentence. A total period of three years’ disqualification (the two years’ benchmark disqualification in addition to the one-year minimum disqualification for driving without insurance) would be proportionate for a first-time offender who drove without a licence: Daryle Seah at [81].

PP v Eng Kwan Meng Garrick

27     In Daryle Seah, the court considered, in respect of Unqualified Drivers, that the total period of three years’ disqualification – comprising the two-year driving disqualification period imposed for the offence under s 35(1) of the RTA and the one-year driving disqualification period imposed for the offence under s 3(1) of the MVA – was “proportionate for a first-time offender who drove without a licence” (Daryle Seah at [81]). This makes clear that the court in Daryle Seah envisioned the driving disqualification periods for the two offences to run consecutively rather than concurrently: Garrick Eng at [63].

28     The driving disqualification periods for the RTA charge and the MVA charge should run consecutively in order to achieve the necessary deterrent effect. This is permissible because the driving disqualification period for an offence under s 35(1) of the RTA is imposed pursuant to s 42(1) of the RTA, which provides that the court may impose a driving disqualification period “for any period that the court thinks fit”. Section 42(1) of the RTA therefore confers on the court the discretion to order the driving disqualification period for the offence under s 35(1) of the RTA to run consecutively to the driving disqualification period for the offence under s 3(1) of the MVA: Garrick Eng at [64].

Decision on sentence

Offence-Specific Factors

(1)   Harm

29     Harm is a measure of the injury caused to society by the commission of the offence (Public Prosecutor v Koh Thiam Huat [2017] 4 SLR 1099 at [41]).

30     The following non-exhaustive factors might be considered (Rizuwan at [63] and Daryle Seah at [82]-[83]):

(a)     The consequences that arose from the offender’s driving (e.g. accident) and

(b)     Whether there were other occupants in the offender’s vehicle.

31     In the present case, the Accused was riding a motorcycle on his own. There was no accident.

32     I was mindful that in assessing the level of harm or potential harm, the sentencing court should be careful not to double-count any factors which may already have been taken into account in assessing the level of culpability: Ye Lin Myint v Public Prosecutor [2019] 5 SLR 1005 at [58] (see also Andrew Ashworth, Sentencing and Criminal Justice (6th Ed, 2015, Cambridge University Press) at [4.3] and [4.5]).

(2)   Culpability

33     Culpability is a measure of the degree of relative blameworthiness disclosed by an offender’s actions and is measured chiefly in relation to the extent and manner of the offender’s involvement in the criminal act: Public Prosecutor v Aw Tai Hock [2017] 5 SLR 1141 at [35] (see Andrew Ashworth, Sentencing and Criminal Justice (Cambridge University Press, 6th Ed, 2015) at [4.5]).

34     The following non-exhaustive factors might be considered (Rizuwan at [63] and Daryle Seah at [82]-[83]):

(a)     The offender’s reason for driving (e.g. drove in order to commit an offence vs drove in an emergency);

(b)     The offender’s manner and length of driving (e.g. failed to obey traffic rules); and

(c)     The offender’s conduct after the offence had been committed (e.g. attempted to evade arrest).

35     In the present case, there was no culpability-increasing factor. The Accused had been riding the motorcycle to his workplace at Woodlands before he was stopped by the complainant for checks.[note: 12] He did not attempt to evade arrest.

Offender-Specific Factors

(1)   Antecedents

36     The Accused had a clean driving record.

(2)   Guilty plea

37     The SAP Guidelines for Guilty Pleas applied: Ng En You Jeremiah v Public Prosecutor [2025] SGHC 135 at [110]-[111] and [115]-[117] (see also Edwin Lim Wei Keat, A Critical Analysis of the Application of Guidelines on Reduction in Sentences for Guilty Pleas in Singapore, SAcLJ (10 October 2025, e-First) at [37]-[43]).

38     I gave full weight to the Accused’s guilty plea: Angliss Singapore Pte Ltd v Public Prosecutor [2006] 4 SLR(R) 653 at [77]. This saved the criminal justice system resources that would have been expended with a full trial. He pleaded guilty at his first court mention.

39     Accordingly, I gave the Accused the full 30% discount (Stage 1) for his early plea of guilt.

40     All things considered, including the harm and culpability factors, the starting point for the sentence was about 3 weeks’ imprisonment. After considering the mitigating factors and the PG discount, in the round, the sentence would be 2 weeks’ imprisonment.

41     For completeness, the evidence against the Accused was overwhelming and lends itself to the conclusion that he had little choice but to plead guilty: Vasentha d/o Joseph v Public Prosecutor [2015] SGHC 197 at [71] and [73], and Public Prosecutor v BDB [2017] SGCA 69 at [74].

(3)   Cooperation with the authorities

42     I gave due weight to the Accused’s cooperation with the authorities: Public Prosecutor v Siew Boon Loong [2005] 1 SLR(R) 611 at [16]-[18].

Other points

(1)   Driving disqualification order

43     Driving disqualification orders meld the three sentencing objectives of punishment, protection of the public and deterrence: Edwin s/o Suse Nathen v Public Prosecutor [2013] 4 SLR 1139 at [13]-[14], Public Prosecutor v Koh Thiam Huat [2017] 4 SLR 1099 at [64] and Chen Song v Public Prosecutor [2024] SGHC 129 at [143].

44     The most important sentencing principles engaged in driving disqualification orders are to:

(a)      protect society, because disqualification orders are meant to prevent future harm that the offender may cause to the public, and to

(b)      deter, because such orders deprive offenders of the freedom to drive: Public Prosecutor v Ong Heng Chua [2018] SGHC 95 at [61].

45     As stated in Public Prosecutor v Mohd Isa [1963] MLJ 135, the “most satisfactory penalty for most motoring offences is disqualification” because a fine is paid once and then forgotten. For instance, a 12-month disqualification order would mean that for the entire year in which the order is in effect, the offender is reminded every day of his offence and the unwarranted risks in which he had placed ordinary members of the public: Sivakumar s/o Rajoo v Public Prosecutor [2002] 1 SLR(R) 265 at [28].

46     Where a person is disqualified for a period of 12 months or longer, that person’s driving licence shall be “of no effect” and the person is further prevented from driving a motor vehicle after the disqualification period unless he passes the prescribed test of competence to drive: s 43(1)(b) of the Road Traffic Act.

(2)   Special reasons

47     An offender would be disqualified from driving under s 3(3) of the MVA unless he shows “special reasons”.

48     In this connection, the two-stage framework for “special reasons” is as follows:

(a)     First Stage: Show special reasons, viz. reasons relating to the facts or circumstances of an offence and not to the offender herself; and

(b)     Second Stage: Even if special reasons are established, the court will consider whether the discretion not to disqualify must be exercised in favour of the offender.

49     Under the two-stage framework, the first stage is offence-specific (not offender-specific). When an offender seeks to come within the special reasons exception, the facts to back up such circumstances must be proved to the court’s satisfaction: Toh Yong Soon v Public Prosecutor [2011] 3 SLR 147 at [5].

50     Even if special reasons are established, it does not automatically follow that the offender would not be disqualified from driving. For the second stage, the court’s discretion not to disqualify can only be made in very exceptional circumstances: Sivakumar s/o Rajoo v Public Prosecutor [2002] 1 SLR(R) 265 at [25] (see also Prathib s/o M Balan v Public Prosecutor [2017] SGHC 303 at [9]-[11]).

(i)   First Stage

51     What are “special reasons” not to impose a driving disqualification? The special reasons have to be reasons relating to the facts or circumstances of an offence and not to the offender himself – this would be the clearest means of giving effect to Parliament’s intention: M V Balakrishnan v Public Prosecutor [1998] 2 SLR(R) 846 at [9], Muhammad Faizal bin Rahim v Public Prosecutor [2012] 1 SLR 116 at [41] and Rafael Voltaire Alzate at [38].

52     In other words, a special reason is a mitigating or extenuating circumstance, not amounting in law to a defence to the charge, yet directly connected with the commission of the offence, and one which the court ought properly to take into consideration when imposing punishment: Whittall v Kirby [1947] 1 KB 194 at 201, as endorsed by Muhammad Faizal bin Rahim at [30].

53     Offender-specific factors, such as the fact that the defendant is of a good character or has a good driving record, cannot be accepted as special reasons: Wilkinson’s Road Traffic Offences, Sweet & Maxwell, (32nd Ed, 2025, General Editor: Kevin McCormac) at [21-10]. Circumstances peculiar to the offender do not go towards reducing his moral culpability; they are essentially extrinsic facts about the offender which are unrelated to the offence but are produced to elicit sympathy from the court. These circumstances are morally distinguishable from circumstances peculiar to the offence: Muhammad Faizal bin Rahim at [43].

54     Even if an offender requires his driving licence for his livelihood, this would not constitute a special reason (see also Tan Yock Lin and S. Chandra Mohan, Criminal Procedure (LexisNexis: March 2019; Binder 3, Loose-leaf, Chapter XVII: Sentencing) at [3751]).

55     This is because in the Malaysian Criminal Appeal Court case of Public Prosecutor v Hiew Chin Fong [1988] 1 MLJ 467 – which was endorsed in Chua Chye Tiong v Public Prosecutor [2004] 1 SLR(R) 22 at [61] and [62] – a 12-month disqualification period was imposed on the offender despite the fact that his livelihood depended on him having a driving licence.

56     The Criminal Appeal Court in Public Prosecutor v Hiew Chin Fong laid down several statements of law on what should not be considered special reasons:

(a)     Financial hardship to the offender;

(b)     The offender knew no other means of earning his livelihood;

(c)     That the effect of the disqualification must necessarily and consequently deprive the offender of his livelihood or occupation; and

(d)     That the offender was a poor man and would have difficulty to get to his work.

57     The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs, Ms Sun Xueling, had stated as follows (Singapore Parliamentary Debates, Official Report (8 July 2019) vol 94):

… Actually, if an individual depends on driving to make a living, that is all the more reason for him to drive safely and for him to be off the roads if he is unable or unwilling to do so.

58     Before an emergency is capable of amounting to a special reason under law, a crucial prerequisite is for the offender to show that there was no alternative but for him to drive, and that he had explored every reasonable alternative before driving: Sivakumar s/o Rajoo v Public Prosecutor [2002] 1 SLR(R) 265 at [17], affirmed in Siti Hajar bte Abdullah v Public Prosecutor [2006] 2 SLR(R) 248 at [13] (see also Fan Lei v Public Prosecutor [2024] SGHC 278 at [16]).

59     When an offender seeks to come within the special reasons exception, the facts to back up such circumstances must be proved to the court’s satisfaction: Toh Yong Soon v Public Prosecutor [2011] 3 SLR 147 at [5]. The onus lies on an accused to raise special reasons for the court’s consideration, if such reasons exist: Chue Woon Wai v Public Prosecutor [1996] 1 SLR(R) 725 at [13], Prathib s/o M Balan v Public Prosecutor [2017] SGHC 303 at [12] and Siti Hajar bte Abdullah v Public Prosecutor [2006] 2 SLR(R) 248 at [12].

(See also Wilkinson’s Road Traffic Offences, Sweet & Maxwell, (32nd Ed, 2025, General Editor: Kevin McCormac) at [21-62])

60      Cheong Wai Keong v Public Prosecutor [2005] SGHC 126 stands for the proposition that the shortness of distance travelled cannot in itself be a “special reason” (Rafael Voltaire Alzate at [41]). A court should be able to have regard to the distance travelled as part of its overall analysis (Rafael Voltaire Alzate at [42]).

61     The High Court in Lee Shin Nan v Public Prosecutor [2023] SGHC 354 at [79] stated that special reasons will generally be found only if the court is satisfied that the offender drove in circumstances that reasonably suggest:

(a)     it was necessary to do so in order to avoid other likely and serious harm or danger; and

(b)     there was no reasonable alternative way to achieve this end.

(see also Chen Song at [138] and Ng En You Jeremiah v Public Prosecutor [2023] SGHC 354 at [82])

(ii)   Second Stage

62     Even if special reasons are established, it does not automatically follow that the offender would not be disqualified. In this regard, there must be a separate process of considering whether the discretion must be exercised in favour of the offender: Sivakumar s/o Rajoo at [22]. The limited discretion not to disqualify can only be made in very exceptional circumstances, having regard to the special circumstances as well as to the whole of the circumstances surrounding the commission of the offence, including the manner in which the offender drove and the alcohol content in the offender’s body: Sivakumar s/o Rajoo at [25].

63     Pulling the various strands together, the test for special reasons is stringent and is only satisfied in very exceptional circumstances (see also Prathib s/o M Balan v Public Prosecutor [2017] SGHC 303 at [9]-[11]).

64     The Act is construed strictly to preserve its policy of protecting road users: Chua Chye Tiong v Public Prosecutor [2004] 1 SLR (R) 22 at [53]. A less restrictive approach would negate the legislative stipulation of mandatory disqualification and defeat its underlying objectives: Siti Hajar bte Abdullah v Public Prosecutor [2006] 2 SLR(R) 248 at [8]. Widening the special reasons exception would encourage frivolous defences: Muhammad Faizal bin Rahim at [41].

(See also Tan Yock Lin and S. Chandra Mohan, Criminal Procedure (LexisNexis: March 2019; Binder 3, Loose-leaf, Chapter XVII: Sentencing) at [3702], [3751] and [3752])

65     In the present case, I found no special reason to dispense with the driving disqualification order of 12 months for s 3(1) MVA, which is mandatory as well as appropriate.

(3)   Totality principle

66     The sentence was in line with both limbs of the totality principle: Mohamed Shouffee Bin Adam v Public Prosecutor [2014] 2 SLR 998 at [54]-[57] (see also Public Prosecutor v ASR [2019] 1 SLR 941 at [150] where the Court of Appeal considered that the sentence sought by the Prosecution would have violated both limbs of the totality principle).

Conclusion

67     The Accused was sentenced as follows:

Charge

Offence

Sentence

DQ is with effect from

 

 

 

DAC 910753 2026

 

 

 

s 35(1) of the RTA

2 weeks’ imprisonment

and

DQ and Prohibition Order for all classes of driving licences for 24 months

 

 

 

 

10 June 2027

 

 

 

DAC 910754 2026

 

 

 

s 3(1) of the MVA

$600 i/d 1 day’s imprisonment

and

DQ and Prohibition Order for all classes of driving licences for 12 months

 

 

 

10 June 2026



68     The disqualification period for the s 35(1) RTA charge was ordered to commence at the end of the disqualification period for the s 3(1) MVA charge.

69     The total driving disqualification period is three years.

70     I am grateful for the hard work and submissions of both sides.

html:
Nirmala d/o Thangavellu v Acestes Pte. Ltd.

Nirmala d/o Thangavellu v Acestes Pte. Ltd.
[2026] SGDC 195

Case Number:District Court Originating Claim No 1254 of 2024
Decision Date:09 June 2026
Tribunal/Court:District Court
Coram: Evans Ng
Counsel Name(s): Shanthi Elavarasi d/o R Kalamohan (R Kalamohan Law LLC) (instructed) and Mary Magdeline Pereira and R Kalamohan (Whitefield Law Corporation) for the claimant; Hong Heng Leong and Noh Bin Abd Hamid (Just Law LLC) for the defendant.
Parties: Nirmala d/o Thangavellu — Acestes Pte. Ltd.

Civil Procedure – Costs

Civil Procedure – Offer to settle

9 June 2026

Judgment reserved.

District Judge Evans Ng:

1       The Claimant injured her ankle while working as a security officer at a condominium. I dismissed her negligence claim against her employer on 25 May 2026: see Nirmala d/o Thangavellu v Acestes Pte. Ltd. [2026] SGDC 177. The parties were directed to file costs submissions within two weeks if they cannot agree on the costs of the proceedings, and they could not indeed. The Defendant’s solicitors filed submissions that seek, among other things, $20,000[note: 1] or $25,000[note: 2] in party-and-party costs. That two figures should rear up from the same summation done twice by the Defendant’s solicitors holds true to form. They had a tin ear for their own impermissible questions at trial.[note: 3] And their eyes could not alight on the holding in my judgment, prompting them to write to the Court[note: 4] to ask: “For the avoidance of doubt, can we confirm that Your Honour has dismissed the Claimant’s case with costs.” On the other hand, radio silence issued from the Claimant’s lawyers at the close of business on 8 June 2026. So I was left to write the following judgment without either counsel’s assistance.

2       Costs shall follow the event. During the parties’ costs negotiations, the Claimant’s solicitors proposed to the Defendant that the Claimant should not have to bear costs because she is impecunious.[note: 5] But that is rarely a sufficient reason for departing from the general rule. It is not an unfair rule too, especially where a litigant is represented, because their solicitors must have had advised them at the outset that they shall have to pay costs to the other party if they are unsuccessful in the proceedings: r 17(3)(b) of the Legal Profession (Professional Conduct) Rules 2015.

3       One might also doubt the Claimant’s alleged impecuniosity on the face of things. She has been able to pay her own disbursements for court filing fees and transcription fees of around $1,400. She can afford to instruct a quad of senior lawyers (namely, Mr Dube Vinod Kumar (called in 1979), Mr R Kalamohan (called in 1983), Ms Mary Magdeline Pereira (called in 2002), and Ms Shanthi Elavarasi d/o R Kalamohan (called in 2011)) from two different firms to collaborate and work on her claim since May 2022, at the latest. Throughout their labours, her lawyers have not filed an application to discharge themselves on the ground of non-payment of fees. There is also, at present, no allegation from the Claimant that she had taken the “bait” of entering into a contingency fee arrangement with her lawyers — a transaction prohibited in Singapore under s 107(1)(b) and s 107(3) of the Legal Profession Act 1966 — that frees her from paying their legal fees out of her own pocket: Law Society of Singapore v Lau See Jin Jeffrey [2017] 4 SLR 148 at [30(c)]. I now address the Defendant’s position.

4       The Defendant seeks costs on an indemnity basis by relying on an offer of amicable resolution that it served on the Claimant before the trial, pursuant to O 5 r 2 of the Rules of Court 2021.[note: 6] Its terms are that the Claimant shall discontinue the action and pay the Defendant’s costs and disbursements, which means the Claimant is to yield fully. That is the antithesis of a compromise. The offer lacks any element that would induce or facilitate settlement and cannot be considered a “genuine” offer: Singapore Airlines Ltd and anor v Fujitsu Microelectronics (Malaysia) Sdn Bhd and others [2001] 1 SLR(R) 38 at [10] and [11]. It is also hard to tell how the offer’s terms are more favourable to the Claimant than the judicial outcome. The offer therefore fails to alter the Defendant’s entitlement to costs on the standard basis.

5       The Costs Guidelines in the State Courts Practice Directions provide that the range of costs for a negligence claim is: (a) Pre-trial Work - $9,000 to 30,000, (b) Trial Work - $2,500 to $6,000, and (c) Post-trial Work - Up to $8,000. They also state that the “Court may depart from the Costs Guidelines depending on the particular circumstances of each case”.

6       The Claimant raised no real issues of fact or law to be met by the Defendant. In ordinary circumstances, the amount of costs that such a matter attracts would be at the lowest point of the range. I shall award the Defendant costs of $2,500 for trial work and $1,000 for post-trial work. I depart from the Costs Guidelines in respect of the Defendant’s pre-trial work.

7       The affidavit of evidence-in-chief of the Defendant’s sole witness (Mr Haresh) was inadequately prepared. The evidence contained therein was sparse. Yet it comprised mainly hearsay and raised unfairly prejudicial or irrelevant points. This prolonged Mr Haresh’s cross-examination. All the exhibits to the affidavit were absent and improperly tendered as a separate bundle. The key piece of evidence (a video recording) was not prepared and tendered to Court in the correct medium ahead of the trial. This prevented the Court from fully reading in beforehand. Further, the photographs of the condominium’s premises adduced by the Defendant were undated and it could not be established when they were taken — these were issues that should have been detected and sorted out way before trial. Initial copies of the photographs provided to the participants of the trial were of such inferior quality that they could not resolve their contents. It is unfair to award the same measure of costs to a litigant who prepares his papers in a deficient way as one who does so properly. I therefore apply a 25% discount to $9,000 and award $6,750 for pre-trial work.

8       The Defendant also claims disbursements of $1,327.70, particularised in a list,[note: 7] which I agree is a reasonable amount.

9       In sum, I fix costs of DC/OC 1254/2024 at $11,577.70 (all-in) to be paid by the Claimant to the Defendant. As a pre-condition to demanding or enforcing payment of costs and any related interest, I order the Defendant’s solicitors to send hardcopies of the two relevant judgments to the Claimant directly, with her solicitors in copy: see r 7(3)(d) of the Legal Profession (Professional Conduct) Rules 2015.

10     Despite some misgivings I have about the way in which the Claimant’s case was brought, I do not think it is appropriate to invite the Claimant’s lawyers to show cause under O 21 r 6(2) of the Rules of Court 2021, regarding whether they should be liable to repay to the Claimant costs which the Claimant has been ordered to pay to the Defendant; or be disallowed solicitor-and-client costs as between them and the Claimant. If there were any problems with the Claimant’s lawyers’ treatment of this case, they ran to the root. For instance, in their letter before action written on 22 March 2024[note: 8] to request compensation from the Defendant’s insurer, the solicitors alleged:

On the material day, when our client together with his co-worker needed to go up to the 3rd level to unhook the lifting chain on the container, our client was using the ladder and when he was coming down from the 2nd level, our client slipped and fell down when the ladder slipped off at about the height of 2.5 metre, landing on his backside. As a result, our client sustained serious injuries to his left knee.

[Emphasis in bold in original]

These allegations were not even wrong since they concerned a different client.

11     It is more appropriate for the Claimant to consider whether her lawyers have fulfilled their duties set out by the High Court in Mookan Sadaiyakumar v Kim Hock Corp Pte Ltd and another appeal [2020] 4 SLR 555 at [49], since only she would know the instructions she gave and the advice she received, and thereafter to proceed as she thinks fit.

[note: 2]Defendant’s Costs Submissions, para 10.

[note: 3]Notes of Evidence, 18 March 2026, 96/1-97/9.

[note: 4]Other Hearing Related Requests filed by the Defendant’s solicitors on 25 May 2026.

[note: 5]Other Supporting Document filed by the Defendant’s solicitors on 4 June 2026.

[note: 6]Defendant’s Costs Submissions, paras 5 and 6, pages 16 and 17.

html:
Public Prosecutor v Koh Hong Rui Kendrick

Public Prosecutor v Koh Hong Rui Kendrick
[2026] SGDC 194

Case Number:District Arrest Case No 901186 of 2026 & 2 Others
Decision Date:09 June 2026
Tribunal/Court:District Court
Coram: Paul Quan
Counsel Name(s): Ernest Goh (Attorney-General's Chambers) for the Public Prosecutor; Kalaithasan S/O Karuppaya/ B Rajendraprasad (Regent LLC) for the Accused.
Parties: Public Prosecutor — Koh Hong Rui Kendrick

Criminal Law – Offences – Property – Criminal trespass – House-breaking

Criminal Law – Offences – Property – Theft

Criminal Law – Offences – Unlawful assembly – Rioting

Criminal Procedure and Sentencing – Sentencing – Young offenders

9 June 2026

District Judge Paul Quan:

Introduction

1       This is a case of a recalcitrant young offender, who committed a fresh spate of more serious offences barely six months after his discharge from a juvenile home where he was detained for previously bringing a chopper knife to school and for committing other property-related offences.

Brief facts

2       The accused, Koh Hong Rui Kendrick (“Mr Koh”), an 18-year-old Singaporean, was previously ordered by the Youth Court in August 2023 to be detained at the Singapore Boys’ Home for 21 months for committing the offences of public possession of an offensive weapon and theft-in-dwelling, with other theft-in-dwelling and dishonest misappropriation of property charges to be taken into consideration for the purpose of sentence (“TIC”).[note: 1] Barely six months after his discharge from the juvenile home on 7 May 2025, he committed the present set of offences that were more serious in nature.

Charges

3       Mr Koh has pleaded guilty to two charges of house-breaking and rioting under sections 451 and 147 of the Penal Code 1871 (2020 Rev Ed) (“PC”) respectively,[note: 2] committed merely a week apart in January 2026. He also faces a TIC charge of theft-in-dwelling under section 380 PC,[note: 3] where he stole his father’s bracelet worth S$10,000 at their residence in November 2025 that was unrecovered.

Parties’ positions

4       I convicted Mr Koh on 19 May 2026. Agreeing with the parties, I called for a reformative training (“RT”) pre-sentence report (“PSR”) on him. I have since received his PSR from the Singapore Prison Service (“SPS”) on 4 June 2026,[note: 4] recommending him to undergo “Level 2 intensity of rehabilitation” if he were sentenced to RT. Parties have now sought such a sentence to be imposed on Mr Koh. Mr Koh was also reportedly prepared to accept such a sentence.[note: 5]

Court’s decision

5       I agree and explain in this ex tempore judgment why I sentence Mr Koh to RT with a minimum detention period of 12 months, or level 2 intensity of rehabilitation.

Why RT but not probation PSR called

6       I delivered brief reasons on 19 May 2026 explaining why I called for an RT but not a probation PSR on Mr Koh. I outline these reasons by way of background.

7       I am cognisant that I should generally call for a probation PSR before sentencing a young offender who is aged 21 or below but I did not do so in Mr Koh’s case because I did not think probation is viable or realistic although the basic prerequisites for probation are met: A Karthik v PP [2018] 5 SLR 1289 at [20] and [21]. This is for two reasons: first, the severity of the offences committed by Mr Koh; and second, the recalcitrant and escalating nature of his offending behaviour. This effectively rules out probation as a sentencing option altogether.

Basic prerequisites for probation met

8       In Mr Koh’s case, the basic prerequisites for probation are met:

(a)     Mr Koh’s offences are not offences for which the sentences are “fixed by law”: section 5(1) of the Probation of Offenders Act 1951 (2020 Rev Ed) (“POA”) –

(i)       for his house-breaking offence, Mr Koh faces mandatory imprisonment for a term which may extend to ten years that can be coupled with a fine. For his rioting offence, it is seven years coupled with caning, and

(ii)       the sentences are fixed in type but not in quantum; the court must impose imprisonment with or without a fine or caning, but has the discretion to decide on the length of imprisonment, quantum of the fine, and the number of strokes to be imposed: Mohamad Fairuuz bin Saleh v PP [2015] 1 SLR 1145 at [17(c)]; and

(b)     the proviso to section 5(1) of the POA also does not apply as the offences are not punishable with either a specified minimum sentence or mandatory minimum sentence.

Probation not viable or realistic

9       Be that as it may, I must still preliminarily assess whether probation is viable or realistic on the facts of Mr Koh’s case, and the court should order a probation PSR if the accused is young (that is, between 16 and 21 years old), a first offender and convicted of a relatively less serious crime: Wong Shan Shan v PP [2008] SGHC 49 at [20]-[21].

10     Mr Koh is a young offender being 18 at the time of the offences, conviction and sentencing. But he is not a first-time offender despite his spent convictions having completed his juvenile home detention because he is no longer a young person (14 or older but below 18 as defined by section 2(1) of the Children and Young Persons Act 1993): section 7DA(2)(a) read with 7E(2)(c) and section 7E(3) of the Registration of Criminals Act 1949 (2020 Rev Ed). I also found that probation is not viable or realistic given the severity of Mr Koh’s offences. In comparison, the offenders in A Karthik and Wong Shan Shan were arguably convicted of charges of the same severity or more charges: Cheah Bernice [2024] SGDC 220 at [14]. In both cases, the appellate court thought that probation PSRs ought to have been called on the offenders. However, the consideration of the nature and gravity of any offence is necessarily a fact-specific exercise and the severity of Mr Koh’s offences must be properly appreciated in its particular context and not by mere reference to the maximum punishments prescribed by the offences: Cheah Bernice at [15].

11     As it is, house-breaking and rioting are serious by their very nature, having regard to the prescribed punishments for the offences. The context in which they were committed was also egregious. Mr Koh’s offending behaviour escalated in this regard as he had committed more serious property-related offences, barely six months after being discharged from the juvenile home. Prior to the house-breaking offence, he stole a S$10,000 bracelet from his father, which was an exponential increase in the economic value of his previous property-related offences. Two months later, he went on to commit house-breaking by brazenly climbing into his neighbour’s ground-floor unit in the wee hours of the morning, upon noticing that one of its windows was opened, and searched the unit for valuable items to steal. He had been targeting the unit for two days. He evaded apprehension by fleeing the scene when he was discovered but was eventually caught by the occupant. While awaiting the arrival of the police, he fled again but subsequently returned and was arrested. He was charged in court the next day and released on bail on 23 January 2026. Four days later, while on bail, his offending behaviour further escalated as he went on to commit a further offence of rioting with co-accused persons whom he met at the juvenile home and affiliated with a gang. They decided to take revenge on the victim who had beaten up a fellow gang member. One of them ended up punching the person accompanying the victim twice in the head.

RT PSR ordered

12     In this case, there is a clear need to incorporate a sufficient element of deterrence, both general and specific, within any overarching focus on the goal of rehabilitation. RT affords a possible rehabilitative-deterrent/punitive sentencing option because it incorporates a minimum incarceration period of six or 12 months that is not a feature of probation: PP v Koh Wen Jie Boaz [2016] 1 SLR 334 (“Boaz Koh”) at [34] and [39]; it meets the goal of rehabilitation without sending the offender to prison: A Karthik at [67]. I therefore called for a report pursuant to section 305(3) of the Criminal Procedure Code 2010 (2020 Rev Ed) on Mr Koh’s physical and mental condition, his suitability for RT, and the nature of the rehabilitation that is recommended for him, in order for me to assess RT as a sentencing option. I ordered for him to be remanded for about a week at the reformative training centre (“RTC”) to enable his PSR to be submitted to the court. He continues to be in remand on a no-bail order because he re-offended while on bail.

13     As Mr Koh was remanded for more than three months then, SPS has promptly submitted his PSR in three weeks in time for today’s mention at my request. In fact, SPS did so in very good time four days before today’s mention, with a recommendation that Mr Koh undergo level 2 intensity of rehabilitation if he were sentenced to RT. I retain the full discretion to decide whether he should be sentenced to RT or other forms of punishment, applying my mind based on all the information and facts before me in this case: Ng Jun Xian v PP [2017] 3 SLR 933 at [54].

Approach to sentencing young offender

14     When sentencing a young offender, the first stage is to identify and prioritise the primary sentencing considerations appropriate to the offender having regard to all the circumstances including those of the offence. The second stage is to select the appropriate sentence that would best meet those identified and prioritised sentencing considerations: PP v Mohammad Al-Ansari bin Basri [2008] 1 SLR(R) 449 at [77]-[78] and PP v Koh Wen Jie Boaz [2016] 1 SLR 334 (“Boaz Koh”) at [28] as affirmed and explained in PP v ASR [2019] 1 SLR 941 at [94], [101]-[102]. The inquiry proceeds from the foremost question of whether rehabilitation remains the dominant sentencing principle.

15     I apply the same approach and adopt the same language that I used in PP v Elyana Binte Amraiy [2025] SGDC 152 mainly for consistency and I am cognisant of the differences between the cases.

Stage 1: Identify and prioritise primary sentencing considerations

16     At the first stage, the question is whether in all the circumstances, the presumptive emphasis on rehabilitation has been displaced: See Li Quan Mendel v PP [2020] 2 SLR 630 (“Mendel See”) at [15]. If an offender is 21 years old or below at both the time of the offence and the time of sentencing, the law takes the presumptive view that the primary sentencing consideration in such cases will generally be rehabilitation, because both the retrospective and prospective rationales underlying such presumptive primacy of rehabilitation would apply: A Karthik v PP [2018] 5 SLR 1289 at [44].

Presumptive primacy of rehabilitation not displaced in this case

17     In this case, Mr Koh is 18 at the time of the offences and sentencing. The primacy of rehabilitation is therefore presumptive. But the focus on rehabilitation can be diminished or even eclipsed by such considerations as deterrence or retribution where the circumstances warrant. Broadly speaking, this happens in cases where:

(a)     the offence is serious,

(b)     the harm caused is severe,

(c)     the offender is hardened and recalcitrant, or

(d)     the conditions do not exist to make rehabilitative sentencing options viable: Boaz Koh at [30].

Mr Koh’s offences are serious, it was fortuitous that the harm caused by his offences were not severe, and he is recalcitrant: see [11], above.

18     Rehabilitation may not have been displaced as the normative sentencing consideration in his case but there is clear need to incorporate a sufficient element of deterrence within any overarching focus on the goal of rehabilitation.

Stage 2: How sentencing considerations ought to be achieved

19     Having determined that Mr Koh should be rehabilitated, I next have to ascertain how rehabilitation ought to be achieved and his suitability to undergo a specific form of rehabilitation: ASR at [99]. The second stage is to select the appropriate sentence that would best meet this concern of prioritising rehabilitation and yet have the requisite deterrent effect.

RT appropriate sentence to meet rehabilitative and deterrent needs

20     In Mr Koh’s case, RT is appropriate because:

(a)     RT lies within the spectrum of rehabilitative sentences: Mandel See at [13]. However, it also incorporates a significant element of deterrence because there is a minimum detention period of either six or 12 months depending on the intensity of the RT ordered: Boaz Koh at [38];

(b)     where there is a need for both deterrence and rehabilitation, RT may be the most suitable sentence, given that it offers a useful middle ground between sending Mr Koh to prison and meeting the desire to rehabilitate him: A Karthik at [67]. RT allows the court to sentence him to a rehabilitative programme under a structured environment, while avoiding the danger of exposing him to the potentially unsettling influence of an adult prison environment: Boaz Koh at [38]; and

(c)     the conditions exist to make RT a viable rehabilitative sentencing option as is evident from Mr Koh’s RT PSR.

(1)   Mr Koh assessed to be suitable for RT

21     Mr Koh was found to be in general good physical condition with no known major illnesses,[note: 6] and also of normal mental condition with no current indication of any major mental illness.[note: 7] He was therefore assessed to be suitable to undergo RT. The upshot of his PSR was that he: [note: 8]

presented with multiple needs that require structured intervention and supervision, namely his antisocial attitudes that support the use of violence and crimes, association with peers of negative influence, and use of drugs. In addition, he would require interventions that address his lack of meaningful engagement in employment and recreational activities. [Mr Koh] and his parents could also benefit from support to help the parents better supervise and manage him.

On this basis, the recommendation is for him to undergo level 2 intensity of rehabilitation if he were sentenced to RT.

22     An RT PSR does not contain a positive recommendation for an offender to undergo RT, and understandably so because the law does not confer any mandate for the prison authorities to make any such recommendation as to whether an offender ought to be sentenced to RT as opposed to other forms of punishment. Such a report is meant to reflect whether an offender is physically and mentally fit, and in that sense suitable, for RT: Ng Jun Xian at [54]. Even though Mr Koh has been found suitable for RT by SPS, I must apply my mind to whether he should be sentenced to RT.

(2)   Sentence of RT of Level 2 intensity appropriate

23     The rehabilitation plan of the RT PSR is premised on adequate sources of information.[note: 9] I see no good reason to depart from the finding that Mr Koh presented intervention needs and his parents could benefit from guidance on exercising better oversight over him: see [21], above.

24     Mr Koh presented himself with a concerning plethora of criminogenic needs:[note: 10]

(a)     the chief of which are concerning attitudes and an overall orientation supportive of crime,[note: 11] driven by a misguided sense that there was utility in committing crime and violence and took pride in this as it would allow him to gain respect and status, and as such he wanted to “really do big [cases]” and “make a name” for himself. His mother’s account that he had wanted to be a criminal leader with power and authority over others corroborated this. He also lacked empathy towards the victim of his offences as well as remorse for his actions and said he would have committed the same crime if given the choice to do so again. He had a skewed perception that doubling down on his offending behaviour with the subsequent rioting offence would make any eventual incarceration worthwhile when he did not reap any financial gain from his earlier house-breaking offence;

(b)     he has negative peer influence, undesirable leisure/recreation activities, and engaged in drug use, namely ‘Kpods’;[note: 12]

(c)     he displayed personality and behavioural patterns associated with antisocial behaviour,[note: 13] and a history of conduct disorder diagnosed by the Institute of Mental Health in 2023.[note: 14] During the period of remand, Mr Koh reported he was involved in several disciplinary incidents, such as assaulting his cellmate and vandalism;[note: 15]

(d)     he stopped attending school at the Institute of Technical Education and had not engaged in any other long-term education or employment pursuits;[note: 16] and

(e)     his parents have limited control over him but appeared to still be supportive of him.[note: 17]

25     It is clear to me that substantial work needs to be done and a level 2 intensity of psychology-based correctional programmes to be delivered over a 12-month period[note: 18] is necessary to address Mr Koh’s criminogenic needs to course correct:

(a)     his attitudes and orientation supportive of committing crime and the use of violence;

(b)     his association with negative peer influence and lack of insight into its impact and in this regard, he should be kept away from such influence in RTC whom he is reportedly excited to meet if he were sentenced to RT;[note: 19]

(c)     his Kpod drug use with psychology-based interventions;

(d)     his lack of meaningful engagement in employment and recreational activities with vocational training aligned to his interests in cooking and art;[note: 20] and

(e)     his lack of meaningful engagement in education with shorter term academic studies as he expressed an intention to further his studies in RTC should he be sentenced to RT.[note: 21]

26     Family programmes are also needed because they are beneficial, in particular those that guide Mr Koh’s parents in exercising oversight over Mr Koh’s activities.

Sentence of RT of Level 2 intensity also proportionate

27     Mr Koh should undergo RT to reform him and to prevent crime, having regard to his character, previous conduct and the circumstances of the offences: section 305(1) of the CPC. Considerations of proportionality have been imported into the “circumstances of the offences” limb of this provision: PP v Saiful Rizam bin Assim [2014] 2 SLR 495 (“Saiful Rizam”) at [38]. Even if the minimum detention periods might not be proportionate to the underlying offence, the principle of proportionality legitimately takes a back seat with a view to reforming the young offender and deterring him at an early stage: Sim Yeow Kee v PP [2016] 5 SLR 936 at [95]. However, as much as the rehabilitative effect of RT is a valuable and important sentencing goal, a measure of proportionality in making orders for RT is also imperative so that offenders are not unduly punished: Saiful Rizam at [41].

(1)   Expected sentence of at least 15 months’ imprisonment if Mr Koh not sentenced to RT

28     As for the sentence that Mr Koh can expect if he were not sentenced to RT, I would have sentenced him to 12 months’ imprisonment for the house-breaking offence and 15 months’ imprisonment for the rioting offence.

(A)   Sentence of 12 months’ imprisonment for house-breaking offence

29     I would have imposed a sentence of 12 months’ imprisonment for Mr Koh’s house-breaking offence based on the following offence-specific harm-culpability factors and offender-specific aggravating and mitigating factors:

(a)     offence-specific harm-culpability factors –

(i)       although the harm caused by Mr Koh’s offence is low in that he did not manage to steal anything and he did not cause any damage to the house that he broke into: Lim Wei Ho at [29] and [35(b)], this does not reduce his culpability in any way because he had clearly intended to cause loss to the occupants as he searched for valuable items to steal once he was inside the house. He was only foiled in his attempt by the occupant who discovered him,

(ii)       there was also planning and premeditation on his part as he had targeted the house for two days and also committed the offence during the wee hours of the morning under the cover of night: Lim at [35(d)] and [35(f)], and

(iii)       he also evaded apprehension by fleeing the scene, first upon being discovered by the occupant, and second, while awaiting the police after he was apprehended by the occupant: Lim [35(e)];

(b)     offender-specific aggravating and mitigating factors –

(i)       his similar and recent property-related antecedents,

(ii)       the aggravating presence of another theft-in-dwelling TIC charge with a significant economic value of S$10,000,

(iii)       his youth as a mitigating factor, and

(iv)       the mitigatory weight to be accorded to his early guilty plea.

(B)   Sentence of at least 15 months’ imprisonment for rioting offence

30     I would have imposed a sentence of at least 15 months’ imprisonment for the rioting offence. The offence is aggravated in that injury, though minor, was caused and the offence was gang-affiliated. He played a minor role in that he was one of the pairs who would surround the victim and any of his accompanying companions. He did not take part in the violence or caused injury. His culpability was therefore low. His related and recent antecedent of public possession of an offensive weapon that impacts on public safety and tranquillity is a personal aggravating factor; so is the fact that he committed this offence while on court bail, just days after he was charged and released for his house-breaking offence. Against this is the mitigatory weight to be given for his youth and early guilty plea.

(2)   Sentence of RT with minimum detention period of 12 months not comparatively disproportionate

31     A sentence of imprisonment does not make for easy and direct comparison with that of RT because it is fundamentally a very different and more severe punitive sentence. However, given that Mr Koh faces the prospect of a sentence of at least 15 months’ imprisonment if he were not sentenced to RT, a sentence of RT with a minimum detention period of 12 months would therefore not be comparatively disproportionate.

Conclusion

Sentence of RT for minimum detention period of 12 months imposed

32     I therefore sentence Mr Koh to RT for a minimum detention period of 12 months from today. This is to reform him and prevent crime given the specific rehabilitation plan that has been drawn up for him. It is not only a viable and feasible but the appropriate sentence to impose on Mr Koh that is both sufficient and proportionate.

33     Given that Mr Koh is in remand for slightly more than four months now, it remains for me to thank SPS for its prompt submission of Mr Koh’s PSR despite having only a three-week lead-time with a slightly shorter remand period because of an intervening public holiday. I acknowledge the efforts of medical officer Dr Rodney Bay, psychiatrist Dr Claire Law and lead correctional rehabilitation specialist Cheryl Wong in this regard.
